CaseA_TestA: Hearsay admissibility under the “principled approach”: hearsay (including evidence said to fit a traditional exception) is admissible only if it meets the twin requirements of “reliability and necessity”; traditional exceptions “must therefore yield to comply with the principled approach” (Khan/Smith framework as applied in Starr).
BaselineA: Common law (hearsay rule and exceptions; principled approach from R. v. Khan and R. v. Smith; present intentions exception discussed in R. v. Smith).
CaseB_TestB: Public interest standing (Downtown Eastside framework): court “must assess and weigh three factors” — (i) “serious justiciable issue”; (ii) “genuine interest”; and (iii) “reasonable and effective means” — and “weigh the factors cumulatively, flexibly and purposively”; no “particular weight” to legality/access to justice; no requirement of an individual co-plaintiff if a “sufficiently concrete and well-developed factual setting” will be forthcoming.
BaselineB: Common law (public interest standing test from Canada (Attorney General) v. Downtown Eastside Sex Workers United Against Violence Society, 2012 SCC 45).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Limited-liability/non-assessability constraint on corporate articles: a company cannot, by amending articles or resolution, impose any pecuniary obligation on holders of fully paid shares; and any share transfer fee is valid only to the extent of the "reasonable and proper cost" of the transfer (excess is an illegal levy).
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law principle: The Companies Act (Alberta) (e.g., s. 42(1) power to amend articles; definitions/limited liability provisions; s. 68(4) deeming no-par shares "fully paid and non-assessable"; winding-up contribution limit) plus the common-law "basic jural principle" of limited liability/non-assessability (citing Ooregum Gold Mining Co. of India v. Roper; Bisgood v. Henderson’s Transvaal Estates; Shalfoon v. Cheddar Valley Co-operative Dairy Co.).
JudgeA: Dickson J. (for Ritchie, Pigeon and Dickson JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Van der Peet aboriginal-rights identification test (as applied): (1) characterize the precise claim (considering the action, the impugned regulation, and the practice relied on); (2) ask whether, prior to contact, the practice was "integral to the distinctive culture" (i.e., a "central, significant or defining feature") of the claimant group; appellate deference to trial findings absent "palpable and overriding error".
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine under Constitution Act, 1982, s. 35(1), applying the framework articulated contemporaneously in R. v. Van der Peet (and situated within Sparrow’s s. 35 framework).
JudgeB: The Chief Justice (Lamer C.J., for the majority)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Reviewability of a consensual labour arbitrator’s award for error of law on the face: no “specific question of law” reference (binding/ouster) where the issue arises in the ordinary grievance process under a collective agreement that limits the arbitrator to decisions consistent with the agreement; therefore courts may review and quash for error of law on the face
BaselineA: Common law (scope of judicial review of consensual arbitration awards), drawing on Government of Kelantan v. Duff Development Co. Ltd.; F.R. Absalom Ltd. v. Great Western (London) Garden Village Society Ltd.; Faubert and Watts v. Temagami Mining Co. Ltd.; City of Vancouver v. Brandram-Henderson of B.C. Ltd.; and Bell Canada v. Office and Professional Employees’ International Union, Local 131
JudgeA: Martland J. (for Martland, Judson, Ritchie, Pigeon, Dickson and de Grandpré JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Morin framework for s. 11(b) “reasonable time” delay: assess (1) length of delay minus defence waiver, then consider (2) reasons for delay, (3) prejudice (including that “prejudice may be inferred from the length of the delay”), and (4) the interests s. 11(b) protects, in an overall balancing rather than a “mathematical or administrative formula”
BaselineB: Combination: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 11(b), as applied through the common-law/constitutional framework in R. v. Morin and R. v. Askov
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 3(4) possession framework (including joint possession): for Code purposes, possession is personal possession or knowingly having it in another’s custody or in any place for use/benefit; and where one of two or more persons, with the knowledge and consent of the rest, has it, it is deemed in the custody and possession of each
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 3(4)(a)-(b) (quoted in reasons). SCC interprets scope of “For the purposes of this Act” and confirms applicability in all proceedings under the Code, including where possession is used as an evidentiary link (citing Reference re R. v. Coffin, [1956] S.C.R. 191).
CaseB_TestB: Adverse possession in British Columbia: possession must be “open and notorious, adverse, exclusive, peaceful (not by force), actual (generally), and continuous”; SCC rejects any additional ‘inconsistent use’ requirement as not part of BC law
BaselineB: Combination: common law adverse possession elements as summarized in the reasons (citing Ziff) plus statutory limitations framework in British Columbia (received 1833 English limitations codification; applied through BC limitation statutes). SCC contribution is chiefly interpretive: the ‘inconsistent use’ doctrine “forms no part of the law of British Columbia governing adverse possession”.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Quantum meruit for hospital services where no remuneration agreed: municipality must pay “reasonable rates” (and OICs only bar recovery if validly authorized and if rates were actually “established under the Social Assistance Act”; no retroactive extinguishment absent clear authority).
BaselineA: Common law (quantum meruit/quasi-contract) plus statutory/regulatory interpretation of Hospital Act s. 37(2), Social Assistance Act, and Residence and Responsibility Act s. 3 (and OICs 3103, 4399, 4400).
CaseB_TestB: Voluntariness/“operating mind” test for admissibility of inculpatory statements by an allegedly insane accused: the “underlying and controlling question” is whether the statement was “freely and voluntarily made,” including whether the words were “the utterances of an operating mind.”
BaselineB: Common law confession voluntariness doctrine (Boudreau v. The King; Ward v. The Queen; with discussion of R. v. Santinon).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Effect of breach of a witness-exclusion order: witness not automatically disqualified; admissibility is discretionary; weight is assessed by trier of fact (and no legal requirement that the judge expressly state a self-caution for each such witness)
BaselineA: Common law practice on exclusion of witnesses (cited through Moore v. Lambeth County Court Registrar; Cook v. Nethercotte; Thomas v. David; Chandler v. Home; R. v. Briggs; R. v. Thompson; Black v. Besse; R. v. Carefoot)
CaseB_TestB: Clear-and-unequivocal-language requirement to lift Crown immunity from discovery; CLPA s. 27 applies only when the Crown is a party, so immunity from discovery remains when the Crown is not a party
BaselineB: Statutory interpretation of Crown immunity starting point in Interpretation Act, s. 17, and scope of CLPA, s. 27 (with common law Crown immunity as the background rule)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Disqualification/bias in Law Society discipline: whether benchers who sat on the Discipline Committee may participate in Convocation when Convocation considers the Committee’s report (two-stage process vs appeal; expressio unius re s. 39(4))
BaselineA: Statute and regulation: The Law Society Act, 1970 (Ont.), ss. 33(12), 34, 37, 39 (especially s. 39(4) disqualification on an appeal from a reprimand) and Reg. 556, s. 13(6)-(7); interpreted using the maxim expressio unius est exclusio alterius
CaseB_TestB: Criminal Code s. 731(1)(b) probation eligibility: “imprisonment for a term not exceeding two years” refers to the term imposed by the sentencing court at a single sitting (not the aggregate of other sentences), with the exception that probation cannot attach where sentences imposed at the same session result in continuous custody over two years
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 731(1)(b) (and related context in ss. 732.2, 743.1)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “operation of a mine” and when a separate “mine” exists for the 36‑month tax exemption: (1) “operation of a mine” in s. 83(5) “refers only to the extraction of ore from an ore body and does not include the processing of the ore after it has been produced”; and (2) “there is ‘a mine’ within the meaning of s. 83(5) if there is a body of ore together with the workings, equipment and machinery capable of producing it” — a separate mine arises when a separate ore body “commenced to be extracted by means of its separate and distinct extraction facilities.”
BaselineA: Statute: Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1952, c. 148 as amended, s. 83(5) and s. 83(6) (definitions of “mine” and “production”); interpreted in light of SCC authorities North Bay Mica Company Limited v. M.N.R., [1958] S.C.R. 597 and M.N.R. v. MacLean Mining Co., [1970] S.C.R. 877.
CaseB_TestB: Leave to sue a receiver/trustee under s. 215 BIA (Mancini test): leave should be refused only for “frivolous or vexatious” or “manifestly unmeritorious” claims; the evidence must provide the required support and “disclose a cause of action” — “If the evidence discloses a prima facie case, leave should be granted”; and “The court is not required to make a final assessment of the merits of the claim before granting leave.”
BaselineB: Statute: Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. B-3, s. 215 (leave requirement), with related context in ss. 47(2) and 72(1); common-law/appellate baseline: Mancini (Bankrupt) v. Falconi (1993), 61 O.A.C. 332 (C.A.) adopted as the governing approach.
JudgeB: Abella J. (McLachlin C.J. and Bastarache, Binnie, LeBel, Fish and Charron JJ. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Education Act s. 373: when school commissioners must amend municipal valuation rolls—if valuations are "not uniform", they must amend the rolls "so as to re-establish on the basis of its real value the valuation of the taxable property of all the parts of the school municipality" (i.e., equalize valuations by real value of what is taxable in each municipality, not by importing another municipality’s tax base choices like machinery exemptions).
BaselineA: Statute: Education Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 235, s. 373 (and its interaction with municipal power under Cities and Towns Act s. 488 to exclude machinery from taxable immovables).
CaseB_TestB: Criminal Code s. 426(1)(a)(ii) (secret commissions): actus reus has three elements—(1) agency relationship; (2) agent accepts a benefit "as consideration" for acting/forbearing in relation to the principal’s affairs; and (3) "failure by the agent to make adequate and timely disclosure of the source, amount and nature of the benefit"; "corruptly" in this context means "secretly or without the requisite disclosure" and no "corrupt bargain" with the giver is required.
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 426(1)(a) (formerly s. 383(1)(a)).
JudgeB: Cory J. (for L'Heureux-Dubé, Gonthier, Cory and Iacobucci JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Extradition-crime classification by “essence of the crime charged”: “The test is what is the essence of the crime charged” (i.e., whether the offence is, in substance, a crime “against the laws for the suppression of the traffic in narcotics” under the extradition arrangement).
BaselineA: Statute + extradition arrangement: Extradition Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-21, s. 2 (definition of “extradition crime”), including crimes “described in such arrangement”; Supplementary Convention (1925) classification added to the Act: “Crimes and offences against the laws for the suppression of the traffic in narcotics”.
CaseB_TestB: Section 13 “incriminate” vs “impeach credibility” distinction for use of prior testimony at a later proceeding: prior testimony may be used on cross-examination if its “sole purpose” is “undermining… credibility”, but not if used “to incriminate” (to establish guilt).
BaselineB: Constitution + statute: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 13 (and context of s. 11(c), (d) discussed); Canada Evidence Act, s. 5(2) (interpreted as offering “virtually identical protection” to s. 13).
JudgeB: Lamer C.J. (for Dickson C.J. and Lamer C.J. and Gonthier and McLachlin JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Negligence foreseeability/remoteness test for highway authority liability: whether “a reasonable person should have anticipated that what happened might be a natural result of that act or omission”; not necessary to foresee the “precise concatenation of events”, only “in a general way the class or character of injury which occurred”.
BaselineA: Common law (foreseeability/remoteness in negligence), applied alongside the Highway Improvement Act, R.S.O. 1960, s. 33(1) (duty to maintain highway). Baseline case cited: University Hospital Board v. Lépine, [1966] S.C.R. 561; also Wagon Mound No. 2.
CaseB_TestB: CEAA “tracking” rule: the environmental assessment track is determined by the “project as proposed” (not “project as scoped”); if the project as proposed is listed in the Comprehensive Study List, s. 21 requirements are mandatory and the responsible authority cannot reduce the scope below what is proposed (though it may enlarge scope under s. 15(2)-(3)).
BaselineB: Statute/regulation: Canadian Environmental Assessment Act, S.C. 1992, c. 37 (especially ss. 2 “project”, 15, 18, 21, 21.1, 58(1)(i)) and Comprehensive Study List Regulations, SOR/94-638 (e.g., Sch., s. 16).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Using res ipsa loquitur to infer (and support a finding of) gross negligence for a gratuitous passenger claim: (1) instrumentality under defendant’s sole management/control; (2) occurrence would not have happened without negligence; and (3) no evidence as to why/how it occurred — but if an explanation is given and is not a valid answer, the inference may still apply.
BaselineA: Combination: statute (Highway Traffic Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 202, s. 132(3) requiring “gross negligence” for gratuitous passengers) + common law evidentiary rule (res ipsa loquitur as described via Clerk & Lindsell; applied to gross negligence per Walker v. Coates, [1968] S.C.R. 599; and discussion of skidding as a “neutral fact” from Gauthier & Co. Ltd. v. The King, [1945] S.C.R. 143).
CaseB_TestB: Criteria for recognizing a vested (acquired) right protected by the presumption against legislative interference: a vested right exists where (1) the person’s legal situation is “tangible and concrete” (not “general and abstract”), and (2) the situation was “sufficiently constituted at the time of the new statute’s commencement”; if so, absent clear legislative intent, amendments will not be read to impair the right (including where statutory terms were incorporated into a private contract).
BaselineB: Combination: statutory interpretation baseline (Interpretation Act, R.S.Q., c. I-16, s. 12 on “rights acquired”; plus the student-loan statutory scheme AFAS and amending Acts, including s. 13 “juridical situations in progress”) + common law/codified presumption against interference with vested rights (e.g., Spooner Oils Ltd. v. Turner Valley Gas Conservation Board, [1933] S.C.R. 629).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Mechanics’ lien owner-liability/holdback interpretation: s. 19(2) does not prevent the owner deducting completion costs; it only bars deductions for extraneous set-off/counterclaim so owner liability remains limited by s. 6 to “the sum payable by the owner to the contractor” (i.e., no lien fund beyond the statutory holdback for completion-cost purposes).
BaselineA: Statute: Mechanics’ Lien Act, R.S.B.C. 1960, c. 238, ss. 6, 19(2), 21(1), 21(6). Key text: s. 6 limits owner liability to “the sum payable by the owner to the contractor”; s. 19(2) says the contract price “shall not be diminished by any prior or subsequent indebtedness, set-off, or counterclaim”.
CaseB_TestB: Choice of law in tort (general rule): apply lex loci delicti — “the law of the place where the activity occurred”; with only a narrowly confined possibility of exception (rare) and recognition that limitation periods under the lex loci can be substantive where they create an accrued right to plead a time bar.
BaselineB: Common law (conflict of laws in tort), reformulating/overruling prior SCC approach in McLean v. Pettigrew; also applied alongside statutory schemes where relevant (e.g., Quebec Automobile Insurance Act, ss. 3-4; Saskatchewan Vehicles Act, s. 180(1) for limitation characterization).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Constitutional (territorial) validity test for provincial legislation with extra-provincial effects: Manitoba cannot, by s. 4(2) of The Fishermen’s Assistance and Polluters’ Liability Act, nullify a permission/licence granted by another jurisdiction; the Act is inapplicable/ultra vires insofar as it purports to legislate in relation to conduct and rights outside Manitoba (interprovincial pollution is a federal matter). Key statutory trigger: s. 4(2) makes it 'not a lawful excuse' that the discharge 'was permitted' where the discharge occurred if that authority lacked jurisdiction where damage occurred.
BaselineA: Statute (The Fishermen’s Assistance and Polluters’ Liability Act, 1970 (Man.), c. 32, especially ss. 4(1) and 4(2)) interpreted against constitutional limits under the B.N.A. Act, 1867 (division of powers/territoriality; majority also invokes federal residual/POGG for interprovincial concern).
JudgeA: Pigeon J. (for Martland, Pigeon and Beetz JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Judicial review standard under a privative clause: court may intervene only for jurisdictional error; an administrative decision warrants intervention only if it is 'so patently unreasonable that its construction cannot be rationally supported by the relevant legislation' (C.U.P.E. test). Related: 'good and sufficient cause' is not a prerequisite to jurisdiction but 'the very subject of the inquiry' (intra-jurisdictional).
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law administrative law: Act respecting labour standards, R.S.Q., c. N-1.1, ss. 124-129 (esp. ss. 128-129) plus Labour Code, s. 139 (privative clause) and the SCC’s prior 'patently unreasonable' jurisprudence (e.g., C.U.P.E.).
JudgeB: Lamer J. (reasons for McIntyre and Lamer JJ.; Beetz, Chouinard and Wilson JJ. concur in result)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Collective agreement not terminable by common-law repudiation/fundamental breach during its term; illegal strike does not per se terminate employment—employer remains bound unless it takes positive disciplinary action (e.g., discharge) under the collective agreement/legislation
BaselineA: Combination: statute (Mediation Services Act, 1968 (B.C.), ss. 6 and 23; referenced s. 8 on term) plus SCC/common-law labour jurisprudence rejecting individual-contract framing (Syndicat catholique des employés de magasins de Québec Inc. v. Compagnie Paquet Ltée; C.P.R. Co. v. Zambri; also Re Polymer)
CaseB_TestB: Limits on cross-examination using a complainant’s diary: relevant defence cross-examination may be excluded only if prejudice substantially outweighs probative value; omission evidence is probative only if defence establishes a reasonable expectation the event would have been recorded (Seaboyer/Osolin standard, not O’Connor production balancing)
BaselineB: Common law (Seaboyer; Osolin; clarified against misapplication of O’Connor/Mills production framework); statutory context noted but held inapplicable to admissibility/use (Criminal Code ss. 278.1–278.9)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Admissibility of evidence that an accused refused to participate in an identification line-up: admissible where needed to explain the absence of a line-up (and resulting confrontation/show-up), but not automatically—"Admissibility will depend upon the circumstances of the case"; if the Crown must explain the omission of a line-up or risk an adverse inference, refusal evidence is "relevant and admissible"; otherwise it "should not normally be tendered" due to risk to the presumption of innocence.
BaselineA: Common law evidence (relevance/admissibility) and common law privilege against self-incrimination as limited to testimonial compulsion (as discussed with reference to Curr v. The Queen and A.-G. (Que.) v. Begin).
CaseB_TestB: Division of powers limit on provincial commissions of inquiry: a provincial inquiry is ultra vires if, in pith and substance, it is "a substitute police investigation and preliminary inquiry" into a specific Criminal Code offence by named private individuals—i.e., the inquiry process "cannot be used to circumvent the federally prescribed criminal procedure" and must be "firmly anchored to a provincial head of power" and not used "as a means to investigate and determine the criminal responsibility of specific individuals for specific offences".
BaselineB: Constitution Act, 1867 division of powers (s. 91(27) criminal law/procedure vs provincial heads) applied through the pith-and-substance doctrine; applied to an Order in Council under Ontario's Public Inquiries Act, R.S.O. 1980, c. 411 (especially s. 2).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Punitive damages in tort: whether this is a “very proper case for punitive damages”, assessed by the “circumstances of the case” and what “substantial justice” requires (including the nature of the tortious scheme and its impact)
BaselineA: Common law (punitive/exemplary damages in tort; no specific baseline case or statutory provision is identified in the reasons provided)
CaseB_TestB: Anns/Cooper duty of care framework for recognizing a new duty (pure economic loss): Stage 1 asks (1) “reasonable foreseeability” and (2) “proximity” including party-specific policy; Stage 2 asks whether “residual policy considerations” (e.g., indeterminate liability) negate the duty
BaselineB: Common law (Anns v. Merton London Borough Council; adopted in Kamloops (City of) v. Nielsen; recast/applied in Cooper v. Hobart and Childs v. Desormeaux)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Railway Act s. 275(2)/(4): any Commission order enlarging the 30-day notice period for an advance-tolls freight tariff must be made before the tariff’s stated effective date; after that date, the tariff takes effect under s. 275(4) and a post-effective-date “extension” is an impermissible indirect postponement (ultra vires).
BaselineA: Statute: Railway Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. R-2, s. 275(2) and s. 275(4) (with context from National Transportation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. N-17, s. 64(5)).
CaseB_TestB: Palmer fresh-evidence test (criminal appeals): admit fresh evidence in the “interests of justice” considering (1) due diligence (less strict in criminal cases), (2) relevance to a decisive/potentially decisive issue, (3) credibility, and (4) whether it could reasonably be expected to have affected the result.
BaselineB: Common law: Palmer v. The Queen, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 759 (applied), in the context of Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 683.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Effectiveness/finality of a court order still within the appeal period: despite being subject to appeal, it may be treated as fully effective (even against third parties) where there is only an “ephemeral prospect of an appeal”; assess finality contextually by considering “the purpose” for which finality is urged, “who is affected”, and “in what context” finality is asserted
BaselineA: Statute (The Conveyancing and Law of Property Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 85, s. 62) applied in the vendor–purchaser/title requisition context; with common-law/background principles about the effect of appealable orders (cases discussed: Re West; Leonard v. Wharton (distinguished))
CaseB_TestB: Preliminary inquiry committal test under Criminal Code s. 548(1): ask “whether or not there is any evidence upon which a reasonable jury properly instructed could return a verdict of guilty”; if Crown evidence is circumstantial, the judge must do a “limited weighing” of the whole evidence (including defence evidence) to assess whether the Crown’s evidence, if believed, could reasonably support the inferences of guilt (without drawing inferences or assessing credibility)
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 548(1) (and related preliminary inquiry provisions), interpreted through the common law rule from United States of America v. Shephard, [1977] 2 S.C.R. 1067 (reaffirmed/clarified with reference to Mezzo and Monteleone)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Discretionary public-interest standing (taxpayer/citizen) to challenge legislation: standing may be granted where (1) a “serious, a substantial constitutional issue” is raised; (2) the plaintiff is “directly affected” or has a “direct interest” (here, the public’s interest in what it may view); and (3) “there appears to be no other way, practically speaking, to subject the challenged Act to judicial review”, such that it is “enough ... to support the claim ... to have the discretion of the Court exercised in his favour to give him standing”.
BaselineA: Common law (standing/locus standi doctrine), drawing on SCC authorities including Thorson v. Attorney General of Canada (No. 2), [1975] 1 S.C.R. 138 and Smith v. Attorney General of Ontario, [1924] S.C.R. 331.
CaseB_TestB: Interpretation of ASRA Program s. 88(3) (government-assistance “linkage”): because s. 88(3) “does not specify how ... is to be linked” and states only that La Financière must consider “any amounts to which a participant is entitled”, it must be interpreted under C.C.Q. arts. 1425-1432; read with the contract as a whole (art. 1427) and past practices (art. 1426), s. 88(3) “does not require that amounts be linked individually but, on the contrary, gives La Financière the discretion to decide what linkage method to employ”, subject to exercise “in accordance with the requirements of good faith and contractual fairness” (arts. 6, 7, 1375, 1434 C.C.Q.).
BaselineB: Statute/regulation and civil code interpretation rules: Programme d’assurance stabilisation des revenus agricoles, s. 88(3); Civil Code of Québec, arts. 1425-1432 (interpretation), plus arts. 6, 7, 1375, 1434 (good faith/contractual fairness).
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Rebuttable presumption of mens rea for trafficking once actus reus proved: when it is proved the accused trafficked in the restricted drug, “a rebuttable presumption arises” that the conduct was voluntary and the accused “is guilty ... and must be convicted unless other evidence is adduced which raises a reasonable doubt” (applied here to LSD trafficking; no defence evidence meant mens rea not negated).
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Food and Drugs Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. F-27, ss. 40 (definitions incl. “traffic”) and 42 (trafficking offence), plus SCC mens rea principles from Beaver v. The Queen and the rebuttable-presumption approach from R. v. King (as quoted and applied).
CaseB_TestB: Limits on trial-judge intervention / appearance of impartiality: a judge may question and interrupt witnesses, but “must do so within certain limits and in such a way that justice is seen to be done”; if the judge’s conduct “raised some doubt as to his impartiality”, a new trial is required.
BaselineB: Common law principles of procedural fairness and judicial impartiality, grounded in R. v. Sussex Justices; Ex parte McCarthy (“justice should not only be done, but ... be seen to be done”) and related authorities (e.g., Jones v. National Coal Board; Torbiak and Campbell; Darlyn; Yuill; Bateman).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Interpretation of “burglary” in Criminal Code s. 213 (constructive murder): despite later drafting/revision ambiguities, “burglary” retains the meaning of the offence defined in Criminal Code 1892 s. 410, read with the 1892 definitions of “dwelling-house” and “break” in s. 407 (i.e., burglary limited to breaking/entering a dwelling-house at night, as statutorily defined).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 213 and 306; Interpretation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-23, s. 36(f); with historical reference to Criminal Code, 1892, ss. 228, 407, 410).
JudgeA: Pigeon J. (for Laskin C.J. and Martland, Spence, Pigeon, Dickson and Beetz JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Damages for repudiation where contract allows alternative modes of performance: adopt the mode “least profitable to the plaintiff, and least burdensome to the defendant”; the test is not what the defendant would likely have done but for repudiation, but what performance the contract entitled the plaintiff to (minimum/least-burdensome performance).
BaselineB: Common law (general principle traced to Cockburn v. Alexander (1848) and explained in Withers v. General Theatre Corp. (1933)).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Lease interpretation test for shifting fire-loss risk to landlord/insurer where tenant covenants to pay “insurance rates”: read the lease “reasonably and in a business sense”; if tenant has discharged its obligation to pay for fire insurance (at least once the landlord presents “the insurance bill”), the tenant “is entitled to rest in respect of loss by fire” and the landlord’s insurer has “no basis” for subrogation against the tenant for that fire loss (including tenant-negligence-caused fire).
BaselineA: Common law contract/lease interpretation ("ordinary test of reading it reasonably and in a business sense"), applied in the landlord-tenant/insurance context; with statutory backdrop noted (Ontario Insurance Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 224, s. 118, as confirming standard fire coverage includes third-party negligence).
CaseB_TestB: Civil Code art. 1053 “fault” liability for banks paying on unauthorized endorsements: a bank commits a “fault” by accepting cheques payable to a company for deposit to an individual’s personal benefit “without examining it, and without verifying the sufficiency of the endorsement”; if that fault deprives the payee of money that belonged to it and causes damage, damages are recoverable (typically equal to the cheque amounts where the payee has no remaining remedy against the drawer).
BaselineB: Statute and civil law: Bills of Exchange Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. B-5 (notably s. 51 on signature by procuration as notice of limited authority; also s. 10 mentioned) plus Civil Code (Quebec) art. 1053 (fault/damage/causation), as developed in Norwich Union Fire Insurance Society Ltd. v. La Banque Canadienne Nationale, [1934] S.C.R. 596.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 15(1) adverse-effects discrimination (prima facie breach): (1) law creates a distinction on an enumerated/analogous ground, including by effects where it has a “disproportionate impact” on a protected group; and (2) it “imposes burdens or denies a benefit” in a way that “reinforc[es], perpetuat[es], or exacerbat[es] disadvantage” (with guidance that statistical disparity and/or group-disadvantage evidence may prove disproportionate impact, and no need to prove intent or that the protected characteristic ‘caused’ the impact).
BaselineA: Constitution (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 15(1)) and prior SCC s. 15 jurisprudence (e.g., Withler; Taypotat; Alliance; Centrale) articulating the two-step s. 15(1) framework.
CaseB_TestB: Division of powers “pith and substance” analysis: (1) determine the law’s “essential character” by examining “purpose and the legal effect”; then (2) ask whether that character “relate[s] to an enumerated head of power” (here, whether s. 27 is in pith and substance related to federal fisheries power rather than provincial property and civil rights).
BaselineB: Constitution (Constitution Act, 1867, ss. 91(12), 91(27), 92(13)) and the established constitutional doctrine of pith and substance (as summarized with reference to prior cases such as Reference re Firearms Act; Global Securities; Morgentaler).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Lease interpretation test for whether tenant’s covenant to pay “insurance rates” shifts the fire-loss risk (including tenant negligence) to the landlord, barring insurer subrogation: apply “the ordinary test of reading [the lease] reasonably and in a business sense”; if so, “the risk of loss by fire passed to the landlord, at least upon the presentation by the landlord of the insurance bill”.
BaselineA: Common law contract/lease interpretation ("reading it reasonably and in a business sense"), in the context of landlord-tenant fire-loss liability; with statutory context that standard fire coverage includes third-party negligence (Ontario Insurance Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 224, s. 118).
CaseB_TestB: Warsaw Convention limitation entitlement under Art. 3(2): limitation is lost “only where no ticket is delivered”; “The absence, irregularity or loss of the passenger ticket does not affect the existence or the validity of the contract of carriage… Nevertheless, if the carrier accepts a passenger without a passenger ticket having been delivered he shall not be entitled” to limit liability.
BaselineB: Statute/treaty text: Carriage by Air Act, R.S.C. 1952, c. 45, Schedule I (Warsaw Convention), especially Arts. 3(1)-(2), 4(4), and 22 (limitations).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Negligent misrepresentation (heating-cost estimate): plaintiff must prove more than error—must show the estimate was wrong because of a lack of reasonable care/skill/competence/diligence (i.e., failure to exercise “such care as the circumstances required”); failure to qualify is not itself negligence but may ground responsibility if the opinion is given carelessly
BaselineA: Common law (negligent misrepresentation / duty of care for advice): Hedley Byrne & Co. Ltd. v. Heller & Partners Ltd. (Lord Reid’s “three courses” and duty to exercise “such care as the circumstances require”); Mutual Life and Citizens’ Assurance Co. Ltd. v. Evatt (Lord Diplock on an “ascertainable standard of skill, competence and diligence”)
JudgeA: Ritchie J. (majority reasons; Laskin C.J. concurring on different approach)
CaseB_TestB: Extra-territoriality / s. 92 territorial limits for intangible pith-and-substance: (1) identify pith and substance and a provincial head of power; (2) decide if pith and substance is “in the Province”; if intangible, assess “relationships among the enacting territory, the subject matter of the legislation and the persons made subject to it” to see if the law has a “meaningful connection” to the province and respects other jurisdictions’ sovereignty
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine interpreting Constitution Act, 1867, s. 92 (territorial limits) and s. 92(13) (“Property and Civil Rights in the Province”), drawing on Reference re Upper Churchill Water Rights Reversion Act (Churchill Falls) and Unifund Assurance Co. v. ICBC (relationships/meaningful connection approach)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Parole suspension/revocation under the Parole Act: suspension requires a written warrant and may be issued when the decision-maker is “satisfied that the arrest of the inmate is necessary or desirable” for specified purposes; revocation may occur “in [the Board’s] discretion” including after sentence expiry if the inmate is “in custody pursuant to a warrant issued under section 16” (ss. 16(1)-(2), 10(1)(e)).
BaselineA: Statute (Parole Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. P-2, ss. 16(1)-(2), 10(1)(e); also discussed: Canadian Bill of Rights, s. 2(c)(i), s. 2(e); prior SCC approach in Ex p. McCaud and Howarth).
JudgeA: Ritchie J. (for Judson, Ritchie, Pigeon and Beetz JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Approach to equitable compensation for Crown breach of fiduciary duty over reserve land: the court must assess the beneficiary’s “lost opportunity” by asking “what position would the beneficiary be in had the fiduciary fulfilled its obligations?”, with factual causation but no foreseeability/remoteness limit; assess at trial “with the benefit of hindsight”; apply equitable presumptions (e.g., “most favourable use”); and in this context the Crown “ought to have first attempted to negotiate a surrender” and compensation must reflect “the value of the land to the hydroelectricity project”.
BaselineB: Common law (equitable compensation for breach of fiduciary duty: Guerin; Canson; Blueberry River; Osoyoos; Wewaykum; Williams Lake) applied in the statutory/treaty context (Indian Act, R.S.C. 1927, c. 98, ss. 48, 50, 51; Treaty No. 3).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Sales tax exemption for machinery/apparatus used “directly in the manufacture or production of goods”: regulators are not exempt where they merely control/transmit gas in distribution and cannot be considered used in “production” (distinguishing Hydro-Québec transformers as “no mere transmission”).
BaselineA: Statute: Excise Tax Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-13, s. 29(1) and Schedule III, Part XIII, para. 1(a)(i) (exemption for machinery/apparatus used directly in “the manufacture or production of goods”); interpreted in light of Hydro-Québec v. Dep. Min. of Nat. Revenue for Customs and Excise, [1970] S.C.R. 30.
JudgeA: Pigeon J. (for Martland, Judson, Pigeon, Dickson and Beetz JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Appellate review of a trial judge’s finding on the scope of a solicitor’s retainer: the scope of the retainer is “purely a factual question” and should not be upset on appeal “save for error arising from misapprehension of the evidence”.
BaselineB: Common law appellate standard of review for findings of fact (as stated in the decision: deference to trial findings; interference only for error such as misapprehension of evidence).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Whether an invention relates to a substance “prepared or produced by chemical processes” under Patent Act s. 41(1): apply the “popular” (informed layman) sense and assess the character of the entire process; chemical reactions are neither necessary nor sufficient, but it is enough if chemical operations play a significant part
BaselineA: Statute (Patent Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. P-4, s. 41(1)) as interpreted through prior SCC cases Continental Soya Co. Ltd. v. J.R. Short Milling Co. (Canada) Ltd., [1942] S.C.R. 187 and Laboratoire Pentagone Ltée v. Parke, Davis & Co., [1968] S.C.R. 307
CaseB_TestB: Adequacy/sufficiency of an indictment (including in multiple-conspiracy situations): an indictment is adequate if it gives the accused “reasonable information” to identify the transaction and prepare a defence; sufficiency depends on the offence and facts; time need not be exact unless essential and no prejudice; a charge is generally established if the offence occurred within the time period alleged; a proven conspiracy lies within the indictment if it included some accused, occurred sometime within the alleged span, and had as its object the type of crime alleged
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 510, 512, 516(1)(g)) informed by prior SCC guidance including R. v. Côté, [1978] 1 S.C.R. 8; R. v. Wis Development Corp., [1984] 1 S.C.R. 485; R. v. Cotroni, [1979] 2 S.C.R. 256; R. v. B. (G.), [1990] 2 S.C.R. 30
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 1 Charter justification (Oakes proportionality) applied contextually: pressing and substantial objective + proportionality (rational connection, minimal impairment, overall proportionality), with emphasis that the state must show a total ban is necessary and that justification must be “reasonable” and “demonstrably justified”.
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional text (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 1) as structured by common law (R. v. Oakes, [1986] 1 S.C.R. 103). Key quotes: s. 1 requires limits “as can be demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society”; Oakes proportionality has three aspects: measures must be “rationally connected”, “impair ... as little as possible”, and have proportionality between “deleterious” and “salutary” effects.
JudgeA: McLachlin J. (reasons adopted for disposition by Lamer C.J.; Sopinka, Major concurring; Iacobucci concurring in result)
CaseB_TestB: Duty to accommodate in the presence of a collectively bargained automatic-termination clause: the negotiated absence period is a relevant factor/evidence of accommodation/undue hardship but is not determinative; accommodation remains individualized and undue hardship is assessed globally from the start of the absence.
BaselineB: Common law human-rights accommodation framework from Meiorin (BCGSEU) and related cases, applied in labour arbitration context; also informed by Quebec Charter of human rights and freedoms (ss. 10, 20) and the collective agreement clause. Key quote (Meiorin test as reproduced): employer must show (1) purpose “rationally connected” to job performance; (2) adopted in “honest and good faith”; (3) “reasonably necessary” meaning “impossible to accommodate ... without imposing undue hardship”.
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Indian Act s. 88 provincial-law applicability/paramountcy inquiry: provincial law applies to Indians (via s. 88 reference) except to the extent it is "inconsistent" with the Indian Act; here, interpret Adoption Act s. 10(2) "for all purposes" so it does not remove an Indian child’s entitlement to registration under Indian Act s. 11(1)(d) (i.e., no inconsistency on registrability).
BaselineA: Statute: Indian Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-6, s. 88 (and s. 11(1)(d) registrability definition of "Indian"); applied to Adoption Act, R.S.B.C. 1960, c. 4, s. 10(2) ("for all purposes").
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 24(2) Collins framework for exclusion of evidence: assess whether admission would bring the administration of justice into disrepute by considering (1) fairness of the trial, (2) seriousness of the Charter breach, and (3) the effect of exclusion on the repute of justice; in this case, emphasize seriousness (including whether police had "reasonable and probable grounds" and good/bad faith) and exclude where cumulative breaches are serious.
BaselineB: Combination: Statute/constitutional text—Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 24(2) (and related ss. 8, 10); common law baseline from SCC precedent—R. v. Collins (three-category framework), as applied/organized in this decision.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Termination of a continuing guarantee by “notice in writing”: notice need not use set words but must be explicit and unequivocal (not merely an expression of “wish” or “preference”) so the creditor is left in no doubt
BaselineA: Contract/common law interpretation of the guarantee’s termination clause (Guarantee and Postponement of Claim, s. 4: liability may be determined “by notice in writing delivered to the Manager...”)
CaseB_TestB: Admissibility/use of an accused’s post-caution silence: unless the Crown establishes “real relevance and a proper basis”, questions about silence and evidence of ensuing silence should not be admitted; if admitted, the jury must be instructed to ignore it (no adverse inference)
BaselineB: Common law right to silence as protected by Charter s. 7, and prior case law on relevance/admissibility of silence (e.g., Rothman; Robertson; Symonds; Hebert)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Validity/regularity of an interim cease-and-desist order under Trade Union Act s. 49(2): Board may issue an interim order "if satisfied after investigation" of a s. 48 breach, "notwithstanding any provision of this Act"; investigation may be done through Board officers; interim order need not be limited to relief requested so long as it is related/connected to the illegal work stoppage
BaselineA: Statute (Trade Union Act, 1972 (N.S.), c. 19, ss. 48, 49(2), 15(9)-(10)) and constitutional constraint (British North America Act, 1867, s. 96) as interpreted in prior cases (e.g., John East Iron Works; Tremblay)
CaseB_TestB: YCJA youth-sentencing interpretation: general deterrence is not a sentencing principle because Part XXIII of the Criminal Code does not apply (YCJA s. 50(1) omits Code s. 718(b)) and deterrence cannot be implied from YCJA ss. 3 and 38; plus s. 42(2)(o) does not require a fixed 2/3 custody and 1/3 supervision split (unlike s. 42(2)(n))
BaselineB: Statute (Youth Criminal Justice Act, S.C. 2002, c. 1, ss. 3, 38, 42(2)(n), 42(2)(o), 50(1); Criminal Code, s. 718(b) referenced via s. 50(1) exclusion)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Relief from municipal notice requirement: if the plaintiff proves they were prevented from giving notice within 15 days for a reason “deemed sufficient by the court”, then the notice condition “ceased to exist” and (once the time is exceeded) the plaintiff is “permanently released” from any obligation to give notice before suing
BaselineA: Statute — Cities and Towns Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 193, s. 622(1), (3), (4), (5) (especially s. 622(4) “any reason deemed sufficient by the court or judge” and s. 622(5) prescription starting points)
CaseB_TestB: Judicial review of labour arbitration award on collective agreement interpretation: court asks whether the arbitrator’s conclusion is a “patently unreasonable” interpretation / whether it is “one which the agreement would reasonably bear” (and not whether the court would decide it differently)
BaselineB: Common law (as applied in labour arbitration/judicial review) — relying on Bell Canada v. Office and Professional Employees' Union, [1974] S.C.R. 335; McLeod v. Egan, [1975] 1 S.C.R. 517; and CUPE v. New Brunswick Liquor Corp., [1979] 2 S.C.R. 227 (patently unreasonable criterion)
JudgeB: Pigeon J. (reasons concurred in by Martland, Ritchie, Beetz and Pratte JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal negligence causing death under Criminal Code ss. 191-192: Crown must prove (a) breach of a legal duty and (b) that the breach showed "wanton or reckless disregard for the lives or safety of other persons"; similar-fact evidence admissible if relevant to guilty intent (not propensity) per Makin/Noor Mohamed/Wray
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code ss. 191-192 (now 202-203)) plus common-law evidence principles on similar fact evidence (Makin; Thompson; Noor Mohamed; adopted/limited discretion per Wray)
CaseB_TestB: Municipal valuation: where "special circumstances make it impossible to fix the realizable value of property by the usual methods", "whatever method is appropriate in the circumstances may be used" to estimate "actual value" (including the 'developer’s approach')
BaselineB: Statute (Charter of the City of Montreal, S.Q. 1959-60, c. 102, including ss. 873-874 appeal scheme) as interpreted through prior valuation jurisprudence (e.g., Sun Life Assurance; related SCC/PC cases)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Admissibility of similar-fact evidence on criminal negligence: similar acts admissible to establish mens rea (not propensity) if relevant to an issue such as whether the act was “designed or accidental” or to rebut a defence; Crown must prove (a) breach of a legal duty and (b) that the breach showed “wanton or reckless disregard”.
BaselineA: Combination: Criminal Code ss. 191-192 (now ss. 202-203) defining criminal negligence (“wanton or reckless disregard” and “duty” imposed by law) plus common-law similar-fact admissibility principles from Makin v. Attorney General for New South Wales and related cases (Thompson; Noor Mohamed; Wray).
CaseB_TestB: Issue estoppel as a defence to perjury after an acquittal: on a perjury charge, the Crown is estopped from re-litigating an issue decided in the accused’s favour unless it tenders evidence “not available by the exercise of reasonable diligence at the time of the first trial”.
BaselineB: Common law doctrine of res judicata/issue estoppel and fraud exception (e.g., Duchess of Kingston’s Case; Gushue; Humphrys), as adapted to criminal proceedings and perjury/double jeopardy concerns.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory interpretation of “tetracycline and its derivatives”: apply the common/primary meaning in both official languages; “derivative” means a thing actually “obtained from another” (not merely in the same scientific ‘family’).
BaselineA: Combination: (1) regulation/order-in-council tariff text (“Tetracycline and its derivatives” in Schedule A to SOR/69-8 made under the Customs Tariff Act) plus (2) interpretive rule that statutes use common-language meaning even in technical contexts; plus bilingual interpretation under Official Languages Act, s. 8(2)(b).
CaseB_TestB: Limits of inherent/implied jurisdiction re amici remuneration: courts may appoint amici only exceptionally when essential, but (absent statutory authority or a constitutional/Charter basis) inherent/implied jurisdiction does not extend to fixing amici compensation rates or ordering the Attorney General to pay a particular rate.
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine of inherent jurisdiction / implied powers of statutory courts (as described via prior cases such as MacMillan Bloedel and Caron), constrained by constitutional structure (separation of powers) and subject to statutory limits; with an explicit carve-out for authority “flowing from a constitutional challenge or a statutory provision”.
JudgeB: Karakatsanis J. (McLachlin C.J. and Rothstein, Moldaver and Wagner JJ. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Bankruptcy trustee’s statutory duty to insure: under Bankruptcy Act s. 9(1)-(2), trustee must keep in force existing insurance and insure/keep insured “all the insurable property of the bankrupt” (including hypothec-encumbered property), and if unable to obtain insurance must at least notify the secured (hypothecary) creditor; failure can ground personal liability (and s. 171 leave requirement does not apply to omissions).
BaselineA: Statute — Bankruptcy Act, R.S.C. 1952, c. 14, ss. 9(1)-(2) (insurance duty; proceeds payable to trustee) and s. 171 (leave to sue trustee), read with s. 2 definitions of “property” and “secured creditor”.
CaseB_TestB: Charitable status under ITA via common law Pemsel (4th head) as applied in Vancouver Society: to be charitable, an organization’s purposes must be (a) for “public benefit/beneficial to the community” and (b) “in a way the law regards as charitable”; under the D’Aguiar/Vancouver Society approach, assess (1) trend of prior decisions by reasonable extension/analogy, (2) accepted anomalies, and (3) cross-check whether property could be applied to non-charitable purposes; plus benefit must be to the community or an appreciably important class (not private advantage).
BaselineB: Combination — Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), ss. 149.1(1) and 248(1) (registration framework) relying on common law charity definition: Pemsel; Vancouver Society; D’Aguiar (test for 4th head).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Eligibility for a Quebec seat under Supreme Court Act s. 6 requires current membership: appointee must be appointed “from among” current judges of the Quebec Court of Appeal/Superior Court or current Quebec advocates (and must meet s. 5’s 10-year standing requirement). The Court held s. 6 “impliedly excludes former members” and “imposes a requirement of current membership” (paras. 42, 45, 70).
BaselineA: Statute (Supreme Court Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. S-26, ss. 5 and 6; also constitutional entrenchment analysis under Constitution Act, 1982, Part V, esp. s. 41(d)).
JudgeA: McLachlin C.J. and LeBel, Abella, Cromwell, Karakatsanis and Wagner JJ. (Joint Reasons)
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 15(1) equality test (as applied to Pay Equity Act s. 38): (1) does the law, on its face or in impact, draw a distinction based on an enumerated/analogous ground; and (2) does it impose burdens/deny a benefit in a way that “reinforc[es], perpetuat[es] or exacerbat[es]” disadvantage (Abella J., para. 22, citing Quebec v. A and Taypotat).
BaselineB: Common law / constitutional doctrine (Charter s. 15(1) framework from Quebec (Attorney General) v. A and Kahkewistahaw First Nation v. Taypotat, as quoted/applied at para. 22; applied to statute: Pay Equity Act, CQLR, c. E-12.001, s. 38).
JudgeB: Abella J. (Moldaver, Karakatsanis and Gascon JJ. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Highway Victims Indemnity Fund must satisfy a qualifying final judgment upon timely application; the claimant need not first exhaust remedies against the tortfeasor’s insurer, and the applicable prescription is 30 years because the claim is based on the judgment (not the underlying bodily injury). Key statutory requirements: creditor holds a qualifying final judgment (s. 36), applies within one year (s. 36), files a sworn declaration showing the judgment is unsatisfied and that “no insurer will benefit” (s. 37), after which the Fund “shall satisfy the judgment” within seven days (s. 38) and is subrogated to the creditor’s rights (s. 39).
BaselineA: Statute (Highway Victims Indemnity Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 232, ss. 36-39) plus Civil Code prescription provisions (arts. 2262, 2265).
CaseB_TestB: Fatal Accidents Act damages assessment framework: determine the dependants’ annual dependency (including deducting income tax to reach “take-home pay”), then calculate the present value of a lump sum that will replace that stream over the relevant period using a discount rate based on long-term investment returns adjusted for inflation, with a further reduction for contingencies. (E.g., “The object here is to award a sum which will replace present day payments of $7,000 per year for a future period of 31 years, with some reduction for contingencies”; discount rate “should be calculated on the basis of present rates of return on long-term investments with an allowance for the effects of future inflation”.)
BaselineB: Statute (The Fatal Accidents Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 164) as interpreted through common-law damages principles (including the Court’s contemporaneous trilogy on discounting/present value: Andrews, Thornton, Arnold).
JudgeB: Dickson J. (for Laskin C.J. and Martland, Ritchie, Pigeon, Dickson and Beetz JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Equitable/common-law test for awarding pre-judgment interest as compensation where a “just debt has been improperly withheld” and it is “fair and equitable” to award interest, with the rate set as the creditor’s borrowing rate on the facts
BaselineA: Common law/equitable principle (Toronto Railway Co. v. City of Toronto, [1906] A.C. 117; followed in The Custodian v. Blucher, [1927] S.C.R. 420) applied alongside statutory context (Interest Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-18, ss. 3, 12, 13; Supreme Court Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. S-19, s. 52)
CaseB_TestB: Two-step post-conviction non-disclosure framework: (1) reasonable possibility undisclosed info affects reliability of conviction; if not, (2) reasonable possibility non-disclosure affected overall trial fairness (lost lines of inquiry), with defence due diligence weighed in the fairness analysis
BaselineB: Common law/Charter jurisprudence on disclosure and remedies (R. v. Stinchcombe; R. v. Egger; R. v. Chaplin; R. v. Carosella) applying Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 7 and 24(1)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Doctrine/rule of recent possession (jury instruction): once Crown proves recent theft + accused’s possession, jury may infer guilt unless an explanation that may reasonably be true raises a reasonable doubt; Crown need not prove absence of explanation
BaselineA: Common law rule of evidence (as repeatedly approved), especially R. v. Schama; R. v. Abramovitch (Lord Reading’s formulation) as adopted/approved in SCC cases including Richler v. The King, Ungaro v. The King, Graham v. The Queen, Tremblay v. The Queen, and R. v. Graham
CaseB_TestB: Imperial Tobacco extraterritoriality framework for provincial legislation: (1) identify pith and substance by purpose/effects; (2) assess territorial limits by asking whether the law has a “meaningful connection” to the province and respects other governments’ sovereignty (applied to ORA s. 11)
BaselineB: Common law constitutional division-of-powers framework from British Columbia v. Imperial Tobacco Canada Ltd., 2005 SCC 49 (applied to Constitution Act, 1867, s. 92 territorial limits)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Mulligan (majority): psychiatric “dissociative reaction” evidence need not be re-put on the drunkenness defence where it is directed to insanity and (if accepted) would establish insanity; drunkenness is considered only if insanity is not proved
BaselineA: Combination: Criminal Code s. 212(a) (mens rea for murder) and common law intoxication/incapacity doctrine as in DPP v. Beard (1920) (adopted in the jury charge and treated as governing the drunkenness defence)
JudgeA: Martland J. (for Martland, Judson, Ritchie, Pigeon, Beetz and de Grandpré JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Ibanescu: “straddle evidence” is admissible to rebut the Criminal Code s. 258(1)(d.1) presumption, and its probative value is assessed under Gibson—i.e., whether the straddle range “may be capable of raising a reasonable doubt”, weighed in light of all the evidence
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code s. 258(1)(d.1) (statutory presumption from breathalyser readings) as interpreted through R. v. Gibson, 2008 SCC 16
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Drunkenness and mens rea for murder: intoxication only negates murder if it renders the accused “incapable of forming the specific intent”; psychiatric ‘dissociative reaction’ evidence need not be re-put on drunkenness if it is directed to insanity and would only matter if it showed a pre-existing susceptibility to alcohol incapacity
BaselineA: Combination: statute (Criminal Code, s. 212(a) (as then in force)) + common law intoxication doctrine (DPP v. Beard)
JudgeA: Martland J. (for Martland, Judson, Ritchie, Pigeon, Beetz and de Grandpré JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Section 23 ‘numbers warrant’ sliding-scale placement: (1) determine long-term number who will eventually avail themselves; (2) compare province-wide to majority schools to assess pedagogy/cost, with a rebuttable presumption from comparably sized majority schools; (3) determine level of services (homogeneous school if comparable and presumption not rebutted; otherwise range of services with deference to minority board)
BaselineB: Combination: constitutional text (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 23) + prior SCC framework (Mahe v. Alberta) refined/clarified
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: BC Labour Code s. 108(1)(b) review: court may intervene only for an “error of law affecting the jurisdiction” of the arbitrator; no such jurisdictional error where the arbitrator “applied himself to the problem at hand” and answered the question submitted after considering “all the circumstances” (i.e., no “sin of omission” amounting to jurisdictional error).
BaselineA: Statute: Labour Code of British Columbia Act, 1973, s. 108(1)(b) (limited appellate review; intervention only for “error of law affecting the jurisdiction of the arbitration board”).
CaseB_TestB: Garofoli leave (threshold) test for cross-examining a wiretap affiant: defence must show a “reasonable likelihood” that cross-examination “will elicit testimony of probative value to the issue for consideration by the reviewing judge” (relevance/materiality-focused threshold).
BaselineB: Common law: R. v. Garofoli, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 1421 (leave requirement/threshold for cross-examining affiant on a wiretap review).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Appellate restraint on concurrent findings of fact: SCC will not interfere "unless we are satisfied that the decision of the learned trial judge was wrong and that there was no evidence on which he could have reached his conclusion".
BaselineA: Common law (appellate standard of review for concurrent findings of fact; articulated in the reasons without specific prior SCC case citation).
JudgeA: de Grandpré J. (for Laskin C.J. and Judson, Beetz and de Grandpré JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Division of powers “integral element” test for federal jurisdiction over s. 92(10) undertakings: Parliament may displace provincial law only where the matter is "an integral part" of the core federal undertaking; otherwise provincial laws of general application apply.
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine (integral element approach) drawn from Construction Montcalm Inc. v. Minimum Wage Commission and Northern Telecom Ltd. v. Communications Workers of Canada, applied to s. 92(10) railways and s. 342(1) Railway Act.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory condition 10(a) / art. 2571 C.C. (fire insurance): policy not void for failure to state insured’s interest so long as insured has an insurable interest; “owned/possédée” read broadly (includes tenant/possessor). Key holding: “All that is necessary to satisfy statutory condition 10(a) of the policy is that the insured have an insurable interest.”
BaselineA: Statute + civil law: Insurance Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 295, s. 240 (statutory conditions incl. 10(a)); Civil Code art. 2571 (and related arts. 2480, 2572). Also relies on prior interpretation of similar statutory condition (Wandlyn Motels v. Commerce General Insurance Company, [1970] S.C.R. 992).
CaseB_TestB: Section 8 ‘piggybacking’ principle for bodily samples: when a non-police actor (e.g., coroner) seizes a bodily sample but it is later used for criminal prosecution, the court must assess whether police conduct constitutes an independent state seizure or renders the initial seizure unreasonable; once evidence is appropriated for law-enforcement use, it becomes unreasonable absent Hunter-style prior judicial authorization. Key statement: the court must “go beyond the initial non-police seizure” and determine whether police actions “constitute a seizure by the state in and of themselves or make the initially valid seizure by the coroner unreasonable.”
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine under Charter s. 8, building on Hunter v. Southam Inc. (prior judicial authorization requirement for criminal-law seizures) and R. v. Dyment (privacy in bodily samples/information). Statutory context: Coroners Act, R.S.O. 1980, c. 93, s. 16(2), (5).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Adjournment to secure counsel: an adjournment needed to exercise the s. 577(3) right to defend by counsel may be refused only for a reason based on established facts; refusal is reviewable if based on reasons not well founded in law (especially where it deprives a party of rights)
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 577(3) (right to make full defence personally or by counsel) and appellate review under s. 613; applied with reference to Talbot v. R. and distinguished from Spataro v. R.)
CaseB_TestB: Equitable compensation for breach of fiduciary duty: assess plaintiff’s actual loss with hindsight; foreseeability is irrelevant, but recovery is limited to losses which, on a common-sense view of causation, were caused by the breach (no recovery for unrelated third-party losses absent a direct link; no duty to mitigate in the tort sense, but losses from clearly unreasonable plaintiff conduct are attributed to that conduct)
BaselineB: Common law / equity (fiduciary duty and equitable compensation), drawing on Guerin v. The Queen and Nocton v. Lord Ashburton (and related authorities on equitable compensation)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Quebec Superior Court jurisdiction in a personal action (declinatory exception): under art. 68 C.C.P., jurisdiction lies in the court of the defendant’s domicile, or failing that, of his residence; filing a declinatory exception does not automatically shift the burden to the plaintiff to prove jurisdiction
BaselineA: Statute: Code of Civil Procedure (Quebec), arts. 68 and 70; plus Canadian Citizenship Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-19, s. 10 (presumption tied to citizenship/principal residence)
CaseB_TestB: When (and how) police/state misconduct can reduce a criminal sentence: if the misconduct relates to the circumstances of the offence or the offender, the sentencing judge may treat it as a mitigating factor within Criminal Code sentencing (ss. 718–718.2) without resort to Charter s. 24(1); sentence reductions must stay within statutory limits (e.g., mandatory minimums), save possibly in exceptional egregious cases
BaselineB: Combination of statute and constitutional text: Criminal Code, ss. 718–718.2 (sentencing principles) and statutory minimums; Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 24(1) (remedies)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Contractual interpretation of warranty: construe “depreciation” in para. 3(g) and the auditor’s letter as an accounting concept (write-off over useful life), not “full capital cost allowance” under the Income Tax Act; the bracketed phrase “(using capital cost allowance rates)” refers to rates only, not the tax ‘system’, and “at least” must be given effect—there is no breach if the books show full depreciation computed using those rates for the period assets were in service.
BaselineA: Common law (interpretation/construction of contractual warranty terms, using the contract text and incorporated auditor’s letter).
CaseB_TestB: Youth court power under Young Offenders Act: even though s. 19(2) says the court may “find ... guilty or not guilty or make an order dismissing the charge”, it does not authorize dismissing a charge merely because the judge thinks it “ought never to have been laid”; absent clear legislative intent, prosecutorial discretion governs, subject only to exceptional remedies like a stay for abuse of process (“clearest of cases”).
BaselineB: Statute (Young Offenders Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. Y-1, especially ss. 19(2) and 3(1), read against the common-law principle of prosecutorial discretion and limited judicial control via abuse of process/stay jurisprudence).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Crown appeal from acquittal (error of law): Crown must show the verdict "would not necessarily have been the same" absent the misdirection (White v. R. test)
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 613(4) (appeal from acquittal powers) plus the common-law test from White v. R., [1947] S.C.R. 268 (also applied in R. v. Gauthier, [1977] 1 S.C.R. 441).
CaseB_TestB: Group defamation in Quebec civil liability: plaintiff must prove personal injury to each member by showing an "ordinary person" would believe the remarks, viewed as a whole, damaged each member’s reputation; assessed contextually using non-exhaustive factors (size, homogeneity, identifiability, etc.)
BaselineB: Statute/civil code framework: Civil Code of Québec, art. 1457 (fault, injury, causal connection) and related C.C.Q. arts. 1607, 1611; plus procedural context under Code of Civil Procedure class action provisions (e.g., arts. 1002-1003, 1028, 1034, 1051). The injury standard draws on SCC Quebec defamation cases Prud’homme v. Prud’homme and Néron.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Interpretation of standard auto policy exclusion: whether an insured is “entitled to receive the benefits of any workmen’s compensation law or plan” (exclusion applies based on entitlement on the admitted facts, not on whether a claim/award was made). Key holding: “a workman’s entitlement ‘to receive’ payments is not dependent upon a formal application for workmen’s compensation having been made and approved”; thus a workman “who is ‘entitled to benefits’ ... is to be taken as being ‘entitled to receive benefits’ within the meaning of Exclusion 2(a)(ii)”.
BaselineA: Statute (Ontario): Insurance Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 224, s. 232(1) and Schedule E, Exclusion 2(a)(ii) (mandatory standard policy wording), interpreted in light of Workmen’s Compensation Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 505 (including ss. 3 and 8).
CaseB_TestB: Section 8 framework applied (mutatis mutandis) to cross-border disclosure under Criminal Code s. 193(2)(e): (1) disclosure must be authorized by law; (2) the law must be reasonable; (3) disclosure must be carried out in a reasonable manner. Authorization requires compliance with s. 193(2)(e)’s two conditions: recipient is “a person or authority with responsibility in a foreign state for the investigation or prosecution of offences” and disclosure is “intended to be in the interests of the administration of justice in Canada or elsewhere”; the discloser must “subjectively believe” this, “honestly and genuinely held”, with credibility “tested against objective facts”.
BaselineB: Combination: Charter s. 8 reasonableness framework from R. v. Collins / R. v. Caslake, applied to statutory disclosure power in Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 193(2)(e).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Service ex juris under Federal Court Rule 307: discretion guided primarily by forum conveniens—"the overriding consideration ... must ... be the existence of some other forum more convenient and appropriate for the pursuit of the action and for securing the ends of justice"; refusal is an error in principle if based solely on "no relation or connection with Canada".
BaselineA: Statute and regulation: Federal Court Act, R.S.C. 1970 (2nd Supp.), c. 10, ss. 22(2)(a), 43(1), 44; Federal Court Rules, Rule 307 (service ex juris).
JudgeA: Ritchie J. (for Ritchie, Pigeon, Beetz and de Grandpré JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Quebec civil liability (medical malpractice) causation: reject "loss of chance" as a substitute for causation where death/sickness has occurred; causation "must be established on the balance of probabilities, taking into account all the evidence: factual, statistical and that which the judge is entitled to presume"; in some cases a court may presume causation where a clear danger materializes unless strongly indicated otherwise.
BaselineB: Civil law (Quebec) principles of civil responsibility (fault, causation, damage) plus Civil Code of Lower Canada, art. 1205 (presumptions), as applied/clarified in SCC jurisprudence cited in the reasons (e.g., Snell v. Farrell; Morin v. Blais; Shawinigan Engineering v. Naud).
JudgeB: Gonthier J. (for Lamer C.J. and L'Heureux-Dubé, Sopinka, Gonthier, Cory and McLachlin JJ.)
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Breach of municipal development agreement sewer-servicing obligation: developer must prove a specific failure to provide sewers/enlargements “required to properly service” the redevelopment stage (i.e., evidence of actual or foreseeable inadequacy); a general sewer-upgrading report/charge is irrelevant absent evidence connecting it to serviceability of the project sewers
BaselineA: Contract (development agreement) interpretation and breach: s. 31(a)(iii) of the August 31, 1966 development agreement (City/CMHC “Partnership” covenanting to undertake “the construction of all public sewers in each stage and the enlargement of any public sewers located outside such stage that may be required to properly service such stage”)
CaseB_TestB: Presumption of advancement and rebuttal in husband-to-wife gratuitous transfer: presumption applies unless husband rebuts it; it is not rebutted by saying the transfer was only to defeat creditors, and surrounding conduct may confirm rather than rebut the presumption
BaselineB: Common law presumptions in property ownership between spouses: (1) resulting/constructive trust principle where property is put in another’s name without consideration; (2) rebuttable presumption of advancement when a husband conveys to his wife (court notes this is subject to later statutory change in Ontario, but not applicable retrospectively)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 613(1)(b)(iii) curative proviso: uphold conviction despite trial error if the Crown satisfies the appellate court that the jury, properly charged, "could not, as reasonable men, have done otherwise than find the appellant guilty" (i.e., no "substantial wrong or miscarriage of justice")
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, s. 613(1)(b)(iii)) as applied through SCC precedent (Colpitts v. R., quoting Brooks v. The King)
CaseB_TestB: Marshall treaty right framework: Mi’kmaq treaty right to fish and trade for "necessaries" (modern "moderate livelihood"), with (i) treaty interpretation allowing extrinsic evidence absent ambiguity and (ii) regulatory limits either (a) accommodated by regulation (e.g., catch limits for moderate livelihood) or (b) otherwise requiring justification under the Badger/Sparrow s. 35 infringement/justification approach
BaselineB: Combination: constitutional and common law (Constitution Act, 1982, s. 35; Sparrow prima facie infringement questions; Badger treaty-right justification; treaty-interpretation jurisprudence including Sioui/Simon/Sundown) applied to the Mi’kmaq Treaties of 1760-61 and fisheries regulatory scheme (Fisheries Act s. 7(1); Maritime Provinces Fishery Regulations ss. 4(1)(a), 20; Fishery (General) Regulations s. 35(2))
JudgeB: Binnie J. (for Lamer C.J. and L’Heureux-Dubé, Cory, Iacobucci and Binnie JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Carrier can invoke Hague Protocol/Warsaw liability limits (Art. 22) only if the passenger ticket/baggage check includes the required Protocol “notice” (Arts. 3(1)(c), 4(1)(c)) — i.e., something “in a form calculated to attract attention”; 4.5-point, inconspicuous print is not a “notice”.
BaselineA: Statute (Carriage by Air Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-14 incorporating the Hague Protocol amending the Warsaw Convention): Hague Protocol Arts. 3(1)(c), 3(2), 4(1)(c) and 22 (and contrasted with Warsaw Convention Arts. 3 and 4).
CaseB_TestB: Rebutting Criminal Code breathalyzer presumptions after St‑Onge Lamoureux: for s. 258(1)(c) (after severance), the accused must raise a reasonable doubt that “the approved instrument was malfunctioning or was operated improperly”; for s. 258(1)(d.1), the accused must adduce evidence tending to show alcohol consumption consistent with both (i) BAC not exceeding .08 at the time of the offence and (ii) the test results.
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, ss. 258(1)(c), (d.01), (d.1)) as reviewed under Charter s. 11(d) and s. 1; SCC severs parts of s. 258(1)(c) and upholds remaining scheme.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Municipal notice period under Montreal Charter art. 1088 runs from the claimant’s discovery of the accident’s causal significance (not necessarily the accident date) where starting from the accident date would make the right of action practically illusory
BaselineA: Statute: An Act to revise and consolidate the Charter of the City of Montreal, 1959-60 (Que.), c. 102, art. 1088 (notice requirement: city must have “received” notice within 15 days for sidewalk/roadway falls); related interpretive context: Interpretation Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 1, ss. 52 and 61; Post Office Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. P-14, s. 41 (rejected as deeming receipt absent agency)
CaseB_TestB: Discretionary test for discharging a civil jury after a reference to insurance: discharge only if the reference likely caused real prejudice amounting to a substantial wrong/miscarriage of justice and the prejudice cannot be cured (usually by instructions)
BaselineB: Common law baseline from Bowhey v. Theakston, [1951] S.C.R. 679 (automatic discharge once jury might infer insurance), which the SCC overruled in part; applied within the trial-management discretion context
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Admissibility of an accused’s prior in-court testimony (judicial statement under oath) at a later trial without a voir dire: such testimony is admissible as of right even if alleged to have been induced by unlawful threats/violence; voluntariness goes to weight for the jury, not admissibility. Key holdings include: “it is never necessary to hold a voir dire with respect to the voluntariness of a previous statement of the accused given in court” and “several considerations make the accused’s previous testimony admissible as of right, even if its voluntariness is disputed”.
BaselineA: Common law (distinction between extra-judicial confessions to persons in authority requiring a voir dire and judicial statements). The Court relies on longstanding authority that compelled prior judicial testimony is admissible, especially R. v. Scott (1856) 169 E.R. 909; also references Reg. v. Coote (1873) L.R. 4 P.C. 599; R. v. Brown (No. 2) (1963) 40 C.R. 105; Tass v. The King, [1947] S.C.R. 103. Statutory context noted: Canada Evidence Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-10, s. 5(2) (protection against subsequent use if claimed) and Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 17 (duress/perjury context).
CaseB_TestB: Appellate intervention for trial judge’s failure to consider relevant evidence: while an appellate court has “neither the duty nor the right to reassess evidence… for the purpose of determining guilt or innocence”, it must review the record to ensure the trial court “properly directed itself to all the evidence bearing on the relevant issues”; “Where the record… discloses a lack of appreciation of relevant evidence and more particularly the complete disregard of such evidence, then it falls upon the reviewing tribunal to intercede.”
BaselineB: Common law principles on appellate review of criminal convictions, drawn from SCC authorities including MacDonald v. The Queen, [1977] 2 S.C.R. 665 and Ungaro v. R., [1950] S.C.R. 430 (and related cases cited therein). (Statutory setting: Criminal Code appeal on a question of law under s. 618(1)(b), but the operative test is framed as common-law appellate duty/standard.)
JudgeB: Estey J. (for Martland, Dickson, Beetz, Estey, McIntyre and Lamer JJ.)
