Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Admissibility of Crown rebuttal evidence to an alibi/credibility: Crown may contradict an alibi only by attacking its “material points”; and the Crown may not contradict an accused on a “collateral fact” elicited in cross-examination
BaselineA: Common law evidence rules (rebuttal evidence limits; collateral-fact rule; similar fact evidence limits), as reflected in R. v. Cargill, R. v. Hrechuk, R. v. Rafael; and SCC similar-fact cases Leblanc v. The Queen and Boulet v. The Queen
CaseB_TestB: Self-induced intoxication and rape: rape is an offence of “general/basic intent”, so drunkenness has “no application” as a defence (subject to the narrow ‘incapable of forming specific intent’ doctrine for specific-intent crimes)
BaselineB: Common law intoxication doctrine and the specific-intent/general-intent distinction (The Queen v. George; DPP v. Beard; DPP v. Majewski applied/relied on)
JudgeB: Pigeon J. (for Martland, Judson, Ritchie, Pigeon, Beetz and de Grandpré JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Applicability of mandatory supervision under Parole Act s. 15(1) to an inmate with multiple sentences: if s. 15(1) is in force at release and the inmate falls within the proclamation class (sentenced to penitentiary on/after Aug. 1, 1970), then—because s. 14(1) deems multiple terms to be 'one sentence'—s. 15(1) applies to the inmate’s release on remission (over 60 days). Key statutory language: s. 15(1) 'Where an inmate ... is released ... as a result of remission ... and the term of such remission exceeds sixty days, he shall ... be subject to mandatory supervision'; s. 14(1) terms 'shall ... be deemed to constitute one sentence'.
BaselineA: Statute: Parole Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. P-2, ss. 14(1) and 15(1)-(2), as enacted/triggered by Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1968-69 (Can.), c. 38, s. 101(2) and the July 30, 1970 proclamation (SOR/70-339) fixing Aug. 1, 1970.
CaseB_TestB: Interpretation of Succession Duties Act s. 26(1): insurance proceeds are taxable succession property if they are 'proceeds of insurance policies ... due by an insurer by reason or on account of the death of the person on whose life the insurance was effected'—and this includes accident insurance where death is accidental ('a death does not cease to be a death because it is accidental') and 'sur la tête de' / 'on whose life' is not limited to life insurance.
BaselineB: Statute: Succession Duties Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 70, s. 26(1) (with related discussion of ss. 45(f) and 46(1)); interpretive support from Civil Code arts. 1902, 1903, 1905, 1906.
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Estate Tax Act: whether community property with a full survivorship stipulation involves a taxable “passing” on death / whether the deceased was “competent to dispose” of the property. Holding: survivor is owner retroactively so “no passing”; husband’s administrative powers do not make him “competent to dispose” within ss. 3(1)(a), 3(2)(a) and 58(1)(i) ("he is not free, not competent to dispose of such assets in any sense contemplated").
BaselineA: Statute (Estate Tax Act, 1958 (Can.), c. 29), especially ss. 3(1)(a), 3(2)(a), 3(2)(e) and 58(1)(i), applied with prior SCC interpretations in Sura v. MNR, [1962] S.C.R. 65 and The Royal Trust Company v. MNR, [1968] S.C.R. 505.
CaseB_TestB: Treaty/NRTA hunting right on private land: geographic limit based on “visible, incompatible land use” (case-by-case). If land is “occupied”, i.e., “put to visible use which is incompatible with hunting”, no right of access; if “unoccupied and not put to visible use”, right of access exists. Any prima facie infringement of the treaty/NRTA right must be justified using the Sparrow test (valid objective; then honour of the Crown/special trust; then possible further factors like minimal impairment, compensation, consultation).
BaselineB: Combination of constitutional/statutory instruments and common-law framework: Treaty No. 8 and Natural Resources Transfer Agreement, 1930 (Constitution Act, 1930, Schedule 2), para. 12; justification framework taken from R. v. Sparrow, [1990] 1 S.C.R. 1075 (applied to treaty/NRTA infringements).
JudgeB: Cory J. (majority reasons on the key tests)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Contractual price-adjustment clause for tax changes applies only where a “tax, duty, charge or fee” is imposed on the seller (Imperial) “in respect of bunker fuel oil” (the product) or its “production, manufacture, sale or delivery” by the seller; it does not extend to upstream cost increases (e.g., higher crude oil prices from foreign taxes/royalties borne by affiliates).
BaselineA: Common law (contract interpretation) applied to clause 9 of the parties’ supply agreement (price adjustment for taxes/duties/charges/fees borne by Seller; excluding income/profits taxes).
CaseB_TestB: Van der Peet test (as applied to self-government/gambling claim): (1) correctly characterize the claimed right by considering “the nature of the action”, “the nature of the governmental regulation ... being impugned”, and “the practice, custom or tradition” relied on; then (2) determine whether the activity is “an element of a practice, custom or tradition integral to the distinctive culture” and whether it was “a defining feature of the culture in question” prior to European contact.
BaselineB: Constitution Act, 1982, s. 35(1) (aboriginal rights), applying the common-law constitutional framework from R. v. Van der Peet, [1996] 2 S.C.R. 507.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Foreseeability-based duty/standard of care for occupier/railway: liability only if the injury was a "reasonably foreseeable result" of the situation created by the defendant; mere possibility is insufficient (no duty to prevent unforeseeable child act of boarding a moving train).
BaselineA: Common law negligence/occupier’s liability principles (foreseeability and duty of care), with a statutory fencing backdrop (Railway Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. R-2, s. 214) rejected as causative here; cases cited include Ouellet v. Cloutier, University Hospital Board v. Lepine, Mitchell v. C.N.R., Paskivski v. Canadian Pacific Ltd.
CaseB_TestB: Section 7 "fair hearing" requirements in IRPA security-certificate proceedings: a fair judicial process must include (1) a hearing, (2) an independent and impartial decision-maker, (3) a decision on the facts and the law, and (4) the right to know and answer the case; if full disclosure is impossible, there must be a "substantial substitute" (IRPA provided neither).
BaselineB: Constitutional/Charter baseline: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7 (and related analysis under s. 1), applied to the statutory IRPA security-certificate scheme (IRPA ss. 77-85, especially s. 78 secrecy provisions and s. 80 reasonableness determination).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory interpretation of Highway Victims Indemnity Act s. 43: Fund must satisfy judgment for unknown driver only "to the same extent as if [judgment] had been rendered against the author of the accident", meaning (i) Fund liability is capped at $35,000 (s. 14) and (ii) payment by another liable party does not extinguish the Fund’s capped liability where the victim received nothing from the unknown driver (no s. 38 deduction).
BaselineA: Statute: Highway Victims Indemnity Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 232, especially ss. 43 (unknown driver), 14 ($35,000 financial responsibility cap), 38 (deduction rule in Fund recourse), and 49 (Fund powers).
CaseB_TestB: Sentencing treatment of collateral immigration consequences: a judge "may exercise his or her discretion to take collateral immigration consequences into account", but only if the sentence remains proportionate (Criminal Code, s. 718.1); such consequences are "but one relevant factor" and "must not be allowed to dominate" or "skew" sentencing; appellate intervention is available where the sentencing judge was unaware of the collateral consequences or counsel failed to advise (fitness assessed without a relevant factor).
BaselineB: Statute and common law sentencing framework: Criminal Code ss. 718, 718.1, 718.2 (proportionality/individualization/parity) as applied through prior SCC sentencing jurisprudence (e.g., R. v. M. (C.A.); R. v. Wust; R. v. Ipeelee).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Whether the trial judge must give the accomplice-evidence caution (danger of convicting on uncorroborated testimony) when a witness may be an accomplice (and/or accessory after the fact), and whether the jury can realistically find “accessory after the fact but not accomplice” on the evidence
BaselineA: Common law rule of practice/caution on accomplice testimony (as discussed via Horsburgh v. The Queen and Davies v. D.P.P.; debate informed by R. v. Gratton and R. v. Riezebos) and related appellate harmless-error approach (The Queen v. Vézeau)
JudgeA: Pigeon J. (for Spence, Pigeon and de Grandpré JJ.; Martland J. concurs in disposition)
CaseB_TestB: Interpretation/application of Criminal Code s. 212(c) murder (“unlawful object” constructive murder): (i) meaning of “unlawful object”; (ii) no need that the dangerous act be unlawful; (iii) if dangerous act is unlawful, require a further unlawful object distinct from the immediate object; (iv) objective ‘ought to know’ applied using the accused’s actual knowledge of surrounding circumstances; intoxication relevant to that knowledge
BaselineB: Statute—Criminal Code, ss. 205(5)(a) and 212(c) (and context of ss. 212(a)(i)-(ii)); interpreted in light of prior SCC cases including Graves v. The King and R. v. Hughes et al.
JudgeB: Lamer J. (for Martland, Dickson, Estey, McIntyre, Chouinard and Lamer JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Construction of Manitoba auto insurance exclusion s. 31(3)(h): the phrase “the death of, an insured” must be read contract-specifically, because the owner’s and driver’s certificates are “separate contracts”; therefore the exclusion applies only to “an insured under that particular certificate” under which indemnity is claimed.
BaselineA: Regulation (Manitoba Automobile Insurance Regulation, Man. Reg. 333/74 under The Manitoba Public Insurance Corporation Act): s. 31(3)(h) (exclusion), read with ss. 30 (definition of “insured”), 31(1) (coverage), and 31(2) (“DRIVER’S POLICY”).
JudgeA: Pigeon J. (for Laskin C.J. and Ritchie, Spence, Pigeon and Beetz JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Treaty 8 / NRTA para. 12 “for food” limit: determine whether the impugned conduct is hunting “for food” (i.e., “for sustenance for the individual Indian or the Indian’s family”) or instead “an act of commerce”; if it is commerce (including a “multi-stage process” of selling to obtain funds), the treaty right does not protect it and provincial Wildlife Act s. 42 applies via Indian Act s. 88.
BaselineB: Constitutional/statutory interpretation of Treaty No. 8 (1899) and Natural Resources Transfer Agreement, 1930 (Alberta), para. 12, applied through Indian Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-6, s. 88, to Alberta Wildlife Act, R.S.A. 1980, c. W-9, ss. 1(s) and 42.
JudgeB: Cory J. (for Lamer, La Forest, Gonthier and Cory JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 287(2) “telecommunication” definition: theft of a “telecommunication service” applies only where the transmission/emission/reception is “by wire or cable” (not by Hertzian waves/radio); no “partly wire” vs “entirely wire” distinction
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 287(1)(b) and definition in s. 287(2) (“telecommunication” means transmission etc. “by wire or cable”)
CaseB_TestB: Immigration Act s. 19(1)(a)(ii) “excessive demands” assessment for social services: must be individualized and consider both medical and non-medical factors (including family ability/willingness to pay); threshold is “reasonable probability, not remote possibility” (more likely than not) that excessive demands will materialize
BaselineB: Statute: Immigration Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. I-2, s. 19(1)(a)(ii) (and noted parallel in IRPA s. 38(1)(c))
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Limits on municipal discretion to refuse a business licence under Municipal Act s. 455: discretion must be exercised “judicially”, not on “extraneous”/“irrelevant or alien” grounds; “in any particular case” means peculiar to the applicant (not a blanket prohibition of a business type), and refusal must not be “unreasonably” withheld
BaselineA: Statute (Municipal Act, R.S.B.C. 1960, c. 255, s. 455) interpreted in light of the Act’s overall scheme and common law limits on licensing/prohibition (e.g., Municipal Corporation of the City of Toronto v. Virgo, [1896] A.C. 88; Sunshine Valley Co-operative Society v. City of Grand Forks; Wilcox v. Township of Pickering)
CaseB_TestB: IRPA security-certificate disclosure/fairness standard under Charter s. 7: the named person must receive an “incompressible minimum” of disclosure and is “reasonably informed” only if they have “sufficient disclosure” to give “meaningful instructions” to public counsel and “meaningful guidance and information” to special advocates; if non-disclosure prevents this, the Minister must withdraw the information/evidence and the judge must quash the certificate
BaselineB: Statute + Charter (IRPA, especially ss. 77(2), 78, 83(1)(e), 83(1)(i); Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7) building on prior SCC constitutional requirements for security certificates (Charkaoui v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2007 SCC 9)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Appellate deference to trial findings of fact: an appellate court should not disturb findings of fact where there was “credible evidence” on which the trial judge could “reasonably base his conclusion”, and it is “not the function of an appellate court to reconsider that evidence … and come to a different conclusion, unless it can be shown that the evidence reasonably could not result in justifying the conclusion of the trial judge”.
BaselineA: Common law (appellate review standard for findings of fact; articulated as a “well-known principle” in the reasons, with reference to Cook v. Lewis and Mann v. Balaban).
CaseB_TestB: Bona fide occupational qualification (BFOQ) under Ontario Human Rights Code s. 4(6): (1) subjective good faith—limitation “must be imposed honestly, in good faith, and in the sincerely held belief” it serves adequate performance “with all reasonable dispatch, safety and economy” and not for “ulterior or extraneous reasons”; and (2) objective necessity—must be “related in an objective sense” and “reasonably necessary to assure the efficient and economical performance of the job without endangering” the employee, co-workers, or the public; employer bears the burden on a balance of probabilities once a prima facie case is shown.
BaselineB: Statute: The Ontario Human Rights Code, R.S.O. 1970, c. 318, ss. 4(1) and 4(6) (and procedural context under ss. 14a, 14d).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Unlawful act manslaughter causation: Crown must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused’s unlawful act was “at least a contributing cause of death, outside the de minimis range” (not necessary to prove it caused each intermediate mechanism like vomiting/aspiration).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code), especially s. 205(1) (“A person commits homicide ... when directly or indirectly, by any means, he causes the death of a human being”), applied with common law causation principles (incl. thin skull).
CaseB_TestB: Anns two-stage duty-of-care framework for novel pure economic loss claims: (1) prima facie duty based on foreseeability and “proximity”; (2) whether “policy considerations ... negative or limit” the duty—applied to hold generally no duty of care in commercial negotiations and no duty in drafting tender specifications in these circumstances.
BaselineB: Common law (Anns v. Merton London Borough Council; adopted in Kamloops (City of) v. Nielsen) applied to pure economic loss categories (Norsk; D’Amato; Bow Valley).
JudgeB: Iacobucci and Major JJ. (for the Court)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Crown bound by legislation/regulations only if expressly mentioned or (at common law) by “necessary implication” (i.e., the statute’s purpose would be “wholly frustrated” unless the Crown were bound); SCC holds current Interpretation Act s. 16 requires the Crown be “mentioned or referred to,” excluding necessary implication
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Interpretation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-23, s. 16 ("No enactment is binding on Her Majesty... except only as therein mentioned or referred to") and common law rule from Bombay Province v. Bombay Municipal Corporation, [1947] A.C. 58 (Crown bound by necessary implication only where purpose would be "wholly frustrated" otherwise)
CaseB_TestB: Breach of contract where a stipulated term (here, cargo weight) is “material if not a critical term”; excessive deviation from the stipulated weight constitutes breach, engaging Civil Code art. 1065 (damages for breach) rather than nullity for error under art. 992
BaselineB: Statute (Civil Code of Quebec): arts. 992 (error as cause of nullity only in specified circumstances) and 1065 ("Every obligation renders the debtor liable in damages in case of a breach of it on his part")
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Lord’s Day Act s. 11(x) exemption scope: CTC must assess only whether (given the Act’s object of preventing Sunday gainful work) the Sunday freight work is "necessary to permit" "with the object of preventing undue delay"; impacts on local peace/quiet (congestion, noise, pollution, safety) are irrelevant to the s. 11(x) inquiry
BaselineA: Statute: Lord’s Day Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. L-13, ss. 4 and 11(x) (interpreting "having regard to the object of this Act" and the Commission’s mandate); reference to Minister of Transportation and Communications (Ont.) v. C.T.C. et al., [1974] 2 F.C. 164
CaseB_TestB: Meaning of "bona fide" pension plan under Human Rights Code s. 3(6)(a) (Abella J. majority): plan must be "subjectively and objectively bona fide"—"a legitimate plan, adopted in good faith and not for the purpose of defeating protected rights"; inquiry is into the plan’s overall bona fides (registration under pension legislation is a helpful indicator), not actuarial details
BaselineB: Statute: Human Rights Code, R.S.N.B. 1973, c. H-11, s. 3(6)(a) (interpreting "bona fide" in the pension-plan exemption); discussed in relation to s. 3(5) (Meiorin) and Zurich but not importing those tests
JudgeB: Abella J. (Binnie, LeBel and Rothstein JJ. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “unduly” in Combines Investigation Act conspiracy: Crown must prove (1) intent to enter the agreement and (2) that the agreement, “if it were carried into effect would prevent or lessen competition unduly”; “best if not the only way” is “considering whether competition would be unduly prevented or lessened if the design evidenced by the agreement were carried into effect”; reject per se ‘meaningful segment’ approach
BaselineA: Statute (Combines Investigation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-23, s. 32(1)(c)) as interpreted in prior SCC cases (Howard Smith Paper Mills v. The Queen, [1957] S.C.R. 403; Weidman v. Shragge (1912), 46 S.C.R. 1; Stinson-Reeb Builders Supply Co. v. The King, [1929] S.C.R. 276; Container Materials Ltd. v. The King, [1942] S.C.R. 147)
CaseB_TestB: Unreasonable verdict (Criminal Code s. 686(1)(a)(i)): appellate court asks whether “the verdict is one that a properly instructed jury or a judge could reasonably have rendered”; may also find unreasonableness if an essential inference/finding “(1) is plainly contradicted by the evidence relied on ... or (2) is ... incompatible with evidence that has not otherwise been contradicted or rejected”; credibility findings cannot be disturbed unless they “cannot be supported on any reasonable view of the evidence”
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(a)(i)) plus SCC common-law gloss from R. v. Yebes, [1987] 2 S.C.R. 168; R. v. Biniaris, 2000 SCC 15; R. v. Sinclair, 2011 SCC 40; R. v. Beaudry, 2007 SCC 5; R. v. Burke, [1996] 1 S.C.R. 474
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Hodge’s Case circumstantial-evidence formula does not apply to proving intent; for intent the jury asks only whether guilt is proven beyond a reasonable doubt (Hodge applies only to the act/identity).
BaselineA: Combination: Criminal Code s. 110(1)(b) (requires intent to confer a benefit “with respect to those dealings”) plus common-law jury-instruction doctrine on circumstantial evidence (Hodge’s Case as limited by R. v. Mitchell).
CaseB_TestB: Insurance contract interpretation: give effect to the parties’ intent by construing policy references so they have meaning (art. 1014 C.C.); here “See Garage Policy” in the fleet policy refers to limits/premium, not to importing the garage policy’s restrictive coverage/exclusion.
BaselineB: Civil law/statutory interpretation of insurance contracts: Civil Code arts. 1014 (clause given meaning), 1013 (intent of parties) applied to the garage/fleet policies and rider Q.E.F. 73; also context of Highway Victims Indemnity Act ss. 10, 12 (insurance card) discussed.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Impossibility of performance as a defence in a mandate/contract claim: plaintiff must prove fault, damage, and causality; if defendant alleges the obligation was impossible (object impossible), defendant bears the burden to prove impossibility (not mere difficulty) under art. 1203 C.C.
BaselineA: Statute (Civil Code of Quebec): arts. 1701 (mandate), 984 and 1062 (object of contract/obligation must be possible), and 1203 (burden: 'he who alleges facts in avoidance or extinction of the obligation must prove them')
CaseB_TestB: Municipal office disqualification for conflict of interest: under Moncton Consolidation Act, s. 6, a mayor/alderman is disqualified if he 'directly or indirectly ... have[s] any interest in any contract' with the City (other than 'as a shareholder'); 'interested in' is given its ordinary meaning so that a director/officer is at least indirectly interested in the company’s municipal contracts.
BaselineB: Statute: Moncton Consolidation Act, 1946 (N.B.), c. 101, s. 6 (interpreted with reference to Interpretation Act, R.S.N.B. 1973, c. I-13, s. 17; and considered alongside Municipalities Act, R.S.N.B. 1973, c. M-22, ss. 71-72)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Interpretation of para. 12 Alberta Natural Resources Transfer Agreement: “Indians of the Province” (Alberta Indians) vs “Indians within the boundaries” (all Indians physically in Alberta, irrespective of residence), so non-resident treaty Indians in Alberta are subject to provincial game laws but retain the proviso right to hunt/fish for food on unoccupied Crown lands/lands of access
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional instrument and treaty: Indian Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-6, s. 88; Alberta Natural Resources Transfer Agreement, 1930, para. 12 (confirmed by British North America Act, 1930); Treaty No. 6
CaseB_TestB: Qualified privilege in libel: an occasion is privileged where the maker has an “interest or a duty, legal, social or moral” to communicate and the recipient has a corresponding interest/duty; on a privileged occasion, liability requires proof of malice, and the defendant is protected even if language is “violent or excessively strong” if he “might have honestly and on reasonable grounds believed” it true (Adam v. Ward; applied via Netupsky v. Craig)
BaselineB: Common law of defamation/qualified privilege (Adam v. Ward; Netupsky v. Craig)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory obscenity definition in Criminal Code s. 159(8) is the exclusive test for sex-based obscenity across the Code (displacing Hicklin): a work is obscene if it is a “publication” whose “dominant characteristic” is the “undue exploitation of sex” (alone or with crime/horror/cruelty/violence) and this s. 159(8) test should be applied wherever “the allegation of obscenity revolves around sex considerations”.
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, s. 159(8) (and its interaction with ss. 159(1), 163, 164) against the common law Hicklin obscenity rule (R. v. Hicklin (1868)) as discussed via Brodie v. The Queen, [1962] S.C.R. 681.
CaseB_TestB: Duty to accommodate in adverse-effect discrimination: employer (and, where it is a party to discrimination, the union) must take “reasonable measures short of undue hardship”; “undue hardship” is assessed contextually (non-exhaustive factors include “financial cost, disruption of a collective agreement, problems of morale of other employees, interchangeability of work force and facilities”, and safety), and the union’s duty depends on whether it (1) co-created the discriminatory rule or (2) impeded a reasonable accommodation; complainant must also facilitate and accept reasonable accommodation.
BaselineB: Combination: Statute (Human Rights Act, S.B.C. 1984, c. 22, ss. 8(1)(a),(b),(4), 9) as interpreted through common law/precedent on accommodation (O'Malley v. Simpsons-Sears; Central Alberta Dairy Pool; Etobicoke; Bhinder).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory obscenity test in Criminal Code s. 159(8) is the exclusive test for sexual-obscenity across the Code (Hicklin displaced): a work is obscene if it is a “publication a dominant characteristic of which is the undue exploitation of sex, or of sex and … crime, horror, cruelty and violence” and it “shall be deemed to be obscene”; this s. 159(8) test should be applied in other Code provisions (e.g., ss. 159, 163, 164) where the allegation “revolves around sex considerations”.
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, s. 159(8) (definition deeming certain publications obscene) and its relationship to other Code offences (ss. 159(1), 163, 164); common-law backdrop discussed: R. v. Hicklin (1868) as prior common-law obscenity definition; Brodie v. The Queen, [1962] S.C.R. 681 on exclusivity for publications.
CaseB_TestB: Duty-to-accommodate analysis for termination-after-absence clauses: apply Meiorin BFOR/justification framework; a collectively bargained maximum-absence/termination clause is “a factor to consider” and “evidence” in assessing accommodation/undue hardship, but “does not definitively determine” entitlement because “each case must be evaluated” individually; undue hardship from absence must be assessed “globally starting from the beginning of the absence, not from the expiry” of the negotiated period.
BaselineB: Common law / human-rights framework: Meiorin (BCGSEU) test (three-step BFOR/justification including accommodation to undue hardship) applied in the labour/human-rights context; also informed by Quebec Charter of human rights and freedoms (ss. 10, 20) and collective agreement clause 12.11.5 (36-month absence termination).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Federal jurisdiction over cable TV as a single interprovincial/international “undertaking” (no constitutional demarcation at the antenna/technology change): federal power extends to reception and onward transmission, and “programme content regulation is inseparable” from regulating the undertaking
BaselineA: Combination: Constitution (B.N.A. Act ss. 91 and 92(10)(a)) interpreted through precedent, especially the Radio Reference (In re Regulation and Control of Radio Communication in Canada, [1932] A.C. 304) and Winner ([1954] A.C. 541)
CaseB_TestB: Income tax “proceeds of disposition” treatment of assumed obligations: purchaser’s assumption is included only if it is a distinct existing vendor liability; if the obligation is an embedded future cost that “runs with”/is inseverable from the property, it merely depresses value and is excluded from proceeds
BaselineB: Statute: Income Tax Act, s. 13(21) (“proceeds of disposition” includes “the sale price of property that has been sold”), applied with the general principle that “the assumption of a vendor’s liability by a purchaser may constitute part of the sale price” (citing Telus Communications (Edmonton) Inc. v. MNR, Loyens v. The Queen, etc.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Immovable by nature (Civil Code): a structure is immovable if it adheres (directly or indirectly) to land or a building so as to acquire a fixed foundation; vertical attachment of a wire network to the ground is sufficient, and separation of ownership is irrelevant
BaselineA: Statute + civil law: Retail Sales Tax Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 71, ss. 2(3) ("moveable property" = all property not considered immoveable by the laws of Quebec) and 6 (tax on purchase price of moveable property), interpreted by reference to Civil Code arts. 374 et seq. (esp. arts. 375-378/376 on immovables by nature) and SCC precedents (Montreal Light, Heat and Power Consolidated v. Westmount, [1926] S.C.R. 515; Lower St. Lawrence Power Co. v. L’Immeuble Landry Ltée, [1926] S.C.R. 655; Bélair v. Ste-Rose (1922), 63 S.C.R. 526)
CaseB_TestB: Punitive damages for breach of contract (wrongful dismissal): available but rare; require an actionable wrong (typically tort) and conduct that is "harsh, vindictive, reprehensible and malicious" / "extreme" and "deserving of full condemnation"
BaselineB: Common law of contract damages and punitive damages: Addis v. Gramophone Co. (H.L.) and SCC’s application in Peso Silver Mines Ltd. (N.P.L.) v. Cropper, [1966] S.C.R. 673; plus general punitive damages principles (incl. Rookes v. Barnard (H.L.) discussed; McElroy v. Cowper-Smith and Woodman, [1967] S.C.R. 425; H. L. Weiss Forwarding Ltd. v. Omnus, [1976] 1 S.C.R. 776)
JudgeB: McIntyre J. (for Beetz, McIntyre and Lamer JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Assessment of a parent’s contributory negligence/obligation to contribute: whether the parent departed from the “generally accepted standard of care” of parents in the community (i.e., the conduct expected of a “reasonably prudent” parent in the circumstances)
BaselineA: Common law negligence (duty/standard of care), framed through Donoghue v. Stevenson’s reasonable foreseeability/“reasonable care” concept and prior negligence/contribution cases referenced in the reasons (e.g., Ware’s Taxi Ltd. v. Gilliham; Gambino v. Dileo; Beckerson v. Dougherty; Cowle v. Filion; McCallion v. Dodd)
CaseB_TestB: Repudiation by insisting on different terms: where a purchaser’s purported “election” under a fire/insurance clause goes beyond the clause and effectively dictates new conditions, it is “a refusal to complete the agreement as written” and constitutes repudiation that the vendor may accept
BaselineB: Combination of (1) contract interpretation of the parties’ agreement (standard form clause 5 and clause 9) and (2) common law contract doctrine of repudiation/acceptance of repudiation; also contrasted with the common law risk rule for damage between contract and closing (as described by the Court)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Matrimonial property beneficial interest via resulting trust (presumed common intention from contribution) and, alternatively, constructive trust for unjust enrichment (enrichment + corresponding deprivation + no juristic reason; causal connection to asset)
BaselineA: Common law (trusts/restitution): resulting trust presumption from contribution (e.g., Dyer v. Dyer; Thompson v. Thompson; Murdoch v. Murdoch; Pettitt v. Pettitt; Gissing v. Gissing) and constructive trust/unjust enrichment (Deglman v. Guaranty Trust; Murdoch v. Murdoch (Laskin J. dissent); Peter Kiewit Sons' Co. v. Eakins Construction)
JudgeA: Dickson J. (for Laskin C.J. and Spence and Dickson JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Discretionary access-to-exhibits test: presumptive openness subject to curtailment where needed to protect superordinate values (especially protecting the innocent), with court entitled to inquire into and regulate proposed use; balance privacy/prejudice vs public access
BaselineB: Common law (open courts/access to judicial records) as applied/extended from Attorney General of Nova Scotia v. MacIntyre; also considered alongside Nova Scotia Civil Procedure Rule 30.11(6) (return of exhibits)
JudgeB: Stevenson J. (for Lamer C.J. and Wilson, La Forest, Sopinka, Gonthier and Stevenson JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Limitation Act s. 6(4)(b) postponement test: time runs only when a properly advised reasonable person would conclude the plaintiff could reasonably sue, given the plaintiff’s own circumstances and interests; postponement only if those interests/circumstances are “serious, significant, and compelling” and not “purely tactical” (McLachlin J., para. 39).
BaselineA: Statute (Limitation Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 266, s. 6(4)(b) (and the s. 6(4) framework including s. 6(4)(a))).
CaseB_TestB: Arbitration Act s. 15 stay framework in receivership: (1) applicant shows an arguable case for four technical prerequisites for a mandatory stay; (2) resisting party must prove a s. 15(2) exception (e.g., agreement “void, inoperative or incapable of being performed”); in receivership, an agreement may be “inoperative” if enforcing it would “compromise the orderly and efficient resolution of the receivership”, assessed using a non-exhaustive factor list (effect on insolvency integrity, relative prejudice, urgency, insolvency stay, other factors) (Côté J., paras. 76-89, 155).
BaselineB: Statute (Arbitration Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 55, s. 15(1)-(2), interpreted alongside Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. B-3, ss. 183(1) and 243(1)(c)).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Start of 5-year extinctive prescription for engineers’ fees: prescription runs only when the fee is due—i.e., either “on completion of the work” or “at the time it was suspended, after a decision clearly communicated” to the engineers (and, under the tariff, generally not before the call for tenders or clear termination making tenders impossible).
BaselineA: Combination of statute/civil code and regulation, interpreted through general civil law principles: Civil Code art. 2260(6) (5-year prescription) plus the Quebec “Tariff of fee for Professional Engineers” (O.C. 891, Sept. 4, 1957, adopted under s. 4(2) of the Professional Engineers’ Act), and general principles of bilateral contracts (payment not demandable before performance/delivery absent agreement).
CaseB_TestB: Whether to enforce foreign letters rogatory under Canada Evidence Act s. 43: enforcement is “in [the court’s] discretion” and may be refused where Canadian public policy/sovereignty concerns outweigh comity; the court should not “take issue with the government’s determination of public policy or to measure its impact.”
BaselineB: Statutory discretion under Canada Evidence Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-10, s. 43 (court “may, in its or his discretion” order examination/production), informed by comity principles and public policy limits; considered alongside the Uranium Information Security Regulations (C.R.C., c. 366) and Atomic Energy Control Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. A-19, s. 9.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 170 nudity offence: s. 170(2) is a deeming provision that extends (does not restrict) “nude”; for complete nudity in a public place the Crown need not prove “offend against public decency or order”
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, s. 170(1)(a) (offence of being nude in a public place without lawful excuse) and s. 170(2) ("For the purpose of this section a person is nude who is so clad as to offend against public decency or order"); interpreted in light of predecessor s. 205A ("shall be deemed to be nude")
CaseB_TestB: Application of the Criminal Code s. 613(1)(b)(iii) proviso (“no substantial wrong or miscarriage of justice”): cannot be used where Crown improperly split its case and the appellate court cannot realistically assess the residual case after excising the improper reply evidence
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 613(1)(b)(iii) (curative proviso: appeal may be dismissed if “no substantial wrong or miscarriage of justice” occurred)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 170 nudity offence: complete nudity in a public place is established by the fact of being "completely bare"; s. 170(2) is a deeming provision that only extends "nude" to being "so clad as to offend against public decency or order" (no need for Crown to prove offence to decency/order in cases of total nudity)
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, s. 170(1)(a) and s. 170(2) (interpreting "a person is nude who is so clad as to offend against public decency or order" as a deeming provision; historical comparison to predecessor s. 205A)
CaseB_TestB: Availability of certiorari in criminal proceedings: for parties, certiorari lies "only for a jurisdictional error by a provincial court judge"; jurisdictional errors occur where the court fails to observe a mandatory statutory provision or breaches natural justice (legal errors, including disclosure errors, are not enough)
BaselineB: Common law extraordinary remedy constrained by Criminal Code s. 674 (no interlocutory appeals) and prior SCC jurisprudence (e.g., Cohen; Skogman; Dagenais; Cunningham) defining limits of certiorari
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Workmen’s Compensation Act s. 8 “additional sum” claim where the Commission is subrogated: if the dependant’s civil claim (reduced for the victim’s contributory fault) is fully covered by compensation, there is no further “additional sum” and the Commission has priority to recover up to what it paid
BaselineA: Statute and Civil Code: Workmen’s Compensation Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 159, ss. 7(3) (subrogation pleno jure) and 8 (right to claim “any additional sum required”); Civil Code arts. 1056 (wrongful death claim), 1157 (partial payment and subrogation priority). Prior SCC authorities on contributory fault reducing the civil claim: Rainville Automobile Ltd. v. Primiano; Hôpital Notre-Dame de l’Espérance and Théoret v. Laurent; distinguished Brink’s Express v. Plaisance (no victim fault).
CaseB_TestB: Employer’s obligation to pay under a service contract after purported termination: payment obligation depends on the employee being “available and willing to provide the services”; entering a conflicting contract and playing elsewhere is a breach that frees the employer from further payment
BaselineB: Common law contract principles applied to the parties’ written employment contract (interpretation of contractual terms on termination/guarantee; breach/repudiation).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Workmen’s compensation subrogation/priority where victim contributorily at fault: if the dependant’s civil claim against the third party is reduced by the victim’s fault so that the Commission’s compensation is not merely a “part payment”, the dependant cannot claim an “additional sum” under s. 8; the Commission is subrogated pleno jure and is reimbursed first up to what it paid (here, because the art. 1056 claim was only 50% of the loss).
BaselineA: Statute and Civil Code: Workmen’s Compensation Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 159, ss. 7(3) (subrogation pleno jure) and 8 (right to claim “any additional sum required”); Civil Code art. 1157 (partial payment rule) and art. 1056 (wrongful death claim reduced by victim’s fault). Prior SCC authorities applied/distinguished: Rainville Automobile Ltd. v. Primiano; Hôpital Notre-Dame de l’Espérance and Théoret v. Laurent; Brink’s Express v. Plaisance.
CaseB_TestB: Institutional financial security requirement for judicial independence: “Any measure taken by a government that affects any aspect of the remuneration conditions of judges will automatically trigger” the duty to use an “independent, effective and objective” commission process; if recommendations are ignored, the decision must be justified on a “simple rationality test”.
BaselineB: Constitutional doctrine under Charter s. 11(d) and the Preamble to the Constitution Act, 1867, building on Valente v. The Queen and the Provincial Court Judges Reference (Reference re Remuneration of Judges of the Provincial Court of Prince Edward Island).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Suspensive effect of serving a prohibition/quash notice with a Rule 7 command to make a return forthwith: the inferior criminal court’s jurisdiction is suspended (and it cannot take further steps) pending disposition; non-compliance with the return obligation cannot improve the inferior court’s position.
BaselineA: Combination: Ontario Criminal Rules 4-8 (esp. Rules 6-8 requiring a return “forthwith” and giving it “the same effect as a return to a writ of certiorari”) plus Criminal Code, s. 714; informed by common law certiorari suspension principles discussed in the reasons (e.g., R. v. Foster; R. v. Titchmarsh).
CaseB_TestB: Section 15(1) equality analysis (La Forest J. majority): (1) distinction; (2) disadvantage; (3) whether the distinction rests on an enumerated/analogous ground and, if so, whether it is an “irrelevant personal characteristic” by assessing the ground’s relevancy to the law’s “functional values” in its broader context.
BaselineB: Common law/constitutional doctrine under Charter s. 15(1), drawing on Andrews v. Law Society of British Columbia and Miron v. Trudel (as cited in the reasons).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Defence of fair comment in libel requires proof that the defamatory comment is the honest expression of the real opinion of the writer/publisher; absent evidence of the writers’ honest belief (and where the newspaper disavows belief), the defence cannot go to the jury. Key statements: “A defence of fair comment is dependent upon the fact that the words in issue represent an honest expression of the real view of the person making the comment”; “it is an essential ingredient to the defence of fair comment that it must be the honest expression of the writer's opinion, and each publisher in relying on the defence of fair comment is in exactly the same position as the original writer.”
BaselineA: Common law (defamation; fair comment defence), drawing on authorities cited in the reasons including Turner v. Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer Pictures Ltd., Jones v. Skelton, Slim v. Daily Telegraph Ltd., and Silkin v. Beaverbrook Newspapers Ltd.
CaseB_TestB: Section 2(a) freedom of religion infringement threshold for indirect burdens: state action that “increases the cost of practising or otherwise manifesting religious beliefs” can infringe s. 2(a), but “is not prohibited if the burden is trivial or insubstantial”; all coercive burdens (direct/indirect, intentional/unintentional) are “potentially within the ambit of s. 2(a).”
BaselineB: Statute/constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 2(a) (and interpretive context s. 27); developed in light of R. v. Big M Drug Mart Ltd. and applied alongside s. 1 (Oakes framework referenced but not selected as the key test here).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Fair comment defence requires proof that the defamatory comment was an honest expression of the real opinion of the writer/publisher (each publisher is in the same position as the original writer); absent evidence of the writers’ honest belief (and with the newspaper’s denial of belief), the defence is unavailable
BaselineA: Common law defamation (fair comment) as described in authorities cited in the reasons (e.g., Turner v. Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer Pictures Ltd.; Jones v. Skelton; Slim v. Daily Telegraph; Silkin v. Beaverbrook Newspapers; and related cases discussed).
CaseB_TestB: Contempt of court: liability requires personal service or actual personal knowledge of the order (proved beyond a reasonable doubt); service on a solicitor does not, without supporting circumstances, fix ministers with knowledge; vicarious liability/delegation/identification do not apply to natural persons in contempt
BaselineB: Common law contempt (knowledge requirement) plus interpretation of Federal Court Rules (C.R.C. 1978, c. 663, Rules 308, 311, 355) as not altering the common-law elements of contempt.
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Fair comment in defamation requires proof that the impugned comment was an honest expression of the real view of the person making/publishing the comment; absent evidence of the writers' honest belief (and with the newspaper/editor denying honest belief), the defence is not available. Key quotes: "A defence of fair comment is dependent upon the fact that the words in issue represent an honest expression of the real view of the person making the comment"; "it is an essential ingredient to the defence of fair comment that it must be the honest expression of the writer's opinion, and each publisher in relying on the defence of fair comment is in exactly the same position as the original writer".
BaselineA: Common law defamation (fair comment) as described through prior authorities cited in the reasons, including Silkin v. Beaverbrook Newspapers Ltd.; Turner v. Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer Pictures Ltd.; Jones v. Skelton; Slim v. Daily Telegraph Ltd.
CaseB_TestB: Garofoli review of wiretap authorizations: errors in the information to the authorizing judge "are only factors" and "do not by themselves lead to automatic vitiation"; the reviewing judge should excise the tainted material and ask whether the remaining, independent information provides "sufficient reliable" and "independently verifiable" grounds on which an authorization "could reasonably be based".
BaselineB: Statutory wiretap authorization regime (Criminal Code interception of private communications) as applied through the SCC framework in R. v. Garofoli, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 1421.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Intra vires test for CRTC regulations under Broadcasting Act s. 16: validity is tested by determining objectively whether the regulation "deals with a class of subject referred to in s. 3" (i.e., is "in furtherance of its objects" implementing the s. 3 broadcasting policy).
BaselineA: Statute (Broadcasting Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. B-11, ss. 3, 15, 16(1) including 16(1)(b)(i) and (ix)) and subordinate legislation (Radio (A.M.) Broadcasting Regulations, s. 5(1)(k)).
CaseB_TestB: Quasi-delict/negligence and jury review framework: fault under art. 1053 C.C. is assessed by whether conduct matches "a reasonable person concerned about the interests of others and placed in the same external situation"; a jury verdict stands unless "unreasonable" (art. 380 C.C.P.), with the judge setting the legal criterion and the jury translating the prudent-and-reasonable-person standard to the case.
BaselineB: Statute/civil law (Civil Code art. 1053; Code of Civil Procedure arts. 363, 380) plus prior jurisprudence referenced in reasons (notably Metropolitan Railway Co. v. Jackson (1877), 3 A.C. 193; Gagné v. Côté, [1970] S.C.R. 25).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Limits on a provincial commission of inquiry’s coercive powers vis-à-vis federal institutions/Crown: a province may inquire into specific criminal acts by RCMP members as part of “administration of justice”, but cannot (directly or indirectly) inquire into RCMP administration/management; and a minister’s s. 41(2) Federal Court Act national-security certificate is binding on a commissioner (not a superior court) so production “shall be refused without any examination”.
BaselineA: Combination: Constitution (B.N.A. Act ss. 91, 92, esp. s. 92(14) vs s. 91(27)); Quebec Public Inquiry Commission Act (s. 7); Federal Court Act, R.S.C. 1970 (2nd Supp.), c. 10, s. 41(1)-(2); common law Crown immunity/privilege principles (as discussed via cases such as Quebec North Shore Paper; Alberta v. C.T.C.).
CaseB_TestB: Contested custody between natural parent and adoptive parents: exercising parens patriae (via s. 39), the court must treat “the welfare of the child” as “the predominant factor” and decide it on “all relevant factors” (including “psychological, spiritual and emotional welfare”); parental claims are considered but “must be set aside where the welfare of the child requires it”.
BaselineB: Combination: Domestic Relations Ordinance, R.O.N.W.T. 1974, c. D-9, ss. 28(1), 35(2), 37, 39 (equity rules preserved); common law/equity parens patriae approach as reflected in cited authorities (e.g., Re Moores and Feldstein; Beson; Racine; J. v. C.).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Public Authorities Protection Act s. 11: whether the impugned act/omission falls within a "statutory or other public duty or authority" by segregating statutory functions into (1) those with a "public aspect or connotation" vs (2) "private executive or private administrative" / "managerial, internal or operational" matters that are "subordinate or incidental" (only the former get s. 11’s six-month bar).
BaselineA: Statute: The Public Authorities Protection Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 374, s. 11, interpreted in relation to The Housing Development Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 213, s. 6(2); with interpretive support from Bradford Corporation v. Myers and McGonegal v. Gray (as discussed in the reasons).
CaseB_TestB: Non-delegable statutory duty (Indian Act): determine whether a statute creates a mandatory non-delegable duty by starting with the statutory text and asking whether it "clearly places" the government under such a duty; permissive language ("may" not "shall") and express power to contract out/enter agreements indicate no non-delegable duty.
BaselineB: Statute: Indian Act, S.C. 1951, c. 29, ss. 113-114 (and related context), applying the approach referenced to E.D.G. v. Hammer and contrasting Lewis (Guardian ad litem of) v. British Columbia.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Exemption-from-seizure for insurance proceeds: an exemption clause in a life insurance policy can operate only in favour of a “true beneficiary” (a third party); a universal legatee/heir is not a third party and therefore cannot rely on the policy clause or C.C.P. art. 553(3). Key holdings: “respondent definitely cannot be considered as the ‘beneficiary’ of the policy”; “In order for there to be a stipulation for the benefit of a third person, a benefit must be stipulated for a third party. In the eyes of the law a person’s heirs are not third parties.”
BaselineA: Statute/civil law codal provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, art. 553(3) (exemption from seizure for property declared exempt by donor/testator); Civil Code (C.C.) arts. 597 (heir not a third party), 1028 (contract binds heirs/legal representatives), 735 (limits on bequests protecting against creditors).
CaseB_TestB: No-fault liability for neighbourhood disturbances under art. 976 C.C.Q.: liability turns on whether neighbours suffered “abnormal or excessive annoyances” beyond “the limit of tolerance” owed “according to the nature or location of their land or local custom”, and does not require proof of wrongful conduct. Key statements: “conduct is not the deciding criterion when it comes to abnormal annoyances under art. 976 C.C.Q.”; “there is… a no-fault liability regime based on art. 976 C.C.Q.”
BaselineB: Statute/civil code: Civil Code of Québec, art. 976 (neighbours must tolerate normal annoyances not beyond the limit of tolerance). The Court also situates this alongside arts. 1457 (fault-based liability) and 7 (abuse of rights), but the key test is grounded in art. 976.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Superior Court jurisdiction not ousted: a provincial superior court may decide a federal-utility statutory-interpretation issue (e.g., whether s. 5(4) imposes an obligation) when it arises incidentally in a properly brought tort/injunction action, absent a clear exclusive-jurisdiction grant to the regulator
BaselineA: Statute + provincial procedural law: Quebec Code of Civil Procedure, art. 31 (general original jurisdiction unless exclusively assigned elsewhere) and federal scheme in An Act respecting The Bell Telephone Company of Canada, s. 5(4)-(6), plus National Transportation Act, s. 45(1) (argued as ousting jurisdiction)
CaseB_TestB: Test for reopening the Crown’s case: the keystone is prejudice to the accused; discretion narrows by trial stage—(1) before Crown closes: broad latitude; (2) after Crown closes but before defence elects: allowed to correct oversight/inadvertent omission if justice requires and no prejudice; (3) after defence has started to answer: reopening only in the narrowest/most exceptional circumstances (generally limited to matters of form or where defence conduct contributed), to protect against self-incrimination
BaselineB: Common law discretion on reopening (including Robillard v. The Queen) informed/constitutionalized by Charter principle against self-incrimination (ss. 7, 11(c), 13 referenced in reasons)
JudgeB: Lamer C.J. (for Lamer C.J. and Sopinka, Cory, Iacobucci and Major JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Admissibility of cross-examining an accused/witness on juvenile delinquency record as “convictions” under s. 12 Canada Evidence Act (and rebuttal of good character under s. 593 Criminal Code): (1) “any offence” in s. 12(1) includes Criminal Code violations dealt with under the Juvenile Delinquents Act; (2) a juvenile “finding of delinquency” is “equivalent to a conviction” for s. 12; (3) an admitted prior conviction/delinquency need not be proved by the official record unless exceptional circumstances show the admission was erroneous; and (4) where the accused says he has never been convicted/arrested, he “put his character in issue” so the Crown may contradict with proof of prior convictions.
BaselineA: Statute: Canada Evidence Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-10, s. 12(1)-(2); Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 593; interpreted in light of Juvenile Delinquents Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. J-3 (esp. ss. 3, 20(1), 38).
JudgeA: Pratte J. (for Martland, Ritchie, Pigeon, Beetz and Pratte JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Whether an indictment may be amended to cure a variance between a particular and the proof: under Criminal Code s. 529(4)-(5), the court considering amendment must consider (a) preliminary inquiry evidence, (b) trial evidence, (c) circumstances, (d) whether the accused was “misled or prejudiced in his defence”, and (e) whether the amendment can be made “without injustice”; if prejudice exists but can be removed, the court may adjourn (s. 529(5)); if no (irreparable) prejudice, amendment should be made, and on appeal the SCC may amend and dismiss under s. 613(1)(b)(i) and (3).
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 529(4)-(5), 613(1)(b)(i), 613(3); applied in context of Narcotic Control Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. N-1, ss. 2, 4 and Schedule item 3.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Dickson J.’s four-criteria test for whether an administrative decision is required by law to be made on a judicial or quasi-judicial basis (for Federal Court Act s. 28 reviewability): (1) whether the statutory language/context suggests a hearing; (2) whether the decision affects rights/obligations; (3) whether an adversary process is involved; (4) whether there is an obligation to apply substantive rules to individual cases — “These are all factors to be weighed and evaluated, no one of which is necessarily determinative.”
BaselineA: Common law / administrative law (duty to act judicially / natural justice) applied within the statutory framework of Federal Court Act s. 28 and Income Tax Act s. 231(4)-(5).
CaseB_TestB: Stillman s. 24(2) ‘trial fairness’ framework: classify Charter-breached evidence as non-conscriptive vs conscriptive; if conscriptive, ask whether Crown proves on a balance of probabilities it would have been discovered by alternative non-conscriptive means (independent source/inevitable discovery). If conscriptive and not discoverable, “the court, as a general rule, will exclude the evidence without considering” other Collins factors.
BaselineB: Statute/constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 24(2), building on Collins (s. 24(2) factors) and related SCC jurisprudence (e.g., Hebert, Black, Burlingham, Colarusso).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory limits on interim rate-setting: s. 31 “losses” means lost revenue after the rate application, and the legality question is whether interim rates will prospectively over-recover by including pre-application shortfalls; plus s. 8 duty to give reasons (findings of fact + reasons).
BaselineA: Statute: The Gas Utilities Act, R.S.A. 1970, c. 158, ss. 27-28 (rate-setting generally) and especially s. 31 (excess revenues/losses after application due to undue delay); and The Administrative Procedures Act, R.S.A. 1970, c. 2, s. 8 (written decision with findings of fact and reasons). Prior SCC reference: City of Edmonton et al. v. Northwestern Utilities Limited, [1961] S.C.R. 392 (Locke J. on s. 31 meaning of “losses”).
CaseB_TestB: Cuerrier fraud-vitiated consent test under Criminal Code s. 265(3)(c): non-disclosure of HIV status vitiates consent if (1) dishonesty (including non-disclosure) related to obtaining consent, assessed objectively, and (2) deprivation via exposing the complainant to a “significant risk of serious bodily harm”; plus proof the complainant would have refused unprotected sex if informed.
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, ss. 265(3)(c) (fraud vitiating consent) and 268 (aggravated assault). Common-law/criminal-fraud concepts used as baseline for “fraud”: R. v. Olan, [1978] 2 S.C.R. 1175; R. v. Théroux, [1993] 2 S.C.R. 5; R. v. Zlatic, [1993] 2 S.C.R. 29; and rejection of the older “nature and quality of the act” limitation associated with R. v. Clarence (1888).
JudgeB: Cory J. (for Cory, Major, Bastarache and Binnie JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory interpretation of Parole Act ss. 10 and 20 (as amended in 1977): day parole may be ended by either (i) revocation under s. 10(1)(e) triggering s. 20 consequences, or (ii) termination under s. 10(2); the phrase “any parole” in s. 20(2) includes day parole and “recommitment” in s. 20(1) creates no operative ambiguity
BaselineA: Statute: Parole Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. P-2 (as amended 1977), especially ss. 2 (definition of “parole” includes day parole), 10(1)(e), 10(2), and 20(1)-(3); also Penitentiary Act remission context (s. 22(1))
CaseB_TestB: Palmer criteria (applied to sentence appeals) for admitting fresh evidence on appeal: (1) generally not admitted if could have been adduced at trial by due diligence; (2) relevant; (3) credible; (4) if believed, could reasonably, with the trial record, be expected to have affected the result
BaselineB: Common law: Palmer v. The Queen, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 759 (fresh evidence test), applied within the statutory appellate context (Criminal Code ss. 683 and 687)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Exercise of SCC discretion under Supreme Court Act s. 52 to vary interest on an SCC judgment: default is interest runs as it would on the trial judgment "[u]nless otherwise ordered by the Court", but the Court may limit interest based on the circumstances (here, limiting pre-SCC-judgment interest to the trial award due to appellant-caused delay).
BaselineA: Statute (Supreme Court Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. S-19, s. 52 (as amended in 1976) and Interest Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-18, ss. 13-14; plus SCC Rules r. 61 procedure for varying an unsettled/unentered judgment).
CaseB_TestB: Whether procedural fairness/natural justice applies to Governor in Council review under National Transportation Act s. 64(1): on proper construction, s. 64(1) imposes no implied duty of fairness (no hearing/reasons/disclosure required) because the Governor in Council’s discretion is "complete" within the "jurisdictional boundaries" of s. 64(1).
BaselineB: Statute (National Transportation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. N-17, s. 64(1)-(2), contrasted; with context from Railway Act ss. 320-321 and Interpretation Act s. 28; common-law fairness/natural justice principles considered but held not implied on this statutory scheme).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory-limit rule for groundwater pumping: under Ontario Water Resources Commission Act s. 37, pumping above 10,000 gallons/day (absent a permit) is deemed unreasonable and can ground nuisance/negligence; no pumping right is a defence for excess pumping
BaselineA: Combination of common law nuisance/negligence (including the prior “English Rule” for percolating water) and statute: Ontario Water Resources Commission Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 332, s. 37 (and discussion of s. 47 / Expropriations Act context).
CaseB_TestB: Meaning of “unlawful and intentional interference” for exemplary damages under Quebec Charter s. 49(2): intent exists where the actor (1) desires/intends the consequences of the wrongful conduct, or (2) acts with full knowledge of the “immediate and natural or at least extremely probable” consequences
BaselineB: Statute: Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms (Quebec), R.S.Q., c. C-12, s. 49(2) (and s. 1 context), as interpreted through SCC jurisprudence including Quebec (Public Curator) v. Syndicat national des employés de l’hôpital St-Ferdinand.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Highway Code s. 13(6) irrebuttable presumption: if the registered owner has not complied with s. 13(1)-(2), he "shall be deemed to be the owner for purposes of responsibility and for purposes of insurance against the responsibility resulting from the ownership or use of such vehicle"; therefore, for liability coverage the transfer is treated as not having occurred and the buyer/driver can be covered under the transferor’s omnibus clause (driving with the deemed owner’s consent).
BaselineA: Statute (Highway Code, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 231, s. 13(6) (and related compliance duties in s. 13(1)-(2)); applied to the civil liability section/omnibus clause of the auto policy).
CaseB_TestB: Garofoli leave/threshold test for cross-examining a wiretap affiant: defence must show a "reasonable likelihood" that cross-examination "will elicit testimony of probative value" on the issue for the reviewing judge (i.e., tending to undermine a statutory precondition/basis for the authorization).
BaselineB: Common law (R. v. Garofoli, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 1421), applied in the context of Criminal Code wiretap authorizations (including s. 184.2) and Charter s. 8 review.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Direct action under Highway Victims Indemnity Act s. 6: insurer is directly liable to third parties only for “damage covered by liability insurance”; s. 6 removes only “causes of nullity or of lapse” defences and “does not extend the insurance contract to what it does not cover”, so coverage turns on the policy’s definition of “automobile” and whether the damage was caused “first and foremost” by use of an excluded trailer rather than the insured automobile.
BaselineA: Statute (Highway Victims Indemnity Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 232, s. 6) as interpreted in General Security Insurance Company of Canada v. Bélanger, [1977] 1 S.C.R. 802, applied to the insurance contract’s coverage definition (policy definition of “automobile” for Section A “Civil Liability”).
CaseB_TestB: Lease interpretation re fire insurance/subrogation: a landlord’s covenant to insure “with the Lessee” runs to the tenant’s benefit (barring the insurer’s subrogated claim for tenant-negligence fire loss) unless there is “another explanation” in the lease (e.g., option-to-purchase provisions) sufficient to show the covenant was not meant to shift the negligence-fire risk off the tenant.
BaselineB: Common law (landlord-tenant/insurance allocation) drawing on Ross Southward Tire Ltd. v. Pyrotech Products Ltd., [1976] 2 S.C.R. 35 and Agnew-Surpass Shoe Stores Ltd. v. Cummer-Yonge Investments Ltd., [1976] 2 S.C.R. 221, and distinguishing United Motors Service Inc. v. Hutson, [1937] S.C.R. 294.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Qualified privilege in defamation defeated only by malice; privilege protects even excessive language if the defendant "might have honestly and on reasonable grounds believed" it was true (Adam v. Ward / Netupsky v. Craig)
BaselineA: Common law (qualified privilege and malice; definition of privileged occasion from Adam v. Ward; scope of protection and 'honestly and on reasonable grounds believed' language from Adam v. Ward as applied in Netupsky v. Craig)
CaseB_TestB: Sheppard/Braich test for appellate intervention based on insufficient reasons: (1) are the reasons inadequate; (2) if so, do they prevent appellate review (i.e., are they not "sufficiently amenable to appellate review")
BaselineB: Common law (R. v. Sheppard; R. v. Braich; related deference principles such as 'palpable and overriding error')
JudgeB: Bastarache and Abella JJ. (LeBel J. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Fault for unlawful arrest by police: (1) coroner’s s. 38 warrant is invalid if used to detain a suspect rather than ensure attendance as a witness; and (2) warrantless arrest power requires “reasonable and probable grounds” that must “take into account all the information available” (police may disregard only what they have good reason to believe is unreliable).
BaselineA: Combination of statute and civil law delict: Civil Code arts. 1053, 1054 (fault and employer liability) plus Coroners’ Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 29, s. 38 (detention of witnesses) and Criminal Code 1965 s. 435 (warrantless arrest on reasonable and probable grounds).
CaseB_TestB: Validity of dismissal of a probationary constable: dismissal is ineffective unless made by the Board (non-delegable statutory/contractual authority), and the Board cannot “fulfil its statutory function” where it does not even notify the constable that his case will be considered (no effective discharge under the law).
BaselineB: Statute/regulation and collective agreement: Regulation 680 under The Police Act, s. 27(b) (board authority “to dispense with the services of any constable within eighteen months”) and s. 9 of the collective agreement (dismissal power in the Board), with reference to Nicholson v. Haldimand-Norfolk Regional Board of Commissioners of Police.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Municipal office disqualification for having an “interest” in a municipal contract: interpret “interested in” broadly (common usage) so that a director/officer of a contracting company has at least an indirect interest, notwithstanding disclosure/recusal
BaselineA: Statute (Moncton Consolidation Act, 1946 (N.B.), c. 101, s. 6) interpreted using the Angrignon principle that “interested in” has no technical meaning and must be given its common usage; also considered interaction with Municipalities Act, R.S.N.B. 1973, c. M-22, ss. 71-72
CaseB_TestB: Statutory interpretation of OLA s. 22: determine whether a municipality is an “institution” under OLA s. 1 for the duty to use the other party’s chosen official language in civil proceedings; and limit “oral or written pleadings”/“process” to exclude evidence and case-law translations
BaselineB: Statute (Official Languages Act, S.N.B. 2002, c. O-0.5, ss. 1 “institution”, 22) applying the modern principle of interpretation (Driedger) and the Bell ExpressVu rule that Charter values apply only where there is genuine ambiguity
JudgeB: Charron J. (McLachlin C.J. and Major, Fish and Abella JJ. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Qualified privilege in libel: malice goes to the jury only if the evidence "raises a probability" of express malice (more than a mere scintilla/possibility; "more consistent with its existence than with its non-existence")
BaselineA: Common law (defamation/qualified privilege and malice), drawing on Adam v. Ward; Somerville v. Hawkins; Spill v. Maule; and SCC authority Sun Life Assurance Co. v. Dalrymple
CaseB_TestB: Blood Tribe clarity requirement for statutory abrogation of solicitor-client privilege: only where legislative language shows a "clear" and "unequivocal" intent may privilege be abrogated; open-textured production powers are read not to include privileged material
BaselineB: Statutory interpretation of Income Tax Act ss. 231.2(1), 231.7(1), and definition in s. 232(1) (in light of the common-law/constitutional status of solicitor-client privilege and the Blood Tribe interpretive principle)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Priority/attachment rule for B.C. Payment of Wages Act s. 5A lien: the wage lien arises "from the date wages were earned" and takes priority over later dispositions, but does not defeat mortgages made before the lien attached; it "will only attach to the employer’s equity" in the property
BaselineA: Statute: Payment of Wages Act, 1962 (B.C.), c. 45, ss. 5 and 5A (especially s. 5A(1)-(2))
CaseB_TestB: Suppletive application test for forced dissolution of a Part III Companies Act legal person: where no special statutory scheme is applicable, the Civil Code of Québec fills the gaps (art. 334/300), and dissolution may be ordered under art. 355(2) if the court confirms (i) fulfilment of a condition, (ii) accomplishment of the object, (iii) impossibility of accomplishing the object, or (iv) "some other legitimate cause"
BaselineB: Statute/codified law: Civil Code of Québec, arts. 300, 334, 355 (and related arts. 355-364); considered alongside Companies Act (Quebec) and Code of Civil Procedure art. 829
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Residual discretion/inherent jurisdiction to remedy unfairness from Crown’s closing address: (1) usually by curative jury instruction; (2) in rare ‘clearest cases of unfairness’, a limited defence reply confined to the improper issue(s)
BaselineA: Combination: statute + common law. Statutory baseline is Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 651(3)-(4) (order of addresses). Common-law baseline is superior courts’ inherent jurisdiction to prevent unfairness/abuse of process (e.g., Selvey v. DPP; R. v. Osborn; Amato v. The Queen, as cited in the reasons).
JudgeA: Cory, Iacobucci and Bastarache JJ. (for Gonthier, Cory, Iacobucci and Bastarache JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 11(d) validity of a statutory presumption: a presumption is constitutional only if the substituted fact leads ‘inexorably’ to the essential element it replaces; plus (post-s. 172.1(3) invalidity) the s. 172.1(4) ‘reasonable steps’ framework as a defence-limiting, three-stage approach (air of reality → Crown disproves defence beyond a reasonable doubt → Crown must still prove belief beyond a reasonable doubt)
BaselineB: Combination: statute + constitutional/common-law doctrine. Statutory baseline is Criminal Code, s. 172.1(3) (presumption re age) and s. 172.1(4) (no defence unless reasonable steps). Constitutional/common-law baseline is Charter s. 11(d) presumption-of-innocence jurisprudence on presumptions (Whyte; Downey; Audet) and the Oakes s. 1 framework.
JudgeB: Moldaver J. (Wagner C.J. and Gascon, Côté, Brown, Rowe and Martin JJ. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Adjudicator’s remedial power to substitute a lesser penalty for discharge: where the adjudicator finds “just and sufficient cause for some disciplinary action, but not for discharge”, the adjudicator may replace discharge with a lesser penalty (e.g., suspension) because s. 92(1)(b) subjects “disciplinary action resulting in discharge, suspension or a financial penalty” to full review and treats discipline as a continuum.
BaselineA: Statute + collective agreement: Public Service Labour Relations Act, R.S.N.B. 1973, c. P-25, s. 92(1)(b) (and s. 101 privative clause context) together with the collective agreement’s “just and sufficient cause” discipline provisions (Art. V(d), XVII(c)); contrasted with Port Arthur Shipbuilding Co. v. Arthurs, [1969] S.C.R. 85.
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 24(2) exclusion analysis (Collins guidelines): whether, “having regard to all the circumstances”, admission of evidence obtained through a Charter breach “would bring the administration of justice into disrepute”; applied by considering (as framed in Collins) trial fairness and the seriousness of the Charter violation (here, good-faith reliance on an unchallenged writ of assistance; dwelling-house search).
BaselineB: Constitutional text + common law framework: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 24(2) (“having regard to all the circumstances… bring the administration of justice into disrepute”), applying the SCC’s framework from R. v. Collins, [1987] 1 S.C.R. 265.
JudgeB: Lamer J. (for Dickson C.J. and Lamer, Wilson, Le Dain and La Forest JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Will-construction test: give effect to the testator’s overriding intention on a fair reading of the will; administrative/boilerplate clauses should not defeat a clearly expressed intention (legacy payable on disposition of the business, however effected)
BaselineA: Common law (will construction/ascertaining testator’s intention from the will as a whole; no specific statutory provision identified in the reasons)
CaseB_TestB: Manslaughter legal causation with intervening acts: the test remains whether the accused’s dangerous and unlawful acts were a “significant contributing cause of death”; foreseeability/independence are non-determinative analytical aids
BaselineB: Common law causation test from Smithers v. The Queen ("a contributing cause of death, outside the de minimis range") as confirmed in R. v. Nette (significant contributing cause), applied alongside Criminal Code ss. 222, 224, 225
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Labour-relations division of powers: provincial jurisdiction is the rule; federal jurisdiction is the exception limited to labour relations that are an integral part of a federal undertaking—assessed by the “functional test” of the undertaking’s “nature of their operations and their normal activities” (i.e., whether it can be “characterized as federal”).
BaselineA: Common law constitutional division-of-powers doctrine for labour relations (functional/undertaking characterization), as summarized from Toronto Electric Commissioners v. Snider and the Stevedoring Reference line of cases.
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 15(1) equality test (post-Kapp/Withler): (1) Does the law create a distinction based on an enumerated or analogous ground? (2) Does the distinction create a disadvantage by perpetuating prejudice or stereotyping—assessed contextually without requiring a “mirror comparator group”.
BaselineB: Common law Charter equality jurisprudence interpreting Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 15(1) (notably Andrews, Law, and Kapp).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Bankruptcy Act s. 107(1)(j) interpretation: Crown provincial tax 'privilege' cannot be treated as a 'secured creditor' right to escape s. 107(1)(j); Crown tax claims (not otherwise mentioned) rank pari passu 'notwithstanding any statutory preference to the contrary'.
BaselineA: Statute: Bankruptcy Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. B-3, ss. 2 (definition of 'secured creditor') and 107(1)(j) (scheme of distribution); applied against Quebec Retail Sales Tax Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 71, s. 30 and Civil Code art. 1989 (registration of Crown privilege).
JudgeA: Pigeon J. (for Martland, Ritchie, Pigeon, Beetz, Pratte and McIntyre JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Public interest standing (purposive, flexible, discretionary): weigh three interrelated factors—(1) serious justiciable issue; (2) real stake/genuine interest; (3) whether the proposed suit is, 'in all of the circumstances', a 'reasonable and effective means' to bring the issue to court (not a strict 'no other way' requirement).
BaselineB: Common law doctrine of public interest standing from SCC cases (as cited in the reasons): Borowski; Finlay; Canadian Council of Churches; Thorson; McNeil; Hy and Zel’s.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Crown prerogative priority applies only where Crown and subject claims are “of equal degree”; a prior registered second/collateral mortgage is of a higher degree than a later-registered Crown judgment, so Registry Act registration-date priorities govern
BaselineA: Combination: common law Crown prerogative priority for debts “of equal degree” (The Queen v. Bank of Nova Scotia (1885), 11 S.C.R. 1) plus Nova Scotia Registry Act, R.S.N.S. 1967, c. 265, ss. 17-18 and Nova Scotia Civil Procedure Rule 47.11
CaseB_TestB: International jurisdiction by extension of domestic territorial jurisdiction: under art. 71 C.C.P., an incidental action in warranty “must be taken before the court in which the principal action is pending”, and this rule applies to a foreign defendant without limitation
BaselineB: Statute/civil law: Code of Civil Procedure (Quebec), arts. 71 (and discussed alongside arts. 68-75, including art. 75); Civil Code, art. 27; plus the private international law principle that international jurisdiction is determined by extending domestic territorial jurisdiction rules (as reflected in Alimport and Trower and Sons)
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “detained” under Canadian Bill of Rights s. 2(c): “detain”/“detention” connote “some form of compulsory restraint” (i.e., held in custody/physical restraint), so a motorist stopped and asked to do sobriety/roadside screening steps but then “allowed to go away” is not “detained” and cannot claim a right to counsel as a “reasonable excuse” for refusing a roadside breath demand.
BaselineA: Statute (Canadian Bill of Rights, 1960, s. 2(c)(ii)-(iii), interpreted alongside Criminal Code s. 234.1(1)-(2); with reference to prior SCC breath-demand cases including Brownridge v. The Queen and Hogan v. The Queen).
