CaseB_TestB: Tort of civil conspiracy (two-branch test): liability exists (1) where “the predominant purpose of the defendants’ conduct is to cause injury to the plaintiff” (means lawful or unlawful); or (2) where defendants’ conduct is “unlawful”, “directed towards the plaintiff (alone or together with others)”, and defendants “should know in the circumstances that injury to the plaintiff is likely to and does result” (constructive intent), with actual damage required in both cases.
BaselineB: Common law (tort of conspiracy), drawing on authorities including Lonrho Ltd. v. Shell Petroleum Co. Ltd., Crofter Hand Woven Harris Tweed Co. v. Veitch, Sorrell v. Smith, and SCC cases including Gagnon v. Foundation Maritime Limited and International Brotherhood of Teamsters v. Therien.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 492 re-election validity: effective re-election occurs where the accused (1) notifies the sheriff of the desire to re-elect (s. 492(1)); (2) attends at the time/place fixed (s. 492(2)-(3)); and (3) after the actual charge faced at trial is read, communicates the re-election (which may be done through counsel in the accused’s presence), with the court permitted to proceed directly to the communication of the election; failure to prefer a new Form 4 indictment under s. 496 after re-election does not invalidate proceedings where the indictment is already in Form 4.
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, ss. 492 and 496)
CaseB_TestB: Injurious affection where no land is taken (Loiselle conditions) and actionable-at-common-law requirement: claimant must satisfy four conditions—(1) damage results from an act rendered lawful by statutory powers; (2) damage would have been actionable at common law but for statutory powers; (3) injury is to the land itself (not personal/business); (4) damage is occasioned by construction, not use—and here the actionable common-law inquiry turns on private nuisance requiring an unreasonable interference assessed "in the light of all the surrounding circumstances" (reasonable user/balancing).
BaselineB: Combination: Statute (Expropriations Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 154, ss. 1(e)(ii), 21) plus common law (injurious affection conditions from The Queen v. Loiselle; nuisance reasonableness framework)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Ontario Municipal Board jurisdiction under s. 137(1): referential incorporation of Municipal Act s. 14(11)(a),(b),(d) applies (without the qualifying words in s. 14(11)’s introduction), empowering the Board to make “adjustments of assets and liabilities … as the Board may consider equitable” in relation to the County’s dissolution
BaselineA: Statute: The Regional Municipality of Ottawa-Carleton Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 407, ss. 135-137, incorporating by reference The Municipal Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 284, s. 14(11)(a),(b),(d)
JudgeA: Estey J. (for Dickson, Estey and McIntyre JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Charter ss. 7 and 11(d) mens rea requirement for murder: “a conviction for murder cannot rest on anything less than proof beyond a reasonable doubt of subjective foresight of death” (therefore s. 213(a) is unconstitutional)
BaselineB: Combination: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 7 and 11(d) (principles of fundamental justice) applied to Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 213(a); building from R. v. Vaillancourt, [1987] 2 S.C.R. 636
JudgeB: Lamer C.J. (for Dickson C.J. and Lamer C.J. and Wilson, Gonthier and Cory JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Valid consent to intercept a private communication under Criminal Code s. 178.11(2)(a): consent must be "voluntary (i.e. free from coercion)" and "made knowingly, with an awareness of the significance of the consent"; promised/expected leniency does not by itself amount to coercion; if valid consent exists, the interception is "lawfully made" for s. 178.16(1)(a) admissibility.
BaselineA: Statute (Protection of Privacy Act amendments to Criminal Code): interpretation/application of Criminal Code ss. 178.1 ("private communication"), 178.11(2)(a) (consent interception), and 178.16(1)(a) (admissibility where interception "lawfully made").
CaseB_TestB: Proving the target identifiable group under Criminal Code s. 319(2): the trial judge must assess the "totality of the evidence" to decide whether the statements, "as a matter of fact, promoted hatred" of the particularized group; it is not necessary to prove strict "interchangeability" of labels (e.g., "gypsies" and "Roma").
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code): application of s. 319(2) (wilful promotion of hatred) and s. 318(4) ("identifiable group"), with evidentiary principle of judicial notice referenced via R. v. Find (SCC) for when courts may accept facts without proof.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Audi alteram partem in administrative appeals: an appellate tribunal must not receive evidence/representations ex parte after the hearing; if it does, the decision is invalid if the material might have caused prejudice
BaselineA: Common law natural justice / procedural fairness (audi alteram partem), applied in the statutory university discipline/appeal context
CaseB_TestB: Workers’ compensation occupational-disease causation under s. 250(4): causation may be inferred from circumstantial evidence; expert opinion is not determinative; if evidence is evenly weighted, resolve causation in the worker’s favour
BaselineB: Statute (Workers Compensation Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 492) and mandatory policy incorporated by statute
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Appellate intervention in a trial damages award: an appellate court may not substitute its own figure unless a wrong principle of law was applied or the overall award is a wholly erroneous estimate of damages (mere view that award is 'on the high side' is insufficient).
BaselineA: Common law (as stated in Andrews et al. v. Grand & Toy Alberta Ltd. et al., [1978] 2 S.C.R. 229 at p. 235).
JudgeA: Martland J. (for the Court, oral reasons)
CaseB_TestB: Videotape-only identification: once it is established the videotape has not been altered/changed and depicts the crime, it is admissible; the trier of fact may identify and convict on the videotape alone if, considering the tape’s clarity/quality (and to a lesser extent time of depiction), they are satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt it identifies the accused (no corroboration required).
BaselineB: Common law evidence principles (drawing on R. v. Leaney, [1989] 2 S.C.R. 393 and related admissibility/real evidence authorities).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Quebec Labour Code s. 16 rebuttal: employer must show the “other good and sufficient reason” is substantial, not a pretext, and the true (real and determining) reason for dismissal; commissioner/court cannot review the severity/appropriateness of the penalty once a real reason is established
BaselineA: Statute (Quebec Labour Code, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 141 as am., ss. 13-16, especially s. 16 presumption and “another good and sufficient reason”)
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 12 “gross disproportionality” test (Smith): assess whether punishment is “so excessive as to outrage standards of decency” by considering gravity of offence, personal characteristics of offender, and particular circumstances; plus a two-aspect approach (actual offender, then reasonable hypotheticals) for assessing statutory minimums
BaselineB: Combination: Constitutional text (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 12) + common law/precedent (R. v. Smith; reaffirmed in Lyons and Luxton, as discussed and applied)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Summary conviction appeal costs against the Crown: ss. 758 and 771(3) of the Criminal Code are implicitly binding on Her Majesty, so the appeal court may order costs against the Crown where it considers it "just and reasonable" (s. 758) / "proper" (s. 771(3))
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, Part XXIV; interpreted in light of Interpretation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-23, s. 16, and common law background on Crown costs)
CaseB_TestB: Statutory mortgage prepayment right under Interest Act s. 10(1): mortgagors have a right to pay off at the end of each five-year period; in a renewal that "deems" a new mortgage date and is itself ≤ 5 years, prepayment is only at the end of that renewal term; purported relinquishment of the five-year statutory right is unenforceable
BaselineB: Statute (Interest Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-18, s. 10(1)-(2); also considered alongside Manitoba Mortgage Act s. 20(6)-(7) and Real Property Act s. 103(1)(c))
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Wrongful dismissal damages: no deduction for income tax not payable; and unemployment insurance benefits are not deductible because they are a consequence of the employment contract (akin to contributory pension/insurance benefits)
BaselineA: Common law contract damages (wrongful dismissal) principles, applied with reference to SCC authority on non-deductibility of contributory benefits (Guy v. Trizec Equities Ltd.)
CaseB_TestB: Identification of Criminals Act s. 2 applies to juveniles: a juvenile in lawful custody for a delinquency that relates to a Criminal Code indictable offence is a person “charged with, or under conviction of an indictable offence”, so police may use necessary reasonable force to fingerprint
BaselineB: Statute (Identification of Criminals Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-1, s. 2(1)-(2)) interpreted in light of the Juvenile Delinquents Act; relying on Morris v. The Queen for meaning of “offence/conviction” in the juvenile context
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: “Air of reality / sense of reality” threshold for whether a trial judge must leave a defence (here, mistake of fact as to consent) with the jury: there must be “in the record some evidence which would convey a sense of reality in the submission”; for mistake of fact here, “some evidence which, if believed, would support the existence of a mistaken but honest belief” in consent (and, on these facts, the majority adds that the evidence must be “from or be supported by sources other than the appellant” to give it “any air of reality”).
BaselineA: Common law (jury-charge duty / defences left to jury) drawing on SCC authorities: Kelsey v. The Queen, [1953] 1 S.C.R. 220; Wu v. The King, [1934] S.C.R. 609; R. v. Workman and Huculak, [1963] S.C.R. 266.
CaseB_TestB: Section 7 abuse-of-process test (as the remedy framework for appellate delay, per Sopinka J.): a court may stay proceedings where “compelling an accused to stand trial would violate those fundamental principles of justice which underlie the community’s sense of fair play and decency and to prevent the abuse of a court’s process through oppressive or vexatious proceedings” (adopted from R. v. Young and reaffirmed in R. v. Jewitt and R. v. Keyowski).
BaselineB: Constitutional (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7) incorporating the common-law abuse of process doctrine as a principle of fundamental justice; key SCC baselines cited: R. v. Jewitt, [1985] 2 S.C.R. 128; R. v. Keyowski, [1988] 1 S.C.R. 657 (and quotation from R. v. Young (1984), 40 C.R. (3d) 289 (Ont. C.A.)).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Standard of review framework: presumptive reasonableness for a tribunal interpreting its home statute, rebutted only by Dunsmuir correctness categories (statutory appeal is not a new correctness category)
BaselineA: Common law (judicial review standard of review framework from Dunsmuir v. New Brunswick; applied to statutory appeal context per Saguenay/Dr. Q/Ryan line of cases)
CaseB_TestB: Framework for Crown sui generis fiduciary duty (as applied in specific claims): fiduciary duty arises from Crown discretionary control over a specific/cognizable Aboriginal interest; breach assessed by whether Crown met fiduciary standard of conduct (loyalty/good faith/full disclosure/ordinary prudence), not by achieving a particular result
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law (Specific Claims Tribunal Act, s. 14(1)(b), 14(1)(c), 14(2) plus common law fiduciary doctrine from Wewaykum/Guerin/Haida/Manitoba Metis Federation)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Necessarily incidental doctrine for federal legislation that prima facie trenches on provincial jurisdiction: to uphold it, it must be shown to be "necessarily incidental to effective legislation" on an enumerated federal head (here, s. 91(12) fisheries); a broad "blanket prohibition" with "no attempt to link the proscribed conduct to actual or potential harm to fisheries" is not necessarily incidental and is ultra vires.
BaselineA: Common law constitutional division-of-powers doctrine (Lord Tomlin’s proposition (3) in Attorney-General for Canada v. Attorney-General for British Columbia and others, [1930] A.C. 111) applied to s. 33(3) of the Fisheries Act in light of B.N.A. Act, 1867 ss. 91(12) and 92(13).
CaseB_TestB: Colour of right in theft: the defence turns on whether the trier of fact is satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused did NOT have, at the time of the taking/conversion, an "honest belief that he had the right to that money"; it is not dependent on what the jury thinks the accused’s legal rights actually were.
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code theft provisions: "fraudulently and without colour of right" in ss. 283 and 294 (as referenced in the reasons)).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “unlawful purpose” in Criminal Code s. 423(2)(a): it means “contrary to law”, i.e., conduct “prohibited by federal or provincial legislation” (so a conspiracy charge under s. 423(2)(a) requires that the alleged purpose be prohibited by legislation, not merely undesirable or non-criminal).
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 423(2)(a) (conspiracy “to effect an unlawful purpose”); also considered in context of s. 8 (abolition of common law offences) and prior conspiracy jurisprudence (e.g., Wright, McDermott & Feeley v. The Queen).
CaseB_TestB: Quebec defamation fault under art. 1457 C.C.Q.: a “contextual analysis” where “the guiding principle of liability for defamation is that there will not be fault until it has been shown that the journalist or media outlet ... has fallen below professional standards”; “the conduct of the reasonable journalist becomes the all-important guidepost”.
BaselineB: Statute (civil law): Civil Code of Québec, art. 1457 (general extra-contractual liability), as applied through Quebec defamation jurisprudence (notably Société Radio-Canada v. Radio Sept-Îles Inc. and Prud’homme v. Prud’homme).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Rabey (majority) internal-cause vs external-factor approach to whether automatism is excluded because the accused had a "disease of the mind" under Criminal Code s. 16 (ordinary life stresses are not an external cause)
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 16) interpreted through common-law automatism/insanity jurisprudence (e.g., Bratty v. A.G. Northern Ireland, R. v. K.)
CaseB_TestB: Conflict/supersession test: where a standard mortgage clause says it "shall supersede any policy provisions in conflict therewith" (to the mortgagee’s interest), Statutory Condition 4 (material change to risk) cannot be used to void mortgagee coverage if it conflicts with the mortgage clause
BaselineB: Combination of statute and contract: Insurance Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. I.8, Part IV (Statutory Condition 4) plus the policy’s standard mortgage clause (interpreted with reference to National Bank of Greece (Canada) v. Katsikonouris)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Prescription characterization for damages: if damages flow from a single cause of action that is breach of a contractual obligation, they are contractual (30-year prescription); if they flow from separate and independent causes of action, each head is characterized as contractual or delictual and prescribed accordingly
BaselineA: Statute/civil code (Civil Code arts. 2242, 2260(4), 2261(2), plus arts. 1024, 1057) and Quebec jurisprudence on contractual vs delictual characterization of damages
CaseB_TestB: Priority between mechanic’s lien and mortgage for past indebtedness: where the Mechanics’ Lien Act does not prescribe priority (s. 14(1) inapplicable), an unregistered lien has no priority and priority is determined by registration under the Registry Act (ss. 69(1), 70), i.e., first registered interest prevails absent actual notice
BaselineB: Statute (The Mechanics’ Lien Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 267, especially ss. 14(1), 16, 20-22; and The Registry Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 409, ss. 69(1), 70)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Accrued-rights preservation on statutory repeal/amendment: apply Interpretation Act s. 35(c) so repeal "does not… affect any right, privilege, obligation or liability acquired, accrued, accruing or incurred"; read the amending Unemployment Insurance Act s. 31 together with s. 35(c) to preserve only the pre-amendment accrued benefit and continue pre-amendment disqualifications (here, pension-payable) for that preserved period.
BaselineA: Statute (Interpretation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-23, s. 35(c) and Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, S.C. 1970-71-72, c. 48, s. 31 as amended by S.C. 1974-75-76, c. 80, s. 10; also s. 38 benefit-period limit).
CaseB_TestB: Compellability of judges before a public inquiry under Public Inquiries Act ss. 3-4: read ss. 3 and 4 together so the Commission may "summon" but cannot "enforce" attendance beyond what a superior court judge could compel; because of judicial independence, judges have immunity from being compelled to testify about (1) "how and why" they reached a decision and (2) why a particular judge sat on a particular case (assignment/composition).
BaselineB: Combination of statute and constitutional/common law principles: Public Inquiries Act, R.S.N.S. 1967, c. 250, ss. 3-4, interpreted in light of the constitutional principle of judicial independence (as summarized in Valente v. The Queen and Beauregard v. Canada, and the common law tradition of judicial immunity).
JudgeB: McLachlin J. (for L'Heureux-Dubé, Gonthier and McLachlin JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Interpretation of Motor Vehicle Transport Act s. 3: s. 3(2) (“into or through the province”) authorizes provincial boards, acting under federal authority, to license extra‑provincial undertakings “in, across, into and out of the province” and to apply provincial “terms and conditions” and enforcement (including seizure) as for local undertakings; s. 6 does not displace provincial seizure powers.
BaselineA: Statute (Motor Vehicle Transport Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. M-14, ss. 3(1)-(2), 5, 6; definition in s. 2) with incorporated provincial statute (The Public Service Vehicles Act, R.S.A. 1970, c. 300, including s. 58 seizure power) via s. 3(2) “upon the like terms and conditions and in the like manner as if ... a local undertaking”.
CaseB_TestB: Charter scope test for corporate claimants under s. 12: a claimant must show an interest “falling within the scope of the guarantee, and one which accords with the purpose of that provision”; purposive interpretation begins with the text, and because “cruel and unusual” denotes human pain and suffering, s. 12’s protective scope is limited to human beings (corporations cannot claim s. 12).
BaselineB: Constitutional text and purposive interpretation framework (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 12; purposive approach from R. v. Big M Drug Mart Ltd.; corporate standing/scope principle from R. v. CIP Inc.).
JudgeB: Brown and Rowe JJ. (Wagner C.J. and Moldaver and Côté JJ. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Applicability of an exclusion/waiver clause after fundamental breach: determined by the "true construction of the contract" (waiver ceases to bind if, on construction in context, it is tied to the contract’s fate and the innocent party elects to treat the contract as at an end).
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Mechanics’ Lien Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 267, s. 5(1) (lien unless person "signs an express agreement to the contrary") plus the common-law approach from Suisse Atlantique and Photo Production that whether an exception/exclusion clause applies after fundamental breach is a matter of contractual construction.
CaseB_TestB: Collateral attack on an administrative order in penal proceedings: determine legislature’s intended forum by considering (non-exhaustively) (1) wording of the statute, (2) purpose of the legislation, (3) availability of an appeal, (4) nature of the collateral attack in light of the appeal tribunal’s expertise/raison d’être, and (5) penalty for non-compliance.
BaselineB: Statutory interpretation of the Environmental Protection Act, R.S.O. 1980, c. 141 (notably ss. 17, 122-123, 146(1a)) informed by common-law principles about collateral attack/rule of law (e.g., Wilson; Litchfield; Sarson) but operationalized through the Act’s scheme.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Constructive trust based on unjust enrichment: claimant must show (1) an enrichment, (2) a corresponding deprivation, and (3) absence of any juristic reason; and in spousal-like relationships it is unjust where one prejudices herself in a reasonable expectation of an interest and the other accepts benefits knowing/ought to know of that expectation; remedy proportionate to contribution
BaselineA: Common law (constructive trust/unjust enrichment framework drawn from Murdoch v. Murdoch and Rathwell v. Rathwell, as discussed and applied)
CaseB_TestB: Solicitor-client confidentiality/privilege in search-warrant context: confidentiality applies to communications made to obtain legal advice (including pre-retainer and administrative info), except crime/fraud communications; justice of the peace lacks jurisdiction to authorize seizure of privileged evidence and should refuse a warrant to search a lawyer’s office unless no reasonable alternative exists, and must impose protective execution terms
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law (Criminal Code, s. 443(1)(b) search warrant power, interpreted in light of common law solicitor-client privilege/confidentiality as reaffirmed in Solosky v. The Queen and related authorities)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Informed-consent negligence: (1) duty to disclose “all material risks” (answer specific questions; disclose nature/gravity, “any material risks and any special or unusual risks”); and (2) causation assessed objectively — whether “a reasonable person in the patient’s position would have” declined the treatment if properly informed (including reasonably-based “special considerations” of that patient).
BaselineA: Common law (medical negligence/duty of disclosure and causation), drawing on Hopp v. Lepp (duty of disclosure summary) and rejecting a battery-based approach to non-disclosure (disclosure failures generally go to negligence, not battery).
CaseB_TestB: Division-of-powers “integral element” test for s. 92(10) undertakings: federal legislation affecting a provincial matter is valid/applicable only if it regulates something “vital”, “essential” or “integral” to the “core” of the federal undertaking; otherwise provincial law of general application applies. Applied to hold Railway Act s. 342(1) ultra vires as to provincial personal-injury actions, and “read down” to valid federal statutory causes of action.
BaselineB: Constitutional law (Constitution Act, 1867 ss. 91(29), 92(10), 92(13), 92(14)) and the “integral element” approach from Construction Montcalm Inc. v. Minimum Wage Commission and Northern Telecom Ltd. v. Communications Workers of Canada; applied to Railway Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. R-2, s. 342(1).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Natural Resources Agreement (para. 12) “right of access” test for treaty Indian hunting for food: if provincial law permits any (even limited) hunting on the land, that constitutes a “right of access” for hunting, which triggers the proviso and guarantees Indians may hunt for food “at all seasons of the year” (so provincial season limits cannot apply). Key language: “once any hunting is permitted, then Indians (and other members of the public) have a right of access for the purpose of hunting” and “the laws in force ... contemplated a limited right to hunt ... This constituted a ‘right of access’ and engaged the proviso in paragraph 12”.
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional instrument: Natural Resources Agreement (Canada–Saskatchewan), 1930, para. 12 (confirmed by British North America Act, 1930). Baseline interpretation applied from R. v. Sutherland, Wilson and Wilson, [1980] 2 S.C.R. 451 (definition/operation of “right of access”).
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 2(a) constitutionality ‘purpose-first’ framework: “the legislation's purpose is the initial test of constitutional validity”; only if the law “has passed the purpose test” do courts consider effects; “effects can never be relied on to save legislation with an invalid purpose.”
BaselineB: Constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 2(a) (and related remedial/supremacy provisions, especially Constitution Act, 1982, s. 52(1)).
JudgeB: Dickson J. (for Dickson, Beetz, McIntyre, Chouinard and Lamer JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: No implied power to retroactively revoke an allowed unemployment insurance premium reduction; officer’s decision under Regs s. 24(2) is a judicial/quasi-judicial decision made under prescribed standards, and even legal error does not make it a nullity (no suo motu reopening absent express authority).
BaselineA: Statute and regulation: Unemployment Insurance Act, 1970-71-72, ss. 64(4), 64(6) (regulation-making re premium reductions) and Unemployment Insurance Regulations, s. 24 (decision and employer-initiated review/appeal).
CaseB_TestB: Mens rea for Criminal Code s. 121(1)(a): Crown must prove the accused (1) knew he/she was an official, (2) intentionally demanded/accepted a loan, reward, advantage or benefit, and (3) knew it was “in consideration for” cooperation/assistance/exercise of influence in connection with government business; no additional “corrupt” purpose required.
BaselineB: Statute (interpreted): Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 121(1)(a) (and s. 19 re ignorance of law).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Ward s. 24(1) Charter damages — countervailing factors analysis applied categorically to quasi-judicial regulator: Charter damages are never an “appropriate and just” remedy against this Board because (collectively) (1) judicial review is an effective alternative remedy, (2) good governance concerns, and (3) case-by-case damages litigation would undermine tribunal immunity ("Charter damages could never be an appropriate and just remedy for Charter breaches by the Board" (para. 24); "when such countervailing factors are considered collectively, they negate the appropriateness" (summary; see also paras. 30-31)).
BaselineA: Common law (Charter remedial framework) applying Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 24(1), as set out in Vancouver (City) v. Ward, 2010 SCC 27 ("The leading case about when Charter damages are an appropriate and just remedy is Vancouver (City) v. Ward" (para. 26)). Also interacts with statute: Energy Resources Conservation Act, R.S.A. 2000, c. E-10, s. 43 (immunity clause).
CaseB_TestB: Duty to consult does not apply to the law-making process: "no aspect of the law-making process — from the development of legislation to its enactment — triggers a duty to consult" (para. 50); the law-making process "does not constitute 'Crown conduct' that triggers the duty to consult" (para. 2).
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine of the duty to consult grounded in the honour of the Crown (Haida Nation v. British Columbia (Minister of Forests), 2004 SCC 73) and s. 35 of the Constitution Act, 1982; plus statutory jurisdictional framework under the Federal Courts Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. F-7 (ss. 2(1), 2(2), 17, 18, 18.1).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Workers’ compensation statutory bar does not extend to a motor-vehicle owner who is only a deemed employer under Motor-vehicle Act s. 70(1): WCA s. 10(1) bars actions only against the worker’s employer/covered employers/other workers; the tort remains actionable against a non-covered vicariously liable owner
BaselineA: Statute (Workers’ Compensation Act, 1968 (B.C.), s. 10(1) and Motor-vehicle Act, R.S.B.C. 1960, s. 70(1))
CaseB_TestB: Operational conflict / precedence framework for conflicting administrative decisions: (1) determine if there is a true operational conflict (compliance with one necessitates violation of the other); (2) ask whether either decision would be overturned on its ordinary standard of review; (3) if both would stand, courts may declare one inoperative to the extent of conflict and decide precedence using a pragmatic and functional approach considering legislative purpose, centrality to tribunal mandate, and policy-making/implementation role
BaselineB: Common law administrative law (curial deference/standard of review and pragmatic & functional approach) applied in context of statutory schemes (e.g., Railway Act ss. 335, 340; NTPPA; Canada Labour Code)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Priority between a mechanics’ lien and a subsequent mortgage for past indebtedness: absent an applicable statutory priority (s. 14(1)), priority is determined by registration (Registry Act ss. 69(1), 70) once the lien is registered under Mechanics’ Lien Act s. 20; an unregistered (or later-registered) lien has no general priority over a prior-registered mortgage without notice
BaselineA: Statute: The Mechanics’ Lien Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 267 (especially ss. 14(1), 16, 20, 21, 22) and The Registry Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 409 (ss. 69(1), 70)
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 2(b)/s. 1 assessment of PIPA’s restriction on union expression: whether the statute achieves a “constitutionally acceptable balance” between privacy control and freedom of expression; although rationally connected to a pressing objective, the limit fails because the impact on expression is “disproportionate” (i.e., the Act lacks mechanisms to accommodate/balance expressive purposes in lawful labour disputes)
BaselineB: Constitution (Charter): Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms ss. 2(b) and 1, applied to statute Personal Information Protection Act, S.A. 2003, c. P-6.5 (notably ss. 3, 4(1), 7(1) and exemptions) and Regulation s. 7
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Quebec civil liability “choice” test: a contracting party may sue in delict (art. 1053 C.C.) despite a contract only if the contractual fault is independently a delictual fault—i.e., it “must in itself be a fault sanctioned by art. 1053 C.C. even in the absence of a contract”.
BaselineA: Statute (Civil Code art. 1053; Code of Civil Procedure art. 68) as interpreted through SCC jurisprudence (e.g., Ross v. Dunstall; Alliance Assurance).
CaseB_TestB: Reasonable apprehension of bias consequence rule: where “a reasonable apprehension of bias is demonstrated the trial judge has no further jurisdiction” and “the only appropriate remedy is a new trial”; appellate finding of bias “retroactively renders all the decisions and orders made during the trial void and without effect”.
BaselineB: Common law procedural fairness / bias doctrine, relying on Newfoundland Telephone Co. v. Newfoundland (Board of Commissioners of Public Utilities) and general criminal trial fairness principles.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Bills of Exchange Act “sum certain”/negotiability requirement: principal and interest must be certain on the face of the instrument (interest must be ascertainable in gross or by numerical calculation from materials in the document); extrinsic evidence is generally not permitted unless necessary to implement a specific Act provision
BaselineA: Statute (Bills of Exchange Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. B-5, ss. 28, 176(1), 186; plus s. 10 incorporating common law/law merchant)
CaseB_TestB: Criminal Code s. 172(3) “disturbs” threshold: to convict, conduct must be “disorderly in itself or productive of disorder”; mere “annoyance, anxiety or emotional upset” from “brief, essentially passive and peaceful” conduct voluntarily desisted from is insufficient
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 172(3))
JudgeB: Dickson J. (for Dickson, Beetz, McIntyre, Chouinard and Lamer JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Bills of Exchange Act “sum certain”/negotiability test for promissory notes: the amount (principal + interest) must be certain on the face of the instrument (or calculable from it); extrinsic evidence is generally not permitted unless necessary to implement a specific Act provision, and a term like interest “from the date of advance” (date not on the instrument) creates inherent uncertainty defeating negotiability.
BaselineA: Statute: Bills of Exchange Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. B-5, ss. 176(1) (definition of promissory note), 28 (sum certain; interest), 186 (application to notes), plus s. 10 (common law/law merchant applies unless inconsistent).
CaseB_TestB: Civil Code of Lower Canada test for when the 2-year suicide exclusion limit runs (arts. 2516, 2532): identify the contract’s effective date (including permissible retroactive effect from a backdated policy date if favourable and if no change in insurability when premium paid), and determine whether later changes are a mere variation of the same contract or a new contract (a fact-specific continuity inquiry) for whether a new exclusion period can run.
BaselineB: Statute (civil law): Civil Code of Lower Canada, arts. 2516 (life insurance becomes effective when three conditions met concurrently), 2532 (suicide clause ineffective after two years of uninterrupted insurance), and art. 2500 (limits on derogation).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: When a statute creates a specific tribunal/procedure to decide an issue, the Superior Court should not intervene by declaratory judgment to decide that very issue (and a declaration should be refused if it would be of little or no practical use).
BaselineA: Combination: Code of Civil Procedure, art. 453 (declaratory judgment) plus common-law/precedent discretion limiting declarations where a statute assigns the matter to another tribunal (e.g., Barraclough v. Brown; City of Lethbridge v. Canadian Western Natural Gas; Cassidy v. Stuart).
CaseB_TestB: Minister’s s. 7 Fisheries Act power to “authorize to be issued” licences is a continuing power, so the Minister may revoke an authorization any time before the licence is actually issued; discretion is constrained only by natural justice (relevant considerations, no arbitrariness, good faith).
BaselineB: Statute: Fisheries Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. F-14, s. 7 (and s. 9 for post-issuance revocation) interpreted with Interpretation Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. I-21, s. 31(3).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Excise Tax Act machinery exemption: claimant must be a “manufacturer or producer of goods” and the machinery must be “purchased and used directly in the manufacture of goods”; “manufacturing” includes generating electricity when generators are in operation and the Court rejects any restrictive definition not found in the Act
BaselineA: Statute: Excise Tax Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-13, ss. 27(1), 29(1), and Schedule III, Part XIII, s. 1 (plus acceptance of a prior definition of “manufacture” from R. v. York Marble, Tile and Terrazzo Ltd., [1968] S.C.R. 140, and analogy to Bank of Nova Scotia v. The King, [1930] S.C.R. 174)
CaseB_TestB: Vesting of appeal-as-of-right under former Criminal Code s. 691(2): a right is “acquired, accrued or accruing” only when the court of appeal renders judgment because “a right cannot accrue, be acquired, or be accruing until all conditions precedent to the exercise of the right have been fulfilled” (charge, acquittal/stay tantamount to acquittal, reversal, and new trial order)
BaselineB: Statute: Interpretation Act, R.S.C., 1985, c. I-21, ss. 43(c) and 44(c),(d), applied to amended Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 691(2)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: No common-law tort/civil action for discrimination where the Ontario Human Rights Code provides a comprehensive enforcement and remedial scheme (the Code “foreclose[s] any civil action based directly upon a breach thereof” and “also excludes any common law action based on an invocation of the public policy expressed in the Code”).
BaselineA: Statute (Ontario Human Rights Code, R.S.O. 1970, c. 318, especially s. 4(1)(a)-(b) on employment discrimination; plus the Code’s administrative/board-of-inquiry and appeal provisions described by the Court).
CaseB_TestB: Undue-obstacle/undue-hardship (reasonable accommodation) analysis under CTA s. 172: discriminatory barrier must be removed unless the carrier proves accommodation would impose “undue hardship” (i.e., the obstacle is not “undue”); what is “undue” depends on contextual factors like “cost, economic viability, safety, and the quality of service to all passengers” (CTA s. 5 factors).
BaselineB: Statute (Canada Transportation Act, S.C. 1996, c. 10, ss. 5, 170-172) interpreted consistently with human rights reasonable-accommodation jurisprudence (e.g., Meiorin/Grismer) as incorporated into the CTA context.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Bill of Rights limit on reverse-onus: a reverse onus (balance of probabilities) is compatible with s. 2(f) only if the fact the accused must prove is "rationally open" to proof/disproof and not an "impossible" burden; for Customs Act s. 248(1) the Crown must first adduce facts showing the accused had "some knowledge or means of knowledge of the circumstances of importation"—otherwise applying the reverse onus would create an "irrebuttable presumption of guilt" and the Crown must prove unlawful importation beyond a reasonable doubt
BaselineA: Statute (Customs Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-40, ss. 205(1),(3), 248(1)) as constrained by statute (Canadian Bill of Rights, R.S.C. 1970, App. III, s. 2(f)); prior SCC guidance referenced: R. v. Appleby, [1972] S.C.R. 303
CaseB_TestB: Interested-party status/right to be heard at bargaining-unit stage under Labour Code s. 32: because s. 32 requires the bargaining-unit investigation be held "in the presence of every association concerned and the employer", the list is exhaustive and "the legislator indicated his intent to divest the employee of the status of an interested party"; on judicial review under a privative clause, the commissioners/Labour Court interpretation stands unless "patently unreasonable" (i.e., not "manifestly unreasonable")
BaselineB: Statute (Quebec Labour Code, especially s. 32, with related context in ss. 28, 39, 129; and Code of Civil Procedure art. 846) plus administrative-law judicial review doctrine (privative clause; CUPE v. NB Liquor and related cases cited) applying a patently unreasonable/manifestly unreasonable standard
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Intoxication (drunkenness) and mens rea for murder: evidence of drunkenness is relevant only if it "rendered an accused incapable of forming the intent to kill or to cause bodily harm that he knew was likely to cause death"; "The accused’s capacity is a question of fact for you" and the Crown must satisfy the jury beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused had that capacity.
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 212(a)(ii) (murder intent) plus the common-law intoxication 'capacity' approach from Director of Public Prosecutions v. Beard, as applied/clarified in SCC cases MacAskill v. The King; Perrault v. The Queen; Mulligan v. The Queen.
CaseB_TestB: Interjurisdictional immunity (constitutional inapplicability) for provincial laws of general application: provincial law applies to federal works/undertakings/services unless it bears on what makes them specifically federal; for a federal service, inapplicability arises if the provincial statute "touches on a vital or essential aspect of its establishment, management or operation".
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine (interjurisdictional immunity) as stated in Construction Montcalm and Bell Canada v. Quebec (CSST), and related cases (e.g., Clark v. CNR). Applied to the Quebec Transport Act permit scheme (R.S.Q., c. T-12) and Bus Transport Regulation.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Availability of Criminal Code s. 116(1) charge for disobeying a court order: s. 116(1) applies unless a penalty/punishment/other mode of proceeding is "expressly provided by law" meaning "by statute law" (not inherent/common law contempt powers).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 116(1); also considered s. 8 and Manitoba Queen’s Bench Rules 483, 485, 492).
CaseB_TestB: Public law promissory estoppel in regulatory/penal context: requires (1) a "clear and unambiguous promise" by a public authority intended to induce action, (2) reliance and change of conduct, but estoppel "must yield" to overriding public interest and "may not be invoked to prevent the application of an express legislative provision" (so it cannot defeat a clear strict-liability zoning by-law offence).
BaselineB: Common law doctrine of promissory estoppel as applied in public law (citing Mount Sinai (paras. 45-47) and Maracle), applied against the backdrop of express municipal by-law penal provisions and enabling statutes (Cities and Towns Act, s. 576; zoning by-law art. 359; Act respecting land use planning and development, s. 227).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Insurance policy interpretation to fix the policy’s “effective date”: read the policy and application “in entirety” and, on the “true construction of the entire contract”, select the single effective date “for the purpose of calculating any of the time periods contemplated, including the application of the self-destruction clause” (here, January 23, 1968).
BaselineA: Combination of statute and contract interpretation: Insurance Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 224, s. 148(2) (application + policy form the contract) and general common-law principles of construing the insurance contract as a whole (including discussion of contra proferentem only if ambiguity).
CaseB_TestB: Access in conjunction with permanent guardianship: access is legally possible but “the decision as to whether or not to grant access is a delicate exercise” requiring the judge to “weigh the various components of the best interests of the child”; “access is the exception and not the rule” and “should not be granted if its exercise would have negative effects on the physical or psychological health of the child” or would jeopardize an adoption in the child’s best interests.
BaselineB: Statute: Family Services Act, S.N.B. 1980, c. F-2.2, especially s. 1 (definition of “best interests of the child”), s. 53(2) (best interests paramount), s. 56 (permanent guardianship), s. 60(6) (court may make any order it considers appropriate if in best interests), and s. 85(2) (court may preserve access after adoption).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 16(2) insanity: meaning of “incapable of appreciating the nature and quality of an act” — an accused “appreciates” if he “knows what he is doing” and “is aware of the physical consequences which will result from his acts” (excluding mere emotional/moral indifference).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 16(2)); interpreted consistently with SCC authorities including Cooper v. The Queen and R. v. Barnier (as discussed in the reasons).
CaseB_TestB: Extradition: (1) Committal—restrained role/reliability screening: ROC evidence is “presumptively reliable” and committal is refused on reliability only if evidence is “so defective or appears so unreliable that it would be dangerous or unsafe to act on it”; defences generally not considered at committal. (2) Surrender—unavailable-defence threshold: before a defence-difference can engage s. 44(1)(a), the person sought must show (1) a substantive difference (defence in Canada but no comparable defence abroad), (2) a reasonable prospect of success in Canada, and (3) significantly greater jeopardy abroad; if met, Minister then weighs all circumstances.
BaselineB: Statute (Extradition Act, S.C. 1999, c. 18, ss. 29(1)(a), 32(1)(c), 44(1)(a)); built on prior SCC extradition jurisprudence including United States of America v. Ferras and Lake v. Canada (Minister of Justice) (as discussed in the reasons).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Non-pecuniary damages in severe personal injury: apply the functional approach and a “rough upper limit” of $100,000, exceedable only rarely (not merely because injuries seem worse), with increases only on proof/agreement of inflation’s effect
BaselineA: Common law (damages assessment principles from the “trilogy” and subsequent refinement): Andrews v. Grand & Toy Alberta Ltd.; Arnold v. Teno; Thornton v. Board of School Trustees of School District No. 57; Lewis v. Todd
CaseB_TestB: OPCF 44R / Insurance Act s. 239 “arising directly or indirectly from the use or operation of an automobile”: indemnity coverage requires the tortfeasor be liable “as a motorist” and an “unbroken chain of causation”; coverage denied where the tort is an intervening, “severable” act (more than mere “but for” connection)
BaselineB: Statute/contract interpretation: Insurance Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. I.8, s. 239(1)(a) (tracked by OPCF 44R wording) and prior causation/nexus jurisprudence including Amos v. ICBC (distinguished for no-fault context)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Workmen’s Compensation Act subrogation/election effect on (i) who may sue and for what, and (ii) whether the Commission has “interest” to intervene and benefit from interruption of prescription: once the worker elects compensation, “only the Commission can claim the amounts which it has paid or will have to pay” and the worker “can claim… only the additional sum provided for in s. 8”; a worker’s improper claim for the whole loss “does not have the effect of validly introducing… the object of the Commission’s claim” for intervention or interruption purposes.
BaselineA: Statute (Workmen’s Compensation Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 159, ss. 7(1)-(3), 8; plus Civil Code art. 1056a and Code of civil procedure art. 208, applied to intervention/prescription consequences).
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 24(2) Collins framework for excluding evidence: balance three categories—(1) fairness of the trial, (2) seriousness of the Charter violation, and (3) effect of exclusion on the repute of the justice system—i.e., whether “having regard to all the circumstances, the admission… would bring the administration of justice into disrepute.”
BaselineB: Combination of statute/constitutional text and common law framework: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 24(2), applying the Collins/Jacoy/Simmons line (R. v. Collins, [1987] 1 S.C.R. 265, as organized into three categories).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Public access to executed search warrants/informations: presumption of openness; in camera issuance permitted; post-execution access unless superordinate values (notably protection of the innocent where nothing is found) justify restriction
BaselineA: Combination: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 443 and 446, plus common law/open court principle and court supervisory power over records (e.g., Scott v. Scott; McPherson v. McPherson; Gazette Printing Co. v. Shallow, as discussed in the reasons)
CaseB_TestB: Bona fide occupational qualification (BFOQ) under BC Human Rights Code s. 8: two-branch test—(1) subjective good faith/no ulterior purpose; (2) objective reasonable necessity to accomplish the job/employer’s legitimate objectives (adapted to denominational school context)
BaselineB: Combination: Human Rights Code, R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 186, ss. 8 and 22, applying the common-law/precedential BFOQ framework from Ontario Human Rights Commission v. Etobicoke (Borough of), [1982] 1 S.C.R. 202
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Validity of a Quebec deed of donation and trust benefiting unborn (non-existent) primary beneficiaries: interpret art. 981a C.C. “subject to the special characteristics of the trust” and uphold validity where (i) trustee acceptance makes the trust irrevocable and (ii) trustee is owner of the trust property during the trust, so beneficiaries need not exist at creation; only public-order prohibitions on gifts carry over to trusts.
BaselineA: Statute (Civil Code of Quebec provisions on trusts and gifts): arts. 981a, 981b, 981l (trusts) read with arts. 754, 755, 765, 771, 772, 929 (gifts/substitutions). Key prior SCC baseline points relied on: Curran v. Davis, [1933] S.C.R. 283 (trustee acceptance suffices; beneficiaries are not ordinary donees/legatees).
CaseB_TestB: When a civil-court injunction can effectively bind non-parties (enforceable by contempt): courts have jurisdiction to make orders binding on non-parties; but because non-parties may be held in contempt, they must be (i) apprised of the existence and terms of the order and (ii) given an opportunity to comply; additionally it is desirable that (iii) the order’s terms speak of the duty of non-parties to respect it, and (iv) orders be “carefully worded and constrained” so they are “fair and not unduly broad”.
BaselineB: Common law equitable/inherent jurisdiction over injunctions and contempt (e.g., Seaward v. Paterson; International Longshoremen’s Association, Local 273 v. Maritime Employers’ Association) plus statutory confirmation of interlocutory injunction power (Law and Equity Act, R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 224, s. 36) and Criminal Code, s. 11 (civil remedies not suspended by criminality).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory displacement of the Kienapple rule: s. 83 permits multiple convictions/punishments for the same event where a firearm is used, because Parliament gave a clear indication (including consecutive sentencing) that s. 83 is a distinct offence; and s. 21 party liability applies to s. 83
BaselineA: Combination of common law and statute: common law Kienapple principle (Kienapple v. The Queen; also nemo debet bis puniri) plus interpretation/application of Criminal Code ss. 83 and 21
JudgeA: Dickson J. (for Martland, Dickson, Estey, McIntyre and Chouinard JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Division of powers validity (pith and substance) and interjurisdictional immunity: characterize purpose and effects; if measure trenches on the core of a federal power and its effect is sufficiently serious (impairs, not merely affects), it is inapplicable
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrines (pith and substance; interjurisdictional immunity) applied in light of constitutional text (Constitution Act, 1867) and federal statutory context (Radiocommunication Act s. 5(1)(f))
JudgeB: Wagner and Côté JJ. (for McLachlin C.J. and Abella, Cromwell, Moldaver, Karakatsanis and Brown JJ. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Labour arbitration remedial authority under s. 25(3): where the collective agreement lacks a specific penalty for the infraction, an arbitrator/board that finds discharge/discipline occurred may substitute a lesser penalty that "seems just and reasonable in the circumstances" (including reinstatement without back pay) when dismissal is not sustainable
BaselineA: Statute: The Trade Union Act, R.S.S. 1978, c. T-17, s. 25(3) (interpreting when it applies alongside collective agreement provisions on dismissal/remedy)
CaseB_TestB: Article 1F(a) refugee exclusion for complicity (contribution-based test): exclusion requires "serious reasons for considering" the claimant "has voluntarily made a significant and knowing contribution to the organization’s crime or criminal purpose"; guided by a non-exhaustive, contextual list of factors (size/nature of organization; relevant part; duties; rank; time in organization after knowledge; recruitment and opportunity to leave)
BaselineB: Statute + treaty: Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, S.C. 2001, c. 27, s. 98 incorporating Refugee Convention, art. 1F(a) (informed by international criminal law sources such as the Rome Statute)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 43 Canada Evidence Act letters rogatory: court should give s. 43 a “broad, liberal construction in the interests of comity”; s. 43 is “wide enough to support the request here for production of documents alone”, and judicial assistance is guided by comity limits including: (1) evidence required for trial not discovery; (2) relevancy (for commissioner/foreign court); (3) scope permitted by local law; (4) documents adequately defined.
BaselineA: Statute (Canada Evidence Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-10, s. 43) plus common-law/comity guidelines (notably Zingre v. The Queen, [1981] 2 S.C.R. 392, applied).
CaseB_TestB: Admissibility of defence-led unknown third party suspect evidence: admissible where (1) relevant to a fact in issue and (2) “the probative value of the evidence is not substantially outweighed by its prejudicial effects” (Seaboyer). Logical relevance/air of reality is shown by a “sufficient connection” (similarity) between the charged crime and another incident plus evidence the accused “could not have committed the other offence”; trial judge must not assess credibility/weight or require proof on a balance of probabilities.
BaselineB: Common law (general admissibility principles from R. v. Corbett; balancing test from R. v. Seaboyer; air of reality from R. v. Cinous; sufficient connection concept from McMillan/Grandinetti).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Civil Code art. 1055 C.C. “ruin of a building” liability applies only if the defect/want of repairs is assessed “in light of the purpose for which the building is to be used”; if the victim uses the building/part “contrary to the purpose for which it was intended”, the owner is not liable under art. 1055
BaselineA: Statute (Civil Code of Quebec (as then in force), arts. 1053, 1054, 1055; especially art. 1055) as interpreted in prior SCC authority (Leznek v. City of Verdun, [1940] S.C.R. 313)
JudgeA: Beetz J. (for Beetz, Chouinard and Lamer JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: “Operating mind” / limited cognitive capacity standard for admissibility and Charter choice-rights: accused must have “sufficient cognitive capacity to understand what he or she is saying and what is said”, including understanding a caution that it “can be used against” him; no separate “awareness of consequences” test, and “inner compulsion” alone does not negate an operating mind absent police conduct making the statement involuntary
BaselineB: Common law confession voluntariness/operating-mind doctrine (Ibrahim v. The King; Ward; Horvath; Nagotcha; Hebert) plus constitutional baseline (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 7 and 10(b)) and statutory fitness concept (Criminal Code, s. 2 “unfit to stand trial”) used to harmonize the mental-capacity threshold
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Judicial review of a labour board’s interpretation under a privative clause: intervene only if the interpretation is “plainly unreasonable” / “patently unreasonable” (certiorari is “a long way from an appeal”)
BaselineA: Combination: statute + common law. Statutory baseline is The Public Service Employee Relations Act, 1977 (Alta.), especially ss. 9(1), 11, 89 and the arbitrability limits in s. 48(2). Common-law baseline is CUPE v. New Brunswick Liquor Corp. (1979) and related SCC deference cases (Volvo; Douglas Aircraft) articulating the patently unreasonable standard.
CaseB_TestB: Adverse-effect discrimination and duty to accommodate: discrimination under Quebec Charter s. 10 requires (1) a “distinction, exclusion or preference”, (2) based on an enumerated ground, and (3) having the effect of “nullifying or impairing” the right; once adverse-effect discrimination is shown, employer must take “reasonable steps to accommodate ... short of undue hardship” (no de minimis test)
BaselineB: Combination: statute + common law. Statutory baseline is Quebec Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms, ss. 10 and 16 (and related provisions), applied in the employment context. Common-law baseline is O’Malley (duty to accommodate) and subsequent SCC cases (Central Alberta Dairy Pool; Renaud) on accommodation/undue hardship.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Similar fact evidence admissibility: (1) apply Makin/Boardman principle that admissibility depends on probative value balanced against prejudice; and (2) threshold requirement that there be an evidentiary link (direct or circumstantial) connecting the alleged similar acts to the accused (similarity alone is insufficient).
BaselineA: Common law (Makin v. A-G for New South Wales; Boardman v. DPP; Harris v. DPP).
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 7 vagueness test: a law is unconstitutionally vague if it "so lacks in precision as not to give sufficient guidance for legal debate" (i.e., for reaching a conclusion by reasoned analysis applying legal criteria).
BaselineB: Common law / constitutional doctrine under Charter s. 7 (building on the Prostitution Reference and related SCC vagueness jurisprudence).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 16(2) insanity — “first arm” requires incapacity to appreciate the nature and quality of the act in the sense of perceiving the physical consequences of the act; failure to appreciate penal consequences (punishment) does not satisfy s. 16(2).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 16(2)), as interpreted in Cooper v. The Queen, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 1149; Schwartz v. The Queen, [1977] 1 S.C.R. 673; R. v. Barnier, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 1124; Kjeldsen v. The Queen, [1981] 2 S.C.R. 617.
CaseB_TestB: Administrative tribunal jurisdiction to decide constitutional issues (including s. 35) — “essential question” is whether the empowering legislation “implicitly or explicitly grants to the tribunal the jurisdiction to interpret or decide any question of law”; if yes, the tribunal is presumed to have concomitant jurisdiction to decide the constitutional issue unless a “clear implication” rebuts it.
BaselineB: Common law / constitutional doctrine on tribunal jurisdiction to decide constitutional questions, applied through interpretation of the Forest Practices Code of British Columbia Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 159 (notably s. 131(8) allowing submissions as to “facts, law and jurisdiction”), and relying on Nova Scotia (Workers’ Compensation Board) v. Martin, 2003 SCC 54; Cooper v. Canada (Human Rights Commission), [1996] 3 S.C.R. 854 (discussed).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Patentability of a new use for an old compound as a “new and useful art” (and permissibility of claiming compositions as the practical embodiment): the invention is “the application of this new knowledge to effect a desired result which has an undisputed commercial value” and thus falls within “any new and useful art”; s. 36 does not bar composition claims where the composition is required to give practical effect to the new use/idea.
BaselineA: Statute (Patent Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. P-4), especially s. 2 definition of “invention” (“any new and useful art...”) and s. 36 claim/specification requirements; interpreted against prior case law including Farbwerke Hoechst, Jules R. Gilbert, Agripat, Ciba, Tennessee Eastman, and Hickton’s Patent Syndicate.
CaseB_TestB: Party liability for drug trafficking by aiding/abetting under Criminal Code s. 21(1): (1) actus reus—“to aid... means to assist or help the actor” (s. 21(1)(b)); “to abet... includes encouraging, instigating, promoting or procuring” (s. 21(1)(c)); (2) mens rea—under s. 21(1)(b) “purpose” is “intention” (not “desire”): Crown must prove the accused “intended the consequences that flowed from his or her aid”; under s. 21(1)(c) Crown must prove the accused encouraged and “intended to do so”; purchaser is excluded from trafficking by purchase alone, but one who assists the purchaser can be liable if they in fact assist/encourage the sale with the requisite intent.
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, s. 21(1)(b),(c); Narcotic Control Act, s. 2 “traffic”, s. 4(1), and related possession provisions), with interpretive reliance on Hibbert (meaning of “purpose”) and Poitras/Meston (purchaser not a trafficker by purchase alone).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory incompatibility/repugnancy test for whether a permissive municipal discretion (Police Act s. 24(6)) excludes a collectively bargained/arbitrated working-condition clause under s. 29(2): ask whether the provisions are "incompatible or inconsistent"; if not, "each has its own area of operation" and the clause is not excluded
BaselineA: Statute (The Police Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 351, ss. 24(6) and 29(2))
CaseB_TestB: State Immunity Act statutory-exception applicability test (especially s. 6(a)): (1) the s. 6(a) exception applies only where "the tort causing the personal injury or death has occurred in Canada"; and (2) "personal or bodily injury" requires a "physical breach of personal integrity"—"Only when psychological distress manifests itself after a physical injury will the exception" apply
BaselineB: Statute (State Immunity Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. S-18, ss. 3(1), 6(a), and related definition in s. 2)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory incompatibility/repugnancy test between Police Act s. 24(6) (municipal discretion to pay costs) and s. 29(2) (collective bargaining over “working conditions”): whether the provisions are “incompatible or inconsistent” such that s. 24(6) would exclude a bargained/arbitrated clause like art. 17.06; held no—s. 24(6) is “an empowering provision only” and “does not prescribe exclusivity”.
BaselineA: Statute: The Police Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 351, ss. 24(6) and 29(2) (with analogy to IBEW v. Town of Summerside, [1960] S.C.R. 591 on repugnancy).
CaseB_TestB: Corporate attribution for BIA s. 96(1)(b)(ii)(B) transfers at undervalue: for s. 96, the attribution test is “simply whether the person was the directing mind and whether their actions were performed within the sector of corporate responsibility assigned to them”; the “fraud” and “no benefit” exceptions do not apply in this context.
BaselineB: Combination: Statute (Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act, s. 96(1)(b)(ii)(B)) plus common law corporate attribution doctrine (Canadian Dredge & Dock Co. v. The Queen; Deloitte & Touche v. Livent; DeJong).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Jennings test for establishing a constitutional convention, emphasizing that the key requirement is acceptance/recognition by the actors in the precedents (precedents + belief/acceptance of being bound + reason for the rule)
BaselineA: Common law (constitutional conventions doctrine), as articulated in Re: Resolution to amend the Constitution, [1981] 1 S.C.R. 753, adopting Sir W. Ivor Jennings’ three questions: “first, what are the precedents; secondly, did the actors in the precedents believe that they were bound by a rule; and thirdly, is there a reason for the rule?”
CaseB_TestB: Reasonable suspicion standard for sniffer-dog (sniff) searches under Charter s. 8: police may deploy a drug detection dog without prior authorization where there is “reasonable suspicion based on objective, ascertainable facts” assessed on the “totality of the circumstances” (a sufficiently particularized constellation, not generalized suspicion), plus the dog must be sufficiently reliable
BaselineB: Common law Charter search framework (R. v. Collins) and prior SCC sniffer-dog cases (R. v. Kang-Brown; R. v. A.M.) establishing reasonable suspicion as the threshold for dog deployment
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory tribunal test for labour arbitrators under art. 846 C.C.P.: even if parties were not compelled by statute to choose arbitration, an arbitrator is a “statutory tribunal” where, once chosen, the arbitrator is “invested with wide duties and powers by statute” (e.g., Canada Labour Code s. 157) and thus subject to evocation; refusal to hear “admissible and relevant evidence” is “so clear a case of excess or refusal to exercise jurisdiction” that evocation is justified.
BaselineA: Combination of common law/prerogative-writ doctrine (Howe Sound; Port Arthur; R. v. National Joint Council for the Craft of Dental Technicians) and statute (Code of Civil Procedure, art. 846; Canada Labour Code ss. 156(2), 157, 159, 160(5)).
CaseB_TestB: Sublicence characterization test in patent licensing: a sublicence exists only if the licensee “granted, either expressly or impliedly, the right to do something which [the third party] would otherwise be prohibited from doing, and which [the licensee] was permitted to do only by virtue of its compulsory licence”; interpret the contract from its text (parol evidence excluded if unambiguous) and ask whether the agreement is “more than merely an elaborate arrangement under which future contracts for purchase and sale might be completed.”
BaselineB: Common law principles of patent licensing and contractual interpretation (including Consolidated-Bathurst; parol evidence rule) applied in the statutory context of the Patent Act compulsory licensing regime and NOC Regulations.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Kienapple remedy direction: where Kienapple applies, enter a stay of proceedings rather than an acquittal
BaselineA: Common law (Kienapple v. The Queen, [1975] 1 S.C.R. 729)
CaseB_TestB: Removing/replacing a litigation guardian: the Rule 49(1) test turns on the dependent adult’s “best interests”, guided by the Szwydky criteria (including required “indifference”/no conflict)
BaselineB: Combination of regulation and statute, interpreted and applied: Queen’s Bench Rules (Saskatchewan) r. 49(1) (“best interests”); The Dependent Adults Act, S.S. 1989-90, c. D-25.1, ss. 19(4)-(6), 20(3)(a); plus common-law guidance from Szwydky v. Magiera (1988) (QB)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Contract interpretation of the 1905 power-supply agreement: reconcile general language (“to such an extent as the said Town… may require”) with specific allocation clauses (paras. 6 and 8), yielding a fixed entitlement of 4,000 horsepower at $14 per horsepower per annum (and no broader right to all output). Key quotes: para. 8 requires the Company to “retain and reserve… Four Thousand Horse Power… permanently available”; the Court holds the Company’s commitment “is to provide… to the extent of 4,000 horsepower per annum… at the contract price of $14 per horsepower per annum.”
BaselineA: Contract (1905 agreement) interpretation; key provisions are paras. 1, 5, 6, 8 (and arbitration clauses 5/13 considered but found not to expand quantity entitlement).
CaseB_TestB: General Motors indicia for validity under the general trade and commerce power (Constitution Act, 1867, s. 91(2)): ask (1) part of a general regulatory scheme; (2) oversight by a regulatory agency; (3) concerned with trade as a whole rather than a particular industry; (4) provinces acting alone or together would be constitutionally incapable of enacting it; (5) failure to include one or more provinces would jeopardize successful operation. Quote: validity “may be ascertained by asking (1)… (2)… (3)… (4)… (5)…; these indicia… are not exhaustive, nor is it necessary that they be present in every case.”
BaselineB: Common law constitutional test from General Motors of Canada Ltd. v. City National Leasing, [1989] 1 S.C.R. 641, applied to s. 91(2) of the Constitution Act, 1867.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Contract interpretation of the 1905 power agreement: the Company’s obligation to supply Fort Frances is limited to the 4,000 horsepower reserve at the fixed ceiling price ($14 per horsepower per annum), with no entitlement to additional uncommitted power absent availability under the agreement
BaselineA: Common law (contract interpretation principles) applied to the January 9, 1905 agreement (especially paras. 1, 5, 6, 8, 13); related statutes were found to have no direct bearing on the issue
CaseB_TestB: Kidnapping as a continuing offence + party liability for latecomers: kidnapping continues while the victim remains unlawfully confined, and a person who later joins the confinement is a party if, with knowledge (or wilful blindness) of the kidnapping and the principal’s intention to see it through, they intentionally aid/abet the ongoing offence (Criminal Code s. 21(1))
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, ss. 279(1) and 21(1)) interpreted in light of the common law understanding of kidnapping as an aggravated form of unlawful confinement/false imprisonment
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Trigger for municipality’s mandatory acquisition duty under Planning Act s. 70(1): land must be “designated under a land use by-law” (not merely identified in statutory plans); statutory plans are “policy documents” and “the land use by-law was the instrument which triggered s. 70”.
BaselineA: Statute: The Planning Act, 1977 (Alta.), s. 70(1) (and definition of “land use by-law” in s. 1(14)).
CaseB_TestB: O’Connor framework for production of private third-party records in criminal cases: (1) accused must show records are “likely to be relevant” to an issue at trial or witness competence; (2) if so, court balances salutary vs deleterious effects (privacy/equality vs full answer and defence) to decide whether/what to produce (including in-camera review and tailored disclosure).
BaselineB: Common law/Charter-informed discretion: builds on disclosure jurisprudence (e.g., Stinchcombe) and Charter values (ss. 7, 24(1)) while emphasizing third-party production is not Crown disclosure; also relies on Criminal Code subpoena mechanism (e.g., ss. 698, 700) as procedural vehicle.
JudgeB: L'Heureux-Dubé J. (reasons joined by La Forest and Gonthier JJ.; McLachlin J. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “has become regularly engaged in some other occupation” under Unemployment Insurance Act s. 44(1)(c): claimant must have worked in the new occupation on a regular (fixed-pattern) schedule; “regularly” concerns regularity of work schedule (contrasted with “casual”/“intermittent”), not duration or an intention to abandon the prior job/strike-related employment
BaselineA: Statute: Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, s. 44(1)(c) (with contextual comparison to s. 44(1)(b) and Regulations s. 49 defining “bona fide employed” as “not less than two weeks duration”)
CaseB_TestB: Whether an ISP “carr[ies] on ... ‘broadcasting undertakings’” under the Broadcasting Act when providing Internet access: “broadcasting undertaking” is not meant to capture entities that “merely provide the mode of transmission”; it contemplates an entity with “some measure of control over programming” (selection/origination/packaging) and a role in the Act’s content-focused policy objectives
BaselineB: Statute: Broadcasting Act, S.C. 1991, c. 11, ss. 2(1) (“broadcasting”), 2(3), 3(1) (interpreted in light of statutory purposes and prior SCC authority such as Electric Despatch and SOCAN v. CAIP)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Cross-border fresh pursuit: a peace officer retains (for Criminal Code s. 25(4)) peace-officer status in another province if the pursuit began lawfully in the officer’s jurisdiction and remains “fresh”; arrest authority depends on whether the suspect would have appeared to a reasonable person in the officer’s circumstances to be committing an offence (reasonable and probable grounds).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 25(4), 450(1)(b), and related ss. 449(1)(b), 25(1),(3)); interpretive baseline includes R. v. Biron, [1976] 2 S.C.R. 56 (apparent commission/reasonable grounds for warrantless arrest).
CaseB_TestB: Arbitrator’s jurisdiction to substitute a lesser penalty under Canada Labour Code s. 157(d): the arbitrator is deprived of substitution power only if the collective agreement contains a “specific penalty” assigned to the particular infraction; a penalty is not “specific” if it is not in the collective agreement or if it can be chosen indiscriminately by the employer.
BaselineB: Statute (Canada Labour Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. L-1, s. 157(d), especially s. 157(d)(ii)) interpreted alongside the collective agreement (Article XI(b)).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Availability/scope of Crown’s per quod servitium amisit action for injuries to Canadian Forces members deemed servants: master may recover costs of lost services (incl. wages/allowances and medical/hospital expenses) where the servant has a valid cause of action; Armed Forces services are not excluded as ‘menial/domestic’ only.
BaselineA: Combination: statute deeming relationship (Federal Court Act, R.S.C. 1970 (2nd Supp.), c. 10, s. 37; and Exchequer Court Act, R.S.C. 1952, c. 98, s. 50) plus common-law per quod action as recognized in SCC precedents (The King v. Richardson, [1948] S.C.R. 57; Attorney-General of Canada v. Jackson, [1946] S.C.R. 489; Nykorak v. Attorney General of Canada, [1962] S.C.R. 331; The Queen v. Murray, [1967] S.C.R. 262).
JudgeA: Ritchie J. (for Ritchie, Estey, Lamer and Wilson JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Mens rea for Criminal Code s. 121(1)(a): no ‘corrupt’ purpose required; guilt requires (1) knowledge one is an official, (2) intentional demand/acceptance of a loan/reward/advantage/benefit, and (3) knowledge the benefit is ‘as consideration for’ cooperation/assistance/exercise of influence in connection with government business.
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 121(1)(a) (and related interpretive context including s. 19); interpreted consistently with SCC authority Martineau v. La Reine, [1966] S.C.R. 103 and distinguished from R. v. Hinchey, [1996] 3 S.C.R. 1128.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Timing rule for Attorney General stay under Criminal Code s. 508(1): the stay power arises only "after a summons or warrant is issued" (i.e., an information is "found" only once the justice decides to issue process after the s. 455.3 hearing).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34 as amended), especially ss. 455, 455.3, 508, plus definitional context in ss. 2 and 503.
CaseB_TestB: Statutory eligibility rule for discharge under Criminal Code s. 662.1(1): a discharge is unavailable if the offence is one "for which a minimum punishment is prescribed by law"; s. 234(a) impaired driving has a minimum because it includes "a fine ... not less than fifty dollars".
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code), interpreting and applying ss. 234(a) and 662.1(1) (with reference to s. 645 discussed but not treated as controlling).
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 508 stay power timing: an information is “found” (and the Attorney General may direct a stay) only after the justice issues process (summons or warrant), not upon mere laying/receipt of the information
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34 as amended): ss. 508(1) (“after an indictment has been found”), with interpretive context from ss. 2 (definition of “indictment”), 503 (“finding an indictment”), and the private information/hearing scheme in ss. 455 and 455.3
CaseB_TestB: Procedural fairness content (Baker factors) for municipal rezoning decisions: apply the five Baker factors to determine the duty’s content; on these facts, fairness required careful evaluation and reasons for refusing the 2nd and 3rd rezoning applications
BaselineB: Common law administrative law duty of procedural fairness, structured by Baker v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), [1999] 2 S.C.R. 817 (five-factor framework for the content of fairness), applied in the municipal rezoning context
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Jurisdictional rule against joint trial of separate informations/indictments: even with consent, a judge is "without jurisdiction to try together separate informations or indictments" (a joint trial on more than one information/indictment is a nullity), unless a provincial statute "expressly provide[s] otherwise".
BaselineA: Common law rule from Crane v. Public Prosecutor (applied/confirmed as incorporated by implication into the Criminal Code; extended to provincial offences absent express statutory authorization).
CaseB_TestB: Credibility assessment limits re (i) absence of evidence of motive to lie and (ii) lack of embellishment: (1) "absence of evidence" of motive cannot be equated with evidence disproving a motive, and (2) the burden of proof cannot be reversed by requiring the accused to show motive; lack of embellishment "cannot be used to bolster" credibility (it "simply does not weigh against it"), though it may be considered regarding motive to lie.
BaselineB: Common law credibility/W.(D.) framework from R. v. W.(D.) and related SCC guidance (including Stirling; Vuradin; G.F.).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Marine insurance “perils of the seas” where loss follows crew negligence: “An act is not negligent in itself but only in relation to a foreseeable risk of harm. If that foreseeable risk of harm is a peculiarly marine risk, then the act, coupled with its foreseeable consequence, is a fortuitous accident of the seas and a peril of the seas and the proximate cause of the loss.”
BaselineA: Statute (Insurance (Marine) Act, R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 203, Schedule “Rules for Construction of Policy”: “The term ‘perils of the seas’ refers only to fortuitous accidents or casualties of the seas.
