It does not include the ordinary action of the winds and waves.”) plus statutory causation rule (Marine Insurance Act, R.S.B.C. 1960, c. 231, s. 57(2)(a) (now s. 56(2)(a)): insurer liable for loss proximately caused by a peril insured against “even though the loss would not have happened but for the misconduct or negligence of the master or crew”), applied with common-law definitions cited from Canada Rice Mills, Ld. v. Union Marine & General Insurance Co. and Cohen, Sons & Co. v. National Benefit Assurance Co.
CaseB_TestB: Section 35(1) threshold for who can claim Aboriginal rights: “the expression ‘aboriginal peoples of Canada’ means the modern-day successors of Aboriginal societies that occupied Canadian territory at the time of European contact” (a “threshold question” before applying Van der Peet).
BaselineB: Constitution Act, 1982, s. 35(1) (“The existing aboriginal and treaty rights of the aboriginal peoples of Canada are hereby recognized and affirmed.”) interpreted purposively; Van der Peet remains the separate baseline test for proving an Aboriginal right once the threshold is met.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory “bridging” of an expired collective agreement: s. 70(1) preserves the parties’ right to invoke interest arbitration after expiry, and the right need only exist when the notice to arbitrate is served (not when the award is issued).
BaselineA: Statute (Ontario Labour Relations Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 232, s. 70(1) (now R.S.O. 1980, c. 228, s. 79)), applied alongside the collective agreement’s interest arbitration clauses (Haldimand art. 16; Perth art. 15).
CaseB_TestB: Test for non-suit / directed verdict: whether there is “any admissible evidence, whether direct or circumstantial, which, if believed by a properly charged jury acting reasonably, would justify a conviction”.
BaselineB: Common law test from United States of America v. Shephard, [1977] 2 S.C.R. 1067, as applied/confirmed in R. v. Monteleone, [1987] 2 S.C.R. 154.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: McKibbon (Lamer J.) conditions for when a non-AG (e.g., AG’s agent) may prefer an indictment under Criminal Code s. 507(2) after the 1969 addition of s. 507(3): (1) a preliminary inquiry has been held; (2) the accused has been committed for trial on at least one charge inquired into; and (3) each count must be for an offence the accused was committed on, or an offence disclosed by the preliminary inquiry evidence and not one the accused was discharged on ("anyone else empowered under s. 507(2) ... can do so only if the following conditions have been met...").
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 507(1)-(3); interpreted in light of related provisions ss. 504-505 and prior SCC discussion in R. v. Chabot, [1980] 2 S.C.R. 985 and Re Criminal Code (1910), 43 S.C.R. 434).
JudgeA: Lamer J. (for Ritchie, Estey and Lamer JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Mitchell (McLachlin C.J.) Van der Peet test (as applied/clarified) for establishing an Aboriginal right under Constitution Act, 1982, s. 35(1): claimant must prove (1) an ancestral practice/custom/tradition supporting the claimed right; (2) that it was "integral" to the distinctive culture (a "defining feature" such that the culture would be "fundamentally altered" without it); and (3) "reasonable continuity" between the pre-contact practice and the modern claim; plus a structured approach to characterizing the claimed right using three factors from Van der Peet (nature of the impugned action; nature of the governmental action/legislation; ancestral practices relied on).
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine under s. 35(1) (test drawn from and applied from R. v. Van der Peet, [1996] 2 S.C.R. 507 and Delgamuukw v. British Columbia, [1997] 3 S.C.R. 1010; also references to Pamajewon, Adams, Côté, etc.).
JudgeB: McLachlin C.J. (for McLachlin C.J. and Gonthier, Iacobucci, Arbour and LeBel JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Planned-and-deliberate first degree murder where s. 212(b) applies: if the accused’s intention to kill (the intended victim) was planned and deliberate, the murder is first degree even if, “by accident or mistake”, someone else is killed; “the identity and character of any victim is entirely irrelevant”.
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 212(b) and 214(2); with s. 214 treated as a sentencing classification per R. v. Farrant, [1983] 1 S.C.R. 24).
CaseB_TestB: Interpretation of Alberta Limitations Act s. 12 in conflicts cases: s. 12 “does not purport to revive an action time-barred by the substantive law of the place where the accident occurred”; if the foreign limitation has expired, “no right of action existed” and the claim is barred.
BaselineB: Statute (Limitations Act, R.S.A. 2000, c. L-12, s. 12) interpreted against the conflicts baseline in Tolofson v. Jensen, [1994] 3 S.C.R. 1022 (lex loci delicti includes foreign limitation as substantive).
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Mens rea for attempted murder: the Crown must prove a specific intent to kill (no lesser/constructive murder intent suffices)
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code) interpreted against prior SCC precedent (Lajoie v. The Queen, [1974] S.C.R. 399) and attempt principles
JudgeA: McIntyre J. (for Dickson, Beetz, Estey, McIntyre, Chouinard, Lamer and Wilson JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: “Establishment” under CHRA s. 11 / Guidelines s. 10: employees are in the same establishment if subject to a “common personnel and wage policy” (a factual inquiry into the employer’s common principles/approach)
BaselineB: Statute and regulation: Canadian Human Rights Act, s. 11, read with Equal Wages Guidelines, 1986, SOR/86-1082, s. 10
JudgeB: LeBel and Abella JJ. (for the Court)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Matrimonial property distribution under Saskatchewan’s Matrimonial Property Act: equal division presumption subject to limited statutory exemptions; pre-marital property exemption is capped at its fair market value at the date of marriage (rejecting the “Capital Base Theory” and use of s. 21(2)(q) to enlarge the s. 23 exemption).
BaselineA: Statute: The Matrimonial Property Act, 1979 (Sask.), c. M-6.1, especially ss. 20, 21(1)-(2), 23(1), 23(4)-(5).
CaseB_TestB: Aggravated assault (s. 268(1) Criminal Code) in HIV non-disclosure cases: because aggravated assault is consequence-based, the Crown must prove the aggravating consequence (here, “endangers the life”) beyond a reasonable doubt; if there is a reasonable doubt the complainant was capable of being endangered (e.g., could already be HIV-positive), no aggravated assault (though attempt may be made out).
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, ss. 268(1) (aggravated assault), with related provisions ss. 265(1)(a), 265(3)(c) (fraud vitiating consent), 24(1) and 660 (attempt).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Mechanics’ lien “owner” test under s. 1(1)(d): a party is an owner if it (a) has an estate/interest in the land, (b) requested the work, and (c) the work was done “upon whose credit, or … on whose behalf, or … with whose privity or consent, or … for whose direct benefit” (overall view of arrangements may show a ‘request’ despite intermediaries/agency).
BaselineA: Statute — The Mechanics’ Lien Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 267, especially ss. 1(1)(d) (definition of “owner”) and 5(1) (lien attaches to owner’s estate/interest; limited to sums “justly due” and “justly owing”).
CaseB_TestB: Challenge for cause (juror partiality) test under Criminal Code s. 638(1)(b): to show a “realistic potential” of partiality generally requires (1) “a widespread bias exists in the community” and (2) “some jurors may be incapable of setting aside this bias, despite trial safeguards, to render an impartial decision” (overarching question: realistic potential for partial juror behaviour).
BaselineB: Statute informed by common law — Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 638(1)(b) (and related jury provisions); framework applied/clarified with reference to R. v. Sherratt, R. v. Williams, R. v. Parks, R. v. Betker.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Anns v. Merton two-stage duty-of-care framework for public authority negligence (proximity + residual policy limits; including policy/operational distinction and bona fide discretion)
BaselineA: Common law (adopting/applying Anns v. Merton London Borough Council, [1978] A.C. 728; also drawing on Donoghue v. Stevenson; Hedley Byrne; Dorset Yacht) in the context of statutory/by-law powers and duties under Municipal Act, R.S.B.C. 1960, c. 255, s. 714 and Kamloops By-law No. 11-1
CaseB_TestB: Implied-limit analysis for s. 10(b) at roadside: a limit is 'prescribed by law' if it arises by necessary implication from statutory operating requirements; roadside sobriety questions/tests are authorized if 'reasonable and necessary' and incompatible with immediate access to counsel, then justified under s. 1 (Oakes proportionality)
BaselineB: Combination of statute and constitutional law: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms ss. 1 and 10(b); Highway Traffic Act (Man.), s. 76.1(1); Criminal Code, ss. 254 (and related impaired driving provisions); building on R. v. Therens and R. v. Thomsen (operating-requirements/necessary-implication approach)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal defence of necessity (as an excuse): requires “urgent situation of clear and imminent peril when compliance with the law is demonstrably impossible”, with limits of (i) imminent/direct peril, (ii) no reasonable legal alternative (“legal way out”), (iii) proportionality (harm inflicted < harm avoided), plus limits on contributory fault and Crown bears burden once air of reality met
BaselineA: Common law defence preserved by Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 7(3), drawing from Morgentaler v. The Queen, [1976] 1 S.C.R. 616 (necessity limited to “urgent situations of clear and imminent peril when compliance with the law is demonstrably impossible”).
CaseB_TestB: Section 8 reasonable expectation of privacy (REP) test applied to online sting: REP assessed on “totality of the circumstances” via four inquiries (subject matter; direct interest; subjective expectation; objective reasonableness), with objective reasonableness a normative inquiry; in this sting context adults have no objectively reasonable REP when communicating online with a child stranger created/controlled by police
BaselineB: Common law/Charter framework for s. 8 REP: “totality of the circumstances” and the four lines of inquiry (as stated in Cole, Marakah, Spencer, Tessling, Edwards, Patrick, etc.), applied under Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 8.
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 613(1)(b)(iii) proviso (harmless error): Crown must satisfy the court the verdict "would necessarily have been the same" absent the legal error; where exculpatory evidence was excluded, assess the entirety of the evidence including the reasonable possible effect of the excluded evidence, with any reasonable effect enuring to the accused
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 613(1)(b)(iii)) as interpreted in Colpitts v. The Queen, [1965] S.C.R. 739 (Cartwright J. at p. 744: Crown must show verdict "would necessarily have been the same")
CaseB_TestB: When an appellate court may raise a new issue on appeal: discretion exercised only rarely; only when failing to do so would risk an injustice (i.e., "good reason to believe" the result would realistically have differed), and the court should also consider jurisdiction, sufficiency of the record, and procedural prejudice; plus notice and opportunity to respond
BaselineB: Common law / appellate practice principles (drawing on prior SCC authority such as R. v. W. (G.) and Quan v. Cusson, as cited in the reasons)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 96 ‘judicial power’ screening test: a power is administrative (not judicial) where there is “no real lis between the parties” and the decision is based “not on considerations of legality but on considerations of expediency” (therefore s. 96 not infringed).
BaselineA: Common law constitutional doctrine under Constitution Act, 1867, s. 96, drawing on Re Residential Tenancies Act, 1979 and related s. 96 jurisprudence (including the ‘judicial power’ concept from John East Iron Works as discussed in Residential Tenancies).
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 12 mandatory-minimum framework (as applied in Hilbach): two-stage inquiry—(1) determine a “fit and proportionate sentence”; (2) ask whether the mandatory minimum is “grossly disproportionate” compared to that fit sentence, assessed via “scope and reach of the offence”, “effects of the penalty on the offender”, and “the penalty and its objectives”; may be assessed on the actual offender or a “reasonably foreseeable case”.
BaselineB: Combination of constitutional text and sentencing statutes: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 12; Criminal Code sentencing principles (e.g., ss. 718, 718.1, 718.2(e)); and SCC precedent on s. 12 mandatory minimums (affirmed/developed in R. v. Hills, 2023 SCC 2; building on Smith, Nur, Lloyd, Bissonnette, Boudreault).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 93(1) denominational schools infringement conditions: a provincial education law is invalid if it “prejudicially affect[s] any Right or Privilege with respect to Denominational Schools which any Class of Persons have by Law in the Province at the Union”; applied via the agreed conditions: “(a) there must be a right or privilege affecting a denominational school; (b) enjoyed by a particular class of persons; (c) by law; (d) in effect at the time of the Union; (e) and which is prejudicially affected.”
BaselineA: Constitution Act, 1867, s. 93(1) (and s. 93(2)); baseline also informed by Privy Council jurisprudence cited in the reasons (e.g., City of Winnipeg v. Barrett; Hirsch; Tiny).
CaseB_TestB: Young Offenders Act non-disclosure “link” test: the “nub” is whether the communication “links the identity of the young person with a charge, proceeding or disposition under the Act”; “the interpretive exercise is therefore not directed at some formal classification of documents, but at the nature of the information sought to be disclosed. Where the prohibited link is not made, the ban does not apply.”
BaselineB: Statute: Young Offenders Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. Y-1, especially ss. 38(1), 38(1.1), 38(1.13), 40, 44.1, and 46.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 93(1) denominational schools infringement test: s. 93 protection applies where (a) there is a right or privilege affecting a denominational school, (b) enjoyed by a particular class of persons, (c) by law, (d) in effect at the time of the Union, and (e) which is 'prejudicially affected' (applied to proportional grants and referendum/voter-eligibility limits on taxation).
BaselineA: Constitution Act, 1867, s. 93(1) (and s. 93(2)); baseline articulation of the conditions for s. 93 protection as accepted from prior jurisprudence and the trial judge; historical 'by law at the Union' rights identified from C.S.L.C. 1861, c. 15 (ss. 24(1), 55(2), 57(3), 73, 74, 131) and Privy Council/SCC authorities cited (e.g., Barrett; Hirsch; Tiny; Ottawa Separate Schools Trustees).
CaseB_TestB: Federal maritime law (navigation and shipping) scope test for tort claims: the court must examine the 'factual context' and ask whether the allegedly negligent act is 'so integrally connected to maritime matters' / 'integrally connected to the act of navigating the pleasure craft on Canadian waterways' that it is a 'practical necessity' for Parliament to have jurisdiction; 'mere involvement of a pleasure craft' is insufficient.
BaselineB: Common law constitutional/maritime-law framework from ITO—International Terminal Operators Ltd. v. Miida Electronics Inc. ("so integrally connected to maritime matters"), Whitbread v. Walley (practical necessity for uniform law for pleasure craft navigation), and Ordon Estate v. Grail (examine factual context), applied alongside Constitution Act, 1867 ss. 91(10) and 92(13).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Certiorari review of a preliminary inquiry committal: a committal is a reviewable jurisdictional error where there is “no evidence” on an essential element (since “no evidence” can never be “sufficient evidence” under Criminal Code s. 475); reviewing court must independently assess whether there was “any evidence at all” on each essential element
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 475) interpreted through prior certiorari/jurisdiction jurisprudence (Patterson v. The Queen; Martin v. The Queen; Forsythe v. The Queen; Nat Bell Liquors)
CaseB_TestB: Criteria for a compensatory allowance under art. 559 C.C.Q.: claimant must establish (1) contribution, (2) enrichment of spouse’s patrimony, (3) causal link/correlation, and (4) proportion; elements “must be evaluated with great flexibility”; enrichment must “subsist” and be evaluated “at the time of the divorce”
BaselineB: Statute (Civil Code of Quebec, art. 559) informed by unjust enrichment principles (e.g., Cie Immobilière Viger Ltée v. Lauréat Giguère Inc.) and interaction with Bankruptcy Act (R.S.C. 1970, c. B-3, ss. 2, 148)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Estoppel by representation (including by silence): requires a representation (words/conduct, or silence/inaction only where there is a legal duty to speak) that induces detrimental reliance; absent these conditions, estoppel has no application
BaselineA: Common law (estoppel by representation), as summarized from Spencer Bower & Turner and cases such as Greenwood v. Martins Bank, Ltd.
CaseB_TestB: Rebutting the Criminal Code s. 212(3) presumption: jury considers all the evidence about cohabitation and financial arrangements; no need to identify a single “particular and severable” item as “evidence to the contrary”
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 212(3))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Municipal council exceeds jurisdiction (ultra vires) where it does by resolution what enabling legislation requires be done by by-law (including impermissible self-redelegation of a by-law power); such measures are void and can be attacked by direct action in nullity under art. 33 C.C.P.
BaselineA: Statute (Cities and Towns Act, R.S.Q. 1941, c. 233, art. 526 as amended for Dorval; Cities and Towns Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 193, including ss. 385 and 395; Code of Civil Procedure, art. 33).
CaseB_TestB: Causation in negligent blood-donor screening: apply the 'materially contributed' test (not a rebuttable presumption from Hollis and not strict 'but-for' necessity); negligence is a cause if it 'materially contributed' to the injury (i.e., is more than de minimis).
BaselineB: Common law causation in negligence (but-for as general test; material contribution as alternative), drawing on Snell v. Farrell and Athey v. Leonati; Hollis v. Dow Corning distinguished.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 13 self-incrimination bar on using an accused’s prior testimony at a retrial: s. 13 applies when the Crown attempts to use prior testimony to incriminate; incrimination assessed in the second proceeding; a retrial is “any other proceedings”
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 13 (interpreted in light of ss. 11(c) and 11(d)); pre-Charter common law admissibility approach in R. v. Brown (No. 2) (1963) distinguished
CaseB_TestB: Reformed rule for substantive admissibility of a non-accused witness’s prior inconsistent statement: admissible for truth if (threshold) it would have been admissible as the witness’s sole testimony, and (principled hearsay) necessity + reliability shown—typically via (1) oath/affirmation/solemn declaration plus explicit warning, (2) videotaped in entirety, and (3) full opportunity to cross-examine at trial; with possible substitutes; plus voir dire scrutiny including voluntariness/administration-of-justice concerns
BaselineB: Combination: statutory procedure (Canada Evidence Act, s. 9) plus common law hearsay/prior-inconsistent-statement doctrine (the “orthodox rule” from Deacon v. The King) modified through the principled hearsay approach (R. v. Khan; R. v. Smith)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: When a trial judge’s acquittal can be appealed by the Crown as an “error of law alone” on the basis of “no evidence”/“total absence of a foundation” for a finding of fact: only where the law shifts the burden of proof to the accused; otherwise, due to the presumption of innocence, there is always some evidence on which to acquit (so any mistake is factual, not legal).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 605(1)(a)) interpreted in light of SCC jurisprudence on Crown appeals from acquittals (Lampard v. The Queen; Sunbeam Corporation (Canada) Ltd. v. The Queen; discussion of Wild v. The Queen and Lemire).
CaseB_TestB: Criteria for interim relief (stay/interim release) under Supreme Court Act s. 65.1: apply the RJR–MacDonald test—(1) serious question, (2) irreparable harm, and (3) balance of convenience.
BaselineB: Statute (Supreme Court Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. S-26, s. 65.1) applying the common-law/interlocutory relief framework reaffirmed in RJR–MacDonald Inc. v. Canada (Attorney General).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: When a trial judge’s factual finding (esp. reasonable doubt) can be treated as an error of law permitting a Crown appeal from acquittal: only where there is a “total absence of a foundation” and, for acquittals, this occurs only if the law shifts the burden of proof to the accused on that fact
BaselineA: Combination: statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 605(1)(a)) plus SCC common-law/jurisprudential principles on law vs fact (Lampard v. The Queen; Sunbeam Corporation (Canada) Ltd. v. The Queen; discussion of Wild v. The Queen and rejection of Lemire’s broader approach)
CaseB_TestB: Ontario anti-SLAPP dismissal framework under CJA s. 137.1: (1) moving party shows on balance of probabilities the proceeding “arises from” its “expression” that “relates to a matter of public interest” (s. 137.1(3)); then (2) responding party must show “grounds to believe” substantial merit and no valid defence (s. 137.1(4)(a)) and that harm/public-interest in continuing outweighs public-interest in protecting expression (s. 137.1(4)(b))
BaselineB: Statute: Courts of Justice Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.43, s. 137.1 (especially ss. 137.1(3) and (4))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Landry/Eccles warrantless arrest-in-dwelling entry test: arrest on private premises without warrant is lawful only if (1) offence is indictable; (2) suspect committed it or officer has "reasonable and probable grounds" to believe suspect "has committed or is about to commit" it; (3) "reasonable and probable grounds" to believe suspect is within; and (4) "proper announcement" before entry (notice of presence, authority, and purpose).
BaselineA: Combination: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 450(1)(a) (arrest without warrant for indictable offence) plus common law limits/conditions from Eccles v. Bourque, [1975] 2 S.C.R. 739 (itself traced to Semayne’s Case (1604)).
CaseB_TestB: Turpin s. 15 discrimination framework (as applied): (1) show denial of an equality right (e.g., equality before the law) via differential treatment; then (2) show the distinction is "discriminatory"—i.e., "based on grounds relating to personal characteristics" and, in the larger social/political/legal context, imposes burdens or withholds benefits from a disadvantaged group (enumerated or analogous grounds approach).
BaselineB: Combination: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 15(1), interpreted through Andrews v. Law Society of British Columbia, [1989] 1 S.C.R. 143 (definition/approach to discrimination) and related equality jurisprudence (e.g., Drybones under the Bill of Rights for minimal content of “equality before the law”).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Amending an indictment to cure a variance between the particular alleged and the evidence: amendment should be made unless the accused was misled or prejudiced (and any prejudice cannot be cured)
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 529(4)-(5); plus appellate amendment powers in s. 613(1)(b)(i) and s. 613(3))
CaseB_TestB: Ineffective assistance of counsel test: the appellant must show (1) counsel’s acts/omissions constituted incompetence and (2) a miscarriage of justice resulted
BaselineB: Common law (R. v. G.D.B., 2000 SCC 22, at para. 26)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Concurrent liability in tort and contract for professional negligence: a common law duty of care from proximity can coexist with contract, but tort cannot be used to circumvent contractual limits
BaselineA: Common law (duty of care/proximity and negligent misrepresentation principles from Donoghue v. Stevenson; Hedley Byrne; Anns; and SCC discussion of Nunes Diamonds/Smith v. McInnis)
CaseB_TestB: Quebec court must decline jurisdiction in an action in warranty when a valid exclusive choice-of-forum clause applies: art. 3148(2) C.C.Q. prevails over art. 3139, and forum non conveniens (art. 3135) is unavailable unless Quebec jurisdiction is first established
BaselineB: Statute (Civil Code of Québec, arts. 3148 para. 2, 3139, and 3135)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Scope of Quebec Construction Industry Labour Relations Act/Decree: coverage turns on the nature of the work ("construction" vs excluded "maintenance and repair"), not the status of the employer/employee; and no "total wage" set-off—Decree conditions must be paid as specified
BaselineA: Statute and regulation/decree: Construction Industry Labour Relations Act, S.Q. 1968, c. 45 (esp. ss. 1(e), 1(i), 1(j), 1(r), 2(2), 20; also s. 1(p) definition of "wage") and Decree respecting the construction industry (esp. ss. 3.01, 3.02, 18.06, 32.03)
CaseB_TestB: Charter remedy for unconstitutional mandatory minimum sentence: if a mandatory minimum produces a s. 12 breach, the proper remedy is a s. 52 declaration that the law is of no force or effect (no stand-alone s. 24(1) constitutional exemption); s. 12 breach assessed by "grossly disproportionate" punishment
BaselineB: Combination of constitutional text and common law: Charter ss. 12 and 24(1) and Constitution Act, 1982, s. 52(1), applied through prior SCC doctrine (e.g., "grossly disproportionate" test from R. v. Smith; reasonable hypotheticals from R. v. Goltz; remedial framework from Schachter and related cases)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Parens patriae limit: non-therapeutic sterilization of a mentally incompetent person can never be authorized (court lacks jurisdiction); parens patriae discretion must be exercised only for the protected person’s benefit and with great caution
BaselineA: Common law (parens patriae jurisdiction) as received through provincial superior courts’ inherent/Chancery jurisdiction; discussed via English Chancery/wardship authorities (e.g., Wellesley v. Duke of Beaufort; Re X (a minor); Re D (a minor)) and Canadian recognition (e.g., Beson v. Director of Child Welfare (Nfld.))
CaseB_TestB: Residual management rights: whether a unilaterally imposed workplace policy is a reasonable (and fair) exercise of management rights is assessed by a 'balancing of interests' considering all surrounding circumstances and whether the policy strikes a reasonable balance between employer and employee interests
BaselineB: Common law / labour-arbitration doctrine incorporated through collective agreement interpretation (KVP test; endorsed in Irving Pulp & Paper) plus collective agreement clauses requiring the employer to act 'reasonably, fairly and in good faith' (cl. 5.02) and reserving residual management rights (cl. 5.01)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Kienapple (rule against multiple convictions) as clarified in Prince: applies only where there is (1) a sufficient factual nexus (usually: “Does the same act of the accused ground each of the charges?”) and (2) a sufficient legal nexus such that “there is no additional and distinguishing element that goes to guilt” in the offence sought to be barred; plus guidance on when elements are not “distinct” (particularization; alternative methods to prove a single delict; evidentiary proxy) and that for personal violence it is inapplicable for different victims.
BaselineA: Common law Kienapple principle (rule against multiple convictions) from Kienapple v. The Queen, [1975] 1 S.C.R. 729, as developed in cases like Côté v. The Queen, [1975] 1 S.C.R. 303 and Krug v. The Queen, [1985] 2 S.C.R. 255; applied in the Criminal Code context (e.g., ss. 205(5)(a), 206(2), 11, 589).
CaseB_TestB: “Services … to the public” under Yukon Human Rights Act s. 8(a): two-part analysis—(1) determine what constitutes the “service” on the facts; (2) determine whether the service creates a “public relationship” between provider and user (with “public” defined relationally), assessed contextually using non-determinative criteria including “selectivity”, “diversity”, “involvement of non-members”, “commercial nature”, “intimate nature”, and “purpose” of offering the service.
BaselineB: Statutory interpretation of Yukon Human Rights Act, R.S.Y. 1986 (Supp.), c. 11, s. 8(a) (and related context in ss. 6, 11, 10(1)), guided by SCC’s prior approach in University of British Columbia v. Berg, [1993] 2 S.C.R. 353.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Ensite test for whether property is "used or held ... in the course of carrying on a business" (ITA s. 129(4)): property must be "truly employed and risked" in the business; the inquiry is "whether the property was used to fulfil a requirement which had to be met in order to do business"; and the threshold is met when withdrawal would "have a decidedly destabilizing effect on the corporate operations themselves".
BaselineA: Statute — Income Tax Act, especially s. 129(4)(a)(ii) (exclusion for "a property used or held ... in the course of carrying on a business"), applied within the dividend refund/foreign investment income scheme in ss. 129(1), 129(3), 129(4).
CaseB_TestB: Admissibility of prior consistent statements to support credibility (and scope of re-examination): prior out-of-court statements are generally excluded as self-serving, but "may be admitted in support of the credibility of a witness" where the witness is challenged as a "recent fabrication or contrivance"; and re-examination is confined to "matters arising from the cross-examination" (no new facts unless arising from cross).
BaselineB: Common law evidence principles on prior consistent statements and re-examination, as described with reference to R. v. Béland and R. v. Simpson (and general rule against repeating one’s own prior statements).
JudgeB: Cory J. (for Sopinka, Cory, Iacobucci and Major JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Public interest immunity for Cabinet documents: court (not Crown) decides; generally inspect and then balance the public interest in confidentiality against the public interest in the administration of justice (with variables like level/nature of policy, timing, and importance/need in the litigation).
BaselineA: Common law (public interest immunity/Crown privilege doctrine), relying particularly on Smallwood v. Sparling, [1982] 2 S.C.R. 686 (and the general approach in cases like R. v. Snider, [1954] S.C.R. 479; Gagnon v. Commission des valeurs mobilières du Québec, [1965] S.C.R. 73; and Commonwealth authorities discussed).
CaseB_TestB: Review of pre-Lifchus jury charge: whether the charge, read as a whole, was in “substantial compliance” with Lifchus/W.(D.) principles—i.e., whether it gives rise to a “reasonable likelihood that the jury misapprehended” the correct standard of proof and how to deal with conflicting evidence.
BaselineB: Common law (jury-instruction standards) from R. v. Lifchus, [1997] 3 S.C.R. 320; R. v. W. (D.), [1991] 1 S.C.R. 742; and the “substantial compliance” approach in R. v. Starr, 2000 SCC 40.
JudgeB: Major J. (for Major, Binnie, Arbour and LeBel JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 7 limit on extradition: courts may intervene in surrender decisions only where, in the particular circumstances, surrender would violate the principles of fundamental justice—intervention must be exercised "with caution" and "limited to cases of real substance" (generally after the executive surrender order).
BaselineA: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7 ("principles of fundamental justice") applied to extradition; extradition framework under the Extradition Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-21 and the Canada–U.S. Extradition Treaty (1971).
CaseB_TestB: Crown appeal jurisdiction test: on a Crown appeal under Criminal Code s. 605(1)(a), a Court of Appeal may interfere with an acquittal only if the trial court erred "on a question of law alone" (per Schuldt v. The Queen).
BaselineB: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 605(1)(a), as applied in Schuldt v. The Queen, [1985] 2 S.C.R. 592.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 7 limit on extradition: courts may intervene only where surrender would, in the particular circumstances, violate the principles of fundamental justice; intervention must be exercised with caution and be limited to "cases of real substance" (generally after the executive surrender decision).
BaselineA: Statute/Constitution: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7 (and context of extradition under Extradition Act and treaty-based executive surrender).
CaseB_TestB: Income Tax Act s. 20(1)(c)(i) purpose test for interest deductibility: "whether, considering all the circumstances, the taxpayer had a reasonable expectation of income at the time the investment was made" (income = taxable income, not net income; ancillary income-earning purpose suffices absent sham/window dressing).
BaselineB: Statute: Income Tax Act, s. 20(1)(c)(i) (interpreting "used for the purpose of earning income").
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Injurious affection where no land is taken: claimant must satisfy the four Loiselle conditions, including that the construction-caused damage would have been actionable at common law (nuisance) but for statutory authority; loss of prospect/amenities and reasonable highway construction are not actionable nuisances
BaselineA: Statute (Expropriations Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 154, ss. 1(e)(ii), 21) incorporating common-law actionability; four-part test from The Queen v. Loiselle, [1962] S.C.R. 624 at 627
CaseB_TestB: Adequacy of jury instructions on alternative routes to murder liability: jury may convict if satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt the accused "actively participated"/"acted in concert" in the killing; trial judge must correct an erroneous "actual shooter" instruction and may frame liability compendiously where that captures the realistic issues
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, especially s. 21 (parties), with murder provisions ss. 229, 231(5)); informed by prior SCC approach to party liability (e.g., R. v. Thatcher, [1987] 1 S.C.R. 652, as discussed in the reasons)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: s. 10(b) right to counsel: once police promptly advise of the right, no further (correlative) duties arise unless the detainee indicates a desire to exercise it; absent proof of circumstances showing non-understanding, the accused bears the onus to show he asked for counsel and was denied or denied an opportunity to ask
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 10(b) (and remedy context under s. 24(2)); applied approach from R. v. Anderson (Ont. C.A.) as adopted by the SCC
CaseB_TestB: Disgorgement/accounting for employee’s secret profits: where an employee acts in a representative capacity and abuses entrusted authority/funds or receives secret commissions, the employee must account for and turn over profits to the employer (drawing on C.C.L.C. arts. 411 and 1713 and the broader good faith/loyalty principle that no one should profit from wrongdoing)
BaselineB: Statute/civil code: Civil Code of Lower Canada, arts. 411 (possessor in bad faith) and 1713 (mandatary must render account and deliver/pay over what received under authority of mandate), extended by the Court to analogous employment/representative relationships grounded in contractual good faith/loyalty
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Wigglesworth test for when Charter s. 11 applies: a matter falls within s. 11 either (1) because "by its very nature it is a criminal proceeding" (public nature/public order and welfare) or (2) because conviction may lead to a "true penal consequence"; where they conflict, the "by nature" test "must give way" to the "true penal consequence" test
BaselineA: Constitution (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 11; interpretive approach from R. v. Big M Drug Mart Ltd.)
CaseB_TestB: Functional approach to reviewing jury charges: an appellate court asks whether, looking at the charge "as a whole", the jury was left with a "sufficient understanding of the facts as they relate to the relevant issues"; juries must be "properly -- not perfectly -- instructed"
BaselineB: Common law (jury-charge review principles from cases such as Azoulay v. The Queen; Cluett v. The Queen; John v. The Queen)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: s. 577(1) Criminal Code “whole of the trial” test: the accused must be present (able to hear) for jury-selection proceedings that engage juror impartiality; private judge–juror screening for partiality after arraignment/plea breaches s. 577 and vitiates the trial (not curable by s. 613(1)(b)(iii))
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 577(1); also discussed: ss. 569(2), 600, 598-599, 613(1)(b)(iii)) interpreted in light of SCC/CA authorities (e.g., Basarabas and Spek v. The Queen; Vézina and Côté v. The Queen; Hertrich; Meunier)
CaseB_TestB: Common-law test for substituting a conviction on a Crown appeal from acquittal: appellate court may enter guilt (instead of new trial) only if Crown shows (1) with correct law the verdict would not have been the same, (2) the accused should have been found guilty but for the error of law, and (3) all findings necessary for guilt were made explicitly/implicitly or are not in issue
BaselineB: Common law (as stated in Vézeau v. The Queen; applied with reference to Courville v. The Queen) alongside Criminal Code, s. 613(4)(b)(ii) remedial power
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: When a trial judge quashes a voidable charge under Criminal Code s. 529, the quashing is tantamount to an acquittal (supporting autrefois acquit) if and only if the required amendment cannot be made without injustice/irreparable prejudice; otherwise the judge should amend and not quash. Key formulation: the judge must not quash unless he concludes the proposed amendment cannot 'be made without injustice being done'; if amendment 'cannot be made without causing irreparable prejudice', the quashing 'is ... tantamount to an acquittal'.
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, especially ss. 529(1),(3)-(6) (amend/quash), and interaction with ss. 535 and 537 on autrefois acquit/identity).
JudgeA: Lamer J. (for McIntyre, Lamer, Le Dain and La Forest JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Framework to define the scope of an acquired right / legal non-conforming use and decide whether a changed use remains protected: (1) characterize the purpose of the pre-existing use; (2) mere intensification is protected unless it becomes a different use; (3) added activities beyond prior ones may be 'too remote' (then no need to assess neighbourhood effects); (4) if added/altered activities are within the original purpose, balance landowner vs community considering nature of prior use, remoteness, and new/aggravated neighbourhood effects; (5) neighbourhood effects should be proven by evidence unless obvious; (6) definition should be neither too general nor too narrow; (7) criteria aim to ground the inevitably 'subjective judgment' in objective facts.
BaselineB: Combination: statute (Act Respecting Land Use Planning and Development, R.S.Q., c. A-19.1, especially s. 113(18) and s. 227; plus municipal zoning by-law) and common law principles on legal non-conforming uses (e.g., Central Jewish Institute v. City of Toronto, [1948] S.C.R. 101, followed).
JudgeB: Binnie J. (for McLachlin C.J. and Major, Binnie and Arbour JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Workmen’s privilege against an owner’s immovable where work is contracted through a lessee: the lessee is only a “builder/contractor” for arts. 2013e/2013f C.C.L.C. if the owner-lessee agreement is a true construction contract that includes an owner-to-builder “claim” (undertaking by owner to pay a construction contract price) from which the owner can retain funds; absent such a claim/price, no privilege lies against the owner’s immovable
BaselineA: Statute (Civil Code of Lower Canada, arts. 2013e and 2013f (and related arts. 984 et seq., 1060))
CaseB_TestB: Mental distress damages for breach of contract (Hadley v. Baxendale application): plaintiff must show (1) an object of the contract was to secure a psychological benefit so that mental distress on breach was within the parties’ reasonable contemplation at contract formation; and (2) the degree of mental suffering caused by the breach is sufficient to warrant compensation
BaselineB: Common law (Hadley v. Baxendale; as applied/clarified via Vorvis v. I.C.B.C.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Unequal division of marital property under Marital Property Act s. 7(f): court may depart from equal division where equal division would be inequitable; in particular, where property was acquired "exclusively or almost wholly" through one spouse’s efforts and the other made "no, or a negligible" contribution to child care/household management/financial provision, this can justify exercising discretion under s. 7(f).
BaselineA: Statute: New Brunswick Marital Property Act, S.N.B. 1980, c. M-1.1, especially ss. 2, 3(1) (equal division principle) and s. 7 (discretion to depart where equal division would be inequitable), including s. 7(f) ("any other circumstances... rendering it inequitable").
CaseB_TestB: Interjurisdictional immunity (constitutional inapplicability) for a federal service: otherwise-applicable provincial law is inapplicable if it bears on what makes the matter specifically federal; for a federal service, this occurs where the provincial law "touches on a vital or essential aspect of its establishment, management or operation" (here, the provincial transport permit system was constitutionally inapplicable to the federal sightseeing service).
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine (interjurisdictional immunity) as articulated in SCC jurisprudence cited in the reasons, especially Bell Canada v. Quebec (CSST), Construction Montcalm Inc. v. Minimum Wage Commission, and Clark v. Canadian National Railway Co.; applied to provincial Transport Act/Regulation permit scheme.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “financing” in Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971 s. 44(2)(a): claimant is “financing” a labour dispute only where there is “active and voluntary involvement” and a “meaningful connection between the payment and the dispute” (mandatory union dues alone are insufficient).
BaselineA: Statute: Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, S.C. 1970-71-72, c. 48, s. 44(2)(a) (exception to disentitlement where claimant proves he is not “participating in or financing or directly interested in” the labour dispute).
CaseB_TestB: Enforceability/scope of a waiver (exclusion) clause for negligence in a race entry form: in the “context in which it was signed”, the clause is effective where the parties “clearly had a release in mind” and the accident/negligence is within what was reasonably contemplated; clause not avoided as “unfair” or “unreasonable” on these facts.
BaselineB: Common law contract interpretation/enforceability of exclusion/waiver clauses (including arguments framed in terms of fundamental breach, unconscionability, and public policy).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “financing” in Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971 s. 44(2)(a): claimant is “financing” a labour dispute only where there is “active and voluntary involvement” and a “meaningful connection between the payment and the dispute” (mandatory union dues diverted to an international strike fund are not enough).
BaselineA: Statute: Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, S.C. 1970-71-72, c. 48, s. 44(2)(a) (disentitlement exception requiring claimant to prove he is not “participating in or financing or directly interested in” the labour dispute).
CaseB_TestB: Extradition surrender review: whether extraditing the person sought would be contrary to s. 7 fundamental justice so as to “shock the conscience” or otherwise be “unjust or oppressive” under Extradition Act s. 44(1); this requires the Minister to engage in a “balancing exercise”, with refusal only where the “particular treatment” in the requesting state sufficiently violates fundamental justice.
BaselineB: Statute (informed by Charter values and prior SCC extradition jurisprudence): Extradition Act, S.C. 1999, c. 18, s. 44(1) (“unjust or oppressive”); Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7 (“principles of fundamental justice”), as applied through United States v. Burns and Lake v. Canada (Minister of Justice).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 10 “detention” test (Therens criteria): detention occurs when the state “assumes control over the movement of a person by a demand or direction which may have significant legal consequence” and the “compulsion or coercion” arises from “criminal liability for refusal” or a “reasonable belief” there is no choice; applied to a s. 234.1(1) roadside breath demand
BaselineA: Common law/Charter interpretation baseline from R. v. Therens (applied to Charter s. 10(b) detention) plus statutory context of Criminal Code s. 234.1(1)-(2) (roadside demand and offence for refusal)
CaseB_TestB: Criminal Code s. 150.1(4) “all reasonable steps” (mistake of age) framework: once an “air of reality” exists, Crown must prove beyond a reasonable doubt either (1) no honest belief complainant was at least 16, or (2) failure to take “all reasonable steps”; the reasonable-steps inquiry is “highly contextual, fact-specific” and “the more reasonable an accused’s perception of the complainant’s age, the fewer steps reasonably required”
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code s. 150.1(4) (and related scheme s. 150.1(1), s. 150.1(2.1)); SCC clarifies how the statutory “all reasonable steps” requirement operates and how evidence timing/relevance relates to that inquiry
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Extradition specialty/immunity duration: an undertaking not to prosecute for pre-surrender offences does not confer perpetual immunity; it ends once the extraditee has been "restored or has had an opportunity of returning" (i.e., a reasonable opportunity to return) and is no longer in Canada by reason of the surrender but by choice
BaselineA: Statute (Extradition Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-21, s. 33) interpreted in light of the extradition arrangement/undertaking and international law interpretive principles (Vienna Convention, art. 31; specialty principle discussed via United States v. Rauscher)
CaseB_TestB: Criminal appeal scope/curative proviso: where an appeal as of right is properly grounded on a dissent on a question of law, the Crown need not seek leave to also appeal the court of appeal’s refusal to apply the s. 686(1)(b)(iii) proviso because "error of law" and the proviso are "always intertwined" and the SCC will decide whether any found error is "so serious" as to require setting aside the verdict or can be saved
BaselineB: Common law/procedural doctrine from R. v. Keegstra (applied) plus Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(b)(iii)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of "anything" in Criminal Code s. 283(1): to be the object of theft, the thing must (1) be property capable of a proprietary right and (2) be capable of being taken/converted in a way that results in deprivation; confidential information per se fails (and thus cannot be stolen)
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 283(1) (theft definition); also discussed in relation to s. 338(1) (fraud))
CaseB_TestB: Interpretation of "assets" in MVHC rent-subsidy Assistance Application: "assets" means property/interests that can actually be used to discharge debts/liabilities (including rent); a Henson trust interest is a "mere hope" and not an asset for eligibility-to-be-considered
BaselineB: Common law (contractual interpretation framework from Sattva Capital Corp. v. Creston Moly Corp.; ordinary and grammatical meaning read in light of surrounding circumstances/factual matrix) applied to the Tenancy Agreement/Assistance Application documents
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 7 analysis for compelled fingerprinting after charge: (1) deprivation of life/liberty/security; (2) whether deprivation accords with principles of fundamental justice — here, fingerprinting is constitutional where the process does not "unduly invade the rights of the accused" and is not arbitrary, given "reasonable and probable grounds" for the indictable charge and the accepted role of police discretion
BaselineA: Combination: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7 (two-step framework) applied to statutory fingerprinting scheme in Identification of Criminals Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-1, s. 2 and Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 453.3(3), 455.5(5)
CaseB_TestB: Sheppard/Braich test for appellate intervention based on insufficient reasons: two stages — (1) "are the reasons inadequate"; (2) "if so, do they prevent appellate review" (i.e., are they not "sufficiently amenable to appellate review" / do they create an "impediment to appellate review")
BaselineB: Common law (as articulated in R. v. Sheppard, 2002 SCC 26 and R. v. Braich, 2002 SCC 27) governing adequacy of trial reasons for purposes of appellate review
JudgeB: Bastarache and Abella JJ. (LeBel J. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Detention at the border for s. 10(b): a traveller is detained when, taken out of the normal course, they are compelled to submit to a strip search (state assumes control by a demand/direction with significant legal consequences), triggering the right to be informed of and to retain and instruct counsel without delay
BaselineA: Combination of constitutional text (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 10(b)) and common law definition of “detention” from R. v. Therens, [1985] 1 S.C.R. 613 (as reaffirmed in R. v. Hufsky and R. v. Thomsen)
JudgeA: Dickson C.J. (for Dickson C.J. and Beetz, Lamer and La Forest JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Section 11(b) unreasonable delay framework (Morin): a contextual balancing using four factors—(1) length of delay, (2) waiver, (3) reasons for delay (including inherent requirements, actions of accused, actions of Crown, institutional limits, other), and (4) prejudice—with suggested institutional-delay guidelines (8–10 months in Provincial Court; 6–8 months post-committal) that are not fixed ceilings and must yield to other factors
BaselineB: Combination of constitutional text (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 11(b) and s. 24(1)) and common law framework developed in Mills v. The Queen, R. v. Rahey, R. v. Conway, R. v. Smith, and R. v. Askov (all cited in Morin)
JudgeB: Sopinka J. (for La Forest, Sopinka, Stevenson and Iacobucci JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Voluntary intoxication and mens rea for general-intent offences (Leary rule preserved): intoxication evidence only relevant if it raises doubt about voluntariness/intent at an extreme level; Crown may prove mens rea by inference from actus reus or, in rare extreme cases, by proving voluntary self-induced intoxication as blameworthy state
BaselineA: Common law (intoxication defence / general vs specific intent), applied to Criminal Code offence s. 246.2(c) (sexual assault causing bodily harm)
CaseB_TestB: Appellate intervention on Crown appeal from acquittal: (1) no interference with trial judge’s inferences of fact merely because appellate court would draw different inferences; but (2) acquittal may be set aside for error of law where trial judge failed to direct his mind to an issue requiring determination to reach the verdict
BaselineB: Common law appellate review principles (Crown appeals from acquittal), relying on Schuldt v. The Queen; applied in context of Criminal Code appeal provisions and proceeds-of-crime counts under Narcotic Control Act
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Appellate intervention in a trial judge’s discretionary reapportionment of matrimonial property: intervene only if the trial judge “misdirects himself” or the decision is “so clearly wrong as to amount to an injustice” (s. 51 Family Relations Act context).
BaselineA: Combination: statute (Family Relations Act, R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 121, ss. 43 and 51) plus common-law appellate deference standard (as applied in Harper v. Harper; Re Hull Estate).
CaseB_TestB: Duty to comment on prejudicial Crown jury-address remarks and curative proviso: where remarks are “prejudicial to a degree sufficient to impose a legal duty on the trial judge to comment”, failure to do so is an error of law; then consider whether s. 686(1)(b)(iii) applies (no substantial wrong/miscarriage of justice).
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(b)(iii)) plus common-law principles on fair jury trials and improper jury addresses (as reflected through adoption of Ayles J.A.’s formulation).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Wigmore/Slavutych four-part test for recognizing a case-by-case (qualified) privilege against compelled disclosure of confidential communications: (1) communication originates in confidence; (2) confidentiality essential to the relationship; (3) relationship one the community ought to foster; (4) injury from disclosure outweighs benefit to litigation
BaselineA: Common law (Wigmore criteria as discussed by the SCC in Slavutych v. Baker, [1976] 1 S.C.R. 254)
CaseB_TestB: Reasonableness review of Crown corporations’ discretionary PILT calculations: discretion exists to choose the “effective rate”, but it must be exercised within the statutory/regulatory framework—rates must be calculated “as if” the federal property were taxable private property and cannot be based on a “fictitious tax system” (must use the municipality’s actual existing tax system)
BaselineB: Statute and regulation (Payments in Lieu of Taxes Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. M-13, ss. 2 “effective rate”, 2.1, 4(1), 15, sch. II item 10; Crown Corporation Payments Regulations, SOR/81-1030, ss. 2, 7(1))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Patent disclosure/sufficiency under Patent Act s. 36(1): applicant must disclose everything essential for the invention to function properly; completeness requires two conditions — (1) “describe the invention and define the way it is produced or built” and (2) “define the nature of the invention and describe how it is put into operation”; disclosure must enable a skilled person “to produce it using only the instructions contained in the disclosure”; deposit of seed “by itself does not comply” with s. 36(1).
BaselineA: Statute: Patent Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. P-4, s. 36(1) (as interpreted with prior patent-law disclosure principles cited in Minerals Separation North American Corp. v. Noranda Mines Ltd.; Burton Parsons Chemicals Inc. v. Hewlett-Packard (Canada) Ltd.; Monsanto Co. v. Commissioner of Patents; Consolboard Inc. v. MacMillan Bloedel (Saskatchewan) Ltd.).
CaseB_TestB: Standard of review for labour-arbitration awards applying common law/equitable doctrines: apply Dunsmuir categories—correctness only for constitutional issues, “general law” questions of central importance outside expertise, true jurisdiction/vires, or competing-tribunal line-drawing; otherwise reasonableness. Here, an arbitrator’s estoppel remedy does not fall in a correctness category; contextual factors (including LRA privative clause, tribunal purpose, nature of question, expertise) confirm reasonableness.
BaselineB: Common law administrative law standard-of-review framework from Dunsmuir v. New Brunswick (applied via Smith v. Alliance Pipeline Ltd.), plus statutory context: Labour Relations Act, R.S.M. 1987, c. L10, ss. 121 and 128(2).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 96 ‘Residential Tenancies’ three-stage test as refined in Sobeys: (1) historical inquiry with narrow characterization of the power (guided by the nature of the dispute, not the remedy) and a clarified concurrency gloss (shared jurisdiction validates only if inferior-court involvement was ‘broadly co-extensive’); (2) whether the function is judicial (distinguishing Director vs Tribunal); (3) institutional context—whether the judicial power is ‘necessarily incidental’ to a broader regulatory scheme/policy goal
BaselineA: Common law constitutional doctrine under Constitution Act, 1867, s. 96, applying the framework from Re Residential Tenancies Act, 1979, [1981] 1 S.C.R. 714 (and related s. 96 jurisprudence such as Grondin, Tomko, John East)
CaseB_TestB: Downtown Eastside public interest standing framework as applied/clarified: court exercises discretion by cumulatively weighing three factors—(i) serious justiciable issue; (ii) genuine interest; (iii) reasonable and effective means—without giving ‘particular weight’ to legality/access to justice; no requirement of a directly affected co-plaintiff if a ‘sufficiently concrete and well-developed factual setting’ will be forthcoming, and standing may be revisited only on a material change raising serious doubt
BaselineB: Common law test from Canada (Attorney General) v. Downtown Eastside Sex Workers United Against Violence Society, 2012 SCC 45 (public interest standing doctrine)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Bankruptcy Act s. 47(a) vs s. 107(1)(j): a provincial deemed tax “trust” gives the Crown super-priority only if the tax money is still identifiable/traceable as trust property under general trust law; if commingled and untraceable, it is merely a Crown claim ranked under s. 107(1)(j). Key formulation: “the answer ... depends on the facts of the particular case. If the money collected for tax is identifiable or traceable ... [s. 47(a)] ... If ... cannot be traced, there is no ‘property held ... in trust’ ... and s. 107(1)(j) applies.”
BaselineA: Statute: Bankruptcy Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. B-3, ss. 47(a) (“property held ... in trust”) and 107(1)(j) (Crown claims); plus provincial Social Service Tax Act, R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 388, s. 18 (deemed trust/lien). Interpreted through general principles of trust law (identifiability/traceability).
CaseB_TestB: Section 23 “where numbers warrant” / management-and-control framework: relevant numbers are “somewhere between the known demand and the total number of persons who could potentially take advantage of the service”; the service level requires assessing “appropriate services, in pedagogical terms” and “costs”; where a minority-language board exists, defining the relevant area and choosing location of classes/facilities falls within the minority’s management and control, and the Minister’s approval power is limited to verifying compliance with provincial/constitutional requirements (no substitution of his own criteria).
BaselineB: Constitution + prior SCC framework: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 23 (especially s. 23(3)); followed/relied on Mahe v. Alberta and Reference re Public Schools Act (Man.) for the “sliding scale” and “numbers warrant” approach; applied alongside PEI School Act and Regulations (e.g., Reg. s. 6.01(f), 6.07, 6.08, 6.11; School Act s. 128(2)).
JudgeB: Major and Bastarache JJ. (for the Court)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Young Offenders Act s. 16 transfer to ordinary court: whether the judge is satisfied, after "weighing and balancing all the relevant considerations" in s. 16(2), that the case "should be transferred"; Crown bears a persuasive burden but it is "not ... a heavy one"
BaselineA: Statute (Young Offenders Act, S.C. 1980-81-82-83, c. 110, s. 16(1), (2) (and related review provisions s. 16(9), (10)))
CaseB_TestB: Damages for repudiation where contract has alternative modes of performance: adopt the mode "least profitable to the plaintiff, and the least burdensome to the defendant"; the test is not what the defendant would likely have done but for repudiation, but what performance the contract allowed (minimum entitlement)
BaselineB: Common law (general principle traced to Cockburn v. Alexander (1848) and explained in Withers v. General Theatre Corp. (1933))
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Canadian maritime law (agency/mandate): whether an agent of an unnamed/partially disclosed principal is personally liable turns on the parties’ intention as shown by the contract’s construction; there is “no prescribed formality for disclosure” and liability “depends on the will of the contracting parties” (e.g., if the agent indicates it is contracting “as agent only”, it is not liable unless the contract otherwise clearly involves personal liability).
BaselineA: Common law (contract/agency) as part of Canadian maritime law under Federal Court Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. F-7, ss. 2 (“Canadian maritime law”) and 22(2)(m) (stevedoring), building on ITO—International Terminal Operators Ltd. v. Miida Electronics Inc., [1986] 1 S.C.R. 752; with comparative reference to Civil Code of Lower Canada arts. 1715-1716 as sources informing Canadian maritime law.
JudgeA: La Forest J. (majority reasons; Wilson, La Forest, Sopinka and Cory JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Statutory immunity/threshold for child-abuse reporting: under Child Welfare Act, s. 38(6), an informant is protected unless the report is made “maliciously or without reasonable cause”; “reasonable cause” is an objective threshold meaning the informant must have “reasonable cause to ask CPS to consider looking into the matter” (not reasonable grounds to believe abuse occurred), and s. 38(1) requires reporting “information” a child “has been, is or may be” in danger.
BaselineB: Statute: Child Welfare Act, R.S.N. 1990, c. C-12, ss. 38(1) and 38(6), interpreted alongside common-law negligence duty analysis (Cooper v. Hobart; Martel Building).
JudgeB: McLachlin C.J. and Binnie J. (for the Court)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Common-law limits on a warrantless “frisk” search incident to a lawful arrest: no reasonable/probable grounds prerequisite, but (1) discretionary (not a duty) and must be assessed case-by-case; (2) must be for a valid criminal-justice objective (e.g., safety, escape prevention, evidence) and not for an improper purpose; (3) must not be abusive—constraint must be proportionate (otherwise the search is “unreasonable and unjustified at common law”).
BaselineA: Common law (search incident to arrest), drawing on authorities discussed in the reasons including R. v. Brezack (1949), R. v. Morrison (1987), and R. v. Miller (1987).
CaseB_TestB: Section 7 (fundamental justice) minimum for warrantless child apprehension: the “emergency” threshold is not required; rather, “where a statute provides that apprehension may occur without prior judicial authorization in situations of serious harm or risk of serious harm to the child, the statute will not necessarily offend the principles of fundamental justice”, and fundamental justice requires a “fair and prompt post-apprehension hearing” as the minimum procedural protection.
BaselineB: Statute interpreted/assessed under Charter s. 7: Child and Family Services Act, S.M. 1985-86, c. 8, ss. 21(1) (warrantless apprehension on reasonable and probable grounds), 17 (definition of child in need of protection), 27(1) and 29(1) (post-apprehension hearing timelines).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal negligence (s. 219/220): whether the accused’s conduct is a “marked departure from the norm” such that “the conclusion that there is a wanton or reckless disregard is to be drawn from the conduct which falls below the standard”; consequences (death) generally “added nothing” unless “so interwoven” with the conduct as to help characterize it
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34 ss. 202(1)-(2), 203; now Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46 ss. 219, 220) as interpreted in R. v. Tutton, [1989] 1 S.C.R. 1392 (marked departure central to objective/subjective approaches)
CaseB_TestB: Standing/jurisdiction before the CITT under the AIT: a complainant must be a “potential supplier” (CITT Act, s. 30.11(1)) on a “designated contract” (CITT Regulations, s. 3(1)); for an AIT ‘door’, the procurement must be “procurement within Canada” (AIT art. 502), which requires the supplier to be a “Canadian supplier” (AIT art. 518: has “a place of business in Canada”)—otherwise no standing
BaselineB: Statute/regulation plus incorporated trade agreement: Canadian International Trade Tribunal Act ss. 30.1, 30.11(1); Canadian International Trade Tribunal Procurement Inquiry Regulations ss. 3(1), 7(1), 11; interpretation of Agreement on Internal Trade arts. 501, 502, 518 (and scope arts. 100-101)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 8 reasonableness of compelled document production in a regulatory tax audit: s. 231(3) demand is a 'seizure' but is 'reasonable' given the regulatory scheme, low privacy expectation, and need for random monitoring (Hunter criteria not strictly applicable outside criminal/quasi-criminal context).
BaselineA: Combination: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 8 (unreasonable search or seizure) applied to Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1952, c. 148, ss. 231(3), 238(2) (and privacy safeguard in s. 241), with common-law Charter framework from Hunter v. Southam Inc. and related s. 8 jurisprudence (incl. R. v. Simmons).
CaseB_TestB: Public interest standing test (purposive, flexible): weigh three interrelated factors—(1) serious justiciable issue; (2) real stake/genuine interest/engagement; (3) whether the proposed suit is, 'in all of the circumstances', a 'reasonable and effective means' to bring the issue to court (not a strict 'no other way' requirement).
BaselineB: Common law standing doctrine from Minister of Justice of Canada v. Borowski, Finlay v. Canada (Minister of Finance), and Canadian Council of Churches v. Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration) (as discussed/applied).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Insurer’s duty to defend is determined by the pleadings: the duty arises only where the claim seeks “damages which are or may be payable under the terms of this Policy”; i.e., the pleadings must raise at least a possibility of coverage, and there is no duty to defend allegations “clearly beyond the scope of the policy”.
BaselineA: Contract (insurance policy) interpreted using common-law insurance-contract construction principles; key policy wording: Coverage D (defence clause) requiring defence of suits “seeking damages which are or may be payable under the terms of this Policy”.
CaseB_TestB: “Air of reality” threshold for leaving the defence of honest but mistaken belief in consent to the jury under Criminal Code s. 265(4): a defence is not left to the jury unless there is “sufficient evidence” such that “a reasonable jury properly instructed could acquit”; more than a “mere assertion” is required, but no independent evidence is required.
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 265(4)) interpreted as codifying the common-law ‘air of reality’ threshold for defences (citing, inter alia, Pappajohn v. The Queen; R. v. Bulmer; R. v. Robertson).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Deductibility of wage-continuation benefits from tort damages for lost earnings (collateral benefits rule for wages): as a general rule, wages paid while plaintiff unable to work must be deducted; exception where payer has a subrogation/reimbursement entitlement (statute or valid claim), with a narrow discretionary trust possibility where necessary/appropriate in the interests of justice and some obligation to repay is shown.
BaselineA: Common law damages principles (compensatory principle/actual loss; avoidance of double recovery) as discussed through prior cases including Andrews v. Grand & Toy Alberta Ltd., Thornton v. Prince George School Board, and Arnold v. Teno; and collateral benefits jurisprudence including Parry v. Cleaver and Bradburn v. Great Western Rail. Co.
CaseB_TestB: Constitutional characterization/validity of the GST scheme under s. 91(3) (and related questions): GST is valid if, in pith and substance, it is a 'mode or system of taxation' to raise revenue; incidental effects on provincial jurisdiction are permissible, and s. 103 is an appropriations provision that does not create an enforceable right to reimbursement for collection costs.
BaselineB: Constitution Act, 1867 (especially ss. 91(3), 92(13), 103, 125, 126) and the Excise Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. E-15, Part IX (GST provisions including ss. 122, 123, 154, 221, 222, 240, 346).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Art. 559 C.C.Q. compensatory allowance test: claimant must prove (1) contribution, (2) enrichment of spouse’s patrimony, (3) causal link/correlation, and (4) proportion; enrichment must “subsist” and be evaluated “at the time of the divorce”, with “great flexibility” in evaluating the elements (bankruptcy is not irrefutable proof of no subsisting enrichment).
BaselineA: Statute (Civil Code of Quebec, art. 559), informed by unjust enrichment principles (e.g., “correlation” from Cie Immobilière Viger Ltée v. Lauréat Giguère Inc.).
CaseB_TestB: Misapprehension-of-evidence appellate intervention test (Morrissey): to set aside a conviction, the misapprehension must go to “the substance” not “detail”, be “material” not “peripheral”, and the errors must play an “essential part” in the reasoning process leading to conviction (a “stringent” conjunctive standard).
BaselineB: Common law (adopting/affirming R. v. Morrissey; also relying on R. v. C.(R.)), applied within Criminal Code s. 686(1)(a)(iii) miscarriage of justice.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Copyright Act s. 3(1) “reproduction” analysis for computer programs embodied in silicon chips: the chip-embedded program is protected if it is a “reproduction” of the assembly-language program (a “substantial part ... in any material form whatever”), i.e., the chip should be viewed as “a static object encoded with written instructions” rather than “a dynamic interchange of electrical impulses”.
BaselineA: Statute — Copyright Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-30, s. 3(1) (including s. 3(1)(a) and (d) discussed but not decided).
CaseB_TestB: Common law de facto taking (constructive expropriation) test requiring compensation: “two requirements must be met: (1) an acquisition of a beneficial interest in the property or flowing from it, and (2) removal of all reasonable uses of the property”.
BaselineB: Common law — as stated in the decision with reference to Mariner Real Estate Ltd. v. Nova Scotia (Attorney General), Manitoba Fisheries Ltd. v. The Queen, and The Queen in Right of British Columbia v. Tener; applied alongside statute (Vancouver Charter, s. 569) which can negate the remedy.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Novation test (mortgage/assumption context): (1) new debtor assumes complete liability; (2) creditor accepts new debtor as principal debtor (not agent/guarantor); (3) creditor accepts new contract in full satisfaction and substitution for the old; and, absent express agreement, courts should be "loath to find novation unless the circumstances are really compelling" (assent is crucial).
BaselineA: Common law (novation doctrine), with the three-part test stated as being "set out in Polson v. Wulffsohn (1890)"; applied in the mortgage context alongside interpretation of The Limitation of Civil Rights Act, R.S.S. 1978, c. L-16, ss. 2 and 40.
CaseB_TestB: Common law de facto taking (constructive expropriation) test requiring compensation: (1) "an acquisition of a beneficial interest in the property or flowing from it"; and (2) "removal of all reasonable uses of the property".
BaselineB: Common law (de facto taking), as summarized from Manitoba Fisheries Ltd. v. The Queen, Tener, and Mariner Real Estate; applied alongside Vancouver Charter, S.B.C. 1953, c. 55, s. 569 (and related planning provisions ss. 561-563).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Applicability of Criminal Code s. 443 (now s. 487) search-warrant power to offences under "any other Act of Parliament" even where that other Act (e.g., Bankruptcy Act s. 6) also contains search-and-seizure provisions: on a plain reading, s. 443(1)(a)-(b) applies to proceedings under any federal statute; Parliament restricted only para. (e) by the words "subject to any other Act of Parliament".
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 443(1)(a)-(b),(e) (as amended 1985) and Bankruptcy Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. B-3, s. 6 (with interpretive context from Interpretation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-23, s. 27(2)).
CaseB_TestB: Occupiers' Liability Act framework: (1) s. 3(1) imposes a general duty "to take such care as in all the circumstances of the case is reasonable" to see entrants are "reasonably safe"; local custom is only a circumstance and must be proved, and cannot make unreasonable conduct reasonable; (2) s. 4(1) "risks willingly assumed" is a narrow exception embodying volenti—more than mere knowledge is required, i.e., the plaintiff must accept the risk in the sense of waiving legal recourse/assuming the entire risk.
BaselineB: Statute: Occupiers' Liability Act, R.S.O. 1980, c. 322, ss. 3(1) and 4(1) (interpreted in light of common law volenti as described in Dube v. Labar and Crocker v. Sundance Northwest Resorts Ltd.).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 32 applicability to non-core government entities (university): whether there is sufficient government control over the entity’s core functions (distinguishing “ultimate or extraordinary control” from “routine or regular control”) to make the impugned act government action
BaselineA: Common law / constitutional doctrine interpreting Charter s. 32 (applied from McKinney v. University of Guelph; also referencing RWDSU v. Dolphin Delivery Ltd.)
CaseB_TestB: Leave to appeal a commercial arbitral award under Arbitration Act s. 31(2)(a): threshold question of law + (i) importance to the parties and (ii) determination of the point of law may prevent a miscarriage of justice (material issue + arguable merit), with residual discretion factors
BaselineB: Statute (Arbitration Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 55, s. 31(2)(a)) as interpreted by the SCC (building on BCIT and related cases)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Kirkness limit on the Paré “single transaction” analysis: it applies only to murder classification under Criminal Code s. 214(5) and only after the Crown first proves the accused committed (or was a party to) both the underlying offence and the murder; only then ask whether the offences were “sufficiently closely connected in time” to classify the murder as first degree
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 214(5) (now s. 231(5))) as interpreted in R. v. Paré, [1987] 2 S.C.R. 618 ("single transaction" meaning of "while committing")
CaseB_TestB: Forum non conveniens / assumption of jurisdiction in multistate defamation: jurisdiction is established via a presumptive connecting factor (tort of defamation committed in Ontario by publication there), and a stay is granted only if the moving party shows another forum is “clearly more appropriate” after considering multiple contextual factors
BaselineB: Common law framework from Club Resorts Ltd. v. Van Breda, 2012 SCC 17 (real and substantial connection; presumptive connecting factors; forum non conveniens “clearly more appropriate” test)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Abuse of process stay test (Keyowski/Jewitt/Young): stay only in the “clearest of cases” where compelling trial would violate fundamental justice/fair play or proceedings are oppressive or vexatious
BaselineA: Common law (abuse of process stay doctrine from R. v. Jewitt adopting R. v. Young; reaffirmed in R. v. Keyowski and R. v. Conway) applied in context of Criminal Code s. 508 stay/recommencement power
CaseB_TestB: Curative proviso test under Criminal Code s. 686(1)(b)(iii): whether there is any “reasonable possibility” the verdict would have been different but for the error(s)
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(b)(iii)) as interpreted in Colpitts; Wildman; R. v. S.(P.L.); Broyles; R. v. B.(F.F.)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Lippé institutional impartiality test for part-time judges’ outside occupations: (1) ask whether, considering factors including “the nature of the occupation and the parties who appear before this type of judge”, “there [will] be a reasonable apprehension of bias in the mind of a fully informed person in a substantial number of cases”; (2) if yes (occupation “per se incompatible”), assess whether safeguards reduce the risk so that a fully informed person (aware of safeguards) would not have such an apprehension “in a substantial number of cases”; otherwise challenges proceed case-by-case.
