BaselineA: Combination: Charter guarantee of an “independent and impartial tribunal” (Canadian Charter s. 11(d); Quebec Charter s. 23) applied through the common-law reasonable apprehension of bias test from Committee for Justice and Liberty v. National Energy Board (adopted in Valente v. The Queen).
CaseB_TestB: Zundel s. 1 “objective” identification rule in Charter justification: for s. 1, “the Court must look at the intention of Parliament when the section was enacted or amended” and “cannot assign objectives, nor invent new ones according to the perceived current utility of the impugned provision” (rejecting “shifting purpose”); absent a pressing and substantial objective, the limit fails s. 1.
BaselineB: Common law/constitutional doctrine under Charter s. 1 (Oakes framework) and prior rejection of shifting purposes (R. v. Big M Drug Mart Ltd.).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 96 (Constitution Act, 1867) / Residential Tenancies framework — whether jurisdiction can be conferred on an inferior court: (1) characterize the power; (2) historical inquiry whether the power was exercised exclusively by s. 96 courts at Confederation; if yes, (3) (per Wilson J.) ask if the function is judicial and, if so, whether it is "necessarily incidental" to a broader policy scheme rather than a usurpation of s. 96 courts
BaselineA: Common law constitutional test from Re Residential Tenancies Act, 1979, [1981] 1 S.C.R. 714 (three-step s. 96 analysis), as considered in Sobeys Stores Ltd. v. Yeomans, [1989] 1 S.C.R. 238; applied to s. 96 of the Constitution Act, 1867
CaseB_TestB: Interpretation of "sold in any market in Canada" (Patent Act ss. 80(1)(b), 83(1), 85): interpret the phrase contextually and purposively (consumer protection), including SAP sales where the medicine is regulated by Canadian public law, will be delivered/dispensed in Canada, and the cost will be borne by Canadians
BaselineB: Statutory interpretation of Patent Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. P-4, ss. 80(1)(b), 81(1)(a), 83(1), 85, using the modern principle of interpretation (Canada Trustco Mortgage Co. v. Canada, 2005 SCC 54, para. 10)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Adequacy/sufficiency of an indictment (including where evidence shows multiple conspiracies): indictment is adequate if it gives the accused “reasonable information” to identify the transaction and prepare a defence; and a proven conspiracy falls within the indictment if it involved some accused, occurred sometime within the alleged time span, and had as its object the type of crime alleged
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 510, 512, 516(1)(g), plus SCC/common-law principles cited in R. v. Côté, R. v. Wis Development Corp., R. v. B.(G.), and conspiracy-indictment analysis from R. v. Cotroni (and applied discussion of Paterson/Ackworth)
CaseB_TestB: Section 96 constitutionality test (Residential Tenancies framework) applied to s. 38 Canada Evidence Act: (1) does the power conferred on a non‑s.96 body conform to a power exercised by superior/district/county courts at Confederation? If no, “the inquiry ends”; if yes, proceed to (2) whether it is judicial, and (3) whether it is ancillary/incidental to an administrative function
BaselineB: Common law constitutional test from Re Residential Tenancies Act, 1979 (as developed in later cases), applied to the statutory scheme in Canada Evidence Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-5, ss. 38 to 38.16 (and related constitutional provisions Constitution Act, 1867, s. 96; Charter, s. 7 discussed)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Entrapment (Mack) — first-branch clarification: random virtue-testing occurs only if police offer an opportunity without reasonable suspicion of the person OR reasonable suspicion that the associated location is one where the crime is likely occurring; presence in a sufficiently defined bona fide inquiry area counts as being “associated”
BaselineA: Common law (R. v. Mack, [1988] 2 S.C.R. 903 entrapment framework; applied/clarified in Barnes)
CaseB_TestB: Appellate review of voluntariness voir dire — a court of appeal may not reweigh the evidence on whether a statement was “free and voluntary” absent a “serious, specific and determining error”
BaselineB: Common law (confession rule/voluntariness and appellate deference principles; specific prior cases not identified in the reasons provided)
JudgeB: LeBel J. (for the Court, oral reasons)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Duty of trial judge to comment on Crown counsel’s prejudicial jury address: where remarks are “prejudicial to a degree sufficient to impose a legal duty on the trial judge to comment” to ensure the defence position is “fairly put to the jury”; failure is an error of law (then consider whether s. 686(1)(b)(iii) ‘no substantial wrong or miscarriage of justice’ applies).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(b)(iii)) plus common-law principles of fair trial/jury charge (as reflected in adopting Ayles J.A.’s formulation).
CaseB_TestB: Broker commission triggers under Quebec brokerage contract: (1) no “agreement to sell the immovable” unless the accepted promise to purchase is “unconditionally binding” such that it is “possible for one of them to bring an action to compel transfer of title”; and (2) clause mirroring art. 1503 C.C.Q. (“seller voluntarily prevents free performance”) requires proof of seller “fault” preventing fulfilment of the preconditions for commission.
BaselineB: Statute and contract interpretation (Civil Code of Québec, arts. 1396 and 1503; interpreted alongside standard-form brokerage clauses 6.1(3o) and 6.1(4o)).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 16(2) insanity/NCRMD test — focus on the two branches and (per Chaulk) that “wrong” in the second branch means “morally wrong”; first branch is limited to inability to appreciate the physical nature/physical consequences of the act
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 16(2)); interpreted in light of SCC precedents Cooper v. The Queen, Kjeldsen v. The Queen, R. v. Abbey (first branch) and R. v. Chaulk (meaning of “wrong” in second branch)
CaseB_TestB: Reasonable suspicion standard for sniffer-dog searches (and related investigative detention): must be based on “objectively discernible facts” assessed on the “totality of the circumstances”, through the lens of a reasonable officer’s training/experience; focuses on “possibilities, not probabilities”
BaselineB: Common law Charter s. 8/9 framework for sniffer-dog searches and investigative detention, drawing on R. v. Kang-Brown, R. v. A.M., and companion clarification in R. v. Chehil; applied in the Charter context (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 8, 9)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Legitimate expectations doctrine does not apply to the legislative process and cannot create a substantive right (e.g., consent/veto); at most it can require an opportunity to make representations/consultation in administrative decision-making
BaselineA: Common law doctrine of procedural fairness / legitimate expectations (as summarized in Old St. Boniface Residents Assn. Inc. v. Winnipeg (City), and approved principles from Bates v. Lord Hailsham; Inuit Tapirisat; Martineau; Penikett)
CaseB_TestB: Divorce Act s. 17 variation of spousal support: court must be satisfied there has been a post-order “change in the condition, means, needs or other circumstances” (s. 17(4)) and then vary considering the s. 17(7) objectives; pension income may be treated as “means” and “double dipping” does not arise where prior pension division was not a true valuation/division of future pension value
BaselineB: Statute (Divorce Act, 1985, s. 17(4) and s. 17(7))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 7 extradition test: whether surrender (including without death-penalty assurances) would place the fugitive in a situation that “sufficiently shocks” the Canadian conscience / is “simply unacceptable” (considering offence/penalty, foreign justice system safeguards, and comity/security, with latitude to the Minister’s balancing).
BaselineA: Combination: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7 (principles of fundamental justice) as applied to extradition under Extradition Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. E-23, s. 25; and the common-law/Charter extradition standard from Canada v. Schmidt (“shock the conscience”) and United States v. Allard (“simply unacceptable”).
CaseB_TestB: Media search-warrant reasonableness framework: after meeting Criminal Code s. 487(1)(b) requirements, the justice of the peace must assess overall reasonableness by balancing all circumstances (including press function impacts), with a non-mandatory consideration of alternative sources; the “essential question” is whether, “taking into account all the circumstances… the search was reasonable.”
BaselineB: Statute (with Charter backdrop): Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 487(1)(b), (d), (e), interpreted in light of Charter ss. 2(b) and 8; informed by prior jurisprudence including Re Pacific Press Ltd. and Descôteaux v. Mierzwinski.
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Reasonable apprehension of bias (pecuniary interest) test: “Would a reasonably well-informed person consider that the interest might have an influence on the exercise of the official’s public duty?” (Old St. Boniface formulation, applied to Law Society costs provision)
BaselineA: Common law (administrative law/natural justice) reasonable apprehension of bias test as formulated in Old St. Boniface Residents Assn. Inc. v. Winnipeg (City), [1990] 3 S.C.R. 1170; applied within s. 7 “principles of fundamental justice” analysis
CaseB_TestB: Nelles malicious prosecution / lifting prosecutorial immunity test (4 requirements on balance of probabilities): (1) prosecution initiated by defendant; (2) terminated in plaintiff’s favour; (3) absence of reasonable and probable cause (subjective + objective); (4) malice/improper purpose
BaselineB: Common law test from Nelles v. Ontario, [1989] 2 S.C.R. 170 (followed and applied; includes definition of reasonable and probable cause and malice/improper purpose)
JudgeB: Iacobucci and Binnie JJ. (for McLachlin C.J. and Iacobucci, Major and Binnie JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Colour of right / mistake analysis for s. 206(1)(d): colour of right is unavailable where the offence definition does not include it, and a belief that the Criminal Code is inoperative is a mistake of law barred by s. 19 ("a mistake about the law is no defence")
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, ss. 19 and 206(1)(d); plus common law notion that colour of right is only relevant where the offence definition embraces it, as illustrated by theft cases cited)
CaseB_TestB: Modified Taylor definition/test for "hatred" under s. 14(1)(b): apply objectively whether a reasonable person aware of context would view the expression as likely to expose a protected group to "detestation" and "vilification"; focus on likely effects on the audience; intent is irrelevant; and sever "ridicules, belittles or otherwise affronts the dignity of" as unconstitutional
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: Saskatchewan Human Rights Code, s. 14(1)(b) (and related provisions) interpreted through Canada (Human Rights Commission) v. Taylor, [1990] 3 S.C.R. 892
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Test for granting intervener status and managing a new Charter argument/material: intervener must have a “sufficient interest” and bring a “special perspective”; Court considers whether raising Charter for first time would “occasion prejudice” (e.g., if it would have been affected by additional trial evidence); proposed studies/reports should be filed only on respondent’s consent or, absent consent, “with leave of the Court” (especially if they amount to fresh evidence).
BaselineA: Common law / SCC practice on intervention and new issues on appeal (as applied in an application to intervene), with reference to Charter being raised as an interpretive tool and to evidentiary principles about fresh evidence/judicial notice.
CaseB_TestB: Interpretation of Criminal Code s. 182(b) (offering indignities to human remains): (1) physical interference/contact is sufficient but “not a necessary element”; (2) indignities must be offered to “a dead human body or human remains” (not to monuments per se); (3) however, where monuments “mark the presence of human remains”, offering indignities to those monuments constitutes offering indignities to the human remains.
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 182(b) (with related appeal powers in ss. 683(1)(g) and 695(1) for charge amendment).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Applicability trigger for the Environmental Assessment and Review Process Guidelines Order: a project is a “proposal” only if Canada has a “decision making responsibility”, meaning an “affirmative regulatory duty” (a legal duty/obligation under an Act of Parliament), making the responsible federal body the “initiating department” required to apply the assessment process
BaselineA: Regulation + statute: Environmental Assessment and Review Process Guidelines Order, SOR/84-467 (ss. 2 “proposal”, “initiating department”; s. 6; also s. 3) made under Department of the Environment Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. E-10, s. 6; applied alongside Navigable Waters Protection Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. N-22, s. 5 and Fisheries Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. F-14, s. 37
CaseB_TestB: Curative proviso (Criminal Code s. 686(1)(b)(iii)) test: despite an error of law, uphold the conviction if the Crown shows either (1) the error was “so harmless, and so insignificant, that it could not have affected the verdict”; or (2) the case was “so overwhelming that a conviction would have been inevitable even if the error had not been made”
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(b)(iii) (as interpreted in R. v. Khan, 2001 SCC 86 and R. v. Trochym, 2007 SCC 6, cited in the reasons)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 133 “legislative nature” test + anti-circumvention principle: s. 133 applies to statutes and to any instrument of a legislative nature; and where “the net effect of a series of discrete acts has a legislative character, then each of these component acts will also be imbued with this same character” (so s. 133 cannot be avoided by dividing a legislative scheme into steps). Badges of legislative character include: (1) “embodies a rule of conduct”; (2) “has the force of law”; (3) “applies to an undetermined number of persons.”
BaselineA: Constitution Act, 1867, s. 133, as interpreted in Reference re Manitoba Language Rights, [1992] 1 S.C.R. 000 and Reference re Manitoba Language Rights, [1985] 1 S.C.R. 721 (plus analogy to Quebec (Attorney General) v. Brunet, [1990] 1 S.C.R. 260).
CaseB_TestB: Duty to respond to jury question on reasonable doubt: even if the initial reasonable-doubt charge follows Lifchus and is “unassailable”, when the jury asks a question about the standard of proof “the trial judge must attempt to answer the jury’s question in an effort to assist them”; repeating the charge may suffice in some cases, but the judge must not discourage further questions and should “leave the door open” for more questions if confusion remains.
BaselineB: Common law jury-instruction principles from R. v. Lifchus, [1997] 3 S.C.R. 320 and R. v. S. (W.D.), [1994] 3 S.C.R. 521 (also referencing R. v. Starr, 2000 SCC 40).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Mistaken transfer + recipient knowledge + transferor right of recovery ⇒ property does not pass for criminal theft; subsequent fraudulent conversion with intent to deprive ⇒ theft
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 322(1)) interpreted in light of property-law principles about mistake and recovery rights; prior SCC context noted in R. v. Stewart, [1988] 1 S.C.R. 963
CaseB_TestB: Judicial review under IRPA s. 67(1)(c): apply Dunsmuir to select standard (correctness vs reasonableness); for IAD H&C relief decisions the standard is reasonableness and courts ask only whether the outcome falls within a range of reasonable outcomes (no reweighing)
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: Federal Courts Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. F-7, ss. 18 and 18.1 (esp. s. 18.1(4)); Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, S.C. 2001, c. 27, s. 67(1)(c); common-law standard-of-review framework from Dunsmuir v. New Brunswick, 2008 SCC 9
JudgeB: Binnie J. (McLachlin C.J. and LeBel, Abella and Charron JJ. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: s. 11(b) unreasonable delay analysis (Morin factors + institutional-delay guideline): a "judicial determination balancing" (1) length of delay; (2) waiver; (3) reasons for delay (incl. inherent time requirements, actions of accused/Crown, institutional resources, other); and (4) prejudice, with an administrative guideline of 8–10 months for Provincial Court institutional delay (not a fixed ceiling) and prejudice potentially inferred from length of delay
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional text + prior SCC framework: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 11(b) (and remedy via s. 24(1)); factors distilled in R. v. Smith, [1989] 2 S.C.R. 1120 and applied/extended in R. v. Askov, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 1199 (also drawing on Mills, Rahey, Conway)
JudgeA: Sopinka J. (for La Forest, Sopinka, Stevenson and Iacobucci JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Contractor/subcontractor liability for collapse under Quebec Civil Code: even if supports yielded first, subcontractor not liable where "true cause" is contractor’s contractual fault of overloading; subcontractor may defend by showing damage due to "the fault of the owner [contractor]" (and is not obliged to provide supports for an unforeseeable, undisclosed overload)
BaselineB: Statute/civil code + prior SCC statement of principle: Civil Code arts. 1684, 1688, 1065; and Hill, Clarke-Francis Ltd. v. Northland Groceries (Quebec) Ltd., [1941] S.C.R. 437 (builder can avoid responsibility by proving damage due to force majeure/Act of God/fault of owner/act of third party)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Secret commissions offence (Criminal Code s. 426(1)(a)(ii)): actus reus requires (1) agency relationship; (2) agent accepts a benefit as consideration for an act/forbearance in relation to the principal’s affairs; and (3) failure to make “adequate and timely disclosure of the source, amount and nature of the benefit”; mens rea requires awareness of each element, including awareness of the extent of disclosure/lack thereof; “corruptly” means “secretly or without the requisite disclosure” and there is no “corrupt bargain” requirement.
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 426(1)(a) (as applied to s. 426(1)(a)(ii)); framework followed from R. v. Kelly (1992).
CaseB_TestB: Criminal Code s. 686(1)(b)(iii) curative proviso: ask “whether a jury properly instructed could, acting reasonably, have come to a different conclusion absent the error”; jury findings may inform the hypothetical reasonable jury if not tainted by the error.
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(b)(iii).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: State Immunity Act s. 5 “commercial activity” exception: two-step, contextual inquiry — (1) determine the “nature” of the foreign state activity (with purpose/context relevant), then (2) assess whether the Canadian proceedings “relate to” that activity by a sufficient “nexus” (more than incidental) when the activity is viewed “in its entire context”
BaselineA: Statute (State Immunity Act, S.C. 1980-81-82-83, c. 95, ss. 2 and 5) codifying the common law restrictive immunity doctrine (acts jure imperii vs jure gestionis), discussed via I Congreso del Partido
CaseB_TestB: Compatibility of Quebec “pay-and-retain/compensation” mechanisms with the BIA scheme of distribution: determine whether the provincial right is merely subrogation/compensation within BIA s. 97(3) and civil law rules, using a timing-based analysis (pre-bankruptcy payment with liquid debts; pre-bankruptcy payment with non-liquid debt; post-bankruptcy payment) and rejecting equitable set-off in Quebec bankruptcy
BaselineB: Statutes and civil law: Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. B-3 (esp. ss. 97(3), 121, 136-147, 67, 71(2)); Quebec statutes (AIAOD s. 316; ALRCI s. 54) interpreted through Civil Code of Québec provisions on subrogation/compensation/solidarity (e.g., arts. 1651, 1656(3), 1672-1673, 1681, 1523, 1536) and prior SCC conflict jurisprudence including Husky Oil
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Quebec civil law “obligation to inform” (duty of disclosure) in contracts of enterprise: duty arises where (1) the debtor has “knowledge of the information, whether actual or presumed”; (2) the information is “of decisive importance”; and (3) it is “impossible for the party to whom the duty to inform is owed to inform itself, or that the creditor is legitimately relying on the debtor of the obligation”; in large projects its content varies with “allocation of risk, the relative expertise of the parties and the continuing formation of the contract”.
BaselineA: Civil Code of Lower Canada (arts. 1024, 1053) and existing Quebec jurisprudence recognizing good faith and delictual liability to third parties for unreasonable conduct in a contractual context (e.g., Houle v. Canadian National Bank; National Bank of Canada v. Soucisse; Bank of Montreal v. Kuet Leong Ng).
CaseB_TestB: Canadian maritime law reform: contributory negligence is no longer a complete bar in maritime tort; instead, contributory negligence “may reduce recovery but does not bar the plaintiff’s claim”, with defendants “jointly and severally liable” for the non-plaintiff-fault portion, “subject to a right of contribution between defendants”.
BaselineB: Common law of Canadian maritime tort (contributory negligence as a bar) as part of Canadian maritime law (relying on ITO—International Terminal Operators Ltd. v. Miida Electronics Inc. for the scope of Canadian maritime law; and historical common law authorities on contributory negligence).
JudgeB: McLachlin J. (reasons agreed with on this point by Gonthier, Cory, Iacobucci and Major JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Duty to accommodate (employer/union) to the point of “reasonable measures short of undue hardship”, including when and how a union becomes liable (co-discriminator vs. impeding accommodation) and the complainant’s duty to facilitate/accept reasonable accommodation
BaselineA: Combination: statute (Human Rights Act, S.B.C. 1984, c. 22, ss. 8(1)(a),(b),(4)) plus common-law human-rights framework from O'Malley and Central Alberta Dairy Pool. Core baseline formulation: employer must take “reasonable measures short of undue hardship” (O'Malley) and undue hardship assessed with non-exhaustive factors (Central Alberta Dairy Pool).
CaseB_TestB: Exclusive arbitral jurisdiction under s. 45(1): courts are ousted where the dispute’s “essential character” arises from the “interpretation, application, administration or alleged violation” of the collective agreement
BaselineB: Statute: Ontario Labour Relations Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. L.2, s. 45(1) (mandatory “final and binding settlement by arbitration ... of all differences ... arising from the interpretation, application, administration or alleged violation of the agreement”), interpreted in light of SCC labour-arbitration exclusivity jurisprudence (notably St. Anne Nackawic).
JudgeB: McLachlin J. (for L'Heureux-Dubé, Gonthier, McLachlin and Major JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Trial judge’s discretion to exclude cross-examination on a collateral credibility matter: admit only if its (tenuous) relevance outweighs its prejudicial value/misleading effect
BaselineA: Common law (trial management/evidence discretion), as applied in R. v. Meddoui, [1991] 3 S.C.R. 320
JudgeA: McLachlin J. (for the Court, oral reasons)
CaseB_TestB: Income Tax Act s. 20(1)(c)(i) purpose requirement for interest deductibility: whether, considering all the circumstances, the taxpayer had a reasonable expectation of income at the time the investment was made (income = taxable income, not net income; ancillary income-earning purpose suffices absent sham/window dressing)
BaselineB: Statute (Income Tax Act, s. 20(1)(c)(i); also discussed with reference to s. 85 rollover linkage) interpreted in light of prior SCC cases including Bronfman Trust and Tennant
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 10(b) “detention” at a port of entry: routine secondary immigration examination is not detention unless the restriction goes beyond routine screening into a restraint of liberty (Therens/Simmons applied; factors include routine screening purpose, no “action” indicating escalation, and “absence of stigma”).
BaselineA: Combination: constitutional text (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 10(b)) interpreted through common law/precedent. Baseline definition of “detention” from R. v. Therens (psychological compulsion; state agent assumes control by demand/direction with significant legal consequence) and border-screening context from R. v. Simmons (routine questioning not detention; intrusive measures like strip search are detention).
CaseB_TestB: Elements of civil contempt (no “contumacious intent” required): civil contempt is established by proof beyond a reasonable doubt of (1) a clear and unequivocal order, (2) actual knowledge of the order, and (3) an intentional act/omission that breaches the order; intent to interfere with the administration of justice is not an element (goes to penalty).
BaselineB: Common law. Baseline elements drawn from prior authorities cited in the reasons, including Bhatnager v. Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration) and related appellate authorities (e.g., Prescott-Russell; Sheppard) as summarized and affirmed by the SCC.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Admissibility and required limiting instruction for bad-character/disposition evidence: admissible if (1) relevant to an issue other than disposition/character and (2) probative value outweighs prejudicial effect; if admitted, jury must be specifically warned not to use it as propensity proof of guilt
BaselineA: Common law (bad character/disposition exclusion and probative-prejudicial balancing from Morris v. The Queen; limiting-instruction requirement from R. v. D. (L.E.)); also applied alongside Criminal Code s. 686(1)(b)(iii) curative proviso jurisprudence (e.g., R. v. S. (P.L.), R. v. Broyles)
CaseB_TestB: Recent fabrication exception for prior consistent statements: where cross-examination amounts to an allegation of recent fabrication, prior complaint evidence is admissible only to show the fact the complaint was made, not the truth of its contents
BaselineB: Common law (rule against prior consistent statements with the recent-fabrication exception)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Substantive admissibility of a non-accused witness’s prior inconsistent statement (reformed rule): threshold that the statement “would have been admissible as the witness’s sole testimony”, plus principled hearsay “reliability” and “necessity” adapted to this context; reliability is met where there are “sufficient circumstantial guarantees of reliability” such as “(1) [made] under oath, solemn affirmation or solemn declaration following an explicit warning…; (2) …videotaped in its entirety; and (3) …full opportunity to cross-examine… at trial”, with a voir dire to confirm indicia and screen for voluntariness/administration-of-justice concerns.
BaselineA: Common law hearsay/prior inconsistent statement doctrine (the “orthodox rule” from Deacon v. The King) as modified by the principled hearsay approach in R. v. Khan and R. v. Smith; applied procedurally through Canada Evidence Act, s. 9 (voir dire/cross-examination of own witness).
CaseB_TestB: Interpretive rule for insurer’s obligation to pay “interest” under a liability policy: the insurer’s promise to pay “interest accrued on the amount of its guarantee from the date when the action was instituted” is “necessarily the interest which the insured may be ordered to pay”; because art. 1056c C.C. ‘interest’ is “in reality damages due to delay”, the second-paragraph “indemnity… is of the same nature” and is therefore included in the policy’s “interest”.
BaselineB: Statute/civil code provision governing interest/additional indemnity on delictual damages: Civil Code (Quebec), art. 1056c (both paragraphs), applied through interpretation of the insurance contract’s “interest” clause.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal fraud (Criminal Code s. 380(1)) — “other fraudulent means”: actus reus requires (1) a prohibited act (deceit/falsehood/“other fraudulent means”) and (2) deprivation (actual loss or “placing of the victim’s pecuniary interests at risk”); for “other fraudulent means” the “fundamental question” is whether the conduct “can properly be stigmatized as dishonest”, assessed objectively: “Would the reasonable person stigmatize what was done as dishonest?”; mens rea requires (1) “subjective knowledge of the prohibited act” and (2) “subjective knowledge that the prohibited act could have as a consequence the deprivation of another (… including … pecuniary interests … put at risk)”.
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 380(1)), as interpreted through SCC jurisprudence including R. v. Olan and (released concurrently) R. v. Théroux.
CaseB_TestB: Union duty of representation in collective bargaining (Labour Code s. 47.2): union must not act “in bad faith or in an arbitrary or discriminatory manner or show serious negligence”; the duty “as a general rule constitutes an obligation of means” (not a result), and in bargaining the union “may therefore have to take the interests” of employees who have left the unit into account, but their prior work “would not … create rights … that would take precedence” and their presence “certainly did not impose an obligation of result on the Union requiring that it obtain” retroactive pay for them.
BaselineB: Statute (Labour Code, R.S.Q., c. C-27, s. 47.2; also discussed alongside ss. 59, 62, 67) and related SCC labour-law jurisprudence on the duty of representation (e.g., Noël; Centre hospitalier Régina).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Crown appeal from acquittal/new trial test under Criminal Code s. 686(4): Crown must show the verdict "would not necessarily have been the same" but for the legal error (a "very heavy onus")
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(4)) as interpreted in prior SCC cases (Vézeau v. The Queen; R. v. Morin)
JudgeA: Cory J. (for Sopinka, Cory, Iacobucci and Major JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Implied contractual duty of reasonable notice before enforcing security/appointing receiver: creditor must give "reasonable notice of its intention to enforce the security" and "reasonable time to pay"; reasonableness assessed using the Mister Broadloom criteria
BaselineB: Common law (Lister (R.E.) Ltd. v. Dunlop Canada Ltd.; Mister Broadloom Corporation (1968) Ltd. v. Bank of Montreal; Massey v. Sladen)
JudgeB: McLachlin and Bastarache JJ. (for the Court)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Engineer/design professional preparing tender documents owes no duty to advise/warn contractors about permits or difficulties tied to the contractor’s chosen method of performing the work, absent specific arrangements to the contrary (contractor bears responsibility for its chosen method).
BaselineA: Common law (duty/standard of care in construction/tendering context; negligent misrepresentation/duty to warn). Key authorities cited: R. v. Paradis and Farley Inc., [1942] S.C.R. 10; Vermont Construction Inc. v. Beatson, [1977] 1 S.C.R. 758; Temar Construction Ltd. v. West Hill Redevelopment Co. (1986), 21 C.L.R. 156 (Ont. H.C.).
CaseB_TestB: Framework for reviewing Crown decision-making: (1) identify whether the decision is prosecutorial discretion (decisions about the nature/extent of the prosecution) or (2) tactics/conduct before the court; exercises of prosecutorial discretion are reviewable only for abuse of process, meaning conduct that is “egregious and seriously compromises trial fairness and/or the integrity of the justice system,” with a threshold requirement that the accused first establish a “proper evidentiary foundation” before the Crown must justify its decision.
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law/constitutional doctrine. Statutory context: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, ss. 255(1)(a)(iii) and 727(1) (Notice triggering mandatory minimums); Charter s. 7 raised but Court rejects a new s. 7 duty. Common law baseline on prosecutorial discretion/review: Krieger v. Law Society of Alberta, 2002 SCC 65; R. v. Nixon, 2011 SCC 34; abuse of process jurisprudence.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 8 reasonableness of a warrantless search: a warrantless search is reasonable only if it is (1) "authorized by law", (2) "the law itself is reasonable", and (3) "the manner in which the search was carried out is reasonable"; and (SCC contribution) s. 10 Narcotic Control Act can constitutionally authorize a warrantless search only where "exigent circumstances render it impracticable to obtain prior judicial authorization".
BaselineA: Combination of common law/Charter doctrine and statute: Collins (S.C.C.) for the 3-part s. 8 reasonableness test; statutory baseline was Narcotic Control Act, R.S.C., 1985, c. N-1, s. 10 (warrantless search power) and s. 12 (warrant).
CaseB_TestB: Income Tax Act s. 241(3) disclosure exception: the confidentiality bar in s. 241(1)-(2) does not apply "in respect of proceedings relating to the administration or enforcement" of the Income Tax Act; (SCC contribution) this includes not only proceedings brought under the Act but also other proceedings sufficiently connected to enforcement (here, a trustee’s bankruptcy action), given the broad scope of "in respect of" and "relating to".
BaselineB: Statute: interpretation of Income Tax Act, S.C. 1970-71-72, c. 63, s. 241(1)-(4) (especially s. 241(3)); contextual support from s. 222 (tax debts recoverable in court).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Screen for child complainant under Criminal Code s. 486(2.1): judge may order testimony behind a screen if (1) accused is charged with an enumerated offence, (2) complainant is under 18, and (3) judge is of the opinion the exclusion is "necessary to obtain a full and candid account of the acts complained of"; constitutionally valid because it does not render the trial "fundamentally unfair" (ss. 7, 11(d)) and confrontation is not absolute but "subject to qualification in the interests of justice".
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 486(2.1)) applied against Charter ss. 7 and 11(d) fair trial/fundamental justice requirements.
CaseB_TestB: Similar fact evidence (identity) — use of prior conviction on voir dire: under Arp, Crown must show (1) sufficient similarity ("striking similarity") and (2) "some evidence" linking accused to the prior act; a prior conviction may be tendered to establish an essential element (e.g., identity) where put in issue and is "presumptively reliable" unless overturned or later shown wrong; overall admissibility still requires probative value exceeding prejudicial effect (Handy).
BaselineB: Common law similar fact admissibility framework from R. v. Arp and R. v. Handy (with SCC clarification on admissibility/use of prior convictions as proof of the Arp "some evidence" link).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Party liability for manslaughter where the principal is guilty of murder (ss. 21(1) aiding/abetting and 21(2) common unlawful purpose): manslaughter mens rea is objective foreseeability of non-trivial harm; death need not be foreseeable; included offence liability under s. 21(2) is available
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, ss. 21(1)(b),(c) and 21(2)) interpreted in light of SCC manslaughter jurisprudence (R. v. Kirkness; R. v. Creighton; R. v. Trinneer; also R. v. DeSousa; R. v. Logan)
CaseB_TestB: Entitlement to GST rebate for overpayment under Excise Tax Act: s. 261(1) turns on actual payment of an amount 'not payable', not legal liability; s. 261(2)(c) only bars double payment where a rebate 'is payable' under ss. 215.1/216(6); s. 296(2.1) requires applying an 'allowable rebate' on assessment even if the limitation period in s. 261(3) expired
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Government tort liability: classify the impugned conduct as a protected “true policy decision” (immune) versus “operational implementation” (ordinary negligence applies); policy includes decisions “involve or are dictated by financial, economic, social or political factors or constraints” (e.g., “budgetary allocations”), while operational matters are those to which “the standard of negligence ... can be applied”
BaselineA: Common law (Just v. British Columbia; also drawing on Anns v. Merton and Kamloops v. Nielsen) applied alongside enabling statutes (Public Highways Act, ss. 4-5; Proceedings against the Crown Act, s. 5(1)(a); Expropriation Act, ss. 70(f), 71)
CaseB_TestB: Damages in lieu of specific performance: where the plaintiff maintains a claim for specific performance and elects damages instead, damages may be assessed at the date of trial/judgment (not necessarily breach) so they are a “true substitute for specific performance”; “Specific performance should ... not be granted as a matter of course absent evidence that the property is unique”
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: Courts of Justice Act (Ontario), s. 99 (damages in substitution for specific performance) applied with common-law compensatory damages principles and authorities (e.g., Johnson v. Agnew; Wroth v. Tyler; Asamera Oil)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Abuse of process threshold in criminal cases: stay/remedy only in the “clearest of cases” (conduct that “shocks the conscience of the community” and is “so detrimental to the proper administration of justice” that intervention is warranted; requires “overwhelming evidence” of unfairness; courts intervene only with “conspicuous evidence of improper motives or of bad faith” or an act “so wrong that it violates the conscience of the community”).
BaselineA: Common law (abuse of process doctrine as affirmed in R. v. Jewitt and reiterated in R. v. Keyowski, R. v. Conway, etc.)
CaseB_TestB: Mr. Big confessions admissibility rule: confessions to the state during a Mr. Big operation are “presumptively inadmissible”; Crown must show (balance of probabilities) that “the probative value of the confession outweighs its prejudicial effect”, with probative value assessed mainly via reliability (circumstances of the operation + markers of reliability in the confession).
BaselineB: Common law (party admissions exception to hearsay; plus existing common-law probative value vs prejudicial effect discretion; SCC creates a new common-law evidentiary rule specific to Mr. Big confessions)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 16(1) “knowing that it was wrong”: incapacity includes inability to rationally apply right/wrong to the particular act (capacity for rational perception and rational choice), not merely abstract knowledge
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 16(1) (as amended 1991, c. 43, s. 2)), interpreted in light of M'Naghten's Case and SCC’s R. v. Chaulk
CaseB_TestB: Palmer criteria (applied to sentence appeals): fresh evidence admissible only if (1) due diligence (flexible factor), (2) relevance, (3) credibility, and (4) could reasonably, with trial record, have affected the result; overall “interests of justice”
BaselineB: Common law (Palmer v. The Queen) applied within statutory appellate powers (Criminal Code ss. 683 and 687)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Mohan test for admissibility of expert evidence (and added reliability/distinctiveness screening for expert disposition/profile evidence): expert evidence admissible only if (a) "relevance"; (b) "necessity in assisting the trier of fact"; (c) "the absence of any exclusionary rule"; and (d) "a properly qualified expert"; and for disposition/profile evidence the judge must be satisfied "as a matter of law" that the perpetrator or accused has "distinctive behavioural characteristics" and that the profile is "in common use as a reliable indicator" / that "the scientific community [has] developed a standard profile" (threshold reliability).
BaselineA: Common law (expert opinion and character evidence rules), drawing on and synthesizing prior cases cited in the reasons including R. v. Abbey, R. v. Lupien, R. v. Morin, R. v. Béland, R. v. Lavallee, and related authorities; applied in a criminal proceeding under the Criminal Code (procedural appeal provision s. 693).
CaseB_TestB: Section 745 Criminal Code parole ineligibility review decision framework: the jury determines whether ineligibility "ought to be reduced" "having regard to" (1) "the character of the applicant", (2) "his conduct while serving his sentence", (3) "the nature of the offence", and (4) "such other matters as the judge deems relevant"; the factors "must be assessed and weighed as a whole" in a discretionary decision (not element-by-element proof).
BaselineB: Statute — Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 745(1)-(4) (especially s. 745(2) listing factors and discretion).
JudgeB: Lamer C.J. (for Lamer C.J. and Gonthier and Cory JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 10(b) informational/implementational duties: no duty to mention duty counsel where none exists; further police duties are triggered only if detainee asserts a desire to speak to counsel
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional text (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 10(b)), as interpreted in prior SCC cases (R. v. Brydges; confirmed in R. v. Bartle; applied alongside the contemporaneous reasoning in R. v. Prosper)
CaseB_TestB: Criminal Code s. 347 framework for late payment penalties: (1) determine if charge is “interest” (a charge “paid or payable for the advancing of credit under an agreement or arrangement”); (2) apply s. 347(1)(a) ex ante and s. 347(1)(b) ex post with Nelson ‘voluntary act of debtor’ limit
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 347(1)-(2)) interpreted with reference to Nelson v. C.T.C. Mortgage Corp. and the companion interpretation in Degelder Construction Co. v. Dancorp Developments Ltd.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 7 overbreadth (principles of fundamental justice) test: a law violates s. 7 if it limits life, liberty or security of the person in a manner that is "unnecessarily broad, going beyond what is needed to accomplish the governmental objective"; courts ask whether the means are "necessary to achieve the State objective" and "reasonably tailored" so the limit "should not go beyond what is necessary".
BaselineA: Combination: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7 (principles of fundamental justice) plus prior SCC articulation of overbreadth/vagueness relationship and s. 7 scope (notably Re B.C. Motor Vehicle Act; R. v. Nova Scotia Pharmaceutical Society).
CaseB_TestB: Transfer pricing “reasonable amount in the circumstances” test under Income Tax Act s. 69(2): determine whether the non-arm’s-length price exceeds what "would have been reasonable in the circumstances" at arm’s length; "If transactions other than the purchasing transaction are relevant ... they must not be ignored"; comparability requires considering "economically relevant characteristics" and linked agreements conferring rights/benefits, with the court exercising "best informed judgment" because "transfer pricing is not an exact science" and a price within a "reasonable range" may suffice.
BaselineB: Statute: Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), s. 69(2) (now replaced by s. 247(2)).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Inference of possession from fingerprint evidence: whether an accused’s fingerprint on an article/container will support an inference of possession is “not subject to a hard and fast rule” but “depends on all of the circumstances of the case and all of the evidence adduced” (a totality-of-the-evidence assessment); adverse inference from silence only once Crown evidence “would support a conclusion of guilt beyond a reasonable doubt”.
BaselineA: Common law evidentiary principles on circumstantial proof of possession and adverse inference from failure to testify, as discussed through R. v. O'Keefe (1958) and R. v. Johnson (1993) (cited with approval in R. v. François, [1994] 2 S.C.R. 827).
CaseB_TestB: Scope of Review Board power under Criminal Code Part XX.1: Boards may make conditions binding on hospital authorities and may impose conditions “regarding”/supervising treatment (including ordering re-evaluations and exploration of alternatives) but have “no power to ‘prescribe’ treatment”; s. 672.55(1) is not a true exception but an example of supervisory power.
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, Part XX.1), primarily ss. 672.54 and 672.55(1) (also interpreted in light of related provisions including ss. 672.1, 672.38(1), 672.39, 672.41(1), 672.42, 672.72–672.78).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 7 compellability / exemption from compulsion test: whether the “predominant purpose” of compelling the witness is to obtain incriminating evidence against them rather than to further a legitimate public purpose; if predominant purpose is incrimination, compulsion must be justified and witness not compellable if other significant prejudice to fair trial is shown
BaselineA: Combination: Charter (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7; also s. 13) plus common-law/Charter framework from R. v. S. (R.J.), [1995] 1 S.C.R. 451, applied in the regulatory setting created by Securities Act, S.B.C. 1985, c. 83, s. 128(1)
CaseB_TestB: Timing rule for Corbett applications: the defence’s application to exclude prior convictions under s. 12 Canada Evidence Act “should be made after the close of the Crown’s case” and decided then; if necessary, a voir dire is held where defence outlines intended evidence, with possible later modification if defence evidence departs significantly
BaselineB: Combination: statute (Canada Evidence Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-5, s. 12 as interpreted in R. v. Corbett, [1988] 1 S.C.R. 670) plus common-law/Charter “case-to-meet” principle under Charter s. 7
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 7 compellability / exemption from compulsion test: whether the "predominant purpose" of compelling the witness is to obtain incriminating evidence against them rather than to further a legitimate public purpose; if predominant purpose is incrimination, compulsion must be justified and the witness may still be compellable if only prejudice is derivative use (protected by immunity), but not if other significant prejudice jeopardizes a fair trial
BaselineA: Combination: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7 (principles of fundamental justice) and prior SCC common-law/Charter framework from R. v. S. (R.J.), [1995] 1 S.C.R. 451 (compellability and self-incrimination protections)
CaseB_TestB: Section 15(1) prima facie discrimination test (Quebec v. A framework): (1) does the law create a distinction on an enumerated or analogous ground (on its face or in impact); and (2) does it impose "arbitrary — or discriminatory — disadvantage" by failing to respond to actual capacities/needs and instead reinforcing, perpetuating or exacerbating disadvantage; claimant must show a "disproportionate effect" based on group membership
BaselineB: Combination: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 15(1) and prior SCC jurisprudence, especially Quebec (Attorney General) v. A, 2013 SCC 5 (paras. 319-47) (also Withler, Kapp, Andrews, etc.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Tax-treaty residency under Article IV(1): a person is a “resident of a Contracting State” only if “liable to tax therein by reason of” an enumerated connecting factor (domicile, residence, place of management, place of incorporation) or a “criterion of a similar nature”; “similar nature” means a basis for comprehensive (world-wide) taxation, not mere source taxation (e.g., being “engaged in a trade or business” effectively connected to the U.S.)
BaselineA: Statute (Canada-United States Tax Convention Act, 1984, Schedule I: Canada-United States Income Tax Convention (1980), Article IV(1) (and related Articles I, XII))
CaseB_TestB: Trigger for Ontario auto-insurance limitation period: the two-year period in Insurance Act s. 281(5) runs only after a “valid refusal”; “no such refusal is given if there has not been adequate compliance with s. 71” SABS, which requires notice of the dispute-resolution process in “straightforward and clear language, directed towards an unsophisticated person” and, “at a minimum”, including mediation, arbitration/litigation if mediation fails, mandatory mediation first, and the “relevant time limits”
BaselineB: Statute and regulation (Insurance Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. I.8, s. 281(5) and related ss. 279-283; Statutory Accident Benefits Schedule, O. Reg. 776/93, ss. 71, 72 (and context ss. 62(8), 94))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Weber exclusive arbitral jurisdiction test under s. 45(1) OLRA: courts are ousted if the dispute’s “essential character” arises from the “interpretation, application, administration or alleged violation” of the collective agreement
BaselineA: Statute (Ontario Labour Relations Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. L.2, s. 45(1)) interpreted in light of SCC labour-arbitration exclusivity jurisprudence (notably St. Anne Nackawic Pulp & Paper Co. v. Canadian Paper Workers Union, Local 219, [1986] 1 S.C.R. 704)
CaseB_TestB: Criminal Code s. 744 parole-ineligibility extension framework: trial judge may extend beyond 10 years “having regard to (1) the character of the offender, (2) the nature of the offence, and (3) the circumstances surrounding its commission”; 10 years is the general rule but can be “ousted” if those criteria justify longer
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 744 (and related sentencing provisions including s. 742(b)); plus appellate review under s. 687(1) “fitness”/“clearly unreasonable” standard)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “loss of employment” for a retiring allowance: an employee is only “in the service” of the employer once under an obligation to provide services; therefore “loss of employment” cannot occur before that moment (no prospective/intended employment).
BaselineA: Statute: Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1952, c. 148 (now R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.)), ss. 56(1)(a)(ii) and 248(1) definitions of “employment” (“position of an individual in the service of some other person”) and “retiring allowance” (incl. amounts received “in respect of a loss of an office or employment”).
CaseB_TestB: Whether improper Crown closing submissions (personal anecdote not in evidence) caused an unfair trial/miscarriage of justice, assessed contextually using the “relevant factors” (from R. v. Stephan) such as seriousness, prominence, objections, and adequacy of the jury charge.
BaselineB: Common law: contextual trial-fairness/miscarriage-of-justice assessment for improper jury addresses, relying on factors referenced from R. v. Stephan (ABCA) and related authorities (Pisani; Boucher; Manasseri; Abdullahi).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Pragmatic and functional approach to whether a labour board acted within its jurisdiction (and, if within jurisdiction, review only for patent unreasonableness/clear irrationality)
BaselineA: Combination: common law administrative-law standards of review + statute (Canada Labour Code privative clause and certification provisions). Key baseline cases cited: U.E.S., Local 298 v. Bibeault (pragmatic and functional approach); CUPE v. New Brunswick Liquor (deference/patently unreasonable). Key statutory provisions applied: Canada Labour Code ss. 22 (privative clause), 24, 27, 28 (certification/unit determination), 33 (multi-employer units).
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 8 reasonableness test for DNA data bank orders under Criminal Code s. 487.055: (1) Collins prerequisites for a reasonable search; (2) contextual balancing of state interest vs privacy; (3) Hunter criteria generally not applicable; (4) procedural fairness assessed contextually (ex parte permissible)
BaselineB: Combination: constitutional common law under Charter s. 8 (Hunter v. Southam; R. v. Collins; R. v. Stillman; R. v. McKinlay Transport; R. v. Beare) + statute (Criminal Code s. 487.055(1), s. 487.055(3.1), s. 487.06(2), s. 487.057(1), s. 487.07; DNA Identification Act ss. 3-4).
JudgeB: Charron J. (McLachlin C.J. and Bastarache and Abella JJ. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Gladstone refinement of Sparrow s.35 justification/priority for commercial Aboriginal rights: government must show (1) a valid legislative objective and (2) consistency with fiduciary duty; where the Aboriginal right has no internal limit, priority is not exclusivity but requires the Crown to allocate the resource in a way that reflects the prior interest of Aboriginal right-holders, both procedurally and substantively
BaselineA: Common law constitutional framework under Constitution Act, 1982, s. 35(1) (Sparrow justification test: valid legislative objective + fiduciary duty/priority; also informed by Jack v. The Queen on priority)
CaseB_TestB: Admissibility of Crown rebuttal evidence: rebuttal may be admitted where it is relevant to an issue raised by the defence (here, it went to the 'context and the essential fabric of the alibi defence') and the Crown could not have known in advance the defence evidence; admission is within the trial judge’s discretion
BaselineB: Common law trial-evidence principles on rebuttal evidence and trial judge discretion (as applied by the Court, relying on the Court of Appeal’s approach)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Implied waiver of Charter s. 11(d) in regulatory ticketing scheme: legislature may infer waiver from failure to pay/appear only if (1) accused is "fully aware of the consequences of failing to act" and (2) the scheme has "sufficient safeguards to ensure that the conduct of the accused was not due to events over which he or she had no control" (including ability to set aside conviction if failure to appear was not the accused’s fault).
BaselineA: Combination: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 11(d) (and contextual role of s. 7 liberty), plus common-law/Charter waiver principles as discussed through SCC precedent (notably R. v. Lee) applied to the statutory ticketing/conviction scheme in Provincial Offences Procedure Act, S.N.B. 1987, c. P-22.1, s. 16 (and related safeguards such as ss. 10(1)(h), 11(1), 117, 48(1)).
CaseB_TestB: Procedural fairness/natural justice for CHRC dismissal under s. 36(3)(b): Commission must act "on a quasi-judicial basis"; fairness requires (1) an opportunity to make submissions "at least in writing" before the decision, and (2) prior disclosure of "the substance of the case against the party" so submissions are informed (a hearing "is not necessarily required").
BaselineB: Combination: statute (Canadian Human Rights Act, 1976-77 (Can.), c. 33, ss. 35 and 36(3)(b)) plus common-law procedural fairness/natural justice requirements applied to the Commission’s decision-making process.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Patently unreasonable standard on judicial review of a labour arbitration award (including the 'no evidence' constraint on factual inferences)
BaselineA: Common law (administrative law standard of review) applied in labour arbitration context; key baseline cases cited include CUPE v. New Brunswick Liquor Corp. (patently unreasonable interpretation), PSAC No. 2 (high deference), and Lester (evidence incapable of supporting findings).
CaseB_TestB: Statutory 'equivalent in value' test under Reorg. Act s. 15(2)(a): equivalence requires comparing both benefits and the funding mechanism as of the implementation date
BaselineB: Statute: Manitoba Telephone System Reorganization and Consequential Amendments Act, S.M. 1996, c. 79, s. 15(2)(a) (and related context in s. 15(3)); interpreted alongside the Civil Service Superannuation Act definition of 'pension benefit' (s. 1(1)) but not treated as determinative.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Doctrine of part performance prevents the Crown from relying on a statutory writing requirement (s. 21(1)(a) Public Highways Act) to deny an equitable permission/right to cross the highway where the agreement has been carried out by conduct
BaselineA: Combination: statute (Public Highways Act, R.S.N.S. 1954, c. 235, s. 21(1)(a); Expropriation Act, R.S.N.S. 1954, c. 91, ss. 1(c), 21(1), 25) and equitable common law doctrine (part performance / Statute of Frauds principles, as described via Steadman v. Steadman)
CaseB_TestB: Quebec annulment/homologation ‘public order’ test for arbitration awards: under art. 946.5 C.C.P., the court examines the award ‘as a whole’ and annuls/refuses only if the outcome (disposition) violates public order; mere legal error on a mandatory rule is insufficient unless the result conflicts with ‘fundamental principles of public order’
BaselineB: Statute/civil code framework: Code of Civil Procedure, R.S.Q., c. C-25, arts. 946.2, 946.4, 946.5, 947.2; Civil Code of Québec, art. 2639; plus interpretation of Copyright Act, s. 37 (re arbitrability context)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Southam reasonableness simpliciter standard of review: on statutory appeal from an expert tribunal, the reviewing court asks whether the tribunal decision is "unreasonable" (i.e., "not supported by any reasons that can stand up to a somewhat probing examination"), a middle standard between correctness and patent unreasonableness
BaselineA: Common law (standard-of-review jurisprudence), applied in the context of a statutory appeal under the Competition Tribunal Act; key baseline cases cited include Pezim v. British Columbia (Superintendent of Brokers) and CUPE v. New Brunswick Liquor Corp.
CaseB_TestB: Temporal-effect framework for suspended s. 52(1) declarations: declarations are presumptively retroactive, but the presumption is rebutted ("explicitly or by necessary implication") where the purpose of the suspension would be defeated by retroactivity; then the declaration must operate "purely prospectively"; individual relief may still be available under s. 24(1)
BaselineB: Constitutional text and remedial doctrine: Constitution Act, 1982, s. 52(1) and Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 24(1), building on prior SCC remedial cases including Ontario (Attorney General) v. G and Canada (Attorney General) v. Hislop (and interpreting the effect of Bedford’s suspended declaration)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: CCA “purpose of producing income” test under Reg. 1102(1)(c): (1) “Does the property produce income? In the affirmative, the deduction is allowable.” (2) If not, “was it acquired for the purpose of producing income?”, determined by “an objective evaluation of the specific facts and circumstances… having regard to whether the taxpayer acted in accordance with reasonably acceptable principles of commerce and business practices.”
BaselineA: Statute and regulation: Income Tax Act, s. 20(1)(a) (deductions “as is allowed by regulation”) and Income Tax Regulations, s. 1102(1)(c) (“property… not acquired… for the purpose of gaining or producing income”).
CaseB_TestB: Bail denial under s. 515(10)(c) (post-severance): detention may be ordered “where the detention is necessary in order to maintain confidence in the administration of justice, having regard to all the circumstances, including” (i) “the apparent strength of the prosecution’s case”, (ii) “the gravity of the nature of the offence”, (iii) “the circumstances surrounding its commission” and (iv) “the potential for a lengthy term of imprisonment”; applied through whether “a reasonable member of the community would be satisfied that denial of bail is necessary to maintain confidence in the administration of justice.”
BaselineB: Statute interpreted/partly invalidated: Criminal Code, s. 515(10)(c), read with Charter s. 11(e) (“not to be denied reasonable bail without just cause”) and Constitution Act, 1982, s. 52 (severance of unconstitutional wording).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: When an appeal right is “acquired, accrued or accruing” under Interpretation Act s. 43(c): the right to appeal as of right vests only once all conditions precedent are fulfilled (here, when the court of appeal renders judgment reversing the acquittal and ordering a new trial)
BaselineA: Statute (Interpretation Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. I-21, ss. 43(c) and 44(c),(d), applied to Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 691(2) (as amended))
CaseB_TestB: Sherman Estate v. Donovan test for discretionary limits on the open court principle (publication bans): (1) serious risk to an important public interest; (2) necessity because reasonable alternatives will not prevent the risk; (3) proportionality—benefits outweigh negative effects
BaselineB: Common law (Sherman Estate v. Donovan, 2021 SCC 25, para. 38 open court/publication ban framework)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Income-tax profit computation framework under ITA s. 9(1): taxpayer may use any method consistent with the Act, case law, and well-accepted business principles that yields an “accurate picture” of profit; on reassessment, once taxpayer shows an accurate picture, the onus shifts to the Minister to show it is not accurate or that another method is more accurate (Canderel summary at para. 53(3)-(6)).
BaselineA: Statute (Income Tax Act, S.C. 1970-71-72, c. 63, ss. 9(1), 18(1)(a), 18(9)) as interpreted through prior case law (including Symes v. Canada; M.N.R. v. Irwin; Associated Investors of Canada Ltd. v. M.N.R.; Johnston v. M.N.R.).
CaseB_TestB: Interpretation of Partnership Act s. 55(b): without unanimous limited-partner consent, a general partner has no authority to “do any act which makes it impossible to carry on the ordinary business of the limited partnership”; “does not require that all facets” be impossible, but refers to a “substantial portion” of the ordinary business (Estey J., paras. 23-24).
BaselineB: Statute (Partnership Act, R.S.A. 1980, c. P-2, s. 55(b)) interpreted by the Court; related equitable/common-law fiduciary principles discussed but the key test applied is the statutory s. 55(b) standard.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Post-conviction Crown non-disclosure: two-step “reasonable possibility” test for impairment of full answer and defence/new trial (reliability of result, then overall trial fairness, with defence due diligence as a key factor)
BaselineA: Combination: Charter ss. 7 and 24(1) plus common-law disclosure framework from R. v. Stinchcombe (as explained in Egger, Chaplin) and post-conviction remedy analysis (C. (M.H.), Carosella). Key formulations: disclosure relevance threshold—information is relevant if it “can reasonably be used by the accused either in meeting the case for the Crown, advancing a defence or otherwise in making a decision which may affect the conduct of the defence” (Egger, quoted at para. 20).
CaseB_TestB: Standard-form insurance interpretation: if clause unambiguous (ordinary meaning to the average insured, reading contract as a whole), give effect to clear language; here “policy of insurance” in SEF 44 cl. 4(b)(vii) means private insurance contract and excludes CPP
BaselineB: Common law (contract/insurance interpretation) applied to a standard-form contract term (SEF 44 Endorsement cl. 4(b)(vii)). Baseline principles stated via Ledcor/Progressive Homes/Scalera/Gibbens: “where the language of the disputed clause is unambiguous, reading the contract as a whole, effect should be given to that clear language” (para. 12) and words given their ordinary meaning as understood by the “average person applying for insurance” (para. 13).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Caslake ‘truly incidental to arrest’ limit on search-incident-to-arrest: police must have a purpose connected to the arrest (e.g., safety, evidence preservation, discovery of evidence) and it must be objectively reasonable; delay/distance may support a negative inference rebuttable by explanation
BaselineA: Common law (search incident to arrest) as discussed in Cloutier v. Langlois, [1990] 1 S.C.R. 158, within the Charter s. 8 reasonableness framework from Hunter v. Southam and R. v. Collins
CaseB_TestB: Admissibility framework for defence-led unknown third party suspect evidence: (1) logical relevance to an available defence shown by a sufficient connection/similarity between the charged crime and another incident plus evidence the accused could not have committed the other offence; and (2) admit unless prejudicial effects substantially outweigh probative value (Seaboyer balancing), without credibility findings or balance-of-probabilities proof
BaselineB: Common law evidence principles, especially R. v. Seaboyer, [1991] 2 S.C.R. 577 (defence evidence excluded only if prejudice substantially outweighs probative value), with relevance/air of reality guidance from Corbett and Cinous
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Schreiber (L’Heureux‑Dubé J.) — s. 8 is not engaged by a Canadian “letter of request” alone; only the foreign search/seizure (state compulsion) would engage s. 8, but it is done by foreign authorities and is not subject to Charter scrutiny
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 8 and 32(1), applied with prior SCC jurisprudence on extraterritoriality and s. 8 (e.g., R. v. Terry; R. v. Harrer; Hunter v. Southam). Key formulation: s. 8 protects against unreasonable use of the power of search or seizure by the government of Canada (Hunter, at p. 160).
CaseB_TestB: Fullowka (Cromwell J.) — Anns/Cooper duty-of-care framework for negligence in omissions/third-party harm: prima facie duty requires foreseeability + proximity; if established, ask whether residual policy considerations negate/limit the duty
BaselineB: Common law: Anns/Cooper duty of care framework as developed in SCC cases (Cooper v. Hobart; Edwards v. Law Society; Odhavji Estate; Childs v. Desormeaux; Hill v. Hamilton‑Wentworth). Core statement: duty analysis asks “whether the relationship ... discloses sufficient foreseeability and proximity to establish a prima facie duty of care and, if so, whether there are any residual policy considerations which ought to negate or limit that duty of care” (para. 18).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Pushpanathan framework for interpreting Refugee Convention art. 1F(c): exclusion applies where there is (1) an international consensus that the acts are “sufficiently serious and sustained violations of fundamental human rights as to amount to persecution”, or (2) the acts are “explicitly recognized as contrary to the purposes and principles of the United Nations”; with two main categories: (i) widely accepted international agreement/UN resolution explicitly so declaring (designation “determinative” if reflecting a reasonable consensus), and (ii) acts a court can itself characterize as “serious, sustained and systemic violations of fundamental human rights constituting persecution” (even an isolated violation may suffice if near the core of human rights and e.g. a universal jurisdiction offence).
BaselineA: Statute + treaty: Immigration Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. I-2, s. 2(1) (incorporating Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees, Can. T.S. 1969 No. 6, art. 1F(c)); interpretive baseline includes Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, arts. 31-32 (as applied to treaty interpretation).
CaseB_TestB: Contract damages remoteness test (Hadley v. Baxendale) as applied to employment-contract breach: damages are those that “arise either naturally” or “may reasonably be supposed to have been in the contemplation of both parties, at the time they made the contract, as the probable result of a breach”; applied by asking whether, at contract formation, if the parties had directed their minds to the possibility of the breach, they would have contemplated the type of loss claimed.
BaselineB: Common law: Hadley v. Baxendale (1854) remoteness/foreseeability-in-contemplation rule for contract damages (as adopted in Canadian contract law).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Hodgson confessions/voir dire framework: (1) whether the recipient is a “person in authority” (including those the accused “reasonably believes are acting on behalf of the police or prosecuting authorities”), and (2) if so, Crown must prove the statement was voluntary; plus when a trial judge must hold a voir dire of their own motion (only in “extremely rare cases” where evidence “clearly demonstrates” a close connection to authorities). Key quotes: “no statement made out of court by an accused to a person in authority can be admitted… unless… made freely and voluntarily” (para 12, citing Erven); “the accused’s belief… must also be reasonable” (para 34); “In extremely rare cases… the trial judge must of his or her own motion direct a voir dire” (para 48(9)).
BaselineA: Common law confessions rule (voluntariness requirement for statements to a person in authority), as stated in Erven v. The Queen, [1979] 1 S.C.R. 926 and Ibrahim v. The King, [1914] A.C. 599 (P.C.) (adopted in Prosko v. The King (1922), 63 S.C.R. 226).
CaseB_TestB: McClurg s. 56(2) attribution test (anti-avoidance “diversion” principle): s. 56(2) targets cases where a taxpayer “seeks to avoid receipt” of income by arranging it be received by another; generally, “a dividend payment does not fall within the scope of s. 56(2)” because until declared profits belong to the corporation and otherwise would be retained earnings. Key quotes: s. 56(2) applies where a taxpayer “seeks to avoid receipt of what in his hands would be income by arranging to have the amount received by some other person” (quoting Miller v. M.N.R., 62 D.T.C. 1139); “Consequently, as a general rule, a dividend payment cannot reasonably be considered a benefit diverted… within the contemplation of s. 56(2).”
BaselineB: Statute: Income Tax Act, S.C. 1970-71-72, c. 63, s. 56(2) (interpreted in light of prior case law including Miller v. M.N.R., 62 D.T.C. 1139, and Perrault v. The Queen, [1979] 1 F.C. 155).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Depletion allowance profit computation under Income Tax Regulations, reg. 1201(2): determine profits “reasonably attributable” to production in the normal way (receipts attributable to production minus expenses of earning those receipts), and deduct only the items enumerated in reg. 1201(4) (no implied deduction for long-term research expenses deductible for income under ITA ss. 11(1)(j) and 72).
BaselineA: Regulation (Income Tax Regulations (Can.), reg. 1201(2) and 1201(4)) and related statutory context (Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1952, c. 148, ss. 11(1)(j), 72); interpretive reliance on MNR v. Imperial Oil Ltd., [1960] S.C.R. 735.
CaseB_TestB: Sherman Estate v. Donovan test for discretionary limits on the open court principle (publication bans): applicant must establish (1) openness poses a serious risk to an important public interest; (2) the order is necessary because reasonably alternative measures will not prevent the risk; and (3) proportionality—benefits outweigh negative effects.
BaselineB: Common law discretionary open court/publication ban framework as articulated in Sherman Estate v. Donovan, 2021 SCC 25 (applied).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Kienapple (res judicata) multiple-convictions rule where counts differ in gravity: if the same delict underlies both, convict on the more serious count and acquit/strike the less serious; if a guilty plea is entered to the less serious count first, it must be held in abeyance pending trial of the more serious count and then struck with an acquittal if the more serious conviction is entered
BaselineA: Common law (Kienapple v. The Queen, [1975] 1 S.C.R. 729, rule against multiple convictions for the same delict; with reference to theft/possession line such as R. v. Siggins and Côté v. The Queen)
CaseB_TestB: Availability of habeas corpus to challenge continued detention in parole context: continuation of a valid deprivation of liberty is reviewable only if it becomes unlawful, which occurs only once the inmate has acquired parolee status—i.e., when the parole decision takes effect; if parole is conditional, status arises only if/when the condition is fulfilled
BaselineB: Combination of common law habeas corpus principles as developed in R. v. Miller, Cardinal v. Director of Kent Institution, and Morin v. National Special Handling Unit Review Committee, applied in the statutory parole context (Parole Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. P-2, as amended)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 672.54 disposition test for NCR accused: absolute discharge unless the court/Review Board makes a positive finding the accused poses a “significant threat to the safety of the public”; if significant threat, impose the “least onerous and least restrictive” conditional discharge or detention after considering the four statutory factors
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, Part XX.1, especially s. 672.54; interpreted in light of Charter s. 7 principles and Swain)
CaseB_TestB: Westbank test for characterizing a levy under Constitution Act, 1867 s. 125: a levy is generally a “tax” if it is (1) compulsory/enforceable by law, (2) imposed under legislative authority, (3) levied by a public body, (4) for a public purpose, and (5) unconnected to any regulatory scheme; otherwise it may be a regulatory charge/user fee (pith and substance inquiry)
BaselineB: Constitutional text and doctrine (Constitution Act, 1867, s. 125; drawing on Lawson and Eurig Estate; applied to Indian Act s. 83(1)(a) by-laws)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 2(d) (freedom of association) infringement in labour-relations context: s. 2(d) protects only (1) “the freedom to establish, belong to and maintain an association” and (2) “the exercise in association of the lawful rights of individuals”; it “does not include the right to establish a particular type of association defined in a particular statute”, and (absent exceptional circumstances) imposes no positive obligation on government to provide a statutory labour-relations framework; exclusion from a statutory regime violates s. 2(d) only if it interferes with forming/maintaining an independent association or with exercising lawful rights in association.
BaselineA: Combination: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 2(d) (and s. 32(1) re government action), plus prior SCC jurisprudence defining s. 2(d) in labour context (Reference re Public Service Employee Relations Act (Alta.); PSAC v. Canada; RWDSU v. Saskatchewan; Professional Institute of the Public Service of Canada v. Northwest Territories (Commissioner); Canadian Egg Marketing Agency v. Richardson).
JudgeA: Bastarache J. (for Gonthier, McLachlin, Major and Bastarache JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Joint/co-principal liability in group assaults (manslaughter): “Joint/co‑principal liability flows whenever two or more individuals come together with an intention to commit an offence, are present during the commission of the offence, and contribute to its commission.” For manslaughter, triers should focus on whether the accused’s actions were “a significant contributing cause of death”; in group assaults, “absent a discrete or intervening event, the actions of all assailants can constitute a significant contributing cause to all injuries sustained.”
BaselineB: Statute-focused: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 21(1)(a) (co-principal) and s. 21(1)(c) (abetting), as interpreted in prior case law (notably R. v. Pickton; clarification of implication from R. v. Cabrera / R. v. Shlah).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 4 Federal Child Support Guidelines: when the Table amount is “inappropriate” for incomes over $150,000 (presumption in favour of Table; deviation only if rebutted; assess all circumstances including s. 4(b)(ii) factors)
BaselineA: Regulation/statute: Federal Child Support Guidelines, SOR/97-175, ss. 3 and 4 (especially s. 4(b)(i)-(ii)); interpreted consistently with Divorce Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 3 (2nd Supp.), s. 26.1(2). Key interpretive holding: “the word 'inappropriate' in this section must be broadly defined to mean 'unsuitable' rather than merely 'inadequate'” and there is “a presumption in favour of the Table amounts” rebuttable only on sufficient evidence after examining “all of the circumstances of the case, including the factors expressly listed in s. 4(b)(ii)”.
CaseB_TestB: Classification of an all-risks/multi-peril policy under the B.C. Insurance Act for limitation purposes: if the policy does not fit within Part 5 (Fire Insurance) via s. 119, it is governed by Part 2 (general provisions), and contractual terms cannot undercut Part 2 due to s. 3(a)
BaselineB: Statute/regulation: Insurance Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 226, s. 119 (scope of Part 5) and s. 3(a) (Part 2’s mandatory “floor”); plus statutory condition 14 (Part 5 limitation) and the Insurance Classes Regulation, B.C. Reg. 337/90 (definition of “fire insurance”).
