Key holding: multi-risk policies “cannot be shoehorned into” Part 5; “Since the insured’s policy does not fit into a specific category, it is governed by Part 2”; and s. 3(a) “does not permit the insurer to substitute harsher terms than those provided in Part 2.”
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meiorin unified BFOR test (Human Rights Code s. 13): employer must prove on a balance of probabilities (1) the standard was adopted for a purpose “rationally connected to the performance of the job”; (2) it was adopted “in an honest and good faith belief” it was necessary; and (3) it is “reasonably necessary” — i.e., “it is impossible to accommodate individual employees sharing the characteristics of the claimant without imposing undue hardship upon the employer” (para. 54).
BaselineA: Statute (British Columbia Human Rights Code, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 210, ss. 13(1)(a), (b), (4)), building on prior SCC human-rights/BFOR and accommodation jurisprudence (e.g., O’Malley; Etobicoke; Central Alberta Dairy Pool; Renaud).
CaseB_TestB: Stewart source-of-income test under the Income Tax Act: reject REOP as a stand-alone test; apply a two-stage approach—(i) “Is the activity of the taxpayer undertaken in pursuit of profit, or is it a personal endeavour?”; (ii) if not personal, “is the source of the income a business or property?” (para. 50). Where there is a personal/hobby element, ask: “Does the taxpayer intend to carry on an activity for profit and is there evidence to support that intention?” (para. 54); REOP is only “a factor” (para. 55).
BaselineB: Statute (Income Tax Act, especially ss. 3(a), 9(1)-(2), 18(1)(a), (h), 20(1)(c)(i), 67, 248(1) “personal or living expenses”), with the Court restricting/clarifying prior case-law use of Moldowan’s REOP discussion.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Staged analysis for availability/appropriateness of a conditional sentence under Criminal Code s. 742.1, including when and how s. 718.2(e) (Gladue factors) must be considered for Aboriginal offenders
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, ss. 742.1 and 718-718.2, especially s. 718.2(e)); interpreted through SCC sentencing jurisprudence including R. v. Proulx and R. v. Gladue
CaseB_TestB: Quebec Charter s. 9.1 balancing of a freedom of religion claim (s. 3) against countervailing rights/values/harms to determine whether a party is immune from civil consequences (damages) for breaching a valid contract with religious aspects
BaselineB: Statute (Quebec Charter of human rights and freedoms, ss. 3 and 9.1; applied alongside Civil Code of Québec contract-validity provisions including arts. 1373, 1385, 1412, 1413)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Unreasonable verdict review under Criminal Code s. 686(1)(a)(i): whether the verdict is one that a properly instructed jury (or trial judge) acting judicially could reasonably have rendered; appellate court must thoroughly re-examine the evidence and cannot intervene based only on a vague “lurking doubt” without articulating why the verdict is inconsistent with a judicial appreciation of the evidence.
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(a)(i)) as interpreted in SCC common law (R. v. Yebes; reaffirmed in R. v. Biniaris).
CaseB_TestB: Institutional consultation / natural justice on judicial review: consultation is permissible and does not create apprehension of bias or lack of independence if (1) it is not imposed by a superior authority, (2) it is limited to questions of policy and law, and (3) decision-makers remain free to decide; for audi alteram partem, an applicant must show an actual breach (not merely an apprehended breach), and if the rules are met a presumption of regularity applies so a change from draft to final reasons alone does not imply impropriety.
BaselineB: Common law procedural fairness/natural justice framework from SCC cases (IWA v. Consolidated-Bathurst Packaging Ltd.; Tremblay v. Quebec (Commission des affaires sociales)).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: “Functional and structural” approach to whether a statutory court/tribunal has jurisdiction to grant a Charter remedy under s. 24(1) (i.e., the third branch of the Mills ‘court of competent jurisdiction’ test: ‘power to grant the remedy sought’). Key formulation: the ‘paramount question’ is whether, ‘by virtue of its function and structure, [it] is an appropriate forum for ordering the Charter remedy in issue’; if so, ‘it can reasonably be inferred, in the absence of any contrary indication, that the legislature intended’ it to have that remedial power (paras. 35, 43-46).
BaselineA: Combination: Charter + common law. Baseline is Charter s. 24(1) (“court of competent jurisdiction”) and the common-law/constitutional test from Mills v. The Queen defining such a court as having (1) jurisdiction over the person; (2) jurisdiction over the subject matter; and (3) jurisdiction to grant the remedy (para. 15).
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 11(d) ‘inexorable connection’ test for statutory presumptions: a presumption complies with s. 11(d) ‘solely if proof of the substituted fact leads inexorably to the existence of the essential element it replaces’; the nexus must be ‘nothing less than inexorable’ and must ‘necessarily hold true in all cases’ (paras. 52-53). Applied to strike down Criminal Code s. 172.1(3) (presumption of belief from representation of age).
BaselineB: Combination: Charter + common law. Baseline is Charter s. 11(d) (presumption of innocence) and SCC jurisprudence on presumptions (Whyte; Downey; Audet) requiring an “inexorable” link between the basic/substituted fact and the presumed essential element (paras. 52-53).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Existence of a valid partnership (for s. 96 ITA loss deduction): at formation, evidence must show alleged partners were “(1) carrying on a business, (2) in common, (3) with a view to profit”; tax motivation does not negate partnership if these ingredients are present; courts take a pragmatic approach and “weigh the relevant factors in the context of all the surrounding circumstances”.
BaselineA: Combination: Income Tax Act, s. 96 (loss deduction depends on being a partner) + common-law partnership test from Continental Bank Leasing Corp. v. Canada, [1998] 2 S.C.R. 298 (as reiterated in Backman v. Canada, 2001 SCC 10).
CaseB_TestB: Adequacy of jury instructions on credibility and reasonable doubt (W.(D.) context): where credibility is central, the judge must explain the relationship between credibility assessment and the Crown’s burden; a general reasonable-doubt instruction is insufficient; the charge must make it “crystal clear” the burden never shifts and must avoid the “credibility contest” error; failure to use W.(D.)’s exact three questions is not fatal if, read as a whole, the jury “could not have been under any misapprehension as to the correct burden and standard of proof to apply”.
BaselineB: Common law: jury-charge framework from R. v. W. (D.), [1991] 1 S.C.R. 742 (and subsequent SCC applications such as S. (W.D.) and Avetysan).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Customs Act s. 48(5)(a)(iv) “condition of sale” test for dutiable royalties/licence fees: royalties/licence fees are dutiable only if paid “as a condition of the sale of the goods for export to Canada”; “Unless a vendor is entitled to refuse to sell licensed goods to the purchaser or repudiate the contract of sale where the purchaser fails to pay royalties or licence fees, s. 48(5)(a)(iv) is inapplicable.”
BaselineA: Statute: Customs Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (2nd Supp.), s. 48(5)(a)(iv) (and related definition in s. 45(1) “price paid or payable”).
CaseB_TestB: ITA s. 224 “requirement to pay” trigger (bank liability) in cheque-deposit context: a bank is not “liable to make a payment” to the tax debtor merely because the debtor is named as payee; “What is on the back of the cheque — the instructions or the endorsement — is crucial”; where instructions are to deposit to a joint account, the bank’s obligation is to the joint account holders, and “the mere fact that cheques payable to [the tax debtor] were delivered to the Bank for deposit did not make the latter liable to make a payment to the former within the meaning of s. 224(1) of the ITA.”
BaselineB: Statute: Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), s. 224(1), interpreted alongside Bills of Exchange Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. B-4 (notably ss. 84(1), 84(3), 86(1), 126, 138(2), 165(3)).
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Quebec Labour Code s. 45 successorship in subcontracting: s. 45 may apply where the transferee, beyond performing similar functions, receives a "right to operate part of the transferor’s undertaking" and has a "sufficient degree of autonomy" assessed contextually (including by the "criterion of the subordination of the employees to the contractors").
BaselineA: Statute (Labour Code, R.S.Q., c. C-27, ss. 45-46) as interpreted in U.E.S., Local 298 v. Bibeault and Lester (W.W.) (1978) Ltd.; applied through Labour Court post-Bibeault principles.
CaseB_TestB: Jarvis "predominant purpose" test for when a CCRA audit becomes a penal investigation: the adversarial relationship is engaged where the "predominant purpose" of the inquiry is determining penal liability; "no one factor is determinative" and the judge must assess the "totality of the circumstances" (with Jarvis factors applied).
BaselineB: Common law/Charter framework from R. v. Jarvis interpreting use of Income Tax Act requirement powers (ss. 231.1(1), 231.2(1)) in light of Charter ss. 7 and 8.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Anns/Cooper duty of care test for statutory regulators: (1) prima facie duty requires reasonably foreseeable harm + proximity (starting with analogous categories; if none, whether a new duty should be recognized; proximity grounded in the governing statute); (2) if prima facie duty, ask whether residual policy considerations negate the duty
BaselineA: Common law (Anns v. Merton London Borough Council; Kamloops (City of) v. Nielsen), as clarified/applied in Cooper v. Hobart; applied in a statutory-regulator context with reference to the Law Society Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. L.8 (notably s. 9 immunity and the Act’s public-interest/client-protection scheme)
JudgeA: The Chief Justice and Major J.
CaseB_TestB: Section 1 (Oakes) justification analysis, applied to a fiscal-crisis justification: pressing and substantial objective; rational connection; minimal impairment; proportionality of effects (including weighing salutary vs deleterious effects), with rejection of adding a separate ‘separation of powers’ step
BaselineB: Constitution (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 1) and the Oakes framework (R. v. Oakes), as developed in subsequent s. 1 jurisprudence
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Pragmatic and functional approach (Pushpanathan) to select the standard of review: (1) privative clause/statutory appeal, (2) relative expertise, (3) purpose of the Act/provision, (4) nature of the problem; applied to hold correctness for CRTC’s interpretation of Telecommunications Act s. 43(5)
BaselineA: Common law (judicial review standard of review framework) applied to a statutory appeal under Telecommunications Act, S.C. 1993, c. 38, s. 64(1); key baseline case cited: Pushpanathan v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), [1998] 1 S.C.R. 982
CaseB_TestB: Sentencing treatment of collateral consequences and related mitigating considerations: collateral consequences may be considered if they “relate to the offence and the circumstances of the offender”, but “the fundamental principle of proportionality must prevail”; plus defined limits on (i) mistake of law mitigation (requires “honest but mistaken belief” in legality; “confusion or uncertainty” is not enough) and (ii) non-impairment mitigation (must be “limited”; offender bears onus on balance of probabilities)
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code sentencing framework): ss. 718 to 718.2 (including proportionality in s. 718.1) and offence provision s. 255(3.2)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 2(b) infringement for sign restrictions: a by-law that restricts the use of an "optimum means of communication" (posting signs) to certain places directly infringes expression; then the government must justify under Charter s. 1 (pressing objective, rational connection, minimal impairment, proportionality of effects). Key quotes: "By restricting the right to use this optimum means of expression to certain designated places, the impugned by-law directly infringes freedom of expression" (para. 26); and s. 1 requires the law be "proportionate to the goal in the sense of furthering the goal, being carefully tailored to avoid excessive impairment of the right, and productive of benefits that outweigh the detriment" (para. 28).
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 2(b) and 1 (Oakes proportionality framework as refined in Dagenais and Thomson Newspapers, as summarized in Sharpe and adopted at para. 28).
CaseB_TestB: Canadian Bill of Rights property due process limits: (1) no due process right to notice/hearing before Parliament enacts expropriative legislation; (2) procedural due process (notice/opportunity to contest) arises only "in the context of an adjudication" of individual rights/obligations; (3) no substantive due process protection against "unambiguous" legislative expropriation—Parliament may expropriate (even without compensation) if intent is "clear and unambiguous". Key quotes: "the Bill of Rights guarantees notice and some opportunity to contest ... only in the context of an adjudication" (para. 42); "no adjudicative procedure is necessary for the non-discretionary application of a law to incontestable facts" (para. 45); "does not protect against the expropriation of property by the passage of unambiguous legislation" (para. 51); and expropriation is permitted where intent is "clear and unambiguous" (paras. 52-57).
BaselineB: Statute: Canadian Bill of Rights, ss. 1(a) and 2(e), applied to Department of Veterans Affairs Act, s. 5.1(4).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Copyright Act s. 3(1) “reproduction” requires copying that brings an additional/new copy into existence; a purely physical transfer of the same ink layer to a new substrate, with no multiplication, is not “production (or reproduction) ... in any material form”
BaselineA: Statute (Copyright Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-42, especially ss. 3(1), 38(1); also the Act’s moral rights provisions ss. 28.2(1), 28.2(3) used to maintain the economic/moral rights boundary)
CaseB_TestB: Reasonableness simpliciter on judicial review: a decision is unreasonable only if “there is no line of analysis within the given reasons that could reasonably lead the tribunal from the evidence before it to the conclusion at which it arrived”; if any sufficient reasons are “tenable” on a “somewhat probing examination”, the court must not interfere
BaselineB: Common law (pragmatic and functional approach and standards of review jurisprudence, especially Pushpanathan v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration); Canada (Director of Investigation and Research) v. Southam Inc.; U.E.S., Local 298 v. Bibeault; also applied in the context of the Law Society Act, 1996, S.N.B. 1996, c. 89)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Privacy Act s. 22(1)(b) exemption: refusal to disclose personal information only if disclosure “could reasonably be expected” to be injurious to the conduct of lawful investigations (including future investigations), requiring a “clear and direct connection” between the specific disclosure and the alleged injury, supported by case-specific “real grounds” (not mere non-consent or general assertions).
BaselineA: Statute (Privacy Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. P-21, ss. 12(1), 22(1)(b), 22(3), 47, 49; applied harmoniously with Official Languages Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 31 (4th Supp.), ss. 60, 72-74).
CaseB_TestB: Adverse inference / presumption of fact in medical causation (CCQ art. 2849): even where defendant negligence undermines proof and plaintiff adduces “some” evidence, the trier of fact is not required to draw an adverse inference; any presumption of fact is discretionary and must be “serious, precise and concordant”, assessed on a legal (not scientific) standard, and reviewed on palpable and overriding error.
BaselineB: Statute/civil code evidence rules (Civil Code of Québec, art. 2849) as informed by SCC causation jurisprudence (Snell v. Farrell; St-Jean v. Mercier).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Validity/effect of a zoning “holding regulation”: interpret the by-law’s substance—if it clearly implements a lawful development freeze, superfluous wording about future amendment does not invalidate the operative prohibition (i.e., “Notwithstanding any other provisions… no building… may be… erected to contain three or more dwelling units…”).
BaselineA: Statute (The Planning Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 349, s. 35(1) and related appeal mechanism in s. 35(22)) applied to/through the municipal zoning by-law (By-law 306-480 as amended by 306(bc)-504, especially s. 4 inserting “11. Holding Regulation”).
CaseB_TestB: Custody determination under the Infants Act: the “paramount consideration” is the welfare of the children; parental conduct/fault in the marriage breakdown is relevant only as one factor bearing on “relative fitness” and “each particular case must be judged on its own circumstances.”
BaselineB: Statute (The Infants Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 222, s. 1(1)) plus prior custody jurisprudence referenced (e.g., McKee v. McKee; Bickley v. Bickley; Retzer v. Retzer; Re L.).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: OSC s. 17(1) disclosure of compelled investigation material: apply Stinchcombe-style relevance (“reasonable possibility” of relevance to full answer and defence) within a s. 17(1) “public interest” balancing; disclosure may be ordered globally unless a party shows “no reasonable possibility” a particular item is relevant
BaselineA: Statute/regulation: Securities Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. S.5, ss. 16(1) (confidentiality) and 17(1) (OSC may order disclosure if it considers it “in the public interest”), plus OSC Rules of Practice r. 3.3(2) (staff must disclose all “relevant” material). SCC uses the Stinchcombe relevance standard (“reasonable possibility” of relevance) as the meaning of “relevant” for disclosure scope.
CaseB_TestB: Framework to classify requested state-held information as first-party (Stinchcombe/McNeil) vs third-party (O’Connor) disclosure: ask (1) is it in prosecuting Crown possession/control? (2) if not, should police/other Crown entity have supplied it because it is “fruits of the investigation” or “obviously relevant”? If neither, O’Connor applies and accused must show “likely relevance” (“reasonable possibility” the info is logically probative)
BaselineB: Common law disclosure regimes: Stinchcombe (first-party disclosure), McNeil (police/Crown inquiry duties; “fruits of the investigation”/“obviously relevant”), and O’Connor (third-party disclosure; “likely relevant” threshold). Also statutory context discussed: Criminal Code, s. 258(1)(c) presumption of accuracy (but the key test is the common-law disclosure-classification framework).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Misfeasance in public office (defining elements): (1) “deliberate and unlawful conduct in the exercise of public functions”; and (2) “awareness that the conduct is unlawful and likely to injure the plaintiff” (plus causation and compensable loss).
BaselineA: Common law (tort of misfeasance in public office), developed with reference to cases including Roncarelli v. Duplessis and comparative authorities (e.g., Three Rivers). Statutory breaches (Police Services Act, ss. 41(1)(b), 113(9)) supply the alleged unlawfulness but do not create a standalone statutory-breach tort.
CaseB_TestB: Eligibility for Quebec seats under Supreme Court Act, s. 6: appointee must be a current member “from among” the Quebec Court of Appeal/Superior Court or “from among the advocates” of Quebec (i.e., current Barreau du Québec member) and meet the 10-year standing requirement via s. 5; plus constitutional rule that changes to SCC “composition” (including ss. 4(1), 5, 6 eligibility) require unanimity under Constitution Act, 1982, s. 41(d).
BaselineB: Statutory/constitutional interpretation: Supreme Court Act, ss. 5 and 6 (and attempted ss. 5.1, 6.1), interpreted in light of Constitution Act, 1982, Part V (ss. 41(d), 42(1)(d)) and Constitution Act, 1867, s. 101.
JudgeB: McLachlin C.J. and LeBel, Abella, Cromwell, Karakatsanis and Wagner JJ.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Public-interest administrative penalty under Securities Act, s. 162: once a contravention is found, the Commission may consider the full context (including general deterrence and settlements) and a reviewing court asks whether there is a rational basis and reviews the order globally for reasonableness
BaselineA: Statute (Securities Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 418, s. 162; also s. 167(3) on appeal powers). Key statutory trigger: s. 162 applies if the Commission (a) determines a contravention and (b) considers it in the public interest to order an administrative penalty up to $100,000.
CaseB_TestB: Adequacy of jury instructions on alternative routes to murder liability where others may be involved: the trial judge must instruct on routes to liability arising on the evidence; here, liability could be found if the accused "acted in concert" / was an "active participant in the killing" (and correcting an erroneous 'actual shooter' direction did not cause a miscarriage of justice)
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 21 (party liability); also ss. 229, 231(5), 686(1)(b)(iii)). The case applies the duty to instruct the jury on routes to liability supported by the evidence, including party liability concepts.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Cross-examination on unproven facts requires only a "good faith basis" (no evidentiary foundation/undertaking to call evidence required); judge may inquire only where factual predicate is "manifestly tenuous or suspect"
BaselineA: Common law (scope/limits of cross-examination and counsel’s duties), as reflected in authorities the Court relies on including R. v. Bencardino (Ont. C.A.) and this Court’s discussion of R. v. Howard (SCC) and Browne v. Dunn (H.L.)
CaseB_TestB: Federal paramountcy test: provincial law is inoperative only if (1) operational conflict (impossible dual compliance) or (2) frustration of federal purpose (requires "clear proof of purpose" and incompatibility); apply a restrained, cooperative-federalism approach
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine of federal paramountcy (operational conflict / frustration of purpose) applied to statutes including Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. B-3, ss. 243, 243(1.1), 244, 72(1) and The Saskatchewan Farm Security Act, S.S. 1988-89, c. S-17.1, Part II, ss. 9-22
JudgeB: Abella and Gascon JJ. (for the majority)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Parliamentary privilege existence/scope test (authoritative precedent first; otherwise necessity): court asks if the claimed category/scope of privilege is authoritatively established for Canada or Westminster; if not, claimant must show the activity is "so closely and directly connected" to legislative/deliberative functions (incl. holding government to account) that outside interference would undermine required autonomy to do the work "with dignity and efficiency" (Vaid, paras. 39-40, 46).
BaselineA: Combination: constitutional/statutory privilege framework (Constitution Act, 1867, s. 18; Parliament of Canada Act, s. 4) plus common-law/constitutional doctrine of necessity from privilege jurisprudence (e.g., New Brunswick Broadcasting; Harvey) as synthesized in Vaid.
CaseB_TestB: Interpretive test for Tobacco Act s. 22(3) ban on ads appealing to youth: s. 22(3) "requires the prosecution in a given case to prove that there are reasonable grounds to believe that the advertisement ... could be appealing to young persons", meaning "particularly attractive and of interest to young persons, as distinguished from the general population" (JTI-Macdonald, para. 89).
BaselineB: Statute: Tobacco Act, S.C. 1997, c. 13, s. 22(3) (interpreted bilingually/purposively), applied within Charter s. 1 proportionality framework (Oakes) but with the key SCC contribution being the statutory meaning of s. 22(3).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: GAAR “abusive tax avoidance” (s. 245(4)) analysis: after tax benefit and avoidance transaction are established, ask whether it “cannot be reasonably concluded that a tax benefit would be consistent with the object, spirit or purpose of the provisions relied upon by the taxpayer” (para. 31(1)(3)); courts use a “unified textual, contextual and purposive analysis” (para. 31(4)) and may find abuse where transactions “lack a proper basis relative to the object, spirit or purpose” or are “wholly dissimilar” to what the provisions contemplate (para. 31(6)).
BaselineA: Statute (Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.)): GAAR framework in ss. 245(1)-(4) (especially s. 245(4)); interaction with ss. 18(13) and 96(1). The Court follows the companion SCC framework in Canada Trustco Mortgage Co. v. Canada, 2005 SCC 54 (paras. 31-33).
CaseB_TestB: Vancouver Sun informer-privilege procedure / guiding rule: apply a two-stage procedure where (1) the court verifies privilege—“evidence that a person is a police informer automatically engages the privilege” (para. 48) and “even the claim of informer privilege must not be disclosed” (para. 48); then (2) having established privilege, the judge must conduct proceedings giving “full effect” to the “complete and total bar on any disclosure of the informer’s identity” while “limiting, as much as possible, any impairment of the open court principle” (paras. 47, 72-73), generally by measures such as creating a sealed “parallel proceeding” with its own record number and releasing a redacted public judgment where feasible (paras. 75, 79, 82).
BaselineB: Common law (informer privilege and open court principle) as structured by Named Person v. Vancouver Sun, 2007 SCC 43 (applied; paras. 47-51).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “lawful authority” for whistleblower protection under s. 74(1)(a): includes internal employer authorities who can address the wrongdoing (“up the ladder” reporting)
BaselineA: Statute: The Labour Standards Act, R.S.S. 1978, c. L-1, s. 74(1)(a) (and s. 74(2))
CaseB_TestB: Waiver of insurer’s right to rely on dishonoured-cheque non-payment rule: waiver requires “express and unequivocal language or conduct”
BaselineB: Statute plus common law: The Alberta Insurance Act, R.S.A. 1970, c. 187, s. 238(1) (dishonoured cheque deemed not payment) applied with the common-law waiver requirement as reflected in McGeachie v. North American Life Insurance Company (1893), 23 S.C.R. 148
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “lawful authority” for whistleblower protection under s. 74(1)(a): includes internal employer authorities who can address the wrongdoing (“up the ladder” reporting)
BaselineA: Statute — The Labour Standards Act, R.S.S. 1978, c. L-1, s. 74(1)(a) (and s. 74(2)); interpreted using the modern purposive/contextual approach (Rizzo & Rizzo Shoes; Bell ExpressVu) and Saskatchewan Interpretation Act, 1995, s. 10
CaseB_TestB: Common law joinder test (Clunas) for a joint trial of provincial offences and summary conviction Criminal Code offences: (1) sufficient factual nexus (functional approach to “could initially have been jointly charged”); and (2) joint trial is in the interests of justice (weighing costs/benefits)
BaselineB: Common law — R. v. Clunas, [1992] 1 S.C.R. 595 (two-part joinder test), applied alongside statutory context (Provincial Offences Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. P.33, ss. 2(1), 47(1); Criminal Code provisions on summary conviction procedure)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal indecency (bawdy-house) two-step harm-based test: Crown must prove beyond a reasonable doubt (1) conduct “causes harm or presents a significant risk of harm” (e.g., unwanted public exposure; predisposition to anti-social behaviour; physical/psychological harm) and (2) the harm/risk is “of a degree that is incompatible with the proper functioning of society” (R. v. Kouri, para. 10, following Labaye/Butler).
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 210(1) (and related definition context in s. 197(1)); test structure stated as “based on the guidelines emerging from R. v. Butler, [1992] 1 S.C.R. 452” and elaborated in the companion case R. v. Labaye, 2005 SCC 80.
CaseB_TestB: Pointe Gourde / s. 27(1)(a) scheme-disregard test for expropriation compensation: to decide whether a regulation’s value-impact is ignored, the “key question is whether the enactment was made with a view to the expropriation or, conversely, was an independent enactment”; the inquiry “involves examining the purposes and effects of the enactment”, and “causation does not drive the inquiry” (St. John’s (City) v. Lynch, 2024 SCC 17, paras. 46-54).
BaselineB: Statute informed by common law: Expropriation Act, R.S.N.L. 1990, c. E-19, s. 27(1)(a) (“no account shall be taken of the compulsory acquisition of the land”), incorporating the common law Pointe Gourde principle (Pointe Gourde Quarrying and Transport Co. v. Sub-Intendent of Crown Lands, [1947] A.C. 565).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Interpretation of Alberta Limitations Act, s. 12 in conflicts cases: s. 12 applies Alberta’s limitations law only to "live" foreign causes of action and does not revive claims already time-barred under the applicable foreign substantive law (lex loci delicti, including its limitation period)
BaselineA: Combination: statute (Limitations Act, R.S.A. 2000, c. L-12, s. 12) interpreted against common law conflicts rule from Tolofson v. Jensen (lex loci delicti includes the foreign limitation period as substantive law)
CaseB_TestB: Ancillary powers doctrine (Waterfield/Dedman framework) for common law police powers: define the asserted power and liberty interest; then (1) whether conduct falls within scope of a police duty; (2) whether conduct is a justifiable exercise—i.e., "reasonably necessary" assessed by weighing (i) importance of the duty, (ii) necessity of the liberty interference, and (iii) extent of the interference; onus on the state; no common law power to arrest a lawful person to prevent an apprehended breach of the peace by others
BaselineB: Common law: ancillary powers doctrine from Dedman v. The Queen (adopting Waterfield), as applied/structured in R. v. MacDonald (three-factor reasonable necessity analysis)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Palmer/Lévesque test for admitting fresh evidence on a sentence appeal (interests of justice): (1) due diligence; (2) relevance to a decisive/potentially decisive sentencing issue; (3) credibility; (4) could reasonably be expected to have affected the result
BaselineA: Common law (Palmer v. The Queen; adapted to sentence appeals in R. v. Lévesque) applied under Criminal Code, s. 687(1)
CaseB_TestB: Section 8 reasonable expectation of privacy (REP) analysis: REP assessed on the totality of the circumstances along four lines of inquiry—(1) subject matter; (2) claimant’s direct interest; (3) subjective expectation; (4) objective reasonableness (normative) having regard to the totality of the circumstances
BaselineB: Common law Charter s. 8 framework (e.g., Edwards; Tessling; Spencer; Cole; Marakah) applied to Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 8
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Secondary infringement under Copyright Act s. 27(2)(e): requires “hypothetical infringement” and an exclusive licensee cannot establish it where the hypothetical maker is the copyright owner (owner cannot infringe its own copyright; licensee’s remedy is in contract, not infringement).
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 11(h) “punished … again” for retrospective parole changes: “dominant consideration” is the extent to which “an offender’s settled expectation of liberty has been thwarted”; “retrospective frustration of an expectation of liberty … constitutes punishment”; automatic lengthening of incarceration is a “clearest of cases”; otherwise ask whether the change “substantially increase[s] the risk of additional incarceration” (with indicators like individualized decision-making and procedural safeguards).
BaselineB: Constitution (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 11(h); applied to Abolition of Early Parole Act, S.C. 2011, c. 11, s. 10(1))
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Sentencing of hybrid offences prosecuted summarily: treat as summary conviction for sentencing; maximum sentence available without “worst offender/worst offence” constraint; appellate intervention only for error of principle/relevant factor/overemphasis or demonstrably unfit sentence
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, Part XXIII sentencing principles; especially ss. 716, 718.1, 718.2(d),(e), 787(1)) plus prior SCC rejection of “worst offender/worst offence” as a constraint (R. v. Cheddesingh; R. v. L.M.)
CaseB_TestB: Admissibility of Mr. Big confessions (new common law rule): presumptively inadmissible unless Crown proves (balance of probabilities) probative value (reliability) outweighs prejudicial effect; reliability assessed via circumstances and markers; plus separate abuse-of-process scrutiny for coercive/abusive operations
BaselineB: Common law evidence (party admissions exception to hearsay: R. v. Evans; existing PV>PE discretion; related doctrines including abuse of process and bad character balancing: R. v. Handy; plus confessions/right-to-silence limits noted via R. v. McIntyre, R. v. Hebert, R. v. Grandinetti)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Adequacy of jury charge (Azoulay principle): trial judge must (except rare needless cases) review substantial parts of the evidence and present the defence theory so the jury can appreciate the evidence and apply the law; trial judge has considerable latitude in how much evidence to review, so long as jurors get an adequate understanding of the relationship between essential evidence and the issues
BaselineA: Common law (Azoulay v. The Queen; R. v. Jacquard)
CaseB_TestB: Trade-marks Act s. 6 confusion test: whether, having regard to 'all the surrounding circumstances' (including s. 6(5) factors), use of both marks in the same area would be likely to lead the 'casual consumer somewhat in a hurry' to the mistaken inference that the wares/services come from the same source; no requirement of 'resemblance or linkage' between wares/services and no single factor (including fame or difference in wares) is determinative
BaselineB: Statute (Trade-marks Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. T-13, ss. 6(2) and 6(5))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 172.1(1)(c) “luring a child”: three essential elements — (1) intentional communication by computer; (2) with a person the accused “knows or believes” is under 14; (3) “for the specific purpose of facilitating” a listed secondary offence; intent is subjective and “facilitating” means “helping to bring about and making easier or more probable” (Legare, paras. 3, 28, 31-32, 36, 42).
BaselineA: Statute — Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 172.1(1)(c) (as then worded), with listed secondary offences including ss. 151 and 152.
CaseB_TestB: Enforcement of a forum selection clause: absent specific legislation, the court should enforce the clause unless there is “strong cause” to displace the chosen forum; the test is “discretionary in nature” (Momentous.ca, para. 9, citing Pompey).
BaselineB: Common law — Z.I. Pompey Industrie v. ECU-Line N.V., 2003 SCC 27 (“strong cause” test), applied within the procedural setting of Ontario Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 21.01(3)(a).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Leave to appeal under Supreme Court Act s. 40(1): SCC may grant leave only if it is of the opinion the question is “by reason of its public importance or the importance of any issue of law or any issue of mixed law and fact… one that ought to be decided by the Supreme Court or is, for any other reason, of such a nature or significance as to warrant decision by it” (s. 40(1)); jurisdiction extends to “any final or other judgment” (including an order granting/refusing an extension of time) unless excluded by s. 40(3).
BaselineA: Statute: Supreme Court Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. S-26, ss. 2, 40(1), 40(3) (with reference to Criminal Code ss. 691-693 for exclusions).
CaseB_TestB: Access to Information Act s. 27(1) third-party notice threshold: disclose without notice only in “clear cases” where there is “no reason to believe that the record might contain” s. 20(1) exempt material; refuse without notice where there is “no reason to believe that the information is subject to disclosure”; otherwise notice is required, including where the head “is in doubt about whether the information is exempt” or “intends to disclose severed material pursuant to s. 25” (paras. 72-78, 84).
BaselineB: Statute: Access to Information Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. A-1, ss. 20(1), 25, 27(1), 28, 44.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Reasonableness of departing from the common law “knock and announce” rule when executing a dwelling-house search warrant: police must ordinarily give (i) notice of presence, (ii) notice of authority, and (iii) notice of purpose (Eccles), but if they depart, “there is an onus on them to explain why”; if challenged, “the Crown must lay an evidentiary framework” showing “reasonable grounds to be concerned about the possibility of harm ... or about the destruction of evidence” (Cornell, paras. 18-20).
BaselineA: Common law + constitutional baseline: Charter s. 8 reasonableness framework from R. v. Collins (search must be authorized by law, law reasonable, and search conducted reasonably) and the common law “knock and announce” rule from Eccles v. Bourque; also relies on Genest/Gimson for justification requirements when departing from announced entry.
CaseB_TestB: Implied assertions are hearsay when tendered for the truth of their contents; such hearsay is “presumptively inadmissible” unless within a traditional exception or admitted under the principled approach requiring “indicia of reliability and necessity ... established on a voir dire” (Mapara framework; Baldree, paras. 34, 48).
BaselineB: Common law hearsay rule and the SCC’s principled hearsay framework: R. v. Khan (move to principled approach) and R. v. Mapara (four-part framework for exceptions/necessity/reliability), with defining features of hearsay from R. v. Khelawon.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: State Immunity Act commercial activity exception: determine whether proceedings “relate to any commercial activity of the foreign state” by examining “the nature of the acts ... in their full context, which includes the purpose of the acts” (not merely whether authorized by the state or aimed at public interests).
BaselineA: Statute: State Immunity Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. S-18, ss. 3 (general immunity), 5 (commercial activity exception), and s. 2 (“commercial activity” definition). Interpreted in light of SCC precedent Re Canada Labour Code, [1992] 2 S.C.R. 50 (contextual nature+purpose approach).
CaseB_TestB: Miscarriage of justice / curative proviso framework under Criminal Code s. 686(1): (1) determine whether an irregularity rendered the trial unfair or created an appearance of unfairness (case-by-case, guided by factors such as centrality, gravity/likely impact, jury vs judge-alone, remedial steps, cumulative effect, and counsel’s response); (2) if curable, apply the proviso only where conviction was “inevitable” (no reasonable possibility the verdict would have differed).
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(a)(ii)-(iii) and s. 686(1)(b)(iii)-(iv) (curative proviso). Built on prior SCC proviso jurisprudence cited (e.g., Colpitts; Wildman; Bevan; S. (P.L.)).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Journalist-source privilege in civil proceedings (Quebec): threshold relevance + Wigmore 4-factor test with context-specific balancing at factor 4
BaselineA: Common law (Wigmore case-by-case privilege framework as applied in R. v. National Post, 2010 SCC 16) plus Quebec civil evidence/procedure context (C.C.Q. art. 2857 relevance; C.C.P. art. 46 general powers)
CaseB_TestB: Court jurisdiction to review voluntary association decisions: requires an underlying legal right; contract exists only if general contract formation (especially objective intention to create legal relations) is shown
BaselineB: Common law (Highwood Congregation of Jehovah’s Witnesses (Judicial Committee) v. Wall, 2018 SCC 26; general contract formation principles including objective intention to create legal relations)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Quebec Charter s. 49(2) punitive (exemplary) damages: admissible autonomously (not dependent on compensatory damages) and awarded where there is (1) “unlawful” and (2) “intentional” interference with a Charter right; “intentionality refers not to the intent to commit the fault but rather to the intent to cause the result thereof” (paras. 57, 60).
BaselineA: Statute (Quebec Charter, s. 49(2)) interpreted alongside Civil Code of Québec, art. 1621; and prior SCC interpretation of s. 49(2) in St-Ferdinand (unlawful interference/intentionality) and debate in Béliveau St-Jacques (autonomy/incidental nature).
CaseB_TestB: YCJA jurisdiction for youth judicial interim release on s. 469 charges after election: (1) “the proceeding” in YCJA ss. 13(2)-(3) “is not confined to the trial” but “includes any step taken ... after the young person elects to be tried at the superior court, including any pre-trial application for judicial interim release, until trial” (paras. 9, 15); and (2) YCJA s. 33(8) gives release power to “a youth justice court judge” (including both s. 13(1) designated youth court judges and ss. 13(2)-(3) deemed superior court judges), so jurisdiction is concurrent (paras. 23-25).
BaselineB: Statute (Youth Criminal Justice Act ss. 13(1)-(3), 28, 33(8), 67) interpreted in relation to Criminal Code ss. 469 and 522(1).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Miscarriage of justice on appeal: whether trial defects “affected the trial judge’s appreciation of the evidence or rendered the proceedings unfair, so as to give rise to a miscarriage of justice” (para. 8); plus jurisdiction point that failure to plead it “does not deprive a court of appeal of jurisdiction” (para. 4).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code appeal powers; appeal as of right under s. 693(1)(a), and the appellate concept of “miscarriage of justice” as the governing standard for intervention).
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 13 engagement turns on whether prior compelled testimony is “incriminating evidence”: s. 13 applies only if the witness gave “incriminating evidence” under compulsion; “incriminating evidence” means evidence the Crown could use “to prove or assist in proving one or more of the essential elements of the offence” (paras. 8-10). Non-incriminating prior evidence used only for impeachment does not trigger s. 13 (paras. 22-25).
BaselineB: Statute/constitutional text (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 13) as interpreted in prior SCC jurisprudence (notably R. v. Henry, R. v. Kuldip, R. v. Noël, Dubois v. The Queen).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “in association with” a criminal organization (Criminal Code s. 467.12): offence must (1) advance, at least to some degree, the interests of a criminal organization (a nexus between predicate offence and organization, not merely accused’s association), and (2) be committed while the accused knowingly dealt with the criminal organization (subjective mens rea; knowledge or wilful blindness).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 467.12(1) “for the benefit of, at the direction of, or in association with, a criminal organization”; related definition in s. 467.1).
CaseB_TestB: Test for “compulsion” under Motor Vehicle Act s. 61(1) (for Charter s. 7 use-immunity): whether, at the time the accident was reported, the driver gave the report on the basis of an “honest and reasonably held belief” that they were required by law to report the accident to the person to whom it was given; accused bears burden on balance of probabilities to show compulsion.
BaselineB: Combination: statute and Charter (Motor Vehicle Act, R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 288, s. 61(1) and (1.1) reporting duty; Charter, s. 7 principle against self-incrimination as applied to compelled statements).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 8 sniffer-dog search: police need “reasonable suspicion” grounded in “objectively discernible facts” assessed on the “totality of the circumstances” (a “constellation of factors”), through the lens of a reasonable officer; the question is whether facts indicate the “possibility of criminal behaviour” (not probability) — “If so, the objective component of the test will have been met. If not, the inquiry is at an end.”
BaselineA: Common law Charter s. 8 framework for sniffer-dog searches and “reasonable suspicion” from R. v. Kang-Brown, 2008 SCC 18 and R. v. A.M., 2008 SCC 19 (as clarified in companion R. v. Chehil, 2013 SCC 49).
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 11(i) “punishment” test (reformulated from Rodgers): a measure is punishment if (1) it is a consequence of conviction forming part of the “arsenal of sanctions”, and either (2) it is imposed in furtherance of the “purpose and principles of sentencing”, or (3) it has a “significant impact on an offender’s liberty or security interests” (i.e., “significantly constrain[s]” lawful conduct or imposes “significant burdens” not imposed on the public).
BaselineB: Common law Charter s. 11(i) “punishment” test from R. v. Rodgers, 2006 SCC 15 (applied to Criminal Code s. 161(1)(c), (d)).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Civil law ‘rectification’ via interpretation under art. 1425 C.C.Q.: where the evidence proves a discrepancy between the parties’ proven common intention and the intention declared in the written instruments, the court may recognize the parties’ mutual amendments/corrections to remedy the error (subject to third-party rights). Key quotes: the court must seek the parties’ intention and resolve the discrepancy — “the determination of the common intention, or will, of the parties represents a true exercise of interpretation” and “If such a writing contains an error, the court must, once the error is proved ... note the error and ensure that it is remedied.”
BaselineA: Statute (Civil Code of Québec, art. 1425; also relies on general C.C.Q. contract principles such as consensualism and amendment/annulment (e.g., art. 1439))
CaseB_TestB: Bank ‘put upon inquiry’ constructive trust/breach of trust test: “A banker may be a constructive trustee of money in his customer’s account and in breach of that trust if he pays the money away, even on the customer’s mandate, in circumstances which put him upon inquiry.” Applied by asking whether the bank had “sufficient notice ... to put the Bank on its inquiry” such that it was required “to take steps to ascertain the character of the funds”.
BaselineB: Common law (constructive trustee / bank on inquiry doctrine; summarized from Halsbury’s Laws of England and illustrated by cases discussed in the reasons, e.g., White v. Dominion Bank and Cartwright v. Lyster & Bank of Nova Scotia)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Applicability of Quebec’s 1974 retrospective prescription amendments to a case pending in the SCC: s. 5 makes C.C. art. 2262(2) (one-year prescription) inapplicable to a “suit pending before a court on 1 January 1975”, so the SCC may dismiss the appeal on that basis (notwithstanding Supreme Court Act s. 47).
BaselineA: Statute (Act to amend certain prescriptions, 1974 (Que.), c. 80, ss. 1, 3, 5; and Supreme Court Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. S-19, s. 47 (also discussed: ss. 50, 67); applied against the Civil Code prescription provisions (arts. 2261(2), 2262(2))).
CaseB_TestB: Ministerial refusal of extradition/surrender: the person sought must show surrender would “shock the conscience” (s. 7 Charter) or be “unjust or oppressive” (Extradition Act, s. 44(1)); the Minister’s core inquiry is whether surrender to the “particular treatment” awaiting the person would be contrary to principles of fundamental justice.
BaselineB: Statute and Charter (Extradition Act, S.C. 1999, c. 18, s. 44(1); Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7; informed by SCC precedent including United States v. Burns and Argentina v. Mellino).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Hart ‘Mr. Big’ confessions admissibility rule: presumptive inadmissibility rebutted only if Crown shows (on balance) probative value (reliability) outweighs prejudicial effect; plus separate abuse-of-process backstop for coercive/abusive operations
BaselineA: Common law evidence (party admissions exception to hearsay; trial judge discretion to exclude where prejudicial effect exceeds probative value; abuse of process doctrine). Baseline cases cited in the decision include R. v. Evans (party admissions), R. v. Handy (PV vs prejudice/bad character), and R. v. Babos / R. v. Mack (abuse of process).
CaseB_TestB: Meaning of ‘her mind is then disturbed’ in Criminal Code s. 233 (infanticide): apply ‘disturbed’ in its ordinary sense; no need for mental disorder/defined illness; must be present at time of act/omission and ‘by reason of’ childbirth/lactation; no causation requirement between disturbance and killing
BaselineB: Statute — Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 233 (with contextual reference to ss. 2, 16, 663(b), 672.11(c)).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Penile swab as a search incident to arrest: police may take a penile swab incident to arrest if (i) the arrest is lawful and the swab is truly incidental to arrest for a valid purpose, (ii) police have "reasonable grounds to believe that a penile swab will afford evidence of the offence for which the accused was arrested" (independent of arrest grounds), and (iii) the swab is "conducted in a reasonable manner" guided by specified factors (e.g., station-house, supervisory authorization, privacy, same gender, minimal officers, record-keeping).
BaselineA: Common law (search incident to arrest) as framed in R. v. Fearon (general framework) and tailored by analogy to R. v. Golden (strip-search reasonable-grounds threshold and manner guidelines); reasonableness structure referenced from R. v. Caslake (s. 8 reasonableness requirements).
CaseB_TestB: Joint/co-principal liability in group assaults (manslaughter): "Joint/co-principal liability flows whenever two or more individuals come together with an intention to commit an offence, are present during the commission of the offence, and contribute to its commission"; for manslaughter, focus on whether the accused’s actions were a "significant contributing cause of death" rather than who inflicted which wound; in group assaults, "absent a discrete or intervening event", all assailants’ actions can be a significant contributing cause to all injuries.
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, s. 21(1)(a) (parties—common intention/co-principal) and s. 21(1)(c) (abetting)), with consistency noted with R. v. Pickton (party liability discussion).
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Whether a damages claim for breach of a no-strike clause is a “grievance” subject to compulsory arbitration: no distinction between (i) employer vs employee monetary claims and (ii) “interpretation/application” vs “violation” of the collective agreement (either can ground a grievance). Key quote: “no distinction can be made between a dispute relating to the ‘application’ of an agreement and a dispute relating to its ‘violation’, because these are simply two ways of looking at the same problem.”
BaselineA: Statute (Quebec Labour Code, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 141, ss. 1(g) definition of “grievance” and 88 mandatory arbitration), as interpreted through SCC precedent (General Motors of Canada Ltd. v. Brunet, [1977] 2 S.C.R. 537; also Imbleau et al. v. Laskin et al., [1962] S.C.R. 338).
CaseB_TestB: Enforceability/scope of a waiver (exclusion) clause for negligence in a sporting event: construed “in the context in which it was signed”; clause effective where the parties “clearly had a release in mind” and the accident/negligence was within what was reasonably contemplated; clause not avoided as “unfair” or “unreasonable” on these facts. Key quotes: “in the context in which it was signed, the waiver clause… exonerated the Association”; and the clause was not “so unusual as to make it fall outside the contemplation of the clause”; “does not appear to be unreasonable.”
BaselineB: Common law contract principles governing construction/enforcement of exclusion/waiver clauses (including arguments framed in terms of fundamental breach, unconscionability, and public policy, though the Court found it unnecessary to develop fundamental breach).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: When a s. 119 Canada Labour Code “review” application must be treated like a new certification (vs mere updating/clarification): if the Board’s changes “alter the nature and scope of the certificate of certification and of the bargaining unit” it is effectively a new unit; if the changes “do not alter the nature and scope”, it remains an order of review and the Board “must simply be satisfied that these changes are in order.”
BaselineA: Statute (Canada Labour Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. L-1, s. 119 (power to “review, rescind, amend, alter or vary any order or decision made by it”)), as operationalized by the Board’s prior framework in The Employees of the Regional Comptroller and the Canadian National Railways (1975), 9 D.I. 20 (three categories of s. 119 review applications).
CaseB_TestB: Appellate intervention with trial findings: it is wrong to set aside a trial judgment “where there is not palpable and overriding error, and the only point at issue is the interpretation of the evidence as a whole”; the appellate court must be able to say the trial judge was “plainly wrong.”
BaselineB: Common law (as stated in prior SCC cases cited: Schreiber Brothers Ltd. v. Currie Products Ltd. and Gulf Oil Canada Ltd., Stein v. “Kathy K.”, and Lewis v. Todd).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Ernst (Cromwell J.) — Ward Charter-damages framework applied to a quasi-judicial regulator: even if Ward’s functional objectives are met, countervailing factors (alternative remedy + good governance + immunity’s purpose) mean Charter damages are never “appropriate and just” against this Board, so the statutory immunity clause bars the claim
BaselineA: Combination: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 24(1) ("appropriate and just" remedy) + common-law Charter damages framework from Vancouver (City) v. Ward, 2010 SCC 27
CaseB_TestB: Bird (Moldaver J.) — Maybrun/Klippert framework for when an accused charged with breaching an administrative order may collaterally attack the order: determine legislative intent using five non-exhaustive factors (statutory wording; purpose; appeal/other effective review mechanisms; nature of attack vs expertise/raison d’être; penalty)
BaselineB: Common law framework from R. v. Consolidated Maybrun Mines Ltd., [1998] 1 S.C.R. 706 and R. v. Al Klippert Ltd., [1998] 1 S.C.R. 737 (applied in context of CCRA s. 134.1(2) and related review mechanisms)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Art. 2930 C.C.Q. applies (3-year prescription) where the action is based on the obligation to make reparation for bodily injury caused to another: courts must "characterize the basis for the action"; the basis is the "wrongful act that gave rise to interference with the [victim’s] physical integrity", and if the plaintiff’s losses are the "direct and immediate consequences" of that interference, the action falls under art. 2930 (even if the heads of damages are moral/material).
BaselineA: Statute: Civil Code of Québec, arts. 2925 and 2930 (in interaction with Cities and Towns Act, s. 586).
CaseB_TestB: Appellate non-intervention in trial fact-finding/credibility: once the trial judge’s oral reasons are in the record, the Court of Appeal’s substitution of its view of the evidence for the trial judge’s is an "unwarranted intrusion" into an area "exclusive to the trial judge" (who had the advantage of seeing/hearing witnesses).
BaselineB: Common law/jurisprudence on appellate deference to trial findings of fact and credibility (as cited: Latour v. Grenier; Maze v. Empson; Dorval v. Bouvier; Métivier v. Cadorette; Hood v. Hood).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Schrenk “sufficient nexus with the employment context” test for whether discrimination is “regarding employment” under s. 13(1)(b): Tribunal must do a contextual analysis considering all relevant circumstances; non-exhaustive factors include (1) whether the respondent was integral to the complainant’s workplace; (2) whether the impugned conduct occurred in the complainant’s workplace; and (3) whether the complainant’s work performance or work environment was negatively affected (paras. 67-68).
BaselineA: Statute: Human Rights Code, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 210, s. 13(1)(b) (“discriminate against a person regarding employment”), with interpretive context from ss. 1 (“person”, “employment”) and 3 (purposes).
CaseB_TestB: Groia in-court incivility/professional misconduct framework: a context-specific, multi-factor approach considering “what the lawyer said, the manner and frequency in which it was said, and the presiding judge’s reaction” (para. 79-80). In particular, allegations impugning opposing counsel’s integrity “cross the line into professional misconduct unless they are made in good faith and have a reasonable basis” (para. 81), where “reasonable basis” is satisfied if there is “a sufficient factual foundation” even if the lawyer’s legal position is sincerely held but incorrect (paras. 88-91, 132-133).
BaselineB: Regulation/statutory scheme: Rules of Professional Conduct made under the Law Society Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. L.8 (and predecessor Professional Conduct Handbook), as interpreted/applied by the Law Society disciplinary bodies; SCC clarifies how the “good faith” and “reasonable basis” requirements operate within that framework.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Ontario anti-SLAPP dismissal framework under CJA s. 137.1: (1) defendant must show on a balance of probabilities the proceeding “arises from an expression” that “relates to a matter of public interest” (s. 137.1(3)); then (2) plaintiff must show both (a) “grounds to believe” the proceeding has “substantial merit” and defendant has “no valid defence” (s. 137.1(4)(a)), and (b) the harm is “sufficiently serious” that the public interest in letting the proceeding continue “outweighs” the public interest in protecting the expression (s. 137.1(4)(b)). Key clarifications include: “grounds to believe” requires “a basis in the record and the law” (para. 39); “substantial merit” means a “real prospect of success” (para. 49); and s. 137.1(4)(b) is a qualitative public-interest weighing where one side must “outweigh” the other (paras. 61-67).
BaselineA: Statute: Courts of Justice Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.43, s. 137.1(3) and (4) (and related ss. 137.1(1)-(2), 137.2).
CaseB_TestB: Corporate attribution doctrine (including for one-person corporations) and the discretionary “public interest” refusal to attribute: attribution may apply where (1) the wrongdoer was the corporation’s directing mind and (2) acted within their sector of corporate responsibility; attribution is generally inappropriate where the directing mind acted “totally in fraud of the corporation” or with “no benefit” to it; and, additionally, courts have discretion to refrain from attribution where doing so would be “in the public interest, in the sense that it would promote the purpose of the law under which attribution is sought” (Aquino summary adopted at para. 62; applied at paras. 75-81). The SCC held the same purposive/contextual/pragmatic approach applies to one-person corporations (paras. 64-71).
BaselineB: Common law corporate attribution doctrine from SCC cases (Canadian Dredge & Dock; Livent; DeJong), as summarized in Aquino v. Bondfield Construction Co., 2024 SCC 31, and applied in the statutory context of Limitations Act, 2002 (ss. 5, 12) and BIA.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Duty of trial judge to comment on Crown counsel’s prejudicial jury-address remarks: where remarks are “prejudicial to a degree sufficient to impose a legal duty on the trial judge to comment” to ensure the defence position is “fairly put to the jury”; failure to do so is an error of law (and no curative proviso applied here).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(b)(iii) “no substantial wrong or miscarriage of justice” proviso) applied to the common-law fairness duty in jury instructions regarding improper counsel remarks.
CaseB_TestB: Section 43(2) Federal Courts Act in rem jurisdiction — “identifiability” test: reject “physical nexus”; property is “subject of the action” if it is identifiable as the cargo designated in the contract of affreightment alleged to be breached.
BaselineB: Statute (Federal Courts Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. F-7, s. 43(2) — in rem jurisdiction over “ship, aircraft or other property that is the subject of the action”).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Threshold for summary dismissal of criminal applications: an application should only be summarily dismissed if it is “manifestly frivolous”, with the judge assuming alleged facts/inferences as true and taking the applicant’s arguments “at their highest”
BaselineA: Common law (criminal procedure/case management power to summarily dismiss applications; Vukelich/Kutynec line of authority, with comparison to civil strike standard in Imperial Tobacco)
CaseB_TestB: Combined effect of Criminal Code s. 172.1(3) presumption and s. 172.1(4) “reasonable steps” requirement: representation of underage triggers presumption of belief; rebuttal requires evidence including objectively reasonable steps to ascertain age; evidential burden on accused, persuasive burden on Crown
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 172.1(3) and s. 172.1(4), read harmoniously with s. 172.1’s purpose; with reference to R. v. Legare, 2009 SCC 56)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Two-step framework for whether a sentencing judge may grant credit for a pre-sentence driving prohibition despite a mandatory minimum: (1) identify the applicable common law rule allowing credit; (2) specify the statute’s effect on that common law (displaced expressly or by necessary implication). Applied here by interpreting s. 259(1)(a) as a minimum 'punishment' (global) not a minimum 'sentence' (prospective), so credit may be granted after imposing the mandatory minimum.
BaselineA: Combination of common law (credit for pre-sentence driving prohibition recognized in R. v. Lacasse; analogy to pre-sentence custody credit in R. v. Wust) and statute (Criminal Code, ss. 259(1)(a) and 719(1), with discussion of s. 719(3)).
CaseB_TestB: Mitigation in breach of contract where plaintiff claims specific performance: defendant must prove (i) plaintiff failed to take reasonable steps to mitigate and (ii) mitigation was possible; plaintiff’s inaction may be reasonable only if it had a 'fair, real, and substantial justification' / 'substantial and legitimate interest' in specific performance (typically requiring land’s 'peculiar and special value' such that damages are not a complete remedy).
BaselineB: Common law mitigation doctrine and specific performance context from Asamera Oil Corp. v. Seal Oil & General Corp. (mitigation and 'fair, real, and substantial justification') and Semelhago v. Paramadevan (specific performance only where land has 'peculiar and special value').
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Hearsay admissibility under the principled approach (necessity + threshold reliability), which can override traditional hearsay exceptions (e.g., present intention) where the statement is made in “circumstances of suspicion” or otherwise lacks sufficient indicia of reliability
BaselineA: Common law (hearsay rule and exceptions; principled approach from R. v. Khan and R. v. Smith; present intentions/state of mind exception discussed in R. v. Smith)
CaseB_TestB: Public interest standing (Downtown Eastside) — discretionary, cumulative weighing of three factors: (i) serious justiciable issue; (ii) genuine interest; (iii) reasonable and effective means (including whether a “sufficiently concrete and well-developed factual setting” will be forthcoming, without requiring an individual co-plaintiff)
BaselineB: Common law (Canada (Attorney General) v. Downtown Eastside Sex Workers United Against Violence Society, 2012 SCC 45)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Limited-liability/non-assessability constraint on corporate articles: an amendment/resolution is ultra vires if it seeks to impose on holders of fully paid shares “any financial burden whatsoever in respect of those shares”; and a share transfer fee is unlawful “to the extent that it exceeded the reasonable and proper cost of the transfer” (an “illegal levy” in respect of shares).
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common-law company-law principle: The Companies Act (Alberta) (notably ss. 42(1), 68(4), and provisions defining limited liability and non-assessability) plus the “basic jural principle ... that a shareholder who has paid for his shares is thereafter free of pecuniary obligation in respect of those shares” (supported by authorities cited in the reasons, e.g., Ooregum Gold Mining Co. v. Roper; Bisgood v. Henderson’s Transvaal Estates; Shalfoon v. Cheddar Valley Co-operative Dairy Co.).
CaseB_TestB: Van der Peet test (as applied) for an Aboriginal right to sell/exchange fish: the court must (1) “determine the precise nature of the claim being made” (considering the action, the impugned regulation, and the relied-on practice), and (2) decide whether, “prior to contact with Europeans,” the practice was “an integral part of the distinctive ... society” — i.e., “a central, significant or defining feature” of the group’s culture.
BaselineB: Constitutional/common-law framework under Constitution Act, 1982, s. 35(1), applying the test articulated in R. v. Van der Peet (and situated within the Sparrow framework, though this case turns on the first/definition stage).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Reviewability of a consensual labour arbitrator’s award for error of law on the face: no “specific question of law” reference where the issue arises in the ordinary grievance process under a collective agreement that restricts the arbitrator from making any decision inconsistent with the agreement
BaselineA: Common law (judicial review of consensual arbitration awards; distinction between a specific question of law referred vs. a general dispute where law arises). Key authorities discussed: Government of Kelantan v. Duff Development Co. Ltd.; F.R. Absalom Ltd. v. Great Western (London) Garden Village Society Ltd.; Faubert and Watts v. Temagami Mining Co. Ltd.; Bell Canada v. Office and Professional Employees’ International Union, Local 131.
CaseB_TestB: Morin framework for s. 11(b) “reasonable time” analysis: assess (1) length of delay minus defence waiver, then consider (2) reasons for delay, (3) prejudice, and (4) the interests s. 11(b) protects; prejudice may be inferred from length of delay
BaselineB: Combination: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 11(b), applied through common-law/constitutional framework from R. v. Morin (and R. v. Askov).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 3(4) possession attribution (including joint possession): for Code purposes, possession is established by personal possession, knowing custody/possession by another or in any place for use/benefit, and is deemed shared where one has custody/possession with the knowledge and consent of the others; s. 3(4) applies in all proceedings under the Code (including where possession is only an evidentiary link).
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 3(4) (now s. 4(3) in later consolidations).
CaseB_TestB: Adverse possession in British Columbia: possession must be “open and notorious, adverse, exclusive, peaceful (not by force), actual (generally), and continuous”; and the “inconsistent use” requirement is not part of BC law (it “forms no part of the law of British Columbia governing adverse possession”).
BaselineB: Combination: common law adverse possession elements as received/understood in BC, applied within BC limitations legislation history (e.g., Real Property Limitation Act, 1833 (U.K.) as received via Law and Equity Act, and BC Statute of Limitations provisions).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Quantum meruit for services rendered without agreed remuneration: where the recipient continues to request/authorize and accept services, it is obligated to pay a reasonable rate (subject only to clear statutory/regulatory bar).
BaselineA: Common law (quasi-contract/quantum meruit), as applied in King George Highway Hospital Ltd. v. District of Surrey, [1971] S.C.R. vi; plus statutory interpretation of whether Orders in Council under the Hospital Act s. 37(2) and the Residence and Responsibility Act s. 3 validly bar recovery.
CaseB_TestB: Voluntariness/operating mind test for admissibility of inculpatory statements by an allegedly insane accused: the controlling question is whether the statement was "freely and voluntarily made", including whether it represents the utterances of an "operating mind"; no fixed formula required.
BaselineB: Common law confession voluntariness doctrine (Boudreau v. The King, [1949] S.C.R. 262; Ward v. The Queen, [1979] 2 S.C.R. 30) with consideration of mental condition/"operating mind"; also engages Criminal Code s. 16(2) only as contextual reference in Santinon.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Effect of breach of a witness-exclusion order: witness not automatically disqualified; admissibility is discretionary; weight is for trier of fact (and no legal requirement that the judge expressly state a self-caution for each such witness)
BaselineA: Common law (practice/rule on exclusion of witnesses and consequences of breach, as reflected in cases cited such as Moore v. Lambeth County Court Registrar; Cook v. Nethercotte; Thomas v. David; Chandler v. Home; R. v. Carefoot)
CaseB_TestB: Crown immunity from discovery when not a party: immunity persists unless lifted by clear and unequivocal legislative language; CLPA s. 27 lifts immunity only in proceedings where the Crown is a party
BaselineB: Statute interpreted against common law backdrop (Interpretation Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. I-21, s. 17; Crown Liability and Proceedings Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-50, s. 27 (and related structure/ss. 23-27, 34))
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Bencher disqualification/bias in Law Society discipline: members of the Discipline Committee are not disqualified from participating in Convocation’s consideration of the Committee’s report (two-step procedure; s. 39(4) disqualification limited to the statutory reprimand-appeal).
BaselineA: Statute/regulation interpretation: The Law Society Act, 1970 (Ont.), ss. 33(12), 34, 37, 39 (especially s. 39(4)); and Reg. 556, s. 13(6)-(7).
JudgeA: Spence J. (for Martland, Judson, Spence, Pigeon, Beetz and de Grandpré JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Criminal Code s. 731(1)(b) probation availability: “imprisonment for a term not exceeding two years” refers to the term imposed by the sentencing court at a single sitting (not the aggregate of other sentences), but probation is unavailable if sentences imposed at the same session produce continuous custody over two years.
BaselineB: Statutory interpretation: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 731(1)(b) (with related context in ss. 732.2 and 743.1).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “operation of a mine” / when a separate “mine” exists for s. 83(5) exemption: “operation of a mine” is only extraction (not processing); a “mine” exists where there is “a body of ore together with the workings, equipment and machinery capable of producing it”, and a separate mine arises when a separate ore body “commenced to be extracted by means of its separate and distinct extraction facilities” (shared mill does not matter).
BaselineA: Statute: Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1952, c. 148 as amended, s. 83(5) and s. 83(6) (definitions of “mine” and “production”); interpreted in light of SCC authorities North Bay Mica Co. Ltd. v. M.N.R., [1958] S.C.R. 597 and M.N.R. v. MacLean Mining Co. Ltd., [1970] S.C.R. 877.
CaseB_TestB: Leave to sue a receiver/trustee under s. 215 BIA (Mancini test): leave should be refused only for “frivolous or vexatious” or “manifestly unmeritorious” claims; the evidence must disclose a cause of action and provide facts supporting it; “If the evidence discloses a prima facie case, leave should be granted”; court does not finally assess merits.
BaselineB: Statute: Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. B-3, s. 215 (leave requirement), with related statutory context in ss. 47(2) and 72(1); common-law/appellate baseline: Mancini (Bankrupt) v. Falconi (1993), 61 O.A.C. 332 (C.A.) adopted as governing approach.
JudgeB: Abella J. (McLachlin C.J. and Bastarache, Binnie, LeBel, Fish and Charron JJ. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Education Act s. 373 school-board roll revision: if municipal valuations are not uniform, commissioners must amend the rolls only to “re-establish on the basis of its real value the valuation of the taxable property” in each part of the school municipality (i.e., value what is taxable in each municipality; no cross-municipality override of a town’s choice to exclude machinery from taxable immovables).
BaselineA: Statute (Quebec Education Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 235, s. 373; with context from Cities and Towns Act s. 488 (as amended) allowing a by-law excluding machinery from taxable immovables).
CaseB_TestB: Criminal Code s. 426(1)(a)(ii) “secret commission” offence (agent/taker): actus reus requires (1) agency relationship, (2) acceptance of a benefit “as consideration” for acting in relation to the principal’s affairs, and (3) failure to make “adequate and timely disclosure” of the benefit; “corruptly” in this context means “secretly or without the requisite disclosure” and no “corrupt bargain” with the giver is required.
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 426(1)(a), especially s. 426(1)(a)(ii)).
JudgeB: Cory J. (for L’Heureux-Dubé, Gonthier, Cory and Iacobucci JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Extradition-crime classification under an extradition arrangement: “The test is what is the essence of the crime charged” (i.e., whether the charged offence is, in substance, a crime “against the laws for the suppression of the traffic in narcotics”).
BaselineA: Statute + extradition arrangement: Extradition Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-21, s. 2 (definition of “extradition crime”), and the 1925 Supplementary Convention classification “Crimes and offences against the laws for the suppression of the traffic in narcotics”.
CaseB_TestB: Section 13 “incrimination” purpose test for use of prior testimony at a later proceeding: prior testimony may be used on cross-examination if its “sole purpose” is to impeach credibility, but not if used “to incriminate” (to establish guilt).
BaselineB: Constitution + statute: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 13 (and its interpretation in R. v. Dubois and R. v. Mannion as discussed in the reasons); also interpreted alongside Canada Evidence Act, s. 5(2).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Negligence/causation foreseeability test for highway authority liability: “whether a reasonable person should have anticipated that what happened might be a natural result of that act or omission”; not necessary to foresee the “precise concatenation of events”, only “in a general way the class or character of injury”.
BaselineA: Common law foreseeability/remoteness in negligence (University Hospital Board v. Lépine; Wagon Mound No. 2 referenced/applied) plus statutory highway-maintenance duty under The Highway Improvement Act, R.S.O. 1960, s. 33(1).
JudgeA: Dickson J. (for Laskin C.J. and Spence J.)
CaseB_TestB: CEAA “tracking” rule: assessment track is determined by the “project as proposed” (not “project as scoped”); if the proposed project is on the Comprehensive Study List, s. 21 requirements are mandatory and the responsible authority cannot reduce scope below what the proponent proposed (only enlarge under s. 15(2)-(3)).
BaselineB: Statutory interpretation of the Canadian Environmental Assessment Act, S.C. 1992, c. 37 (especially ss. 2 “project”, 15, 18, 21, 58(1)(i)) and the Comprehensive Study List Regulations, SOR/94-638.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Res ipsa loquitur as a rule of evidence to infer (gross) negligence: applies where (1) the thing causing damage was under the defendant’s “sole management and control”; (2) the occurrence is such that it “would not have happened without negligence”; and (3) there is “no evidence as to why or how the occurrence took place” (but an offered explanation that is “no answer, even if believed in full” does not bar the inference).
