BaselineA: Common law evidentiary doctrine (res ipsa loquitur), as described via Clerk & Lindsell and recognized in SCC cases including Walker v. Coates et al. and Gauthier & Co. Ltd. v. The King; applied in the statutory context of Highway Traffic Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 202, s. 132(3) (gross negligence requirement for gratuitous passengers).
CaseB_TestB: Criteria for recognizing a vested (acquired) right against legislative interference: an individual has a vested right where (1) the person’s legal situation is “tangible and concrete rather than general and abstract”; and (2) the situation was “sufficiently constituted at the time of the new statute’s commencement” (with the presumption that legislation does not interfere with vested rights absent clear contrary intent, assessed in light of the “entire context”).
BaselineB: Statutory interpretation doctrine grounded in Interpretation Act, R.S.Q., c. I-16, s. 12 (acquired rights), and SCC jurisprudence on vested rights/retroactivity (e.g., Spooner Oils; Gustavson Drilling; Venne; Attorney General of Quebec v. Expropriation Tribunal), applied to amendments to the Act respecting financial assistance for students (including s. 13 “juridical situations in progress”).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Mechanics’ lien owner-liability/holdback interpretation: s. 19(2) does not prevent the owner deducting completion costs from amounts otherwise payable to the head contractor; s. 19(2) only bars deductions for extraneous “prior or subsequent indebtedness, set-off, or counterclaim” not arising under the contract
BaselineA: Statute (Mechanics’ Lien Act, R.S.B.C. 1960, c. 238, ss. 6, 19(2), 21(1), 21(6)) plus prior SCC approach in Canadian Comstock Co. Ltd. v. Toronto Transit Commission, [1970] S.C.R. 205 (approving S.I. Guttman Ltd. v. Mokry and Freedman v. Guaranty Trust re non-completion)
CaseB_TestB: Choice of law in tort: apply lex loci delicti as the general rule (“the law to be applied in torts is the law of the place where the activity occurred”), with only narrowly confined/rare exceptions; limitation periods under the applicable foreign law are treated as substantive when they create an accrued right to plead a time bar
BaselineB: Common law conflict-of-laws doctrine (overruling McLean v. Pettigrew) and related characterization doctrine (substance vs procedure), with application alongside relevant statutes in the cases (e.g., Saskatchewan Vehicles Act, s. 180(1); Quebec Automobile Insurance Act, ss. 3-4)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Constitutional (territorial) validity test for provincial legislation affecting extra-provincial conduct: Manitoba’s statutory pollution-liability scheme is ultra vires insofar as it purports to regulate/attach consequences to acts done outside the province (e.g., discharge of contaminant outside Manitoba into waters carried into Manitoba), engaging an interprovincial matter beyond provincial competence
BaselineA: Statute + constitutional division of powers: The Fishermen’s Assistance and Polluters’ Liability Act, 1970 (Man.), especially s. 4(1) (liability where contaminant discharged “into waters in the province or into any waters whereby it is carried into waters in the province”) and s. 4(2) (no lawful excuse based on a permit from the place of discharge unless that authority also had jurisdiction where damage occurred), assessed against B.N.A. Act, 1867 territorial limits and federal residual/interprovincial concern principles
JudgeA: Pigeon J. (for Martland, Pigeon and Beetz JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Privative-clause judicial review threshold: with a privative clause, courts intervene only for jurisdictional error; an administrative decision loses protection only if it is “patently unreasonable”/an “unreasonable finding” (or an “abuse of authority amounting to fraud and of such a nature as to cause a flagrant injustice”)
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common-law administrative law: Act respecting labour standards, R.S.Q., c. N-1.1, ss. 128-129 (arbitrator may make any decision “fair and reasonable, taking into account all the circumstances” where he considers no “good and sufficient cause”); Labour Code, s. 139 (privative clause); Code of Civil Procedure, art. 846; plus SCC privative-clause jurisprudence (e.g., CUPE) referenced in reasons
JudgeB: Lamer J. (reasons for McIntyre and Lamer JJ.; Beetz J. concurs in result and largely in Monet J.A.’s approach)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Collective agreement in force: common law repudiation/fundamental breach inapplicable; illegal strike does not itself terminate employment, and absent employer disciplinary termination, closure triggers severance obligations under the collective agreement
BaselineA: Combination: labour relations statute (Mediation Services Act, 1968 (B.C.), ss. 6 and 23(1), and related statutory collective bargaining scheme) plus prior SCC labour-law characterization of collective agreements (Syndicat catholique des employés de magasins de Québec Inc. v. Compagnie Paquet Ltée; C.P.R. Co. v. Zambri)
CaseB_TestB: Limits on cross-examination using a complainant’s diary: relevant defence evidence may be excluded only if its prejudicial effect substantially outweighs its probative value; O’Connor production balancing is not the test for cross-examination; omission evidence is probative only if a foundation shows a reasonable expectation the event would have been recorded
BaselineB: Common law (Seaboyer; Osolin; explained distinction from O’Connor production framework; also notes Criminal Code ss. 278.1–278.9 are about production, not admissibility/use)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Admissibility of evidence that an accused refused to participate in an identification line-up: admissible only where, in the circumstances, it is relevant (e.g., to explain the omission of a line-up) and not normally otherwise; jury assesses significance on the “totality of the evidence”. Key quotes: “Admissibility will depend upon the circumstances of the case”; “If, at trial, it unfolds that the Crown must explain the omission of a line-up… then… evidence of refusal is both relevant and admissible. In other circumstances I do not think such evidence should normally be tendered.”
BaselineA: Common law evidence relevance/admissibility principles and the common law privilege against self-incrimination (as limited to testimonial compulsion), discussed with reference to Curr v. The Queen and A.-G. (Que.) v. Begin; also analogies to identification-parade practice (e.g., R. v. Brager).
CaseB_TestB: Division-of-powers (pith and substance) limit on provincial commissions of inquiry: an inquiry is ultra vires if, in purpose/effect, it is “a substitute police investigation and preliminary inquiry with compellable accused” into a specific Criminal Code offence by named private individuals. Key quotes: “The inquiry process cannot be used to circumvent the federally prescribed criminal procedure”; “The pith and substance of a provincial commission must be firmly anchored to a provincial head of power and cannot be used… to investigate and determine the criminal responsibility of specific individuals for specific offences.”
BaselineB: Constitution Act, 1867 division of powers analysis (s. 91(27) vs provincial heads) using the pith-and-substance framework; applied to an Order in Council under Ontario’s Public Inquiries Act.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Punitive damages in tort: whether the circumstances justify an additional punitive award “in the interests of justice” (here, tortious inducement of breach plus a scheme to take over and end the plaintiff’s business), and if so, the quantum
BaselineA: Common law (punitive/exemplary damages principles; no specific baseline case articulated in the reasons provided)
CaseB_TestB: Negligence duty of care for pure economic loss in tendering: (1) does the claim fit a recognized pure economic loss category (incl. relational economic loss requiring third-party personal injury/property damage), and if not (2) should a new duty be recognized under the Anns/Cooper framework (foreseeability + proximity, including party-specific policy at stage 1; residual policy like indeterminate liability at stage 2)
BaselineB: Common law (Anns v. Merton; Kamloops; Cooper; Childs; Norsk categories of pure economic loss; tendering Contract A/B from Ron Engineering and related cases)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Railway Act s. 275 notice/effective-date rule: even if the Commission can extend the 30-day notice period, it must do so before the tariff’s stated effective date; after that date, an ‘extension’ is an impermissible indirect postponement and is ultra vires
BaselineA: Statute (Railway Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. R-2, ss. 275(2) and 275(4); also National Transportation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. N-17, s. 64(5) on implementation of FCA opinion/ultra vires effect)
CaseB_TestB: Fresh evidence (Palmer) test: admit fresh evidence on appeal where (1) due diligence (flexible in criminal cases), (2) relevance to a decisive/potentially decisive issue, (3) credibility, and (4) could reasonably be expected to have affected the result; overriding consideration is the ‘interests of justice’
BaselineB: Common law (Palmer v. The Queen, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 759, at p. 775; applied under Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 683)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Effectiveness/finality of an order still within the appeal period: despite being appealable, it may be treated as fully effective (even against third parties) where there is only an “ephemeral prospect of an appeal”; assess “the purpose” for which finality is urged, “who is affected”, and “in what context” finality is asserted
BaselineA: Statute (The Conveyancing and Law of Property Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 85, s. 62) plus general/common-law principles about the effect of appealable orders; prior Ontario authorities Re West (1928) and Leonard v. Wharton (1921) are distinguished
CaseB_TestB: Preliminary inquiry committal test under Criminal Code s. 548(1): whether there is “any evidence upon which a reasonable jury properly instructed could return a verdict of guilty”; if Crown evidence is circumstantial, the judge must do a “limited weighing” of the whole evidence to see if, assuming the Crown evidence is believed, it would be reasonable for a jury to infer guilt (without drawing inferences or assessing credibility)
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 548(1) (and Part XVIII generally) interpreted through the common law rule from United States of America v. Shephard, [1977] 2 S.C.R. 1067 (also discussed: Mezzo; Monteleone; Charemski)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Discretionary public-interest standing (taxpayer/citizen) to challenge legislation: standing may be granted where a serious constitutional issue is raised, the plaintiff is arguably directly affected (including as a member of the public), and there is otherwise no practical way to bring the legislation to judicial review
BaselineA: Common law (standing/locus standi doctrine), drawing on Smith v. Attorney General of Ontario, [1924] S.C.R. 331 and Thorson v. Attorney General of Canada (No. 2), [1975] 1 S.C.R. 138
CaseB_TestB: Interpretation of ASRA Program s. 88(3) and review of La Financière’s choice of linkage method: s. 88(3) gives La Financière discretion to choose collective or individual linkage, but it must exercise that discretion in accordance with good faith and contractual fairness
BaselineB: Regulation/contract interpreted through Quebec private law: Programme d’assurance stabilisation des revenus agricoles, s. 88(3), applying Civil Code of Québec arts. 1425-1432 (interpretation), and arts. 6, 7, 1375, 1434 (good faith/contractual fairness)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Rebuttable presumption of mens rea for trafficking once actus reus proved: when it is proved the accused trafficked in the restricted drug, “a rebuttable presumption arises” that he “intended to traffic” and “is guilty” unless other evidence raises a reasonable doubt (applied here: “No evidence having been tendered by the accused, it is not possible to find that he had an honest belief amounting to a non-existence of mens rea”).
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Food and Drugs Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. F-27, ss. 40 (definitions) and 42 (trafficking offence), plus SCC mens rea/mistake jurisprudence (Beaver v. The Queen; R. v. King) and narcotics mens rea approach (Blondin).
CaseB_TestB: Limits on trial-judge intervention / appearance of impartiality: a judge may and sometimes must question and interrupt witnesses, but “must do so within certain limits and in such a way that justice is seen to be done”; if the judge’s conduct “raised some doubt as to his impartiality”, a new trial is required.
BaselineB: Common law principles of procedural fairness and judicial impartiality, grounded in the maxim from R. v. Sussex Justices; Ex parte McCarthy that justice must “manifestly and undoubtedly be seen to be done”, and related case law on judicial interventions (e.g., Jones v. National Coal Board; Torbiak; Darlyn; Yuill; Bateman).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Interpreting “burglary” in Criminal Code s. 213 (constructive murder): because of bilingual/revision ambiguity, “burglary” retains the meaning of the offence defined in Criminal Code, 1892, s. 410 (dwelling-house burglary) read with s. 407 definitions
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 213 (and related breaking and entering provisions, s. 306) interpreted using Interpretation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-23, s. 36; historical baseline traced to Criminal Code, 1892, s. 228 (constructive murder) and s. 410 (definition of burglary) plus s. 407 (definitions of “dwelling-house” and “break”). Key interpretive direction quoted: Interpretation Act s. 36(f): where a former enactment is repealed and a new enactment substituted, “except to the extent that the provisions of the new enactment are not in substance the same as those of the former enactment, the new enactment shall not be held to operate as new law, but shall be construed and have effect as a consolidation and as declaratory of the law as contained in the former enactment”.
CaseB_TestB: Damages for repudiation where contract allows alternative modes of performance: assess damages on the least burdensome mode to the defendant (least profitable to plaintiff), not on a hypothetical “what would likely have happened but for breach” inquiry
BaselineB: Common law damages principle for contracts with alternative performances, traced to Cockburn v. Alexander (1848) and explained in Withers v. General Theatre Corp. (1933). Core formulation adopted: “where there are several ways in which the contract might be performed, that mode is adopted which is the least profitable to the plaintiff, and the least burthensome to the defendant.”
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Lease interpretation test for shifting fire-loss risk to landlord: applying “the ordinary test of reading [the lease] reasonably and in a business sense”, the tenant’s covenant to pay “insurance rates” means the “risk of loss by fire passed to the landlord, at least upon the presentation by the landlord of the insurance bill”, so the landlord’s insurer has no subrogated claim against the tenant for negligent fire loss.
BaselineA: Common law contract/lease interpretation (read reasonably and in a business sense) plus statutory context that standard fire insurance covers third-party negligence (Insurance Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 224, s. 118).
CaseB_TestB: Civil Code art. 1053 “fault causing damage” framework for bank liability on unauthorized endorsements: a bank/manager commits a “fault” by accepting payment/deposit of cheques payable to a company “without examining it, and without verifying the sufficiency of the endorsement”; if this fault “depriv[es] [the payee] of money that belonged to it” and causes damage, damages are recoverable (typically equal to the cheque amounts), especially where the payee has no remaining recourse against the drawer.
BaselineB: Combination of statute and civil law: Bills of Exchange Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. B-5 (notably s. 51 on signature by procuration as notice of limited authority; also referenced s. 10) and Civil Code (Quebec) art. 1053 (fault-based extra-contractual liability), as developed in Norwich Union Fire Insurance Society Ltd. v. La Banque Canadienne Nationale, [1934] S.C.R. 596.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 15(1) adverse impact discrimination (prima facie breach): claimant must show (1) a distinction based on an enumerated/analogous ground, including by effects where the law has a “disproportionate impact” on a protected group, and (2) the law’s impact “reinforc[es], perpetuat[es], or exacerbat[es] disadvantage”; for adverse effects, “both evidence of statistical disparity and of broader group disadvantage may demonstrate disproportionate impact; but neither is mandatory”.
BaselineA: Constitution (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 15(1)) and prior SCC s. 15 jurisprudence (e.g., Withler; Taypotat; Alliance; Centrale) articulating the two-step s. 15(1) test.
JudgeA: Abella J. (for Wagner C.J. and Abella, Moldaver, Karakatsanis, Martin and Kasirer JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Division of powers “pith and substance” analysis: (1) determine the law’s “essential character” by examining “purpose and the legal effect”; (2) classify whether that character relates to an enumerated head of power (here, whether s. 27 is “in pith and substance concerned with the management of the Canadian fishery” under s. 91(12)).
BaselineB: Constitution (Constitution Act, 1867, ss. 91(12), 91(27), 92(13)) and the established pith and substance doctrine (as summarized in the decision, including Reference re Firearms Act).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Lease interpretation test for shifting fire-loss risk to landlord where tenant covenants to pay “insurance rates”: read the lease “reasonably and in a business sense”; if tenant pays for fire insurance (at least once the landlord presents “the insurance bill”), the tenant is “entitled to rest in respect of loss by fire on the discharge of its obligation to pay for fire insurance”, so the landlord/insurer cannot pursue subrogation against the tenant for fire loss caused by the tenant’s negligence.
BaselineA: Combination: common-law/contract interpretation approach (“ordinary test of reading it reasonably and in a business sense”) plus statutory insurance context (Ontario Insurance Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 224, s. 118, noted as making third-party-negligence fire loss part of standard coverage).
CaseB_TestB: Warsaw Convention limitation entitlement under Art. 3(2): limitation is lost “only where no ticket is delivered”; “absence, irregularity or loss” of the passenger ticket does not remove the limitation. For baggage under Art. 4(4), limitation is lost only if luggage accepted without a delivered luggage ticket or if the ticket lacks particulars (d), (f) and (h); compliance assessed by whether the ticket is “legible by the ordinary person using ordinary diligence” and content is adequate.
BaselineB: Statute/treaty text: Carriage by Air Act, R.S.C. 1952, c. 45, Schedule I (Warsaw Convention), especially Arts. 3, 4 and 22 (and discussion distinguishing the Hague Protocol amendments).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Negligent misrepresentation in giving an estimate/opinion: plaintiff must prove more than that the estimate was wrong; must show the error resulted from a lack of "skill, competence or diligence" / failure to exercise "such care as the circumstances required" (and failure to qualify is not itself negligence, but may ground responsibility if the opinion was given carelessly).
BaselineA: Common law (negligent misrepresentation duty of care and standard of care), drawing on Hedley Byrne & Co. Ltd. v. Heller & Partners Ltd. and Mutual Life & Citizens’ Assurance Co. Ltd. v. Evatt (as cited in the reasons).
JudgeA: Ritchie J. (for Martland, Judson, Ritchie, Pigeon, Beetz and de Grandpré JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Extra-territoriality / territorial limits on provincial competence for intangible matters: (1) determine pith and substance and a provincial head of power; (2) determine whether the pith and substance is "in the Province"—if intangible, assess "relationships among the enacting territory, the subject matter of the legislation and the persons made subject to it" to see if there is a "meaningful connection" and respect for other jurisdictions’ sovereignty.
BaselineB: Constitutional text and doctrine: Constitution Act, 1867, s. 92 (including s. 92(13) "Property and Civil Rights in the Province"), and prior SCC jurisprudence on territorial limits/pith and substance (e.g., Churchill Falls; Unifund; Global Securities; Firearms Reference, as cited).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Scope of habeas corpus review of parole detention: on habeas corpus the court is confined to the face of the warrants/committal and cannot use certiorari to review the Parole Board’s administrative acts; Bill of Rights s. 2(c)(i) satisfied if detainee is told parole was suspended/revoked
BaselineA: Statute (Parole Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. P-2, especially ss. 10(1)(e), 16, 18, 20, 23; Federal Court Act, 1970-71-72 (Can.), c. 1, s. 18) plus common law limits on certiorari/habeas corpus (as applied in Re Shumiatcher; Security Export Co. v. Hetherington; Commonwealth of Puerto Rico v. Hernandez) and prior SCC treatment of parole revocation as administrative (Ex p. McCaud; Howarth v. National Parole Board)
JudgeA: Ritchie J. (for Judson, Ritchie, Pigeon and Beetz JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Equitable compensation for Crown breach of fiduciary duty over reserve land: assess the beneficiary’s “lost opportunity” by first defining what Canada “ought to have done as a fiduciary” (not merely what it could have done legally), then valuing the loss (with hindsight; no remoteness/foreseeability limit) on the basis of the best compensation that could realistically have been negotiated, including the land’s value to the hydroelectricity project
BaselineB: Common law of Crown fiduciary duty and equitable compensation (Guerin; Canson; Blueberry River; Wewaykum; Osoyoos; Williams Lake; etc.) applied alongside statutory/treaty context (Indian Act, R.S.C. 1927, c. 98, ss. 48, 50, 51; Treaty No. 3 (1873); Royal Proclamation, 1763)
JudgeB: Karakatsanis J. (for Wagner C.J. and Abella, Moldaver, Brown, Rowe, Martin and Kasirer JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Sales tax exemption for machinery/apparatus: whether the item is used “directly in … the manufacture or production of goods” (and not merely in distribution); gas pressure regulators that “merely cause the gas to pass … from the higher pressure pipes to lower pressure pipes” are not used in “production” “within the usual meaning of those words”.
BaselineA: Statute: Excise Tax Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-13, s. 29(1) and Schedule III, Part XIII, para. 1(a)(i) (exemption for machinery/apparatus used directly in “the manufacture or production of goods”); interpreted in light of Hydro-Québec v. Dep. Min. of Nat. Revenue for Customs and Excise, [1970] S.C.R. 30.
JudgeA: Pigeon J. (for Martland, Judson, Pigeon, Dickson and Beetz JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Scope-of-retainer test for solicitor/counsel liability: the “crucial question” is “the nature and scope of [counsel’s] retainer”, a “purely … factual question” not to be disturbed on appeal absent “error arising from misapprehension of the evidence”.
BaselineB: Common law appellate review principle for factual findings (deference to trial judge on factual findings/inferences absent misapprehension of evidence), applied to professional negligence/retainer-scope determination.
JudgeB: The Chief Justice (Laskin C.J.) (for Laskin C.J. and Martland, Spence, Dickson and Estey JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Whether an invention relates to a food substance “prepared or produced by chemical processes” under Patent Act s. 41(1): apply the term “chemical process” in its ordinary/popular sense, assess the process “as a whole”, and treat it as a factual question; chemical reactions are neither necessary nor sufficient, but it is enough if chemical operations play a “significant part” in producing the substance.
BaselineA: Statute (Patent Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. P-4, s. 41(1)), interpreted through prior SCC cases Continental Soya Co. Ltd. v. J.R. Short Milling Co. (Canada) Ltd., [1942] S.C.R. 187 and Laboratoire Pentagone Ltée v. Parke, Davis & Co., [1968] S.C.R. 307.
JudgeA: Dickson J. (for Laskin C.J. and Martland, Judson, Spence and Dickson JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Adequacy of an indictment (including in multiple-conspiracies situations): an indictment is adequate if it contains “sufficient details to give the accused reasonable information” and to “identify the transaction” for defence preparation; sufficiency depends on the offence and facts; time need not be exact unless essential and no prejudice; and a conspiracy proven falls within the indictment if it included some accused, occurred sometime within the alleged time span, and had as its object the type of crime alleged (with the Crown’s opening address relevant to construing the charge).
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 510, 512, 516) plus prior SCC guidance on indictments and conspiracy construction (notably R. v. Cotroni, [1979] 2 S.C.R. 256; also R. v. Côté, [1978] 1 S.C.R. 8; R. v. Wis Development Corp., [1984] 1 S.C.R. 485; R. v. B. (G.), [1990] 2 S.C.R. 30).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 1 justification (Oakes proportionality) applied contextually: infringement must be a "reasonable limit" that can be "demonstrably justified"; requires (1) pressing and substantial objective and (2) proportionality: "rationally connected", "impair the guaranteed right or freedom as little as possible" (minimal impairment), and proportionality of effects (RJR-MacDonald).
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 1 ("reasonable limits ... demonstrably justified") as structured by R. v. Oakes, [1986] 1 S.C.R. 103 (pressing/substantial objective + proportionality with rational connection, minimal impairment, and overall proportionality).
CaseB_TestB: Duty to accommodate/undue hardship where a collective agreement has an automatic termination clause: the negotiated period is "a factor to consider" but "does not definitively determine" accommodation; "each case must be evaluated on the basis of its particular circumstances"; undue hardship from absence must be assessed "globally starting from the beginning of the absence" (McGill University Health Centre).
BaselineB: Common law (human rights accommodation framework): Meiorin test (BCGSEU) requiring employer to justify a standard by showing (1) rational connection to job performance, (2) good faith, and (3) reasonable necessity, meaning "impossible to accommodate ... without imposing undue hardship"; applied in the context of Quebec Charter of human rights and freedoms (ss. 10, 20) and collective agreement clause 12.11(5) (36-month absence).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Indian Act s. 88 provincial-law applicability/paramountcy analysis: provincial law applies to Indians (via s. 88 reference) but is inoperative "to the extent" it is "inconsistent" with the Indian Act; here, assess whether Adoption Act s. 10(2) ("for all purposes" severing natural-parent relationship) negates Indian Act s. 11 registrability/entitlement to be registered as an "Indian" (it does not).
BaselineA: Statute: Indian Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-6, s. 88 (and s. 11 definition/entitlement to registration) applied against Adoption Act, R.S.B.C. 1960, c. 4, s. 10(2) ("for all purposes").
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 24(2) Collins framework (as organized in Greffe): exclude evidence if, "having regard to all the circumstances", its admission would "bring the administration of justice into disrepute"; factors organized into three categories—(1) fairness of the trial, (2) seriousness of the Charter violations (including whether police had "reasonable and probable grounds"; informant-tip reliability factors), and (3) effect of exclusion on the repute of the justice system.
BaselineB: Combination: Statute/constitutional text—Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 24(2) (and ss. 8, 10); common-law/precedent baseline—R. v. Collins (framework) as applied/organized here.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Termination/determination of a continuing guarantee by “notice in writing”: notice need not use set words, but must be explicit and unequivocal (not merely a “wish” or “preference”) so the creditor is left in no doubt
BaselineA: Contract (guarantee instrument) — clause (4) providing the guarantor may “by notice in writing delivered to the Manager ... determine ... liability ... in respect of liabilities thereafter incurred or arising”
CaseB_TestB: Admissibility/use of an accused’s silence: unless the Crown establishes “real relevance and a proper basis”, questions about post‑caution silence and evidence of ensuing silence should not be admitted; if admitted, the jury must be instructed to ignore it (no adverse inference)
BaselineB: Common law right to silence (as discussed via Rothman; Robertson; Symonds) and Charter s. 7 recognition; applied in the context of Criminal Code s. 613(1)(b)(iii) (curative proviso) on appeal
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Validity/regularity of an interim “cease and desist” order under Trade Union Act, s. 49(2): Board may issue an interim order “if satisfied after investigation of the complaint that Section 48 has not been complied with”, “notwithstanding any provision of this Act”; investigation may be done through Board officers; interim order need not be limited to relief requested so long as it is “related to or connected with the illegal work stoppage”.
BaselineA: Statute (Trade Union Act, 1972 (N.S.), c. 19, ss. 48, 49(2), 15(9)-(10); plus constitutional constraint discussion under B.N.A. Act, 1867, s. 96).
CaseB_TestB: YCJA youth-sentencing interpretation: general deterrence is not a permissible sentencing principle because (i) YCJA s. 50(1) excludes Criminal Code Part XXIII and does not incorporate s. 718(b) (“to deter the offender and other persons”), and (ii) “deter/deterrence” is absent from YCJA ss. 3 and 38 and cannot be implied; additionally, YCJA s. 42(2)(o) does not require a 2/3 custody and 1/3 supervision split (unlike s. 42(2)(n)’s “one half as long” supervision requirement).
BaselineB: Statute (Youth Criminal Justice Act, S.C. 2002, c. 1, ss. 3, 38, 42(2)(n), 42(2)(o), 50(1); contrasted with Criminal Code, s. 718(b)).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Cities and Towns Act s. 622 notice: failure to give notice is excused if the victim proves they were prevented from giving it for a reason “deemed sufficient” by the court; if so, after the 15-day period the victim is permanently released from any obligation to give notice and may sue without further notice
BaselineA: Statute — Cities and Towns Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 193, s. 622(1), (3), (4), (5) (especially s. 622(4) “prevented… for any reason deemed sufficient by the court or judge”)
CaseB_TestB: Judicial review of labour grievance arbitration award: court should ask whether the arbitrator’s interpretation is “patently unreasonable” / “one which the agreement would reasonably bear” (and not re-decide the merits or treat a sub-issue as a ‘wrong question’ unless the main issue was not addressed)
BaselineB: Common law (judicial review of arbitration awards) as developed in prior cases cited in the reasons, especially Bell Canada v. Office and Professional Employees' Union, [1974] S.C.R. 335; Canadian Union of Public Employees Local 963 v. New Brunswick Liquor Corp., [1979] 2 S.C.R. 227; Metropolitan Toronto Police Association v. Board of Commissioners, [1975] 1 S.C.R. 630
JudgeB: Pigeon J. (with Martland, Ritchie, Beetz and Pratte JJ. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Admissibility of similar fact evidence: other acts are inadmissible to show propensity, but are admissible if "relevant to an issue" such as whether the act was "designed or accidental" or to "rebut a defence"; and (per Noor Mohamed/Wray) the trial judge should exclude if the probative value for that purpose is only "trifling" given the grave prejudice
BaselineA: Common law evidence rule on similar fact evidence (general exclusionary rule and its exception), as stated in Makin v. Attorney General for New South Wales and refined in Thompson v. The King, Noor Mohamed v. The King; applied with reference to R. v. Wray
CaseB_TestB: Municipal valuation in exceptional cases: where "special circumstances make it impossible to fix the realizable value of property by the usual methods", "whatever method is appropriate in the circumstances may be used" to estimate "actual value" (including the 'developer’s approach')
BaselineB: Statutory municipal valuation requirement of "actual value" under the Charter of the City of Montreal, S.Q. 1959-60, c. 102 (appeal provisions noted at ss. 873-874), interpreted through prior valuation jurisprudence (notably Sun Life Assurance Co. of Canada v. City of Montreal)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Admissibility of similar fact evidence to prove mens rea in criminal negligence: similar acts are admissible (not to show disposition) if relevant to an issue such as whether the act was “designed or accidental” or to rebut a defence otherwise open; in criminal negligence the Crown must prove (a) “breach of an obligation imposed by law” and (b) that the breach showed “wanton or reckless disregard for the lives or safety of other persons”.
BaselineA: Common law evidence rule on similar fact evidence (general exclusionary rule and its exception), as discussed via Makin v. Attorney General for New South Wales and related authorities; applied in the context of Criminal Code ss. 191-192 (now 202-203).
CaseB_TestB: Issue estoppel as a defence to a perjury charge after an acquittal: the Crown is estopped from re-litigating an issue decided in the accused’s favour “unless it is tendering, in addition to or in lieu of the evidence previously adduced, evidence that was not at the time of the first trial available by the exercise of reasonable diligence”.
BaselineB: Common law doctrine of res judicata/issue estoppel and the fraud exception (e.g., Duchess of Kingston’s Case; Gushue v. The Queen; DPP v. Humphrys), adapted to criminal proceedings/perjury context.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory interpretation of technical terms: construe words by their primary/common meaning (in both official languages); here, “derivative/dérivé” means a thing actually obtained from another (not merely in the same scientific ‘family’).
BaselineA: Regulation/statutory interpretation: Order in Council SOR/69-8, Schedule A (tariff item 92944-1: “Tetracycline and its derivatives” / “tétracycline et ses dérivés”); plus Official Languages Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. O-2, s. 8(2)(b) (shared bilingual ‘concept’).
CaseB_TestB: Scope of inherent/implied jurisdiction re amici: courts may appoint amici only exceptionally where “essential” to permit a proceeding to be “successfully and justly adjudicated”, but (absent statutory or constitutional authority) that jurisdiction does not extend to fixing amici compensation rates or ordering the province to pay a particular rate.
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine of inherent jurisdiction / implied powers of statutory courts (as discussed with reference to cases like MacMillan Bloedel and Caron), subject to constitutional structure (separation of powers) and any statutory limits.
JudgeB: Karakatsanis J. (McLachlin C.J. and Rothstein, Moldaver and Wagner JJ. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Bankruptcy trustee’s statutory duty to insure: under Bankruptcy Act s. 9(1)-(2), trustee must keep existing insurance in force and insure/replace coverage for all the bankrupt’s insurable property (including hypothec-encumbered property), and if insurance cannot be obtained must notify the secured (hypothecary) creditor; failure can ground personal liability (and s. 171 leave requirement does not apply to omissions).
BaselineA: Statute (Bankruptcy Act, R.S.C. 1952, c. 14, ss. 9(1)-(2), 171; definitions in s. 2 of “property” and “secured creditor”).
CaseB_TestB: Charitable status under the fourth Pemsel head (for ITA registration): organization’s purposes must be (a) of “public benefit/beneficial to the community” and (b) “in a way the law regards as charitable”; applied via the D’Aguiar/Vancouver Society approach (trend by analogy, anomalies, and cross-check whether property can be applied to non-charitable purposes).
BaselineB: Common law (Pemsel categories as adopted in SCC charity jurisprudence; Vancouver Society applying D’Aguiar framework) applied within the statutory context of the Income Tax Act, ss. 149.1(1) and 248(1).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Eligibility for a Quebec seat on the SCC under Supreme Court Act s. 6: appointee must be a current member of the Quebec bar/bench (and meet s. 5’s 10-year standing) — s. 6 “impliedly excludes former members” by requiring appointment “from among” current members
BaselineA: Statute (Supreme Court Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. S-26, ss. 5 and 6; plus constitutional constraints in Constitution Act, 1982, Part V, especially s. 41(d))
JudgeA: McLachlin C.J. and LeBel, Abella, Cromwell, Karakatsanis and Wagner JJ.
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 15(1) equality test (two-step): (1) does the law, on its face or in impact, draw a distinction based on an enumerated/analogous ground; and (2) does it impose burdens/deny benefits in a way that “reinforc[es], perpetuat[es] or exacerbat[es]” disadvantage (applied to Pay Equity Act s. 38 delay)
BaselineB: Constitution (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 15(1); framework applied from prior SCC cases cited in the reasons, including Quebec (AG) v. A and Taypotat)
JudgeB: Côté J. (Wagner, Brown and Rowe JJ. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Highway Victims Indemnity Fund must satisfy a qualifying final judgment upon timely application; 30-year prescription applies and claimant need not first exhaust remedies against the insurer (no insurer 'benefit' because s. 39 transfers rights to the Fund)
BaselineA: Statute (Highway Victims Indemnity Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 232, ss. 36-39) plus Civil Code prescription rules (arts. 2262, 2265)
CaseB_TestB: Fatal Accidents Act damages methodology: determine dependants’ annual loss (including deducting income tax), then calculate present value using a discount rate based on long-term investment returns adjusted for inflation, with a reduction for contingencies
BaselineB: Statute (The Fatal Accidents Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 164) as interpreted through SCC damages jurisprudence (including reconsideration of Gehrmann v. Lavoie and reference to Andrews/Thornton/Arnold methodology)
JudgeB: Dickson J. (for Laskin C.J. and Martland, Ritchie, Pigeon and Beetz JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Equitable prejudgment interest for improper withholding of a just debt: where (in the court’s opinion) “the payment of a just debt has been improperly withheld” and “it seems to be fair and equitable” to compensate, the court “allow[s] interest for such time and at such rate as the Court may think right”; in this case, the compensatory rate should be “equivalent to the bank borrowing rates of [the creditor]”.
BaselineA: Common law/equitable principle from Toronto Railway Co. v. City of Toronto, [1906] A.C. 117 (applied via The Queen’s Bench Act, R.S.S. 1965, c. 73, s. 46; and with discussion of Interest Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-18, ss. 3, 12, 13; plus authority to direct interest under Supreme Court Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. S-19, s. 52).
CaseB_TestB: Post-conviction remedy for Crown non-disclosure (s. 7 / s. 24(1) Charter): (1) disclosure breach if there is a “reasonable possibility” the undisclosed information “could have been used” by the defence; (2) impairment/new trial requires a two-step analysis—first, whether there is a “reasonable possibility” the undisclosed information “on its face” affects the reliability of the conviction; second, if not, whether there is a “reasonable possibility” non-disclosure affected overall trial fairness by lost lines of inquiry/opportunities; defence counsel’s due diligence is a “significant factor” in the fairness stage and requires counsel to “diligently pursue disclosure”.
BaselineB: Common law Charter disclosure framework from R. v. Stinchcombe, [1991] 3 S.C.R. 326 (and related SCC cases Egger, Chaplin, Carosella), applied under Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 7 and 24(1).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Doctrine/rule of recent possession: once Crown proves (1) goods were recently stolen and (2) accused possessed them, jury may infer guilt; if an explanation is given that “may reasonably be true”, it must be considered and can raise a reasonable doubt; Crown need not adduce evidence of absence of explanation and proper instruction is not a prohibited comment on silence
BaselineA: Common law rule of evidence (recent possession) as stated in R. v. Schama; R. v. Abramovitch and applied/approved in SCC cases including Richler v. The King; Ungaro v. The King; Graham v. The Queen; Tremblay v. The Queen; R. v. Graham; plus statutory context Canada Evidence Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-10, s. 4(5) (no comment on failure to testify)
CaseB_TestB: Imperial Tobacco extraterritoriality framework for provincial legislation: (1) identify pith and substance by purpose and effects (intrinsic/extrinsic; legal/practical); (2) assess territorial limits by asking whether the law has a “meaningful connection” to the province (connection to enacting territory, subject matter, and those made subject to it) and whether it respects other governments’ sovereignty
BaselineB: Common law constitutional division-of-powers framework from British Columbia v. Imperial Tobacco Canada Ltd., 2005 SCC 49 (applied to Constitution Act, 1867, s. 92 territorial limits, including ss. 92(13) and 92(14))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Mulligan (majority): psychiatric “dissociative reaction” evidence need not be re-put on the drunkenness defence unless it bears on a pre-existing condition making the accused more likely to become incapable from alcohol; otherwise, if accepted it goes to insanity and if rejected drunkenness is assessed on the drinking evidence
BaselineA: Common law (drunkenness negates specific intent/incapacity framework from DPP v. Beard) applied alongside Criminal Code s. 212(a) mens rea for murder
JudgeA: Martland J. (for Martland, Judson, Ritchie, Pigeon, Beetz and de Grandpré JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Ibanescu/Gibson: “straddle evidence” is admissible and, when weighed with all the evidence, may raise a reasonable doubt and rebut the Criminal Code s. 258(1)(d.1) presumption that BAC exceeded 80 mg/100 mL at the time of driving
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, s. 258(1)(d.1) presumption) as interpreted through SCC precedent R. v. Gibson
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Drunkenness negating mens rea for murder: intoxication must render the accused “incapable of forming the specific intent” to murder; mere impairment/greater propensity to violence is insufficient
BaselineA: Common law (as adopted in the jury charge from Director of Public Prosecutions v. Beard, [1920] A.C. 479 (H.L.)) and applied to Criminal Code s. 212(a) (“means to cause his death” / intent for murder)
JudgeA: Martland J. (for Martland, Judson, Ritchie, Pigeon, Beetz and de Grandpré JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Section 23 “numbers warrant” sliding-scale placement: (1) determine long-term number who will eventually avail themselves; (2) compare province-wide to majority schools and apply a rebuttable presumption of pedagogical/cost appropriateness where comparably sized majority schools exist; (3) determine level of services (homogeneous school if comparable and presumption not rebutted)
BaselineB: Constitutional text (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 23) as interpreted in Mahe v. Alberta, [1990] 1 S.C.R. 342 (sliding scale; pedagogy and cost factors)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory judicial-review threshold under BC Labour Code s. 108(1)(b): court may intervene only for an "error of law affecting the jurisdiction" of the arbitrator; no such jurisdictional error where the arbitrator addressed the submitted question by considering the circumstances and giving an answer (i.e., no "sin of omission" amounting to jurisdictional error).
BaselineA: Statute: Labour Code of British Columbia Act, 1973 (B.C.) (2d Sess.), c. 122, s. 108(1)(b) (and s. 108(1) generally).
CaseB_TestB: Garofoli leave (threshold) test for cross-examining a wiretap affiant: leave should be granted only where the defence shows a "reasonable likelihood" that cross-examination will elicit testimony of "probative value" on a material issue for the reviewing judge (relevance/materiality within the narrow Garofoli review).
BaselineB: Common law: R. v. Garofoli, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 1421 (applied/affirmed); applied in the context of Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 184.2 (consent wiretap authorization) and Charter s. 8.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Appellate non-intervention with concurrent findings of fact: SCC will not interfere unless the trial decision was wrong and there was no evidence to support it
BaselineA: Common law (appellate review/deference to concurrent findings of fact; no specific prior SCC case cited in the reasons provided)
CaseB_TestB: ‘Integral element’ test for whether federal legislation affecting a s. 92(10) undertaking is within Parliament’s jurisdiction (and thus can displace provincial law): federal authority must be an integral element of the core federal competence
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine interpreting Constitution Act, 1867 ss. 91(29) and 92(10), drawing on Construction Montcalm Inc. v. Minimum Wage Commission and Northern Telecom Ltd. v. Communications Workers of Canada
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Fire policy statutory condition 10(a): the policy is not void for failure to state the insured’s interest in property “owned by any other person” so long as the insured has an insurable interest (i.e., “All that is necessary to satisfy statutory condition 10(a) of the policy is that the insured have an insurable interest”).
BaselineA: Statute (Quebec Insurance Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 295, s. 240 statutory conditions, especially condition 10(a)) and Civil Code art. 2571 C.C. (requirement that “the nature of the interest must be specified”).
JudgeA: Pigeon J. (for Laskin C.J. and Martland, Judson, Ritchie, Spence, Pigeon, Dickson and Beetz JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Section 8 “piggybacking” rule for bodily samples: even if a coroner’s seizure is initially valid for non-criminal purposes, “once the evidence or the information derived from it is appropriated by the state's criminal law enforcement arm for use against the person from whom it was seized, the seizure will become unreasonable and run afoul of s. 8”; courts must “go beyond the initial non-police seizure” to assess whether police conduct constitutes an independent seizure or makes the coroner’s seizure unreasonable.
BaselineB: Constitutional/common law Charter framework under s. 8 (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 8) as developed in Hunter v. Southam Inc. (prior authorization requirement for criminal-law seizures) and R. v. Dyment (privacy in bodily samples), applied in the context of the Coroners Act, R.S.O. 1980, c. 93, s. 16(2).
JudgeB: La Forest J. (for La Forest, L'Heureux-Dubé, Sopinka, Gonthier and Iacobucci JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Refusing an adjournment that is necessary to exercise the s. 577(3) right to counsel: the refusal is reviewable and improper unless based on established facts; an adjournment may be refused only for a legally available reason grounded in evidence, and prejudice from being forced to proceed without counsel cannot be assumed away
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 577(3) (right to make full defence personally or by counsel) and 613 (miscarriage of justice/appellate intervention))
JudgeA: Pigeon J. (for Laskin C.J. and Judson, Spence, Pigeon, Dickson and Beetz JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Equitable compensation for breach of fiduciary duty (non-disclosure): assess the plaintiff’s actual loss with hindsight; foreseeability is irrelevant, but recovery is limited to losses that, on a common-sense view of causation, were caused by the breach (including third-party losses only where the breach permitted them by a direct link)
BaselineB: Common law / equity (fiduciary duty and equitable compensation), drawing on cases including Nocton v. Lord Ashburton and Guerin v. The Queen (as discussed in the reasons)
JudgeB: McLachlin J. (for Lamer C.J. and L'Heureux-Dubé and McLachlin JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Quebec Superior Court jurisdiction on a declinatory exception: in a personal action (art. 68 C.C.P.), jurisdiction lies in the court of the defendant’s domicile, or failing this, his residence; filing a declinatory exception does not automatically shift the burden to the plaintiff, and the court determines residence/domicile on the evidence as a whole (including statutory presumptions such as Canadian Citizenship Act, s. 10).
BaselineA: Statute (Quebec Code of Civil Procedure, arts. 68 and 70; plus Canadian Citizenship Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-19, s. 10 presumption re principal residence/domicile).
CaseB_TestB: When (and how) state/police misconduct can reduce a criminal sentence: if the misconduct "relates to the circumstances of the offence or the offender", the sentencing judge may treat it as a relevant mitigating factor within the Criminal Code sentencing regime (ss. 718–718.2) without resort to Charter s. 24(1); as a general rule sentence reduction must remain within statutory limits (cannot go below mandatory minimums), with only a narrow possibility of exceptional s. 24(1) relief outside statutory limits for particularly egregious misconduct.
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code ss. 718–718.2 and mandatory minimum constraints; Charter s. 24(1) as remedial backdrop).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Contractual warranty interpretation: construe “depreciation” in the warranty/auditor’s letter as an accounting concept (write-off over useful life) and not “full capital cost allowance”; the parenthetical “(using capital cost allowance rates)” refers to rates only, not adoption of the tax ‘system’, so no breach if full depreciation was taken on the books for the period assets were in service
BaselineA: Common law (contract interpretation of a warranty clause, read with the incorporated auditor’s letter; no specific SCC baseline case cited in the reasons)
CaseB_TestB: Youth court power under Young Offenders Act: s. 19(2) does not give jurisdiction to dismiss a charge merely because the judge thinks it “ought never to have been laid”; absent clear statutory language, the court must decide guilt/not guilt on the proved elements (with only exceptional control via abuse-of-process stay in the “clearest of cases”)
BaselineB: Statute (Young Offenders Act, R.S.C., 1985, c. Y-1, especially ss. 19(2) and 3(1); interpreted against the background principle of prosecutorial discretion recognized in cases such as Smythe v. The Queen and R. v. Jewitt)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Crown appeal from acquittal (error of law): Crown must satisfy the court that the verdict "would not necessarily have been the same" absent the misdirection (White v. R. test)
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 613(4) (appeal from acquittal) plus the common-law test from White v. R., [1947] S.C.R. 268 (as applied in R. v. Gauthier, [1977] 1 S.C.R. 441)
CaseB_TestB: Group defamation/personal injury in Quebec civil liability: plaintiff must prove that an "ordinary person" would believe the remarks, in context, damaged the reputation of each group member personally; assessed using a non-exhaustive list of contextual factors (size, homogeneity, identifiability, precision, plausibility, etc.)
BaselineB: Combination of statute and civil-law jurisprudence: Civil Code of Québec, art. 1457 (fault, injury, causation) and prior SCC defamation cases applying the "ordinary person" injury standard (Prud’homme v. Prud’homme, 2002 SCC 85; Néron, 2004 SCC 53)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Workmen’s compensation exclusion in standard auto policy: an insured is excluded if, on the admitted facts, they are "entitled to receive the benefits of any workmen’s compensation law or plan"—entitlement to receive is not dependent on having applied for, or obtained, a compensation award
BaselineA: Statute (Ontario): Insurance Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 224, s. 232(1) and Schedule E, Exclusion 2(a)(ii) (mandatory standard policy wording), interpreted in light of the Workmen’s Compensation Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 505 (e.g., ss. 3, 8)
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 8 reasonableness framework (mutatis mutandis) for cross-border disclosure of lawfully intercepted wiretap communications under Criminal Code s. 193(2)(e): (1) authorized by law; (2) law is reasonable; (3) disclosure carried out in a reasonable manner
BaselineB: Combination: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 193(2)(e)) assessed under Charter s. 8 using the established s. 8 framework from R. v. Collins and R. v. Caslake (authorized by law / reasonable law / reasonable manner), applied to disclosures "mutatis mutandis"
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Discretion to order service ex juris under Federal Court Rules, Rule 307 guided by forum conveniens: the “overriding consideration” is whether there exists “some other forum more convenient and appropriate for the pursuit of the action and for securing the ends of justice”; refusal is an error in principle if based solely on “no relation or connection with Canada”.
BaselineA: Statute and regulation: Federal Court Act, R.S.C. 1970 (2nd Supp.), c. 10, ss. 22(2)(a), 43(1), 44; Federal Court Rules, Rule 307 (service ex juris).
JudgeA: Ritchie J. (for Ritchie, Pigeon, Beetz and de Grandpré JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Quebec medical civil liability causation (rejecting “loss of chance” as a substitute for causation where death/sickness has occurred): plaintiff must prove fault, damage, and causation “on the balance of probabilities”, considering “all the evidence: factual, statistical and that which the judge is entitled to presume”; in some cases a court may presume causation where a fault creates a “clear danger” that materializes, unless there is a “strong indication to the contrary”; if not satisfied causation of “any real damage” is proven, “recovery should be denied”.
BaselineB: Civil law (Quebec delictual responsibility) with evidentiary presumptions under Civil Code of Lower Canada, art. 1205; SCC causation approach referenced in Snell v. Farrell, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 311 (as cited in the reasons).
JudgeB: Gonthier J. (for Lamer C.J. and L'Heureux-Dubé, Sopinka, Gonthier, Cory and McLachlin JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Breach of municipal development agreement sewer-servicing obligation: developer must prove a specific failure to provide sewers/enlargements “required to properly service” the redevelopment stage (i.e., evidence of actual or foreseeable inadequacy); a general sewer-upgrading report/charge is not enough without evidence connecting it to serviceability
BaselineA: Contract (development agreement) interpretation and breach: s. 31(a)(iii) of the August 31, 1966 development agreement requiring “the construction of all public sewers in each stage and the enlargement of any public sewers located outside such stage that may be required to properly service such stage”
CaseB_TestB: Presumption of advancement on gratuitous transfer from husband to wife and rebuttal: presumption applies unless husband rebuts it; it is not rebutted by saying he transferred “only … to defeat his creditors”; rebuttal assessed from the parties’ conduct and intention
BaselineB: Common law presumption of advancement (and resulting/constructive trust principles), with statutory context noted but not applied retroactively: The Family Law Reform Act, 1975 (Ont.), c. 41, s. 1(3)(d) (abolishing presumption prospectively only)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 613(1)(b)(iii) curative proviso: uphold conviction despite trial error if the Crown satisfies the appellate court that a properly charged jury "could not, as reasonable men, have done otherwise than find the appellant guilty" (i.e., no substantial wrong or miscarriage of justice).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, s. 613(1)(b)(iii)) as applied through SCC precedent (Colpitts v. R. adopting Brooks v. The King formulation).
CaseB_TestB: Sparrow prima facie infringement test (as applied to treaty rights) for whether fisheries regulations infringe Mi’kmaq treaty rights: ask "First, is the limitation unreasonable? Second, does the regulation impose undue hardship? Third, does the regulation deny to the holders of the right their preferred means of exercising that right?"; if infringement, regulation inoperative unless justified under the Badger/Sparrow justification framework.
BaselineB: Constitutional/common law framework under Constitution Act, 1982, s. 35(1), applying Sparrow (prima facie infringement) and Badger (treaty-rights justification) to federal fisheries regulatory scheme.
JudgeB: Binnie J. (for Lamer C.J. and L’Heureux-Dubé, Cory, Iacobucci and Binnie JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Hague Protocol carrier-liability limitation: carrier may invoke Art. 22 only if the passenger ticket/baggage check includes the required Art. 3(1)(c)/4(1)(c) “notice” in a form “calculated to attract attention” (i.e., “noticeable”), strictly construed; 4.5-point inconspicuous print is not a “notice”.
BaselineA: Statute (Carriage by Air Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-14 incorporating the Warsaw Convention as amended by the Hague Protocol), especially Hague Protocol Arts. 3(1)(c), 3(2), 4(1)(c), and 22 (and contrasted with Warsaw Convention Arts. 3 and 4).
CaseB_TestB: Charter validity of Criminal Code breathalyzer presumptions: s. 258(1)(c) “conclusive proof” presumptions are constitutional only after severing the 2nd and 3rd rebuttal requirements; accused need only raise a reasonable doubt that the approved instrument “was functioning and was operated properly” (with s. 258(1)(d.01) excluding Carter evidence for that purpose).
BaselineB: Statute + constitutional review (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, ss. 258(1)(c), (d.01), (d.1) as amended; assessed under Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms ss. 11(d), 7, 11(c), and s. 1).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Municipal notice-of-accident limitation in Charter art. 1088 runs from the claimant’s discovery of the accident/cause (not necessarily the accident date) where otherwise the short delay would practically deny the right of action
BaselineA: Statute: An Act to revise and consolidate the Charter of the City of Montreal, 1959-60 (Que.), c. 102, art. 1088 (notice must be received within 15 days for sidewalk/roadway falls); plus interpretive context from City of Ile Perrot v. Goulet-Wiseman, [1977] 1 S.C.R. 175 (exceptions/justification for failure to give notice)
CaseB_TestB: Discretionary test for discharging a civil jury after a reference to insurance: discharge only if the reference likely caused real prejudice (a “substantial wrong or miscarriage of justice”) and the prejudice cannot be cured by instructions
BaselineB: Common law (overruling Bowhey v. Theakston, [1951] S.C.R. 679 on automatic discharge; adopting a discretionary prejudice-based approach drawn from later case law such as Michaud v. Wales (1991))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Admissibility of an accused’s prior in-court testimony: prior judicial testimony under oath is admissible at a later trial without a voir dire on voluntariness (jury assesses weight), even if unlawful compulsion is alleged; protection against self-incrimination must be claimed at the time (cannot be claimed after the event). Key holdings: “it is never necessary to hold a voir dire with respect to the voluntariness of a previous statement of the accused given in court” and “the witness may request the protection of the law … at the time he is testifying … [but] is not allowed to request the protection of the law after the event”.
BaselineA: Common law distinction between extra-judicial confessions (require voir dire voluntariness) and judicial statements; authorities including R. v. Scott (1856) (judicial testimony admissible though compelled) and related cases; statutory context noted: Canada Evidence Act, s. 5(2) (protection if claimed).
CaseB_TestB: Appellate intervention for failure to consider relevant evidence: appellate courts do not reassess guilt, but must review the record to ensure the trial court directed itself to all evidence on relevant issues; if reasons/record show “lack of appreciation” or “complete disregard” of relevant evidence, the reviewing court “must intercede”. Key statement: “Where the record … discloses a lack of appreciation of relevant evidence and more particularly the complete disregard of such evidence, then it falls upon the reviewing tribunal to intercede.”
BaselineB: Common law/appellate criminal procedure principles as articulated in prior SCC cases (MacDonald v. The Queen; Ungaro v. R. and others cited) on when misdirection/self-misdirection or overlooking a vital issue/evidence warrants appellate intervention.
JudgeB: Estey J. (for Martland, Dickson, Beetz, Estey, McIntyre and Lamer JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Admissibility of Crown rebuttal evidence to an alibi: Crown may contradict an alibi only by attacking its “material points”; and Crown cannot contradict an accused on a “collateral fact” elicited in cross-examination (so rebuttal evidence on a collateral fact is inadmissible).
BaselineA: Common law evidence principles (rebuttal to alibi; collateral fact rule), with appellate review/curative proviso under Criminal Code s. 613(1)(b)(iii). Cases cited for baseline include R. v. Cargill, R. v. Hrechuk, R. v. Rafael (collateral fact rule) and The Queen v. Vézeau (Crown burden on no substantial wrong/miscarriage).
CaseB_TestB: Drunkenness and rape via the specific-intent/general-intent distinction: rape is an offence of “general intent” so “the defence of drunkenness can have no application” (subject to the separate inquiry whether there is evidence of incapacity and whether any miscarriage of justice occurred).
BaselineB: Common law intoxication doctrine and the specific intent/general (basic) intent framework as stated in The Queen v. George and DPP v. Beard, and affirmed in DPP v. Majewski; with Criminal Code s. 613(1)(b)(iii) for miscarriage/curative proviso analysis.
JudgeB: Pigeon J. (for Martland, Judson, Ritchie, Pigeon, Beetz and de Grandpré JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Applicability of mandatory supervision under Parole Act s. 15(1) to an inmate with multiple sentences: if the inmate falls within the post‑Aug. 1, 1970 class (via a later penitentiary sentence) and is released by remission exceeding 60 days, then s. 15(1) applies to the single deemed sentence under s. 14(1) (mandatory supervision attaches).
BaselineA: Statute (Parole Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. P-2, ss. 14(1) and 15(1)-(2), as enacted via Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1968-69 (Can.), c. 38, s. 101(2) and brought into force by proclamation SOR/70-339 (effective Aug. 1, 1970)).
CaseB_TestB: Succession Duties Act s. 26(1) inclusion test for insurance proceeds: proceeds are taxable if they are “due by an insurer by reason or on account of the death of the person on whose life the insurance was effected”, which includes accident insurance death benefits (no life/accident distinction; accidental death is still death).
BaselineB: Statute (Succession Duties Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 70, s. 26(1); with related discussion of ss. 45(f) and 46(1) and bilingual interpretation of “sur la tête” / “on whose life”).
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Estate Tax Act: no “passing” of community property to surviving spouse (and deceased not “competent to dispose”) where marriage contract gives survivor ownership retroactive to marriage
BaselineA: Statute (Estate Tax Act, 1958 (Can.), c. 29, ss. 3(1)(a), 3(2)(a), 3(2)(e), 58(1)(i); applied with SCC precedents Sura v. MNR, [1962] S.C.R. 65 and Royal Trust Co. v. MNR, [1968] S.C.R. 505)
CaseB_TestB: Treaty/NRTA hunting right on private land: geographic limit turns on “visible, incompatible land use” (case-by-case), and any prima facie infringement must be justified under the Sparrow test
BaselineB: Combination of constitutional/statutory instruments and common law: para. 12 of the Natural Resources Transfer Agreement, 1930 (Constitution Act, 1930, Schedule 2) and Treaty No. 8; justification framework from R. v. Sparrow, [1990] 1 S.C.R. 1075
JudgeB: Cory J. (for La Forest, L'Heureux-Dubé, Gonthier, Cory and Iacobucci JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Contractual price-adjustment (tax-escalation) clause applies only where there is an “increase or decrease” or “imposition of any new tax, duty, charge or fee” that is “applicable to the product or its production, manufacture, sale or delivery” and “is or will be borne by Seller”; it does not extend to upstream crude-oil cost increases from foreign taxes/royalties or affiliate pricing, and crude-oil imports are not deliveries of “the product”.
BaselineA: Common law (contract interpretation) applied to the parties’ agreement, especially clause 9 (and the defined term “the product”).
CaseB_TestB: Van der Peet test for an Aboriginal right under s. 35(1): “in order to be an aboriginal right an activity must be an element of a practice, custom or tradition integral to the distinctive culture of the aboriginal group claiming the right”; the Court must (1) “first identify the exact nature of the activity claimed to be a right” and then (2) determine whether it was “a defining feature of the culture in question” prior to contact with Europeans (including, at the characterization stage, considering “the nature of the action”, “the nature of the governmental regulation… being impugned”, and “the practice, custom or tradition being relied upon”).
BaselineB: Constitution (Constitution Act, 1982, s. 35(1)) as operationalized by the common-law framework in R. v. Van der Peet (applied here to a claimed self-government/gambling right).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Foreseeability-based duty/standard of care in negligence (no liability unless the injury was a reasonably foreseeable result of the situation created by the defendant; here, no duty to take additional precautions against a child attempting to board a moving train)
BaselineA: Common law negligence/occupiers’ liability principles, with a statutory fencing backdrop (Railway Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. R-2, s. 214) discussed but found not breached; foreseeability principles cited from Ouellet v. Cloutier, [1947] S.C.R. 521 and University Hospital Board v. Lepine, [1966] S.C.R. 561; railway-crossing ‘special circumstances’ approach referenced from Paskivski v. Canadian Pacific Ltd., [1976] 1 S.C.R. 687; child/railway occupier cases discussed including Mitchell v. C.N.R., [1975] 1 S.C.R. 592
CaseB_TestB: Section 7 ‘fair hearing’ requirements for IRPA security-certificate reasonableness/detention review: a fair judicial process must include (in substance) a hearing before an independent and impartial decision-maker, a decision on the facts and law, and the right to know and answer the case; if full disclosure is impossible, there must be a ‘substantial substitute’ (IRPA provided neither)
BaselineB: Constitutional baseline under the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7 (and related ss. 1, 9, 10(c)), applied to the statutory scheme in the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, S.C. 2001, c. 27, ss. 77-85 (especially ss. 78, 80(1), 80(3), 82-84); prior SCC procedural fairness/fundamental justice authorities cited include Singh v. Minister of Employment and Immigration, [1985] 1 S.C.R. 177; Suresh v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2002 SCC 1; United States of America v. Ferras, 2006 SCC 33; R. v. Rodgers, 2006 SCC 15
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Highway Victims Indemnity Fund liability for unknown-driver accidents: under Highway Victims Indemnity Act s. 43 the Fund must satisfy judgment only "to the same extent as if [judgment] had been rendered against the author of the accident", meaning liability is capped by s. 14 at $35,000 and is not extinguished by payments from other liable parties (no s. 38 deduction where victim received nothing from the unknown driver).
BaselineA: Statute: Highway Victims Indemnity Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 232, especially ss. 43 (unknown driver), 14 ("financial responsibility" = $35,000 cap), 38 (deduction rule in Division XII), and 49(b) ("to the extent prescribed").
CaseB_TestB: Collateral immigration consequences in sentencing and appellate intervention: a sentencing judge may consider collateral immigration consequences only if the final sentence remains proportionate (Criminal Code s. 718.1) and consequences must not "skew" sentencing; an appellate court may vary sentence where the sentencing judge was unaware of those consequences or counsel failed to advise, subject to evidentiary requirements where not raised below and Crown does not consent.
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: Criminal Code ss. 718, 718.1, 718.2 (sentencing principles) plus SCC sentencing jurisprudence (e.g., R. v. M. (C.A.) on appellate intervention for failure to consider a relevant factor) and interaction with Immigration and Refugee Protection Act s. 64 (collateral consequence trigger).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Whether the trial judge must give the accomplice-corroboration caution where a key witness may be an accomplice (and/or accessory after the fact): the jury decides accomplice status; if the witness is likely to be considered an accomplice, the judge must warn of the danger of convicting on uncorroborated testimony
BaselineA: Common law rule of practice on accomplice evidence/corroboration caution (as discussed via Horsburgh v. The Queen and Davies v. D.P.P.; also contrasted with R. v. Gratton and R. v. Riezebos) and Criminal Code s. 23 definition of accessory after the fact (referred to in the jury-instruction discussion)
CaseB_TestB: Interpretation/application of Criminal Code s. 212(c) murder (“unlawful object” murder): (1) no requirement the dangerous act be unlawful; (2) if the dangerous act is unlawful, there must be a further unlawful object distinct from the immediate object of the dangerous act; (3) “unlawful object” means an object which, if prosecuted fully, would amount to an indictable mens rea offence; (4) objective ‘ought to know’ is applied using the accused’s actual knowledge of surrounding circumstances, and intoxication is relevant to that actual knowledge
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code ss. 205(5)(a) and 212(c) (and related ss. 212(a)(i)-(ii)); interpreted in light of prior SCC cases Graves v. The King and R. v. Hughes et al. (with Graves not followed)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Construction of Manitoba auto insurance exclusion s. 31(3)(h): “an insured” is read contract-specifically (owner’s vs driver’s certificate are separate contracts), so the exclusion applies only if the bodily injury/death is to an insured under the particular certificate under which indemnity is claimed
BaselineA: Regulation (Manitoba Automobile Insurance Regulation, Man. Reg. 333/74 under The Manitoba Public Insurance Corporation Act), especially ss. 30 (definition of “insured”), 31(1), 31(2) and 31(3)(h)
JudgeA: Pigeon J. (for Laskin C.J. and Ritchie, Spence, Pigeon and Beetz JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Treaty 8 / NRTA para. 12 limit on hunting rights: determine whether the impugned conduct is “hunting… for food” (i.e., for sustenance) versus an “act of commerce”; if it is commerce, provincial Wildlife Act s. 42 applies via Indian Act s. 88
BaselineB: Statute/constitutional instruments: Indian Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-6, s. 88; Alberta Wildlife Act, R.S.A. 1980, c. W-9, ss. 1(s), 42; Treaty No. 8 (1899); Natural Resources Transfer Agreement, 1930 (Alberta), para. 12 (confirmed by Constitution Act, 1930)
JudgeB: Cory J. (for Lamer, La Forest, Gonthier and Cory JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 287(2) “telecommunication” definition: theft of a “telecommunication service” applies only where the transmission/emission/reception is “by wire or cable” (not by Hertzian waves/radio); no “partly wire” vs “entirely wire” distinction
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 287(1)(b) and definition in s. 287(2) (“telecommunication” means transmission/emission/reception “by wire or cable”).
CaseB_TestB: Immigration Act s. 19(1)(a)(ii) “excessive demands” assessment: decision-makers must make an individualized assessment of likely demands (not mere eligibility) and consider both medical and non-medical factors, including the family’s ability and willingness to pay/mitigate; threshold is “reasonable probability, not remote possibility” (“more likely than not” that contingencies will materialize)
BaselineB: Statute: Immigration Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. I-2, s. 19(1)(a)(ii) (medical inadmissibility where admission “would cause or might reasonably be expected to cause excessive demands on health or social services”).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Limits on municipal discretion to refuse a business licence under Municipal Act s. 455: discretion must be exercised “judicially”, not on “extraneous”/“irrelevant or alien” grounds; “in any particular case” means peculiar to the applicant (not a type of business) and cannot be used as a de facto prohibition of a lawful trade/land use.
BaselineA: Statute (Municipal Act, R.S.B.C. 1960, c. 255, s. 455) interpreted in light of the Act’s overall scheme; plus common-law/authority limits on licensing-as-prohibition (Municipal Corporation of the City of Toronto v. Virgo, [1896] A.C. 88; and the “irrelevant/alien grounds” constraint reflected in Sunshine Valley Co-operative Society v. City of Grand Forks, [1949] 1 W.W.R. 165).
CaseB_TestB: IRPA security-certificate procedural fairness/disclosure standard under Charter s. 7: the named person must receive an “incompressible minimum” of disclosure—i.e., be “reasonably informed” by receiving enough to give “meaningful instructions” to public counsel and “meaningful guidance and information” to special advocates; if non-disclosure prevents this, the Minister must withdraw the information/evidence and the judge must quash the certificate.
BaselineB: Statute + Charter: Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, ss. 77(2), 78, 83(1)(e), 83(1)(i) (and related Division 9 provisions) interpreted to comply with Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7, building on Charkaoui v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2007 SCC 9 (Charkaoui I).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Appellate deference to trial findings of fact: an appellate court should not disturb findings of fact where there was credible evidence on which the trial judge could reasonably base the conclusion; it is not the function of an appellate court to reconsider the evidence and reach a different conclusion unless the evidence reasonably could not justify the trial judge’s conclusion.
BaselineA: Common law (appellate review standard for findings of fact; articulated in this decision as a “well-known principle” rather than tied to a specific statute).
CaseB_TestB: Bona fide occupational qualification (BFOQ) under Ontario Human Rights Code s. 4(6): (1) subjective good faith—limitation “must be imposed honestly, in good faith, and in the sincerely held belief” it serves adequate performance “with all reasonable dispatch, safety and economy” and not for “ulterior or extraneous reasons”; and (2) objective necessity—must be “related in an objective sense” and “reasonably necessary to assure the efficient and economical performance of the job without endangering” the employee, co-workers, or the public; employer bears the burden on a balance of probabilities once prima facie discrimination is shown.
BaselineB: Statute: The Ontario Human Rights Code, R.S.O. 1970, c. 318, ss. 4(1) and 4(6) (and related procedure/appeal provisions including s. 14d).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Unlawful act manslaughter causation: Crown must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused’s unlawful act was “at least a contributing cause of death, outside the de minimis range” (not necessary to prove it caused each intermediate mechanism like vomiting/aspiration).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code), especially s. 205(1) (“A person commits homicide ... when directly or indirectly, by any means, he causes the death of a human being”), applied with common-law causation principles (incl. thin skull).
CaseB_TestB: Anns two-stage duty-of-care framework for recognizing a novel duty for pure economic loss: (1) proximity/foreseeability → prima facie duty; (2) residual policy considerations may negate/limit the duty; applied to reject a negligence duty in commercial negotiations (and to reject a duty in drafting tender specs).
