BaselineB: Common law (Anns v. Merton London Borough Council; adopted in Canada via Kamloops (City of) v. Nielsen) applied to pure economic loss categories (Norsk; Bow Valley; D’Amato).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Crown bound by legislation/regulations only if expressly mentioned/referred to (Interpretation Act, s. 16), otherwise only (at common law) by “necessary implication” where the statute’s purpose would be “wholly frustrated” without binding the Crown
BaselineA: Combination: statute (Interpretation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-23, s. 16; s. 28) plus common law rule from Bombay Province v. Bombay Municipal Corporation ([1947] A.C. 58) on “necessary implication”
CaseB_TestB: Breach of contract (Civil Code art. 1065) where a stipulated term (here, cargo weight) is “material if not a critical term”; excessive deviation from the stipulated weight constitutes breach (not nullity for error under art. 992)
BaselineB: Statute (Civil Code of Quebec provisions: arts. 992 and 1065) applied to a contract of carriage
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Lord’s Day Act s. 11(x) exemption scope: CTC must assess only whether (given the Act’s object of preventing Sunday gainful work) Sunday freight work is 'necessary to permit' to prevent 'undue delay'; impacts on local peace/quiet (noise, congestion, pollution, safety) are irrelevant to the statutory mandate
BaselineA: Statute: Lord’s Day Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. L-13, ss. 4 and 11(x) (interpretation of 'object of this Act' and the scope of the CTC’s inquiry under s. 11(x))
CaseB_TestB: Meaning of 'bona fide pension plan' under Human Rights Code s. 3(6)(a) (Abella J. majority): plan must be 'subjectively and objectively bona fide'—i.e., 'a legitimate plan, adopted in good faith and not for the purpose of defeating protected rights'; inquiry is into the plan’s overall bona fides (registration under pension legislation is a helpful indicator), not actuarial mechanics
BaselineB: Statute: Human Rights Code, R.S.N.B. 1973, c. H-11, s. 3(6)(a) (interpretation of 'bona fide' in the pension-plan exemption from age-discrimination provisions)
JudgeB: Abella J. (Binnie, LeBel and Rothstein JJ. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: “Undueness” under Combines Investigation Act s. 32(1)(c): Crown must prove (1) an agreement/conspiracy and (2) that, if carried into effect, it would “prevent or lessen competition unduly”; “only by assessing what the result would be if the agreement were implemented” can undueness be measured; reject per se ‘meaningful segment’ approach
BaselineA: Statute: Combines Investigation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-23, s. 32(1)(c), interpreted in light of SCC jurisprudence on “unduly” (Howard Smith Paper Mills; Weidman v. Shragge; Stinson-Reeb; Container Materials)
JudgeA: Ritchie J. (for Martland, Ritchie, Pigeon, Dickson and Beetz JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Unreasonable verdict (Criminal Code s. 686(1)(a)(i)): appellate court asks whether the verdict is one a properly instructed jury or judge “could reasonably have rendered”; may find unreasonableness where an essential inference/finding is (1) “plainly contradicted” by the evidence relied on, or (2) “incompatible” with uncontradicted/unrejected evidence; credibility findings only disturbed if they “cannot be supported on any reasonable view of the evidence”
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(a)(i), as applied through SCC precedents (Yebes; Biniaris; Sinclair; Beaudry; Burke)
JudgeB: Deschamps J. (Abella, Cromwell, Moldaver and Karakatsanis JJ. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Hodge’s Case circumstantial-evidence formula does not apply to proving the accused’s intent; intent must be proved beyond a reasonable doubt without the Hodge ‘only rational inference’ direction
BaselineA: Common law jury-charge doctrine on circumstantial evidence (Hodge’s Case) as limited by SCC precedent in R. v. Mitchell (1964) and reaffirmed in R. v. John (1971)
CaseB_TestB: Interpretation of linked insurance policies: a reference in the fleet policy to the garage policy (“See Garage Policy”) should be construed to have effect (art. 1014 C.C.), i.e., as referring to limits/premium, leaving fleet-policy third-party liability coverage intact despite a garage-policy rider excluding owned autos
BaselineB: Statutory/civil-law contract interpretation under Quebec Civil Code, especially art. 1014 C.C. (and related interpretive provisions discussed: arts. 1013, 1234, 2480; plus context of insurance documentation)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Burden of proof when a mandatary (insurance broker) alleges “impossibility of performance” to avoid contractual liability: plaintiff must prove fault, damage, causality; but under C.C. art. 1203 the defendant who pleads impossibility bears the onus to prove impossibility (not mere difficulty).
BaselineA: Statute (Civil Code of Quebec provisions governing mandate/contract validity and proof): arts. 1701 (mandate), 984 and 1062 (object must be possible), and 1203 (“he who alleges facts in avoidance or extinction of the obligation must prove them”).
CaseB_TestB: Meaning of “directly or indirectly… have any interest in any contract” for municipal disqualification: interpret “interested in” broadly (non-technical, ordinary meaning) so that a director/officer of a contracting company has at least an indirect interest; disclosure/non-participation does not avoid the statutory disqualification.
BaselineB: Statute (Moncton Consolidation Act, 1946 (N.B.), c. 101, s. 6; plus interpretive direction in Interpretation Act, R.S.N.B. 1973, c. I-13, s. 17; considered alongside Municipalities Act, R.S.N.B. 1973, c. M-22, ss. 71-72).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Interpretation of para. 12 Alberta Natural Resources Transfer Agreement: “Indians of the Province” (Alberta Indians) vs “Indians within the boundaries” (all Indians physically in Alberta, regardless of residence), so non-resident treaty Indians may hunt “for food” on “unoccupied Crown lands”/lands of access despite provincial game laws
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional instrument interpretation: Indian Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-6, s. 88; Alberta Natural Resources Transfer Agreement, 1930, para. 12 (confirmed by British North America Act, 1930 (U.K.)); Treaty No. 6 (1876)
CaseB_TestB: Qualified privilege in libel: communication on a privileged occasion is protected unless plaintiff proves malice; even “violent or excessively strong” language is protected if the defendant “might have honestly and on reasonable grounds believed that what he wrote or said was true” (Adam v. Ward; applied via Netupsky v. Craig)
BaselineB: Common law qualified privilege and malice (Adam v. Ward; Netupsky v. Craig, as cited in the reasons)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code obscenity definition: s. 159(8) is the exclusive test for sexual obscenity across Code offences (displacing Hicklin); i.e., a work is obscene if it is a “publication a dominant characteristic of which is the undue exploitation of sex (or sex plus crime/horror/cruelty/violence)”.
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, s. 159(8) (definition of obscene publication) applied/extended for Code-wide consistency; contrasted with common law Hicklin test (R. v. Hicklin (1868)) and SCC discussion in Brodie v. The Queen.
CaseB_TestB: Duty to accommodate in employment discrimination: employer (and, in defined circumstances, union) must take “reasonable measures short of undue hardship”; undue hardship assessed contextually (e.g., cost, disruption of collective agreement, morale/rights of other employees, interchangeability, size, safety).
BaselineB: Combination: Statute (Human Rights Act, S.B.C. 1984, c. 22, ss. 8(1), 8(4), 9) interpreted through SCC common-law/human-rights jurisprudence on accommodation (O'Malley; Central Alberta Dairy Pool).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 159(8) statutory obscenity test is exhaustive for sex-based obscenity across the Code: a work is obscene if it is a “publication” whose “dominant characteristic” is the “undue exploitation of sex (or sex plus crime, horror, cruelty, violence)”, and the common law Hicklin test is displaced in sex-based obscenity cases
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, s. 159(8) definition of obscenity; interpreted alongside ss. 159(1), 163, 164 and s. 8; prior SCC discussion in Brodie v. The Queen and the common law Hicklin rule referenced as the competing baseline)
CaseB_TestB: Duty to accommodate analysis for termination-after-absence clauses: apply Meiorin (BFOQ) framework; a collectively bargained maximum-absence/termination clause is a relevant factor/evidence in assessing reasonable accommodation and undue hardship, but is not determinative because accommodation must be individualized and undue hardship assessed globally from the start of the absence
BaselineB: Common law / quasi-constitutional human rights framework (Meiorin test for justification of discriminatory standards; applied in the context of Quebec Charter equality rights and collective agreement termination clause)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Federal jurisdiction over cable TV as a single interprovincial/international “undertaking”: no constitutional demarcation at the antenna; content regulation is inseparable from regulating the undertaking
BaselineA: Common law constitutional division of powers under the B.N.A. Act, ss. 91 and 92(10)(a), relying on the Privy Council’s Radio Reference (In re Regulation and Control of Radio Communication in Canada, [1932] A.C. 304) and related “undertaking” jurisprudence (e.g., Winner)
CaseB_TestB: Income tax “proceeds of disposition” characterization: purchaser’s assumed obligation is included only if it is a distinct existing liability; embedded future costs that run with the property merely depress value and are excluded
BaselineB: Statute — Income Tax Act, s. 13(21) definition of “proceeds of disposition” (including “the sale price of property that has been sold”), applied with the general principle that assumption of a vendor’s liability may form part of sale price (e.g., mortgage-assumption cases cited)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Immovable by nature (Civil Code arts. 374 et seq.): a structure is immovable where it is a construction that adheres (directly or indirectly) to land/building; for wire networks, “the vertical attachment of a network of wires to the ground is in itself enough to make these wires immovable”; “the criterion for being immovable by nature is met when a structure that may be described as a building adheres to something that is immovable by nature, whether land or a building”.
BaselineA: Combination: statute + civil law. Retail Sales Tax Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 71, ss. 2(3) ("moveable property" = what is not immoveable by Quebec law) and 6 (tax on purchase of moveable property), applied by reference to Civil Code arts. 374 et seq.; prior SCC authorities applied/clarified include Montreal Light, Heat and Power Consolidated v. City of Westmount, [1926] S.C.R. 515 and Lower St. Lawrence Power Co. v. L’Immeuble Landry Ltée, [1926] S.C.R. 655.
CaseB_TestB: Punitive damages for breach of contract (wrongful dismissal): punitive damages are available but “will be rare” in contract; they require “the commission of an actionable wrong which caused the injury complained of” (i.e., “unless the conduct constituting the breach is also a tort for which punitive damages are recoverable”), and in any event the conduct must be “extreme… deserving of full condemnation” (e.g., “harsh, vindictive, reprehensible and malicious”).
BaselineB: Common law. Baseline authorities discussed include Addis v. Gramophone Co. and SCC’s Peso Silver Mines Ltd. (N.P.L.) v. Cropper; the majority also relies on the Restatement (Contracts) s. 355 formulation (punitive damages not for breach of contract unless also a tort).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Negligence duty/standard of care for an ice-cream truck operator/company attracting young children: once they "put the truck in operation" and attract children, they become the children’s "neighbours" and "must take reasonable care to avoid acts or omissions which you can reasonably foresee would be likely to injure your neighbour" (Donoghue v. Stevenson applied); failure to take obvious precautions for child safety can ground liability.
BaselineA: Common law negligence duty of care (Donoghue v. Stevenson “neighbour”/reasonable foreseeability and proximity approach), applied to a child-attracting street-vending enterprise.
CaseB_TestB: Interpretation of real-estate APS fire/insurance clause (cl. 5): after damage, purchaser has a binary election—"either have the proceeds of the insurance and complete the purchase, or may cancel the Agreement"—and has a right to reasonable time to decide and obtain insurance details, but "does not accord the purchaser the right to wait and see if the insurer will pay"; attempting to impose extra conditions is repudiation.
BaselineB: Contract interpretation of the parties’ agreement (standard-form Nova Scotia Real Estate Association APS), specifically clause 5 (risk/insurance proceeds election) and clause 9 (time of the essence), against the background common law risk rule for damaged property pending closing.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Matrimonial property beneficial interest via resulting trust from joint account contributions: where spouses intend a joint “common purse”, “in the absence of agreement to the contrary, a one-half interest in any investment purchased by a husband from a common pool of funds ... will be considered to be held by him for the benefit of his wife” (rebuttable presumption of resulting trust based on contribution in money or money’s worth).
BaselineA: Common law (resulting trust/common intention and constructive trust/unjust enrichment), drawing on Murdoch v. Murdoch; Thompson v. Thompson; Pettitt v. Pettitt; Gissing v. Gissing; and joint-account authority Jones v. Maynard.
CaseB_TestB: Access to court exhibits (audio/video) test: court balances open court/access against privacy/protection of the innocent; “curtailment of public accessibility can only be justified where there is present the need to protect social values of superordinate importance. One of these is the protection of the innocent” (MacIntyre, applied), and the court “is bound to inquire into the use to be made of [exhibits] and is fully entitled to regulate that use.”
BaselineB: Common law open court/access doctrine from Attorney General of Nova Scotia v. MacIntyre, applied in the context of exhibits; procedural backdrop includes Nova Scotia Civil Procedure Rule 30.11(6) (return of exhibits).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Limitation Act s. 6(4)(b) postponement: time runs only when a properly advised reasonable person would conclude the plaintiff, in light of their own circumstances and interests, could reasonably bring an action; postponement beyond accrual requires interests/circumstances that are “serious, significant, and compelling” and excludes “purely tactical concerns” (McLachlin J., para. 39).
BaselineA: Statute — Limitation Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 266, s. 6(4)(b) (within the s. 6(4) postponement scheme, including s. 6(4)(a) and s. 6(5) “appropriate advice”).
CaseB_TestB: Arbitration Act s. 15 stay framework in receivership: (1) applicant shows an “arguable case” for four technical prerequisites (arbitration agreement; court proceeding by a party; matter within scope; no “step” taken); (2) if met, stay is mandatory unless, on a balance of probabilities in a “clear case”, the agreement is “void, inoperative or incapable of being performed”; in receivership, an agreement may be “inoperative” where enforcing it would “compromise the orderly and efficient resolution of the receivership”, assessed using non-exhaustive factors (effect on insolvency integrity; relative prejudice; urgency; insolvency stay; other material factors) (Côté J., paras. 76-89, 155).
BaselineB: Statute — Arbitration Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 55, s. 15(1)-(2), interpreted alongside Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. B-3, ss. 183(1) and 243(1)(c) (statutory jurisdiction supporting inoperability in receivership).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Start of 5-year extinctive prescription for engineers’ fees: prescription runs only when the fee is due—i.e., “on completion of the work” or “at the time it was suspended, after a decision clearly communicated” to the engineers (and, under the tariff, generally not before the call for tenders or clear termination/no-tenders notice).
BaselineA: Combination of statute/civil code and regulation, informed by civil law principles: Civil Code art. 2260(6) (5-year prescription) plus the Quebec “Tariff of fee for Professional Engineers” (O.C. 891, Sept. 4, 1957) and general bilateral-contract principles (contract for work; payment due on delivery/termination).
CaseB_TestB: Discretionary test for enforcing foreign letters rogatory under Canada Evidence Act s. 43: even if statutory preconditions are met, the court “may, in its or his discretion” refuse enforcement where Canadian public policy/sovereignty concerns outweigh comity; it is “not for a Court…to take issue with the government’s determination of public policy or to measure its impact.”
BaselineB: Statute-based discretion under Canada Evidence Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-10, s. 43 (order may be made “in its or his discretion”), applied alongside comity principles and public policy considerations (including interaction with Uranium Information Security Regulations under Atomic Energy Control Act s. 9, though validity not decided).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 170 nudity offence: “nude” in s. 170(1)(a) means complete bareness; s. 170(2) is a deeming provision extending “nude” to being “so clad as to offend against public decency or order”, and the Crown need not prove offensiveness where there is total nudity
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, s. 170(1)(a) (nude in a public place without lawful excuse) and s. 170(2) (“For the purpose of this section a person is nude who is so clad as to offend against public decency or order”), interpreted in light of predecessor s. 205A (“shall be deemed to be nude”)
CaseB_TestB: Application of Criminal Code s. 613(1)(b)(iii) proviso: despite trial error (splitting the Crown’s case / improper reply evidence), an appeal may be dismissed only if there was “no substantial wrong or miscarriage of justice”; here the proviso cannot apply because the appellate court cannot realistically assess the case after extracting the improperly adduced evidence
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, s. 613(1)(b)(iii) (curative proviso: dismiss appeal if “no substantial wrong or miscarriage of justice”) applied to trial error involving reply evidence / splitting the Crown’s case
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 170 nudity offence: “nude” in s. 170(1)(a) keeps its ordinary meaning of complete bareness; s. 170(2) is a deeming provision that only extends nudity to being “so clad as to offend against public decency or order”, so the Crown need not prove offensiveness where there is total nudity (absent lawful excuse).
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, s. 170(1)(a) and s. 170(2) (interpreting “a person is nude who is so clad as to offend against public decency or order” as a deeming provision).
CaseB_TestB: Availability of certiorari in criminal proceedings: for parties, certiorari lies only for a provincial court judge’s jurisdictional error (not mere errors of law, including disclosure/evidentiary rulings); jurisdictional error occurs where the court fails to observe a mandatory statutory provision or breaches natural justice.
BaselineB: Common law constrained by statute: Criminal Code, s. 674 (no interlocutory appeals) plus SCC jurisprudence on certiorari/jurisdictional error (e.g., Skogman; Cohen; Dagenais; Cunningham).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Workmen’s Compensation Act s. 8 “additional sum” entitlement where the Commission is subrogated: if the compensation paid equals or exceeds the dependant’s civil claim (as reduced by the victim’s contributory fault), there is no “additional sum” to claim; the Commission has priority to recover up to what it paid (s. 7(3) subrogation pleno jure).
BaselineA: Statute and Civil Code: Workmen’s Compensation Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 159, ss. 7(3) (subrogation pleno jure) and 8 (right to claim an “additional sum”); Civil Code art. 1157 (partial payment/subrogation priority) and art. 1056 (wrongful death claim, reduced by victim fault per cited SCC cases).
CaseB_TestB: Employee’s right to continued salary under a service contract after being “cut”: the club’s obligation to pay “depended upon the plaintiff’s being available and willing to provide the services”; by signing/playing for another club without consent, the player breached and the club was “freed ... of any further obligation to pay salary under the contract.”
BaselineB: Common law contract principles applied to the parties’ written employment contract (interpretation of contractual terms on termination/guarantee and effect of breach/repudiation).
JudgeB: McIntyre J. (for Dickson, Beetz and McIntyre JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Workmen’s compensation subrogation/priority where victim contributorily at fault: if the Commission’s compensation equals or exceeds the dependant’s reduced civil claim (e.g., 50% under art. 1056 C.C.), the dependant has not received only “part payment” and cannot claim an “additional sum” under s. 8; the Commission is subrogated pleno jure to that extent and is reimbursed first
BaselineA: Statute and Civil Code: Workmen’s Compensation Act (R.S.Q. 1964, c. 159) ss. 7(3) (subrogation pleno jure) and 8 (right to claim “any additional sum required”); Civil Code art. 1157 (partial payment rule) and art. 1056 (wrongful death claim reduced by victim’s fault). Prior SCC authorities referenced: Rainville Automobile Ltd. v. Primiano; Hôpital Notre-Dame de l’Espérance and Théoret v. Laurent; Brink’s Express v. Plaisance (distinguished).
CaseB_TestB: Institutional financial security requirement for judicial independence: any government measure affecting judges’ remuneration conditions (including eliminating an office conferring a clear economic benefit) must be preceded by an “independent, effective and objective” commission process; if recommendations are ignored, the government must justify that decision on a “simple rationality test”
BaselineB: Constitutional doctrine under Charter s. 11(d) and the Preamble to the Constitution Act, 1867, building on Valente v. The Queen and the Reference re Remuneration of Judges of the Provincial Court of Prince Edward Island (Provincial Court Judges Reference) (commission requirement; rationality review if recommendations rejected).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Suspensive effect on an inferior criminal court’s power once served with a prohibition/quash notice endorsed to require a Rule 7 return: “there must be a suspension of jurisdiction when an application to quash or a combined application to prohibit and to quash is served on the inferior court with the command, under the Rules, to make a return forthwith”; failure to return “had the same effect as if a return was properly made whereupon jurisdiction was suspended.”
BaselineA: Combination of (i) Ontario Criminal Rules 4-8 (esp. Rules 6-8) and (ii) Criminal Code, s. 714, informed by common law certiorari suspension principles (e.g., R. v. Foster; R. v. Titchmarsh discussed).
JudgeA: Laskin C.J. (for Laskin C.J. and Judson, Spence and Dickson JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Section 15(1) equality analysis (La Forest J.): three-step test—(1) whether the law draws a distinction; (2) whether the distinction results in disadvantage (imposes a burden/withholds a benefit); (3) whether the distinction is based on an “irrelevant personal characteristic” enumerated or analogous, assessed by “relevancy…to the functional values underlying the law” in a contextual comparative analysis.
BaselineB: Common law Charter framework from Andrews v. Law Society of British Columbia and related s. 15 jurisprudence (as discussed in the reasons), applied to Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 15(1).
JudgeB: La Forest J. (for Lamer C.J. and La Forest, Gonthier and Major JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Defence of fair comment requires proof that the impugned comment was the honest expression of the real opinion of the writer/publisher; each publisher is in the same position as the original writer, so absent proof of the writers’ honest belief (and with defendants’ denial of honest belief), the defence cannot go to the jury. Key quotes: fair comment protection applies only when the opinion is honest — “such protection is afforded only when the opinion represents the honest expression of the view of the person who expresses it”; “Comment must be published honestly in that it is the expression of the defendant's real opinion”; and “each publisher in relying on the defence of fair comment is in exactly the same position as the original writer.”
BaselineA: Common law (defamation—fair comment defence), drawing on authorities cited in the reasons including Turner v. Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer Pictures Ltd., Slim v. Daily Telegraph Ltd., Jones v. Skelton, and Lyon & Lyon v. Daily Telegraph Ltd.
JudgeA: Ritchie J. (reasons concurred in by Laskin C.J., Pigeon and Pratte JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Section 2(a) infringement threshold for indirect burdens: state action that increases the cost of practising/manifesting religious belief is within s. 2(a) unless the burden is “trivial or insubstantial”; then s. 1 justification applies using the Oakes framework (pressing and substantial objective; proportionality including rational connection, minimal impairment, and overall proportionality). Key quotes: “All coercive burdens on the exercise of religious beliefs are potentially within the ambit of s. 2(a)”; but “action which increases the cost of practising or otherwise manifesting religious beliefs is not prohibited if the burden is trivial or insubstantial”; and under s. 1, the objective must be a “pressing and substantial concern” and the means must be “proportional or appropriate to the ends” (rational connection, minimal impairment, and proportionality of effects).
BaselineB: Statute + constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms ss. 1 and 2(a) (and related interpretive use of s. 27), applied to the Retail Business Holidays Act, R.S.O. 1980, c. 453 (notably ss. 2 and 3(4)); s. 1 analysis follows R. v. Oakes as referenced in the reasons.
JudgeB: Dickson C.J. (for Dickson C.J. and Chouinard and Le Dain JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Fair comment defence requires proof that the defamatory comment was an honest expression of the real opinion of the writer/publisher (each publisher is in the same position as the original writer); absent evidence of the writers’ honest belief (and with the newspaper’s denial of belief), the defence is unavailable
BaselineA: Common law defamation (fair comment) as described in authorities cited in the reasons (e.g., Turner v. Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer Pictures Ltd.; Jones v. Skelton; Slim v. Daily Telegraph; Silkin v. Beaverbrook Newspapers; and related cases discussed)
CaseB_TestB: Contempt of court: the party alleging contempt must prove beyond a reasonable doubt the constituent elements, including the alleged contemnor’s actual personal knowledge of the order (personal service or actual knowledge); service on a solicitor does not, without supporting circumstances, fix ministers with knowledge; vicarious liability does not apply
BaselineB: Common law contempt (knowledge/personal service requirement) plus interpretation of Federal Court Rules on service (Rules 308, 311, 355) as not altering contempt’s knowledge element
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Fair comment in defamation requires proof that the impugned comment was an honest expression of the real view of the person making/publishing it; each publisher is in the same position as the original writer, so without proof of the writers' honest belief (and with the newspaper/editor denying honest belief) the defence cannot go to the jury.
BaselineA: Common law (defence of fair comment in defamation), drawing on authorities cited in the reasons including Turner v. Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer Pictures Ltd. and Silkin v. Beaverbrook Newspapers Ltd.
CaseB_TestB: Garofoli review of wiretap authorizations: errors in the affidavit (even advertent or fraudulent) are only factors and do not automatically vitiate the authorization; the court should excise the tainted material and ask whether the remaining independent information provides sufficient reliable grounds on which an authorization could reasonably be based.
BaselineB: Common law framework from R. v. Garofoli (applied to Criminal Code wiretap authorizations).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Validity (intra vires) of a CRTC regulation under Broadcasting Act s. 16: a regulation is valid if, objectively, it "deals with a class of subject referred to in s. 3" (i.e., is "in furtherance of its objects" implementing the s. 3 broadcasting policy).
BaselineA: Statute (Broadcasting Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. B-11, ss. 3, 15, 16; applied to Radio (A.M.) Broadcasting Regulations, s. 5(1)(k))
CaseB_TestB: Quebec civil fault (art. 1053 C.C.) and appellate deference to jury: fault is whether conduct matches "a reasonable person concerned about the interests of others and placed in the same external situation"; a jury verdict stands unless "unreasonable" (and the jury translates the prudent-and-reasonable-person criterion into concrete terms).
BaselineB: Statute/civil law (Civil Code art. 1053; Code of Civil Procedure arts. 363, 380; with supporting jurisprudence including Metropolitan Railway Co. v. Jackson (1877), 3 A.C. 193, followed)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Limits on a provincial commission of inquiry’s coercive powers vis-à-vis federal institutions/Crown: province may inquire into specific criminal acts by RCMP members, but cannot (directly or indirectly) inquire into RCMP administration/management; and a minister’s s. 41(2) Federal Court Act national-security certificate binds a commissioner (not a superior court) so production/discovery is refused without examination
BaselineA: Combination: (1) Constitution (B.N.A. Act, ss. 91/92, esp. s. 92(14) “administration of justice” vs federal jurisdiction); (2) statute: Federal Court Act, R.S.C. 1970 (2nd Supp.), c. 10, s. 41(2) (and s. 41 generally); (3) common law Crown immunity/privilege principles (e.g., Crown not compellable for discovery) as discussed in Quebec North Shore Paper, Alberta v. C.T.C., etc.
CaseB_TestB: Contested custody (natural parent vs adoptive parents): exercising parens patriae/equitable jurisdiction, the court must treat the child’s welfare as the predominant/paramount consideration, decided on “all relevant factors” (including psychological, spiritual and emotional welfare); parental claims are considered but set aside where welfare requires
BaselineB: Statute plus equity/common law: Domestic Relations Ordinance, R.O.N.W.T. 1974, c. D-9, ss. 28(1), 35(2), 37, and especially s. 39 (rules of equity prevail where not conflicting), together with parens patriae jurisprudence (e.g., Racine v. Woods; Beson v. Director of Child Welfare; Re Moores and Feldstein; and discussion of the SCC “trilogy” cases).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Public Authorities Protection Act s. 11: classify the impugned act as part of a “statutory or other public duty or authority” only if it has a “public aspect or connotation”; exclude acts that are “private executive or private administrative” or “subordinate or incidental” (public/private segregation of statutory functions)
BaselineA: Statute: The Public Authorities Protection Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 374, s. 11 (six-month limitation for acts/neglect in execution of “any statutory or other public duty or authority”), read with The Housing Development Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 213, s. 6(2) (power to “plan, construct and manage” housing projects). Interpreted in light of Bradford Corporation v. Myers and McGonegal v. Gray (as discussed in the reasons).
JudgeA: Estey J. (for Laskin C.J. and Spence, Dickson, Beetz, Estey and Pratte JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Non-delegable statutory duty inquiry: determine from the statute’s text whether it “clearly places” the defendant under a mandatory, non-delegable duty (here, no such duty where the Indian Act uses “may” not “shall” and expressly contemplates delegation via agreements)
BaselineB: Statute: Indian Act, S.C. 1951, c. 29, ss. 113-114 (and related scheme). The Court applies the approach that the inquiry “begins with the words of the statute” and asks whether it “clearly places” Canada under a non-delegable duty (citing E.D.G. v. Hammer; contrasting Lewis (Guardian ad litem of) v. British Columbia).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Exemption-from-seizure via insurance policy clause only applies if claimant is a true third-party beneficiary (not a universal legatee/heir); heirs are not “third parties” so cannot invoke art. 553(3) C.C.P. through the policy
BaselineA: Statute/civil code provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, art. 553(3) (exemption from seizure for property declared exempt by donor/testator); Civil Code (C.C.) arts. 597 (heir not a third party), 1028 (contract binds heirs/legal representatives), 735 (limits on bequests shielding from creditors).
CaseB_TestB: No-fault liability for neighbourhood disturbances under art. 976 C.C.Q.: liability turns on whether neighbours suffered “abnormal or excessive annoyances” beyond the “limit of tolerance” (result-focused, not conduct/fault-focused)
BaselineB: Statute/civil code provision: Civil Code of Québec, art. 976 (duty to tolerate normal neighbourhood annoyances; liability for excessive/abnormal annoyances).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Superior Court jurisdiction not ousted: a provincial superior court retains jurisdiction (per art. 31 C.C.P.) to decide whether Bell’s s. 5(4) imposes a legal obligation, when the issue arises in properly instituted court proceedings (e.g., a tort/fault-based injunction action), absent a clear statutory indication of exclusive Commission jurisdiction
BaselineA: Statute and regulation (Quebec Code of Civil Procedure, art. 31; An Act respecting The Bell Telephone Company of Canada, s. 5(4)-(6) as amended; National Transportation Act, s. 45(1); Bell General Regulations/Rules 2, 7, 9)
CaseB_TestB: Reopening the Crown’s case: the “keystone principle” is prejudice to the accused; discretion tightens by trial stage—(1) before Crown closes: broad latitude; (2) after Crown closes but before defence elects: generally to correct an “oversight or inadvertent omission” if justice requires and no prejudice; (3) after defence has started to answer: reopening only in the “narrowest or most exceptional of circumstances” (e.g., defence contributed to omission or matter of form), to avoid undermining self-incrimination principles
BaselineB: Common law discretion on reopening (considering Robillard v. The Queen and related reopening jurisprudence) informed by Charter self-incrimination principles (ss. 7, 11(c), 13) and discussed alongside Criminal Code amendment provisions (s. 601) though the holding turns on reopening
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Admissibility of cross-examining an accused/witness on juvenile delinquency record as “convictions” under s. 12 Canada Evidence Act (and related character issue under s. 593 Criminal Code): (1) “any offence” in s. 12(1) includes a delinquency consisting of a Criminal Code violation enforceable under the Juvenile Delinquents Act; (2) a finding/adjudication of delinquency is “equivalent to a conviction” for s. 12; (3) an admitted prior conviction/delinquency need not be proved by the official record unless exceptional circumstances show the admission was erroneous; and (4) where the accused says he has never been convicted/arrested, he “put his character in issue” so the Crown may contradict with proof of prior convictions.
BaselineA: Statute (Canada Evidence Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-10, s. 12(1)-(2); Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 593; interpreted alongside Juvenile Delinquents Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. J-3, ss. 3, 20(1), 38).
JudgeA: Pratte J. (for Martland, Ritchie, Pigeon, Beetz and Pratte JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Criminal Code indictment amendment for variance between a particular and the proof (drug specified vs drug proved): where the Crown has particularized the narcotic but proves a different scheduled form, the charge should be amended under s. 529; the court “shall” consider s. 529(4)(a)-(e), especially whether the accused “has been misled or prejudiced in his defence” and whether the amendment can be made “without injustice”; if prejudice exists but can be cured, s. 529(5) permits adjournment; if no (or no irreparable) prejudice, amendment may be made, including by the SCC on appeal under s. 613(1)(b)(i) and (3).
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 529(4)-(5), 613(1)(b)(i), 613(3); applied in context of Narcotic Control Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. N-1, ss. 2, 4 and Schedule item 3).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Dickson J.’s four-factor test for whether an administrative decision/order is required by law to be made on a judicial or quasi-judicial basis (for Federal Court Act s. 28 reviewability): (1) whether the statutory language/context suggests a hearing; (2) whether the decision affects rights/obligations; (3) whether an adversary process is involved; (4) whether there is an obligation to apply substantive rules to many individual cases (vs broad policy). These are “factors to be weighed and evaluated, no one of which is necessarily determinative.”
BaselineA: Statute (Federal Court Act, s. 28; definition in s. 2) interpreted using common-law natural justice/duty-to-act-judicially jurisprudence (e.g., Guay v. Lafleur; Randolph; Wiseman; Pearlberg; Russell v. Duke of Norfolk).
CaseB_TestB: Stillman (Cory J.) s. 24(2) “trial fairness” framework: first classify evidence as non-conscriptive vs conscriptive; if non-conscriptive, proceed to other Collins factors; if conscriptive, ask whether Crown proves on a balance of probabilities the evidence would have been discovered by alternative non-conscriptive means (independent source/inevitable discovery). If conscriptive and not discoverable, “as a general rule” exclude without considering other Collins factors.
BaselineB: Statute/constitutional text (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 24(2)) building on prior SCC framework in R. v. Collins (and related cases like Black, Burlingham, Borden).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory limits on interim rate-setting: s. 31 “losses” means lost revenue after the rate application, and the legality question is whether interim rates will prospectively over-recover by including pre-application shortfalls; plus s. 8 duty to give written findings of fact and reasons
BaselineA: Statute: The Gas Utilities Act, R.S.A. 1970, c. 158, ss. 27-28 (rate-setting framework) and especially s. 31 (excess revenues/losses after application due to undue delay); and The Administrative Procedures Act, R.S.A. 1970, c. 2, s. 8 (written decision with findings of fact and reasons). Prior SCC reference: City of Edmonton et al. v. Northwestern Utilities Limited, [1961] S.C.R. 392 (re s. 31 meaning of “losses”).
CaseB_TestB: Cuerrier fraud-vitiated consent test under Criminal Code s. 265(3)(c): consent to unprotected sex is vitiated if (1) dishonesty (including non-disclosure of HIV status, assessed objectively) and (2) deprivation via exposure to a “significant risk of serious bodily harm”, and the Crown must prove the complainant would have refused unprotected sex if informed
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, ss. 265(3)(c) (fraud vitiating consent) and 268 (aggravated assault). Common-law/criminal-fraud concepts used as baseline for “fraud”: R. v. Olan, [1978] 2 S.C.R. 1175; R. v. Théroux, [1993] 2 S.C.R. 5; R. v. Zlatic, [1993] 2 S.C.R. 29.
JudgeB: Cory J. (for Cory, Major, Bastarache and Binnie JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory interpretation of Parole Act ss. 10 and 20 (as amended in 1977): day parole may be ended by (i) revocation under s. 10(1)(e) triggering s. 20 consequences, or (ii) termination under s. 10(2); “any parole” in s. 20(2) includes day parole and “recommitment” in s. 20(1) creates no operative ambiguity
BaselineA: Statute: Parole Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. P-2 (as amended by 1977 amendments), especially s. 2 definition of “parole” ("includes day parole"), s. 10(1)(e) (revocation), s. 10(2) (termination), and s. 20(1)-(3) (revocation consequences and Board discretion to recredit remission)
CaseB_TestB: Palmer criteria (applied to sentence appeals) for admitting fresh evidence on appeal: (1) generally not admitted if, by due diligence, it could have been adduced at trial; (2) relevant; (3) credible; (4) if believed, could reasonably, with the trial record, be expected to have affected the result
BaselineB: Common law test from Palmer v. The Queen, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 759, applied within the statutory appellate-evidence framework (Criminal Code, ss. 683 and 687) under the overriding “interests of justice” criterion
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Exercise of SCC discretion under Supreme Court Act s. 52 to vary interest on an SCC judgment: default is interest as if from the trial judgment date, but the Court may order otherwise; here, limit pre-SCC-judgment interest to the trial award amount where delay is attributable to the successful appellant
BaselineA: Statute (Supreme Court Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. S-19, s. 52 (as amended 1976) and Interest Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-18, ss. 13-14; plus Supreme Court Rules, r. 61 procedure)
CaseB_TestB: Whether procedural fairness/natural justice applies to Governor in Council decisions under National Transportation Act s. 64(1): construe the statute; where s. 64(1) confers broad, quasi-legislative discretion with no procedural standards, no duty of fairness is implied beyond staying within jurisdictional boundaries/conditions precedent
BaselineB: Statute (National Transportation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. N-17, s. 64(1)-(2); related context: Railway Act, ss. 320-321; Interpretation Act, s. 28) interpreted against common-law fairness/natural justice jurisprudence (e.g., Nicholson)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory-limit rule for groundwater pumping: “any pumping above 10,000 gallons a day is unreasonable unless a permit has been granted”; “any pumping in violation of s. 37 is to be considered as a nuisance when causing damage to other properties” (and no right to pump is a defence for pumping exceeding the quantity authorized).
BaselineA: Statute + common law (private nuisance/negligence). Baseline statute: The Ontario Water Resources Commission Act / Ontario Water Resources Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 332, s. 37 (10,000 gallons/day limit; permits). Baseline common law backdrop: the “English Rule” on percolating water (e.g., Langbrook Properties) and nuisance reasonableness concepts.
CaseB_TestB: Meaning of “unlawful and intentional interference” for exemplary damages under Quebec Charter s. 49(2): intent exists where the actor “has a state of mind that implies a desire or intent to cause the consequences of his or her wrongful conduct, or … acts with full knowledge of the immediate and natural or at least extremely probable consequences that his or her conduct will cause”.
BaselineB: Statute (quasi-constitutional) + prior SCC interpretation. Baseline statute: Quebec Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms, ss. 1 and 49 (especially s. 49(2)). Baseline case cited for the test: Quebec (Public Curator) v. Syndicat national des employés de l’hôpital St-Ferdinand, [1996] 3 S.C.R. 211.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Highway Code s. 13(6) irrebuttable presumption: if the registered owner has not complied with s. 13(1)-(2), he "shall be deemed to be the owner for purposes of responsibility and for purposes of insurance against the responsibility resulting from the ownership or use of such vehicle"; therefore, for liability coverage, the transfer is deemed not to have occurred and the buyer/driver remains covered under the transferor’s omnibus clause (driving with the deemed owner’s consent).
BaselineA: Statute (Highway Code, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 231, s. 13(6), with compliance duties in s. 13(1)-(2); applied in relation to the civil liability section/omnibus clause of the auto policy).
CaseB_TestB: Garofoli leave/threshold test for cross-examining a wiretap affiant: leave requires the defence to show a "reasonable likelihood" that cross-examination "will elicit testimony of probative value" on a material issue for the reviewing judge (i.e., tending to undermine a statutory precondition/basis for the authorization).
BaselineB: Common law (R. v. Garofoli, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 1421), applied in the context of Criminal Code wiretap authorizations (including s. 184.2).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Direct action under Highway Victims Indemnity Act s. 6: insurer is directly liable to third parties only for “damage covered by liability insurance”; s. 6 removes only nullity/lapse defences and “does not extend the insurance contract to what it does not cover”, so coverage turns on the policy’s defined scope (including whether the trailer falls within the policy definition of “automobile” and whether the damage was caused “first and foremost” by the trailer’s use).
BaselineA: Statute (Highway Victims Indemnity Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 232, s. 6) as interpreted alongside the insurance contract’s definition of coverage; relying on General Security Insurance Co. of Canada v. Bélanger, [1977] 1 S.C.R. 802.
CaseB_TestB: Landlord covenant to insure and insurer subrogation against negligent tenant: tenant escapes liability for negligently caused fire only if the landlord’s covenant to insure “runs to the benefit of the tenant”; the covenant is treated as benefiting the tenant “unless the option to purchase provisions ... provide an explanation consistent with the risk of fires being on the tenant.”
BaselineB: Common law of landlord-tenant/contract interpretation and subrogation, building on Agnew-Surpass Shoe Stores Ltd. v. Cummer-Yonge Investments Ltd., [1976] 2 S.C.R. 221 and Ross Southward Tire Ltd. v. Pyrotech Products Ltd., [1976] 2 S.C.R. 35 (and distinguishing United Motors Service Inc. v. Hutson, [1937] S.C.R. 294).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Qualified privilege in defamation defeated only by malice; privilege protects even excessive language if the defendant "might have honestly and on reasonable grounds believed" the statement was true (Adam v. Ward / Netupsky v. Craig).
BaselineA: Common law (qualified privilege and malice), drawing on Adam v. Ward, [1917] A.C. 309 and Netupsky v. Craig, [1973] S.C.R. 55.
CaseB_TestB: Sufficiency of reasons (Sheppard/Braich): two-stage inquiry—(1) are the reasons inadequate; and (2) if so, do they prevent appellate review (i.e., are they not "sufficiently amenable to appellate review").
BaselineB: Common law appellate review doctrine from R. v. Sheppard, 2002 SCC 26 and R. v. Braich, 2002 SCC 27 (with Criminal Code, s. 686 as the appellate intervention backdrop).
JudgeB: Bastarache and Abella JJ. (LeBel J. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Fault for unlawful arrest by police: arrest power requires lawful authority; for warrantless arrest, officer must have reasonable grounds and the belief must take into account all information available (including potentially exculpatory information)
BaselineA: Combination of statute and civil law delict: Civil Code arts. 1053, 1054 (fault and employer liability) plus Criminal Code 1953-54 s. 435 (warrantless arrest on reasonable and probable grounds) and Coroners' Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 29, s. 38 (detention of witnesses)
CaseB_TestB: Validity of dismissal of probationary constable: dismissal power is exclusively vested in the Police Board and cannot be delegated; Board must actually exercise the power (not merely have the chief act) and must at least inform the constable that the Board is considering dismissal—otherwise there is no effective discharge
BaselineB: Statute/regulation (and related collective agreement): The Police Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 351, s. 29; Regulation 680, s. 27(b) (authority of board to dispense with services within 18 months); s. 9 of the collective agreement (dismissal during probation)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Municipal office disqualification for having a direct or indirect “interest in any contract” with the city (broad, ordinary-meaning approach: directors/officers are “interested” in their company’s municipal contracts)
BaselineA: Statute (Moncton Consolidation Act, 1946 (N.B.), c. 101, s. 6), interpreted using the broad principle from Angrignon (SCC) that “interested in” has no technical meaning and must be given effect “according to the common usage of men”
CaseB_TestB: Statutory interpretation of whether a municipality is an “institution” under the New Brunswick Official Languages Act for s. 22 (duty to use the other party’s chosen official language in civil pleadings/processes)
BaselineB: Statute (Official Languages Act, S.N.B. 2002, c. O-0.5, ss. 1 “institution” and 22), applying the modern principle of interpretation (Driedger) and limiting “Charter values” to cases of genuine ambiguity (Bell ExpressVu)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Qualified privilege in libel: malice goes to the jury only if the evidence “raises a probability” of express malice (more than a mere scintilla/possibility; “more consistent with its existence than with its non-existence”).
BaselineA: Common law (defamation/qualified privilege and malice), drawing on authorities including Somerville v. Hawkins and SCC’s Sun Life Assurance Co. of Canada v. Dalrymple.
CaseB_TestB: Blood Tribe clear-intent requirement for statutory abrogation of solicitor-client privilege: privilege “cannot be abrogated by inference”; only “clear intent” in legislative language permits abrogation (applied to ITA s. 232(1) accounting-records exception).
BaselineB: Statute (Income Tax Act, ss. 231.2(1), 231.7(1), and especially s. 232(1) definition of “solicitor-client privilege”), interpreted under the common-law/constitutional principle from Blood Tribe that abrogation requires clear legislative language.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Priority of B.C. Payment of Wages Act s. 5A lien: the lien arises "from the date wages were earned" and takes priority only over dispositions after it attaches; if a mortgage predates the lien, it is "not affected" and the lien "will only attach to the employer’s equity" in the property.
BaselineA: Statute — Payment of Wages Act, 1962 (B.C.), c. 45, ss. 5 and 5A (especially s. 5A(1)-(2)).
CaseB_TestB: Suppletive dissolution of a Quebec legal person: arts. 355-364 C.C.Q. apply "insofar as it is necessary to fill the gaps of a special statute"; dissolution may be ordered under art. 355(2) where the court confirms (i) fulfilment of a condition, (ii) accomplishment of the object, (iii) "impossibility of accomplishing that object", or (iv) "some other legitimate cause".
BaselineB: Statute/Codified law — Civil Code of Québec, arts. 300, 334, 355 (and related arts. 355-364); considered alongside Companies Act and Code of Civil Procedure art. 829.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Residual discretion/inherent jurisdiction to remedy unfairness from Crown’s closing address: normally by curative jury instruction; in rare cases by a limited defence reply only in the clearest cases of unfairness
BaselineA: Combination: statute and common law. Statutory baseline is Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 651(3) and s. 651(4) (order of addresses). Common law baseline is the superior court’s inherent jurisdiction to control its process to prevent unfairness/abuse (e.g., Selvey v. DPP; R. v. Osborn; Amato v. The Queen, as cited).
JudgeA: Cory, Iacobucci and Bastarache JJ. (for Gonthier, Cory, Iacobucci and Bastarache JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Charter-validity test for a statutory presumption under s. 11(d): a presumption is constitutional only if proof of the substituted fact leads “inexorably” to the essential element it replaces (and s. 172.1(3) fails because representation of age does not inexorably prove belief)
BaselineB: Combination: statute and common law/constitutional doctrine. Statutory baseline is Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 172.1(3) (presumption re age) in the context of s. 172.1(1)(b). Constitutional baseline is Charter, s. 11(d). The governing SCC doctrine is drawn from prior SCC cases cited (e.g., R. v. Whyte; R. v. Downey; R. v. Audet) requiring an “inexorable” connection.
JudgeB: Moldaver J. (Wagner C.J. and Gascon, Côté, Brown, Rowe and Martin JJ. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Adjudicator’s remedial authority to substitute a lesser penalty for discharge: where the adjudicator finds “just and sufficient cause for some disciplinary action, but not for discharge”, the adjudicator has power to replace discharge with a lesser penalty (e.g., suspension).
BaselineA: Statute + collective agreement: Public Service Labour Relations Act, R.S.N.B. 1973, c. P-25, s. 92(1)(b) (adjudication of “disciplinary action resulting in discharge, suspension or a financial penalty”) and s. 101 (privative clause), plus collective agreement art. V(d) (“Discipline, suspension, demotion or discharge ... shall be for just and sufficient cause”) and art. XVII(c) (management rights subject to “just and sufficient cause”). Prior SCC baseline discussed/distinguished: Port Arthur Shipbuilding Co. v. Arthurs, [1969] S.C.R. 85.
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 24(2) exclusion test (Collins guidelines): exclude evidence only if, “having regard to all the circumstances”, its admission “would bring the administration of justice into disrepute”; applied via Collins factors (including trial fairness and seriousness of the Charter breach, e.g., good-faith reliance on then-unchallenged writ of assistance).
BaselineB: Statute/constitutional text + prior SCC framework: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 24(2) (and ss. 7, 8 context), applying the SCC’s then-newly articulated common-law-like framework in R. v. Collins, [1987] 1 S.C.R. 265.
JudgeB: Lamer J. (for Dickson C.J. and Lamer, Wilson, Le Dain and La Forest JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Will-construction test: give effect to the testator’s overriding intention on a fair reading of the will clause (do not let administrative/technical wording defeat a clearly expressed intention)
BaselineA: Common law (will construction/interpretation principles; applied to the will’s clause 4(i) and related administrative clauses)
CaseB_TestB: Manslaughter legal causation with intervening acts: the accused’s dangerous and unlawful acts must be a “significant contributing cause of death”; foreseeability/independent-act analyses are non-determinative “analytical aids”
BaselineB: Common law causation test from Smithers v. The Queen and R. v. Nette (interpreting/applying Criminal Code ss. 222, 224, 225 in the homicide context)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Functional/operational test for whether labour relations fall under exclusive federal jurisdiction (exception) or provincial jurisdiction (rule): federal only if the undertaking’s “nature of [its] operations and [its] normal activities” can be “characterized as federal”, i.e., if federal labour jurisdiction is “an integral part of primary federal jurisdiction over some other federal object”.
BaselineA: Common law constitutional division-of-powers doctrine for labour relations (functional/operational test), as stated through prior cases cited in the reasons (e.g., Toronto Electric Commissioners v. Snider; the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act Reference (Stevedoring case)).
CaseB_TestB: Section 15(1) Charter equality test (post-Kapp/Withler): (1) “Does the law create a distinction based on an enumerated or analogous ground?” and (2) “Does the distinction create a disadvantage by perpetuating prejudice or stereotyping?”, assessed contextually without needing a “mirror comparator group”.
BaselineB: Combination of constitutional text (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 15(1)) and prior SCC equality jurisprudence (especially Andrews; Law; Kapp).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Bankruptcy Act s. 107(1)(j) overrides provincial Crown “privileges”/priorities: provincial tax claims (not otherwise mentioned) rank pari passu “notwithstanding any statutory preference to the contrary”, so a registered provincial tax privilege cannot be treated as a “secured creditor” right to escape s. 107(1)(j). Key move: treat the opening “Subject to the rights of secured creditors” as a general rule, but the “notwithstanding” clause in s. 107(1)(j) as an exception that prevails where applicable.
BaselineA: Statute: Bankruptcy Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. B-3, s. 2 (definition of “secured creditor”) and s. 107(1)(j) (scheme of distribution: Crown claims pari passu “notwithstanding any statutory preference to the contrary”); applied against Quebec Retail Sales Tax Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 71, s. 30 and Civil Code art. 1989 (registration of Crown privilege).
JudgeA: Pigeon J. (for Martland, Ritchie, Pigeon, Beetz, Pratte and McIntyre JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Public interest standing (purposive, flexible, discretionary): courts weigh three interrelated factors—(1) serious justiciable issue; (2) plaintiff has a real stake/genuine interest/engagement; and (3) whether, “in all of the circumstances”, the proposed suit is a “reasonable and effective means” to bring the issue to court (not a strict ‘no other way’ requirement). The third factor is assessed by considering (illustratively) judicial economy, suitability for adversarial determination, and the principle of legality, plus practical realities and alternatives.
BaselineB: Common law standing doctrine from SCC cases (e.g., Borowski; Finlay; Canadian Council of Churches; Hy and Zel’s; Thorson; McNeil), reformulated/clarified in this decision.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Crown prerogative priority applies only where Crown and subject claims are “of equal degree”; a prior registered second/collateral mortgage is of a higher degree than a later registered Crown judgment, so Registry Act registration-date priorities govern
BaselineA: Combination: common law Crown prerogative priority for debts “of equal degree” (The Queen v. Bank of Nova Scotia (1885), 11 S.C.R. 1) plus Nova Scotia Registry Act, R.S.N.S. 1967, c. 265, ss. 17-18 (and N.S. Civil Procedure Rule 47.11 distribution “according to their priorities”)
CaseB_TestB: International jurisdiction in Quebec is determined by extending domestic territorial jurisdiction rules; under art. 71 C.C.P., an incidental action in warranty “must be taken before the court in which the principal action is pending” and this rule applies to a foreign defendant without limitation
BaselineB: Statute/civil law: Code of Civil Procedure, art. 71 (and discussion of arts. 68-75, incl. art. 75) and Civil Code, art. 27; applied through the private international law principle that international jurisdiction is defined by extension of domestic territorial jurisdiction (as recognized in Alimport, Trower and Sons, etc.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “detained” under Canadian Bill of Rights s. 2(c): “detain”/“detention” “connote some form of compulsory restraint” and contemplate a person “detained by due process of law”; roadside sobriety screening where the driver is then “allowed to go away” is not detention, so no Bill of Rights right to counsel is triggered and no “reasonable excuse” exists for refusing the breath demand.
BaselineA: Statute: Canadian Bill of Rights, 1960, s. 2(c)(ii)-(iii) (right to retain and instruct counsel without delay when “arrested or detained”; habeas corpus language) applied in relation to Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 234.1(1)-(2) (roadside breath demand; offence to refuse “without reasonable excuse”).
CaseB_TestB: Two-branch test for civil conspiracy: liability exists (1) where “the predominant purpose of the defendants’ conduct is to cause injury to the plaintiff” (means lawful or unlawful); or (2) where “the conduct of the defendants is unlawful”, is “directed towards the plaintiff (alone or together with others)”, and defendants “should know in the circumstances that injury to the plaintiff is likely to and does result” (constructive intent), with actual damage required.
BaselineB: Common law tort of conspiracy to injure, drawing on and synthesizing prior authorities discussed in the reasons (including International Brotherhood of Teamsters v. Therien; Gagnon v. Foundation Maritime; and applying Lonrho Ltd. v. Shell Petroleum).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 492 re-election validity: effective re-election occurs where the accused (1) notifies the sheriff of the desire to re-elect (s. 492(1)); (2) attends at the time/place fixed (s. 492(2)-(3)); and (3) after the charge actually faced at trial is read, communicates the re-election (which may be done through counsel in the accused’s presence). SCC clarifies that s. 492(3) requires reading the operative indictment/charge then faced, and that failure to prefer a new Form 4 indictment under s. 496 after re-election does not invalidate proceedings where the indictment is already in Form 4.
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, s. 492 (re-election procedure) and related s. 496 (Form 4 indictment after re-election).
CaseB_TestB: Injurious affection where no land is taken (Loiselle conditions): compensation requires proof that (1) damage results from an act rendered lawful by statutory powers; (2) damage would have been actionable at common law but for statutory powers; (3) damage is an injury to the land itself (not personal/business); and (4) damage is occasioned by construction of the public work, not its use. SCC applies this by asking whether the construction would be actionable in private nuisance (unreasonable interference), and holds loss of prospect/amenities from adjacent highway construction is not actionable.
BaselineB: Statute plus common law: Expropriations Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 154, ss. 1(e)(ii), 21, incorporating the common-law requirement of actionable nuisance; four-part test quoted from The Queen v. Loiselle, [1962] S.C.R. 624.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Interpretation of s. 137(1): Ontario Municipal Board may exercise Municipal Act s. 14(11)(a),(b),(d) powers (including to “make all such adjustments of assets and liabilities…as the Board may consider equitable”) “in relation to the dissolution of the County of Carleton” (not limited to annexation/amalgamation under Municipal Act s. 14(2)); referential incorporation is “restricted entirely to…subclauses (a), (b) and (d), without the qualifying or delimiting words in the introduction to subs. (11)”.
BaselineA: Statute: The Regional Municipality of Ottawa-Carleton Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 407, ss. 135, 137 (incorporating by reference The Municipal Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 284, s. 14(11)(a),(b),(d)).
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 7/11(d) mens rea requirement for murder: “it is a principle of fundamental justice that a conviction for murder cannot rest on anything less than proof beyond a reasonable doubt of subjective foresight of death”; therefore Criminal Code s. 213(a) is unconstitutional because it “expressly removes from the Crown the burden of proving beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused had subjective foresight of death”.
BaselineB: Combination: Constitutional baseline (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms ss. 7, 11(d)) applied to statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 213(a)); prior SCC authority discussed/applied: R. v. Vaillancourt, [1987] 2 S.C.R. 636.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Validity of one-party consent interception and resulting admissibility: (1) determine whether statements are “private communications” by asking whether the speaker/originator reasonably expected no interception; (2) an interception is “lawfully made” under s. 178.16(1)(a) if it falls within s. 178.11(2)(a) consent; (3) consent is valid if “voluntary (i.e. free from coercion)” and “made knowingly, with an awareness of the significance of the consent”
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, Part IV.1 as enacted by the Protection of Privacy Act): ss. 178.1 (definition of “private communication”), 178.11(2)(a) (consent interception), 178.16(1) (admissibility: “unless (a) the interception was lawfully made; or (b) ... expressly consented to the admission”)
JudgeA: McIntyre J. (for Martland, Ritchie, Pigeon, Dickson, Beetz, Estey, Pratte and McIntyre JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Proving the “identifiable group” element under Criminal Code s. 319(2): the trial judge must assess “the totality of the evidence” to decide whether the accused’s statements “as a matter of fact, promoted hatred” of the particularized group; it is “not necessary for the Crown to prove that the terms ‘gypsies’ and ‘Roma’ were interchangeable” and “the reference to ‘gypsies’ was but one item of evidence to consider”
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code): s. 319(2) (wilful promotion of hatred), s. 318(4) (definition of “identifiable group”); plus common-law evidence doctrine of judicial notice as summarized from R. v. Find, 2001 SCC 32 (facts may be accepted if notorious or “capable of immediate and accurate demonstration by resort to readily accessible sources of indisputable accuracy”)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Audi alteram partem in administrative appeals: an appellate tribunal must not receive evidence/representations ex parte after the hearing; if it does, the decision is invalid if the material might have prejudiced the party (no need to show actual prejudice)
BaselineA: Common law natural justice (audi alteram partem) applied in a statutory university discipline/appeal setting; statutory context: Universities Act, 1974 (B.C.), c. 100, ss. 58(1)-(3) (suspension and appeal) and s. 61 (President is a Board member and must attend meetings)
CaseB_TestB: Workers’ compensation occupational-disease causation on judicial review: causation may be inferred from circumstantial evidence (even with inconclusive/contrary expert evidence), and under s. 250(4) evenly weighted evidence on causation must be resolved in the worker’s favour; reviewing courts may intervene only if the finding is patently unreasonable (evidence incapable of supporting it)
BaselineB: Statutory scheme and policy: Workers Compensation Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 492, ss. 6 and 250(4) (plus s. 250(2) requiring application of Board policy on “causative significance”); judicial review constraint via Administrative Tribunals Act, S.B.C. 2004, c. 45, s. 58(2)(a) (patent unreasonableness). Common law causation inference principle referenced (Snell v. Farrell)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Appellate intervention in a trial damages award: an appellate court may not substitute its own figure unless "a wrong principle of law was applied" or "the overall award is a wholly erroneous estimate of damages" (Andrews v. Grand & Toy, applied).
BaselineA: Common law (as stated in Andrews et al. v. Grand & Toy Alberta Ltd. et al., [1978] 2 S.C.R. 229 at p. 235).
JudgeA: Martland J. (for the Court, oral reasons)
CaseB_TestB: Videotape-only identification: once it is established the videotape "has not been altered or changed" and "depicts the scene of a crime", it is admissible; a trier of fact may identify and convict on the videotape alone if satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt, assessing (i) "clarity and quality" and (ii) (to a lesser extent) "the length of time" the accused appears, with appropriate cautions/directions.
BaselineB: Common law evidence principles on admissibility/weight of recordings and SCC use of videotape identification (notably R. v. Leaney, [1989] 2 S.C.R. 393; also drawing on general relevance/admissibility principles).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Quebec Labour Code s. 16 presumption rebuttal: employer must show the dismissal was for “another good and sufficient reason” meaning a “substantial” reason that is “not a pretext” and is the “true reason” (causa causans); commissioner/court cannot review the severity/appropriateness of the penalty once a real reason is established
BaselineA: Statute (Quebec Labour Code, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 141 as am., ss. 13-16, especially s. 16; also discussed alongside s. 14 and s. 98)
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 12 “gross disproportionality” test (and its two-aspect application): assess whether punishment is “so excessive as to outrage standards of decency” by considering “the gravity of the offence, the personal characteristics of the offender and the particular circumstances of the case” (plus other non-decisive factors); if not grossly disproportionate on the facts, assess validity via “reasonable hypothetical circumstances”
BaselineB: Combination of constitutional text and common law/precedent (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 12; test drawn from and clarified from R. v. Smith, reaffirmed in R. v. Lyons and R. v. Luxton)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Summary conviction appeal costs: under Criminal Code ss. 758 and 771(3), the appeal court "may make any order with respect to costs that it considers just and reasonable" / "proper" and these provisions implicitly bind the Crown (Her Majesty) when read in the context of Part XXIV despite Interpretation Act s. 16.
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 758 ("may make any order with respect to costs that it considers just and reasonable") and 771(3) ("may make any order with respect to costs that it considers proper"), interpreted in light of Part XXIV (including s. 720(1) definition of "prosecutor") and Interpretation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-23, s. 16 (Crown not bound unless mentioned or referred to).
CaseB_TestB: Mortgage prepayment under Interest Act s. 10(1): mortgagors have a right to pay off at the end of each five-year period; Court sets categorical rules for when the right arises across renewal/extension scenarios (including that a valid renewal that "deems" the mortgage date to the maturity of the existing loan and is itself ≤ 5 years means no prepayment until the end of that renewal term).
BaselineB: Statute: Interest Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-18, s. 10(1) (and related provincial analogues, esp. Manitoba Mortgage Act s. 20(6); discharge procedure referenced via Real Property Act s. 103(1)(c)).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Wrongful dismissal damages: no deduction for (i) income tax not payable and (ii) unemployment insurance benefits arising from the employment contract (collateral benefits not deductible)
BaselineA: Common law contract damages principle (put plaintiff in same position as if contract performed) and SCC collateral-benefits approach (Guy v. Trizec Equities Ltd.)
CaseB_TestB: Identification of Criminals Act s. 2 applies to juveniles: a juvenile in lawful custody for a delinquency relating to a Criminal Code indictable offence is a person 'charged with, or under conviction of an indictable offence', so necessary reasonable force may be used to fingerprint
BaselineB: Statute: Identification of Criminals Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-1, s. 2(1)-(2) (interpreted alongside the Juvenile Delinquents Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. J-3)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: “Air of reality” / “sense of reality” test for whether a trial judge must leave a defence (here, mistake of fact as to consent) with the jury: there must be “some evidence or matter apt to convey a sense of reality” to the defence; for mistake as to consent, “some evidence which, if believed, would support the existence of a mistaken but honest belief” in consent.
BaselineA: Common law (jury-charge/defence-leaving doctrine from Kelsey v. The Queen and applied in R. v. Workman and Huculak; also discussed with reference to Wu v. The King).
CaseB_TestB: Morin s. 11(b) “reasonable time” framework (as applied to pre-trial delay): assess (1) length of delay; (2) waiver; (3) reasons for delay; and (4) prejudice; overall reasonableness determined by balancing these factors.
BaselineB: Constitution (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 11(b); framework drawn from R. v. Morin).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Presumption of reasonableness on review of a tribunal’s interpretation of its home statute (Dunsmuir framework), and statutory interpretation of MGA s. 467(1) that “change” includes an “increase”
BaselineA: Combination: common law standard-of-review framework (Dunsmuir v. New Brunswick) applied to interpretation of Municipal Government Act, R.S.A. 2000, c. M-26, ss. 467(1), 460(3), 305(1), 305(5), 470
CaseB_TestB: Framework for Crown sui generis fiduciary duty: duty arises from Crown discretionary control over a specific/cognizable Aboriginal interest; breach assessed by whether Crown met fiduciary standard of conduct (loyalty/good faith/full disclosure/ordinary prudence), not by achieving a particular result
BaselineB: Combination: common law fiduciary law (e.g., Wewaykum; Guerin; Haida Nation; Manitoba Metis Federation) applied within Specific Claims Tribunal Act, S.C. 2008, c. 22, s. 14(1)(b), (c) and s. 14(2)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Necessarily incidental (ancillary) doctrine for validity of federal law that prima facie intrudes on provincial jurisdiction: where legislation is not directly about a s. 91 head of power, it must be shown to be "necessarily incidental to effective legislation" on that federal subject; here, s. 33(3) failed because it was a "blanket prohibition" that "makes no attempt to link the proscribed conduct to actual or potential harm to fisheries" and was therefore "not necessarily incidental" to s. 91(12) fisheries power.
BaselineA: Common law constitutional division-of-powers doctrine (ancillary/necessarily incidental) drawn from Lord Tomlin’s proposition (3) in Attorney-General for Canada v. Attorney-General for British Columbia and others, [1930] A.C. 111, applied to s. 91(12) and s. 92 (esp. property and civil rights) of the British North America Act, 1867.
CaseB_TestB: Colour of right in theft: the defence turns on whether the trier of fact is satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused did not have, at the time of the taking/transfer, an "honest belief" (a "bona fide belief") that he had a right to the money; it is not determined by what the jury thinks the accused’s legal rights actually were (e.g., when commissions were payable).
BaselineB: Statute—Criminal Code theft provisions (R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 283 and 294 as referenced in the reasons), specifically the statutory phrase "without colour of right" within the definition of theft.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “unlawful purpose” in Criminal Code conspiracy (s. 423(2)(a)): “unlawful purpose means contrary to law, that is prohibited by federal or provincial legislation”; if the alleged purpose is not itself prohibited by legislation, an information under s. 423(2)(a) does not disclose an offence
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 423(2)(a) (conspiracy “to effect an unlawful purpose”); also considered in light of Criminal Code s. 8 (no common law offences) and related conspiracy jurisprudence (e.g., Wright, McDermott & Feeley; Frey v. Fedoruk; Celebrity Enterprises)
CaseB_TestB: Quebec defamation fault under art. 1457 C.C.Q.: fault is determined by a contextual analysis, with the “guiding principle” that there is no fault “until it has been shown that the journalist or media outlet in question has fallen below professional standards”; “the conduct of the reasonable journalist becomes the all‑important guidepost”
BaselineB: Statute (civil law): Civil Code of Québec, art. 1457 (extra-contractual liability) as applied to defamation; informed by prior Quebec jurisprudence (Radio Sept-Îles) and SCC guidance (Prud’homme) on contextual fault analysis
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Rabey (majority) disease-of-the-mind classification for automatism: distinguish internal-cause malfunctioning of the mind (disease of the mind/insanity) from transient effects of a specific external factor (non-insane automatism); ordinary stresses and disappointments of life are not an external cause
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 16) interpreted through common-law insanity/automatism jurisprudence (e.g., Bratty v. A.G. Northern Ireland, R. v. K.)
CaseB_TestB: Conflict/supersession analysis between standard mortgage clause and Statutory Condition 4: if a policy term (including Statutory Condition 4) conflicts with the mortgage clause, it is superseded and cannot be used to void the mortgagee’s coverage
BaselineB: Statute and contract: Insurance Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. I.8, Part IV (Statutory Condition 4) plus the policy’s standard mortgage clause, interpreted in light of National Bank of Greece (Canada) v. Katsikonouris
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.
