CaseA_TestA: Single-cause vs multiple-causes characterization for prescription: if damages result from a single cause of action that is a breach of contractual obligation, they are contractual and prescribe in 30 years; if they result from several separate and independent causes, each is characterized as contractual or delictual and prescribes accordingly
BaselineA: Statute (Civil Code of Quebec provisions on prescription and contractual effects: arts. 2242 (30-year prescription), 2261(2) (2-year delictual prescription), and art. 1024 (contract extends to consequences by equity, usage or law))
CaseB_TestB: Priority between mechanics’ lien and competing registered interests where the Act does not prescribe priority: absent s. 14(1) priority, an unregistered lien has no priority; once registered (s. 20), the lien claimant is deemed a purchaser pro tanto and priority is determined under Registry Act ss. 69(1) and 70 by priority of registration (subject to actual notice)
BaselineB: Statute (The Mechanics’ Lien Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 267, ss. 14(1) and 20; and The Registry Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 409, ss. 69(1) and 70)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Accrued-rights preservation on statutory repeal/amendment: apply Interpretation Act s. 35(c) so repeal does not “affect any right, privilege, obligation or liability acquired, accrued, accruing or incurred” under the repealed enactment; here, reading the amended Unemployment Insurance Act with s. 35(c) preserves benefits only to the extent of the pre-amendment accrued entitlement and leaves the claimant subject to the pre-amendment disqualification (pension payable), ending benefits when the pension becomes payable (Jan. 31, 1976).
BaselineA: Statute: Interpretation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-23, s. 35(c) (effect of repeal) applied to Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, S.C. 1970-71-72, c. 48, s. 31 (as amended by S.C. 1974-75-76, c. 80, s. 10) and s. 38; also considers Unemployment Insurance Entitlements Adjustment Act, 1976-77, c. 11, s. 2.
CaseB_TestB: Compellability of judges before a commission under the Public Inquiries Act: read ss. 3 and 4 together so the commission’s power to compel testimony is no greater than a superior court judge’s in a civil case; because of judicial independence/judicial immunity, judges cannot be compelled to testify “as to how and why they arrived at their decisions” or “as to why a particular judge sat on a particular case”; general statutory language is insufficient to override this immunity.
BaselineB: Combination: Statute (Public Inquiries Act, R.S.N.S. 1967, c. 250, ss. 3-4) interpreted in light of common law/constitutional principle of judicial independence and judicial immunity (as discussed with reference to Valente v. The Queen and Beauregard v. Canada, and historical authority like Knowles' Trial).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Interpretation of Motor Vehicle Transport Act s. 3(2): provincial board may license extra‑provincial undertakings “into or through” a province as including operations “into and out of” the province; and s. 6 does not displace provincial enforcement (including seizure) incorporated via “like terms and conditions”
BaselineA: Statute: Motor Vehicle Transport Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. M-14, ss. 2 (definitions), 3(1)-(2), 5, 6; and incorporated provincial scheme under The Public Service Vehicles Act, R.S.A. 1970, c. 300 (notably s. 58 seizure).
CaseB_TestB: Purposive-scope test for Charter standing under s. 12: claimant must show an interest within the guarantee’s scope and consistent with its purpose; s. 12’s protection (“cruel and unusual”) is limited to human beings, so corporations cannot claim s. 12
BaselineB: Constitution (Charter): Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 12, applying the purposive-interpretation framework (Big M Drug Mart) and the standing/scope requirement from R. v. CIP Inc. (as cited in the reasons).
JudgeB: Brown and Rowe JJ. (Wagner C.J. and Moldaver and Côté JJ. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Applicability of an exclusion/waiver clause after fundamental breach: whether the clause continues to bind is determined by the “true construction of the contract” (waiver clause’s fate is tied to the contract’s fate; here it ceased to bind once the innocent party elected to treat the contract as at an end).
BaselineA: Combination of common law and statute: common-law approach to exclusion clauses after fundamental breach (Suisse Atlantique; Photo Production) applied alongside statutory lien context (The Mechanics’ Lien Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 267, s. 5(1)).
CaseB_TestB: Collateral attack on an administrative order in penal proceedings: depends on the statute and is determined by legislative intent as to the appropriate forum, assessed using non-exhaustive factors (statutory wording, purpose, availability of appeal, nature of attack in light of tribunal expertise/raison d’être, and penalty).
BaselineB: Primarily common law administrative-law principles (rule against collateral attack adapted to administrative orders) applied through interpretation of the Environmental Protection Act, R.S.O. 1980, c. 141 (notably ss. 17, 122-123, 146(1a)).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Constructive trust based on unjust enrichment: claimant must show (1) an enrichment, (2) a corresponding deprivation, and (3) absence of any juristic reason for the enrichment; plus the Court must find retention of the benefit would be “unjust” in the circumstances (including reasonable expectation and knowing acceptance).
BaselineA: Common law (equitable constructive trust/unjust enrichment), drawing on Rathwell v. Rathwell and Murdoch v. Murdoch as discussed in the reasons.
CaseB_TestB: Solicitor-client confidentiality/privilege and search warrants: (1) confidentiality may be raised whenever communications risk disclosure; (2) conflicts are resolved in favour of confidentiality unless law provides otherwise; (3) exercises of legal authority must interfere only to the extent “absolutely necessary”; (4) derogations are interpreted restrictively; plus for Criminal Code s. 443 searches of lawyers’ offices, the justice should refuse a warrant unless there is “no reasonable alternative” and must impose protective execution terms; crime/fraud communications are excepted.
BaselineB: Combination: statute (Criminal Code, s. 443(1)(b) search warrant power) interpreted in light of common law solicitor-client privilege/confidentiality (including Solosky v. The Queen and the crime-fraud exception).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Reibl v. Hughes — Objective causation test in informed-consent negligence: whether “a reasonable person in the patient’s position would have” declined the treatment if “proper disclosure” of “all material and special risks” (of doing/foregoing treatment) had been made; patient’s “particular concerns must also be reasonably based”.
BaselineA: Common law (medical negligence / duty of disclosure and causation), building from Hopp v. Lepp, [1980] 2 S.C.R. 192 (duty to disclose “any material risks and any special or unusual risks” and answer specific questions).
CaseB_TestB: Clark v. Canadian National Railway Co. — “Integral element” test for federal legislative competence over s. 92(10) undertakings: federal law displacing provincial law is valid only if it regulates an aspect “integral” (i.e., “vital”, “essential” or “integral”) to the “core” of the federal undertaking; otherwise provincial laws of general application apply.
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine (division of powers / interjurisdictional immunity analysis) as articulated in Construction Montcalm Inc. v. Minimum Wage Commission, [1979] 1 S.C.R. 754 and Northern Telecom Ltd. v. Communications Workers of Canada, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 115.
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Natural Resources Agreement (para. 12) “right of access” test for treaty Indian hunting for food: if provincial law/regulations contemplate any limited hunting on the land, that constitutes a “right of access” and then Indians may hunt for food “at all seasons of the year” (not limited to the particular day’s open season).
BaselineA: Constitutional instrument / agreement confirmed by statute: Natural Resources Agreement (Canada–Saskatchewan), para. 12 (confirmed by British North America Act, 1930 and implementing statutes); interpreted in light of R. v. Sutherland, Wilson and Wilson, [1980] 2 S.C.R. 451 (and references to R. v. Smith; R. v. Strongquill).
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 2(a) constitutionality “purpose-first” framework: “The initial test of constitutionality must be whether or not the legislation’s purpose is valid”; effects are considered only if the law “has passed the purpose test,” and “effects can never be relied on to save legislation with an invalid purpose.”
BaselineB: Constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 2(a) (and s. 1 framework discussed but not treated as the key test per instructions); developed with reference to prior cases including Robertson and Rosetanni and Hunter v. Southam.
JudgeB: Dickson J. (for Dickson, Beetz, McIntyre, Chouinard and Lamer JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: No implied power for the Commission/officer to retroactively revoke an allowed premium reduction; review is only at the employer’s instance, and an erroneous grant is not a “nullity” absent express statutory/regulatory authority
BaselineA: Regulation/statute: Unemployment Insurance Act, 1970-71-72, ss. 64(4), 64(6) (regulation-making and prescribed standards) and Unemployment Insurance Regulations, s. 24 (decision and employer-initiated review/appeal); also argued (rejected on these facts) s. 70 of the Act
CaseB_TestB: Mens rea for Criminal Code s. 121(1)(a): intent to commit the prohibited act plus knowledge of the circumstances; no additional requirement of a “corrupt” state of mind
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 121(1)(a) (interpreted), with supporting interpretation from SCC precedent (Martineau v. La Reine) on the scope of the offence
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Ernst (Cromwell J.) — Ward s. 24(1) Charter damages: even if damages are functionally justified, they are not an “appropriate and just” remedy where countervailing factors (alternative remedies + good governance + immunity’s purpose) collectively negate damages; for this Board, “Charter damages could never be an appropriate and just remedy” (paras. 26-31, 58).
BaselineA: Combination of Charter and common law: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 24(1) (“appropriate and just” remedy) applied through the common-law framework in Vancouver (City) v. Ward, 2010 SCC 27 (paras. 26-33). Also interacts with statutory immunity: Energy Resources Conservation Act, s. 43.
CaseB_TestB: Mikisew Cree (Karakatsanis J.) — Duty to consult does not apply to the law-making process: “no aspect of the law-making process — from the development of legislation to its enactment — triggers a duty to consult” (paras. 32-41, 50).
BaselineB: Combination of constitutional text and common law: duty to consult doctrine from Haida Nation v. British Columbia (Minister of Forests), 2004 SCC 73 (trigger elements) grounded in Constitution Act, 1982, s. 35; limited here by constitutional principles (separation of powers, parliamentary sovereignty/privilege) and by the Federal Courts Act jurisdictional scheme (ss. 2(1)-(2), 17, 18, 18.1) (paras. 13-19, 32-41).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Workers’ compensation statutory bar does not extend to a non-employer car owner deemed a master/servant under motor-vehicle legislation: s. 10(1) WCA bars actions only against the worker’s employer/covered employers/workers; a deemed vicarious-liability ‘employer’ under s. 70(1) MVA who is outside s. 10(1) remains suable in tort
BaselineA: Statute (Workers’ Compensation Act, 1968 (B.C.), c. 59, s. 10(1) and Motor-vehicle Act, R.S.B.C. 1960, c. 253, s. 70(1))
CaseB_TestB: Operational-conflict framework for conflicting administrative decisions: an ‘operational conflict’ exists where compliance with one decision necessitates violation of the other; if both decisions would otherwise withstand review, courts may intervene and, using a ‘pragmatic and functional’ approach (legislative purpose, centrality to tribunal mandate, and policy-making/implementation role), determine which decision the legislature intended to take precedence
BaselineB: Common law administrative law (building on Domtar and the pragmatic and functional approach from Bibeault) applied in the context of statutory schemes governing the tribunals
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Priority between a mechanics’ lien and a subsequent mortgage for past indebtedness: absent s. 14(1) applicability, an unregistered lien has no priority; once the lien is registered (s. 20), priority is determined under the Registry Act by priority of registration unless the prior registrant had actual notice
BaselineA: Statute (The Mechanics’ Lien Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 267, ss. 14(1), 16, 20, 21, 22; and The Registry Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 409, ss. 69(1), 70)
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 2(b)/s. 1 analysis of privacy legislation in the labour-picketing context: whether the statute achieves a “constitutionally acceptable balance” between informational privacy and freedom of expression; infringement not justified where the impact on expression is “disproportionate” to the privacy objective
BaselineB: Combination (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 2(b), 1; and statutory scheme under Personal Information Protection Act, S.A. 2003, c. P-6.5, especially ss. 3, 4(1), 4(3), 7(1) and related exemptions; plus Personal Information Protection Act Regulation, Alta. Reg. 366/2003, s. 7)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Election between contractual and delictual liability in Quebec: a plaintiff may sue in delict despite a contract only if the alleged contractual fault is independently a delictual fault under art. 1053 C.C. (i.e., it would be a fault 'even in the absence of a contract')
BaselineA: Statute (Quebec Civil Code, art. 1053; and jurisdictional context under Code of Civil Procedure, art. 68), as interpreted through SCC jurisprudence (e.g., Ross v. Dunstall; Alliance Assurance)
CaseB_TestB: Reasonable apprehension of bias in a criminal trial: where it is demonstrated, the trial judge has 'no further jurisdiction' and 'the only appropriate remedy is a new trial'; appellate finding of apprehension of bias retroactively renders subsequent orders 'void and without effect'
BaselineB: Common law procedural fairness / bias doctrine, relying on Newfoundland Telephone Co. v. Newfoundland (Board of Commissioners of Public Utilities), [1992] 1 S.C.R. 623
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Bills of Exchange Act “sum certain/negotiability” requirement: the principal + interest must be ascertainable on the face of the instrument (or by numerical calculation from materials in it); certainty on the face is the general rule and recourse to extrinsic evidence is not allowed unless a specific Act provision cannot operate without it (so an interest clause running “from the date of advance” makes the instrument non-negotiable/non-promissory note).
BaselineA: Statute: Bills of Exchange Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. B-5, ss. 176(1) (definition of promissory note: “sum certain”), 28 (sum certain though payable with interest; interest runs from date of bill unless otherwise provides), 186 (application to promissory notes), plus s. 10 (common law/law merchant applies unless inconsistent).
CaseB_TestB: Criminal Code s. 172(3) “disturbs” threshold: to convict, the accused’s act must be “disorderly in itself or productive of disorder”; mere “annoyance, anxiety or emotional upset” is insufficient, and where acts are “brief, essentially passive and peaceful” and “voluntarily desisted from, upon request”, “then there is no crime”.
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 172(3) (and context from ss. 169-175 heading “Disorderly Conduct”).
JudgeB: Dickson J. (for Dickson, Beetz, McIntyre, Chouinard and Lamer JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Bills of Exchange Act “sum certain”/negotiability requirement: principal + interest must be ascertainable on the face of the instrument (or by numerical calculation from materials in it); extrinsic evidence is generally not permitted unless necessary to implement a specific Act provision
BaselineA: Statute (Bills of Exchange Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. B-5, ss. 28, 176(1), 186; plus s. 10 incorporating common law/law merchant)
CaseB_TestB: Start of the Civil Code suicide-exclusion period (arts. 2516, 2532 C.C.L.C.) in backdating/coverage-increase situations: determine the contract’s effective date (including permissible retroactivity) and whether later changes are a mere variation or a new contract; the exclusion period cannot run more than once within a single contract
BaselineB: Statute (Civil Code of Lower Canada, arts. 2516, 2532; also arts. 2500, 1018; interpreted with reference to General Trust of Canada v. Artisans Coopvie, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 1185)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Declaratory judgment should not be used to decide issues the legislature has specifically confided to another tribunal (here, an arbitration committee); courts should decline to intervene where a complete statutory procedure exists and the declaration would be of limited usefulness
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law principles: Code of Civil Procedure (Quebec) art. 453 (declaratory judgment) applied alongside the principle from Barraclough v. Brown and City of Lethbridge that a party must use the statutory procedure and courts should decline declaratory relief where the legislature created a specialized tribunal/remedy
CaseB_TestB: Minister’s s. 7 Fisheries Act power to “authorize to be issued” licences is a continuing power, revocable any time before issuance; exercise is constrained only by natural justice (relevant considerations, no arbitrariness, good faith)
BaselineB: Statutory interpretation of Fisheries Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. F-14, s. 7 (and interaction with s. 9), supported by Interpretation Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. I-21, s. 31(3)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Excise Tax Act machinery exemption: claimant must be a “manufacturer or producer of goods” and the machinery must be “purchased and used directly in the manufacture or production of goods”; “manufacture” not restrictively defined—operating generators to produce electricity qualifies as manufacturing
BaselineA: Statute: Excise Tax Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-13, ss. 27(1), 29(1), and Schedule III, Part XIII, s. 1 (plus acceptance of a prior SCC definition of “manufacture” from R. v. York Marble, Tile and Terrazzo Ltd.)
CaseB_TestB: Vesting of appeal-as-of-right: a right is “acquired, accrued or accruing” only when all conditions precedent are fulfilled; for former Criminal Code s. 691(2), the right arises only when the court of appeal reverses an acquittal (or equivalent) and orders a new trial
BaselineB: Statute: Interpretation Act, R.S.C., 1985, c. I-21, ss. 43(c) and 44(c),(d), applied to Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 691(2) (as amended effective May 14, 1997)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: No common-law tort or direct civil action for employment discrimination where the Ontario Human Rights Code provides a comprehensive enforcement/remedial scheme (the Code “foreclose[s] any civil action based directly upon a breach thereof” and “also excludes any common law action based on an invocation of the public policy expressed in the Code”).
BaselineA: Statute (Ontario Human Rights Code, R.S.O. 1970, c. 318, especially s. 4(1)(a)-(b) on employment discrimination; plus the Code’s administrative/board-of-inquiry and appeal provisions discussed by the Court, including ss. 14b(6), 14c, 14d(4)).
CaseB_TestB: “Undue obstacle” / reasonable accommodation analysis under CTA s. 172: the barrier “must be removed unless there is a bona fide justification for its retention, which is proven by establishing that accommodation imposes undue hardship”; what is “undue” depends on contextual factors (e.g., “cost, economic viability, safety, and the quality of service to all passengers”) assessed in the federal transportation context.
BaselineB: Statute (Canada Transportation Act, S.C. 1996, c. 10, ss. 5 and 172(1), (3)), interpreted consistently with human rights reasonable-accommodation/undue-hardship principles (e.g., Meiorin/Grismer line).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Bill of Rights s. 2(f) limit on statutory reverse onus: a reverse onus (balance of probabilities) is compatible only if the fact is "rationally open" to the accused to prove/disprove; if the Crown’s proved facts have "no rational or necessary connection" to unlawful importation and the accused lacks "some knowledge or means of knowledge" of importation circumstances, the reverse onus is an "impossible burden" amounting to an irrebuttable presumption, so the Crown must prove unlawful importation beyond a reasonable doubt
BaselineA: Statute (Customs Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-40, ss. 205(1),(3), 248(1)) as constrained by statute (Canadian Bill of Rights, R.S.C. 1970, App. III, s. 2(f)); prior SCC guidance in R. v. Appleby, [1972] S.C.R. 303 on reverse onus and s. 2(f)
CaseB_TestB: Interested-party status/right to be heard under Quebec Labour Code s. 32 for bargaining-unit definition: because s. 32 requires the investigation be held "in the presence of every association concerned and the employer", the list is exhaustive and "indicated [the] intent to divest the employee of the status of an interested party" for bargaining-unit issues; on judicial review under a privative clause, the tribunal’s interpretation stands unless "patently unreasonable"
BaselineB: Statute (Quebec Labour Code, R.S.Q. 1977, c. C-27, s. 32 (and related ss. 28, 39, 129)) plus common-law/administrative-law principles of natural justice and privative-clause judicial review ("patently unreasonable" standard, e.g., CUPE v. N.B. Liquor)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Trial judge’s duty to put defences to the jury: (1) whether a defence is revealed by the evidence or can reasonably be inferred; and (2) if so, whether the charge adequately put that defence to the jury (R. v. Squire).
BaselineA: Common law (jury-charge/defence-leaving duty as restated in R. v. Squire, citing Mancini v. DPP and other authorities)
CaseB_TestB: Interjurisdictional immunity (constitutional inapplicability) for federal services: a provincial law of general application is inapplicable if it touches a “vital or essential aspect” of the federal service’s “establishment, management or operation”.
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine (interjurisdictional immunity) as articulated in Construction Montcalm and Bell Canada v. Quebec (CSST), applied to a federal service
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Availability of Criminal Code s. 116(1) charge for disobeying a court order: s. 116(1) applies unless statute law expressly provides a penalty/punishment or other mode of proceeding; inherent/common law contempt powers do not qualify as 'expressly provided by law'.
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 116(1); also considers s. 8 and Manitoba Queen’s Bench Rules 483, 485, 492 as potential 'express' alternatives).
CaseB_TestB: Public law promissory estoppel in regulatory/penal enforcement: requires (1) a clear and unambiguous promise by a public authority intended to induce action, and (2) reliance/change of conduct; but estoppel cannot be invoked to prevent application of a clear express legislative provision (including a strict liability zoning offence).
BaselineB: Common law (public law promissory estoppel as described in Mount Sinai, incorporating Maracle; plus the limiting principle that estoppel cannot override an express legislative provision).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Insurance policy interpretation to determine the policy’s “effective date”: construe the entire contract (policy + application) as a whole, not by a “mechanical reading of two phrases set apart”; where the policy is structured around an antedated date, that date is the effective date “for the purpose of calculating any of the time periods contemplated, including the application of the self-destruction clause”.
BaselineA: Combination: statute + contract interpretation. Statutory baseline: The Insurance Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 224, s. 148(2) (application and policy form part of the contract). The operative interpretive baseline is common-law contractual construction (reading the contract as a whole).
CaseB_TestB: Access in conjunction with permanent guardianship: (1) court has jurisdiction under the Family Services Act to consider/grant access when making (or varying) a permanent guardianship order; and (2) access is discretionary and “the exception and not the rule”, granted only if, on a “best interests of the child” analysis, it is beneficial—access “should not be granted if its exercise would have negative effects on the physical or psychological health of the child” and must not jeopardize an adoption that is in the child’s best interests.
BaselineB: Statute. Family Services Act, S.N.B. 1980, c. F-2.2, especially s. 1 (definition of “best interests of the child”), ss. 53(2), 56, 60(2), 60(6), 61(1), and 85(2).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 16(2) insanity: meaning of “incapable of appreciating the nature and quality of an act” — the accused must (at the time of the offence) know what he is doing and be able to foresee/understand the physical consequences (not emotional/moral reactions).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 16(2)), as interpreted in SCC cases including Cooper v. The Queen, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 1149 and R. v. Barnier, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 1124.
CaseB_TestB: Extradition Act committal/surrender framework: (1) committal—s. 29(1)(a) requires evidence that would justify committal for trial in Canada; ROC is presumptively reliable and can be rejected only if so defective/unreliable it would be “dangerous or unsafe” to act on; defences generally not considered at committal. (2) surrender—s. 44(1)(a) “unjust or oppressive” and, for defence-unavailability claims, a 3-part threshold: (i) substantive difference in defences, (ii) reasonable prospect of success in Canada, (iii) significantly greater jeopardy abroad, then weigh with all circumstances.
BaselineB: Statute (Extradition Act, S.C. 1999, c. 18, ss. 29(1)(a), 32(1)(c), 44(1)(a)), building on Ferras, 2006 SCC 33 and related extradition jurisprudence.
JudgeB: Cromwell J. (McLachlin C.J. and Moldaver and Wagner JJ. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Non-pecuniary damages in severe personal injury: apply the functional approach and a “rough upper limit” of $100,000, exceedable only rarely (not merely because injuries seem worse), with any increase requiring proof/agreement of inflation’s effect on money value
BaselineA: Common law (the personal injury damages “trilogy”: Andrews v. Grand & Toy Alberta Ltd.; Arnold v. Teno; Thornton v. Board of School Trustees; as refined in Lewis v. Todd)
CaseB_TestB: OPCF 44R / Insurance Act s. 239(1)(a) “use or operation” indemnity coverage: claimant must show an unbroken chain of causation linking the tortfeasor’s conduct as a motorist to the injury; coverage fails where the tort is an intervening, severable act (more than mere “but for” connection)
BaselineB: Statute and standard-form policy language (Insurance Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. I.8, s. 239(1)(a); OPCF 44R s. 3), interpreted in light of (but distinguished from) Amos v. ICBC
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Effect of workers’ compensation election/subrogation on who may sue (and thus Commission’s interest to intervene and interruption of prescription): once election for compensation is made, only the Commission may claim the compensated portion; the worker may claim only the s. 8 “additional sum”, and a worker’s overbroad action does not create Commission interest or interrupt prescription for the Commission
BaselineA: Statute and civil law: Workmen’s Compensation Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 159, ss. 7(3) ("The subrogation takes place by the mere making of the election"), 8 (worker may claim only "any additional sum required"), plus Civil Code art. 1056a (recourse only "to the extent permitted" by the Act) and Code of civil procedure art. 208 (intervention by a person "interested" in the action)
CaseB_TestB: Collins s. 24(2) Charter exclusion framework (as applied/organized in Greffe): balance three categories—(1) fairness of the trial, (2) seriousness of the Charter breach (including good/bad faith; here emphasizing need for proven reasonable and probable grounds and assessing informant-tip reliability), and (3) effect of exclusion on the repute of the justice system
BaselineB: Constitution (Charter) and common-law framework: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 24(2) (exclude evidence if, "having regard to all the circumstances", admission would "bring the administration of justice into disrepute"), applying R. v. Collins, [1987] 1 S.C.R. 265 (three-category approach)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Public access to executed search warrants/informations: presumption of openness; curtailment only where needed to protect social values of superordinate importance (notably protection of the innocent where nothing is found); issuance may be in camera to protect administration of justice, but after execution public may inspect
BaselineA: Combination: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 443 and 446 (statutory search warrant scheme) plus common law/open court principle and courts' supervisory power over records (e.g., Scott v. Scott; McPherson v. McPherson; Gazette Printing Co. v. Shallow)
CaseB_TestB: Bona fide occupational qualification (BFOQ) test (Etobicoke) as applied to denominational-school teachers: two branches—(1) subjective good faith/no ulterior purpose; (2) objective reasonable necessity to accomplish the employer’s legitimate objectives (here, religious conformity reasonably necessary to provide Catholic education)
BaselineB: Statute interpreted through prior SCC common-law-like framework: Human Rights Code, R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 186, s. 8 (and related s. 22); BFOQ framework taken from Ontario Human Rights Commission v. Etobicoke (Borough of), [1982] 1 S.C.R. 202
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Validity of a Quebec inter vivos trust benefiting unborn (non-existent) primary beneficiaries: interpret art. 981a C.C. “subject to the special characteristics of the trust”, so that (i) trustee acceptance suffices to make the trust irrevocable and (ii) ownership vests in the trustee during the trust, meaning it is “not necessary that there be beneficiaries in whom ownership of the property conveyed is vested”; arts. 981a et seq. must be given a “wide and liberal interpretation” and are invalid only where a true public-order prohibition applies.
BaselineA: Statute (Civil Code provisions governing Quebec trusts and gifts): arts. 981a, 981b, 981l (trusts) read with arts. 754, 755, 765, 771, 772, 929 (gifts/substitutions) and related capacity rules; plus prior SCC interpretation in Curran v. Davis, [1933] S.C.R. 283 (trustee acceptance; nature of trustee’s rights).
CaseB_TestB: When an injunction in private litigation can effectively bind non-parties (enforceable by contempt): courts have jurisdiction to make such orders, but because “members of the public can be held in contempt”, they “must first be apprised of the existence and terms of the order and be given an opportunity to comply”; it is “desirable that the order’s terms speak of the duty of non-parties to respect it”; and orders must be “carefully worded and constrained to ensure that they are fair and not unduly broad.”
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law/equity: Law and Equity Act, R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 224, s. 36 (interlocutory injunctions “just or convenient” on “terms and conditions the court thinks just”) and the common law contempt principle that non-parties who violate court orders may be punished for contempt (supported by cases such as International Longshoremen’s Association, [1979] 1 S.C.R. 120, and English authorities discussed).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory displacement of the Kienapple rule for s. 83 firearm-use offences: s. 83(2) is a “clear indication” Parliament intended multiple convictions and consecutive sentences for firearm use arising from the same event; and s. 21 party liability applies to s. 83
BaselineA: Combination of common law and statute: common law Kienapple principle (Kienapple v. The Queen; also Quon; Cox and Paton) plus Criminal Code provisions s. 83(1)-(2) (use of a firearm; consecutive sentence) and s. 21 (parties to an offence)
CaseB_TestB: Division of powers pith-and-substance analysis (purpose + effects) for a municipal measure, and (in the alternative) interjurisdictional immunity: (1) characterize pith and substance by examining “both its purpose and its effects”; (2) for interjurisdictional immunity, ask whether the measure trenches on the “core” of the federal power and whether the effect is sufficiently serious to “impair” (not merely “affect”) that core
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrines (pith and substance; interjurisdictional immunity) applied in light of federal statutory context (Radiocommunication Act, s. 5(1)(f)) and constitutional heads of power (Constitution Act, 1867, ss. 91(29), 92(10)(a), 92(13), 92(16))
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Labour arbitration remedial authority under s. 25(3): where the collective agreement lacks a specific penalty for the infraction, an arbitrator who finds dismissal cannot be sustained may substitute a lesser penalty (including reinstatement without back pay) that "seems just and reasonable in the circumstances"; if cause under a clause mandating dismissal is established, dismissal must be sustained; if no cause/discipline is established, reinstatement with full compensation follows.
BaselineA: Statute (The Trade Union Act, R.S.S. 1978, c. T-17, s. 25(3)) applied alongside the collective agreement (notably arts. 6(4) and 12(12)(a)); Port Arthur Shipbuilding Company v. Arthurs, [1969] S.C.R. 85 distinguished.
CaseB_TestB: Article 1F(a) complicity (contribution-based test): exclusion from refugee protection requires "serious reasons for considering" the claimant has "voluntarily made a significant and knowing contribution to the organization’s crime or criminal purpose"; assessment is contextual and may consider non-exhaustive factors (size/nature of organization; part involved; duties; rank; time in organization after knowledge; recruitment and opportunity to leave).
BaselineB: Statute + treaty: Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, s. 98 incorporating Refugee Convention art. 1F(a) (interpreted in light of international criminal law sources, including Rome Statute arts. 25, 30, 31(1)(d)).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 43 Canada Evidence Act letters rogatory: s. 43 supports production of documents alone; judicial assistance granted on comity subject to limits (trial-not-discovery; relevance; permissible scope; adequate definition).
BaselineA: Statute (Canada Evidence Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-10, s. 43) interpreted in light of comity (Zingre v. The Queen, [1981] 2 S.C.R. 392) and prior letters rogatory jurisprudence.
CaseB_TestB: Admissibility of defence-led unknown third party suspect evidence: admissible where (1) relevant to a fact in issue (logical relevance shown by a sufficient connection/similarity between charged crime and other incident plus evidence accused could not have committed other offence) and (2) probative value is not substantially outweighed by prejudicial effects (Seaboyer balancing); no balance-of-probabilities proof of the other incident and no credibility weighing by the judge.
BaselineB: Common law evidence principles (R. v. Seaboyer, [1991] 2 S.C.R. 577; R. v. Corbett, [1988] 1 S.C.R. 670; air of reality from R. v. Cinous, 2002 SCC 29; sufficient connection concept from McMillan/Grandinetti) applied to unknown third party suspect evidence.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Civil Code art. 1055 C.C. (building owner liability for ruin): the defect/want of repairs is assessed by the building’s intended purpose; if the victim used the building/part for a purpose contrary to that intended, the owner is not liable under art. 1055
BaselineA: Statute (Civil Code of Quebec (as then in force), arts. 1053, 1054, 1055), as interpreted in prior SCC authority (esp. Leznek v. City of Verdun, [1940] S.C.R. 313)
JudgeA: Beetz J. (for Beetz, Chouinard and Lamer JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Mental capacity standard for confessions/right to silence/s. 10(b) waiver: the accused need only have an “operating mind” (limited cognitive capacity) — understand what is said/said to him and that it may be used against him; for s. 10(b) waiver, capacity aligns with fitness-to-stand-trial (can communicate with and understand the function of counsel), with no separate “awareness of consequences” test
BaselineB: Combination: common law confession rule/right to silence (Ibrahim; Ward; Horvath; Nagotcha; Hebert) plus constitutional/statutory provisions (Charter ss. 7, 10(b); Criminal Code s. 2 definition of “unfit to stand trial” used to set the competency benchmark)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Judicial review on certiorari of a labour board’s “home statute” interpretation: intervene only if the interpretation is “plainly unreasonable” / “patently unreasonable” (CUPE standard). Key formulation: “was the Board’s interpretation so patently unreasonable that its construction cannot be rationally supported by the relevant legislation and demands intervention by the court upon review?”
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law. Statutory baseline: The Public Service Employee Relations Act, 1977 (Alta.), c. 40, ss. 9(1), 11, 48, 89 (esp. s. 89(2) preserving certiorari/mandamus; ss. 9 and 11 as strong privative/finality provisions). Common-law baseline: CUPE v. New Brunswick Liquor Corp., [1979] 2 S.C.R. 227 (patently unreasonable standard), adopted in Volvo Canada Ltd. v. U.A.W., Local 720, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 178 and Douglas Aircraft Co. of Canada v. McConnell, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 245.
CaseB_TestB: Adverse-effect religious discrimination and duty to accommodate: discrimination under Quebec Charter requires (1) a “distinction, exclusion or preference”; (2) based on a listed ground (e.g., religion); and (3) having the effect of “nullifying or impairing” the equal exercise of a right. Once adverse-effect discrimination is shown, employer must take “reasonable steps to accommodate ... short of undue hardship” (no de minimis threshold).
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law. Statutory baseline: Quebec Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms, R.S.Q., c. C-12, ss. 10 (definition/elements of discrimination), 16 (employment discrimination), plus related freedom provisions (ss. 3, 9.1). Common-law baseline: Ontario Human Rights Commission v. Simpsons-Sears (O’Malley), [1985] 2 S.C.R. 536 (adverse-effect discrimination; accommodation “short of undue hardship”); Central Alberta Dairy Pool v. Alberta (Human Rights Commission), [1990] 2 S.C.R. 489 (non-exhaustive undue-hardship factors); Central Okanagan School District No. 23 v. Renaud, [1992] 2 S.C.R. 970 (rejecting de minimis; framing undue hardship).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Similar fact evidence admissibility: (1) apply the Makin principle (relevance to an issue, not propensity) and (2) admit only where probative value outweighs prejudice, but (3) as a threshold, “Before evidence may be admitted as evidence of similar facts, there must be a link between the allegedly similar facts and the accused” — i.e., “some evidentiary link, direct or circumstantial, with the accused.”
BaselineA: Common law (Makin v. A-G for New South Wales; Harris v. DPP; Boardman v. DPP)
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 7 vagueness test: “a law will be found unconstitutionally vague if it so lacks in precision as not to give sufficient guidance for legal debate” (i.e., for reaching its meaning “by reasoned analysis applying legal criteria”).
BaselineB: Combination of statute and constitutional doctrine (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7; building on the Court’s vagueness jurisprudence including the Prostitution Reference and Irwin Toy)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 16(2) insanity (first arm): incapacity to "appreciate the nature and quality" is limited to inability to perceive the "consequences, impact and results of a physical act"; failure to appreciate "penal sanctions" does not qualify (and "wrong" in the second arm means "wrong according to law").
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 16(2)); interpreted in light of SCC cases including Cooper v. The Queen, R. v. Barnier, Kjeldsen v. The Queen, and Schwartz v. The Queen.
CaseB_TestB: Tribunal jurisdiction to decide constitutional issues (including s. 35): "The essential question is whether the empowering legislation implicitly or explicitly grants to the tribunal the jurisdiction to interpret or decide any question of law"; if yes, it is presumed to have jurisdiction to decide the issue in light of s. 35/other constitutional provisions unless a "clear implication" rebuts that presumption.
BaselineB: Common law / constitutional doctrine on tribunal constitutional jurisdiction, applying Nova Scotia (Workers’ Compensation Board) v. Martin (2003 SCC 54) and discussing Cooper v. Canada (Human Rights Commission); applied to Forest Practices Code of British Columbia Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 159, especially s. 131(8) ("make submissions as to facts, law and jurisdiction").
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Patentability of a new use for an old compound as a “new and useful art” (and permissibility of claiming compositions as the practical embodiment): an invention exists where the discovery is a new use “capable of practical application” with “undisputed commercial value”, and nothing in the Patent Act (including s. 36) precludes claiming the compositions that embody that new knowledge.
BaselineA: Statute (Patent Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. P-4, ss. 2 (definition of “invention”), 36 (specification/claims requirements), and discussion of s. 41 limits) plus prior SCC patentability jurisprudence (e.g., Farbwerke Hoechst; Ciba; Burton Parsons) and Hickton’s Patent (UK CA) by analogy.
CaseB_TestB: Party liability for drug trafficking by aiding/abetting under Criminal Code s. 21(1): to aid is to “assist or help the actor” (s. 21(1)(b)) and to abet includes “encouraging, instigating, promoting or procuring” (s. 21(1)(c)); for s. 21(1)(b) the Crown must prove the accused “intended the consequences that flowed from his or her aid” (purpose = intention, not desire), and for s. 21(1)(c) the Crown must prove the accused encouraged and “intended to do so”; applied to whether assisting a purchaser can make one a party to trafficking.
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, s. 21(1)(b),(c); Narcotic Control Act, ss. 2 “traffic”, 3(1), 4(1),(2)) as interpreted through SCC precedent (notably Hibbert on “for the purpose of”).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory incompatibility/repugnancy test for whether a permissive municipal discretion (Police Act, s. 24(6)) excludes a collectively-bargained/arbitrated “working condition” under s. 29(2): does s. 24(6) “prescribe exclusivity” or is there “no incompatibility or inconsistency” so “each has its own area of operation”?
BaselineA: Statute (The Police Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 351, ss. 24(6) and 29(2))
CaseB_TestB: State Immunity Act interpretation rules: (1) s. 3(1) is exhaustive (“[e]xcept as provided by this Act” ousts common law/international-law exceptions); (2) s. 6(a) territorial tort requirement—exception applies only where “the tort causing the personal injury or death has occurred in Canada”; and (3) s. 6(a) requires a “physical breach of personal integrity” (mental distress only if “linked to a physical injury”).
BaselineB: Statute (State Immunity Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. S-18, ss. 3(1), 6(a), and related definition in s. 2)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory incompatibility/repugnancy test for whether a permissive municipal discretion (Police Act, s. 24(6)) excludes a collectively bargained/arbitrated working-condition clause under s. 29(2): s. 24(6) is "an empowering provision only" and does not preclude bargaining unless the provisions are "incompatible or inconsistent"; here "there is no incompatibility or inconsistency" and "each has its own area of operation".
BaselineA: Statute (The Police Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 351, ss. 24(6) and 29(2))
CaseB_TestB: Corporate attribution test for BIA s. 96(1)(b)(ii)(B) (transfers at undervalue): for this statutory context, the "fraud" and "no benefit" exceptions do not apply; "the test for corporate attribution under s. 96 is simply whether the person was the directing mind and whether their actions were performed within the sector of corporate responsibility assigned to them" (and if so, intent is attributed).
BaselineB: Combination: Statute (Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act, s. 96(1)(b)(ii)(B); CCAA, s. 36.1) plus common law corporate attribution doctrine (Canadian Dredge; Livent; DeJong) as adapted for the s. 96 context
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Jennings test for establishing a constitutional convention: (1) what are the precedents; (2) did the actors in the precedents believe they were bound by a rule; (3) is there a reason for the rule — with the Court emphasizing that "acceptance or recognition by the actors in the precedents" is "the most important element" (normative/formal) distinguishing convention from expediency.
BaselineA: Common law / constitutional convention doctrine as adopted in Re: Resolution to amend the Constitution, [1981] 1 S.C.R. 753 (quoting Sir W. Ivor Jennings, The Law and the Constitution (5th ed., 1959), at p. 136; and approving Freedman C.J.M./Hogg definition that a convention is a rule "regarded as obligatory by the officials to whom it applies").
CaseB_TestB: Reasonable suspicion standard for sniffer-dog searches under s. 8: police may deploy a drug detection dog without prior authorization where they have "reasonable suspicion based on objective, ascertainable facts" that evidence will be discovered; suspicion is assessed on the "totality of the circumstances" (a "constellation of factors"), avoiding "generalized" suspicion; exculpatory/neutral facts cannot be ignored, but police have no duty to investigate to rule out innocent explanations; dog reliability is assessed contextually using controlled testing and field deployment evidence.
BaselineB: Common law Charter search framework: R. v. Collins, [1987] 1 S.C.R. 265 (unauthorized search criteria) and sniffer-dog authorization threshold from R. v. Kang-Brown, 2008 SCC 18 and R. v. A.M., 2008 SCC 19 (reasonable suspicion for sniff searches).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory tribunal (art. 846 C.C.P.) test for labour arbitrators: even if parties are not compelled by statute to choose arbitration, an arbitrator is a “statutory tribunal” where, once chosen, the arbitrator is “invested with wide powers by statute” (i.e., has “duties and powers conferred by statute”), such that the tribunal is not purely consensual; here, Canada Labour Code ss. 156(2), 157, 159, 160(5) show statutory powers/duties and a privative clause.
BaselineA: Combination of common law criteria for certiorari/evocation against arbitrators (Howe Sound Co. v. International Union of Mine, Mill and Smelter Workers; Port Arthur Shipbuilding Co. v. Arthurs; R. v. National Joint Council for the Craft of Dental Technicians) and statutory context (Code of Civil Procedure, art. 846; Canada Labour Code, ss. 156, 157, 159, 160(5)).
CaseB_TestB: Sublicence characterization test in patent licensing: a sublicence exists only if the licensee “granted, either expressly or impliedly, the right to do something which [the third party] would otherwise be prohibited from doing, and which [the licensee] was permitted to do only by virtue of its compulsory licence”; assess whether this occurs by (1) express provisions or (2) the agreement’s “actual legal effect” (not subjective intent).
BaselineB: Common law principles of patent licensing and contractual interpretation (including Consolidated-Bathurst; parol evidence rule) applied within the statutory setting of the Patent Act compulsory licensing regime and the Patented Medicines (Notice of Compliance) Regulations.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Kienapple remedy modification: when Kienapple applies, enter a stay of proceedings rather than an acquittal
BaselineA: Common law (Kienapple v. The Queen, [1975] 1 S.C.R. 729)
CaseB_TestB: Removing/replacing a litigation guardian: the Rule 49(1) test is the dependent adult’s “best interests”, informed by the Szwydky criteria (including required “indifference”/no conflict)
BaselineB: Statute/regulation (Queen’s Bench Rules (Saskatchewan), r. 49(1); informed by Szwydky v. Magiera (1988) criteria as guidance)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Contract interpretation to determine the extent of the supplier’s obligation and fixed-price entitlement: reconcile general ‘to such an extent as the Town may require’ language with specific allocation clauses, concluding the Town is entitled to 4,000 horsepower per annum at $14 per horsepower per annum (and no more at that price). Key holding: the Company’s commitment “is to provide electrical energy ... to the extent of 4,000 horsepower per annum ... at the contract price of $14 per horsepower per annum.”
BaselineA: Common law (interpretation of the January 9, 1905 agreement/contract; the Court holds the relevant issues “stand to be settled entirely on the interpretation of the 1905 agreement”).
CaseB_TestB: General Motors indicia for validity under the general trade and commerce power (Constitution Act, 1867, s. 91(2)): ask (1) whether the law is part of a general regulatory scheme; (2) whether the scheme is under the oversight of a regulatory agency; (3) whether it is concerned with trade as a whole rather than a particular industry; (4) whether provinces acting alone or in concert are constitutionally incapable of enacting it; and (5) whether failure to include one or more provinces would jeopardize successful operation elsewhere (indicia “not exhaustive” and “not ... necessary that they be present in every case”).
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine applying Constitution Act, 1867, s. 91(2) (general trade and commerce power), using the General Motors of Canada Ltd. v. City National Leasing indicia.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Contract interpretation of the 1905 agreement: the Company’s obligation is limited to supplying Fort Frances with electricity from the Rainy River Canadian generating facilities up to the 4,000 horsepower reserve at the fixed ceiling price of $14 per horsepower per annum (and no broader entitlement to all municipal requirements). Key language: para. 8 requires the Company to “retain and reserve for use on the Canadian side ... Four Thousand Horse Power”; para. 5 sets the price that “shall not in any event exceed ... Fourteen Dollars ($14.00) per Horse Power per annum”; the Court declares the commitment “is to provide ... to the extent of 4,000 horsepower per annum ... at the contract price of $14 per horsepower per annum.”
BaselineA: Common law (contract interpretation) applied to the 1905 agreement (a contract). The Court holds the relevant statutes (1905 Can. c.139; 1906 Ont. c.132; 1911 Ont. c.7) have no direct bearing on the issue and the matter is “settled entirely on the interpretation of the 1905 agreement.”
CaseB_TestB: Kidnapping as a continuing offence + party liability for latecomers: (1) “So long as the victim of the kidnapping remains unlawfully confined, the crime of kidnapping continues” and ends when the victim is freed; (2) for s. 21(1) party liability in a continuing offence, “where an accused — with knowledge of the principal’s intention to see a continuing offence through to its completion — does (or omits to do) something, with the intention of aiding or abetting the commission of the ongoing offence, party liability is established.”
BaselineB: Statute interpreted in light of common law: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, ss. 279(1) (kidnapping) and 21(1) (party liability), with the meaning of “kidnapping” informed by its common law origins as an aggravated form of unlawful confinement/false imprisonment.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Trigger for municipality’s mandatory acquisition duty under Planning Act s. 70(1): land must be “designated under a land use by-law” (not merely in statutory plans); statutory plans are proposals and do not trigger s. 70
BaselineA: Statute: The Planning Act, 1977 (Alta.), s. 70(1) (and related scheme/definitions including s. 1(14) defining “land use by-law”)
CaseB_TestB: O’Connor framework for production of private third-party records in criminal cases: (1) accused must show records are “likely to be relevant” to an issue at trial or witness competence; (2) if so, judge balances salutary vs deleterious effects (privacy/equality vs full answer and defence) to decide whether/what to produce (often via in camera review)
BaselineB: Common law/Charter-based procedural framework drawing on prior SCC cases (notably R. v. Stinchcombe; abuse of process line including R. v. Jewitt) and Charter ss. 7 and 24(1) as Charter values guiding discretion; also interacts with Criminal Code subpoena provisions (e.g., ss. 698, 700) as procedural vehicle
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “has become regularly engaged in some other occupation” under Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, s. 44(1)(c): focuses on regularity of work schedule (a “fixed pattern”), not duration or intent to abandon former job
BaselineA: Statute: Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, s. 44(1)(c) (with contextual comparison to s. 44(1)(b) and Regulations s. 49 defining “bona fide employed” as “not less than two weeks duration”)
CaseB_TestB: Whether an ISP “carr[ies] on ... ‘broadcasting undertakings’” under the Broadcasting Act when providing Internet access: entities that merely provide the mode of transmission (with no control over programming—no selection, origination, or packaging) are not “broadcasting undertakings”
BaselineB: Statute: Broadcasting Act, S.C. 1991, c. 11, ss. 2(1) (“broadcasting”), 2(3), 3(1) (interpreted purposively in light of the Act’s content-focused objectives)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 450(1)(b) / s. 25 justification in cross-border fresh pursuit: (1) arrest without warrant is lawful if, on the circumstances apparent at the time, the suspect would have appeared to a reasonable person in the officer’s position to be committing an offence (i.e., officer acted on “reasonable and probable grounds”); and (2) for s. 25(4), an officer who began a lawful pursuit in-province retains peace-officer status in another province “inasmuch as the pursuit had commenced lawfully in his jurisdiction and as long as such pursuit is fresh” (with the reservation that he should contact local police ASAP and once they take over he becomes a person assisting under s. 449(1)(b)).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34), especially ss. 450(1)(b), 25(4), and related ss. 449(1)(b), 25(1), 25(3); interpretive baseline includes R. v. Biron, [1976] 2 S.C.R. 56 (apparent-at-the-time / reasonable-and-probable-grounds approach).
CaseB_TestB: Canada Labour Code s. 157(d)(ii) ‘specific penalty’ jurisdiction test: an arbitrator is deprived of substitution power only if “a specific penalty must be assigned to the particular infraction in the collective agreement”; a penalty is not “specific” if it is not in the collective agreement or if it “can be chosen indiscriminately by the employer” (e.g., a discretionary range in an employer rule book).
BaselineB: Statute (Canada Labour Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. L-1, s. 157(d), especially s. 157(d)(ii)) interpreted alongside the collective agreement (Article XI(b)).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Availability of Crown per quod servitium amisit action for injured Canadian Forces members deemed Crown servants (and scope not limited to domestic/menial services)
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Federal Court Act, R.S.C. 1970 (2nd Supp.), c. 10, s. 37 (and analogous Exchequer Court Act, R.S.C. 1952, c. 98, s. 50) plus the common-law per quod action as applied in SCC cases (The King v. Richardson; Attorney-General of Canada v. Jackson; Nykorak v. Attorney General of Canada; The Queen v. Murray).
JudgeA: Ritchie J. (for Ritchie, Estey, Lamer and Wilson JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Mens rea for Criminal Code s. 121(1)(a): intent to commit the prohibited act plus knowledge of the relevant circumstances; no additional requirement of 'corruption'
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 121(1)(a) (interpreted in light of Martineau v. La Reine and distinguished from Hinchey).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Timing rule for Attorney General stay under Criminal Code s. 508: an information is “found” only after the justice decides to issue process; therefore the AG’s stay power “starts as of the moment a summons or warrant is issued” (not merely upon laying/receiving the information).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34 as amended), especially ss. 455, 455.3, 503, 508 (interpreting “after an indictment has been found” and its application to informations).
CaseB_TestB: Statutory eligibility rule for discharge under Criminal Code s. 662.1(1): discharge is unavailable where the offence is one “for which a minimum punishment is prescribed by law”; impaired driving under s. 234(a) has a minimum fine (“not less than fifty dollars”), so s. 662.1(1) does not apply.
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code), primarily ss. 234(a) and 662.1(1) (interpreting “minimum punishment is prescribed by law”).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 508 stay power timing: an information is “found” only after the justice decides to issue process; therefore the Attorney General’s power to stay “starts as of the moment a summons or warrant is issued” (not merely upon laying/receiving the information).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34 as amended): ss. 508(1) (stay “after an indictment has been found and before judgment”), plus interpretive context in ss. 2 (“indictment” includes “information”) and 503 (“finding an indictment includes (a) preferring an indictment, and (b) presentment of an indictment by a grand jury”), and the private information/hearing scheme in ss. 455 and 455.3.
CaseB_TestB: Procedural fairness content (Baker factors) requiring reasons: when an administrative decision affects “individual rights, privileges or interests”, the duty of fairness’s content “varies according to five factors” from Baker, and here those factors required the municipality to “give reasons for refusing” the second and third rezoning applications.
BaselineB: Common law administrative law duty of procedural fairness, structured by Baker v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), [1999] 2 S.C.R. 817 (five-factor framework), applied to municipal rezoning decisions under the Act respecting land use planning and development (R.S.Q., c. A-19.1).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Jurisdictional rule against joint trial on separate informations/indictments: a trial judge is without jurisdiction to try together separate informations or indictments (even with consent), unless an applicable statute expressly provides otherwise
BaselineA: Common law rule from Crane v. Public Prosecutor, [1921] 2 A.C. 299 (applied/confirmed); also treated as incorporated by implication into Criminal Code procedure
CaseB_TestB: Credibility assessment guidance re (i) absence of evidence of motive to lie and (ii) lack of embellishment: absence of motive evidence is relevant but must not reverse burden; lack of embellishment cannot bolster credibility (only not weigh against it) and may relate to motive-to-lie assessment
BaselineB: Common law (credibility/W.(D.) framework and appellate review principles), drawing on R. v. W.(D.), R. v. Stirling, and related cases cited in the reasons
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Marine insurance “perils of the seas” causation test for negligent acts: an act is negligent only relative to a foreseeable risk of harm; if the foreseeable risk is a “peculiarly marine risk”, then the negligent act “coupled with its foreseeable consequence” is a “fortuitous accident of the seas” and thus a “peril of the seas” and the proximate cause of the loss
BaselineA: Statute (Insurance (Marine) Act, R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 203, Schedule “Rules for Construction of Policy”: “The term ‘perils of the seas’ refers only to fortuitous accidents or casualties of the seas”; and Marine Insurance Act, R.S.B.C. 1960, c. 231, s. 57(2)(a) (now s. 56(2)(a)): insurer liable for loss proximately caused by a peril insured against “even though the loss would not have happened but for the misconduct or negligence of the master or crew”), applied with common-law definitions from Canada Rice Mills, Ld. v. Union Marine & General Insurance Co., [1941] A.C. 55 and Cohen, Sons & Co. v. National Benefit Assurance Co. (1924), 18 Ll. L. Rep. 199
CaseB_TestB: Section 35(1) threshold test for who qualifies as an “aboriginal peopl[e] of Canada”: “the modern-day successors of Aboriginal societies that occupied Canadian territory at the time of European contact” (which “may include Aboriginal groups that are now outside Canada”); if met, proceed to Van der Peet
BaselineB: Constitution (Constitution Act, 1982, s. 35(1): “The existing aboriginal and treaty rights of the aboriginal peoples of Canada are hereby recognized and affirmed”), interpreted purposively; built on existing s. 35 jurisprudence (e.g., Sparrow; Van der Peet) but creating a distinct threshold inquiry not previously decided
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Jurisdiction to proceed with interest arbitration after collective agreement expiry: s. 70(1) preserves the parties’ contractual right to invoke interest arbitration if notice is served within the statutory freeze period; the right need only exist at the time of the notice to arbitrate (not when the award issues).
BaselineA: Statute + collective agreement (Ontario Labour Relations Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 232, s. 70(1) (now s. 79, R.S.O. 1980, c. 228) interpreted alongside the agreements’ interest arbitration clauses (Haldimand art. 16; Perth art. 15); SCC also relies on its prior interpretation in Bradburn v. Wentworth Arms Hotel Limited, [1979] 1 S.C.R. 846.
CaseB_TestB: Directed verdict / non-suit test: whether there is “any admissible evidence, whether direct or circumstantial, which, if believed by a properly charged jury acting reasonably, would justify a conviction”.
BaselineB: Common law test as stated in R. v. Monteleone, [1987] 2 S.C.R. 154, derived from United States of America v. Shephard, [1977] 2 S.C.R. 1067.
JudgeB: Iacobucci J. (for La Forest, L’Heureux-Dubé, Sopinka, Gonthier, Cory and Iacobucci JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: McKibbon conditions for when a non-AG (agent/other person under s. 507(2)) may prefer an indictment in a non-grand-jury province: (1) a preliminary inquiry has been held; (2) the accused has been committed for trial on at least one charge inquired into; and (3) each count must be for an offence the accused was committed on, or an offence disclosed by the preliminary inquiry evidence and not one the accused was discharged on.
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 507(1)-(3), interpreted alongside ss. 504-505 and contrasted with s. 496).
CaseB_TestB: Van der Peet / Mitchell test for establishing an Aboriginal right under s. 35(1): claimant must prove (1) an ancestral practice, custom or tradition; (2) that it was integral to the distinctive culture (a defining feature such that the culture would be “fundamentally altered” without it); and (3) reasonable continuity between the pre-contact practice and the modern claim; plus initial characterization of the claimed right using three factors (nature of the impugned action, the conflicting government action/legislation, and the ancestral practices relied on).
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine under Constitution Act, 1982, s. 35(1), applying/clarifying the Van der Peet framework (as developed in R. v. Van der Peet and Delgamuukw, as cited in the reasons).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: First degree murder classification under Criminal Code ss. 212(b) + 214(2): if the murder is established under s. 212(b) (intent to kill A but by accident/mistake causes death of B), it is first degree under s. 214(2) where the planning and deliberation relates to the s. 212(b) mens rea (the intent to kill A), and the identity of the actual victim is irrelevant ("planning and deliberation ... makes the offence first degree murder when ... the accused in fact kills someone else"; "When s. 214(2) is combined with s. 212(b) the identity and character of any victim is entirely irrelevant").
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 212(b) (murder by accident/mistake killing another) and 214(2) ("Murder is first degree murder when it is planned and deliberate"), interpreted in light of R. v. Farrant, [1983] 1 S.C.R. 24 (s. 214 is a sentencing classification, not a separate offence).
CaseB_TestB: Interpretation of Alberta Limitations Act s. 12 in conflicts cases: s. 12 applies Alberta limitation law only to "live" causes of action; it "does not purport to revive an action time-barred by the substantive law of the place where the accident occurred"—so if the lex loci delicti limitation has expired, "no right of action existed" and the claim is barred.
BaselineB: Statute: Limitations Act, R.S.A. 2000, c. L-12, s. 12, interpreted against the common-law conflicts rule from Tolofson v. Jensen, [1994] 3 S.C.R. 1022 (lex loci delicti governs, including its limitation period as substantive).
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Mens rea for attempted murder: the Crown must prove a specific intent to kill (no lesser/constructive murder intent suffices)
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code) interpreted against prior SCC precedent
JudgeA: McIntyre J. (for Dickson, Beetz, Estey, McIntyre, Chouinard, Lamer and Wilson JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: “Same establishment” under CHRA s. 11 / Guidelines s. 10: whether employees are subject to a “common personnel and wage policy” (a factual inquiry into the employer’s common principles/approach)
BaselineB: Statute + regulation/guidelines (Canadian Human Rights Act, s. 11; Equal Wages Guidelines, 1986, s. 10)
JudgeB: LeBel and Abella JJ. (for the Court)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Matrimonial property distribution: pre-marital property exemption is limited to its fair market value at the time of marriage; s. 21(2)(q) cannot be used to expand s. 23; Capital Base Theory rejected
BaselineA: Statute: The Matrimonial Property Act, 1979 (Sask.), c. M-6.1, especially ss. 20-23 (equal distribution presumption; unequal distribution factors; pre-marital exemption and its limits)
CaseB_TestB: Aggravated assault (s. 268(1) endangering life) requires proof beyond a reasonable doubt of the aggravating consequence; if there is a reasonable doubt the complainant was capable of being endangered (e.g., may already be HIV-positive), no aggravated assault (though attempt may be made out)
BaselineB: Statute (as interpreted in prior SCC cases): Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, ss. 265(1), 265(3)(c), 268(1), and attempt provisions ss. 24(1), 660; informed by SCC authorities including R. v. Cuerrier and R. v. DeSousa (as cited in the reasons)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Mechanics’ lien “owner” test under s. 1(1)(d): a party is an owner if it (a) has an estate or interest in the land, (b) requested the work, and (c) the work was done “upon whose credit, or … on whose behalf, or … with whose privity or consent, or … for whose direct benefit” (overall view of arrangements; request can be through an agent/development structure).
BaselineA: Statute: The Mechanics’ Lien Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 267, s. 1(1)(d) (definition of “owner”) (applied with s. 5(1) lien entitlement; also discussed: ss. 7, 11).
CaseB_TestB: Challenge for cause (juror partiality) test under s. 638(1)(b): must show a “realistic potential” of partiality, generally by (1) establishing a “widespread bias” in the community and (2) showing some jurors may be unable to set aside the bias despite trial safeguards; overarching question is whether there is a realistic potential for partial juror behaviour.
BaselineB: Statute interpreted/applied: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 638(1)(b) (challenge for cause: juror “not indifferent”); framework drawn from SCC cases including R. v. Sherratt and R. v. Williams.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Anns-based duty of care for public authorities: (1) proximity/foreseeability plus (2) residual policy considerations; with policy/operational distinction and no immunity for inaction where there is a duty to act (nonfeasance/misfeasance irrelevant once duty exists)
BaselineA: Common law (adopting/applying Anns v. Merton London Borough Council, [1978] A.C. 728, including Lord Wilberforce’s two questions: (1) sufficiently close relationship/proximity; (2) considerations to negative/limit duty; plus policy vs operational distinction)
CaseB_TestB: Implied s. 1 limit on Charter s. 10(b) at roadside: a limit is “prescribed by law” if it “results by necessary implication” from a statute’s “operating requirements”; roadside sobriety questions/tests are authorized if “reasonable and necessary” to fulfill police duty and are “incompatible with the exercise of the right to counsel”
BaselineB: Combination of statute and constitutional law: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms ss. 1 and 10(b); Manitoba Highway Traffic Act s. 76.1(1); Criminal Code ss. 253, 254; plus prior SCC interpretation of “prescribed by law” in R. v. Therens and implied-limit reasoning in R. v. Thomsen
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal defence of necessity (as an excuse): requires “urgent situation of clear and imminent peril when compliance with the law is demonstrably impossible”, including no reasonable legal alternative and proportionality; Crown must disprove voluntariness beyond a reasonable doubt once properly raised
BaselineA: Common law defence of necessity preserved by Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 7(3), with the Morgentaler v. The Queen, [1976] 1 S.C.R. 616 formulation (“urgent situations of clear and imminent peril when compliance with the law is demonstrably impossible”) as the starting point
CaseB_TestB: Section 8 reasonable expectation of privacy (REP) analysis: REP assessed on the “totality of the circumstances” via four inquiries (subject matter; direct interest; subjective expectation; objective reasonableness), with objective reasonableness being a normative assessment; in this sting context, no objectively reasonable REP so s. 8 not engaged
BaselineB: Common law/Charter jurisprudence under Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 8, applying the established REP framework (as reiterated in R. v. Marakah, 2017 SCC 59 and R. v. Spencer, 2014 SCC 43) including the “totality of the circumstances” and four lines of inquiry
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 613(1)(b)(iii) proviso (harmless error): Crown must satisfy the court the verdict “would necessarily have been the same if such error had not occurred”; where the error is exclusion of exculpatory evidence, assess the entirety of the evidence including the reasonable possible effect of the excluded evidence, which “should… enure to the benefit of the accused”.
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 613(1)(b)(iii)), as interpreted in Colpitts v. The Queen, [1965] S.C.R. 739 (Cartwright J.: Crown must show verdict “would necessarily have been the same”).
CaseB_TestB: Appellate court raising a new issue on appeal: a “new issue” is one that raises “a new basis for potentially finding error… beyond the grounds… framed by the parties”; discretion to raise it only in rare cases where failing to do so “would risk an injustice” (i.e., “good reason to believe that the result would realistically have differed”), and only if the court has jurisdiction, the record is sufficient, and no procedural prejudice results; notice and opportunity to respond required.
BaselineB: Common law / appellate practice principles (party presentation/adversarial system; impartiality/bias constraints), drawing on cases such as R. v. W. (G.), [1999] 3 S.C.R. 597 and Quan v. Cusson, 2009 SCC 62.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 96 ‘judicial power’ screening test: a power is administrative (not judicial) where there is “no real lis between the parties” and the decision is based “not on considerations of legality but on considerations of expediency” (therefore s. 96 not infringed).
BaselineA: Combination: Constitution Act, 1867, s. 96, applied through the s. 96 jurisprudence (Re Residential Tenancies Act, 1979; Massey-Ferguson; Grondin) and the ‘judicial power’ indicia from John East Iron Works as quoted in Residential Tenancies Act.
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 12 mandatory-minimum framework (as applied to robbery MMPs): “two-stage inquiry” — (1) determine a “fit and proportionate sentence”; (2) ask whether the law requires a sentence “grossly disproportionate” to that fit sentence, assessed via “scope and reach of the offence, the effects of the penalty on the offender, and the penalty and its objectives”; may be based on the actual offender or a “reasonably foreseeable case”.
BaselineB: Combination: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 12, applied through existing SCC s. 12 mandatory-minimum jurisprudence (especially R. v. Hills, 2023 SCC 2; also Nur, Lloyd, Smith, Bissonnette, Boudreault).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 93(1) denominational schools infringement test: s. 93 protection applies only if (a) there is a right/privilege affecting a denominational school, (b) enjoyed by a particular class of persons, (c) by law, (d) in effect at the time of the Union, and (e) it is 'prejudicially affected' (trial judge’s formulation adopted at para. 16).
BaselineA: Constitution Act, 1867, s. 93(1) (and s. 93(2)); baseline articulation of the conditions is taken from the trial judge and Privy Council/SCC s. 93 jurisprudence referenced in the reasons (e.g., Barrett; Hirsch; Tiny; Ottawa Separate Schools Trustees).
CaseB_TestB: Young Offenders Act non-disclosure analysis focused on the 'prohibited link': the 'nub' is whether the information 'links the identity of the young person with a charge, proceeding or disposition under the Act'—the interpretive exercise is 'not directed at some formal classification of documents, but at the nature of the information sought to be disclosed' (paras. 26-27). If the link is made, disclosure is prohibited unless a specific statutory exception authorizes it (e.g., s. 44.1 or s. 38 exceptions).
BaselineB: Statute: Young Offenders Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. Y-1, especially ss. 38(1), 38(1.1), 38(1.13) and ss. 40-46 (including s. 44.1 and s. 46).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 93(1) denominational schools guarantee: a provincial education law is invalid if it "prejudicially affect[s]" a protected denominational-school "Right or Privilege" that a "Class of Persons" had "by Law" "at the Union" (conditions: (a) right/privilege affecting a denominational school; (b) enjoyed by a particular class of persons; (c) by law; (d) in effect at the time of the Union; (e) prejudicially affected).
BaselineA: Constitution Act, 1867, s. 93(1) (and s. 93(2)); applied with reference to Privy Council/SCC s. 93 jurisprudence cited in the reasons (e.g., City of Winnipeg v. Barrett; Hirsch; Tiny; Ottawa Separate Schools Trustees v. Ottawa Corporation).
CaseB_TestB: Canadian maritime law / navigation and shipping scope test: the "mere involvement of a pleasure craft" is insufficient; courts must examine the "factual context" and ask whether the allegedly negligent act is "so integrally connected to the act of navigating the pleasure craft on Canadian waterways" that it is a "practical necessity" for Parliament to have jurisdiction (otherwise provincial property and civil rights applies).
BaselineB: Common law constitutional characterization of Canadian maritime law scope under Constitution Act, 1867, ss. 91(10) and 92(13), drawing on ITO — International Terminal Operators Ltd. v. Miida Electronics Inc.; Whitbread v. Walley; Ordon Estate v. Grail (as cited in the reasons).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Certiorari review of a preliminary inquiry committal: a committal is a jurisdictional error reviewable on certiorari where there is "no evidence" on an essential element ("No evidence" on an essential element "can never amount to 'sufficient evidence'" under s. 475); reviewing court asks whether there is "any evidence at all"/"some evidence" on each essential element.
