BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, s. 475) as interpreted through prior certiorari/jurisdiction jurisprudence (Patterson v. The Queen; Martin v. The Queen; Forsythe v. The Queen; and the 'any evidence' principle from R. v. Nat Bell Liquors Ltd.).
CaseB_TestB: Criteria for a compensatory allowance under art. 559 C.C.Q.: claimant must establish (1) contribution; (2) enrichment of spouse's patrimony; (3) causal link; and (4) proportion of contribution to enrichment; "Each of these elements must be evaluated with great flexibility" and the enrichment "must subsist" and be evaluated at the time of divorce.
BaselineB: Statute (Civil Code of Quebec, art. 559) informed by unjust enrichment principles (e.g., correlation concept from Cie Immobilière Viger Ltée v. Lauréat Giguère Inc.).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Estoppel by representation (including by silence): requires (1) a representation by words/conduct, or by “silence or inaction” only where the representor is “under a duty ... to speak or act”; (2) intended (actual or presumptive) to induce reliance; (3) that in fact induces the representee to “alter his position to his detriment” (detrimental reliance).
BaselineA: Common law (estoppel by representation), as summarized from Spencer Bower & Turner and cases such as Greenwood v. Martins Bank, Ltd.
CaseB_TestB: Rebutting the Criminal Code s. 212(3) presumption (“evidence to the contrary”): the jury should consider “all of the evidence” about how the accused and prostitute lived together and how finances were handled; the judge need not identify a “particular and severable” item of rebuttal evidence.
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 212(3))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Municipal taxing power must be exercised in the form required by the enabling statute (no self-redelegation from by-law to resolution); if statute requires a by-law, a resolution fixing the tax rate is ultra vires and void
BaselineA: Statute (Cities and Towns Act, R.S.Q. 1941, c. 233, s. 526 as amended for Dorval; plus procedural requirements in Cities and Towns Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 193 including ss. 385 and 395; remedy context: Code of Civil Procedure, art. 33)
CaseB_TestB: Causation in negligent blood-donor screening: apply the 'material contribution' test (not a rebuttable presumption and not strict 'but-for')—whether the defendant’s negligence materially contributed to the occurrence of the injury (i.e., contribution outside the de minimis range)
BaselineB: Common law (causation in negligence; but-for as general test; material contribution as alternative—citing Snell v. Farrell and Athey v. Leonati; distinguishing Hollis v. Dow Corning Corp.)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 13 self-incrimination bar on using an accused’s prior testimony at a retrial: s. 13 “precludes the admission at the second trial of the evidence given by the appellant at his first trial”; the protection “inures to an individual at the moment an attempt is made to utilize previous testimony to incriminate him”; “any evidence the Crown tenders as part of its case against an accused is, for the purpose of s. 13, incriminating evidence”; and “A retrial of the same offence ... is therefore ‘other proceedings’ within the meaning of s. 13.”
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 13 (interpreted purposively in light of ss. 11(c) and 11(d)).
CaseB_TestB: Reformed rule for substantive admissibility of a non-accused witness’s prior inconsistent statement (B.(K.G.)): prior inconsistent statements are substantively admissible on a principled basis (reliability + necessity), with a threshold that the statement “will only be admissible if [it] would have been admissible as the witness’s sole testimony”; reliability is satisfied where there are “sufficient circumstantial guarantees of reliability” (typically: (1) statement under oath/affirmation/solemn declaration plus explicit warning re criminal sanctions; (2) videotaped in its entirety; (3) full opportunity to cross-examine at trial), though “other circumstantial guarantees ... may suffice”; and on a voir dire the judge must be satisfied the indicia are “present and genuine” and that the statement was obtained without voluntariness/administration-of-justice concerns (generally on a balance of probabilities).
BaselineB: Combination: statutory procedure (Canada Evidence Act, s. 9) plus common law hearsay/prior inconsistent statement doctrine (the former “orthodox rule” from Deacon v. The King), reformed using the principled hearsay approach (Khan; Smith).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Crown appeal from acquittal on a “question of law alone”: a trial judge’s finding of fact is only an error of law for “total absence of a foundation” and, for an acquittal, that can “only occur if there has been a transfer to the accused by the law of the burden of proof of a given fact” (otherwise “there is always some evidence” to acquit due to the presumption of innocence).
BaselineA: Combination: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 605(1)(a) (appeal on question of law alone) plus common-law/SCC appellate-jurisdiction principles from Lampard v. The Queen, Sunbeam Corporation (Canada) Ltd. v. The Queen, and discussion of Wild v. The Queen and R. v. Lemire.
CaseB_TestB: Test for interim relief (stay/interim release) under Supreme Court Act s. 65.1: the RJR-MacDonald criteria—(1) “serious question”, (2) “irreparable harm”, and (3) “balance of convenience”.
BaselineB: Combination: Supreme Court Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. S-26, s. 65.1 (and s. 65) as interpreted/applied through the common-law framework reaffirmed in RJR-MacDonald Inc. v. Canada (Attorney General).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: When a trial judge’s factual finding (esp. reasonable doubt) can be treated as an error of law on a Crown appeal from acquittal: only where there is a 'total absence of a foundation' and, for acquittals, this can 'only occur if there has been a transfer to the accused by the law of the burden of proof of a given fact' (otherwise 'there is always some evidence' to acquit due to the presumption of innocence).
BaselineA: Combination: statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 605(1)(a) (appeal on 'question of law alone')) plus SCC common-law appellate-jurisdiction principles from Lampard v. The Queen, [1969] S.C.R. 373 and Sunbeam Corporation (Canada) Ltd. v. The Queen, [1969] S.C.R. 221 (and discussion of Wild v. The Queen, [1971] S.C.R. 101).
CaseB_TestB: Ontario anti-SLAPP dismissal framework under Courts of Justice Act, s. 137.1: (1) moving party must 'satisf[y]' the judge on a balance of probabilities that the proceeding 'arises from' the moving party’s 'expression' that 'relates to a matter of public interest' (s. 137.1(3)); if met, (2) responding party must show (a) 'grounds to believe' the proceeding has 'substantial merit' and the moving party has 'no valid defence' (s. 137.1(4)(a)), and (b) the harm from the expression is 'sufficiently serious' that the public interest in permitting the proceeding to continue 'outweighs' the public interest in protecting the expression (s. 137.1(4)(b))—a public-interest weighing exercise described as the 'fundamental crux' of the analysis.
BaselineB: Statute: Courts of Justice Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.43, s. 137.1(3) and (4) (anti-SLAPP provisions).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Landry/Eccles warrantless arrest-in-dwelling entry test: arrest on private premises without warrant is lawful only if all four questions are answered “yes” (indictable offence; reasonable and probable grounds the person committed/is about to commit it; reasonable and probable grounds the person is within; and “proper announcement” before entry).
BaselineA: Combination: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 450(1)(a) (arrest without warrant for indictable offence) plus common law entry limits from Eccles v. Bourque, [1975] 2 S.C.R. 739 (itself drawing on Semayne’s Case).
CaseB_TestB: Turpin s. 15 discrimination framework (as applied): (1) determine whether the law denies an equality right (e.g., equality before the law); (2) if so, determine whether the denial is “with discrimination” (i.e., a distinction based on personal characteristics, assessed in the larger social/political/legal context, typically via enumerated/analogous grounds).
BaselineB: Constitutional/Charter baseline: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 15, interpreted through Andrews v. Law Society of British Columbia, [1989] 1 S.C.R. 143 (and related equality jurisprudence discussed in the reasons).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Amending an indictment/conviction to cure a variance in a particular: amendment should be made where it does not mislead or prejudice the accused (Criminal Code, s. 529(4)-(5)); SCC may itself amend on appeal (s. 613(1)(b)(i), (3)). Key point: the only question is whether the amendment would prejudice the accused and, if so, whether it can be cured.
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 529(4)-(5) (amendment considering prejudice/misleading and injustice; possible adjournment to cure), and ss. 613(1)(b)(i), 613(3) (SCC appellate power to amend). Also interpretation of Narcotic Control Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. N-1, ss. 2, 4 and Schedule item 3 (what counts as the charged 'narcotic').
CaseB_TestB: Ineffective assistance of counsel test (G.D.B.): to set aside a verdict, the appellant must show "first, that counsel’s acts or omissions constituted incompetence and second, that a miscarriage of justice resulted".
BaselineB: Common law: R. v. G.D.B., 2000 SCC 22, [2000] 1 S.C.R. 520 at para. 26 (two-part incompetence + miscarriage of justice test).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Concurrent liability in tort and contract for professional negligence: a common law duty of care from a relationship of sufficient proximity can coexist with contract, but tort cannot be used to evade contractual limits. Key propositions: (1) proximity-based duty of care is "not confined to relationships that arise apart from contract"; (2) tort duty must be "independent of the contract" in the sense that it must not depend on "specific obligations or duties created by the express terms of the contract" (distinction between "what is to be done and how it is to be done"); (3) concurrent tort liability "will not be admitted" if it would "permit the plaintiff to circumvent or escape a contractual exclusion or limitation of liability"; otherwise plaintiff may choose the more advantageous cause of action.
BaselineA: Common law (duty of care/proximity and negligent misrepresentation principles from Donoghue v. Stevenson; Hedley Byrne & Co. v. Heller; Anns v. Merton London Borough Council; plus SCC discussion of Nunes Diamonds and related authorities on contractual limits).
CaseB_TestB: Jurisdiction in Quebec action in warranty with a choice-of-forum clause: art. 3148 para. 2 C.C.Q. prevails over art. 3139 C.C.Q. where the clause shows a clear intention to oust Quebec jurisdiction; in that case "the Quebec authority must decline jurisdiction". Art. 3139 is "permissive" and "procedural" and must be interpreted narrowly; art. 3135 (forum non conveniens) is "suppletive" and applies only after Quebec jurisdiction is first established.
BaselineB: Statute (Civil Code of Québec, S.Q. 1991, c. 64, arts. 3148 para. 2, 3139, and 3135).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Scope of Quebec Construction Industry Labour Relations Act/Decree turns on the nature of the work (construction vs. maintenance/repair exception), not the status of the employer/industry; and Decree minimums cannot be avoided by “total wage” set-off. Key formulation: “in order to determine whether a particular employer or employees are covered, one must look at the nature of the work done and not simply at the status of the parties” (para. 30); and “The question is not one of the total wage but of the specific conditions determined by the decree” (para. 76).
BaselineA: Statute and regulation/decree: Construction Industry Labour Relations Act, S.Q. 1968, c. 45 (now R.S.Q., c. R-20), especially ss. 1(e),(i),(j),(r) and 2(2); and Decree respecting the construction industry (1973) 105 O.G. II 5837, ss. 3.01-3.02; plus Act s. 20 and Decree ss. 18.06, 32.03 on public order.
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 12 mandatory-minimum analysis and remedy: a sentence violates s. 12 only if “grossly disproportionate” — “so excessive as to outrage standards of decency” such that Canadians “would find the punishment abhorrent or intolerable” (para. 14); and if a mandatory minimum is unconstitutional in a particular case, the proper remedy is s. 52 invalidity, not a s. 24(1) constitutional exemption: “If a mandatory minimum sentence would create an unconstitutional result in a particular case, the minimum sentence must be struck down” (para. 13) and “constitutional exemptions should not be recognized” (para. 74).
BaselineB: Combination of constitutional text and prior common law: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 12 and 24(1); Constitution Act, 1982, s. 52(1); and the gross disproportionality test from R. v. Smith (cited at para. 14), with related mandatory-minimum jurisprudence (e.g., Goltz, Morrisey).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Parens patriae limit: a court may not authorize non-therapeutic sterilization of a mentally incompetent person (sterilization for non-therapeutic purposes should never be authorized; discretion must be exercised only for the protected person’s benefit)
BaselineA: Common law (parens patriae jurisdiction as inherited from the English Court of Chancery/Lord Chancellor; also discussed alongside P.E.I. Chancery Act, s. 3 and Chancery Jurisdiction Transfer Act, s. 2 as the source vesting that jurisdiction in the superior court)
CaseB_TestB: Residual management rights: whether a unilaterally imposed workplace policy is a reasonable exercise of management rights is assessed by a 'balancing of interests' considering all surrounding circumstances and whether the policy strikes a reasonable balance between employer and employee interests
BaselineB: Common law / labour arbitration doctrine (KVP test; endorsed in Irving Pulp & Paper) applied to interpretation of collective agreement management-rights clause (including clause 5.02 requiring the employer to act 'reasonably, fairly and in good faith')
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Kienapple (rule against multiple convictions) applicability: requires (1) sufficient factual nexus (usually: “Does the same act of the accused ground each of the charges?”) and (2) sufficient legal nexus—“only be satisfied if there is no additional and distinguishing element that goes to guilt” in the offence sought to be barred; with guidance on when an element is not “additional or distinct” (particularization; alternative methods to prove a single delict; evidentiary proxy).
BaselineA: Common law Kienapple principle from Kienapple v. The Queen, [1975] 1 S.C.R. 729 (also discussed with related SCC cases like Côté v. The Queen and Krug v. The Queen).
JudgeA: The Chief Justice (Dickson C.J., for the Court)
CaseB_TestB: Meaning of “services … to the public” under Yukon Human Rights Act s. 8(a): two-part analysis—(1) determine what constitutes the “service” on the facts; (2) determine whether the service creates a “public relationship” between provider and user, assessing contextual criteria “including, but not limited to, selectivity… diversity… involvement of non-members… commercial nature… intimate nature… purpose”; “None of these criteria operate determinatively.”
BaselineB: Statute: Yukon Human Rights Act, R.S.Y. 1986 (Supp.), c. 11, s. 8(a) (interpreted in light of analogous human rights statutes and UBC v. Berg, [1993] 2 S.C.R. 353).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Ensite test for whether property is “used or held ... in the course of carrying on a business” (ITA s. 129(4)(a)(ii) exclusion): ask whether the property was used to fulfil a requirement that had to be met to do business; property must be “truly employed and risked” in the business, with “risk” meaning more than a remote risk or mere business purpose; threshold met when withdrawal would “have a decidedly destabilizing effect on the corporate operations themselves”.
BaselineA: Statute — Income Tax Act, s. 129(4)(a)(ii) (as amended) (and related dividend refund scheme in ss. 129(1), 129(3), 129(4)); interpreted using prior jurisprudence including The Queen v. Marsh & McLennan, Ltd. (FCA) and March Shipping Ltd.
CaseB_TestB: Vézeau/Morin test for ordering a new trial on a Crown appeal from acquittal under Criminal Code s. 686(4): the Crown must satisfy the appellate court that “the verdict would not necessarily have been the same if the trial judge had properly directed the jury” (a “very heavy onus”).
BaselineB: Statute + common law gloss — Criminal Code, s. 686(4), as interpreted in Vézeau v. The Queen and reaffirmed in R. v. Morin.
JudgeB: Cory J. (for Sopinka, Cory, Iacobucci and Major JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Public interest immunity for Cabinet documents: court must (often after judicial inspection) balance the public interest in confidentiality against the public interest in the administration of justice; Cabinet documents are not absolutely immune and class protection is only one variable (e.g., level of decision-making, nature of policy, timing, importance/need for litigation). Key quotes: the court must "determine the balance to be struck between the public interest in the proper administration of justice and the public interest in withholding" (para. 36); "it is for the court and not the Crown to determine the issue" (para. 39); "Cabinet documents like other evidence must be disclosed unless such disclosure would interfere with the public interest" and the level of decision-making is "only one of many variables" (para. 79); "Cabinet documents ought not to be disclosed without a preliminary judicial inspection to balance the competing interests" (para. 86).
BaselineA: Common law public interest immunity / Crown privilege doctrine as developed in cases discussed in the reasons, especially Smallwood v. Sparling, [1982] 2 S.C.R. 686; also R. v. Snider, [1954] S.C.R. 479; Gagnon v. Commission des valeurs mobilières du Québec, [1965] S.C.R. 73; and comparative authorities (Conway v. Rimmer; Burmah Oil; Sankey v. Whitlam).
CaseB_TestB: Appellate review of (pre-Lifchus) jury instructions on reasonable doubt / conflicting evidence: "the test is whether there was substantial compliance with the principles set out in Lifchus" (para. 12) and "the basic question remains: does the charge, read as a whole, give rise to a reasonable likelihood that the jury misapprehended the correct standard of proof?" (para. 12).
BaselineB: Common law jury-charge standards from R. v. Lifchus, [1997] 3 S.C.R. 320 (reasonable doubt instruction) and R. v. W. (D.), [1991] 1 S.C.R. 742 (how to deal with competing versions/credibility), as applied through R. v. Starr, 2000 SCC 40.
JudgeB: Major J. (for Major, Binnie, Arbour and LeBel JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 7 limit on extradition/surrender: courts may intervene only where surrender would, in the particular circumstances, violate the principles of fundamental justice; intervention must be exercised with caution and be limited to "cases of real substance" (generally after the executive surrender decision).
BaselineA: Statute/treaty framework plus Charter: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7 (and discussion of s. 11(h), s. 32); Extradition Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-21 (ss. 3, 13, 18) and Extradition Treaty Between Canada and the United States (esp. art. 4(1)(i)).
CaseB_TestB: Crown appeal jurisdiction test: a Court of Appeal may interfere with an acquittal on a Crown appeal only if the trial court erred "on a question of law alone" (Criminal Code, s. 605(1)(a); applying Schuldt).
BaselineB: Statute plus precedent: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 605(1)(a), as interpreted/applied in Schuldt v. The Queen, [1985] 2 S.C.R. 592.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 7 limit on extradition/surrender: courts may intervene only where surrender would, in the particular circumstances, violate the principles of fundamental justice (intervention limited to 'cases of real substance')
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional text (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7) applied in the extradition context (Extradition Act and treaty framework)
CaseB_TestB: Income Tax Act s. 20(1)(c)(i) interest deductibility (purpose element): whether, considering all the circumstances, the taxpayer had a reasonable expectation of income at the time the investment was made
BaselineB: Statute (Income Tax Act, s. 20(1)(c)(i)) interpreted using modern statutory interpretation; built on prior SCC discussion in Bronfman Trust and Shell Canada
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Injurious affection where no land is taken: claimant must show the construction-caused loss would have been actionable at common law (nuisance), applying the Loiselle four conditions and rejecting claims for mere loss of amenities (e.g., loss of view) where the public work is a reasonable use
BaselineA: Statute (Expropriations Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 154, ss. 1(e)(ii), 21) incorporating the common-law requirement of actionability; common-law nuisance concepts (as described in Fleming/Street) and the SCC’s prior four-condition framework in The Queen v. Loiselle, [1962] S.C.R. 624
CaseB_TestB: Adequacy of jury instructions on alternative routes to murder liability: no miscarriage of justice where the charge, read as a whole, allowed conviction if the accused “actively participated”/“acted in concert with others” in the killing (not merely present or minor role), even if not proven to be the actual shooter
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, ss. 21, 229, 686(1)(b)(iii)) and common-law principles on assessing jury charges as a whole and party liability (including R. v. Thatcher, [1987] 1 S.C.R. 652, as discussed in the reasons)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 10(b) right to counsel: after police promptly advise of the right, no further (correlative) duties arise unless the detainee indicates a desire to exercise the right; absent proof of circumstances showing non-understanding, the accused bears the onus to show he asked for counsel and was denied or denied an opportunity to ask
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 10(b) (and remedy context under s. 24(2)); applied approach endorsed from R. v. Anderson (Ont. C.A.) as adopted by the SCC
CaseB_TestB: Employee/representative must disgorge profits obtained through abuse of position or secret commissions: applying C.C.L.C. arts. 411 (possessor in bad faith must remit capital plus 'any increase in value and fruits') and 1713 (mandatary must 'deliver and pay over all that he has received under the authority of the mandate, even if it were not due'), extended to senior employees acting in a representative capacity based on good faith/loyalty and the principle that no one should profit from wrongdoing
BaselineB: Statute/civil code: Civil Code of Lower Canada, arts. 411 and 1713 (and related good-faith/loyalty principles discussed through the Code); supported by jurisprudence including Thompson v. Sénécal and analogy to Canadian Aero Service Ltd. v. O'Malley
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Wigglesworth s. 11 Charter applicability test: a matter falls within s. 11 if (1) it is, "by its very nature" a criminal/quasi-criminal/public proceeding, OR (2) it exposes the person to a "true penal consequence"; where the two conflict, the "by nature" test "must give way" to the "true penal consequence" test.
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 11 (opening words "Any person charged with an offence"); interpreted in light of Charter interpretation approach from R. v. Big M Drug Mart Ltd.
CaseB_TestB: Functional approach to reviewing jury charges: "As long as an appellate court, when looking at a trial judge’s charge to the jury as a whole, concludes that the jury was left with a sufficient understanding of the facts as they relate to the relevant issues, the charge is proper."
BaselineB: Common law (jury-charge review principles) drawing on Azoulay v. The Queen; John v. The Queen; Cluett v. The Queen (and related appellate review jurisprudence).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: s. 577(1) Criminal Code “whole of the trial” / right to be present: jury selection (including questioning prospective jurors about partiality after arraignment and plea) is part of the trial; exclusion (including inability to hear) is a fundamental breach not cured by curative provisions
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 577(1); also discussed: ss. 569(2), 598, 599, 600, 613(1)(b)(iii)) interpreted in light of prior SCC guidance (Basarabas and Spek v. The Queen; Vézina and Côté v. The Queen) and related appellate authority (Hertrich; Meunier)
CaseB_TestB: Common-law test for when an appellate court may set aside an acquittal and enter a conviction (instead of ordering a new trial): Crown must show the verdict would not have been the same but for the error of law and that the accused should have been found guilty; all findings necessary for guilt must have been made (explicitly/implicitly) or not be in issue
BaselineB: Common law (as stated with reference to Vézeau v. The Queen and Courville v. The Queen) applied alongside Criminal Code, s. 613(4)(b)(ii)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: When a trial judge quashes a voidable charge under Criminal Code s. 529, the quashing is tantamount to an acquittal (triggering autrefois acquit) unless the charge was an absolute nullity; quashing is only permitted where the required amendment cannot be made without injustice/irreparable prejudice
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 529, 535, 537) interpreted in light of SCC jurisprudence on autrefois acquit and final dispositions (e.g., Petersen v. The Queen; Doyle v. The Queen)
CaseB_TestB: Framework to define the scope of an acquired right/legal non-conforming use and decide whether a modified use remains protected: characterize the purpose of the pre-existing use; treat mere intensification as protected unless it becomes a different use; treat added activities as unprotected if too remote; otherwise balance remoteness and neighbourhood effects, supported by evidence, to define the acquired right without being too broad or too narrow
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: Act Respecting Land Use Planning and Development, R.S.Q., c. A-19.1, s. 113(18) (and s. 227) plus common law principles on legal non-conforming uses (e.g., Central Jewish Institute v. City of Toronto, [1948] S.C.R. 101)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Workmen’s privilege against an owner’s immovable where work is done for a lessee: a lessee is not a “builder/contractor” for arts. 2013e–2013f C.C.L.C. unless the owner–lessee agreement is a true construction contract that includes a claim by the builder against the owner (i.e., an undertaking by the owner to pay a construction contract price) from which the owner can retain funds to satisfy privileged claims
BaselineA: Statute (Civil Code of Lower Canada), especially arts. 2013e and 2013f (workmen/materialmen privileges), with related contract provisions (arts. 984 et seq., 1060)
CaseB_TestB: Mental distress damages for breach of contract (Hadley v. Baxendale remoteness): recoverable where (1) an object of the contract was to secure a psychological benefit bringing mental distress on breach within the parties’ reasonable contemplation at contract formation, and (2) the plaintiff proves mental suffering of a degree sufficient to warrant compensation; no independent actionable wrong required
BaselineB: Common law (contract damages/remoteness), anchored in Hadley v. Baxendale and this Court’s prior approach in Vorvis v. I.C.B.C.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Unequal division of marital property under NB Marital Property Act s. 7(f): depart from equal division where equal division would be inequitable; in particular, where property was acquired “exclusively or almost wholly through the efforts of one spouse” and the other made “no, or a negligible, contribution to child care, household management or financial provision”, the court may exercise discretion to depart from equal shares
BaselineA: Statute: Marital Property Act, S.N.B. 1980, c. M-1.1, ss. 2, 3(1), 7 (especially s. 7(f) “any other circumstances ... rendering it inequitable for the division ... to be in equal shares”)
CaseB_TestB: Interjurisdictional immunity (constitutional inapplicability) for a federal service: provincial laws of general application apply unless they bear on what makes the federal thing/service “specifically of federal jurisdiction”; for a federal service, inapplicability arises if the provincial law “touches on a vital or essential aspect of its establishment, management or operation”
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine (interjurisdictional immunity) as articulated in prior SCC cases cited, especially Bell Canada v. Quebec (CSST), [1988] 1 S.C.R. 749; Construction Montcalm Inc. v. Minimum Wage Commission, [1979] 1 S.C.R. 754; Clark v. CNR, [1988] 2 S.C.R. 680
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “financing” in Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971 s. 44(2)(a): claimant is “financing” only where there is “active and voluntary involvement” and a “meaningful connection between the payment and the dispute” (mandatory union dues alone are not enough).
BaselineA: Statute: Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, S.C. 1970-71-72, c. 48, s. 44(2)(a) (exception to disentitlement where claimant proves he is not “participating in or financing or directly interested in” the labour dispute).
CaseB_TestB: Enforceability/scope of a waiver (exclusion) clause for negligence: construed “in the context in which it was signed”; clause applies unless the alleged negligence is outside what reasonable parties would have contemplated, and the clause is not avoided merely as “unfair” or “unreasonable” on these facts.
BaselineB: Common law: contractual interpretation and enforceability of exclusion/waiver clauses (including arguments framed as fundamental breach/unconscionability/public policy).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “financing” in Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971 s. 44(2)(a): claimant is “financing” a labour dispute only where there is “active and voluntary involvement” and a “meaningful connection between the payment and the dispute”; mandatory union dues diverted to a strike fund are not enough
BaselineA: Statute: Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, S.C. 1970-71-72, c. 48, s. 44(2)(a) (exception to disentitlement where claimant proves he is not “participating in or financing or directly interested in” the labour dispute)
CaseB_TestB: Extradition surrender refusal threshold under Extradition Act s. 44(1) / Charter s. 7: Minister must conduct a “balancing exercise”; surrender should be refused only where the requesting state’s “particular treatment” would “shock the conscience” or be “unjust or oppressive” such that it “tilt[s] the balance against extradition”
BaselineB: Statute + constitutional standard: Extradition Act, S.C. 1999, c. 18, s. 44(1) (“unjust or oppressive”) interpreted in light of Charter s. 7 principles of fundamental justice and prior SCC guidance (United States v. Burns; Lake v. Canada (Minister of Justice))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 10 “detention” test (Therens criteria as restated/applied): detention exists where (1) s. 10 targets a “restraint of liberty other than arrest” where one “may reasonably require the assistance of counsel”; (2) beyond physical constraint, detention occurs when the state “assumes control over the movement of a person by a demand or direction which may have significant legal consequence and which prevents or impedes access to counsel”; (3) the needed “compulsion or coercion” may arise from “criminal liability for refusal” or a “reasonable belief” there is no choice; and (4) s. 10 applies to detentions “of varying duration”.
BaselineA: Common law/Charter interpretation baseline from R. v. Therens, [1985] 1 S.C.R. 613 (interpreting Charter s. 10 “detention”), applied to Criminal Code s. 234.1(1) roadside breath demand context.
CaseB_TestB: Mistake-of-age defence under Criminal Code s. 150.1(4) (“all reasonable steps”)—Crown must prove beyond a reasonable doubt either (1) accused “did not honestly believe the complainant was at least 16” or (2) accused “did not take ‘all reasonable steps’ to ascertain the complainant’s age”; the “reasonable steps inquiry is contextual” and “highly contextual, fact-specific”; with a general rule that “the more reasonable an accused’s perception of the complainant’s age, the fewer steps reasonably required of them.”
BaselineB: Statutory baseline: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 150.1(4) (and related scheme ss. 150.1(1), 150.1(2.1), 151, 271).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Extradition specialty/immunity duration: an undertaking not to prosecute for pre-surrender offences does not bar prosecution once the extraditee has been “restored or has had an opportunity of returning” to the surrendering state; the undertaking is construed as “related to the surrender” and not perpetual where the person remains in Canada by choice
BaselineA: Statute (Extradition Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-21, s. 33) plus interpretation of the ad hoc extradition arrangement/undertaking with Brazil (read in light of international law interpretive principles, incl. Vienna Convention art. 31 as referenced)
CaseB_TestB: Criminal appeal procedure: where an appeal is properly before the SCC on an alleged error of law, the Court will also decide (if the Crown invokes it) whether the conviction can be “saved” by the curative proviso in Criminal Code s. 686(1)(b)(iii); it is “unnecessary for the Crown to seek leave” on the proviso because error-of-law and proviso are “always intertwined”
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(b)(iii)) as applied through SCC precedent on scope of arguments in criminal appeals (R. v. Keegstra, [1995] 2 S.C.R. 381)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “anything” in Criminal Code theft (s. 283(1)): to be the object of theft, the thing must (1) be “property of some sort” (capable of a proprietary right) and (2) be “capable of being taken or converted in a manner that results in the deprivation of the victim”; confidential information per se fails (not property for theft; and in any event not capable of taking/conversion with deprivation).
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 283(1) (theft definition: “takes, or ... converts ... anything whether animate or inanimate” with specified intents).
CaseB_TestB: Interpretation of “assets” in MVHC rent-subsidy Assistance Application: “assets” means an applicant’s “property or interest(s) in property that can actually be used to discharge his or her debts and liabilities, including the monthly rent”; a Henson trust interest is a “mere hope” and not an “asset” for this purpose.
BaselineB: Common law contractual interpretation (Sattva: read contract as a whole, ordinary and grammatical meaning, consistent with surrounding circumstances/factual matrix) applied to the Tenancy Agreement/Assistance Application documents.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 7 analysis for compelled fingerprinting: (1) deprivation of life/liberty/security; (2) whether deprivation accords with principles of fundamental justice — i.e., whether fingerprinting/appearance requirement "unduly invades the rights of the accused" and is not arbitrary (discretion permitted; "sense of proportion" required).
BaselineA: Statute + constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7; Identification of Criminals Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-1, s. 2; Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 453.3(3) and 455.5(5) (deeming lawful custody for fingerprinting).
CaseB_TestB: Sheppard/Braich test for appellate intervention based on insufficient reasons: two stages — (1) "are the reasons inadequate"; (2) "if so, do they prevent appellate review" (i.e., are they "inscrutable" such that review is impeded).
BaselineB: Common law (as stated in the decision): R. v. Sheppard, 2002 SCC 26; R. v. Braich, 2002 SCC 27 (also discussed alongside Burns).
JudgeB: Bastarache and Abella JJ. (LeBel J. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Detention at the border for s. 10(b): a traveller is "detained" when a state agent "assumes control over the movement of a person by a demand or direction which may have significant legal consequence" (Therens, adopted), applied here to a compelled strip search where the person "could not have refused and continued on her way" and was "subject to external restraint".
BaselineA: Common law / Charter interpretation baseline from R. v. Therens, [1985] 1 S.C.R. 613 interpreting Charter s. 10(b) "detention" (applied/affirmed; also referenced: Hufsky, Thomsen).
CaseB_TestB: s. 11(b) unreasonable delay framework (Morin factors + institutional-delay guideline): determine unreasonableness by a "judicial determination balancing" interests using (1) length of delay; (2) waiver; (3) reasons for delay (including inherent requirements, actions of accused/Crown, institutional resources, other reasons); and (4) prejudice; with a non-binding guideline of "between 8 and 10 months" for institutional delay in Provincial Courts.
BaselineB: Statutory/constitutional baseline: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 11(b) ("to be tried within a reasonable time"), developed through prior SCC cases (Mills, Rahey, Conway, Smith, Askov) as synthesized and refined here.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Voluntary intoxication and mens rea for general-intent offences (Leary rule as applied): intoxication evidence is excluded unless it is so extreme as to negate the minimal intent/voluntariness; Crown may prove mens rea by inference from actus reus or, in extreme cases, by proving voluntary self-induced intoxication as substituted fault
BaselineA: Common law (applied/affirmed from Leary v. The Queen, [1978] 1 S.C.R. 29; also relying on R. v. George, [1960] S.C.R. 871; Swietlinski v. The Queen, [1980] 2 S.C.R. 956; and Majewski (H.L.))
JudgeA: McIntyre J. (for Beetz and McIntyre JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Appellate intervention on Crown appeal from acquittal: an appellate court cannot interfere with a trial judge’s inferences of fact merely because it would draw different inferences, but may intervene where the trial judge failed to direct his mind to an issue requiring determination (error of law)
BaselineB: Common law (limits on Crown appeals from acquittal and deference to inferences of fact, relying on Schuldt v. The Queen, [1985] 2 S.C.R. 592; also referencing R. v. Morin, [1992] 3 S.C.R. 286 and R. v. C. (R.), [1993] 2 S.C.R. 226)
JudgeB: Major J. (for Lamer C.J. and Sopinka and Major JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Appellate intervention in trial judge’s discretionary reapportionment of family assets: intervene only if the trial judge “misdirects himself” or the decision is “so clearly wrong as to amount to an injustice” (in applying Family Relations Act, s. 51 unfairness criteria; no requirement to assess each asset individually or to make division proportionate to contribution).
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Family Relations Act, R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 121, ss. 43 and 51 (equal division unless “unfair” having regard to listed criteria) plus appellate deference standard from Harper v. Harper, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 2 (and Re Hull Estate (Ont. C.A.) quoted).
CaseB_TestB: Duty to comment on improper Crown jury address: where Crown counsel’s remarks are “prejudicial to a degree sufficient to impose a legal duty on the trial judge to comment” to ensure the defence position is “fairly put to the jury”; failure is an error of law, and the curative proviso (Criminal Code, s. 686(1)(b)(iii)) does not apply absent no substantial wrong/miscarriage of justice.
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(b)(iii)) applied through common-law principles of fair trial/jury charge; the Court adopts the dissenting appellate formulation (Ayles J.A.) as the governing standard in this case.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Wigmore/Slavutych four-part test for recognizing a (qualified) common law privilege against compelled disclosure of communications (including claimed journalist-source privilege): (1) communication originates in confidence; (2) confidentiality essential to the relationship; (3) relationship one the community ought to foster; (4) injury from disclosure greater than benefit for correct disposal of litigation
BaselineA: Common law (Wigmore criteria as discussed with approval in Slavutych v. Baker, [1976] 1 S.C.R. 254, at p. 260)
CaseB_TestB: Reasonableness review of Crown corporations’ discretionary PILT calculations: discretion exists to choose the 'effective rate', but it must be exercised within the statutory/regulatory framework—rates must be calculated 'as if the federal property were taxable property belonging to a private owner' and cannot be based on a 'fictitious tax system' (must use the tax system that actually exists in the municipality)
BaselineB: Statute and regulation (Payments in Lieu of Taxes Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. M-13, ss. 2 (definitions incl. “effective rate”), 2.1, 4(1), sch. II item 10; Crown Corporation Payments Regulations, SOR/81-1030, ss. 2 (definitions), 7(1))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Patent Act s. 36(1) disclosure/sufficiency test: applicant must disclose everything essential for the invention to function properly; completeness requires (1) describing the invention and defining how it is produced/built, and (2) defining the nature of the invention and describing how it is put into operation; disclosure must enable a person skilled in the art to produce it using only the instructions in the specification (a mere deposit of seed, by itself, is not enough).
BaselineA: Statute (Patent Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. P-4, s. 36(1)), as interpreted through prior patent-law authorities cited in the reasons (e.g., Minerals Separation; Burton Parsons; Monsanto; Consolboard).
CaseB_TestB: Dunsmuir standard-of-review framework applied to labour arbitration: arbitral awards are presumptively reviewed for reasonableness; correctness applies only to established exceptional categories (constitutional questions, questions of central importance to the legal system and outside expertise, true jurisdiction/vires, or competing-tribunal jurisdictional lines). Applying an equitable/common law doctrine (like estoppel) does not, by itself, trigger correctness; contextual factors confirm reasonableness.
BaselineB: Common law administrative-law framework from Dunsmuir v. New Brunswick and Smith v. Alliance Pipeline Ltd., applied in the labour-arbitration/statutory context (Labour Relations Act, R.S.M. 1987, c. L10, ss. 121, 128(2)).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 96 ‘Residential Tenancies’ three-stage test, clarified: (1) historical ‘broad conformity’ with s. 96 courts in 1867 using a narrow characterization of the dispute (not the remedy); (2) whether the function is judicial; (3) whether, in institutional context, the judicial power is merely ancillary/necessarily incidental to a broader regulatory scheme. Added glosses: stage 1 asks whether superior-court jurisdiction was exclusive; if shared, it validates only where inferior-court involvement was ‘broadly co-extensive’ (e.g., consider geographic/pecuniary limits). Historical inquiry is national (four original provinces; if tie, look to U.K.).
BaselineA: Common law constitutional doctrine applying Constitution Act, 1867, s. 96; baseline framework from Re Residential Tenancies Act, 1979, [1981] 1 SCR 714 (three-step test).
CaseB_TestB: Public interest standing (Downtown Eastside) framework, applied and clarified: court ‘must assess and weigh three factors’ — (i) serious justiciable issue; (ii) genuine interest; (iii) reasonable and effective means — and ‘courts flexibly and purposively weigh the factors’. Clarifications include: legality/access to justice do not get ‘particular weight’; no directly affected co-plaintiff is required if a ‘concrete and well-developed factual setting’ can be shown; what suffices is context-specific; and standing may be revisited only on a ‘material change’ raising serious doubt about a forthcoming factual setting (most likely after pleadings/discovery).
BaselineB: Common law test from Canada (Attorney General) v. Downtown Eastside Sex Workers United Against Violence Society, 2012 SCC 45 (three-factor discretionary framework for public interest standing).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Bankruptcy priority for provincial “statutory trust” tax claims: s. 47(a) applies only if the tax money is identifiable/traceable as trust property under general trust law; if not traceable, the province has only a Crown claim under s. 107(1)(j). (“If the money collected for tax is identifiable or traceable... s. 47(a)... If... cannot be traced... s. 107(1)(j) applies.”)
BaselineA: Statute (Bankruptcy Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. B-3, ss. 47(a), 107(1)(j)) interpreted alongside provincial statute (Social Service Tax Act, R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 388, s. 18)
CaseB_TestB: Section 23 “numbers warrant” / minority-language facilities & management-control analysis: relevant numbers are “somewhere between the known demand and the total number of persons who could potentially take advantage of the service”; the service level is determined on a case-by-case “sliding scale” considering pedagogical requirements and costs; where a minority-language board exists, defining the area and choosing location/mode of delivery falls within the minority’s exclusive management and control, with the Minister’s discretion limited to verifying compliance with objective provincial norms consistent with s. 23.
BaselineB: Constitution (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 23) plus common-law/precedent framework (Mahe v. Alberta) and related provincial statute/regulations (P.E.I. School Act and School Act Regulations) as applied/limited by s. 23
JudgeB: Major and Bastarache JJ. (for the Court)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Young Offenders Act s. 16 transfer to ordinary court: whether, after weighing and balancing all relevant s. 16(2) factors, the judge is satisfied transfer is appropriate (onus on applicant, but 'not ... a heavy one')
BaselineA: Statute (Young Offenders Act, S.C. 1980-81-82-83, c. 110, s. 16(1) and s. 16(2); also review provisions s. 16(9)-(10))
CaseB_TestB: Damages for breach where contract has alternative modes of performance: adopt the mode 'least profitable to the plaintiff, and the least burdensome to the defendant' (not a 'would likely have performed' counterfactual inquiry)
BaselineB: Common law (general principle traced to Cockburn v. Alexander (1848) and explained in Withers v. General Theatre Corp. (1933), as adopted in Canadian appellate authority cited)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Canadian maritime law (agency/mandate): whether an agent of an unnamed/partially disclosed principal is personally liable turns on the parties’ intention as shown by the contract’s construction; there is “no prescribed formality for disclosure” and liability “depends on the will of the contracting parties” (e.g., if the agent indicates it is contracting “as agent only”, it is not liable unless the contract otherwise clearly involves personal liability).
BaselineA: Common law (contract/agency) as part of Canadian maritime law under Federal Court Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. F-7, ss. 2 and 22(2)(m), building on ITO—International Terminal Operators Ltd. v. Miida Electronics Inc., [1986] 1 S.C.R. 752; with comparative reference to Civil Code of Lower Canada arts. 1715-1716 (as a source, not governing provincial law).
JudgeA: La Forest J. (for Wilson, La Forest, Sopinka and Cory JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Child Welfare Act reporting immunity: s. 38(6) bars actions by informants only if the report is not made “maliciously or without reasonable cause”; “reasonable cause” is an objective threshold meaning reasonable cause to ask CPS to look into the matter (not reasonable grounds to believe abuse occurred), and the duty to report in s. 38(1) and immunity in s. 38(6) are “co-extensive” and read together.
BaselineB: Statute: Child Welfare Act, R.S.N. 1990, c. C-12, ss. 38(1) and 38(6) (interpreted alongside common law negligence duty analysis from Cooper v. Hobart and Martel Building Ltd. v. Canada).
JudgeB: McLachlin C.J. and Binnie J. (for the Court)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Common-law limits on a warrantless “frisk” search incident to a lawful arrest: no reasonable/probable grounds prerequisite, but (1) discretionary (not a duty), (2) must pursue a valid criminal-justice objective (safety/escape/evidence; not intimidation), and (3) must be non-abusive with force/constraint proportionate to objectives and circumstances
BaselineA: Common law (search incident to arrest), drawing on Canadian and British authorities discussed in the reasons (e.g., R. v. Brezack; R. v. Morrison; R. v. Miller; Leigh v. Cole; Bessell v. Wilson; Lindley v. Rutter)
CaseB_TestB: Section 7 “principles of fundamental justice” minimum for warrantless child apprehension: no prior judicial authorization required if statute permits apprehension in situations of “serious harm or risk of serious harm” to the child, coupled with a fair and prompt post-apprehension hearing (with the constitutional assessment reached via balancing interests/risks)
BaselineB: Statute + Charter interpretation: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7 applied to Manitoba Child and Family Services Act, S.M. 1985-86, c. 8, ss. 17, 21(1), 27(1), 29(1)
JudgeB: L’Heureux-Dubé J. (for the majority: L’Heureux-Dubé, Gonthier, Major, Bastarache and Binnie JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal negligence (s. 219): whether the accused’s conduct is a “marked departure from the norm” such that “the conclusion that there is a wanton or reckless disregard is to be drawn from the conduct which falls below the standard”; consequences (death) generally “added nothing” unless “so interwoven” with the acts as to help characterize the conduct
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 202(1)-(2), 203 (now ss. 219, 220); interpreted in light of R. v. Tutton, [1989] 1 S.C.R. 1392)
CaseB_TestB: Standing/jurisdiction before the CITT under the AIT: a non-Canadian supplier has no standing; for AIT coverage the procurement must be “procurement within Canada”, which requires the supplier to be a “Canadian supplier” (AIT art. 518: supplier with “a place of business in Canada”)—otherwise the AIT is inapplicable and the contract is not a “designated contract” for CITT Act purposes
BaselineB: Statute and regulation incorporating a trade agreement (Canadian International Trade Tribunal Act, ss. 30.1, 30.11(1); Canadian International Trade Tribunal Procurement Inquiry Regulations, ss. 3(1), 7(1), 11; interpreting Agreement on Internal Trade, especially arts. 501, 502, 518)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 8 reasonableness of compelled document production in a regulatory/tax audit context: a s. 231(3) demand is a “seizure” but is reasonable given the regulatory scheme, low expectation of privacy, and need for random monitoring (Hunter criteria not strictly applicable outside criminal/quasi-criminal context).
BaselineA: Combination: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 8 (unreasonable search or seizure) applied to Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1952, c. 148, s. 231(3) (demand for information/documents) with enforcement in s. 238(2); baseline Charter reasonableness framework from Hunter v. Southam Inc. and related s. 8 jurisprudence (incl. Simmons) as discussed in the reasons.
CaseB_TestB: Public interest standing test (purposive, flexible, discretionary): courts weigh (1) serious justiciable issue, (2) real stake/genuine interest, and (3) whether the proposed suit is, “in all of the circumstances”, a “reasonable and effective means” to bring the issue to court (not a rigid ‘no other way’ requirement).
BaselineB: Common law standing doctrine from SCC cases (as cited and discussed): Borowski (three-factor formulation), Finlay, Canadian Council of Churches, Hy and Zel’s, Thorson, McNeil, etc.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Duty to defend is determined by the pleadings: insurer must defend only if the suit seeks damages that "are or may be payable under" the policy (i.e., claims that potentially fall within indemnity coverage); no duty where allegations are clearly outside coverage (e.g., only fraud alleged and fraud excluded).
BaselineA: Contract (insurance policy) interpreted using common-law insurance contract construction principles; key policy wording: duty to "[d]efend any suit ... seeking damages which are or may be payable under the terms of this Policy" and exclusion for "dishonest, fraudulent, criminal or malicious act or omission".
CaseB_TestB: Criminal Code s. 265(4) “air of reality” threshold for honest but mistaken belief in consent: a defence is left to the jury only if there is "sufficient evidence" such that "a reasonable jury properly instructed could acquit"; requires evidence beyond a bare assertion of belief (though not necessarily independent of the accused).
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 265(4)) codifying/reflecting common-law threshold for leaving defences with the jury (cases discussed include Pappajohn, Bulmer, Robertson).
JudgeB: Cory J. (for Cory and Major JJ.; majority on key points)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Deductibility of wage-continuation benefits from tort damages for lost earnings (collateral benefits rule): "As a general rule, wage benefits paid while a plaintiff is unable to work must be brought into account and deducted from the claim for lost earnings"; exception where payer has a subrogation/reimbursement entitlement, and (rarely) trust where "necessary and appropriate in the interests of justice" with some "obligation, moral if not legal, to repay".
BaselineA: Common law damages principles (compensation for "actual loss"; no double recovery) and prior collateral-benefits jurisprudence cited in the reasons, including Andrews v. Grand & Toy Alberta Ltd.; Thornton v. Prince George School Board; Arnold v. Teno; and discussion of Bradburn v. Great Western Rail. Co. and Parry v. Cleaver.
CaseB_TestB: Constitutional "necessarily incidental" (integration) test for federal provisions intruding on provincial jurisdiction: after finding a valid federal head of power, impugned provisions must be "sufficiently integrated with the scheme" (a "high degree of integration") to be upheld; applied to uphold GST collection/input-credit scheme under s. 91(3).
BaselineB: Constitution Act, 1867 (especially ss. 91(3) and 92(13)) and the common-law/constitutional doctrine articulated in prior SCC cases cited, especially General Motors of Canada Ltd. v. City National Leasing and Reference re Exported Natural Gas Tax.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Art. 559 C.C.Q. compensatory allowance test: claimant must prove (1) contribution, (2) enrichment of spouse’s patrimony, (3) causal link/correlation, and (4) proportion in which the contribution made possible the enrichment; enrichment must subsist and is evaluated at the time of divorce, with the elements assessed “with great flexibility”.
BaselineA: Statute (Civil Code of Quebec, art. 559), informed by unjust enrichment principles (e.g., Cie Immobilière Viger Ltée v. Lauréat Giguère Inc.).
CaseB_TestB: Misapprehension of evidence (Morrissey) test for setting aside a conviction: misapprehension must go to “the substance” not “detail”, be “material” not “peripheral”, and the errors must play an “essential part” in the reasoning process resulting in conviction (a “stringent” conjunctive standard).
BaselineB: Common law appellate standard adopted/affirmed from R. v. Morrissey (Ont. C.A.) and R. v. C. (R.) (SCC), applied in the context of Criminal Code, s. 686(1)(a)(iii) (miscarriage of justice).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Copyright Act s. 3(1) reproduction analysis for software embedded in silicon chips: the chip-embedded program is protected if it is a "reproduction" of the copyrightable program in written form (the chip should be viewed as "a static object encoded with written instructions"; thus "the programs embedded in the silicon chip are a reproduction of the programs in assembly language and as such are protected by copyright under s. 3(1)").
BaselineA: Statute: Copyright Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-30, s. 3(1) (including s. 3(1)(a) and (d) discussed but not decided).
CaseB_TestB: Common law de facto taking test (compensation): "two requirements" — (1) "an acquisition of a beneficial interest in the property or flowing from it" and (2) "removal of all reasonable uses of the property".
BaselineB: Common law: de facto taking doctrine as stated with reference to Mariner Real Estate Ltd. v. Nova Scotia (Attorney General), Manitoba Fisheries Ltd. v. The Queen, and The Queen in Right of British Columbia v. Tener (and applied alongside Vancouver Charter, s. 569).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Novation (substitution of debtor) test in mortgage/assumption context: (1) “The new debtor must assume the complete liability”; (2) “The creditor must accept the new debtor as principal debtor and not merely as an agent or guarantor”; and (3) “The creditor must accept the new contract in full satisfaction and substitution for the old contract” (from Polson v. Wulffsohn (1890)), with the SCC emphasizing that assent is crucial and courts should be “loath to find novation unless the circumstances are really compelling”.
BaselineA: Common law (Polson v. Wulffsohn (1890), 2 B.C.R. 39, as quoted/applied in the reasons).
CaseB_TestB: De facto taking (constructive expropriation) test for compensation at common law: requires (1) “an acquisition of a beneficial interest in the property or flowing from it”, and (2) “removal of all reasonable uses of the property”.
BaselineB: Common law (as stated and supported by Mariner Real Estate Ltd. v. Nova Scotia (A.G.); Manitoba Fisheries Ltd. v. The Queen; and The Queen in Right of British Columbia v. Tener).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Applicability of Criminal Code s. 443 (now s. 487) search-warrant power to offences under “any other Act of Parliament” even where that other Act (e.g., Bankruptcy Act s. 6) also contains search-and-seizure provisions: on a plain reading, s. 443(1)(a)-(b) applies to proceedings under any federal statute; Parliament restricted only para. (e) by making it “subject to any other Act of Parliament”.
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 443(1)(a), (b), (e) (as amended 1985, c. 19, s. 69) and Bankruptcy Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. B-3, s. 6 (plus interpretive context from Interpretation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-23, s. 27(2)).
CaseB_TestB: Meaning of “risks willingly assumed” in Occupiers’ Liability Act s. 4(1): s. 4(1) embodies the volenti doctrine, so more than mere knowledge/appreciation of danger is required—there must be consent to the legal risk/waiver of legal rights (plaintiff assumes both physical and legal risk), making s. 4(1) a “very narrow exception” to the s. 3(1) duty of reasonable care.
BaselineB: Statute interpreted in light of common law: Occupiers’ Liability Act, R.S.O. 1980, c. 322, ss. 3(1) and 4(1), with the common law volenti doctrine as articulated in SCC cases (e.g., Dube v. Labar; Crocker v. Sundance Northwest Resorts Ltd.).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 32 applicability to an entity (Wilson J.’s three-part criteria): (1) whether government exercises “general control” over the entity; (2) whether it performs a “traditional government function”/state responsibility; and (3) whether it acts under “statutory authority” to further a public-interest governmental objective.
BaselineA: Combination: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 32(1), applied through prior SCC jurisprudence (McKinney v. University of Guelph; RWDSU v. Dolphin Delivery Ltd.).
CaseB_TestB: Leave to appeal a commercial arbitral award under Arbitration Act, s. 31(2)(a): threshold “question of law”; plus (i) result “important to the parties” and (ii) determination “may prevent a miscarriage of justice”, meaning the legal issue is material and has “arguable merit”; with residual discretion factors (conduct, alternative remedies, undue delay, urgent need for finality).
BaselineB: Statute: Arbitration Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 55, s. 31(2)(a) (and related s. 31(1)); interpreted with reference to BCIT and other appellate guidance.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Limits on applying the s. 214(5) “single transaction” analysis: it applies only to murder classification under s. 214(5) and only after the Crown first proves the accused committed (or was a party to) both the underlying offence and the murder; only then ask whether the offences were “sufficiently closely connected in time” to classify the murder as first degree
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 214(5) (now s. 231(5))) as interpreted in R. v. Paré, [1987] 2 S.C.R. 618 (including the “single transaction” understanding of “while committing”); also references to party-liability concepts under s. 21 in explaining prerequisites for party cases
CaseB_TestB: Forum non conveniens test: once jurisdiction is properly assumed, the party seeking a stay must show another forum is “clearly a more appropriate forum”; the court considers numerous, context-specific factors and asks whether one forum “ultimately emerge[s] as clearly more appropriate”
BaselineB: Common law (Club Resorts Ltd. v. Van Breda, 2012 SCC 17) governing forum non conveniens and jurisdiction; with reference to codified factor-lists (e.g., CJPTA s. 11(2) as persuasive) but applied as common-law doctrine
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Abuse of process stay of proceedings test (Keyowski/Jewitt/Young): a stay is granted only in the “clearest of cases” where compelling the accused to stand trial would violate fundamental principles of justice/fair play and decency, or where proceedings are “oppressive or vexatious”; also framed as whether the “affront to fair play and decency is disproportionate to the societal interest in the effective prosecution of criminal cases”.
BaselineA: Common law (as articulated in R. v. Jewitt adopting R. v. Young; reaffirmed/clarified in R. v. Keyowski and R. v. Conway). Statutory context: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 508 (stay/recommencement power) was the procedural setting but the abuse-of-process test itself is common law.
CaseB_TestB: When a Vetrovec “clear, sharp warning” is required: the trial judge has discretion to decide whether any witness is “for some reason untrustworthy to such an extent that a warning to the jury is necessary”; but in some cases the circumstances are such that a Vetrovec caution “must be given”. If given, detailed identification of corroborative evidence is not mandatory in all cases; whether to refer to specific supportive evidence (and how) remains within the trial judge’s discretion, especially where supportive evidence is highly prejudicial.
BaselineB: Common law (Vetrovec v. The Queen; refinement discussed via R. v. Babinski and Sellars v. The Queen).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Lippé institutional impartiality test for part-time judges’ outside occupations: (1) ask whether, considering factors including “the nature of the occupation and the parties who appear before this type of judge”, “there [will] be a reasonable apprehension of bias in the mind of a fully informed person in a substantial number of cases”; (2) if yes (occupation “per se incompatible”), ask whether safeguards reduce the risk so that, with knowledge of safeguards, there is no longer a reasonable apprehension of bias “in a substantial number of cases” (otherwise proceed case-by-case).
BaselineA: Combination: constitutional text (Canadian Charter s. 11(d); Quebec Charter s. 23) plus common-law reasonable apprehension of bias test from Committee for Justice and Liberty v. National Energy Board (adopted in Valente v. The Queen).
CaseB_TestB: Zundel s. 2(b) infringement framework (Irwin Toy) applied to Criminal Code s. 181: expression is protected if it “convey[s] or attempt[s] to convey meaning” unless excluded by “physical form” (e.g., violence); then ask whether the law’s “purpose or effect” restricts expression (if so, s. 2(b) is infringed).
BaselineB: Common law/constitutional doctrine: Irwin Toy Ltd. v. Quebec (Attorney General) s. 2(b) framework interpreting Canadian Charter s. 2(b).
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Section 96 “core jurisdiction” / Residential Tenancies step-one historical inquiry (with required characterization): determine whether the impugned jurisdiction was exercised exclusively by s. 96 superior courts at Confederation; if not, the grant to an inferior court is valid
BaselineA: Common law constitutional test from Re Residential Tenancies Act, 1979, [1981] 1 S.C.R. 714 (as applied to s. 96 of the Constitution Act, 1867) and Sobeys Stores Ltd. v. Yeomans, [1989] 1 S.C.R. 238; applied to Constitution Act, 1867, s. 96
CaseB_TestB: Interpretation of “sold in any market in Canada” (Patent Act ss. 80(1)(b), 83(1), 85): include sales of medicines regulated by Canadian public law, delivered/dispensed in Canada, and whose cost is borne by Canadians
BaselineB: Statutory interpretation of Patent Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. P-4, ss. 80(1)(b), 83(1), 85 (and related information power in s. 81(1)(a)); applying the modern principle of interpretation (Canada Trustco)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Adequacy of an indictment (incl. multiple-conspiracies context): an indictment is adequate if it gives the accused reasonable information and enables identification of the transaction; and a proven conspiracy falls within the indictment if it included some accused, occurred sometime within the alleged time span, and had as its object the type of crime alleged
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 510, 512, 516) plus SCC/common-law principles (R. v. Côté; R. v. Wis Development Corp.; R. v. B.(G.); R. v. Cotroni; R. v. Ackworth)
CaseB_TestB: Constitutional validity of the Canada Evidence Act s. 38 scheme under s. 96: apply the Re Residential Tenancies Act, 1979 test (historical conformity at Confederation as the first step; if no conformity, the inquiry ends) and, separately, assess whether the impugned power trenches on the protected 'core jurisdiction' of superior courts (properly characterized narrowly)
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine (Re Residential Tenancies Act, 1979; MacMillan Bloedel; Reference re Amendments to the Residential Tenancies Act (N.S.); Babcock) applied to a statutory scheme (Canada Evidence Act, ss. 38 to 38.16; Constitution Act, 1867, s. 96)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Entrapment (Mack) — random virtue-testing / bona fide inquiry: entrapment where police provide an opportunity without (a) reasonable suspicion the person is already engaged in the crime or (b) acting pursuant to a bona fide inquiry; and, even if suspicion/bona fide inquiry exists, entrapment where police go beyond opportunity and induce the offence. Barnes clarifies that within a bona fide inquiry, police may randomly offer the opportunity to anyone 'associated' with the defined area, and 'associated' requires no more than presence; random virtue-testing arises only if neither (a) nor (b) is met.
BaselineA: Common law (R. v. Mack, [1988] 2 S.C.R. 903 entrapment test; applied/clarified in Barnes).
CaseB_TestB: Appellate review of trial judge’s voluntariness ruling on a statement: a court of appeal errs by reweighing the voir dire evidence and refusing to admit a statement absent a 'serious, specific and determining error' in the trial judge’s assessment of whether the statement was 'free and voluntary'.
BaselineB: Common law (voluntariness of statements and appellate deference to trial-level voir dire findings; no statute identified in the reasons).
JudgeB: LeBel J. (for the Court, oral reasons)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Duty to comment on Crown counsel’s prejudicial jury address: where remarks are “prejudicial to a degree sufficient to impose a legal duty on the trial judge to comment” to ensure the defence position is “fairly put to the jury”; failure is an error of law (with no curative proviso applied here under s. 686(1)(b)(iii)).
BaselineA: Statute + common law fairness principles: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(b)(iii) (curative proviso) applied to an alleged error of law arising from non-direction in jury instructions.
CaseB_TestB: Broker commission triggers under brokerage contract: (1) “agreement to sell” requires an unconditional promise to purchase—“so long as a promise to purchase is not unconditionally binding ... there is no ‘agreement to sell’”; and (2) “seller voluntarily prevents free performance” mirrors art. 1503 C.C.Q. and requires proof of seller fault preventing fulfilment of the condition.
BaselineB: Statute + contract interpretation: Civil Code of Québec, arts. 1396 and 1503 (and related arts. 1723, 1725), applied to standard-form brokerage clauses 6.1(3o) and 6.1(4o).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 16(2) insanity test — second branch: whether, due to “disease of the mind”, the accused was “incapable … of knowing that an act or omission is wrong” (with “wrong” meaning “morally wrong” per Chaulk, applied in Landry); first branch limited to inability to appreciate the “physical consequences” of the act
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 16(2)); prior SCC interpretations: Cooper v. The Queen; Kjeldsen v. The Queen; R. v. Abbey (first branch = physical character/consequences) and R. v. Chaulk (redefining “wrong” in s. 16(2))
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 8 sniffer-dog search threshold — “reasonable suspicion” requires more than a hunch: it must be “grounded in objectively discernible facts” and assessed on the “totality of the circumstances” (a “constellation of factors”), viewed through the lens of a reasonable officer’s training/experience; asks whether facts indicate the “possibility” (not probability) of criminal behaviour
BaselineB: Common law Charter s. 8 framework for sniffer-dog searches (building on R. v. Kang-Brown and R. v. A.M.; clarified with reference to R. v. Chehil) applying Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 8 (and related detention analysis under s. 9)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Legitimate expectations cannot constrain the legislative process: the doctrine is procedural only (consultation/representations) and does not apply to introducing legislation (especially money bills)
BaselineA: Common law administrative-law doctrine of legitimate expectations as an aspect of procedural fairness (as summarized in Old St. Boniface Residents Assn. Inc. v. Winnipeg (City))
CaseB_TestB: Divorce Act s. 17 variation framework: court must be satisfied of a post-order change in the spouses’ “condition, means, needs or other circumstances” and then vary support considering the s. 17(7) objectives; pension income may be treated as “means” where prior property division did not truly divide the pension’s future value (no actionable “double dipping” on these facts)
BaselineB: Statute (Divorce Act, 1985, s. 17(4) and s. 17(7))
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Extradition under Charter s. 7: surrender (including without death-penalty assurances) violates fundamental justice only if the fugitive faces a situation that “sufficiently shocks” the Canadian conscience / is “simply unacceptable”, assessed contextually (offence/penalty, foreign justice system safeguards, comity and security, and “due latitude” to the Minister’s balancing).
BaselineA: Combination: statute (Extradition Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. E-23, s. 25; Canada–U.S. Extradition Treaty, Art. 6) + common-law/Charter s. 7 framework from Canada v. Schmidt ("shock the conscience") and United States v. Allard ("simply unacceptable").
CaseB_TestB: Search warrants for media premises: no special constitutional preconditions beyond Criminal Code s. 487; s. 2(b) is a “backdrop” and the key question is whether, “taking into account all the circumstances and viewing them fairly and objectively”, the search is reasonable (with a non-exhaustive list of factors, and alternative sources ordinarily disclosed but not required).
BaselineB: Combination: statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 487(1)(b),(d),(e)) + common-law/Charter reasonableness framework (including discussion of Re Pacific Press and Descôteaux v. Mierzwinski).
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Reasonable apprehension of bias (pecuniary interest) test for tribunal impartiality: “Would a reasonably well-informed person consider that the interest might have an influence on the exercise of the official's public duty?” (Old St. Boniface formulation applied to Law Society costs provision)
BaselineA: Common law (administrative law/natural justice) as formulated in Old St. Boniface Residents Assn. Inc. v. Winnipeg (City), [1990] 3 S.C.R. 1170; applied in the s. 7 Charter “principles of fundamental justice” context
CaseB_TestB: Nelles test for malicious prosecution / lifting prosecutorial immunity: plaintiff must prove on a balance of probabilities (1) prosecution initiated by defendant; (2) terminated in plaintiff’s favour; (3) absence of reasonable and probable cause (subjective + objective); and (4) malice/improper purpose (“deliberate and improper use of the office … inconsistent with the status of ‘minister of justice’”)
BaselineB: Common law (tort of malicious prosecution and prosecutorial immunity) from Nelles v. Ontario, [1989] 2 S.C.R. 170
JudgeB: Iacobucci and Binnie JJ. (for McLachlin C.J. and Iacobucci, Major and Binnie JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Colour of right / mistake analysis for s. 206(1)(d) lottery offence: colour of right is unavailable where the offence definition does not include it, and in any event a belief that the Criminal Code is inoperative is a mistake of law barred by s. 19 ("Ignorance of the law ... is not an excuse").
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, ss. 19 and 206(1)(d); plus the general common law principle that mistake of law is no defence, expressed in s. 19).
CaseB_TestB: Modified Taylor definition/test for "hatred" under s. 14(1)(b) hate-publications prohibition: apply objectively whether "a reasonable person, aware of the context and circumstances" would view the expression as likely to expose a protected group to "detestation" and "vilification"; focus on effects (likely exposure to hatred by others), not intent; and strike "ridicules, belittles or otherwise affronts the dignity of" as unconstitutional.
BaselineB: Statute (Saskatchewan Human Rights Code, S.S. 1979, c. S-24.1, s. 14(1)(b)) interpreted in light of prior SCC hate-speech jurisprudence, especially Canada (Human Rights Commission) v. Taylor, [1990] 3 S.C.R. 892.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Test for granting intervener status and managing prejudice from a new Charter argument/fresh evidence: intervener must have a sufficient interest and bring a special perspective; Court considers whether raising a new Charter argument would prejudice the respondent (prejudice if the Charter argument would have been affected by additional trial evidence / respondent might have adduced other material evidence); proposed materials should be filed only on respondent’s consent or, absent consent, with leave (especially if they constitute fresh evidence rather than judicial notice).
BaselineA: Common law / SCC practice on intervention and fresh evidence (as applied in an application to intervene in an appeal involving the Limitations Act and Charter interpretive arguments).
CaseB_TestB: Interpretation of Criminal Code s. 182(b) (offering indignities to human remains): (1) physical interference/contact is sufficient but not necessary; (2) the indignities must be offered to a dead human body or human remains (not to monuments per se); (3) where monuments mark the presence/final resting place of human remains, offering indignities to those monuments constitutes offering indignities to the human remains.
BaselineB: Statute — Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 182(b) (with related appeal powers in ss. 683(1)(g) and 695(1) discussed).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.
