CaseA_TestA: When the federal Environmental Assessment and Review Process Guidelines Order applies: there must be a “proposal” (an “initiative, undertaking or activity for which the Government of Canada has a decision making responsibility”), and “responsibility” means an “affirmative regulatory duty”/“legal duty or obligation” under an Act of Parliament; once that duty exists, identify the “initiating department” as the federal “decision making authority” (Guidelines Order ss. 2, 6; Oldman River: Transport yes via NWPA s. 5; Fisheries no because s. 37 is only an ad hoc discretionary power).
BaselineA: Regulation + statute: Environmental Assessment and Review Process Guidelines Order, SOR/84-467 (ss. 2 “proposal”, “initiating department”; s. 3; s. 6) made under Department of the Environment Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. E-10, s. 6; applied alongside Navigable Waters Protection Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. N-22, s. 5 and Fisheries Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. F-14, ss. 35, 37.
CaseB_TestB: Post-offence conduct and intent/culpability: where post-offence conduct “may be equally explained by reference to consciousness of guilt of two or more offences”, the jury must be instructed that it “has no probative value with respect to any particular offence” (Arcangioli); this limiting instruction is “most likely” required where the accused admits the actus reus but denies a “specific level of culpability” (White).
BaselineB: Common law (SCC precedent): R. v. Arcangioli, [1994] 1 S.C.R. 129 at p. 145; R. v. White, [1998] 2 S.C.R. 72 at para. 28 (applied in the context of appellate review under Criminal Code, s. 686(1)(a), (b)(iii)).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 133 “legislative nature” test (including anti-circumvention principle): an instrument is legislative if its form/content/effect show sufficient legislative connection and it (1) embodies a rule of conduct, (2) has the force of law, and (3) applies to an undetermined number of persons; and if “the net effect of a series of discrete acts has a legislative character, then each of these component acts will also be imbued with this same character”.
BaselineA: Constitution Act, 1867, s. 133 as interpreted in Reference re Manitoba Language Rights (1992) and (1985); applied with analogy to Quebec (Attorney General) v. Brunet, [1990] 1 S.C.R. 260.
CaseB_TestB: Responsive-answer requirement on a jury question about reasonable doubt: even with an unassailable Lifchus/model charge, when the jury asks about the standard of proof the trial judge “must attempt to answer the jury’s question”; repeating the charge may suffice in some cases, but the judge must not discourage further questions and must provide meaningful assistance responsive to the confusion raised.
BaselineB: Common law jury-instruction framework from R. v. Lifchus, [1997] 3 S.C.R. 320 and R. v. S. (W.D.), [1994] 3 S.C.R. 521 (with reference to R. v. Starr, 2000 SCC 40).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Mistaken transfer + recipient knowledge: property does not pass for criminal theft purposes if property law gives transferor a right of recovery; subsequent fraudulent conversion with intent to deprive = theft
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 322(1)) interpreted in light of property-law principles; prior approach in R. v. Dawood, [1976] 1 W.W.R. 262 (overruled)
CaseB_TestB: Judicial review standard for IAD humanitarian & compassionate relief decisions: apply Dunsmuir reasonableness (deference; court asks whether outcome falls within a range of reasonable outcomes and does not reweigh evidence)
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: Federal Courts Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. F-7, s. 18.1 (esp. s. 18.1(4)) plus common-law standard-of-review framework from Dunsmuir v. New Brunswick, 2008 SCC 9; applied to IRPA, S.C. 2001, c. 27, s. 67(1)(c)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 11(b) unreasonable delay analysis: a non-mathematical "balancing" of (1) length of delay; (2) waiver; (3) reasons for delay (inherent time requirements, actions of accused, actions of Crown, limits on institutional resources, other reasons); and (4) prejudice to the accused, with an institutional-delay guideline of 8–10 months in Provincial Court (not a fixed ceiling and must yield to other factors).
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 11(b) (and remedy via s. 24(1)); common-law/precedential baseline from SCC cases distilled in R. v. Smith, [1989] 2 S.C.R. 1120 and R. v. Askov, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 1199 (also Mills, Rahey, Conway).
CaseB_TestB: Contractor/subcontractor liability for construction collapse: even if supports yielded first, the subcontractor is not liable where the "true cause" is the contractor’s fault in overloading contrary to contract/specifications; the subcontractor may at least raise defences analogous to the builder’s defences (force majeure/act of God/owner’s fault/third party), including the contractor’s own fault, and is under no obligation to provide supports for an unforewarned, unforeseeable overload.
BaselineB: Civil Code (Quebec) and contract: C.C. arts. 1684, 1688, 1065, plus incorporated "General Conditions" (notably cl. 33 "OVERLOADING"); SCC baseline statement in Hill, Clarke-Francis Ltd. v. Northland Groceries (Quebec) Ltd., [1941] S.C.R. 437 (builder can avoid liability by proving force majeure/act of God/owner’s fault/third party act).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Secret commissions offence (Criminal Code s. 426(1)(a)(ii)): actus reus requires (1) agency relationship; (2) agent accepts a benefit as consideration for an act/forbearance in relation to principal’s affairs; and (3) failure to make “adequate and timely disclosure of the source, amount and nature of the benefit”; mens rea requires awareness of each element, and “if the accused was aware that some disclosure was made then it will be for the court to determine whether, in all the circumstances of the particular case, it was in fact adequate and timely”; “corruptly” means “secretly or without the requisite disclosure” and there is “no ‘corrupt bargain’ requirement.”
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 426(1)(a) (as applied to s. 426(1)(a)(ii) secret commissions); interpreted and applied following R. v. Kelly, [1992] 2 S.C.R. 000 (released concurrently).
JudgeA: Cory J. (for L'Heureux-Dubé, Cory and Iacobucci JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Criminal Code s. 686(1)(b)(iii) curative proviso: ask “whether a jury properly instructed could, acting reasonably, have come to a different conclusion absent the error”; jury findings may inform the hypothetical reasonable jury “provided those findings are not tainted by the error.”
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(b)(iii).
JudgeB: Sopinka J. (for the Court, oral reasons)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: State Immunity Act s. 5 “commercial activity” exception: two-step, contextual inquiry—(1) determine the nature of the foreign state’s activity (considering its context, including purpose where helpful), and (2) assess whether the Canadian proceedings “relate” to the commercial aspect by a sufficient “nexus” (more than merely ‘touch on’ or ‘incidentally affect’), considering competing nexus to sovereign aspects
BaselineA: Statute (State Immunity Act, S.C. 1980-81-82-83, c. 95), interpreted in light of common law restrictive immunity (acts jure imperii vs jure gestionis; contextual approach from I Congreso del Partido)
CaseB_TestB: Compatibility of Quebec “pay-and-retain/compensation” mechanisms with the BIA distribution scheme: characterize the provincial mechanism as subrogation/compensation and apply a timing-based set-off framework—pre-bankruptcy payment may allow legal compensation (or BIA s. 97(3) set-off if not liquid); post-bankruptcy subrogatory payment cannot ground compensation; equitable set-off is inapplicable in Quebec bankruptcy
BaselineB: Combination of statute and civil law: Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act (notably ss. 97(3), 121, 136–147) plus Quebec civil law rules on subrogation/compensation (C.C.Q. arts. 1651, 1656(3), 1672–1673, 1681) applied to provincial statutes (AIAOD s. 316; ALRCI s. 54)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Quebec civil law “obligation to inform” (duty of disclosure) in contracts: elements are (1) debtor’s knowledge (actual or presumed), (2) information of “decisive importance”, and (3) creditor cannot inform itself or legitimately relies on debtor; in large-project contracts of enterprise, scope varies with risk allocation, relative expertise, and the contract’s “continuing formation”.
BaselineA: Combination: Civil Code of Lower Canada arts. 1024 (good faith implied obligations) and 1053 (delictual fault standard), plus existing Quebec jurisprudence on good faith/obligation to inform (e.g., National Bank of Canada v. Soucisse; Bank of Montreal v. Kuet Leong Ng; Houle v. Canadian National Bank; Ross v. Dunstall; Air Canada v. McDonnell Douglas).
CaseB_TestB: Test for when a contract exclusion/limitation clause negates tort liability (here, duty to warn): if the contract language makes the parties’ intention clear that liability “shall extend only to” a specified head (here, negligent installation), then other tort heads (like duty to warn) are excluded by necessary implication; interpret by the contract as a whole and the “natural meaning” of the clauses (Miida Electronics approach).
BaselineB: Common law (tort-in-contractual-matrix / effect of exclusion clauses on negligence), relying on ITO—International Terminal Operators Ltd. v. Miida Electronics Inc. and related exclusion-clause jurisprudence (also referencing BG Checo; Giffels).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Duty to accommodate in adverse-effect discrimination: employer/union must take "reasonable measures short of undue hardship"; union is liable if it (1) helped create the discriminatory rule (e.g., collective agreement term) or (2) "impedes the reasonable efforts" to accommodate; undue hardship assessed contextually (e.g., cost, collective agreement disruption, morale/rights of others).
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Human Rights Act, S.B.C. 1984, c. 22, ss. 8(1)(a),(b),(4), 9(a)-(c), interpreted through SCC duty-to-accommodate jurisprudence (Ontario Human Rights Commission and O'Malley v. Simpsons-Sears Ltd.; Central Alberta Dairy Pool v. Alberta (Human Rights Commission)).
CaseB_TestB: Exclusive arbitral jurisdiction under s. 45(1) OLRA: courts are ousted where the dispute, in its "essential character", arises from the "interpretation, application, administration or alleged violation" of the collective agreement; focus is on the facts/dispute ("differences"), not the legal labels (tort/Charter).
BaselineB: Statute: Ontario Labour Relations Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. L.2, s. 45(1), interpreted in light of SCC labour-arbitration exclusivity jurisprudence (notably St. Anne Nackawic Pulp & Paper Co. v. Canadian Paper Workers Union, Local 219).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Trial judge’s discretion to exclude cross-examination on a collateral credibility matter where its (tenuous) relevance is outweighed by prejudicial effect (risk of misleading the jury)
BaselineA: Common law (trial management/evidence discretion), as applied in R. v. Meddoui, [1991] 3 S.C.R. 320
JudgeA: McLachlin J. (for the Court, oral reasons)
CaseB_TestB: Income Tax Act s. 20(1)(c)(i) interest deductibility: whether, considering all the circumstances, the taxpayer had a reasonable expectation of income at the time the investment was made (and “income” means income subject to tax, not net income)
BaselineB: Statute: Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), s. 20(1)(c)(i) (interpreting “purpose” and “income”); built on prior SCC discussion in Bronfman Trust and Shell Canada
JudgeB: Iacobucci J. (for Gonthier, Iacobucci, Major, Bastarache, Binnie and Arbour JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 10(b) “detention” at a port of entry: routine secondary immigration examination is not detention unless the restriction goes beyond routine processing into a restraint of liberty (Therens/Simmons applied)
BaselineA: Combination: constitutional text (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 10(b)) interpreted through common-law/Charter jurisprudence defining “detention” (R. v. Therens; R. v. Simmons; also discussed: R. v. Jacoy; R. v. Kwok)
CaseB_TestB: Elements of civil contempt: proof beyond a reasonable doubt of (1) a clear order, (2) actual knowledge, and (3) an intentional act/omission that breaches the order; no “contumacious intent” required
BaselineB: Common law (civil contempt doctrine), as summarized from prior authorities cited in the reasons (e.g., Bhatnager v. Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration); Prescott-Russell; Sheppard; TG Industries)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Curative proviso (Criminal Code s. 686(1)(b)(iii)) — an appellate court may dismiss despite legal error only if the Crown satisfies it that the verdict "would necessarily have been the same" absent the error; i.e., if properly instructed, any other verdict would have been "unreasonable or not supported by the evidence" / conviction "inevitable" (no reasonable possibility of reasonable doubt).
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(b)(iii) (interpreted with reference to SCC cases including Colpitts v. The Queen; Wildman v. The Queen; R. v. Yebes; Mahoney v. The Queen; R. v. S. (P.L.); R. v. Broyles).
JudgeA: Lamer C.J. (concurring with Iacobucci J.; key test articulated in Lamer C.J.’s reasons on s. 686(1)(b)(iii))
CaseB_TestB: Recent fabrication exception for prior consistent statements — where cross-examination amounts to an "allegation of recent fabrication", prior consistent statements (e.g., to a social worker/doctor) are admissible to rebut it, but only "to establish the fact that the complaints were made" and "not for the purpose of establishing the truth of the contents".
BaselineB: Common law: rule against prior consistent statements, with the recognized exception permitting admission to rebut an allegation of recent fabrication (as applied by the Court).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Substantive admissibility of a non-accused witness’s prior inconsistent statement (reformed rule): threshold that the statement "would have been admissible as the witness's sole testimony"; then, on a s. 9 CEA voir dire, admit for truth where reliability and necessity are met—reliability satisfied where there are "sufficient circumstantial guarantees" (typically: (1) statement made "under oath, solemn affirmation or solemn declaration" after an "explicit warning" about criminal sanctions; (2) statement "videotaped in its entirety"; and (3) opposing party has a "full opportunity to cross-examine" at trial), with possible substitutes if the judge is satisfied they provide "adequate assurances of reliability"; plus screening for voluntariness/administration-of-justice concerns.
BaselineA: Common law hearsay/prior inconsistent statement rule (the "orthodox rule" from Deacon v. The King) as affected by the principled hearsay approach in R. v. Khan and R. v. Smith, and applied procedurally through Canada Evidence Act, s. 9.
CaseB_TestB: Interpretation of insurer’s obligation to pay "interest" under a liability policy: the policy promise to pay "interest accrued on the amount of its guarantee from the date when the action was instituted" includes the art. 1056c C.C. second-paragraph "indemnity" because both the first-paragraph "interest" and the second-paragraph indemnity are "in reality damages due to delay" and are of the "same nature" (computed as a percentage of the capital sum).
BaselineB: Statutory/civil law damages provision (Civil Code art. 1056c) applied through interpretation of the insurance contract’s "interest" clause; supported by SCC discussion in R. v. Nord-Deutsche Versicherungs-Gesellschaft and distinguishing Highway Victims Indemnity Fund v. Martineau.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal fraud (Criminal Code s. 380(1)) — “other fraudulent means”: actus reus is conduct that a reasonable person would “properly ... stigmatize as dishonest”, i.e., “the wrongful use of something in which another person has an interest, in such a manner that this other's interest is extinguished or put at risk”; mens rea requires (1) “subjective knowledge of the prohibited act” and (2) “subjective knowledge that the prohibited act could have as a consequence the deprivation of another (… including … putting [the victim’s] pecuniary interests … at risk)”, and does not require subjective appreciation of dishonesty.
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 380(1)) as interpreted through SCC precedent (R. v. Olan; R. v. Théroux).
CaseB_TestB: Union duty of representation in collective bargaining (Labour Code s. 47.2): union must not act “in bad faith or in an arbitrary or discriminatory manner or show serious negligence”; duty is “as a general rule … an obligation of means” and in bargaining the union may have to consider interests of former employees, but their work does not create “acquired rights” to retroactivity nor an “obligation of result” to obtain it.
BaselineB: Statute (Labour Code, R.S.Q., c. C-27, s. 47.2; also discussed alongside ss. 59, 62, 67) and related SCC labour jurisprudence (e.g., Noël; Centre hospitalier Régina; Royal Oak Mines).
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Crown appeal from acquittal/new trial test (s. 686(4)): Crown must show the verdict "would not necessarily have been the same" but for the legal error
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(4)) as interpreted in SCC precedent (Vézeau v. The Queen; reaffirmed in R. v. Morin)
JudgeA: Cory J. (for Sopinka, Cory, Iacobucci and Major JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Reasonable notice before enforcing security/appointing receiver: debtor must receive "reasonable notice of [the] intention to enforce the security" and "reasonable time to pay"; reasonableness assessed by the Mister Broadloom criteria
BaselineB: Common law (Lister (R.E.) Ltd. v. Dunlop Canada Ltd.; criteria for reasonable notice from Mister Broadloom; also citing Massey v. Sladen)
JudgeB: McLachlin and Bastarache JJ. (for the Court)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Engineer/design professional preparing tender documents owes no duty to advise/warn contractors about permits or difficulties tied to the contractor’s chosen method of performing the work, absent specific arrangements to the contrary (method choice is contractor’s responsibility).
BaselineA: Common law (construction/tendering duty-allocation rule): "barring specific arrangements to the contrary, the method by which a contractor chooses to execute the work falls within its sphere of responsibility"; supported by R. v. Paradis and Farley Inc., [1942] S.C.R. 10; Vermont Construction Inc. v. Beatson, [1977] 1 S.C.R. 758 (and referenced Temar Construction Ltd. v. West Hill Redevelopment Co.).
CaseB_TestB: Framework for reviewing Crown decisions: (1) classify the decision as prosecutorial discretion (decisions about the "nature and extent of the prosecution") vs tactics/conduct before the court; (2) if prosecutorial discretion, it is reviewable only for abuse of process (egregious conduct seriously compromising trial fairness or integrity of the justice system) and the accused must first establish a proper evidentiary foundation on a balance of probabilities before the Crown may be required to justify its decision.
BaselineB: Common law/constitutional doctrine governing prosecutorial discretion and judicial review, clarifying Krieger v. Law Society of Alberta, 2002 SCC 65, and applying the abuse of process standard (with evidentiary-threshold guidance drawn from R. v. Nixon, 2011 SCC 34). Also arises in the context of Criminal Code ss. 255 and 727(1) (Notice triggering mandatory minimums) and Charter s. 7 arguments, but the key test is the common-law standard of review for prosecutorial discretion.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Constitutional validity of warrantless search under s. 8: a warrantless search is reasonable only if it is "authorized by law"; s. 10 NCA authorizes warrantless searches only where "exigent circumstances render it impracticable to obtain prior judicial authorization" (otherwise the search is not authorized and is unreasonable).
BaselineA: Combination of common law/Charter jurisprudence and statute: R. v. Collins, [1987] 1 S.C.R. 265 ("A search will be reasonable if it is authorized by law, if the law itself is reasonable and if the manner in which the search was carried out is reasonable"; Crown bears burden once warrantless search shown) applied to Narcotic Control Act, R.S.C., 1985, c. N-1, s. 10, as constitutionally limited by R. v. Grant, [1993] 3 S.C.R. 000.
CaseB_TestB: Income Tax Act s. 241(3) disclosure exception: ss. 241(1)-(2) non-disclosure "do not apply" "in respect of proceedings relating to the administration or enforcement" of the Act; interpret "in respect of"/"relating to" broadly (wide connection/relationship) so bankruptcy-related proceedings aimed at tax collection can qualify.
BaselineB: Statute: Income Tax Act, S.C. 1970-71-72, c. 63, s. 241(1)-(4) (especially s. 241(3)); interpreted in light of s. 222 (tax debts recoverable in court) and prior case Glover v. Minister of National Revenue, [1981] 2 S.C.R. 561.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 486(2.1) screen order: judge may allow a child complainant to testify behind a screen if the judge is of the opinion it is “necessary to obtain a full and candid account of the acts complained of from the complainant”; this limited procedure does not, in itself, infringe Charter ss. 7 or 11(d) because confrontation/cross-examination remain (accused can still see the witness) and the right to face one’s accuser is “subject to qualification in the interests of justice”.
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 486(2.1)) applied/assessed under Charter ss. 7 and 11(d).
CaseB_TestB: Similar fact (identity) — use of prior conviction on voir dire: where the accused puts identity for the prior act in issue, the Crown may tender the prior conviction as “some evidence” linking the accused to the similar act; verdicts are “presumptively reliable” on identity “unless overturned on appeal or later shown to be wrong”. Challenge to the conviction on the voir dire is not automatic and will be rare; it may be refused where there is “no reasonable likelihood” the challenge will affect admissibility (trial judge’s control of proceedings).
BaselineB: Common law similar fact admissibility framework (R. v. Arp; R. v. Handy) including the “some evidence” linkage requirement; plus evidentiary treatment of prior verdicts (rejecting Hollington; relying on Malik).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Objective mens rea for manslaughter liability of a party under Criminal Code s. 21(1) and s. 21(2) where the principal is guilty of murder: manslaughter if a reasonable person in all the circumstances would foresee non-trivial bodily harm from the dangerous act/common purpose (no foreseeability of death required).
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, ss. 21(1)(b),(c) and 21(2), interpreted in light of SCC manslaughter jurisprudence (R. v. Kirkness; R. v. Creighton; R. v. Trinneer; also R. v. DeSousa).
CaseB_TestB: Entitlement to GST rebate for overpayment under Excise Tax Act s. 261(1) (as applied via s. 296(2.1)): the claimant need not be legally liable for the tax; it is enough that the claimant actually paid an amount on account of GST that was not payable/remittable, and s. 261(2)(c) only blocks s. 261(1) where a rebate is actually payable under ss. 215.1 or 216(6).
BaselineB: Statute: Excise Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. E-15, ss. 261(1), 261(2)(c), 261(3), 296(2.1) (and related context in ss. 215.1, 216(6), 225(1)); with reference to West Windsor Urgent Care Centre Inc. v. R.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Policy vs. operational decision framework for governmental tort liability in highway maintenance/inspections: prima facie duty of care applies unless excluded by (i) explicit statutory exemption or (ii) the impugned conduct being a “true policy decision”; policy decisions (e.g., “decisions which involve or are dictated by financial, economic, social or political factors or constraints” such as “budgetary allocations”) are immune, while operational implementation is subject to ordinary negligence standards (Just v. British Columbia applied).
BaselineA: Common law (Just v. British Columbia; also drawing on Anns v. Merton; Kamloops v. Nielsen) applied alongside interpretation of statutory context (Public Highways Act, ss. 4-5; Proceedings against the Crown Act, s. 5(1)(a); and authority to enter adjoining land under Public Highways Act s. 4 / Expropriation Act ss. 70(f), 71).
CaseB_TestB: Damages in lieu of specific performance—assessment date and uniqueness: where a purchaser has a legitimate claim to specific performance for a “unique” asset and elects damages instead, it is permissible to assess damages as of the date of trial/judgment (not necessarily breach) so damages are a “true substitute” for specific performance; and no deduction is made for the plaintiff’s unrelated gain in value of their retained property.
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: Courts of Justice Act (Ontario) s. 99 (damages “in substitution for” specific performance) applied with common law damages principles and authorities (Johnson v. Agnew; Wroth v. Tyler; Asamera Oil; etc.).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Abuse of process threshold in criminal proceedings: stay/remedy only in the “clearest of cases” (conduct that “shocks the conscience of the community” and is “so detrimental to the proper administration of justice” that intervention is warranted; requires “overwhelming evidence” of unfairness, with intervention only where there is “conspicuous evidence of improper motives or of bad faith” or an act violating the community’s conscience).
BaselineA: Common law doctrine of abuse of process (as affirmed in R. v. Jewitt; reiterated in R. v. Keyowski; discussed with R. v. Conway, R. v. Mack, R. v. Scott).
CaseB_TestB: Mr. Big confessions admissibility rule (new common law): confessions to the state during a Mr. Big operation are “presumptively inadmissible”; Crown must show on a “balance of probabilities” that “the probative value of the confession outweighs its prejudicial effect”, with probative value assessed via reliability (circumstances of the operation + markers of reliability in the confession) and prejudice assessed as moral/reasoning prejudice; plus separate abuse-of-process backstop for coercive/abusive operations.
BaselineB: Common law evidence (party admissions exception to hearsay) and existing common law doctrines (probative value vs prejudicial effect; abuse of process).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 16(1) “knowing that it was wrong”: incapacity includes inability to rationally apply right/wrong to the particular act (capacity for rational perception and rational choice)
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 16(1)), interpreted in light of M'Naghten's Case and R. v. Chaulk
CaseB_TestB: Palmer criteria for admitting fresh evidence on appeal (including sentence appeals): (1) due diligence (flexible factor), (2) relevance, (3) credibility, (4) could reasonably be expected to have affected the result
BaselineB: Common law test from Palmer v. The Queen, applied within Criminal Code appellate powers (ss. 683 and 687)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Mohan test for admissibility of expert evidence (relevance, necessity, no exclusionary rule, properly qualified expert) plus special threshold for expert disposition/profile evidence: trial judge must be satisfied the perpetrator or accused has “distinctive behavioural characteristics” and that the profile is “in common use as a reliable indicator”/a “standard profile” developed by the scientific community
BaselineA: Common law (expert opinion and character evidence rules; abnormal/distinctive group exception discussed through prior cases including R. v. Lupien, R. v. Abbey, R. v. Morin, and Ontario CA cases R. v. McMillan and R. v. Robertson (aff’d [1977] 2 S.C.R. 824))
CaseB_TestB: Section 745 Criminal Code parole ineligibility review: jury must decide whether ineligibility “ought to be reduced” by weighing listed factors “as a whole” (character, conduct in custody, nature of offence, and “such other matters as the judge deems relevant”), with fairness constraints on Crown submissions (must not undermine s. 745 or invite consideration of irrelevant in terrorem material)
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 745(2) (and related s. 745(1), (3), (4)); plus common-law fair hearing/prosecutorial conduct principles applied in this statutory context)
JudgeB: Lamer C.J. (for Lamer C.J. and Gonthier and Cory JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 10(b) informational/implementational duties: police must give a compliant s. 10(b) caution (right to counsel without delay + legal aid info); if no duty counsel system exists, no duty-counsel advice is required; further police duties arise only if the detainee asserts the right to counsel
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional text (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 10(b)); interpreted in light of SCC precedents R. v. Brydges and R. v. Bartle (and the concurrently released R. v. Prosper)
CaseB_TestB: Criminal Code s. 347 framework for late payment penalties: a charge is “interest” only if it is “paid or payable for the advancing of credit under an agreement or arrangement”; “credit advanced” includes deferral of payment for goods/services; s. 347(1)(a) assessed at time of contracting, s. 347(1)(b) at time of payment with a ‘voluntary act of debtor’ limitation
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 347(1)-(2)); interpreted with reference to Nelson v. C.T.C. Mortgage Corp. and Degelder Construction Co. v. Dancorp Developments Ltd.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 7 overbreadth (principles of fundamental justice) test: a law is unconstitutional if it limits life, liberty or security of the person in a manner that is "unnecessarily broad, going beyond what is needed to accomplish the governmental objective"; courts ask whether the means are "necessary to achieve the State objective" and "reasonably tailored" to the law’s purpose (applied to strike down Criminal Code s. 179(1)(b) as overbroad).
BaselineA: Combination: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms s. 7 (principles of fundamental justice) applied to Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 179(1)(b); baseline jurisprudence referenced includes Re B.C. Motor Vehicle Act and R. v. Nova Scotia Pharmaceutical Society on overbreadth/vagueness under s. 7.
CaseB_TestB: Income Tax Act s. 69(2) transfer-pricing “reasonable amount in the circumstances” test: determine whether the non-arm’s-length price exceeds what "would have been reasonable in the circumstances" if dealing at arm’s length; "If transactions other than the purchasing transaction are relevant ... they must not be ignored" and comparability requires considering "economically relevant characteristics" and linked agreements conferring rights/benefits.
BaselineB: Statute: Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), s. 69(2) (now s. 247(2)).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Inference of possession from fingerprint evidence: whether an accused’s fingerprint on an article supports an inference of possession is “not subject to a hard and fast rule” but “depends on all of the circumstances of the case and all of the evidence adduced” (including that the fingerprint was on a container rather than the contraband itself as merely “another factor”).
BaselineA: Common law evidentiary inference re fingerprint evidence and possession (as discussed through R. v. O'Keefe (1958) and approved via R. v. Mehrabnia (1993)); applied in context of statutory possession definition (Criminal Code, s. 4(3), incorporated by Food and Drugs Act, s. 46).
CaseB_TestB: Scope of Review Board power under Criminal Code s. 672.54: Boards may make conditions binding on hospital authorities and may impose conditions “regarding”/supervising treatment (including ordering re-evaluation/exploration of alternatives) but have no power to “prescribe” or “impose” treatment; s. 672.55(1) is not a true exception but an example of supervisory power.
BaselineB: Statutory interpretation of Criminal Code Part XX.1, especially ss. 672.54 and 672.55(1) (with related context from ss. 672.1, 672.38, 672.72-672.78, 672.9-672.94).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 7 compellability / exemption from compulsion test: whether the “predominant purpose” of compelling the witness is to obtain incriminating evidence against them rather than to further a legitimate public purpose (with justification and prejudice analysis if predominant purpose is improper). Key directions include: “the crucial question is whether the predominant purpose for seeking the evidence is to obtain incriminating evidence ... or rather some legitimate public purpose”; if predominant purpose is to incriminate, the party seeking to compel “must justify the potential prejudice”; witness bears burden to show improper predominant purpose; and compellability may be assessed at subpoena and later trial stages.
BaselineA: Common law / Charter-based doctrine (s. 7 principles of fundamental justice) building on R. v. S. (R.J.), [1995] 1 S.C.R. 451 (compellability and self-incrimination framework) and related Charter provisions (ss. 7 and 13).
CaseB_TestB: Timing rule for Corbett applications: “a Corbett application should be made by the defence and decided by the trial judge immediately after the close of the Crown’s case”; if needed, a pre-defence voir dire may be held where defence outlines intended evidence so the judge can apply Corbett’s probative-value-vs-prejudice discretion; ruling may be modified only if defence evidence “departs significantly” from what was disclosed.
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: Canada Evidence Act, s. 12 (as interpreted in R. v. Corbett, [1988] 1 S.C.R. 670, creating discretion to exclude prior convictions where probative value is outweighed by prejudice), plus common law/Charter “case-to-meet” fairness principle (linked to s. 7).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 7 compellability / exemption from compulsion test: whether the "predominant purpose" of compelling the witness is to obtain incriminating evidence against them or to further a legitimate public purpose (with possible justification and fair-trial prejudice analysis)
BaselineA: Combination: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7 (principles of fundamental justice) and the Court’s prior framework in R. v. S. (R.J.), [1995] 1 S.C.R. 451 (compellability/exemptions and derivative use immunity context)
CaseB_TestB: Section 15(1) prima facie equality test (Quebec v. A framework): (1) distinction on an enumerated/analogous ground (on its face or in impact) and (2) discriminatory disadvantage—i.e., perpetuating arbitrary disadvantage; claimant must show disproportionate impact linked to group membership
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine interpreting Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 15(1), as set out most recently in Quebec (Attorney General) v. A, 2013 SCC 5 (and related s. 15 jurisprudence)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Tax-treaty residency under Canada–U.S. Income Tax Convention (1980) Art. IV(1): entity is a "resident of a Contracting State" only if it is "liable to tax therein by reason of" an enumerated connecting factor ("domicile, residence, place of management, place of incorporation") or a "criterion of a similar nature"—interpreted as a criterion grounding comprehensive (world-wide) tax liability, not mere source-based liability; a factor that merely informs domestic tax liability cannot be elevated into the treaty residency criterion
BaselineA: Statute/treaty: Canada-United States Tax Convention Act, 1984, Schedule I (Canada–United States Income Tax Convention (1980)), especially Article IV(1) (definition of "resident of a Contracting State") and its interaction with Article XII; applied against Income Tax Act s. 212(1)(d) withholding tax context
CaseB_TestB: Trigger for Ontario Insurance Act s. 281(5) two-year limitation: the limitation "only begins to run upon the issuance by the insurer of a valid refusal"; "No such refusal is given if there has not been adequate compliance with s. 71" of the SABS—insurer must inform claimant of the dispute-resolution procedure (ss. 279–283) in "straightforward and clear language" for an "unsophisticated person"; "At a minimum" include key steps (mediation; arbitration/litigation if mediation fails; mediation prerequisite; and relevant time limits)
BaselineB: Statute/regulation: Insurance Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. I.8, s. 281(5) (two-year limitation after insurer’s refusal) interpreted together with Statutory Accident Benefits Schedule (O. Reg. 776/93), s. 71 (duty to inform of dispute-resolution procedure) (and related context ss. 279–283 of the Insurance Act)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Weber exclusive arbitral jurisdiction test: courts are ousted where the dispute’s “essential character” arises from the “interpretation, application, administration or alleged violation” of the collective agreement (s. 45(1)); focus on facts of the dispute, not legal labels (tort/Charter).
BaselineA: Statute (Ontario Labour Relations Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. L.2, s. 45(1)) interpreted in light of SCC labour-arbitration exclusivity jurisprudence (notably St. Anne Nackawic Pulp & Paper Co. v. Canadian Paper Workers Union, Local 219, [1986] 1 S.C.R. 704).
CaseB_TestB: Criminal Code s. 744 parole ineligibility extension framework: judge may substitute >10 and ≤25 years “having regard to (1) the character of the offender, (2) the nature of the offence, and (3) the circumstances surrounding its commission”; “as a general rule” 10 years, but this is “ousted” if those criteria justify longer; no “unusual circumstances” requirement.
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 744 (and related sentencing provisions such as s. 742(b)); also appellate review under s. 687(1) for sentence fitness).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “loss of employment” for a retiring allowance: an employee is only “in the service” of the employer (and can only suffer a “loss of employment”) once the employee is under an obligation to provide services under the contract; intended/prospective employment is excluded
BaselineA: Statute: Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1952, c. 148 (now R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.)), ss. 56(1)(a)(ii) and 248(1) definitions of “retiring allowance” and “employment” (plus contextual use of “intended office or employment” in s. 80.4(1))
CaseB_TestB: Whether improper Crown closing submissions (personal anecdote not in evidence) caused an unfair trial/miscarriage of justice assessed contextually using the “relevant factors” (as in R. v. Stephan), including seriousness, prominence, objection, and adequacy of jury instructions
BaselineB: Common law: trial fairness/miscarriage of justice analysis for improper jury addresses, relying on Pisani v. The Queen; Boucher v. The Queen; and contextual “relevant factors” approach referenced from R. v. Stephan (ABCA) and R. v. Manasseri (ONCA), with jury-charge adequacy framed by R. v. Abdullahi
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Pragmatic and functional approach to whether a labour board has jurisdiction to determine an “appropriate” bargaining unit (and may suggest an alternative unit), followed by deference unless the decision is “patently unreasonable” (i.e., “clearly irrational”). Key points: Board “shall determine the unit that, in the opinion of the Board, is appropriate” (Canada Labour Code, s. 27(1)); if the proposed unit is not appropriate “it cannot be certified”; and once within jurisdiction, the decision stands unless “patently unreasonable” meaning “not clearly irrational”.
BaselineA: Statute (Canada Labour Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. L-2, ss. 24, 27, 28, 22, 33) plus administrative-law common law on jurisdiction/standard of review (U.E.S., Local 298 v. Bibeault (pragmatic and functional approach); CUPE; National Corn Growers; PSAC).
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 8 “reasonableness” of DNA data bank sampling under Criminal Code s. 487.055 assessed contextually by balancing: per Hunter v. Southam, “whether in a particular situation the public’s interest in being left alone by government must give way to the government’s interest in intruding on the individual’s privacy”; and per Collins/Stillman, a search is reasonable if (a) authorized by law, (b) the law is reasonable, and (c) the manner is reasonable. SCC holds Hunter’s investigative ‘reasonable and probable grounds’ paradigm is “not applicable” here; instead, reasonableness turns on the identification purpose, reduced privacy expectations of convicted offenders, and statutory safeguards limiting use to identification only.
BaselineB: Combination: Charter s. 8 (and related s. 7 procedural fairness considerations folded into s. 8) and statute (Criminal Code, s. 487.055; DNA Identification Act, ss. 3-4). Key common-law baselines cited: Hunter v. Southam (balancing conception of reasonableness), R. v. Collins / R. v. Stillman (three-part reasonableness requirements), R. v. Beare (identification measures analogy).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Gladstone refinement of Sparrow s.35 justification/priority for Aboriginal commercial fishing rights: government must show (1) a valid legislative objective and (2) consistency with fiduciary duty; where the Aboriginal right has no internal limit, priority is not exclusivity but requires the Crown to show both the allocation process and the resulting allocation reflect the prior interest of Aboriginal right-holders, with the content of priority remaining “somewhat vague” and assessed case-by-case
BaselineA: Common law constitutional framework under Constitution Act, 1982, s. 35(1) as set out in R. v. Sparrow (two-part justification test and priority concept), applied in the context of the Fisheries Act and Pacific Herring Fishery Regulations, SOR/84-324, s. 20(3)
CaseB_TestB: Admissibility of Crown rebuttal evidence: rebuttal may be admitted where it is “clearly relevant to an issue raised in the defence” and the Crown “could not have known in advance” the defence evidence; admission is a matter of trial-judge discretion
BaselineB: Common law evidentiary rule on rebuttal evidence and trial-judge discretion (as applied by the Court, largely endorsing the Alberta Court of Appeal’s approach)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Implied waiver of Charter s. 11(d) in regulatory ticket schemes: legislature may infer waiver from failure to pay/appear only if accused is fully aware of consequences and scheme has sufficient safeguards to ensure omission was not due to events beyond the accused’s control
BaselineA: Combination: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 11(d) (and contextual s. 7 liberty analysis) plus common-law/Charter waiver principles as applied in R. v. Lee, [1989] 2 S.C.R. 1384
CaseB_TestB: Procedural fairness for CHRC dismissal under s. 36(3)(b): Commission must act quasi-judicially; fairness requires (1) opportunity to make submissions (at least in writing, hearing not necessarily required) before decision, and (2) prior disclosure of the substance of the case to ensure informed submissions
BaselineB: Combination: Canadian Human Rights Act, 1976-77 (Can.), c. 33, ss. 35 and 36(3)(b) (decision to dismiss as unsubstantiated) interpreted through common-law natural justice/procedural fairness requirements
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Patently unreasonable standard on judicial review of labour arbitration (including the “no evidence” constraint): decision must be quashed where there is “no evidence” supporting a key inference; patently unreasonable means “clearly irrational”/“evidently not in accordance with reason”
BaselineA: Common law (administrative law standard of review) applied in labour arbitration context; key baselines cited include CUPE v. New Brunswick Liquor Corp. (patently unreasonable), PSAC No. 2 (deference/patently unreasonable), and Lester (evidence “incapable of supporting” findings)
CaseB_TestB: Statutory “equivalent in value” test under Reorg. Act s. 15(2)(a): equivalence requires comparing both (i) benefits paid and (ii) the funding mechanism; if employee contributions exceed employer’s on implementation date (e.g., unmatched Initial Surplus), there is a prima facie breach unless the surplus is reserved for members’ exclusive benefit or members receive compensatory benefits of equivalent value
BaselineB: Statute: The Manitoba Telephone System Reorganization and Consequential Amendments Act, S.M. 1996, c. 79, s. 15(2)(a) (“benefits which on the implementation date are equivalent in value”); interpreted in light of related statutory context (s. 15(3)) and pension-plan statutes (CSSA) as context
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Doctrine of part performance prevents the Crown from relying on a statutory writing requirement (s. 21(1)(a) Public Highways Act) to deny an equitable permission/right of way created by the parties’ carried-out agreement: where the agreement has been carried out, strict adherence to writing would not prevent fraud but would defraud; equity enforces the oral arrangement (“equity recognizes as done that which ought to have been done”).
BaselineA: Combination: statute (Public Highways Act, s. 21(1)(a); Expropriation Act, ss. 1(c), 21(1), 25) plus equitable/common law doctrine of part performance (as described via Steadman v. Steadman).
CaseB_TestB: Quebec arbitration/public order framework for annulment/homologation: (1) interpret arbitrator’s mandate liberally—mandate includes what is “closely connected” to the arbitration agreement; (2) s. 37 Copyright Act does not bar arbitration; (3) under art. 946.5 C.C.P., court reviews the award “as a whole” and annuls for public order only if the outcome/disposition violates public order—mere legal error on a mandatory rule is insufficient unless the result conflicts with “fundamental principles of public order.”
BaselineB: Statutory: Civil Code of Québec art. 2639; Code of Civil Procedure arts. 946.2, 946.4, 946.5 (and related arbitration provisions); plus interpretation of Copyright Act s. 37 and Act respecting the professional status of artists s. 37.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Southam standard of review framework: in statutory appeals from an expert tribunal, apply reasonableness simpliciter (a third standard between correctness and patent unreasonableness); an "unreasonable" decision is one "not supported by any reasons that can stand up to a somewhat probing examination" (vs. patently unreasonable where the defect is "apparent on the face" of the reasons).
BaselineA: Common law (standard of review jurisprudence), applied in the context of a statutory appeal under Competition Tribunal Act, ss. 12-13.
CaseB_TestB: Albashir temporal-effect test for suspended s. 52(1) declarations: declarations are presumptively retroactive, but the presumption is rebutted (even without explicit wording) where, by necessary implication, retroactivity would defeat the purpose/compelling public interest that justified the suspension; then the declaration must operate "purely prospectively".
BaselineB: Constitutional text and remedial doctrine: Constitution Act, 1982, s. 52(1) and Charter, s. 24(1), building on prior SCC remedial cases (e.g., Hislop; Ontario (AG) v. G; Bedford).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: CCA “purpose of producing income” test under Reg. 1102(1)(c): (1) “does the property produce income? In the affirmative, the deduction is allowable”; (2) if not, “was it acquired for the purpose of producing income?”, determined by “an objective evaluation of the specific facts and circumstances ... having regard to whether the taxpayer acted in accordance with reasonably acceptable principles of commerce and business practices” (L’Heureux‑Dubé J.).
BaselineA: Statute and regulation: Income Tax Act, s. 20(1)(a) (deductions “from a business or property” and “wholly applicable to that source”); Income Tax Regulations, s. 1102(1)(c) (“property ... not acquired ... for the purpose of gaining or producing income”).
CaseB_TestB: Bail denial under s. 515(10)(c) (post-severance): detention may be ordered where it is “necessary in order to maintain confidence in the administration of justice”, assessed objectively “having regard to all the circumstances, including the apparent strength of the prosecution’s case, the gravity of the nature of the offence, the circumstances surrounding its commission and the potential for a lengthy term of imprisonment”; the judge must be satisfied “a reasonable member of the community would be satisfied that denial of bail is necessary” (McLachlin C.J.).
BaselineB: Statute interpreted/partly invalidated: Criminal Code, s. 515(10)(c), read with Charter s. 11(e) (“not to be denied reasonable bail without just cause”) and Constitution Act, 1982, s. 52 (severance).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Vesting/accrual of an appeal-as-of-right: the right is only “acquired”, “accrued” or “accruing” once all conditions precedent are fulfilled — i.e., when the court of appeal renders judgment reversing the acquittal and ordering a new trial (so Interpretation Act, s. 43(c) does not protect it and s. 44 applies).
BaselineA: Statute (Interpretation Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. I-21, ss. 43(c) and 44(c),(d), applied to Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 691(2) (as amended)).
CaseB_TestB: Sherman Estate test for discretionary limits on the open court principle (publication bans): applicant must establish (1) court openness poses a serious risk to an important public interest; (2) the order is necessary because reasonable alternatives will not prevent the risk; and (3) proportionality: benefits outweigh negative effects.
BaselineB: Common law (Sherman Estate v. Donovan, 2021 SCC 25, para. 38).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Canderel profit-computation framework under ITA s. 9(1): taxpayer may use any method consistent with the Act/case law/well-accepted business principles that yields an “accurate picture” of profit; on reassessment, once taxpayer shows an accurate picture, the onus shifts to the Minister to show it is not accurate or that another method is more accurate
BaselineA: Statute (Income Tax Act) interpreted through existing case law on profit computation (notably Symes v. Canada; also M.N.R. v. Irwin; Associated Investors of Canada Ltd. v. M.N.R.)
CaseB_TestB: Interpretation of Partnership Act s. 55(b): a general partner breaches the statute only if its act “makes it impossible to carry on the ordinary business” of the limited partnership, meaning it must render impossible a “substantial portion” (not every facet) of the partnership’s ordinary business
BaselineB: Statute (Partnership Act, R.S.A. 1980, c. P-2, s. 55(b))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Dixon two-step test for post-conviction Crown non-disclosure: (1) reasonable possibility undisclosed info affects reliability of conviction; (2) if not, reasonable possibility non-disclosure affected overall trial fairness (lost lines of inquiry/opportunities), with defence due diligence weighed
BaselineA: Combination: Charter ss. 7 and 24(1) plus common-law disclosure framework from R. v. Stinchcombe (relevance/"reasonable possibility" usefulness threshold), as applied/clarified through R. v. C. (M.H.) and R. v. Carosella
CaseB_TestB: Standard-form insurance contract interpretation (Ledcor framework) applied to SEF 44 cl. 4(b)(vii): give effect to clear, unambiguous language as understood by the average insured; only if ambiguous use general rules, then contra proferentem; here “policy of insurance” means private insurance contract, so CPP disability benefits are not deductible
BaselineB: Common law of contract/insurance interpretation (Ledcor; Progressive Homes; Scalera; Gibbens) applied to the SEF 44 Endorsement, specifically cl. 4(b)(vii) (and related cl. 4(b) structure)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Search incident to arrest must be “truly incidental”: police must have a purpose connected to the arrest (e.g., “protecting the police, protecting the evidence, discovering evidence”) and “must have had some reason related to the arrest ... and that reason must be objectively reasonable” (subjective + objective requirement; delay may support a negative inference rebuttable by explanation)
BaselineA: Common law (search incident to arrest doctrine) applied within Charter s. 8 reasonableness framework
CaseB_TestB: Admissibility of defence-led unknown third party suspect evidence: (1) relevance to a fact in issue (logical relevance shown by a “sufficient connection”/similarity between the charged crime and another incident the accused could not have committed), and (2) admissible unless “its prejudicial effects substantially outweigh its probative value” (Seaboyer balancing; no balance-of-probabilities proof of the other incident; judge must not assess credibility/weight)
BaselineB: Common law evidence principles (Seaboyer; Corbett; Cinous; Grandinetti distinguished/limited in unknown-suspect context)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Schreiber (Lamer C.J.) — s. 8 Charter is only triggered if claimant shows a reasonable expectation of privacy; for foreign-held records, expectation generally corresponds to protection under foreign law (Plant contextual factors + foreign-law limitation)
BaselineA: Combination: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 8 (and s. 32(1) applicability) + common-law s. 8 framework from Hunter v. Southam and contextual REOP factors from R. v. Plant
CaseB_TestB: Fullowka — Cooper/Anns duty-of-care framework (foreseeability + proximity, then residual policy) for negligence in failing to prevent third-party intentional harm
BaselineB: Common law: duty of care analysis from Cooper v. Hobart (as applied/clarified through Edwards, Odhavji Estate, Childs, Hill)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Pushpanathan framework for applying Refugee Convention art. 1F(c): exclusion applies where there is (1) an international-law consensus that the acts are “sufficiently serious and sustained violations of fundamental human rights as to amount to persecution”, or (2) the acts are “explicitly recognized as contrary to the purposes and principles of the United Nations”; with two main categories: (i) a “widely accepted international agreement or United Nations resolution explicitly declares” the acts contrary to UN purposes/principles (designation “determinative” if it reflects a “reasonable consensus”); or (ii) a court can itself characterize the conduct as “serious, sustained and systemic violations of fundamental human rights constituting persecution” (even an isolated violation may suffice if the violated norm is near the core of human rights and e.g. a universal-jurisdiction offence).
BaselineA: Statute incorporating treaty: Immigration Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. I-2, s. 2(1) (definition of “Convention refugee” incorporating Refugee Convention art. 1F(c)); interpreted using treaty-interpretation rules (Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, arts. 31-32).
CaseB_TestB: Hadley v. Baxendale remoteness/proximity test for contract damages: damages are those that “arise either naturally” or “may reasonably be supposed to have been in the contemplation of both parties, at the time they made the contract, as the probable result of a breach”; applied to employment-contract breach of an implied duty of good faith (branch manager’s implied term to retain supervised employees) and to reject a general post-employment non-competition duty during the notice period.
BaselineB: Common law contract damages (Hadley v. Baxendale (1854), as adopted in Canadian contract law) applied to implied terms in employment contracts (common law).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Hodgson confessions/voir dire framework: (1) whether the recipient is a “person in authority” (including those the accused “reasonably believes are acting on behalf of the police or prosecuting authorities”), and (2) if so, Crown must prove the statement was voluntary; plus when a trial judge must hold a voir dire on their own motion (only in “extremely rare cases” where evidence “clearly demonstrates” a close connection to authorities). Key quotes: “no statement made out of court by an accused to a person in authority can be admitted… unless… made freely and voluntarily” (para 12); “the accused’s belief… must also be reasonable” (para 34); “In extremely rare cases… the trial judge must of his or her own motion direct a voir dire” (para 48(9)).
BaselineA: Common law confessions rule (voluntariness + person in authority), drawing on Ibrahim v. The King; Erven v. The Queen; Rothman v. The Queen (as cited in the reasons).
CaseB_TestB: McClurg s. 56(2) attribution (anti-avoidance) approach: s. 56(2) targets situations where a taxpayer “seeks to avoid receipt” of income by diverting it to another; as a general rule, “a dividend payment does not fall within the scope of s. 56(2)” because until declared profits belong to the corporation. Key quotes: s. 56(2) text (“A payment or transfer of property… pursuant to the direction of, or with the concurrence of, a taxpayer… for the benefit of the taxpayer…”); purpose statement: “designed to prevent avoidance… of receipts which he or she otherwise would have obtained”; rule statement: “Consequently, as a general rule, a dividend payment cannot reasonably be considered a benefit diverted… within the contemplation of s. 56(2).”
BaselineB: Statute: Income Tax Act, S.C. 1970-71-72, c. 63, s. 56(2) (interpreted in light of prior case law cited, including Miller v. M.N.R.).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Depletion allowance profit computation under Income Tax Regulations, reg. 1201(2) and (4): compute profits “reasonably attributable” to production in the normal way (receipts attributable to production minus expenses of earning those receipts), and deduct only the items enumerated in reg. 1201(4) (courts cannot read in additional deductions such as long-term research expenses deductible for income under ITA ss. 11(1)(j) and 72).
BaselineA: Regulation (Income Tax Regulations, reg. 1201(2) and 1201(4)) interpreting interaction with statute (Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1952, c. 148, ss. 11(1)(j) and 72); prior SCC approach referenced from Minister of National Revenue v. Imperial Oil Ltd., [1960] S.C.R. 735.
CaseB_TestB: Sherman Estate v. Donovan test for discretionary limits on the open court principle (publication bans): applicant must establish (1) openness poses a serious risk to an important public interest; (2) the order is necessary because reasonable alternatives will not prevent the risk; and (3) proportionality—benefits outweigh negative effects.
BaselineB: Common law (Sherman Estate v. Donovan, 2021 SCC 25, para. 38) governing discretionary court orders limiting openness.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Kienapple (res judicata / rule against multiple convictions) where counts differ in gravity: if same delict underlies both, convicting on the more serious count requires acquittal on the less serious; if guilty plea entered on the less serious first, it must be held in abeyance pending trial of the more serious and struck if the more serious results in conviction
BaselineA: Common law (Kienapple v. The Queen, [1975] 1 S.C.R. 729; also discussed: R. v. Siggins; Côté v. The Queen; R. v. St-Jean; R. v. Cole)
CaseB_TestB: Availability of habeas corpus to challenge continued detention in parole context: continuation of a valid detention is reviewable only if it becomes unlawful, which occurs only once the inmate has acquired 'parolee' status (i.e., when the parole decision takes effect; if conditional, only when the condition is fulfilled)
BaselineB: Combination of common law habeas corpus principles as developed in R. v. Miller, [1985] 2 S.C.R. 613 (and related cases Cardinal; Morin) and the statutory parole scheme (Parole Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. P-2, as amended)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 672.54 disposition test for NCR accused: absolute discharge is mandatory unless the court/Review Board makes a positive finding on the evidence that the accused poses a “significant threat to the safety of the public”; if significant threat is found, impose the “least onerous and least restrictive” conditional discharge or detention after considering public protection, mental condition, reintegration, and other needs (McLachlin J.’s 9-point summary, incl. definition of “significant threat”).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, Part XX.1, especially s. 672.54; interpreted against Charter s. 7 principles and Swain).
CaseB_TestB: Section 125 “tax vs regulatory charge/user fee” characterization test: determine the levy’s primary purpose (pith and substance) as (1) tax, (2) regulatory charge (ancillary/adhesive to a regulatory scheme), or (3) user fee; a levy is generally a “tax” if it is (1) compulsory/enforceable by law, (2) imposed under legislative authority, (3) levied by a public body, (4) for a public purpose, and (5) unconnected to any regulatory scheme.
BaselineB: Constitution + common law characterization framework (Constitution Act, 1867, s. 125; applied with indicia from Lawson and Eurig Estate; regulatory-charge distinction from Re Exported Natural Gas Tax; in context of Indian Act s. 83(1)(a)).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 2(d) freedom of association (labour context): only protects (1) the freedom to establish/belong to/maintain an independent association and (2) the exercise in association of members’ lawful rights; it does not include a right to be included in a particular statutory labour-relations regime (no positive obligation), and exclusion from a statutory scheme is not itself an infringement absent state interference with associational activity
BaselineA: Combination: constitutional text (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 2(d), with related discussion of s. 2 generally and s. 32(1)) plus prior SCC jurisprudence defining s. 2(d) (Reference re Public Service Employee Relations Act (Alta.), PSAC v. Canada, RWDSU v. Saskatchewan; Professional Institute of the Public Service of Canada v. Northwest Territories (Commissioner); Canadian Egg Marketing Agency v. Richardson). Statutory context: Public Service Staff Relations Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. P-35, s. 2 “employee” (e) (exclusion of RCMP members).
JudgeA: Bastarache J. (for Gonthier, McLachlin, Major and Bastarache JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Joint/co-principal liability in group assaults (manslaughter): co-principal liability applies where (1) two or more individuals come together with an intention to commit an offence, (2) are present during its commission, and (3) contribute to its commission; in manslaughter, the focus is whether the accused’s actions were a “significant contributing cause of death” (not which perpetrator inflicted which wound), and in group assaults (absent a discrete/intervening event) all assailants’ actions can be a significant contributing cause of all injuries
BaselineB: Statute interpreted/applied: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 21(1)(a) (common intention/co-principal) and s. 21(1)(c) (abetting), in the context of unlawful act manslaughter; with consistency noted with prior SCC authority (R. v. Pickton).
JudgeB: Rowe J. (for the Court, oral reasons)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Federal Child Support Guidelines s. 4 ‘inappropriateness’ framework for incomes over $150,000: Table amount presumptively applies; deviation only if ‘inappropriate’ meaning ‘unsuitable’ is shown, assessed on all circumstances including s. 4(b)(ii) factors
BaselineA: Regulation/statute: Federal Child Support Guidelines, SOR/97-175, ss. 3 and 4 (especially s. 4(b)(i)-(ii)); interpretive context includes Divorce Act, s. 26.1(2)
CaseB_TestB: Classification approach for all-risks/multi-peril policies under the B.C. Insurance Act: if the policy does not fit within Part 5 (Fire Insurance) via s. 119, it is governed by Part 2 (general provisions), so the Part 2 limitation period applies; contractual shorter limitation cannot undercut Part 2 due to s. 3(a)
BaselineB: Statute: Insurance Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 226, ss. 119 and 3(a) (and Part 2 vs Part 5 structure; statutory condition 14 relevant to Part 5)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meiorin unified BFOR test (3 steps) for justifying a prima facie discriminatory employment standard: (1) purpose rationally connected to job performance; (2) adopted in honest and good faith belief it was necessary; (3) reasonably necessary—i.e., “impossible to accommodate ... without imposing undue hardship” (paras. 54-55).
BaselineA: Statute (British Columbia Human Rights Code, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 210, s. 13(1)(a), (b), (4)) interpreted in light of prior SCC human rights jurisprudence (e.g., O’Malley; Etobicoke; Central Alberta Dairy Pool; Renaud).
CaseB_TestB: Stewart source-of-income test (2-stage) under the Income Tax Act: (i) “Is the activity ... undertaken in pursuit of profit, or is it a personal endeavour?”; (ii) if not personal, “is the source ... a business or property?”; where personal/hobby is possible, ask: “Does the taxpayer intend to carry on an activity for profit and is there evidence to support that intention?” (paras. 50, 54-55).
BaselineB: Statute (Income Tax Act, especially ss. 3(a), 9(1)-(2); also discussed: ss. 18(1)(a), (h), 20(1)(c)(i), 248(1)) with prior SCC/common-law “REOP” line traced to Moldowan v. The Queen.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Staged analysis for whether a conditional sentence is available/appropriate (s. 742.1) and when/how s. 718.2(e) (Gladue factors) must be considered for Aboriginal offenders: (1) preliminarily exclude probation and a penitentiary term; (2) confirm s. 742.1 prerequisites (incl. community safety risk assessment); (3) at the “most substantial stage”, decide if a conditional sentence is consistent with ss. 718–718.2, and if incarceration is in issue, the judge is “required to consider s. 718.2(e)” including “unique systemic or background circumstances” and “types of practicable procedures and sanctions” (paras. 27-30).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, ss. 742.1 and 718–718.2, especially s. 718.2(e)) as interpreted in R. v. Proulx and R. v. Gladue.
CaseB_TestB: Quebec Charter s. 9.1 balancing for a freedom of religion claim raised to avoid civil liability: even if there is a prima facie religious-freedom impact, the claim “must be balanced and reconciled with countervailing rights, values, and harm” (para. 77) and assessed through a “complex, nuanced, fact-specific exercise that defies bright-line application” (para. 2); here, any impairment is “significantly outweighed” by harms and public interests (paras. 17, 70, 92).
BaselineB: Statute (Quebec Charter of human rights and freedoms, ss. 3 and 9.1) plus prior SCC freedom of religion framework (Syndicat Northcrest v. Amselem) applied in the private-law context.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Unreasonable verdict review under Criminal Code s. 686(1)(a)(i): whether the verdict is one that a properly instructed jury (or trial judge) acting judicially could reasonably have rendered; appellate court must thoroughly re-examine the evidence and cannot intervene based only on a vague “lurking doubt” without articulating why the verdict is inconsistent with a judicial appreciation of the evidence.
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(a)(i)) as interpreted in SCC common law (R. v. Yebes; reaffirmed in R. v. Biniaris).
CaseB_TestB: Institutional consultation / natural justice framework: consultation does not create apprehension of bias or lack of independence if (1) not imposed by a superior authority, (2) limited to questions of policy and law, and (3) decision-makers remain free; for audi alteram partem, applicant must show an actual breach (not merely apprehended), and if the rules are met a presumption of regularity applies so a change from draft to final reasons alone does not imply impropriety.
BaselineB: Common law natural justice/procedural fairness principles from IWA v. Consolidated-Bathurst Packaging Ltd. and Tremblay v. Quebec (Commission des affaires sociales) (applied/clarified in this case).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 24(1) “court of competent jurisdiction” — Mills three-part test plus the SCC’s “functional and structural” approach to whether a statutory court/tribunal has jurisdiction to grant the Charter remedy sought (here, costs): infer remedial power where, by its function and structure, the body is an appropriate forum and the legislature can be taken to have intended it to grant the remedy absent contrary indication
BaselineA: Combination of common law and constitutional text: Charter s. 24(1) (“court of competent jurisdiction”) interpreted through the common-law Mills framework. Baseline test: Mills v. The Queen, [1986] 1 S.C.R. 863 — a “court of competent jurisdiction” possesses (1) jurisdiction over the person; (2) jurisdiction over the subject matter; and (3) jurisdiction to grant the remedy (para. 15).
JudgeA: The Chief Justice (McLachlin C.J.) for the Court
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 11(d) validity of a statutory presumption — “inexorable connection” test: a presumption complies with s. 11(d) only if proof of the substituted (basic) fact leads “inexorably” to the essential element it replaces; plus (in sting cases post-striking s. 172.1(3)) the clarified single pathway to conviction and the structured operation of the s. 172.1(4) ‘reasonable steps’ defence (air of reality → Crown disproves defence → Crown still must prove belief beyond a reasonable doubt)
BaselineB: Combination of statute and constitutional text: Criminal Code, s. 172.1(3) (presumption re age) and s. 172.1(4) (no defence unless reasonable steps), assessed under Charter ss. 11(d), 7, and remedied under Constitution Act, 1982, s. 52(1). The s. 11(d) presumption baseline draws on SCC cases cited in the reasons (e.g., Whyte; Downey; Audet) requiring an “inexorable” link (paras. 52-53).
JudgeB: Moldaver J. (for Wagner C.J. and Gascon, Côté, Brown, Rowe and Martin JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Existence of a valid partnership (for s. 96 ITA loss allocation): at formation, alleged partners must be “(1) carrying on a business, (2) in common, (3) with a view to profit”; tax motivation does not negate partnership if these essentials are present; “view to profit” is not a strictly quantitative net-gain test and may be supported by an ancillary profit intention assessed on objective evidence in all the circumstances
BaselineA: Combination: Income Tax Act, s. 96 (loss allocation depends on existence of a partnership) + common law partnership test from Continental Bank Leasing Corp. v. Canada, [1998] 2 S.C.R. 298 (as reiterated with Backman v. Canada, 2001 SCC 10)
CaseB_TestB: Adequacy of jury instructions on credibility and reasonable doubt (W.(D.) context): where credibility is central, the judge must explain the relationship between credibility assessment and the Crown’s burden; instructions must make it “crystal clear” the burden never shifts and must avoid the “credibility contest” (not a choice between two versions); failure to recite W.(D.) verbatim is not fatal if, read as a whole, the charge leaves the jury under no misapprehension about the correct burden/standard
BaselineB: Common law: R. v. W. (D.), [1991] 1 S.C.R. 742 (and subsequent SCC guidance such as R. v. Avetysan, 2000 SCC 56, on substance-over-form in jury charges)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Customs Act s. 48(5)(a)(iv) “condition of sale” test for dutiable royalties/licence fees: royalties/licence fees are added to value for duty only if paid “as a condition of the sale of the goods for export to Canada”; “Unless a vendor is entitled to refuse to sell licensed goods to the purchaser or repudiate the contract of sale where the purchaser fails to pay royalties or licence fees, s. 48(5)(a)(iv) is inapplicable” (paras. 54-55, 68).
BaselineA: Statute — Customs Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (2nd Supp.), s. 48(5)(a)(iv) (and related definition in s. 45(1) “price paid or payable”).
CaseB_TestB: ITA s. 224 “requirement to pay” trigger (bank liability) in cheque-deposit context: a requirement to pay applies only where the person served “is ... liable to make a payment to” the tax debtor (ITA s. 224(1)); for cheques deposited to a joint account, “the fact that a person is designated as payee on the face of a cheque does not on its own mean that the bank is liable to make a payment to the person”; liability turns on “to whom the drawee may make the payment” and “what is on the back of the cheque — the instructions or the endorsement” (paras. 46, 51).
BaselineB: Combination — Statute (Income Tax Act, s. 224(1)) interpreted through Bills of Exchange Act presentment/holder rules (e.g., BEA ss. 84(1), 84(3), 86(1), 138(2), 165(3), 126) and common law banking principles (e.g., Foley v. Hill; Schroeder).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Quebec Labour Code s. 45 successorship in subcontracting: s. 45 may apply where the transferee, beyond performing similar functions, receives a "right to operate" part of the undertaking and has a "sufficient degree of autonomy" assessed contextually (including by the "criterion of the subordination of the employees" to the contractor); specialized decision-makers "weigh the applicable criteria" to decide if a transfer of operation occurred.
BaselineA: Statute (Labour Code, R.S.Q., c. C-27, ss. 45-46) as interpreted in SCC jurisprudence including U.E.S., Local 298 v. Bibeault and Lester (W.W.) (1978) Ltd.
CaseB_TestB: Jarvis/Ling audit vs investigation test: the Charter-protected "adversarial relationship" is engaged when the "predominant purpose" of the inquiry is determining penal liability under ITA s. 239; "no one factor is determinative" and the judge assesses the "totality of the circumstances" (with factors such as grounds to lay charges, decision to investigate, file transfer, and auditor acting as agent).
BaselineB: Combination of statute and constitutional law: Income Tax Act, ss. 231.1(1), 231.2(1), 239(1) and Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 7, 8, 24(2), applying the SCC framework from R. v. Jarvis.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Anns/Cooper duty of care test for statutory regulators: (1) prima facie duty—reasonable foreseeability + proximity (starting with analogous categories; if none, whether a new duty should be recognized, with proximity grounded in the statute); (2) residual policy considerations may negate the duty
BaselineA: Common law (Anns v. Merton London Borough Council; Kamloops (City of) v. Nielsen), as clarified in Cooper v. Hobart; applied in light of the Law Society Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. L.8 (notably ss. 9, 33, 51, 61)
JudgeA: The Chief Justice and Major J.
CaseB_TestB: Section 1 (Oakes) justification analysis, as applied to a fiscal-crisis justification: pressing and substantial objective; rational connection; minimal impairment; proportionality of effects (including weighing salutary vs deleterious effects), with strong skepticism of budget-only justifications but allowance for exceptional fiscal emergencies
BaselineB: Constitution (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 1 and 15(1)); Oakes framework (R. v. Oakes) and subsequent s. 1 jurisprudence
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Pragmatic and functional approach (Pushpanathan) to select the standard of review: (1) privative clause/statutory appeal, (2) relative expertise, (3) purpose of the Act/provision, (4) nature of the problem; applied to hold correctness for CRTC’s interpretation of Telecommunications Act s. 43(5)
BaselineA: Common law (standard of review framework) applied to a statutory interpretation question under Telecommunications Act, S.C. 1993, c. 38, ss. 43(5) and 64(1)
CaseB_TestB: Sentencing treatment of collateral consequences and related mitigating considerations: collateral consequences may be considered if they “relate to the offence and the circumstances of the offender”, but “the fundamental principle of proportionality must prevail”; plus specific sub-rules that (i) vigilante violence is a collateral consequence to be considered “to a limited extent”, (ii) mistake of law mitigates only with an “honest but mistaken belief” in legality (mere “confusion or uncertainty” is insufficient), and (iii) non-impairment can mitigate refusal sentencing but its effect “must be limited” and the offender bears the onus on a balance of probabilities
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, ss. 718 to 718.2, 718.1, and s. 255(3.2)) with common-law sentencing principles as applied/clarified
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.
