CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 2(b) infringement for sign restrictions: a by-law that restricts the use of an “optimum means of expression” (posting signs) to certain designated places “directly infringes freedom of expression” (para. 26), especially where its literal effect makes it “impossible for any individual to post signs criticising the practices, products or services of a business” (para. 27).
BaselineA: Combination of constitutional text and common-law Charter doctrine: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 2(b) (and s. 1 referenced but not treated as the key test per instructions); baseline freedom-of-expression approach drawn from SCC cases cited in the reasons (e.g., Irwin Toy; Ramsden; Sharpe).
CaseB_TestB: Canadian Bill of Rights “due process” limits in property expropriation: s. 1(a) does not require (i) notice/hearing before Parliament enacts expropriative legislation (paras. 37-41); (ii) an individual hearing where there is “non-discretionary application of a law to incontestable facts” (para. 45); and (iii) provides no substantive protection against expropriation by “clear and unambiguous” legislation—Parliament may expropriate without compensation if intent is “clear and unambiguous” (paras. 51-57).
BaselineB: Statutory interpretation of the Canadian Bill of Rights, ss. 1(a) and 2(e), applied to Department of Veterans Affairs Act, s. 5.1(4); baseline principles drawn from cited authorities on Bill of Rights operation and expropriation (e.g., Drybones; Miller; Wells; Manitoba Fisheries).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Copyright Act s. 3(1) “reproduction” requires copying (typically the making of an additional/new copy); mere physical transfer of the same ink layer to a new substrate, with no multiplication, is not “production (or reproduction) ... in any material form”
BaselineA: Statute: Copyright Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-42, ss. 3(1) (definition of copyright: “sole right to produce or reproduce the work ... in any material form whatever”), 38(1) (seizure of “infringing copies”), plus the definition of “infringing” in s. 2; related moral rights provisions discussed (ss. 14.1, 28.2).
JudgeA: Binnie J. (for McLachlin C.J. and Iacobucci, Major and Binnie JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Reasonableness simpliciter on judicial review: a decision is unreasonable “only if there is no line of analysis within the given reasons that could reasonably lead the tribunal from the evidence before it to the conclusion at which it arrived”; if any sufficient reasons are “tenable” on a “somewhat probing examination”, the court must not interfere
BaselineB: Common law (judicial review standards and the pragmatic and functional approach), drawing on SCC precedents including Pushpanathan v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) and Canada (Director of Investigation and Research) v. Southam Inc.; applied in the context of the Law Society Act, 1996, S.N.B. 1996, c. 89 (notably ss. 66(1), 68).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Privacy Act s. 22(1)(b) exemption: access to personal information may be refused only if disclosure “could reasonably be expected to be injurious” to the conduct of lawful investigations (including future investigations), requiring a “clear and direct connection” between the specific disclosure and the alleged injury, supported by “concrete reasons” tied to the case
BaselineA: Statute (Privacy Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. P-21, ss. 12(1), 22(1)(b), 22(3), 47, 49; applied harmoniously with Official Languages Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 31 (4th Supp.), ss. 60(1), 72-74)
CaseB_TestB: Adverse inference / presumption of fact in medical causation: even where defendant negligence undermines proof and plaintiff adduces “some” evidence, the trier of fact is not required to draw an adverse inference; any presumption of fact under art. 2849 C.C.Q. is discretionary and must be “serious, precise and concordant”
BaselineB: Statute/civil code evidence rules (Civil Code of Québec, art. 2849 (and arts. 2846-2849 generally)), informed by SCC causation jurisprudence (Snell v. Farrell; St-Jean v. Mercier)
JudgeB: Wagner J. (McLachlin C.J. and Karakatsanis and Gascon JJ. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Validity/effect of a zoning “holding regulation”: a by-law clause stating “Notwithstanding any other provisions... no building... may be... erected to contain three or more dwelling units until this by-law has been amended...” operates as a valid freeze on apartment development; superfluous added words about future amendment do not invalidate the effective prohibitory words where the City’s freeze policy is clear and within its powers.
BaselineA: Statute + municipal by-law: The Planning Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 349, s. 35(1) (zoning power) and s. 35(22) (appeal to Municipal Board), applied to City of London zoning by-law 306-480 as amended by by-law 306(bc)-504, s. 4 (new s. 11 “Holding Regulation”).
CaseB_TestB: Custody decision-making under s. 1(1) of The Infants Act: the court must consider the parties’ conduct only as it bears on “relative fitness” to have custody; conduct (including fault for marriage breakdown) is “only one factor” and “each particular case must be judged on its own circumstances” with the “paramount consideration... the welfare of the children.”
BaselineB: Statute + prior custody jurisprudence: The Infants Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 222, s. 1(1) (welfare/fitness inquiry), with guidance from McKee v. McKee; Bickley v. Bickley; Retzer v. Retzer; and discussion alongside Talsky v. Talsky and Re L.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: OSC disclosure of compelled investigation material under Securities Act s. 17(1): apply Stinchcombe-style relevance (“reasonable possibility of being relevant” to full answer and defence) and then determine whether disclosure is “in the public interest” by balancing confidentiality/privacy against fair-hearing/full-answer-and-defence needs; disclosure may be ordered globally unless a party shows “no reasonable possibility” a particular item is relevant
BaselineA: Statute/regulation: Securities Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. S.5, ss. 16(1) (confidentiality) and 17(1) (OSC may authorize disclosure if it considers it “in the public interest”); OSC Rules of Practice r. 3.3(2) (staff must disclose all “relevant” material). The SCC-approved relevance threshold is taken from common law criminal disclosure in R. v. Stinchcombe, [1991] 3 S.C.R. 326 (“reasonable possibility” of relevance).
CaseB_TestB: Framework to classify requested state-held records as first-party (Stinchcombe) vs third-party (O’Connor) disclosure: consider (1) whether the information is in the possession/control of the prosecuting Crown; and (2) if not, whether the police/other Crown entity ought to have supplied it because it is part of the “fruits of the investigation” or “obviously relevant”; if neither, O’Connor applies and the accused must show the record is “likely relevant” (a “reasonable possibility” it is logically probative to an issue at trial or witness competence)
BaselineB: Common law disclosure regimes: R. v. Stinchcombe (first-party disclosure), R. v. O’Connor (third-party disclosure), and R. v. McNeil (duties re police/Crown entities). Statutory context discussed: Criminal Code, s. 258(1)(c) (presumption of accuracy for approved instruments).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Misfeasance in public office (Iacobucci J.): (1) “deliberate and unlawful conduct in the exercise of public functions”; and (2) “awareness that the conduct is unlawful and likely to injure the plaintiff” (plus causation and compensable loss).
BaselineA: Common law tort of misfeasance in public office (discussing/endorsing Three Rivers District Council v. Bank of England (No. 3) and referencing Roncarelli v. Duplessis; applied in context of statutory duties under Police Services Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. P.15, ss. 113(9) and 41(1)(b)).
CaseB_TestB: Eligibility for Quebec seats under Supreme Court Act, s. 6: s. 6 “narrows the pool” and requires “current membership” — appointees must be “current members of the Barreau du Québec, the Quebec Court of Appeal or the Superior Court of Quebec” (and meet s. 5’s 10-year standing requirement).
BaselineB: Statutory interpretation of Supreme Court Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. S-26, ss. 5 and 6 (and constitutional constraint analysis under Constitution Act, 1982, Part V, especially s. 41(d), for Parliament’s ability to amend).
JudgeB: McLachlin C.J. and LeBel, Abella, Cromwell, Karakatsanis and Wagner JJ.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Securities Act s. 162 administrative-penalty ‘public interest’ analysis: s. 162 is triggered by a breach, and in deciding whether/what penalty is ‘in the public interest’ the Commission may consider the full context; ‘general deterrence is an appropriate factor to consider, albeit not the only one’; reviewing courts assess whether there is a ‘rational basis’ and review the order ‘globally’ (no single factor in isolation).
BaselineA: Statute (Securities Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 418, s. 162 (and related public-interest context in ss. 161, 167); interpreted in light of Committee for the Equal Treatment of Asbestos Minority Shareholders v. Ontario (Securities Commission), 2001 SCC 37).
CaseB_TestB: Adequacy of jury instructions on alternative routes to murder liability where others may have participated: the trial judge must instruct on routes to liability that arise on the evidence; it is not necessary to find the accused acted alone—he may be convicted if he ‘acted in concert with other persons’ and the jury is satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that he ‘actively participated in the killing’; the erroneous ‘actual shooter’ direction was properly corrected to: ‘If you find that Mr. Pickton shot [the victim] or was otherwise an active participant in her killing ...’
BaselineB: Statute and common law: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 21 (party liability) and s. 686(1)(b)(iii) (curative proviso), applied with guidance from cases including R. v. Thatcher, [1987] 1 S.C.R. 652 and R. v. Rose, [1998] 3 S.C.R. 262.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Cross-examination on unproven facts: counsel may put a question if there is a “good faith basis” (no evidentiary foundation required), subject to limited judicial screening where the factual predicate is “manifestly tenuous or suspect”
BaselineA: Common law (scope/ethics of cross-examination), as reflected in authorities like R. v. Bencardino (Ont. C.A.) and this Court’s discussion of R. v. Howard; also linked to Charter-protected full answer and defence (ss. 7, 11(d))
CaseB_TestB: Federal paramountcy (two-branch test): (1) operational conflict (“impossible to comply with both”); or (2) frustration of federal purpose (party must prove federal purpose with “clear proof” and show provincial law is incompatible; apply a restrained/cooperative-federalism approach)
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine of federal paramountcy (as articulated in cases such as Rothmans, Benson & Hedges; COPA; Canadian Western Bank; Ryan Estate)
JudgeB: Abella and Gascon JJ. (Cromwell, Moldaver, Karakatsanis and Wagner JJ. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Parliamentary privilege existence/scope test: (1) ask whether the claimed privilege’s “existence and scope ... have been authoritatively established” in Canada or at Westminster; if not, (2) apply the necessity test—privilege exists only if the activity is “so closely and directly connected” to legislative/deliberative functions (including holding government to account) that “outside interference would undermine the level of autonomy required” for Parliament to do its work “with dignity and efficiency” (paras. 39-40, 46).
BaselineA: Combination: Constitution Act, 1867, s. 18 and Parliament of Canada Act, s. 4 (benchmarking to Westminster) plus common-law constitutional doctrine of parliamentary privilege/necessity (e.g., New Brunswick Broadcasting; Harvey; Stockdale v. Hansard).
CaseB_TestB: Interpretive test for Tobacco Act s. 22(3) (“appealing to young persons”): s. 22(3) “requires the prosecution ... to prove that there are reasonable grounds to believe that the advertisement ... could be appealing to young persons, in the sense that it could be particularly attractive and of interest to young persons, as distinguished from the general population” (para. 89).
BaselineB: Statute: Tobacco Act, S.C. 1997, c. 13, s. 22(3) (interpreted using modern statutory interpretation and bilingual common meaning).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: GAAR “abusive tax avoidance” (s. 245(4)) analysis: three requirements (tax benefit, avoidance transaction, and abuse) with abuse determined by whether it “cannot be reasonably concluded that a tax benefit would be consistent with the object, spirit or purpose of the provisions relied upon by the taxpayer” (para. 31(1)(3)); applied here to hold that using s. 18(13) and s. 96 to sell losses to arm’s length parties is abusive (para. 58).
BaselineA: Statute (Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), ss. 245(1)-(4) (GAAR), plus the provisions relied on for the benefit: ss. 18(13) and 96(1); interpretive approach and GAAR framework followed from Canada Trustco Mortgage Co. v. Canada, 2005 SCC 54 (paras. 31, 35).
CaseB_TestB: Vancouver Sun informer-privilege procedure and “single guiding rule”: (1) verify existence of informer privilege (in camera/ex parte if needed) where “evidence that a person is a police informer automatically engages the privilege” (para. 48); (2) once established, conduct proceedings by “giving full effect” to the “complete and total bar” on disclosure of identity while “limiting, as much as possible, any impairment of the open court principle” (paras. 47-49, 72-75), including generally creating a sealed parallel proceeding so the existence of the hearing/decision is public (paras. 73-75, 79).
BaselineB: Common law (informer privilege and the Vancouver Sun procedure from Named Person v. Vancouver Sun, 2007 SCC 43; reaffirmed and applied here, with added guidance on how to implement the guiding rule when proceeding totally in camera (paras. 47-49, 71-79)).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “lawful authority” for whistleblower protection under s. 74(1)(a): includes internal authorities who can lawfully address the wrongdoing (“up the ladder” reporting)
BaselineA: Statute: The Labour Standards Act, R.S.S. 1978, c. L-1, s. 74(1)(a) (and s. 74(2)); interpreted using the modern principle of statutory interpretation (Driedger/Rizzo/Bell ExpressVu) and Saskatchewan Interpretation Act, 1995, s. 10
CaseB_TestB: Waiver of insurer’s right to rely on dishonoured-cheque non-payment rule: waiver requires “express and unequivocal language or conduct”
BaselineB: Combination: Statute (The Alberta Insurance Act, R.S.A. 1970, c. 187, s. 238(1) deeming dishonoured-cheque premium “not to have been made”) plus common-law waiver principles as applied/followed in McGeachie v. North American Life Insurance Company (1893), 23 S.C.R. 148
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “lawful authority” for whistleblower protection under s. 74(1)(a): includes not only police/public enforcement but also internal persons who “exercise lawful authority over the employee(s) complained about, or over the activity that is or is likely to result in the offence” (para. 38).
BaselineA: Statute: The Labour Standards Act, R.S.S. 1978, c. L-1, s. 74(1)(a) (and s. 74(2)); interpreted using the modern principle of statutory interpretation (Rizzo; Bell ExpressVu) and Saskatchewan Interpretation Act, 1995, s. 10.
CaseB_TestB: Common law joinder test (Clunas) applied to joint trial of provincial and summary conviction criminal charges: (1) offences “could initially have been jointly charged” satisfied by a functional “sufficient factual nexus” inquiry (paras. 35-40); and (2) joint trial must be “in the interests of justice”, requiring “weighing of the costs and benefits” (paras. 41-43).
BaselineB: Common law: R. v. Clunas, [1992] 1 S.C.R. 595 (two-part joinder test), reaffirmed in R. v. S.J.L., 2009 SCC 14; applied alongside statutory context (POA s. 2(1), s. 47(1); Criminal Code s. 591(3)).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal indecency (bawdy-house) — two-step harm-based test: Crown must prove beyond a reasonable doubt (1) conduct "causes harm or presents a significant risk of harm" in specified ways (autonomy/liberty; predisposition to anti-social behaviour; physical/psychological harm) and (2) the harm/risk is "of a degree that is incompatible with the proper functioning of society" (R. v. Kouri, paras. 9-10).
BaselineA: Combination: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 210(1) (and definition context in s. 197(1) "public place"); common law guidance from R. v. Butler, [1992] 1 S.C.R. 452 and companion case R. v. Labaye, 2005 SCC 80 (Kouri, paras. 1, 9-10).
CaseB_TestB: Pointe Gourde / s. 27(1)(a) valuation exclusion — whether a land-use enactment is ignored in compensation: "the key question is whether the enactment was made with a view to the expropriation or, conversely, was an independent enactment"; inquiry examines "purposes and effects" and "causation does not drive the inquiry" (Lynch, paras. 46, 48, 50-54).
BaselineB: Combination: statute and common law. Statutory baseline is Expropriation Act, R.S.N.L. 1990, c. E-19, s. 27(1)(a) ("no account shall be taken of the compulsory acquisition of the land"); common law baseline is the Pointe Gourde principle from Pointe Gourde Quarrying and Transport Co. v. Sub-Intendent of Crown Lands, [1947] A.C. 565 (Lynch, paras. 2, 34-38).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Interpretation of Limitations Act, s. 12 (Alberta): it applies Alberta’s limitations law only to "live" foreign causes of action and does not revive an action already time-barred under the applicable foreign substantive law (lex loci delicti, including its limitation period)
BaselineA: Combination: statute (Limitations Act, R.S.A. 2000, c. L-12, s. 12) interpreted against common law conflict-of-laws baseline from Tolofson v. Jensen (lex loci delicti includes the foreign limitation period as substantive)
CaseB_TestB: Ancillary powers doctrine (Waterfield/Dedman framework) for common law police powers: define the asserted power and liberty interest; then (1) is the conduct within the general scope of a police duty; (2) is it a justifiable exercise—i.e., "reasonably necessary"—weighing (i) importance of the duty, (ii) necessity of the liberty interference, and (iii) extent of the interference; onus on the state
BaselineB: Common law: ancillary powers doctrine / Waterfield test as adopted in Dedman v. The Queen and applied/structured in R. v. MacDonald (including the three-factor "reasonably necessary" inquiry)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Palmer/Lévesque test for admitting fresh evidence on a sentence appeal (interests of justice): (1) due diligence; (2) relevance; (3) credibility; (4) could reasonably have affected the result
BaselineA: Common law (Palmer v. The Queen; adapted to sentence appeals in R. v. Lévesque) applied under Criminal Code, s. 687(1)
CaseB_TestB: Section 8 reasonable expectation of privacy test (totality of the circumstances) with four lines of inquiry: (1) subject matter; (2) direct interest; (3) subjective expectation; (4) objective reasonableness
BaselineB: Common law/Charter jurisprudence under Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 8 (as articulated in cases such as Edwards, Tessling, Spencer, Cole, Marakah)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Copyright Act s. 27(2)(e) “hypothetical infringement” requirement: to prove secondary infringement by importation, plaintiff must show the imported copy “would infringe copyright if it had been made in Canada by the person who made it”; no liability where the foreign maker would be the Canadian copyright owner (owner cannot infringe its own copyright, and an exclusive licensee cannot sue the owner-licensor for infringement).
CaseB_TestB: Section 11(h) Charter “punished again” test for retrospective parole changes: “the dominant consideration” is “the extent to which an offender’s settled expectation of liberty has been thwarted by retrospective legislative action”; “a retrospective change ... will not be considered punitive if it does not substantially increase the risk of additional incarceration”, but a change that “automatically lengthen[s] the offender’s period of incarceration” is a “clearest of cases” of double punishment.
BaselineB: Constitutional text and statutory context — Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 11(h) (and s. 1 justification framework); applied to Abolition of Early Parole Act, S.C. 2011, c. 11, s. 10(1) and related CCRA provisions.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Sentencing/appellate review for hybrid offences prosecuted summarily: treat as summary conviction; any sentence within the statutory range (including the maximum) stands absent error of principle/relevant-factor error/overemphasis, unless demonstrably inadequate or excessive; “worst offender, worst offence” no longer a constraint
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, Part XXIII sentencing principles and summary conviction limit for hybrid offences proceeded with summarily)
CaseB_TestB: Admissibility of “Mr. Big” confessions (new common law rule): presumptively inadmissible; Crown must show on balance that probative value (a function of reliability) outweighs prejudicial effect; reliability assessed via circumstances of the operation and markers in the confession; plus separate abuse-of-process scrutiny for coercive/abusive police conduct
BaselineB: Common law (party admissions exception to hearsay; discretionary exclusion where prejudice exceeds probative value; abuse of process doctrine)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Adequacy of jury charge (Azoulay principle): trial judge must (except in rare needless cases) review the substantial parts of the evidence and put the defence theory so the jury can appreciate the evidence and apply the law; with latitude as to how much evidence to review so long as jurors get an adequate understanding of the relationship between essential evidence and the issues
BaselineA: Common law (Azoulay v. The Queen; R. v. Jacquard)
CaseB_TestB: Trade-marks Act s. 6 confusion test: whether use of both marks in the same area is likely to lead the 'casual consumer somewhat in a hurry' to the mistaken inference that the wares/services come from the same source, assessed under 'all the surrounding circumstances' including the s. 6(5) factors (no requirement of 'resemblance or linkage' between wares/services)
BaselineB: Statute (Trade-marks Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. T-13, ss. 6(2) and 6(5))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 172.1(1)(c) “luring a child”: three essential elements — (1) intentional communication by computer; (2) with a person the accused knows or believes is under 14; (3) for the specific purpose of facilitating a listed secondary offence (with “facilitating” meaning helping to bring about or making easier/more probable, and intent assessed subjectively at time of communication).
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 172.1(1)(c) (as then numbered), with related secondary offences in ss. 151 and 152 (and others listed in s. 172.1(1)(c)).
CaseB_TestB: Enforcement of forum selection clause: absent legislation, a court should enforce the clause unless the party resisting shows “strong cause” to displace the chosen forum (a discretionary test).
BaselineB: Common law: “strong cause” test for enforcing forum selection clauses from Z.I. Pompey Industrie v. ECU-Line N.V., 2003 SCC 27; applied within the procedural framework of Ontario Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 21.01(3)(a).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: SCC leave-to-appeal test under Supreme Court Act s. 40(1): leave only if the Court is of the opinion the question is of sufficient importance (public importance/importance of an issue of law or mixed fact and law) such that it “ought to be decided” by the SCC or is otherwise of such “nature or significance” as to warrant decision; plus jurisdiction extends to “any final or other judgment” not excluded by s. 40(3).
BaselineA: Statute: Supreme Court Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. S-26, ss. 40(1), 40(3) (and definition of “judgment” in s. 2); interaction with Criminal Code ss. 691-693 for exclusions.
CaseB_TestB: Access to Information Act third-party notice threshold under s. 27(1): notice is required unless disclosure/refusal is clear—i.e., disclose without notice only in “clear cases” where there is “no reason to believe” the record might contain s. 20(1) exempt material; refuse without notice only where there is “no reason to believe” disclosure could be required; otherwise give notice (including where severance under s. 25 is intended).
BaselineB: Statute: Access to Information Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. A-1, especially ss. 20(1), 25, 27(1) (and related notice/review provisions ss. 28, 44).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Reasonableness of an unannounced forced entry (departure from “knock and announce”): except in exigent circumstances police should give (i) notice of presence, (ii) notice of authority, and (iii) notice of purpose; if they depart, “there is an onus on them to explain why” and the Crown must show “reasonable grounds to be concerned about the possibility of harm ... or about the destruction of evidence” (Eccles/Genest framework as applied in Cornell).
BaselineA: Common law + constitutional baseline: knock-and-announce rule from Eccles v. Bourque (1975) and justification/onus language from R. v. Genest (1989), applied within Charter s. 8 reasonableness (R. v. Collins (1987)); also statutory context considered (Criminal Code, s. 29(1) and CDSA ss. 11-12).
CaseB_TestB: Implied assertions are hearsay when tendered for the truth of their contents; admissible only if within a traditional exception or, failing that, under the principled approach on a voir dire with “sufficient indicia of reliability and necessity” (Mapara/Khelawon framework applied to drug purchase calls).
BaselineB: Common law: principled hearsay framework from R. v. Khan (1990), R. v. Khelawon (2006) and R. v. Mapara (2005); SCC clarifies that implied assertions are not exempt from the hearsay rule and must satisfy necessity and reliability.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: State Immunity Act commercial activity exception: determine whether proceedings “relate to any commercial activity of the foreign state” by examining the act’s “nature ... in [its] full context, which includes the purpose of the acts” (not merely whether authorized by the state or pursuing public interests); if commercial, s. 5 removes s. 3 immunity
BaselineA: Statute: State Immunity Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. S-18, ss. 3 (general immunity), 5 (commercial activity exception), and s. 2 (“commercial activity” definition). SCC relies on and applies Re Canada Labour Code, [1992] 2 S.C.R. 50 (contextual nature+purpose approach).
CaseB_TestB: Criminal Code s. 686 curative proviso / miscarriage of justice framework: (i) miscarriage of justice if irregularity “severe enough to render the trial unfair or create the appearance of unfairness”; (ii) reference points include whether irregularity was central, its gravity/likely influence, jury vs judge-alone, whether remedied, and counsel’s response; (iii) curative proviso applies only if conviction was “inevitable”/no “reasonable possibility that the verdict would have been different”
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(a)(ii)-(iii) and s. 686(1)(b)(iii)-(iv). SCC synthesizes prior SCC authorities cited in the reasons (e.g., Bevan; S. (P.L.); Colpitts; Wildman; Fanjoy).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Journalist-source privilege (civil proceedings in Quebec): threshold relevance + four Wigmore factors, with context-specific balancing at factor 4. Quote: requesting party must show questions are relevant; if relevant, court applies Wigmore: (1) confidence of non-disclosure; (2) anonymity essential; (3) relationship should be sedulously fostered; (4) public interest in confidentiality outweighs public interest in getting at the truth; at factor 4 court must balance 'the importance of disclosure to the administration of justice' against 'the public interest in maintaining journalist-source confidentiality' (paras. 65-66).
BaselineA: Common law (Wigmore case-by-case privilege framework as applied to journalist-source privilege in R. v. National Post, 2010 SCC 16), adapted/confirmed for Quebec civil litigation; with relevance gatekeeping consistent with Civil Code of Québec art. 2857 (relevance/admissibility) and Superior Court powers under Code of Civil Procedure art. 46.
CaseB_TestB: Court jurisdiction to review voluntary association decisions: jurisdiction exists only if plaintiff seeks to vindicate an underlying legal right; for contract, membership is contractual only if general contract formation is met, especially objective intention to create legal relations. Quote: 'Jurisdiction ... depends on the existence of a legal right which the court is asked to vindicate' (para. 3); and 'the test is whether parties have indicated ... in the form of the objective reasonable bystander, their intention to contract' (para. 36).
BaselineB: Common law (Highwood Congregation of Jehovah’s Witnesses (Judicial Committee) v. Wall, 2018 SCC 26 on legal-right requirement for jurisdiction; and general common-law contract formation principles, including objective intention to create legal relations, drawn from Scotsburn and Crystal Square as cited).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Quebec Charter s. 49(2) punitive (exemplary) damages: admissible autonomously (not dependent on compensatory damages) and awardable where there is (1) unlawful interference with a Charter right and (2) intentional interference; punitive damages may pursue denunciation even if the wrongdoer is deceased
BaselineA: Statute: Charter of human rights and freedoms (Quebec), s. 49(2) ("in case of unlawful and intentional interference ... the tribunal may, in addition, condemn ... to exemplary damages"), informed by Civil Code of Québec, art. 1621 (preventive purpose of punitive damages). Prior SCC guidance discussed: St-Ferdinand (definition of "unlawful interference" and "intentional"), Béliveau St-Jacques (scope limited to public compensation systems).
CaseB_TestB: YCJA jurisdiction framework for youth judicial interim release on s. 469 charges after election: (1) interpret "the proceeding" in YCJA ss. 13(2)-(3) as including any step after election up to trial (including bail), so superior court judge is deemed a youth justice court judge for bail; (2) YCJA s. 33(8) gives exclusive release power to "a youth justice court judge" (including both s. 13(1) designated youth court judges and ss. 13(2)-(3) deemed superior court judges), yielding concurrent jurisdiction
BaselineB: Statute: Youth Criminal Justice Act, ss. 13(1)-(3), 28, 33(8), 67, read with Criminal Code, ss. 469 and 522, and Interpretation Act, s. 33(2).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Miscarriage of justice on appeal: whether trial defects "affected the trial judge’s appreciation of the evidence or rendered the proceedings unfair, so as to give rise to a miscarriage of justice" (para. 8); leading questions cross the line only if they "suggest an answer or assume a state of facts that is in dispute" (para. 9).
BaselineA: Combination: Criminal Code appeal power (s. 693(1)(a)) plus common-law/Charter-informed appellate concept of "miscarriage of justice" and evidentiary rule on leading questions (no specific originating SCC case named in the reasons).
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 13 engagement turns on whether the prior compelled testimony is "incriminating evidence": s. 13 applies only if the witness gave "incriminating evidence" under compulsion; "incriminating evidence" means evidence the Crown could use at the later proceeding "to prove or assist in proving one or more of the essential elements of the offence" (paras. 8-10). Non-incriminating compelled evidence used only to impeach does not trigger s. 13 (paras. 22-25).
BaselineB: Statute/constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 13 (interpreted in light of prior SCC cases including R. v. Henry, R. v. Kuldip, R. v. Noël, and Dubois v. The Queen).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 467.12 “in association with” test: the Crown must show (1) the predicate offence “advance[s], at least to some degree, the interests of a criminal organization” and thus has a required “connection between the predicate offence and the organization” (not merely between the accused and the organization), and (2) the accused “knowingly dealt with a criminal organization” (subjective mens rea, including wilful blindness).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 467.12(1) phrase “for the benefit of, at the direction of, or in association with, a criminal organization”; related definition in s. 467.1).
CaseB_TestB: Compulsion test for Motor Vehicle Act accident reports (s. 61) for Charter s. 7 use-immunity: “whether, at the time that the accident was reported by the driver, the driver gave the report on the basis of an honest and reasonably held belief that he or she was required by law to report the accident to the person to whom the report was given”; accused bears the onus on a balance of probabilities to show compulsion.
BaselineB: Combination: Statute (Motor Vehicle Act, R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 288, s. 61(1), (1.1), (4), (7)) interpreted through Charter s. 7 principle against self-incrimination (with discussion of prior SCC cases including R. v. Fitzpatrick, Thomson Newspapers, R. v. S. (R.J.), R. v. Jones).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Reasonable suspicion standard for sniffer-dog search (and investigative detention): must be based on objectively discernible facts assessed under the totality of the circumstances, through the lens of a reasonable officer; focuses on possibility not probability
BaselineA: Common law Charter s. 8 sniffer-dog jurisprudence (R. v. Kang-Brown; R. v. A.M.; clarified alongside R. v. Chehil) and common law investigative detention (R. v. Mann); applied in Charter context (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 8, 9)
CaseB_TestB: Reformulated s. 11(i) Charter test for whether a consequence is 'punishment': (1) consequence of conviction within the arsenal of sanctions, and either (2) imposed in furtherance of sentencing purposes/principles, or (3) has a significant impact on liberty/security (significantly constrains lawful conduct or imposes significant burdens)
BaselineB: Combination of Charter and common law: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 11(i) (and s. 1 context) interpreted through the prior common-law test in R. v. Rodgers (two-part punishment test)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Quebec civil-law “rectification” via interpretation under art. 1425 C.C.Q.: where a discrepancy is proved between the parties’ common intention and the intention declared in the written acts, the court may recognize and give effect to amendments correcting the writings (subject to third-party rights). Key passages: the court must determine the parties’ “common intention” and resolve “the discrepancy ... between the common intention of the parties and the expression of that intention” (para. 48); if a private writing contains an error, “the court must, once the error is proved ... note the error and ensure that it is remedied” (para. 52); and “it was open to the courts to intervene to find that the amendments ... were legitimate and necessary” (para. 51).
BaselineA: Statute: Civil Code of Québec, art. 1425 (interpretation: “In interpreting a contract, the common intention of the parties rather than adherence to the literal meaning of the words shall be sought.”) (as applied/relied on throughout, esp. paras. 48-52).
CaseB_TestB: Bank “put upon inquiry” constructive-trust/breach test: “A banker may be a constructive trustee of money in his customer’s account and in breach of that trust if he pays the money away, even on the customer’s mandate, in circumstances which put him upon inquiry.” The bank is liable where it has “sufficient notice ... to put the Bank on its inquiry” and fails to take steps “to ascertain the character of the funds”.
BaselineB: Common law (banking/constructive trust doctrine), as summarized from Halsbury’s Laws of England and illustrated by cases cited in the reasons (e.g., White v. Dominion Bank; Cartwright v. Lyster & Bank of Nova Scotia).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Applicability of Quebec’s 1974 retrospective prescription amendments to a case pending in the SCC: s. 5 makes art. 2262(2) C.C. inapplicable to a “suit pending before a court” on Jan. 1, 1975, and the SCC may rely on that to dismiss the appeal (not to vary the Court of Appeal judgment) under Supreme Court Act s. 47
BaselineA: Statute (Supreme Court Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. S-19, s. 47; and Quebec Act to amend certain prescriptions, 1974 (Que.), c. 80, ss. 1, 3, 5, affecting Civil Code arts. 2260a, 2261(2), 2262(2))
CaseB_TestB: Ministerial refusal of extradition/surrender threshold: surrender must be refused only if it would “shock the conscience” (s. 7 Charter) or be “unjust or oppressive” (Extradition Act s. 44(1)); otherwise it is reasonable to leave due process/delay issues to the foreign court
BaselineB: Statute and constitutional text (Extradition Act, S.C. 1999, c. 18, s. 44(1); Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7; as informed by United States v. Burns and Argentina v. Mellino)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Hart ‘Mr. Big’ confessions admissibility rule: confession to state in Mr. Big operation is “presumptively inadmissible”; Crown must show (balance of probabilities) “the probative value of the confession outweighs its prejudicial effect”, with probative value assessed via reliability (circumstances of operation + markers in confession) and prejudice assessed as moral/reasoning prejudice; plus separate abuse-of-process backstop for coercive/abusive operations
BaselineA: Common law evidence (party admissions exception to hearsay) and existing discretionary exclusion/abuse of process doctrines; SCC cites party admissions in R. v. Evans and R. v. Osmar, and notes confessions rule inapplicable per R. v. Grandinetti and right to silence limits per R. v. McIntyre/R. v. Hebert
CaseB_TestB: Meaning of “her mind is then disturbed” in Criminal Code s. 233 (infanticide): apply “disturbed” in its “grammatical and ordinary sense” (e.g., “mentally agitated”, “mentally unstable” or “mental discomposure”); no need for defined mental illness/mental disorder or significant impairment; disturbance must exist at time of act/omission and be “by reason of” childbirth effects or lactation; no need to prove the act was caused by the disturbance
BaselineB: Statute — Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 233 (with contextual reference to ss. 2, 16, 663(b), 672.11(c))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Penile swab as a search incident to arrest: police may take a penile swab incident to arrest if (i) the arrest is lawful and the swab is truly incidental to arrest for a valid purpose, (ii) police have "reasonable grounds to believe that a penile swab will afford evidence of the offence for which the accused was arrested" (independent of arrest grounds), and (iii) the swab is "conducted in a reasonable manner" guided by specified factors (e.g., station-house, supervisory authorization, privacy, same gender officers, minimal force, record-keeping).
BaselineA: Common law (search incident to arrest) as framed in R. v. Fearon (general framework) and R. v. Golden (strip-search modifications/guidelines), within the s. 8 Charter reasonableness structure from R. v. Caslake.
CaseB_TestB: Joint/co-principal liability in group assaults (manslaughter): "Joint/co-principal liability flows whenever two or more individuals come together with an intention to commit an offence, are present during the commission of the offence, and contribute to its commission"; for manslaughter, focus is whether the accused’s actions were a "significant contributing cause of death" (not who inflicted which wound), and in group assaults "absent a discrete or intervening event" all assailants’ actions can be a significant contributing cause to all injuries.
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, s. 21(1)(a) and s. 21(1)(c)) as interpreted in the party-liability jurisprudence referenced (notably R. v. Pickton).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Whether an employer’s damages claim for breach of a no-strike clause is a “grievance” subject to compulsory arbitration: no distinction between “interpretation/application” and “violation” of a collective agreement (a violation can ground a grievance).
BaselineA: Statute (Quebec Labour Code, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 141): definition of “grievance” in s. 1(g) (“disagreement respecting the interpretation or application of a collective agreement”) and mandatory arbitration in s. 88; interpreted in light of SCC precedent General Motors of Canada Ltd. v. Brunet, [1977] 2 S.C.R. 537 (and followed alongside Imbleau et al. v. Laskin et al., [1962] S.C.R. 338).
CaseB_TestB: Enforceability/scope of a waiver (exclusion) clause releasing liability for negligence: construed in its context; clause applies unless the negligence is outside what reasonable parties would have contemplated, and it will not be set aside as “unfair/unreasonable” absent unconscionability or public policy grounds.
BaselineB: Common law contract principles governing interpretation/enforcement of exclusion/waiver clauses (including arguments framed via “fundamental breach”, unconscionability, and public policy).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: When a s. 119 Canada Labour Code “review” application must be treated like a new certification versus a mere update/clarification: if the Board’s changes “do not alter the nature and scope of the certificate of certification and of the bargaining unit”, it is a review/update; only where the review would “enlarge or otherwise alter the bargaining unit” so the revised order is “substantially different” is it “basically of the same nature as an application for certification” requiring the “basic requirements” for certification.
BaselineA: Statute (Canada Labour Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. L-1, s. 119 (Board may “review, rescind, amend, alter or vary any order or decision made by it”); applied in light of the Board’s prior articulation in The Employees of the Regional Comptroller (1975), 9 D.I. 20, and referenced Board practice in Canadian Overseas Telecommunications Union v. Teleglobe (1979), 32 D.I. 270).
CaseB_TestB: Appellate intervention with trial findings of fact: it is wrong to set aside a trial judgment absent “palpable and overriding error” where “the only point at issue is the interpretation of the evidence as a whole”; the appellate court should not interfere unless the trial judge was “plainly wrong”.
BaselineB: Common law (appellate standard of review for factual findings), relying on Schreiber Brothers Ltd. v. Currie Products Ltd. and Gulf Oil Canada Ltd., [1980] 2 S.C.R. 78; Stein v. "Kathy K.", [1976] 2 S.C.R. 802; and Lewis v. Todd, [1980] 2 S.C.R. 694.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Ward s. 24(1) Charter damages analysis as applied to a quasi-judicial regulator: even if damages are functionally justified (compensation/vindication/deterrence), the state may show countervailing factors (alternative remedies; good governance) that negate appropriateness; here, considering these factors collectively, Charter damages could never be an “appropriate and just” remedy against this Board (Cromwell J., paras. 26-31). Key quotes: damages are limited to situations in which it is “appropriate and just” (para. 27); countervailing factors include “the existence of alternative remedies and concerns for good governance” (para. 28); “when these countervailing factors are considered collectively… they negate the appropriateness… [so] Charter damages could never be an appropriate and just remedy for Charter breaches by the Board” (paras. 31, 58).
BaselineA: Common law Charter remedial framework from Vancouver (City) v. Ward, 2010 SCC 27 (applied), interpreting/operating within Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 24(1), alongside the statutory immunity clause Energy Resources Conservation Act, R.S.A. 2000, c. E-10, s. 43.
CaseB_TestB: Maybrun framework for when an accused charged with breaching an administrative order may collaterally attack the order: focus on legislative intent, assessed using five non-exhaustive factors—“(1) the wording of the statute…; (2) the purpose of the legislation; (3) the existence of a right of appeal; (4) the kind of collateral attack in light of the expertise or raison d’être of the administrative appeal tribunal; and (5) the penalty on a conviction” (Moldaver J., para. 32). The factors are “not independent and absolute criteria, but important clues” (para. 32).
BaselineB: Common law framework from R. v. Consolidated Maybrun Mines Ltd., [1998] 1 S.C.R. 706 and R. v. Al Klippert Ltd., [1998] 1 S.C.R. 737 (applied/‘revisited’), in the statutory context of Corrections and Conditional Release Act, S.C. 1992, c. 20, s. 134.1(2) and Criminal Code, s. 753.3(1).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Art. 2930 C.C.Q. applies (3-year prescription) where the action is based on the obligation to make reparation for the direct and immediate consequences of interference with a person’s physical integrity; the court must characterize the action’s basis by the nature of the initial interference (bodily injury), not by the heads of damages claimed (paras. 26-27, 55).
BaselineA: Statute: Civil Code of Québec, arts. 2925 and 2930 (in conflict context with Cities and Towns Act, s. 586).
CaseB_TestB: Appellate non-intervention in trial fact-finding/credibility: once the trial judge’s reasons are available, the Court of Appeal should not substitute its view of the evidence for the trial judge’s; doing so is an “unwarranted intrusion” into an area “exclusive to the trial judge”.
BaselineB: Common law principle of appellate deference/non-intervention in factual and credibility findings (as reflected in Latour v. Grenier; Maze v. Empson; Dorval v. Bouvier; Métivier v. Cadorette; Hood v. Hood, cited in the reasons).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Schrenk “sufficient nexus with the employment context” test for whether discrimination is “regarding employment” under s. 13(1)(b): Tribunal must do a contextual analysis considering all relevant circumstances; non-exhaustive factors include (1) whether the respondent was integral to the complainant’s workplace; (2) whether the impugned conduct occurred in the complainant’s workplace; and (3) whether the complainant’s work performance or work environment was negatively affected (paras. 67-68).
BaselineA: Statute: Human Rights Code, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 210, s. 13(1)(b) (“discriminate against a person regarding employment”), with interpretive context from ss. 1 (definitions of “employment”, “person”) and s. 3 (purposes).
CaseB_TestB: Groia contextual approach to when in-court incivility amounts to professional misconduct: assess context-specific factors (what was said; manner and frequency; presiding judge’s reaction). Allegations impugning opposing counsel’s integrity “cross the line into professional misconduct unless they are made in good faith and have a reasonable basis” (paras. 59, 81, 88).
BaselineB: Regulatory/statutory: Law Society Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. L.8 (home statute) and Rules of Professional Conduct made under it (plus earlier Professional Conduct Handbook) governing civility/professional misconduct.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Ontario anti-SLAPP dismissal framework (CJA s. 137.1): threshold (s. 137.1(3)) plus plaintiff’s merits hurdle (s. 137.1(4)(a)) and public-interest weighing (s. 137.1(4)(b), requiring that permitting the proceeding 'outweighs' protecting the expression)
BaselineA: Statute: Courts of Justice Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.43, s. 137.1(3)-(4) (and related ss. 137.2-137.5).
CaseB_TestB: Corporate attribution doctrine for a one-person corporation: apply Aquino/Livent guiding principles and exercise discretion to attribute (or not) the directing mind’s knowledge based on whether attribution would promote the purpose of the law under which attribution is sought (public-interest/purposive, contextual, pragmatic approach)
BaselineB: Common law corporate attribution doctrine from Canadian Dredge & Dock Co. v. The Queen; Deloitte & Touche v. Livent Inc. (Receiver of); Christine DeJong Medicine Professional Corp. v. DBDC Spadina Ltd.; and Aquino v. Bondfield Construction Co., applied in the context of the Limitations Act, 2002 (ss. 4, 5, 12) and the Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Duty to comment on prejudicial Crown jury address: where Crown counsel’s remarks are “prejudicial to a degree sufficient to impose a legal duty on the trial judge to comment” to ensure the defence position is “fairly put to the jury”; failure to do so is an error of law (and no curative proviso applied here).
BaselineA: Common law principles of fair trial/jury charge duties, applied through Criminal Code s. 686(1)(b)(iii) (curative proviso) in assessing whether the error can be cured.
CaseB_TestB: “Identifiability” test for Federal Court in rem jurisdiction under Federal Courts Act s. 43(2): reject “physical nexus”; cargo is “subject of the action” if it is the cargo designated in the contract of affreightment alleged to be breached.
BaselineB: Statute — Federal Courts Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. F-7, s. 43(2) (meaning of “property ... that is the subject of the action”).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Threshold for summary dismissal of a criminal application: the underlying application may be summarily dismissed only if it is “manifestly frivolous”; on the motion the judge must assume alleged facts are true and take the applicant’s arguments “at their highest”, without weighing evidence or choosing among competing inferences (Haevischer, paras. 3, 71, 82-85, 90).
BaselineA: Common law / judge-made criminal procedure (Vukelich-type hearings), drawing on prior jurisprudence including R. v. Vukelich (BCCA) and SCC comments in Jordan/Cody; clarified and unified by the SCC in this case.
CaseB_TestB: Combined effect of Criminal Code s. 172.1(3) presumption and s. 172.1(4) “reasonable steps” requirement for child luring: if underage is represented, accused is presumed to believe it; presumption is rebutted only by “evidence to the contrary” that includes reasonable steps to ascertain age; if reasonable steps were taken and accused believed interlocutor not underage, Crown fails (Levigne, para. 32).
BaselineB: Statute — Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 172.1(3) and s. 172.1(4) (interpreted harmoniously with s. 172.1’s purpose; relying on R. v. Legare).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Two-step framework for whether legislation displaces the common law discretion to grant credit for a pre-sentence driving prohibition; and holding that s. 259(1)(a) imposes a minimum 'punishment' (global) not a minimum 'sentence' (prospective), so credit may be granted after imposing the mandatory minimum
BaselineA: Combination of common law and statute: common law discretion to credit pre-sentence driving prohibitions (R. v. Lacasse, 2015 SCC 64; analogy to pre-sentence custody credit discussed in R. v. Wust, 2000 SCC 18) plus Criminal Code ss. 259(1)(a) and 719(1) (and consideration of s. 719(3))
CaseB_TestB: Mitigation in contract where plaintiff sought specific performance: defendant must prove failure to mitigate and that mitigation was possible; plaintiff’s inaction may be reasonable only if it had a 'fair, real, and substantial justification' / 'substantial and legitimate interest' in specific performance (typically requiring land’s 'peculiar and special value')
BaselineB: Common law mitigation doctrine and specific-performance-related mitigation principles from Asamera Oil Corp. v. Seal Oil & General Corp., [1979] 1 SCR 633 (and related mitigation authorities cited in the reasons)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Hearsay admissibility under the principled approach (necessity + reliability) applies even to traditional hearsay exceptions; statements of present intention inadmissible if made in “circumstances of suspicion” and cannot be used to prove a third party’s intentions absent an exception for each hearsay level
BaselineA: Common law (hearsay rule/exceptions and the principled approach from R. v. Khan and R. v. Smith; present intentions exception discussed in Smith; co-conspirator exception referenced via R. v. Carter)
CaseB_TestB: Public interest standing (Downtown Eastside) three-factor discretionary framework: (i) serious justiciable issue; (ii) genuine interest; (iii) reasonable and effective means, weighed cumulatively, flexibly and purposively; no individual co-plaintiff required if a sufficiently concrete and well-developed factual setting will be forthcoming
BaselineB: Common law (public interest standing framework from Canada (Attorney General) v. Downtown Eastside Sex Workers United Against Violence Society, 2012 SCC 45)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Limited-liability/non-assessability constraint on corporate amendments: an alteration of articles is ultra vires if it seeks to impose on fully paid shareholders “any financial burden whatsoever in respect of those shares”; and a share transfer fee is invalid “to the extent that it exceeded the reasonable and proper cost of the transfer” (an “illegal levy” in respect of shares).
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common-law company-law principle: The Companies Act (Alberta) (notably s. 42(1) special resolution power; limited liability/non-assessability provisions including s. 68(4), and related limited-liability definitions/sections cited) plus the fundamental common-law/jural principle that fully paid shares are non-assessable (authorities cited include Ooregum Gold Mining Co. v. Roper; Bisgood v. Henderson’s Transvaal Estates; Shalfoon v. Cheddar Valley Co-operative Dairy Co.).
CaseB_TestB: Van der Peet aboriginal-rights identification test (as applied): (1) characterize the precise claim (considering the action, the impugned regulation, and the practice/custom/tradition relied on); (2) determine whether, prior to European contact, the practice was “integral to the distinctive culture” (i.e., a “central, significant or defining feature”); with appellate deference absent “palpable and overriding error.”
BaselineB: Common law constitutional test under s. 35(1) of the Constitution Act, 1982 as articulated in R. v. Van der Peet (applied here), with the constitutional text (s. 35(1)) and the impugned regulatory context (BC Fishery (General) Regulations, ss. 4(5), 27(5)) framing the claim.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Reviewability of a consensual labour arbitrator’s award for error of law on the face: no “specific question of law” reference where the issue arises in the ordinary grievance process under a collective agreement that limits the arbitrator to decisions consistent with the agreement; therefore courts may review and quash for error of law on the face
BaselineA: Common law (scope of judicial review of consensual arbitration awards), drawing on Government of Kelantan v. Duff Development Co. Ltd.; F.R. Absalom Ltd. v. Great Western (London) Garden Village Society Ltd.; Faubert and Watts v. Temagami Mining Co. Ltd.; and Bell Canada v. Office and Professional Employees’ International Union, Local 131
CaseB_TestB: Morin framework for s. 11(b) “reasonable time” analysis: assess (1) length of delay minus defence waiver, then consider (2) reasons for delay, (3) prejudice to the accused, and (4) the interests protected by s. 11(b); with prejudice potentially inferred from length of delay
BaselineB: Statute/constitutional text plus common law framework: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 11(b), as applied through R. v. Morin and R. v. Askov
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 3(4) possession attribution: possession is established where a person has an item in personal possession or knowingly has it in another’s custody/possession or in a place for use/benefit (s. 3(4)(a)); and where one of two or more persons, with the knowledge and consent of the rest, has anything in custody/possession, it is deemed to be in the custody and possession of each and all (s. 3(4)(b)). SCC held s. 3(4) applies broadly 'for the purposes of this Act' to all proceedings under the Code, including using possession as a circumstantial evidentiary link.
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 3(4) (now s. 4(3) in later consolidations).
CaseB_TestB: Adverse possession in British Columbia: to establish adverse possession, possession must be 'open and notorious, adverse, exclusive, peaceful (not by force), actual (generally), and continuous'; SCC contribution includes rejecting any additional mandatory 'inconsistent use' requirement in B.C. (i.e., no need to show the possessor’s use was inconsistent with the true owner’s intended present/future use).
BaselineB: Common law adverse possession test (as described in the reasons, citing Ziff) operating within B.C. limitations legislation that reproduces the 1833 English codification; SCC interprets this legislative history to exclude an 'inconsistent use' add-on.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Quantum meruit for services accepted without an agreed price: where there is "no agreement as to remuneration", the recipient "must pay reasonable rates" (subject to any valid statutory/regulatory bar, construed restrictively and not retroactive absent clear authority).
BaselineA: Common law (quantum meruit/quasi-contract), with statutory/regulatory overlay considered as potential bars (Hospital Act s. 37(2) and O.C. 3103; Residence and Responsibility Act s. 3 and O.C. 4399/4400). Key SCC baseline case cited: King George Highway Hospital Ltd. v. District of Surrey, [1971] S.C.R. vi.
CaseB_TestB: Voluntariness/"operating mind" test for admissibility of inculpatory statements by an allegedly insane accused: the "underlying and controlling question" is whether the statement is "freely and voluntarily made", including whether it represents "the utterances of an operating mind" (no fixed formula required).
BaselineB: Common law confessions rule (voluntariness) as articulated in Boudreau v. The King, [1949] S.C.R. 262 and Ward v. The Queen, [1979] 2 S.C.R. 30 (with discussion of R. v. Santinon (BCCA) as consistent guidance).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Effect of breach of a witness-exclusion order: witness not necessarily disqualified; admissibility discretionary; weight assessed by trier of fact (and no legal requirement that the judge expressly state a self-caution for each such witness)
BaselineA: Common law (practice/rule on exclusion of witnesses and consequences of breach, as reflected in cases cited such as Moore v. Lambeth County Court Registrar; Cook v. Nethercotte; Thomas v. David; Chandler v. Home; Black v. Besse; R. v. Carefoot)
CaseB_TestB: Clear-and-unequivocal-language requirement to lift Crown immunity from discovery; s. 27 CLPA applies only where the Crown is a party (so immunity from discovery remains when Crown is not a party)
BaselineB: Statute + common law: Interpretation Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. I-21, s. 17 (starting point that enactments do not bind the Crown absent clear lifting) and Crown Liability and Proceedings Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-50, s. 27 (scope interpreted against common law immunity backdrop)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory disqualification/bias in Law Society discipline: benchers who sat on the Discipline Committee are NOT disqualified from participating in Convocation’s consideration of that Committee’s report (a two-step process, not an appeal), and s. 39(4) disqualification applies only to the specific statutory appeal from a reprimand
BaselineA: Statute and regulation: The Law Society Act, 1970 (Ont.), ss. 33(12), 34, 37, 39 (especially s. 39(4) “No bencher who sat on the committee ... shall take any part in the hearing of the appeal in Convocation”); Reg. 556, s. 13(6)-(7) (report to Convocation and notice procedure). Common-law natural justice/bias principles are discussed (nemo judex; reasonable apprehension of bias) but the majority resolves the issue primarily by statutory interpretation (expressio unius).
CaseB_TestB: Criminal Code s. 731(1)(b) probation eligibility rule: “imprisonment for a term not exceeding two years” refers to the term imposed by the sentencing court at a single sitting; it does not include other sentences from other occasions, and later sentences do not invalidate an existing probation order (but probation is barred where sentences imposed at the same session result in continuous custody over two years)
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 731(1)(b) (and related context in ss. 732.2, 743.1).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “operation of a mine” and when a separate “mine” exists for the s. 83(5) 36‑month tax exemption: (1) “operation of a mine” refers only to extraction/production of ore (not milling/processing); (2) “there is ‘a mine’ ... if there is a body of ore together with the workings, equipment and machinery capable of producing it”; a separate mine arises when a separate ore body “commenced to be extracted by means of its separate and distinct extraction facilities” (shared mill does not negate separate mines).
BaselineA: Statute (Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1952, c. 148 as amended, s. 83(5) and s. 83(6)); interpreted with reference to SCC precedents North Bay Mica Co. Ltd. v. M.N.R., [1958] S.C.R. 597 and M.N.R. v. MacLean Mining Co. Ltd., [1970] S.C.R. 877.
CaseB_TestB: Mancini test (s. 215 BIA leave to sue a receiver/trustee): leave should be refused only for frivolous/vexatious/manifestly unmeritorious claims or where the evidence does not disclose a cause of action; the court does not decide the merits—“If the evidence discloses a prima facie case, leave should be granted.”
BaselineB: Statute (Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. B-3, s. 215) applied through the common-law/precedential framework from Mancini (Bankrupt) v. Falconi (1993), 61 O.A.C. 332 (C.A.) (as adopted/endorsed by the SCC here).
JudgeB: Abella J. (for McLachlin C.J. and Bastarache, Binnie, LeBel, Fish and Charron JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Education Act, s. 373: when school commissioners must amend municipal valuation rolls—if valuations are “not uniform”, they “shall amend such various rolls so as to re-establish on the basis of its real value the valuation of the taxable property of all the parts of the school municipality”; this requires valuing only what is taxable in each municipality (no priority to another municipality’s choice to exempt machinery).
BaselineA: Statute (Education Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 235, s. 373; interpreted in light of municipal power under Cities and Towns Act (then s. 488) to exclude machinery from taxable immovables).
CaseB_TestB: Criminal Code s. 426(1)(a)(ii) (secret commissions): actus reus has three elements—(1) agency relationship; (2) agent accepts a benefit “as consideration” for acting/forbearing in relation to the principal’s affairs; (3) “corruptly” adds non-disclosure—failure to make “adequate and timely disclosure” of the benefit (source/amount/nature) to the principal; no “corrupt bargain” with the giver is required.
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 426(1)(a), especially s. 426(1)(a)(ii); with interpretive reliance on prior case law such as R. v. Brown (1956) and R. v. Morris (1988) as discussed in the reasons).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Extradition-crime classification under an extradition arrangement: “The test is what is the essence of the crime charged” (i.e., whether the offence is, in substance, a crime “against the laws for the suppression of the traffic in narcotics”).
BaselineA: Statute + extradition arrangement: Extradition Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-21, s. 2 (definition of “extradition crime”), plus the 1925 Supplementary Convention classification added to the Act (“Crimes and offences against the laws for the suppression of the traffic in narcotics”).
CaseB_TestB: Section 13 self-incrimination limit on use of prior testimony at a later proceeding: prior testimony may be used on cross-examination to impeach credibility but not “to incriminate” (i.e., to establish guilt); the key distinction is the “purpose” of the use (impeaching credibility vs incriminating).
BaselineB: Constitution + statute: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 13 (and its interpretation in R. v. Dubois and R. v. Mannion as discussed), and Canada Evidence Act, s. 5(2) (interpreted as coextensive in protection against incriminating use).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Foreseeability/remoteness test for highway authority negligence: whether “a reasonable person should have anticipated that what happened might be a natural result of that act or omission”; not necessary to foresee the “precise concatenation of events”, only the “class or character of injury”
BaselineA: Common law foreseeability/remoteness in negligence (University Hospital Board v. Lépine; Wagon Mound No. 2 referenced) applied in context of Highway Improvement Act, R.S.O. 1960, s. 33(1) duty to maintain
CaseB_TestB: CEAA “project as proposed” rule for determining assessment track: if the project as proposed is described in the Comprehensive Study List, s. 21 requirements are mandatory and the responsible authority cannot “reduce the scope of the project to less than what is proposed by the proponent” to avoid a comprehensive study
BaselineB: Statutory interpretation of Canadian Environmental Assessment Act, S.C. 1992, c. 37 (especially ss. 2 “project”, 15, 18, 21, 58(1)(i)) and Comprehensive Study List Regulations, SOR/94-638
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Res ipsa loquitur as a rule of evidence to infer (and support a finding of) gross negligence for a gratuitous passenger claim: applies where (1) the thing causing damage was under defendant’s sole management/control; (2) the occurrence is such that it would not have happened without negligence; and (3) there is “no evidence as to why or how the occurrence took place” — but an offered explanation that is “no answer, even if believed in full” does not bar using the maxim.
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Highway Traffic Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 202, s. 132(3) (gratuitous passenger requires “gross negligence”); common law res ipsa loquitur framework as quoted from Clerk & Lindsell and recognized in Walker v. Coates, [1968] S.C.R. 599; discussion of skidding as a “neutral fact” from Gauthier & Co. Ltd. v. The King, [1945] S.C.R. 143.
CaseB_TestB: Two-criteria test for a vested right (acquired right) and presumption against legislative interference: a vested right exists where (1) the individual’s legal situation is “tangible and concrete rather than general and abstract”; and (2) it was “sufficiently constituted at the time of the new statute’s commencement”; absent “a clear indication in a statute to the contrary in light of the entire context”, legislation is not read to prejudicially affect such rights.
BaselineB: Statutory interpretation baseline (Interpretation Act, R.S.Q., c. I-16, s. 12; transitional provision in Amending Act, 1998, s. 13; AFAS provisions incorporated into the loan contract) plus common law/statutory-interpretation jurisprudence on vested rights (e.g., Spooner Oils; Gustavson Drilling) as discussed in the reasons.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Mechanics’ lien owner-liability/holdback test on contractor abandonment: s. 19(2) does not prevent the owner deducting completion costs from amounts otherwise payable; s. 19(2) only bars deductions for extraneous “prior or subsequent indebtedness, set-off, or counterclaim” not arising under the contract
BaselineA: Statute (Mechanics’ Lien Act, R.S.B.C. 1960, c. 238, especially ss. 6, 19(2), 21(1), 21(6); interpreted in light of SCC approval of Guttman/Comstock)
CaseB_TestB: Choice of law in tort: apply lex loci delicti (law of the place where the activity/wrong occurred) as the general rule; includes applying the locus limitation period as substantive where it creates an accrued right to plead a time bar
BaselineB: Common law (conflict of laws in tort; overruling McLean v. Pettigrew and rejecting lex fori/double-actionability approaches) plus characterization of limitation periods in conflicts; applied alongside relevant statutes in the cases (e.g., Vehicles Act, R.S.S. 1978, c. V-3, s. 180(1); Quebec Automobile Insurance Act, L.Q. 1977, c. 68, ss. 3-4)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Constitutional (territorial) validity test for provincial legislation with extraterritorial operation: Manitoba cannot, by s. 4(2) of The Fishermen’s Assistance and Polluters’ Liability Act, “nullify the effect of permission duly granted by the regulatory authority of another jurisdiction”; a province may protect its property, but “in respect of injury caused by acts performed outside its territory, [it] cannot be treated as a matter within its legislative authority” (Act held inapplicable/ultra vires as applied to out-of-province discharges).
BaselineA: Statute + constitutional division of powers/territorial limits: The Fishermen’s Assistance and Polluters’ Liability Act, 1970 (Man.), especially s. 4(2) (and s. 4(1) context), assessed against B.N.A. Act, 1867 provincial territorial limits (e.g., s. 92 heads; discussion of federal residual/POGG and interprovincial concern).
JudgeA: Pigeon J. (for Martland, Pigeon and Beetz JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Privative-clause judicial review threshold: with a privative clause, courts intervene only for jurisdictional error; an “unreasonable finding, whatever its origin, impairs the jurisdiction of the tribunal”, i.e., intervention only if the decision is “so patently unreasonable that its construction cannot be rationally supported by the relevant legislation”.
BaselineB: Common law administrative law standard of review under a privative clause, anchored in CUPE: “so patently unreasonable that its construction cannot be rationally supported by the relevant legislation”; applied alongside the statutory scheme (Act respecting labour standards, R.S.Q., c. N-1.1, ss. 128-129; Labour Code, s. 139).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Collective agreement not terminable by common-law repudiation/fundamental breach during its term; an illegal strike does not, by itself, terminate the employment relationship, so employer remains bound by collective-agreement obligations (e.g., severance) absent lawful disciplinary termination
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law labour jurisprudence: Mediation Services Act, 1968 (B.C.), including s. 6 (collective agreement binding) and s. 23 (prohibition on strikes during term), plus SCC labour-law approach in Syndicat catholique des employés de magasins de Québec Inc. v. Compagnie Paquet Ltée and C.P.R. Co. v. Zambri (as discussed by the Court)
CaseB_TestB: Limits on cross-examination using a complainant’s diary: relevant defence cross-examination may be excluded only if its prejudicial effect substantially outweighs its probative value; omission evidence is probative only if the defence establishes a reasonable expectation the event would have been recorded (and O’Connor production balancing is not the test for cross-examination scope)
BaselineB: Common law evidence principles governing cross-examination limits and admissibility (Seaboyer; Osolin), with clarification that O’Connor applies to production not admissibility/use; statutory context noted but not applied to admissibility: Criminal Code ss. 278.1–278.9 (production regime) held inapplicable to use/admissibility here
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Admissibility of evidence that an accused refused to participate in a police line-up: admissible where needed to explain the absence of a line-up (and resulting confrontation/showup), but not normally tendered otherwise; admissibility depends on the circumstances (relevance/prejudice).
BaselineA: Common law evidence (relevance/admissibility principles) informed by the common law privilege against self-incrimination (testimonial compulsion only) and related jurisprudence (e.g., Curr v. The Queen; A.-G. (Que.) v. Begin; U.S. cases Holt, Schmerber, Wade).
CaseB_TestB: Division of powers limit on provincial commissions of inquiry: an inquiry is ultra vires if, in pith and substance, it is a substitute police investigation/preliminary inquiry into specific alleged criminal conduct by named individuals (i.e., it circumvents federally prescribed criminal procedure).
BaselineB: Constitution Act, 1867 division of powers analysis (pith and substance; assignment to s. 91(27) vs s. 92 heads) applied to commissions of inquiry, drawing on prior SCC jurisprudence (e.g., Faber; Di Iorio; Keable; O'Hara) and the statutory scheme of Ontario's Public Inquiries Act.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Punitive damages in tort: whether the circumstances justify an additional punitive award “in the interests of justice” (here, tortious inducement/conspiracy coupled with a scheme to take over and end the plaintiff as a going concern)
BaselineA: Common law (punitive/exemplary damages principles; no specific prior SCC test case is identified in the reasons provided)
CaseB_TestB: Duty of care for pure economic loss: (1) does the claim fit within a recognized category (including relational economic loss requiring third-party physical injury/property damage), and if not (2) should a new duty be recognized under the Anns/Cooper two-stage test (foreseeability + proximity, then residual policy such as indeterminate liability)
BaselineB: Common law (Anns v. Merton London Borough Council; Kamloops (City of) v. Nielsen; Cooper v. Hobart; Childs v. Desormeaux; and the recognized pure economic loss categories from Norsk)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory limits on Canadian Transport Commission power re freight tariff effective dates: once a freight tariff advancing tolls is duly filed/published and the effective date arrives, it takes effect under s. 275(4); any Commission order to “extend” the s. 275(2) notice period must be made before the effective date, otherwise it is an impermissible attempt to postpone the effective date (ultra vires).
BaselineA: Statute: Railway Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. R-2, s. 275(2) and s. 275(4) (with context from National Transportation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. N-17, s. 3(a) and s. 64(5)).
CaseB_TestB: Palmer test for admitting fresh evidence on appeal (“interests of justice”): (1) due diligence (relaxed in criminal cases), (2) relevance to a decisive/potentially decisive issue, (3) credibility, and (4) whether, if believed, it could reasonably be expected to have affected the result.
BaselineB: Common law: Palmer v. The Queen, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 759 (applied), in the context of Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 683.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Effectiveness/finality of an order still within the appeal period: despite being appealable, the order may be treated as fully effective (even against third parties) where there is only an “ephemeral prospect of an appeal”; assess (1) the purpose for which finality is invoked, (2) who is affected, and (3) the context in which finality is asserted before the appeal period expires.
BaselineA: Statute (Ontario) — The Conveyancing and Law of Property Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 85, s. 62 (order discharging building restrictions), with the Court addressing the practical effect of such an order while appeal time remains.
CaseB_TestB: Preliminary inquiry committal test (s. 548 Criminal Code / Shephard): ask whether there is “any evidence upon which a reasonable jury properly instructed could return a verdict of guilty”; if Crown evidence is circumstantial, the judge must do a “limited weighing” of the whole evidence (including defence evidence) to assess whether the Crown’s evidence, if believed, could reasonably support the inferences of guilt (without drawing inferences or assessing credibility).
BaselineB: Combination — Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 548(1)) interpreted through common law (United States of America v. Shephard, [1977] 2 S.C.R. 1067; also discussed: Mezzo; Monteleone; Charemski).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Discretionary public-interest standing (taxpayer/citizen) to challenge legislation: standing may be granted where (1) a “serious, a substantial constitutional issue” is raised; (2) the plaintiff has taken “all the steps that he could reasonably be required to take” so the standing issue is “ripe”; (3) the plaintiff is arguably “directly affected” (here, as a member of the public affected by censorship); and (4) there is “no other way, practically speaking, to subject the challenged Act to judicial review”, such that the court may “exercise[] its discretion to grant standing”.
BaselineA: Common law (standing/locus standi doctrine), drawing on Smith v. Attorney General of Ontario, [1924] S.C.R. 331 and Thorson v. Attorney General of Canada, [1975] 1 S.C.R. 138.
