CaseB_TestB: Interpretation of ASRA Program s. 88(3) and review of La Financière’s choice of linkage method: s. 88(3) “does not specify how ... is to be linked” and, interpreted under C.C.Q. arts. 1425-1432 (esp. art. 1427 ‘contract as a whole’ and art. 1426 ‘past practices/usage’), it “does not require that amounts be linked individually but, on the contrary, gives La Financière the discretion to decide what linkage method to employ”; that discretion must be exercised “in accordance with the requirements of good faith and contractual fairness” (C.C.Q. arts. 6, 7, 1375, 1434).
BaselineB: Regulation/contract text and civil law: Programme d’assurance stabilisation des revenus agricoles, s. 88(3), interpreted through Civil Code of Québec arts. 1425-1432 (interpretation) and arts. 6, 7, 1375, 1434 (good faith/contractual fairness).
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Rebuttable presumption of mens rea for trafficking once actus reus proved: when it is proved the accused trafficked in a restricted drug (here, LSD), “a rebuttable presumption arises” that the condition/intent was voluntarily induced and the accused “must be convicted unless other evidence is adduced which raises a reasonable doubt” (applied from R. v. King) — here, no defence evidence, so mens rea not negated.
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Food and Drugs Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. F-27, ss. 40 (definitions incl. “traffic”) and 42(1)-(3) (trafficking offence/penalty), plus SCC mens rea/mistake framework from Beaver v. The Queen and rebuttable-presumption approach from R. v. King (and related drug mens rea cases such as Blondin).
JudgeA: de Grandpré J. (for Martland, Judson, Ritchie, Pigeon, Dickson, Beetz and de Grandpré JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Limits on trial-judge intervention / appearance of impartiality test: a judge may question and interrupt witnesses to ensure justice is done, but “must do so within certain limits and in such a way that justice is seen to be done”; if the judge’s conduct “raised some doubt as to his impartiality”, a new trial is required.
BaselineB: Common law principles of procedural fairness and judicial impartiality/appearance of justice (e.g., R. v. Sussex Justices; Ex parte McCarthy: justice must “manifestly and undoubtedly be seen to be done”), developed through case law on permissible judicial intervention (e.g., Jones v. National Coal Board; Torbiak; Darlyn; Yuill; Bateman).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory-interpretation rule for s. 213 constructive murder: despite bilingual/revision ambiguities, “burglary” retains its 1892 Criminal Code meaning (s. 410) (dwelling-house, by night) as preserved by revision/consolidation principles (Interpretation Act, s. 36(f))
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 213; Interpretation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-23, s. 36(f); with historical reference to Criminal Code, 1892, ss. 228, 410, 407)
CaseB_TestB: Damages for repudiation where contract has alternative modes of performance: assess on the basis of the mode “least profitable to the plaintiff, and the least burdensome to the defendant” (not a ‘what would likely have happened’ inquiry)
BaselineB: Common law (general principle traced to Cockburn v. Alexander (1848) and explained in Withers v. General Theatre Corp. (1933))
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Lease interpretation test for shifting fire-loss risk to landlord where tenant covenants to pay “insurance rates”: read the lease “reasonably and in a business sense”; if tenant pays for fire insurance (at least once the landlord presents “the insurance bill”), the tenant is “entitled to rest in respect of loss by fire on the discharge of its obligation to pay for fire insurance”, so the landlord/insurer cannot pursue the tenant by subrogation.
BaselineA: Common law contract/lease interpretation ("ordinary test of reading it reasonably and in a business sense") plus statutory context that standard fire insurance covers third-party negligence (The Insurance Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 224, s. 118).
CaseB_TestB: Civil Code art. 1053 “fault” framework for bank liability on unauthorized endorsements: a bank commits a compensable “fault” by accepting payment/deposit of cheques on an unauthorized endorsement “without examining it, and without verifying the sufficiency of the endorsement”; if that fault deprives the payee of its money and causes damage, damages are recoverable (typically equal to the cheque amounts), with the key limitation that Norwich Union bars recovery only where the beneficiary still has full recourse against the drawer.
BaselineB: Combination of statute and civil law: Bills of Exchange Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. B-5 (notably s. 51 on signatures by procuration; also s. 10 mentioned) and Civil Code art. 1053, as developed in Norwich Union Fire Insurance Society Ltd. v. La Banque Canadienne Nationale, [1934] S.C.R. 596.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 15(1) adverse impact discrimination (prima facie breach) — claimant must show (1) a distinction on an enumerated/analogous ground through effects shown by “disproportionate impact” and (2) that the law’s impact “reinforc[es], perpetuat[es], or exacerbat[es] disadvantage”; with guidance that “both evidence of statistical disparity and of broader group disadvantage may demonstrate disproportionate impact; but neither is mandatory”.
BaselineA: Constitution (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 15(1); applied via existing SCC s. 15 framework from cases cited in the reasons, including Withler v. Canada (Attorney General) and Kahkewistahaw First Nation v. Taypotat).
CaseB_TestB: Division of powers “pith and substance” analysis — “two questions: first, what is the essential character of the law? Second, does that character relate to an enumerated head of power”; essential character determined by “looking at the purpose and the legal effect” of the measure.
BaselineB: Constitution (Constitution Act, 1867, ss. 91 and 92; applied through the established pith and substance doctrine as described with reference to cases such as Reference re Firearms Act (Can.) and R. v. Morgentaler).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Lease interpretation test for whether tenant’s covenant to pay “insurance rates” shifts the risk of fire loss (including tenant negligence) to the landlord, barring insurer subrogation: apply “the ordinary test of reading [the lease] reasonably and in a business sense”; if tenant pays for fire insurance (at least once the landlord presents “the insurance bill”), “the risk of loss by fire passed to the landlord” and “the landlord’s insurer has no basis for asserting a subrogated claim”.
BaselineA: Common law contract/lease interpretation ("reading it reasonably and in a business sense"), in the landlord-tenant/insurance context; with statutory backdrop that fire policies cover third-party negligence (Ontario Insurance Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 224, s. 118).
JudgeA: Laskin C.J. (for Laskin C.J. and Judson and Spence JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Warsaw Convention limitation entitlement turns on strict statutory conditions: under Art. 3(2) the carrier loses limitation “only where no ticket is delivered” (illegibility/irregularity does not equal non-delivery); under Art. 4(4) limitation is lost if no luggage ticket is delivered or if it lacks particulars (d), (f), (h), and compliance includes that the ticket’s print is “legible by the ordinary person using ordinary diligence” and content is adequate.
BaselineB: Statute/treaty text: Carriage by Air Act, R.S.C. 1952, c. 45, Schedule I (Warsaw Convention), especially Arts. 3, 4, and 22.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Negligent misrepresentation (opinion/estimate): plaintiff must prove more than that the estimate was wrong; must show the error resulted from a lack of reasonable care/skill (“lack of skill, competence or diligence” / failure to exercise “such care as the circumstances required”).
BaselineA: Common law (negligent misrepresentation duty of care and standard of care), relying on Hedley Byrne & Co. Ltd. v. Heller & Partners Ltd. and Mutual Life & Citizens’ Assurance Co. Ltd. v. Evatt as discussed in the reasons.
CaseB_TestB: Extra-territoriality / s. 92 territorial limits for intangible pith-and-substance: (1) identify pith and substance and a provincial head of power; (2) determine if pith and substance is “in the Province”; if intangible, assess “relationships among the enacting territory, the subject matter of the legislation and the persons made subject to it” to see if the law has a “meaningful connection” to the province and respects other jurisdictions’ sovereignty.
BaselineB: Common law / constitutional doctrine interpreting Constitution Act, 1867, s. 92 (esp. s. 92(13)) and territorial limits, drawing on cases including Churchill Falls (Reference re Upper Churchill Water Rights Reversion Act) and Unifund as cited in the reasons.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Parole Act s. 10(1)(e): the National Parole Board may revoke parole after sentence expiry if, at the time of revocation, the person is “in custody pursuant to a warrant issued under section 16” (and habeas corpus review is confined to the face of the warrants; no duty to give reasons beyond ‘parole suspended/revoked’).
BaselineA: Statute (Parole Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. P-2, ss. 10(1)(e), 16; plus Canadian Bill of Rights, s. 2(c)(i), s. 2(e) as argued). Key prior cases referenced: Ex p. McCaud; Howarth v. National Parole Board; Re Shumiatcher.
JudgeA: Ritchie J. (for Judson, Ritchie, Pigeon and Beetz JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Equitable compensation for Crown breach of fiduciary duty over reserve land: assess the beneficiary’s “lost opportunity” by asking “what position would the beneficiary be in had the fiduciary fulfilled its obligations?”, with factual causation (not limited by foreseeability/remoteness), assessed with hindsight, and guided by equitable presumptions (e.g., most favourable use); here, compensation must reflect the lost opportunity to negotiate on the basis of the land’s value to the hydroelectricity project.
BaselineB: Common law of Crown fiduciary duty and equitable compensation (Guerin; Canson; Osoyoos; Wewaykum; Blueberry River; etc.), applied in the statutory/treaty context (Indian Act, R.S.C. 1927, c. 98, ss. 48, 50, 51; Treaty No. 3).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Excise Tax Act sales-tax exemption: whether machinery/apparatus is used by a manufacturer/producer 'directly in the manufacture or production of goods' (excludes mere distribution; regulators that merely control flow/pressure are not 'production')
BaselineA: Statute: Excise Tax Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-13, s. 29(1) and Schedule III, Part XIII, para. 1(a)(i) ("machinery and apparatus ... for use by them directly in (i) the manufacture or production of goods")
CaseB_TestB: Scope-of-retainer determination for solicitor/counsel negligence: the 'crucial question' is the nature and scope of the adviser’s retainer (a factual finding not to be disturbed on appeal absent misapprehension of evidence), which determines whether a duty included advising on limitation periods
BaselineB: Common law (professional negligence/solicitor-client duty) applied through appellate review principle: findings of fact on scope of retainer should not be upset "save for error arising from misapprehension of the evidence"
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Patent Act s. 41(1): whether an invention relates to a food substance “prepared or produced by chemical processes” — apply a “popular” (ordinary) meaning assessed by an “informed layman” looking at the process “as a whole”, asking whether chemical operations play a “significant part” (not merely incidental) in producing the substance
BaselineA: Statute: Patent Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. P-4, s. 41(1), interpreted through SCC precedents Continental Soya Co. Ltd. v. J.R. Short Milling Co. (Canada) Ltd., [1942] S.C.R. 187 and Laboratoire Pentagone Ltée v. Parke, Davis & Co., [1968] S.C.R. 307
JudgeA: Dickson J. (for Laskin C.J. and Martland, Judson, Spence and Dickson JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Adequacy of an indictment: it is sufficient if it gives the accused “reasonable information” to identify the transaction and prepare a defence; sufficiency depends on the offence and facts; time need not be exact unless essential and no prejudice; in multiple-conspiracy proof, a conspiracy lies within the indictment if it included some accused, occurred sometime within the alleged time span, and had as its object the type of crime alleged
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 510, 512, 516(1)(g), informed by SCC/common law principles in R. v. Côté, [1978] 1 S.C.R. 8; R. v. Wis Development Corp., [1984] 1 S.C.R. 485; R. v. Cotroni, [1979] 2 S.C.R. 256; R. v. B. (G.), [1990] 2 S.C.R. 30
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 1 justification (Oakes proportionality) applied contextually: infringement must be a "reasonable limit" that can be "demonstrably justified"; requires (1) pressing and substantial objective and (2) proportionality: "rationally connected", "impair ... as little as possible" (minimal impairment), and proportionality of salutary vs deleterious effects
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional text + common law framework: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 1 (and s. 2(b)); baseline framework from R. v. Oakes, [1986] 1 S.C.R. 103 (pressing/substantial objective + proportionality: rational connection, minimal impairment, overall proportionality)
JudgeA: McLachlin J. (reasons leading to the Court’s disposition on s. 1)
CaseB_TestB: Meiorin justification test for a workplace standard alleged to be discriminatory, and how a collective-agreement termination clause fits: employer must justify by showing (1) purpose rationally connected to job performance; (2) adopted in honest and good faith belief it was necessary; (3) "reasonably necessary"—i.e., "impossible to accommodate" affected employees "without imposing undue hardship"; the negotiated absence period is a relevant factor but "does not definitively determine" accommodation and undue hardship is assessed "globally" from the start of the absence
BaselineB: Common law / human rights jurisprudence applying human rights legislation: baseline from British Columbia (Public Service Employee Relations Commission) v. BCGSEU ("Meiorin"), [1999] 3 S.C.R. 3 (para. 54) and related duty-to-accommodate cases (e.g., O’Malley; Central Okanagan v. Renaud); applied in light of Quebec Charter of human rights and freedoms (ss. 10, 20) and the collective agreement clause (e.g., termination after "thirty-sixth (36th) month of absence")
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Indian Act s. 88 provincial-law applicability/inconsistency analysis: provincial law of general application applies to Indians (via s. 88) except to the extent it is "inconsistent" with the Indian Act; here, adoption under B.C. Adoption Act s. 10(2) ("for all purposes" severing natural-parent relationship) does not remove an Indian child’s entitlement to be registered under Indian Act s. 11(1)(d), so no inconsistency on the key issue of registrability
BaselineA: Statute: Indian Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-6, s. 88 (and s. 11(1)(d) registrability); interacting with Adoption Act, R.S.B.C. 1960, c. 4, s. 10(2) ("for all purposes")
CaseB_TestB: Collins s. 24(2) exclusion framework (as organized in Greffe): whether admitting evidence would bring the administration of justice into disrepute, assessed by three categories—(1) fairness of the trial, (2) seriousness of the Charter breach (including whether police had "reasonable and probable grounds"; conclusory informer tips insufficient without detail/reliability indicia), and (3) effect of exclusion on the repute of justice—applied to exclude evidence where cumulative ss. 8/10 breaches were serious
BaselineB: Statute/constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 24(2) (exclusion if admission would "bring the administration of justice into disrepute"), applying the common-law/precedential framework from R. v. Collins
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Termination (determination) of a continuing guarantee by “notice in writing”: notice need not use set words but must be explicit and unequivocal (not merely a ‘wish’ or ‘preference’) so the creditor is left in no doubt
BaselineA: Contract (guarantee) term: clause (4) allowing the guarantor to “by notice in writing delivered to the Manager ... determine ... liability ... in respect of liabilities thereafter incurred or arising”
CaseB_TestB: Admissibility/use of an accused’s post-caution silence: unless the Crown establishes “real relevance and a proper basis”, questions about silence and evidence of ensuing silence should not be admitted; if admitted, the jury must be instructed to ignore it (no adverse inference)
BaselineB: Common law right to silence (as discussed via Rothman v. The Queen; R. v. Robertson; R. v. Symonds) and Charter s. 7 recognition (Hebert v. The Queen)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Tomko s. 49(2) interim cease-and-desist order validity: Board/Panel may issue an interim order ex parte if "satisfied after investigation" that s. 48 was breached; "notwithstanding any provision of this Act"; investigation may be done through Board officers; interim order may be directed to "any person" and against "any activity or action" so long as related to the illegal work stoppage
BaselineA: Statute (Trade Union Act, 1972 (N.S.), c. 19, ss. 48, 49(2), 15(9)-(10))
CaseB_TestB: YCJA youth sentencing interpretation: general deterrence is not a sentencing principle under the YCJA (no statutory basis to impose a harsher sanction "to deter others"); and s. 42(2)(o) does not require a 2/3 custody and 1/3 supervision split (unlike s. 42(2)(n))
BaselineB: Statute (Youth Criminal Justice Act, S.C. 2002, c. 1, ss. 3, 38, 42(2)(n), 42(2)(o), 50(1); Criminal Code, s. 718(b) referenced via s. 50(1) exclusion)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Cities and Towns Act s. 622 notice: if the plaintiff proves they were “prevented from giving such notice for any reason deemed sufficient by the court or judge” (s. 622(4)), then after the 15-day period the plaintiff is “permanently released from the obligation to give notice” and may sue without later giving notice
BaselineA: Statute — Cities and Towns Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 193, s. 622(1), (3), (4), (5) (especially s. 622(4) and (5))
CaseB_TestB: Judicial review of a consensual labour arbitrator’s collective-agreement interpretation: courts must ask whether the arbitrator’s conclusion is a “patently unreasonable” interpretation / whether it is “one which the agreement would reasonably bear”
BaselineB: Common law (judicial review of arbitration awards), drawing on SCC labour-arbitration review jurisprudence including Bell Canada v. Office and Professional Employees' Union, [1974] S.C.R. 335 and CUPE v. New Brunswick Liquor Corp., [1979] 2 S.C.R. 227 (as cited in the reasons)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Admissibility of similar fact evidence: other misconduct is inadmissible to show propensity, but is admissible if "relevant to an issue before the jury" (e.g., whether the act was "designed or accidental" or to rebut a defence), and is admitted "not to prove commission of the crime" but "to establish guilty intent"; with only a very limited discretion to exclude gravely prejudicial evidence of trifling probative value (Noor Mohamed/Wray).
BaselineA: Common law evidence rule on similar fact evidence (Makin v. Attorney General for New South Wales; Thompson v. The King; Noor Mohamed v. The King) as applied in Canada via R. v. Wray; applied in context of Criminal Code ss. 191-192 (now 202-203).
CaseB_TestB: Municipal valuation—choice of method: where "special circumstances make it impossible to fix the realizable value of property by the usual methods", "whatever method is appropriate in the circumstances may be used" to estimate "actual value" (including the "developer’s approach").
BaselineB: Statutory municipal valuation requirement of "actual value" under the Charter of the City of Montreal, S.Q. 1959-60, c. 102, informed by prior valuation jurisprudence (Sun Life Assurance Co. of Canada v. City of Montreal and related cases).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Admissibility of similar fact evidence to prove mens rea (guilty intent) in criminal negligence: similar acts are admissible if relevant to an issue (e.g., whether the act was “designed or accidental” or to rebut a defence otherwise open), and are admitted “not to prove commission of the crime mentioned in the indictment but to establish guilty intent”.
BaselineA: Common law evidence rule on similar fact evidence (general exclusionary rule and its exception), as stated in Makin v. Attorney General for New South Wales and discussed with Thompson v. The King, Noor Mohamed v. The King, and R. v. Wray; applied in context of Criminal Code ss. 191-192 (now 202-203).
CaseB_TestB: Issue estoppel on a subsequent perjury charge: the Crown is estopped from re-litigating an issue decided in the accused’s favour “unless it is tendering, in addition to or in lieu of the evidence previously adduced, evidence that was not at the time of the first trial available by the exercise of reasonable diligence”.
BaselineB: Common law doctrine of res judicata/issue estoppel and fraud exception (e.g., Duchess of Kingston’s Case; Gushue v. The Queen; DPP v. Humphrys), adapted to criminal proceedings and perjury prosecutions.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory interpretation of technical terms: apply the common/ordinary meaning shared by both official-language versions; here, “tetracycline and its derivatives” captures only things actually “obtained from” tetracycline (not merely in the same scientific ‘group’). Key quotes: “statutes are to be construed according to the meaning of the words in common language”; “the primary meaning in common language is that of a thing obtained from another”; under the Official Languages Act the “concept” must be one “to which in its expression in both versions … the reference is apt”, so select “a thing actually derived from another.”
BaselineA: Statute/regulation interpretation: Customs Tariff Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-41, s. 12 and Schedule A (tariff item 92944-1) as amended by Order in Council (SOR/69-8) exempting antibiotics except “tetracycline and its derivatives”; bilingual-interpretation baseline from Official Languages Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. O-2, s. 8(2)(b).
CaseB_TestB: Limits of inherent/implied jurisdiction re amici remuneration: courts may appoint amici only exceptionally where “necessary to permit a particular proceeding to be successfully and justly adjudicated”, but “absent authority flowing from a constitutional challenge or a statutory provision” courts’ inherent/implied jurisdiction “does not extend to setting rates of compensation for amici and ordering the provinces to pay.” If payment cannot be agreed, the judge’s recourse may be a stay until an amicus can be found.
BaselineB: Common law / constitutional principles governing inherent and implied jurisdiction (as described via prior cases such as MacMillan Bloedel and Caron) and separation of powers; the majority frames the key limit as applying “absent authority flowing from a constitutional challenge or a statutory provision.”
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Trustee’s statutory duty to insure bankrupt’s “insurable property” (including hypothecated property) and resulting personal liability for omission: under Bankruptcy Act s. 9(1)-(2), trustee must “forthwith temporarily insure and keep insured ... all the insurable property of the bankrupt” and, if insurance is cancelled/insufficient, must replace it and at least notify the secured (hypothecary) creditor; failure is a fault grounding personal liability.
BaselineA: Statute: Bankruptcy Act, R.S.C. 1952, c. 14, ss. 9(1)-(2) (duty/automatic payable-to-trustee effect), s. 171 (leave requirement), and definitions in s. 2 ("property", "secured creditor").
CaseB_TestB: Charitable status under the fourth Pemsel head for ITA registration: purposes must be (a) of “public benefit”/“beneficial to the community” and (b) “in a way the law regards as charitable”; applied via the Vancouver Society/D’Aguiar approach (trend/analogy, anomalies, and cross-check whether property can be applied to non-charitable purposes).
BaselineB: Combination: Statute (Income Tax Act, ss. 149.1(1) “charitable organization”, 248(1) “registered charity”/RCAAA) relying on common law meaning of charity (Pemsel; Vancouver Society adopting D’Aguiar framework).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Eligibility for a Quebec seat under Supreme Court Act s. 6 requires current membership: appointee must be appointed “from among” current judges of the Quebec Court of Appeal/Superior Court or current Quebec advocates (with the s. 5 ten-year standing requirement applying). The Court holds s. 6 “impliedly excludes former members of those institutions and imposes a requirement of current membership” and that “at the time of appointment, the appointee [must] be a current member of the Quebec bar with at least 10 years standing”.
BaselineA: Statute (Supreme Court Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. S-26, ss. 5 and 6; interpreted in light of constitutional entrenchment under Constitution Act, 1982, Part V, esp. s. 41(d))
JudgeA: The Chief Justice and LeBel, Abella, Cromwell, Karakatsanis and Wagner JJ.
CaseB_TestB: Section 15(1) Charter equality test (two-step): (1) whether the law “on its face or in its impact, draw[s] a distinction based on an enumerated or analogous ground”; and (2) whether it “impose[s] burdens or den[ies] a benefit in a manner that has the effect of reinforcing, perpetuating or exacerbating . . . disadvantage” (Taypotat/Quebec v. A framework), applied to the s. 38 Pay Equity Act delay/retroactivity issue.
BaselineB: Common law / constitutional doctrine (Charter s. 15(1) framework from Quebec (Attorney General) v. A and Kahkewistahaw First Nation v. Taypotat; applied to Pay Equity Act, CQLR, c. E-12.001, s. 38)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Highway Victims Indemnity Fund payment obligation and limitation period: claimant must meet HVIA ss. 36-38 requirements (apply within 1 year; sworn declaration that judgment unsatisfied and “no insurer will benefit”; authentic copy of judgment), after which the Fund “has no choice” and “shall satisfy the judgment” within 7 days; action against Fund is prescribed by 30 years (C.C. art. 2265) because it is “based on the judgments obtained, not on the liability”.
BaselineA: Statute (Highway Victims Indemnity Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 232, ss. 36-39) plus Civil Code prescription rules (arts. 2262, 2265).
CaseB_TestB: Fatal Accidents Act damages assessment methodology: determine dependants’ annual loss of support (net of income tax per majority), then calculate the present value of a lump sum that will replace that annual amount over the relevant period using a discount rate based on “present rates of return on long-term investments with an allowance for the effects of future inflation”, and then make “some reduction for contingencies”.
BaselineB: Statute (The Fatal Accidents Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 164) as interpreted through common-law damages principles; SCC references to Andrews v. Grand & Toy Alberta Ltd., Thornton v. Board of School Trustees, Arnold v. Teno, and overruling/not following Gehrmann v. Lavoie on tax treatment.
JudgeB: Dickson J. (for Laskin C.J. and Martland, Ritchie, Pigeon, Dickson and Beetz JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Equitable prejudgment interest for improper withholding of a just debt: where payment of a just debt has been improperly withheld and it is fair and equitable to compensate, the court should award interest for such time and at such rate as it thinks right (here: contractor’s bank borrowing rate).
BaselineA: Common law/equitable principle from Toronto Railway Co. v. City of Toronto, [1906] A.C. 117 (as followed in The Custodian v. Blucher, [1927] S.C.R. 420), applied alongside statutory context (Interest Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-18, ss. 3, 12, 13; Supreme Court Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. S-19, s. 52).
CaseB_TestB: Dixon two-step test for post-conviction remedy for Crown non-disclosure: (1) is there a reasonable possibility the undisclosed information affects the reliability of the conviction? If yes, new trial. (2) if not, is there a reasonable possibility the non-disclosure affected overall trial fairness (lost lines of inquiry/opportunities), considering defence due diligence? If yes, new trial.
BaselineB: Charter-based doctrine under Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 7 and 24(1), building on common law disclosure framework from R. v. Stinchcombe, [1991] 3 S.C.R. 326 (and related SCC cases cited: Egger, Chaplin, Carosella, etc.).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Doctrine/rule of recent possession: once Crown proves (1) goods were recently stolen and (2) accused possessed them, jury may infer guilt; if an explanation “may reasonably be true”, it must be considered and can raise a reasonable doubt; Crown need not adduce evidence of ‘no explanation’ and the jury instruction is not barred by Canada Evidence Act s. 4(5).
BaselineA: Common law rule of evidence (recent possession) as stated in R. v. Schama; R. v. Abramovitch and applied/approved in SCC cases including Richler v. The King; Ungaro v. The King; Graham v. The Queen; Tremblay v. The Queen; R. v. Graham.
CaseB_TestB: Imperial Tobacco extraterritoriality framework for provincial legislation: (1) identify pith and substance by purpose and effects; (2) assess territorial limits by asking whether the law has a “meaningful connection” to the province and respects other governments’ sovereignty (applied to uphold ORA s. 11 as procedural under s. 92(14)).
BaselineB: Common law constitutional division-of-powers framework from British Columbia v. Imperial Tobacco Canada Ltd. (2005 SCC 49), applied to Constitution Act, 1867 s. 92 territorial limits.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Drunkenness negating mens rea for murder: intoxication must render the accused "incapable of forming the specific intent"; mere drink-induced propensity to violence "falling short of incapacity" is insufficient (Beard approach as charged to jury).
BaselineA: Common law (Director of Public Prosecutions v. Beard) applied alongside Criminal Code s. 212(a) intent requirement for murder.
CaseB_TestB: Rebutting the Criminal Code s. 258(1)(d.1) presumption with "straddle evidence": evidence placing BAC in a range that straddles 80 mg/100 mL "may be capable of raising a reasonable doubt" and is weighed "in the light of all of the evidence at trial" (Gibson).
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code s. 258(1)(d.1)) as interpreted/applied through R. v. Gibson, 2008 SCC 16.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Drunkenness and mens rea for murder: intoxication negatives intent only if it renders the accused incapable of forming the specific intent; mere impairment/greater propensity to violence is insufficient
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code s. 212(a) (as referenced)) plus common law intoxication doctrine (DPP v. Beard)
CaseB_TestB: Section 23 “numbers warrant” sliding-scale placement: (1) determine long-term number of students who will eventually avail; (2) compare to majority-language schools (province-wide if needed) with a rebuttable presumption of pedagogical/cost appropriateness; (3) determine level of services (homogeneous school if comparable and presumption not rebutted)
BaselineB: Constitution (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 23) as interpreted in Mahe v. Alberta (sliding scale; pedagogy and cost factors)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Labour Code s. 108(1)(b) judicial review limit: court may intervene only for an "error of law affecting the jurisdiction" of a labour arbitrator; no such jurisdictional error where the arbitrator addressed the submitted question and considered the relevant circumstances (no "sin of omission" amounting to jurisdictional error).
BaselineA: Statute: Labour Code of British Columbia Act, 1973, s. 108(1)(b) (and s. 108 generally limiting review to specified grounds).
CaseB_TestB: Garofoli leave/threshold test for cross-examining a wiretap affiant: leave requires showing a "reasonable likelihood" that cross-examination "will elicit testimony of probative value" on the issue for the reviewing judge (i.e., tending to undermine a statutory precondition/basis for the authorization).
BaselineB: Common law: R. v. Garofoli, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 1421 (threshold/leave requirement for cross-examining the affiant on a wiretap review).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Appellate non-interference with concurrent findings of fact: SCC will not interfere unless satisfied the trial decision was wrong and there was no evidence to support it
BaselineA: common law (appellate review/deference doctrine for concurrent findings of fact; articulated in this case as a general proposition without specific prior SCC case citation)
CaseB_TestB: Division of powers “integral element” test for federal jurisdiction over matters affecting s. 92(10) undertakings: federal regulation is permissible only if the matter is an integral element of the core federal competence; otherwise provincial law of general application applies
BaselineB: common law constitutional doctrine (integral element approach) applied to s. 92(10) undertakings; key baseline cases cited include Construction Montcalm Inc. v. Minimum Wage Commission and Northern Telecom Ltd. v. Communications Workers of Canada
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Fire policy statutory condition 10(a): insurer not relieved of liability for property “owned by any other person” unless insured’s interest stated — satisfied if insured has an insurable interest (no need to specify nature of interest where not required)
BaselineA: Statute (Quebec Insurance Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 295, s. 240 statutory conditions; especially statutory condition 10(a)) and Civil Code art. 2571 C.C.
CaseB_TestB: Section 8 coroner/police ‘piggyback’ framework for bodily samples: when non-police seizure later used in criminal prosecution, court must assess whether police actions constitute an independent state seizure or render the initial coroner seizure unreasonable (Hunter warrant requirement applies once appropriated for law enforcement)
BaselineB: Common law/constitutional doctrine under Charter s. 8 (Hunter v. Southam; R. v. Dyment) applied alongside statute (Coroners Act, R.S.O. 1980, c. 93, s. 16(2), (5))
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Adjournment to permit representation by counsel: an adjournment necessary to exercise the s. 577(3) right to make full defence by counsel may be refused only for a reason based on established facts; refusal is reviewable if based on reasons not well founded in law (especially where it deprives a party of rights).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 577(3) and 613) plus prior case law on review of discretion (e.g., Spataro v. Regina; Talbot v. Regina referenced).
JudgeA: Pigeon J. (for Laskin C.J. and Judson, Spence, Pigeon, Dickson and Beetz JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Equitable compensation for breach of fiduciary duty (solicitor non-disclosure): compensate actual loss assessed with hindsight; foreseeability not required; but recovery is limited to losses which, on a common-sense view of causation, were caused by the breach (no recovery for independent third-party losses absent a direct link).
BaselineB: Common law/equity (fiduciary duty and equitable compensation), drawing on cases discussed in the reasons (notably Nocton v. Lord Ashburton; Guerin v. The Queen; Jacks v. Davis; Doyle v. Olby).
JudgeB: McLachlin J. (for Lamer C.J. and L'Heureux-Dubé and McLachlin JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Quebec declinatory exception to jurisdiction: filing the exception does not automatically shift the burden to the plaintiff; court determines jurisdiction (domicile/residence) on the whole record (art. 68 C.C.P.), with a citizenship-based presumption of principal residence in Canada (Canadian Citizenship Act, s. 10) supporting Montreal residence
BaselineA: Statute (Quebec Code of Civil Procedure, arts. 68 and 70; Canadian Citizenship Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-19, s. 10)
CaseB_TestB: When (and how) state/police misconduct can reduce sentence: if misconduct relates to the circumstances of the offence or the offender, it may be treated as a mitigating factor within Criminal Code sentencing; generally unnecessary to invoke Charter s. 24(1), and sentence reductions must stay within statutory limits (no going below mandatory minimums absent constitutional invalidity), save possibly exceptional egregious cases
BaselineB: Statute/constitutional text (Criminal Code, ss. 718–718.2 and mandatory minimum provisions; Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 24(1))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Contractual interpretation of warranty: “depreciation” in the clause/letter means accounting depreciation (write-off over useful life), not “full capital cost allowance” under the Income Tax Act; the parenthetical “(using capital cost allowance rates)” refers to rates only, not adoption of the CCA system, so no breach if depreciation was taken on all vehicles for the period in service at those rates.
BaselineA: Common law (interpretation/construction of a contractual warranty clause, read with the incorporated auditor’s letter).
CaseB_TestB: Youth court power under Young Offenders Act: despite s. 19(2) (“find ... guilty or not guilty or make an order dismissing the charge”), a youth court judge has no jurisdiction to dismiss a charge merely because it “ought never to have been laid”; absent abuse of process/constitutional exception, prosecutorial discretion governs unless Parliament makes a contrary intention “manifest” with “irresistible clearness”.
BaselineB: Statute (Young Offenders Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. Y-1, especially ss. 19(2) and 3(1), read with general criminal procedure principles of prosecutorial discretion).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Crown appeal from acquittal after legal error: Crown must show the verdict "would not necessarily have been the same" absent the misdirection (White v. R. test), applied where jury was wrongly told it could not draw an unfavourable inference from accused’s failure to testify (especially on alibi).
BaselineA: Combination: statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 613(4) (appeal from acquittal) and s. 618(2)) plus common law gloss from White v. R., [1947] S.C.R. 268 (as followed in R. v. Gauthier, [1977] 1 S.C.R. 441). Also interprets Canada Evidence Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-10, s. 4(5) (no comment on failure to testify).
CaseB_TestB: Group defamation/personal injury in Quebec civil liability: plaintiff must prove that an "ordinary person" would believe the remarks, viewed as a whole, brought discredit on each member’s reputation; for group comments, court conducts a contextual, non-exhaustive multi-factor analysis (e.g., group size, homogeneity/organization, identifiability, stigma, plaintiff’s relationship to group, precision of allegations, seriousness/extravagance, plausibility, extrinsic context) to decide if each member suffered personal injury.
BaselineB: Statute/civil code framework: Civil Code of Québec, art. 1457 (fault, injury, causal connection) and related provisions on compensable injury (arts. 1607, 1611), plus procedural context under Code of Civil Procedure class action provisions (e.g., arts. 1002-1003, 1028, 1034, 1051). The key defamation injury standard is drawn from SCC civil-law defamation cases (Prud’homme v. Prud’homme; Néron).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Insurance Act standard auto policy exclusion: an insured is excluded if, on the admitted facts, they are "entitled to receive the benefits of any workmen’s compensation law or plan"—entitlement to receive is not dependent on having applied for and obtained a Board award
BaselineA: Statute (Ontario): Insurance Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 224, s. 232(1) and Schedule E, Exclusion 2(a)(ii) (standard auto policy wording mandated by statute), interpreted in light of the Workmen’s Compensation Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 505 (esp. ss. 3 and 8)
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 8 reasonableness framework (mutatis mutandis) for cross-border disclosure under Criminal Code s. 193(2)(e): (1) disclosure authorized by law (recipient is proper foreign authority + disclosure intended "in the interests of the administration of justice"), (2) the law is reasonable (not overbroad/vague; adequate safeguards), and (3) disclosure carried out in a reasonable manner (including, in risky contexts, whether the discloser knew/should have known of human-rights misuse risks)
BaselineB: Combination: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 193(2)(e)) assessed under Charter s. 8 using the common-law/Charter reasonableness framework from R. v. Collins and R. v. Caslake ("authorized by law, the law itself must be reasonable, and [it] must be carried out in a reasonable manner")
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Discretion to order service ex juris under Federal Court Rule 307 guided by forum conveniens: the “overriding consideration” is whether there exists “some other forum more convenient and appropriate for the pursuit of the action and for securing the ends of justice”; error to refuse solely because the cause of action has “no relation or connection with Canada”.
BaselineA: Statute + regulation/rules: Federal Court Act, R.S.C. 1970 (2nd Supp.), c. 10, ss. 22(2)(a), 43(1), 44; Federal Court Rules, Rule 307 (service ex juris).
JudgeA: Ritchie J. (for Ritchie, Pigeon, Beetz and de Grandpré JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Quebec medical malpractice causation (rejecting “loss of chance” as a substitute for causation where death/sickness has occurred): plaintiff must prove fault, damage, and causation “on the balance of probabilities”, considering “all the evidence: factual, statistical and that which the judge is entitled to presume”; in some cases a court may presume causation where a fault presents “clear danger” and the danger materializes, unless there is a “strong indication to the contrary”; if not satisfied the fault caused “any real damage”, recovery is denied.
BaselineB: Civil law (Civil Code of Lower Canada) principles of civil responsibility and proof, including art. 1205 C.C.L.C. (presumptions), as applied/clarified in SCC causation jurisprudence (e.g., Snell v. Farrell referenced).
JudgeB: Gonthier J. (for Lamer C.J. and L'Heureux-Dubé, Sopinka, Gonthier, Cory and McLachlin JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Breach of municipal development agreement sewer-servicing obligation: developer must prove an actual or foreseeable inadequacy in sewer service to show the City failed to provide sewers/enlargements “required to properly service” the stage (a long-term master plan/report and a general development charge are not enough without evidence connecting them to serviceability of the project sewers).
BaselineA: Common law (contract interpretation/application of the parties’ 1966 development agreement, especially s. 31(a)(iii) requiring sewer construction/enlargement “required to properly service” each stage).
CaseB_TestB: Presumption of advancement in husband-to-wife gratuitous transfer: the presumption applies and stands unless the husband rebuts it; it is not rebutted by asserting the transfer was only to defeat creditors, and post-transfer conduct may confirm (rather than rebut) an intention to advance.
BaselineB: Common law (equitable presumptions in resulting trust/advancement; discussed with reference to Goodfriend v. Goodfriend and Tinker v. Tinker).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 613(1)(b)(iii) curative proviso: despite trial error(s), uphold conviction if the Crown satisfies the appellate court that the jury, properly charged, "could not, as reasonable men, have done otherwise than find the appellant guilty" (i.e., no "substantial wrong or miscarriage of justice")
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, s. 613(1)(b)(iii)) as applied through SCC precedent (Colpitts v. R., [1965] S.C.R. 739, quoting Brooks v. The King, [1927] S.C.R. 633)
CaseB_TestB: Treaty right to fish and trade for "necessaries" ("moderate livelihood") and infringement analysis: interpret treaty in historical/cultural context (including extrinsic evidence even absent ambiguity) and recognize a regulated treaty right to obtain necessaries through hunting/fishing and trading, with limits and any infringements requiring justification under the Badger/Sparrow framework
BaselineB: Combination: constitutional/statutory framework (Constitution Act, 1982, s. 35; Fisheries Act and regulations) plus common-law treaty-interpretation and s. 35 infringement/justification jurisprudence (e.g., Badger; Sparrow; Adams; Sioui; Sundown)
JudgeB: Binnie J. (for Lamer C.J. and L’Heureux-Dubé, Cory, Iacobucci and Binnie JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Hague Protocol ‘notice’ requirement for carrier to invoke liability limitation: carrier may rely on Art. 22 only if the passenger ticket/baggage check includes the required ‘notice’ in a form ‘calculated to attract attention’ (i.e., “noticeable”, not merely “reasonably readable”); otherwise limitation is unavailable
BaselineA: Statute (Carriage by Air Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-14 incorporating the Warsaw Convention as amended by the Hague Protocol): Hague Protocol Art. 3(1)(c) (required ‘notice’), Art. 3(2) (sanction: if ticket lacks required notice, carrier cannot avail itself of Art. 22), Art. 4(1)(c) (baggage check ‘notice’), and Art. 22 (liability limitation)
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 11(d) analysis of Criminal Code breathalyzer presumptions and rebuttal requirements, with severance: statutory presumptions risk conviction despite reasonable doubt; under s. 1, only the first rebuttal requirement (evidence tending to show the approved instrument malfunctioned or was operated improperly) is justified, while the additional causal-connection and ‘actual BAC under .08’ requirements are unconstitutional and severed
BaselineB: Statute + constitutional baseline: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, ss. 258(1)(c), 258(1)(d.01), 258(1)(d.1) (as amended by Tackling Violent Crime Act, S.C. 2008, c. 6), assessed under Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms ss. 11(d) and 1 (Oakes framework referenced but not treated as the ‘important test’ per instructions)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Municipal notice-of-accident limitation: the 15-day period in Montreal Charter art. 1088 runs from the claimant’s discovery/knowledge of the accident’s causal significance (not necessarily the accident date) where starting from the accident date would make the right of action practically illusory
BaselineA: Statute (An Act to revise and consolidate the Charter of the City of Montreal, 1959-60 (Que.), c. 102, art. 1088; plus interpretive context from Interpretation Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 1, ss. 52 and 61; and related SCC approach to notice provisions referenced via City of Ile Perrot v. Goulet-Wiseman)
CaseB_TestB: Discretionary test for discharging a civil jury after a reference to insurance: no automatic discharge; trial judge assesses whether the reference likely caused a “substantial wrong or miscarriage of justice” (real prejudice) making it unfair to continue, considers whether insurance is generally well known, and discharges only if prejudice cannot be cured (usually by instructions)
BaselineB: Common law (overruling Bowhey v. Theakston on automatic discharge; replacing it with a discretionary prejudice/miscarriage-of-justice approach; procedural context includes Supreme Court Rules, B.C. Reg. 310/76, Rule 41(6))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Admissibility of an accused’s prior in-court testimony (judicial statement under oath) without a voir dire: prior testimony given in a judicial proceeding is admissible as of right; voluntariness (including alleged unlawful compulsion) goes to weight for the jury, not admissibility, and the witness cannot claim s. 5(2) protection after the fact
BaselineA: Common law evidence rule on use of prior judicial testimony; key baseline authority relied on is R. v. Scott (1856) (and the long line of cases following it). Statutory context noted: Canada Evidence Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-10, s. 5(2) (protection against subsequent use if claimed at the time).
CaseB_TestB: Appellate intervention where trial reasons show failure to consider relevant evidence: an appellate court does not reassess guilt, but must review the record to ensure the trial court directed itself to all evidence on relevant issues; where reasons/record disclose a lack of appreciation or complete disregard of relevant evidence, the reviewing court must intercede (new trial)
BaselineB: Common law appellate review principles as articulated in prior SCC cases, especially MacDonald v. The Queen, [1977] 2 S.C.R. 665 and Ungaro v. The King, [1950] S.C.R. 430.
JudgeB: Estey J. (for Martland, Dickson, Beetz, Estey, McIntyre and Lamer JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Admissibility of Crown rebuttal evidence against an alibi / credibility: Crown may contradict an alibi only by attacking its “material points”; and the Crown may not contradict a collateral fact elicited in cross-examination (so rebuttal evidence of a different-date robbery was inadmissible).
BaselineA: Common law evidence principles (rebuttal to alibi must go to material points; collateral-fact rule barring Crown contradiction of collateral matters), with remedial overlay of Criminal Code s. 613(1)(b)(iii) (no substantial wrong/miscarriage).
CaseB_TestB: Intoxication and rape (majority): apply the specific-intent vs general/basic-intent distinction; rape is an offence of general intent, so self-induced intoxication is not a defence (subject to the narrow ‘incapable of forming intent’ idea, found not to arise on the facts).
BaselineB: Common law intoxication doctrine and the specific/general intent framework as stated in R. v. George (SCC) and Beard/Majewski (UK), with remedial overlay of Criminal Code s. 613(1)(b)(iii).
JudgeB: Pigeon J. (for Martland, Judson, Ritchie, Pigeon, Beetz and de Grandpré JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Applicability of mandatory supervision under Parole Act s. 15(1) where an inmate has multiple sentences: if the inmate falls within the proclaimed class (sentenced to penitentiary on/after Aug. 1, 1970), then s. 15(1) applies to the inmate’s release; and by s. 14(1) the multiple terms are “deemed to constitute one sentence” for purposes of applying s. 15(1). Key statutory trigger: an inmate released by remission where “the term of such remission exceeds sixty days” “shall… be subject to mandatory supervision”.
BaselineA: Statute: Parole Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. P-2, ss. 14(1), 15(1)-(2), as enacted/limited by Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1968-69 (Can.), c. 38, s. 101(2) and proclamation SOR/70-339 (effective Aug. 1, 1970).
CaseB_TestB: Whether insurance proceeds are deemed property transmitted on death under Succession Duties Act s. 26(1): apply s. 26(1) according to its “categorical, precise and general” text—“the proceeds of insurance policies… due by an insurer by reason or on account of the death of the person on whose life the insurance was effected”—which includes accident insurance; and “a death does not cease to be a death because it is accidental.”
BaselineB: Statute: Succession Duties Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 70, s. 26(1) (and related discussion of ss. 45(f), 46(1)); interpretive support from Civil Code arts. 1902, 1903, 1905, 1906 (terminology “sur la tête”/“on whose life”).
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Estate Tax Act: no “passing” (and no inclusion under s. 3(1)(a)) where a marriage contract gives the survivor ownership of the whole community retroactively; deceased not “competent to dispose” of community assets in the statutory sense
BaselineA: Statute (Estate Tax Act, 1958 (Can.), c. 29), especially ss. 3(1)(a), 3(2)(a), 3(2)(e) and 58(1)(i), applied with SCC precedents Sura v. MNR, [1962] S.C.R. 65 and The Royal Trust Company v. MNR, [1968] S.C.R. 505
CaseB_TestB: Treaty 8/NRTA geographic limit: treaty right of access to hunt for food on private land turns on “visible, incompatible land use” (case-by-case); plus Sparrow justification framework applies to prima facie infringements
BaselineB: Constitutional/treaty instruments and common-law framework: Treaty No. 8 (1899) and Natural Resources Transfer Agreement, 1930, para. 12 (Constitution Act, 1930, Schedule 2), with justification analysis drawn from R. v. Sparrow, [1990] 1 S.C.R. 1075
JudgeB: Cory J. (majority reasons on the key test)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Contractual tax-adjustment clause applies only to a “tax, duty, charge or fee” imposed on the seller (Imperial) “in respect of bunker fuel oil” (the product) or its “production, manufacture, sale or delivery” by the seller; it does not cover upstream crude-oil cost increases (including foreign taxes/royalties passed through by affiliates) and does not treat crude-oil imports as deliveries of “the product”.
BaselineA: Common law (contract interpretation) applied to clause 9 of the parties’ supply agreement (price adjustment for tax changes).
CaseB_TestB: Van der Peet test (applied to self-government/gambling claim under s. 35(1)): “in order to be an aboriginal right an activity must be an element of a practice, custom or tradition integral to the distinctive culture of the aboriginal group claiming the right”; court must (1) “identify the exact nature of the activity claimed” and (2) determine whether it was “a defining feature of the culture in question” prior to European contact.
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine interpreting Constitution Act, 1982, s. 35(1), as set out in R. v. Van der Peet (applied here to asserted self-government/gambling regulation).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Negligence duty/foreseeability limit for occupier/railway: liability only if the injury was a "reasonably foreseeable result"; no duty where "no reasonable occupier could have reasonably foreseen" the child would leave safety and attempt to board a moving train
BaselineA: Common law negligence/occupiers’ liability principles (foreseeability and duty of care), with a statutory fencing reference to Railway Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. R-2, s. 214 (found not breached/decisive). Prior SCC cases referenced as baseline context include Mitchell v. C.N.R., [1975] 1 S.C.R. 592; Paskivski v. Canadian Pacific Ltd., [1976] 1 S.C.R. 687; Amos v. New Brunswick Electric Power Commission, [1977] 1 S.C.R. 500; Ouellet v. Cloutier, [1947] S.C.R. 521; University Hospital Board v. Lepine, [1966] S.C.R. 561.
JudgeA: de Grandpré J. (for Martland, Judson, Ritchie, Pigeon, Beetz and de Grandpré JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Section 7 "fair hearing" requirements in security-certificate proceedings: a fair process must include (1) a hearing, (2) an independent and impartial magistrate, (3) a decision on the facts and the law, and (4) the right to know and answer the case; if full disclosure is impossible, "either the person must be given the necessary information, or a substantial substitute for that information must be found"
BaselineB: Constitutional/Charter baseline applying Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7 (and related analysis under s. 1), in the statutory context of Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, S.C. 2001, c. 27, ss. 77-85 (especially ss. 78, 80, 83-84).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory interpretation of Highway Victims Indemnity Act s. 43: Fund must satisfy judgment for unknown driver only up to the s. 14 cap ($35,000), and prior recovery from another liable party does not extinguish the Fund’s capped liability (no s. 38 deduction where victim received nothing from unknown driver). Key language: Fund satisfies judgment “to the same extent as if it had been rendered against the author of the accident”; this imports the s. 14 limit.
BaselineA: Statute: Highway Victims Indemnity Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 232, especially ss. 43 (unknown driver), 14 ($35,000 financial responsibility cap), 38 (deduction rule in Division XII), and 49(b),(e) (Fund powers).
CaseB_TestB: Sentencing treatment of collateral immigration consequences and appellate intervention: a sentencing judge may consider collateral immigration consequences only if the final sentence remains proportionate (Criminal Code s. 718.1); such consequences are “but one” relevant factor and must not “skew” sentencing. An appellate court may vary a sentence where the sentencing judge was unaware of the collateral immigration consequences (or counsel failed to advise), because a relevant factor was not considered.
BaselineB: Statute-informed common law sentencing framework: Criminal Code, ss. 718, 718.1, 718.2 (proportionality, parity, individualization) and the collateral consequence at issue under Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, s. 64; appellate sentencing intervention principle drawn from R. v. M. (C.A.).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Whether the trial judge must give the accomplice-evidence caution (danger of convicting on uncorroborated testimony) when a key witness may be an accomplice (and/or accessory after the fact); here, because the jury could not find the witness an accessory after the fact without also finding him an accomplice, the caution was required in any event
BaselineA: Common law rule of practice/caution on accomplice testimony (as discussed via Horsburgh v. The Queen and Davies v. DPP; also Vézeau on Crown appeal from acquittal/harmless error)
CaseB_TestB: Interpretation/application of Criminal Code s. 212(c) murder: (1) no requirement the dangerous act be unlawful; (2) if the dangerous act is unlawful, there must be a further unlawful object distinct from the immediate object of the dangerous act; (3) 'unlawful object' means an object which, if prosecuted fully, would amount to an indictable mens rea offence; (4) objective 'ought to know' is applied using the accused’s actual knowledge of surrounding circumstances, and intoxication is relevant to that knowledge
BaselineB: Statute — Criminal Code, ss. 205(5)(a) and 212(c) (with interpretation informed by prior SCC cases including Graves v. The King and R. v. Hughes)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Construction of Manitoba auto insurance exclusion: in s. 31(3)(h) (“death of, an insured”), “an insured” is read as referring to an insured under the particular certificate/contract under which indemnity is claimed; owner’s and driver’s certificates are “separate contracts” with “distinct coverages” and must be construed separately
BaselineA: Regulation/Statute: The Manitoba Public Insurance Corporation Act, C.S.M. c. A180 and Man. Reg. 333/74 (Manitoba Automobile Insurance Regulation), especially ss. 30 (definition of “insured”), 31(1), 31(2) and 31(3)(h) (“The Corporation shall not pay… (h) for loss or damages resulting from… the death of, an insured”)
CaseB_TestB: Treaty 8/NRTA limitation test for provincial game-law applicability: Treaty 8 hunting rights are limited by NRTA 1930, para. 12 to hunting “for food” (i.e., “for sustenance for the individual Indian or the Indian’s family”); if the activity is a “multi-stage process” involving sale/trafficking, it is an “act of commerce” and no longer protected, so provincial Wildlife Act s. 42 applies via Indian Act s. 88
BaselineB: Statute/Constitution/Treaty: Wildlife Act, R.S.A. 1980, c. W-9, ss. 42 and 1(s) (definition of “traffic”); Indian Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-6, s. 88; Treaty No. 8 (1899); Natural Resources Transfer Agreement, 1930 (Alberta), para. 12 (hunting “for food”)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 287 (as then worded): “telecommunication” requires transmission “by wire or cable” (not Hertzian waves/radio); no ‘partly by wire’ extension
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 287(1)(b) and definition in s. 287(2) (“telecommunication” means transmission “by wire or cable”).
CaseB_TestB: Immigration Act s. 19(1)(a)(ii) “excessive demands” on social services: individualized assessment of likely demands (reasonable probability, not remote possibility) requiring consideration of both medical and non-medical factors including family ability/willingness to pay
BaselineB: Statute: Immigration Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. I-2, s. 19(1)(a)(ii) (medical inadmissibility where admission “would cause or might reasonably be expected to cause excessive demands on health or social services”).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Municipal Act s. 455 licence-refusal discretion must be exercised judicially: refusal cannot rest on extraneous/irrelevant grounds (e.g., morality) and “in any particular case” means peculiar to the applicant (not a blanket prohibition of a business type).
BaselineA: Statute: Municipal Act, R.S.B.C. 1960, c. 255, s. 455 (and its “shall not be unreasonably refused” limit), read in the context of the Act’s other express by-law powers (e.g., ss. 870(n), 870(m), zoning provisions).
CaseB_TestB: IRPA security-certificate disclosure/fairness standard under Charter s. 7: the named person must receive an “incompressible minimum” of disclosure—“reasonably informed” means enough disclosure to give meaningful instructions to public counsel and meaningful guidance to special advocates; if non-disclosure prevents this, the Minister must withdraw the information/evidence (or the certificate must be quashed).
BaselineB: Statute interpreted in light of Charter s. 7: Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, S.C. 2001, c. 27, Division 9 (notably ss. 77(2), 78, 83(1)(e), 83(1)(i), 85.4(2)), as constrained by Charkaoui v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2007 SCC 9.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Appellate deference to trial findings of fact: an appellate court should not disturb findings of fact where there was credible evidence on which the trial judge could reasonably base the conclusion; it is not the function of an appellate court to reconsider the evidence and reach a different conclusion unless the evidence reasonably could not justify the trial judge’s conclusion.
BaselineA: Common law appellate review principle (as stated in the decision: “a well-known principle that appellate tribunals should not disturb findings of fact made by a trial judge if there were credible evidence before him on which he could reasonably base his conclusion”).
CaseB_TestB: Bona fide occupational qualification (BFOQ) under Ontario Human Rights Code s. 4(6): (1) subjective good-faith requirement—must be imposed honestly, in good faith, and in the sincerely held belief it is for adequate performance with reasonable dispatch, safety and economy and not for ulterior/extraneous reasons; and (2) objective requirement—must be objectively related and “reasonably necessary” to assure efficient and economical performance without endangering the employee, co-workers, or the public (with the employer bearing the burden on a balance of probabilities once prima facie discrimination is shown).
BaselineB: Statute: The Ontario Human Rights Code, R.S.O. 1970, c. 318, ss. 4(1) and 4(6) (and related procedure provisions including s. 14d).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal causation for unlawful act manslaughter: Crown must prove the unlawful act was “at least a contributing cause of death, outside the de minimis range” (not necessary to prove it caused each intermediate mechanism like vomiting/aspiration).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code), especially s. 205(1) (“A person commits homicide ... when directly or indirectly, by any means, he causes the death of a human being”), applied with common-law causation principles (incl. thin skull).
CaseB_TestB: Anns two-stage duty-of-care framework for recognizing a novel duty for pure economic loss (proximity/foreseeability → then residual policy factors may negate/limit duty); applied to reject a duty of care in commercial negotiations and in drafting tender specifications.
BaselineB: Common law: Anns v. Merton London Borough Council (two-stage duty of care analysis), as adopted in Kamloops (City of) v. Nielsen and applied in later SCC negligence/economic loss cases.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Crown bound by legislation/regulations only if expressly mentioned/referred to; otherwise (at common law) only by “necessary implication” where the statute’s purpose would be “wholly frustrated” if the Crown were not bound
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Interpretation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-23, s. 16 (and s. 28 definition of “Her Majesty”); common law rule from Bombay Province v. Bombay Municipal Corporation, [1947] A.C. 58 (“necessary implication”/“wholly frustrated”)
CaseB_TestB: Breach of contract where a stipulated term (here, cargo weight) is “material if not a critical term”; excessive deviation from the stipulated weight constitutes breach, engaging Civil Code art. 1065 damages (not nullity under art. 992 / not “mutual mistake”)
BaselineB: Statute (Civil Code): arts. 992 (error as cause of nullity) and 1065 (damages for breach of obligation)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Scope of CTC’s s. 11(x) exemption inquiry under the Lord’s Day Act: Commission must focus on the Act’s object (preventing gainful Sunday work) and whether exempting the work is needed to prevent undue delay in freight traffic; broader impacts on Sunday quiet/congestion are irrelevant
BaselineA: Statute: Lord’s Day Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. L-13, ss. 4 and 11(x) (interpreting “having regard to the object of this Act” and the Commission’s mandate under s. 11(x))
CaseB_TestB: Meaning of “bona fide pension plan” under Human Rights Code s. 3(6)(a): plan must be “subjectively and objectively bona fide” — “a legitimate plan, adopted in good faith and not for the purpose of defeating protected rights” (overall plan bona fides, not actuarial details)
BaselineB: Statute: Human Rights Code, R.S.N.B. 1973, c. H-11, s. 3(6)(a) (interpreting “bona fide retirement or pension plan”)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Combines conspiracy “undueness” test: an agreement is criminal only if, if carried into effect, it would prevent or lessen competition “unduly” — i.e., impose “improper, inordinate, excessive or oppressive restrictions” or “virtually reliev[e] the conspirators from the influence of free competition”; assess undueness by “considering whether competition would be unduly prevented or lessened if the design evidenced by the agreement were carried into effect”.
BaselineA: Statute: Combines Investigation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-23, s. 32(1)(c) (“prevent, or lessen, unduly, competition ... or in the price of insurance upon persons or property”). Interpreted with reference to SCC cases including Howard Smith Paper Mills v. The Queen, Weidman v. Shragge, Stinson-Reeb, and Container Materials.
CaseB_TestB: Unreasonable verdict (s. 686(1)(a)(i)) test: an appellate court asks whether the verdict is one “that a properly instructed jury or a judge could reasonably have rendered”; and may find unreasonableness where an essential inference/finding “is plainly contradicted by the evidence” relied on, or “is shown to be incompatible with evidence that has not otherwise been contradicted or rejected”; credibility findings are not to be disturbed unless they “cannot be supported on any reasonable view of the evidence”.
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(a)(i) (unreasonable verdict). Framework drawn from SCC precedents: Yebes; Biniaris; Sinclair; Beaudry; Burke.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Limits of the Hodge’s Case circumstantial-evidence instruction: it applies to proof of the act/identity, not to proof of intent; intent is assessed under the ordinary reasonable-doubt standard
BaselineA: Common law (jury instruction on circumstantial evidence) as treated in R. v. Mitchell, [1964] S.C.R. 471, and Hodge’s Case (1838)
CaseB_TestB: Interpretation of linked insurance policies: a reference in the fleet policy schedule to “See Garage Policy [number]” should be construed to give it effect (C.C. art. 1014), i.e., as referring to limits/premium, not negating the fleet policy’s third-party liability coverage; surrounding facts (including the liability card) may confirm intended coverage
BaselineB: Statute/civil law: Civil Code of Quebec arts. 1014 (and related interpretive provisions discussed, incl. arts. 1013, 1234, 2480) plus the insurance contract documents
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Burden of proof for alleged “impossibility of performance” (as a defence avoiding a contractual obligation): plaintiff proves fault, damage, causality; defendant who pleads impossibility must prove it under art. 1203 C.C. (difficulty is not enough).
BaselineA: Statute (Civil Code of Quebec): arts. 1701 (mandate), 984 and 1062 (object must be possible), and especially art. 1203 (“he who alleges facts in avoidance or extinction of the obligation must prove them”).
CaseB_TestB: Disqualification for municipal office under s. 6 Moncton Consolidation Act: whether an office-holder “directly or indirectly… have[s] any interest in any contract” with the City (other than as a shareholder) is assessed by giving “interested in” its ordinary meaning; a director/officer is ordinarily “interested” in the company’s municipal contracts.
BaselineB: Statute: Moncton Consolidation Act, 1946 (N.B.), c. 101, s. 6 (interpreted with reference to New Brunswick Interpretation Act, R.S.N.B. 1973, c. I-13, s. 17; and considered alongside Municipalities Act, R.S.N.B. 1973, c. M-22, ss. 71-72).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Interpretation of para. 12 Alberta Natural Resources Transfer Agreement: “Indians within the boundaries” includes all Indians physically in Alberta (not only Alberta residents), so they are subject to provincial game laws but retain the proviso right to hunt “for food at all seasons” on “unoccupied Crown lands” and other lands with a “right of access”.
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional instrument and treaty: Indian Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-6, s. 88 (provincial laws of general application apply to Indians “subject to the terms of any treaty”); Alberta Natural Resources Transfer Agreement, 1930, para. 12 (as confirmed by British North America Act, 1930); Treaty No. 6 hunting clause.
CaseB_TestB: Qualified privilege in libel: a communication is privileged where the maker has an “interest or a duty, legal, social or moral” to make it and the recipient has a corresponding interest/duty; on a privileged occasion, liability requires proof of malice, and the publisher is protected even if language is “violent or excessively strong” if, “having regard to all the circumstances”, he “might have honestly and on reasonable grounds believed” it was true/necessary.
BaselineB: Common law qualified privilege and malice: Adam v. Ward, [1917] A.C. 309 (definition and scope of privilege) and Netupsky v. Craig, [1973] S.C.R. 55 (malice inquiry), as applied to libel.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory obscenity test in Criminal Code s. 159(8) is exhaustive for sex-based obscenity across the Code (displacing Hicklin): a work is obscene if it is a “publication a dominant characteristic of which is the undue exploitation of sex (or sex plus crime, horror, cruelty, violence)” and this standard should be applied wherever “the allegation of obscenity revolves around sex considerations”.
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, s. 159(8) definition of obscenity) in tension with common law Hicklin obscenity test (R. v. Hicklin (1868)) as discussed via Brodie v. The Queen, [1962] S.C.R. 681.
CaseB_TestB: Duty to accommodate (employer/union) in adverse-effect discrimination: take “reasonable measures short of undue hardship”; undue hardship assessed contextually (e.g., “financial cost, disruption of a collective agreement, problems of morale of other employees, interchangeability of work force and facilities… [and] safety”), with union liability where it (1) helped create the discriminatory rule or (2) blocks a reasonable accommodation needed to remove the discriminatory effect.
BaselineB: Statute (Human Rights Act, S.B.C. 1984, c. 22, ss. 8(1), 8(4), 9) as interpreted through prior SCC duty-to-accommodate jurisprudence (O'Malley; Central Alberta Dairy Pool; Etobicoke; Bhinder).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 159(8) obscenity test as the exclusive standard for sex-based obscenity across the Code: a work is obscene if it is a “publication a dominant characteristic of which is the undue exploitation of sex, or of sex and … crime, horror, cruelty and violence” (s. 159(8)); Hicklin is displaced and s. 159(8) should be applied wherever “the allegation of obscenity revolves around sex considerations”.
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, s. 159(8) (and its interaction with ss. 159(1), 163, 164); contrasted with common law Hicklin test from R. v. Hicklin (1868) as discussed in Brodie v. The Queen).
CaseB_TestB: Meiorin duty-to-accommodate/undue hardship analysis applied to time-limited termination clauses: the negotiated absence period in a collective agreement is a relevant factor/evidence in assessing reasonable accommodation and undue hardship, but “does not definitively determine” entitlement because “each case must be evaluated on the basis of its particular circumstances”; undue hardship from absence is assessed “globally starting from the beginning of the absence”.
BaselineB: Common law / human rights framework (Meiorin test from BCGSEU; related accommodation jurisprudence such as Bergevin/Renaud) applied in the context of human rights legislation (Quebec Charter of human rights and freedoms) and a collective agreement clause.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Federal jurisdiction over cable television/broadcasting undertakings: no constitutional demarcation at the antenna; cable distribution receiving and retransmitting extra-provincial signals is a single interprovincial/international “undertaking”, and “programme content regulation is inseparable” from regulating that undertaking
BaselineA: Common law constitutional division-of-powers doctrine under the B.N.A. Act, ss. 91 and 92(10)(a), relying on the Privy Council’s Radio Reference (In re Regulation and Control of Radio Communication in Canada, [1932] A.C. 304) and related “undertaking” jurisprudence (e.g., Winner)
CaseB_TestB: Income Tax Act “proceeds of disposition” analysis for assumed obligations: purchaser’s assumption is included only if it is assumption of a distinct existing vendor liability; where the obligation is “embedded in the [property]” as a future cost that depresses value, it is not part of the “sale price” and is excluded regardless of contingency or contractual valuation
BaselineB: Statute — Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), s. 13(21) definition of “proceeds of disposition” (including “the sale price of property that has been sold”), applied with existing tax principle that assumption of a vendor’s liability may form part of sale price (e.g., Telus Communications (Edmonton) Inc.; Loyens; Lord Elgin Hotel)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Immovable by nature (Civil Code arts. 374 et seq.): a structure is immovable where it is a construction that adheres (directly or indirectly) to land or a building; for wire networks, “the vertical attachment of a network of wires to the ground is in itself enough to make these wires immovable”; ownership separation is irrelevant (“not a physical characteristic ... but a legal characteristic, which is irrelevant”).
BaselineA: Statute + civil law: Retail Sales Tax Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 71, ss. 2(3) (definition of “moveable property” by reference to what is immoveable “by the laws of this Province”) and 6 (tax on purchase of moveable property), interpreted by reference to Civil Code, arts. 374 et seq. (immovables), and prior SCC cases on networks as immovables by nature (Montreal Light, Heat and Power Consolidated v. Westmount; Lower St. Lawrence Power Co. v. L’Immeuble Landry Ltée).
CaseB_TestB: Punitive damages for breach of contract (wrongful dismissal): available but “rare”; require an actionable wrong beyond the breach (e.g., tort) and conduct that is “extreme ... deserving of full condemnation and punishment” (e.g., “harsh, vindictive, reprehensible and malicious”); in this case no punitive damages because the employer’s conduct was “not sufficiently offensive, standing alone, to constitute actionable wrong”.
BaselineB: Common law of damages for wrongful dismissal and punitive damages, relying on cases including Addis v. Gramophone Co. and Peso Silver Mines Ltd. (N.P.L.) v. Cropper (limits on dismissal damages), and punitive damages jurisprudence including Rookes v. Barnard, McElroy v. Cowper-Smith and Woodman, and H. L. Weiss Forwarding Ltd. v. Omnus; also referenced Restatement (Second) of Contracts s. 355 (punitive damages not for breach unless conduct is also a tort).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Parent’s contributory negligence / duty of care assessed by the “accepted standard of care by parents generally in the community” (a reasonably prudent parent in the circumstances)
BaselineA: Common law negligence (reasonableness standard), with the Court expressly grounding duty/standard analysis in Donoghue v. Stevenson (neighbour principle) and using prior negligence/contribution cases as reference points (e.g., Ware’s Taxi Ltd. v. Gilliham; Gambino v. Dileo; Beckerson v. Dougherty; Cowle v. Filion).
