CaseB_TestB: Interpretation of fire/insurance clause in land sale: purchaser must elect either (i) complete and take whatever insurance proceeds are owing, or (ii) cancel; attempting to impose extra conditions is repudiation the vendor may accept
BaselineB: Common law contract principles (election under contract terms; repudiation/acceptance) applied through interpretation of the parties’ agreement (standard-form clause 5 and “time of the essence” clause 9).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Matrimonial property beneficial interest via resulting trust from a common pool/joint account: where spouses intend a joint “common purse”, “in the absence of agreement to the contrary, a one-half interest in any investment purchased by a husband from a common pool of funds … will be considered to be held by him for the benefit of his wife” (legal title held in trust jointly); resulting trust presumption from contribution in “money or money’s worth” (rebuttable by proof of contrary intention).
BaselineA: Common law (resulting trust/common intention doctrine from Pettitt v. Pettitt; Gissing v. Gissing; Murdoch v. Murdoch; Thompson v. Thompson; and joint-account resulting trust reasoning from Jones v. Maynard; also general resulting trust principles such as Dyer v. Dyer).
CaseB_TestB: Access to court exhibits (audio/video tapes) test: apply MacIntyre balancing—presumptive openness subject to curtailment to protect “social values of superordinate importance” (notably “protection of the innocent”); for exhibits, the court as custodian must inquire into and may regulate the proposed use, and may deny unrestricted access where an acquitted person’s privacy interests outweigh public access, especially for exhibits “judicially determined to be inadmissible against him”.
BaselineB: Common law (open courts/access to judicial records framework from Attorney General of Nova Scotia v. MacIntyre; applied and extended to exhibits; with reference to Nova Scotia Civil Procedure Rule 30.11(6) on return of exhibits).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Limitation Act s. 6(4)(b) postponement test: time starts when a properly advised reasonable person would conclude the plaintiff could reasonably sue, considering the plaintiff’s serious, significant, and compelling interests/circumstances (no tactical delay)
BaselineA: Statute: Limitation Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 266, s. 6(4)(b) (within the broader s. 6(4) postponement scheme, including s. 6(4)(a) and s. 6(5) “appropriate advice” definition)
CaseB_TestB: Arbitration Act s. 15 stay framework in receivership: (1) technical prerequisites (arguable case) then (2) exceptions (balance of probabilities); arbitration agreement may be “inoperative” if enforcing it would compromise the orderly and efficient resolution of a court-ordered receivership (non-exhaustive factors)
BaselineB: Statute: Arbitration Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 55, s. 15(1)-(2), interpreted in light of Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. B-3, ss. 183(1) and 243(1)(c)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Start of 5-year prescription for engineers’ fees: prescription runs only when the fee is due—i.e., “on completion of the work” or, if suspended, “at the time it was suspended, after a decision clearly communicated” to the engineers (and, under the tariff, generally not before the call for tenders or clear termination/no-tenders notice).
BaselineA: Combination: Civil Code art. 2260(6) (extinctive prescription) + general principles of bilateral contracts/contract for work + Tariff of fee for Professional Engineers of the Province of Quebec (O.C. 891, 4/9/57) incorporated into the contract.
CaseB_TestB: Discretionary enforcement of letters rogatory under Canada Evidence Act s. 43: even if statutory/regulatory bars are uncertain, a court may refuse enforcement where doing so would run counter to asserted Canadian public policy/sovereignty; comity yields to public policy, and it is “not for a Court…to take issue with the government’s determination of public policy or to measure its impact.”
BaselineB: Statute: Canada Evidence Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-10, s. 43 (court “may, in its or his discretion” order examination/production), informed by comity principles and public policy limits discussed in the reasons (including Rio Tinto Zinc v. Westinghouse and Re Westinghouse (Ont. H.C.) as persuasive authorities).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 170 nudity offence: “nude” in s. 170(1)(a) means complete nudity; s. 170(2) is a deeming (enlarging) provision (“is” = “shall be deemed to be”) extending nudity to being “so clad as to offend against public decency or order”; therefore, for complete nudity the Crown need not prove offence to public decency/order and the accused cannot defend by showing compatibility with decency/order (lawful excuse remains a separate defence).
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, s. 170(1)(a) and s. 170(2) (with historical comparison to former s. 205A deeming language).
CaseB_TestB: Application of the Criminal Code s. 613(1)(b)(iii) proviso (“no substantial wrong or miscarriage of justice”): where the Crown improperly splits its case by calling reply evidence that raises new issues/attacks credibility and forces the accused to testify again, the proviso cannot be invoked because the appellate court cannot realistically assess the verdict after extracting the improperly adduced evidence; a new trial is required.
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, s. 613(1)(b)(iii) (appellate curative proviso) applied in light of criminal process principles against splitting the Crown’s case.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 170 nudity offence: for complete nudity in a public place, the Crown need not prove the nudity "offended against public decency or order"; s. 170(2) is a deeming (enlarging) provision so that "a person is nude" means "shall be deemed to be" nude when "so clad as to offend against public decency or order"
BaselineA: Statute — Criminal Code, s. 170(1)(a) and s. 170(2) (and interpretive comparison to predecessor s. 205A). Key interpretive holding: in s. 170(2) the verb "is" means "shall be deemed to be"; "nude" retains its ordinary meaning of "completely bare" and is only extended (not restricted) by s. 170(2).
CaseB_TestB: Availability of certiorari in criminal proceedings: certiorari is available to parties only for a "jurisdictional error" by a provincial court judge; jurisdictional errors occur where the court "fails to observe a mandatory provision of a statute" or "acts in breach of the principles of natural justice" (legal errors, including errors of law on the face of the record, are not enough for parties)
BaselineB: Common law constrained by statute — Criminal Code, s. 674 (general prohibition on interlocutory appeals) plus SCC jurisprudence on certiorari/extraordinary remedies (e.g., Cohen; Skogman; Dagenais; Cunningham). SCC contribution: categorical rule that for parties, certiorari lies only for jurisdictional error, and definition of jurisdictional error in the criminal context (mandatory statutory provision or natural justice breach).
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Workmen’s Compensation Act s. 8 “additional sum” entitlement where the Commission is subrogated: if the dependant’s civil claim (reduced for the victim’s contributory fault) is fully met or exceeded by compensation, there is no further “additional sum” claim; the Commission has priority to recover up to what it paid (s. 7(3) subrogation pleno jure).
BaselineA: Statute + Civil Code: Workmen’s Compensation Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 159, ss. 7(3) (subrogation pleno jure) and 8 (right to claim “any additional sum required”); Civil Code art. 1157 (partial payment and creditor priority) and art. 1056 (wrongful death claim reduced by victim fault).
CaseB_TestB: Employer’s obligation to pay under a contract of service after purported termination: payment obligation “depended upon the plaintiff’s being available and willing to provide the services”; by contracting to play for another team, the employee breached/repudiated and this “freed the respondent of any further obligation to pay salary under the contract.”
BaselineB: Common law contract principles applied to an employment contract (repudiation/anticipatory breach and dependency of payment on availability to perform), as applied through interpretation of the parties’ written contract terms (notably exclusivity/consent and termination/guarantee clauses).
JudgeB: McIntyre J. (for Dickson, Beetz and McIntyre JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Workmen’s Compensation Act s. 8 “additional sum” entitlement where Commission is subrogated: if the dependant’s civil claim (reduced for the victim’s contributory fault) is fully met or exceeded by compensation, there is no “additional sum” and the Commission has priority to recover up to what it paid
BaselineA: Statute + Civil Code (Workmen’s Compensation Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 159, ss. 7(3), 8; Civil Code arts. 1056, 1157; plus SCC cases on contributory fault and subrogation cited in the reasons: Rainville Automobile Ltd. v. Primiano; Hôpital Notre-Dame de l’Espérance and Théoret v. Laurent; Brink’s Express v. Plaisance distinguished)
CaseB_TestB: Institutional financial security requirement for judicial independence: any government measure affecting judges’ remuneration conditions (including eliminating an office conferring a clear economic benefit) must be preceded by an independent, effective and objective commission process; if recommendations are ignored, the decision must be justified on a “simple rationality test”
BaselineB: Constitution + Charter + prior SCC framework (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 11(d); Constitution Act, 1867, Preamble; applying/expanding Valente v. The Queen and Reference re Remuneration of Judges of the Provincial Court of Prince Edward Island (Provincial Court Judges Reference))
JudgeB: Gonthier J. (for L’Heureux-Dubé, Gonthier, Iacobucci, Major and Arbour JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Suspensive effect of serving an originating notice for prohibition/quash with a Rule 7 command to make a return forthwith: service (and, a fortiori, return) suspends the inferior court’s ability to proceed; non-compliance cannot improve the inferior court’s position
BaselineA: Regulation/rules + statute + common law (Ontario Criminal Rules 4-8, especially Rules 6-8; Criminal Code, s. 714; common law certiorari suspension principle as discussed via R. v. Foster and related authorities)
CaseB_TestB: Section 15(1) equality analysis (La Forest J. majority): three-step test—(1) distinction, (2) disadvantage, (3) whether distinction is based on an enumerated/analogous ground and is an ‘irrelevant personal characteristic’ assessed by ‘relevancy to the functional values underlying the law’ in its larger context
BaselineB: Common law/constitutional doctrine (Charter s. 15(1) framework from Andrews v. Law Society of British Columbia and Miron v. Trudel, as applied to the Old Age Security Act definition of “spouse” in ss. 2 and 19(1))
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Fair comment defence in defamation requires proof of honest belief/real opinion by the publisher (each publisher in same position as original writer); absent evidence of the writers’ honest belief (and with publisher/editor denying belief), the defence cannot go to the jury
BaselineA: Common law (defamation—fair comment defence), drawing on authorities cited in the reasons (e.g., Turner v. Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer Pictures Ltd.; Slim v. Daily Telegraph Ltd.; Lyon & Lyon v. Daily Telegraph Ltd.; and SCC reference Globe and Mail Ltd. v. Boland)
CaseB_TestB: Section 2(a) freedom of religion infringement threshold for indirect burdens (“trivial or insubstantial” burdens not caught) and s. 1 justification applying Oakes proportionality to Sunday-closing law (pressing and substantial objective; proportional means including minimal impairment and overall proportionality)
BaselineB: Constitution/Charter (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms ss. 2(a), 1, 27) and prior SCC framework for s. 1 (R. v. Oakes) plus freedom of religion principles from R. v. Big M Drug Mart Ltd.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Fair comment requires proof that the defamatory comment was an honest expression of the real opinion of the writer/publisher; absent evidence of the writers’ honest belief (and with publisher/editor denying belief), the defence is unavailable
BaselineA: Common law defence of fair comment in defamation (as described via authorities cited in the reasons, including Silkin v. Beaverbrook Newspapers Ltd.; Turner v. Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer Pictures Ltd.; Slim v. Daily Telegraph Ltd.)
CaseB_TestB: Contempt of court: liability requires proof beyond a reasonable doubt of personal service or actual personal knowledge of the order; service on a solicitor does not, without supporting circumstances, fix ministers with knowledge, and vicarious liability does not apply
BaselineB: Common law contempt requirements (personal service or actual personal knowledge) plus interpretation of Federal Court Rules (C.R.C. 1978, c. 663, Rules 308, 311, 355) as not altering contempt’s knowledge element absent express language
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Fair comment in defamation requires proof the impugned comment was an honest expression of the real opinion of the writer/publisher; absent evidence of the writers’ honest belief (and with publisher/editor denying honest belief), the defence is unavailable and need not be left to the jury
BaselineA: Common law defamation (fair comment defence), drawing on authorities including Turner v. Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer Pictures Ltd. and Slim v. Daily Telegraph Ltd. (as discussed in the reasons)
JudgeA: Ritchie J. (with concurrence of Laskin C.J., Pigeon and Pratte JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Garofoli review of wiretap authorizations: errors in the ITO/affidavit (even advertent or fraudulent) are only factors and do not automatically vitiate; after excising affected material, ask whether remaining independent information provides sufficient reliable grounds on which an authorization could reasonably be based
BaselineB: Common law/Charter criminal procedure framework for reviewing wiretap authorizations as stated in R. v. Garofoli, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 1421
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Intra vires test for CRTC regulations under Broadcasting Act s. 16: validity "must be tested by determining whether the regulation deals with a class of subject referred to in s. 3" (i.e., objectively in furtherance of the Commission’s objects/implementing the s. 3 broadcasting policy).
BaselineA: Statute (Broadcasting Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. B-11, ss. 3, 15, 16; applied to Radio (A.M.) Broadcasting Regulations, s. 5(1)(k))
CaseB_TestB: Quasi-delict (art. 1053 C.C.) assessed by the "prudent and reasonable man" standard, with appellate deference to a jury verdict unless it is "unreasonable" (and the judge/jury division: judge states the criterion; jury decides whether conduct meets it).
BaselineB: Statute/civil law (Civil Code art. 1053; Code of Civil Procedure arts. 363, 380; with supporting jurisprudence including Metropolitan Railway Co. v. Jackson (1877))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Limits on provincial commissions of inquiry vis-à-vis federal institutions and Crown privilege: a province may inquire into specific criminal acts within provincial 'administration of justice' but cannot, directly or indirectly, inquire into the administration/management of a federal institution (RCMP); and a minister’s s. 41(2) Federal Court Act national-security certificate requires refusal of production without examination and is binding on a commissioner
BaselineA: Combination: Constitution (B.N.A. Act ss. 91, 92, especially s. 92(14) 'Administration of Justice in the Province' vs federal heads), statute (Federal Court Act, R.S.C. 1970 (2nd Supp.), c. 10, s. 41(1)-(2); Public Inquiry Commission Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 11, s. 7), and common law Crown immunity/privilege (as discussed via cases such as Quebec North Shore Paper; Alberta v. C.T.C.)
CaseB_TestB: Custody contest (natural parent vs adoptive parents): under parens patriae/equity preserved by statute, the court must treat the child’s welfare as the predominant/paramount consideration, decided on 'all relevant factors' (including psychological, spiritual and emotional welfare), with parental claims considered but set aside where welfare requires
BaselineB: Statute (Domestic Relations Ordinance, R.O.N.W.T. 1974, c. D-9, ss. 28(1), 35(2), 37, 39) plus equitable parens patriae jurisdiction (rules of equity preserved by s. 39; supported by cases including Re Moores and Feldstein; Racine v. Woods; Beson)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Public Authorities Protection Act s. 11 scope: whether the impugned act/omission is in the execution of a "statutory or other public duty or authority"—i.e., segregate statutory functions into (1) those with a "public aspect or connotation" (covered) vs (2) "private executive or private administrative" / "managerial, internal or operational" matters that are "subordinate or incidental" (not covered).
BaselineA: Statute: The Public Authorities Protection Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 374, s. 11, interpreted in relation to The Housing Development Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 213, s. 6(2) (and informed by prior case law such as Bradford Corporation v. Myers and McGonegal v. Gray).
CaseB_TestB: Non-delegable statutory duty inquiry under the Indian Act: determine from the statute’s text whether it "clearly places" Canada under a mandatory, non-delegable duty to ensure student safety—here, permissive "may" language and express power to contract with religious organizations indicate no such non-delegable duty.
BaselineB: Statute: Indian Act, S.C. 1951, c. 29, ss. 113-114 (and related regulations considered but found insufficient); interpretive approach referenced to E.D.G. v. Hammer and contrasted with Lewis v. British Columbia.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Exemption-from-seizure for insurance proceeds: a policy’s exemption clause can operate only in favour of a “true beneficiary” (a third party); a universal legatee/heir is not a third party and therefore cannot invoke the policy clause or C.C.P. art. 553(3)
BaselineA: Statute/civil law codal provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, art. 553(3) (exemption from seizure for property declared exempt by donor/testator); Civil Code (C.C.) arts. 597 (heir not a third party), 1028 (contract binds heirs/legal representatives), 735 (limits on bequests protecting against creditors)
CaseB_TestB: No-fault liability for neighbourhood disturbances under art. 976 C.C.Q.: liability turns on whether neighbours suffered “abnormal or excessive annoyances” beyond the “limit of tolerance” owed according to the nature/location of the land or local custom (conduct/fault not required)
BaselineB: Statute/civil law codal provision: Civil Code of Québec, art. 976 (neighbours must suffer normal annoyances not beyond the limit of tolerance); contrasted with fault-based liability under arts. 1457 and 7 C.C.Q.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Superior court jurisdiction not ousted absent a specific statutory provision assigning the matter exclusively elsewhere; a provincial superior court may decide a federal-law issue (here, whether Bell has a legal obligation under s. 5(4) to prescribe reasonable requirements) when it arises incidentally in a properly constituted tort/injunction action
BaselineA: Statute + provincial procedural law: Code of Civil Procedure (Quebec), art. 31 (general original jurisdiction unless 'assigned exclusively' by specific law) applied against Bell’s constituent Act (An Act respecting The Bell Telephone Company of Canada, s. 5(4)-(6) as amended) and National Transportation Act, s. 45(1)
CaseB_TestB: Reopening the Crown’s case: prejudice-to-the-accused is the keystone; discretion narrows by trial stage—(1) before Crown closes: broad latitude; (2) after Crown closes but before defence elects: allowed to correct oversight/inadvertent omission if justice requires and no prejudice; (3) after defence has started to answer/meet the case: reopening only in the narrowest/most exceptional circumstances (generally limited to matters of form or where defence conduct contributed), to avoid undermining self-incrimination principles
BaselineB: Common law discretion on reopening (cases discussed include Robillard v. The Queen; R. v. Kishen Singh; R. v. Cachia; R. v. Dunn; etc.), informed by Charter self-incrimination principles (ss. 7, 11(c), 13) as rationale for restricting late reopening
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Admissibility of cross-examining an accused/witness on juvenile delinquency record as “convictions” under s. 12 Canada Evidence Act (and related proof by admission): “any offence” includes Criminal Code violations dealt with under the Juvenile Delinquents Act, and a juvenile “finding of delinquency” is “equivalent to a conviction” for s. 12; an admitted conviction need not be proved by the official record absent exceptional circumstances showing the admission was in error.
BaselineA: Statute: Canada Evidence Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-10, s. 12(1)-(2) (plus interpretive interaction with Juvenile Delinquents Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. J-3, ss. 2(1), 3, 20(1), 38; and discussion of Criminal Code, s. 593).
CaseB_TestB: Criminal Code indictment amendment for variance in a particular: where the Crown particularizes the narcotic but proves a different scheduled form, the court should amend under s. 529 if it can be done “without injustice” by assessing prejudice/misleading per s. 529(4) (including whether the accused “has been misled or prejudiced”) and, if prejudice exists, whether it can be cured by adjournment under s. 529(5); if no prejudice, appellate court/SCC may amend and dismiss under s. 613(1)(b)(i) and (3).
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 529(4)-(5), 613(1)(b)(i), 613(3), applied in context of Narcotic Control Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. N-1, ss. 2, 4 and Schedule item 3.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Coopers & Lybrand criteria for whether an administrative decision is required by law to be made on a judicial or quasi-judicial basis (and thus reviewable): (1) hearing contemplated; (2) affects rights/obligations; (3) adversary process; (4) obligation to apply substantive rules to individual cases — “factors to be weighed and evaluated, no one of which is necessarily determinative.”
BaselineA: Common law / judicial review doctrine (duty to act judicially / natural justice) applied within the statutory setting of Federal Court Act s. 28 and Income Tax Act s. 231(4)-(5).
CaseB_TestB: Stillman s. 24(2) trial-fairness framework: classify evidence as non-conscriptive vs conscriptive; if conscriptive, Crown must prove on balance of probabilities it would have been discovered by alternative non-conscriptive means (independent source/inevitable discovery) or else evidence is excluded as a general rule.
BaselineB: Statute/constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 24(2), building on Collins (s. 24(2) factors) and related SCC jurisprudence cited in the reasons.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory limits on interim rate-setting under s. 31 Gas Utilities Act: the Board may not set prospective interim rates that (in effect) recover pre-application revenue shortfalls, except for post-application losses due to undue delay; the proper inquiry is whether interim rates will "produce an amount in excess of the estimated total revenue requirements" for the period because of including pre-application shortfalls.
BaselineA: Statute (Alberta): The Gas Utilities Act, R.S.A. 1970, c. 158, s. 31 (and related prospective rate-setting scheme incl. ss. 27-28, 35); also The Public Utilities Board Act, R.S.A. 1970, c. 302, s. 52(2) (interim orders).
CaseB_TestB: Cuerrier fraud-vitiated consent test (s. 265(3)(c) Criminal Code) for HIV non-disclosure: consent is vitiated if (1) the accused’s non-disclosure/deceit is objectively dishonest and (2) it results in deprivation by exposing the complainant to a "significant risk of serious bodily harm"; plus the Crown must prove the complainant would have refused unprotected sex if informed.
BaselineB: Statute (federal): Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, ss. 265(3)(c) (fraud vitiating consent) and 268 (aggravated assault), interpreted using criminal fraud jurisprudence (e.g., R. v. Olan; R. v. Théroux; R. v. Zlatic) and rejecting the older "nature and quality of the act" limitation associated with R. v. Clarence.
JudgeB: Cory J. (for Cory, Major, Bastarache and Binnie JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory interpretation of Parole Act ss. 10 and 20 (1977 amendments): day parole may be ended by either (i) revocation under s. 10(1)(e) triggering s. 20 consequences, or (ii) termination under s. 10(2) (no s. 20 consequences); s. 20 applies to “any parole” including day parole and “recommitment” wording creates no operative ambiguity
BaselineA: Statute (Parole Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. P-2, as amended effective Oct. 15, 1977): definition of “parole” in s. 2 (“includes day parole”); s. 10(1)(e) (Board may revoke parole) and s. 10(2) (Board may terminate day parole); s. 20(1)-(3) (recommitment and sentence/remission consequences on revocation). Interpreted against prior case-law discussed (Hales; Carlson; Zong) and ambiguity principle (Marcotte).
CaseB_TestB: Palmer criteria (applied to sentence appeals): fresh evidence on appeal is admissible only if (1) generally not admissible if could have been adduced at trial with due diligence (flexibly applied in criminal cases), (2) relevant, (3) credible, and (4) such that, if believed, it could reasonably be expected (with the trial record) to have affected the result; overriding consideration is the “interests of justice”
BaselineB: Common law test from Palmer v. The Queen, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 759 (fresh evidence on appeal), applied within the statutory appellate-evidence discretion in Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, ss. 683 and 687.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: SCC discretion under Supreme Court Act s. 52 to vary interest on an SCC judgment: default interest runs as it would on the trial judgment "[u]nless otherwise ordered by the Court", and the Court may limit/adjust interest based on the circumstances (here, limiting pre-SCC interest to the trial award due to appellant-caused delay).
BaselineA: Statute (Supreme Court Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. S-19, s. 52 (as amended); Interest Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-18, ss. 13-14; plus Supreme Court Rules, r. 61 procedure).
CaseB_TestB: Whether procedural fairness/natural justice applies to Governor in Council decisions under National Transportation Act s. 64(1): on a proper construction of s. 64(1), the Governor in Council’s discretion is "complete" (no implied procedural fairness duties) so long as it stays within the statute’s "jurisdictional boundaries"; courts review only for failure to meet conditions precedent/jurisdictional limits, not for fairness of the procedure.
BaselineB: Statute (National Transportation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. N-17, s. 64(1)-(2); with context from Railway Act ss. 320-321 and Interpretation Act s. 28).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory-limit rule for groundwater pumping: Ontario Water Resources Act s. 37 defines what is “reasonable”; pumping above 10,000 gallons/day (absent a permit) is “unreasonable” and “any pumping in violation of s. 37 is to be considered as a nuisance when causing damage to other properties”; likewise, for negligence, “for any pumping of subterranean water over the legal limit, no one may claim to have been acting in the exercise of a right and consequently free of negligence.”
BaselineA: Statute (The Ontario Water Resources Commission Act / Ontario Water Resources Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 332, s. 37 (and related permitting scheme); applied within common-law nuisance/negligence concepts)
CaseB_TestB: Exemplary damages under Quebec Charter s. 49(2) (“unlawful and intentional interference”): intent exists where the wrongdoer “has a state of mind that implies a desire or intent to cause the consequences of his or her wrongful conduct, or … acts with full knowledge of the immediate and natural or at least extremely probable consequences that his or her conduct will cause.”
BaselineB: Statute (Quebec Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms, s. 49(2); test adopted/applied from Quebec (Public Curator) v. Syndicat national des employés de l’hôpital St-Ferdinand, [1996] 3 S.C.R. 211)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Effect of Quebec Highway Code s. 13(6) on auto liability coverage after transfer: if the registered owner has not complied with s. 13(1)-(2), they are "deemed to be the owner for purposes of responsibility and for purposes of insurance"; therefore, for liability coverage the transfer is treated as not having occurred and the buyer/driver with the deemed-owner’s consent is covered under the omnibus clause
BaselineA: Statute: Highway Code, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 231, s. 13(6) (with s. 13(1)-(2) as the triggering non-compliance); applied to the civil liability section/omnibus clause of the auto policy
CaseB_TestB: Garofoli leave (threshold) test for cross-examining a wiretap affiant: leave requires the defence to show a "reasonable likelihood" that cross-examination "will elicit testimony of probative value" on a material issue for the reviewing judge (i.e., tending to undermine a statutory precondition/basis for the authorization)
BaselineB: Common law: R. v. Garofoli, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 1421 (threshold/leave requirement for cross-examination on a Garofoli review), applied in the context of Criminal Code wiretap authorizations (including s. 184.2)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: s. 6 Highway Victims Indemnity Act direct action: insurer is directly liable to third parties only for “damage covered by liability insurance”; s. 6 removes only nullity/lapse defences and “does not extend the insurance contract to what it does not cover”, so coverage turns on the policy’s definition of “automobile” (including when a trailer is or is not included) and whether the damage was caused “first and foremost” by the excluded trailer rather than the insured automobile
BaselineA: Statute (Highway Victims Indemnity Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 232, s. 6) interpreted alongside the insurance contract’s coverage-defining terms (especially the policy definition of “automobile” in the Civil Liability section); guided by General Security Insurance Co. of Canada v. Bélanger, [1977] 1 S.C.R. 802 (scope of s. 6 exception vs coverage definition)
CaseB_TestB: Landlord covenant-to-insure effect on subrogation/tenant liability: tenant remains liable for negligently caused fire unless the lease shows the landlord’s covenant to insure “runs to the benefit of the tenant”; majority approach—tenant gets the benefit of the landlord’s fire-insurance covenant “unless there is another explanation” (e.g., option-to-purchase provisions) consistent with leaving the risk on the tenant
BaselineB: Common law of landlord-tenant/contract interpretation and insurer subrogation, drawing on United Motors Service Inc. v. Hutson, [1937] S.C.R. 294, and applying/analogizing Agnew-Surpass Shoe Stores Ltd. v. Cummer-Yonge Investments Ltd., [1976] 2 S.C.R. 221 and Ross Southward Tire Ltd. v. Pyrotech Products Ltd., [1976] 2 S.C.R. 35
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Qualified privilege in defamation: a privileged communication is protected unless the plaintiff proves malice; even “violent or excessively strong” language remains protected if, “having regard to all the circumstances”, the defendant “might have honestly and on reasonable grounds believed that what he wrote or said was true” (Adam v. Ward; applied via Netupsky v. Craig).
BaselineA: Common law (qualified privilege and malice), drawing on Adam v. Ward and Netupsky v. Craig as cited in the reasons.
CaseB_TestB: Sufficiency of reasons (Sheppard/Braich): two-stage inquiry—(1) are the reasons inadequate; (2) if so, do they prevent appellate review? The functional question is whether the reasons are “sufficiently amenable to appellate review” / whether there is an “impediment to appellate review”.
BaselineB: Common law appellate review doctrine on reasons (R. v. Sheppard; R. v. Braich; also discussed alongside Burns and Burke).
JudgeB: Bastarache and Abella JJ. (LeBel J. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Reasonable and probable grounds for warrantless arrest: an officer may arrest without warrant only if they have reasonable and probable grounds, and that belief "must take into account all the information available" (cannot focus only on incriminating facts and ignore exculpatory information unless there is good reason to think it unreliable).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code 1953-54, c. 51, s. 435 warrantless arrest power; plus Civil Code arts. 1053, 1054 for fault/employer liability).
CaseB_TestB: Validity of dismissal of a probationary constable: dismissal is ineffective unless made by the legally authorized decision-maker (the Board, not the chief), and the Board must actually exercise its function (it cannot silently "confirm" a chief’s unauthorized dismissal without informing the constable or giving any meaningful opportunity to respond to the proper authority).
BaselineB: Statute/regulation (The Police Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 351, s. 29; Regulation 680, s. 27(b); plus collective agreement s. 9 allocating dismissal power to the Board).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Municipal office disqualification for having a direct or indirect “interest in any contract” with the city (broad, ordinary-meaning approach; directors/officers are “interested” in company contracts)
BaselineA: Statute: Moncton Consolidation Act, 1946 (N.B.), c. 101, s. 6 (interpreting “directly or indirectly ... have any interest in any contract ... otherwise than as a shareholder in an incorporated company”), informed by Angrignon v. Bonnier, [1935] S.C.R. 38 (Duff C.J.: “The phrase ‘interested in’ has no technical signification; effect must be given to it according to the common usage of men.”) and Interpretation Act, R.S.N.B. 1973, c. I-13, s. 17 (liberal/remedial construction).
CaseB_TestB: Statutory interpretation of whether a municipality is an “institution” under New Brunswick’s Official Languages Act for s. 22 (civil pleadings must use the other party’s chosen official language only if the party is “Her Majesty ... or an institution”)
BaselineB: Statute: Official Languages Act, S.N.B. 2002, c. O-0.5, ss. 1 (“institution”), 22 (duty to use the other party’s chosen official language in “oral or written pleadings” or “process”).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Qualified privilege—threshold for leaving express malice to the jury: malice should not be put to the jury unless the evidence “raises a probability” of malice (more than a mere scintilla/possibility; “more consistent with its existence than with its non-existence”).
BaselineA: Common law (defamation/qualified privilege and malice), drawing on authorities including Somerville v. Hawkins (1851), Spill v. Maule (1869), Adam v. Ward (1917), and SCC’s Sun Life Assurance Co. of Canada v. Dalrymple (1965).
CaseB_TestB: Blood Tribe clarity requirement for statutory abrogation of solicitor-client privilege: only “clear” and “unequivocal” legislative language can abrogate privilege; applied to ITA s. 232(1) to conclude Parliament clearly excluded “an accounting record of a lawyer” from the statutory definition of privilege.
BaselineB: Statute—Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), ss. 231.2(1), 231.7(1), and especially s. 232(1) (“solicitor-client privilege” definition), interpreted using the Blood Tribe interpretive principle.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Priority/attachment rule for B.C. Payment of Wages Act lien: s. 5A lien arises "from the date wages were earned" and takes priority only over dispositions after attachment; if a mortgage predates attachment, it is "not affected" and the lien "will only attach to the employer’s equity"
BaselineA: Statute: Payment of Wages Act, 1962 (B.C.), c. 45, ss. 5 and 5A (especially s. 5A(1)-(2))
CaseB_TestB: Suppletive application framework for forced dissolution of a Quebec legal person: under art. 300 C.C.Q., look first to special statutes; if no specific scheme applies, arts. 355-364 C.C.Q. fill the gaps (art. 334 C.C.Q. does not bar application merely because special rules are incomplete); dissolution may be ordered under art. 355(2) where, e.g., "it is impossible to accomplish" the object or there is "some other legitimate cause"
BaselineB: Statute (civil code): Civil Code of Québec, arts. 300, 334, 355-364 (and consideration of Companies Act and C.C.P. art. 829 to determine if a special scheme applies)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Residual discretion/inherent jurisdiction to remedy unfairness from an improper closing address: (1) usually by curative jury instructions; (2) in rare cases, a limited reply confined to the improper issues, granted only in the clearest cases of unfairness
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Criminal Code, s. 651(3)-(4) (order of addresses) plus common law inherent jurisdiction of superior courts to ensure trial fairness
CaseB_TestB: Charter-validity test for a basic-fact presumption under s. 11(d): a presumption is constitutional only if proof of the substituted fact leads 'inexorably' to the essential element it replaces; plus (post-s. 172.1(3) invalidity) the structured framework for s. 172.1(4) 'reasonable steps' as a threshold to raising the defence of belief in legal age (air of reality → Crown disproves beyond reasonable doubt → ultimate Crown burden to prove belief/wilful blindness beyond reasonable doubt)
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law/constitutional doctrine: Criminal Code, s. 172.1(3)-(4) interpreted under Charter ss. 7 and 11(d); presumption jurisprudence (Whyte/Downey/Audet) and prior SCC interpretation of s. 172.1 in Levigne
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Adjudicator’s remedial power to substitute a lesser penalty for discharge: where the adjudicator finds "just and sufficient cause" for some discipline but "not for discharge", the adjudicator may vary the employer’s penalty (i.e., not an "all or nothing" choice).
BaselineA: Statute and collective agreement: Public Service Labour Relations Act, R.S.N.B. 1973, c. P-25, s. 92(1)(b) (adjudication of "disciplinary action resulting in discharge, suspension or a financial penalty") and s. 101 (privative clause), plus collective agreement art. V(d) ("Discipline, suspension, demotion or discharge ... shall be for just and sufficient cause") and art. XVII(c) (management right to discipline "for just and sufficient cause"). Prior SCC baseline discussed/distinguished: Port Arthur Shipbuilding Co. v. Arthurs, [1969] S.C.R. 85.
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 24(2) exclusion (Collins guidelines): whether, "having regard to all the circumstances", admission of evidence obtained through a Charter breach "would bring the administration of justice into disrepute" (applied here to an assumed unreasonable search under a writ of assistance).
BaselineB: Constitutional text and SCC common law framework: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 24(2) ("shall be excluded if ... the admission of it ... would bring the administration of justice into disrepute"), applying the SCC’s framework from R. v. Collins, [1987] 1 S.C.R. 265.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Will-construction test: give effect to the testator’s overriding intention on a fair reading of the will; administrative/boilerplate clauses should not defeat a clearly expressed intention (here, legacy payable on disposition of the business ‘however that disposition was made’).
BaselineA: Common law (will construction/ascertaining testator’s intention from the will read as a whole; no specific statutory provision identified in the reasons).
CaseB_TestB: Manslaughter legal causation with intervening acts: the Smithers/Nette test remains whether the accused’s dangerous unlawful acts were a ‘significant contributing cause of death’; ‘reasonable foreseeability’ and ‘intentional, independent act’ are non-determinative analytical aids.
BaselineB: Combination of common law and statute: common law causation test from Smithers v. The Queen and R. v. Nette; statutory context in Criminal Code ss. 222, 224, 225 (and discussion of s. 21).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Functional (and traditional) test for whether labour relations fall under exclusive federal jurisdiction: federal jurisdiction is the exception and applies only where the undertaking’s “nature of [its] operations and [its] normal activities” can be “characterized as federal”; otherwise provincial labour law applies
BaselineA: Common law constitutional division-of-powers doctrine for labour relations (functional test), as stated with reference to Toronto Electric Commissioners v. Snider and the Stevedoring Reference line of cases
CaseB_TestB: Section 15(1) Charter equality test (post-Kapp/Withler): (1) distinction based on enumerated/analogous ground; (2) disadvantage by perpetuating prejudice/disadvantage or stereotyping, assessed contextually without requiring a “mirror comparator group”
BaselineB: Common law Charter s. 15(1) framework from Andrews v. Law Society of British Columbia, Law v. Canada, and R. v. Kapp (two-step discrimination inquiry)
JudgeB: McLachlin C.J. and Abella J. (for the Court)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Bankruptcy Act s. 107(1)(j) interpretation: Crown tax claims rank pari passu notwithstanding provincial statutory preferences; provincial tax “privilege” cannot be used to escape s. 107(1)(j) by characterizing the Crown as a “secured creditor”
BaselineA: Statute: Bankruptcy Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. B-3, ss. 2 (definition of “secured creditor”) and 107(1)(j) (scheme of distribution); interacting with Quebec Retail Sales Tax Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 71, s. 30 and Civil Code art. 1989 (registration of Crown privilege)
JudgeA: Pigeon J. (for Martland, Ritchie, Pigeon, Beetz, Pratte and McIntyre JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Public interest standing (purposive, flexible 3-factor framework): (1) serious justiciable issue; (2) plaintiff has a real stake/genuine interest/engagement; (3) proposed suit is, “in all of the circumstances”, a “reasonable and effective means” to bring the issue to court (not a rigid ‘no other way’ requirement)
BaselineB: Common law standing doctrine from SCC cases (e.g., Borowski; Finlay; Canadian Council of Churches; Thorson; McNeil; Hy and Zel’s), as reformulated/clarified in this decision
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Crown prerogative priority applies only where Crown and subject claims are “of equal degree”; a prior registered second/collateral mortgage is of a higher degree than a later-registered Crown judgment, so priority is determined by Registry Act registration dates (ss. 17-18) rather than prerogative
BaselineA: Combination: common law Crown prerogative priority for debts/claims “of equal degree” (The Queen v. Bank of Nova Scotia (1885), 11 S.C.R. 1) plus Nova Scotia Registry Act, R.S.N.S. 1967, c. 265, ss. 17-18 (and related civil procedure distribution rule 47.11)
CaseB_TestB: International jurisdiction by extension of domestic territorial jurisdiction: art. 71 C.C.P. applies to foreign defendants, so an incidental action in warranty “must be taken before the court in which the principal action is pending” and this rule is “not subject to any limitation”
BaselineB: Statute/civil law: Code of Civil Procedure art. 71 (and discussion of arts. 68-75, including art. 75) and Civil Code art. 27, applied through the private-international-law principle that international jurisdiction is determined by extending domestic territorial jurisdiction rules (as recognized in Alimport and Trower and Sons)
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “detained” under Canadian Bill of Rights s. 2(c) in roadside breath-demand context: “detain”/“detention” “connote some form of compulsory restraint” and contemplate detention “by due process of law” (i.e., associated with “actual physical restraint”); if not arrested/detained, no Bill of Rights right to counsel and thus no “reasonable excuse” to refuse s. 234.1(1) demand
BaselineA: Statute (Canadian Bill of Rights, 1960, s. 2(c)(ii)-(iii)) applied to Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 234.1(1)-(2) (and by analogy s. 235); with reference to prior SCC cases Brownridge v. The Queen and Hogan v. The Queen
CaseB_TestB: Two-branch test for civil conspiracy: liability exists (1) where “the predominant purpose of the defendants’ conduct is to cause injury to the plaintiff” (means lawful or unlawful); or (2) where defendants’ conduct is “unlawful”, “directed towards the plaintiff (alone or together with others)”, and defendants “should know in the circumstances that injury to the plaintiff is likely to and does result” (constructive intent), with actual damage required
BaselineB: Common law tort of conspiracy, drawing on Crofter Hand Woven Harris Tweed Co. v. Veitch and Sorrell v. Smith, and considering/using SCC authorities International Brotherhood of Teamsters v. Therien and Gagnon v. Foundation Maritime Limited; also applying Lonrho Ltd. v. Shell Petroleum Co. Ltd.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 492 re-election validity: accused may re-elect judge-alone by (1) notifying the sheriff of the desire to re-elect; (2) attending at the time/place fixed; and (3) after the charge is read, communicating the re-election (which may be done through counsel in the accused’s presence). SCC clarifies that s. 492(3) requires reading the actual charge the accused faces (the preferred indictment), and that failure to prefer a new Form 4 indictment under s. 496 after re-election does not invalidate proceedings where the indictment is already in Form 4.
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, s. 492 (re-election procedure) and related s. 496 (Form 4 indictment after re-election).
CaseB_TestB: Injurious affection where no land is taken (Expropriations Act, s. 1(e)(ii), s. 21): compensation requires that the construction-caused damage would have been actionable at common law (typically nuisance). SCC applies nuisance as requiring an unreasonable interference—i.e., a “substantia[l] interfer[ence] with the use or enjoyment of land ... where, in the light of all the surrounding circumstances, this injury or interference is held to be unreasonable”—and holds loss of view/prospect and related amenity loss from highway construction is not actionable.
BaselineB: Statute: Expropriations Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 154, ss. 1 (definition of injurious affection) and 21 (compensation), incorporating common law nuisance/actionability requirements (including the Loiselle four conditions).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Ontario Municipal Board jurisdiction under s. 137(1): referential incorporation of Municipal Act s. 14(11)(a),(b),(d) applies (without the introductory limiting words) so the Board may adjust assets/liabilities on dissolution of the County as it considers “equitable”
BaselineA: Statute: The Regional Municipality of Ottawa-Carleton Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 407, ss. 135-137, incorporating by reference The Municipal Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 284, s. 14(11)(a),(b),(d) (not the introductory words of s. 14(11))
CaseB_TestB: Charter ss. 7 and 11(d) minimum mens rea for murder: conviction for murder requires proof beyond a reasonable doubt of “subjective foresight of death”; constructive murder provision s. 213(a) is unconstitutional because it removes that requirement
BaselineB: Constitution/common law principle under Charter ss. 7 and 11(d) (fundamental justice) applied to Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 213(a); building from R. v. Vaillancourt, [1987] 2 S.C.R. 636
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Valid consent to intercept a private communication under Criminal Code s. 178.11(2)(a): consent must be "voluntary (i.e. free from coercion)" and "made knowingly, with an awareness of the significance of the consent"; and if there is valid consent, a consent interception is "lawfully made" for s. 178.16(1)(a) admissibility purposes
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, Part IV.1 as enacted by the Protection of Privacy Act): ss. 178.1 (definition of "private communication"), 178.11(2)(a) (consent interception), 178.16(1)(a) (admissibility if interception "lawfully made")
CaseB_TestB: Proving the "identifiable group" element under Criminal Code s. 319(2) where the information particularizes the group: the trial judge must assess "the totality of the evidence" to decide whether the statements "as a matter of fact, promoted hatred" of the particularized group; it is "not necessary" to prove strict "interchangeability" of labels (e.g., "gypsies" and "Roma")
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code): s. 319(2) (wilful promotion of hatred), s. 318(4) (definition of "identifiable group"); plus evidentiary doctrine of judicial notice as summarized from R. v. Find (facts "so notorious" or "capable of immediate and accurate demonstration")
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Audi alteram partem / natural justice rule against receiving evidence or representations ex parte after the hearing: unless expressly or by necessary implication empowered to act ex parte, an appellate authority must not hear evidence in the absence of the affected party; if it does, the decision is invalid if the evidence 'might' have caused prejudice
BaselineA: Common law (procedural fairness / natural justice) applied in a statutory university-appeal setting; statute does not abrogate natural justice absent express language or necessary implication
CaseB_TestB: Workers’ compensation occupational-disease causation under s. 250(4): causation may be inferred from other (including circumstantial) evidence and is not determined by the presence/absence of expert opinion; where evidence is 'evenly weighted' on causation, the issue must be resolved in the worker’s favour
BaselineB: Statute (Workers Compensation Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 492, ss. 6 and 250(4)) plus mandatory Board policy via s. 250(2) (RSCM II: 'causative significance' meaning 'more than a trivial or insignificant aspect')
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Appellate intervention in a trial damages award: an appellate court may not substitute its own figure unless a wrong principle of law was applied or the overall award is a wholly erroneous estimate of damages (Andrews v. Grand & Toy).
BaselineA: Common law (as stated in Andrews et al. v. Grand & Toy Alberta Ltd. et al., [1978] 2 S.C.R. 229 at p. 235).
JudgeA: Martland J. (oral reasons for the Court)
CaseB_TestB: Videotape-only identification: once it is established the videotape has not been altered and depicts the crime, it is admissible; identity may be found on the tape alone if the trier of fact, exercising care, is satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt (considering clarity/quality and, to a lesser extent, time of depiction).
BaselineB: Common law evidence principles (building on R. v. Leaney, [1989] 2 S.C.R. 393 and related admissibility/real-evidence authorities; no specific statutory test governs admissibility here).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Quebec Labour Code s. 16 rebuttal of presumption: employer must show the “other” reason is substantial, not a pretext, and the true (real and determining) reason for dismissal; commissioner/court cannot review the severity/appropriateness of the penalty once a real reason is established
BaselineA: Statute (Quebec Labour Code, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 141 as am., ss. 13-16, especially s. 16 presumption and “another good and sufficient reason”)
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 12 “gross disproportionality” test (as applied to mandatory minimums): assess gravity of offence, personal characteristics of offender, and particular circumstances; plus possible informing factors; and a two-aspect approach (actual offender first, then reasonable hypotheticals if needed)
BaselineB: Common law constitutional test under Charter s. 12 (from R. v. Smith; reaffirmed in R. v. Lyons and R. v. Luxton) applied to statutory minimum sentence in Motor Vehicle Act, s. 88(1)(c)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Summary conviction appeal costs: under Criminal Code ss. 758 and 771(3), the appeal court "may make any order with respect to costs that it considers just and reasonable" / "proper" and these provisions implicitly bind the Crown when read in the context of Part XXIV
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 758, 771(3) (interpreted in context of Part XXIV, incl. ss. 720(1), 738(4), 748, 752.1, 755, 759) and Interpretation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-23, s. 16
CaseB_TestB: Mortgage statutory prepayment right (Interest Act s. 10(1)): determine when prepayment is available across renewals by treating the "mortgage" as "the mortgage (as amended)" and applying the Court’s four-scenario framework; plus: a mortgagor who knowingly chooses renewal does not "contract out of" or "waive" the right, but any clause purporting to relinquish the right at the end of a five-year period is unenforceable
BaselineB: Statute: Interest Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-18, s. 10(1), (2) (and parallel provincial provisions: The Mortgage Act, R.S.M. 1970, c. M200, s. 20(6), (7); remedy context: The Real Property Act, R.S.M. 1970, c. R30, s. 103(1)(c))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Wrongful dismissal damages: no deduction for (i) income tax not payable and (ii) unemployment insurance benefits that are a consequence of the employment contract (collateral benefits rule as applied to UI)
BaselineA: Common law contract damages for wrongful dismissal (mitigation/collateral benefits), with analogy to contributory pension benefits in Guy v. Trizec Equities Ltd.; income-tax point discussed against uncertain Income Tax Act treatment (ss. 3, 5, 25 referenced) but resolved as a damages-assessment principle
CaseB_TestB: Statutory authorization to fingerprint juveniles: under Identification of Criminals Act s. 2, a juvenile in lawful custody for a delinquency relating to a Criminal Code indictable offence is a person 'charged with'/'under conviction of' an indictable offence, so 'such force may be used as is necessary' to take fingerprints
BaselineB: Statute: Identification of Criminals Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-1, s. 2(1)-(2), interpreted in light of Juvenile Delinquents Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. J-3; guided by Morris v. The Queen (SCC) on meaning of 'offence'/'conviction' for juvenile delinquencies
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: “Air of reality / sense of reality” test for whether a defence must be left with the jury: there must be “in the record some evidence which would convey a sense of reality in the submission”; for mistake of fact as to consent, there must be “some evidence which, if believed, would support the existence of a mistaken but honest belief” (and, here, the majority adds that to require leaving the alternative defence, the evidence must be supported by sources other than the accused to give it “any air of reality”).
BaselineA: Common law (jury-instruction/defence-leaving doctrine), drawing the “sense of reality” formulation from Kelsey v. The Queen and applied as in R. v. Workman and Huculak (both cited in the reasons).
JudgeA: McIntyre J. (for Martland, Pigeon, Beetz, McIntyre and Chouinard JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Morin s. 11(b) “reasonable time” framework (as described by McLachlin J.): assess delay by (1) length of delay; (2) waiver; (3) reasons for delay; and (4) prejudice to the subject of the criminal process.
BaselineB: Statute/constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 11(b) (and related discussion of ss. 7 and 24(1)); the multi-factor approach is taken from R. v. Morin (cited).
JudgeB: McLachlin J. (for Lamer C.J. and Major J., dissenting on the s. 11(b) applicability issue)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Presumption of reasonableness on review of a tribunal’s interpretation of its home statute (Dunsmuir framework): start by asking whether the issue is interpretation of the tribunal’s own statute; if so, reasonableness is presumed unless a Dunsmuir correctness category applies or the presumption is rebutted by context; statutory right of appeal is not a new correctness category
BaselineA: Common law (standard of review framework from Dunsmuir v. New Brunswick and subsequent SCC cases) applied in the context of a statutory appeal under Municipal Government Act, R.S.A. 2000, c. M-26, ss. 467(1), 470
CaseB_TestB: Framework for Crown sui generis fiduciary duty (and breach) in specific claims: a sui generis fiduciary obligation arises from the Crown’s discretionary control over a specific/cognizable Aboriginal interest; breach assessed by whether the Crown exercised that control with loyalty/good faith/full disclosure and “ordinary prudence” in managing its own affairs, reconciling competing interests fairly; duty is met by standard of conduct, not a particular result
BaselineB: Common law fiduciary doctrine (e.g., Wewaykum; Guerin; Haida Nation; Manitoba Metis Federation) applied within the statutory specific-claims scheme (Specific Claims Tribunal Act, S.C. 2008, c. 22, ss. 14(1)(b), 14(1)(c), 14(2))
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Necessarily incidental doctrine for sustaining federal legislation that prima facie regulates provincial property and civil rights: to be valid under s. 91(12) (fisheries), the impugned provision must be shown to be "necessarily incidental to effective legislation" on fisheries; a "blanket prohibition" not linked to "actual or potential harm to fisheries" is not necessarily incidental and is ultra vires.
BaselineA: Common law constitutional division-of-powers doctrine (necessarily incidental/ancillary powers) applied to Parliament’s s. 91(12) fisheries power; articulated via Lord Tomlin’s proposition (3) in Attorney-General for Canada v. Attorney-General for British Columbia and others, [1930] A.C. 111, and related fisheries jurisprudence (e.g., R. v. Robertson).
CaseB_TestB: Colour of right in theft: the defence turns on whether the trier of fact is satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused did NOT have, at the time of the taking/transfer, an "honest belief that he had the right to that money" (not on what the accused’s rights actually were).
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code theft provisions using the phrase "without colour of right"; Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 283 and 294 (as referenced in the reasons)).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “unlawful purpose” in Criminal Code s. 423(2)(a): it means “contrary to law, that is prohibited by federal or provincial legislation”; if the alleged purpose is not prohibited by legislation (and the charge is not framed as “lawful purpose by unlawful means” under s. 423(2)(b) or another specific offence), the information discloses no offence known to law.
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 423(2)(a), in light of s. 8 and prior conspiracy jurisprudence such as Wright, McDermott & Feeley v. The Queen, [1964] S.C.R. 192; and discussion of R. v. Celebrity Enterprises Ltd.).
CaseB_TestB: Quebec defamation fault under C.C.Q. art. 1457 for journalists/media: fault is determined by a “contextual analysis” and the “guiding principle” is that “there will not be fault until it has been shown that the journalist or media outlet in question has fallen below professional standards”; the “conduct of the reasonable journalist becomes the all-important guidepost.”
BaselineB: Statute/civil code (Civil Code of Québec, art. 1457), as developed in Quebec jurisprudence (notably Société Radio-Canada v. Radio Sept-Îles Inc., [1994] R.J.Q. 1811; Prud’homme v. Prud’homme, 2002 SCC 85).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Rabey (majority): Disease-of-the-mind classification for automatism — internal cause vs transient external factor; “ordinary stresses and disappointments of life” are not an external cause taking the condition out of “disease of the mind”.
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 16) interpreted through common-law automatism/insanity jurisprudence (incl. Bratty v. A.G. Northern Ireland).
CaseB_TestB: RBC v. State Farm: Conflict/supremacy analysis — where the standard mortgage clause says it “shall supersede any policy provisions in conflict therewith”, Statutory Condition 4 cannot be used to void mortgagee coverage if it conflicts with the mortgage clause (including for vacancy/non-occupancy).
BaselineB: Statute and contract text (Insurance Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. I.8, Part IV; Statutory Condition 4) plus the policy’s standard mortgage clause, interpreted in light of Katsikonouris.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Single vs multiple causes of action test for characterizing damages (contractual vs delictual) and applicable prescription: if damages result from a single cause of action that is breach of a contractual obligation, they are contractual and prescribe in 30 years; if they result from several separate and independent causes of action, each is characterized (contract/delict) by its source and prescribes accordingly (e.g., separate ‘typical offences’ prescribe in 2 years).
BaselineA: Statute/civil code (Civil Code arts. 2242, 2261(2), 1024, 1057) plus contractual characterization of corporate by-laws/natural justice in member-corporation relations (supported by prior jurisprudence cited, e.g., Vancouver Real Estate Board v. Moscrop Realty Ltd.).
CaseB_TestB: Priority between mechanic’s lien and subsequent mortgage for past indebtedness where s. 14(1) does not apply: an unregistered lien has no general priority; when priorities are not prescribed by the Mechanics’ Lien Act, the lien claimant must register and priority is determined under s. 20 (lien claimant deemed ‘purchaser pro tanto’) and the Registry Act—‘priority according to priority of registration’ (ss. 69(1), 70), absent actual notice.
BaselineB: Statute (Mechanics’ Lien Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 267, especially ss. 14(1), 20, and registration scheme ss. 16, 21, 22) and Registry Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 409, ss. 69(1), 70.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Accrued-rights/anti-retroactivity analysis on statutory repeal: apply Interpretation Act s. 35(c) to preserve a claimant’s “right or privilege … acquired, accrued, accruing” under the pre-amendment Unemployment Insurance Act, so the amendment does not strip accrued benefits; read the amending Act “in the light of s. 35(c)” such that the claimant keeps the pre-1976 benefit for January 1976 but remains subject to the old disqualification when “a retirement pension … becomes payable” (benefits end Jan. 31, 1976).
BaselineA: Statute: Interpretation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-23, s. 35(c) (effect of repeal on accrued rights) applied to Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, S.C. 1970-71-72, c. 48, ss. 31, 38 as amended by S.C. 1974-75-76, c. 80, s. 10; and considering Unemployment Insurance Entitlements Adjustment Act, 1976-77, S.C. 1976-77, c. 11, s. 2.
CaseB_TestB: Compellability of judges before a commission under the Public Inquiries Act: read ss. 3 and 4 together so the Commission may “summon” but cannot “compel” beyond what a superior court judge could compel; because of judicial independence/immunity, a judge cannot be compelled to testify “as to how and why” a decision was reached or “as to why a particular judge sat on a particular case”; general language in s. 3 is “not specific enough to override” this immunity.
BaselineB: Combination: Statute (Public Inquiries Act, R.S.N.S. 1967, c. 250, ss. 3-4) interpreted in light of constitutional/common law principles of judicial independence and judicial immunity (as discussed via Valente v. The Queen and Beauregard v. Canada, and historical common law authorities).
JudgeB: McLachlin J. (for L'Heureux-Dubé, Gonthier and McLachlin JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Interpretation of Motor Vehicle Transport Act, s. 3(2): provincial transport board may license extra‑provincial undertakings “into or through” a province as including operations “in, across, into and out of” the province; and s. 6 does not displace provincial enforcement (including seizure) incorporated via “like terms and conditions”
BaselineA: Statute: Motor Vehicle Transport Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. M-14, ss. 3(1)-(2), 5, 6; definitions in s. 2 (“extra-provincial undertaking”, “law of the province”). Related incorporated provincial scheme: The Public Service Vehicles Act, R.S.A. 1970, c. 300 (notably s. 58 seizure power). Prior SCC interpretation referenced: Coughlin v. Ontario Highway Transport Board, [1968] S.C.R. 569; R. v. Smith, [1972] S.C.R. 359.
CaseB_TestB: Charter scope test for corporate claimants under s. 12: a claimant must show an interest within the guarantee’s scope and purpose; s. 12 (“cruel and unusual”) is limited to human beings and therefore corporations cannot invoke s. 12
BaselineB: Constitutional text and purposive interpretation framework: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 12; purposive interpretation approach from R. v. Big M Drug Mart Ltd., [1985] 1 S.C.R. 295; corporate-claimant scope principle from R. v. CIP Inc., [1992] 1 S.C.R. 843; interpretive reliance on Irwin Toy Ltd. v. Quebec (Attorney General), [1989] 1 S.C.R. 927 (text indicates “only human beings can enjoy” certain rights).
JudgeB: Brown and Rowe JJ. (joint reasons; Wagner C.J. and Moldaver and Côté JJ. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Effect of fundamental breach on an exclusion/waiver clause: whether the clause continues to bind is determined by the “true construction of the contract” (no automatic rule that fundamental breach nullifies the clause); here, the lien waiver “ceased to bind” once the subcontractor communicated its election to treat the contract as at an end.
BaselineA: Combination: common law on exclusion clauses and fundamental breach (Suisse Atlantique; Photo Production) plus statutory lien baseline in The Mechanics’ Lien Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 267, s. 5(1) (lien exists unless an express agreement to the contrary is signed).
CaseB_TestB: When a penal court may entertain a collateral attack on an administrative order: depends on legislative intent as to the appropriate forum, assessed using non-exhaustive factors—“the wording of the statute”, “the purpose of the legislation”, “the availability of an appeal”, “the nature of the collateral attack taking into account the appeal tribunal’s expertise and raison d’être”, and “the penalty on a conviction”.
BaselineB: Statutory/interpretive framework under the Environmental Protection Act, R.S.O. 1980, c. 141 (notably ss. 17, 122-123, 146(1a)) and the common-law rule against collateral attacks on court orders (Wilson; Litchfield; Sarson) adapted to administrative orders via legislative-intent analysis.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Constructive trust based on unjust enrichment: claimant must show (1) an enrichment, (2) a corresponding deprivation, and (3) absence of any juristic reason for the enrichment; plus the enrichment must be unjust in the circumstances (e.g., where one in a spousal-like relationship prejudices herself in reasonable expectation of an interest and the other knowingly accepts the benefit).
BaselineA: Common law (equitable constructive trust/unjust enrichment), drawing on Rathwell v. Rathwell and Murdoch v. Murdoch as discussed in the reasons.
CaseB_TestB: Solicitor-client confidentiality/privilege and search warrants: (i) confidentiality may be raised whenever communications are likely to be disclosed without consent; (ii) conflicts are resolved in favour of confidentiality unless law provides otherwise; (iii) authorized interferences must be limited to what is 'absolutely necessary'; (iv) enabling statutes derogating from confidentiality are interpreted restrictively; plus for Criminal Code s. 443 searches of lawyers’ offices, the justice should refuse a warrant unless there is 'no reasonable alternative' and must impose protective execution terms; crime/fraud communications are excepted.
BaselineB: Combination: statute (Criminal Code, s. 443 (and related execution context)) plus common law solicitor-client privilege/confidentiality (including Solosky v. The Queen and common law crime-fraud exception).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Objective causation test for failure-to-disclose (informed consent in negligence): whether a reasonable person in the patient’s position would have declined the treatment if properly informed of all material (and special) risks
BaselineA: Common law (medical negligence duty of disclosure and causation), drawing on Hopp v. Lepp, [1980] 2 S.C.R. 192 (material risks disclosure) and addressing causation approaches discussed in lower courts and U.S. cases
CaseB_TestB: “Integral element” test for federal jurisdiction over s. 92(10) undertakings: federal legislation displacing provincial law is valid only if it regulates an aspect that is “vital/essential/integral” to the core of the federal undertaking
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine (division of powers) applying Constitution Act, 1867 ss. 91(29), 92(10), (13), (14), and relying on Construction Montcalm Inc. v. Minimum Wage Commission, [1979] 1 S.C.R. 754 and Northern Telecom Ltd. v. Communications Workers of Canada, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 115
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Natural Resources Agreement (para. 12) “right of access” rule for treaty Indian hunting for food: province may deny hunting access to all, but if any hunting is permitted on the land (even at limited times), that constitutes a “right of access” engaging the proviso so Indians may hunt for food “at all seasons of the year” (not just open seasons)
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional instrument: Natural Resources Agreement (Canada–Saskatchewan, 1930), para. 12 (confirmed by British North America Act, 1930) plus SCC interpretation in R. v. Sutherland, Wilson and Wilson, [1980] 2 S.C.R. 451 (defining “right of access” as access for hunting/trapping/fishing and holding that once limited hunting is allowed, the proviso is engaged)
CaseB_TestB: Charter validity “purpose-first” framework: “The initial test of constitutionality must be whether or not the legislation’s purpose is valid; the legislation’s effects need only be considered when the law under review has passed the purpose test. The effects test can never be relied on to save legislation with an invalid purpose.”
BaselineB: Constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 2(a) (freedom of conscience and religion) and Constitution Act, 1982, s. 52(1) (supremacy/invalidity). The Court articulates a general method for assessing Charter invalidity by reference to legislative purpose and effects.
JudgeB: Dickson J. (for Dickson, Beetz, McIntyre, Chouinard and Lamer JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: No retroactive revocation of premium-reduction decisions absent express statutory/regulatory authority; officer’s decision under prescribed standards is not a nullity merely because legally wrong
BaselineA: Statute and regulation: Unemployment Insurance Act, 1970-71-72, ss. 64(4), 64(6) (regulation-making re premium reductions) and Regulations s. 24 (decision and employer-initiated review/appeal); also discussed: Act s. 70 (Minister’s assessment powers) and Federal Court Act s. 28 (review jurisdiction context)
CaseB_TestB: Mens rea for Criminal Code s. 121(1)(a): intent to commit the prohibited act plus knowledge of the circumstances; no additional requirement of a “corrupt” state of mind
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 121(1)(a) (and s. 19 noted re ignorance of law); interpreted in light of SCC precedent including Martineau v. La Reine
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Ernst (Cromwell J.): Ward s. 24(1) Charter damages ‘appropriate and just’ analysis — countervailing factors (alternative remedies + good governance) can categorically negate Charter damages against a quasi-judicial regulator (AER), so damages could never be appropriate
BaselineA: Common law / constitutional (Charter) framework from Vancouver (City) v. Ward, 2010 SCC 27 interpreting Charter s. 24(1) (“appropriate and just” remedy); applied alongside statutory immunity clause Energy Resources Conservation Act, s. 43
CaseB_TestB: Mikisew Cree (Karakatsanis J.): Duty to consult (Haida) is triggered only by executive ‘Crown conduct’; the law-making process (development, passage, enactment of legislation) is legislative and does not trigger the duty to consult
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine of the duty to consult from Haida Nation v. British Columbia (Minister of Forests), 2004 SCC 73 (and related cases), grounded in the honour of the Crown and s. 35; applied in light of constitutional principles (separation of powers, parliamentary sovereignty/privilege) and Federal Courts Act jurisdictional provisions (ss. 2(1)-(2), 17, 18, 18.1)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Workers’ compensation statutory bar does not extend to a non-employer car owner deemed an employer/servant relationship under motor-vehicle legislation: s. 10(1) WCA bars actions only against the worker’s employer/covered employers/other workers; a Motor-vehicle Act deemed agency/employment (s. 70(1)) creates vicarious liability but does not make the owner an 'employer' under s. 10(1), so the tort claim against the owner proceeds
BaselineA: Statute: Workers’ Compensation Act, 1968 (B.C.), c. 59, s. 10(1) (exclusive-remedy bar) and Motor-vehicle Act, R.S.B.C. 1960, c. 253, s. 70(1) (deeming driver to be owner’s 'agent or servant' and 'in the course of his employment')
CaseB_TestB: Operational conflict framework for conflicting administrative tribunal decisions: an 'operational conflict' exists where 'compliance with the decision of one tribunal necessitates violation of the other'; if both decisions would normally withstand review, courts may declare one decision inoperative to the extent of conflict and, using a 'pragmatic and functional' approach, decide which decision the legislature intended to take precedence (considering factors like each tribunal’s legislative purpose, centrality of the decision to that purpose, and whether the decision is policy-making/implementation)
BaselineB: Common law administrative law (judicial review/standard of review and conflict-resolution between tribunals), building on cases cited in the reasons including Domtar Inc. v. Quebec (CALP) and U.E.S., Local 298 v. Bibeault; applied in the context of statutory schemes including the Railway Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. R-3, ss. 335, 340 and related telecom legislation
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Priority between a mechanics’ lien and a subsequent collateral mortgage for past indebtedness: where the Mechanics’ Lien Act does not prescribe priority (s. 14(1) inapplicable), an unregistered lien has no general priority and priority is determined by registration under the Registry Act once the lien is registered and deemed a purchaser (Mechanics’ Lien Act, s. 20; Registry Act, ss. 69(1), 70).
BaselineA: Statute (Ontario Mechanics’ Lien Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 267, especially ss. 14(1) and 20, plus registration/enforcement provisions; and Ontario Registry Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 409, ss. 69(1) and 70).
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 2(b) / s. 1 analysis of privacy legislation in the labour-strike context: PIPA violates s. 2(b) and is not justified under s. 1 because its broad restrictions are disproportionate—PIPA lacks any mechanism to balance a union’s expressive rights with privacy interests, so its limits on expression are disproportionate to its benefits.
BaselineB: Combination (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 2(b) and 1; applied to Alberta’s Personal Information Protection Act, S.A. 2003, c. P-6.5, especially ss. 3, 4(1), 4(3), 7(1) and related exemptions; and PIPA Regulation, Alta. Reg. 366/2003, s. 7).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Quebec civil liability “choice” test: a contracting party may sue in delict (art. 1053 C.C.) despite a contract only if the alleged contractual fault is independently a delictual fault that would exist “even in the absence of a contract”
BaselineA: Statute (Civil Code art. 1053; Code of Civil Procedure art. 68) as interpreted alongside SCC jurisprudence (Ross v. Dunstall; Ross v. Emery; Alliance Assurance)
CaseB_TestB: Reasonable apprehension of bias consequence rule: once a reasonable apprehension of bias is demonstrated, the trial judge has “no further jurisdiction” and “the only appropriate remedy is a new trial”; appellate finding of bias retroactively renders orders “void and without effect”
BaselineB: Common law procedural fairness / bias doctrine (as reflected in Newfoundland Telephone Co. v. Newfoundland (Board of Commissioners of Public Utilities)) applied in the criminal trial context
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Bills of Exchange Act “sum certain” / negotiability requirement: principal + interest must be ascertainable on the face of the instrument (no extrinsic evidence for an inherently uncertain interest start date like “from the date of advance”)
BaselineA: Statute (Bills of Exchange Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. B-5, ss. 28, 176(1), 186; plus s. 10 incorporating common law/law merchant)
