CaseB_TestB: Criminal Code s. 172(3) “disturbs” threshold: to convict, conduct must be “disorderly in itself or productive of disorder”; mere “annoyance, anxiety or emotional upset” from brief, passive, peaceful conduct voluntarily desisted from is insufficient
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 172(3), interpreted in context of ss. 169-175 heading “Disorderly Conduct”)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Negotiable instrument “sum certain” / certainty-on-the-face rule: a promissory note must disclose on its face a sum certain (principal + interest), meaning interest must be ascertainable from the instrument itself (by “numerical calculation from materials contained in the document”); extrinsic evidence is generally not permitted to cure inherent uncertainty (e.g., “interest ... from the date of advance” where that date is not on the instrument).
BaselineA: Statute (Bills of Exchange Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. B-5, ss. 176(1) (definition of promissory note), 28 (sum certain; interest), 186 (application to notes), plus s. 10 incorporating common law/law merchant).
CaseB_TestB: Start of the 2-year suicide exclusion period under Quebec life insurance: determine the contract’s effective date for “two years of uninterrupted insurance” (art. 2532 C.C.L.C.) by applying art. 2516’s three concurrent conditions, while allowing (if favourable to the policyholder) retroactive effect to a backdated policy date; and decide whether later increased coverage is a mere variation within the same contract (so the exclusion period cannot “run more than once”) or a new contract based on continuity factors.
BaselineB: Statute (Civil Code of Lower Canada, arts. 2516 (conditions for life insurance to become effective), 2532 (suicide clause ineffective after two years of uninterrupted insurance), and art. 2500 (relative public order / non-derogation except if favourable), with interpretive support from prior SCC case law (e.g., General Trust; McClelland).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: When a statute creates a specific tribunal/procedure to decide an issue, the Superior Court should not intervene by declaratory judgment to decide that very issue (and declaratory relief is discretionary and may be refused if it would be of little use).
BaselineA: Combination: Quebec Code of Civil Procedure, art. 453 (declaratory judgment) plus common-law/precedential limits on declaratory relief where a statute provides a specific forum (e.g., Barraclough v. Brown; City of Lethbridge v. Canadian Western Natural Gas; Cassidy v. Stuart) and the special statutory scheme in the Act respecting the Olympic Village, 1976 (Qué.), c. 43 (notably ss. 10 and Division III; s. 27).
CaseB_TestB: Minister’s s. 7 Fisheries Act power to “authorize to be issued” licences is a continuing power, so the Minister may revoke an authorization any time before the licence is actually issued; discretion is constrained only by natural justice (relevant considerations, no arbitrariness, good faith).
BaselineB: Statute: Fisheries Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. F-14, s. 7 (and s. 9 for issued-licence cancellation) interpreted with Interpretation Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. I-21, s. 31(3) (“from time to time as occasion requires”).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Excise Tax Act machinery exemption: taxpayer must be a “manufacturer or producer” and the machinery must be used “directly in” the manufacture/production of “goods”; “manufacturing” not to be restrictively defined where the Act provides no such restriction (generation of electricity by on-site generators qualifies).
BaselineA: Statute: Excise Tax Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-13, ss. 27(1), 29(1), and Schedule III, Part XIII, s. 1 (plus acceptance of a general definition of “manufacture” from R. v. York Marble, Tile and Terrazzo Ltd.).
CaseB_TestB: Vesting/accrual of appeal-as-of-right: a right to appeal as of right is only “acquired,” “accrued” or “accruing” when the lower court judgment is rendered and all conditions precedent are fulfilled; until then, Interpretation Act s. 43(c) does not protect it and s. 44 applies (proceedings continue under the new enactment).
BaselineB: Statute: Interpretation Act, R.S.C., 1985, c. I-21, ss. 43(c) and 44(c),(d), applied to the amended Criminal Code, s. 691(2).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: No common law tort/civil action for employment discrimination where the Ontario Human Rights Code provides a comprehensive, exclusive remedial scheme (Code forecloses both a direct statutory cause of action and a common law action based on Code policy).
BaselineA: Statute — The Ontario Human Rights Code, R.S.O. 1970, c. 318 (notably s. 4(1)(a)-(b) and the Code’s complaint/board of inquiry/appeal scheme, including s. 14b(6), s. 14c, s. 14d(4)).
CaseB_TestB: Undue obstacle/undue hardship (reasonable accommodation) analysis under CTA s. 172: remove the discriminatory barrier unless the carrier proves accommodation would impose undue hardship; factors include cost, economic viability, safety, and quality of service (as informed by CTA s. 5 and human rights principles).
BaselineB: Statute — Canada Transportation Act, S.C. 1996, c. 10, ss. 5, 170(1), 171, 172(1), 172(3), interpreted consistently with human rights reasonable-accommodation/undue-hardship principles (e.g., Meiorin/Grismer).
JudgeB: Abella J. (for McLachlin C.J. and Bastarache, LeBel and Charron JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Bill of Rights limit on reverse-onus: a reverse onus (balance of probabilities) is compatible with s. 2(f) only if the fact the accused must prove is "rationally open" to proof/disproof by the accused; if the burden is "impossible to meet" (beyond the accused’s knowledge/what they can reasonably be expected to know) it becomes an "irrebuttable presumption of guilt". For Customs Act s. 248(1) to operate on unlawful importation, Crown must at least prove foreign origin + possession + "some knowledge or means of knowledge of the circumstances of importation" on the accused’s part; otherwise Crown must prove unlawful importation beyond a reasonable doubt.
BaselineA: Statute (Customs Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-40, ss. 205(1),(3), 248(1)) as constrained by statute (Canadian Bill of Rights, R.S.C. 1970, App. III, s. 2(f)); relying on SCC interpretation in R. v. Appleby, [1972] S.C.R. 303
CaseB_TestB: Interested-party status/right to be heard under Quebec Labour Code s. 32 in bargaining-unit definition: because s. 32 requires the investigation on the bargaining unit be held "in the presence of every association concerned and the employer", the list is exhaustive and "the legislator indicated his intent to divest the employee of the status of an interested party" for bargaining-unit issues; therefore no audi alteram partem right for individual employees at that stage. On judicial review under a privative clause, the commissioners/Labour Court interpretation stands unless "patently unreasonable" (i.e., not "manifestly unreasonable").
BaselineB: Statute (Quebec Labour Code, R.S.Q. 1977, c. C-27, s. 32 (and related provisions ss. 28, 39, 129); Code of Civil Procedure, art. 846) plus common-law/administrative-law principles (audi alteram partem; privative-clause deference per CUPE v. NB Liquor)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Intoxication (drunkenness) and mens rea for murder: intoxication is relevant only if it rendered the accused "incapable of forming the intent" to kill or to cause bodily harm "that he knows is likely to cause death"; Crown must prove capacity beyond a reasonable doubt and the accused gets the benefit of any reasonable doubt
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 212(a)(ii) (murder definition) plus the intoxication 'capacity' approach from Director of Public Prosecutions v. Beard and SCC cases MacAskill v. The King; Perrault v. The Queen; Mulligan v. The Queen
CaseB_TestB: Interjurisdictional immunity (constitutional inapplicability) for federal services: a provincial law of general application is inapplicable if it "touches on a vital or essential aspect" of a federal service's "establishment, management or operation" (i.e., bears on what makes it specifically federal)
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine (interjurisdictional immunity) as stated in Construction Montcalm Inc. v. Minimum Wage Commission and Bell Canada v. Quebec (CSST), applied to a federal service; applied against Quebec Transport Act permit scheme (e.g., s. 36) and Bus Transport Regulation
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 116(1) applies to disobedience of a lawful court order unless a penalty/punishment/mode of proceeding is expressly provided by statute law (common law contempt power does not qualify as 'expressly provided by law')
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 116(1) (and interpretive context including s. 8); issue is meaning of 'unless some penalty or punishment or other mode of proceeding is expressly provided by law'
CaseB_TestB: Public law promissory estoppel (clear and unambiguous promise + reliance/change of conduct) cannot be invoked to avoid liability under a clear legislative provision creating a strict liability regulatory offence (e.g., zoning by-law)
BaselineB: Common law doctrine of public law promissory estoppel as described in Mount Sinai (quoting Maracle): requires 'a clear and unambiguous promise' intended to induce action, plus reliance and change of conduct; limited by rule that estoppel cannot prevent application of an express legislative provision
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Insurance policy “effective date” for time-limited clauses is determined by the true construction of the entire contract (read policy and application as a whole), avoiding an incongruous split effective date; here, the policy was “entirely structured around” January 23 so that date governs “for the purpose of calculating any of the time periods contemplated, including the application of the self-destruction clause”.
BaselineA: Statute + contract interpretation: Insurance Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 224, s. 148(2) (application and policy form the contract) (with general common-law contractual interpretation principles applied to the insurance contract).
CaseB_TestB: Access in conjunction with permanent guardianship: (1) court has jurisdiction under the Family Services Act to grant/deny access when making the initial permanent guardianship order (since access can be considered on review under s. 60(6), “a fortiori” it can be considered initially); and (2) whether to grant access is a best-interests assessment where “access is the exception and not the rule” and “access should not be granted if its exercise would have negative effects on the physical or psychological health of the child” (including where it would jeopardize adoption).
BaselineB: Statute: Family Services Act, S.N.B. 1980, c. F-2.2, especially ss. 1 (best interests factors), 53(2) (best interests paramount), 56(1) (permanent guardianship), 60(2), 60(6) (variation/review and “such order ... appropriate” if in best interests), 85(2) (post-adoption access preservation).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 16(2) insanity: meaning of “incapable of appreciating the nature and quality of an act” — an accused “appreciates” if he “knows what he is doing” and “is aware of the physical consequences which will result from his acts” (emotional/moral indifference is irrelevant).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 16(2)); interpreted in light of SCC authorities including Cooper v. The Queen, R. v. Barnier, and Schwartz v. The Queen.
CaseB_TestB: Extradition Act committal and surrender frameworks: (1) Committal under s. 29(1)(a) — judge asks whether there is admissible evidence of conduct that “would justify committal for trial in Canada” (prima facie case), with ROC evidence “presumptively reliable” and rebuttable only if “so defective or appears so unreliable that it would be dangerous or unsafe to act on it”; defences generally not considered. (2) Surrender under s. 44(1)(a) — unavailability of a Canadian defence may matter only if the person sought shows: (1) a substantive difference (defence in Canada, no comparable defence abroad), (2) a reasonable prospect of success in Canada, and (3) significantly greater jeopardy abroad; then the Minister weighs this with all circumstances.
BaselineB: Statute (Extradition Act, S.C. 1999, c. 18, ss. 29(1)(a), 44(1)(a)); built on prior SCC extradition jurisprudence including United States of America v. Ferras and Canada v. Schmidt.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Non-pecuniary damages in severe personal injury: apply the functional approach and a “rough upper limit” of $100,000, exceedable only rarely (e.g., on proof/agreement of inflationary erosion). The award “should not depend alone upon the seriousness of the injury but upon its ability to ameliorate the condition of the victim”; the $100,000 figure is reaffirmed as an upper limit “save in exceptional circumstances” and “should be subject to increase upon proof of, or agreement as to, the effect of inflation”.
BaselineA: Common law (damages for non-pecuniary loss) as set out in the SCC “trilogy” and refined in Lewis v. Todd: Andrews v. Grand & Toy Alberta Ltd.; Arnold v. Teno; Thornton v. Board of School Trustees of School District No. 57; Lewis v. Todd.
CaseB_TestB: OPCF 44R / Insurance Act s. 239(1)(a) “arising directly or indirectly from the use or operation of an automobile”: for indemnity (inadequately insured motorist) coverage, the tortfeasor must be liable “as a motorist” and there must be an “unbroken chain of causation” linking the conduct “as a motorist” to the injuries; coverage fails where the tort is an “intervening event” and a “severable activity” (more than mere “but for” connection).
BaselineB: Statutory/contractual interpretation: Insurance Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. I.8, s. 239(1)(a) (and matching OPCF 44R wording), with Amos v. ICBC distinguished as a no-fault benefits context.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Effect of workers’ compensation election/subrogation on who may sue and whether the Commission has an “interest” to intervene or benefit from interruption of prescription: once s. 7(3) subrogation occurs (on election), only the Commission may claim amounts it paid/will pay; the worker may claim only the s. 8 “additional sum”; a worker’s action for the whole loss does not introduce the Commission’s claim and does not create intervention interest or interrupt prescription for the Commission.
BaselineA: Statute and civil law provisions: Workmen’s Compensation Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 159, ss. 7(3) ("The subrogation takes place by the mere making of the election"), 8 (worker may claim only the "additional sum"); Civil Code art. 1056a; Code of civil procedure art. 208 ("Any person interested in an action... may intervene").
CaseB_TestB: Collins s. 24(2) Charter exclusion framework (as organized in Greffe): balance three categories—(1) fairness of the trial, (2) seriousness of the Charter violation (police conduct, incl. good/bad faith), and (3) effect of exclusion on the repute of the administration of justice; in Greffe the Court emphasizes the second category and requires an evidentiary basis for “reasonable and probable grounds” (a conclusory informer tip is insufficient; assess detail, source/means of knowledge, and indicia of reliability).
BaselineB: Constitutional/statutory: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 24(2) ("shall be excluded if... the admission... would bring the administration of justice into disrepute"), applying the common-law/Charter framework from R. v. Collins.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Public access to search-warrant materials: issuance may be in camera, but after execution (and if items are seized and brought before a justice) the public may inspect; access may be curtailed only to protect superordinate social values (notably protection of the innocent where nothing is found).
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law principles: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 443 (issuance of warrant) and 446 (bringing/detention of seized items), plus common law/open court principle and court’s supervisory power over records.
CaseB_TestB: Bona fide occupational qualification (BFOQ) test (Etobicoke) applied to denominational-school teacher: two branches—(1) subjective good faith/no ulterior purpose; (2) objective reasonable necessity to accomplish the employer’s legitimate objectives (here, religious conformity reasonably necessary to provide Catholic education).
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: Human Rights Code, R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 186, s. 8 (equality of opportunity based on bona fide qualifications; no discrimination unless reasonable cause), with the BFOQ framework taken from Ontario Human Rights Commission v. Etobicoke (Borough of), [1982] 1 S.C.R. 202.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Validity of a Quebec deed of donation and trust benefiting unborn (non-existent) primary beneficiaries: trustee acceptance suffices and trustee holds ownership; art. 981a must be interpreted liberally subject to trust’s special characteristics (not ordinary gift rules)
BaselineA: Statute (Civil Code of Quebec provisions on trusts and gifts): arts. 981a, 981b, 981l (trusts) read with arts. 754, 755, 608, 765, 771, 772, 929 (gifts/legacies/capacity). Key prior SCC baseline cases discussed: Curran v. Davis (acceptance by trustee; nature of trust gift) and related jurisprudence on trustee ownership (e.g., Greenshields; Reford).
CaseB_TestB: When an injunction in private litigation can effectively bind non-parties (enforceable by contempt): courts may issue such orders, but fairness requires notice/opportunity to comply and careful, constrained wording
BaselineB: Common law equitable injunction and contempt principles, with statutory confirmation of interlocutory injunction power and civil/criminal overlap: Law and Equity Act, R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 224, s. 36 ("just or convenient"), and Criminal Code, s. 11 (civil remedies not affected by criminality). Key prior SCC baseline case cited: International Longshoremen's Association, Local 273 v. Maritime Employers' Association (practice of wording affecting non-parties).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory displacement of the Kienapple rule: s. 83 permits multiple convictions/punishment where Parliament gives a clear indication (here, consecutive sentence for firearm-use offence) and s. 21 party liability applies to s. 83
BaselineA: Combination of common law and statute: common law Kienapple principle (Kienapple v. The Queen; Cox and Paton v. The Queen; R. v. Quon) applied/limited by Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 83(1)-(2) (use of a firearm; consecutive sentence) and s. 21 (parties to an offence)
JudgeA: Dickson J. (for Martland, Dickson, Estey, McIntyre and Chouinard JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Division of powers validity (pith and substance) and interjurisdictional immunity: (1) characterize purpose and effects to identify pith and substance; (2) for interjurisdictional immunity, ask whether the measure trenches on the core of the other power and whether it 'impairs' (seriously/significantly) rather than merely 'affects' it
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrines (pith and substance; interjurisdictional immunity) applied in light of Constitution Act, 1867, ss. 91(29), 92(10)(a), 92(13), 92(16), and the federal Radiocommunication Act, s. 5(1)(f) (Ministerial siting approval)
JudgeB: Wagner and Côté JJ. (joint reasons; McLachlin C.J. and Abella, Cromwell, Moldaver, Karakatsanis and Brown JJ. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Labour arbitration remedial authority under s. 25(3): where the collective agreement lacks a specific penalty for the infraction, an arbitrator/board may substitute a lesser penalty (including reinstatement without back pay) that “seems just and reasonable in the circumstances”; in discharge cases, “unless the infraction carries a specified penalty which may be discharge”, s. 25(3) applies when dismissal “could not be sustained”.
BaselineA: Statute — The Trade Union Act, R.S.S. 1978, c. T-17, s. 25(3) (interacting with the collective agreement’s discharge/reinstatement provisions).
CaseB_TestB: Article 1F(a) complicity (contribution-based test): exclude from refugee protection only if there are “serious reasons for considering” the claimant has “voluntarily made a significant and knowing contribution to the organization’s crime or criminal purpose”; contextual factors may guide the assessment (size/nature of organization; part involved; duties; rank; time in organization after knowledge; recruitment/opportunity to leave).
BaselineB: Statute + treaty — IRPA, s. 98 incorporating Refugee Convention, art. 1F(a) (informed by international criminal law concepts).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 43 Canada Evidence Act (letters rogatory): s. 43 authorizes production of documents alone (not merely ancillary to viva voce testimony) and should be construed broadly in the interests of comity; court applies comity guidelines (trial not discovery; relevance; scope permitted domestically; adequate precision of request).
BaselineA: Statute: Canada Evidence Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-10, s. 43 (letters rogatory/judicial assistance). Related statutory context discussed: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 178.2, 178.16, 446. Prior SCC guidance referenced: Zingre v. The Queen, [1981] 2 S.C.R. 392 (liberal/comity approach).
CaseB_TestB: Admissibility of defence-led unknown third party suspect evidence: (1) evidence must be relevant to a fact in issue (logical relevance shown by a sufficient connection/similarity between the charged crime and another incident plus evidence the accused could not have committed the other offence); and (2) evidence is admissible unless its prejudicial effects substantially outweigh its probative value (Seaboyer balancing), without the judge weighing credibility or requiring proof on a balance of probabilities.
BaselineB: Common law: general admissibility principles and balancing from R. v. Seaboyer, [1991] 2 S.C.R. 577; logical relevance from R. v. Corbett, [1988] 1 S.C.R. 670; air of reality threshold from R. v. Cinous, 2002 SCC 29; sufficient connection concept from third-party suspect jurisprudence (R. v. Grandinetti, 2005 SCC 5; McMillan v. The Queen, [1977] 2 S.C.R. 824).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Civil Code art. 1055 C.C. “ruin of a building” liability is assessed by the intended purpose/use of the building/part; if the victim used it for a purpose contrary to that intended, art. 1055 does not apply (and art. 1054 presumption applies only where damage is caused by the thing’s “positive and independent action”).
BaselineA: Statute (Civil Code of Quebec (as then in force), arts. 1053, 1054, 1055), as interpreted in prior SCC authority (notably Leznek v. City of Verdun, [1940] S.C.R. 313; Curley v. Latreille (1920), 60 S.C.R. 131).
CaseB_TestB: Mental capacity standard for confessions/right to silence/s. 10(b) waiver: the accused must have an “operating mind” (limited cognitive capacity) — understand what is being said/said by them and that it may be used against them; for s. 10(b) waiver, capacity aligns with fitness-to-stand-trial (can communicate with and understand the function of counsel), and no separate “awareness of consequences” test applies.
BaselineB: Combination of common law (confessions voluntariness/“operating mind” line: Ward; Horvath; Nagotcha; Hebert) and statute/constitutional text (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 7 and 10(b); Criminal Code definition of “unfit to stand trial”, s. 2).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Judicial review of a labour board’s “home statute” interpretation: intervene only if the interpretation is “patently unreasonable” / “plainly unreasonable” (certiorari is “a long way from an appeal”).
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law (deference on review in presence of privative/finality clauses). Statutory baseline: The Public Service Employee Relations Act, 1977 (Alta.), c. 40, ss. 9(1), 11, 48, 89. Common-law baseline as cited: Canadian Union of Public Employees Local 963 v. New Brunswick Liquor Corporation, [1979] 2 S.C.R. 227; Volvo Canada Ltd. v. U.A.W., Local 720, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 178; Douglas Aircraft Co. of Canada v. McConnell, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 245.
CaseB_TestB: Adverse-effect religious discrimination and duty to accommodate: discrimination is shown by the three s. 10 Quebec Charter elements, and the employer must take “reasonable steps to accommodate ... short of undue hardship” (no de minimis threshold).
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law. Statutory baseline: Quebec Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms, R.S.Q., c. C-12, ss. 10, 16 (and related rights provisions). Common-law baseline as cited: Ontario Human Rights Commission and O'Malley v. Simpsons-Sears Ltd., [1985] 2 S.C.R. 536 (adverse effect discrimination; accommodation “short of undue hardship”); Central Okanagan School District No. 23 v. Renaud, [1992] 2 S.C.R. 970; Central Alberta Dairy Pool v. Alberta (Human Rights Commission), [1990] 2 S.C.R. 489.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Similar fact evidence admissibility: (1) apply the Makin principle (relevance to an issue other than propensity) with probative value vs prejudice balancing; and (2) threshold requirement that there be an evidentiary link connecting the similar acts to the accused (not mere similarity). Key holding: “Before evidence may be admitted as evidence of similar facts, there must be a link between the allegedly similar facts and the accused… some evidence upon which the trier of fact can make a proper finding that the similar facts… were in fact the acts of the accused.”
BaselineA: Common law (similar fact evidence doctrine), drawing on Makin v. Attorney-General for New South Wales and Boardman v. DPP; link requirement supported by Harris v. DPP.
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 7 vagueness test (“legal debate” standard): “a law will be found unconstitutionally vague if it so lacks in precision as not to give sufficient guidance for legal debate — that is, for reaching a conclusion as to its meaning by reasoned analysis applying legal criteria.” (Applied to s. 32(1)(c) Combines Investigation Act: “unduly” not vague.)
BaselineB: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7 (principles of fundamental justice) and s. 1 in limine (“prescribed by law”), as developed in prior SCC vagueness jurisprudence (notably the Prostitution Reference).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 16(2) insanity — “first arm” requires incapacity to appreciate the nature and quality of the act in the sense of perceiving the physical consequences; failure to appreciate penal consequences (punishment) does not qualify
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 16(2)), as interpreted in Cooper v. The Queen, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 1149; Schwartz v. The Queen, [1977] 1 S.C.R. 673; R. v. Barnier, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 1124; Kjeldsen v. The Queen, [1981] 2 S.C.R. 617
CaseB_TestB: Administrative tribunal jurisdiction to decide constitutional issues (including s. 35): if empowering legislation “implicitly or explicitly grants ... jurisdiction to interpret or decide any question of law”, the tribunal is presumed to have concomitant jurisdiction to decide the constitutional question unless a “clear implication” rebuts it
BaselineB: Common law / constitutional doctrine on tribunal constitutional jurisdiction, applied from Nova Scotia (Workers’ Compensation Board) v. Martin, 2003 SCC 54; interpreted alongside Forest Practices Code of British Columbia Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 159, s. 131(8) (and related appeal provisions)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Patentability of a new use for an old compound as a “new and useful art” (and permissibility of claiming compositions as the practical embodiment): the invention is “the application of this new knowledge to effect a desired result which has an undisputed commercial value” and, once such a new use is discovered, “I can find nothing in the statute which would preclude a claim for these compositions” (Patent Act, ss. 2 and 36).
BaselineA: Statute (Patent Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. P-4, ss. 2 (definition of “invention”), 36 (specification/claims requirements), and discussion of s. 41 limits); informed by prior patent jurisprudence including Hickton’s Patent Syndicate (1909) and SCC cases such as Farbwerke Hoechst, Ciba, Burton Parsons.
CaseB_TestB: Party liability for drug trafficking by aiding/abetting under Criminal Code s. 21(1): to aid is “to assist or help the actor” (s. 21(1)(b)) and to abet includes “encouraging, instigating, promoting or procuring” (s. 21(1)(c)); mens rea—under s. 21(1)(b) “purpose” means “intention” (not “desire”), i.e., Crown must prove the accused “intended the consequences that flowed from his or her aid”; under s. 21(1)(c) Crown must prove the accused encouraged and “intended to do so.”
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, s. 21(1)(b),(c); Narcotic Control Act, ss. 2 “traffic”, 3(1), 4(1),(2)); with interpretive reliance on Hibbert (meaning of “purpose”) and Poitras/Meston (purchaser not a trafficker by purchase alone).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory incompatibility/repugnancy test: whether a permissive statutory discretion (Police Act s. 24(6)) excludes a collectively bargained/arbitrated clause otherwise authorized as a “working condition” under s. 29(2); i.e., whether the provisions are “incompatible or inconsistent” such that s. 24(6) prescribes exclusivity. The Court holds the discretion is “an empowering provision only” and “does not prescribe exclusivity”; thus “no incompatibility or inconsistency ...; each has its own area of operation.”
BaselineA: Statute: The Police Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 351, ss. 24(6) and 29(2) (plus the general statutory-interpretation concept of incompatibility/repugnancy between provisions, with analogy to International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers v. Town of Summerside, [1960] S.C.R. 591).
CaseB_TestB: State Immunity Act interpretation framework (key applied sub-test: s. 6(a) territorial tort/physical-integrity limits): the s. 6(a) “death or personal or bodily injury ... that occurs in Canada” exception applies only where (1) “the tort causing the personal injury or death has occurred in Canada” (the impugned events/tort must “occur in Canada”), and (2) the claimed injury must stem from “a physical breach of personal integrity” (per Schreiber: “limited to instances where mental distress and emotional upset were linked to a physical injury”; “some form of a breach of physical integrity must be made out”).
BaselineB: Statute: State Immunity Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. S-18, ss. 3(1), 6(a) (interpreted in light of the Act’s purpose and prior SCC authority in Schreiber v. Canada (Attorney General), 2002 SCC 62).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory incompatibility/repugnancy test between Police Act s. 24(6) (permissive indemnification discretion) and s. 29(2) (collective bargaining over “working conditions”): s. 24(6) does not exclude a bargained/arbitrated clause unless the provisions are “incompatible or inconsistent”; s. 24(6) is “an empowering provision only” and “does not prescribe exclusivity”.
BaselineA: Statute (The Police Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 351, ss. 24(6) and 29(2))
CaseB_TestB: Corporate attribution for BIA s. 96(1)(b)(ii)(B) transfers at undervalue: for s. 96, the “fraud” and “no benefit” exceptions do not apply; “the test for corporate attribution under s. 96 is simply whether the person was the directing mind and whether their actions were performed within the sector of corporate responsibility assigned to them.”
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law (BIA s. 96(1)(b)(ii)(B) and common law corporate attribution doctrine from Canadian Dredge; refined in Livent and DeJong)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Jennings test for establishing a constitutional convention (with emphasis that recognition/acceptance by the actors is the most important, normative requirement): (1) precedents; (2) did the actors believe they were bound; (3) reason for the rule; and a convention requires acceptance/recognition by the relevant political actors
BaselineA: Common law / constitutional convention doctrine as adopted in Re: Resolution to amend the Constitution, [1981] 1 S.C.R. 753 (quoting Jennings, The Law and the Constitution, and Freedman C.J.M./Hogg definition of convention)
CaseB_TestB: Reasonable suspicion standard for sniffer-dog (sniff) searches under Charter s. 8: police may deploy a drug detection dog without prior authorization where there is a reasonable suspicion, assessed on the totality of the circumstances, based on objective, ascertainable facts, and the dog used is sufficiently reliable
BaselineB: Common law Charter search framework (R. v. Collins) and prior SCC sniffer-dog cases (R. v. Kang-Brown; R. v. A.M.) defining authorization on “reasonable suspicion”
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory tribunal (art. 846 C.C.P.) test for labour arbitrators: even if parties were not compelled to choose arbitration, an arbitrator is a statutory tribunal once selected where statute confers wide duties/powers; refusal to hear admissible and relevant evidence is an excess/refusal of jurisdiction
BaselineA: Combination of common law and statute: prior certiorari/evocation jurisprudence (Howe Sound; Port Arthur; R. v. National Joint Council for the Craft of Dental Technicians) applied to Quebec Code of Civil Procedure, art. 846, in light of Canada Labour Code provisions (ss. 156(2), 157, 159, 160(5))
CaseB_TestB: Sublicence characterization test in patent licensing: a sublicence exists only if the licensee grants (expressly or impliedly) the right to do something the third party would otherwise be prohibited from doing and which the licensee may do only by virtue of the licence; interpret contract from its text (parol evidence excluded if unambiguous) and assess legal effect vs mere purchase-and-sale/supply arrangement
BaselineB: Primarily common law (licence/sublicence concepts and contract interpretation/parol evidence rule), applied in the statutory context of the Patent Act and Patented Medicines (Notice of Compliance) Regulations (notably Patent Act ss. 39(4), 39.11, 39.14; Regulations ss. 5-7)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Kienapple remedy direction: where Kienapple applies, enter a stay of proceedings rather than an acquittal
BaselineA: Common law (Kienapple v. The Queen, [1975] 1 S.C.R. 729)
CaseB_TestB: Removing/replacing a litigation guardian: the Rule 49(1) 'best interests' test, informed by the six Szwydky criteria (including required 'indifference' / no conflict)
BaselineB: Combination: statute/rules plus prior case guidance (Queen’s Bench Rules (Saskatchewan), r. 49(1); Szwydky v. Magiera (1988), 71 Sask. R. 273 (Q.B.))
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Contract-interpretation test for the extent of the Company’s obligation to supply electricity at the contract rate: reconcile the general words in para. 1 (“to such an extent as the said Town… may require”) with the specific allocation provisions in paras. 6 and 8, yielding a fixed entitlement of 4,000 horsepower at $14/hp/year (and no broader right to the whole output). Key holding: the Company’s commitment “is to provide electrical energy… to the extent of 4,000 horsepower per annum… at the contract price of $14 per horsepower per annum.”
BaselineA: Common law (contract interpretation) applied to the January 9, 1905 agreement; the Court treats the federal/provincial statutes as having “no direct bearing” on the dispositive issue.
CaseB_TestB: General Motors indicia for validity under the general branch of the federal trade and commerce power (s. 91(2)): ask (1) general regulatory scheme; (2) oversight by a regulatory agency; (3) concerned with “trade as a whole rather than with a particular industry”; (4) provinces “acting alone or in concert, would be constitutionally incapable of enacting it”; (5) failure to include one or more provinces would “jeopardize its successful operation in other parts of the country” (indicia “not exhaustive” and “not necessary that they be present in every case”).
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine interpreting Constitution Act, 1867, s. 91(2) (general trade and commerce power), based on General Motors of Canada Ltd. v. City National Leasing and related jurisprudence.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Contract-interpretation framework for extent of obligation to supply power at fixed price: reconcile general clause (“to such an extent as the said Town… may require”) with specific allocation clauses (paras. 6 and 8), yielding a fixed entitlement of 4,000 horsepower/year at $14 per horsepower/year
BaselineA: Common law (contract interpretation principles) applied to the 1905 Agreement (esp. paras. 1, 5, 6, 8, 13); statutes held not to govern the issue
CaseB_TestB: Continuing-offence/party-liability test for kidnapping: kidnapping continues while victim remains unlawfully confined; a latecomer is a party under s. 21(1) if, with knowledge of the ongoing kidnapping (or wilful blindness) and intent to assist, they do/omit something to aid or abet the ongoing offence
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, ss. 279(1), 279(2), 21(1)) interpreted in light of common law meaning of kidnapping as aggravated unlawful confinement; party-liability principles from R. v. Briscoe and R. v. Thatcher
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Hartel s. 70(1) trigger: land is “designated under a land use by-law” only if the designation is made in the land use by-law itself (not merely in statutory plans), so the s. 70(1) duty to acquire/expropriate is not triggered by statutory plans
BaselineA: Statute: The Planning Act, 1977 (Alta.), s. 70(1) (and definition of “land use by-law” in s. 1(14))
CaseB_TestB: O’Connor (L’Heureux-Dubé J.) framework: (1) stay for Crown non-disclosure only where s. 7 prejudice to full answer and defence is shown on a balance of probabilities and the case is among the “clearest of cases”; and (2) two-stage production of private third-party records—accused must show “likely relevance”, then the judge balances salutary/deleterious effects (privacy, equality, etc.) to decide whether/what to produce
BaselineB: Combination: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms ss. 7 and 24(1) (stay/remedy) plus common law abuse-of-process jurisprudence (e.g., R. v. Jewitt) and Criminal Code subpoena provisions (e.g., ss. 698, 700) for third-party records
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “has become regularly engaged in some other occupation” under Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, s. 44(1)(c): focuses on regularity of work schedule (a “fixed pattern”) rather than duration or intent to abandon former job
BaselineA: Statute: Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, s. 44(1)(c) (with contextual comparison to s. 44(1)(b) and Regulations s. 49 defining “bona fide employed” as “not less than two weeks duration”)
CaseB_TestB: Whether an entity is a “broadcasting undertaking” under the Broadcasting Act when it merely provides the mode of transmission: requires some measure of control over programming (selection/origination/packaging) and a role in advancing the Act’s content-focused policy objectives
BaselineB: Statute: Broadcasting Act, S.C. 1991, c. 11, ss. 2(1) (“broadcasting”), 2(3), 3(1)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Cross-border fresh pursuit & s. 25(4) protection: an officer retains peace-officer status in another province (for s. 25(4)) if the pursuit began lawfully in his jurisdiction and remains “fresh”; plus arrest authority/justification turns on whether the suspect would have “appeared to a reasonable person, placed in the same circumstances” to be committing the offence (reasonable and probable grounds).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code): ss. 450(1)(b) (arrest without warrant), 25(4) (force to prevent escape by flight), and related ss. 449(1)(b), 25(1),(3). Baseline interpretation drawn from R. v. Biron, [1976] 2 S.C.R. 56 (arrest validity assessed by circumstances apparent at the time / “apparently committing” read with objective reasonableness).
CaseB_TestB: “Specific penalty” threshold under Canada Labour Code s. 157(d)(ii): an arbitrator is deprived of substitution jurisdiction only if “a specific penalty must be assigned to the particular infraction in the collective agreement”; a penalty is not “specific” if it is not in the collective agreement or if it “can be chosen indiscriminately by the employer.”
BaselineB: Statute (Canada Labour Code, s. 157(d), especially s. 157(d)(ii)) interpreted against the collective agreement (Article XI(b)).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Per quod servitium amisit availability for the Crown re Armed Forces: Crown may recover for loss of services where (i) the injured person is the Crown’s servant (here, deemed by statute) and (ii) the servant has a valid cause of action against the wrongdoer; damages include necessary costs such as wages/allowances and medical/hospital expenses (and the action is not confined to domestic/menial services).
BaselineA: Combination: statute + common law. Statutory baseline is Federal Court Act, R.S.C. 1970 (2nd Supp.), c. 10, s. 37 (and the parallel Exchequer Court Act, R.S.C. 1952, c. 98, s. 50) deeming Forces members to be servants of the Crown; common-law baseline is the per quod servitium amisit action as recognized in SCC cases (The King v. Richardson; Nykorak v. Attorney General of Canada; Attorney-General of Canada v. Jackson; The Queen v. Murray).
JudgeA: Ritchie J. (for Ritchie, Estey, Lamer and Wilson JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Mens rea for Criminal Code s. 121(1)(a): guilt requires (1) the accused knows he/she is an official; (2) intentionally demands/accepts (etc.) a loan, reward, advantage or benefit; and (3) knows the benefit is given “as consideration for cooperation, assistance or exercise of influence” in connection with “the transaction of business with or relating to the government”; no additional “corrupt” purpose is required and the Crown need not prove the benefit was conferred because of official status.
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 121(1)(a) (and related interpretive context including s. 19). The Court also relies on prior SCC interpretation in Martineau v. La Reine regarding acting in an “official capacity” not being required.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Timing rule for Attorney General stay under Criminal Code s. 508(1): an information is “found” only after the justice decides to issue process; therefore the AG’s power to stay “starts as of the moment a summons or warrant is issued” (not merely upon laying/receiving the information).
CaseB_TestB: Statutory eligibility rule for discharge under Criminal Code s. 662.1(1): discharge is unavailable if the offence is one “for which a minimum punishment is prescribed by law”; s. 234(a) prescribes a minimum ($50 fine), so s. 662.1(1) does not apply.
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, ss. 234(a), 662.1(1); discussed alongside s. 645(2))
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 508 stay power timing: an information is “found” (triggering the AG’s stay power) only after the justice decides to issue process; “The Attorney General’s power to stay starts as of the moment a summons or warrant is issued.”
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34 as amended), especially ss. 455, 455.3, 503, 508
CaseB_TestB: Procedural fairness content (Baker factors) requiring reasons: duty of fairness “varies according to five factors” and, on these facts, “require[s] the Municipality to articulate reasons” for refusing the 2nd and 3rd rezoning applications
BaselineB: Common law administrative law duty of fairness framework from Baker v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), [1999] 2 S.C.R. 817 (five-factor test)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Jurisdictional rule against joint trial on separate indictments/informations: even with consent, a judge is "without jurisdiction to try together separate informations or indictments"; applies under the Criminal Code and provincial statutes unless the statute "expressly provide[s] otherwise" (Crane v. Public Prosecutor applied).
BaselineA: Common law rule from Crane v. Public Prosecutor, [1921] 2 A.C. 299 (also applied in R. v. Dennis; R. v. Parker, [1924] 1 K.B. 867), treated as incorporated by implication into the Criminal Code; extended to provincial summary conviction procedure absent express statutory authorization.
CaseB_TestB: Credibility-assessment guidance on (1) absence of evidence of motive to lie and (2) lack of embellishment: absence of motive evidence may be relevant but judges must avoid (a) treating "no evidence either way" as proof disproving a motive and (b) reversing the burden by requiring the accused to show a motive; lack of embellishment "cannot be used to bolster" credibility and "simply does not weigh against it" (may be considered only regarding motive-to-lie).
BaselineB: Common law credibility/reasoning principles in criminal trials, drawing on R. v. W.(D.) and prior SCC guidance (R. v. Stirling; R. v. Vuradin; R. v. G.F.).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Marine insurance “perils of the seas” causation test for negligent acts: an act is negligent only relative to a foreseeable risk; if the foreseeable risk is a “peculiarly marine risk”, then the act plus its foreseeable consequence is a “fortuitous accident of the seas” and thus a “peril of the seas” and the proximate cause of the loss ("If that foreseeable risk of harm is a peculiarly marine risk, then the act, coupled with its foreseeable consequence, is a fortuitous accident of the seas and a peril of the seas and the proximate cause of the loss.").
BaselineA: Statute (Insurance (Marine) Act, R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 203, Schedule “Rules for Construction of Policy” defining perils of the seas as “fortuitous accidents or casualties of the seas”; and Marine Insurance Act, R.S.B.C. 1960, c. 231, s. 57(2)(a) (now s. 56(2)(a)) on insurer liability despite crew negligence) plus common-law/authorities applied (Canada Rice Mills, Ld. v. Union Marine & General Insurance Co., [1941] A.C. 55; Cohen, Sons & Co. v. National Benefit Assurance Co. (1924), 18 Ll. L. Rep. 199).
CaseB_TestB: Section 35(1) threshold test for who can assert Aboriginal rights: an Aboriginal group must be an “aboriginal peopl[e] of Canada”, meaning “the modern-day successors of Aboriginal societies that occupied Canadian territory at the time of European contact” (and this “may include Aboriginal groups that are now outside Canada”).
BaselineB: Constitution (Constitution Act, 1982, s. 35(1): “The existing aboriginal and treaty rights of the aboriginal peoples of Canada are hereby recognized and affirmed.”), interpreted purposively in light of prior s. 35 jurisprudence (e.g., Sparrow; Van der Peet; Mitchell) but addressing a previously undecided threshold question.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory “bridging” of an expired collective agreement preserves the right to invoke interest arbitration: s. 70(1) preserves “any right” (including interest arbitration) if notice to arbitrate is given within the s. 70 window; the right need only exist at the time of notice, not when the award issues.
BaselineA: Statute + collective agreement interpretation (Ontario Labour Relations Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 232, s. 70(1) (now R.S.O. 1980, c. 228, s. 79) and the interest-arbitration clauses in the collective agreements; prior SCC reference: Bradburn v. Wentworth Arms Hotel Limited, [1979] 1 S.C.R. 846).
CaseB_TestB: Directed verdict / non-suit test: whether there is “any admissible evidence, whether direct or circumstantial, which, if believed by a properly charged jury acting reasonably, would justify a conviction” (from U.S.A. v. Shephard as applied in Monteleone).
BaselineB: Common law (as stated in R. v. Monteleone, [1987] 2 S.C.R. 154, deriving the test from United States of America v. Shephard, [1977] 2 S.C.R. 1067).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: McKibbon (Lamer J.) conditions for an Attorney General’s agent (or other non-AG under s. 507(2)) to prefer an indictment adding counts: (1) a preliminary inquiry has been held; (2) the accused has been committed for trial on at least one charge inquired into; and (3) each added count must be for an offence the accused was committed on, or an offence disclosed by the preliminary inquiry evidence and not one the accused was discharged on
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 507(1)-(3), interpreted in light of ss. 504-505 and contrasted with s. 496)
CaseB_TestB: Mitchell / Van der Peet test for establishing an Aboriginal right under s. 35(1): claimant must prove (1) existence of an ancestral practice, custom or tradition; (2) that it was integral to the distinctive culture (a defining feature, such that the culture would be “fundamentally altered” without it); and (3) reasonable continuity between the pre-contact practice and the modern claim
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine under Constitution Act, 1982, s. 35(1), applying Van der Peet and Delgamuukw (and related s. 35 jurisprudence)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Planned-and-deliberate first degree murder where s. 212(b) applies: if the accused planned and deliberated the intention to kill A, and in carrying out that plan “by accident or mistake causes death to another human being” (B), the murder of B is first degree; “the identity and character of any victim is entirely irrelevant” when s. 214(2) is combined with s. 212(b).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 212(b) and 214(2), within the homicide scheme including s. 205; with reliance on SCC interpretation in R. v. Farrant, [1983] 1 S.C.R. 24 that s. 214 is a sentencing classification provision).
CaseB_TestB: Interpretation of Alberta Limitations Act, s. 12 in conflicts cases: s. 12 “does not purport to revive an action time-barred by the substantive law of the place where the accident occurred”; where lex loci delicti applies (Tolofson) and the foreign limitation has expired, “there was no right of action” and the claim is barred.
BaselineB: Statute (Limitations Act, R.S.A. 2000, c. L-12, s. 12) interpreted against the common-law conflicts baseline from Tolofson v. Jensen, [1994] 3 S.C.R. 1022 (lex loci delicti and foreign limitation as substantive).
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Mens rea for attempted murder: the Crown must prove a specific intent to kill (no constructive/lesser intent under ss. 212/213 can ground an attempt).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code) plus prior SCC precedent (Lajoie v. The Queen, [1974] S.C.R. 399). Key provisions: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 24(1) (attempt), 212 (murder intents), 213(d) (constructive murder), and s. 222 (attempted murder penalty provision).
CaseB_TestB: “Establishment” for pay equity under CHRA s. 11 / Guidelines s. 10: determine whether employees are subject to a “common personnel and wage policy” (a factual inquiry into the employer’s common principles/approach, not a term-by-term comparison of collective agreements).
BaselineB: Statute and regulation/guidelines: Canadian Human Rights Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. H-6, ss. 11 and 27(2), read with Equal Wages Guidelines, 1986, SOR/86-1082, s. 10.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory limits on unequal matrimonial property distribution: pre-marital property exemption under s. 23 is capped at fair market value at marriage; s. 21(2)(q) cannot be used to expand the exemption (rejecting the “Capital Base Theory”)
BaselineA: Statute: The Matrimonial Property Act, 1979 (Sask.), c. M-6.1, especially ss. 21 and 23 (equal distribution presumption; pre-marital exemption and its limited discretion)
CaseB_TestB: Aggravated assault (s. 268(1) “endangers life”) in HIV non-disclosure cases requires proof beyond a reasonable doubt of the aggravating consequence (endangerment) at the time of the assault; if there is a reasonable doubt the complainant was already HIV-positive, aggravated assault is not made out (attempt may be)
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, ss. 268(1) (aggravated assault), 265(1)(a) and 265(3)(c) (assault/consent/fraud), and attempt provisions ss. 24(1), 660; informed by SCC cases cited in the reasons (e.g., Cuerrier; DeSousa; Cooper)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Mechanics’ lien Act “owner” test (s. 1(1)(d)): a party is an owner if it (a) has an estate or interest in the land, (b) requested the work, and (c) the work was done “upon whose credit”, “on whose behalf”, “with whose privity or consent”, or “for whose direct benefit” (overall view of the arrangements may establish the ‘request’).
BaselineA: Statute: The Mechanics’ Lien Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 267, s. 1(1)(d) (and applied with s. 5(1), plus discussion of ss. 7 and 11).
CaseB_TestB: Challenge for cause (Criminal Code s. 638(1)(b)) “realistic potential for juror partiality” test: generally requires (1) a “widespread bias” in the community and (2) that some jurors may be unable to set aside the bias despite trial safeguards; overarching question is whether there is a “realistic potential for partial juror behaviour”.
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 638(1)(b), as interpreted through prior SCC cases (notably R. v. Sherratt and R. v. Williams).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Anns duty-of-care framework for municipal liability in negligent building inspection/enforcement: (1) proximity/foreseeability — “is there a sufficiently close relationship between the parties ... so that, in the reasonable contemplation of the authority, carelessness on its part might cause damage to that person?”; (2) residual policy limits — “are there any considerations which ought to negative or limit (a) the scope of the duty and (b) the class of persons to whom it is owed or (c) the damages to which a breach of it may give rise?”; plus the policy/operational distinction (no liability for bona fide policy decisions; liability may attach in the operational sphere, including where the authority fails to act without a bona fide policy decision).
BaselineA: Common law (adopting and applying Anns v. Merton London Borough Council, [1978] A.C. 728; also drawing on Donoghue v. Stevenson; Hedley Byrne; Dorset Yacht). Applied in the statutory context of Municipal Act, R.S.B.C. 1960, c. 255, s. 714 and the City’s building by-law imposing an enforcement duty.
CaseB_TestB: “Prescribed by law” via necessary implication from statutory operating requirements (Therens) for a s. 10(b) roadside-counsel limit: a limit is prescribed if it is “expressly provided for by statute or regulation, or results by necessary implication from the terms of a statute or regulation or from its operating requirements”; applied to hold that reasonable roadside sobriety questions/tests are within implied police authority and “incompatible with the exercise of the right to counsel,” and then justified under s. 1 using the Oakes proportionality criteria (important objective; rational connection; minimal impairment; proportionality of effects).
BaselineB: Combination of statute and constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 1 and 10(b); Highway Traffic Act (Manitoba), s. 76.1(1); Criminal Code, ss. 253 and 254. Interprets “prescribed by law” using R. v. Therens and extends the Thomsen implied-limit approach.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal defence of necessity (as an excuse): requires “urgent situation of clear and imminent peril when compliance with the law is demonstrably impossible”, with limits including (i) imminent risk/direct and immediate peril, (ii) no reasonable legal alternative (“legal way out”), (iii) proportionality (harm inflicted < harm avoided), plus limits on contributory fault and Crown must disprove voluntariness beyond a reasonable doubt once properly raised
BaselineA: Common law defence preserved by Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 7(3), building from Morgentaler v. The Queen, [1976] 1 S.C.R. 616 (quoted formulation: “urgent situation of clear and imminent peril when compliance with the law is demonstrably impossible”)
CaseB_TestB: Section 8 Charter “reasonable expectation of privacy” (REP) inquiry: REP assessed on the “totality of the circumstances” via four lines of inquiry (subject matter; direct interest; subjective expectation; and whether that expectation is objectively reasonable as a normative question), applied to determine whether police screen-capture of online communications in a child-luring sting engages s. 8
BaselineB: Common law/constitutional doctrine under Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 8, using the established REP framework from cases cited in the reasons (e.g., R. v. Edwards; R. v. Tessling; R. v. Spencer; R. v. Cole; R. v. Marakah)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 613(1)(b)(iii) proviso (harmless error): Crown must satisfy the court the verdict "would necessarily have been the same" absent the legal error; where exculpatory evidence was excluded, assess the entirety of the evidence including the reasonable possible effect of the excluded evidence, with any reasonable effect enuring to the accused
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 613(1)(b)(iii)), as interpreted in Colpitts v. The Queen, [1965] S.C.R. 739 (Cartwright J.: Crown must satisfy the court the verdict "would necessarily have been the same if such error had not occurred")
CaseB_TestB: Appellate court raising a new issue on appeal: a "new issue" is one that raises a new basis for finding error beyond the parties’ grounds; discretion to raise it should be exercised only rarely—only when failing to do so would risk an injustice (i.e., there is "good reason to believe" the result would realistically have differed), and the court must also consider jurisdiction, sufficiency of the record, and procedural prejudice, with notice and opportunity to respond
BaselineB: Common law / appellate practice principles (building on prior SCC guidance such as R. v. W. (G.), [1999] 3 S.C.R. 597 and Quan v. Cusson, 2009 SCC 62, referenced in the reasons) recognizing appellate courts’ jurisdiction to invite submissions on issues not raised by the parties
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Threshold s. 96 ‘judicial power’ characterization: a power is administrative (not judicial) where there is no real lis between parties and the decision is based on expediency rather than legality
BaselineA: Common law / constitutional doctrine under Constitution Act, 1867, s. 96, drawing on Re Residential Tenancies Act, 1979; Massey-Ferguson; Grondin; and the ‘judicial power’ indicia from John East Iron Works and related cases
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 12 mandatory-minimum framework (as applied in Hilbach): two-stage inquiry—(1) determine a fit and proportionate sentence; (2) ask whether the mandatory minimum is ‘grossly disproportionate’, assessed via scope/reach of offence, effects on offender, and the penalty/objectives; may be based on actual offender or a reasonably foreseeable case
BaselineB: Combination of constitutional text and precedent: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 12 (and related sentencing provisions in the Criminal Code), applying/clarifying the Hills/Nur/Smith/Lloyd line of cases
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 93(1) denominational schools protection test: s. 93 applies where (a) there is a "right or privilege affecting a denominational school" (b) "enjoyed by a particular class of persons" (c) "by law" (d) "in effect at the time of the Union" and (e) "which is prejudicially affected"; if so, the provincial law is ultra vires to the extent of the prejudicial effect.
BaselineA: Constitution Act, 1867, s. 93(1) (and s. 93(2)); applied by reference to rights existing "by law" at Confederation (e.g., C.S.L.C. 1861, c. 15) and Privy Council jurisprudence cited in the reasons (e.g., Barrett; Hirsch; Tiny).
CaseB_TestB: Young Offenders Act non-disclosure ‘link’ test for dockets/communications: the "nub" is whether the information "links the identity of the young person with a charge, proceeding or disposition"; if the prohibited link is made, disclosure/publication is barred unless it fits within enumerated statutory exceptions (notably ss. 38(1.1), 38(1.13), or record-disclosure under s. 44.1).
BaselineB: Statute: Young Offenders Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. Y-1, especially ss. 38(1), 38(1.1), 38(1.13), 40-46 (including s. 44.1 and s. 46).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 93(1) denominational schools protection test: s. 93 applies where (a) there is a right or privilege affecting a denominational school, (b) enjoyed by a particular class of persons, (c) by law, (d) in effect at the time of the Union, and (e) which is 'prejudicially affected' (applied to school financing/grants/taxation measures).
BaselineA: Constitution Act, 1867, s. 93(1) (and s. 93(2)); baseline articulation of the conditions for protection as stated by the trial judge and accepted by the parties, plus historical 'by law at the Union' rights drawn from the 1861 Act (C.S.L.C. 1861, c. 15) and Privy Council/SCC authorities cited (e.g., Hirsch; Tiny; Barrett; Ottawa Separate Schools Trustees).
CaseB_TestB: Canadian maritime law / navigation-and-shipping scope test: the 'mere involvement of a pleasure craft' is insufficient; courts must examine the factual context and ask whether the allegedly negligent act is 'so integrally connected' to navigation/shipping that it is a 'practical necessity' for Parliament to have jurisdiction (otherwise provincial property and civil rights applies).
BaselineB: Common law constitutional/maritime-law framework from ITO — International Terminal Operators Ltd. v. Miida Electronics Inc. ("so integrally connected"), Whitbread v. Walley (practical necessity for uniform law re pleasure craft navigation), and Ordon Estate v. Grail (examine factual context), applied alongside Constitution Act, 1867, ss. 91(10) and 92(13).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Certiorari can quash a committal for trial under Criminal Code s. 475 where there is “no evidence” on an essential element: “'No evidence' on an essential element of the charge against the accused cannot amount to 'sufficient evidence' under s. 475”; reviewing court must “independently assess the record to determine whether there was any evidence to support the committal”.
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 475) as interpreted through SCC certiorari/jurisdiction jurisprudence (e.g., Patterson v. The Queen; Martin v. The Queen; Forsythe v. The Queen) cited in the reasons.
JudgeA: Estey J. (for Dickson, Estey, Lamer and Wilson JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Art. 559 C.C.Q. compensatory allowance requirements: claimant must establish “(1) his or her contribution; (2) the enrichment of his or her spouse's patrimony; (3) the causal link between the two; and (4) the proportion in which the contribution made possible the enrichment”; “Each of these elements must be evaluated with great flexibility”; enrichment “must subsist and must be evaluated at the time of the divorce”.
BaselineB: Statute/civil code (Civil Code of Quebec, art. 559) informed by unjust enrichment principles (e.g., Cie Immobilière Viger Ltée v. Lauréat Giguère Inc. on “correlation”) and interacting with Bankruptcy Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. B-3, ss. 2 and 148 (provable claims/discharge).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Estoppel by representation (including by silence): requires (1) a representation by words/conduct, or by silence/inaction only where there is a legal duty to speak; (2) intention (actual or presumptive) and result of inducing reliance; and (3) the representee alters position to its detriment (detrimental reliance).
BaselineA: Common law (estoppel by representation), as summarized from Spencer Bower & Turner and cases such as Greenwood v. Martins Bank, Ltd.
CaseB_TestB: Rebutting the Criminal Code s. 212(3) presumption: the jury should consider all the evidence about cohabitation and financial arrangements to decide whether the presumption has been rebutted; the judge need not identify a single “particular and severable” item of “evidence to the contrary”.
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 212(3)).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Municipal taxing power must be exercised in the form required by the enabling statute (by-law vs resolution); self-delegation to set a tax rate by resolution when the statute requires a by-law is ultra vires (excess of jurisdiction) and supports a direct action in nullity
BaselineA: Statute (Cities and Towns Act, R.S.Q. 1941, c. 233, art. 526 as amended for Dorval; plus Code of Civil Procedure, art. 33 (formerly art. 50))
CaseB_TestB: Causation in negligent blood-donor screening: apply the 'material contribution' test (not a rebuttable presumption from Hollis and not strict 'but-for' necessity); plaintiff must prove the defendant’s negligence 'materially contributed' to the injury (i.e., more than de minimis)
BaselineB: Common law (causation in negligence; Court applies Snell v. Farrell and Athey v. Leonati; distinguishes Hollis v. Dow Corning)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 13 bar on using an accused’s prior testimony to incriminate them at a retrial: a retrial is “any other proceedings”; incrimination assessed in the second proceeding
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 13 (interpreted in light of ss. 11(c) and 11(d))
CaseB_TestB: Reformed rule for substantive admissibility of a non-accused witness’s prior inconsistent statement: threshold ‘would be admissible as sole testimony’ plus principled hearsay reliability/necessity with specified reliability indicia and a voir dire
BaselineB: Combination: Statute (Canada Evidence Act, s. 9) plus common law ‘orthodox rule’ limiting prior inconsistent statements to credibility only (e.g., Deacon v. The King), modified via principled hearsay approach (Khan; Smith)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: When a trial judge’s acquittal can be appealed by the Crown as a “question of law alone”: a “total absence of evidence” is an error of law only where the law has shifted the burden of proof to the accused; otherwise “there is always some evidence upon which to make a finding of fact favourable to the accused” (presumption of innocence).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 605(1)(a) (Crown appeal on a question of law alone)) plus SCC common law on law/fact distinction in Crown appeals (Lampard v. The Queen; Sunbeam Corporation (Canada) Ltd. v. The Queen; discussion of Wild v. The Queen and Lemire).
CaseB_TestB: Test for interim relief/stay under Supreme Court Act s. 65.1 (RJR–MacDonald): applicant must show (1) a serious question, (2) irreparable harm, and (3) balance of convenience favours relief.
BaselineB: Statute (Supreme Court Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. S-26, s. 65.1) as applied through the common-law/interlocutory-relief framework reaffirmed in RJR–MacDonald Inc. v. Canada (Attorney General).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Crown appeal from acquittal: when an alleged “no evidence”/“no foundation” finding becomes an error of law (only where the burden has shifted to the accused)
BaselineA: Combination: statute (Criminal Code, s. 605(1)(a) (appeal on question of law alone)) plus SCC common-law/jurisprudential principles on law vs fact from Lampard v. The Queen, Sunbeam Corporation (Canada) Ltd. v. The Queen, and discussion of Wild v. The Queen (and not following Lemire to the extent inconsistent)
CaseB_TestB: Ontario anti-SLAPP dismissal framework under CJA s. 137.1: threshold (s. 137.1(3)) plus plaintiff’s merits hurdles and public-interest weighing (s. 137.1(4))
BaselineB: Statute: Courts of Justice Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.43, s. 137.1(3) and s. 137.1(4) (and related ss. 137.2-137.5 as context)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Lawfulness of warrantless arrest on private premises (forcible entry) under Criminal Code s. 450(1)(a) + Eccles v. Bourque conditions: arrest is lawful if (1) offence is indictable; (2) officer has committed/believes on reasonable and probable grounds the person committed/is about to commit it; (3) reasonable and probable grounds the person is within the premises; (4) “proper announcement” before entry (notice of presence, authority, and purpose). “An affirmative answer to all of these questions will mean that the arrest is lawful.”
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 450(1)(a) (arrest without warrant for indictable offence) interpreted against common law spatial limits from Eccles v. Bourque, [1975] 2 S.C.R. 739 (itself drawing on Semayne’s Case (1604)).
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 15 discrimination analysis (as applied in Turpin): even if a law denies an equality right (e.g., “equality before the law”), there is no s. 15 breach unless the distinction is “discriminatory” in purpose or effect—i.e., a distinction “based on grounds relating to personal characteristics of the individual or group” that imposes burdens or withholds benefits; requires examining the “larger social, political and legal context” and typically looking for disadvantage beyond the impugned distinction.
BaselineB: Constitutional/Charter baseline: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 15(1), as interpreted in Andrews v. Law Society of British Columbia, [1989] 1 S.C.R. 143 (definition/approach to discrimination), applied to Criminal Code ss. 427, 429, 430.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code indictment amendment for variance: amend to conform to evidence unless accused was misled/prejudiced or injustice would result (s. 529(4)-(5)); appellate court may amend conviction/indictment on dismissal (s. 613(1)(b)(i), (3))
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 529(4)-(5) (amendment criteria; prejudice/adjournment cure) and ss. 613(1)(b)(i), (3) (SCC power to amend on appeal); plus interpretation of offence element under Narcotic Control Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. N-1, ss. 2, 4 and Schedule item 3 ("narcotic" includes cannabis resin and marihuana).
CaseB_TestB: Ineffective assistance of counsel (G.D.B.) test: appellant must show (1) counsel’s acts/omissions constituted incompetence and (2) a miscarriage of justice resulted
BaselineB: Common law: R. v. G.D.B., 2000 SCC 22, [2000] 1 S.C.R. 520 at para. 26 (two-part incompetence + miscarriage of justice test).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Concurrent liability in contract and tort for professional negligence: a common law duty of care arises from a relationship of sufficient proximity even if created by contract, but tort cannot be used to circumvent contractual limits; plus discoverability for limitation periods (cause of action arises when material facts are discovered or ought to be discovered by reasonable diligence). Key formulations: (1) proximity not confined to non-contract: "The question is whether there is a relationship of sufficient proximity, not how it arose." (2) tort duty must not depend on express contractual specification: "between what is to be done and how it is to be done"; and (3) no circumvention: "will not be admitted if its effect would be to permit the plaintiff to circumvent or escape a contractual exclusion or limitation of liability"; (4) discoverability: "A cause of action arises for purposes of a limitation period when the material facts on which it is based have been discovered or ought to have been discovered ... by the exercise of reasonable diligence."
BaselineA: Common law (duty of care/proximity and concurrent liability principles from Donoghue v. Stevenson; Hedley Byrne; Anns v. Merton; plus Kamloops v. Nielsen for discoverability), applied alongside a provincial limitations statute (Nova Scotia Statute of Limitations, R.S.N.S. 1967, c. 168, s. 2(1)(e)).
CaseB_TestB: Jurisdiction in Quebec over an action in warranty where there is an exclusive choice-of-forum clause: art. 3148 para. 2 C.C.Q. prevails over art. 3139 C.C.Q. if the clause shows a clear intention to oust Quebec jurisdiction; in that case "the Quebec authority must decline jurisdiction" and forum non conveniens (art. 3135) is unavailable because it is only "applicable only where the jurisdiction of the Quebec court has first been established."
BaselineB: Statute/codified private international law: Civil Code of Québec, arts. 3148 para. 2 (choice of forum), 3139 (incidental demand), and 3135 (forum non conveniens).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Scope of Quebec Construction Industry Labour Relations Act/Decree: coverage turns on the nature of the work ("construction" vs excluded "maintenance and repair"), not the status of the employer/employee; and Decree minimum conditions cannot be displaced by a "total wage" set-off
BaselineA: Statute and regulation/decree: Construction Industry Labour Relations Act, S.Q. 1968, c. 45 (notably ss. 1(e) ("construction"), 1(i) ("employer"), 1(j) ("professional employer"), 1(r) ("permanent employee"), 2(2) (exception)); and Decree respecting the construction industry (1973) 105 O.G. II 5837 (notably ss. 3.01, 3.02; plus public order clauses such as s. 18.06 and s. 32.03)
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 12 mandatory minimum sentencing analysis and remedy: a sentence violates s. 12 only if "grossly disproportionate" ("so excessive as to outrage standards of decency" / "abhorrent or intolerable"), and if a mandatory minimum is unconstitutional the proper remedy is s. 52 invalidity (no stand-alone constitutional exemption under Charter s. 24(1))
BaselineB: Combination of constitutional text and common law: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 12 and 24(1); Constitution Act, 1982, s. 52(1); Criminal Code, s. 236(a) (four-year minimum). Common-law baseline for the s. 12 test: R. v. Smith (gross disproportionality) and related mandatory-minimum jurisprudence (e.g., Goltz; Morrisey) as cited in the reasons.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Parens patriae limit: a court should never authorize non-therapeutic sterilization of a mentally incompetent person (because it can never safely be determined to be for the person’s benefit)
BaselineA: Common law (parens patriae jurisdiction as inherited from the English Court of Chancery/Lord Chancellor; exercised on the basis of necessity and for the protected person’s benefit/welfare)
CaseB_TestB: Residual management rights ‘balancing of interests’ assessment: arbitrator considers all surrounding circumstances and decides whether the employer policy strikes a reasonable balance between management and employees’ interests (reasonableness/fairness under the collective agreement)
BaselineB: Common law / labour arbitration doctrine incorporated through the collective agreement’s management-rights limits (notably the KVP framework as endorsed in Irving)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Kienapple (rule against multiple convictions) — applies only where there is (1) a sufficient factual nexus (usually: “Does the same act of the accused ground each of the charges?”) and (2) a sufficient legal nexus such that “there is no additional and distinguishing element that goes to guilt” in the second offence; plus, for personal-violence offences, Kienapple is inapplicable where convictions relate to different victims
BaselineA: Common law (Kienapple v. The Queen; also developed through cases like Côté v. The Queen and Krug v. The Queen, as discussed in the reasons)
JudgeA: The Chief Justice (Dickson C.J., for the Court)
CaseB_TestB: Meaning of “services … to the public” under Yukon Human Rights Act s. 8(a): two-step analysis — (1) identify the “service”; (2) determine whether it creates a “public relationship” between provider and user, assessed contextually using non-determinative criteria (e.g., selectivity, diversity of the public, non-member involvement, commercial nature, intimate nature, purpose)
BaselineB: Statute (Yukon Human Rights Act, R.S.Y. 1986 (Supp.), c. 11, s. 8(a); interpreted in light of analogous Canadian human rights provisions and UBC v. Berg)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Ensite test for whether property is "used or held ... in the course of carrying on a business" (ITA s. 129(4)(a)(ii) exclusion): ask whether the property was used to fulfil a requirement that had to be met to do business; the property must be "truly employed and risked" in the business, with "risk" meaning more than a remote risk or mere business purpose; the threshold is met when withdrawal would "have a decidedly destabilizing effect on the corporate operations themselves".
BaselineA: Statute (Income Tax Act, S.C. 1970-71-72, c. 63, s. 129(4)(a)(ii) as amended by S.C. 1974-75-76, c. 26, s. 86(2); interpreting "property used or held ... in the course of carrying on a business").
