CaseB_TestB: Test for when prior consistent statements may be admitted on re-examination to support credibility: although a witness generally cannot repeat prior out-of-court statements, they "may be admitted in support of the credibility of a witness" where the witness is challenged as a "recent fabrication or contrivance"; and the "right to re-examine must be confined to matters arising from the cross-examination" (i.e., questions permitted as of right must relate to new matters arising out of cross-examination or matters needing explanation).
BaselineB: Common law (credibility/prior consistent statements and scope of re-examination), drawing on R. v. Béland, R. v. Simpson, and related authorities cited in the reasons.
JudgeB: Cory J. (for Sopinka, Cory, Iacobucci and Major JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Public interest immunity for Cabinet documents: court must (1) conduct a preliminary judicial inspection (in doubtful class-claims) and then (2) balance the competing public interests (confidentiality of Cabinet/government decision-making vs proper administration of justice), considering variables like the level and nature of the policy, timing/staleness, and importance of the litigation; the party resisting inspection/production bears the onus once documents are admitted to relate to the case. Key quotes: (i) "Cabinet documents like other evidence must be disclosed unless such disclosure would interfere with the public interest"; (ii) "the level of the decision-making process concerned is only one of many variables"; (iii) "the time when a document or information is to be revealed is an extremely important factor"; (iv) "Cabinet documents ought not to be disclosed without a preliminary judicial inspection to balance the competing interests"; and (v) where documents are admitted to relate to the case, they "should be available for inspection unless there is some reason shown why in the interests of public policy that course should not be followed" and "the onus of establishing that they should not be produced for inspection must lie on the party which seeks a departure from the general rule".
BaselineA: Common law public interest immunity ("Crown privilege"); baseline cases discussed/applied include Smallwood v. Sparling (SCC) ("it is the role of the courts, not the administration to determine whether disclosure of documents would be injurious to the public interest"), plus earlier SCC authorities R. v. Snider and Gagnon v. Commission des valeurs mobilières du Québec; comparative Commonwealth authorities include Conway v. Rimmer and Burmah Oil.
CaseB_TestB: Review test for adequacy of a (pre-Lifchus) jury charge on reasonable doubt and conflicting evidence: the charge is assessed for "substantial compliance" with Lifchus/W.(D.) principles; the "basic question" is whether the charge, read as a whole, creates "a reasonable likelihood that the jury misapprehended the correct standard of proof". For conflicting versions, the jury must be directed to the W.(D.) third alternative (acquit even if accused not believed if a reasonable doubt remains). Key quotes: (i) "the test is whether there was substantial compliance with the principles set out in Lifchus"; (ii) "The basic question remains: does the charge, read as a whole, give rise to a reasonable likelihood that the jury misapprehended the correct standard of proof?"; and (iii) W.(D.) requires: "First, if you believe the evidence of the accused, obviously you must acquit. Second, if you do not believe the testimony of the accused but you are left in reasonable doubt by it, you must acquit. Third, even if you are not left in doubt by the evidence of the accused, you must ask yourself whether... you are convinced beyond a reasonable doubt".
BaselineB: Common law (criminal jury instruction doctrine) grounded in prior SCC cases: R. v. Lifchus (reasonable doubt instruction), R. v. W.(D.) (credibility/conflicting evidence instruction), and R. v. Starr (pre-Lifchus review uses substantial compliance).
JudgeB: Major J. (for Major, Binnie, Arbour and LeBel JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 7 limit on extradition/surrender: courts may intervene only where the executive’s decision to surrender, in the particular circumstances, would violate the principles of fundamental justice (intervention limited to “cases of real substance” and exercised with caution).
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7 (and s. 32 re application); applied in the extradition context alongside the Extradition Act and the Canada–U.S. Extradition Treaty.
CaseB_TestB: Crown appeal jurisdiction limit: a Court of Appeal may interfere with an acquittal on a Crown appeal only if the trial court erred “on a question of law alone” (Criminal Code, s. 605(1)(a); applying Schuldt).
BaselineB: Statute and precedent: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 605(1)(a), as interpreted/applied in Schuldt v. The Queen, [1985] 2 S.C.R. 592.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 7 limit on extradition/surrender: courts may intervene only where surrender would, in the particular circumstances, violate the principles of fundamental justice (judicial intervention limited to cases of real substance/compelling situations, generally after executive surrender decision)
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7 (and related extradition framework under Extradition Act and treaty context)
CaseB_TestB: ITA s. 20(1)(c)(i) interest deductibility (purpose element): whether, considering all the circumstances, the taxpayer had a reasonable expectation of income at the time the investment was made (income = income subject to tax, not net income; ancillary income-earning purpose suffices absent sham/window dressing)
BaselineB: Statute: Income Tax Act, s. 20(1)(c)(i) (interpreting “used for the purpose of earning income” and “income”)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Injurious affection (no land taken): claimant must show the construction damage would have been actionable at common law (nuisance), i.e., an indirect physical injury to land or a substantial interference with use/enjoyment that is unreasonable in light of all surrounding circumstances; loss of prospect/view is not compensable and highway construction is generally a reasonable user.
BaselineA: Statute (Expropriations Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 154, ss. 1(e)(ii), 21) incorporating common-law actionability; SCC relies on Loiselle’s four conditions for injurious affection when no land is taken and applies common-law nuisance concepts (including Street’s definition; historical rule denying recovery for loss of prospect).
CaseB_TestB: Adequacy of jury instructions on alternative routes to murder liability: it is sufficient if the jury is instructed that the accused may be convicted if he “actively participated”/“acted in concert with others” in the killing (not merely present or minor role), and the trial judge may correct an erroneous “actual shooter” instruction by adding “or was otherwise an active participant in her killing”.
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, including ss. 21, 229, 686(1)(b)(iii)) and prior SCC authority on party liability/jury charges (notably R. v. Thatcher).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 10(b) right to counsel: once police promptly advise of the right, no further correlative duties arise unless the detainee indicates a desire to exercise it; absent proof of circumstances showing non-understanding, the accused bears the onus to show he asked for counsel and was denied or denied an opportunity to ask ("absent proof of circumstances indicating that the accused did not understand... the onus has to be on him to prove that he asked for the right but it was denied or he was denied any opportunity to even ask for it").
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 10(b) (and remedy context s. 24(2)); applied approach from R. v. Anderson (Ont. C.A.) as adopted by the SCC here.
CaseB_TestB: Disgorgement/accounting for employee’s secret profits: where an employee acts in a representative capacity and breaches good faith/loyalty (including by abusing authority or using employer funds/position), the principle in Civil Code of Lower Canada art. 1713 (and art. 411 for bad-faith possession) requires the employee to "deliver and pay over all that he has received" and to remit profits so that no one profits from wrongdoing ("the intensity of the employee's obligation of good faith increases with the responsibility attached to the position held").
BaselineB: Statute/civil code: Civil Code of Lower Canada, arts. 1713 (mandatary must account and deliver all received under authority of mandate) and 411 (possessor in bad faith must remit fruits/increase), extended by the Court to senior employees acting representatively in employment context.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Wigglesworth s. 11 Charter applicability test: a matter falls within s. 11 if (1) by its very nature it is a criminal/quasi-criminal/public proceeding (“If a particular matter is of a public nature, intended to promote public order and welfare within a public sphere of activity, then that matter falls within s. 11”), OR (2) it exposes the person to a “true penal consequence” (“imprisonment or a fine which by its magnitude would appear to be imposed for the purpose of redressing the wrong done to society at large”); if the two branches conflict, “the ‘by nature’ test must give way to the ‘true penal consequence’ test.”
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 11 (opening words “Any person charged with an offence”) and s. 11(h) (double jeopardy protection).
CaseB_TestB: Jacquard appellate review test for jury charges (functional approach): “As long as an appellate court, when looking at a trial judge’s charge to the jury as a whole, concludes that the jury was left with a sufficient understanding of the facts as they relate to the relevant issues, the charge is proper”; juries must be “properly — not perfectly — instructed.”
BaselineB: Common law approach to reviewing jury charges, relying on prior SCC authorities (e.g., Azoulay v. The Queen; Cluett v. The Queen; John v. The Queen) and applied in the context of Criminal Code provisions governing the issues at trial (e.g., ss. 16, 231(2)) and appeal (s. 686(1)(b)(iii)).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 577(1) “presence during the whole of the trial” includes jury selection: questioning/excusing prospective jurors for partiality after arraignment and plea is part of the trial and must occur with the accused able to hear/participate; breach is fundamental and not cured by later challenge-for-cause or curative provisions
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 577(1); also engaged: ss. 569(2), 598, 599, 600, 613(1)(b)(iii); provincial context: Juries Act, S.N.S. 1969, c. 12, s. 4(2))
JudgeA: Dickson C.J. (for Dickson C.J. and Beetz, Estey, Wilson and La Forest JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Common-law test for when an appellate court may set aside an acquittal and enter a conviction (instead of ordering a new trial): Crown must show (1) with correct law the verdict would not have been the same, (2) the accused should have been found guilty but for the error of law, and (3) all findings necessary to support guilt were made explicitly/implicitly or are not in issue
BaselineB: Common law (as stated in the decision, relying on Vézeau v. The Queen and R. v. Courville/Courville v. The Queen; applied alongside Criminal Code s. 613(4)(b)(ii))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: When a trial judge quashes a voidable charge under Criminal Code s. 529, the quashing is tantamount to an acquittal (supporting autrefois acquit) unless the charge was an absolute nullity/lack of jurisdiction; quashing is only proper where the required amendment cannot be made without injustice/irreparable prejudice
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 529, 535, 537) plus common law requirements for autrefois acquit (jeopardy + final determination) as reflected in SCC cases (e.g., Petersen v. The Queen; Doyle v. The Queen)
CaseB_TestB: Framework to define the scope of an acquired right/legal non-conforming use: characterize the purpose of the pre-existing use, then assess intensification/remoteness/neighbourhood effects (with balancing) to decide whether the modified activity remains within the protected use
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: Act Respecting Land Use Planning and Development, R.S.Q., c. A-19.1, s. 113(18) (and related municipal by-law context), plus common law/non-conforming use jurisprudence (e.g., Central Jewish Institute v. City of Toronto)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Workmen’s privilege against an owner’s immovable where work is contracted through a lessee: the owner–lessee agreement must be a true construction contract, which requires a claim by the builder against the owner (an undertaking by the owner to pay a construction-contract price). Absent such a claim/price, the lessee is not a ‘builder’ for arts. 2013e/2013f and the subcontractor/supplier has no privilege on the owner’s immovable.
BaselineA: Statute (Civil Code of Lower Canada), especially arts. 2013e and 2013f (workmen’s/suppliers’ privileges), with related contract provisions (arts. 984 et seq., 1060).
CaseB_TestB: Mental distress damages for breach of contract (Hadley v. Baxendale application): plaintiff must show (1) an object of the contract was to secure a psychological benefit bringing mental distress on breach within the parties’ reasonable contemplation at formation; and (2) the mental suffering caused by the breach was sufficiently serious to warrant compensation (proved on the evidence). No independent actionable wrong is required.
BaselineB: Common law remoteness/foreseeability in contract damages (Hadley v. Baxendale), as developed in SCC jurisprudence (e.g., Vorvis referenced) and related common law authorities.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Unequal division of marital property under NB Marital Property Act s. 7(f): depart from equal division only in “clear cases” where equal division would be “inequitable”, including where property was acquired “exclusively or almost wholly” by one spouse and the other made “no, or a negligible, contribution” to child care/household management/financial provision
BaselineA: Statute: Marital Property Act, S.N.B. 1980, c. M-1.1, ss. 2, 3, 7 (especially s. 7(f))
CaseB_TestB: Interjurisdictional immunity (constitutional inapplicability): a provincial law of general application applies to federal works/undertakings/services unless it bears on what makes them “specifically federal”; for a federal service, inapplicability arises if the provincial law touches a “vital or essential aspect” of the service’s “establishment, management or operation”
BaselineB: Common law/constitutional doctrine (interjurisdictional immunity) as articulated in prior SCC cases (notably Bell Canada v. Quebec (CSST); Construction Montcalm; Clark v. CNR; Dick v. The Queen) and applied in light of Constitution Act, 1867, s. 91(1A)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “financing” in Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971 s. 44(2)(a): claimant is disentitled only if their payment shows “active and voluntary involvement” and a “meaningful connection between the payment and the dispute” (mere mandatory union dues diverted to a strike fund are not enough).
BaselineA: Statute: Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, S.C. 1970-71-72, c. 48, s. 44(2)(a) (interpreting the word “financing” in the disentitlement exception).
JudgeA: L'Heureux-Dubé J. (for Dickson C.J. and Wilson, La Forest and L'Heureux-Dubé JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Enforceability/scope of a negligence waiver in a race entry form: in the “context in which it was signed”, the clause is effective if it clearly contemplates releasing/indemnifying for the type of negligence that occurred; attempts to avoid it fail where the clause is not “unfair” or “unreasonable” and the negligence is not “radically different from anything reasonable men could have contemplated”.
BaselineB: Common law contract interpretation/enforcement of exclusion/waiver clauses (including arguments framed as fundamental breach, unconscionability, and public policy).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “financing” in Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971 s. 44(2)(a): claimant is “financing” a labour dispute only where there is “active and voluntary involvement” and a “meaningful connection between the payment and the dispute” (mandatory union dues alone are insufficient).
BaselineA: Statute — Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, S.C. 1970-71-72, c. 48, s. 44(2)(a) (disentitlement exception where claimant proves he is not “participating in or financing or directly interested in” the labour dispute).
CaseB_TestB: Extradition surrender review: whether extraditing the person sought would be contrary to s. 7 fundamental justice so as to “shock the conscience” or be “unjust or oppressive” under Extradition Act s. 44(1); requires a Ministerial “balancing exercise” and deference/comity absent “exceptional cases of ‘real substance’”.
BaselineB: Statute (informed by Charter values and prior SCC extradition jurisprudence) — Extradition Act, S.C. 1999, c. 18, s. 44(1) (“unjust or oppressive”), and Charter s. 7 (“principles of fundamental justice”), applying United States v. Burns and Lake v. Canada (Minister of Justice).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 10 “detention” test for roadside breath demand: detention exists where the state “assumes control over the movement of a person by a demand or direction which may have significant legal consequence” and there is “compulsion or coercion” (from criminal liability for refusal or a reasonable belief one has no choice)
BaselineA: Common law/Charter interpretation baseline from R. v. Therens (applied to Charter s. 10(b) detention) plus application to Criminal Code s. 234.1(1) roadside screening demand
CaseB_TestB: Mistake-of-age (s. 150.1(4)) “all reasonable steps” framework: once an air of reality exists, Crown must prove beyond a reasonable doubt either no honest belief complainant was at least 16 or failure to take “all reasonable steps”; the inquiry is “highly contextual, fact-specific” and “the more reasonable an accused’s perception of the complainant’s age, the fewer steps reasonably required”
BaselineB: Statutory baseline: Criminal Code s. 150.1(4) (and related scheme) governing mistake of age and the “all reasonable steps” requirement
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Extradition specialty/undertaking immunity ends once the extradited person has been “restored or has had an opportunity of returning” to the surrendering state; an unqualified specialty undertaking is construed as related to the surrender and not perpetual (requires a “reasonable opportunity” to return).
BaselineA: Statute (Extradition Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-21, s. 33) plus interpretation of the Canada–Brazil extradition arrangement/undertaking in light of international law principles (incl. Vienna Convention, art. 31).
CaseB_TestB: Criminal appeal scope: where an appeal is properly before the SCC on an alleged error of law, the Court may also determine whether the error is cured under the s. 686(1)(b)(iii) proviso; the Crown need not seek separate leave because “error of law and application of the curative proviso” are “always intertwined”.
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(b)(iii)) as interpreted through SCC precedent (R. v. Keegstra, [1995] 2 S.C.R. 381).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of "anything" in Criminal Code s. 283(1) (theft): to be the object of theft, the thing must (1) be "property" (capable of a proprietary right) and (2) be capable of being "taken or converted" in a way that results in "deprivation"; confidential information per se fails these requirements
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 283(1))
CaseB_TestB: Interpretation of "assets" in MVHC rent-subsidy Assistance Application: "assets" means property/interests that can actually be used to discharge debts (including rent); a Henson trust interest is a "mere hope" and not an "asset" for eligibility-to-be-considered
BaselineB: Common law (contractual interpretation principles, incl. Sattva; applied to tenancy agreement/assistance application documents)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 7 analysis for compelled fingerprinting pre‑conviction: (1) deprivation of life/liberty/security; (2) whether deprivation accords with principles of fundamental justice—i.e., whether fingerprinting/attendance requirement "unduly invades the rights of the accused" and is not arbitrary (police discretion permitted) given "reasonable and probable grounds" for the charge
BaselineA: Combination: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7 (two-step framework) plus statutory fingerprinting scheme (Identification of Criminals Act, s. 2; Criminal Code, ss. 453.3(3), 455.5(5))
CaseB_TestB: Sheppard/Braich test for appellate intervention based on insufficient reasons: two stages—(1) "are the reasons inadequate"; (2) "if so, do they prevent appellate review" (i.e., are they "inscrutable" / do they create an "impediment to appellate review")
BaselineB: Common law (as articulated in R. v. Sheppard and R. v. Braich, applied in this appeal context under Criminal Code, s. 686)
JudgeB: Bastarache and Abella JJ. (LeBel J. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Detention at the border (s. 10(b) Charter): a traveller is “detained” when a state agent “assumes control over the movement of a person by a demand or direction which may have significant legal consequence” (Therens), applied to hold that being “taken out of the normal course and forced to submit to a strip search” is detention requiring advice of the right to counsel
BaselineA: Combination: constitutional text (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 10(b)) + common law definition of “detention” from R. v. Therens, [1985] 1 S.C.R. 613 (as reaffirmed in Hufsky and Thomsen)
JudgeA: Dickson C.J. (for Dickson C.J. and Beetz, Lamer and La Forest JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: s. 11(b) “reasonable time” analysis: “not by the application of a mathematical or administrative formula but rather by a judicial determination balancing” using factors: (1) length of delay; (2) waiver; (3) reasons for delay (inherent time requirements, actions of accused, actions of Crown, limits on institutional resources, other reasons); and (4) prejudice to the accused; with a non-binding guideline of “between 8 and 10 months for institutional delay in Provincial Courts”
BaselineB: Combination: constitutional text (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 11(b) and s. 24(1)) + common law framework distilled from Mills, Rahey, Conway, Smith, and Askov (as discussed in the reasons)
JudgeB: Sopinka J. (for La Forest, Sopinka, Stevenson and Iacobucci JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Leary intoxication rule for general-intent offences (as applied to sexual assault causing bodily harm): voluntary intoxication is generally irrelevant to mens rea; mens rea may be inferred from the actus reus, and in extreme cases the Crown may prove voluntary self-induced intoxication to establish the blameworthy mental state
BaselineA: Common law (Leary v. The Queen, [1978] 1 S.C.R. 29; also relying on R. v. George, [1960] S.C.R. 871; DPP v. Majewski [1977] A.C. 443) applied in the context of Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 246.2(c)
CaseB_TestB: Appellate intervention on Crown appeal from acquittal: (1) appellate court cannot interfere with inferences of fact merely because it would draw different inferences (Schuldt); but (2) it may overturn where the trial judge failed to direct his or her mind to an issue requiring determination to reach the verdict (error of law)
BaselineB: Common law appellate review principles (Schuldt v. The Queen, [1985] 2 S.C.R. 592; also referencing R. v. Morin, [1992] 3 S.C.R. 286) in the context of Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 675 and proceeds offences under the Narcotic Control Act, ss. 11.1, 11.2
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Appellate intervention in a trial judge’s discretionary reapportionment of family assets: intervene only if the trial judge “misdirects himself” or the decision is “so clearly wrong as to amount to an injustice” (and s. 51 does not require asset-by-asset contribution comparison or separate ‘business’/‘domestic’ pools).
BaselineA: Combination: statute (Family Relations Act, R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 121, ss. 43 and 51) plus common-law appellate deference to discretion (as applied in Harper v. Harper, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 2; also citing Re Hull Estate (Ont. C.A.)).
CaseB_TestB: Duty to comment on prejudicial Crown jury-address remarks: where remarks are “prejudicial to a degree sufficient to impose a legal duty on the trial judge to comment” to ensure the defence is “fairly put to the jury”; failure is an error of law and (here) not cured by the s. 686(1)(b)(iii) proviso.
BaselineB: Combination: statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(b)(iii)) plus common-law fairness control of jury addresses/charge (as adopted via the dissenting reasons of Ayles J.A. in the court below).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Wigmore/Slavutych four-part test for recognizing a (qualified) common law privilege against compelled disclosure of communications (applied to journalist-source claim): (1) communication originates in confidence; (2) confidentiality essential to the relationship; (3) relationship one the community ought to foster; (4) injury from disclosure greater than benefit for correct disposal of litigation
BaselineA: Common law (Wigmore criteria as discussed with approval in Slavutych v. Baker, [1976] 1 S.C.R. 254)
CaseB_TestB: Reasonableness review of Crown corporations’ discretionary decisions setting PILT “effective rate”: discretion exists but must be exercised within the statutory/regulatory framework—rate must be calculated “as if the federal property were taxable property belonging to a private owner” and based on the municipality’s actual existing tax system (not a “fictitious tax system” such as reintroducing an abolished occupancy tax)
BaselineB: Statute and regulation (Payments in Lieu of Taxes Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. M-13, ss. 2 ("effective rate"), 2.1, 4(1), sch. II; Crown Corporation Payments Regulations, SOR/81-1030, ss. 2, 7(1))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Patent Act s. 36(1) disclosure/sufficiency test: applicant must disclose everything essential for the invention to function properly; completeness requires (1) describing the invention and defining how it is produced/built, and (2) defining the nature of the invention and describing how it is put into operation, in terms enabling a skilled person to make/produce it from the disclosure alone (deposit of seed alone is not enough).
BaselineA: Statute (Patent Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. P-4, s. 36(1)), as interpreted through prior patent-law authorities cited in the reasons (e.g., Consolboard; Minerals Separation; Burton Parsons; Monsanto).
CaseB_TestB: Dunsmuir standard-of-review framework applied to labour arbitration: arbitral awards (including those applying/adapting common law/equitable doctrines like estoppel) are reviewed on reasonableness unless they fall within correctness categories (constitutional questions, central questions of law outside expertise, true jurisdiction/vires, or competing-tribunal jurisdictional lines); contextual factors confirm deference.
BaselineB: Common law / administrative law framework from Dunsmuir v. New Brunswick and subsequent SCC standard-of-review cases (e.g., Smith v. Alliance Pipeline), applied in the labour-arbitration statutory context (Labour Relations Act, R.S.M. 1987, c. L10, ss. 121, 128(2)).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 96 ‘Residential Tenancies’ three-stage test, clarified: (1) historical inquiry with narrow characterization; (2) judicial function; (3) institutional context/ancillary-to-broader-policy goal — plus new guidance on shared jurisdiction and national (1867) yardstick
BaselineA: Constitution Act, 1867, s. 96; common-law/constitutional framework from Re Residential Tenancies Act, 1979, [1981] 1 S.C.R. 714
JudgeA: Wilson J. (for Dickson C.J. and McIntyre, Lamer and Wilson JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Public interest standing (Downtown Eastside) framework: discretionary, cumulative weighing of (i) serious justiciable issue, (ii) genuine interest, (iii) reasonable and effective means — with guidance that no factor has ‘particular weight’, no individual co-plaintiff is required if a sufficiently concrete factual setting will be forthcoming, and standing may be revisited on a ‘material change’
BaselineB: Common law test from Canada (Attorney General) v. Downtown Eastside Sex Workers United Against Violence Society, 2012 SCC 45
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Bankruptcy Act s. 47(a) vs s. 107(1)(j): a provincial “deemed trust” only removes assets from the bankrupt’s estate under s. 47(a) if the tax money is identifiable/traceable as true trust property under general trust law; if commingled and untraceable, the province has only a Crown claim (secured by lien/charge) ranked under s. 107(1)(j). Key formulation: “If the money collected for tax is identifiable or traceable... the money is exempt... by reason of s. 47(a). If... cannot be traced, there is no ‘property held... in trust’ under s. 47(a)... and s. 107(1)(j) applies.”
BaselineA: Statute (Bankruptcy Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. B-3, ss. 47(a), 107(1)(j)) interpreted alongside provincial statute (Social Service Tax Act, R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 388, s. 18(1)-(2)) and general trust law principles (identifiability/traceability).
CaseB_TestB: Section 23 “numbers warrant” / sliding-scale and local facilities with minority management and control: determine the relevant number as “somewhere between the known demand and the total number of persons who could potentially take advantage of the service”; define the service area case-by-case (not confined to existing school boundaries) within the minority’s management/control subject to objective provincial norms consistent with s. 23; then determine what the numbers warrant by assessing (1) appropriate services “in pedagogical terms” for the number of students and (2) costs. Ministerial approval is constrained: “The Minister’s discretion was limited to verifying whether the Board had met provincial requirements; he had no power to substitute his own criteria or decision.”
BaselineB: Constitution (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 23) plus prior SCC framework (Mahe v. Alberta) and related provincial statute/regulations (School Act and School Act Regulations) applied/limited by s. 23.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Young Offenders Act s. 16 transfer to ordinary court: whether, after weighing and balancing all relevant s. 16(2) factors, the judge is satisfied transfer is appropriate (onus not “heavy”)
BaselineA: Statute: Young Offenders Act, S.C. 1980-81-82-83, c. 110, s. 16(1) and s. 16(2) (and related review provisions s. 16(9)-(10)); applied as explained in the companion SCC decision R. v. M. (S.H.), [1989] 2 S.C.R. 000
CaseB_TestB: Damages for repudiation where contract has alternative modes of performance: assess damages on the basis of the least profitable mode to the plaintiff and least burdensome to the defendant (not a ‘what would likely have happened’ inquiry)
BaselineB: Common law principle (traced to Cockburn v. Alexander (1848) and explained in Withers v. General Theatre Corp. (1933)) adopted/confirmed for Canadian contract damages
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Canadian maritime law (agency): whether an agent of an unnamed/partially disclosed principal is personally liable turns on the parties’ intention as shown by the contract—“a matter of construction of a particular contract”; “there is no prescribed formality for disclosure” and liability “depends on the will of the contracting parties” (e.g., clear wording like “as agent only” negates personal liability).
BaselineA: Common law of contract/agency as part of Canadian maritime law under Federal Court Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. F-7, ss. 2 (“Canadian maritime law”) and 22(2)(m) (stevedoring); with reference to ITO—International Terminal Operators Ltd. v. Miida Electronics Inc., [1986] 1 S.C.R. 752 and common-law agency authorities discussed in the reasons.
CaseB_TestB: Child Welfare Act reporting immunity threshold: s. 38(6) bars actions by informants only if the report is not “maliciously or without reasonable cause”; “reasonable cause” means reasonable cause to ask CPS to look into the matter (not reasonable grounds to believe abuse occurred), and requires “information” that a child “has been, is or may be” in danger—mere “speculation and conjecture” is insufficient.
BaselineB: Statute: Child Welfare Act, R.S.N. 1990, c. C-12, ss. 38(1) and 38(6) (interpreted alongside common-law negligence duty analysis referenced from Cooper v. Hobart and Martel Building).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Common-law limits on a warrantless “frisk” search incident to a lawful arrest: no reasonable/probable grounds prerequisite, but (1) discretionary (not a duty), (2) must be for a valid criminal-justice objective, and (3) must be conducted non-abusively with proportionate force/constraint
BaselineA: Common law police power of search incident to arrest (as discussed through common law authorities and Canadian cases such as R. v. Brezack; R. v. Morrison; R. v. Miller; and SCC obiter in R. v. Beare and R. v. Debot)
CaseB_TestB: Section 7 fundamental-justice minimum for warrantless child apprehension in non-emergency situations: statute is constitutionally acceptable where apprehension without prior judicial authorization is limited to “serious harm or risk of serious harm” to the child, with a fair and prompt post-apprehension hearing as the minimum procedural protection
BaselineB: Statutory scheme under The Child and Family Services Act, S.M. 1985-86, c. 8 (notably ss. 17 and 21(1), plus post-apprehension hearing timelines in ss. 27(1) and 29(1)), assessed under Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal negligence: whether the accused’s conduct is a “marked departure from the norm” such that “wanton or reckless disregard” can be inferred; consequences (death) generally add nothing unless “so interwoven” with the conduct as to help characterize it
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 202(1)-(2), 203 (now ss. 219-220)) as interpreted in R. v. Tutton, [1989] 1 S.C.R. 1392 (marked departure central under both objective and subjective approaches)
CaseB_TestB: CITT standing/jurisdiction under AIT procurement regime: a non-Canadian supplier has no standing; for a procurement to be “within Canada” under AIT art. 502, the supplier must be a “Canadian supplier” (AIT art. 518: has a “place of business in Canada”), otherwise the AIT is inapplicable and the contract is not a “designated contract” for CITT Act purposes
BaselineB: Statute and regulation incorporating a trade agreement: Canadian International Trade Tribunal Act, ss. 30.1, 30.11(1) and Canadian International Trade Tribunal Procurement Inquiry Regulations, ss. 3(1), 7(1), interpreted by reference to Agreement on Internal Trade, especially arts. 101, 501, 502 and 518
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 8 reasonableness of compelled document production in a regulatory/tax audit context: apply a flexible standard (not full Hunter criteria) by weighing the state’s compliance-monitoring interest against the taxpayer’s privacy interest; s. 231(3) is reasonable as a minimally intrusive demand with low privacy expectation and confidentiality protection (s. 241).
BaselineA: Combination: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 8 (unreasonable search or seizure) + common-law/constitutional framework from Hunter v. Southam Inc. (criteria for reasonableness in criminal/quasi-criminal searches) and related SCC s. 8 jurisprudence (e.g., Simmons; Thomson Newspapers (concurrent)). Also applied to Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1952, c. 148, ss. 231(3), 238(2), and confidentiality safeguard s. 241.
CaseB_TestB: Public interest standing test (purposive, flexible, discretionary): weigh three interrelated factors—(1) serious justiciable issue, (2) plaintiff has a real stake/genuine interest, and (3) the proposed suit is, “in all of the circumstances”, a “reasonable and effective means” to bring the issue to court—assessed by non-exhaustive considerations (judicial economy, adversarial suitability, legality, realistic alternatives, etc.).
BaselineB: Common law: prior SCC standing framework from Borowski and Canadian Council of Churches (and related cases such as Finlay, Thorson, McNeil, Hy and Zel’s).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Duty to defend is determined by the pleadings: insurer must defend only claims that, on the allegations, seek damages that "are or may be payable under" the policy (i.e., potentially within coverage); no duty where allegations are clearly outside coverage (e.g., only fraud alleged and fraud excluded).
BaselineA: Contract (insurance policy) interpreted using common-law principles of insurance contract construction; key policy wording: insurer must "[d]efend any suit ... seeking damages which are or may be payable under the terms of this Policy"; exclusion: policy "DOES NOT APPLY ... to any dishonest, fraudulent, criminal or malicious act or omission".
CaseB_TestB: Section 265(4) Criminal Code “air of reality” threshold for honest but mistaken belief in consent: defence goes to jury only if there is "sufficient evidence" such that "a reasonable jury properly instructed could have acquitted"; requires evidence beyond a bare assertion of belief (though it need not be independent of the accused).
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 265(4)) interpreted in light of prior SCC jurisprudence on the air-of-reality requirement for defences (e.g., Pappajohn; Bulmer; Robertson).
JudgeB: Cory J. (for Cory and Major JJ.; majority on key test)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Collateral wage benefits and tort damages for lost earnings: as a general rule, wage benefits paid while the plaintiff is unable to work "must be brought into account and deducted from the claim for lost earnings"; exception where the payer has a subrogation/reimbursement entitlement (and, rarely, a discretionary trust where "necessary and appropriate in the interests of justice").
BaselineA: Common law (tort damages principles and collateral benefits jurisprudence). Key baselines cited include the SCC damages trilogy (Andrews v. Grand & Toy Alberta Ltd.; Thornton v. Prince George School Board; Arnold v. Teno) and collateral-benefit authorities (Bradburn v. Great Western Rail. Co.; Parry v. Cleaver; Browning v. War Office; Hussain v. New Taplow Paper Mills Ltd.).
CaseB_TestB: GST supplier reimbursement under Constitution Act, 1867, s. 103 and common law: s. 103 is an appropriations provision and "was never intended to create a legally enforceable right in third parties" to reimbursement; absent contract, suppliers (statutory agents) have no common-law right to remuneration/reimbursement for GST collection costs (and restitution fails where the statute supplies a "juridical reason").
BaselineB: Combination of constitutional text and statute, plus common law agency/restitution. Constitution Act, 1867, s. 103; Excise Tax Act (GST) provisions appointing suppliers as agents/trustees and addressing compensation: ss. 221, 222 (agency/trust), and s. 346 (transitional credit). Common law baselines discussed include Pettkus v. Becker (unjust enrichment framework) and agency principles (as summarized via Fridman, The Law of Agency).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Art. 559 C.C.Q. compensatory allowance test: claimant must prove (1) contribution, (2) enrichment of spouse’s patrimony, (3) causal link/correlation, and (4) proportion; enrichment must subsist and is evaluated at the time of divorce, with the elements assessed “with great flexibility”
BaselineA: Statute (Civil Code of Quebec, art. 559), informed by unjust enrichment principles (e.g., Cie Immobilière Viger Ltée v. Lauréat Giguère Inc.)
CaseB_TestB: Misapprehension of evidence (Morrissey) test for setting aside a conviction: misapprehension must go to “the substance” not “detail”, be “material” not “peripheral”, and the errors must play an “essential part” in the reasoning process resulting in conviction (conjunctive hurdles)
BaselineB: Common law appellate standard adopted from R. v. Morrissey and R. v. C. (R.), applied in the context of Criminal Code s. 686(1)(a)(iii) (miscarriage of justice)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Copyright infringement where a computer program is embodied in a silicon chip: the chip-embedded program is protected if it is a “reproduction” of the copyrightable program in a “material form” under s. 3(1) (i.e., view the chip as a “static object encoded with written instructions”, not merely a dynamic “sequence of electrical impulses”).
BaselineA: Statute — Copyright Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-30, s. 3(1) (including s. 3(1)(a) and (d) discussed but not decided).
CaseB_TestB: Common law de facto taking (constructive expropriation) test requiring compensation: (1) “an acquisition of a beneficial interest in the property or flowing from it”, and (2) “removal of all reasonable uses of the property”.
BaselineB: Common law — as stated in the decision with reference to Mariner Real Estate Ltd. v. Nova Scotia (Attorney General), Manitoba Fisheries Ltd. v. The Queen, and The Queen in Right of British Columbia v. Tener (and applied alongside Vancouver Charter, s. 569).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Novation (substitution of debtor) test: (1) “The new debtor must assume the complete liability”; (2) “The creditor must accept the new debtor as principal debtor and not merely as an agent or guarantor”; and (3) “The creditor must accept the new contract in full satisfaction and substitution for the old contract” (Polson v. Wulffsohn). SCC adds that, absent express agreement, courts should be “loath to find novation unless the circumstances are really compelling”, and that an assumption agreement does not “per se” effect a novation.
BaselineA: Common law (novation doctrine; three-part test from Polson v. Wulffsohn (1890), 2 B.C.R. 39, as adopted/applied in this decision)
CaseB_TestB: De facto (constructive) taking test requiring compensation at common law: two requirements — “(1) an acquisition of a beneficial interest in the property or flowing from it, and (2) removal of all reasonable uses of the property”.
BaselineB: Common law (as stated with reference to Mariner Real Estate; Manitoba Fisheries; Tener) and applied alongside statute (Vancouver Charter, s. 569, which deems no taking)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Availability of Criminal Code search warrant power for federal statutory offences: on a plain reading, s. 443(1)(a)-(b) applies to proceedings under "any" federal statute ("any other Act of Parliament"), regardless of whether that statute also contains search-and-seizure provisions; limits must be express (e.g., s. 443(1)(e) "subject to any other Act of Parliament").
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 443(1)(a), (b), (e) (as amended 1985, c. 19, s. 69) interpreted alongside Bankruptcy Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. B-3, s. 6.
CaseB_TestB: Meaning of "risks willingly assumed" under Occupiers' Liability Act s. 4(1): s. 4(1) embodies the volenti doctrine, so more than mere knowledge is required; the plaintiff must assume the risk in the sense of accepting the entire risk of injury without recourse (i.e., consent to the legal risk/waiver of legal rights).
BaselineB: Statute interpreted in light of common law: Occupiers' Liability Act, R.S.O. 1980, c. 322, ss. 2, 3(1), 4(1); common law volenti as clarified in SCC cases Dube v. Labar, [1986] 1 S.C.R. 649 and Crocker v. Sundance Northwest Resorts Ltd., [1988] 1 S.C.R. 1186.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 32 applicability to an entity: Wilson J.’s three-part ‘government’ criteria (general control; government function; statutory authority/public interest objective)
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 32(1) (and related Charter applicability jurisprudence referenced in the reasons, including McKinney v. University of Guelph and RWDSU v. Dolphin Delivery Ltd.)
CaseB_TestB: Leave to appeal an arbitral award under Arbitration Act s. 31(2)(a): threshold ‘question of law’ + ‘may prevent a miscarriage of justice’ (materiality + arguable merit) + residual discretion factors
BaselineB: Statute: Arbitration Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 55, s. 31(2)(a) (interpreted with reference to BCIT and related cases)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Kirkness limit on the Paré “single transaction” analysis: applies only to murder classification under Criminal Code s. 214(5) and only after Crown first proves accused committed (or was party to) both the underlying offence and the murder; only then ask whether offences are sufficiently closely connected in time to classify as first degree
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 214(5) (now s. 231(5))) as interpreted in R. v. Paré, [1987] 2 S.C.R. 618 ("single transaction" meaning of “while committing”); also interacts with party liability under Criminal Code s. 21
CaseB_TestB: Forum non conveniens test (post-Van Breda): once jurisdiction is properly assumed, the party seeking a stay must show an alternative forum is a “clearly more appropriate” forum; court considers multiple non-exhaustive factors and one forum must “ultimately emerge as clearly more appropriate”
BaselineB: Common law (Club Resorts Ltd. v. Van Breda, 2012 SCC 17) forum non conveniens framework; referenced statutory analogues include CJPTA s. 11(2) and Civil Code of Québec art. 3135 (as comparative guides, not the governing source in Ontario)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Abuse of process stay test (Jewitt/Young/Keyowski): a stay is granted only in the “clearest of cases” where compelling the accused to stand trial would violate fundamental principles of justice/fair play and decency, or where proceedings are “oppressive or vexatious” (with Conway framing: stay where the “affront to fair play and decency is disproportionate to the societal interest” in prosecution).
BaselineA: Common law (abuse of process stay doctrine from R. v. Jewitt adopting R. v. Young; reiterated in R. v. Keyowski and R. v. Conway) applied in the context of Criminal Code s. 508 stay/recommencement power.
CaseB_TestB: When a Vetrovec “clear, sharp warning” is required and what it must contain: trial judge has discretion to warn where a witness is sufficiently untrustworthy; in some cases the caution is mandatory; and if given, the judge need not always detail corroborative evidence, though usually should make some reference to supportive evidence unless unfairly prejudicial.
BaselineB: Common law (Vetrovec v. The Queen; refinement discussed via R. v. Babinski; accessory-after-the-fact caution context via Sellars v. The Queen).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Lippé institutional impartiality test for part-time judges’ outside occupations: (1) ask whether, considering factors like “the nature of the occupation and the parties who appear before this type of judge”, there is “a reasonable apprehension of bias in the mind of a fully informed person in a substantial number of cases”; if no, only case-by-case challenges; if yes, the occupation is “per se incompatible” unless safeguards reduce the apprehension so that, with knowledge of the safeguards, a fully informed person would not have an apprehension of bias “in a substantial number of cases”.
BaselineA: Combination of common law and constitutional text: s. 11(d) Canadian Charter and s. 23 Quebec Charter; reasonable apprehension of bias test from Committee for Justice and Liberty v. National Energy Board (adopted in Valente v. The Queen).
CaseB_TestB: Zundel s. 1 ‘objective’ identification rule in Charter justification: for s. 1, the Court must look to “the intention of Parliament when the section was enacted or amended” and “cannot assign objectives, nor invent new ones according to the perceived current utility of the impugned provision” (rejecting ‘shifting purpose’); without a sufficiently pressing and substantial objective, the limit fails s. 1.
BaselineB: Common law/constitutional doctrine under s. 1 Canadian Charter (Oakes framework) and the anti–shifting purpose principle from R. v. Big M Drug Mart Ltd.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Residential Tenancies (s. 96) test — Step 1 historical inquiry with required characterization: determine whether the impugned jurisdiction was exercised exclusively by superior courts at Confederation; if not, s. 96 is not infringed (here, characterize as “jurisdiction over young persons charged with a criminal offence” and find it “did not exist at Confederation”).
BaselineA: Common law constitutional doctrine under Constitution Act, 1867, s. 96, applying Re Residential Tenancies Act, 1979, [1981] 1 S.C.R. 714 (and considering Sobeys Stores Ltd. v. Yeomans, [1989] 1 S.C.R. 238) to assess whether jurisdiction can be conferred on an inferior court/tribunal.
CaseB_TestB: Interpretation of “sold in any market in Canada” (Patent Act, ss. 80(1)(b), 83(1), 85): for PMPRB jurisdiction, interpret the phrase purposively to include sales of medicines “regulated by the public laws of Canada, ... delivered in Canada, ... dispensed in Canada, and where ... the cost ... will be borne by Canadians”.
BaselineB: Statutory interpretation of Patent Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. P-4, ss. 80(1)(b), 81(1)(a), 83(1), 85, using the Canada Trustco textual-contextual-purposive approach; rejecting a strict commercial-law locus-of-sale meaning in this context.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Adequacy of an indictment (and whether a proven conspiracy falls within the scope of the conspiracy charged): indictment is adequate if it gives the accused “reasonable information” and identifies the “transaction”; and a specific conspiracy is within the indictment if it “included some of the accused”, occurred “at some time within the time frame alleged”, and had “as its object the type of crime alleged”
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 510(1)-(3), 512(g), 516(1)(g)) as interpreted through SCC/common-law principles (notably R. v. Côté; R. v. Wis Development Corp.; R. v. B.(G.); and conspiracy-indictment principles from R. v. Cotroni)
CaseB_TestB: Constitutional validity of the Canada Evidence Act s. 38 scheme: (i) s. 96 analysis applies the Re Residential Tenancies Act, 1979 test—first ask whether the power “broadly conforms” to a superior court power at Confederation (if not, “the inquiry ends”); and (ii) trial fairness is protected because the trial judge retains remedial power under s. 38.14—if the judge cannot conclude non-disclosure has not compromised fairness, “a stay of proceedings under s. 38 must issue”
BaselineB: Combination of statute and constitutional/common law: Canada Evidence Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-5, ss. 38-38.16 (especially ss. 38.04, 38.06, 38.14) interpreted against Constitution Act, 1867, s. 96 and Charter, s. 7, using the common-law s. 96 framework from Re Residential Tenancies Act, 1979 and core-jurisdiction cases (e.g., MacMillan Bloedel; Babcock)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Entrapment (random virtue-testing) — first branch of Mack: police may offer an opportunity only with (a) reasonable suspicion of the person’s involvement, or (b) a bona fide inquiry tied to a sufficiently precise location; random virtue-testing exists only if neither (a) nor (b) is present
BaselineA: Common law (R. v. Mack, [1988] 2 S.C.R. 903)
CaseB_TestB: Appellate intervention in trial judge’s voluntariness ruling on a statement: absent a “serious, specific and determining error”, an appellate court should not reassess the weighing of the evidence from the voir dire on whether the statement was “free and voluntary”
BaselineB: Common law (confession rule/voluntariness; specific baseline cases not identified in the reasons provided)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Duty to comment on Crown counsel’s prejudicial jury address: where remarks are “prejudicial to a degree sufficient to impose a legal duty on the trial judge to comment” to ensure the defence is “fairly put to the jury”; failure is an error of law (with s. 686(1)(b)(iii) curative proviso not available on these facts).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(b)(iii)) plus common-law principles of fair trial/jury charge (as reflected in the Court’s adoption of Ayles J.A.’s formulation).
CaseB_TestB: Broker commission—meaning of “agreement to sell” and “voluntarily prevents free performance”: (1) no “agreement to sell” unless the accepted promise to purchase is “unconditional” such that it is possible to compel transfer of title; and (2) clause mirroring art. 1503 C.C.Q. requires proof of seller “fault” (failure to do what it was obliged to do or doing what it was obliged not to do) to show the seller voluntarily prevented performance.
BaselineB: Statute (Civil Code of Québec, arts. 1396 and 1503) applied through interpretation of standard-form brokerage contract clauses 6.1(3o) and 6.1(4o).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 16(2) insanity defence — second branch: whether, because of “disease of the mind”, the accused was “incapable … of knowing that an act or omission is wrong”, with “wrong” (per Chaulk, applied here) meaning “morally wrong” rather than “legally wrong”; first branch limited to inability to “appreciat[e] the physical consequences of his act”.
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 16(2)); interpreted in light of SCC precedents including R. v. Chaulk, [1990] 3 S.C.R. 1303 (redefining “wrong”), and Cooper v. The Queen, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 1149; Kjeldsen v. The Queen, [1981] 2 S.C.R. 617; R. v. Abbey, [1982] 2 S.C.R. 24 (limiting first branch to physical nature/consequences).
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 8 sniffer-dog search — “reasonable suspicion” standard: must be based on “objectively discernible facts” assessed on the “totality of the circumstances” (a “constellation of factors”), asking whether facts are “objectively indicative of the possibility of criminal behaviour”; assessment is through the lens of a reasonable person “standing in the shoes of the police officer” (training/experience relevant but not accepted uncritically).
BaselineB: Common law Charter s. 8 framework for sniffer-dog searches (building on R. v. Kang-Brown, 2008 SCC 18 and R. v. A.M., 2008 SCC 19; clarified alongside R. v. Chehil, 2013 SCC 49) applying Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 8 (and related detention analysis under s. 9).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Legitimate expectations: (1) creates only procedural rights (consultation/representations), not substantive rights (no veto); and (2) does not apply to the legislative process (so cannot constrain introducing legislation, especially a money bill)
BaselineA: Common law administrative law doctrine of legitimate expectations as an extension of procedural fairness (citing Old St. Boniface Residents Assn. Inc. v. Winnipeg (City); also Bates v. Lord Hailsham; Inuit Tapirisat; Martineau; Penikett) applied in light of constitutional principles (parliamentary sovereignty; Constitution Act, 1867, s. 54) and statutory interpretation (Interpretation Act, s. 42(1))
CaseB_TestB: Divorce Act s. 17 variation framework: court must be satisfied of a post-order “change in the condition, means, needs or other circumstances” (s. 17(4)) and then vary support considering the s. 17(7) objectives; pension income may be treated as “means” and “double dipping” is not engaged where the pension was not truly valued/divided as future property
BaselineB: Statute (Divorce Act, 1985, s. 17(4) and s. 17(7))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Extradition/death-penalty s. 7 test: whether surrender without assurances is "simply unacceptable" / "sufficiently shocks" the Canadian conscience (a contextual balancing considering offence/penalty, foreign justice system safeguards, comity and security, with latitude to the Minister)
BaselineA: Combination: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7 (principles of fundamental justice) as applied to extradition under Extradition Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. E-23, s. 25, informed by prior SCC extradition cases (Canada v. Schmidt; United States v. Allard; Argentina v. Mellino) and the Canada–U.S. Extradition Treaty, Art. 6
CaseB_TestB: Media search-warrant reasonableness framework: after meeting Criminal Code s. 487(1)(b) grounds, the justice must assess overall reasonableness by balancing state interests and press functions/privacy, considering a non-exhaustive list of factors; alternative sources are ordinarily disclosed but are not constitutional prerequisites
BaselineB: Statute plus Charter backdrop: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 487(1)(b), (d), (e) (issuance of search warrants) applied with Charter ss. 2(b) and 8 informing reasonableness; draws on prior jurisprudence including Re Pacific Press Ltd. and Descôteaux v. Mierzwinski
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Reasonable apprehension of bias (pecuniary interest) test for tribunal impartiality: “Would a reasonably well-informed person consider that the interest might have an influence on the exercise of the official’s public duty?” (Old St. Boniface), applied contextually to Law Society discipline/costs
BaselineA: Common law (administrative law / natural justice), as formulated in Old St. Boniface Residents Assn. Inc. v. Winnipeg (City), [1990] 3 S.C.R. 1170 (and related bias jurisprudence)
CaseB_TestB: Nelles malicious prosecution / prosecutorial immunity test (four cumulative elements): (1) prosecution initiated by defendant; (2) terminated in plaintiff’s favour; (3) absence of reasonable and probable cause (subjective + objective); (4) malice/improper purpose (“deliberate and improper use” of prosecutorial office)
BaselineB: Common law tort framework from Nelles v. Ontario, [1989] 2 S.C.R. 170 (applied to Crown/prosecutors; balance of probabilities)
JudgeB: Iacobucci and Binnie JJ. (for McLachlin C.J. and Iacobucci, Major and Binnie JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Colour of right / mistake analysis for s. 206(1)(d) lottery offence: colour of right unavailable where offence definition does not include it, and a mistake that the Criminal Code is inoperative is a mistake of law barred by s. 19 ("Ignorance of the law ... is not an excuse")
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, ss. 19 and 206(1)(d)) plus common law principle that mistake of law is no defence (as reflected in s. 19)
CaseB_TestB: Modified Taylor definition/test for "hatred" under human rights hate-speech prohibitions: apply objectively whether a reasonable person aware of context would view the expression as likely to expose a protected group to "detestation" and "vilification"; focus on likely effects on audience; intent irrelevant; and strike "ridicules, belittles or otherwise affronts the dignity of" from s. 14(1)(b)
BaselineB: Combination: statute (Saskatchewan Human Rights Code, S.S. 1979, c. S-24.1, s. 14(1)(b)) interpreted through prior SCC common law/constitutional framework (Canada (Human Rights Commission) v. Taylor, [1990] 3 S.C.R. 892)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Intervention test where intervener raises a new Charter argument: allow intervention if the applicant has a “sufficient interest” and will bring a “special perspective”, while leaving to the appeal panel whether the new Charter issue should be entertained given possible “prejudice” (i.e., whether respondent might have adduced additional evidence) and controlling proposed materials as potential “fresh evidence” (file only on consent or, absent consent, with leave).
BaselineA: Common law / SCC practice on intervention and new issues on appeal (no specific statute-based test articulated in the reasons).
CaseB_TestB: Meaning of “offers any indignity” under Criminal Code s. 182(b): (1) physical interference/contact is sufficient but not necessary; (2) the offence targets indignities to “a dead human body or human remains” and not “monuments per se”; but (3) where a monument marks the presence/final resting place of human remains, offering indignities to the monument constitutes offering indignities to the human remains.
BaselineB: Statute — Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 182(b) (interpreted by the Court).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Applicability trigger for the Environmental Assessment and Review Process Guidelines Order: a project is a “proposal” only if Canada has a “decision making responsibility”, meaning an “affirmative regulatory duty” (a legal duty/obligation under an Act of Parliament) — not merely a potential effect on a federal head of power
BaselineA: Regulation and statute: Environmental Assessment and Review Process Guidelines Order, SOR/84-467 (ss. 2 “proposal”, “initiating department”; s. 6; also s. 3) made under Department of the Environment Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. E-10, s. 6; applied in context of Navigable Waters Protection Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. N-22, s. 5 and Fisheries Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. F-14, s. 37
CaseB_TestB: Curative proviso (Criminal Code s. 686(1)(b)(iii)) test: uphold conviction despite legal error if Crown shows either (1) the error was “so harmless, and so insignificant, that it could not have affected the verdict”; or (2) despite the error, the case was “so overwhelming that a conviction would have been inevitable”
BaselineB: Statute and precedent: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(b)(iii), as articulated in R. v. Khan, 2001 SCC 86 and applied in this appeal
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 133 “legislative nature” test + anti-circumvention principle: s. 133 applies to statutes and to any instrument of a legislative nature; and where “the net effect of a series of discrete acts has a legislative character, then each of these component acts will also be imbued with this same character” (so s. 133 cannot be avoided by dividing the legislative process). Badges of legislative character include: (1) “embodies a rule of conduct”; (2) “has the force of law”; (3) “applies to an undetermined number of persons”.
BaselineA: Constitution Act, 1867, s. 133, as interpreted in Reference re Manitoba Language Rights (1992) and (1985); also applied by analogy to Quebec (Attorney General) v. Brunet (1990).
CaseB_TestB: Responsive-answer requirement on jury question about reasonable doubt: even where the initial Lifchus/model reasonable doubt charge is correct, if the jury asks about the standard of proof, “the trial judge must attempt to answer the jury’s question in an effort to assist them”; repeating the charge may suffice in some cases, but the judge must not discourage further questions—failure to respond and discouraging follow-up raises concern the verdict was not based on a proper understanding of the standard of proof (miscarriage of justice).
BaselineB: Common law jury-instruction framework from R. v. Lifchus (1997) and the duty to answer jury questions from R. v. S. (W.D.) (1994) (with reference to Starr (2000) and other appellate authorities).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Mistaken transfer + recipient knowledge + transferor right of recovery ⇒ property does not pass for criminal-law theft; subsequent fraudulent conversion with intent to deprive is theft (void/voidable distinction irrelevant)
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 322(1)) interpreted with reference to property-law principles about mistaken transfers and rights of recovery
CaseB_TestB: Dunsmuir reasonableness review applied under Federal Courts Act s. 18.1: court asks whether outcome falls within a 'range of possible, acceptable outcomes' and does not reweigh evidence; s. 18.1 sets grounds (not standards) and preserves remedial discretion
BaselineB: Combination: common law (Dunsmuir v. New Brunswick) applied alongside statute (Federal Courts Act, R.S.C., 1985, c. F-7, ss. 18, 18.1; and context of IRPA, S.C. 2001, c. 27, s. 67(1)(c))
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 11(b) unreasonable delay analysis: a non-mathematical balancing of (1) length of delay, (2) waiver, (3) reasons for delay (incl. inherent requirements, accused/Crown actions, institutional limits, other), and (4) prejudice; with an institutional-delay guideline of 8–10 months in Provincial Court (not a fixed ceiling)
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional text (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 11(b) and 24(1)) plus prior SCC s. 11(b) jurisprudence (Mills; Rahey; Conway; Smith; Askov)
CaseB_TestB: Contractor/subcontractor liability for construction collapse: even if supports yielded first, subcontractor is not liable where the true cause is contractor’s contractual fault of overloading beyond the contemplated/design load (contractor may be liable under Civil Code/contract; subcontractor not obliged to foresee or withstand undisclosed overload)
BaselineB: Statute/civil law (Civil Code arts. 1684, 1688, 1065) and SCC statement in Hill, Clarke-Francis Ltd. v. Northland Groceries (Quebec) Ltd. on builder’s ability to exonerate by proving force majeure/Act of God/owner’s fault/third party act; applied by analogy to contractor–subcontractor relationship
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 426(1)(a)(ii) secret commissions (agent/taker): actus reus requires (1) agency relationship; (2) agent accepts a benefit as consideration for an act/forbearance in relation to the principal’s affairs; and (3) failure to make “adequate and timely disclosure of the source, amount and nature of the benefit”; mens rea requires awareness of each element, and “corruptly” means “secretly or without the requisite disclosure” (no “corrupt bargain” requirement).
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 426(1)(a) (as applied to s. 426(1)(a)(ii)); framework followed from R. v. Kelly, [1992] 2 S.C.R. 000 (released concurrently).
CaseB_TestB: Criminal Code s. 686(1)(b)(iii) curative proviso: ask “whether a jury properly instructed could, acting reasonably, have come to a different conclusion absent the error”; jury findings may be considered if not tainted by the error.
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(b)(iii).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: State Immunity Act s. 5 “commercial activity” exception — two-step contextual inquiry: (1) determine the nature of the foreign state activity (context may include purpose); (2) assess whether the Canadian proceedings “relate to” that activity by a sufficient “nexus” (more than incidental), considering competing nexus to sovereign attributes
BaselineA: Statute (State Immunity Act, S.C. 1980-81-82-83, c. 95, ss. 2 and 5) codifying the common law restrictive immunity doctrine (acts jure imperii vs jure gestionis), discussed via I Congreso del Partido
CaseB_TestB: Compatibility test for provincial “pay-and-retain/compensation” mechanisms with the BIA scheme of distribution: determine whether the provincial mechanism goes beyond BIA s. 97(3) set-off/compensation; apply a timing-based rule—pre-bankruptcy payment may permit compensation (if mutual debts pre-exist and meet civil law conditions), but post-bankruptcy subrogatory payment cannot create compensation; equitable set-off is inapplicable in Quebec bankruptcy
BaselineB: Combination of statute and civil law: Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. B-3 (esp. ss. 97(3), 121, 136-147) plus Civil Code of Québec (arts. 1651, 1656(3), 1672-1673, 1681) interpreting provincial statutes (AIAOD s. 316; ALRCI s. 54) against the federal distribution scheme; guided by Husky Oil
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Quebec civil law “obligation to inform” (duty to disclose) in contracts of enterprise, enforceable via delict by a subcontractor: (1) debtor’s actual or presumed knowledge of the information; (2) information of “decisive importance”; (3) creditor cannot inform itself or legitimately relies on the debtor; with scope varying in large projects by risk allocation, relative expertise, and the contract’s “continuing formation”.
BaselineA: Combination: Civil Code of Lower Canada arts. 1024 (good faith implied terms) and 1053 (delictual fault) as the normative base; plus existing Quebec/SCC jurisprudence recognizing good faith and delict in contractual settings (cited: Houle v. Canadian National Bank; National Bank of Canada v. Soucisse; Bank of Montreal v. Kuet Leong Ng).
CaseB_TestB: Test for when a construction contract’s “owner-directed supply” limitation clause excludes a tort duty to warn: where the contract specifies the builder’s liability “shall extend only to installation” of owner-directed supply, the parties have (by necessary implication) excluded other heads of liability (including duty to warn), because the clause can ‘bite’ only on negligence in installation (Miida Electronics approach).
BaselineB: Common law of contract interpretation/exclusion clauses in a tort ‘contractual matrix’ (cited: ITO—International Terminal Operators Ltd. v. Miida Electronics Inc.; Giffels Associates Ltd. v. Eastern Construction Co.).
JudgeB: Iacobucci J. (for Gonthier, Cory, Iacobucci and Major JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Duty to accommodate in adverse-effect discrimination (employer/union/complainant): take “reasonable measures short of undue hardship”; union liable if it (1) participated in the discriminatory rule (e.g., collective agreement term) or (2) impeded reasonable accommodation; complainant must facilitate and accept reasonable accommodation
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Human Rights Act, S.B.C. 1984, c. 22, ss. 8(1)(a),(b),(4) and 9; common-law/precedential duty to accommodate from Ontario Human Rights Commission and O'Malley v. Simpsons-Sears Ltd. and Central Alberta Dairy Pool v. Alberta (Human Rights Commission)
CaseB_TestB: Exclusive arbitral jurisdiction under s. 45(1) OLRA: courts are ousted if the dispute, in its “essential character”, arises from the “interpretation, application, administration or alleged violation” of the collective agreement
BaselineB: Statute interpreted in light of precedent: Ontario Labour Relations Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. L.2, s. 45(1), building on St. Anne Nackawic Pulp & Paper Co. v. Canadian Paper Workers Union, Local 219 (and related labour-arbitration jurisprudence)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Trial judge’s discretion to exclude cross-examination on a collateral credibility matter: admit only if its relevance outweighs its prejudicial effect (including potential to mislead the jury), especially where relevance is tenuous absent an indication the collateral evidence might be false.
BaselineA: Common law (trial judge’s discretion over cross-examination/evidence; applied from R. v. Meddoui, [1991] 3 S.C.R. 320).
CaseB_TestB: Income Tax Act s. 20(1)(c)(i) purpose test for interest deductibility: whether, considering all the circumstances, the taxpayer had a reasonable expectation of income at the time the investment was made (income meaning income subject to tax, not net income; ancillary income-earning purpose suffices absent sham/window dressing).
BaselineB: Statute (Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), s. 20(1)(c)(i); interpreted in light of prior SCC cases including Bronfman Trust and Shell Canada).
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 10(b) “detention” at the border: routine secondary immigration examination is not detention unless state action goes beyond what is required for processing entry and becomes a restraint of liberty (state compulsion alone is insufficient; absence of stigma supports no detention)
BaselineA: Common law/constitutional interpretation of Charter s. 10(b) “detention”, grounded in R. v. Therens (definition of detention incl. psychological compulsion) and applied in border context via R. v. Simmons and related cases
CaseB_TestB: Elements of civil contempt: proof beyond a reasonable doubt of (1) a clear and unequivocal order, (2) actual knowledge (or wilful blindness), and (3) an intentional act/omission that breaches the order; no “contumacious intent” required (goes only to penalty)
BaselineB: Common law of civil contempt (as summarized from prior authorities) alongside Ontario Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 60.11 (procedural framework for contempt motions)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Admissibility of bad character/disposition evidence: admissible only if (1) relevant to an issue other than disposition/character, and (2) its probative value outweighs its prejudicial effect (with heightened scrutiny for “morally repugnant” acts); plus mandatory limiting jury instruction against propensity reasoning
BaselineA: Common law (as stated in Morris v. The Queen; also applied with guidance from R. v. B. (C.R.) and R. v. D. (L.E.))
CaseB_TestB: Recent fabrication exception for prior consistent statements: where cross-examination amounts to an allegation of recent fabrication, prior consistent statements may be admitted only to rebut that allegation, limited to proving the fact the complaint was made (not the truth of its contents)
BaselineB: Common law (prior consistent statements / recent fabrication doctrine)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: R. v. B. (K.G.) reformed rule for substantive admissibility of a non-accused witness’s prior inconsistent statement (principled hearsay: necessity + threshold reliability with specified safeguards, plus voir dire screening)
BaselineA: Common law hearsay/orthodox rule (prior inconsistent statements only for credibility) as recognized in Deacon v. The King; adapted through the principled hearsay approach in R. v. Khan and R. v. Smith, applied in the s. 9 Canada Evidence Act context
CaseB_TestB: Interpretive test for whether the insurer’s promise to pay “interest” includes the art. 1056c C.C. second-paragraph additional indemnity (characterized as damages for delay and therefore included in “interest” payable under the policy)
BaselineB: Statute/civil code interpretation applied to an insurance contract: Civil Code art. 1056c (both paragraphs) and its characterization in R. v. Nord-Deutsche Versicherungs-Gesellschaft; contract clause promising to pay “interest accrued on the amount of its guarantee from the date when the action was instituted”
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal fraud (Criminal Code, s. 380(1)) — “other fraudulent means”: actus reus requires objectively dishonest conduct (reasonable person) involving the “wrongful use of something in which another person has an interest” that extinguishes or puts that interest “at risk”; mens rea requires subjective knowledge of the prohibited act and subjective knowledge that it could cause deprivation (including risk).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 380(1)), as interpreted through SCC fraud jurisprudence including R. v. Olan and the concurrently released R. v. Théroux.
CaseB_TestB: Union duty of representation (Labour Code, s. 47.2) in collective bargaining: the duty is generally an “obligation of means”; breach requires showing the union acted “in bad faith or in an arbitrary or discriminatory manner or show[ed] serious negligence”; former employees may be an affected interest but have no “acquired rights” to retroactivity and the union has no “obligation of result” to obtain it.
BaselineB: Statute (Labour Code, R.S.Q., c. C-27, s. 47.2; also discussed alongside s. 67 on single collective agreement).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Crown appeal from acquittal/new trial test under Criminal Code s. 686(4): Crown must show the verdict "would not necessarily have been the same" but for the legal error (a "very heavy onus")
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(4)) as interpreted in SCC precedent (Vézeau v. The Queen; reaffirmed in R. v. Morin)
JudgeA: Cory J. (for Sopinka, Cory, Iacobucci and Major JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Reasonable notice to enforce security: creditor must give "reasonable notice of its intention to enforce the security" and "reasonable time to pay"; reasonableness assessed using the Mister Broadloom criteria (7-factor list)
BaselineB: Common law (Lister (R.E.) Ltd. v. Dunlop Canada Ltd.; reasonableness factors from Mister Broadloom Corporation (1968) Ltd. v. Bank of Montreal; also citing Massey v. Sladen)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Engineer/design professional preparing tender documents owes no duty to advise/warn bidders about permits or difficulties tied to the contractor’s chosen method of performance, absent specific arrangements to the contrary (method of execution is the contractor’s responsibility).
