BaselineA: Common law (construction/tendering duty of care allocation): “barring specific arrangements to the contrary, the method by which a contractor chooses to execute the work falls within its sphere of responsibility” (citing R. v. Paradis and Farley Inc., [1942] S.C.R. 10; Vermont Construction Inc. v. Beatson, [1977] 1 S.C.R. 758; Temar Construction Ltd. v. West Hill Redevelopment Co. (1986), 21 C.L.R. 156).
CaseB_TestB: Framework for reviewing Crown decision-making: (1) classify the decision as prosecutorial discretion vs. tactics/conduct before the court; (2) if prosecutorial discretion, it is reviewable only for abuse of process (egregious conduct seriously compromising trial fairness or integrity of the justice system), with a threshold requirement that the accused first establish a proper evidentiary foundation before the Crown must justify its decision.
BaselineB: Combination of common law/constitutional doctrine and statute context: prosecutorial discretion jurisprudence (explaining Krieger v. Law Society of Alberta, 2002 SCC 65; applying Nixon, 2011 SCC 34; etc.) in the setting of Criminal Code s. 727(1) notice triggering mandatory minimums under s. 255, and Charter s. 7 arguments.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Validity of a search warrant where the ITO includes Charter-tainted information: the warrant remains valid if it "would have issued even if the inadmissible facts had been excised" (Garofoli excision test), assessed on whether the authorizing judge "could have granted the authorization" on the remaining record
BaselineA: Common law/Charter jurisprudence applying s. 8 and warrant review doctrine from R. v. Garofoli, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 1421 (and the s. 8 reasonableness framework from R. v. Collins, [1987] 1 S.C.R. 265), in the context of a warrant under Narcotic Control Act, s. 12
CaseB_TestB: Scope of the Income Tax Act confidentiality exception in s. 241(3): whether disclosure is permitted "in respect of proceedings relating to the administration or enforcement" of the Act, interpreted broadly using the "widest possible scope" of the connecting phrases "in respect of" and "relating to"
BaselineB: Statute — Income Tax Act, S.C. 1970-71-72, c. 63, s. 241(1)-(4) (especially s. 241(3)); interpreted in light of s. 222 (tax debts recoverable in court) and prior case law (e.g., Nowegijick; Glover)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 486(2.1) screen order: judge may permit a child complainant (<18) to testify behind a screen only if the judge is of the opinion it is "necessary to obtain a full and candid account of the acts complained of"; this limited procedure does not infringe Charter ss. 7 or 11(d) where confrontation/cross-examination remain intact
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 486(2.1)) applied/assessed under Charter ss. 7 and 11(d)
CaseB_TestB: Similar fact (identity) admissibility—use of prior conviction: where the accused puts identity for the prior act in issue, the Crown may tender the prior conviction as "some evidence" linking the accused to the similar act (Arp second test); challenging the conviction on the voir dire is not automatic and will be rare—may be refused where there is "no reasonable likelihood" the challenge will affect admissibility
BaselineB: Common law similar fact admissibility framework from R. v. Arp and R. v. Handy (including the "some evidence" link requirement and probative value vs prejudicial effect balancing)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Party liability for manslaughter where the principal is guilty of murder (ss. 21(1) aiding/abetting and 21(2) common unlawful purpose): manslaughter available if the accused lacked murder mens rea but, objectively, a reasonable person would foresee non-trivial bodily harm from the dangerous act/common purpose
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, ss. 21(1)(b),(c) and 21(2)) as interpreted through SCC manslaughter jurisprudence (R. v. Kirkness; R. v. Creighton; R. v. Trinneer; also R. v. DeSousa referenced)
CaseB_TestB: Entitlement to GST rebate for overpayment under Excise Tax Act: s. 261(1) turns on actual payment of an amount 'not payable', not legal liability; s. 261(2)(c) only bars double recovery where a rebate 'is payable' under ss. 215.1/216(6); and s. 296(2.1) requires the Minister to apply an 'allowable rebate' on assessment even if not claimed within s. 261(3)'s two-year limit
BaselineB: Statute (Excise Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. E-15, ss. 261(1)-(3), 296(2.1), and related ss. 215.1, 216(6), 225(1))
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Policy vs. operational decision framework for Crown tort liability in highway maintenance (policy decisions immune; operational implementation subject to negligence standard)
BaselineA: Common law (Just v. British Columbia; also drawing on Anns v. Merton and Kamloops v. Nielsen) applied alongside statutory context (Public Highways Act, ss. 4-5; Proceedings against the Crown Act, s. 5(1)(a); Expropriation Act, ss. 70(f), 71)
CaseB_TestB: Damages in lieu of specific performance: assess as of date of trial (judgment) where specific performance legitimately pursued; specific performance not granted as a matter of course absent evidence of uniqueness
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: Courts of Justice Act (Ontario), s. 99 (damages in substitution for specific performance) applied with common law damages principles (Johnson v. Agnew; Wroth v. Tyler; and SCC guidance in Asamera Oil)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Abuse of process threshold (“clearest of cases”): court may intervene only where conduct “shocks the conscience of the community” and there is “overwhelming evidence” the proceedings are unfair; otherwise no residual appellate discretion under s. 686(4) beyond allowing/dismissing the appeal
BaselineA: Common law doctrine of abuse of process (as affirmed in R. v. Jewitt; reiterated in R. v. Keyowski; discussed with R. v. Conway, R. v. Mack, R. v. Scott, R. v. Potvin) plus statutory interpretation of Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(4)
CaseB_TestB: Mr. Big confessions admissibility rule: presumptively inadmissible unless Crown proves (balance of probabilities) probative value (reliability) outweighs prejudicial effect; reliability assessed via operation circumstances and “markers of reliability” in the confession; plus abuse-of-process backstop for coercive/abusive operations
BaselineB: Common law evidence (party admissions exception to hearsay: R. v. Evans; existing limited tools of prejudice vs probative value and abuse of process; confessions rule inapplicable per R. v. Grandinetti; right to silence not engaged absent detention per R. v. McIntyre and R. v. Hebert)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 16(1) “knowing it was wrong”: incapacity includes inability to rationally apply right/wrong to the particular act (capacity for rational perception and rational choice by ordinary-person standards)
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 16(1)), interpreted in light of prior insanity jurisprudence (notably R. v. Chaulk and the M'Naghten Rules)
CaseB_TestB: Palmer criteria for admitting fresh evidence on appeal (including sentence appeals): (1) due diligence (flexible factor), (2) relevance, (3) credibility, (4) could reasonably be expected to have affected the result, all under the overriding “interests of justice”
BaselineB: Common law test from Palmer v. The Queen, applied/confirmed for sentence appeals alongside Criminal Code ss. 683 and 687 (“interests of justice” discretion)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Mohan test for admissibility of expert evidence (and added threshold for expert disposition/profile evidence): expert evidence admissible only if (a) relevant, (b) necessary to assist trier of fact, (c) not barred by an exclusionary rule, and (d) tendered by a properly qualified expert; for expert disposition/profile evidence, the judge must be satisfied "as a matter of law" that the perpetrator or accused has "distinctive behavioural characteristics" and that the profile is in common use as a reliable indicator (i.e., "Has the scientific community developed a standard profile").
BaselineA: Common law (expert opinion admissibility and character/disposition evidence), drawing on and synthesizing prior cases cited in the reasons including R. v. Abbey, R. v. Béland, R. v. Morin, R. v. Lupien, and related authorities; not primarily statutory (Criminal Code s. 693 is procedural only).
CaseB_TestB: Section 745 Criminal Code parole ineligibility review framework: jury determines whether ineligibility "ought to be reduced" by weighing listed factors "as a whole"—"having regard to the character of the applicant, his conduct while serving his sentence, the nature of the offence ... and such other matters as the judge deems relevant"—a discretionary, holistic assessment (not element-by-element proof).
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 745(1)-(4) (especially s. 745(2) listing factors and conferring discretion).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 10(b) informational/implementational duties: no duty-counsel advice required where no duty counsel exists; further police duties are only triggered if detainee asserts desire to speak to counsel (a clear 'No' triggers no further obligations)
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 10(b) (and related jurisprudence interpreting its informational and implementational components, including R. v. Brydges and R. v. Bartle; addressed alongside R. v. Prosper)
CaseB_TestB: Criminal Code s. 347 framework for late payment penalties: (1) determine whether the charge is 'interest'—i.e., 'paid or payable for the advancing of credit under an agreement or arrangement' (including deferral of payment for goods/services as 'credit advanced'); (2) apply s. 347(1)(a) ex ante (narrow) vs s. 347(1)(b) ex post (broad), with Nelson 'voluntary act of debtor' limitation
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 347(1)-(2) (definitions of 'interest', 'credit advanced', 'criminal rate'); interpreted in light of Nelson v. C.T.C. Mortgage Corp. and Degelder Construction Co. v. Dancorp Developments Ltd.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 7 overbreadth (principles of fundamental justice) test: a law is unconstitutional if it limits life, liberty or security of the person in a manner that is "unnecessarily broad, going beyond what is needed to accomplish the governmental objective"; courts ask whether the means are "necessary" and "reasonably tailored" to the objective (Heywood).
BaselineA: Combination: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7 (principles of fundamental justice) applied to Criminal Code, s. 179(1)(b); baseline jurisprudence referenced includes Re B.C. Motor Vehicle Act and R. v. Nova Scotia Pharmaceutical Society on overbreadth/vagueness.
CaseB_TestB: ITA s. 69(2) transfer pricing “reasonable amount in the circumstances” test: determine whether the non-arm’s-length price exceeds what "would have been reasonable in the circumstances" at arm’s length; consider "all the circumstances" relevant to price, including linked agreements conferring rights/benefits, and ensure comparators are "sufficiently comparable" in their "economically relevant characteristics" (GlaxoSmithKline).
BaselineB: Statute: Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), s. 69(2) (now s. 247(2)); OECD 1979/1995 Transfer Pricing Guidelines treated as non-binding interpretive aids.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Inference of possession from fingerprint evidence: whether an accused’s fingerprint on an article supports an inference of possession is “not subject to a hard and fast rule” but “depends on all of the circumstances of the case and all of the evidence adduced” (including that the bag-vs-contents distinction is “merely another factor” in the totality analysis).
BaselineA: Common law (circumstantial-evidence approach to inferring possession from fingerprints), drawing on R. v. O'Keefe (1958) and approving R. v. Mehrabnia (1993).
CaseB_TestB: Review Board jurisdiction under Criminal Code s. 672.54: Boards may impose binding conditions on hospital authorities and may impose conditions “regarding”/supervising treatment, but cannot “prescribe” or “impose” treatment; supervisory power includes ordering re-evaluations/exploration of alternatives, and s. 672.55(1) is not a true exception to the no-prescription rule.
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, Part XX.1), primarily ss. 672.54 and 672.55(1) (with related appeal/enforcement provisions).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Predominant purpose test for exemption from compulsion to testify (s. 7 self-incrimination): whether the “predominant purpose” of seeking the evidence is “to obtain incriminating evidence against the person compelled to testify or rather some legitimate public purpose”; if predominant purpose is to incriminate, compulsion must be justified and witness not compellable if other significant prejudice jeopardizes fair trial
BaselineA: Common law / Charter-based doctrine from R. v. S. (R.J.) interpreting and applying Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 7 and 13, in the context of Securities Act, S.B.C. 1985, c. 83, s. 128(1)
CaseB_TestB: Timing rule for Corbett applications: the defence “should” bring, and the trial judge “should” decide, a Corbett application “immediately after the close of the Crown’s case”; if necessary, hold a pre-defence voir dire where defence discloses intended evidence; ruling may be modified if defence evidence departs significantly from what was disclosed
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: Canada Evidence Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-5, s. 12 as interpreted in R. v. Corbett; procedural fairness principles under Charter s. 7 (case-to-meet) referenced via R. v. S. (R.J.)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 7 compellability / exemption from compelled testimony: whether the “predominant purpose” of seeking the evidence is to obtain incriminating evidence against the witness or to further a legitimate public purpose (with derivative-use-immunity backdrop and burden on the witness)
BaselineA: Combination: Charter (ss. 7 and 13) applied to statutory compulsion under Securities Act, S.B.C. 1985, c. 83, s. 128(1), building on SCC common-law/Charter self-incrimination framework from R. v. S. (R.J.), [1995] 1 S.C.R. 451
CaseB_TestB: Section 15(1) prima facie equality test (Quebec v. A framework): (1) distinction on an enumerated/analogous ground (on its face or in impact) and (2) discriminatory/arbitrary disadvantage—claimant must show disproportionate impact tied to group membership
BaselineB: Constitutional: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 15(1), applying the SCC’s existing framework from Quebec (Attorney General) v. A, 2013 SCC 5 (and related s. 15 jurisprudence)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Tax-treaty residency under Article IV(1): entity must be “liable to tax” in the contracting state “by reason of” an enumerated connecting factor (domicile, residence, place of management, place of incorporation) or a “criterion of a similar nature”; “similar nature” means a basis for comprehensive (world-wide) taxation, not mere source taxation (e.g., being engaged in a U.S. trade or business with effectively connected income).
BaselineA: Statute/treaty: Canada-United States Tax Convention Act, 1984, Schedule I (Canada–U.S. Income Tax Convention (1980)), Article IV(1) (and related context Articles I, XII).
CaseB_TestB: “Valid refusal” trigger for the two-year limitation: the s. 281(5) Insurance Act limitation period “only begins to run upon the issuance by the insurer of a valid refusal”; no valid refusal if inadequate compliance with SABS s. 71, which requires notice of the dispute-resolution process in “straightforward and clear language” and, “at a minimum”, key items (mediation right, arbitration/litigation if mediation fails, mediation prerequisite, and relevant time limits).
BaselineB: Statute/regulation: Insurance Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. I.8, s. 281(5) and Statutory Accident Benefits Schedule (O. Reg. 776/93), ss. 71 (and related ss. 72, 62(8), 94).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Weber exclusive arbitral jurisdiction test: courts are ousted where the dispute’s “essential character” arises from the “interpretation, application, administration or violation” of the collective agreement (s. 45(1) OLRA), regardless of how pleaded (tort/Charter), subject to residual court jurisdiction only where the tribunal lacks power to grant the needed remedy
BaselineA: Statute (Ontario Labour Relations Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. L.2, s. 45(1)) interpreted in light of SCC labour-arbitration exclusivity jurisprudence (notably St. Anne Nackawic Pulp & Paper Co. v. Canadian Paper Workers Union, Local 219, [1986] 1 S.C.R. 704)
CaseB_TestB: Criminal Code s. 744 parole-ineligibility extension framework: trial judge “may, having regard to (1) the character of the offender, (2) the nature of the offence, and (3) the circumstances surrounding its commission … substitute for ten years” a longer period (10–25); 10 years is the general rule but can be “ousted” where those criteria justify longer; appellate intervention only if sentence is “clearly unreasonable”/outside the “acceptable range”
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, ss. 744 and 687(1))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Retiring allowance for loss of employment: an employee is only “in the service” of the employer once under an obligation to provide services; therefore “loss of employment” cannot occur before that moment (no retiring allowance for loss of intended/prospective employment)
BaselineA: Statute (Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1952, c. 148 (now R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.)), s. 56(1)(a)(ii) and s. 248(1) definitions of “employment” and “retiring allowance”; also contrasted with s. 80.4(1) “intended office or employment”)
CaseB_TestB: Whether improper Crown closing submissions (personal anecdote not in evidence) caused an unfair trial/miscarriage of justice assessed contextually using the “relevant factors” (from R. v. Stephan), including seriousness vis-à-vis core issues, prominence, objections, and adequacy of the jury charge
BaselineB: Common law (trial fairness/miscarriage of justice analysis for improper jury addresses; factors referenced from R. v. Stephan; also relying on Pisani, Boucher, Manasseri, Abdullahi)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Pragmatic and functional approach to whether a labour board has jurisdiction (and thus whether its decision is reviewable only for patent unreasonableness): consider (a) wording of the enactment, (b) purpose of the statute, (c) reason for the tribunal’s existence, (d) tribunal expertise, (e) nature of the problem (U.E.S., Local 298 v. Bibeault factors).
BaselineA: Combination: common law administrative-law framework (U.E.S., Local 298 v. Bibeault) applied to the Canada Labour Code jurisdiction/privative-clause scheme (ss. 16(p)(v), 22, 24, 27, 28, 33).
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 8 reasonableness of DNA data bank sampling of convicted offenders: assess reasonableness contextually by balancing state interest in identification against privacy impact; Hunter v. Southam ‘reasonable and probable grounds’ requirements are not applicable to DNA data bank orders; key question becomes whether the offender has a reasonable expectation of privacy in the identifying information derived from DNA sampling.
BaselineB: Combination: statute (Criminal Code s. 487.055; related provisions including s. 487.055(3.1)) plus Charter s. 8 common law/constitutional framework (Collins/Stillman reasonableness requirements; Hunter v. Southam balancing concept).
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Gladstone refinement of Sparrow s.35 justification: for Aboriginal commercial rights without internal limits, Crown must justify infringement by (1) valid legislative objective and (2) consistency with fiduciary duty, including a non-exclusive but priority-respecting allocation that is both procedurally and substantively fair
BaselineA: Common law / constitutional doctrine under Constitution Act, 1982, s. 35(1) (Sparrow framework). Baseline test from R. v. Sparrow: justification requires (1) valid legislative objective and (2) consistency with fiduciary duty (including priority).
CaseB_TestB: Admissibility of Crown rebuttal evidence: rebuttal may be admitted where Crown could not have anticipated the defence evidence and the rebuttal is clearly relevant to an issue raised (e.g., going to the 'context and the essential fabric' of an alibi); admission is discretionary
BaselineB: Common law (trial judge discretion over rebuttal evidence; relevance and proper rebuttal scope). Also references Criminal Code, s. 686(1)(b)(iii) only for curative proviso on appeal, not as the admissibility test itself.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Implied waiver of Charter s. 11(d) in ticketed regulatory offences: legislature may infer waiver from failure to pay/appear only if (1) accused is fully aware of consequences of failing to act and (2) the procedural scheme has sufficient safeguards to ensure the failure was not due to events beyond the accused’s control (R. v. Richard, para. 8; reiterated at para. 32).
BaselineA: Combination of Charter interpretation (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 11(d), with contextual reference to s. 7 liberty) and common-law/Charter waiver principles as discussed through SCC precedent (notably R. v. Lee, [1989] 2 S.C.R. 1384, and general waiver requirements of voluntariness and full knowledge: para. 22).
CaseB_TestB: Procedural fairness for CHRC dismissal of a complaint as unsubstantiated: Commission acts quasi-judicially and must (1) give parties an opportunity to make submissions (at least in writing; a hearing not necessarily required) before deciding, and (2) before the decision, disclose “the substance of the case” to ensure submissions are informed (Radulesco, reasons of Lamer J.).
BaselineB: Statutory decision under the Canadian Human Rights Act, 1976-77 (Can.), c. 33, ss. 35 and 36(3)(b), informed by common-law natural justice/procedural fairness principles (quasi-judicial duty of fairness).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Patently unreasonable standard on judicial review of labour arbitration (including the 'no evidence' basis): decision must be 'clearly irrational' / 'evidently not in accordance with reason'; a finding based on 'no evidence' is patently unreasonable
BaselineA: Common law (administrative law standard of review) applied in labour arbitration context; also influenced by a broad privative clause in School Boards and Teachers Collective Negotiations Act, s. 72
CaseB_TestB: Statutory 'equivalent in value' test for successor pension plan: s. 15(2)(a) requires comparing both (1) benefits paid and (2) the funding mechanism; not enough that monthly payments are equal
BaselineB: Statute: The Manitoba Telephone System Reorganization and Consequential Amendments Act, S.M. 1996, c. 79, s. 15(2)(a) ('equivalent in value'); interpreted in context with s. 15(3) and related pension legislation background
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Doctrine of part performance defeats a statutory writing requirement (Statute of Frauds analogue): where an oral agreement for an interest in land has been carried out/partly performed, equity will enforce it and prevent the Crown from relying on the absence of writing to deny the interest
BaselineA: Combination: statute + equitable/common law doctrine. Statutory baseline is Public Highways Act, R.S.N.S. 1954, c. 235, s. 21(1)(a) (written permit requirement) (and argued Expropriation Act, R.S.N.S. 1954, c. 91, ss. 21(1), 25). Common law/equity baseline is the doctrine of part performance as described via Steadman v. Steadman, [1976] A.C. 536 (H.L.) (and related authorities).
CaseB_TestB: Quebec arbitration/public order framework for annulment/homologation: (1) interpret arbitration agreements liberally to include matters “closely connected” to the dispute; (2) an award is annulled for public order only if the outcome/disposition violates public order—mere legal error on a mandatory rule is insufficient
BaselineB: Statute/civil code: Civil Code of Québec, art. 2639 (arbitrability/public order) and Code of Civil Procedure, arts. 946.2 and 946.5 (no merits review; refuse homologation/annul only if matter not arbitrable or award contrary to public order). Also interprets Copyright Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-42, s. 37 (concurrent jurisdiction) as not excluding arbitration.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Southam standard of review framework and the “reasonableness simpliciter” test: on statutory appeal, determine the standard by considering “the nature of the problem”, “the applicable law properly interpreted in the light of its purpose” and “the expertise of the tribunal”; where a middle ground is required, review for whether the tribunal decision is “unreasonable” (i.e., “not supported by any reasons that can stand up to a somewhat probing examination”).
BaselineA: Common law (standard of review jurisprudence), applied in the context of a statutory right of appeal under the Competition Tribunal Act, ss. 12-13.
CaseB_TestB: Albashir temporal-effect test for suspended s. 52(1) declarations: declarations are “presumptively retroactive” but the presumption is rebutted “explicitly or by necessary implication”; for suspended declarations, courts must look to “the purpose of a suspension” and if retroactivity would “defeat the compelling public interests that required the suspension”, “the declaration must apply purely prospectively”.
BaselineB: Constitutional text and remedial doctrine: Constitution Act, 1982, s. 52(1) and Charter, s. 24(1), building on prior SCC remedial jurisprudence (including Bedford, Hislop, and Ontario (Attorney General) v. G).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: CCA “purpose of producing income” test under Reg. 1102(1)(c): (1) “Does the property produce income? In the affirmative, the deduction is allowable.” (2) If not, “was it acquired for the purpose of producing income?”, determined by “an objective evaluation of the specific facts and circumstances ... having regard to whether the taxpayer acted in accordance with reasonably acceptable principles of commerce and business practices.”
BaselineA: Statute and regulation: Income Tax Act, s. 20(1)(a) (deductions “from a business or property” as “allowed by regulation”); Income Tax Regulations, s. 1102(1)(c) (property excluded if “not acquired ... for the purpose of gaining or producing income”).
CaseB_TestB: Bail denial under Criminal Code s. 515(10)(c) (post-severance): detention may be ordered where “necessary in order to maintain confidence in the administration of justice”, assessed objectively “having regard to all the circumstances, including the apparent strength of the prosecution’s case, the gravity of the nature of the offence, the circumstances surrounding its commission and the potential for a lengthy term of imprisonment”, i.e., whether “a reasonable member of the community would be satisfied that denial of bail is necessary to maintain confidence in the administration of justice.”
BaselineB: Statute and constitutional constraint: Criminal Code, s. 515(10)(c) (tertiary bail ground) interpreted in light of Charter, s. 11(e) (“not to be denied reasonable bail without just cause”).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Vesting/accrual of an appeal-as-of-right: the right is only “acquired”, “accrued” or “accruing” once all conditions precedent are fulfilled (in this context, when the court of appeal renders judgment reversing the acquittal and ordering a new trial)
BaselineA: Statute: Interpretation Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. I-21, ss. 43(c) and 44(c),(d), applied to Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 691(2) (as amended effective May 14, 1997)
CaseB_TestB: Sherman Estate test for discretionary limits on the open court principle (publication bans): (1) serious risk to an important public interest; (2) necessity because reasonable alternatives will not prevent the risk; (3) proportionality—benefits outweigh negative effects
BaselineB: Common law: Sherman Estate v. Donovan, 2021 SCC 25 (para. 38 framework for discretionary orders limiting court openness)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Canderel profit-computation framework under ITA s. 9(1): taxpayer may use any method consistent with the Act, case law, and well-accepted business principles that yields an “accurate picture” of profit; once taxpayer shows this, onus shifts to Minister to show inaccuracy or a more accurate alternative
BaselineA: Statute (Income Tax Act, S.C. 1970-71-72, c. 63, ss. 9(1), 18(1)(a), 18(9)) plus prior SCC/common-law profit principles (e.g., M.N.R. v. Irwin; Symes v. Canada; Friesen v. Canada)
CaseB_TestB: Interpretation/application of Partnership Act s. 55(b): a general partner breaches only if it does an act that “makes it impossible to carry on the ordinary business” of the limited partnership—meaning impossibility as to a “substantial portion” of the ordinary business, not every facet
BaselineB: Statute (Partnership Act, R.S.A. 1980, c. P-2, s. 55(b))
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Dixon two-step test for Charter remedy/new trial for Crown non-disclosure: (1) reasonable possibility undisclosed info affects reliability of conviction; if not, (2) reasonable possibility non-disclosure affected overall fairness via lost lines of inquiry/opportunities, with defence due diligence as a significant balancing factor
BaselineA: Combination of common law disclosure doctrine and Charter: Stinchcombe relevance threshold (as explained in Egger; also Chaplin) and Charter ss. 7 and 24(1) (with Carosella, C.(M.H.), Collins referenced)
CaseB_TestB: Standard-form insurance contract interpretation (Ledcor framework) applied to SEF 44 cl. 4(b)(vii): give effect to clear, unambiguous language as understood by the average insured; only if ambiguous apply general rules, then contra proferentem—leading to conclusion CPP is not a 'policy of insurance'
BaselineB: Common law principles of standard-form insurance contract interpretation (Ledcor; Progressive Homes; Scalera; Gibbens) applied to the SEF 44 Endorsement clause 4(b)(vii) wording
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Caslake ‘truly incidental to arrest’ limit on search-incident-to-arrest: police must have a purpose related to the arrest (within Cloutier purposes or other valid purpose) and it must be objectively reasonable; delay/distance may support a negative inference rebuttable by explanation
BaselineA: Common law (search incident to arrest doctrine) as explained in Cloutier v. Langlois, [1990] 1 S.C.R. 158 (and referenced in R. v. Stillman, [1997] 1 S.C.R. 607); applied within Charter s. 8 reasonableness framework from Hunter v. Southam and R. v. Collins
CaseB_TestB: Admissibility of defence-led unknown third party suspect evidence under Seaboyer: (1) logical relevance to an available defence shown by a sufficient connection/similarity between the charged crime and another incident plus evidence the accused could not have committed the other offence; and (2) admit unless prejudicial effects substantially outweigh probative value (no balance-of-probabilities proof; judge must not assess credibility/weight)
BaselineB: Common law evidence admissibility principles from R. v. Seaboyer, [1991] 2 S.C.R. 577 (probative value vs prejudicial effect; defence evidence excluded only if prejudice substantially outweighs value), with relevance principles from R. v. Corbett and the air of reality threshold from R. v. Cinous; draws on (but distinguishes/does not apply) Grandinetti and Handy frameworks
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Schreiber (Lamer C.J.) — s. 8 Charter is only triggered if claimant shows a reasonable expectation of privacy; for foreign-held records, expectation generally corresponds to the degree of protection under the foreign law (contextual Plant factors, with a foreign-law ceiling).
BaselineA: Combination: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 8 (and s. 32(1) on application) + common-law s. 8 jurisprudence (Hunter v. Southam; R. v. Plant; R. v. Terry).
CaseB_TestB: Fullowka — Anns/Cooper duty-of-care framework for negligence (foreseeability + proximity → prima facie duty; then residual policy to negate/limit), applied to omissions to prevent third-party intentional harm.
BaselineB: Common law (Anns/Cooper duty of care framework as developed in Cooper v. Hobart; Edwards v. Law Society; Childs v. Desormeaux; Hill v. Hamilton-Wentworth).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Pushpanathan Art. 1F(c) exclusion framework: Art. 1F(c) applies where there is international-law consensus that the acts are "sufficiently serious and sustained violations of fundamental human rights as to amount to persecution", or where acts are "explicitly recognized as contrary to the purposes and principles of the United Nations"; includes (1) determinative UN/international instruments explicitly designating acts as contrary to UN purposes/principles, and (2) acts a court can itself characterize as "serious, sustained and systemic violations of fundamental human rights constituting persecution" (with indicators like proximity to core human rights and universal-jurisdiction status).
BaselineA: Statute incorporating treaty: Immigration Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. I-2, s. 2(1) (definition of "Convention refugee" incorporating Refugee Convention Art. 1F(c)); interpreted using treaty-interpretation rules (Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, Arts. 31-32).
CaseB_TestB: Hadley v. Baxendale remoteness/proximity test for contract damages (as applied to employment implied duties): damages are those that arise "either naturally" or that "may reasonably be supposed to have been in the contemplation of both parties, at the time they made the contract, as the probable result of a breach"; applied to assess damages for breach of an implied duty of good faith by a branch manager orchestrating a mass exit.
BaselineB: Common law contract damages: Hadley v. Baxendale (1854) (remoteness/foreseeability-in-contemplation rule) as the governing baseline for breach-of-contract damages.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Hodgson/Wells framework for when a trial judge must hold a voir dire (proprio motu) on whether an accused’s statement was made to a “person in authority” (and thus must be proven voluntary): duty arises only in “extremely rare cases” where the evidence, viewed objectively, clearly shows the receiver was a conventional person in authority or was closely connected to authorities such that the accused could reasonably have believed the receiver was acting as an agent of the police/prosecution; otherwise defence must raise the issue.
BaselineA: Common law (confessions rule; person-in-authority requirement; voir dire practice)
CaseB_TestB: McClurg interpretation of Income Tax Act s. 56(2) in the dividend context: as a general rule, corporate dividends (including allocations under a discretionary dividend clause) are not “payments/benefits diverted” from the taxpayer within s. 56(2) because, absent declaration/allocation, profits remain corporate retained earnings; s. 56(2) targets diversion of amounts the taxpayer otherwise would have received.
BaselineB: Statute (Income Tax Act, S.C. 1970-71-72, c. 63, s. 56(2))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Reg. 1201 depletion-base profit computation: determine profits “reasonably attributable” to production in the normal way (receipts attributable to production minus expenses of earning those receipts), then deduct only the items enumerated in Reg. 1201(4) (no implied deduction for scientific research expenses deductible for income under ITA ss. 11(1)(j) and 72).
BaselineA: Regulation (Income Tax Regulations, reg. 1201(2) and 1201(4)) and related statutory context (Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1952, c. 148, ss. 11(1)(j) and 72); interpretive reliance on MNR v. Imperial Oil Ltd., [1960] S.C.R. 735.
CaseB_TestB: Sherman Estate test for discretionary limits on the open court principle (publication bans): applicant must establish (1) openness poses a serious risk to an important public interest; (2) the order is necessary because reasonable alternatives will not prevent the risk; and (3) proportionality—benefits outweigh negative effects.
BaselineB: Common law (Sherman Estate v. Donovan, 2021 SCC 25, para. 38).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Guidelines for applying the Kienapple (res judicata / rule against multiple convictions) principle where multiple counts arise from the same delict but differ in gravity: convict on the more serious count and acquit/hold in abeyance the less serious count (cannot use a guilty plea to the lesser to bar trial/conviction on the greater).
BaselineA: Common law (Kienapple v. The Queen, [1975] 1 S.C.R. 729) applied in the context of Criminal Code charges (ss. 83, 302(d), 421(a)).
CaseB_TestB: Habeas corpus availability to challenge continued detention in parole context: continuation of a valid deprivation of liberty is reviewable only if it becomes unlawful; in parole cases detention becomes unlawful only once the inmate has acquired parolee status, which occurs when the parole decision takes effect (including fulfillment of any condition).
BaselineB: Common law habeas corpus principles as developed in R. v. Miller, [1985] 2 S.C.R. 613; Cardinal v. Director of Kent Institution, [1985] 2 S.C.R. 643; Morin v. National Special Handling Unit Review Committee, [1985] 2 S.C.R. 662, applied alongside the Parole Act (R.S.C. 1970, c. P-2, as amended).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Winko interpretation of Criminal Code s. 672.54: absolute discharge is mandatory unless the court/Review Board makes a positive finding that the NCR accused poses a “significant threat to the safety of the public”; “significant threat” = “a real risk of physical or psychological harm ... that is serious ... beyond the merely trivial or annoying” and the conduct “must be criminal in nature” (plus the s. 672.54 factors and least- onerous/least-restrictive requirement).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, Part XX.1, especially s. 672.54(a)-(c); also Charter ss. 7 and 15 context).
CaseB_TestB: Westbank test for characterizing a levy under Constitution Act, 1867 s. 125: ask whether the charge is “(1) compulsory and enforceable by law; (2) imposed under the authority of the legislature; (3) levied by a public body; (4) intended for a public purpose; and (5) unconnected to any form of a regulatory scheme”; if all yes, it “will generally be described as a tax” (otherwise may be regulatory charge/user fee).
BaselineB: Constitutional text and statutory context (Constitution Act, 1867, s. 125; also Indian Act, s. 83(1)(a) as the by-law authority; building on prior SCC tax/fee jurisprudence such as Lawson and Re Exported Natural Gas Tax as cited in the reasons).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 2(d) (freedom of association) in labour context: s. 2(d) protects only (1) the freedom to establish/belong to/maintain an association and (2) the exercise in association of members’ lawful rights; it generally does not impose a positive obligation to include a group in a statutory labour-relations regime. Key quote: “only the establishment of an independent employee association and the exercise in association of the lawful rights of its members are protected under s. 2(d)” and “the fundamental freedoms protected by s. 2 of the Charter do not impose a positive obligation of protection or inclusion on Parliament or the government, except perhaps in exceptional circumstances”.
BaselineA: Common law / constitutional jurisprudence interpreting Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 2(d), drawing on the 1987 labour trilogy (Reference re Public Service Employee Relations Act (Alta.); PSAC v. Canada; RWDSU v. Saskatchewan) and Professional Institute of the Public Service of Canada v. Northwest Territories (Commissioner), as confirmed in Canadian Egg Marketing Agency v. Richardson.
JudgeA: Bastarache J. (for Gonthier, McLachlin, Major and Bastarache JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Joint/co-principal liability in group assaults (Criminal Code, s. 21(1)(a)): co-principal liability “flows whenever” (1) “two or more individuals come together with an intention to commit an offence”, (2) “are present during the commission of the offence”, and (3) “contribute to its commission”; for manslaughter, focus is whether the accused’s actions were “a significant contributing cause of death” (and in group assaults, “absent a discrete or intervening event, the actions of all assailants can constitute a significant contributing cause to all injuries sustained”).
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 21(1)(a) and (c)) as interpreted in SCC jurisprudence (notably R. v. Pickton, referenced).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Francis v. Baker framework for s. 4 Federal Child Support Guidelines (high-income payor): Table amount presumptively applies; deviation only if Table amount is shown to be “inappropriate” meaning “unsuitable”, assessed on all circumstances (including s. 4(b)(ii) factors), with a rebuttable presumption in favour of the Table amount and requiring “clear and compelling evidence” to depart
BaselineA: Regulation/statute: Federal Child Support Guidelines, SOR/97-175, s. 4 (esp. s. 4(b)(i)-(iii)) and related scheme (ss. 1, 3, 7, 21); Divorce Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 3 (2nd Supp.), s. 26.1(2)
CaseB_TestB: KP Pacific classification approach under B.C. Insurance Act: determine whether a multi-risk/all-risks policy “fits into a specific category” under Part 5 (Fire Insurance) via s. 119; if it does not fit, it is governed by Part 2 (general provisions), and s. 3(a) prevents contracting out of Part 2’s minimum protections (including the longer limitation period)
BaselineB: Statute: Insurance Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 226, ss. 119 (Part 5 applicability) and 3(a) (Part 2 paramountcy/floor); plus statutory condition 14 (Part 5 limitation) and Part 2 limitation tied to proof of loss
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meiorin unified BFOR test (3-step): employer must prove (1) standard adopted for a purpose “rationally connected to the performance of the job”; (2) adopted “in an honest and good faith belief” it was necessary; and (3) standard is “reasonably necessary” — i.e., “impossible to accommodate” affected employees “without imposing undue hardship” on the employer.
BaselineA: Statute (British Columbia Human Rights Code, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 210, ss. 13(1)(a), (b), (4)) plus prior SCC human rights/BFOR jurisprudence (e.g., O’Malley; Etobicoke; Central Alberta Dairy Pool; Renaud).
CaseB_TestB: Stewart source-of-income test (2-stage): (i) “Is the activity ... undertaken in pursuit of profit, or is it a personal endeavour?”; (ii) if not personal, “is the source ... a business or property?”; where hobby/personal elements exist, ask whether taxpayer has “subjective intention to profit” plus “evidence of businesslike behaviour” supporting it (REOP is only “a single factor”).
BaselineB: Statute (Income Tax Act, S.C. 1970-71-72, c. 63 / R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), especially ss. 3(a), 9(1)-(2), 18(1)(a),(h), 20(1)(c)(i), 248(1)) and prior SCC case law on “reasonable expectation of profit” (Moldowan v. The Queen).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Staged analysis for whether a conditional sentence is appropriate for an Aboriginal offender (s. 742.1 with mandatory consideration of s. 718.2(e) once incarceration is in play): (1) preliminarily exclude probation and a penitentiary term; (2) confirm s. 742.1 prerequisites (no minimum; <2 years; community safety—risk of reoffending and gravity of harm); (3) then determine whether a conditional sentence is consistent with ss. 718–718.2, including that when the choice narrows to incarceration the judge is 'obliged to consider the unique systemic or background circumstances' and 'the types of practicable procedures and sanctions' tied to Aboriginal heritage (Gladue).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, ss. 742.1 and 718.2(e), interpreted through R. v. Proulx and R. v. Gladue)
CaseB_TestB: Quebec Charter s. 9.1 balancing for a freedom-of-religion claim raised to avoid civil liability: even if there is a prima facie religious-freedom claim, it 'must be balanced and reconciled with countervailing rights, values, and harm' and determining when it yields is a 'complex, nuanced, fact-specific exercise'; here, any impairment is 'significantly outweighed' by harms and public interests (equality, autonomy in marriage/divorce, and enforcing valid contracts).
BaselineB: Statute (Quebec Charter of human rights and freedoms, ss. 3 and 9.1; informed by SCC freedom of religion jurisprudence including Syndicat Northcrest v. Amselem and R. v. Big M Drug Mart)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Unreasonable verdict review under Criminal Code s. 686(1)(a)(i): whether the verdict is one that a properly instructed jury (or trial judge) acting judicially could reasonably have rendered; appellate court must thoroughly re-examine the evidence and cannot overturn based on a mere “lurking doubt” without articulating why the verdict is inconsistent with a judicial appreciation of the evidence
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(a)(i)) as interpreted in SCC common law (R. v. Yebes; reaffirmed/followed via R. v. Biniaris)
CaseB_TestB: Institutional consultation / natural justice limits and evidentiary threshold on judicial review: consultation is permissible if (1) not imposed by a superior authority, (2) limited to questions of policy and law, and (3) decision-makers remain free; for audi alteram partem, applicant must prove an actual breach (not merely an apprehended breach), and a change between draft and final reasons does not by itself rebut the presumption of regularity
BaselineB: Common law procedural fairness/natural justice doctrine, especially IWA v. Consolidated-Bathurst Packaging Ltd. and Tremblay v. Quebec (Commission des affaires sociales) (with discussion alongside statutory context in Ontario Labour Relations Act, 1995, ss. 114(1), 117)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: “Functional and structural” approach to whether a statutory court/tribunal has the third Mills attribute (“power to grant the remedy sought”) and is therefore a “court of competent jurisdiction” under Charter s. 24(1) (here, power of a POA justice to order costs for a Charter breach)
BaselineA: Combination: Charter s. 24(1) (“court of competent jurisdiction”) plus common-law/constitutional jurisprudence defining that phrase (Mills v. The Queen three-part test; affirmed in Weber; Mooring). Also considered: Provincial Offences Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. P.33 (notably s. 90(2)) as enabling legislation context for implied powers.
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 11(d) “inexorable connection” test for statutory presumptions: a presumption is constitutional “solely if proof of the substituted fact leads inexorably to the existence of the essential element it replaces” (applied to strike down Criminal Code s. 172.1(3) presumption of belief about age in sting operations)
BaselineB: Combination: Charter s. 11(d) (presumption of innocence) applied to Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 172.1(3) (and context of s. 172.1(1)(b)); baseline SCC cases for the presumption test include Whyte, Downey, and Audet (as cited).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Existence of a valid partnership (for s. 96 ITA loss deduction): at formation, alleged partners must be “(1) carrying on a business, (2) in common, (3) with a view to profit”; tax motivation does not negate partnership if these ingredients are present, and “view to profit” is not a strictly quantitative net-gain-over-loss inquiry (ancillary profit intention can suffice).
BaselineA: Combination: statute (Income Tax Act, s. 96) applied through common-law partnership test from Continental Bank Leasing Corp. v. Canada, [1998] 2 S.C.R. 298 (as reiterated with Backman v. Canada, 2001 SCC 10).
CaseB_TestB: Adequacy of jury instructions on credibility and reasonable doubt (W.(D.) context): where credibility is central, the judge must explain the relationship between credibility assessment and the Crown’s burden; the charge is sufficient if, read as a whole, it is “crystal clear” the burden never shifts and the jury is not left with a “credibility contest” (not required to recite W.(D.) as a “magic incantation”; ultimate question is whether the jury “could not have been under any misapprehension as to the correct burden and standard of proof to apply”).
BaselineB: Common law: jury-charge framework from R. v. W. (D.), [1991] 1 S.C.R. 742 (and subsequent SCC applications such as S. (W.D.) and Avetysan).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Customs Act s. 48(5)(a)(iv) “condition of sale” test for dutiable royalties/licence fees: royalties/licence fees are added to value for duty only if they are paid “as a condition of the sale of the goods for export to Canada”; “Unless a vendor is entitled to refuse to sell licensed goods to the purchaser or repudiate the contract of sale where the purchaser fails to pay royalties or licence fees, s. 48(5)(a)(iv) is inapplicable.”
BaselineA: Statute — Customs Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (2nd Supp.), s. 48(5)(a)(iv) (and related context in ss. 45(1), 48(4), 48(5)(a)(v)); interpreted using common law/sale of goods concepts of “condition of sale”.
CaseB_TestB: ITA s. 224 “requirement to pay” trigger (bank liability): a requirement to pay applies only if the third party is “liable to make a payment” to the tax debtor; for cheques, “The fact that a person is designated as payee on the face of a cheque does not on its own mean that the bank is liable to make a payment to the person”; liability turns on cheque mechanics (e.g., presentment/holder status and deposit instructions/endorsement).
BaselineB: Combination — Statute (Income Tax Act, s. 224) applied through statutory/common-law rules of negotiable instruments (Bills of Exchange Act, including ss. 84, 86, 126, 138(2), 165(3)) and banking common law (debtor-creditor relationship).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: s. 45 Labour Code successorship in subcontracting: s. 45 may apply where the transferee, beyond performing similar functions, receives a "right to operate part of the transferor’s undertaking" and has a "sufficient degree of autonomy" assessed contextually (including by the "criterion of the subordination of the employees" to the contractor); no rigid "total control" requirement
BaselineA: Statute (Quebec Labour Code, R.S.Q., c. C-27, ss. 45-46) as interpreted in SCC jurisprudence (U.E.S., Local 298 v. Bibeault; Lester (W.W.) (1978) Ltd.)
CaseB_TestB: Jarvis/Ling audit vs. investigation test: the Charter-protected adversarial relationship is engaged where the "predominant purpose" of the inquiry is determining penal liability under s. 239; "no one factor is determinative" and the judge assesses the "totality of the circumstances" (with non-exhaustive factors) to decide when an investigation begins
BaselineB: Combination of statute and constitutional law (Income Tax Act, ss. 231.1(1), 231.2(1), 239; Charter ss. 7, 8, 24(2)) as interpreted in R. v. Jarvis (followed)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Anns/Cooper duty of care test for recognizing a novel duty of care (foreseeability + proximity at stage 1; residual policy at stage 2). Key points: at stage 1, ask whether there is “reasonably foreseeable harm and proximity sufficient to establish a prima facie duty of care”; “Mere foreseeability is not enough... The plaintiff must also show proximity”; and where a statute governs, “Factors giving rise to proximity must be grounded in the governing statute”. If stage 1 is met, stage 2 asks whether “residual policy considerations... justify denying liability”.
BaselineA: Common law (Anns v. Merton London Borough Council; Kamloops (City of) v. Nielsen), as clarified/applied in Cooper v. Hobart; proximity analysis also grounded in the Law Society Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. L.8 (notably s. 9 immunity and the Act’s regulatory scheme).
JudgeA: The Chief Justice and Major J.
CaseB_TestB: Section 1 (Oakes) justification analysis, articulated here as “five related questions with close attention to the factual context”: (1) pressing and substantial objective; (2) rational connection; (3) minimal impairment (“as little as possible” / no more than reasonably necessary); (4) proportionality between effects and objective; (5) whether deleterious effects outweigh “actual salutary effects”. The Court rejects adding a separate ‘separation of powers’ step to Oakes.
BaselineB: Constitutional text and doctrine: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 1 (and s. 15(1) as the infringed right), applying the Oakes framework from R. v. Oakes.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Pragmatic and functional approach (Pushpanathan) to select the standard of review for the CRTC’s interpretation of s. 43(5) Telecommunications Act (correctness here): consider (1) statutory right of appeal/privative clause, (2) relative expertise, (3) purpose of the Act/provision, (4) nature of the problem
BaselineA: Common law (standard-of-review framework from Pushpanathan v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), [1998] 1 S.C.R. 982; also referenced Dr. Q v. College of Physicians and Surgeons of British Columbia, 2003 SCC 19) applied in the context of Telecommunications Act, S.C. 1993, c. 38, ss. 43(5) and 64(1)
CaseB_TestB: Sentencing: how to treat collateral consequences, mistake of law, and non-impairment when fixing a fit sentence for refusal causing death (s. 255(3.2)); includes (i) collateral consequences must relate to the offence/offender and cannot make the sentence disproportionate, (ii) mistake of law requires an honest but mistaken belief in legality (mere confusion/uncertainty is not enough though may still mitigate), (iii) non-impairment is mitigating but its effect must be limited and the offender bears the onus to prove non-impairment on a balance of probabilities
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, ss. 255(3.2), 718 to 718.2, 718.1) with common-law sentencing principles/cases (e.g., R. v. Lacasse, 2015 SCC 64; R. v. Pham, 2013 SCC 15; R. v. Pontes, [1995] 3 S.C.R. 44; R. v. MacDonald, 2014 SCC 3)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 2(b) infringement and s. 1 justification (Oakes proportionality) applied to a municipal sign by-law restricting “counter-advertising”
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional text (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 2(b) and 1) plus existing SCC s. 1 framework (Oakes, as refined in Dagenais and Thomson Newspapers)
CaseB_TestB: Canadian Bill of Rights due process analysis for property: no pre-enactment hearing required; procedural protections only in adjudicative application; no substantive protection against clear, unambiguous legislative expropriation
BaselineB: Statute (Canadian Bill of Rights, ss. 1(a) and 2(e)) and its interpretive rule (Bill of Rights prevails unless an express notwithstanding declaration), with prior SCC Bill of Rights jurisprudence (e.g., Drybones, Miller, Burnshine) and constitutional principle of parliamentary privilege/procedure
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Copyright infringement by “reproduction” under s. 3(1): “Reproduction” generally requires “producing additional or new copies”; a “literal physical, mechanical transfer in which no multiplication takes place” is not a reproduction (so s. 38(1) seizure for “infringing copies” is unavailable).
BaselineA: Statute (Copyright Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-42, ss. 3(1), 2 “infringing”, 38(1); with related discussion of moral rights limits in ss. 14.1, 28.2 and Quebec C.C.P. art. 734 for seizure before judgment).
CaseB_TestB: Reasonableness simpliciter on judicial review: the standard does not “float”; a decision is unreasonable “only if there is no line of analysis within the given reasons that could reasonably lead the tribunal from the evidence before it to the conclusion at which it arrived”; if any sufficient reasons are “tenable” on a “somewhat probing examination”, the court must not interfere.
BaselineB: Common law (pragmatic and functional approach and standards of review framework from SCC cases including Pushpanathan v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) and Canada (Director of Investigation and Research) v. Southam Inc.; applied in context of statutory appeal under Law Society Act, 1996, S.N.B. 1996, c. 89).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Privacy Act s. 22(1)(b) exemption: government institution may refuse access only if disclosure “could reasonably be expected” to be injurious to the conduct of lawful investigations; requires a “clear and direct connection” between disclosure of the specific information and the alleged injury, supported by “concrete reasons” tied to the specific case (not general assertions or mere lack of consent).
BaselineA: Statute (Privacy Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. P-21, ss. 22(1)(b), 22(3), 47, 49; applied harmoniously with Official Languages Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 31 (4th Supp.), ss. 60, 72-74).
CaseB_TestB: Adverse inference / presumption of fact in medical causation (CCQ art. 2849): even where defendant negligence undermines proof of causation and plaintiff adduces “some” evidence, the trier of fact is not required to draw an adverse inference; it is discretionary and only “serious, precise and concordant” presumptions may be relied on, assessed legally (not scientifically) and reviewable only for palpable and overriding error.
BaselineB: Statute and jurisprudence: Civil Code of Québec, art. 2849 (presumptions of fact), informed by SCC causation/inference cases Snell v. Farrell and St-Jean v. Mercier.
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Validity of a zoning “holding regulation”/development freeze: give effect to the substance of the by-law where the policy is clear and within municipal powers; superfluous drafting about future amendment does not invalidate the operative prohibition (i.e., “Notwithstanding… no building… to contain three or more dwelling units until this by-law has been amended…”).
BaselineA: Statute and municipal by-law: The Planning Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 349, s. 35(1) (zoning power) and s. 35(22) (appeal to Municipal Board), applied to City of London zoning by-law 306-480 as amended by by-law 306(bc)-504, s. 4 (new s. 11 “Holding Regulation”).
CaseB_TestB: Custody assessment under The Infants Act: the trial judge must consider the parties’ conduct only as it bears on their relative fitness, but it is “only one factor” and “each particular case must be judged on its own circumstances” with “the paramount consideration… the welfare of the children.”
BaselineB: Statute: The Infants Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 222, s. 1(1) (welfare/paramount consideration; direction to consider conduct), as applied in custody jurisprudence referenced in the reasons (including McKee v. McKee; Bickley v. Bickley; Retzer v. Retzer; and the Court’s contemporaneous discussion in Talsky v. Talsky).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: OSC disclosure of compelled investigation material under Securities Act s. 17(1): apply Stinchcombe-style relevance (“reasonable possibility of relevance” to full answer and defence) within the s. 17(1) “public interest” balancing; disclosure may be ordered globally unless a party shows “no reasonable possibility” a particular item is relevant
BaselineA: Statute (Ontario Securities Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. S.5, ss. 16(1) confidentiality and 17(1) disclosure if Commission considers it “in the public interest”), informed by common-law relevance standard from R. v. Stinchcombe
CaseB_TestB: Framework to classify requested state-held records as first-party (Stinchcombe) vs third-party (O’Connor) disclosure: ask (1) is the information in prosecuting Crown possession/control? and (2) should police/another Crown entity have supplied it because it is “fruits of the investigation” or “obviously relevant”? If yes to either, Stinchcombe applies; otherwise O’Connor applies and accused must show “likely relevance” (“reasonable possibility” logically probative) to obtain production
BaselineB: Common law (Stinchcombe; O’Connor; McNeil) applied in light of Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 258(1)(c) (presumption of accuracy context)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Misfeasance in public office (defining elements): (1) “deliberate and unlawful conduct in the exercise of public functions”; and (2) “awareness that the conduct is unlawful and likely to injure the plaintiff” (plus causation and compensable loss).
BaselineA: Common law tort (misfeasance in public office), developed from cases including Ashby v. White and Roncarelli v. Duplessis; with unlawful conduct here pleaded as breaches of Police Services Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. P.15, ss. 113(9) and 41(1)(b).
CaseB_TestB: Eligibility for Quebec seats under Supreme Court Act, s. 6: appointee must be a current member “from among” the Quebec institutions (current judge of Quebec CA/Superior Court or current Quebec advocate with 10 years standing via s. 5); former Quebec advocates are excluded.
BaselineB: Statute/constitutional interpretation: Supreme Court Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. S-26, ss. 5 and 6 (and constitutional constraints under Constitution Act, 1982, Part V, especially s. 41(d) on “composition”).
JudgeB: McLachlin C.J. and LeBel, Abella, Cromwell, Karakatsanis and Wagner JJ.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Securities Act s. 162 administrative penalty in the public interest: once a contravention is found, the Commission may consider the full context (including general deterrence and settlements) and courts review the sanction globally for reasonableness (rational basis in light of statutory framework and circumstances). Key quotes: s. 162 is triggered by a breach, but the Commission may consider 'the context surrounding the breach' (para. 63); 'General deterrence is an appropriate factor to consider, albeit not the only one' (para. 61); 'Courts should review the order globally... No one factor should be considered in isolation' (para. 64).
BaselineA: Statute (Securities Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 418, s. 162; also context of ss. 161-162).
CaseB_TestB: Adequacy of jury instructions on routes to liability where other participants may be involved: the trial judge must instruct on 'all routes to liability which arise from the evidence' (para. 19) and, in this case, it was sufficient to tell the jury it could convict if satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt the accused 'actively participated' / 'acted in concert with others' in the killing; correcting the erroneous 'actual shooter' instruction to 'shot... or was otherwise an active participant' did not cause a miscarriage of justice (paras. 23-35).
BaselineB: Combination: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 21 party liability; s. 686(1)(b)(iii) curative proviso) and common law on jury-charge adequacy/party liability (e.g., R. v. Thatcher, R. v. Rose, as cited).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Good faith basis test for putting unproven factual suggestions in cross-examination (no evidentiary foundation required unless predicate is manifestly tenuous or suspect)
BaselineA: Common law (cross-examination principles), as explained through R. v. Howard, [1989] 1 S.C.R. 1337 and R. v. Bencardino (1973), 15 C.C.C. (2d) 342; also discussed alongside Browne v. Dunn (1893), 6 R. 67
CaseB_TestB: Federal paramountcy test (operational conflict or frustration of federal purpose; frustration requires clear proof of federal purpose and incompatibility)
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine of federal paramountcy, as summarized with reference to Rothmans, Benson & Hedges Inc. v. Saskatchewan, 2005 SCC 13; Canadian Western Bank v. Alberta, 2007 SCC 22; Quebec (Attorney General) v. Canadian Owners and Pilots Association (COPA), 2010 SCC 39; and related cases
JudgeB: Abella and Gascon JJ. (for the majority)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Vaid framework for determining existence/scope of parliamentary privilege: (1) is the claimed category/scope authoritatively established in Canada or at Westminster? If not, (2) apply the necessity test requiring a close/direct connection to legislative functions such that outside interference would undermine required autonomy
BaselineA: Combination of constitutional text and common law of parliamentary privilege: Constitution Act, 1867, s. 18; Parliament of Canada Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. P-1, s. 4; and prior SCC privilege jurisprudence (notably New Brunswick Broadcasting Co. v. Nova Scotia (Speaker of the House of Assembly) and Harvey v. New Brunswick (Attorney General))
CaseB_TestB: Interpretive test for Tobacco Act ss. 18-19: construe “promotion” as “commercial promotion directly or indirectly targeted at consumers” to avoid an overbroad ban on funded scientific works
BaselineB: Statutory interpretation of Tobacco Act, S.C. 1997, c. 13, ss. 18(1), 18(2)(a), 19 (in light of Charter s. 2(b) and s. 1 justification framework, but the key test is the statutory narrowing construction of “promotion”)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: GAAR “abusive tax avoidance” (s. 245(4)) — deny a tax benefit where it “cannot be reasonably concluded that a tax benefit would be consistent with the object, spirit or purpose of the provisions relied upon by the taxpayer”, determined through a “unified textual, contextual and purposive analysis” (applied to s. 18(13) and s. 96 to bar arm’s-length loss trading).
BaselineA: Statute: Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), especially ss. 245(1)-(4) (GAAR) applied with ss. 18(13) and 96(1); interpretive approach and GAAR framework followed from Canada Trustco Mortgage Co. v. Canada, 2005 SCC 54 (summarized at para. 31).
CaseB_TestB: Vancouver Sun informer-privilege procedure and “single guiding rule”: give “full effect” to informer privilege (a “complete and total bar on any disclosure of the informer’s identity”) while “limiting, as much as possible, any impairment of the open court principle”; two stages: (1) verify privilege (in camera/ex parte if needed; evidence of informer status “automatically engages the privilege”); (2) conduct proceedings and craft confidentiality measures to protect privilege while accommodating openness as much as possible (including, generally, making at least the existence of the in camera hearing and any decision public, often via a parallel sealed proceeding with a public redacted judgment).
BaselineB: Common law: Named Person v. Vancouver Sun, 2007 SCC 43 (procedure and guiding rule for informer privilege vs. open court principle), reaffirmed and applied; also relies on common-law informer privilege doctrine (e.g., Leipert; Basi) as described in the reasons.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “lawful authority” for whistleblower protection under s. 74(1)(a): includes not only police/public enforcement but also internal persons who “exercise lawful authority over the employee(s) complained about, or over the activity that is or is likely to result in the offence” (i.e., an “up the ladder” internal reporting route can qualify).
BaselineA: Statute: The Labour Standards Act, R.S.S. 1978, c. L-1, s. 74(1)(a) (and s. 74(2)); interpreted using the modern principle of statutory interpretation (Driedger/Rizzo) and Saskatchewan Interpretation Act, 1995, s. 10.
CaseB_TestB: Waiver of insurer’s right to rely on dishonoured-cheque non-payment rule: despite demand for replacement cheque, “Before one can find waiver there must be express and unequivocal language or conduct”; absent that, s. 238(1) deems premium unpaid if cheque dishonoured and policy terminates after grace period.
BaselineB: Combination: Statute (The Alberta Insurance Act, R.S.A. 1970, c. 187, s. 238(1)) plus common-law waiver principle as applied/followed from McGeachie v. North American Life Insurance Company (1893), 23 S.C.R. 148.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “lawful authority” for whistleblower protection under s. 74(1)(a): includes internal employer authorities who can address the wrongdoing (“up the ladder” reporting). The Court held that “the expression ‘lawful authority’ in s. 74 includes not only the police or other agents of the state ... but also individuals within the employer organization who exercise lawful authority over the employee(s) complained about, or over the activity that is or is likely to result in the offence” (para. 38).
BaselineA: Statute: The Labour Standards Act, R.S.S. 1978, c. L-1, s. 74(1)(a) (and interpretive context including The Interpretation Act, 1995, S.S. 1995, c. I-11.2, s. 10).
CaseB_TestB: Common law joinder test (Clunas) applied to joint trials of provincial offences and summary conviction Criminal Code offences: (1) offences “could initially have been jointly charged” (interpreted functionally as requiring a “sufficient factual nexus” rather than the same physical charging document) (paras. 35-40); and (2) joinder must be “in the interests of justice”, involving “a weighing of the costs and benefits of a joint trial” (paras. 41-43).
BaselineB: Common law: R. v. Clunas, [1992] 1 S.C.R. 595 (two-part joinder test), applied alongside statutory context (Provincial Offences Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. P.33; Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Two-step harm-based test for criminal indecency (Labaye/Butler framework): Crown must prove beyond a reasonable doubt (1) conduct "causes harm or presents a significant risk of harm" (e.g., to public autonomy/liberty, predisposition to anti-social behaviour, or physical/psychological harm) and (2) the harm/risk is "of a degree that is incompatible with the proper functioning of society" (R. v. Kouri, para. 10).
BaselineA: Combination: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 210(1) (keeping a common bawdy-house for the practice of acts of indecency) interpreted through SCC common law guidance from R. v. Butler, [1992] 1 S.C.R. 452 and the companion case R. v. Labaye, 2005 SCC 80.
CaseB_TestB: Pointe Gourde / s. 27(1)(a) compensation inquiry: when deciding whether a land-use enactment’s effect on value must be ignored, the "key question is whether the enactment was made with a view to the expropriation or, conversely, was an independent enactment"; the inquiry examines the enactment’s "purposes and effects" and "causation does not drive the inquiry" (St. John’s (City) v. Lynch, 2024 SCC 17, paras. 46, 48, 50-54).
BaselineB: Statute plus common law: Expropriation Act, R.S.N.L. 1990, c. E-19, s. 27(1)(a) ("no account shall be taken of the compulsory acquisition of the land") incorporating the common law Pointe Gourde principle (Pointe Gourde Quarrying and Transport Co. v. Sub-Intendent of Crown Lands, [1947] A.C. 565).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Interpretation of Alberta Limitations Act, s. 12 in conflicts cases: s. 12 applies Alberta’s limitation law only to “live actions” and does not revive a claim already time-barred under the applicable foreign substantive law (lex loci delicti, including its limitation period). Key holdings: “Since the California limitations period applied and had expired ... there was no right of action ... Section 12 does not purport to revive an action time-barred by the substantive law of the place where the accident occurred” (Major J., paras. 4, 8).
BaselineA: Statute (Alberta Limitations Act, R.S.A. 2000, c. L-12, s. 12) interpreted against the common law conflicts baseline from Tolofson v. Jensen (lex loci delicti includes the foreign limitation period as substantive).
CaseB_TestB: Ancillary powers doctrine (Waterfield/Dedman framework) for common law police powers interfering with liberty: preliminary step define the asserted power and liberty interests; then (1) whether conduct falls within scope of a police duty; (2) whether conduct is a justifiable exercise of powers—i.e., “reasonably necessary” assessed by weighing (1) importance of the duty, (2) necessity of the interference, (3) extent of the interference (paras. 46-48). Applied to reject a purported power: “there is no common law power to arrest someone who is acting lawfully in order to prevent an apprehended breach of the peace by others” (paras. 7, 101-102).
BaselineB: Common law (ancillary powers doctrine from Dedman v. The Queen and Waterfield; factors articulated in R. v. MacDonald).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Palmer/Lévesque test for admitting fresh evidence on a sentence appeal (interests of justice): (1) due diligence; (2) relevance; (3) credibility; (4) could reasonably be expected to have affected the result
BaselineA: Common law test from Palmer v. The Queen, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 759, as adapted to sentence appeals in R. v. Lévesque, 2000 SCC 47; applied under Criminal Code, s. 687(1) (appellate power to receive additional evidence)
CaseB_TestB: Section 8 reasonable expectation of privacy (REP) framework: REP assessed on the totality of the circumstances via four inquiries (subject matter; direct interest; subjective expectation; objective reasonableness)
BaselineB: Common law/Charter framework for s. 8 REP from cases cited in the reasons (e.g., R. v. Edwards, [1996] 1 S.C.R. 128; R. v. Tessling, 2004 SCC 67; R. v. Spencer, 2014 SCC 43; R. v. Cole, 2012 SCC 53; R. v. Marakah, 2017 SCC 59)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Copyright Act s. 27(2)(e) “hypothetical infringement” requirement: to prove secondary infringement by importation, the plaintiff must show the imported copy “would have infringed copyright if it had been made in Canada by the person who made it”; no liability where the foreign maker is the Canadian copyright owner because “a copyright owner cannot be liable to its exclusive licensee for infringement” (so no hypothetical infringement).
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 11(h) double-punishment test for retrospective parole changes: “The dominant consideration ... will be the extent to which an offender’s settled expectation of liberty has been thwarted by retrospective legislative action”; “It is the retrospective frustration of an expectation of liberty that constitutes punishment”; a change that “automatically lengthen[s] the offender’s period of incarceration” is a “clearest of cases”; otherwise, generally not punitive if it “does not substantially increase the risk of additional incarceration” (with indicators like individualized decision-making and procedural safeguards).
BaselineB: Constitution (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 11(h); applied to Abolition of Early Parole Act, S.C. 2011, c. 11, s. 10(1))
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Sentencing of hybrid offences prosecuted summarily: treat as summary conviction for sentencing; maximum sentence available without “worst offender/worst offence”; appellate intervention only for error of principle/relevant factor/overemphasis or demonstrably unfit sentence
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, Part XXIII sentencing principles and summary conviction limits)
CaseB_TestB: Admissibility of “Mr. Big” confessions: presumptive inadmissibility rebutted only if Crown proves (balance of probabilities) probative value (reliability) outweighs prejudicial effect; plus separate abuse-of-process scrutiny for coercive/abusive operations
BaselineB: Common law (party admissions exception to hearsay; probative value vs prejudicial effect discretion; abuse of process doctrine) as discussed with reference to Evans, Handy, Mohan, Mack, Babos, etc.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Adequacy of jury charge on evidence/defence theory (Azoulay/Jacquard): trial judge must (except rare needless cases) review substantial evidence and put the defence theory so jury can appreciate the evidence and apply the law; judge has considerable latitude as to how much evidence to review so long as jury has an adequate understanding of the relationship between essential evidence and issues
BaselineA: Common law (Azoulay v. The Queen; R. v. Jacquard)
CaseB_TestB: Trade-marks Act s. 6 confusion test: whether, having regard to 'all the surrounding circumstances' (including s. 6(5) factors), it is likely the 'casual consumer somewhat in a hurry' would be led to the mistaken inference that the wares/services come from the same source; no requirement of 'resemblance or linkage' between wares/services and no single factor (including fame or difference in wares) 'trumps' the others
BaselineB: Statute (Trade-marks Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. T-13, ss. 6(2) and 6(5))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 172.1(1)(c) “luring a child” — three essential elements: (1) “an intentional communication by computer”; (2) “with a person whom the accused knows or believes to be under 14 years of age”; (3) “for the specific purpose of facilitating the commission of a specified secondary offence” (subjective intent; “facilitating” includes “helping to bring about and making easier or more probable”; content of communication “not necessarily determinative”; no need to meet or intend to meet).
BaselineA: Statute — Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 172.1(1)(c) (as it read at trial), with related secondary offences in ss. 151 and 152.
