CaseB_TestB: Enforcement of forum selection clause — “strong cause” test: absent “strong cause” to displace the chosen forum, “order and fairness are better achieved when parties are held to their bargains” (discretionary; applied on a Rule 21.01(3)(a) motion).
BaselineB: Common law (as confirmed in Z.I. Pompey Industrie v. ECU-Line N.V., 2003 SCC 27) applied within the procedural framework of Ontario Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 21.01(3)(a).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: SCC leave jurisdiction and leave-importance test under Supreme Court Act s. 40(1): jurisdiction over “any final or other judgment” (incl. extension-of-time orders) unless excluded by s. 40(3), but leave only if the question is of “public importance” or otherwise “of such a nature or significance as to warrant decision”
BaselineA: Statute: Supreme Court Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. S-26, ss. 40(1), 40(3) (and definition of “judgment” in s. 2); interpreted in light of SCC jurisprudence including Hill v. The Queen, R. v. Gardiner, MacDonald v. City of Montreal, R. v. Hinse, R. v. Mentuck
CaseB_TestB: Threshold for third-party notice under Access to Information Act s. 27(1): disclose without notice only in “clear cases” where there is “no reason to believe” the record might contain s. 20(1) exempt material; refuse without notice where there is “no reason to believe” disclosure could be required; otherwise notice is required (including whenever severance under s. 25 is intended)
BaselineB: Statute: Access to Information Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. A-1, ss. 20(1), 25, 27(1), 28, 44; interpreted with reference to prior jurisprudence (e.g., Twinn; Air Atonabee; H.J. Heinz) and statutory purpose in s. 2(1)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 8 reasonableness of executing a dwelling-house search warrant: “knock and announce” is the norm; police may depart only if they had (ex ante) reasonable grounds to be concerned about harm or destruction of evidence, and the Crown must provide an evidentiary basis for that departure
BaselineA: Common law + constitutional baseline (Charter s. 8) drawing on Eccles v. Bourque (knock-and-announce content) and R. v. Genest (onus/evidentiary framework for departures), within the Collins s. 8 framework
CaseB_TestB: Implied assertions are hearsay when tendered for their truth; admissible only if within a traditional exception or, failing that, if the principled approach establishes “sufficient indicia of reliability and necessity” on a voir dire
BaselineB: Common law hearsay rule and the SCC’s principled approach (Khan; Starr; Khelawon; Mapara) as applied to implied assertions
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: State Immunity Act “commercial activity” exception: determine whether the proceeding “relate[s] to any commercial activity of the foreign state” by examining the acts’ “nature ... in their full context, which includes the purpose of the acts” (not merely whether authorized by the state or pursuing public interests).
BaselineA: Statute: State Immunity Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. S-18, ss. 2 (“commercial activity”), 3 (general immunity), 5 (commercial activity exception); applied within Quebec recognition/enforcement framework (C.C.Q., arts. 3076, 3155, 3158). Key baseline case referenced for approach: Re Canada Labour Code, [1992] 2 S.C.R. 50 (contextual nature+purpose approach).
CaseB_TestB: Miscarriage-of-justice assessment for trial irregularities (tainted material reaching jury): evaluate whether the irregularity was “severe enough to render the trial unfair or create the appearance of unfairness”, using non-exhaustive “reference points” (centrality, gravity/likely influence, jury vs judge-alone, remedial steps, appearance of fairness, defence counsel’s response).
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1) (especially s. 686(1)(a)(iii) “miscarriage of justice” and related curative proviso provisions).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Journalist-source privilege in Quebec civil proceedings: threshold relevance + Wigmore factors (with context-specific balancing at factor 4)
BaselineA: Common law (Wigmore case-by-case privilege framework as applied in R. v. National Post, 2010 SCC 16) plus Quebec civil evidence/procedure context (C.C.Q. art. 2857 relevance/admissibility; C.C.P. art. 46 general powers)
CaseB_TestB: Court jurisdiction to review voluntary association decisions: requires an underlying legal right; contract exists only with objective intention to create legal relations
BaselineB: Common law (Highwood Congregation of Jehovah’s Witnesses (Judicial Committee) v. Wall, 2018 SCC 26; general contract formation principles including objective intention to create legal relations)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Quebec Charter s. 49(2) punitive (exemplary) damages: admissible autonomously (no need for compensatory damages) and available against a deceased wrongdoer’s succession if there is (1) “unlawful” and (2) “intentional” interference with a Charter right; denunciation is a valid objective (in addition to punishment/deterrence). Key quotes: s. 49(2) requires the act be “both unlawful and intentional” (para. 57); “the fact that no compensatory damages were awarded ... does not in itself bar the claim” (para. 46); “denunciation contributes to the preventive objective of art. 1621 C.C.Q.” (para. 53).
BaselineA: Statute (Quebec Charter, s. 49(2)) interpreted alongside Civil Code of Québec, art. 1621; prior SCC guidance on s. 49 punitive damages in Augustus v. Gosset, Quebec (Public Curator) v. Syndicat national des employés de l’hôpital St-Ferdinand, and Béliveau St-Jacques.
CaseB_TestB: YCJA jurisdiction framework for youth judicial interim release on s. 469 Criminal Code charges after election: (1) “the proceeding” in YCJA ss. 13(2)-(3) is not confined to trial but includes “any step ... after the young person elects ... including any pre-trial application for judicial interim release, until trial” (para. 9, 15); and (2) release jurisdiction under YCJA s. 33(8) is held concurrently by superior court judges deemed youth justice court judges (ss. 13(2)-(3)) and provincially designated youth justice court judges (s. 13(1)) (paras. 24-25).
BaselineB: Statute (Youth Criminal Justice Act, ss. 13(1)-(3), 28, 33(8), 67; Criminal Code, ss. 469, 522/Part XVI; Interpretation Act, s. 33(2))—statutory interpretation of “the proceeding” and interaction between YCJA and Criminal Code.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Miscarriage of justice on appeal: whether trial defects "affected the trial judge’s appreciation of the evidence or rendered the proceedings unfair" (and thus "give rise to a miscarriage of justice")
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code appeal jurisdiction) plus common-law/Charter-informed appellate concept of "miscarriage of justice"
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 13 threshold: s. 13 is engaged only if the prior compelled testimony was "incriminating evidence"—i.e., evidence the Crown could use (if permitted) "to prove or assist in proving one or more of the essential elements of the offence"; non-incriminating compelled evidence may be used for impeachment
BaselineB: Statute/constitutional text (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 13) interpreted in light of prior SCC jurisprudence (R. v. Henry; R. v. Kuldip; R. v. Noël; Dubois v. The Queen)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “in association with” in Criminal Code s. 467.12: the offence must (1) have a nexus/connection to a criminal organization and (2) be committed with subjective knowledge (or wilful blindness) that one is dealing with a criminal organization; “in association with” captures offences that “advance, at least to some degree, the interests of a criminal organization” and “requires a connection between the predicate offence and the organization, as opposed to simply an association between the accused and the organization”.
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 467.12(1) (phrase “in association with”); related context in ss. 467.1, 467.13)
CaseB_TestB: Test for statutory “compulsion” (Motor Vehicle Act s. 61) triggering Charter s. 7 use-immunity: “whether, at the time that the accident was reported by the driver, the driver gave the report on the basis of an honest and reasonably held belief that he or she was required by law to report the accident to the person to whom the report was given”; accused bears the onus on a balance of probabilities to show compulsion.
BaselineB: Combination: Statute (Motor Vehicle Act, R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 288, s. 61(1)) interpreted through Charter s. 7 principle against self-incrimination (with contextual guidance from SCC cases including R. v. Fitzpatrick, [1995] 4 S.C.R. 154, as discussed in the reasons).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Reasonable suspicion standard for sniffer-dog searches (s. 8): subjective suspicion plus objective grounds assessed on the totality of the circumstances, through the lens of a reasonable officer with training/experience
BaselineA: Common law Charter s. 8 sniffer-dog framework from R. v. Kang-Brown and R. v. A.M., as clarified in companion R. v. Chehil; investigative detention authority from R. v. Mann
CaseB_TestB: Reformulated s. 11(i) 'punishment' test: consequence of conviction within the arsenal of sanctions, and either imposed in furtherance of sentencing purposes/principles or having a significant impact on liberty/security
BaselineB: Common law Charter s. 11(i) punishment test from R. v. Rodgers (two-part test)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: CCQ art. 1425 “common intention prevails” interpretation/rectification: where evidence proves a discrepancy between the parties’ proven common intention and the intention declared in the written instruments, and the parties mutually correct the error (subject to third-party rights), the court may recognize the amendments as “legitimate and necessary” and ensure the error “is remedied”. Key quotes: “the determination of the common intention… represents a true exercise of interpretation” (para. 48); “If such a writing contains an error, the court must, once the error is proved… note the error and ensure that it is remedied” (para. 52); “It was open to the courts to intervene to find that the amendments… were legitimate and necessary” (para. 51).
BaselineA: Statute (Civil Code of Québec, art. 1425; also discussed alongside arts. 2818, 2829, 1439 and related contract/evidence provisions).
CaseB_TestB: Bank “put upon inquiry” constructive trust/breach of trust test: “A banker may be a constructive trustee of money in his customer’s account and in breach of that trust if he pays the money away… in circumstances which put him upon inquiry.” Once on inquiry, the bank must take steps “to ascertain the character of the funds” before dealing with them.
BaselineB: Common law (constructive trustee/bank on inquiry doctrine; summarized from Halsbury’s Laws of England and illustrated by cases cited in the reasons such as White v. Dominion Bank and Cartwright v. Lyster & Bank of Nova Scotia).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Applicability of Quebec’s 1974 prescription amendments to a case pending in the SCC: s. 5 makes art. 2262(2) C.C. inapplicable to a “suit pending before a court on 1 January 1975”, and the SCC may rely on that intervening provincial statute to dismiss the appeal (not to substitute a different judgment under Supreme Court Act, s. 47).
BaselineA: Statute: Supreme Court Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. S-19, s. 47 (power to dismiss an appeal or give the judgment the court below should have given), plus Quebec Act to amend certain prescriptions, 1974 (Que.), c. 80, ss. 1, 3, 5 and Civil Code arts. 2261(2), 2262(2) (and the prior SCC approach in Boulevard Heights v. Veilleux and K.V.P. Co. Ltd. v. McKie).
CaseB_TestB: Refusal of extradition/surrender: the person sought must show surrender would “shock the conscience” (s. 7 Charter) or be “unjust or oppressive” (Extradition Act, s. 44(1)); the Minister’s decision is reviewed for reasonableness, focusing on whether the “particular treatment” awaiting the person would be contrary to Canadian principles of fundamental justice.
BaselineB: Combination of statute and constitutional standard: Extradition Act, S.C. 1999, c. 18, s. 44(1) (“unjust or oppressive”) and Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7 (“shock the conscience”/fundamental justice), as framed by United States v. Burns and Argentina v. Mellino.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Hart ‘Mr. Big’ confessions admissibility rule: presumptive inadmissibility rebutted only if Crown proves (on balance) probative value (reliability) outweighs prejudicial effect; plus separate abuse-of-process backstop for coercive/abusive operations
BaselineA: Common law evidence (party admissions exception to hearsay) and residual common law exclusion for prejudice/abuse; prior SCC cases noted as baseline limits: R. v. Evans (party admissions), R. v. McIntyre and R. v. Hebert (right to silence not engaged absent detention), R. v. Grandinetti (confessions rule inoperative where accused unaware of person in authority)
CaseB_TestB: Borowiec interpretation of Criminal Code s. 233 ‘her mind is then disturbed’: apply ‘disturbed’ in its ordinary sense (e.g., mentally agitated/unstable/discomposed), not requiring a defined mental illness or substantial impairment; must be present at time of act/omission and be ‘by reason of’ childbirth effects or lactation; no causation required between disturbance and killing
BaselineB: Statute — Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 233 (infanticide) (with contextual reference to related Code provisions ss. 2, 16, 663(b), 672.11(c))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Penile swab incident to arrest is Charter-compliant if (1) lawful arrest and truly incidental purpose; (2) police have "reasonable grounds to believe that a penile swab will afford evidence of the offence" (independent of arrest grounds; factors include timing, nature of allegations, and whether evidence already destroyed); and (3) swab is conducted "in a reasonable manner" guided by enumerated safeguards (station-house as general rule; supervisory authorization; notice of procedure/purpose/authority; option to self-swab; same-gender officers absent necessity; minimal officers; privacy; speed/partial undress; record-keeping).
BaselineA: Common law (search incident to arrest under s. 8 Charter reasonableness framework). Baseline cases cited for the general framework and tailoring: R. v. Caslake (three-part s. 8 reasonableness requirements), R. v. Fearon (general search-incident-to-arrest framework), and R. v. Golden (strip-search modifications: reasonable grounds + manner guidelines). Stillman is distinguished as not governing this context.
CaseB_TestB: Joint/co-principal liability in group assaults: "Joint/co-principal liability flows whenever two or more individuals come together with an intention to commit an offence, are present during the commission of the offence, and contribute to its commission." For manslaughter, the trier should focus on whether the accused’s actions were "a significant contributing cause of death" (and, in group assaults, "absent a discrete or intervening event, the actions of all assailants can constitute a significant contributing cause to all injuries sustained").
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 21(1)(a) (co-principal) and s. 21(1)(c) (abetting) as the party-liability provisions applied/clarified). The Court also situates the clarification as consistent with R. v. Pickton and corrects an implication from Cabrera.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Whether a claim is a “grievance” subject to compulsory arbitration: no distinction between (i) employer vs employee monetary claims for breach of the collective agreement, and (ii) disputes about “interpretation/application” vs “violation” of the collective agreement (either can ground a grievance).
BaselineA: Statute (Quebec Labour Code, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 141, ss. 1(g) definition of “grievance” and s. 88 mandatory arbitration), as interpreted in SCC precedents General Motors of Canada Ltd. v. Brunet, [1977] 2 S.C.R. 537 and Imbleau et al. v. Laskin et al., [1962] S.C.R. 338.
CaseB_TestB: Enforceability/scope of a waiver (exclusion) clause for negligence in a sporting event: construed “in the context in which it was signed”; clause applies unless the negligence is of a kind “radically different from anything reasonable men could have contemplated” (i.e., outside the contemplation of the clause), and absent grounds such as unconscionability or public policy (clause must not be “unfair”/“unreasonable” in the circumstances).
BaselineB: Common law contract principles governing interpretation and enforceability of exclusion/waiver clauses (including arguments framed via fundamental breach, unconscionability, and public policy), applied contextually.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: When a s. 119 Canada Labour Code “review” of a certification order is merely an updating/clarification (not a new certification): the Board need only be satisfied the changes are “in order” and the review must not “alter the nature and scope” of the certificate/bargaining unit; if it would substantially alter/enlarge the unit, it is “basically of the same nature as an application for certification” requiring the basic certification requirements
BaselineA: Statute (Canada Labour Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. L-1, s. 119; with the Court relying on the Board’s prior articulation in The Employees of the Regional Comptroller (1975), 9 D.I. 20 distinguishing types of s. 119 review applications)
CaseB_TestB: Appellate intervention with trial findings: an appellate court should not set aside a trial judgment absent “palpable and overriding error” where the only issue is “the interpretation of the evidence as a whole” (i.e., cannot intervene unless the trial judge was “plainly wrong”)
BaselineB: Common law (as stated through prior SCC authorities: Schreiber Brothers Ltd. v. Currie Products Ltd. and Gulf Oil Canada Ltd.; Stein v. "Kathy K."; Lewis v. Todd)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Ernst (Cromwell J.) — Ward Charter-damages framework applied to quasi-judicial regulators: even if damages are functionally justified, countervailing factors (alternative remedies + good governance + immunity’s purpose) mean Charter damages are never “appropriate and just” against this Board, so the statutory immunity clause bars the claim
BaselineA: Combination of common law/Charter remedial doctrine and statute: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 24(1) (“appropriate and just” remedy) as interpreted in Vancouver (City) v. Ward, 2010 SCC 27; applied in the presence of Energy Resources Conservation Act, R.S.A. 2000, c. E-10, s. 43 (immunity clause: “No action or proceeding may be brought against the Board... in respect of any act or thing done purportedly in pursuance of this Act...”).
CaseB_TestB: Bird — Maybrun framework for when an accused charged with breaching an administrative order may collaterally attack the order: determine legislative intent using five non-exhaustive factors
BaselineB: Common law framework from R. v. Consolidated Maybrun Mines Ltd., [1998] 1 S.C.R. 706 and R. v. Al Klippert Ltd., [1998] 1 S.C.R. 737, applied in the statutory context of Corrections and Conditional Release Act, S.C. 1992, c. 20, s. 134.1(2) (Parole Board may impose conditions it considers “reasonable and necessary”).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Art. 2930 C.C.Q. applies (3-year prescription) where the action is based on the obligation to make reparation for the direct and immediate consequences of interference with a person’s physical integrity: courts must “characterize the basis for the action” by looking to “the nature of the initial interference rather than the head of damages being claimed” (paras. 26, 55).
BaselineA: Statute: Civil Code of Québec, arts. 2925 and 2930 (in interaction with Cities and Towns Act, s. 586).
CaseB_TestB: Appellate non-intervention in trial fact-finding/credibility: once the trial judge’s oral reasons are in the record, the Court of Appeal’s substitution of its view of the evidence is “an unwarranted intrusion” into an area “exclusive to the trial judge”.
BaselineB: Common law principle of appellate deference/non-intervention in findings of fact and credibility (as reflected in Latour v. Grenier; Maze v. Empson; Dorval v. Bouvier; Métivier v. Cadorette; Hood v. Hood, cited).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Schrenk “sufficient nexus with the employment context” test for whether discrimination is “regarding employment” under s. 13(1)(b): Tribunal must conduct a “contextual analysis that considers all relevant circumstances”; non-exhaustive factors include “(1) whether the respondent was integral to the complainant’s workplace; (2) whether the impugned conduct occurred in the complainant’s workplace; and (3) whether the complainant’s work performance or work environment was negatively affected” (paras. 67-68).
BaselineA: Statute: Human Rights Code, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 210, s. 13(1)(b) (“discriminate against a person regarding employment”), with interpretive context from ss. 1 (definitions), 3 (purposes), 27(1)(a) (jurisdiction dismissal).
CaseB_TestB: Groia in-court incivility/professional misconduct framework: a “context-specific” approach considering “what the lawyer said, the manner and frequency in which it was said, and the presiding judge’s reaction” (paras. 79-81, 98-110). For integrity-impugning allegations, they “cross the line into professional misconduct unless they are made in good faith and have a reasonable basis” (para. 81), with “reasonable basis” meaning not speculative and not defeated merely by an honest legal error if there is “a sufficient factual foundation” (paras. 88-91).
BaselineB: Statute/regulatory: Law Society Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. L.8 (discipline mandate) and Law Society Rules of Professional Conduct (incl. civility obligations), as applied through administrative-law reasonableness review (Ryan; Doré).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Ontario anti-SLAPP dismissal framework (Courts of Justice Act, s. 137.1): (1) defendant must show on a balance of probabilities the proceeding “arises from an expression” that “relates to a matter of public interest” (s. 137.1(3)); then (2) plaintiff must satisfy the judge that (a) there are “grounds to believe” the proceeding has “substantial merit” and the defendant has “no valid defence” (s. 137.1(4)(a)), and (b) the harm from the expression is “sufficiently serious” that the public interest in allowing the proceeding to continue “outweighs” the public interest in protecting the expression (s. 137.1(4)(b)). Key SCC clarifications include: “grounds to believe” requires “a basis in the record and the law”; “substantial merit” means a “real prospect of success”; and s. 137.1(4)(b) is an open-ended “public interest weighing exercise” requiring one side to “outweigh” the other.
BaselineA: Statute: Courts of Justice Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.43, s. 137.1(3) and s. 137.1(4) (including s. 137.1(2) definition of “expression”).
CaseB_TestB: Corporate attribution doctrine (as applied to one-person corporations) for limitation/discoverability purposes: corporate attribution must be applied “purposively, contextually, and pragmatically” to the law under which attribution is sought; even where the directing mind conditions are met, courts have discretion to refrain from attribution where it would not be “in the public interest, in the sense that it would promote the purpose of the law under which attribution is sought” (Aquino summary adopted). In this case, the Court upheld refusing to attribute the sole directing mind’s knowledge because it would undermine the purposes of the Limitations Act discoverability rules and the BIA.
BaselineB: Common law corporate attribution doctrine (Canadian Dredge & Dock; Deloitte & Touche v. Livent; DeJong; summarized in Aquino v. Bondfield Construction Co., 2024 SCC 31) applied in the statutory context of the Limitations Act, 2002 (ss. 4, 5, 12) and the Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Duty to comment on Crown counsel’s prejudicial jury address: where remarks are “prejudicial to a degree sufficient to impose a legal duty on the trial judge to comment” to ensure the defence position is “fairly put to the jury”; failure is an error of law and (here) not cured by the s. 686(1)(b)(iii) proviso
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(b)(iii)) plus common-law principles on fair jury charge / improper jury addresses (as applied via the Court of Appeal dissent adopted by Lamer C.J.)
CaseB_TestB: “Identifiability” test for Federal Court in rem jurisdiction under s. 43(2): reject “physical nexus”; cargo is “property … subject of the action” if it is the cargo designated in the contract of affreightment alleged to be breached
BaselineB: Statute (Federal Courts Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. F-7, s. 43(2))
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Threshold for summary dismissal of a criminal application: the application may be summarily dismissed only if it is “manifestly frivolous”; on the motion the judge must assume alleged facts are true and take the applicant’s arguments “at their highest”, without weighing evidence or choosing among competing inferences (unless an inference is itself manifestly frivolous).
BaselineA: Common law (criminal procedure/case management power to summarily dismiss applications; Vukelich-type hearings).
CaseB_TestB: Combined effect of Criminal Code s. 172.1(3) presumption and s. 172.1(4) “reasonable steps” requirement in child luring: where underage is represented, accused is presumed to believe underage; presumption is rebutted only by “evidence to the contrary” that must include objectively reasonable steps to ascertain age; evidential burden on accused, persuasive burden on Crown.
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 172.1(3) and s. 172.1(4), read harmoniously with s. 172.1’s purpose).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Two-step framework for statute–common law interaction in sentencing, applied to credit for pre-sentence driving prohibitions despite a mandatory minimum: (1) identify the applicable common law rule (credit may be granted); (2) determine the statute’s effect (displaced only if expressly or by necessary implication). On interpretation, s. 259(1)(a) sets a minimum 'punishment' (global deprivation), not a minimum prospective 'sentence', so credit may be granted after imposing the mandatory minimum.
BaselineA: Combination of common law and statute: common law discretion to grant credit for pre-sentence driving prohibitions (R. v. Lacasse, 2015 SCC 64; analogy to pre-sentence custody credit discussed in R. v. Wust, 2000 SCC 18) plus statutory provisions Criminal Code ss. 259(1)(a) and 719(1) (and consideration of s. 719(3)).
CaseB_TestB: Mitigation in contract damages where plaintiff claims specific performance: defendant must prove (i) plaintiff failed to take reasonable steps to mitigate and (ii) mitigation was possible; a plaintiff’s inaction may be reasonable only if it had a 'fair, real, and substantial justification' / 'substantial and legitimate interest' in specific performance—investment property generally requires showing land has 'a peculiar and special value' such that damages are not a complete remedy.
BaselineB: Common law mitigation doctrine and specific-performance-related mitigation principles from Asamera Oil Corp. v. Seal Oil & General Corp., [1979] 1 S.C.R. 633, read with Semelhago v. Paramadevan, [1996] 2 S.C.R. 415 (uniqueness/adequacy of damages).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Principled approach to hearsay admissibility prevailing over traditional exceptions: hearsay is admissible only if it meets the twin criteria of threshold reliability and necessity; even hearsay within a traditional exception may be excluded if it fails these criteria (e.g., statements of present intention inadmissible if made in “circumstances of suspicion”; statements cannot be used to prove a third party’s intentions absent an exception for each hearsay level).
BaselineA: Common law (hearsay rule and exceptions; principled approach from R. v. Khan and R. v. Smith; present intentions/state of mind exception discussed in R. v. Smith).
CaseB_TestB: Downtown Eastside public interest standing framework: discretionary, cumulative weighing of three factors—(i) serious justiciable issue, (ii) genuine interest, (iii) reasonable and effective means—without giving “particular weight” to legality/access to justice; no requirement for a directly affected co-plaintiff if a sufficiently concrete and well-developed factual setting will be forthcoming; standing may be revisited only after a material change raising serious doubt about the factual setting.
BaselineB: Common law (public interest standing test from Canada (Attorney General) v. Downtown Eastside Sex Workers United Against Violence Society, 2012 SCC 45).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Limited-liability/non-assessability constraint on corporate amendments: an alteration/resolution is ultra vires if it seeks to impose on holders of fully paid shares “any financial burden whatsoever in respect of those shares”; and a share transfer fee is invalid “to the extent that it exceeded the reasonable and proper cost of the transfer” (an “illegal levy” in respect of shares).
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law principle: The Companies Act (Alberta) (notably s. 42(1) power to alter articles “subject to the provisions of this Act and to the conditions contained in its memorandum”; plus limited-liability/non-assessability provisions including s. 68(4) and winding-up contribution limit in s. 193(1)(d)), together with the common law ‘basic jural principle’ of limited liability/non-assessability (citing Ooregum Gold Mining Co. v. Roper; Bisgood v. Henderson’s Transvaal Estates; Shalfoon v. Cheddar Valley Co-operative Dairy Co.).
CaseB_TestB: Van der Peet Aboriginal-rights identification test (as applied): to be recognized as an Aboriginal right, an activity must be “an element of a practice, custom or tradition integral to the distinctive culture of the aboriginal group claiming the right”; the court must (1) “determine the precise nature of the claim” (considering the action, the impugned regulation, and the relied-on practice), and (2) ask whether, “prior to contact with Europeans,” the practice was a “central, significant or defining feature” of the group’s distinctive culture.
BaselineB: Common law/constitutional doctrine under Constitution Act, 1982, s. 35(1), applying the framework articulated contemporaneously in R. v. Van der Peet (and situated within the Sparrow s. 35 framework, though this case turns on the first/right-identification stage).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Reviewability of a consensual labour-arbitration award for error of law on the face: no ‘specific question of law’ reference where the issue arises in the ordinary grievance process and the arbitrator is contractually bound to decide consistently with the agreement
BaselineA: Common law (judicial review of consensual arbitration awards; distinction between a ‘specific question of law’ reference vs a general dispute where a legal question arises), drawing on Government of Kelantan v. Duff Development Co. Ltd.; F.R. Absalom Ltd. v. Great Western (London) Garden Village Society Ltd.; Faubert and Watts v. Temagami Mining Co. Ltd.; and Bell Canada v. Office and Professional Employees’ International Union, Local 131
CaseB_TestB: Morin framework for s. 11(b) ‘reasonable time’ analysis: assess (1) length of delay minus defence waiver, then consider (2) reasons for delay, (3) prejudice, and (4) the interests s. 11(b) protects; prejudice may be inferred from length of delay
BaselineB: Constitution (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 11(b)) as interpreted through the common-law/constitutional framework in R. v. Morin (and Askov)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 3(4) possession framework (including joint possession): possession is established for Code purposes where a person has something personally or knowingly via another person/place for use/benefit, and where one of multiple persons has custody/possession with the knowledge and consent of the rest it is deemed in the custody and possession of each
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 3(4))
CaseB_TestB: Adverse possession elements in British Columbia: to establish adverse possession, the act of possession must be “open and notorious, adverse, exclusive, peaceful (not by force), actual (generally), and continuous”; and the SCC rejects any additional mandatory “inconsistent use” requirement in BC
BaselineB: Common law adverse possession test as received in British Columbia (via 1833 English codification) plus provincial limitations legislation reproducing that scheme (e.g., Statute of Limitations (1924), ss. 16-17; Law and Equity Act, s. 2 (reception))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Quantum meruit for services rendered without agreed remuneration: where a party accepts authorized services in the absence of an agreement as to remuneration, it must pay a reasonable rate (and statutory/regulatory instruments will not bar recovery absent clear authority, including no retroactive impairment of existing rights without express/necessary implication).
BaselineA: Common law (quantum meruit/quasi-contract) plus statutory/regulatory interpretation limits (Hospital Act s. 37(2) and regulations; Social Assistance Act; Residence and Responsibility Act s. 3; O.C. 3103/4399/4400). Key SCC baseline authority referenced: King George Highway Hospital Ltd. v. District of Surrey, [1971] S.C.R. vi; interpretive principle against taking away private rights without clear legislative intent.
CaseB_TestB: Voluntariness/operating mind for admissibility of inculpatory statements by an allegedly insane accused: the “underlying and controlling question” is whether the statement was “freely and voluntarily made”, including considering whether, due to mental condition, the words were “the utterances of an operating mind” (no fixed formula required).
BaselineB: Common law confession rule (voluntariness) as articulated in Boudreau v. The King, [1949] S.C.R. 262 and Ward v. The Queen, [1979] 2 S.C.R. 30 (with discussion of Santinon).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Effect of breach of a witness-exclusion order: witness not automatically disqualified; admissibility is discretionary; weight is for trier of fact
BaselineA: Common law (practice/rule on exclusion of witnesses and consequences of breach, as reflected in cases cited such as Moore v. Lambeth County Court Registrar; Cook v. Nethercotte; Thomas v. David; Chandler v. Home; Black v. Besse; R. v. Carefoot)
CaseB_TestB: Clear-and-unequivocal legislative language required to lift Crown immunity from discovery; CLPA s. 27 lifts immunity only when Crown is a party
BaselineB: Statute + common law: Interpretation Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. I-21, s. 17 (starting point for Crown immunity) and Crown Liability and Proceedings Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-50, s. 27 (scope of procedural rules applying to Crown), against the backdrop of common law Crown immunity from discovery
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Disqualification/bias in Law Society discipline: whether benchers who sat on the Discipline Committee may participate in Convocation when Convocation considers the Committee’s report (majority: permitted; dissent: barred by reasonable apprehension of bias where prior adjudication of guilt)
BaselineA: Statute and regulation (The Law Society Act, 1970 (Ont.), ss. 33(12), 34, 37, 39; Reg. 556, s. 13) plus common-law natural justice/bias principles (nemo judex / reasonable apprehension of bias)
CaseB_TestB: Criminal Code s. 731(1)(b) probation eligibility: “imprisonment for a term not exceeding two years” means the term imposed by the sentencing court at that sitting (not aggregated with other sentences), but probation is unavailable if sentences imposed at the same session result in continuous custody over two years
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 731(1)(b), with related context in ss. 732.2 and 743.1)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “operation of a mine” and when a separate “mine” exists for the 36‑month tax exemption: (1) “operation of a mine” in s. 83(5) “refers only to the extraction of ore from an ore body and does not include processing of the ore after it has been produced”; and (2) “there is ‘a mine’ within the meaning of s. 83(5) if there is a body of ore together with the workings, equipment and machinery capable of producing it” (a separate mine arises when a separate ore body “commenced to be extracted by means of its separate and distinct extraction facilities”).
BaselineA: Statute — Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1952, c. 148 as amended, s. 83(5) and s. 83(6) (definitions of “mine” and “production”); interpreted with reference to SCC authorities North Bay Mica Co. Ltd. v. M.N.R., [1958] S.C.R. 597 and M.N.R. v. MacLean Mining Co. Ltd., [1970] S.C.R. 877.
CaseB_TestB: Leave to sue a receiver/trustee under s. 215 BIA (Mancini test): leave should be refused only for “frivolous or vexatious” or “manifestly unmeritorious” claims; leave should not be granted if the evidence (typically affidavit evidence plus draft pleading) “does not disclose a cause of action”; and the court “is not required to make a final assessment of the merits” — the question is whether the evidence provides the required support, i.e., “If the evidence discloses a prima facie case, leave should be granted.”
BaselineB: Statute — Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. B-3, s. 215 (leave requirement), with related statutory context in ss. 47(2) and 72(1); test drawn from Ontario CA decision Mancini (Bankrupt) v. Falconi (1993), 61 O.A.C. 332 (applied/affirmed as governing s. 215).
JudgeB: Abella J. (for McLachlin C.J. and Bastarache, Binnie, LeBel, Fish and Charron JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Education Act s. 373 school-tax valuation roll adjustment: if valuations across municipalities are "not uniform", commissioners must amend rolls "so as to re-establish on the basis of its real value the valuation of the taxable property" (i.e., value only what is taxable in each municipality; no cross-municipality priority for a town’s machinery-exemption by-law).
BaselineA: Statute: Education Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 235, s. 373 (plus interaction with Cities and Towns Act, s. 488 (as amended) allowing a by-law excluding machinery from taxable immovables).
CaseB_TestB: Criminal Code s. 426(1)(a)(ii) “secret commission” offence (agent/taker): actus reus requires (1) agency relationship; (2) agent accepts a benefit "as consideration" for acting/forbearing in relation to the principal’s affairs; and (3) "failure by the agent to make adequate and timely disclosure of the source, amount and nature of the benefit"—with "corruptly" meaning "secretly or without the requisite disclosure" and no requirement to prove a "corrupt bargain" with the giver.
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 426(1)(a) (interpreting "corruptly" and elements of s. 426(1)(a)(ii)).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Extradition Act classification: whether the offence is an “extradition crime” turns on “what is the essence of the crime charged” (i.e., whether it is, in substance, a crime “against the laws for the suppression of the traffic in narcotics” under the 1925 Supplementary Convention).
BaselineA: Statute + extradition arrangement: Extradition Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-21, s. 2 (“extradition crime” definition) and the 1925 Supplementary Convention category “Crimes and offences against the laws for the suppression of the traffic in narcotics” (added to the Act).
CaseB_TestB: Section 13 Charter self-incrimination limit on use of prior testimony at retrial: prior testimony may be used on cross-examination only if its purpose is to impeach credibility; it is barred if used “to incriminate” (to establish guilt).
BaselineB: Constitution + statute: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 13 (and its interpretation in R. v. Dubois and R. v. Mannion, as discussed); also interpreted alongside Canada Evidence Act, s. 5(2).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Negligence/foreseeability (remoteness) test for highway authority liability: “whether a reasonable person should have anticipated that what happened might be a natural result of that act or omission”; not necessary to foresee the “precise concatenation of events”, only “in a general way the class or character of injury”.
BaselineA: Common law foreseeability/remoteness in negligence (as applied to statutory highway-maintenance duty): University Hospital Board v. Lépine, [1966] S.C.R. 561; also Wagon Mound No. 2 applied.
CaseB_TestB: CEAA “tracking” rule: the environmental assessment track (screening vs comprehensive study) is determined by the “project as proposed” by the proponent; if the proposed project is in the Comprehensive Study List, s. 21 requirements are mandatory and the responsible authority cannot reduce scope below what is proposed (scoping may only enlarge under s. 15(2)-(3)).
BaselineB: Statute/regulations: Canadian Environmental Assessment Act, S.C. 1992, c. 37 (especially ss. 2 “project”, 15, 18, 21, 21.1) and Comprehensive Study List Regulations, SOR/94-638 (e.g., Sch., s. 16).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Using res ipsa loquitur to infer (and prove) gross negligence of a driver toward a gratuitous passenger under Highway Traffic Act s. 132(3): applies where (1) the thing causing damage was under defendant’s “sole management and control”; (2) the occurrence “would not have happened without negligence”; and (3) there is “no evidence as to why or how the occurrence took place” — but if an explanation is given and is “no answer, even if believed in full”, the maxim may still apply.
BaselineA: Combination: statute (Ontario Highway Traffic Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 202, s. 132(3) requiring “gross negligence” for gratuitous passengers) plus common-law evidentiary rule (res ipsa loquitur as described via Clerk & Lindsell; and SCC recognition in Walker v. Coates that it can aid proof of gross negligence).
CaseB_TestB: Vested-rights test (acquired rights) for whether new legislation can affect existing contractual rights: a vested right exists where (1) the individual’s legal situation is “tangible and concrete rather than general and abstract”; and (2) it was “sufficiently constituted at the time of the new statute’s commencement” (rights under a contract are “usually created at the same time as the contract itself”). Absent “a clear indication in a statute to the contrary in light of the entire context”, legislation is not read as “prejudicially affecting accrued rights”.
BaselineB: Combination: statutory interpretation baseline (Interpretation Act, R.S.Q., c. I-16, s. 12; and presumption from Spooner Oils) plus common-law/statutory-interpretation jurisprudence (e.g., Gustavson Drilling; Venne; Attorney General of Quebec v. Expropriation Tribunal).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Mechanics’ lien holdback/contract-price rule on contractor abandonment: s. 19(2) does not prevent the owner deducting completion costs; it only bars deductions for extraneous set-off/counterclaims not arising under the contract. As Spence J. held, s. 19(2) was meant to prevent deductions for items "not arising under the terms of the contract but outside the terms of the contract" and therefore "does not bar the owner from deducting from the amounts payable upon the bankruptcy the cost of completion of the contract" (reconciling s. 19(2) with s. 6’s limit that the owner’s liability is no greater than "the sum payable by the owner to the contractor").
BaselineA: Statute: Mechanics’ Lien Act, R.S.B.C. 1960, c. 238, ss. 6, 19(2), 21(1), 21(6) (interpreted in light of Comstock and Guttman).
CaseB_TestB: Choice of law in tort (general rule): apply lex loci delicti. La Forest J.: "the law to be applied in torts is the law of the place where the activity occurred, i.e., the lex loci delicti"; and in Tolofson, this includes treating the foreign limitation period as substantive where it "created an accrued right in the defendant to plead a time bar".
BaselineB: Common law (conflict of laws in tort), with the SCC overruling McLean v. Pettigrew and reformulating the governing common-law choice-of-law rule; also applied alongside statutory limitation provisions in issue (e.g., Vehicles Act, R.S.S. 1978, c. V-3, s. 180(1)).
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Constitutional (territorial) validity test for provincial legislation with extraterritorial operation: a province cannot legislate in relation to acts done outside the province (e.g., by nullifying another jurisdiction’s permission/licence), even if damage is felt in-province; interprovincial pollution is a matter of federal concern. Key point applied: Manitoba’s s. 4(2) “purported to nullify the effect of permission duly granted by the regulatory authority of another jurisdiction” and thus “purported to legislate with respect to conduct and rights of the [defendants] outside the territorial limits of the Province of Manitoba”.
BaselineA: Statute + constitutional division of powers: The Fishermen’s Assistance and Polluters’ Liability Act, 1970 (Man.), especially s. 4(2) (and s. 4(1) context), assessed against B.N.A. Act, 1867 territorial limits on provincial heads of power (e.g., s. 92) and federal competence over interprovincial matters (including s. 91(12) fisheries / residual POGG as discussed).
JudgeA: Pigeon J. (for Martland, Pigeon and Beetz JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Privative-clause judicial review threshold: intervention only if the tribunal’s decision is “patently unreasonable” / an “unreasonable finding” that “impairs the jurisdiction of the tribunal”; courts should not intervene where the decision is reasonable. Key formulation: “was the Board’s interpretation so patently unreasonable that its construction cannot be rationally supported by the relevant legislation and demands intervention by the court upon review?”
BaselineB: Statute + prior SCC administrative law: Act respecting labour standards, R.S.Q., c. N-1.1, ss. 128-129 (arbitrator’s remedial powers; reasons requirement) and Labour Code, R.S.Q. 1977, c. C-27, s. 139 (privative clause), interpreted through CUPE and related SCC jurisprudence on “patently unreasonable” review.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Collective agreement primacy: common law repudiation/fundamental breach inapplicable during subsisting collective agreement; illegal strike does not per se terminate employment, and absent employer disciplinary action, plant closure triggers severance obligations
BaselineA: Statute + labour-relations common law: Mediation Services Act, 1968 (B.C.) (notably s. 6 binding effect of collective agreement; s. 23 strike prohibition) and SCC labour jurisprudence rejecting individual-contract framing (Syndicat catholique des employés de magasins de Québec Inc. v. Compagnie Paquet Ltée; C.P.R. Co. v. Zambri; with reference to Re Polymer Corp.)
CaseB_TestB: Limits on cross-examination using a complainant’s diary: relevant defence evidence may be excluded only if prejudice substantially outweighs probative value; omission evidence is probative only if a reasonable expectation of recording is established; O’Connor production balancing is not the admissibility/cross-examination test
BaselineB: Common law evidence/Charter-informed admissibility and cross-examination limits: Seaboyer and Osolin ("prejudice must substantially outweigh" probative value); clarification that O’Connor governs production, not admissibility/cross-examination; statutory context noted but held inapplicable to admissibility/use (Criminal Code ss. 278.1-278.9)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Admissibility of evidence that an accused refused to participate in a police line-up: admissible where the Crown must explain the absence of a line-up (or avoid an adverse inference), otherwise normally not tendered; always depends on the circumstances
BaselineA: Common law evidence (relevance/admissibility) and common law privilege against self-incrimination (testimonial compulsion only), as discussed via Curr v. The Queen and A.-G. (Que.) v. Begin
CaseB_TestB: Division of powers limit on provincial commissions of inquiry: an inquiry is ultra vires if, in pith and substance, it is a substitute police investigation/preliminary inquiry into a specific Criminal Code offence by named private individuals (i.e., it circumvents federally prescribed criminal procedure)
BaselineB: Constitution Act, 1867 (ss. 91(27) and 92 heads) applied through the pith-and-substance characterization framework; applied to an Order in Council under Ontario’s Public Inquiries Act
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Punitive damages in tort: whether the circumstances justify an additional punitive award “in the interests of justice” (here, tortious inducement/conspiracy to take over business) and, if so, the appropriate quantum
BaselineA: Common law (punitive/exemplary damages principles in tort; no specific baseline case articulated in the reasons provided)
JudgeA: Laskin C.J. (for Laskin C.J. and Spence and Beetz JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Duty of care for pure economic loss in negligence: (1) does the claim fit within a recognized pure economic loss category (incl. relational economic loss requiring injury/property damage to a third party)?; if not, (2) should a new duty be recognized under the Anns/Cooper framework (foreseeability + proximity, including party-specific policy at stage 1; residual policy such as indeterminate liability at stage 2)
BaselineB: Common law (Anns v. Merton; Kamloops; Cooper; Childs; Norsk categories of pure economic loss; tendering contract framework from Ron Engineering, M.J.B., Martel)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory limits on Canadian Transport Commission power over filed freight tariffs: once a tariff is duly filed/published, it takes effect on the stated effective date under s. 275(4); even if s. 275(2) permits extending the 30-day notice, any extension must be ordered before the effective date—an after-the-fact “extension” is an impermissible postponement (ultra vires).
BaselineA: Statute: Railway Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. R-2, s. 275(2) and s. 275(4) (with context from National Transportation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. N-17, s. 64(5) and s. 3(a)).
CaseB_TestB: Directed verdict / sufficiency limit on single-eyewitness identification: a jury should not be instructed it may convict on eyewitness testimony alone where that testimony, even if believed, would necessarily leave reasonable doubt; if the Crown’s case consists solely of such eyewitness evidence, the trial judge must direct an acquittal on a directed-verdict motion.
BaselineB: Common law (as synthesized from SCC authorities cited): Arcuri; Reitsma; Zurowski; United States of America v. Shephard; plus identification-evidence caution duty from Mezzo/Turnbull/Nikolovski.
JudgeB: Rothstein J. (McLachlin C.J. and LeBel, Abella, Cromwell and Wagner JJ. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Effectiveness/finality of an order still within the appeal period: despite being appealable, it may be treated as fully effective (even against third parties) where there is only an “ephemeral prospect of an appeal”; assess (1) the purpose for which finality is invoked, (2) who is affected, and (3) the context in which finality/lack of finality is asserted
BaselineA: Statute (The Conveyancing and Law of Property Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 85, s. 62) plus general/common-law principles about the effect of appealable orders (discussing and distinguishing Re West (1928) and Leonard v. Wharton (1921))
CaseB_TestB: Preliminary inquiry committal test under Criminal Code s. 548(1) (Shephard): ask whether there is “any evidence upon which a reasonable jury properly instructed could return a verdict of guilty”; if Crown evidence is circumstantial, the judge must do a “limited weighing” of the whole evidence (including defence evidence) to assess whether, if the Crown’s evidence is believed, it would be reasonable for a jury to infer guilt (without drawing inferences or assessing credibility)
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 548(1) (and Part XVIII procedure) interpreted through the common-law sufficiency rule from United States of America v. Shephard, [1977] 2 S.C.R. 1067 (also discussing Mezzo and Monteleone)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Discretionary test for granting public interest/taxpayer standing to challenge legislation: standing may be granted where (1) the plaintiff has taken all reasonable steps to make standing “ripe” ("took all the steps that he could reasonably be required to take"), (2) a “serious, substantial constitutional issue” is raised, (3) the plaintiff has an arguable direct interest (here, the public arguably directly affected), and (4) there is “no other way in practical terms” to subject the Act to judicial review, justifying the court’s discretion to grant standing.
BaselineA: Common law (standing/locus standi doctrine), drawing on Smith v. Attorney General of Ontario, [1924] S.C.R. 331 and Thorson v. Attorney General of Canada (No. 2), [1975] 1 S.C.R. 138.
JudgeA: The Chief Justice (Laskin C.J.) for the Court
CaseB_TestB: ASRA Program linkage discretion constrained by private-law duties: interpret s. 88(3) using C.C.Q. arts. 1425-1432 (esp. arts. 1427 and 1426) so that s. 88(3) “does not require that amounts be linked individually” but “gives La Financière the discretion to decide what linkage method to employ”; that discretion must be exercised “in accordance with the requirements of good faith and contractual fairness” (arts. 6, 7, 1375, 1434 C.C.Q.).
BaselineB: Regulation and civil law: Programme d’assurance stabilisation des revenus agricoles, s. 88(3), interpreted through Civil Code of Québec arts. 1425-1432 (interpretation) and arts. 6, 7, 1375, 1434 (good faith/contractual fairness).
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Rebuttable presumption of mens rea for drug trafficking once actus reus proved: when it has been proved the accused trafficked in the restricted drug, “a rebuttable presumption arises” that the conduct was voluntary and the accused “is guilty ... and must be convicted unless other evidence is adduced which raises a reasonable doubt” (applied here to LSD trafficking).
BaselineA: Combination of statute (Food and Drugs Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. F-27, ss. 40, 42) and common law/SCC precedent on mens rea and presumptions (Beaver v. The Queen; R. v. King; Blondin).
CaseB_TestB: Limits on trial-judge intervention / appearance of impartiality: a judge may question and interrupt witnesses, but “must do so within certain limits and in such a way that justice is seen to be done”; if the judge’s conduct “raised some doubt as to his impartiality”, a new trial is required.
BaselineB: Common law principles of procedural fairness and judicial impartiality (notably R. v. Sussex Justices; Ex parte McCarthy; and related appellate guidance such as Jones v. National Coal Board; Torbiak; Yuill; Darlyn; Bateman).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “burglary” in Criminal Code s. 213 (constructive murder): despite later revisions, “burglary” retains the 1892 Code meaning (s. 410) — i.e., breaking and entering a dwelling-house by night (or breaking out) with intent to commit an indictable offence, read with the 1892 definitions of “dwelling-house” and “break” (s. 407).
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 213 (and related context s. 306); Interpretation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-23, s. 36(f) (repeal/substitution—consolidation rule). Historical baseline used to fix meaning: Criminal Code, 1892, s. 228 (constructive murder) and s. 410 (definition of burglary), with s. 407 definitions.
CaseB_TestB: Damages for repudiation where contract allows alternative performances: adopt the least burdensome mode to the defendant (and least profitable to the plaintiff) — “where there are several ways in which the contract might be performed, that mode is adopted which is the least profitable to the plaintiff, and the least burdensome to the defendant”; not a “but for repudiation” likelihood inquiry, but the position the plaintiff would have been in “had the contract been performed”.
BaselineB: Common law damages for breach of contract with alternative modes of performance, traced to Cockburn v. Alexander (1848) and explained in Withers v. General Theatre Corp. (1933) (as cited and adopted).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Lease interpretation test for shifting fire-loss risk to landlord where tenant covenants to pay “insurance rates”: read the lease “reasonably and in a business sense”; if tenant pays the fire insurance bill, “the risk of loss by fire passed to the landlord, at least upon the presentation by the landlord of the insurance bill”, barring the landlord’s insurer’s subrogated claim against the tenant
BaselineA: Common law contract/lease interpretation ("ordinary test of reading it reasonably and in a business sense") applied to the lease covenant; with statutory context noted (Ontario Insurance Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 224, s. 118, confirming fire policies ordinarily cover third-party negligence)
CaseB_TestB: Civil Code art. 1053 “fault–damage” liability for banks paying on unauthorized endorsements: a bank commits a compensable “fault” by accepting/processing cheques payable to a company for deposit to an individual’s personal benefit “without examining it, and without verifying the sufficiency of the endorsement”; damages equal the cheque amounts where the payee is thereby deprived of its money and has no effective recourse against the drawer
BaselineB: Combination of statute and civil law: Bills of Exchange Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. B-5 (notably s. 51 on signature by procuration as notice of limited authority; s. 10 mentioned) plus Civil Code (Quebec) art. 1053 (fault causing damage)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 15(1) adverse impact discrimination (prima facie breach): (1) distinction on an enumerated/analogous ground shown by disproportionate impact; (2) burden/benefit denial that has the effect of “reinforcing, perpetuating, or exacerbating disadvantage”, with guidance on proving disproportionate impact (group-situation evidence and/or statistical outcome evidence; no intent; no need to prove the ground “caused” the impact). Key quotes: “To prove a prima facie violation of s. 15(1), a claimant must demonstrate that the impugned law or state action: • on its face or in its impact, creates a distinction based on enumerated or analogous grounds; and • imposes burdens or denies a benefit in a manner that has the effect of reinforcing, perpetuating, or exacerbating disadvantage” (para. 27). “In order for a law to create a distinction based on prohibited grounds through its effects, it must have a disproportionate impact on members of a protected group” (para. 52). “Both evidence of statistical disparity and of broader group disadvantage may demonstrate disproportionate impact; but neither is mandatory” (para. 67). “Whether the legislature intended to create a disparate impact is irrelevant” (para. 69). “If claimants successfully demonstrate that a law has a disproportionate impact on members of a protected group, they need not independently prove that the protected characteristic ‘caused’ the disproportionate impact” (para. 70).
BaselineA: Combination: constitutional text (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 15(1)) plus SCC common-law/constitutional jurisprudence (two-step s. 15 framework as stated in Quebec (AG) v. Alliance, 2018 SCC 17, para. 25; Centrale des syndicats du Québec v. Quebec (AG), 2018 SCC 18, para. 22; and adverse-impact recognition in Withler v. Canada (AG), 2011 SCC 12, para. 64; Taypotat, 2015 SCC 30).
JudgeA: Abella J. (for Wagner C.J. and Abella, Moldaver, Karakatsanis, Martin and Kasirer JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Division of powers “pith and substance” analysis for validity of legislation: “The pith and substance analysis asks two questions: first, what is the essential character of the law? Second, does that character relate to an enumerated head of power granted to the legislature in question by the Constitution Act, 1867?” (para. 16). Essential character determined by “looking at the purpose and the legal effect” (para. 17), and the court must consider the law’s context and “should not be concerned with the efficacy of the law” (para. 18).
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine (pith and substance) applied to constitutional text: Constitution Act, 1867, ss. 91(12), 91(27), 92(13). The Court cites as baseline authorities Reference re Firearms Act (Can.), 2000 SCC 31; Global Securities, 2000 SCC 21; R. v. Morgentaler, [1993] 3 SCR 463; Whitbread v. Walley, [1990] 3 SCR 1273 (para. 16-18).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Lease interpretation test for shifting fire-loss risk to landlord where tenant covenants to pay “insurance rates”: read the lease “reasonably and in a business sense”; if tenant pays for fire insurance (at least once the landlord presents “the insurance bill”), “the risk of loss by fire passed to the landlord” and the landlord/insurer cannot pursue the tenant by subrogation for that fire loss (including tenant negligence).
BaselineA: Common law contract/lease interpretation ("ordinary test of reading it reasonably and in a business sense") plus statutory context that standard fire coverage includes third-party negligence (Ontario Insurance Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 224, s. 118).
CaseB_TestB: Warsaw Convention limitation entitlement: under Art. 3(2) the carrier loses limitation “only where no ticket is delivered” (ticket “absence, irregularity or loss” does not remove limitation); under Art. 4(4) limitation is lost if luggage accepted without a delivered luggage ticket or if the ticket lacks particulars (d), (f) and (h), but compliance is met where the ticket’s print is “legible by the ordinary person using ordinary diligence” and its content is adequate.
BaselineB: Statute/international convention: Carriage by Air Act, R.S.C. 1952, c. 45, Schedule I (Warsaw Convention), especially Arts. 3(1)-(2), 4(1)-(4), and 22.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Negligent misrepresentation (heating-cost estimate): plaintiff must prove more than a wrong estimate—must show the error resulted from a lack of reasonable care/skill/competence/diligence; duty is to exercise “such care as the circumstances required” in giving the unqualified opinion
BaselineA: Common law (negligent misrepresentation / duty of care for advice): Hedley Byrne & Co. Ltd. v. Heller & Partners Ltd. (Lord Reid’s “three courses” and duty to exercise “such care as the circumstances require”); Mutual Life and Citizens’ Assurance Co. Ltd. v. Evatt (Lord Diplock on an “ascertainable standard of skill, competence and diligence”)
CaseB_TestB: Extra-territoriality / s. 92 territorial limits for intangible pith-and-substance: if pith and substance is intangible, locate it by examining “the relationships among the enacting territory, the subject matter of the legislation and the persons made subject to it” to see if the law has a “meaningful connection” to the province and respects other jurisdictions’ sovereignty
BaselineB: Common law / constitutional doctrine interpreting Constitution Act, 1867, s. 92 territorial limits (building on cases like Churchill Falls and Unifund as cited in the reasons)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Parole Act s. 16(1) suspension warrant requirement: a parole suspension/arrest is valid where the warrant of committal recites that parole “was suspended” by a designated person under s. 16; on habeas corpus the court is confined to the face of the warrants and will not go behind them to test reasons/natural justice for parole suspension/revocation
BaselineA: Statute (Parole Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. P-2, ss. 10(1)(e), 16(1)-(5), 18, 20) plus prior SCC authority on parole revocation as administrative (Ex p. McCaud; Howarth v. National Parole Board) and habeas corpus record limits (Re Shumiatcher)
CaseB_TestB: Equitable compensation for Crown breach of fiduciary duty over reserve land: assess the beneficiary’s “lost opportunity” by asking “what position would the beneficiary be in had the fiduciary fulfilled its obligations?”, requiring a close link between fiduciary obligations and remedy; value the loss on the basis of a negotiated surrender reflecting the land’s value to the hydroelectricity project (not merely expropriation value), with hindsight and equitable presumptions (e.g., most favourable use) and without common-law remoteness limits
BaselineB: Common law of Crown fiduciary duty and equitable compensation (Guerin; Canson; Osoyoos; Wewaykum; Blueberry River; Hodgkinson) applied in the context of statutory/treaty framework (Indian Act, R.S.C. 1927, c. 98, ss. 48, 50, 51; Treaty No. 3 (1873); Royal Proclamation, 1763)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Excise Tax Act sales-tax exemption: whether machinery/apparatus is used “directly in the manufacture or production of goods” (production vs distribution; regulators that merely control flow/pressure are not “production”)
BaselineA: Statute: Excise Tax Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-13, s. 29(1) and Schedule III, Part XIII, para. 1(a)(i) (“machinery and apparatus ... for use by them directly in (i) the manufacture or production of goods”) (interpreted in light of Hydro-Québec v. Dep. Min. of Nat. Revenue for Customs and Excise, [1970] S.C.R. 30)
JudgeA: Pigeon J. (for Martland, Judson, Pigeon, Dickson and Beetz JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Appellate review of solicitor’s negligence claim over against another solicitor: the “crucial question” is the nature and scope of the second solicitor’s retainer, a factual finding not to be disturbed on appeal absent “error arising from misapprehension of the evidence”
BaselineB: Common law: appellate deference to trial findings of fact (trial findings “should not ordinarily be upset on appeal save for error arising from misapprehension of the evidence”) applied to determining the scope of a solicitor’s retainer
JudgeB: The Chief Justice (Laskin C.J.) (for Laskin C.J. and Martland, Spence, Dickson and Estey JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Patent Act s. 41(1): whether an invention relates to a food substance “prepared or produced by chemical processes” — apply the term in its “ordinary and popular sense” and assess the character of the process “as a whole” (an “informed layman” standard; chemical reaction not conclusive; chemical operations must play a “significant part”; essentially a question of fact).
BaselineA: Statute (Patent Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. P-4, s. 41(1)), interpreted through prior SCC cases Continental Soya Co. Ltd. v. J.R. Short Milling Co. (Canada) Ltd., [1942] S.C.R. 187 and Laboratoire Pentagone Ltée v. Parke, Davis & Co., [1968] S.C.R. 307.
JudgeA: Dickson J. (for Laskin C.J. and Martland, Judson, Spence and Dickson JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Adequacy of an indictment (including in multiple-conspiracies situations): an indictment is adequate if it gives the accused “reasonable information” and enables identification of the “transaction” for defence preparation; sufficiency depends on the offence and facts; time need not be exact unless essential and no prejudice; a charge is generally established if the offence occurred within the time period alleged; for a proven conspiracy to fall within the indictment it is sufficient that it included some accused, occurred sometime within the alleged time span, and had as its object the type of crime alleged.
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 510, 512, 516(1)(g)) plus SCC/common-law principles from cases including R. v. Côté, [1978] 1 S.C.R. 8; R. v. Wis Development Corp., [1984] 1 S.C.R. 485; and R. v. Cotroni, [1979] 2 S.C.R. 256.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 1 justification (Oakes proportionality) applied contextually: infringement must be a "reasonable limit" that can be "demonstrably justified"; requires (1) pressing and substantial objective and (2) proportionality: "rationally connected", "impair ... as little as possible" (minimal impairment), and proportionality of effects
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional text (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 1) as structured by common-law Oakes framework (R. v. Oakes, [1986] 1 S.C.R. 103)
JudgeA: McLachlin J. (reasons for the majority disposition on s. 1)
CaseB_TestB: Meiorin justification/undue hardship framework for duty to accommodate, with collective agreement clause as a relevant factor: employer must justify a prejudicial standard by showing (1) rational connection to job performance, (2) adopted in good faith, and (3) "reasonably necessary" meaning "impossible to accommodate ... without imposing undue hardship"; a negotiated absence-termination period is a "factor" but not determinative and "each case must be evaluated on the basis of its particular circumstances"
BaselineB: Common law (Meiorin/BCGSEU test: British Columbia (Public Service Employee Relations Commission) v. BCGSEU, [1999] 3 S.C.R. 3; plus related accommodation cases such as O’Malley and Renaud) applied in the context of Quebec human rights legislation and a collective agreement
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Indian Act s. 88 provincial-law applicability/inconsistency analysis: provincial law applies to Indians (via s. 88 reference) except to the extent it is “inconsistent with” the Indian Act; here, Adoption Act s. 10(2) (“for all purposes” severing natural-parent relationship) does not negate Indian Act s. 11(1)(d) registrability, so no inconsistency on the key issue of entitlement to be registered
BaselineA: Statute: Indian Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-6, s. 88 (and s. 11(1)(d) registrability); provincial Adoption Act, R.S.B.C. 1960, c. 4, s. 10(2) (“for all purposes”)
CaseB_TestB: Collins s. 24(2) exclusion framework (as organized in Greffe): balance three categories—(1) trial fairness, (2) seriousness of Charter breaches (including whether police had “reasonable and probable grounds” and indicia of informant reliability; a “mere conclusory statement” is insufficient), and (3) effect of exclusion/admission on the repute of justice—asking whether, “having regard to all the circumstances”, admission would bring the administration of justice into disrepute
BaselineB: Statute: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 24(2) (and related ss. 8, 10); common-law/Charter baseline case: R. v. Collins, [1987] 1 S.C.R. 265
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Termination (determination) of a continuing guarantee by “notice in writing”: notice need not use set words but must be explicit and unequivocal (not merely a ‘wish’ or ‘preference’) so the creditor is left in no doubt
BaselineA: Contract (guarantee instrument), cl. 4: guarantor may “by notice in writing delivered to the Manager ... determine ... liability ... in respect of liabilities thereafter incurred or arising”
CaseB_TestB: Admissibility/use of an accused’s post-caution silence: unless the Crown establishes “real relevance and a proper basis”, questions about silence and evidence of ensuing silence should not be admitted; if admitted, the jury must be instructed to ignore it (no adverse inference)
BaselineB: Common law right to silence (as discussed via Rothman v. The Queen (Lamer J. dissent), and Ontario CA cases Robertson and Symonds) and Charter s. 7 recognition (via Hebert v. The Queen)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Interim cease-and-desist order under Trade Union Act, s. 49(2): Board may issue ex parte interim order if "satisfied after investigation" that s. 48 breached; "notwithstanding any provision of this Act"; investigation may be done through Board officers; interim order may be directed to "any person" and against "any activity or action" so long as related to the illegal work stoppage
BaselineA: Statute (Trade Union Act, 1972 (N.S.), c. 19, ss. 48, 49(2), 15(9)-(10)) plus constitutional constraint in British North America Act, 1867, s. 96
CaseB_TestB: YCJA youth sentencing interpretation: general (and specific) deterrence is not a sentencing principle under the YCJA because Criminal Code s. 718(b) is excluded by YCJA s. 50(1) and deterrence cannot be implied from YCJA ss. 3 and 38; additionally, YCJA s. 42(2)(o) does not require a 2/3 custody and 1/3 supervision split (unlike s. 42(2)(n))
BaselineB: Statute (Youth Criminal Justice Act, S.C. 2002, c. 1, ss. 3, 38, 42(2)(n), 42(2)(o), 50(1); interpreting omission of Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 718(b))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Cities and Towns Act s. 622(4) excuse for failure to give municipal notice: if the victim proves they were prevented from giving notice within 15 days for a reason “deemed sufficient”, they are permanently relieved of the notice requirement and may sue without later giving notice
BaselineA: Statute — Cities and Towns Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 193, s. 622(1), (3), (4), (5) (especially s. 622(4) and the prescription start points in s. 622(5))
CaseB_TestB: Judicial review standard for a labour grievance arbitration award on collective agreement interpretation: court asks whether the arbitrator’s conclusion is a “patently unreasonable” interpretation / “whether it is one which the agreement would reasonably bear”
BaselineB: Common law (judicial review of arbitration awards) as developed in prior SCC cases cited, especially Bell Canada v. Office and Professional Employees' Union, [1974] S.C.R. 335; also linked to CUPE v. New Brunswick Liquor Corp., [1979] 2 S.C.R. 227 (patently unreasonable) and related arbitral review jurisprudence discussed
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Admissibility of similar fact evidence: other misconduct is inadmissible to show propensity, but is admissible if it is "relevant to an issue before the jury" (e.g., whether the act was "designed or accidental" or to rebut a defence otherwise open), and is admitted "not to prove commission of the crime" but "to establish guilty intent" (Makin/Thompson/Noor Mohamed/Wray as applied).
BaselineA: Common law evidence rule on similar fact evidence (general exclusionary rule and its exception), as stated in Makin v. Attorney General for New South Wales and developed in Thompson v. The King, Noor Mohamed v. The King, and applied in R. v. Wray.
CaseB_TestB: Municipal valuation where usual methods cannot be applied: "Where special circumstances make it impossible to fix the realizable value of property by the usual methods, whatever method is appropriate in the circumstances may be used to estimate the property at its actual value" (including acceptance of the 'developer’s approach' in the circumstances).
BaselineB: Combination of statute and case law: the statutory requirement that property be estimated at its "actual value" under the Charter of the City of Montreal (including appeal provisions ss. 873-874 as discussed), interpreted through prior valuation jurisprudence (notably Sun Life Assurance Co. of Canada v. The City of Montreal and related SCC/PC cases).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Admissibility of similar fact evidence: admissible only if relevant to an issue (e.g., designed vs accidental / to rebut a defence otherwise open), and not to show disposition; in criminal negligence, Crown may prove mens rea by similar conduct of the same type
BaselineA: Common law evidentiary rule on similar fact evidence (general exclusionary rule and its exception), as discussed via Makin v. Attorney General for New South Wales, Thompson v. The King, Noor Mohamed v. The King, and R. v. Wray; applied in context of Criminal Code ss. 191-192 (now 202-203) defining criminal negligence
CaseB_TestB: Issue estoppel on a perjury charge after an acquittal: Crown is estopped from re-litigating an issue necessarily decided in accused’s favour unless it tenders (in addition to or in lieu of prior evidence) evidence not available by the exercise of reasonable diligence at the first trial
BaselineB: Common law doctrine of res judicata/issue estoppel and fraud exception (e.g., Duchess of Kingston’s Case; Gushue v. The Queen; DPP v. Humphrys), adapted to criminal proceedings/perjury context
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory interpretation of technical terms: apply the common/ordinary meaning shared by both official-language versions; here, “tetracycline and its derivatives” captures only things actually “obtained from” tetracycline (not merely in the same drug family)
BaselineA: Statute/regulation interpretation: Order in Council (SOR/69-8) Schedule A (tariff item 92944-1: “Tetracycline and its derivatives” / “dérivés”), plus Official Languages Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. O-2, s. 8(2)(b) (bilingual ‘concept’ must be apt in both versions). The Court also relies on the established interpretive rule that statutes are construed according to common language (citing Continental Soya; Laboratoire Pentagone; Burton Parsons).
CaseB_TestB: Limits on inherent/implied jurisdiction re amici remuneration: absent statutory authority or a constitutional (Charter) basis, courts may appoint amici only exceptionally where essential, but do not have inherent/implied jurisdiction to fix amici compensation rates or order the Attorney General to pay a particular rate
