BaselineB: Common law / constitutional principles governing inherent and implied jurisdiction (as described via prior cases such as MacMillan Bloedel; Caron; Cunningham) and separation of powers; applied in the context of amicus appointments (no specific statute authorizing rate-setting in these cases).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Trustee’s statutory duty to insure bankrupt’s “insurable property” (including hypothec-encumbered property) and resulting personal liability for omission: under Bankruptcy Act s. 9(1)-(2), trustee must “forthwith temporarily insure and keep insured ... all the insurable property of the bankrupt” and, if insurance is cancelled/insufficient, must replace/obtain insurance and at least notify the secured (hypothecary) creditor; failure is a fault grounding personal liability.
BaselineA: Statute — Bankruptcy Act, R.S.C. 1952, c. 14, ss. 9(1)-(2) (insurance duty; policies payable to trustee) and s. 2(o) “property”, s. 2(r) “secured creditor”; also s. 171 (leave requirement) interpreted as inapplicable to omissions.
CaseB_TestB: Charitable status under the fourth Pemsel head (as applied under ITA s. 149.1(1)): purposes must be (a) of “public benefit”/“beneficial to the community” and (b) “in a way the law regards as charitable”; operationalized via the Vancouver Society/D’Aguiar approach—consider the trend of prior decisions by reasonable extension/analogy, examine accepted anomalies, and cross-check whether the property can be applied to non-charitable purposes (if so, charity fails).
BaselineB: Combination — Statute (Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), s. 149.1(1) “charitable organization”, s. 248(1) definitions including “registered charity”/RCAAA) relying on common law meaning of charity (Pemsel; Vancouver Society adopting D’Aguiar test).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Eligibility for a Quebec seat on the SCC under Supreme Court Act s. 6: s. 6 “narrows the pool” and requires current membership in Quebec institutions (current judge of QCCA/QSC or current Quebec advocate with 10 years standing); former Quebec advocates (including Federal Court/FCA judges who were formerly Quebec advocates) are ineligible
BaselineA: Statute (Supreme Court Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. S-26, ss. 5 and 6; plus constitutional constraints in Constitution Act, 1982, Part V, esp. s. 41(d))
JudgeA: McLachlin C.J. and LeBel, Abella, Cromwell, Karakatsanis and Wagner JJ.
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 15(1) equality test (two-step): (1) does the law, on its face or in impact, draw a distinction based on an enumerated/analogous ground; and (2) does it impose burdens/deny a benefit in a way that “reinforc[es], perpetuat[es] or exacerbat[es]” disadvantage (applied to Pay Equity Act s. 38 delay/retroactivity issue)
BaselineB: Common law / constitutional jurisprudence applying Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 15(1) (as summarized from Quebec (AG) v. A and Kahkewistahaw First Nation v. Taypotat) to a statutory scheme (Pay Equity Act, CQLR, c. E-12.001, s. 38)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Highway Victims Indemnity Fund payment obligation and limitation period: claimant must meet HVIA ss. 36-38 requirements (apply within 1 year; sworn declaration that judgment unsatisfied and “no insurer will benefit”), after which the Fund “has no choice” and “shall satisfy the judgment” within 7 days; action against Fund is prescribed by 30 years (C.C. art. 2265) because it is “based on the judgments obtained, not on the liability”.
BaselineA: Statute (Highway Victims Indemnity Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 232, ss. 36-39) plus Civil Code prescription provisions (arts. 2262, 2265).
CaseB_TestB: Fatal Accidents Act damages assessment methodology: determine dependants’ annual loss of support (net of income tax), then award the present value of a lump sum that will replace that stream over the relevant period, using a discount rate based on “present rates of return on long-term investments with an allowance for the effects of future inflation”, with “some reduction for contingencies”.
BaselineB: Statute (The Fatal Accidents Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 164) as informed by SCC damages methodology in Andrews v. Grand & Toy Alberta Ltd.; Thornton v. Board of School Trustees; Arnold v. Teno (all referenced in the reasons).
JudgeB: Dickson J. (for Laskin C.J. and Martland, Ritchie, Pigeon and Beetz JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Equitable interest for improper withholding of a just debt: where payment of a just debt has been improperly withheld and it is fair and equitable to compensate, the court should award interest for such time and at such rate as it thinks right (here: contractor’s bank borrowing rate).
BaselineA: Common law/equitable principle (Toronto Railway Co. v. City of Toronto, [1906] A.C. 117; followed in The Custodian v. Blucher, [1927] S.C.R. 420) plus statutory context (Interest Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-18, ss. 3, 12, 13; Supreme Court Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. S-19, s. 52).
CaseB_TestB: Dixon two-step post-conviction non-disclosure test: (1) reasonable possibility undisclosed info affects reliability of conviction; if not, (2) reasonable possibility non-disclosure affected overall fairness via lost lines of inquiry/opportunities; due diligence of defence counsel is a significant factor in stage (2).
BaselineB: Common law/Charter doctrine from R. v. Stinchcombe, [1991] 3 S.C.R. 326 (disclosure relevance threshold) and related SCC cases (Egger; Chaplin; Carosella), applying Charter ss. 7 and 24(1).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Doctrine/rule of recent possession: once Crown proves (1) goods were recently stolen and (2) accused possessed them, jury may infer guilt; if an explanation “may reasonably be true”, it must be considered and acquittal follows if it raises a reasonable doubt; Crown need not adduce evidence of absence of explanation
BaselineA: Common law rule of evidence (as stated in R. v. Schama; R. v. Abramovitch and repeatedly approved; also R. v. Graham (1974 SCC)) plus statutory constraint Canada Evidence Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-10, s. 4(5) (no comment on failure to testify)
CaseB_TestB: Imperial Tobacco extraterritoriality framework applied to s. 11 ORA: (1) identify pith and substance by purpose and effects; (2) assess territorial limits by asking whether the law has a “meaningful connection” to the province and “respects the sovereignty” of other provinces
BaselineB: Common law constitutional division-of-powers framework from British Columbia v. Imperial Tobacco Canada Ltd., 2005 SCC 49, applied to Constitution Act, 1867, s. 92 territorial limits (esp. ss. 92(13), 92(14)) and to ORA, S.B.C. 2018, c. 35, s. 11 (with CPA, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 50, ss. 4 and 16 referenced)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Drunkenness and mens rea for murder: intoxication is legally relevant only if it renders the accused "incapable of forming the specific intent"; mere impairment/greater propensity to violence is insufficient (Beard approach as charged to jury).
BaselineA: Combination: Criminal Code, s. 212(a) (mens rea for murder) plus common law intoxication doctrine as in Director of Public Prosecutions v. Beard (H.L.), as adopted in the jury charge and accepted by the majority.
CaseB_TestB: Rebutting the s. 258(1)(d.1) BAC presumption with "straddle evidence": evidence placing BAC in a range that crosses 80 mg/100 mL "may be capable of raising a reasonable doubt" and is weighed "in the light of all of the evidence" (Gibson/LeBel J. test).
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, s. 258(1)(d.1) (statutory presumption based on breathalyser readings), as interpreted through R. v. Gibson, 2008 SCC 16.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Drunkenness negating mens rea for murder: intoxication must render the accused incapable of forming the specific intent; mere impairment/greater propensity to violence is insufficient
BaselineA: Combination: Criminal Code s. 212(a) (mens rea for murder) + common law intoxication doctrine (DPP v. Beard)
CaseB_TestB: Section 23 “numbers warrant” sliding-scale placement: (1) determine long-term number who will eventually avail; (2) compare to majority schools (local then province-wide) with a rebuttable presumption from comparators; (3) determine level of services (homogeneous school if comparable; otherwise range with deference to minority board)
BaselineB: Combination: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms s. 23 (and s. 1 context) + prior SCC framework in Mahe v. Alberta (sliding scale) and related cases
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Labour Code s. 108(1)(b) review: court may intervene only for an “error of law affecting the jurisdiction” of a labour arbitrator; no such jurisdictional error where the arbitrator “applied himself to the problem at hand” and answered the question submitted (even if arguably right or wrong on the merits).
BaselineA: Statute: Labour Code of British Columbia Act, 1973 (B.C.) (2d Sess.), c. 122, s. 108(1)(b) (and s. 108(1) generally limiting review to three grounds).
CaseB_TestB: Garofoli leave threshold for cross-examining a wiretap affiant: defence must show a “reasonable likelihood” that cross-examination “will elicit testimony of probative value to the issue for consideration by the reviewing judge” (i.e., relevant and material to whether the authorization had a basis).
BaselineB: Common law: R. v. Garofoli, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 1421 (threshold/leave requirement for cross-examining the affiant on a wiretap review). Also applied in the statutory context of Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 184.2 (consent wiretap authorization).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: ITA s. 83(3) “arrangement with the prospector” / “employer of the prospector” requirement for excluding consideration (mining property interest or shares) from income: taxpayer must have advanced/paid prospecting expenses either (i) “under an arrangement with the prospector made before the prospecting, exploration or development work” or (ii) “as employer of the prospector” (and the prospector must not be prospecting “on behalf of himself”).
BaselineA: Statute: Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1952, c. 148, s. 83(3) (as amended by 1965 (Can.), c. 18, s. 19) (with related definition context in s. 83(1)(c)).
JudgeA: de Grandpré J. (for Laskin C.J. and Judson, Beetz and de Grandpré JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: “Integral element” test for whether Parliament (under Constitution Act, 1867 s. 92(10) railways) can validly enact a special limitation period affecting provincial personal-injury actions: federal jurisdiction over a matter exists only if it is “an integral part” of the core federal competence over the undertaking; otherwise provincial law of general application applies and the federal provision is ultra vires (with s. 342(1) read down to apply only to statutory causes of action validly created by the Railway Act).
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine (division of powers) articulated in prior SCC cases, especially Construction Montcalm Inc. v. Minimum Wage Commission and Northern Telecom Ltd. v. Communications Workers of Canada, applied to Railway Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. R-2, s. 342(1).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Fire policy statutory condition 10(a): the policy is not void for failure to state the insured’s interest so long as the insured has an insurable interest (i.e., “All that is necessary to satisfy statutory condition 10(a) of the policy is that the insured have an insurable interest”).
BaselineA: Statute/standard policy conditions: Insurance Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 295 (including statutory condition 10(a) and s. 240 condition 1) and Civil Code art. 2571; interpreted in light of prior SCC authority (Wandlyn Motels v. Commerce General Insurance Company).
CaseB_TestB: Section 8 ‘coroner-to-police’ bodily sample framework: when a bodily sample is seized by a non-police actor but used in a criminal prosecution, courts must assess whether police conduct constitutes an independent state seizure or renders the initial seizure unreasonable (i.e., must “go beyond the initial non-police seizure” and determine whether police actions “constitute a seizure by the state… or make the initially valid seizure… unreasonable”; once evidence is “appropriated by the state’s criminal law enforcement arm… the seizure will become unreasonable”).
BaselineB: Common law Charter s. 8 framework from Hunter v. Southam Inc. (prior judicial authorization for criminal-law seizures) and R. v. Dyment (privacy in bodily samples), applied alongside the Coroners Act, R.S.O. 1980, c. 93, s. 16(2) and s. 16(5).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Adjournment to secure counsel: refusal is reviewable where it deprives the accused of the right to make full defence by counsel; an adjournment “may be refused only for a reason based on established facts” and discretion must be exercised “judicially” (reviewable if based on reasons “not well founded in law”).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 577(3) right to make full defence personally or by counsel; appellate review/miscarriage of justice under s. 613) with supporting case law (e.g., Spataro v. R.; Talbot v. R.).
JudgeA: Pigeon J. (for Laskin C.J. and Judson, Spence, Pigeon, Dickson and Beetz JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Equitable compensation for breach of fiduciary duty: assess the plaintiff’s “actual loss” with hindsight; “foreseeability is not a concern”, but recovery is limited to losses which, on a “common sense view of causation”, were caused by the breach; third-party losses are recoverable only where the breach “permits” them (direct link), otherwise they are too remote.
BaselineB: Common law/equity (fiduciary duty and equitable compensation), drawing on cases including Nocton v. Lord Ashburton and Guerin v. The Queen; not based on a specific statute for the test.
JudgeB: McLachlin J. (for Lamer C.J. and L’Heureux-Dubé and McLachlin JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Quebec Superior Court jurisdiction on a declinatory exception: in a personal action (art. 68 C.C.P.), jurisdiction lies in the court of the defendant’s domicile, or failing that, of his residence; filing a declinatory exception does not automatically shift the burden to the plaintiff, and the court assesses the evidence to determine the defendant’s (principal) residence.
BaselineA: Statute (Quebec Code of Civil Procedure, arts. 68 and 70; plus Canadian Citizenship Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-19, s. 10 presumption re principal residence for citizenship)
CaseB_TestB: When (and how) police/state misconduct can reduce sentence: if the misconduct relates to the circumstances of the offence or the offender, the sentencing judge may treat it as a relevant mitigating factor within Criminal Code sentencing (ss. 718–718.2) without resort to Charter s. 24(1); sentence must still respect statutory minimums, with only a narrow, exceptional possibility of going outside statutory limits under s. 24(1) for particularly egregious misconduct.
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code ss. 718–718.2 and statutory minimums; Charter s. 24(1) as remedial backdrop)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Contractual interpretation of warranty: “depreciation” in the clause/letter means accounting depreciation (write-off over useful life), not “full capital cost allowance” under the Income Tax Act; the parenthetical “(using capital cost allowance rates)” refers to rates only, not adoption of the CCA system, so no breach if depreciation was taken on all vehicles for the period each was in service at those rates.
BaselineA: Common law (interpretation/construction of a contractual warranty clause, read with the incorporated auditor’s letter).
CaseB_TestB: Youth court power under Young Offenders Act: despite s. 19(2) (“find ... guilty or not guilty or make an order dismissing the charge”), a youth court judge has no jurisdiction to dismiss a charge merely because it “ought never to have been laid”; absent clear statutory language, prosecutorial discretion governs (subject only to exceptional remedies like abuse of process/stay in the “clearest of cases”).
BaselineB: Statute (Young Offenders Act, R.S.C., 1985, c. Y-1, especially ss. 19(2) and 3(1), read in light of the criminal procedure principle of prosecutorial discretion).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Crown appeal from acquittal after legal error: Crown must satisfy the court that the verdict "would not necessarily have been the same" absent the error (White v. R. test)
BaselineA: Common law test from White v. R., [1947] S.C.R. 268, applied in the statutory context of Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 613(4) (appeal from acquittal) and contrasted with s. 613(1)(b)(iii) (curative proviso on conviction appeals)
CaseB_TestB: Group defamation/personal injury in Quebec: plaintiff must prove that an "ordinary person" would believe the remarks, viewed as a whole, discredited each member’s reputation; personal injury assessed contextually using non-exhaustive factors (e.g., group size, homogeneity, identifiability, precision, plausibility)
BaselineB: Statutory civil liability under Civil Code of Québec, art. 1457 (fault, injury, causal connection), with the defamation-injury objective standard drawn from SCC cases Prud’homme v. Prud’homme (2002 SCC 85) and Néron (2004 SCC 53); also engages C.C.Q. arts. 1607, 1611 and C.C.P. class action provisions as procedural context
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Workmen’s compensation exclusion in standard auto policy: insured is excluded if, on the admitted facts, he is “entitled to receive the benefits of any workmen’s compensation law or plan” — entitlement does not depend on having applied for or obtained an award; contra proferentem inapplicable where wording is statutorily mandated
BaselineA: Statute (Ontario): Insurance Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 224, s. 232(1) and Schedule E exclusion 2(a)(ii) (“who is entitled to receive the benefits of any workmen’s compensation law or plan”), interpreted with reference to Workmen’s Compensation Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 505 (e.g., ss. 3, 8). Also common-law interpretive principle: contra proferentem (held inapplicable here because wording mandated by statute).
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 8 reasonableness framework (mutatis mutandis) for cross-border disclosure of wiretap information under Criminal Code s. 193(2)(e): (1) disclosure authorized by law; (2) the law is reasonable; (3) disclosure carried out in a reasonable manner (including case-specific assessment of risks such as torture/unfair trial and whether protocols/caveats mitigate them)
BaselineB: Combination: Charter s. 8 common-law framework from R. v. Collins / R. v. Caslake (“authorized by law / law reasonable / manner reasonable”) applied to statutory disclosure power in Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 193(2)(e) (and Part VI generally).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Discretion to order service ex juris under Federal Court Rule 307 guided by forum conveniens: the “overriding consideration” is whether there exists “some other forum more convenient and appropriate for the pursuit of the action and for securing the ends of justice” (with key factors here including Portland’s participation/waiver via posting bond and Delmar’s lack of other assets beyond the bail bond).
BaselineA: Statute and rules of court: Federal Court Act, R.S.C. 1970 (2nd Supp.), c. 10, ss. 22(2)(a), 43(1), 44; Federal Court Rules, Rule 307 (service ex juris).
JudgeA: Ritchie J. (for Ritchie, Pigeon, Beetz and de Grandpré JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Medical malpractice causation in Quebec civil law (rejecting “loss of chance” as a substitute for causation where death/sickness has occurred): causation “must be established on the balance of probabilities, taking into account all the evidence: factual, statistical and that which the judge is entitled to presume”; in some cases a court may presume causation where a fault creates a “clear danger” that materializes, “unless there is a demonstration or a strong indication to the contrary”; if not satisfied on the balance of probabilities that the fault caused “any real damage”, recovery is denied.
BaselineB: Civil law (Civil Code of Lower Canada causation framework), with reference to art. 1205 (presumptions) and SCC causation jurisprudence (e.g., Snell v. Farrell) as discussed in the reasons.
JudgeB: Gonthier J. (for Lamer C.J. and L'Heureux-Dubé, Sopinka, Gonthier, Cory and McLachlin JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Breach of municipal development agreement sewer-servicing obligation: developer must prove a specific failure to provide sewers/enlargements "required to properly service" the redevelopment stage (i.e., evidence of existing or foreseeable inadequacy); a general sewer-upgrading report/charge is irrelevant absent evidence connecting it to serviceability of the project sewers
BaselineA: Common law (contract interpretation and breach) applied to s. 31(a)(iii) of the 1966 development agreement ("construction" and "enlargement" of sewers "required to properly service" each stage)
CaseB_TestB: Presumption of advancement and rebuttal in husband-to-wife gratuitous transfer: presumption applies unless husband rebuts; it is not rebutted by saying he transferred "only ... to defeat his creditors"; plus the statutory abolition of the presumption (Family Law Reform Act, 1975, s. 1(3)(d)) does not apply retrospectively absent express terms or necessary implication
BaselineB: Common law presumption of advancement (as discussed with reference to Goodfriend v. Goodfriend and Tinker v. Tinker) plus statutory interpretation of The Family Law Reform Act, 1975 (Ont.), s. 1(3)(d) regarding temporal application
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 613(1)(b)(iii) curative proviso: uphold conviction despite trial error only if the Crown satisfies the appellate court that a properly charged jury "could not, as reasonable men, have done otherwise than find the appellant guilty" (i.e., no substantial wrong or miscarriage of justice).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, s. 613(1)(b)(iii)) as applied through SCC precedent (Colpitts v. R., quoting Brooks v. The King).
CaseB_TestB: Marshall treaty right and infringement analysis: (1) interpret the 1760-61 treaties (including extrinsic evidence) to recognize a right to obtain "necessaries" (modern equivalent: a "moderate livelihood") through hunting/fishing and trading; (2) determine prima facie infringement using Sparrow questions ("unreasonable" / "undue hardship" / denial of "preferred means"); (3) if infringed, regulation must be justified under the Badger/Sparrow justificatory standard.
BaselineB: Combination: constitutional and common law framework (Constitution Act, 1982, s. 35(1); Sparrow infringement test; Badger justification; treaty-interpretation principles from Sioui/Badger/Sundown) applied to federal fisheries legislation (Fisheries Act, s. 7(1); Maritime Provinces Fishery Regulations, ss. 4(1)(a), 20; Fishery (General) Regulations, s. 35(2)).
JudgeB: Binnie J. (for Lamer C.J. and L’Heureux-Dubé, Cory, Iacobucci and Binnie JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Hague Protocol ‘notice’ requirement for carrier to invoke liability limitation: limitation in Art. 22 is unavailable unless the passenger ticket/baggage check includes a ‘notice’ in a form ‘calculated to attract attention’ (not merely ‘reasonably readable’).
BaselineA: Statute (Carriage by Air Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-14 incorporating the Warsaw Convention as amended by the Hague Protocol): Hague Protocol Arts. 3(1)(c), 3(2), 4(1)(c), and Art. 22 (limitation of liability).
CaseB_TestB: Post-severance rebuttal of breathalyzer presumptions under Criminal Code s. 258(1)(c) and (d.01): to rebut the presumptions of accuracy/identity, the accused must raise a reasonable doubt that the approved instrument was functioning and was operated properly; Carter-type consumption evidence is legally insufficient for that purpose (s. 258(1)(d.01)).
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, ss. 258(1)(c), 258(1)(d.01), 258(1)(d.1)) as reviewed under Charter s. 11(d) and justified under Charter s. 1 (with severance of the 2nd and 3rd requirements in s. 258(1)(c)).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Municipal notice period under Montreal Charter art. 1088 runs from discovery (when material facts giving rise to the claim become known), not necessarily from the accident date, to avoid making the right of action “aleatory”/practically denied
BaselineA: Statute: Charter of the City of Montreal, 1959-60 (Que.), c. 102, art. 1088 (15-day notice the city must have “received”); plus interpretive context from Interpretation Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 1, ss. 52 and 61; and SCC guidance on notice exceptions referenced from City of Ile Perrot v. Goulet-Wiseman, [1977] 1 S.C.R. 175
CaseB_TestB: Discretionary test for whether to discharge a civil jury after a reference to insurance: discharge only if the reference likely causes “real prejudice”/a “substantial wrong or miscarriage of justice” such that it would be unfair to continue, and the prejudice cannot be cured by instructions
BaselineB: Common law (overruling prior SCC rule): Bowhey v. Theakston, [1951] S.C.R. 679 (automatic discharge once jury might infer insurance); replaced with discretionary approach informed by prejudice/miscarriage-of-justice standard (with reference to Michaud v. Wales as persuasive authority) and general appellate deference to trial-management discretion
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Admissibility of an accused’s prior in-court testimony (judicial statement under oath) at a later trial without a voir dire on voluntariness; voluntariness goes to weight, not admissibility, and protection against self-incrimination must be claimed at the time (Canada Evidence Act s. 5(2)). Key holdings: “it is never necessary to hold a voir dire with respect to the voluntariness of a previous statement of the accused given in court” and such testimony is “admissible as of right, even if its voluntariness is disputed”.
BaselineA: Common law distinction between extra-judicial confessions (require voir dire voluntariness) and judicial statements; authorities cited include R. v. Scott (1856) (principle that compelled prior sworn testimony in a judicial proceeding is admissible), plus related lines of cases; statutory context: Canada Evidence Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-10, s. 5(2) (witness protection against subsequent use if claimed).
CaseB_TestB: Appellate intervention for trial judge’s failure to consider relevant evidence: appellate courts do not reassess guilt, but must review whether the trial court directed itself to all evidence on relevant issues; if the record shows “a lack of appreciation of relevant evidence” or “complete disregard of such evidence”, the reviewing court “must intercede”.
BaselineB: Common law principles on appellate review of reasons/evidence, relying on SCC authorities including MacDonald v. The Queen, [1977] 2 S.C.R. 665 and Ungaro v. R., [1950] S.C.R. 430 (misdirection/overlooking relevant issues/evidence).
JudgeB: Estey J. (for Martland, Dickson, Beetz, Estey, McIntyre and Lamer JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Limits on Crown rebuttal evidence to an alibi / collateral-fact contradiction rule: Crown may contradict an alibi only by attacking its “material points”; and the Crown may not contradict a “collateral fact” elicited on cross-examination to impeach credibility
BaselineA: Common law evidence rules (rebuttal to alibi; collateral fact rule), with appellate-harmless-error overlay under Criminal Code s. 613(1)(b)(iii)
CaseB_TestB: Drunkenness and rape via specific-intent/general-intent classification: rape is an offence of “general or basic intent”, so self-induced intoxication is not a defence (subject to considering whether there was evidence of incapacity and whether any miscarriage of justice occurred)
BaselineB: Common law intoxication doctrine as adopted in SCC jurisprudence (notably The Queen v. George) and English authority (Beard; Majewski), applied in the context of Criminal Code s. 613(1)(b)(iii)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Applicability of mandatory supervision under Parole Act s. 15(1) to an inmate with multiple sentences: if the inmate falls within the proclaimed class (sentenced to penitentiary on/after Aug. 1, 1970) and is released by remission exceeding 60 days, then s. 15(1) applies; by s. 14(1) the multiple terms are deemed “one sentence” for purposes of applying s. 15(1). Key statutory language: s. 15(1) applies where an inmate is released “as a result of remission... and the term of such remission exceeds sixty days, he shall... be subject to mandatory supervision”; s. 14(1) deems multiple terms to “constitute one sentence consisting of a term of imprisonment commencing on the earliest day on which any of those sentences... commences”.
BaselineA: Statute: Parole Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. P-2, ss. 14(1) and 15(1)-(2), as enacted via Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1968-69 (Can.), c. 38, s. 101(2) and proclamation SOR/70-339 (effective Aug. 1, 1970).
CaseB_TestB: Whether insurance proceeds are deemed property transmitted on death under Succession Duties Act s. 26(1): if proceeds are “due by an insurer by reason or on account of the death of the person on whose life the insurance was effected”, they are deemed property passing on death and taxable—this includes accident insurance where payment is triggered by accidental death (“a death does not cease to be a death because it is accidental”), and “insurance policies” is not limited to life insurance; “sur la tête de” / “on whose life” is used broadly for insurance of the person (life/death/health/dismemberment).
BaselineB: Statute: Succession Duties Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 70, s. 26(1) (with related discussion of ss. 45(f) and 46(1)); interpretive support from Civil Code arts. 1902, 1903, 1905, 1906 (usage of “sur la tête” / “upon the life”).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Estate Tax Act: no taxable “passing” (and no inclusion under s. 3(1)(a)) where a marriage contract gives the surviving spouse ownership of the whole community retroactively; deceased not “competent to dispose” of community assets in the Act’s sense
BaselineA: Statute — Estate Tax Act, 1958 (Can.), c. 29, especially ss. 3(1)(a), 3(2)(a), 3(2)(e) and 58(1)(i), as applied with SCC precedents Sura v. MNR, [1962] S.C.R. 65 and The Royal Trust Company et al. v. MNR, [1968] S.C.R. 505
CaseB_TestB: Treaty 8/NRTA geographic limit: treaty right to hunt for food on private land turns on “visible, incompatible land use” (case-by-case); if land is occupied (visible use incompatible with hunting) no right of access, if unoccupied (no visible incompatible use) right of access exists
BaselineB: Constitutional instrument and treaty interpretation — Treaty No. 8 (1899) and Natural Resources Transfer Agreement, 1930, para. 12 (Constitution Act, 1930, Schedule 2), with interpretive principles and prior cases (e.g., Horseman; Frank; Myran; Horse)
JudgeB: Cory J. (for La Forest, L'Heureux-Dubé, Gonthier, Cory and Iacobucci JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Contractual price-adjustment clause for tax changes: clause applies only to a “tax, duty, charge or fee” imposed on the seller (Imperial) “in respect of bunker fuel oil” (the “product”) or its “production, manufacture, sale or delivery” by Imperial; it does not extend to upstream crude-oil cost increases from foreign taxes/royalties or affiliate supply contracts
BaselineA: Common law (contract interpretation) plus the parties’ contract (clause 9) as the operative text being interpreted
CaseB_TestB: Van der Peet test (applied to asserted self-government/gambling right under s. 35(1)): “in order to be an aboriginal right an activity must be an element of a practice, custom or tradition integral to the distinctive culture” of the group; court must (1) “identify the exact nature of the activity claimed” and (2) determine whether it was “a defining feature of the culture in question” prior to contact
BaselineB: Common law / constitutional jurisprudence applying Constitution Act, 1982, s. 35(1), with the governing test taken from R. v. Van der Peet
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Foreseeability-based duty/causation limit in negligence for child injured on railway right-of-way: liability only if the injury was a reasonably foreseeable result of the situation created by the defendant (no duty to prevent unforeseeable ‘train-jumping’ conduct)
BaselineA: Common law negligence/occupiers’ liability principles (foreseeability and duty of care), with discussion of possible statutory fencing duty under Railway Act s. 214 but not determinative
CaseB_TestB: Section 7 ‘fair hearing’ requirements for security-certificate proceedings: a fair hearing requires (i) a hearing, (ii) an independent and impartial decision-maker, (iii) a decision on the facts and the law, and (iv) the right to know and answer the case; if full disclosure is impossible, a ‘substantial substitute’ must be provided
BaselineB: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7 (principles of fundamental justice) applied to IRPA security-certificate scheme (IRPA ss. 77-85, especially s. 78 secrecy provisions)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory interpretation of Highway Victims Indemnity Act s. 43: Fund must satisfy judgment for unknown driver only up to the s. 14 cap ($35,000), and prior recovery from another liable party does not extinguish the Fund’s capped liability (no s. 38 deduction where victim received nothing from unknown driver). Key language: Fund satisfies judgment “to the same extent as if it had been rendered against the author of the accident”; this imports the s. 14 limit.
BaselineA: Statute: Highway Victims Indemnity Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 232, especially ss. 43 (unknown driver), 14 (financial responsibility cap of $35,000), 38 (deduction rule in Fund recourse), and 49 (Fund powers).
CaseB_TestB: Sentencing treatment of collateral immigration consequences and appellate intervention: a sentencing judge may consider collateral immigration consequences as part of individualized sentencing, but the sentence must remain proportionate (Criminal Code s. 718.1) and consequences must not “skew” sentencing; an appellate court may vary a sentence where the sentencing judge was unaware of those consequences or counsel failed to advise, and where not raised below without Crown consent “some evidence should be adduced”.
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law sentencing principles: Criminal Code, ss. 718, 718.1, 718.2 (proportionality, parity, individualization) and the appellate-sentencing intervention framework from R. v. M. (C.A.) (as cited at para. 24). Collateral consequence context: IRPA, s. 64.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Whether the jury must be cautioned about convicting on uncorroborated testimony when a witness may be an accomplice (and the accessory-after-the-fact issue): if the evidence could support finding the witness an accomplice, the trial judge must warn the jury of the danger of relying on that uncorroborated testimony
BaselineA: Common law rule of practice/caution on accomplice evidence (as discussed via Horsburgh v. The Queen and Davies v. DPP; also engages Criminal Code s. 23 definition of accessory after the fact)
CaseB_TestB: Interpretation/application of Criminal Code s. 212(c) murder (“unlawful object” constructive murder): (1) unlawfulness for s. 205(5)(a) is that resulting from prosecuting the unlawful object by a life-dangerous act; (2) dangerous act need not itself be unlawful; (3) if the dangerous act is unlawful, there must be a further unlawful object distinct from the immediate object of the dangerous act; (4) “unlawful object” means an object which, if fully prosecuted, would amount to an indictable mens rea offence; (5) objective ‘ought to know’ is applied using the accused’s actual knowledge of surrounding circumstances; (6) intoxication is relevant to that actual knowledge
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code ss. 205(5)(a) and 212(c) (with related discussion of 212(a)(i)-(ii)); prior SCC authority Graves v. The King reconsidered/not followed on the knowledge/intoxication point
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Construction of Manitoba auto insurance exclusion: the s. 31(3)(h) exclusion for death of “an insured” is applied by reference to the specific contract/certificate under which indemnity is claimed (owner’s vs driver’s), because the certificates evidence “separate contracts” with “distinct coverages”.
BaselineA: Regulation (Manitoba Automobile Insurance Regulation, Man. Reg. 333/74 under The Manitoba Public Insurance Corporation Act, C.S.M. c. A180), especially s. 30 (definition of “insured”), s. 31(1), s. 31(2), and s. 31(3)(h).
CaseB_TestB: Treaty 8 / NRTA para. 12 limit on hunting rights: after the 1930 Natural Resources Transfer Agreement, Treaty 8 hunting rights are limited to hunting “for food” (i.e., “for sustenance for the individual Indian or the Indian’s family”); selling a hide as part of a “multi-stage process” is an “act of commerce” and not protected as hunting “for food”, so provincial Wildlife Act s. 42 applies via Indian Act s. 88.
BaselineB: Constitutional/statutory instruments: Treaty No. 8 (1899) and Natural Resources Transfer Agreement, 1930 (Alberta), para. 12 (confirmed by Constitution Act, 1930), applied alongside Indian Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-6, s. 88 and Alberta Wildlife Act, R.S.A. 1980, c. W-9, ss. 1(s), 42.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 287 (as then worded): “telecommunication” requires transmission “by wire or cable” (not Hertzian waves/radio); no ‘partly wire’ vs ‘entirely wire’ distinction
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 287(1)(b) and definition in s. 287(2) (“telecommunication” means transmission “by wire or cable”)
CaseB_TestB: Immigration Act s. 19(1)(a)(ii) “excessive demands” assessment for social services: individualized assessment considering both medical and non-medical factors (including family ability/willingness to pay); threshold is “reasonable probability, not remote possibility” (“more likely than not”)
BaselineB: Statute: Immigration Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. I-2, s. 19(1)(a)(ii) (and related medical-opinion structure in s. 19(1)(a))
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Limits on municipal discretion to refuse a business licence under Municipal Act s. 455: discretion must be exercised “judicially”, not on “extraneous”/“irrelevant or alien” grounds; “in any particular case” means peculiar to the applicant (not a blanket prohibition of a business type), and refusal must not be “unreasonably” withheld.
BaselineA: Statute (Municipal Act, R.S.B.C. 1960, c. 255, s. 455) interpreted in light of the Act’s scheme; supported by common law principles/cases (e.g., Municipal Corporation of the City of Toronto v. Virgo; Sunshine Valley Co-operative Society v. City of Grand Forks).
CaseB_TestB: IRPA security-certificate procedural fairness under Charter s. 7: the named person must receive an “incompressible minimum” of disclosure—i.e., be “reasonably informed” by receiving “sufficient disclosure to be able to give meaningful instructions” to public counsel and “meaningful guidance and information” to special advocates; if non-disclosure prevents this, the Minister must withdraw the information/evidence and the judge must quash the certificate.
BaselineB: Statute + constitutional baseline: Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (notably ss. 77(2), 78, 83(1)(c),(d),(e),(i), 85.4(2)) interpreted to comply with Charter s. 7, building on Charkaoui I.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Appellate deference to trial findings of fact: an appellate court should not disturb a trial judge’s findings where there was “credible evidence before him on which he could reasonably base his conclusion”, and it is not the function of an appellate court to reconsider the evidence “unless it can be shown that the evidence reasonably could not result in justifying the conclusion of the trial judge”.
BaselineA: Common law (appellate review standard for findings of fact; the Court states it as a “well-known principle” rather than deriving it from a statute).
CaseB_TestB: Bona fide occupational qualification (BFOQ) under Ontario Human Rights Code s. 4(6): the limitation must be imposed “honestly, in good faith, and in the sincerely held belief” it serves adequate performance (dispatch, safety, economy) and not for “ulterior or extraneous reasons”; and it must be objectively related to the job, i.e., “reasonably necessary to assure the efficient and economical performance of the job without endangering” the employee, co-workers, or the public (with the employer bearing the burden on a balance of probabilities once a prima facie case is shown).
BaselineB: Statute: The Ontario Human Rights Code, R.S.O. 1970, c. 318, ss. 4(1), 4(6) (and procedural context in ss. 14a, 14d).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal causation for unlawful act manslaughter: Crown must prove the unlawful act was “at least a contributing cause of death, outside the de minimis range” (not necessary to prove it was the sole cause; thin-skull applies; jury may consider all evidence, expert and lay).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code), especially s. 205(1) (“A person commits homicide ... when directly or indirectly, by any means, he causes the death of a human being”), applied with common law causation principles (incl. thin skull) discussed via cases such as R. v. Larkin and R. v. Blaue.
CaseB_TestB: Anns two-stage duty-of-care framework for recognizing a novel duty for pure economic loss (prima facie duty via foreseeability/proximity; then residual policy considerations may negate/limit duty), applied to reject a general duty of care in commercial negotiations.
BaselineB: Common law negligence duty analysis from Anns v. Merton London Borough Council (as adopted in Kamloops (City of) v. Nielsen) and applied in SCC economic loss jurisprudence (e.g., Norsk, D’Amato, Bow Valley).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Crown bound by legislation/regulations only if expressly mentioned/referred to; common-law 'necessary implication' requires that the statute’s purpose be 'wholly frustrated' unless the Crown is bound
BaselineA: Combination: statute (Interpretation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-23, s. 16 (and s. 28 definition of 'Her Majesty')) plus common law (Bombay Province v. Bombay Municipal Corporation, [1947] A.C. 58: Crown bound by 'necessary implication' only where purpose would be 'wholly frustrated')
CaseB_TestB: Breach of contract where a stipulated term (here, cargo weight) is 'material if not a critical term'; excessive deviation from the stipulated weight constitutes breach, engaging Civil Code art. 1065 (damages for breach) rather than nullity for error under art. 992
BaselineB: Statute (Civil Code, arts. 992 and 1065) applied to a contract of carriage; characterization of the weight term as a contractual term whose breach triggers art. 1065
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Lord’s Day Act s. 11(x) exemption scope: CTC must decide only whether (having regard to the Act’s object of preventing gainful Sunday work) it should exempt “any work” to prevent “undue delay” in freight traffic; impacts on local Sunday quiet/congestion are irrelevant
BaselineA: Statute: Lord’s Day Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. L-13, ss. 4 and 11(x) (interpretation of “object of this Act” and the CTC’s mandate under s. 11(x))
CaseB_TestB: Bona fide pension plan under NB Human Rights Code s. 3(6)(a) (Abella J. for the majority): plan must be “subjectively and objectively bona fide” — “a legitimate plan, adopted in good faith and not for the purpose of defeating protected rights”; inquiry is into the plan’s overall bona fides, not actuarial details
BaselineB: Statute: Human Rights Code, R.S.N.B. 1973, c. H-11, s. 3(6)(a) (interpretation of “bona fide retirement or pension plan”)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: “Undueness” in conspiracy to lessen competition under Combines Investigation Act s. 32(1)(c): agreement is criminal only if, if carried into effect, it would impose “improper, inordinate, excessive or oppressive restrictions” on competition / “virtually reliev[e] the conspirators from the influence of free competition”; assess “what the result would be if the agreement were implemented” and reject any per se ‘meaningful segment’ approach
BaselineA: Statute (Combines Investigation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-23, s. 32(1)(c)) as interpreted in prior SCC cases (Howard Smith Paper Mills; Weidman v. Shragge; Stinson-Reeb; Container Materials)
CaseB_TestB: Unreasonable verdict review (Criminal Code s. 686(1)(a)(i)): appellate court asks whether the verdict is one a properly instructed jury/judge “could reasonably have rendered”; may find unreasonableness where an essential inference/finding is “plainly contradicted” by the evidence relied on or “incompatible with” uncontradicted/unrejected evidence; credibility findings are not disturbed unless they “cannot be supported on any reasonable view of the evidence”
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(a)(i)) plus prior SCC jurisprudence (Yebes; Biniaris; Sinclair; Beaudry; Burke)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Circumstantial-evidence instruction: the Hodge’s Case formula applies to proving the act/identity but not to proving intent; for intent the jury applies the ordinary reasonable-doubt standard (and for circumstantial proof of the act/identity, guilt must be the only reasonable inference).
BaselineA: Combination: statute (Criminal Code s. 110(1)(b) requiring proof beyond a reasonable doubt of conferring a benefit “with respect to those dealings”) plus common law on circumstantial evidence (Hodge’s Case; R. v. Mitchell).
CaseB_TestB: Insurance contract interpretation where a clause/reference is ambiguous: apply C.C. art. 1014 so that a clause is read in the meaning that has effect rather than none; thus “See Garage Policy” in the fleet policy is construed as referring to limits/premium (not importing the garage policy’s restrictive coverage), and the garage rider excluding owned autos does not negate fleet third-party liability coverage.
BaselineB: Statute/civil law: Civil Code of Quebec (esp. art. 1014; also arts. 1013, 2480) applied to interpret the insurance policies; (context includes Highway Victims Indemnity Act ss. 10, 12 and Insurance Act s. 214 but the key interpretive rule is C.C. art. 1014).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Burden of proof for “impossibility of performance” (as distinct from lack of causation) in a mandatary’s liability: plaintiff proves fault, damage, causality; defendant who alleges impossibility to avoid the obligation must prove it (difficulty is insufficient)
BaselineA: Statute (Civil Code of Quebec provisions): arts. 1701 (mandate), 984 and 1062 (object must be possible), and especially art. 1203 C.C. (“he who alleges facts in avoidance or extinction of the obligation must prove them”); applied within the general civil liability triad of fault-damage-causality
CaseB_TestB: Meaning of “directly or indirectly … have any interest in any contract” for municipal office disqualification: interpret “interested in” broadly in ordinary/common usage; a director/officer of a contracting company has at least an indirect interest (shareholding alone is exempt, but directorship/officership triggers disqualification)
BaselineB: Statute: Moncton Consolidation Act, 1946 (N.B.), c. 101, s. 6 (disqualification for having an interest in a contract with the City, except as shareholder); interpretive approach supported by New Brunswick Interpretation Act, R.S.N.B. 1973, c. I-13, s. 17 (fair, large and liberal construction) and SCC guidance in Angrignon (phrase “interested in” has no technical signification; common usage)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Interpretation of para. 12 Alberta Natural Resources Transfer Agreement: “Indians within the boundaries” means all Indians physically within Alberta (not only Alberta residents), so they are subject to provincial game laws but retain the proviso right to hunt/fish for food on unoccupied Crown lands/lands of access
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional instrument and treaty: Indian Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-6, s. 88 (provincial laws of general application apply to Indians “subject to the terms of any treaty”); Alberta Natural Resources Transfer Agreement, 1930, para. 12; Treaty No. 6 hunting right clause
CaseB_TestB: Qualified privilege in libel: a communication is privileged where the maker has an interest/duty to communicate and the recipient has a corresponding interest/duty; if privileged, liability requires proof of malice, and the publisher is protected even if language is “violent or excessively strong” if he “might have honestly and on reasonable grounds believed” it true (and necessary)
BaselineB: Common law: definition of qualified privilege from Adam v. Ward (HL) and SCC discussion in Netupsky v. Craig, [1973] S.C.R. 55
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 159(8) obscenity test as the exclusive standard for sex-based obscenity across the Code (displacing Hicklin): a work is obscene if it is a “publication a dominant characteristic of which is the undue exploitation of sex (or sex plus crime, horror, cruelty, violence)” and this statutory test governs wherever the obscenity allegation “revolves around sex considerations”.
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, s. 159(8) (and its interaction with ss. 159(1), 163, 164) against the backdrop of the common law Hicklin test (R. v. Hicklin (1868)))
CaseB_TestB: Duty to accommodate (employer/union) in adverse-effect discrimination: the discriminator must take “reasonable measures short of undue hardship”; undue hardship is assessed contextually (e.g., “financial cost, disruption of a collective agreement, problems of morale of other employees, interchangeability of work force and facilities, … safety”), and unions are liable where they cause/contribute to the discriminatory rule or impede reasonable accommodation.
BaselineB: Statute (Human Rights Act, S.B.C. 1984, c. 22, ss. 8(1)(a),(b),(4), 9(a)-(c)) as interpreted through SCC common-law/human-rights jurisprudence (notably O'Malley and Central Alberta Dairy Pool)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory obscenity test is exclusive for sex-based obscenity across the Criminal Code: apply Criminal Code s. 159(8) (“any publication a dominant characteristic of which is the undue exploitation of sex ... shall be deemed to be obscene”) and do not apply the common law Hicklin test where the allegation of obscenity “revolves around sex considerations”.
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, s. 159(8) definition of obscenity) in tension with common law Hicklin obscenity test; prior SCC discussion in Brodie v. The Queen.
CaseB_TestB: Duty to accommodate in the presence of a collectively-bargained automatic termination clause: the negotiated absence period is “a factor to consider” and may be evidence of undue hardship, but “does not definitively determine” accommodation because “each case must be evaluated on the basis of its particular circumstances”; undue hardship is assessed “globally starting from the beginning of the absence, not from the expiry” of the negotiated period.
BaselineB: Common law / human rights framework (Meiorin test for justifying a discriminatory standard, including accommodation to the point of undue hardship) applied in labour-arbitration context; informed by Quebec Charter equality norms.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Federal jurisdiction over cable television as a single interprovincial/international “undertaking”: no constitutional demarcation at the point where CATV receives Hertzian waves; content regulation is inseparable from regulating the undertaking
BaselineA: Constitution (B.N.A. Act/Constitution Act, 1867), ss. 91 and 92(10)(a), as interpreted in the Radio Reference (In re Regulation and Control of Radio Communication in Canada, [1932] A.C. 304) and related “undertaking” jurisprudence (e.g., Winner)
CaseB_TestB: Income tax “proceeds of disposition” for sale of forest tenures: purchaser’s assumed reforestation obligations are excluded where they are an embedded future cost that depresses the tenure’s value (not a distinct existing liability assumed as part of sale price)
BaselineB: Statute: Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), s. 13(21) (“proceeds of disposition” includes “the sale price of property that has been sold”), applying the general principle that assumption of a vendor’s liability may form part of sale price (e.g., Telus Communications (Edmonton) Inc.; Loyens; Lord Elgin Hotel)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Immovable by nature (Civil Code): a structure is immovable where it adheres (directly or indirectly) to land or a building so the attachment is not “purely transitory and accidental”; for wire networks, “the vertical attachment of a network of wires to the ground is in itself enough to make these wires immovable”, and separation of ownership of poles/land is irrelevant
BaselineA: Statute + civil law: Retail Sales Tax Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 71, ss. 2(3) ("moveable property" = property not considered immoveable by Quebec law) and 6 (tax on purchase of moveable property), applied by reference to Civil Code arts. 374 et seq. (immovables/movables). Key baseline authorities applied/extended: Montreal Light, Heat and Power Consolidated v. City of Westmount, [1926] S.C.R. 515; Lower St. Lawrence Power Co. v. L’Immeuble Landry Ltée, [1926] S.C.R. 655; Bélair v. City of Ste-Rose (1922), 63 S.C.R. 526
CaseB_TestB: Punitive damages for breach of contract (wrongful dismissal): available only rarely; requires an actionable wrong beyond the breach (typically tortious conduct) and conduct that is “extreme” and “deserving of punishment because of its harsh, vindictive, reprehensible and malicious nature”; Restatement s. 355 approach: punitive damages not recoverable for breach of contract unless the conduct is also a tort for which punitive damages are recoverable
BaselineB: Common law of damages for wrongful dismissal and punitive damages: Addis v. Gramophone Co., [1909] A.C. 488; Peso Silver Mines Ltd. (N.P.L.) v. Cropper, [1966] S.C.R. 673; plus punitive-damages jurisprudence (e.g., Rookes v. Barnard, [1964] A.C. 1129; McElroy v. Cowper-Smith and Woodman, [1967] S.C.R. 425; H. L. Weiss Forwarding Ltd. v. Omnus, [1976] 1 S.C.R. 776) as discussed and applied
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Parent’s contributory negligence / contribution: whether the parent “depart[ed] from the generally accepted standard of care” (i.e., “the accepted standard of care by parents generally in the community”) in supervising the child
BaselineA: Common law negligence (standard of care / contributory negligence), framed through prior authority referenced in the reasons (e.g., Ware’s Taxi Ltd. v. Gilliham, and the general negligence duty language from Donoghue v. Stevenson)
CaseB_TestB: Clause-5 election/repudiation in real estate sale after fire: purchaser may elect either to “have the proceeds of the insurance and complete the purchase” or “cancel the Agreement”; attempting to impose additional conditions is “dictating different terms” and “constituted a repudiation” the vendor may accept
BaselineB: Common law of contracts and interpretation of the parties’ agreement (standard form APS), especially clause 5 (risk/insurance election) and clause 9 (time of the essence), against the background common-law risk rule for purchasers pending closing
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Matrimonial property constructive trust / unjust enrichment: constructive trust may be imposed where the facts show “an enrichment, a corresponding deprivation, and the absence of any juristic reason” (and the court then makes a “fair, equitable distribution having regard to the respective contributions”).
BaselineA: Common law (equitable constructive trust and restitution/unjust enrichment; discussed via Murdoch v. Murdoch, Deglman v. Guaranty Trust Company, and English trust authorities such as Hussey v. Palmer).
CaseB_TestB: Access to court exhibits test: whether to grant access/copying turns on a discretionary balancing in which “N's privacy interests as a person acquitted of a crime outweigh the public right of access” and the court “is bound to inquire into the use to be made of [the exhibits] and is fully entitled to regulate that use”; curtailment is justified where needed to protect “the innocent”.
BaselineB: Common law open court/access principles and the court’s supervisory power over its records (Attorney General of Nova Scotia v. MacIntyre), applied alongside procedural context (Nova Scotia Civil Procedure Rule 30.11(6)).
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Limitation Act s. 6(4)(b) postponement test: time runs only when a properly advised reasonable person would conclude the plaintiff, given their own circumstances and interests, could reasonably bring an action; postponement requires interests/circumstances that are “serious, significant, and compelling” (no tactical concerns)
BaselineA: Statute (Limitation Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 266, s. 6(4)(b) (and the s. 6(4) framework including s. 6(4)(a) and “appropriate advice” in s. 6(5)(a)))
CaseB_TestB: Two-part stay framework under Arbitration Act s. 15 in insolvency/receivership: (1) applicant shows an arguable case for four technical prerequisites; (2) stay is mandatory unless, on a balance of probabilities in a “clear case”, the arbitration agreement is “void, inoperative or incapable of being performed” — including inoperability where enforcing arbitration would compromise the orderly and efficient resolution of a court-ordered receivership (non-exhaustive factors listed)
BaselineB: Statute (Arbitration Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 55, s. 15(1)-(2), interpreted alongside Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. B-3, ss. 183(1) and 243(1)(c))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: When does 5-year extinctive prescription begin for engineers’ percentage-based fees on an uncompleted/suspended project: prescription runs only when the fee is due—either “on completion of the work” or “at the time it was suspended, after a decision clearly communicated” to the engineers (and, under the tariff, generally not before the call for tenders or clear termination).
BaselineA: Combination: Civil Code art. 2260(6) (extinctive prescription) plus general principles of bilateral contracts (payment not demandable before performance absent agreement) and the Quebec “Tariff of fee for Professional Engineers” (O.C. 891, Sept. 4, 1957) governing when/ how percentage fees become due.
CaseB_TestB: Discretionary test for enforcing foreign letters rogatory under Canada Evidence Act s. 43: even if statutory/regulatory bars are uncertain, a court “may, in its or his discretion” refuse enforcement where doing so would run counter to asserted Canadian public policy/sovereignty; the court should not “take issue with the government’s determination of public policy or to measure its impact.”
BaselineB: Statute plus common law discretion/comity: Canada Evidence Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-10, s. 43 (express discretion to order examination/production) informed by comity principles and public policy limits (as discussed with reference to Re Westinghouse Electric Corp. and Duquesne Light Co. and Rio Tinto Zinc Corp. v. Westinghouse).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “nude” in Criminal Code s. 170: s. 170(2) is a deeming provision that extends (does not restrict) s. 170(1)(a); for complete nudity the Crown need not prove it “offend[ed] against public decency or order”
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, s. 170(1)(a) ("Every one who, without lawful excuse, (a) is nude in a public place...") and s. 170(2) ("For the purpose of this section a person is nude who is so clad as to offend against public decency or order"); interpreted in light of predecessor s. 205A ("shall be deemed to be nude")
CaseB_TestB: When the Crown improperly “splits its case” by adducing reply evidence that sandwiches the defence, the curative proviso in Criminal Code s. 613(1)(b)(iii) (“no substantial wrong or miscarriage of justice”) cannot be applied where the appellate court cannot realistically assess the remaining evidence after extracting the improper evidence
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, s. 613(1)(b)(iii) (curative proviso: appeal may be dismissed if “no substantial wrong or miscarriage of justice” occurred) applied to trial error involving reply evidence / splitting the Crown’s case
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 170 nudity offence: “nude” in s. 170(1)(a) keeps its ordinary meaning of complete bareness; s. 170(2) is a deeming provision that extends nudity to being “so clad as to offend against public decency or order”, so the Crown need not prove offence to public decency/order where there is total nudity (absent lawful excuse).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, s. 170(1)(a) and s. 170(2); interpretive comparison to predecessor s. 205A).
CaseB_TestB: Availability of certiorari in criminal proceedings: certiorari is available to parties only for a “jurisdictional error” by a provincial court judge; jurisdictional errors occur where the court fails to observe a mandatory statutory provision or breaches natural justice (legal errors, including errors of law on the face of the record, are not enough).
BaselineB: Common law constrained by statute (Criminal Code, s. 674 prohibition on interlocutory appeals; common-law certiorari principles as synthesized from cases such as Cohen, Skogman, Patterson, Forsythe, Dubois, Deschamplain).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Workmen’s Compensation Act s. 8 “additional sum” claim where victim partly at fault: claimant cannot recover any additional sum from the third party if the compensation received already equals/exceeds the claimant’s reduced civil claim (i.e., the portion of loss attributable to the third party’s fault); Commission is subrogated pleno jure to that extent and has priority
BaselineA: Statute and Civil Code: Workmen’s Compensation Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 159, ss. 7(3) (subrogation pleno jure) and 8 (right to claim “any additional sum required”); Civil Code art. 1157 (partial payment and creditor priority) and art. 1056 (civil claim for death damages), as applied with SCC authorities Rainville Automobile Ltd. v. Primiano; Hôpital Notre-Dame de l’Espérance and Théoret v. Laurent; distinguished Brink’s Express v. Plaisance
CaseB_TestB: Contract of service salary/guarantee enforceability after employee signs with another club: employer’s obligation to pay depends on the employee being “available and willing to provide the services”; signing/playing for another team is a breach that frees the employer from further payment obligations
BaselineB: Common law contract principles applied to an employment contract (repudiation/breach and continuing obligations) plus interpretation of the parties’ written contract terms (notably clauses requiring exclusive services and the “guaranteed” salary language)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Workmen’s Compensation Act s. 8 “additional sum” entitlement where Commission is subrogated: if the compensation received is not merely a partial payment of the claimant’s civil-law claim (e.g., because the victim’s fault reduces the third party’s liability), the dependant cannot claim any “additional sum required” beyond the compensation; the Commission has priority to recover up to what it paid
BaselineA: Statute + Civil Code (Quebec): Workmen’s Compensation Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 159, ss. 7(3) (subrogation) and 8 (additional sum); Civil Code art. 1157 (partial payment/subrogation priority) and art. 1056 (wrongful death claim). SCC also relies on prior SCC cases on contributory fault reducing recovery (Rainville Automobile Ltd. v. Primiano; Hôpital Notre-Dame de l’Espérance and Théoret v. Laurent) and distinguishes Brink’s Express v. Plaisance.
CaseB_TestB: Judicial independence / financial security framework: (1) independence is assessed by whether “a reasonable person who is fully informed of all the circumstances would consider that a particular court enjoyed the necessary independent status”; and (2) any government measure affecting “any aspect of the remuneration conditions of judges” triggers a constitutional duty to use an “independent, effective and objective” commission process, with any rejection of recommendations reviewable on a “simple rationality test”
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine + Charter: Valente v. The Queen (reasonable-person test; three characteristics), and Reference re Remuneration of Judges of the Provincial Court of Prince Edward Island (institutional financial security; commission requirement; simple rationality review). Also grounded in Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms s. 11(d) and the Preamble to the Constitution Act, 1867.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Suspensive effect on an inferior criminal court’s power when served with a prohibition/quash motion endorsed to require a Rule 7 return: “there must be a suspension of jurisdiction when an application to quash or a combined application to prohibit and to quash is served on the inferior court with the command, under the Rules, to make a return forthwith” (and non-return has “the same effect as if a return was properly made”).
BaselineA: Regulation/rules + statute + common law (Ontario Criminal Rules 4-8 (esp. Rules 6-8); Criminal Code, s. 714; common law certiorari suspension principle as discussed via authorities like R. v. Foster and R. v. Titchmarsh).
CaseB_TestB: Section 15(1) equality analysis (La Forest J. majority): three-step test—(1) distinction; (2) disadvantage; (3) whether distinction is based on an “irrelevant personal characteristic” enumerated/analogous, assessed by “relevancy…to the functional values underlying the law” in its larger context.
BaselineB: Common law/Charter jurisprudence (Charter s. 15(1) as interpreted in Andrews v. Law Society of British Columbia and Miron v. Trudel; applied to Old Age Security Act, ss. 2 and 19(1)).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Fair comment in defamation requires proof that the impugned comment was an honest expression of the real opinion of the person making/publishing it; absent evidence of the writer’s honest belief (and where the publisher/editor disavow belief), the defence cannot go to the jury. Key quotes: 'Comment must be published honestly in that it is the expression of the defendant's real opinion.' And: 'in the absence of any proof of the honest belief of the writers ... and having regard to the denial of honest belief by the defendants themselves, the defence of fair comment cannot ... prevail.'
BaselineA: Common law (defamation—defence of fair comment), drawing on authorities cited in the reasons including Turner v. Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer Pictures Ltd. and Slim v. Daily Telegraph Ltd. (as discussed in the SCC reasons).
CaseB_TestB: Section 2(a) freedom of religion—state-imposed burden threshold: indirect burdens can infringe, but only if non-trivial. Key quote: 'Legislative or administrative action which increases the cost of practising or otherwise manifesting religious beliefs is not prohibited if the burden is trivial or insubstantial.'
BaselineB: Constitution/Charter (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 2(a), interpreted in light of R. v. Big M Drug Mart Ltd.; also references to s. 27).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Fair comment in defamation requires proof that the impugned comment was an honest expression of the real opinion of the person making/publishing it (each publisher stands in the position of the original writer); absent evidence of the writers' honest belief (and with the newspaper/editor denying such belief), the defence is unavailable
BaselineA: Common law (defence of fair comment in defamation), drawing on authorities including Turner v. Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer Pictures Ltd. and Slim v. Daily Telegraph Ltd. (as discussed in the reasons)
CaseB_TestB: Contempt of court: the party alleging contempt must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the alleged contemnor had actual personal knowledge of the order (personal service or actual knowledge); service on a solicitor does not, without supporting circumstances, fix ministers with knowledge; vicarious liability does not apply to contempt against natural persons
BaselineB: Common law contempt requirements (personal service or actual personal knowledge) plus interpretation of Federal Court Rules (C.R.C. 1978, c. 663, Rules 308, 311, 355) as not altering contempt elements
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Fair comment defence requires proof that the defamatory comment was an honest expression of the real opinion of the writer/publisher; absent evidence of the letter-writers' honest belief (and with publisher/editor denying belief), the defence cannot go to the jury
BaselineA: Common law defamation (fair comment defence), drawing on authorities including Turner v. Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer Pictures Ltd. and Slim v. Daily Telegraph Ltd. (as discussed in the reasons)
JudgeA: Ritchie J. (with concurrence noted by Laskin C.J., Pigeon and Pratte JJ.; Martland J. and Beetz J. concurring in result)
CaseB_TestB: Garofoli review of wiretap authorizations: errors/misstatements in the ITO are factors only; court must excise affected material and ask whether remaining independent information provides sufficient reliable grounds on which an authorization could reasonably be based (no automatic vitiation)
BaselineB: Common law/Charter criminal procedure framework for reviewing wiretap authorizations as stated in R. v. Garofoli, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 1421
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Intra vires test for CRTC regulations under Broadcasting Act s. 16: validity is tested by determining objectively whether the regulation is made “in furtherance of [the Commission’s] objects” by dealing with “a class of subject referred to in s. 3” (broadcasting policy).
BaselineA: Statute (Broadcasting Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. B-11, ss. 3, 15, 16; applied to Radio (A.M.) Broadcasting Regulations, s. 5(1)(k))
CaseB_TestB: Jury verdict review in Quebec civil liability where fault is assessed by the “prudent and reasonable man”: the verdict is binding unless “unreasonable”; judge sets the legal criterion, jury applies it to decide whether conduct meets the prudent/reasonable-person standard.
BaselineB: Statute/civil law (Civil Code art. 1053; Code of Civil Procedure arts. 363, 380; with reliance on Metropolitan Railway Co. v. Jackson for judge/jury roles)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Limits on a provincial commission of inquiry re federal institutions + effect of Federal Court Act s. 41(2) national security certificate: a province may inquire into specific criminal acts by RCMP members, but cannot (directly or indirectly) inquire into RCMP administration/management; and where a minister certifies under s. 41(2) that production would be injurious to national security, production/discovery is refused without examination and the commissioner must accept the affidavit (not being a superior court).
BaselineA: Combination: Constitution (B.N.A. Act ss. 91, 92), statute (Federal Court Act, R.S.C. 1970 (2nd Supp.), c. 10, s. 41(1)-(2); Public Inquiry Commission Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 11; Code of Civil Procedure arts. 846-850), and common law Crown privilege/immunity principles (as discussed via cases such as Quebec North Shore Paper; Gauthier; Alberta v. C.T.C.).
CaseB_TestB: Contested custody (natural parent vs prospective adoptive parents): applying parens patriae/equity under Domestic Relations Ordinance s. 39, the court must treat the child's welfare as the predominant/paramount consideration, decided on 'all relevant factors' (including psychological, spiritual and emotional welfare), with parental claims considered but set aside where the child's welfare requires.
BaselineB: Statute plus equity/common law: Domestic Relations Ordinance, R.O.N.W.T. 1974, c. D-9, ss. 28(1), 35(2), 37, 39 (equity rules to prevail where not conflicting), informed by parens patriae jurisprudence (citing Re Moores and Feldstein; Beson; Racine; and the SCC 'trilogy' Re Baby Duffell; Hepton; Re Agar).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Public Authorities Protection Act s. 11 scope test: whether the impugned act/omission falls within a "statutory or other public duty or authority" by segregating statutory functions into (1) those with a "public aspect or connotation" vs (2) "private executive or private administrative"/"managerial, internal or operational" matters; only the former get s. 11’s six-month limitation protection
BaselineA: Statute: The Public Authorities Protection Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 374, s. 11, interpreted in relation to The Housing Development Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 213, s. 6(2); informed by prior case law discussed in the reasons (e.g., McGonegal et al. v. Gray et al., [1952] 2 S.C.R. 274; Bradford Corporation v. Myers, [1916] 1 A.C. 242)
CaseB_TestB: Bazley vicarious liability "significant connection" test (with enumerated factors) for intentional torts: vicarious liability may be imposed where there is a "significant connection" between the enterprise/employment and the wrong, assessed via factors including (a) opportunity to abuse power, (b) furtherance of employer’s interests, (c) intimacy/conditions conducive to the wrong, (d) power conferred over the victim, and (e) victim vulnerability
BaselineB: Common law: vicarious liability framework from Bazley v. Curry, [1999] 2 S.C.R. 534 (and related discussion of Jacobi v. Griffiths, [1999] 2 S.C.R. 570)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Exemption-from-seizure in an insurance policy is effective only for a true third-party beneficiary; a universal legatee/heir is not a beneficiary and cannot invoke the policy clause or C.C.P. art. 553(3). Key holding: “respondent definitely cannot be considered as the ‘beneficiary’ of the policy” because “a person’s heirs are not third parties”; therefore the exemption clause “can therefore have effect only in favor of a true beneficiary, that is, a third party on whom the benefit is conferred.”
BaselineA: Statute/civil code provisions governing exemption from seizure and third-party stipulations: Code of Civil Procedure, art. 553(3); Civil Code (C.C.), arts. 597, 735, 1028 (and the concept of stipulation for a third party).
CaseB_TestB: No-fault liability for neighbourhood disturbances under art. 976 C.C.Q.: liability turns on whether neighbours suffered “abnormal or excessive annoyances” beyond “the limit of tolerance” owed “according to the nature or location of their land or local custom”; “conduct is not the deciding criterion” and the regime is “based on the extent of the annoyances suffered by the victim being excessive rather than on the conduct of the person who allegedly caused them.”
BaselineB: Statute (Civil Code of Québec): art. 976 C.C.Q. (neighbourhood annoyances / limit of tolerance).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: When a provincial superior court’s jurisdiction is ousted by a federal regulatory scheme: superior court retains jurisdiction unless a “specific provision of law” assigns the matter exclusively elsewhere; existence of possible Commission proceedings does not preclude a tort/fault action raising the same legal issue
BaselineA: Statute (Quebec Code of Civil Procedure, art. 31; An Act respecting The Bell Telephone Company of Canada, s. 5(4)-(6) as amended; National Transportation Act, s. 45(1); Bell General Regulations/Rules 2, 7, 9)
CaseB_TestB: Test governing whether the Crown may reopen its case: the “keystone principle” is prejudice to the accused; discretion narrows by trial stage, and after the defence has started to answer the case reopening is permitted only in the “narrowest or most exceptional of circumstances” (e.g., defence contributed to omission or matter of form)
BaselineB: Common law discretion on reopening (notably Robillard v. The Queen; also Kishen Singh and related reopening jurisprudence) informed by Charter self-incrimination principles (ss. 7, 11(c), 13)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Admissibility of cross-examining an accused on juvenile delinquencies as “convictions” under s. 12 Canada Evidence Act (and related proof by admission): “any offence” includes Criminal Code violations dealt with under the Juvenile Delinquents Act, and “a finding of delinquency under this Act is equivalent to a conviction within the meaning of s. 12”; an admitted conviction “does not need to be otherwise proven” absent “exceptional circumstances showing clearly that the admission was made in error”.
BaselineA: Statute: Canada Evidence Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-10, s. 12(1)-(2) (plus interaction with Juvenile Delinquents Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. J-3, and also discussed: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 593).
CaseB_TestB: Criminal Code indictment-amendment test for variance between a particular and the proof (s. 529): the court’s “only question” is whether amendment would “prejudice” the accused (and if so whether it can be cured), assessed via s. 529(4) factors including “whether the accused has been misled or prejudiced in his defence” and “whether… the proposed amendment can be made without injustice being done”; if no prejudice, amendment should be made and appellate court may amend under s. 613(1)(b)(i) and (3).
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 529(4)-(5), 613(1)(b)(i), 613(3) (in context of Narcotic Control Act charge).
