Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Dickson J.’s four-factor criteria for whether an administrative decision is required by law to be made on a judicial or quasi-judicial basis (for Federal Court Act s. 28 reviewability): (1) hearing contemplated; (2) affects rights/obligations; (3) adversary process; (4) obligation to apply substantive rules to individual cases (vs broad policy) — “factors to be weighed and evaluated, no one of which is necessarily determinative.”
BaselineA: Statute (Federal Court Act, s. 28; definition in s. 2) informed by common law/natural justice jurisprudence (e.g., Guay v. Lafleur; Russell v. Duke of Norfolk).
CaseB_TestB: Stillman s. 24(2) “trial fairness” framework: classify Charter-breached evidence as non-conscriptive vs conscriptive; if conscriptive, Crown must prove on balance of probabilities it was discoverable by alternative non-conscriptive means (independent source or inevitable discovery); if not discoverable, evidence is excluded “as a general rule” without weighing other Collins factors.
BaselineB: Statute (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 24(2)) building on common law/Charter jurisprudence, especially R. v. Collins.
JudgeB: Cory J. (for Lamer C.J. and La Forest, Sopinka, Cory and Iacobucci JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory limits on interim rate-setting under s. 31 Gas Utilities Act: the Board may not set prospective interim rates that (in effect) recover pre-application revenue shortfalls, except as permitted for post-application losses due to undue delay; the proper inquiry is whether interim rates will "produce an amount in excess of the estimated total revenue requirements" for the period because they include pre-application shortfalls.
BaselineA: Statute: The Gas Utilities Act, R.S.A. 1970, c. 158, ss. 27-28, 31 (plus The Public Utilities Board Act, R.S.A. 1970, c. 302, s. 62; and The Administrative Procedures Act, R.S.A. 1970, c. 2, s. 8).
CaseB_TestB: Cuerrier fraud-vitiated consent test under Criminal Code s. 265(3)(c) (Cory J.): consent to sexual intercourse is vitiated by fraud where (1) dishonesty (including non-disclosure of HIV-positive status) related to obtaining consent is proven objectively, and (2) the dishonesty results in deprivation by exposing the complainant to a "significant risk of serious bodily harm"; plus the Crown must prove the complainant would have refused unprotected sex if informed.
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, ss. 265(3)(c) and 268, interpreted using criminal fraud jurisprudence (e.g., R. v. Olan; R. v. Théroux; R. v. Zlatic) and rejecting the prior "nature and quality of the act" limitation associated with R. v. Clarence.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Interpretation of 1977 Parole Act amendments: day parole may be ended either by revocation (s. 10(1)(e) triggering s. 20 consequences) or by termination (s. 10(2)); “parole” in s. 20 includes day parole and “recommitment” wording creates no operative ambiguity
BaselineA: Statute: Parole Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. P-2 (as amended effective Oct. 15, 1977), especially ss. 2 (definition of “parole” includes day parole), 10(1)(e), 10(2), and 20(1)-(3) (revocation/recommitment and sentence calculation/credits)
CaseB_TestB: Palmer criteria apply to fresh evidence on appeal from sentence: (1) due diligence (flexible factor), (2) relevance, (3) credibility, and (4) evidence such that, if believed, it could reasonably be expected to have affected the result; admission only if in the interests of justice
BaselineB: Common law test from Palmer v. The Queen, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 759 (fresh evidence criteria), applied in the statutory context of Criminal Code, ss. 683 and 687
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Exercise of SCC discretion under Supreme Court Act s. 52 to vary interest: default is interest from the trial-judgment date unless the Court orders otherwise; Court may limit pre-SCC-judgment interest based on case circumstances (e.g., delay attributable to successful party)
BaselineA: Statute: Supreme Court Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. S-19, s. 52 (as amended in 1976) and Interest Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-18, ss. 13-14
CaseB_TestB: Whether procedural fairness/natural justice applies to Governor in Council under National Transportation Act s. 64(1): interpret the statutory scheme; where s. 64(1) confers broad, discretionary, quasi-legislative rate-review power with no procedural standards, no duty of fairness is implied beyond staying within jurisdictional boundaries/conditions precedent
BaselineB: Statute: National Transportation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. N-17, s. 64(1) (contrasted with s. 64(2)); plus common-law fairness/natural justice jurisprudence (e.g., Nicholson) used as interpretive context
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory-limit rule for groundwater pumping: pumping above 10,000 gallons/day (absent a permit) is per se “unreasonable” and thus supports nuisance/negligence liability when it causes damage; no “right to pump” defence for excess pumping
BaselineA: Statute (The Ontario Water Resources Commission Act / Ontario Water Resources Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 332, s. 37) interacting with common-law nuisance/negligence (and the prior “English Rule” on percolating water as background)
CaseB_TestB: Meaning of “unlawful and intentional interference” for exemplary damages under Quebec Charter s. 49(2): intent exists where the actor (1) desires/intends the consequences of the wrongful conduct, or (2) acts with full knowledge of the “immediate and natural” or at least “extremely probable” consequences
BaselineB: Statute/quasi-constitutional statute (Quebec Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms, s. 49(2)) as interpreted in light of SCC precedent (Quebec (Public Curator) v. Syndicat national des employés de l’hôpital St-Ferdinand, [1996] 3 S.C.R. 211)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Effect of transfer of a registered motor vehicle on liability insurance: if the registered owner has not complied with Highway Code s. 13(1)-(2), they are "deemed to be the owner" for liability/insurance purposes (s. 13(6)), so the transfer is treated as not having occurred for civil-liability coverage and the buyer/driver with the deemed-owner’s consent is covered by the omnibus clause
BaselineA: Statute: Highway Code, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 234, s. 13(6) (and related compliance duties in s. 13(1)-(2)); applied to the civil-liability section/omnibus clause of the auto policy
CaseB_TestB: Garofoli leave (threshold) test for cross-examining a wiretap affiant: leave should be granted only where the defence shows a "reasonable likelihood" that cross-examination will elicit testimony of "probative value" on a material issue for the reviewing judge (relevance/materiality) in the s. 8 review of the authorization
BaselineB: Common law: R. v. Garofoli, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 1421 (threshold/leave requirement for cross-examining the affiant on a wiretap authorization review)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Direct action under Highway Victims Indemnity Act, s. 6: insurer is directly liable to third parties only for “damage covered by liability insurance”; s. 6 removes only nullity/lapse defences and “does not extend the insurance contract to what it does not cover” (coverage/excluded-risk analysis via the policy’s definition of “automobile” and whether damage was caused “first and foremost” by the trailer’s use).
BaselineA: Statute + contract interpretation: Highway Victims Indemnity Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 232, s. 6 (and related context ss. 3, 39, 43) applied together with the insurance policy’s contractual definition of “automobile”; guided by General Security Insurance Company of Canada v. Bélanger, [1977] 1 S.C.R. 802 (scope of s. 6 and distinction between lapse and exclusion of risk).
CaseB_TestB: Lease covenant-to-insure/subrogation test: tenant escapes liability for negligently caused fire only if the landlord’s covenant “to insure” runs to the tenant’s benefit; the covenant benefits the tenant “unless there is another explanation” (e.g., option-to-purchase provisions) consistent with leaving the fire-risk on the tenant.
BaselineB: Common law of landlord-tenant/contract interpretation and insurer subrogation, drawing on Ross Southward Tire Ltd. v. Pyrotech Products Ltd., [1976] 2 S.C.R. 35 and Agnew-Surpass Shoe Stores Ltd. v. Cummer-Yonge Investments Ltd., [1976] 2 S.C.R. 221; United Motors Service Inc. v. Hutson, [1937] S.C.R. 294 distinguished.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Qualified privilege in defamation defeated only by proof of malice; privilege protects even excessive language if the defendant "might have honestly and on reasonable grounds believed that what he wrote or said was true" (Adam v. Ward as applied in Netupsky v. Craig)
BaselineA: Common law (qualified privilege and malice), drawing on Adam v. Ward, [1917] A.C. 309 and Netupsky v. Craig, [1973] S.C.R. 55
CaseB_TestB: Sufficiency of reasons (Sheppard/Braich): two-stage inquiry—(1) are the reasons inadequate; (2) if so, do they prevent appellate review? Core question: are the reasons "sufficiently amenable to appellate review" / is there "an impediment to appellate review"
BaselineB: Common law appellate review doctrine on adequacy of reasons, based on R. v. Sheppard, 2002 SCC 26 and R. v. Braich, 2002 SCC 27 (in the context of Criminal Code, s. 686 appellate intervention)
JudgeB: Bastarache and Abella JJ. (LeBel J. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Fault for unlawful arrest: police may arrest without warrant only on "reasonable and probable grounds" that must "take into account all the information available" (cannot ignore exculpatory information); and coroner’s s. 38 detention power cannot be used to jail a suspect (abuse of power).
BaselineA: Combination of statute and civil law: Civil Code arts. 1053, 1054 (fault and employer liability) plus Criminal Code 1953-54 s. 435 (warrantless arrest on reasonable and probable grounds) and Coroners' Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 29, s. 38 (detention of witnesses).
CaseB_TestB: Validity of dismissal of probationary constable: dismissal power is "exclusively" in the Police Board (Reg. 680, s. 27(b) / collective agreement) and cannot be delegated; no effective discharge where the Board does not itself act/notify and does not let the constable know his case will be considered (no meaningful opportunity to respond to the decision-maker).
BaselineB: Statute/regulation and related instruments: The Police Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 351, s. 29 (collective bargaining authority) and Regulation 680, s. 27(b) (authority to dispense with services within 18 months), applied alongside the collective agreement (s. 9).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Municipal office disqualification for having a direct or indirect “interest in any contract” with the city (broad, ordinary-meaning approach; directors/officers have at least an indirect interest beyond mere shareholding)
BaselineA: Statute (Moncton Consolidation Act, 1946 (N.B.), c. 101, s. 6), interpreted using the Angrignon principle that “interested in” has no technical meaning and must be given its ordinary meaning
CaseB_TestB: Statutory interpretation of whether “institution” in OLA s. 22 includes municipalities (contextual/scheme-based coherence analysis; Charter values only if genuine ambiguity)
BaselineB: Statute (Official Languages Act, S.N.B. 2002, c. O-0.5, ss. 1 “institution”, 22) applying the modern principle of statutory interpretation (Driedger) and limiting Charter-values interpretation to genuine ambiguity (Bell ExpressVu)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Qualified privilege—threshold for leaving express malice to the jury: malice must be supported by evidence that "raises a probability of its existence" ("more consistent with its existence than with its non-existence"), not merely "some evidence"/a "scintilla".
BaselineA: Common law (defamation/qualified privilege and malice), drawing on authorities including Adam v. Ward, Somerville v. Hawkins, and SCC confirmation in Sun Life Assurance Co. of Canada v. Dalrymple.
CaseB_TestB: Blood Tribe clear-intent requirement for statutory abrogation of solicitor-client privilege: only where legislative language "evinces a clear intent" may privilege be abrogated; applied to s. 232(1) ITA (accounting records "shall be deemed not" privileged).
BaselineB: Statute (Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), ss. 231.2(1), 231.7(1), and definition in s. 232(1) "solicitor-client privilege"), interpreted through the common-law/constitutional interpretive principle from Canada (Privacy Commissioner) v. Blood Tribe Department of Health.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Priority of B.C. Payment of Wages Act s. 5A wage lien: lien arises when wages are earned and takes priority only over interests created after that date; it does not defeat prior mortgages and therefore attaches only to the employer’s equity in the property
BaselineA: Statute: Payment of Wages Act, 1962 (B.C.), c. 45, ss. 5 and 5A (especially s. 5A(1)-(2))
CaseB_TestB: Suppletive application of C.C.Q. dissolution scheme to legal persons: arts. 355-364 C.C.Q. apply to fill gaps in special statutes (art. 334), and forced dissolution may be ordered under art. 355(2) where the legal person is incapable of accomplishing its objects (impossibility/other legitimate cause)
BaselineB: Statute/Civil code: Civil Code of Québec, arts. 300, 334, 355 (and related arts. 355-364); considered alongside Companies Act (Quebec) and Code of Civil Procedure art. 829
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Residual discretion/inherent jurisdiction to grant a limited right of reply (or curative instruction) where Crown’s closing address causes prejudice: (1) usually cure by specific correcting reference in the jury charge; (2) if curative instructions will not suffice, in the “clearest cases of unfairness” grant a limited reply confined to the improper issues (e.g., Crown dramatically changes/adds theory in closing or misleads defence as to theory).
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 651(3)-(4) (order of addresses) plus common law inherent jurisdiction to ensure trial fairness (e.g., Selvey v. DPP; R. v. Osborn; Amato v. The Queen, as cited).
JudgeA: Cory, Iacobucci and Bastarache JJ. (for Gonthier, Cory, Iacobucci and Bastarache JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Charter-validity test for a statutory presumption under s. 11(d): a presumption complies with the presumption of innocence only if proof of the substituted/basic fact leads “inexorably” (i.e., necessarily in all cases) to the essential element it replaces; otherwise it violates s. 11(d) (and here s. 172.1(3) fails because representation of age online does not inexorably establish belief).
BaselineB: Combination of statute and constitutional/common law doctrine: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 172.1(3) (presumption re age) interpreted under Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 11(d), applying prior SCC presumption jurisprudence (Whyte; Downey; Audet; St-Onge Lamoureux, as cited).
JudgeB: Moldaver J. (Wagner C.J. and Gascon, Côté, Brown, Rowe and Martin JJ. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Adjudicator’s remedial power to substitute a lesser penalty for discharge where there is “just and sufficient cause” for some discipline but not for discharge (discipline as a continuum: financial penalty → suspension → discharge)
BaselineA: Statute + collective agreement: Public Service Labour Relations Act, R.S.N.B. 1973, c. P-25, s. 92(1)(b) (adjudication of “disciplinary action resulting in discharge, suspension or a financial penalty”) and collective agreement art. V(d) (“Discipline, suspension, demotion or discharge ... shall be for just and sufficient cause”) (distinguishing Port Arthur Shipbuilding Co. v. Arthurs, [1969] S.C.R. 85).
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 24(2) exclusion analysis: apply the R. v. Collins guidelines to decide whether, “having regard to all the circumstances”, admission of evidence obtained via a Charter breach would “bring the administration of justice into disrepute”
BaselineB: Statute/constitutional text + common law framework: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 24(2) (and ss. 7, 8) as interpreted by R. v. Collins, [1987] 1 S.C.R. 265 (applied).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Will-construction test: give effect to the testator’s overriding intention on a fair reading of the will; administrative/boilerplate clauses should not defeat a clearly expressed intention (here, legacy payable on disposition of the business ‘however that disposition was made’).
BaselineA: Common law (will construction/ascertaining testator’s intention from the will read as a whole; no specific baseline case cited in the reasons).
CaseB_TestB: Manslaughter legal causation with intervening acts: the Smithers/Nette test remains whether the accused’s dangerous unlawful acts were a ‘significant contributing cause of death’; ‘reasonable foreseeability’ and ‘intentional, independent act’ are non-determinative analytical aids.
BaselineB: Common law causation for manslaughter as set out in Smithers v. The Queen and confirmed in R. v. Nette (in the Criminal Code homicide context, including ss. 222, 224, 225).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Federal vs provincial labour jurisdiction: labour relations are provincially regulated unless the undertaking is a federal undertaking under the functional (operational nature) test; exclusive federal jurisdiction arises only if labour jurisdiction is an integral part of primary federal jurisdiction over another federal head of power
BaselineA: Common law constitutional division-of-powers doctrine for labour relations (functional/operational test; 'integral part of primary federal jurisdiction' principle) as reflected in cases cited including Toronto Electric Commissioners v. Snider and the Stevedoring Reference; applied alongside statutory context (Canada Labour Code s. 108 and definition of 'federal work, undertaking or business' in s. 2; Indian Act s. 88)
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 15(1) equality test (post-Kapp/Withler): (1) does the law create a distinction based on an enumerated or analogous ground? (2) does the distinction create disadvantage by perpetuating prejudice or stereotyping, assessed contextually without requiring a 'mirror comparator group'
BaselineB: Common law Charter jurisprudence interpreting s. 15(1) (Andrews; Law; Kapp) and the constitutional text of Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 15(1)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Bankruptcy Act s. 107(1)(j) overrides provincial Crown “privileges” so that provincial tax claims are paid pari passu as Crown claims, not as “secured creditors”, notwithstanding provincial statutory priority
BaselineA: Statute: Bankruptcy Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. B-3, ss. 2 (definition of “secured creditor”) and 107(1)(j) (scheme of distribution); interacting with Quebec Retail Sales Tax Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 71, s. 30 and Civil Code art. 1989 (registration of Crown privilege)
JudgeA: Pigeon J. (for Martland, Ritchie, Pigeon, Beetz, Pratte and McIntyre JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Public interest standing test (purposive, flexible weighing): (1) serious justiciable issue; (2) plaintiff has a real stake or is engaged; (3) proposed suit is, in all the circumstances, a reasonable and effective means to bring the issue to court
BaselineB: Common law: public interest standing framework from Borowski, Finlay, Canadian Council of Churches, Hy and Zel’s, Thorson, McNeil (as discussed and applied)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Crown prerogative priority applies only where Crown and subject claims are “of equal degree”; a prior registered second/collateral mortgage is of a higher degree than a later-registered Crown judgment, so priority is determined by Registry Act registration date (ss. 17-18).
BaselineA: Combination: common law Crown prerogative priority for debts “of equal degree” (The Queen v. Bank of Nova Scotia (1885), 11 S.C.R. 1) plus Nova Scotia Registry Act, R.S.N.S. 1967, c. 265, ss. 17-18 (and related civil procedure distribution rule).
CaseB_TestB: International jurisdiction by extension of domestic territorial jurisdiction: art. 71 C.C.P. applies to foreign defendants, so an incidental action in warranty “must be taken before the court in which the principal action is pending” and is “not subject to any limitation.”
BaselineB: Statute/civil code: Code of Civil Procedure, art. 71 (and discussion of art. 75); Civil Code, art. 27; plus the private international law principle that international jurisdiction is determined by extending domestic territorial jurisdiction rules (as recognized in Alimport and Trower).
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “detained” under Canadian Bill of Rights s. 2(c): “detain”/“detention” “connote some form of compulsory restraint” (i.e., associated with “actual physical restraint”/custody), so a roadside stop/sobriety screening where the driver is then “allowed to go away” is not “detention” and does not trigger a right to counsel as a “reasonable excuse” to refuse a breath demand
BaselineA: Statute: Canadian Bill of Rights, 1960 (Can.), c. 44, s. 2(c)(ii)-(iii), applied in the context of Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 234.1(1)-(2) (roadside breath demand/refusal “without reasonable excuse”); prior SCC context discussed: Brownridge v. The Queen; Hogan v. The Queen
CaseB_TestB: Tort of civil conspiracy (Canada Cement LaFarge): liability exists (1) where “the predominant purpose of the defendants’ conduct is to cause injury to the plaintiff” (means lawful or unlawful), OR (2) where defendants’ conduct is “unlawful”, “directed towards the plaintiff (alone or together with others)”, and defendants “should know in the circumstances that injury to the plaintiff is likely to and does result” (constructive intent); in both cases “there must be actual damage”
BaselineB: Common law tort of conspiracy to injure, drawing on Crofter Hand Woven Harris Tweed Co. v. Veitch and Sorrell v. Smith; and clarifying Canadian authorities including Gagnon v. Foundation Maritime Limited and International Brotherhood of Teamsters v. Therien; with comparative reliance on Lonrho Ltd. v. Shell Petroleum Co. Ltd.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 492 re-election validity: accused effectively re-elects judge-alone trial where (1) notice of desire to re-elect is given to the sheriff (s. 492(1)); (2) the accused attends at the time/place fixed (s. 492(2)-(3)); and (3) after the charge actually faced at trial is read, the accused (through counsel in the accused’s presence) communicates the re-election—formal reading of the exact s. 492(3) words may be excused where notice already states re-election under s. 492; failure to prefer a new Form 4 indictment under s. 496 after re-election does not invalidate proceedings if the indictment is already in Form 4.
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, s. 492 (re-election procedure) and related s. 496 (Form 4 indictment after re-election).
CaseB_TestB: Injurious affection where no land is taken (Expropriations Act, s. 1(e)(ii), s. 21): claimant must show the construction-caused loss would have been actionable at common law but for statutory authority—i.e., a nuisance meeting the Loiselle conditions, including that damage is to the land itself and is “occasioned by the construction of the public work, not by its user”; loss of prospect/view and general loss of amenities from a neighbouring highway’s construction is not actionable nuisance (reasonable user/balancing).
BaselineB: Statute: Expropriations Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 154, ss. 1 (definition of injurious affection) and 21 (compensation), incorporating common-law actionability; common-law baseline articulated via The Queen v. Loiselle, [1962] S.C.R. 624 (four conditions) and nuisance reasonableness concepts.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory-incorporation/jurisdiction test: under s. 137(1) of The Regional Municipality of Ottawa-Carleton Act, the Ontario Municipal Board may exercise only the incorporated powers in Municipal Act s. 14(11)(a), (b) and (d) (without the prefatory limits tied to s. 14(2) annexation/amalgamation), including power to make asset/liability adjustments the Board "may consider equitable" "in relation to the dissolution of the County of Carleton".
BaselineA: Statute: The Regional Municipality of Ottawa-Carleton Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 407, ss. 135-137, incorporating by reference The Municipal Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 284, s. 14(11)(a), (b), (d) (especially s. 14(11)(a): Board may make adjustments "as the Board may consider equitable").
CaseB_TestB: Constitutional mens rea minimum for murder: "it is a principle of fundamental justice that a conviction for murder cannot rest on anything less than proof beyond a reasonable doubt of subjective foresight of death"; provisions (like Criminal Code s. 213(a)) that "expressly eliminate[] the requirement for proof of subjective foresight" infringe Charter ss. 7 and 11(d).
BaselineB: Constitution (Charter): Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 7 and 11(d), applied to Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 213(a) (now s. 230(a)); built on/extends R. v. Vaillancourt, [1987] 2 S.C.R. 636 (objective foreseeability as constitutional minimum, with Martineau adopting subjective foresight as required).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Validity of one-party consent interception and admissibility: (1) a consent interception under Criminal Code s. 178.11(2)(a) makes the interception “lawfully made” for s. 178.16(1)(a); and (2) consent must be “voluntary (i.e. free from coercion) and made knowingly, with an awareness of the significance of the consent”
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code (Part IV.1, Protection of Privacy Act amendments), especially ss. 178.1 (definition of “private communication”), 178.11(2)(a) (consent to intercept), and 178.16(1) (admissibility: “unless (a) the interception was lawfully made; or (b) ... has expressly consented to the admission thereof”). Also relies on Rosen v. The Queen, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 961 (distinguishing confession voluntariness from consent to admit fixed recordings).
CaseB_TestB: Targeting an identifiable group under Criminal Code s. 319(2): the trier must assess “the totality of the evidence” to decide whether the accused’s statements “as a matter of fact, promoted hatred” of the particularized group; “the reference to ‘gypsies’ was but one item of evidence to consider” and it was not necessary to prove “interchangeability” of terms
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code ss. 319(2) (wilful promotion of hatred), 318(4) (definition of “identifiable group”), and 319(3) (defences). Also applies the common-law evidence doctrine of judicial notice as summarized in R. v. Find, 2001 SCC 32 (facts “so notorious” or “capable of immediate and accurate demonstration”).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Audi alteram partem / no ex parte evidence after the hearing: an appellate tribunal must not receive “necessary facts” or other evidence/representations from one side “behind the back of the other”; if it does, the decision is invalid if the material “might” have caused prejudice (no need to prove actual prejudice).
BaselineA: Common law natural justice (audi alteram partem) applied in a statutory university-appeal setting; statute involved but does not abrogate natural justice absent express language or necessary implication (Universities Act, 1974 (B.C.), ss. 58(1)-(3), 61). Key authorities cited in reasons include Kanda v. Government of the Federation of Malaya; Pfizer Co. Ltd. v. Deputy Minister of National Revenue for Customs and Excise; Board of Education v. Rice; Local Government Board v. Arlidge; Russell v. Duke of Norfolk.
CaseB_TestB: Workers’ compensation occupational-disease causation (and review): causation may be inferred from circumstantial evidence even with inconclusive/contrary expert evidence; under Workers Compensation Act s. 250(4), if evidence on causation is “evenly weighted” it must be resolved “in a manner that favours the worker”; on judicial review, a tribunal’s causation finding stands unless “patently unreasonable” (i.e., evidence viewed reasonably is incapable of supporting it).
BaselineB: Statutory scheme and standard: Workers Compensation Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 492, ss. 6 and 250(4) (plus s. 250(2) re mandatory policy application); Administrative Tribunals Act, S.B.C. 2004, c. 45, s. 58(2)(a) (patent unreasonableness). Common-law causation inference principle referenced from Snell v. Farrell.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Appellate intervention with a trial damages award: an appellate court may not substitute its own figure unless “a wrong principle of law was applied” or “the overall award is a wholly erroneous estimate of damages” (Andrews v. Grand & Toy, applied).
BaselineA: Common law (appellate review standard for damages) from Andrews et al. v. Grand & Toy Alberta Ltd. et al., [1978] 2 S.C.R. 229 at p. 235.
JudgeA: Martland J. (oral reasons for the Court)
CaseB_TestB: Videotape-only identification: once it is established the videotape “has not been altered or changed” and “depicts the scene of a crime”, it is admissible; a trier of fact may identify and convict on the videotape alone if satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt, assessing weight mainly by “clarity and quality” and (to a lesser extent) “length of time” the accused appears, with cautions/directions to exercise care.
BaselineB: Common law evidence principles (admissibility/relevance and use of real evidence) drawing on R. v. Leaney, [1989] 2 S.C.R. 393 and related authorities; also references Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(a)(i) in discussing appellate review, but the key test concerns videotape identification evidence.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Quebec Labour Code s. 16 rebuttal of presumption: employer must show the “other” reason is substantial, not a pretext, and the true (real and determining) reason for dismissal; commissioner/court cannot assess proportionality of the penalty
BaselineA: Statute (Quebec Labour Code, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 141 as am., ss. 13-16 (especially s. 16 “another good and sufficient reason”); presumption/burden scheme)
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 12 “gross disproportionality” test (with Goltz clarification): assess gravity of offence, offender’s personal characteristics, and circumstances; plus permissible informing factors; and a two-aspect approach (actual offender, then reasonable hypotheticals) for mandatory minimum challenges
BaselineB: Common law constitutional test under Charter s. 12 from R. v. Smith (reaffirmed in R. v. Lyons and R. v. Luxton), applied to Motor Vehicle Act, R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 288, s. 88(1)(c) (as applied with s. 88(1)(a) and s. 86(1)(a)(ii))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Whether Criminal Code appeal-costs provisions (ss. 758 and 771(3)) implicitly bind the Crown, giving the appeal court power to order costs against the Attorney General where it considers costs "just and reasonable" / "proper"
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, Part XXIV; Interpretation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-23, s. 16)
CaseB_TestB: Statutory mortgage prepayment/renewal framework under Interest Act s. 10(1): mortgagor may prepay after each five-year period unless a valid renewal "deems" a new mortgage date and itself does not exceed five years; choosing renewal is not "waiver/contracting out" if done with full knowledge
BaselineB: Statute (Interest Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-18, s. 10(1), (2); related provincial analogues discussed)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Wrongful dismissal damages: no deduction for (1) income tax not payable and (2) unemployment insurance benefits that are a consequence of the employment contract (collateral benefits rule as applied to UI)
BaselineA: Common law contract damages / collateral benefits principles (applied by analogy to contributory pension benefits in Guy v. Trizec Equities Ltd., [1979] 2 S.C.R. 756; also engages income tax treatment but resolves deductibility as a damages-assessment issue)
CaseB_TestB: Identification of Criminals Act s. 2 applies to juveniles: a juvenile in lawful custody for a delinquency relating to a Criminal Code indictable offence is a person 'charged with' (and, if found delinquent, 'under conviction of') an indictable offence, so reasonable force may be used to fingerprint
BaselineB: Statute — Identification of Criminals Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-1, s. 2(1)-(2), interpreted alongside the Juvenile Delinquents Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. J-3 (with Morris v. The Queen, [1979] 1 S.C.R. 405 applied)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: “Air of reality / sense of reality” test for whether a trial judge must leave a defence (here, mistake of fact as to consent) with the jury: there must be “in the record some evidence which would convey a sense of reality in the submission”; for mistake-of-fact-as-to-consent, “there must be some evidence which, if believed, would support the existence of a mistaken but honest belief” in consent, and (on these facts) “the evidence must appear from or be supported by sources other than the appellant in order to give it any air of reality.”
BaselineA: Common law (jury-charge duty re defences; “sense of reality” threshold) drawing on Kelsey v. The Queen and R. v. Workman and Huculak (and referenced Wu v. The King). Applied in context of Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 143 (rape).
CaseB_TestB: Section 11(b) “trial within a reasonable time” framework (Morin factors) and its (non-)application to appellate delay: s. 11(b) is assessed by “(1) the length of the delay; (2) waiver, if any, of parts of the delay; (3) the reasons for the delay; and (4) prejudice to the subject of the criminal process”; but (majority) “s. 11(b) does not apply to delay in respect of an appeal” and appellate-delay relief lies, if at all, under s. 7 abuse of process.
BaselineB: Statute/constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 11(b) and 7, as interpreted in R. v. Morin and R. v. Kalanj (and related Charter jurisprudence).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Presumption of reasonableness standard of review for a tribunal interpreting its home statute, rebutted only by Dunsmuir correctness categories (statutory appeal is not a new correctness category)
BaselineA: Common law (standard of review framework from Dunsmuir v. New Brunswick; Saguenay; McLean, etc.)
CaseB_TestB: Framework for Crown sui generis fiduciary duty: fiduciary duty arises from Crown discretionary control over a specific/cognizable Aboriginal interest; breach assessed by fiduciary standard of conduct (loyalty/good faith/full disclosure/ordinary prudence), not by achieving a particular result
BaselineB: Common law (fiduciary duty jurisprudence: Wewaykum; Guerin; Haida Nation; Manitoba Metis Federation) applied within the Specific Claims Tribunal Act scheme
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Necessarily incidental doctrine for validating federal legislation that prima facie intrudes on provincial jurisdiction (s. 91 enumerated power): the impugned provision must be shown to be "necessarily incidental to effective legislation" on the federal head of power; here, s. 33(3) failed because it was a "blanket prohibition" that "makes no attempt to link the proscribed conduct to actual or potential harm to fisheries" and thus was not "necessarily incidental" to s. 91(12) fisheries power.
BaselineA: Common law constitutional division-of-powers doctrine (necessarily incidental/ancillary powers) as articulated in Attorney-General for Canada v. Attorney-General for British Columbia and others, [1930] A.C. 111 (Lord Tomlin’s proposition (3)), applied to Parliament’s s. 91(12) 'Sea Coast and Inland Fisheries' power under the British North America Act, 1867.
CaseB_TestB: Colour of right in theft: the defence turns on whether the jury is satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused did not have, at the time of the taking/transfer, an "honest belief that he had the right to that money" (i.e., 'without colour of right' means lack of bona fide/honest belief), not on what the jury thinks the accused’s legal rights actually were.
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code theft provisions using the phrase 'without colour of right'—Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 283 and 294 (as replaced/substituted)), interpreted by the Court.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “unlawful purpose” in Criminal Code s. 423(2)(a): it “means contrary to law, that is prohibited by federal or provincial legislation”; if the alleged purpose is not prohibited by legislation (and the charge is not framed as “lawful purpose by unlawful means” under s. 423(2)(b)), the information discloses no offence known to law.
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 423(2)(a) (conspiracy to effect an unlawful purpose), read with s. 8 (abolition of common law offences) and contrasted with s. 423(2)(b) and s. 381; prior SCC discussion referenced: Wright, McDermott & Feeley v. The Queen, [1964] S.C.R. 192; Frey v. Fedoruk, [1950] S.C.R. 517.
CaseB_TestB: Quebec defamation fault under C.C.Q. art. 1457: fault is determined by a “contextual analysis of the facts and circumstances”; “the guiding principle of liability for defamation is that there will not be fault until it has been shown that the journalist or media outlet in question has fallen below professional standards” — i.e., the “reasonable journalist” standard is the “all-important guidepost” (truth/public interest are factors but not determinative).
BaselineB: Statute (civil law): Civil Code of Québec, art. 1457 (extra-contractual liability), informed by prior Quebec jurisprudence adopted/applied: Société Radio-Canada v. Radio Sept-Îles Inc., [1994] R.J.Q. 1811 (C.A.), and SCC: Prud’homme v. Prud’homme, 2002 SCC 85.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Rabey (majority): Disease-of-the-mind classification for automatism — internal cause vs transient external factor; “ordinary stresses and disappointments of life” are not an external cause taking the condition out of “disease of the mind”.
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 16) interpreted through common-law automatism/insanity jurisprudence (e.g., Bratty v. A.G. Northern Ireland, R. v. K.)
JudgeA: Ritchie J. (for Martland, Ritchie, Pigeon and Beetz JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: RBC v. State Farm: Conflict/supersession analysis — where the standard mortgage clause says it “shall supersede any policy provisions in conflict therewith BUT ONLY TO THE INTEREST OF THE MORTGAGEE”, Statutory Condition 4 cannot be used to void mortgagee coverage if it conflicts with the mortgage clause.
BaselineB: Statute and contract: Insurance Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. I.8, Part IV (Statutory Condition 4) plus the policy’s standard mortgage clause; interpreted in light of National Bank of Greece (Canada) v. Katsikonouris
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Single-cause vs multiple-causes characterization for prescription: if damages “result from a single cause of action” (breach of contractual obligation) they are contractual and prescribe in 30 years; if they “result from several separate and independent causes of action” they are characterized contract/delict by source and prescribe accordingly (e.g., separate ‘typical offences’ prescribe in 2 years).
BaselineA: Statute/civil code (Civil Code arts. 2242, 2261(2), 1024, 1057) plus contractual characterization of corporate by-laws (voluntary association theory drawn from jurisprudence cited in reasons).
CaseB_TestB: Priority between mechanic’s lien and subsequent mortgage for past indebtedness: absent express priority in Mechanics’ Lien Act (s. 14(1) inapplicable), an unregistered lien has no priority; once registered, lien claimant is “deemed to be a purchaser pro tanto” (s. 20) and priority is determined under Registry Act ss. 69(1) and 70 by priority of registration (subject to actual notice).
BaselineB: Statute (Mechanics’ Lien Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 267, ss. 14(1), 20 (and related registration provisions); Registry Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 409, ss. 69(1), 70).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Accrued-rights/anti-retroactivity analysis on statutory repeal: apply Interpretation Act s. 35(c) so repeal/amendment does not “affect any right, privilege, obligation or liability acquired, accrued, accruing or incurred” under the prior enactment; read the amending Unemployment Insurance Act s. 31 together with s. 35(c) to preserve only the accrued benefit (here, benefits through January 31, 1976) while keeping the prior disqualification (pension-payable) applicable to that accrued right.
BaselineA: Statute: Interpretation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-23, s. 35(c) (effect of repeal) applied to Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, S.C. 1970-71-72, c. 48, ss. 31 and 38 as amended by S.C. 1974-75-76, c. 80, s. 10; also considers Unemployment Insurance Entitlements Adjustment Act, 1976-77, c. 11, s. 2.
CaseB_TestB: Judicial immunity/privilege against compelled testimony before a commission: under Public Inquiries Act ss. 3-4 (read together), a commission may “summon” persons but cannot compel superior court judges to testify about (1) “how and why” they reached a decision (adjudicative process) or (2) why a particular judge sat on a particular case (bench composition/assignment), absent clear statutory language overriding this fundamental principle tied to judicial independence.
BaselineB: Combination of statute and constitutional/common law principle: Public Inquiries Act, R.S.N.S. 1967, c. 250, ss. 3-4 interpreted in light of the constitutional principle of judicial independence (as summarized in Valente v. The Queen and Beauregard v. Canada) and longstanding common law judicial immunity (e.g., Knowles' Trial and subsequent authorities).
JudgeB: McLachlin J. (for L'Heureux-Dubé, Gonthier and McLachlin JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Interpretation of Motor Vehicle Transport Act, s. 3(2): provincial board may license an extra‑provincial undertaking “into or through” a province as including operations “in, across, into and out of the province”, and s. 6 does not displace provincial enforcement (including seizure) incorporated via s. 3(2).
BaselineA: Statute: Motor Vehicle Transport Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. M-14, ss. 3(1)-(2), 5, 6; and incorporated provincial scheme under The Public Service Vehicles Act, R.S.A. 1970, c. 300 (esp. s. 58 seizure power).
CaseB_TestB: Charter scope test for corporate claimants under s. 12: a claimant must show an interest “falling within the scope of the guarantee, and one which accords with the purpose of that provision”; s. 12 (“cruel and unusual”) is limited to human beings and does not protect corporations.
BaselineB: Constitutional text and purposive interpretation framework: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 12, applying the purposive approach (Big M Drug Mart) and the standing/scope requirement from R. v. CIP Inc. (as cited in the reasons).
JudgeB: Brown and Rowe JJ. (Wagner C.J. and Moldaver and Côté JJ. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Effect of fundamental breach/termination on an exclusionary clause (lien waiver): applicability is determined by the “true construction of the contract”; here, the waiver “ceased to bind” once the subcontractor communicated its election to treat the contract as at an end
BaselineA: Combination: common law on exclusion/exception clauses and fundamental breach (Suisse Atlantique; Photo Production) plus statutory lien context (The Mechanics’ Lien Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 267, s. 5(1))
CaseB_TestB: Whether a penal court may hear a collateral attack on an administrative order: determine the legislature’s intended forum, using non-exhaustive factors—“the wording of the statute”, “the purpose of the legislation”, “the availability of an appeal”, “the nature of the collateral attack taking into account the appeal tribunal’s expertise and raison d’être”, and “the penalty”
BaselineB: Statutory/interpretive framework under the Environmental Protection Act, R.S.O. 1980, c. 141 (notably ss. 17, 122-123, 146(1a)) and common-law principles on collateral attack (e.g., Wilson; Litchfield; Sarson) as adapted to administrative orders
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Constructive trust based on unjust enrichment: claimant must show (1) an enrichment, (2) a corresponding deprivation, and (3) absence of any juristic reason for the enrichment; plus the enrichment’s retention must be “unjust” in the circumstances (including reasonable expectation and knowing acceptance) and there must be a causal connection between contribution and the disputed assets; remedy/share is proportionate to contribution
BaselineA: Common law (equitable constructive trust/unjust enrichment), drawing on Rathwell v. Rathwell and Murdoch v. Murdoch (and related trust jurisprudence discussed in the reasons)
CaseB_TestB: Solicitor-client confidentiality/privilege in search-warrant context: (i) confidentiality may be raised whenever communications risk disclosure; (ii) conflicts are resolved in favour of confidentiality unless law provides otherwise; (iii) authorized intrusions must interfere only to the extent “absolutely necessary”; (iv) enabling statutes derogating from confidentiality are interpreted restrictively; plus for Criminal Code s. 443(1)(b) warrants: JP has no jurisdiction to authorize seizure of privileged (inadmissible) documents, should refuse a search of a lawyer’s office unless there is “no reasonable alternative”, and must impose execution terms to protect confidentiality; crime/fraud communications are excepted
BaselineB: Combination: statute (Criminal Code, s. 443(1)(b) search warrant power) interpreted in light of common law solicitor-client privilege/confidentiality (including Solosky v. The Queen and long-standing privilege principles)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Reibl objective causation test for failure-to-disclose (informed consent): whether “a reasonable person in the patient’s position would have done” the treatment if properly informed of “all material and special risks” (and benefits) of undergoing vs. foregoing it
BaselineA: Common law (medical negligence duty of disclosure and causation), drawing on Hopp v. Lepp, [1980] 2 S.C.R. 192 (duty to disclose “any material risks and any special or unusual risks” and answer specific questions; scope depends on circumstances)
CaseB_TestB: Division of powers “integral element” test (s. 92(10) undertakings): federal legislation displacing provincial law is valid/applicable only if the matter is an “integral part” of the core federal undertaking; otherwise provincial laws of general application apply
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine (division of powers) applying the “integral element” approach from Construction Montcalm Inc. v. Minimum Wage Commission, [1979] 1 S.C.R. 754 and Northern Telecom Ltd. v. Communications Workers of Canada, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 115, to assess the constitutional applicability of Railway Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. R-2, s. 342(1)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Natural Resources Agreement para. 12 “right of access” test: if provincial law/regulations contemplate any (even limited) hunting on the land, that constitutes a “right of access” for hunting, which triggers the para. 12 proviso and guarantees treaty Indians the right to hunt for food “at all seasons of the year” (so provincial season limits cannot apply). Key language: “The laws in force ... contemplated a limited right to hunt on the land in question. This constituted a ‘right of access’ and engaged the proviso in paragraph 12 ... [so] unnecessary to consider whether the Cookson unit was ‘unoccupied’ Crown land.”
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional instrument: Natural Resources Agreement (Canada–Saskatchewan) confirmed by British North America Act, 1930 (Imp.), c. 26, para. 12; applied/clarified via SCC precedent R. v. Sutherland, Wilson and Wilson, [1980] 2 S.C.R. 451 (definition of “right of access”).
CaseB_TestB: Charter validity “purpose-first” framework: “the legislation's purpose is the initial test of constitutional validity”; only if the law “has passed the purpose test” are effects considered; “effects can never be relied on to save legislation with an invalid purpose.” Applied to s. 2(a): if the law’s purpose is “the compulsion of religious observance”, it infringes freedom of religion and need not examine actual effects.
BaselineB: Constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 2(a) (and s. 1, s. 52(1)); interpretive approach developed in the decision (with reference to prior cases such as Hunter v. Southam).
JudgeB: Dickson J. (for Dickson, Beetz, McIntyre, Chouinard and Lamer JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: No retroactive, sua sponte revocation of granted premium reductions absent express statutory/regulatory authority; an officer’s legal error in granting a reduction does not make the decision a nullity (no jurisdictional defect). Key points: Regulations provide only a one-way review “at the instance of the employer”; “neither the officer nor the Review Panel nor the Commission itself is given any express power to act on his or its own initiative to set aside an allowed reduction”; and “the fact that the officer may have erred in law... does not mean that he exceeded or failed to exercise his jurisdiction... his errors did not make his decisions nullities.”
BaselineA: Statute and regulation: Unemployment Insurance Act, 1970-71-72, ss. 64(4), 64(6) (regulation-making and prescribed standards/decisions/appeals), and Regulations s. 24 (decision and employer-initiated review/appeal). (Also discussed but rejected as a basis: Act s. 70.)
CaseB_TestB: Mens rea for Criminal Code s. 121(1)(a): no “corrupt” purpose required; guilt requires intentional commission of the prohibited act plus knowledge of the circumstances that are elements of the offence. “Thus, to be guilty... the accused must know that he or she is an official; ... must intentionally demand or accept a loan, reward, advantage or benefit...; and ... must know that the reward is in consideration for cooperation, assistance or exercise of influence in connection with the transaction of business with or relating to the government.”
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 121(1)(a) (interpreting required mens rea; rejecting an added ‘corruption’ element).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Ernst (Cromwell J.) categorical bar on Charter damages against a quasi-judicial regulator: applying Ward, Charter damages are never an “appropriate and just” remedy against this Board because countervailing factors (alternative remedy of judicial review + good governance/immunity rationales + avoiding case-by-case erosion of immunity) negate damages
BaselineA: Common law / constitutional remedial framework under Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 24(1), as articulated in Vancouver (City) v. Ward, 2010 SCC 27 (plus statutory context: Energy Resources Conservation Act, R.S.A. 2000, c. E-10, s. 43 immunity clause)
CaseB_TestB: Mikisew Cree (Karakatsanis J.) rule that the duty to consult does not apply to the law-making process: “no aspect of the law-making process — from the development of legislation to its enactment — triggers a duty to consult” because legislative development is not “Crown conduct” and is shielded by separation of powers/parliamentary sovereignty
BaselineB: Common law / constitutional doctrine of the duty to consult grounded in the honour of the Crown (Haida Nation v. British Columbia (Minister of Forests), 2004 SCC 73; Rio Tinto Alcan Inc. v. Carrier Sekani Tribal Council, 2010 SCC 43; Clyde River (Hamlet) v. Petroleum Geo-Services Inc., 2017 SCC 40) and constitutional principles (Constitution Act, 1867, Part IV; Constitution Act, 1982, s. 35)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Workers’ compensation statutory bar does not extend to a non-employer car owner merely deemed an employer/servant relationship under motor-vehicle legislation (s. 10(1) WCA applies only to actions against the worker’s employer/covered employers/workers).
BaselineA: Statute: Workers’ Compensation Act, 1968 (B.C.), c. 59, s. 10(1) (bar of actions) and Motor-vehicle Act, R.S.B.C. 1960, c. 253, s. 70(1) (deeming driver agent/servant and in course of employment).
CaseB_TestB: Operational conflict framework for conflicting administrative decisions: (1) determine if there is a true operational conflict (compliance with one necessitates violation of the other); (2) if so, ask whether either decision would be quashed under its normal standard of review; (3) if both would stand, courts may declare one inoperative to the extent of conflict and decide precedence using a pragmatic and functional approach (legislative purpose, centrality, policy-making role).
BaselineB: Common law administrative law (judicial review/standard of review and tribunal-jurisdiction principles) informed by prior SCC cases (e.g., Bibeault; Domtar; Pezim; Bell Canada) and statutory schemes governing the tribunals (e.g., Railway Act ss. 335, 340; NTPPA ss. 49, 50, 68(1); Canada Labour Code s. 58).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Priority between a mechanics’ lien and a subsequent collateral mortgage for past indebtedness: absent an express Mechanics’ Lien Act priority rule (s. 14(1) inapplicable), the lien claimant must register and priority is determined by Registry Act registration priority (ss. 69(1), 70), with no special subordination for a “collateral” mortgage
BaselineA: Statute (Ontario): Mechanics’ Lien Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 267 (esp. ss. 14(1), 16, 20, 21, 22) and Registry Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 409 (ss. 69(1), 70)
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 2(b)/s. 1 analysis of privacy legislation in the labour-picketing context: whether PIPA’s limits on collecting/using/disclosing personal information are justified—i.e., whether the infringement is proportionate under s. 1 (pressing and substantial objective; rational connection; minimal impairment; overall proportionality), with emphasis that PIPA lacks a mechanism to balance expression with privacy and is therefore disproportionate
BaselineB: Constitutional + statute: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms ss. 2(b), 1 (Oakes proportionality framework) applied to Personal Information Protection Act, S.A. 2003, c. P-6.5 (notably ss. 3, 4(1), 4(3), 7(1) and exemptions) and Regulation s. 7
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Quebec civil liability “choice” test: a contracting party may sue in delict (art. 1053 C.C.) despite a contract only if the alleged contractual fault is independently a delictual fault that would exist “even in the absence of a contract”
BaselineA: Statute (Civil Code art. 1053; Code of Civil Procedure art. 68) as interpreted alongside prior SCC jurisprudence (Ross v. Dunstall; Alliance Assurance)
CaseB_TestB: Reasonable apprehension of bias in a criminal trial: if demonstrated, the trial judge has “no further jurisdiction” and “the only appropriate remedy is a new trial”; resulting orders are retroactively “void and without effect”
BaselineB: Common law procedural fairness / natural justice (as articulated in Newfoundland Telephone Co. v. Newfoundland (Board of Commissioners of Public Utilities)) applied in the criminal trial context
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Bills of Exchange Act “sum certain” / negotiability requirement: principal + interest must be ascertainable on the face of the instrument (no extrinsic evidence for an inherently uncertain interest start date like “from the date of advance”)
BaselineA: Statute (Bills of Exchange Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. B-5, ss. 28, 176(1), 186; plus s. 10 incorporating common law/law merchant unless inconsistent)
CaseB_TestB: Criminal Code s. 172(3) “disturbs” threshold: conviction requires conduct that is “disorderly in itself or productive of disorder”; mere annoyance/anxiety/emotional upset from brief, passive, peaceful conduct voluntarily desisted from is insufficient
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 172(3), interpreted in context including the “Disorderly Conduct” heading and legislative history)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Negotiable promissory note “sum certain”/certainty-on-the-face test: a note is not a promissory note under the Bills of Exchange Act unless the total sum payable (principal + interest) is ascertainable from the face of the instrument (or by numerical calculation from materials contained in it), with recourse to extrinsic evidence only where necessary to implement a specific Act provision; an interest start date like “from the date of advance” that is not on the face creates disqualifying uncertainty and destroys negotiability.
BaselineA: Statute (Bills of Exchange Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. B-5, ss. 176(1) (definition of promissory note), 28 (sum certain/interest), 186 (application to notes), plus s. 10 incorporating common law/law merchant on negotiability and certainty).
CaseB_TestB: Start-date for the art. 2532 C.C.L.C. two-year suicide exclusion (“two years of uninterrupted insurance”): determine when the life insurance contract is effective under art. 2516 (acceptance without modification + initial premium paid + no change in insurability, concurrently), but parties may validly backdate to an earlier policy effective date favourable to the policyholder so that, once art. 2516 conditions are met, the contract comes into effect retroactively as of the selected policy date; the suicide exclusion period runs from that effective (possibly backdated) date, and does not restart within a single continuous contract (whether a later document is a new contract depends on continuity assessed case-by-case).
BaselineB: Statute/civil code (Civil Code of Lower Canada, arts. 2516 (effectiveness conditions for life insurance), 2532 (suicide clause ineffective after two years uninterrupted insurance), and art. 2500(2) (relative public order); interpretive support from prior SCC interpretation in General Trust of Canada v. Artisans Coopvie).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: When a statute creates a specific tribunal/procedure to decide an issue, the Superior Court should not intervene by declaratory judgment to decide that very issue (and may refuse declarations that would be useless/serve little purpose). Key formulations: “the Superior Court should not intervene by a declaratory judgment when the legislator has specifically provided that the matter is to be decided by some other tribunal”; and declaratory relief is discretionary where it would be “useless or embarrassing or where some other statutory mode of proceeding is provided”.
BaselineA: Combination: statute (Code of Civil Procedure, art. 453; Act respecting the Olympic Village, 1976 (Qué.), c. 43, esp. s. 10 and Division III arbitration scheme) plus common-law/discretionary principles on declaratory relief and statutory-remedy exclusivity (Barraclough v. Brown; City of Lethbridge; Cassidy v. Stuart).
CaseB_TestB: Minister’s power under Fisheries Act s. 7 to “authorize to be issued” licences is a continuing power, so the Minister may revoke an authorization any time before the licence is actually issued; discretion is limited only by natural justice (relevant considerations, no arbitrariness, good faith). Key formulations: “the Minister’s power to authorize the issuance of licences is a continuing power until such time as a licence is actually issued. It follows that he retains the power to revoke the authorization at any time prior to the issuance of the licence”; and discretion is “restricted only by the requirement of natural justice… base his or her decision on relevant considerations, avoid arbitrariness and act in good faith.”
BaselineB: Statute: Fisheries Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. F-14, s. 7 (and contrast with s. 9); Interpretation Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. I-21, s. 31(3) (“from time to time as occasion requires”).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Excise Tax Act machinery exemption: claimant must be a “manufacturer or producer of goods” and the machinery must be “purchased and used directly in the manufacture or production of goods”; “manufacturing” cannot be restrictively defined where the Act does not do so (operating generators to produce electricity = manufacturing goods).
BaselineA: Statute: Excise Tax Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-13, ss. 27(1), 29(1), and Schedule III, Part XIII, s. 1(a)(i) (plus acceptance that electricity is “goods” under Schedule III, Part VI, s. 3).
CaseB_TestB: Vesting/accrual of appeal-as-of-right: a right is only “acquired”, “accrued” or “accruing” when all conditions precedent are fulfilled; for former Criminal Code s. 691(2), the right to appeal as of right arises only when the court of appeal reverses the acquittal and orders a new trial.
BaselineB: Statute: Interpretation Act, R.S.C., 1985, c. I-21, ss. 43(c) and 44(c),(d), applied to Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 691(2) (as amended effective May 14, 1997).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Human rights code exclusivity / no parallel common-law tort or direct civil action: where a statute (Ontario Human Rights Code) provides a comprehensive administrative/adjudicative enforcement scheme, it "foreclose[s]" (1) any civil action "based directly upon a breach" of the Code and (2) any common law action "based on an invocation of the public policy expressed in the Code"
BaselineA: Statute (Ontario Human Rights Code, R.S.O. 1970, c. 318, especially s. 4(1)(a)-(b) and the Code’s complaint/board of inquiry/appeal scheme including s. 14b(6), s. 14c, s. 14d(4))
CaseB_TestB: Undue obstacle / reasonable accommodation under CTA s. 172: an obstacle must be removed unless the carrier proves a bona fide justification by establishing "undue hardship"; what is "undue" is assessed contextually using factors such as "cost, economic viability, safety, and the quality of service to all passengers" (CTA s. 5 factors) and the carrier bears the onus of showing the obstacle is not undue
BaselineB: Statute (Canada Transportation Act, S.C. 1996, c. 10, ss. 5, 170-172) interpreted consistently with human rights reasonable-accommodation jurisprudence (e.g., Meiorin/Grismer) as incorporated into the CTA context
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Bill of Rights limit on reverse onus: a reverse-onus provision is compatible with s. 2(f) only if the fact the accused must prove on a balance of probabilities is "rationally open" to the accused; if it is a fact the accused "cannot reasonably be expected to prove" (beyond his knowledge/means of knowledge), the onus is "impossible to meet" and becomes an irrebuttable presumption of guilt. For Customs Act s. 248(1), the Crown must at least prove foreign origin + possession + "some knowledge or means of knowledge of the circumstances of importation" on the accused’s part before the reverse onus can operate; otherwise the Crown must prove unlawful importation beyond a reasonable doubt.
BaselineA: Statute (Customs Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-40, ss. 205(1), 205(3), 248(1)) interpreted/limited by statute (Canadian Bill of Rights, R.S.C. 1970, App. III, s. 2(f)); prior SCC guidance in R. v. Appleby, [1972] S.C.R. 303 on reverse onus and s. 2(f).
CaseB_TestB: Interested-party status/right to be heard at bargaining-unit stage under Labour Code s. 32: employees included in the proposed bargaining unit are not "interested parties" regarding "any matter relating to the bargaining unit" because s. 32 specifies the investigation is held "in the presence of every association concerned and the employer" (an exhaustive list). On judicial review (evocation) in the face of a privative clause, the tribunal’s interpretation stands unless it is "patently unreasonable"/"not manifestly unreasonable".
BaselineB: Statute (Quebec Labour Code, R.S.Q. 1977, c. C-27, s. 32 (and related ss. 28, 39, 129)) plus common-law administrative law principles on participation rights of interested parties and privative-clause judicial review (CUPE v. New Brunswick Liquor Corp., [1979] 2 S.C.R. 227; Nipawin, [1975] 1 S.C.R. 382).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Duty to leave defences to the jury: the trial judge must put to the jury any defence “revealed by the evidence” or that “can be reasonably inferred from the evidence”, but has “no duty to invite the jury to consider defences of which there is no evidence or which cannot reasonably be inferred from the evidence” (R. v. Squire, quoted by Lamer J., dissenting).
BaselineA: Common law (as restated in R. v. Squire, [1977] 2 S.C.R. 13, quoting Mancini v. DPP; also referencing Lee Chun-Chuen; Wu v. The King and other cases).
CaseB_TestB: Interjurisdictional immunity (constitutional inapplicability) for federal services: provincial laws of general application apply unless they bear on what makes the federal subject “specifically of federal jurisdiction”; for a federal service, inapplicability arises if the provincial statute “touches on a vital or essential aspect of its establishment, management or operation” (Gonthier J.).
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine (interjurisdictional immunity) as articulated in Construction Montcalm; Bell Canada v. Quebec (CSST); Clark v. CNR; Dick; Four B Manufacturing, applied to provincial Transport Act permit scheme.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 116(1) availability test: a charge for disobeying a lawful court order lies unless statute law expressly provides a penalty/punishment/other mode of proceeding; inherent/common law contempt powers do not qualify as 'expressly provided by law'
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 116(1) (and interpretive context including s. 8); plus consideration of Manitoba Queen’s Bench Rules 483, 485, 492)
CaseB_TestB: Public law promissory estoppel in penal/zoning enforcement: requires (1) a clear and unambiguous promise by a public authority intended to induce action, (2) reliance and a change of conduct, but estoppel cannot be invoked to prevent application of an express legislative provision (especially a strict-liability regulatory offence)
BaselineB: Common law doctrine of promissory estoppel as applied in public law (citing Mount Sinai (paras. 45-47) quoting Maracle; also St. Ann’s Island), applied in the context of express municipal by-law penal provisions (By-law VQZ-3, art. 359; Cities and Towns Act, s. 576)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Insurance contract interpretation to fix the policy’s single “effective date” for time-limited clauses: read the policy and application “in entirety” and, on the “true construction of the entire contract”, select the date the policy is “entirely structured around” for “calculating any of the time periods contemplated” (including the suicide clause).
BaselineA: Statute + contract interpretation: Insurance Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 224, s. 148(2) (application and policy form part of the contract) (with the dispute arising against the statutory backdrop of s. 154 on when a contract takes effect).
CaseB_TestB: Access in conjunction with permanent guardianship: (1) court has jurisdiction to grant access because access can be addressed on review/variation and thus “a fortiori” at the initial order; (2) whether to grant access is a “delicate exercise” under the statutory “best interests of the child” factors—access is “the exception and not the rule” and “should not be granted if its exercise would have negative effects on the physical or psychological health of the child” or would jeopardize adoption.
BaselineB: Statute: Family Services Act, S.N.B. 1980, c. F-2.2, especially ss. 1 (best interests definition), 53(2) (best interests paramount), 56(1) (permanent guardianship), 60(2) and 60(6) (variation/review and court may make any appropriate order in best interests), and 85(2) (court may preserve access after adoption).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 16(2) insanity: meaning of being “incapable of appreciating the nature and quality of an act” — an accused appreciates if he “knows what he is doing” and “is aware of the physical consequences which will result from his acts” (i.e., can “estimate and ... understand the physical consequences”); emotional/moral indifference alone is not enough.
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 16(2)); interpreted in light of SCC authorities including Cooper v. The Queen, R. v. Barnier, and Schwartz v. The Queen.
CaseB_TestB: Extradition Act committal and surrender frameworks: (1) Committal under s. 29(1)(a) — extradition judge asks whether there is admissible evidence of conduct that, had it occurred in Canada, “would justify committal for trial”; certified ROC evidence is “presumptively reliable” and committal may be refused on reliability only if evidence is “so defective or appears so unreliable that it would be dangerous or unsafe to act on it”; defences/exculpatory narratives generally not considered. (2) Surrender under s. 44(1)(a) — for defence-unavailability claims, person sought must show (1) a substantive difference (defence in Canada but no comparable defence abroad), (2) a reasonable prospect of success in Canada, and (3) significantly greater jeopardy abroad, before the Minister must weigh that factor with all circumstances.
BaselineB: Statute (Extradition Act, S.C. 1999, c. 18, ss. 29(1)(a), 32(1)(c), 44(1)(a)); built on prior SCC extradition jurisprudence including United States of America v. Ferras, Canada v. Schmidt, and Canada (Justice) v. Fischbacher.
JudgeB: Cromwell J. (McLachlin C.J. and Moldaver and Wagner JJ. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Non-pecuniary damages in severe personal injury: apply the functional approach and a rough $100,000 upper limit, exceedable only rarely (not just because injuries are worse), with increases only on proof/agreement of inflation’s effect
BaselineA: Common law (damages for personal injury), especially the “trilogy” establishing the functional approach and the $100,000 rough upper limit: Andrews v. Grand & Toy Alberta Ltd.; Arnold v. Teno; Thornton v. Board of School Trustees; as refined in Lewis v. Todd
CaseB_TestB: Inadequately insured motorist coverage: (1) vehicle used as a motor vehicle (ordinary and well-known use) and (2) an unbroken chain of causation linking the tortfeasor’s conduct as a motorist to the injuries; coverage denied where the tort is an intervening, severable act (not mere “but for” use), despite the word “indirectly”
BaselineB: Statutory/contractual interpretation of motor vehicle liability language: Insurance Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. I.8, s. 239(1)(a) and the OPCF 44R endorsement using the same “arising directly or indirectly from the use or operation of an automobile” wording; distinguished from Amos v. ICBC (no-fault benefits)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Workmen’s compensation subrogation/election rule: once the worker elects compensation, the Commission alone may claim the compensated portion; the worker may sue only for the s. 8 ‘additional sum’, so the worker’s full-damages action neither gives the Commission an art. 208 C.C.P. interest to intervene nor interrupts prescription for the Commission
BaselineA: Statute and civil law: Workmen’s Compensation Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 159, ss. 7(1)-(3) (subrogation ‘by the mere making of the election’) and 8 (worker may claim only the ‘additional sum’); Civil Code art. 1056a (no civil recourse except as permitted by the Act); Code of Civil Procedure art. 208 (interest to intervene)
CaseB_TestB: Collins s. 24(2) exclusion framework (as applied/organized in Greffe): balance three categories—(1) fairness of the trial, (2) seriousness of the Charter breach, and (3) effect of exclusion on the repute of justice—asking whether, ‘having regard to all the circumstances’, admission would bring the administration of justice into disrepute
BaselineB: Constitution (Charter) and common law framework: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 24(2) (‘shall be excluded if it is established that, having regard to all the circumstances, the admission of it ... would bring the administration of justice into disrepute’), applying R. v. Collins, [1987] 1 S.C.R. 265 (three-category analysis)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Public access to executed search warrants/informations: presumption of access after execution (and objects brought before a justice), with curtailment only where needed to protect “social values of superordinate importance” (notably protecting the innocent where nothing is found); issuance may be in camera to protect the administration of justice
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law/open court principle: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 443 and 446, plus common law policy of openness and court supervisory power over records (e.g., Scott v. Scott; McPherson v. McPherson; Gazette Printing Co. v. Shallow, as discussed)
CaseB_TestB: Two-branch test for bona fide occupational qualification (BFOQ): (1) subjective good-faith/improper-purpose inquiry; and (2) objective reasonable-necessity inquiry (here reframed as whether religious conformity is “reasonably necessary to assure the accomplishment of the objectives” of a Catholic school)
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law test: Human Rights Code, R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 186, s. 8 (and related s. 8(2)(a)); BFOQ framework from Ontario Human Rights Commission v. Etobicoke (Borough of), [1982] 1 S.C.R. 202
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Validity of a Quebec deed of donation and trust benefiting unborn (non-existent) primary beneficiaries: interpret Civil Code art. 981a “subject to the special characteristics of the trust” so that a trust may validly benefit a non-existent person where (i) trustee acceptance suffices to perfect/irrevocably constitute the trust (Curran v. Davis) and (ii) ownership of the trust property vests in the trustee during the trust, so “it is not necessary that there be beneficiaries in whom ownership of the property conveyed in trust be vested”; arts. 981a et seq. must be given a “wide and liberal interpretation” and only public-order prohibitions on gifts carry over through art. 981a.
BaselineA: Statute (Civil Code of Quebec provisions on trusts and gifts): arts. 981a, 981b, 981l (trusts) read with arts. 754, 755, 758, 760, 782, 608, 771, 772, 929; plus SCC precedent on trustee acceptance (Curran v. Davis, [1933] S.C.R. 283).
CaseB_TestB: When a civil injunction may effectively bind non-parties (enforceable by contempt): courts have jurisdiction to make orders binding on non-parties, but fairness constraints apply—because non-parties may be held in contempt, they “must first be apprised of the existence and terms of the order and be given an opportunity to comply”; it is “desirable” that the order’s terms speak of the duty of non-parties to respect it; and orders must be “carefully worded and constrained to ensure that they are fair and not unduly broad.”
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law/equity: Law and Equity Act, R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 224, s. 36 (interlocutory injunctions “just or convenient”); Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 11 (civil remedies not affected by criminality); common law contempt/injunction principles (e.g., International Longshoremen’s Association, Local 273 v. Maritime Employers’ Association, [1979] 1 S.C.R. 120; plus English authorities discussed).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: When multiple convictions are permitted despite Kienapple: interpret Criminal Code s. 83 as creating a distinct offence with mandatory consecutive sentence, so Kienapple (no double punishment for same delict) does not bar a second conviction; and s. 21 party liability applies to s. 83. Key language: s. 83(2) means the sentence 'shall be served consecutively to any other punishment imposed on him for an offence arising out of the same event or series of events' and 'Parliament has in the enactment of s. 83 departed from the fundamental common law principle ... elaborated in Kienapple'.
BaselineA: Combination of common law and statute: common law Kienapple principle (Kienapple v. The Queen; also Cox and Paton v. The Queen; R. v. Quon distinguished) plus Criminal Code provisions s. 83 (use of a firearm; consecutive sentence in s. 83(2)) and s. 21 (parties to an offence).
JudgeA: Dickson J. (for Martland, Dickson, Estey, McIntyre and Chouinard JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Pith and substance analysis for a municipal measure (division of powers): determine the measure’s 'pith and substance' by considering 'both its purpose and its effects' (including 'both the legal ramifications of the words used and the practical consequences'). If pith and substance is the siting of radiocommunication infrastructure, the measure is ultra vires the province/municipality. Key language: 'In analyzing the pith and substance ... the Court must consider both its purpose and its effects' and the evidence 'leads to but one conclusion' about purpose/effects.
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine (pith and substance; double aspect; interjurisdictional immunity) applied in light of the Constitution Act, 1867 heads of power (ss. 91(29), 92(10)(a), 92(13), 92(16)) and the federal Radiocommunication Act, s. 5(1)(f) (Minister’s siting approval power).
JudgeB: Wagner and Côté JJ. (joint reasons; McLachlin C.J. and Abella, Cromwell, Moldaver, Karakatsanis and Brown JJ. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.
