CaseA_TestA: Application of s. 25(3) (Saskatchewan Trade Union Act): in discharge grievances, unless the collective agreement contains a specific penalty for the infraction, an arbitrator who finds dismissal cannot be sustained may substitute a lesser penalty that "seems just and reasonable in the circumstances" (including reinstatement without back pay).
BaselineA: Statute (The Trade Union Act, R.S.S. 1978, c. T-17, s. 25(3)) applied alongside the collective agreement (arts. 6(4) and 12(12)(a)).
CaseB_TestB: Contribution-based complicity test under Refugee Convention art. 1F(a)/IRPA s. 98: exclusion requires "serious reasons for considering" the claimant "has voluntarily made a significant and knowing contribution to the organization’s crime or criminal purpose"; assessed contextually using non-exhaustive factors (size/nature of organization; part involved; duties; rank; time in organization after knowledge; recruitment/opportunity to leave).
BaselineB: Statute and treaty interpretation (IRPA s. 98 incorporating Refugee Convention art. 1F(a)); informed by international criminal law sources (e.g., Rome Statute arts. 25, 30, 31(1)(d)) and prior Canadian approach (Ramirez (FCA) personal and knowing participation test) which the SCC replaces.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 43 Canada Evidence Act (letters rogatory): s. 43 supports production of documents alone; judicial assistance granted subject to comity guidelines (trial not discovery; relevance; scope; precision) and excluding/limiting illegally intercepted communications
BaselineA: Statute: Canada Evidence Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-10, s. 43 (letters rogatory) (with related consideration of Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 178.2, 178.16, 446)
CaseB_TestB: Admissibility of defence-led unknown third party suspect evidence: (1) logical relevance to a fact in issue/available defence shown by a sufficient connection (similarity) between charged crime and other incident(s) plus evidence the accused could not have committed the other offence; and (2) admit unless prejudicial effects substantially outweigh probative value (Seaboyer balancing), without trial judge weighing credibility/strength
BaselineB: Common law: general admissibility and balancing principles (R. v. Corbett; R. v. Seaboyer) and air of reality threshold (R. v. Cinous), with sufficient-connection concept drawn from third-party suspect jurisprudence (McMillan; R. v. Grandinetti)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Civil Code art. 1055 “purpose of the building/part” limitation: owner not liable for ruin/want of repairs where the victim used the building/part for a purpose contrary to that for which it was intended; plus art. 1054 applies only where damage is caused by the “positive and independent action” of the thing
BaselineA: Statute (Civil Code of Quebec (as then in force), arts. 1053, 1054, 1055; with prior SCC interpretation in Leznek v. City of Verdun, [1940] S.C.R. 313 and Curley v. Latreille (1920), 60 S.C.R. 131)
JudgeA: Beetz J. (for Beetz, Chouinard and Lamer JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Mental capacity standard for confessions/right to silence/s. 10(b) waiver: the accused must have an “operating mind” (limited cognitive capacity) — i.e., understand what is being said and that it can be used against him; for s. 10(b) waiver, capacity aligns with fitness-to-stand-trial (can communicate with and understand the function of counsel, and can dispense with counsel)
BaselineB: Combination of common law and statute/constitutional text: common law confession rule and “operating mind” line (Ward; Horvath; Nagotcha; Hebert) plus Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms ss. 7 and 10(b), and Criminal Code s. 2 definition of “unfit to stand trial” used to set the competency threshold
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Judicial review of a labour board’s “home statute” interpretation: intervene only if the interpretation is “patently unreasonable” / “plainly unreasonable” (certiorari is “a long way from an appeal”)
BaselineA: Combination: statute (The Public Service Employee Relations Act, 1977 (Alta.), c. 40, ss. 9, 11, 89) plus common-law/precedent on deference (CUPE v. New Brunswick Liquor Corp.)
CaseB_TestB: Adverse-effect religious discrimination and duty to accommodate: discrimination established by the 3-part Quebec Charter s. 10 test; once adverse-effect discrimination is found, employer must take “reasonable steps to accommodate … short of undue hardship” (no de minimis threshold)
BaselineB: Combination: statute (Quebec Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms, ss. 10, 16; plus Labour Code privative clause context) and common law (O’Malley; Central Alberta Dairy Pool; Renaud)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Similar fact evidence admissibility: must have an evidentiary link connecting the similar acts to the accused (not mere similarity), within the general probative value vs prejudice principle
BaselineA: Common law (similar fact evidence doctrine from Makin v. Attorney-General for New South Wales; applied with Boardman v. DPP and Harris v. DPP)
CaseB_TestB: Charter vagueness test: a law is unconstitutionally vague if it "so lacks in precision as not to give sufficient guidance for legal debate" (fair notice and limiting enforcement discretion)
BaselineB: Common law constitutional principle under Charter s. 7 / s. 1 in limine (building on the Prostitution Reference and related SCC vagueness jurisprudence)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 16(2) insanity — “first arm” requires incapacity to appreciate the physical nature/quality (physical consequences) of the act; failure to appreciate penal consequences (punishment) is irrelevant and does not satisfy s. 16(2)
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 16(2)), as interpreted in Cooper v. The Queen, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 1149; Schwartz v. The Queen, [1977] 1 S.C.R. 673; R. v. Barnier, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 1124; Kjeldsen v. The Queen, [1981] 2 S.C.R. 617
CaseB_TestB: Administrative tribunal jurisdiction to apply the Constitution (including s. 35) — the “essential question” is whether the enabling statute grants jurisdiction to “interpret or decide any question of law”; if yes, the tribunal is presumed to have jurisdiction to decide the issue in light of s. 35/other constitutional provisions unless a “clear implication” rebuts it
BaselineB: Common law framework on tribunal constitutional jurisdiction, applied through Nova Scotia (Workers’ Compensation Board) v. Martin, 2003 SCC 54; also interpreting Forest Practices Code of British Columbia Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 159, especially s. 131(8) (submissions as to “facts, law and jurisdiction”)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Patentability of a new use for an old compound as a “new and useful art”: the “invention” is “the application of this new knowledge to effect a desired result which has an undisputed commercial value”, and the claimed compositions may be the “practical embodiment of the new knowledge” even if mixing with adjuvants is not itself inventive.
BaselineA: Statute (Patent Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. P-4), especially s. 2 definition of “invention” (“any new and useful art...”) and s. 36 claim/specification requirements; interpreted against prior patentability jurisprudence (e.g., Farbwerke Hoechst; Ciba; Tennessee Eastman; Hickton’s Patent).
CaseB_TestB: Party liability for drug trafficking by aiding/abetting: under Criminal Code s. 21(1)(b) “to aid... means to assist or help” and requires acting “for the purpose of” aiding, where “purpose” is equated with “intention” (not “desire”); under s. 21(1)(c) abetting includes “encouraging... promoting... procuring” and requires intent to encourage; purchaser is excluded from trafficking by purchase alone, but an agent/assistant to the purchaser can be liable if they in fact assist/encourage the sale with the requisite intent.
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 21(1)(b),(c); Narcotic Control Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. N-1, ss. 2 “traffic”, 3(1), 4(1),(2)), as interpreted with prior SCC authority (notably Hibbert on “purpose”).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory incompatibility/repugnancy test for whether a permissive municipal discretion (Police Act s. 24(6)) excludes a collectively-bargained/arbitrated working-condition clause under s. 29(2): does s. 24(6) "prescribe exclusivity" or is there "incompatibility or inconsistency" between the provisions? If not, "each has its own area of operation" and the clause is valid.
BaselineA: Statute (The Police Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 351, ss. 24(6) and 29(2))
CaseB_TestB: State Immunity Act interpretation framework: (1) s. 3(1) is exhaustive ("[e]xcept as provided by this Act" ousts common law/international-law exceptions); (2) s. 6(a) territorial tort exception applies only where the tort causing injury/death occurred in Canada and, in any event, requires a physical breach of personal integrity (psychological distress only if linked to physical injury); (3) "government" in s. 2 includes public officials acting in an official capacity, and torture can be an "official act" for immunity purposes.
BaselineB: Statute (State Immunity Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. S-18, ss. 2, 3(1), 6(a))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory incompatibility/inconsistency test: whether a permissive municipal discretion (Police Act, s. 24(6)) excludes a collectively bargained/arbitrated clause authorized as a “working condition” under s. 29(2); clause stands unless the provisions are “incompatible or inconsistent” (s. 24(6) is “an empowering provision only” and “does not prescribe exclusivity”).
BaselineA: Statute (The Police Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 351, ss. 24(6) and 29(2))
CaseB_TestB: Corporate attribution for BIA s. 96 transfers at undervalue: for s. 96(1)(b)(ii)(B), fraudulent intent may be inferred from non-exhaustive “badges of fraud” assessed on “all the circumstances”; and attribution under s. 96 is “simply whether the person was the directing mind and whether their actions were performed within the sector of corporate responsibility assigned to them”, with the “fraud” and “no benefit” exceptions inapplicable.
BaselineB: Combination: Statute (Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act, s. 96(1)(b)(ii)(B) and s. 2; CCAA s. 36.1) plus common law corporate attribution (Canadian Dredge; Livent; DeJong) as adapted for the s. 96 context
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Jennings test for establishing a constitutional convention (precedents; actors’ belief/acceptance they were bound; reason for the rule) — with emphasis that recognition/acceptance by the actors is the “most important element”
BaselineA: Common law / constitutional convention doctrine (as adopted in Re: Resolution to amend the Constitution, [1981] 1 S.C.R. 753, drawing on Sir W. Ivor Jennings and Freedman C.J.M./Hogg definition of convention)
CaseB_TestB: Reasonable suspicion standard for sniffer-dog searches under Charter s. 8: police may deploy a drug detection dog without prior authorization where there is a reasonable suspicion, assessed on the “totality of the circumstances”, based on “objective, ascertainable facts” (with guidance on profiles and dog reliability)
BaselineB: Common law Charter s. 8 search framework (R. v. Collins) and prior sniffer-dog cases (R. v. Kang-Brown; R. v. A.M.)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory tribunal (art. 846 C.C.P.) test for labour arbitrators: even if parties are not compelled by statute to resort to arbitration, an arbitrator is a “statutory tribunal” where, once arbitration is chosen, the arbitrator is “invested with wide duties and powers by statute” (e.g., Canada Labour Code s. 157) and the award is binding; refusal to hear “admissible and relevant evidence” is “so clear a case of excess or refusal to exercise jurisdiction” justifying evocation.
BaselineA: Combination of common-law certiorari principles (Howe Sound; Port Arthur; R. v. National Joint Council for the Craft of Dental Technicians) and statute (Code of Civil Procedure, art. 846; Canada Labour Code, ss. 156(2), 157, 159, 160(5)).
CaseB_TestB: Sublicence characterization test in patent licensing: a sublicence exists only if the licensee “granted, either expressly or impliedly, the right to do something which [the third party] would otherwise be prohibited from doing, and which [the licensee] was permitted to do only by virtue of its [patent] licence”; determine this from the contract’s text (no subjective-intention evidence if unambiguous) and distinguish sublicence from mere purchase-and-sale/supply arrangements.
BaselineB: Common law of patent licensing and contractual interpretation (including parol evidence rule) applied in the context of the Patent Act compulsory licensing regime and NOC Regulations.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Kienapple remedy direction: where Kienapple applies, enter a stay of proceedings rather than an acquittal ("whenever a court is of the view that the principles laid down in Kienapple should be applied, the court should enter a stay of the proceedings, in the stead of entering the acquittal")
BaselineA: Common law (Kienapple v. The Queen, [1975] 1 S.C.R. 729)
CaseB_TestB: Removing/replacing a litigation guardian: the Rule 49(1) test turns on the dependent adult’s “best interests”, informed by the Szwydky criteria including that the proposed guardian be “indifferent as to the outcome of the proceedings” (i.e., no conflict of interest)
BaselineB: Statute/rules-based: Queen’s Bench Rules (Saskatchewan) r. 49(1) (“best interests”); informed by common law guidance from Szwydky v. Magiera (1988), 71 Sask. R. 273
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Contract-interpretation rule for extent of power-supply obligation: reconcile general 'to such an extent as the Town may require' with specific reserve/availability clauses; Town entitled to $14 power only up to the 4,000 horsepower reserve (and no entitlement to additional power unless 'unleased or not in permanent use')
BaselineA: Common law (contract interpretation) applied to the January 9, 1905 agreement; key contractual provisions interpreted: para. 1 ('...to such an extent as the said Town... may require'), para. 5 (price ceiling 'shall not in any event exceed... Fourteen Dollars ($14.00) per Horse Power per annum'), para. 6 (sale/rent of reserved power 'not already in use'), para. 8 (reserve 'Four Thousand Horse Power' and proviso for further power only if 'unleased or not in permanent use')
CaseB_TestB: General Motors indicia for validity under the general trade and commerce power (s. 91(2) general branch): ask (1) general regulatory scheme; (2) oversight by regulatory agency; (3) concerned with trade as a whole not a particular industry; (4) provinces acting alone or together constitutionally incapable; (5) failure to include a province would jeopardize successful operation (indicia not exhaustive and not all required)
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine interpreting Constitution Act, 1867, s. 91(2) (general trade and commerce power), applying the test from General Motors of Canada Ltd. v. City National Leasing, [1989] 1 S.C.R. 641
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Contract-interpretation test for the extent of the Company’s obligation to supply Fort Frances power at the contract rate: reconcile the general words “to such an extent as the said Town… may require” (para. 1) with the specific allocation clauses (paras. 6 and 8), yielding a fixed entitlement of 4,000 horsepower per annum at $14 per horsepower per annum (and no broader right to all output). Key operative language: para. 8 requires the Company to “retain and reserve… Four Thousand Horse Power” and make it “permanently available”; the Court holds the Town’s right does not override this specific scheme and declares the obligation is “to provide… to the extent of 4,000 horsepower per annum… at… $14 per horsepower per annum.”
BaselineA: Common law (contract interpretation) applied to the 1905 Agreement (especially paras. 1, 5, 6, 8, 13); statutes discussed but held not to govern the issue.
CaseB_TestB: Continuing-offence/latecomer party-liability test for kidnapping: (1) Kidnapping under Criminal Code s. 279(1) is a continuing offence that includes ensuing unlawful confinement — “So long as the victim of the kidnapping remains unlawfully confined, the crime of kidnapping continues” and ends when the victim is freed; and (2) party liability under s. 21(1) attaches to a latecomer who, “with knowledge of the principal’s intention to see a continuing offence through to its completion”, does (or omits) something “with the intention of aiding or abetting the commission of the ongoing offence.”
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, ss. 279(1), 279(2), 21(1)) interpreted in light of common law meaning of kidnapping/false imprisonment and prior party-liability jurisprudence (e.g., Briscoe).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Trigger for mandatory municipal acquisition/expropriation under Planning Act s. 70(1): land must be “designated under a land use by-law” (not merely identified in statutory plans); statutory plans are policy/proposals and do not trigger s. 70
BaselineA: Statute — The Planning Act, 1977 (Alta.), s. 70(1) (and related scheme/definitions incl. s. 1(14))
CaseB_TestB: O’Connor framework for production of private third-party records in criminal cases: (1) accused must show records are “likely to be relevant” to an issue at trial or witness competence; (2) if so, court balances salutary vs deleterious effects (privacy/equality vs full answer and defence) and then reviews records to decide what, if anything, to produce
BaselineB: Common law/Charter-informed discretion — production procedure developed under Charter values (ss. 7, 24(1)) and Criminal Code subpoena context (e.g., ss. 698, 700) building from SCC disclosure jurisprudence (notably R. v. Stinchcombe)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “has become regularly engaged in some other occupation” under Unemployment Insurance Act s. 44(1)(c): requires a fixed pattern/regularity of work schedule (contrasted with “casual” or “intermittent”), not long-term duration or intent to abandon former job
BaselineA: Statute (Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, s. 44(1)(c)) and related regulation definition for contrast (Regulations, s. 49 defining “bona fide employed” in s. 44(1)(b) as “employment of not less than two weeks duration”)
CaseB_TestB: Whether an entity is a “broadcasting undertaking” under the Broadcasting Act when providing Internet access: entities that “merely provide the mode of transmission” and take no part in “selection, origination, or packaging of content” (i.e., lack control over programming) are not broadcasting undertakings
BaselineB: Statute (Broadcasting Act, S.C. 1991, c. 11, ss. 2(1) “broadcasting”, 2(3), 3(1)) interpreted purposively in light of the Act’s content-focused objectives
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Cross-border fresh pursuit: for Criminal Code s. 25(4), an officer who lawfully began a warrantless pursuit/arrest in their own province retains “peace officer” status in another province “inasmuch as the pursuit had commenced lawfully in his jurisdiction and as long as such pursuit is fresh”; once local authorities take over, the officer becomes a person assisting under s. 449(1)(b) and still has s. 25(4) protection
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 25(4), 449(1)(b), 450(1)(b); with the arrest-power reasonableness baseline drawn from R. v. Biron, [1976] 2 S.C.R. 56, and A.G. Sask. v. Pritchard (1961) as discussed)
CaseB_TestB: Arbitrator jurisdiction to substitute penalty under Canada Labour Code s. 157(d): an arbitrator is deprived of substitution power only if “the collective agreement does…contain a specific penalty for the infraction”; “a penalty is not specific where it can be chosen indiscriminately by the employer” and “to fall within s. 157(d)(ii) a specific penalty must be assigned to the particular infraction in the collective agreement”
BaselineB: Statute (Canada Labour Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. L-1, s. 157(d), especially s. 157(d)(ii), applied alongside the collective agreement’s Article XI(b))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Availability and scope of the Crown’s action per quod servitium amisit for injuries to Canadian Forces members deemed “servants of the Crown” (requires master-servant relationship; servant must have a valid cause of action; damages include wages/medical expenses)
BaselineA: Combination: statute deeming relationship (Federal Court Act, R.S.C. 1970 (2nd Supp.), c. 10, s. 37; with reference to Exchequer Court Act, R.S.C. 1952, c. 98, s. 50) + common law per quod servitium amisit as recognized in SCC precedents (The King v. Richardson; Nykorak v. Attorney General of Canada; Attorney-General of Canada v. Jackson; The Queen v. Murray)
JudgeA: Ritchie J. (for Ritchie, Estey, Lamer and Wilson JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Mens rea for Criminal Code s. 121(1)(a): no “corrupt” purpose required; guilt requires intentional commission of the prohibited act plus knowledge of the circumstances (official status; intentional demand/acceptance of a benefit; knowledge it is in consideration for cooperation/assistance/exercise of influence in business with/relating to government)
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 121(1)(a) (and s. 19 referenced); interpreted in light of SCC authority Martineau v. La Reine (and distinguished R. v. Hinchey)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Timing limit on Attorney General’s Criminal Code s. 508 stay power: an information is “found” only once the justice decides to issue process; therefore the AG may stay proceedings only after a summons or warrant is issued (not merely after an information is laid/received).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34 as amended), especially ss. 508(1) (“after an indictment has been found”), with interpretive context from ss. 2 (definition of “indictment”), 503 (meaning of “finding an indictment”), and the private information/hearing provisions in ss. 455 and 455.3.
CaseB_TestB: Statutory eligibility threshold for discharge under Criminal Code s. 662.1(1): discharge is unavailable if the offence is one “for which a minimum punishment is prescribed by law”; impaired driving under s. 234(a) qualifies because it prescribes a minimum fine of $50.
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code), interpreting and applying ss. 662.1(1) (discharge available only for an offence “other than an offence for which a minimum punishment is prescribed by law”) and 234(a) (first-offence impaired driving penalty includes “not less than fifty dollars”).
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Timing/trigger for Attorney General stay under Criminal Code s. 508(1): an information is “found” (and stay power begins) only after the justice decides to issue process; “The Attorney General’s power to stay starts as of the moment a summons or warrant is issued.”
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34 as amended): ss. 508(1) (stay “after an indictment has been found and before judgment”), plus interpretive context in ss. 2 (definition of “indictment”), 503 (“finding an indictment”), and the private information/hearing scheme in ss. 455 and 455.3.
CaseB_TestB: Baker procedural fairness framework applied to municipal rezoning decisions: duty of fairness content varies with five factors; here those factors required the Municipality to give reasons for refusing the 2nd and 3rd rezoning applications (“The content of the duty of fairness ... varies according to five factors ... [which] require the Municipality to articulate reasons”).
BaselineB: Common law administrative law duty of procedural fairness, using the Baker v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) five-factor framework (as cited and applied in the reasons).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Jurisdictional rule against joint trial of separate informations/indictments: even with consent, a judge is "without jurisdiction to try together separate informations or indictments" (a joint trial on more than one information/indictment is a nullity), unless a statute expressly provides otherwise
BaselineA: Common law rule from Crane v. Public Prosecutor, [1921] 2 A.C. 299 (applied/confirmed as Canadian law; also treated as incorporated by implication into the Criminal Code); applied as well to provincial summary conviction procedure absent express statutory authorization
CaseB_TestB: Credibility-assessment directions re (i) absence of evidence of motive to lie and (ii) lack of embellishment: motive-to-lie absence may be considered but judges must avoid (1) equating "no evidence either way" with evidence disproving a motive, and (2) reversing the burden by requiring the accused to show motive; lack of embellishment cannot bolster credibility (it "simply does not weigh against it") but may be considered regarding motive to lie
BaselineB: Common law principles governing credibility assessment and burden of proof, drawing on R. v. W.(D.) and related SCC authority (including R. v. Stirling; R. v. G.F.; R. v. Vuradin)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Marine insurance “perils of the seas” (fortuitous accident) where loss follows crew negligence: “An act is not negligent in itself but only in relation to a foreseeable risk of harm. If that foreseeable risk of harm is a peculiarly marine risk, then the act, coupled with its foreseeable consequence, is a fortuitous accident of the seas, a peril of the seas and the proximate cause of the loss.”
BaselineA: Statute + incorporated policy form: Insurance (Marine) Act, R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 203 (Schedule “Rules for Construction of Policy”: “The term ‘perils of the seas’ refers only to fortuitous accidents or casualties of the seas. It does not include the ordinary action of the winds and waves.”) and Marine Insurance Act, R.S.B.C. 1960, c. 231, s. 57(2)(a) (now s. 56(2)(a)) (insurer liable for loss proximately caused by a peril insured against “even though the loss would not have happened but for the misconduct or negligence of the master or crew”). Also applied: Canada Rice Mills, Ld. v. Union Marine & General Insurance Co. and Cohen, Sons & Co. v. National Benefit Assurance Co.
CaseB_TestB: Section 35(1) threshold for who can assert Aboriginal rights: “the expression ‘aboriginal peoples of Canada’ means the modern-day successors of Aboriginal societies that occupied Canadian territory at the time of European contact, and this may include Aboriginal groups that are now outside Canada.” (If threshold met, proceed to Van der Peet.)
BaselineB: Constitution Act, 1982, s. 35(1) (“The existing aboriginal and treaty rights of the aboriginal peoples of Canada are hereby recognized and affirmed.”) interpreted purposively; built on existing s. 35 jurisprudence including R. v. Van der Peet (Aboriginal rights test) and related cases discussed in the reasons.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory “bridging” of collective agreement rights pending renewal bargaining: s. 70(1) preserves the parties’ right to invoke interest arbitration after expiry, so long as the right exists when notice to arbitrate is served (and need not exist when the award is issued). Estey J.: s. 70(1) “provides a mechanism for the preservation of the right to arbitrate the renewal contract”; the right to arbitrate “need exist only at the time of the notice to arbitrate and not at the time the award is handed down.”
BaselineA: Statute: The Labour Relations Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 232, s. 70(1) (now R.S.O. 1980, c. 228, s. 79), applied alongside the collective agreement interest-arbitration clauses (Haldimand art. 16; Perth art. 15).
CaseB_TestB: Test for non-suit / directed verdict in criminal cases: whether there is “any admissible evidence, whether direct or circumstantial, which, if believed by a properly charged jury acting reasonably, would justify a conviction” (from Monteleone/Shephard, reaffirmed and applied).
BaselineB: Common law: R. v. Monteleone, [1987] 2 S.C.R. 154 (deriving the test from United States of America v. Shephard, [1977] 2 S.C.R. 1067).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: McKibbon (Lamer J.) conditions for when a non-AG person (including an AG’s agent) may prefer an indictment under Criminal Code s. 507(2), including additional counts: (1) a preliminary inquiry has been held; (2) the accused has been committed for trial on at least one charge inquired into; and (3) each count must be for (a) an offence for which the accused was committed, or (b) an offence disclosed by the evidence at the preliminary inquiry and not one for which the accused was discharged. (AG or judge’s written consent may prefer for any offence regardless of inquiry/committal/discharge.)
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 507(1)-(3), with comparison to ss. 504-505 and s. 496)
CaseB_TestB: Mitchell / Van der Peet test for establishing an Aboriginal right under Constitution Act, 1982, s. 35(1): claimant must prove (1) an ancestral practice, custom or tradition; (2) that it was “integral to the distinctive culture” (a “defining feature” of the pre-contact society); and (3) “reasonable continuity” between the pre-contact practice and the modern claim; plus the preliminary characterization step using Van der Peet’s three factors (impugned action, conflicting government action, and ancestral practice relied on).
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine under s. 35(1) (Van der Peet; Delgamuukw; Sparrow) interpreting Constitution Act, 1982, s. 35(1)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Planned-and-deliberate first degree murder where s. 212(b) applies: if the accused’s intention to kill (the s. 212(b) mens rea) was “planned and deliberate”, the murder is first degree even if, “by accident or mistake”, someone else is killed; “the identity and character of any victim is entirely irrelevant”.
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 212(b) and 214(2); with s. 214 treated as a sentencing-classification provision per R. v. Farrant, [1983] 1 S.C.R. 24).
CaseB_TestB: Interpretation of Alberta Limitations Act, s. 12 (conflict of laws): s. 12 “does not purport to revive an action time-barred by the substantive law of the place where the accident occurred”; if the foreign (lex loci delicti) limitation has expired, “there was no right of action” and the claim is barred despite Alberta’s longer period.
BaselineB: Statute interpreted against the common-law conflicts baseline from Tolofson v. Jensen, [1994] 3 S.C.R. 1022 (lex loci delicti includes the foreign limitation as substantive), focusing on Limitations Act, R.S.A. 2000, c. L-12, s. 12.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Mens rea for attempted murder: Crown must prove a specific intent to kill (no constructive/lesser murder intents suffice)
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code attempt provision) plus prior SCC interpretation in Lajoie v. The Queen (1974) on attempted murder intent
CaseB_TestB: “Establishment” under CHRA s. 11 / Guidelines s. 10: whether employees are subject to a “common personnel and wage policy” (a factual inquiry into employer’s common principles/approach)
BaselineB: Statute and regulation: Canadian Human Rights Act, s. 11 (read with s. 27(2)) and Equal Wages Guidelines, 1986, s. 10
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory limits on unequal matrimonial property distribution: pre-marital property exemption is capped at fair market value at marriage; s. 21(2)(q) cannot expand s. 23; “Capital Base Theory” rejected as incompatible with the equal-division presumption
BaselineA: Statute: The Matrimonial Property Act, 1979 (Sask.), c. M-6.1, especially ss. 20, 21, 22, 23 (and the interaction of s. 21(2)(q) with s. 23)
CaseB_TestB: Aggravated assault (s. 268(1) “endangers life”) in HIV non-disclosure: Crown must prove the aggravating consequence beyond a reasonable doubt; no conviction where there is a reasonable doubt the complainant was already HIV-positive at the relevant time (but attempt may be made out if intent and more-than-preparatory steps are proven)
BaselineB: Statute (with common-law interpretation): Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, ss. 268(1), 265(1)(a), 265(3)(c), 24(1), 660; interpreted with reference to Cuerrier, Godin, Cooper, Ancio, Dynar
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Mechanics’ lien Act “owner” test: a party is an “owner” if it (a) has an estate or interest in the land, (b) requested the work, and (c) the work was done “upon whose credit, or on whose behalf, or with whose privity or consent, or for whose direct benefit” (overall view of arrangements may establish the “request”).
BaselineA: Statute: The Mechanics’ Lien Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 267, ss. 1(1)(d), 5(1) (also discussed: ss. 7, 11).
CaseB_TestB: Challenge for cause (s. 638(1)(b)) “realistic potential for juror partiality” test: generally requires (1) a “widespread bias” in the community and (2) that some jurors may be unable to set aside the bias despite trial safeguards; overarching question is whether there is a “realistic potential for partial juror behaviour”.
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 638(1)(b) (with Charter context: s. 11(d)).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Anns duty-of-care framework for public authorities (proximity + residual policy considerations), including the policy/operational distinction and the requirement that inaction must at least be a bona fide policy decision to avoid liability
BaselineA: Common law (adopting/applying Anns v. Merton London Borough Council, [1978] A.C. 728; also drawing on Donoghue v. Stevenson; Hedley Byrne; Dorset Yacht) alongside statutory context (Municipal Act, R.S.B.C. 1960, c. 255, s. 714 and the City by-law imposing enforcement duties)
CaseB_TestB: Implied-limit analysis for s. 10(b) at roadside: a limit is 'prescribed by law' if it 'results by necessary implication' from a statute’s 'operating requirements'; roadside sobriety questions/tests are permitted if 'reasonable and necessary' to fulfill the police duty and 'incompatible with the exercise of the right to counsel'
BaselineB: Combination of constitutional text and precedent plus statutory context: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms ss. 1 and 10(b) (and the 'prescribed by law' concept from R. v. Therens; Thomsen) applied to Highway Traffic Act (Man.), s. 76.1(1) and Criminal Code ss. 253-254
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal defence of necessity (as an excuse): requires “moral or normative involuntariness” shown by (i) “imminent risk”/“direct and immediate peril”, (ii) no “reasonable legal alternative” (act “inevitable, unavoidable”), and (iii) proportionality (“harm inflicted must be less than the harm sought to be avoided”); Crown must disprove voluntariness beyond a reasonable doubt once properly raised
BaselineA: Combination: common law necessity as discussed in Morgentaler v. The Queen, [1976] 1 S.C.R. 616 (quoted formulation: “urgent situations of clear and imminent peril when compliance with the law is demonstrably impossible”), preserved via Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 7(3)
CaseB_TestB: Section 8 reasonable expectation of privacy (REP) framework: REP assessed on the “totality of the circumstances” via four inquiries (subject matter; direct interest; subjective expectation; and whether that expectation is “objectively reasonable” as a normative question); in this sting context, no objectively reasonable REP so s. 8 not engaged
BaselineB: Common law/constitutional doctrine under Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 8, applying the REP framework from cases cited in the reasons (e.g., R. v. Edwards; R. v. Tessling; R. v. Spencer; R. v. Cole; R. v. Marakah)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 613(1)(b)(iii) proviso: Crown must satisfy appellate court the verdict “would necessarily have been the same” absent the legal error; where the error is exclusion of exculpatory evidence, assess the entirety of the evidence including the excluded evidence and any reasonable possible effect of the excluded evidence must enure to the accused
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 613(1)(b)(iii)) as interpreted in Colpitts v. The Queen, [1965] S.C.R. 739 (Cartwright J.: Crown must show verdict “would necessarily have been the same if such error had not occurred”)
CaseB_TestB: Appellate court raising a new issue: an issue is “new” if it raises a new basis for finding error beyond the parties’ grounds; discretion to raise is exercised only rarely and only when failing to do so “would risk an injustice” (i.e., “good reason to believe” the result would realistically have differed), plus jurisdiction/record/procedural-prejudice constraints and notice/opportunity to respond
BaselineB: Common law / appellate practice principles (drawing on cases such as Quan v. Cusson and R. v. W.(G.)); articulated as a structured framework in this decision
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Threshold s. 96 ‘judicial power’ characterization: a power is administrative (not judicial) where there is “no real lis between the parties” and the decision is based “not on considerations of legality but on considerations of expediency” (used to uphold Quebec Securities Act s. 112 ministerial takeover power)
BaselineA: Common law / constitutional doctrine under Constitution Act, 1867, s. 96, drawing from Re Residential Tenancies Act, 1979 and related cases (incl. John East Iron Works; Grondin; Coopers and Lybrand) on identifying “judicial power”
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 12 mandatory-minimum framework (as applied in Hilbach): two-stage inquiry—(1) determine a “fit and proportionate sentence”; (2) ask whether the mandatory minimum is “grossly disproportionate” compared to that fit sentence, assessed via “scope and reach of the offence, the effects of the penalty on the offender, and the penalty and its objectives” (and may be based on the actual offender or a reasonably foreseeable case)
BaselineB: Combination of constitutional and statutory sources: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 12 (and s. 1 if reached) plus Criminal Code sentencing provisions (e.g., ss. 718, 718.1, 718.2(e)) and prior SCC s. 12 mandatory-minimum jurisprudence (esp. R. v. Hills, 2023 SCC 2; also Smith; Nur; Lloyd; Bissonnette; Boudreault)
JudgeB: Martin J. (Wagner C.J. and Moldaver, Brown, Rowe and Kasirer JJ. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 93(1) denominational schools protection test: s. 93 applies where (a) there is a 'right or privilege affecting a denominational school' (b) 'enjoyed by a particular class of persons' (c) 'by law' (d) 'in effect at the time of the Union' and (e) 'which is prejudicially affected' (trial judge’s formulation adopted at para. 16).
BaselineA: Constitution Act, 1867, s. 93(1) (and s. 93(2)); content of protected rights determined by law in force at Confederation (e.g., C.S.L.C. 1861, c. 15) and Privy Council jurisprudence cited (Barrett; Brophy; Hirsch; Tiny; Ottawa Separate Schools Trustees).
CaseB_TestB: Young Offenders Act non-disclosure test (docket disclosure): focus is on whether the communication 'create[s] a link between the identity of a young person and an (alleged) offence or hearing under the Act' (para. 27); if so, disclosure is prohibited unless it fits a specific statutory exception (notably s. 44.1 or s. 38(1.1)/(1.13)).
BaselineB: Statute: Young Offenders Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. Y-1, especially ss. 38(1), 38(1.1), 38(1.13), 40-46 and s. 44.1(1)(k).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 93(1) denominational schools protection test: s. 93 applies where “(a) there must be a right or privilege affecting a denominational school; (b) enjoyed by a particular class of persons; (c) by law; (d) in effect at the time of the Union; (e) and which is prejudicially affected.”
BaselineA: Constitution Act, 1867, s. 93(1) (and s. 93(2)); applied with reference to rights “by law in the Province at the Union” (including the 1861 Act respecting Provincial Aid for Superior Education—and Normal and Common Schools, C.S.L.C. 1861, c. 15).
CaseB_TestB: Federal maritime law (navigation and shipping) scope test: “the factual context must be examined to determine whether the allegedly negligent act is integrally connected with the act of navigating the pleasure craft on Canadian waterways such that it is a practical necessity for Parliament to have jurisdiction over the matter”; “the mere involvement of a pleasure craft in an incident is not sufficient to ground Parliament’s jurisdiction.”
BaselineB: Common law constitutional/maritime-law framework from ITO — International Terminal Operators Ltd. v. Miida Electronics Inc. (integral connection), Whitbread v. Walley (practical necessity for uniform law re pleasure craft navigation), and Ordon Estate v. Grail (factual-context examination), applied under Constitution Act, 1867, ss. 91(10) and 92(13).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Certiorari can quash a preliminary inquiry committal for trial where there is “no evidence” on an essential element: “No evidence on an essential element of the charge against the accused cannot amount to ‘sufficient evidence’ under s. 475.” The reviewing court must “independently assess the record to determine whether there was any evidence to support the committal.”
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 475) interpreted through prior certiorari/jurisdiction jurisprudence (Patterson v. The Queen; Martin v. The Queen; Forsythe v. The Queen; Nat Bell Liquors).
CaseB_TestB: Criteria for compensatory allowance under art. 559 C.C.Q.: claimant must establish (1) “contribution”; (2) “enrichment of [the] spouse’s patrimony”; (3) “causal link” between them; and (4) “the proportion in which the contribution made possible the enrichment”; these elements “must be evaluated with great flexibility.” Enrichment “must subsist” and “must be evaluated at the time of the divorce.” Bankruptcy/discharge is not an automatic bar and is not “irrefutable evidence” of no enrichment.
BaselineB: Statute (Civil Code of Quebec, art. 559) with interaction/interpretation of Bankruptcy Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. B-3, ss. 2 (“claim provable in bankruptcy”), 148; informed by unjust enrichment principles (e.g., Cie Immobilière Viger Ltée v. Lauréat Giguère Inc.).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Estoppel by representation (including when silence/inaction can be a representation): requires (1) a representation by words/conduct, or (only if under a duty to speak) by silence/inaction; (2) intended (actual or presumptive) and resulting in inducing the representee to alter position; and (3) detrimental reliance — and silence is not a representation absent a legal duty to disclose
BaselineA: Common law (estoppel by representation; also pleading requirement under Nova Scotia Civil Procedure Rule 14.04 is referenced as a procedural baseline)
CaseB_TestB: Rebutting the Criminal Code s. 212(3) presumption (“living with a prostitute”): jury may consider all the evidence about cohabitation and financial arrangements; no need to identify a single “particular and severable” item as “evidence to the contrary”
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 212(3))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Municipal taxing power must be exercised in the form required by the enabling statute (by-law vs resolution); self-delegation to set a tax rate by resolution where statute requires a by-law is ultra vires/excess of jurisdiction and void
BaselineA: Statute (Cities and Towns Act, R.S.Q. 1941, c. 233, s. 526 as amended for Dorval by its Charter; plus procedural requirements in Cities and Towns Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 193 (e.g., ss. 385, 395))
CaseB_TestB: Causation in negligent blood donor screening: apply the 'material contribution' test (not a rebuttable presumption and not strict 'but-for')—whether the defendant’s negligence 'materially contributed' to the occurrence of the injury (i.e., more than de minimis)
BaselineB: Common law causation in negligence (but-for as general rule; material contribution as alternative), drawing on Snell v. Farrell and Athey v. Leonati; distinguishing Hollis v. Dow Corning
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 13 bar on using an accused’s prior testimony at a retrial: a retrial is “any other proceedings” and any Crown evidence-in-chief is “incriminating” (assessed in the second proceeding)
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 13 (interpreted in light of ss. 11(c) and 11(d))
CaseB_TestB: Reformed rule for substantive admissibility of a non-accused witness’s prior inconsistent statement: admissible for truth if (threshold) it would be admissible as the witness’s sole testimony and (principled hearsay) necessity + reliability shown, typically via oath/affirmation/solemn declaration with warning + videotaping + opportunity to cross-examine at trial (or adequate substitutes), subject to voir dire screening (incl. voluntariness/justice-disrepute concerns)
BaselineB: Combination: Statute (Canada Evidence Act, s. 9 voir dire mechanism) + common law hearsay/prior-inconsistent-statement doctrine (the “orthodox rule” from Deacon v. The King) as reshaped by the principled hearsay approach (R. v. Khan; R. v. Smith)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: When a trial judge’s acquittal can be appealed by the Crown as an “error of law alone”: a “total absence of evidence/foundation” is an error of law only where the law shifts the burden of proof to the accused on the fact in issue; otherwise (given the presumption of innocence) there is always some evidence on which to acquit and any mistake is an error of fact
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 605(1)(a) (Crown appeal on a question of law alone)) interpreted through SCC common-law appellate-jurisdiction jurisprudence (Lampard v. The Queen; Sunbeam Corporation (Canada) Ltd. v. The Queen; discussion of Wild; Lemire not followed on this point)
CaseB_TestB: Test for interim relief (stay/interim release) under Supreme Court Act s. 65.1: (1) serious question to be tried, (2) irreparable harm, and (3) balance of convenience
BaselineB: Combination: Statute (Supreme Court Act, R.S.C., 1985, c. S-26, s. 65.1) applying the common-law/interlocutory-injunction framework reaffirmed in RJR—MacDonald Inc. v. Canada (Attorney General)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Crown appeal from acquittal: when an alleged “no evidence”/“no foundation” finding becomes an error of law (only where the burden has shifted to the accused)
BaselineA: Combination: statute (Criminal Code, s. 605(1)(a) (appeal on question of law alone)) plus common-law/jurisprudential principles from Lampard v. The Queen, Sunbeam Corporation (Canada) Ltd. v. The Queen, and discussion of Wild v. The Queen (and rejecting an overbroad reading of Lemire)
CaseB_TestB: Ontario anti-SLAPP dismissal framework under CJA s. 137.1: threshold (s. 137.1(3)) + plaintiff’s merits/defence hurdle (s. 137.1(4)(a)) + public-interest weighing (s. 137.1(4)(b))
BaselineB: Statute: Courts of Justice Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.43, s. 137.1(3) and s. 137.1(4) (and related ss. 137.2-137.5 as context)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Landry/Eccles test for warrantless arrest on private premises (forcible entry): arrest is lawful if (1) offence is indictable; (2) officer has reasonable and probable grounds the person committed/is about to commit it; (3) reasonable and probable grounds the person is within the premises; and (4) “proper announcement” before entry (notice of presence, authority, and purpose). “An affirmative answer to all of these questions will mean that the arrest is lawful.”
BaselineA: Combination: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 450(1)(a) (arrest without warrant for indictable offences) plus common law limits/authority from Eccles v. Bourque, [1975] 2 S.C.R. 739 (itself grounded in Semayne’s Case (1604) as discussed).
CaseB_TestB: Turpin framework on s. 11(f) Charter “benefit of trial by jury”: (i) s. 11(f) confers a right to the “benefit” of jury trial and therefore permits waiver by the accused; but (ii) “a constitutional right to waive is not a constitutional right to elect” and waiver “does not confer rights, it repudiates them”; thus waiver cannot override Criminal Code s. 429’s mandatory jury trial, and s. 24(1) relief is unavailable absent an infringement.
BaselineB: Constitutional text and interpretation: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 11(f) and 24(1) (with interpretive support from Korponay v. A.G. Canada, [1982] 1 S.C.R. 41 and related waiver jurisprudence).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Amending an indictment to cure a variance between the particular alleged and the evidence: court should amend under Criminal Code s. 529 if it would not mislead or prejudice the accused (and if prejudice exists, consider whether it can be cured, e.g., by adjournment).
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 529(4)-(5) (amendment of indictment; factors include whether accused was misled or prejudiced and whether amendment can be made without injustice). Also applied with SCC authority on particulars/gravamen from Elliott v. The Queen, [1978] 2 S.C.R. 393, and appellate amendment power under s. 613(1)(b)(i) and s. 613(3).
CaseB_TestB: Ineffective assistance of counsel test (G.D.B.): appellant must show (1) counsel’s acts or omissions constituted incompetence and (2) a miscarriage of justice resulted.
BaselineB: Common law: R. v. G.D.B., 2000 SCC 22, [2000] 1 S.C.R. 520 at para. 26 (two-part test: incompetence + resulting miscarriage of justice).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Concurrent liability in tort and contract for professional negligence: a common law duty of care may arise from a contractual relationship of sufficient proximity, but tort cannot be used to circumvent contractual limits; plus discoverability for limitation periods (cause of action arises when material facts are discovered or ought to be discovered by reasonable diligence). Key formulations: (1) proximity not confined to non-contract: "The question is whether there is a relationship of sufficient proximity, not how it arose." (2) tort duty must not depend on express contractual specification: "between what is to be done and how it is to be done"; and "A concurrent or alternative liability in tort will not be admitted if its effect would be to permit the plaintiff to circumvent or escape a contractual exclusion or limitation of liability". (3) discoverability: "A cause of action arises for purposes of a limitation period when the material facts on which it is based have been discovered or ought to have been discovered ... by the exercise of reasonable diligence."
BaselineA: Common law (duty of care/proximity and concurrent liability) drawing on Donoghue v. Stevenson, Hedley Byrne, and Anns; plus statutory limitation period in Nova Scotia Statute of Limitations, R.S.N.S. 1967, c. 168, s. 2(1)(e), interpreted through the common-law discoverability rule as applied in Kamloops (City of) v. Nielsen.
CaseB_TestB: Quebec private international law jurisdiction in warranty actions with a choice-of-forum clause: art. 3148 para. 2 C.C.Q. prevails over art. 3139 C.C.Q. if the clause is valid and shows a clear intention to oust Quebec jurisdiction; forum non conveniens (art. 3135) is inapplicable unless Quebec jurisdiction is first established. Key formulations: "Article 3148, para. 2 C.C.Q. must take precedence over art. 3139 C.C.Q. ... where a choice of forum clause ... indicates a clear intention to oust the jurisdiction of the Quebec authority. In such circumstances, the Quebec authority must decline jurisdiction."
BaselineB: Statute/codified private international law: Civil Code of Québec, arts. 3148 para. 2 (choice of forum), 3139 (incidental demand), and 3135 (forum non conveniens).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Scope of Quebec Construction Industry Labour Relations Act/Decree: coverage turns on the nature of the work (is it “construction” vs excluded “maintenance and repair”), not the status of the employer/employee; and no “total wage” set-off against Decree minima
BaselineA: Statute and regulation/decree: Construction Industry Labour Relations Act, S.Q. 1968, c. 45 (now R.S.Q., c. R-20), especially ss. 1(e) (definition of “construction”), 1(i), 1(j), 1(r), and s. 2(2) (exception for “maintenance and repair work done by permanent employees hired directly by an employer other than a professional employer”); plus Decree respecting the construction industry, (1973) 105 O.G. II 5837, including ss. 3.01-3.02; and Act s. 20 / Decree ss. 18.06, 32.03 (public order effect)
CaseB_TestB: Charter remedy for unconstitutional mandatory minimum sentence: if a mandatory minimum produces a s. 12 breach (gross disproportionality), the proper remedy is s. 52(1) invalidity (no stand-alone s. 24(1) constitutional exemption)
BaselineB: Constitutional text and Charter doctrine: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms ss. 12 and 24(1); Constitution Act, 1982 s. 52(1); plus the s. 12 test that a sentence is unconstitutional only if “grossly disproportionate” (citing R. v. Smith) and related mandatory-minimum jurisprudence (e.g., Goltz, Morrisey)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Parens patriae limit: a court may not authorize non-therapeutic sterilization of a mentally incompetent person; parens patriae discretion must be exercised only for the protected person’s benefit and with great caution, and “sterilization should never be authorized for non-therapeutic purposes under the parens patriae jurisdiction” because “it can never be safely determined that it is for the benefit of that person”.
BaselineA: Common law (parens patriae jurisdiction as inherited from English Chancery and developed in wardship/mental incompetency cases; discussed via authorities such as Wellesley v. Duke of Beaufort, Re X (a minor), Re D (a minor), and Canadian use of parens patriae).
CaseB_TestB: Residual management rights “balancing of interests” assessment: to decide if a unilaterally imposed workplace policy is a reasonable exercise of management rights, arbitrators must “consider all of the surrounding circumstances” and determine whether the policy “strikes a reasonable balance between management and employees’ interests”; the determination is “highly fact-based”.
BaselineB: Common law / labour arbitration doctrine incorporated through the collective agreement’s management-rights clause (cl. 5.02 “act reasonably, fairly and in good faith”), with the SCC grounding the approach in KVP and endorsing it via Irving.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: R. v. Prince refinement of the Kienapple rule against multiple convictions: Kienapple applies only where there is (1) a sufficient factual nexus (usually “Does the same act of the accused ground each of the charges?”) and (2) a sufficient legal nexus such that “there is no additional and distinguishing element that goes to guilt” in the offence sought to be barred; plus guidance on when elements are not ‘additional’ (particularization; alternative methods to prove a single delict; evidentiary proxy/deeming).
BaselineA: Common law (Kienapple v. The Queen, [1975] 1 S.C.R. 729; also discussed through Côté v. The Queen, [1975] 1 S.C.R. 303 and Krug v. The Queen, [1985] 2 S.C.R. 255).
CaseB_TestB: Gould (La Forest J.) two-step test for s. 8(a) “services … to the public” under the Yukon Human Rights Act: (1) identify the relevant “service”; (2) determine whether it creates a “public relationship” between provider and user, with “public” defined relationally; assess contextually non-exhaustive criteria including “selectivity”, “diversity”, “involvement of non-members”, “commercial nature”, “intimate nature”, and “purpose” (none determinative).
BaselineB: Statute (Yukon Human Rights Act, R.S.Y. 1986 (Supp.), c. 11, s. 8(a); interpreted in light of analogous human rights statutes and University of British Columbia v. Berg, [1993] 2 S.C.R. 353).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Ensite test for whether property is “used or held ... in the course of carrying on a business” (ITA s. 129(4)(a)(ii)): property must be “truly employed and risked” in the business; “risk” is met where withdrawal would “have a decidedly destabilizing effect on the corporate operations themselves”; focus is whether property was used to fulfil a requirement that had to be met to do business (not whether taxpayer was forced to use that particular property).
BaselineA: Statute: Income Tax Act, S.C. 1970-71-72, c. 63, s. 129(4)(a)(ii) (as amended by S.C. 1974-75-76, c. 26, s. 86(2)) excluding “a property used or held ... in the course of carrying on a business” from “income ... from a ... property” for investment-income purposes; interpreted with reference to Marsh & McLennan (FCA) and March Shipping (TRB) language adopted/clarified by SCC.
CaseB_TestB: Crown appeal from acquittal/new trial test under Criminal Code s. 686(4): Crown must satisfy the court that “the verdict would not necessarily have been the same if the trial judge had properly directed the jury” (a “very heavy onus”).
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(4), as interpreted in Vézeau v. The Queen and reaffirmed in R. v. Morin (both cited in the reasons).
JudgeB: Cory J. (for Sopinka, Cory, Iacobucci and Major JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Public interest immunity for Cabinet documents: court (not Crown) balances competing public interests; where claim is class-based and relevance is shown, the judge should inspect the documents to decide whether disclosure/production is outweighed by the public interest in confidentiality (considering variables like nature/level of policy, timing, and importance of the litigation). Key quotes: the court must "determine the balance to be struck between the public interest in the proper administration of justice and the public interest in withholding" (para. 36); "it is for the court and not the Crown to determine the issue" (para. 39); "Cabinet documents like other evidence must be disclosed unless such disclosure would interfere with the public interest" and the level of decision-making is "only one of many variables" (para. 79); Cabinet documents "ought not to be disclosed without a preliminary judicial inspection to balance the competing interests" (para. 86).
BaselineA: Common law public interest immunity/Crown privilege doctrine as developed in cases discussed in the reasons, especially Smallwood v. Sparling, [1982] 2 S.C.R. 686 (and also R. v. Snider, [1954] S.C.R. 479; Gagnon v. Commission des valeurs mobilières du Québec, [1965] S.C.R. 73; with comparative discussion of Conway v. Rimmer and Burmah Oil).
CaseB_TestB: Adequacy review of jury instructions (pre-Lifchus / W.(D.)): the charge is assessed "read as a whole" for "substantial compliance" and the "basic question" is whether it creates a "reasonable likelihood that the jury misapprehended the correct standard of proof" (para. 12). For reasonable doubt, Lifchus 'ingredients' must be conveyed "in substance" (para. 10). For conflicting versions, W.(D.) requires the jury be told it must acquit if it believes the accused, or if it does not believe the accused but is left with a reasonable doubt, and even if not left in doubt by the accused's evidence it must ask whether the accepted evidence proves guilt beyond a reasonable doubt (para. 19).
BaselineB: Common law jury-charge requirements from R. v. Lifchus, [1997] 3 S.C.R. 320 and R. v. W. (D.), [1991] 1 S.C.R. 742 (with Starr, Russell, Beauchamp applied/referred to).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 7 limit on extradition/surrender: courts may intervene only where surrender would, in the particular circumstances, violate the principles of fundamental justice—intervention must be exercised "with caution" and "limited to cases of real substance" (generally after the executive surrender decision).
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional text (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7; also extradition framework under the Extradition Act and treaty context).
CaseB_TestB: Crown appeal jurisdiction limit: a Court of Appeal may interfere with an acquittal only if the trial court erred "on a question of law alone" (Criminal Code, s. 605(1)(a); applying Schuldt v. The Queen).
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 605(1)(a)) as interpreted/applied in Schuldt v. The Queen.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 7 limit on extradition/surrender: courts may intervene only where surrender would, in the particular circumstances, violate the principles of fundamental justice (judicial intervention limited to 'cases of real substance')
BaselineA: Statute/Constitution (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7; applied in extradition context alongside Extradition Act and treaty framework)
CaseB_TestB: Income Tax Act s. 20(1)(c)(i) interest deductibility (purpose element): whether, considering all the circumstances, the taxpayer had a 'reasonable expectation of income' at the time the investment was made (income = taxable income, not net income; ancillary income-earning purpose suffices absent sham/window dressing)
BaselineB: Statute (Income Tax Act, s. 20(1)(c)(i))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Injurious affection (no land taken): claimant must satisfy the Loiselle four conditions, including that the damage would have been actionable at common law (nuisance) but for statutory authority; loss of view/amenities from highway construction is not actionable nuisance where the Minister’s use is not unreasonable
BaselineA: Statute (Ontario Expropriations Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 154, ss. 1(e)(ii), 21) incorporating common-law actionability requirement; key baseline test stated in The Queen v. Loiselle, [1962] S.C.R. 624 (four conditions for injurious affection when no land is taken) and common-law nuisance (reasonable user/unreasonableness)
CaseB_TestB: Adequacy of jury instructions on alternative routes to murder liability: it is sufficient to instruct that the accused may be convicted if he acted alone or “acted in concert with others” and “actively participated in the killing”; the trial judge may correct an erroneous ‘actual shooter’ instruction by adding ‘or was otherwise an active participant’ without causing a miscarriage of justice (in context of the charge as a whole)
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, including ss. 21, 229, 686(1)(b)(iii)) and common-law appellate framework for assessing jury charges as a whole / miscarriage of justice; party-liability principles referenced through R. v. Thatcher, [1987] 1 S.C.R. 652
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 10(b) right to counsel: once police promptly advise of the right, no further correlative duties arise unless the detainee indicates a desire to exercise it; absent proof of non-understanding, the accused bears the onus to show he asked for counsel and was denied or denied an opportunity to ask
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 10(b) (and remedy context under s. 24(2)); applied approach from R. v. Anderson (Ont. C.A.) as adopted by the SCC
CaseB_TestB: Disgorgement/accounting for employee’s secret profits: where an employee acting in a representative capacity breaches good faith/loyalty or abuses authority (including using employer funds or taking secret commissions), the employee must account for and turn over the profits to the employer (drawing on C.C.L.C. arts. 411 and 1713 and the principle that no one should profit from wrongdoing)
BaselineB: Civil law statute: Civil Code of Lower Canada, arts. 411 (possessor in bad faith) and 1713 (mandatary’s duty to render an account and deliver what is received under authority of the mandate), extended by the Court to the employment/representative-capacity context
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Wigglesworth s. 11 Charter applicability test: a matter falls within s. 11 either (1) because by its very nature it is a criminal/quasi-criminal/public proceeding, or (2) because conviction may lead to a “true penal consequence”; if the two conflict, the “by nature” test gives way to the “true penal consequence” test
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 11 (opening words “Any person charged with an offence”); interpretive context includes the marginal note “Proceedings in criminal and penal matters” and comparison to Canadian Bill of Rights, s. 2(f)
CaseB_TestB: Jacquard functional approach to reviewing jury charges: a charge is proper “as long as” the appellate court, reading it “as a whole”, concludes the jury had a “sufficient understanding of the facts as they relate to the relevant issues” (juries must be properly, not perfectly, instructed)
BaselineB: Common law (jury-charge review principles) drawing on SCC authorities including Azoulay v. The Queen, John v. The Queen, and Cluett v. The Queen; applied in the context of Criminal Code provisions (e.g., s. 16, s. 231(2), s. 686(1)(b)(iii))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: s. 577(1) Criminal Code “whole of his trial” includes jury selection; accused must be able to hear/participate when jurors are examined for partiality after plea, and breach is fundamental (not curable by proviso)
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 577(1), with related jury-selection provisions incl. ss. 554-573, 569(2), and curative provisions ss. 598-599, 613(1)(b)(iii))
CaseB_TestB: Common-law test for when an appellate court may set aside an acquittal and enter a conviction (instead of ordering a new trial): Crown must show verdict would not have been the same but for error of law, accused should have been found guilty, and all necessary findings of fact were made (explicitly/implicitly) or are not in issue
BaselineB: Common law (as stated in Vézeau v. The Queen and applied with reference to Courville v. The Queen)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 529 quashing/amendment framework and its effect on autrefois acquit: a trial judge must amend unless amendment would cause irreparable prejudice/injustice; if amendment cannot be made without injustice, quashing is tantamount to an acquittal (barring a new information). Key formulation: s. 529 'commands' that 'if the required amendment cannot be made without injustice being done, then and only then the judge is to quash' and 'if ... an amendment cannot be made without causing irreparable prejudice, his quashing ... is ... tantamount to an acquittal' (Lamer J.).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 529, 535, 537) plus prior SCC double-jeopardy/autrefois jurisprudence referenced (e.g., Petersen v. The Queen; Doyle v. The Queen).
CaseB_TestB: Scope of acquired rights / legal non-conforming use (purpose characterization; remoteness and neighbourhood effects): (1) characterize the purpose of the pre-existing use; (2) mere intensification is protected unless it becomes a different use; (3) added activities may be too remote (then no need to assess neighbourhood effects); (4) if within original purpose, balance landowner vs community considering remoteness and new/aggravated neighbourhood effects; plus evidentiary and framing cautions (Binnie J., para. 39).
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law principles: Act Respecting Land Use Planning and Development, R.S.Q., c. A-19.1 (notably s. 113(18)); municipal by-law; and common law/non-conforming use jurisprudence (e.g., Central Jewish Institute v. City of Toronto) used to inform the approach.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Workmen’s privilege against an owner’s immovable where work is done for a lessee: a lessee is not a “builder/contractor” for arts. 2013e/2013f unless the owner–lessee agreement is a true construction contract that includes an owner’s undertaking to pay a construction-contract “price” (i.e., a claim between owner and builder) from which the owner can retain funds; absent such a claim/price, no privilege lies
BaselineA: Statute (Civil Code of Lower Canada, arts. 2013e and 2013f; also art. 1060 definition of contract for services/enterprise)
CaseB_TestB: Mental distress damages for breach of contract: recoverable where (1) an object of the contract was to secure a psychological benefit so that mental distress on breach was within the parties’ reasonable contemplation at contract formation, and (2) the degree of mental suffering caused by the breach is sufficient to warrant compensation; no independent actionable wrong required
BaselineB: Common law (Hadley v. Baxendale remoteness/foreseeability; Vorvis v. I.C.B.C. referenced as SCC authority on contemplation of mental distress in some contracts)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Unequal division under NB Marital Property Act s. 7(f): court may depart from equal division where equal division would be inequitable; in particular, where property was acquired "exclusively or almost wholly" through one spouse’s efforts and the other made "no, or a negligible, contribution" to child care/household management/financial provision, this constitutes circumstances relating to acquisition/maintenance/improvement justifying discretion to depart
BaselineA: Statute: Marital Property Act, S.N.B. 1980, c. M-1.1, ss. 2, 3, 7 (especially s. 7(f) residual factor: "any other circumstances... rendering it inequitable" to divide equally)
CaseB_TestB: Interjurisdictional immunity (constitutional inapplicability) for federal services: otherwise-applicable provincial laws of general application cannot apply where they bear on what makes the matter specifically federal; for a federal service, inapplicability arises if the provincial law touches a "vital or essential aspect" of the service’s "establishment, management or operation"
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine (interjurisdictional immunity) as articulated in prior SCC cases cited (e.g., Bell Canada v. Quebec (CSST); Construction Montcalm; Clark v. CNR; Dick v. The Queen) and applied to the provincial Transport Act/Bus Transport Regulation permit scheme
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “financing” in Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971 s. 44(2)(a): a claimant is “financing” a labour dispute only where there is an “active and voluntary involvement” and a “meaningful connection between the payment and the dispute” (mandatory union dues diverted to a strike fund are not enough).
BaselineA: Statute — Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, S.C. 1970-71-72, c. 48, s. 44(2)(a) (and s. 44 generally).
JudgeA: L'Heureux-Dubé J. (for Dickson C.J. and Wilson, La Forest and L'Heureux-Dubé JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Enforceability/scope of a negligence waiver (exclusion) clause: in the “context in which it was signed”, determine whether the clause (though framed as an indemnity) was intended as a release and whether the negligence causing the injury was within what the parties reasonably contemplated; avoid non-enforcement arguments (fundamental breach/unconscionability/public policy) where the clause is not “unfair” or “unreasonable” in the circumstances.
BaselineB: Common law — contractual interpretation/enforcement of exclusion (waiver) clauses and related doctrines (fundamental breach, unconscionability, public policy) as applied to releases of negligence liability.
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “financing” in Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971 s. 44(2)(a): claimant is “financing” only where there is “active and voluntary involvement” and a “meaningful connection between the payment and the dispute”; mandatory union dues diverted to an international strike fund are not enough
BaselineA: Statute — Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, S.C. 1970-71-72, c. 48, s. 44(2)(a) (“not participating in or financing or directly interested in the labour dispute”)
CaseB_TestB: Extradition surrender review: whether extradition would be contrary to s. 7 principles of fundamental justice so as to “shock the conscience” or be “unjust or oppressive” under Extradition Act s. 44(1); requires a ministerial “balancing exercise” and deference/comity absent “exceptional cases of ‘real substance’”
BaselineB: Statute + Charter — Extradition Act, S.C. 1999, c. 18, s. 44(1) (“unjust or oppressive”) and Charter s. 7; as framed through SCC precedent (United States v. Burns; Lake v. Canada (Minister of Justice))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 10 “detention” test (Therens criteria): detention exists where (1) there is a “restraint of liberty other than arrest” in which a person may reasonably require counsel; and (2) “a police officer ... assumes control over the movement of a person by a demand or direction which may have significant legal consequence and which prevents or impedes access to counsel”; with (3) “compulsion or coercion” arising from “criminal liability for refusal ... or from a reasonable belief that one does not have a choice”.
BaselineA: Common law/Charter interpretation drawing from R. v. Therens (applied) and Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 10(b) (meaning of “detention”).
CaseB_TestB: Mistake of age—“all reasonable steps” requirement: to convict where the defence has an air of reality, Crown must prove beyond a reasonable doubt either (1) accused “did not honestly believe the complainant was at least 16” or (2) “did not take ‘all reasonable steps’ to ascertain the complainant’s age”; the reasonable-steps inquiry is “highly contextual, fact-specific”, and “the more reasonable an accused’s perception of the complainant’s age, the fewer steps reasonably required of them.”
BaselineB: Statute—Criminal Code, s. 150.1(4) (and related scheme), as interpreted and applied by the SCC.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Extradition specialty/undertaking immunity ends once the extradited person has been “restored or has had an opportunity of returning” to the surrendering state; an unqualified specialty undertaking is construed as related to the surrender and not perpetual where the person remains in Canada by choice
BaselineA: Statute (Extradition Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-21, s. 33) plus interpretation of the Brazil-Canada extradition arrangement/undertaking; informed by international law treaty-interpretation principles (Vienna Convention, art. 31) and specialty principle authorities (e.g., United States v. Rauscher)
CaseB_TestB: No separate leave needed to appeal a court of appeal’s refusal to apply the curative proviso: on an appeal as of right on an error of law, the SCC may consider whether the error is saved by Criminal Code s. 686(1)(b)(iii) because “error of law and application of the curative proviso [are] always intertwined”
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(b)(iii)) as interpreted through SCC precedent (R. v. Keegstra)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code theft: meaning of “anything” in s. 283(1) — to be the object of theft, “anything” must (1) be “property of some sort” and (2) be “capable of being taken or converted in a manner that results in the deprivation of the victim”; confidential information per se fails (not property; and in any event not capable of taking/conversion with deprivation) (R. v. Stewart).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 283(1)); with prior case context including R. v. Scallen and R. v. Hardy on intangibles/choses in action.
CaseB_TestB: Contractual interpretation of “assets” in MVHC rent-subsidy Assistance Application: interpret “assets” by “ordinary and grammatical meaning” in context/purpose; a reasonable person would understand “assets” to mean property/interests “that can actually be used to discharge ... debts and liabilities, including monthly rent”; a Henson trust interest is a “mere hope” and not an “asset” for eligibility to be considered (S.A. v. Metro Vancouver Housing Corp.).
BaselineB: Common law (contractual interpretation principles, relying on Sattva Capital Corp. v. Creston Moly Corp. and related cases) applied to a tenancy agreement/assistance application (private contractual documents).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 7 analysis for compelled fingerprinting pre‑conviction: (1) deprivation of life/liberty/security; (2) whether deprivation accords with principles of fundamental justice — i.e., whether fingerprinting/appearance requirement "unduly invades the rights of the accused" and is not arbitrary (reasonable and probable grounds; discretion not constitutionally barred; sufficient safeguards in issuance/confirmation of appearance notice/summons)
BaselineA: Statute + constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7; Identification of Criminals Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-1, s. 2; Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 453.3(3), 455.5(5) (and related issuance/confirmation provisions discussed). Also relies on SCC baseline for s. 7 structure from Re B.C. Motor Vehicle Act and Lyons.
CaseB_TestB: Sheppard/Braich test for appellate intervention based on insufficiency of trial reasons: two stages — (1) "are the reasons inadequate"; (2) "if so, do they prevent appellate review?" (i.e., are the reasons "sufficiently amenable to appellate review" / is there an "impediment to appellate review")
BaselineB: Common law framework from R. v. Sheppard and R. v. Braich (as applied in this case); statutory context noted: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686 (appellate powers).
JudgeB: Bastarache and Abella JJ. (LeBel J. concurring)
