Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Detention at the border triggering s. 10(b): a traveller is “detained” when a customs officer “assumes control over the movement of a person by a demand or direction which may have significant legal consequence” (Therens), applied here because during a strip search the person “could not have refused and continued on her way” and was “subject to external restraint”.
BaselineA: Common law / Charter interpretation baseline from R. v. Therens, [1985] 1 S.C.R. 613 (definition of “detention” for s. 10(b) purposes), applied to a Customs Act strip search context (Customs Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-40, ss. 143, 203).
CaseB_TestB: s. 11(b) “reasonable time” analysis (Morin factors + institutional-delay guideline): not a “mathematical or administrative formula” but a balancing using (1) length of delay; (2) waiver; (3) reasons for delay (including inherent requirements, accused, Crown, institutional resources, other); and (4) prejudice; with a suggested institutional-delay guideline of “between 8 and 10 months for institutional delay in Provincial Courts” (not a fixed ceiling and must not be applied mechanically).
BaselineB: Charter s. 11(b) and prior SCC framework in Mills v. The Queen, [1986] 1 S.C.R. 863; R. v. Rahey, [1987] 1 S.C.R. 588; R. v. Conway, [1989] 1 S.C.R. 1659; R. v. Smith, [1989] 2 S.C.R. 1120; and R. v. Askov, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 1199 (institutional-delay guideline concept).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Voluntary intoxication and mens rea for general-intent offences (Leary rule preserved): intoxication generally irrelevant unless (at most) extreme intoxication akin to insanity/automatism; mens rea may be inferred from actus reus or, in rare cases, established by proof of voluntary self-induced intoxication where voluntariness is in doubt
BaselineA: Common law (as applied to Criminal Code offences): Leary v. The Queen, [1978] 1 S.C.R. 29; also discussed/applied: R. v. George, [1960] S.C.R. 871; Swietlinski v. The Queen, [1980] 2 S.C.R. 956; Director of Public Prosecutions v. Majewski, [1977] A.C. 443
CaseB_TestB: Appellate intervention on Crown appeal from acquittal: (1) appellate court cannot interfere with trial judge’s inferences of fact merely because it would draw different inferences (Schuldt); but (2) it may intervene for an error of law where the trial judge failed to direct his mind to an issue requiring determination to reach the verdict
BaselineB: Common law appellate review principles (Crown appeals from acquittal), relying on Schuldt v. The Queen, [1985] 2 S.C.R. 592; also referenced: R. v. Morin, [1992] 3 S.C.R. 286; R. v. C. (R.), [1993] 2 S.C.R. 226
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Appellate intervention in a trial judge’s discretionary reapportionment of matrimonial property: intervene only if the judge “misdirects himself” or the decision is “so clearly wrong as to amount to an injustice” (and s. 51 does not require asset-by-asset contribution comparison or separate ‘business’/‘domestic’ treatment).
BaselineA: Combination: common law appellate deference to discretion (as applied in Harper v. Harper, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 2; Re Hull Estate (Ont. C.A.) quoted) + statute (Family Relations Act, R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 121, ss. 43 and 51).
CaseB_TestB: Duty to comment on improper Crown jury address: where Crown counsel’s remarks are “prejudicial to a degree sufficient to impose a legal duty on the trial judge to comment” to ensure the defence is “fairly put to the jury”; failure is an error of law (with no s. 686(1)(b)(iii) cure on these facts).
BaselineB: Common law (trial fairness/jury-charge requirements as adopted via the Court of Appeal dissent relied on by the SCC) + statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(b)(iii)).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Wigmore/Slavutych four-part test for recognizing a (qualified) common law privilege against compelled disclosure of communications (including journalist-source): (1) communication originates in confidence; (2) confidentiality essential to the relationship; (3) relationship one the community ought to foster; (4) injury from disclosure greater than benefit to litigation
BaselineA: Common law (Wigmore criteria as discussed by the SCC in Slavutych v. Baker, [1976] 1 S.C.R. 254)
CaseB_TestB: Reasonableness review of Crown corporations’ discretionary decisions setting PILT “effective rate”: discretion exists but must be exercised within the statutory/regulatory framework by basing calculations on the municipality’s actual existing tax system (as if the federal property were taxable private property), not a “fictitious tax system” (e.g., cannot reintroduce an abolished occupancy tax)
BaselineB: Statute and regulation: Payments in Lieu of Taxes Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. M-13 (esp. ss. 2 “effective rate”, 2.1, 4(1), sch. II item 10) and Crown Corporation Payments Regulations, SOR/81-1030 (esp. s. 2 “corporation effective rate”, s. 7(1))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Patent Act s. 36(1) disclosure/sufficiency test: applicant must disclose everything essential for the invention to function properly; completeness requires (1) describing the invention and defining how it is produced/built, and (2) defining the nature of the invention and describing how it is put into operation; disclosure must enable a person skilled in the art to make/produce it using only the specification (deposit of seed alone is not enough).
BaselineA: Statute — Patent Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. P-4, s. 36(1) (as interpreted with prior case law cited in the reasons, incl. Minerals Separation; Burton Parsons; Monsanto; Consolboard).
CaseB_TestB: Standard of review for labour-arbitration awards applying common law/equitable doctrines: reasonableness remains the presumptive standard; correctness applies only if a Dunsmuir correctness category is engaged (e.g., constitutional issue, central question of law outside expertise, true jurisdiction/vires, competing tribunals). Contextual factors (privative clause, purpose, nature of question, expertise) confirm deference; arbitrators may flex/adapt doctrines like estoppel within labour relations, subject to reasonableness.
BaselineB: Common law of judicial review/administrative law — Dunsmuir v. New Brunswick; Smith v. Alliance Pipeline (applied), plus Labour Relations Act, R.S.M. 1987, c. L10, ss. 121 and 128(2) as contextual/statutory anchors for arbitral authority and privative clause.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 96 (Constitution Act, 1867) validity — the three-stage Residential Tenancies test, with Sobeys clarifications on (1) characterization, (2) shared vs. exclusive jurisdiction, and (3) national (1867) historical inquiry: (i) whether the challenged power/jurisdiction 'broadly conform[s]' to s. 96 courts at Confederation; (ii) whether the tribunal is acting in a 'judicial capacity'; and (iii) whether, in its 'institutional context', the power is 'necessarily incidental to the achievement of a broader policy goal' (vs. the tribunal operating 'like a s. 96 Court'). Key Sobeys quotes: stage 1 asks whether the power 'broadly conform[s] to the power or jurisdiction exercised by Superior, District or County Courts at the time of Confederation'; characterization should be narrow and guided by 'the type of dispute' not the remedy; add a 'gloss' that the threshold is whether superior court jurisdiction was 'exclusive' and, if shared, only if inferior court work was 'broadly co-extensive'; and the historical yardstick is national: 'pre-confederation jurisdiction refers to pre-1867 jurisdiction' across the four original provinces (and UK if tied).
BaselineA: Common law constitutional doctrine under Constitution Act, 1867, s. 96, applying and refining Re Residential Tenancies Act, 1979, [1981] 1 S.C.R. 714 (three-stage s. 96 test).
CaseB_TestB: Public interest standing — Downtown Eastside three-factor framework, applied 'cumulatively, flexibly and purposively': (i) 'serious justiciable issue'; (ii) 'genuine interest'; (iii) 'reasonable and effective means' of bringing the issue to court. Key quotes: 'a court must assess and weigh three factors'; 'none of the factors ... are hard and fast requirements or free-standing, independently operating tests'; legality and access to justice 'do not merit particular weight'; and 'a directly affected co-plaintiff ... is not required ... as long as [the litigant] can establish a concrete and well-developed factual setting', which may be shown context-specifically (e.g., by non-plaintiff witnesses) and with a limited ability to revisit standing upon a 'material change' raising 'serious doubt' about a forthcoming factual record.
BaselineB: Common law standing doctrine from Canada (Attorney General) v. Downtown Eastside Sex Workers United Against Violence Society, 2012 SCC 45 (public interest standing framework).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Bankruptcy Act s. 47(a) vs s. 107(1)(j) classification for provincial “deemed trusts”: s. 47(a) applies only if the tax money is “identifiable or traceable”; if commingled/untraceable, there is no “property held ... in trust” and the province has only a Crown claim under s. 107(1)(j)
BaselineA: Statute (Bankruptcy Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. B-3, ss. 47(a), 107(1)(j)) interpreted alongside provincial statute (Social Service Tax Act, R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 388, s. 18); SCC authorities cited include Deputy Minister of Revenue v. Rainville and Deloitte Haskins and Sells Ltd. v. Workers' Compensation Board
CaseB_TestB: Section 23 “numbers warrant” / sliding-scale framework: relevant number is “somewhere between the known demand and the total number of persons who could potentially take advantage of the service”; determining what numbers warrant requires assessing “appropriate services, in pedagogical terms” and “costs”; with a minority-language board, defining the relevant area and choosing location of classes/facilities is within the minority’s management and control (subject to objective provincial norms consistent with s. 23), and the Minister’s discretion is limited to verifying provincial requirements (no substitution of his own criteria)
BaselineB: Constitution (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 23) as developed in Mahe v. Alberta (sliding scale; numbers warrant; management and control) and related s. 23 jurisprudence; applied in the context of P.E.I. School Act and Regulations
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Young Offenders Act s. 16 transfer to ordinary court: whether, after "weighing and balancing all the relevant considerations" in s. 16(2), the judge is satisfied transfer is "appropriate" (onus on applicant but "not ... a heavy one")
BaselineA: Statute: Young Offenders Act, S.C. 1980-81-82-83, c. 110, s. 16(1) (transfer) and s. 16(2) (factors); applied/clarified via R. v. M. (S.H.), [1989] 2 S.C.R. 000 (as referenced in the reasons)
CaseB_TestB: Damages for repudiation where contract has alternative modes of performance: adopt the mode "least profitable to the plaintiff, and the least burdensome to the defendant"; not a factual inquiry into how defendant would likely have performed but for repudiation
BaselineB: Common law principle on damages for contracts with alternative performances, traced to Cockburn v. Alexander (1848) and explained in Withers v. General Theatre Corp. (1933) (as cited in the reasons)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Canadian maritime law (agency): whether an agent of an unnamed/partially disclosed principal is personally liable turns on the parties’ intention as shown by the contract—“a matter of construction of a particular contract”; “there is no prescribed formality for disclosure” and liability “depends on the will of the contracting parties” (e.g., clear wording like signing “as agent only” indicates no personal liability).
BaselineA: Common law (contract/agency) as part of Canadian maritime law under the Federal Court Act, plus comparative use of civil law principles (C.C.L.C. arts. 1715-1716) as sources; statutory framework: Federal Court Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. F-7, ss. 2 (“Canadian maritime law”), 22(2)(m) (stevedoring). Key prior SCC baseline case cited: ITO—International Terminal Operators Ltd. v. Miida Electronics Inc., [1986] 1 S.C.R. 752.
CaseB_TestB: Child Welfare Act reporting immunity: s. 38(6) protects an informant unless the report is made “maliciously or without reasonable cause”; “reasonable cause” is an objective threshold meaning the informant must have “reasonable cause to ask CPS to consider looking into the matter” (not reasonable grounds to believe abuse occurred).
BaselineB: Statute: Child Welfare Act, R.S.N. 1990, c. C-12, ss. 38(1) (duty to report) and 38(6) (immunity unless “maliciously or without reasonable cause”); interpreted alongside common law negligence/duty framework (Cooper v. Hobart; Martel Building).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Common law limits on a warrantless “frisk” search incident to a lawful arrest (no reasonable/probable grounds prerequisite; but three constraints: discretionary, valid objective, non-abusive/proportionate manner)
BaselineA: Common law (police power to search incident to lawful arrest, as recognized in Canadian and UK common law authorities discussed in the reasons, including R. v. Brezack; R. v. Morrison; R. v. Miller; and the Dedman ‘necessary and reasonable’ justification approach to common law police powers)
CaseB_TestB: Section 7 ‘principles of fundamental justice’ minimum for warrantless child apprehension: statute is constitutionally sufficient if it permits apprehension without prior judicial authorization only where there is “serious harm or risk of serious harm” to the child, coupled with a “fair and prompt post-apprehension hearing”
BaselineB: Statute + Charter (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7; Child and Family Services Act, S.M. 1985-86, c. 8, ss. 17 and 21(1), with post-apprehension process in ss. 27(1) and 29(1))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal negligence: whether the accused’s conduct is a “marked departure from the norm” such that “wanton or reckless disregard” can be inferred; consequences (death) generally add nothing unless “so interwoven” with the conduct as to help characterize it
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 202(1)-(2), 203 (now ss. 219, 220) as interpreted in R. v. Tutton, [1989] 1 S.C.R. 1392)
CaseB_TestB: Standing/jurisdiction before the CITT under the AIT: a procurement complaint lies only if the procurement is “within Canada” under AIT art. 502, which requires the supplier to be a “Canadian supplier” (AIT art. 518: supplier with “a place of business in Canada”)
BaselineB: Statute and regulation incorporating a trade agreement: Canadian International Trade Tribunal Act, ss. 30.1, 30.11(1) and Canadian International Trade Tribunal Procurement Inquiry Regulations, s. 3(1), interpreted through the Agreement on Internal Trade (arts. 101, 501, 502, 518)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 8 reasonableness of compelled document production in a regulatory/tax audit: a s. 231(3) demand is a 'seizure' but is reasonable given the regulatory scheme, low expectation of privacy, and need for random monitoring (Hunter criteria not mechanically applicable).
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law/constitutional doctrine: Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1952, c. 148, s. 231(3) (demand for information/documents) with enforcement in s. 238(2); Charter s. 8; reasonableness framework from Hunter v. Southam Inc. and related SCC s. 8 cases (incl. R. v. Simmons; Thomson Newspapers (released concurrently)).
CaseB_TestB: Public interest standing (constitutional/public law): three interrelated factors weighed flexibly—(1) serious justiciable issue; (2) real stake/genuine interest; (3) whether the proposed suit is, in all the circumstances, a reasonable and effective means to bring the issue to court (not a strict 'no other way' requirement).
BaselineB: Common law standing doctrine from SCC precedents (not statute): Borowski; Finlay; Canadian Council of Churches; Thorson; McNeil; Hy and Zel’s; Chaoulli (as discussed).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Duty to defend is determined by the pleadings: insurer must defend only if the suit alleges an act/omission and seeks “damages which are or may be payable under the terms of this Policy”; no duty where allegations are clearly outside coverage (e.g., only fraud alleged and fraud excluded).
BaselineA: Contract (insurance policy) interpreted using common-law principles of insurance contract construction; Court also relies on the general principle that “the pleadings govern the duty to defend” (e.g., Bacon v. McBride; Opron Maritimes Construction Ltd.).
CaseB_TestB: Criminal Code s. 265(4) “air of reality” threshold for honest but mistaken belief in consent: defence goes to jury only if there is “sufficient evidence” such that “a reasonable jury properly instructed could have acquitted”; requires evidence beyond a bare assertion of belief (though it need not be independent of the accused).
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 265(4), treated as codifying the common-law “air of reality” requirement for defences (citing Pappajohn; Bulmer; Robertson; Brisson; Parnerkar).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Deductibility of wage-continuation (collateral) benefits from tort damages for lost earnings: “As a general rule, wage benefits paid while a plaintiff is unable to work must be brought into account and deducted from the claim for lost earnings”, with a limited exception where the payor has a subrogation/reimbursement entitlement (and only rarely via a court-imposed trust where “necessary and appropriate in the interests of justice”).
BaselineA: Common law damages principles (compensation for “actual loss” and no double recovery) and prior collateral-benefits jurisprudence, including the SCC’s personal injury damages trilogy (Andrews v. Grand & Toy Alberta Ltd.; Thornton v. Prince George School Board; Arnold v. Teno) and the insurance/collateral source line (Bradburn v. Great Western Rail. Co.; Parry v. Cleaver).
CaseB_TestB: Constitutional characterization/justification of the GST collection scheme under s. 91(3): determine (1) whether the GST Act is “properly characterized as being in relation to a mode or system of taxation” (pith and substance), and if it intrudes on provincial jurisdiction, (2) whether the impugned features are “sufficiently integrated with the scheme” to be upheld as “necessarily incidental” (high degree of integration).
BaselineB: Constitution Act, 1867 (especially ss. 91(3) and 92(13)) and the SCC’s “necessarily incidental/sufficiently integrated” doctrine as articulated in General Motors of Canada Ltd. v. City National Leasing and Reference re Exported Natural Gas Tax.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Test for entitlement to a compensatory allowance under art. 559 C.C.Q.: claimant must prove (1) contribution, (2) enrichment of the other spouse’s patrimony, (3) causal link/correlation between the two, and (4) the proportion in which the contribution made possible the enrichment; the enrichment must “subsist” and is evaluated “at the time of the divorce”, with “great flexibility” in evaluating the elements (bankruptcy is not irrefutable proof of no subsisting enrichment).
BaselineA: Statute (Civil Code of Quebec, art. 559; with interpretive support from unjust enrichment jurisprudence such as Cie Immobilière Viger Ltée v. Lauréat Giguère Inc., [1977] 2 S.C.R. 67 (correlation) and related civil-law principles).
CaseB_TestB: Morrissey test for setting aside a conviction for misapprehension of evidence: the misapprehension must go to “the substance” (not “detail”), be “material” (not “peripheral”) to the trial judge’s reasoning, and the errors must play an “essential part” not just in the narrative but “in the reasoning process resulting in a conviction” (conjunctive hurdles).
BaselineB: Common law appellate standard adopted from R. v. Morrissey (1995), 97 C.C.C. (3d) 193, and consistent with R. v. C. (R.), [1993] 2 S.C.R. 226; applied in the context of Criminal Code, s. 686(1)(a)(iii) (miscarriage of justice).
JudgeB: Binnie J. (for the Court, oral reasons)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Copyright Act s. 3(1) “reproduction in any material form whatever”: a computer program remains protected when replicated in silicon chip circuitry (chip-embedded machine code is a reproduction of the assembly-language program)
BaselineA: Statute — Copyright Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-30, s. 3(1) (including s. 3(1)(a) and (d) discussed but not decided)
CaseB_TestB: Common law de facto taking (constructive expropriation) test: compensation requires (1) acquisition of a beneficial interest in the property or flowing from it, and (2) removal of all reasonable uses of the property
BaselineB: Common law — test drawn from Mariner Real Estate (N.S.C.A.) and SCC authorities Manitoba Fisheries Ltd. v. The Queen and The Queen in Right of British Columbia v. Tener; applied alongside statute (Vancouver Charter, s. 569) which deems no taking/compensation
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Novation in a mortgage/assumption context: three-part test requiring (1) new debtor assumes complete liability; (2) creditor accepts new debtor as principal debtor; and (3) creditor accepts the new contract "in full satisfaction and substitution for the old contract" (novation not found absent "really compelling" circumstances showing creditor assent).
BaselineA: Common law (novation doctrine; test stated as set out in Polson v. Wulffsohn (1890), 2 B.C.R. 39, and discussed with other authorities).
CaseB_TestB: De facto taking (constructive expropriation) requiring compensation at common law: two requirements—(1) "an acquisition of a beneficial interest in the property or flowing from it" and (2) "removal of all reasonable uses of the property".
BaselineB: Common law (as applied in Mariner Real Estate Ltd. v. Nova Scotia (Attorney General); Manitoba Fisheries Ltd. v. The Queen; The Queen in Right of British Columbia v. Tener), with statutory overlay in Vancouver Charter s. 569 deeming no taking.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Applicability of Criminal Code search-warrant power to offences under other federal statutes: after the 1985 amendment, s. 443(1)(a)-(b) applies to proceedings under “any other Act of Parliament” regardless of whether that Act has its own search-and-seizure provisions (with express limits only where Parliament says “subject to any other Act of Parliament” as in s. 443(1)(e)).
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 443(1)(a)-(b) (as amended in 1985 to add “or any other Act of Parliament”); considered alongside Bankruptcy Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. B-3, s. 6 and Interpretation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-23, s. 27(2).
CaseB_TestB: Meaning of “risks willingly assumed” under Occupiers’ Liability Act s. 4(1): s. 4(1) embodies the volenti doctrine, so “usually more than mere knowledge of the risk is required”; the plaintiff must have assumed the risk in the sense of accepting the legal risk/waiving recourse (i.e., being “prepared to accept the entire risk of injury ... without recourse” to the occupier).
BaselineB: Statute interpreted in light of common law: Occupiers’ Liability Act, R.S.O. 1980, c. 322, ss. 2, 3(1), 4(1); common-law baseline for the defence is volenti non fit injuria as discussed via SCC cases Dube v. Labar and Crocker v. Sundance Northwest Resorts Ltd.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 32 applicability to an entity: Wilson J.’s three-part criteria (general government control; traditional/state responsibility function; statutory authority to further a public-interest government objective)
BaselineA: Common law / constitutional interpretation of Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 32 (as developed in McKinney v. University of Guelph, [1990] 3 S.C.R. 000, and discussed alongside RWDSU v. Dolphin Delivery Ltd., [1986] 2 S.C.R. 573)
CaseB_TestB: Arbitration Act s. 31(2)(a) leave-to-appeal framework: leave only on a question of law; ‘miscarriage of justice’ requires a material legal issue with ‘arguable merit’; plus residual discretion factors (conduct, alternative remedies, undue delay, urgent need for final answer)
BaselineB: Statute: Arbitration Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 55, s. 31(2)(a) (interpreted and structured by the SCC, drawing on BCIT and related jurisprudence)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Kirkness limit on the Paré “single transaction” analysis: applies only to murder classification under Criminal Code s. 214(5) (now s. 231(5)); prerequisites are party/principal liability for both the predicate offence and the murder, then a close temporal connection for first-degree classification; not available for manslaughter
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 214(5) (now R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 231(5))) as interpreted in R. v. Paré, [1987] 2 S.C.R. 618 ("while committing" / single transaction concept)
CaseB_TestB: Forum non conveniens test (as applied to multistate defamation): after jurisdiction is properly assumed, the moving party must show another forum is a “clearly more appropriate forum”; court considers multiple contextual factors and one forum must “ultimately emerge as clearly more appropriate”
BaselineB: Common law (Club Resorts Ltd. v. Van Breda, 2012 SCC 17) forum non conveniens framework; with reference to codified factor lists (e.g., CJPTA s. 11(2); Civil Code of Québec art. 3135) as persuasive guides
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Abuse of process stay test (Keyowski/Jewitt/Young): stay only where compelling trial would violate fundamental principles of justice/fair play and decency or proceedings are oppressive or vexatious, and only in the 'clearest of cases'
BaselineA: Common law (abuse of process stay doctrine) applied alongside Criminal Code s. 508 stay/recommencement power
CaseB_TestB: When a Vetrovec 'clear, sharp warning' is required: trial judge has discretion to warn where a witness is sufficiently untrustworthy, but in some cases the circumstances are such that a Vetrovec caution must be given
BaselineB: Common law (Vetrovec v. The Queen framework for cautioning juries about untrustworthy witnesses)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Institutional impartiality (structural bias) test for part-time judges: (1) ask whether, considering factors including “the nature of the occupation and the parties who appear before this type of judge”, there will be “a reasonable apprehension of bias in the mind of a fully informed person in a substantial number of cases”; (2) if yes (occupation “per se incompatible”), ask whether safeguards sufficiently minimize the risk so that, with knowledge of safeguards, there is not still such a reasonable apprehension “in a substantial number of cases” (otherwise case-by-case challenges remain).
BaselineA: Combination of constitutional text and common-law test: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 11(d) and Quebec Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms, s. 23; applying the reasonable apprehension of bias test from Committee for Justice and Liberty v. National Energy Board (adopted in Valente v. The Queen).
CaseB_TestB: Section 1 justification analysis for Criminal Code s. 181 (“false news”): identify Parliament’s objective as enacted/amended (no “shifting purpose”); if no pressing and substantial objective is shown, the limit fails; even if an objective is assumed, assess proportionality (rational connection, minimal impairment, overall proportionality) given s. 181’s breadth (e.g., “injury or mischief to a public interest”).
BaselineB: Constitutional text and established Charter framework: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 1 and 2(b), applying the Oakes s. 1 test and the Irwin Toy s. 2(b) framework; interpreting Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 181.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 96 “core jurisdiction” / Residential Tenancies step-one historical inquiry (with required characterization): determine whether the impugned jurisdiction was exercised exclusively by s. 96 superior courts at Confederation; if not, it may be conferred on an inferior court/tribunal. Lamer C.J.: characterization must be “sufficiently narrow to avoid large accretions ... but not so narrow as to freeze” inferior-court jurisdiction; here, characterize as “jurisdiction over young persons charged with a criminal offence,” which “did not exist at Confederation” and therefore passes step one.
BaselineA: Common law constitutional test under s. 96 of the Constitution Act, 1867 as formulated in Re Residential Tenancies Act, 1979, [1981] 1 S.C.R. 714 (and discussed with Sobeys Stores Ltd. v. Yeomans, [1989] 1 S.C.R. 238).
CaseB_TestB: Interpretation of “sold in any market in Canada” (Patent Act ss. 80(1)(b), 83(1), 85): Board jurisdiction includes SAP sales where the medicine is “regulated by the public laws of Canada, ... will be delivered in Canada, to be dispensed in Canada, and where ... the cost ... will be borne by Canadians.”
BaselineB: Statutory interpretation of Patent Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. P-4, ss. 80(1)(b), 83(1), 85 (using the modern textual-contextual-purposive approach referenced via Canada Trustco).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Adequacy/sufficiency of an indictment (incl. multiple-conspiracies scope): indictment is adequate if it gives the accused “reasonable information” and identifies the “transaction”; and a proven conspiracy falls within the indictment if it “included some of the accused”, occurred “at some time within the time frame alleged”, and had as its object “the type of crime alleged”.
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 510, 512, 516) as interpreted through SCC/common-law principles (citing R. v. Côté; R. v. Wis Development Corp.; R. v. Cotroni; R. v. B.(G.)).
CaseB_TestB: Constitutional validity of the Canada Evidence Act s. 38 national security disclosure scheme: apply the Re Residential Tenancies Act, 1979 s. 96 test (first ask whether the power “broadly conforms” to a superior court power at Confederation; if not, “the inquiry ends”), plus core-jurisdiction characterization (properly characterize narrowly as authority over disclosure of security-exempt material; trial courts must retain ability to ensure a fair trial via s. 38.14 remedies).
BaselineB: Combination: constitutional doctrine (s. 96 jurisprudence, especially Re Residential Tenancies Act, 1979; MacMillan Bloedel; Babcock) and statute (Canada Evidence Act, ss. 38 to 38.16, especially ss. 38.04, 38.06, 38.14).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Entrapment (random virtue-testing) — first branch of Mack: police may offer an opportunity only with (a) reasonable suspicion of the person, or (b) a bona fide inquiry tied to a sufficiently precise location; random virtue-testing exists if neither (a) nor (b) is met
BaselineA: Common law — R. v. Mack, [1988] 2 S.C.R. 903 (two-branch entrapment test, including the concepts of “reasonable suspicion”, “bona fide inquiry”, and “random virtue-testing”)
CaseB_TestB: Appellate review of trial judge’s voluntariness ruling on a voir dire — a court of appeal should not reweigh the evidence absent a “serious, specific and determining error”
BaselineB: Common law — voluntariness of statements and appellate deference to trial-level weighing of evidence on a voir dire (no specific baseline case cited in the reasons provided)
JudgeB: LeBel J. (for the Court, oral reasons)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Duty to comment on Crown counsel’s prejudicial jury address: where remarks are “prejudicial to a degree sufficient to impose a legal duty on the trial judge to comment” to ensure the defence is “fairly put to the jury”; failure to do so is an error of law (and no curative proviso under s. 686(1)(b)(iii) on these facts).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, s. 686(1)(b)(iii)) plus common-law principles on jury charges/fairness (as reflected in the Court’s adoption of Ayles J.A.’s formulation).
CaseB_TestB: Broker commission triggers under brokerage contract/CCQ: (1) no “agreement to sell” unless the accepted promise to purchase is “unconditional” such that it is “possible for one of them to bring an action to compel transfer of title”; and (2) clause mirroring art. 1503 C.C.Q. requires proof that fulfilment was prevented “through the fault of the seller” (i.e., breach of an obligation to do/not do something).
BaselineB: Statute (Civil Code of Québec, arts. 1396 and 1503) interpreted and applied to standard-form brokerage clauses 6.1(3o) and 6.1(4o).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 16(2) insanity defence — second branch: whether, due to “disease of the mind”, the accused was “incapable … of knowing that an act or omission is wrong”, with “wrong” (per Chaulk) meaning “morally wrong” (not “legally wrong”); first branch limited to inability to appreciate the “physical consequences” of the act
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 16(2)); interpreted in light of SCC precedents including R. v. Chaulk, [1990] 3 S.C.R. 1303 (redefining “wrong”), and Cooper v. The Queen, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 1149; Kjeldsen v. The Queen, [1981] 2 S.C.R. 617; R. v. Abbey, [1982] 2 S.C.R. 24 (limiting first branch to physical nature/consequences)
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 8 sniffer-dog search — “reasonable suspicion” standard: must be more than a hunch; “reasonable suspicion must be grounded in objectively discernible facts” and is assessed on the “totality of the circumstances” (a “constellation of factors”), asking whether facts are “objectively indicative of the possibility of criminal behaviour” (possibilities, not probabilities), viewed through the lens of a reasonable person in the shoes of the trained officer
BaselineB: Common law Charter s. 8 framework for sniffer-dog searches (building on R. v. Kang-Brown, 2008 SCC 18 and R. v. A.M., 2008 SCC 19; clarified alongside R. v. Chehil, 2013 SCC 49) applying Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 8 (and related detention analysis under s. 9 via R. v. Mann, 2004 SCC 52)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Legitimate expectations cannot create substantive rights and do not apply to the legislative process (including introducing a money bill): where applicable, the doctrine only gives a right to make representations/consultation, not consent/veto
BaselineA: Common law doctrine of procedural fairness/legitimate expectations (as summarized in Old St. Boniface Residents Assn. Inc. v. Winnipeg (City)) applied alongside constitutional principles of parliamentary sovereignty and the legislative process (Constitution Act, 1867, s. 54; Interpretation Act, s. 42(1))
CaseB_TestB: Divorce Act s. 17(4) variation threshold and discretion: court must be satisfied of a post-order 'change in the condition, means, needs or other circumstances' and then vary considering that change; pension income may be treated as 'means' and 'double dipping' does not arise where the pension was not truly valued/divided as future property
BaselineB: Statute (Divorce Act, 1985, s. 17(4) and s. 17(7))
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Extradition/death-penalty assurances under Charter s. 7: surrender is unconstitutional only if, considering comity/security and the foreign justice system, the prospective treatment or penalty is "simply unacceptable" / "sufficiently shocks" the Canadian conscience (Schmidt/Allard) and thus violates fundamental justice; otherwise ministerial discretion under Extradition Act s. 25 stands.
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law/Charter: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7; Extradition Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. E-23, s. 25; baseline common-law/constitutional standard from Canada v. Schmidt ("shock the conscience") and United States v. Allard ("simply unacceptable").
CaseB_TestB: Search warrants for media premises: after meeting Criminal Code s. 487(1)(b) requirements, the justice must assess overall reasonableness under Charter s. 8 in light of press interests (s. 2(b)) by weighing all circumstances and striking a "delicate balance"; alternative sources are ordinarily addressed but are not mandatory prerequisites—"[t]he essential question is whether, taking into account all the circumstances... the search was reasonable."
BaselineB: Statute with Charter overlay: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 487(1)(b), (d), (e); Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 2(b) and 8; informed by prior jurisprudence (Re Pacific Press; Descôteaux v. Mierzwinski) but framed as a contextual reasonableness inquiry.
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Reasonable apprehension of bias (pecuniary interest) test: “Would a reasonably well-informed person consider that the interest might have an influence on the exercise of the official’s public duty?” (Old St. Boniface formulation applied to Law Society discipline/costs)
BaselineA: Common law (administrative law/natural justice) as formulated in Old St. Boniface Residents Assn. Inc. v. Winnipeg (City), [1990] 3 S.C.R. 1170
CaseB_TestB: Nelles malicious prosecution / lifting prosecutorial immunity test (4 elements): (1) prosecution initiated by defendant; (2) terminated in plaintiff’s favour; (3) absence of reasonable and probable cause (subjective + objective); (4) malice/improper purpose (“deliberate and improper use” of prosecutorial office)
BaselineB: Common law (tort of malicious prosecution / prosecutorial immunity) from Nelles v. Ontario, [1989] 2 S.C.R. 170
JudgeB: Iacobucci and Binnie JJ. (for McLachlin C.J. and Iacobucci, Major and Binnie JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Colour of right / mistake analysis for s. 206(1)(d): colour of right is unavailable where the offence does not “embrace the concept within its definition”, and in any event a belief that the Criminal Code is inoperative is a mistake of law barred by s. 19 (“Ignorance of the law ... is not an excuse”).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, ss. 19 and 206(1)(d)), plus common-law distinction between mistake of fact and mistake of law as reflected in cited authorities (e.g., Bulmer; DeMarco; Howson; Johnson).
CaseB_TestB: Modified Taylor definition/test for “hatred” under s. 14(1)(b) hate-publications provisions: apply an objective reasonable-person-in-context test; interpret “hatred” as limited to “detestation” and “vilification”; and focus on likely effects on the audience (intent irrelevant).
BaselineB: Statute (Saskatchewan Human Rights Code, S.S. 1979, c. S-24.1, s. 14(1)(b)) interpreted through prior SCC framework in Canada (Human Rights Commission) v. Taylor, [1990] 3 S.C.R. 892 (as modified in this case, including severance of “ridicules, belittles or otherwise affronts the dignity of”).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Test for granting intervener status and managing prejudice from a new Charter argument/fresh evidence: intervener must have a sufficient interest and bring a special perspective; Court considers whether raising a new Charter issue would prejudice the respondent (e.g., whether additional trial evidence might have been led) and restricts/conditions filing of proposed materials (consent or, absent consent, leave; fresh evidence generally disfavoured for interveners).
BaselineA: Common law / SCC practice on intervention and new issues on appeal (as applied in an application to intervene), with reference to potential Charter use as an interpretive tool and concerns about fresh evidence.
CaseB_TestB: Interpretation of Criminal Code s. 182(b) (offering indignities to human remains): (1) physical interference/contact is sufficient but not necessary; (2) the indignity must be offered to a dead human body or human remains (not monuments per se); (3) where monuments mark the presence/final resting place of human remains, offering indignities to those monuments constitutes offering indignities to the human remains.
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 182(b); also applied with ss. 683(1)(g) and 695(1) on amending the indictment).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: When the federal Environmental Assessment and Review Process Guidelines Order applies: there must be a “proposal” (an “initiative, undertaking or activity”) for which the Government of Canada has a “decision making responsibility”, meaning an “affirmative regulatory duty” (a “legal duty or obligation”) under an Act of Parliament; then the responsible “initiating department” must run the mandatory self-assessment process (screening and, if significant, panel review).
BaselineA: Regulation + statute: Environmental Assessment and Review Process Guidelines Order, SOR/84-467 (esp. ss. 2 “proposal”/“initiating department”, 3, 6) made under Department of the Environment Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. E-10, s. 6; applied alongside Navigable Waters Protection Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. N-22, s. 5 (as the source of the Minister of Transport’s affirmative regulatory duty).
CaseB_TestB: Curative proviso (Criminal Code, s. 686(1)(b)(iii)) test: despite an error of law, uphold the conviction if the Crown shows either (1) the error was “so harmless, and so insignificant, that it could not have affected the verdict”; or (2) the case against the accused was “so overwhelming that a conviction would have been inevitable even if the error had not been made”.
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(b)(iii), as explained through SCC precedent (cited in the reasons) including R. v. Khan, 2001 SCC 86 and R. v. Trochym, 2007 SCC 6.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 133 “legislative nature” / anti-circumvention test: if the net effect of a series of discrete acts is legislative, each component act is legislative and must be printed/published in both languages
BaselineA: Constitution Act, 1867, s. 133, as interpreted in Reference re Manitoba Language Rights (1985 and 1992) and Quebec (Attorney General) v. Brunet (1990) (legislative instruments include statutes and other instruments of a legislative nature; badges include: (1) embodies a rule of conduct; (2) has force of law; (3) applies to an undetermined number of persons; plus focus on degree of connection to the legislature)
CaseB_TestB: Responsive-answer requirement on jury question about reasonable doubt: when a jury asks about the standard of proof after a proper Lifchus charge, the trial judge must attempt to answer and must not discourage further questions
BaselineB: Common law jury-instruction framework from R. v. Lifchus (1997) (model reasonable doubt charge) and R. v. S. (W.D.) (1994) (jury questions must be answered “in a complete and careful manner”; recharge must be “correct and comprehensive”)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Milne mistaken-transfer theft rule: where a transferor mistakenly transfers property and the recipient knows of the mistake, property does not pass for criminal-law purposes if property law gives the transferor a right of recovery; if the recipient then converts it fraudulently and without colour of right with intent to deprive, theft is made out
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 322(1)) plus property-law principles about mistake and right of recovery (as discussed in the reasons)
CaseB_TestB: Khosa/Dunsmuir reasonableness review for IAD H&C decisions: apply a reasonableness standard and ask whether the outcome falls within a 'range of possible, acceptable outcomes' and reviewing courts must not reweigh evidence
BaselineB: Combination: common law (Dunsmuir v. New Brunswick) applied within a statutory judicial review scheme (Federal Courts Act, R.S.C., 1985, c. F-7, ss. 18, 18.1; and IRPA, S.C. 2001, c. 27, s. 67(1)(c))
JudgeB: Binnie J. (McLachlin C.J. and LeBel, Abella and Charron JJ. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 11(b) unreasonable delay analysis (Morin factors + institutional-delay guideline): a "judicial determination balancing" (not a formula) considering (1) length of delay; (2) waiver; (3) reasons for delay (inherent time requirements; actions of accused; actions of Crown; limits on institutional resources; other reasons); and (4) prejudice to the accused, with an administrative guideline of "between 8 and 10 months for institutional delay in Provincial Courts" that "is neither a limitation period nor a fixed ceiling" and "must not be applied in mechanical fashion".
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional text + prior SCC framework: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 11(b) (and remedy via s. 24(1)); baseline factors distilled in R. v. Smith, [1989] 2 S.C.R. 1120 and applied/extended in R. v. Askov, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 1199 (also drawing on Mills, Rahey, Conway).
CaseB_TestB: Contractor/subcontractor liability where loss results from overloading: even if the immediate physical failure was the subcontractor’s supports, the subcontractor is not liable where the "true cause" is the general contractor’s fault in overloading contrary to contract/specifications; at minimum the subcontractor may raise defences analogous to the builder’s defences (force majeure/act of God/owner’s fault/third party), including "the fault of the contractor himself"—here, failure to tension lower slabs before pouring above—so the subcontractor had "no obligation to furnish supports capable of withstanding this overload" that it was not forewarned of and not obliged to foresee.
BaselineB: Civil Code (Quebec) + prior SCC articulation of builder’s defences: Civil Code arts. 1684, 1688, 1065; and Hill, Clarke-Francis Ltd. v. Northland Groceries (Quebec) Ltd., [1941] S.C.R. 437 (builder can avoid liability by proving force majeure/act of God/owner’s fault/act of third party).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Secret commissions (Criminal Code s. 426(1)(a)(ii)): actus reus requires (1) agency relationship; (2) agent accepts a benefit as consideration for an act/forbearance in relation to the principal’s affairs; and (3) failure to make “adequate and timely disclosure of the source, amount and nature of the benefit”; mens rea mirrors each element, and “corruptly” means “secretly or without the requisite disclosure” (no “corrupt bargain” requirement); adequacy/timeliness assessed “in all the circumstances of the particular case”.
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 426(1)(a) (as interpreted in R. v. Kelly, [1992] 2 S.C.R. 000, followed here).
JudgeA: Cory J. (for L'Heureux-Dubé, Cory and Iacobucci JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Criminal Code s. 686(1)(b)(iii) curative proviso: ask whether “a jury properly instructed could, acting reasonably, have come to a different conclusion absent the error”; jury findings may inform the hypothetical reasonable jury if “not tainted by the error”; where an included offence was available, conviction of the more serious offence can be relied on (less concern it was a reaction against all-or-nothing acquittal).
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(b)(iii).
JudgeB: Sopinka J. (oral judgment of the Court)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: State Immunity Act s. 5 “commercial activity” exception: two-step contextual inquiry — (1) determine the nature of the relevant state activity (in its full context, with purpose potentially relevant), and (2) assess whether the Canadian proceedings have a sufficient “nexus” to the commercial aspect (more than merely “touch on” or “incidentally affect” it) such that the proceedings “relate to” commercial activity
BaselineA: Statute (State Immunity Act, S.C. 1980-81-82-83, c. 95, ss. 2 and 5) codifying the common law restrictive immunity approach (acts jure imperii vs jure gestionis; contextual approach discussed with reference to I Congreso del Partido)
CaseB_TestB: Compatibility test for provincial “pay-and-retain/compensation” mechanisms with the BIA distribution scheme: determine whether the provincial mechanism grants rights beyond BIA s. 97(3) set-off/compensation (including timing limits) — in particular, compensation is available only where mutual debts arise before bankruptcy; post-bankruptcy subrogatory payment cannot create compensation, leaving only a provable claim under BIA s. 121
BaselineB: Statute (Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. B-3, especially ss. 97(3), 121, 136-147) plus Quebec civil law rules on subrogation/compensation (C.C.Q. arts. 1651, 1656(3), 1672-1673, 1681) and prior SCC guidance (Husky Oil)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Quebec civil law “obligation to inform” (duty of disclosure) in contracts of enterprise: duty arises where (1) the debtor has “knowledge of the information, whether actual or presumed”; (2) the information is “of decisive importance”; and (3) it is “impossible” for the creditor to inform itself or the creditor is “legitimately relying” on the debtor; in large projects the content varies with “allocation of risk”, “relative expertise”, and “continuing formation of the contract”.
BaselineA: Civil Code of Lower Canada (arts. 1024, 1053) and Quebec civil law jurisprudence recognizing good faith and disclosure duties (e.g., National Bank of Canada v. Soucisse; Houle v. Canadian National Bank; Air Canada v. McDonnell Douglas).
CaseB_TestB: Learned intermediary defence to a manufacturer/supplier’s duty to warn: exception applies “generally only” where (1) the product is “highly technical” and used with “expert supervision”, or (2) it is “unrealistic” for the consumer to receive a warning directly; additionally, the intermediary must be “learned” such that its knowledge of the product/risks is “essentially the same” as the manufacturer’s.
BaselineB: Common law products liability duty to warn (Lambert v. Lastoplex; Rivtow; Hollis) and the learned intermediary concept discussed in Hollis.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Duty to accommodate (employer/union) in adverse-effect discrimination: take "reasonable measures short of undue hardship"; union liable if it (1) participated in the discriminatory rule (e.g., collective agreement term) or (2) "impedes the reasonable efforts" to accommodate; undue hardship assessed contextually (e.g., cost, disruption of collective agreement, morale/rights of others) and complainant must "facilitate" and accept reasonable accommodation
BaselineA: Statute (Human Rights Act, S.B.C. 1984, c. 22, ss. 8(1)(a),(b),(4), 9(a)-(c)) as interpreted through SCC common-law human rights jurisprudence (O'Malley; Central Alberta Dairy Pool)
CaseB_TestB: Exclusive arbitral jurisdiction under mandatory arbitration clause: courts are ousted where the dispute, in its "essential character", arises from the "interpretation, application, administration or alleged violation" of the collective agreement (s. 45(1)); focus on facts of the dispute, not legal characterization (tort/Charter), subject to residual court jurisdiction only where necessary to avoid a "real deprivation of ultimate remedy"
BaselineB: Statute (Ontario Labour Relations Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. L.2, s. 45(1)) informed by SCC labour-arbitration exclusivity jurisprudence (St. Anne Nackawic)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Trial judge’s discretion to exclude cross-examination on a collateral credibility matter where its (tenuous) relevance does not outweigh its prejudicial effect/misleading potential
BaselineA: Common law (evidentiary discretion re cross-examination on collateral matters), applied from R. v. Meddoui, [1991] 3 S.C.R. 320
JudgeA: McLachlin J. (for the Court, oral reasons)
CaseB_TestB: Income Tax Act s. 20(1)(c)(i) purpose test: whether, considering all the circumstances, the taxpayer had a reasonable expectation of income at the time the investment was made (ancillary income-earning purpose suffices absent sham/window dressing)
BaselineB: Statute — Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), s. 20(1)(c)(i) (interpreting “purpose” and “income”); building on Bronfman Trust v. The Queen, [1987] 1 S.C.R. 32 and Shell Canada Ltd. v. Canada, [1999] 3 S.C.R. 622
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 10(b) “detention” at a port of entry: routine secondary immigration examination is not detention unless state action goes beyond what is required for entry processing and becomes a restraint of liberty (Therens/Simmons applied; factors include routine screening character and absence of stigma).
BaselineA: Combination: constitutional text (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 10(b)) interpreted through common law/precedent (R. v. Therens; R. v. Simmons; also discussed: R. v. Jacoy; R. v. Kwok).
CaseB_TestB: Elements of civil contempt (common law): proof beyond a reasonable doubt of (1) a clear and unequivocal order, (2) actual knowledge of the order, and (3) an intentional act/omission that breaches the order; no requirement of “contumacious intent” (intent to interfere with administration of justice).
BaselineB: Common law (elements drawn from cases cited in the reasons, including Prescott-Russell; Bhatnager; Sheppard; TG Industries; College of Optometrists; Pro Swing).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Admissibility of bad character/disposition evidence: admissible only if (1) relevant to an issue other than disposition/character and (2) probative value outweighs prejudicial effect; where morally repugnant acts are alleged, prejudice is great so probative value must be high
BaselineA: Common law (as stated in Morris v. The Queen; also applied with guidance from R. v. B. (C.R.))
CaseB_TestB: Recent fabrication exception for prior consistent statements: if cross-examination amounts to an allegation of recent fabrication, prior consistent statements may be admitted to rebut it, but only to prove the fact the complaint was made (not the truth of its contents)
BaselineB: Common law (prior consistent statements / recent fabrication doctrine)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Substantive admissibility of a non-accused witness’s prior inconsistent statement (B. (K.G.) reformed rule): threshold that the statement would be admissible as the witness’s in-court testimony, plus principled hearsay requirements of necessity and reliability adapted via circumstantial guarantees (typically: (1) oath/affirmation/solemn declaration with explicit warning re criminal sanctions, (2) videotaped in entirety, and (3) full opportunity to cross-examine at trial), assessed on a voir dire; substitutes may suffice if the judge is satisfied they provide adequate assurances of reliability.
BaselineA: Common law hearsay/orthodox rule limiting prior inconsistent statements to credibility only (e.g., Deacon v. The King) as applied through Canada Evidence Act, s. 9 procedure; principled hearsay approach from R. v. Khan and R. v. Smith (reliability and necessity).
CaseB_TestB: Characterization/inclusion test for art. 1056c C.C. “additional indemnity” within an insurer’s contractual obligation to pay “interest”: the art. 1056c(2) indemnity is “of the same nature” as art. 1056c(1) interest because both are “in reality damages due to delay”, so the indemnity is included in the policy’s promise to pay interest (up to the policy limit).
BaselineB: Statute/civil code interpretation applied to an insurance contract: Civil Code art. 1056c (and related characterization discussion in R. v. Nord-Deutsche Versicherungs-Gesellschaft; Highway Victims Indemnity Fund v. Martineau distinguished).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal fraud (Criminal Code, s. 380(1)) — “other fraudulent means”: actus reus requires conduct that a reasonable person would “properly ... stigmatize as dishonest”, i.e., “the wrongful use of something in which another person has an interest” that extinguishes or puts that interest “at risk”; mens rea requires subjective knowledge of the prohibited act and subjective knowledge that it could cause deprivation (including risk).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 380(1)) as interpreted in R. v. Théroux (1993) and R. v. Olan (1978) (definition of “other fraudulent means” as conduct that can be “stigmatized as dishonest”).
CaseB_TestB: Union duty of representation in collective bargaining (Labour Code, s. 47.2): union must not act “in bad faith or in an arbitrary or discriminatory manner or show serious negligence”; duty is generally an “obligation of means” and does not impose an “obligation of result” to secure retroactivity for former employees.
BaselineB: Statute (Labour Code, R.S.Q., c. C-27, s. 47.2; also s. 67 on single collective agreement) informed by SCC labour-law jurisprudence on the duty of representation (e.g., Noël v. Société d’énergie de la Baie James; Centre hospitalier Régina Ltée).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Crown appeal from acquittal/new trial test under Criminal Code s. 686(4): Crown must show the verdict "would not necessarily have been the same" but for the legal error
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(4)) as interpreted in SCC precedent (Vézeau v. The Queen; reaffirmed in R. v. Morin)
CaseB_TestB: Implied contractual duty of reasonable notice before enforcing security/appointing receiver: debtor must receive "reasonable notice" of intention to enforce and "reasonable time to pay"; reasonableness assessed by Broadloom factors
BaselineB: Common law (Lister (R.E.) Ltd. v. Dunlop Canada Ltd.; Broadloom criteria from Mister Broadloom; also Massey v. Sladen)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: No duty on owner/engineer to advise bidders about permits or execution method chosen by contractor: absent specific arrangements, the contractor’s chosen method is within its own sphere of responsibility, and design professionals have no duty to advise on method or how to accomplish it
BaselineA: Common law (construction/tendering duty of care allocation). Cited as a settled rule from R. v. Paradis and Farley Inc., [1942] S.C.R. 10; Vermont Construction Inc. v. Beatson, [1977] 1 S.C.R. 758; and Temar Construction Ltd. v. West Hill Redevelopment Co. (1986), 21 C.L.R. 156.
CaseB_TestB: Framework for reviewing Crown decision-making: (1) classify the decision as prosecutorial discretion vs tactics/conduct before the court; (2) if prosecutorial discretion, it is reviewable only for abuse of process (egregious conduct seriously compromising trial fairness and/or integrity of the justice system), with a threshold requirement that the accused first establish a proper evidentiary foundation before the Crown may be required to justify its decision
BaselineB: Common law/constitutional doctrine governing prosecutorial discretion and abuse of process, building on Krieger v. Law Society of Alberta, 2002 SCC 65; R. v. Nixon, 2011 SCC 34; and related cases. (Applied in the context of Criminal Code, s. 727(1) notice triggering mandatory minimums under s. 255, and Charter s. 7 arguments.)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Constitutional limit on warrantless searches under s. 10 Narcotic Control Act: warrantless search is authorized only where exigent circumstances make it impracticable to obtain prior judicial authorization (otherwise s. 8 breach).
BaselineA: Combination of common law Charter s. 8 reasonableness framework (R. v. Collins, [1987] 1 S.C.R. 265: search reasonable if 'authorized by law', the law is reasonable, and the manner is reasonable) and statute (Narcotic Control Act, s. 10) as interpreted through Charter s. 8; SCC also relies on its contemporaneous interpretation in R. v. Grant (1993) limiting s. 10 to exigent circumstances.
CaseB_TestB: Scope of Income Tax Act confidentiality exception: s. 241(3) permits disclosure 'in respect of proceedings relating to the administration or enforcement' of the Act, interpreted broadly to include bankruptcy/trustee proceedings connected to tax collection/enforcement.
BaselineB: Statute (Income Tax Act, S.C. 1970-71-72, c. 63, s. 241(1)-(4), especially s. 241(3) 'in respect of proceedings relating to the administration or enforcement of this Act'; contextual support from s. 222 debt-collection provision).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 486(2.1) screen order: judge may permit a child complainant (<18) in enumerated sexual offences to testify behind a screen if the judge is of the opinion it is "necessary to obtain a full and candid account"; this does not infringe Charter ss. 7 or 11(d) because confrontation/cross-examination remain and the right to face one’s accuser is not absolute but "subject to qualification in the interests of justice".
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 486(2.1)) interpreted in light of Charter ss. 7 and 11(d).
CaseB_TestB: Similar fact (identity) admissibility—use of prior conviction to satisfy Arp’s "some evidence" link: where the accused puts identity for the prior act in issue, the Crown may tender the prior conviction as "some evidence" linking the accused to the similar act; verdicts are "presumptively reliable" and should be treated as such "unless overturned on appeal or later shown to be wrong"; challenge to the conviction on the voir dire is rare and only warranted where there is a "reasonable likelihood" it will affect admissibility.
BaselineB: Common law similar fact framework from R. v. Arp and R. v. Handy (as applied/clarified), plus procedural control principles; (statutory reference only illustratively: Criminal Code s. 696.3(3)(a) as an example of setting aside a conviction).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Party liability for manslaughter (even if principal is guilty of murder) under Criminal Code s. 21(2): accused is guilty of manslaughter if, having formed a common intention to carry out an unlawful purpose and assist, he did not foresee murder but “a reasonable person in all the circumstances would have foreseen at least a risk of harm to another as a result of carrying out the common intention” (objective foresight of harm; included offences available under s. 21(2)).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 21(2)) interpreted in light of SCC authorities on party liability and manslaughter mens rea (R. v. Trinneer; R. v. Kirkness; R. v. Creighton).
CaseB_TestB: Entitlement to GST rebate for overpayment under Excise Tax Act s. 261(1) (as applied via s. 296(2.1)): the “person [who] has paid an amount” is the person who actually paid and was out of pocket; s. 261(1) “does not require an inquiry into liability for payment”, and where the Minister determines an “allowable rebate” would have been payable, s. 296(2.1) requires applying it even if the normal two-year application limit in s. 261(3) has expired.
BaselineB: Statute (Excise Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. E-15, ss. 261(1)-(3), 296(2.1), and related ss. 215.1, 216(6), 225(1)) interpreted and applied.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Government tort liability: distinguishing immune “policy” decisions from actionable “operational” implementation (Just v. B.C. framework) in highway maintenance/inspections
BaselineA: Common law (Just v. British Columbia; also Anns v. Merton; Kamloops v. Nielsen) applied alongside statutory context (Public Highways Act ss. 4-5; Proceedings against the Crown Act s. 5(1)(a); Expropriation Act ss. 70(f), 71)
CaseB_TestB: Damages in lieu of specific performance: when specific performance is (legitimately) available, damages may be assessed as of the date of trial/judgment to be a “true substitute” for specific performance; specific performance not granted as of course absent proof of uniqueness
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: Courts of Justice Act (Ontario) s. 99 (damages in substitution for specific performance) applied with common law damages principles (Johnson v. Agnew; Wroth v. Tyler; Asamera Oil; Adderley v. Dixon)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Abuse of process threshold in criminal proceedings: remedy only in the “clearest of cases” (conduct that “shocks the conscience of the community” and is so unfair/indecent that it would be “contrary to the interest of justice” to proceed)
BaselineA: Common law (abuse of process / stay of proceedings doctrine), as affirmed in R. v. Jewitt and reiterated in R. v. Keyowski, R. v. Conway, R. v. Mack, R. v. Scott
CaseB_TestB: Mr. Big confessions admissibility rule: presumptively inadmissible unless Crown proves (on balance) probative value (reliability) outweighs prejudicial effect; reliability assessed via operation circumstances + markers of reliability in confession
BaselineB: Common law evidence (party admissions exception to hearsay) with a new common law qualification; also relies on common law probative value vs prejudicial effect balancing (e.g., Mohan/Handy concepts) and notes abuse of process as a separate prong
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 16(1) “knowing it was wrong” (NCRMD) requires not only abstract knowledge of right/wrong but capacity to apply that knowledge rationally to the particular act at the time; exemption where mental disorder deprives capacity for rational perception and rational choice about the act’s wrongness by ordinary standards
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 16(1)); interpreted in light of M'Naghten's Case and SCC’s R. v. Chaulk
CaseB_TestB: Palmer criteria govern admission of fresh evidence on appeal from sentence (same as verdict): (1) due diligence (flexible factor), (2) relevance to a decisive/potentially decisive issue, (3) credibility, and (4) if believed, could reasonably be expected (with trial evidence) to have affected the result; overarching ‘interests of justice’
BaselineB: Common law test from Palmer v. The Queen, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 759, applied within statutory appellate powers (Criminal Code ss. 683 and 687)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Mohan test for admissibility of expert evidence (and added threshold for expert disposition/profile evidence): expert evidence admissible only if (a) "relevance"; (b) "necessity in assisting the trier of fact"; (c) "the absence of any exclusionary rule"; and (d) "a properly qualified expert"; and for expert disposition/profile evidence specifically, the judge must be satisfied "that either the perpetrator of the crime or the accused has distinctive behavioural characteristics such that a comparison of one with the other will be of material assistance" and should ask: "Has the scientific community developed a standard profile for the offender who commits this type of crime?"
BaselineA: Common law (law of evidence), drawing on and synthesizing prior authorities including R. v. Abbey, R. v. Béland, R. v. Morin, R. v. Lavallee, and the earlier 'abnormal group' line (R. v. Lupien; R. v. McMillan (aff'd [1977] 2 S.C.R. 824); R. v. Robertson).
CaseB_TestB: Section 745 Criminal Code parole ineligibility review framework: jury must decide whether ineligibility "ought to be reduced" "having regard to the character of the applicant, his conduct while serving his sentence, the nature of the offence ... and such other matters as the judge deems relevant" (s. 745(2)); the SCC emphasizes this is a "broad discretionary power" where listed factors "must be assessed and weighed as a whole" and burden-of-proof concepts are "of very limited value"; fairness review focuses on whether the applicant received a fair hearing (including limits on inflammatory Crown submissions).
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 745(1)-(4), especially s. 745(2) listing factors and discretion; also discussed: s. 735(1.1) and s. 744).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: s. 10(b) informational/implementational duties: no duty-counsel advice required where no duty counsel exists; further police duties are only triggered if detainee asserts desire to speak to a lawyer (a clear 'No' does not trigger further obligations)
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 10(b) (and context of Brydges/Bartle/Prosper jurisprudence on informational and implementational components)
CaseB_TestB: Criminal Code s. 347 framework for late-payment penalties: (1) determine if charge is 'interest' by asking whether it is 'paid or payable for the advancing of credit under an agreement or arrangement' (including deferral of payment for goods/services); (2) apply s. 347(1)(a) ex ante (requires criminal rate on face of agreement) vs s. 347(1)(b) ex post (rate calculated over period credit actually outstanding), subject to Nelson 'voluntary act of debtor' limitation
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 347(1)-(2) (interpreting 'interest', 'credit advanced', and applying Nelson/Dancorp principles)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 7 overbreadth (principles of fundamental justice) test: a law is overbroad where the state’s means are broader than necessary to achieve its objective; s. 179(1)(b) was overbroad (places/people/time/no notice) and thus not in accordance with fundamental justice
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7 (principles of fundamental justice) applied to Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 179(1)(b); baseline articulation of overbreadth/vagueness relationship drawn from R. v. Nova Scotia Pharmaceutical Society, [1992] 2 S.C.R. 606 and related cases cited in the reasons
CaseB_TestB: Transfer pricing “reasonable amount in the circumstances” under ITA s. 69(2): determine whether the non-arm’s-length price exceeds what would be reasonable at arm’s length, considering all relevant circumstances (including linked agreements conferring rights/benefits) and ensuring comparability of “economically relevant characteristics”
BaselineB: Statute: Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), s. 69(2) (now s. 247(2)); interpretive use (non-binding) of OECD Transfer Pricing Guidelines (1979/1995) for methods/comparability concepts
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Inference of possession from fingerprint evidence: whether an inference of possession can be drawn from fingerprints is "not subject to a hard and fast rule" but "depends on all of the circumstances of the case and all of the evidence adduced" (including that fingerprints on a container vs. contents is "merely another factor").
BaselineA: Common law (circumstantial evidence/inference of possession from fingerprints), drawing on R. v. O'Keefe (1958) and approving R. v. Mehrabnia (1993); also applied within the statutory definition of "possession" via Food and Drugs Act, s. 46 incorporating Criminal Code, s. 4(3).
CaseB_TestB: Scope of Review Board power under Criminal Code s. 672.54: Boards may make conditions binding on hospital authorities and may impose conditions "regarding"/supervising treatment (including ordering re-evaluations/exploration of alternatives) but have "no power to 'prescribe' treatment"; s. 672.55(1) is not a true exception but an example of supervisory power.
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, Part XX.1, especially ss. 672.54 and 672.55(1) (with related context from ss. 672.72-672.78, 672.9-672.94, etc.).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Predominant purpose test for exemption from compulsion to testify (s. 7 self-incrimination/right to silence): determine whether the "predominant purpose" of compelling the evidence is "to obtain incriminating evidence" against the witness or "some legitimate public purpose"; if predominant purpose is incrimination, compulsion must be justified and witness not compellable if other significant prejudice to fair trial is shown
BaselineA: Common law / Charter-based doctrine (s. 7 principles of fundamental justice) building on R. v. S. (R.J.), [1995] 1 S.C.R. 451; applied in the statutory context of Securities Act, S.B.C. 1985, c. 83, s. 128(1) (investigatory power to compel testimony/documents)
CaseB_TestB: Timing rule for Corbett applications: a Corbett application "should be made by the defence and decided by the trial judge immediately after the close of the Crown’s case"; if needed, hold a pre-defence voir dire where defence discloses intended evidence, with ruling modifiable only if defence evidence departs significantly from what was disclosed
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: Canada Evidence Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-5, s. 12 (as interpreted in R. v. Corbett, [1988] 1 S.C.R. 670, creating discretion to exclude prior convictions where probative value is outweighed by prejudice), informed by Charter s. 7 "case-to-meet" principle (citing R. v. S. (R.J.))
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 7 compellability / exemption from compelled testimony: whether the "predominant purpose" of seeking the evidence is to obtain incriminating evidence against the witness or to further a legitimate public purpose (with justification required if predominant purpose is incrimination)
BaselineA: Combination of Charter (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7 (and relatedly s. 13)) and common-law/Charter doctrine as developed in R. v. S. (R.J.), [1995] 1 S.C.R. 451; applied in the statutory context of Securities Act, S.B.C. 1985, c. 83, s. 128(1) (investigatory compulsion)
CaseB_TestB: Section 15(1) prima facie discrimination test (Quebec v. A framework): (1) distinction on an enumerated or analogous ground (on its face or in impact) and (2) discriminatory/arbitrary disadvantage—i.e., perpetuating disadvantage; claimant must show disproportionate impact linked to group membership
BaselineB: Charter (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 15(1)) as interpreted by SCC jurisprudence, especially Quebec (Attorney General) v. A, 2013 SCC 5 (and related cases such as Withler, Kapp, Andrews, Corbiere, Law)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Tax-treaty residency under Canada–U.S. Income Tax Convention (1980) Art. IV(1): entity must be “liable to tax” in the U.S. “by reason of” an enumerated residence-type connecting factor (domicile/residence/place of management/place of incorporation) or a “criterion of a similar nature”, which the Court interprets as requiring full (worldwide) tax liability rather than mere source-based liability; a factor that merely informs domestic tax liability cannot itself be the treaty residency criterion
BaselineA: Statute/treaty: Canada-United States Tax Convention Act, 1984, Schedule I (Canada–U.S. Income Tax Convention (1980)), Article IV(1) (definition of “resident of a Contracting State”), applied in context of Article XII; also interacts with Income Tax Act s. 212(1)(d) (withholding tax)
CaseB_TestB: Valid-refusal trigger for Ontario accident-benefits limitation: the two-year limitation in Insurance Act s. 281(5) begins only upon a “valid refusal”; “No such refusal is given if there has not been adequate compliance with s. 71” of the SABS, which requires insurers to inform claimants of the dispute-resolution procedure in “straightforward and clear language, directed towards an unsophisticated person” and, “at a minimum”, to include key points (mediation right; arbitration/litigation if mediation fails; mediation prerequisite; and the relevant time limits)
BaselineB: Statute/regulation: Insurance Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. I.8, s. 281(5) (two-year limitation after insurer’s refusal) and Statutory Accident Benefits Schedule (O. Reg. 776/93), s. 71 (duty to inform of dispute-resolution procedure under ss. 279–283 of the Insurance Act)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Weber exclusive arbitral jurisdiction test: courts are ousted where the dispute’s “essential character” arises from the “interpretation, application, administration or violation” of the collective agreement (s. 45(1) OLRA), regardless of how pleaded (tort/Charter), subject to residual court jurisdiction only where the tribunal lacks power to grant the needed remedy
BaselineA: Statute (Ontario Labour Relations Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. L.2, s. 45(1)) interpreted in light of SCC labour-arbitration exclusivity jurisprudence (notably St. Anne Nackawic Pulp & Paper Co. v. Canadian Paper Workers Union, Local 219, [1986] 1 S.C.R. 704)
CaseB_TestB: Criminal Code s. 744 parole-ineligibility extension framework: trial judge “may, having regard to (1) the character of the offender, (2) the nature of the offence, and (3) the circumstances surrounding its commission … substitute for ten years” a longer period (10–25); 10 years is the general rule but can be “ousted” if, applying the s. 744 criteria, the judge deems a longer period fit (no “unusual circumstances” requirement)
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, ss. 742(b), 744; plus appellate review context under s. 687(1))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Retiring allowance requires a “loss of employment”: an employee is only “in the service” of the employer once under an obligation to provide services; therefore “loss of employment” cannot occur before that moment (Income Tax Act, s. 248(1) “employment”; s. 56(1)(a)(ii); s. 248(1) “retiring allowance”). Key quotes: “employment” is the “position of an individual in the service of some other person”; “An employee is ‘in the service’ of his or her employer from the moment he or she becomes under obligation to provide services under the terms of the contract”; “ ‘loss of employment’ cannot occur before an employee becomes under obligation to provide services”.
BaselineA: Statute (Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1952, c. 148 (now R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.)), s. 56(1)(a)(ii) and definitions in s. 248(1) of “employment” and “retiring allowance”; also contrasted with s. 80.4(1) use of “intended office or employment”).
