CaseB_TestB: Whether improper Crown closing submissions (a personal anecdote not in evidence) rendered the trial unfair / caused a miscarriage of justice is assessed contextually using the “relevant factors” (from R. v. Stephan). Applied factors included: seriousness given the issue at trial; context limiting prejudice (not comparable to allegations; not prominent); absence of defence objection (a factor, not dispositive); and adequacy of the jury charge (general caution that submissions are not evidence; no specific remedial instruction required here). Key quotes: “this error did not result in an unfair trial or a miscarriage of justice”; “relevant factors set out in R. v. Stephan”; “failure ... to object ... is ... a factor to be considered ... (not ... dispositive)”.
BaselineB: Common law (trial fairness / improper jury address analysis drawing on Pisani v. The Queen, Boucher v. The Queen, and the multi-factor approach referenced from R. v. Stephan; also R. v. Manasseri and R. v. Abdullahi).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Pragmatic and functional approach to whether a labour board has jurisdiction (and, if within jurisdiction, review only for patent unreasonableness): consider (a) wording of the enactment, (b) purpose of the statute, (c) reason for tribunal’s existence, (d) tribunal expertise, (e) nature of the problem (Bibeault); then uphold unless “patently unreasonable”/“clearly irrational”.
BaselineA: Combination: common law administrative law standard-of-review framework (U.E.S., Local 298 v. Bibeault) plus statute (Canada Labour Code, esp. ss. 22, 24, 27, 28, 33).
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 8 reasonableness test for DNA data bank orders under Criminal Code s. 487.055: a seizure is constitutional if the authorizing law is “reasonable” by contextual balancing of state objectives vs privacy impact (Hunter v. Southam), with Collins/Stillman structure (authorized by law; law reasonable; manner reasonable); here, no requirement of reasonable and probable grounds linking offender to a particular investigation, and ex parte procedure can satisfy minimal procedural fairness in context.
BaselineB: Combination: Charter s. 8 jurisprudence (Hunter v. Southam; Collins; Stillman) applied to statute (Criminal Code s. 487.055 and related DNA provisions; DNA Identification Act ss. 3-4).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Gladstone modification of Sparrow justification/priority for commercial Aboriginal rights: government must show (1) a valid legislative objective and (2) consistency with fiduciary duty; where the Aboriginal right has no internal limit, priority is “something less than exclusivity” and requires the Crown to show both the allocation process and the resulting allocation reflect the prior interest of Aboriginal right holders
BaselineA: Common law / constitutional doctrine under Constitution Act, 1982, s. 35(1), building on R. v. Sparrow (justification and priority) and R. v. Van der Peet (definition of Aboriginal right); applied in relation to Pacific Herring Fishery Regulations, SOR/84-324, s. 20(3)
CaseB_TestB: Admissibility of Crown rebuttal evidence: rebuttal may be admitted where it is relevant to an issue raised by the defence (here, “the context and the essential fabric of the alibi defence”) and the Crown “could not have known in advance” the defence evidence; admission is within the trial judge’s discretion
BaselineB: Common law trial-evidence principles on rebuttal evidence and trial-judge discretion (as applied in this case); with a separate statutory backstop on appeal via Criminal Code, s. 686(1)(b)(iii) (curative proviso)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Implied waiver of Charter s. 11(d) rights by inaction in a no-imprisonment regulatory ticket scheme: legislature may infer waiver from failure to pay/appear only if (1) the accused is "fully aware of the consequences of failing to act" and (2) the scheme has "sufficient safeguards" ensuring the inaction was not due to events beyond the accused’s control
BaselineA: Combination of constitutional text (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 11(d), with contextual reference to s. 7 liberty) and common-law/Charter waiver principles as discussed through SCC precedent (especially R. v. Lee, [1989] 2 S.C.R. 1384; also references to waiver jurisprudence such as Clarkson and Tran)
CaseB_TestB: Procedural fairness/natural justice for CHRC dismissal of a complaint as unsubstantiated: Commission must act "on a quasi-judicial basis" and fairness requires (1) an opportunity to make submissions "at least in writing" before a decision and (2) prior disclosure of "the substance of the case" so submissions are informed (a hearing "not necessarily required")
BaselineB: Combination of statute (Canadian Human Rights Act, ss. 35 and 36(3)(b)) and common-law procedural fairness/natural justice principles (as applied to quasi-judicial administrative decision-making)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Patently unreasonable standard on judicial review of labour arbitration (including the “no evidence / incapable of supporting” constraint on factual inferences)
BaselineA: Common law (administrative law / labour arbitration judicial review), applied in light of a strong privative clause in School Boards and Teachers Collective Negotiations Act, s. 72
CaseB_TestB: Statutory “equivalent in value” test under Reorg. Act s. 15(2)(a): equivalence requires comparing both benefits and their funding; prima facie breach if employee excess contribution (Initial Surplus) not matched unless reserved exclusively for members or offset by compensatory benefits of equivalent value (as of implementation date)
BaselineB: Statute: The Manitoba Telephone System Reorganization and Consequential Amendments Act, S.M. 1996, c. 79, s. 15(2)(a) (with related context in s. 15(3), (11))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Doctrine of part performance defeats a statutory writing requirement (Statute of Frauds analogue): where an oral agreement for an interest in land has been carried out/partly performed so that insisting on writing would not prevent fraud but would itself work a fraud, equity enforces the agreement and the Crown cannot rely on the absence of writing (creating an “equitable permission”/interest).
BaselineA: Combination of statute and equitable common law: Public Highways Act, R.S.N.S. 1954, c. 235, s. 21(1)(a) (written permit requirement) interpreted as a Statute of Frauds-type writing requirement; equitable doctrine of part performance as described in Steadman v. Steadman, [1976] A.C. 536 (H.L.) (and related equity authorities cited).
CaseB_TestB: Quebec arbitration/public order framework for annulment and arbitrability: (1) interpret the arbitrator’s mandate liberally—mandate includes “everything that is closely connected” with the arbitration agreement; (2) s. 37 Copyright Act does not exclude arbitration unless it expressly does; (3) on annulment for public order under art. 946.5 C.C.P., the court examines the award “as a whole” and asks whether the disposition/outcome violates public order—mere legal error on a mandatory rule is insufficient unless the outcome conflicts with “fundamental principles of public order.”
BaselineB: Statutory: Civil Code of Québec arts. 2638-2643 (esp. art. 2639); Code of Civil Procedure arts. 946.2, 946.4, 946.5, 947.2; Copyright Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-42, s. 37; Act respecting the professional status of artists, R.S.Q., c. S-32.01, s. 37.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Southam standard of review framework: on statutory appeal from an expert tribunal, apply reasonableness simpliciter (a third standard) where warranted by factors (nature of problem, statute/purpose, expertise); an “unreasonable decision” is one “not supported by any reasons that can stand up to a somewhat probing examination” (vs. patently unreasonable where the defect is obvious).
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: statutory right of appeal and tribunal structure under Competition Tribunal Act, ss. 12-13; SCC standard-of-review jurisprudence (e.g., Pezim; CUPE; Bell Canada; Bradco).
CaseB_TestB: Albashir temporal-effect test for suspended s. 52(1) declarations: declarations are presumptively retroactive, but the presumption is rebutted “explicitly or by necessary implication”; for suspended declarations, courts must look to the “purpose of a suspension” and if retroactivity would “defeat the compelling public interests that required the suspension”, the declaration “must apply purely prospectively”.
BaselineB: Constitutional text and remedial doctrine: Constitution Act, 1982, s. 52(1) and Charter, s. 24(1), plus prior SCC remedial jurisprudence (notably Ontario (AG) v. G; Hislop; Manitoba Language Reference; Bedford).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: CCA “purpose of producing income” test under Reg. 1102(1)(c): (1) “does the property produce income [revenue]?” If yes, CCA allowed; (2) if no, “was it acquired for the purpose of producing income?”, assessed objectively “having regard to whether the taxpayer acted in accordance with reasonably acceptable principles of commerce and business practices” (L’Heureux-Dubé J.).
BaselineA: Statute + regulation: Income Tax Act, s. 20(1)(a) (deductions “as is allowed by regulation”) and Income Tax Regulations, s. 1102(1)(c) (property excluded if “not acquired ... for the purpose of gaining or producing income”).
CaseB_TestB: Bail denial under Criminal Code s. 515(10)(c) (post-severance): detention may be ordered “where the detention is necessary in order to maintain confidence in the administration of justice”, assessed objectively “having regard to all the circumstances, including” four listed factors (strength of Crown’s case; gravity of offence; circumstances of commission; potential for lengthy imprisonment), i.e., whether “a reasonable member of the community would be satisfied that denial of bail is necessary” (McLachlin C.J.).
BaselineB: Statute + constitutional constraint: Criminal Code, s. 515(10)(c) interpreted in light of Charter s. 11(e) (“not to be denied reasonable bail without just cause”) and prior SCC bail jurisprudence (Pearson; Morales).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: When an appeal right is “acquired, accrued or accruing” under a repealed/amended enactment: it vests only once all conditions precedent are fulfilled (here, only when the court of appeal renders judgment reversing an acquittal and ordering a new trial)
BaselineA: Statute: Interpretation Act, R.S.C., 1985, c. I-21, ss. 43(c) and 44(c),(d), applied to Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 691(2) (as amended effective May 14, 1997)
CaseB_TestB: Sherman Estate v. Donovan test for discretionary limits on the open court principle (publication bans): (1) serious risk to an important public interest; (2) necessity because reasonable alternatives will not prevent the risk; (3) proportionality—benefits outweigh negative effects
BaselineB: Common law: Sherman Estate v. Donovan, 2021 SCC 25 (para. 38) governing discretionary orders limiting court openness
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Canderel profit-computation framework under ITA s. 9(1): taxpayer may use any method consistent with the Act, case law, and well-accepted business principles that yields an “accurate picture” of profit; once taxpayer shows this, on reassessment the onus shifts to the Minister to show the method is inaccurate or another method is more accurate
BaselineA: Statute (Income Tax Act, S.C. 1970-71-72, c. 63, ss. 9(1), 18(1)(a), 18(9)) interpreted through prior case law (e.g., Symes v. Canada; M.N.R. v. Irwin; Associated Investors)
CaseB_TestB: Interpretation/application of Partnership Act s. 55(b): a general partner breaches only if it does an act that “makes it impossible to carry on the ordinary business” of the limited partnership—meaning impossibility as to a “substantial portion” of the partnership’s ordinary business, not every facet
BaselineB: Statute (Partnership Act, R.S.A. 1980, c. P-2, s. 55(b))
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: R. v. Dixon two-step post-conviction non-disclosure test: (1) reasonable possibility undisclosed info affects reliability of conviction; (2) if not, reasonable possibility non-disclosure affected overall fairness (lost lines of inquiry/opportunities), with defence due diligence as a significant factor
BaselineA: Combination: Charter (ss. 7, 24(1)) + common law disclosure doctrine from R. v. Stinchcombe (relevance/“reasonable possibility of usefulness” threshold) and related SCC cases (Egger; C.(M.H.); Carosella)
CaseB_TestB: Standard-form insurance contract interpretation (Ledcor framework) applied to SEF 44 cl. 4(b)(vii): give effect to clear, unambiguous language as understood by the average insured; only if ambiguous use general rules, then contra proferentem
BaselineB: Common law contract/insurance interpretation principles (Ledcor; Progressive Homes; Scalera; Gibbens) applied to the SEF 44 Endorsement (contract text, especially cl. 4(b)(vii))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Caslake (search incident to arrest): search must be “truly incidental” to the arrest — police must have a purpose connected to the arrest (e.g., “protecting the police, protecting the evidence, discovering evidence”) and “must have had some reason related to the arrest ... and that reason must be objectively reasonable”; delay/distance may support an inference against incidentality but can be rebutted by explanation
BaselineA: Common law (search incident to arrest doctrine), as discussed in Cloutier v. Langlois and applied/linked to s. 8 Charter reasonableness framework from Hunter v. Southam and R. v. Collins
CaseB_TestB: Grant (unknown third party suspect evidence): defence-led evidence admissible where (1) relevant to a fact in issue and (2) “probative value ... is not substantially outweighed by its prejudicial effects” (Seaboyer); for unknown third party suspect relevance, a “sufficient connection — or similarity —” between the charged crime and another incident the accused “could not possibly have committed” can supply the factual foundation/air of reality; trial judge must not assess credibility/weight or require proof on a balance of probabilities
BaselineB: Common law evidence admissibility principles, primarily R. v. Seaboyer (probative value vs prejudicial effect; defence evidence excluded only if prejudice substantially outweighs value), with related relevance/air of reality principles from Corbett and Cinous
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Schreiber (Lamer C.J.) — s. 8 Charter is only triggered if claimant shows a reasonable expectation of privacy; in foreign-search context, expectation generally corresponds to protection under foreign law (Plant contextual factors; foreign-law ceiling).
BaselineA: Constitution (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 8; s. 32(1)) plus common-law/Charter jurisprudence on reasonable expectation of privacy (Hunter v. Southam; R. v. Plant; R. v. Terry).
CaseB_TestB: Fullowka — Anns/Cooper duty-of-care framework: prima facie duty requires foreseeability and proximity; if established, ask whether residual policy considerations negate/limit the duty.
BaselineB: Common law negligence duty framework (Cooper v. Hobart; Edwards v. Law Society; Odhavji Estate; Childs v. Desormeaux; Hill v. Hamilton-Wentworth).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Pushpanathan Art. 1F(c) exclusion framework: Art. 1F(c) applies where there is international-law consensus that the acts are "sufficiently serious and sustained violations of fundamental human rights as to amount to persecution", or where acts are "explicitly recognized as contrary to the purposes and principles of the United Nations"; includes (1) explicit UN/international designation ("determinative" if reflecting reasonable consensus) and (2) court characterization of "serious, sustained and systemic" human-rights violations constituting persecution (with indicators like proximity to the core of human rights and universal-jurisdiction status).
BaselineA: Statute + treaty: Immigration Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. I-2, s. 2(1) incorporating Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees, Can. T.S. 1969 No. 6, Art. 1F(c) (interpreted using Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, Arts. 31-32, as described in the reasons).
CaseB_TestB: Hadley v. Baxendale remoteness/proximity test for contract damages (as applied to employment implied duties): damages are those that arise "either naturally" or that "may reasonably be supposed to have been in the contemplation of both parties, at the time they made the contract, as the probable result of a breach"; applied to assess loss-of-profits damages for breach of an implied duty of good faith by a branch manager.
BaselineB: Common law: Hadley v. Baxendale (1854) remoteness rule for contract damages (as expressly adopted/applied in the reasons).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Hodgson framework for (1) who is a “person in authority” for the confessions rule and (2) when a trial judge must hold a voir dire on their own motion: person in authority includes those the accused reasonably believes can influence/control proceedings; defence must raise issue; judge acts proprio motu only in “extremely rare cases” where evidence objectively shows a close connection to authorities
BaselineA: Common law (confessions rule; voluntariness requirement; person-in-authority concept; voir dire practice)
CaseB_TestB: McClurg approach to Income Tax Act s. 56(2) in corporate dividend context: s. 56(2) targets diversion of amounts the taxpayer “otherwise would have obtained”; “as a general rule, a dividend payment cannot reasonably be considered a benefit diverted from a taxpayer to a third party” because until declared profits belong to the corporation; discretionary dividend allocation treated the same as dividends generally
BaselineB: Statute (Income Tax Act, S.C. 1970-71-72, c. 63, s. 56(2)) interpreted in light of corporate law context
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Reg. 1201 depletion-base profit computation: determine profits “reasonably attributable” to production by subtracting only expenses of earning those receipts, and then deduct only the items enumerated in Reg. 1201(4) (no implied deduction for long-term scientific research under ITA ss. 11(1)(j), 72)
BaselineA: Regulation/statute: Income Tax Regulations, Reg. 1201(2) and 1201(4), in relation to Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1952, c. 148, ss. 11(1)(j) and 72; approach referenced from MNR v. Imperial Oil Ltd., [1960] S.C.R. 735
CaseB_TestB: Sherman Estate test for discretionary limits on the open court principle (publication bans): (1) serious risk to an important public interest; (2) necessity because reasonable alternatives will not prevent the risk; (3) proportionality—benefits outweigh negative effects
BaselineB: Common law: Sherman Estate v. Donovan, 2021 SCC 25 (para. 38) governing discretionary orders limiting court openness
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Guidelines for applying the Kienapple (res judicata / rule against multiple convictions) principle where counts are of different gravity: if same delict underlies both, convict on the more serious and acquit/strike the less serious; if guilty plea entered to the less serious first, hold it in abeyance pending trial on the more serious
BaselineA: Common law (Kienapple v. The Queen, [1975] 1 S.C.R. 729, and related multiple-conviction jurisprudence)
CaseB_TestB: Habeas corpus availability to challenge continuation of detention in parole context: continuation of a valid deprivation of liberty is reviewable only if it becomes unlawful; in parole, unlawfulness arises only once the inmate has acquired parolee status, which occurs when the parole decision takes effect (including fulfillment of any condition precedent)
BaselineB: Common law habeas corpus principles as developed in R. v. Miller, [1985] 2 S.C.R. 613; Cardinal v. Director of Kent Institution, [1985] 2 S.C.R. 643; Morin v. National Special Handling Unit Review Committee, [1985] 2 S.C.R. 662, applied in the statutory parole context (Parole Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. P-2, as amended)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: NCR disposition under Criminal Code s. 672.54: absolute discharge is mandatory unless the court/Review Board makes a positive finding that the NCR accused poses a “significant threat to the safety of the public”; “significant threat” means “a real risk of physical or psychological harm ... that is serious ... going beyond the merely trivial or annoying” and the conduct “must be criminal in nature” (McLachlin J.).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, Part XX.1, especially s. 672.54(a)-(c); interpreted in light of Charter s. 7 and prior SCC guidance in R. v. Swain).
CaseB_TestB: Westbank levy characterization for Constitution Act, 1867 s. 125: a levy is generally a “tax” if it is (1) “compulsory and enforceable by law”; (2) “imposed under the authority of the legislature”; (3) “levied by a public body”; (4) “intended for a public purpose”; and (5) “unconnected to any form of a regulatory scheme” (Gonthier J.).
BaselineB: Constitution + statute: Constitution Act, 1867, s. 125 (and related taxing heads), and Indian Act s. 83(1)(a); building on prior SCC tax/charge jurisprudence (e.g., Lawson; Re Exported Natural Gas Tax; Eurig Estate).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 2(d) (freedom of association) in labour context: s. 2(d) protects only (1) the freedom to establish/belong to/maintain an association and (2) the exercise in association of members’ lawful rights; it generally does not impose a positive obligation to include a group in a statutory labour-relations regime. Key quote: “only the establishment of an independent employee association and the exercise in association of the lawful rights of its members are protected under s. 2(d)” and “the fundamental freedoms protected by s. 2 of the Charter do not impose a positive obligation of protection or inclusion on Parliament or the government, except perhaps in exceptional circumstances”.
BaselineA: Combination: Charter s. 2(d) and prior SCC jurisprudence (1987 labour trilogy; Professional Institute of the Public Service of Canada v. Northwest Territories (Commissioner); Canadian Egg Marketing Agency v. Richardson). Applied to statutory exclusion in Public Service Staff Relations Act, s. 2 “employee” (e) (and relatedly Canada Labour Code, s. 6).
CaseB_TestB: Joint/co-principal liability in group assaults (Criminal Code, s. 21(1)(a)): co-principal liability “flows whenever two or more individuals come together with an intention to commit an offence, are present during the commission of the offence, and contribute to its commission”; for manslaughter, focus on whether the accused’s actions were “a significant contributing cause of death” (not on who inflicted which wound), and in group assaults “absent a discrete or intervening event, the actions of all assailants can constitute a significant contributing cause to all injuries sustained.”
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, ss. 21(1)(a), (c) (party liability). Clarification in light of R. v. Pickton and correcting an implication from R. v. Cabrera (ABCA), aff’d in R. v. Shlah.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Federal Child Support Guidelines s. 4 ‘inappropriate’ analysis for payors over $150,000: Table amount presumptively applies; deviation (up or down) only if rebutted by evidence showing the Table amount is ‘inappropriate’ meaning ‘unsuitable’, assessed on all the circumstances including s. 4(b)(ii) factors
BaselineA: Regulation/statute: Federal Child Support Guidelines, SOR/97-175, s. 4 (and related ss. 1, 3); Divorce Act, s. 26.1(2)
CaseB_TestB: Classification test for all-risks/multi-peril policies under the B.C. Insurance Act: if the policy does not fit coherently within Part 5 (fire insurance) under s. 119, it is governed by Part 2 (general provisions), including Part 2’s limitation period; contractual harsher limitation cannot oust Part 2 due to s. 3(a)
BaselineB: Statute: Insurance Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 226, ss. 119 and 3(a) (and statutory condition 14 in Part 5 as the competing regime)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meiorin unified BFOR test (3-step): employer must prove (1) standard adopted for a purpose “rationally connected to the performance of the job”; (2) adopted “in an honest and good faith belief” it was necessary; and (3) standard is “reasonably necessary” — i.e., “impossible to accommodate” affected employees “without imposing undue hardship” on the employer.
BaselineA: Statute (British Columbia Human Rights Code, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 210, ss. 13(1)(a), (b), (4)) plus prior SCC human rights/BFOR jurisprudence (e.g., O’Malley; Etobicoke; Central Alberta Dairy Pool; Renaud).
CaseB_TestB: Stewart source-of-income test (2-stage): (i) “Is the activity ... undertaken in pursuit of profit, or is it a personal endeavour?”; (ii) if not personal, “is the source of the income a business or property?”; where hobby/personal elements exist, ask whether taxpayer has “subjective intention to profit” supported by “evidence of businesslike behaviour” (REOP is only “a single factor”).
BaselineB: Statute (Income Tax Act, S.C. 1970-71-72, c. 63 / R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), especially ss. 3(a), 9(1)-(2), 18(1)(a), (h), 20(1)(c)(i), 248(1)) and prior SCC case law on REOP/source (notably Moldowan v. The Queen).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Staged analysis for whether a conditional sentence is appropriate for an Aboriginal offender (s. 742.1 with mandatory consideration of s. 718.2(e) once incarceration is in play): (1) preliminarily exclude probation and a penitentiary term; (2) confirm s. 742.1 prerequisites (no minimum; <2 years; community safety—risk of reoffending and gravity of harm); (3) then determine whether a conditional sentence is consistent with ss. 718–718.2, and when narrowing to incarceration the judge must consider Gladue factors (unique systemic/background circumstances and culturally appropriate sanctions).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code) as interpreted in R. v. Proulx and R. v. Gladue
CaseB_TestB: Quebec Charter s. 9.1 balancing for a freedom of religion claim raised to avoid civil liability: even if there is a prima facie religious-freedom impact, the claim "must be balanced and reconciled with countervailing rights, values, and harm" (s. 9.1), a "complex, nuanced, fact-specific exercise"; here, any impairment is outweighed by harms and public interests (equality, autonomy in marriage/divorce, and enforcing valid contracts).
BaselineB: Statute (Quebec Charter of human rights and freedoms, ss. 3 and 9.1) and SCC freedom-of-religion framework from Syndicat Northcrest v. Amselem
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Unreasonable verdict review under Criminal Code s. 686(1)(a)(i): whether the verdict is one that a properly instructed jury (or trial judge) acting judicially could reasonably have rendered; appellate court must thoroughly re-examine the evidence and cannot overturn based on a mere “lurking doubt” without articulating why the verdict is inconsistent with a judicial appreciation of the evidence
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(a)(i)) as interpreted in SCC common law (R. v. Yebes; reaffirmed/followed via R. v. Biniaris)
CaseB_TestB: Institutional consultation / natural justice limits and judicial review threshold: consultation is permissible if (1) not imposed by superiors, (2) limited to law and policy, and (3) decision-makers remain free; for audi alteram partem, applicant must prove an actual breach (not merely an apprehended breach), and a change from draft to final reasons does not by itself rebut the presumption of regularity
BaselineB: Common law procedural fairness/natural justice framework from IWA v. Consolidated-Bathurst Packaging Ltd. and Tremblay v. Quebec (Commission des affaires sociales) (applied in context of judicial review)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: “Functional and structural” approach to the third branch of the Mills ‘court of competent jurisdiction’ test (power to grant the Charter remedy sought under s. 24(1))
BaselineA: Combination: Charter s. 24(1) plus common-law/constitutional jurisprudence defining “court of competent jurisdiction” (Mills v. The Queen; affirmed in Weber; Mooring). Key baseline formulation: a court of competent jurisdiction possesses “(1) jurisdiction over the person; (2) jurisdiction over the subject matter; and (3) jurisdiction to grant the remedy” (Mills, quoted at para. 15).
JudgeA: The Chief Justice (McLachlin C.J.) for the Court
CaseB_TestB: Section 11(d) ‘inexorable connection’ test for statutory presumptions (and resulting invalidity of Criminal Code s. 172.1(3) presumption of belief as to age)
BaselineB: Combination: Charter s. 11(d) (presumption of innocence) applied to a statutory presumption in Criminal Code s. 172.1(3), using prior SCC doctrine (Whyte; Downey; Audet; St‑Onge Lamoureux). Core baseline rule: a presumption complies with s. 11(d) “solely if proof of the substituted fact leads ‘inexorably’ to the existence of the essential element that it replaces” (paras. 52-53).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Existence of a valid partnership (for s. 96 ITA loss allocation): at formation, alleged partners must be (1) carrying on a business, (2) in common, (3) with a view to profit; tax motivation does not negate partnership if these elements are present, and “view to profit” is not a strictly quantitative net-gain inquiry (ancillary profit intention can suffice).
BaselineA: Common law partnership test applied for Income Tax Act, s. 96 purposes; baseline articulated in Continental Bank Leasing Corp. v. Canada, [1998] 2 S.C.R. 298 (and applied via Backman v. Canada, 2001 SCC 10). Statutory context: Income Tax Act, s. 96.
CaseB_TestB: Adequacy of jury instructions on credibility and reasonable doubt (W.(D.) in substance): where credibility is central, the judge must explain the relationship between credibility assessment and the Crown’s burden; instructions must make it “crystal clear” the burden never shifts and must avoid the “credibility contest” error; failure to use W.(D.)’s exact three questions is not fatal if, read as a whole, the charge leaves the jury under no misapprehension about the correct burden/standard.
BaselineB: Common law jury-charge framework from R. v. W. (D.), [1991] 1 S.C.R. 742 (and related cases). Statutory context of the trial: Criminal Code, s. 271(1)(a) (offence charged), but the instruction test is common law.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Customs Act s. 48(5)(a)(iv) “condition of sale” test for dutiable royalties/licence fees: royalties/licence fees are added to value for duty only if they are paid “as a condition of the sale of the goods for export to Canada”; “Unless a vendor is entitled to refuse to sell licensed goods to the purchaser or repudiate the contract of sale where the purchaser fails to pay royalties or licence fees, s. 48(5)(a)(iv) is inapplicable.”
BaselineA: Statute (Customs Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (2nd Supp.), s. 48(5)(a)(iv) (and related context in ss. 45(1), 48(4), 48(5)(a)(v)); interpreted using common law/sale of goods concepts of “condition of sale”.
CaseB_TestB: ITA s. 224 “requirement to pay” trigger in cheque-deposit context: a bank is not “liable to make a payment” to a tax debtor merely because the debtor is named as payee; liability depends on cheque mechanics—“What is on the back of the cheque — the instructions or the endorsement — is crucial”; where instructions are to deposit to a joint account, the bank is not liable to pay the tax debtor personally within s. 224(1).
BaselineB: Combination of statute and commercial law: Income Tax Act, s. 224(1) interpreted through Bills of Exchange Act provisions (including ss. 2, 16(1), 20(3), 84(1),(3), 86(1), 126, 138(2), 165(3)) and common law banking/bills principles (e.g., Foley v. Hill; Schroeder v. Central Bank of London; Capital Associates).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: s. 45 Labour Code successorship in subcontracting: s. 45 may apply where the transferee (1) performs functions similar to those performed by the transferor to which the certification applied and (2) receives a "right to operate part of the transferor’s undertaking"; autonomy is assessed contextually (no rigid "total control" requirement) and may be evaluated using the "criterion of the subordination of the employees to the contractors" to determine whether the transferee has "sufficient authority" to be the new employer
BaselineA: Statute (Quebec Labour Code, R.S.Q., c. C-27, ss. 45-46) as interpreted in SCC jurisprudence including U.E.S., Local 298 v. Bibeault and Lester (W.W.) (1978) Ltd.
CaseB_TestB: Jarvis/Ling audit vs investigation test: CCRA may use ITA ss. 231.1(1)/231.2(1) requirement powers for an audit, but once the "predominant purpose" of the inquiry is "the determination of a taxpayer’s penal liability" under s. 239, officials must stop using those powers; whether that point is reached is assessed on the "totality of the circumstances" ("no one factor is determinative")
BaselineB: Combination of statute and constitutional law: Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), ss. 231.1(1), 231.2(1), 239; Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 7, 8, 24(2), applying the SCC framework in R. v. Jarvis
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Anns/Cooper duty of care framework for recognizing a novel duty of care against a statutory regulator (foreseeability + proximity; then residual policy): at stage 1, ask whether there is “reasonably foreseeable harm and proximity sufficient to establish a prima facie duty of care”; “Mere foreseeability is not enough... [t]he plaintiff must also show proximity”; if established, stage 2 asks whether “residual policy considerations... justify denying liability”.
BaselineA: Common law (Anns v. Merton London Borough Council; Kamloops (City of) v. Nielsen), as clarified in Cooper v. Hobart (2001 SCC 79), applied in light of the Law Society Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. L.8 (notably ss. 9, 33, 51, 61).
JudgeA: The Chief Justice and Major J.
CaseB_TestB: Section 1 (Oakes) justification analysis, emphasizing fiscal-crisis justification: “Demonstration of a reasonable limit involves consideration of five related questions with close attention to the factual context”: (1) pressing and substantial objective; (2) rational connection; (3) minimal impairment (“as little as possible”/“no more than is reasonably necessary”); (4) proportionality between effects and objective; (5) whether deleterious effects outweigh “actual salutary effects”.
BaselineB: Constitution (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 1) and common law framework from R. v. Oakes, with related s. 1 jurisprudence (e.g., Dagenais).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Pragmatic and functional approach to standard of review (correctness vs deference) for CRTC interpretation of s. 43(5): assess (1) privative clause/statutory appeal, (2) relative expertise, (3) purposes of the Act/provision, (4) nature of the problem
BaselineA: Common law (standard of review doctrine) applied to a statutory appeal under Telecommunications Act, S.C. 1993, c. 38, s. 64(1); four-factor framework from Pushpanathan v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), [1998] 1 S.C.R. 982 (also referenced: Dr. Q v. College of Physicians and Surgeons of British Columbia, 2003 SCC 19)
CaseB_TestB: Sentencing framework for considering collateral consequences and mistake of law/non-impairment in sentencing for refusal causing death (s. 255(3.2)): collateral consequences may be considered if they relate to the offence/offender, but proportionality prevails; mistake of law requires honest but mistaken belief in legality; non-impairment is mitigating but its effect must be limited and offender bears onus on balance of probabilities
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, ss. 255(3.2), 718 to 718.2, 718.1; plus existing SCC sentencing jurisprudence (e.g., R. v. Lacasse, 2015 SCC 64; R. v. Pham, 2013 SCC 15) and Criminal Code s. 19 (mistake of law not a defence)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 1 justification (Oakes proportionality) applied to a municipal sign by-law restricting expression: pressing/substantial objective; rational connection; minimal impairment; overall proportionality of effects
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional text (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 1 and 2(b)) plus prior SCC framework (R. v. Oakes; refined in Dagenais and Thomson Newspapers, as summarized in R. v. Sharpe)
CaseB_TestB: Canadian Bill of Rights due process analysis for property: (1) no right to notice/hearing before Parliament enacts expropriative legislation; (2) procedural due process applies only in individualized adjudication; (3) no substantive due process protection against clear and unambiguous legislative expropriation
BaselineB: Statute (Canadian Bill of Rights, ss. 1(a) and 2(e)) applied to statute (Department of Veterans Affairs Act, s. 5.1(4))
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Copyright infringement by “reproduction” under s. 3(1): “Reproduction” generally requires “producing additional or new copies”; a “literal physical, mechanical transfer in which no multiplication takes place” is not a reproduction (so s. 38(1) seizure for “infringing copies” is unavailable).
BaselineA: Statute: Copyright Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-42, ss. 3(1) (definition of copyright: “sole right to produce or reproduce the work or any substantial part thereof in any material form whatever”), 2 (“infringing”), and 38(1) (recovery/seizure of “infringing copies”); applied in context of Code of Civil Procedure, R.S.Q., c. C-25, art. 734 (seizure before judgment).
CaseB_TestB: Reasonableness simpliciter on judicial review: the standard does not “float”; a decision is unreasonable “only if there is no line of analysis within the given reasons that could reasonably lead the tribunal from the evidence before it to the conclusion at which it arrived”; if any sufficient reasons are “tenable” on a “somewhat probing examination”, the court must not interfere.
BaselineB: Common law (judicial review standards) as articulated in prior SCC cases cited in the decision, especially Canada (Director of Investigation and Research) v. Southam Inc. and Pushpanathan v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration); applied in a statutory appeal context under Law Society Act, 1996, S.N.B. 1996, c. 89 (notably ss. 66(1), 68).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Privacy Act s. 22(1)(b) exemption: government institution may refuse access only if disclosure “could reasonably be expected” to be injurious to the conduct of lawful investigations; requires “a clear and direct connection between the disclosure of specific information and the injury that is alleged” and “concrete reasons” tied to the specific case (not general claims of confidentiality). Also, s. 22(1)(b) can apply even after an investigation has concluded (including to protect future investigations).
BaselineA: Statute (Privacy Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. P-21, ss. 12(1), 22(1)(b), 22(3), 47, 49; reconciled with Official Languages Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 31 (4th Supp.), ss. 60(1), 72-74).
CaseB_TestB: Adverse inference / presumption of fact on causation in Quebec medical liability: no rule requires drawing an adverse inference where defendant’s negligence undermines proof and plaintiff adduces some evidence; the trier of fact “may” draw an inference as part of fact-finding, but only within art. 2849 C.C.Q. (“serious, precise and concordant” presumptions) and the decision is discretionary and reviewable only for palpable and overriding error.
BaselineB: Statute and jurisprudence: Civil Code of Québec, art. 2849 (presumptions of fact) as interpreted through SCC causation/inference cases (Snell v. Farrell; St-Jean v. Mercier; also Ediger v. Johnston).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Validity/effect of a zoning “holding regulation”: despite superfluous drafting about future amendment, give effect to the operative prohibition (“Notwithstanding any other provisions... no building... may be... erected to contain three or more dwelling units”) where the municipality’s freeze policy is clear and within its Planning Act powers; do not treat it as an invalid reservation of ad hoc discretion/spot-zoning.
BaselineA: Statute + municipal by-law: The Planning Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 349, s. 35(1) (zoning power) and s. 35(22) (appeal to Municipal Board), applied to City of London zoning by-law 306-480 as amended by by-law 306(bc)-504, s. 4 (new s. 11 “Holding Regulation”).
CaseB_TestB: Custody decision-making under s. 1(1) of The Infants Act: the court must consider the parties’ conduct only as it bears on their relative fitness, but it is “only one factor” and “each particular case must be judged on its own circumstances”, with “the paramount consideration... the welfare of the children.”
BaselineB: Statute + prior custody jurisprudence: The Infants Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 222, s. 1(1) (welfare paramount; conduct considered), with guidance from McKee v. McKee, Bickley v. Bickley, Retzer v. Retzer, and contemporaneous discussion in Talsky v. Talsky (as referenced in the reasons).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: OSC disclosure of compelled investigation material under Securities Act s. 17(1): apply Stinchcombe-style relevance (“reasonable possibility of relevance” to full answer and defence) and order disclosure only to the extent necessary in the public interest (balancing confidentiality/privacy vs fairness/full answer and defence), permitting a global (non document-by-document) relevance assessment where appropriate
BaselineA: Statute (Ontario Securities Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. S.5, ss. 16-17) plus common-law relevance standard from R. v. Stinchcombe for defining “relevant” disclosure
CaseB_TestB: Choosing first-party (Stinchcombe/McNeil) vs third-party (O’Connor) disclosure: ask (1) is the information in the possession or control of the prosecuting Crown? and (2) if not, is it information the police/other Crown entity ought to have supplied because it is part of the “fruits of the investigation” or “obviously relevant”? If yes to either, Stinchcombe applies; otherwise O’Connor applies and the accused must show the record is “likely relevant” (a “reasonable possibility” it is logically probative to an issue at trial or witness competence)
BaselineB: Common law (Stinchcombe; McNeil; O’Connor) applied in the context of Criminal Code s. 258(1)(c) prosecutions
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Misfeasance in public office (Iacobucci J.): plaintiff must prove (1) “deliberate and unlawful conduct in the exercise of public functions”; and (2) “awareness that the conduct is unlawful and likely to injure the plaintiff” (plus causation and compensable loss).
BaselineA: Common law tort (misfeasance in public office), drawing on cases including Roncarelli v. Duplessis and comparative authorities (e.g., Three Rivers); applied in context of statutory duties under Ontario Police Services Act, ss. 113(9) and 41(1)(b).
CaseB_TestB: Eligibility for Quebec seats under Supreme Court Act s. 6 (McLachlin C.J. et al.): s. 6 “impliedly excludes former members” and requires “current membership” in the Barreau du Québec or Quebec superior courts; Parliament cannot unilaterally change these eligibility requirements (Constitution Act, 1982, s. 41(d)).
BaselineB: Statutory interpretation of Supreme Court Act, ss. 5 and 6, plus constitutional constraints under Constitution Act, 1982, Part V (ss. 41(d), 42(1)(d)) and Constitution Act, 1867, s. 101.
JudgeB: McLachlin C.J. and LeBel, Abella, Cromwell, Karakatsanis and Wagner JJ.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Securities Act s. 162 administrative penalty in the public interest: Commission may consider general deterrence (as a factor) and must assess penalty globally in context; reviewing court asks whether there is a rational basis/reasonableness
BaselineA: Statute (Securities Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 418, s. 162 (and related public-interest context in ss. 161-162))
CaseB_TestB: Adequacy of jury instructions on routes to criminal liability where others may be involved: jury may convict if accused "acted in concert with" others / was an "active participant"; trial judge must correct erroneous "actual shooter" instruction and ensure charge as a whole conveys essential elements
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, especially s. 21 party liability; appeal/miscarriage framework includes s. 686(1)(b)(iii))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Good-faith basis (not evidentiary foundation) required to put unproven factual suggestions in cross-examination; judge may require assurance only if predicate is manifestly tenuous or suspect
BaselineA: Common law (scope/limits of cross-examination; ethical duties of counsel), clarified against misreadings of R. v. Howard and consistent with R. v. Bencardino; also linked to Charter-protected full answer and defence (ss. 7, 11(d))
CaseB_TestB: Federal paramountcy test (operational conflict or frustration of federal purpose), with restrained approach and requirement of clear proof of federal purpose before finding frustration
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine of federal paramountcy (as articulated in cases such as Rothmans, Canadian Western Bank, COPA, Ryan Estate) applied to Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act, s. 243 (and related ss. 243(1.1), 244, 72(1)) and The Saskatchewan Farm Security Act, ss. 9-22
JudgeB: Abella and Gascon JJ. (Cromwell, Moldaver, Karakatsanis and Wagner JJ. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Vaid framework for determining existence/scope of parliamentary privilege: (1) if privilege category/scope is authoritatively established in Canada/Westminster, accept; (2) if not, apply necessity test requiring a close/direct connection to legislative functions such that outside interference would undermine required autonomy
BaselineA: Constitution Act, 1867, s. 18 and Parliament of Canada Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. P-1, s. 4 (benchmarking Canadian privilege to Westminster), plus prior SCC privilege jurisprudence (e.g., New Brunswick Broadcasting; Harvey) and the common-law doctrine of necessity
CaseB_TestB: Interpretive rule for Tobacco Act s. 18: construe “promotion” as “commercial promotion directly or indirectly targeted at consumers” (so funded legitimate scientific works are not caught), within the s. 1 Charter proportionality framework
BaselineB: Statute and regulation interpreted/applied under the Charter: Tobacco Act, S.C. 1997, c. 13, ss. 18-19 (and related provisions) and Tobacco Products Information Regulations, SOR/2000-272; Charter s. 1 proportionality (Oakes) as the justificatory framework
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: GAAR (Income Tax Act, s. 245) — three requirements for application, focusing on s. 245(4) “abusive tax avoidance”: (1) tax benefit; (2) avoidance transaction; (3) abuse/misuse assessed by a “unified textual, contextual and purposive analysis” of the provisions relied on, asking whether allowing the benefit would “frustrate or defeat the object, spirit or purpose” of those provisions (here, ss. 18(13) and 96) (paras. 31, 35, 58).
BaselineA: Statute: Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), especially ss. 245(1)-(4) (GAAR), applied with ss. 18(13) and 96(1); interpretive framework explicitly taken from the companion SCC decision Canada Trustco Mortgage Co. v. Canada, 2005 SCC 54 (paras. 1-2, 31).
CaseB_TestB: Vancouver Sun informer-privilege procedure and “single guiding rule”: give “full effect” to informer privilege (a “complete and total bar on any disclosure of the informer’s identity”) while “limiting, as much as possible, any impairment of the open court principle”; two stages: (1) verify privilege (in camera, possibly ex parte; evidence of informer status “automatically engages the privilege”); (2) once privilege exists, determine confidentiality measures to protect it while accommodating openness “to the greatest extent possible” (paras. 47-49, 71-75).
BaselineB: Common law: Named Person v. Vancouver Sun, 2007 SCC 43 (procedure and guiding rule for informer privilege vs open court principle), reaffirmed and applied; also relies on common-law informer privilege doctrine (e.g., Leipert; Basi) as described in the reasons.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “lawful authority” for whistleblower protection under s. 74(1)(a): includes not only police/public enforcement but also internal persons who “exercise lawful authority over the employee(s) complained about, or over the activity that is or is likely to result in the offence” (i.e., an “up the ladder” internal reporting route can qualify).
BaselineA: Statute — The Labour Standards Act, R.S.S. 1978, c. L-1, s. 74(1)(a) (and s. 74(2)); interpreted using the modern principle of statutory interpretation (Driedger/Rizzo) and Saskatchewan Interpretation Act, 1995, s. 10.
CaseB_TestB: Waiver in the face of a dishonoured premium cheque under s. 238(1) Alberta Insurance Act: despite demand for replacement, “before one can find waiver there must be express and unequivocal language or conduct”; a dishonoured cheque means the premium “shall be deemed not to have been made”.
BaselineB: Statute — The Alberta Insurance Act, R.S.A. 1970, c. 187, s. 238(1), applied alongside the common-law waiver requirement as reflected in McGeachie v. North American Life Insurance Company (1893), 23 S.C.R. 148.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “lawful authority” for whistleblower protection under s. 74(1)(a): includes internal employer authorities who can address the wrongdoing (“up the ladder” reporting)
BaselineA: Statute — The Labour Standards Act, R.S.S. 1978, c. L-1, s. 74(1)(a) (and s. 74(2))
CaseB_TestB: Common law joinder test (Clunas) applied to provincial + summary conviction criminal charges: (1) sufficient factual nexus (functional approach to “could initially have been jointly charged”); and (2) joint trial is in the interests of justice (weighing costs/benefits)
BaselineB: Common law — R. v. Clunas, [1992] 1 S.C.R. 595 (two-part joinder test), applied alongside statutory context (POA and Criminal Code)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Two-step harm-based test for criminal indecency under s. 210(1): Crown must prove beyond a reasonable doubt (1) conduct "causes harm or presents a significant risk of harm" (e.g., unwanted public exposure; predisposition to anti-social behaviour; physical/psychological harm) and (2) the harm/risk is "of a degree that is incompatible with the proper functioning of society" (R. v. Kouri, paras. 9-10).
BaselineA: Combination: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 210(1) (keeping common bawdy-house for acts of indecency) interpreted through common-law indecency jurisprudence; Court states the structure is "[b]ased on the guidelines emerging from R. v. Butler" and elaborated in the companion case R. v. Labaye (paras. 1, 9-10).
CaseB_TestB: Pointe Gourde / s. 27(1)(a) compensation inquiry: when deciding whether a land-use enactment’s effect on value must be ignored, "the key question is whether the enactment was made with a view to the expropriation or, conversely, was an independent enactment"; the inquiry examines the enactment’s "purposes and effects" and "causation does not drive the inquiry" (St. John’s (City) v. Lynch, paras. 46, 48, 50-54).
BaselineB: Statute informed by common law: Expropriation Act, R.S.N.L. 1990, c. E-19, s. 27(1)(a) ("no account shall be taken of the compulsory acquisition of the land") incorporating the common-law Pointe Gourde principle from Pointe Gourde Quarrying and Transport Co. v. Sub-Intendent of Crown Lands (paras. 2, 34-38).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Interpretation of Alberta Limitations Act, s. 12 in conflicts cases: s. 12 applies Alberta’s limitations law only to “live” foreign causes of action and does not revive claims already time-barred under the applicable foreign substantive law (lex loci delicti, including its limitation period)
BaselineA: Statute (Limitations Act, R.S.A. 2000, c. L-12, s. 12) interpreted against the common law conflicts rule from Tolofson v. Jensen (lex loci delicti includes the foreign limitation period as substantive)
CaseB_TestB: Ancillary powers doctrine (Waterfield/Dedman) for common law police powers: define the asserted power and liberty interest, then (1) ask if conduct falls within a police duty; (2) ask if conduct is a justifiable exercise—i.e., “reasonably necessary”—weighing (i) importance of the duty, (ii) necessity of the interference, and (iii) extent of the interference; onus on the state
BaselineB: Common law (ancillary powers doctrine from R. v. Waterfield as adopted in Dedman v. The Queen; factors articulated in R. v. MacDonald)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Palmer/Lévesque test for admitting fresh evidence on a sentence appeal (interests of justice): (1) due diligence; (2) relevance; (3) credibility; (4) could reasonably be expected to have affected the result
BaselineA: Common law (Palmer v. The Queen) as adapted for sentence appeals in R. v. Lévesque; applied under Criminal Code, s. 687(1)
CaseB_TestB: Section 8 reasonable expectation of privacy (REP) analysis: REP assessed on the totality of the circumstances along four lines of inquiry (subject matter; direct interest; subjective expectation; objective reasonableness)
BaselineB: Common law/constitutional doctrine under Charter s. 8 (as articulated in cases such as Edwards, Tessling, Spencer, Cole, Marakah) and related statutory context in Criminal Code Part VI (ss. 183, 184.2)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Copyright Act s. 27(2)(e) “hypothetical infringement” requirement: secondary infringement by importation requires that the foreign maker “would infringe copyright if it had been made in Canada by the person who made it”; no liability where the hypothetical maker is the Canadian copyright owner because “a copyright owner cannot be liable to its exclusive licensee for infringement” (so “there is no hypothetical infringement”).
JudgeA: Rothstein J. (Binnie and Deschamps JJ. concurring)
CaseB_TestB: Whaling s. 11(h) “punished again” test for retrospective parole changes: “the dominant consideration” is “the extent to which an offender’s settled expectation of liberty has been thwarted by retrospective legislative action”; “retrospective change that has the effect of automatically lengthening the offender’s period of incarceration” is a “clearest of cases”; otherwise, generally not punitive if it “does not substantially increase the risk of additional incarceration” (with indicators like individualized decision-making and procedural safeguards).
BaselineB: Constitution (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 11(h); with prior SCC punishment/double jeopardy jurisprudence including Wigglesworth and Rodgers).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Sentencing of hybrid offences prosecuted summarily: treat as summary conviction for sentencing; maximum sentence available without “worst offender/worst offence”; appellate intervention only for error of principle/relevant factor/overemphasis or if demonstrably unfit
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, Part XXIII sentencing principles and summary conviction penalty provision)
CaseB_TestB: Mr. Big confessions admissibility rule: presumptively inadmissible; Crown must show (balance of probabilities) probative value (reliability) outweighs prejudicial effect; plus separate abuse-of-process scrutiny for coercive/abusive operations
BaselineB: Common law (party admissions exception to hearsay; trial judge discretion to exclude prejudicial evidence; abuse of process doctrine) as discussed with reference to Evans, Handy, Mohan, Mack, Babos, etc.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Adequacy of jury charge on evidence/defence theory (Azoulay principle): trial judge must (except rare needless cases) review substantial parts of the evidence and give the jury the theory of the defence so they can appreciate the evidence’s value/effect and how law applies; judge should “decant and simplify” and has “considerable latitude” on how much evidence to review, provided jurors get an “adequate understanding” of the relationship between essential evidence and the issues.
BaselineA: Common law (Azoulay v. The Queen; R. v. Jacquard)
CaseB_TestB: Trade-marks Act s. 6 confusion test (likelihood of confusion): confusion exists if use of both marks in the same area would be likely to lead the “casual consumer somewhat in a hurry” to the mistaken inference that the wares/services come from the same source; decision-maker must consider “all the surrounding circumstances” including the s. 6(5) factors, with context-specific weighting; no requirement of “resemblance or linkage” between wares/services beyond what s. 6 provides.
BaselineB: Statute (Trade-marks Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. T-13, ss. 6(2) and 6(5))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 172.1(1)(c) “luring a child” — three essential elements and subjective-purpose focus: (1) “an intentional communication by computer”; (2) “with a person whom the accused knows or believes to be under 14 years of age”; (3) “for the specific purpose of facilitating the commission of a specified secondary offence” (paras. 3, 36). “Facilitating” includes “helping to bring about and making easier or more probable” (para. 28). “What matters is whether the evidence as a whole establishes beyond a reasonable doubt” the communication was for that purpose; objective capability is “neither necessary nor necessarily sufficient” (para. 42).
BaselineA: Statute — Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 172.1(1)(c) (as it read at the time), with related secondary offences in ss. 151 and 152 (and others listed in s. 172.1(1)(c)).
CaseB_TestB: Enforcement of forum selection clause — “strong cause” test: “unless there is a ‘strong cause’ as to why a domestic court should exercise jurisdiction, order and fairness are better achieved when parties are held to their bargains” (para. 9, citing Pompey).
BaselineB: Common law (as confirmed in Z.I. Pompey Industrie v. ECU-Line N.V., 2003 SCC 27) applied within a procedural setting under Ontario Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 21.01(3)(a).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: SCC leave jurisdiction and leave-importance test under Supreme Court Act s. 40(1): jurisdiction over “any final or other judgment” (unless excluded by s. 40(3)), but leave only if the question is of “public importance” or otherwise warrants SCC decision
BaselineA: Statute (Supreme Court Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. S-26, ss. 2, 40(1), 40(3); with interpretive line of cases including Hill v. The Queen and R. v. Gardiner)
CaseB_TestB: Access to Information Act third-party disclosure framework: (1) low-threshold notice duty under s. 27(1) (disclose without notice only in “clear cases”); (2) s. 20(1) exemptions tests (trade secret 4-part definition; confidential info 3-part test; harm test = “reasonable expectation of probable harm”); and (3) s. 25 severance reasonableness (semantic + cost-benefit)
BaselineB: Statute (Access to Information Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. A-1, ss. 20(1), 25, 27, 28, 44; plus common-law/FC jurisprudence incorporated for definitions such as AstraZeneca and Société Gamma)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Departing from the common law “knock and announce” rule when executing a dwelling-house search warrant: police must ordinarily (i) give notice of presence, (ii) notice of authority, and (iii) notice of purpose; if they depart, the Crown must provide an evidentiary basis showing police had “reasonable grounds to be concerned” about harm to persons or destruction of evidence, assessed on what was (or should reasonably have been) known at the time (no ex post facto justifications).
BaselineA: Common law + Charter. Common law “knock and announce” rule from Eccles v. Bourque; justification framework from R. v. Genest and R. v. Gimson; overall s. 8 reasonableness structure from R. v. Collins (Charter, s. 8).
CaseB_TestB: Implied assertions are hearsay when tendered for the truth of their contents; admissible only if within a traditional exception or, failing that, if the principled approach is satisfied on a voir dire by showing “sufficient indicia of reliability and necessity” (principled approach per Mapara/Khelawon).
BaselineB: Common law hearsay rule and the principled approach: R. v. Khelawon (defining features; hearsay dangers), R. v. Mapara (principled framework), and related hearsay jurisprudence (e.g., Starr, Khan).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: State Immunity Act “commercial activity” exception (s. 5): determine whether proceedings “relate to any commercial activity” by examining the nature of the state’s acts “in their full context, which includes the purpose of the acts”; it is “not enough” to ask whether acts were authorized by the state or pursued public interests (Kuwait Airways Corp. v. Iraq, 2010 SCC 40, paras. 17, 30-33).
BaselineA: Statute (State Immunity Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. S-18, ss. 2 “commercial activity”, 3, 5) as interpreted in prior SCC authority (Re Canada Labour Code, [1992] 2 S.C.R. 50).
CaseB_TestB: Criminal Code s. 686(1) curative proviso / miscarriage-of-justice framework: (i) miscarriage of justice turns on whether an irregularity was “severe enough to render the trial unfair or create the appearance of unfairness”, assessed case-by-case with reference points (centrality, gravity/likely impact, jury vs judge-alone, whether remedied, etc.); (ii) curative proviso applies only where conviction was “inevitable” / no “reasonable possibility that the verdict would have been different” (R. v. Khan, 2001 SCC 86, paras. 69, 74-76, 90, 104).
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(a)(ii)-(iii), (b)(iii)-(iv)) as developed in prior SCC cases cited (e.g., Colpitts; Wildman; Bevan; S. (P.L.)).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Journalist-source privilege in Quebec civil proceedings: threshold relevance, then Wigmore 4-factor test with context-specific balancing at factor (4) (Globe and Mail/National Post framework)
BaselineA: Common law (Wigmore privilege framework as applied to journalist-source privilege in R. v. National Post, 2010 SCC 16) applied/extended to Quebec civil litigation; plus Quebec civil evidence context (C.C.Q. art. 2857 relevance/admissibility; C.C.P. art. 46 general powers) and Charter values (Canadian Charter s. 2(b); Quebec Charter ss. 3, 44 as informing values but not creating class privilege).
CaseB_TestB: Court jurisdiction to review decisions of voluntary (religious) associations: jurisdiction only if a legal right is at stake; contract exists only if general contract formation requirements met, especially objective intention to create legal relations
BaselineB: Common law (Highwood Congregation of Jehovah’s Witnesses (Judicial Committee) v. Wall, 2018 SCC 26 on jurisdiction/legal right requirement; general contract law principles including objective intention to create legal relations, citing Scotsburn and Crystal Square).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Quebec Charter s. 49(2) punitive (exemplary) damages: (1) unlawful interference with a Charter right and (2) intentional interference; punitive damages are autonomous (not barred by absence of compensatory damages) and may be awarded against a deceased wrongdoer’s succession, with denunciation recognized as an objective
BaselineA: Statute (Charter of human rights and freedoms, R.S.Q., c. C-12, s. 49(2); Civil Code of Québec, art. 1621; interpreted with prior SCC cases including Béliveau St-Jacques and St-Ferdinand)
CaseB_TestB: YCJA jurisdiction for youth judicial interim release on s. 469 Criminal Code charges after election: “the proceeding” in YCJA ss. 13(2)-(3) includes all steps after election (including pre-trial bail), and jurisdiction to grant release under YCJA s. 33(8) is concurrent between deemed superior court youth justice court judges and provincially designated youth justice court judges
BaselineB: Statute (Youth Criminal Justice Act, ss. 13(1)-(3), 28, 33(8), 67; Criminal Code, ss. 469, 522; Interpretation Act, s. 33(2))
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Miscarriage of justice on appeal: whether trial defects "affected the trial judge’s appreciation of the evidence or rendered the proceedings unfair, so as to give rise to a miscarriage of justice" (including defining a leading question as one that "suggest[s] an answer or assume[s] a state of facts that is in dispute")
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, s. 693(1)(a)) plus common-law appellate concept of "miscarriage of justice"
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 13 engagement turns on whether prior compelled testimony is "incriminating evidence": evidence that the Crown could use at the later proceeding, if permitted, "to prove or assist in proving one or more of the essential elements of the offence"; non-incriminating compelled evidence used only to impeach does not trigger s. 13
BaselineB: Statute/constitutional text (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 13) as interpreted in prior SCC cases (notably R. v. Henry; also Kuldip, Noël, Dubois)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “in association with” in Criminal Code s. 467.12: the offence must (1) have a nexus/connection to a criminal organization and (2) be committed with subjective knowledge (or wilful blindness) of dealing with a criminal organization; “in association with” captures offences that “advance, at least to some degree, the interests of a criminal organization” and “requires a connection between the predicate offence and the organization, as opposed to simply an association between the accused and the organization” (paras. 54-55, 57).
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 467.12(1) (“for the benefit of, at the direction of, or in association with, a criminal organization”) and related organized crime provisions (ss. 467.1, 467.13).
CaseB_TestB: Test for statutory compulsion under Motor Vehicle Act s. 61(1) (for Charter s. 7 use-immunity): “whether, at the time that the accident was reported by the driver, the driver gave the report on the basis of an honest and reasonably held belief that he or she was required by law to report the accident to the person to whom the report was given” (para. 75).
BaselineB: Combination: Statute (Motor Vehicle Act, R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 288, s. 61(1), (1.1), (4), (7)) interpreted through Charter baseline (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7 self-incrimination principle; remedy discussion under s. 24(1)).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Reasonable suspicion standard for sniffer-dog searches (s. 8): subjective suspicion plus objective grounds assessed on the totality of the circumstances through the lens of a reasonable officer (possibility, not probability)
BaselineA: Common law Charter s. 8 framework from R. v. Kang-Brown and R. v. A.M., clarified alongside R. v. Chehil (reasonable suspicion for dog sniffs); also references investigative detention in R. v. Mann
CaseB_TestB: Reformulated s. 11(i) Charter 'punishment' test: consequence of conviction plus (sentencing purpose/principles OR significant liberty/security impact)
BaselineB: Common law Charter s. 11(i) punishment test from R. v. Rodgers (two-part test), applied to Criminal Code s. 161(1)(c),(d) amendments
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: CCQ art. 1425 “common intention prevails” interpretation/rectification: where evidence proves a discrepancy between the parties’ common intention and the written instruments (declared will), and the parties mutually correct the error (subject to third-party rights), the court may recognize the amendments as “legitimate and necessary” and ensure the error is remedied
BaselineA: Statute (Civil Code of Québec, art. 1425; also relies on CCQ contract/obligations provisions including arts. 1378, 1385, 1412, 1439 and evidentiary provisions arts. 2818, 2829)
CaseB_TestB: Bank “put upon inquiry” constructive trust test: “A banker may be a constructive trustee of money in his customer’s account and in breach of that trust if he pays the money away, even on the customer’s mandate, in circumstances which put him upon inquiry” (i.e., where the bank has sufficient notice requiring it to inquire into the character of the funds before dealing with them)
BaselineB: Common law (constructive trust/bank on inquiry doctrine; as summarized from Halsbury’s Laws of England and illustrated by cases discussed in the reasons such as White v. Dominion Bank and Cartwright v. Lyster & Bank of Nova Scotia)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Applicability of Quebec’s 1974 prescription amendments to a case pending in the SCC: s. 5 makes art. 2262(2) C.C. inapplicable to a “suit pending before a court on 1 January 1975”, and the SCC may rely on that intervening provincial statute to dismiss the appeal under Supreme Court Act, s. 47
BaselineA: Statute (Supreme Court Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. S-19, s. 47; plus Quebec Act to amend certain prescriptions, 1974 (Que.), c. 80, ss. 1, 3, 5, and Civil Code arts. 2261(2), 2262(2)); prior SCC approach discussed in Boulevard Heights v. Veilleux and K.V.P. Co. Ltd. v. McKie
CaseB_TestB: Refusal of surrender in extradition: the person must show surrender would “shock the conscience” (s. 7 Charter / fundamental justice) or be “unjust or oppressive” (Extradition Act, s. 44(1)); otherwise the Minister’s surrender decision is upheld as reasonable, with due process concerns generally left to the foreign court
BaselineB: Statute and Charter (Extradition Act, S.C. 1999, c. 18, s. 44(1); Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7) as interpreted in United States v. Burns and Argentina v. Mellino
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Hart ‘Mr. Big’ confessions admissibility rule: presumptive inadmissibility rebutted only if Crown proves (on balance) probative value (reliability) outweighs prejudicial effect; plus separate abuse-of-process backstop for coercive/abusive operations
BaselineA: Common law evidence (party admissions exception to hearsay) and residual common law exclusion for prejudice/abuse; prior SCC cases noted as baseline limits: R. v. Evans (party admissions), R. v. McIntyre and R. v. Hebert (right to silence not engaged absent detention), R. v. Grandinetti (confessions rule inoperative where accused unaware of person in authority)
CaseB_TestB: Borowiec interpretation of Criminal Code s. 233 ‘her mind is then disturbed’: apply ‘disturbed’ in its ordinary sense (e.g., mentally agitated/unstable/discomposure), not requiring mental disorder or substantial impairment; must be present at time of act/omission and ‘by reason of’ childbirth/lactation; no causation between disturbance and act required
BaselineB: Statute — Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 233 (infanticide) (with contextual reference to ss. 16, 2 definitions, 663(b), 672.11(c))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Penile swab incident to arrest is Charter-compliant if (1) lawful arrest and truly incidental purpose; (2) police have "reasonable grounds to believe that a penile swab will afford evidence of the offence"; and (3) the swab is "conducted in a reasonable manner" guided by enumerated factors (e.g., station-house, supervisory authorization, privacy, same gender, minimal officers, record-keeping).
BaselineA: Common law (search incident to arrest) as framed in R. v. Fearon (general framework) and tailored using R. v. Golden (strip-search reasonable-grounds requirement and manner guidelines); reasonableness structure from R. v. Caslake (s. 8: authorized by law / reasonable law / reasonable manner).
CaseB_TestB: Joint/co-principal liability in group assaults: it "flows whenever two or more individuals come together with an intention to commit an offence, are present during the commission of the offence, and contribute to its commission"; for manslaughter, focus on whether the accused’s acts were a "significant contributing cause of death" (not on who inflicted which wound), and in group assaults "absent a discrete or intervening event" all assailants’ actions can be such a cause.
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, s. 21(1)(a) and (c)) applied through existing party-liability jurisprudence referenced in the decision (notably R. v. Pickton).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Quebec Labour Code: a damages claim for breach ("violation") of a collective agreement clause is a "grievance" because no distinction can be made between disputes about "interpretation/application" and "violation" (therefore arbitrable under s. 88).
BaselineA: Statute (Quebec Labour Code, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 141, ss. 1(g) definition of "grievance" and s. 88 mandatory arbitration), as interpreted in SCC precedent (General Motors of Canada Ltd. v. Brunet, [1977] 2 S.C.R. 537; also Imbleau et al. v. Laskin et al., [1962] S.C.R. 338).
CaseB_TestB: Enforceability/scope of a waiver (exclusion) clause: construed in its context, it bars liability for negligence that is within the parties’ contemplation; attempts to avoid it fail absent unreasonableness/unfairness, unconscionability, or public policy grounds.
BaselineB: Common law (contractual interpretation/enforcement of exclusion/waiver clauses; doctrines discussed include fundamental breach, unconscionability, and public policy—no specific baseline case is identified in the SCC reasons provided).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: When a s. 119 Canada Labour Code application to “review, rescind, amend, alter or vary” a certification order must be treated like a new certification: only if the Board’s review “alter[s] the nature and scope” of the existing certificate/bargaining unit; mere updating/clarification that “do[es] not alter the nature and scope” remains a review (and does not trigger fresh representativeness/appropriateness requirements).
BaselineA: Statute — Canada Labour Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. L-1, s. 119 (Board power to “review, rescind, amend, alter or vary” its orders/decisions), in the context of review proceedings under Federal Court Act, R.S.C. 1970 (2nd Supp.), c. 10, s. 28(1)(a)-(c).
CaseB_TestB: Appellate intervention with trial findings: it is wrong to set aside a trial judgment absent “palpable and overriding error” where the only issue is “the interpretation of the evidence as a whole”; the appellate court must be able to say the trial judge was “plainly wrong”.
BaselineB: Common law — appellate standard of review for trial findings as stated in Schreiber Brothers Limited v. Currie Products Limited and Gulf Oil Canada Limited, Stein v. "Kathy K.", and Lewis v. Todd (as cited in the reasons).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Ernst (Cromwell J.) — Ward s. 24(1) Charter damages: even if functionally justified, damages are not an “appropriate and just” remedy where countervailing factors (collectively) negate appropriateness; here, Charter damages could never be appropriate against this quasi-judicial regulator because (1) an effective alternative remedy exists (judicial review) and (2) “good governance” concerns (including quasi-judicial independence/impartiality, chilling effects, resource diversion, collateral attack) and (3) case-by-case damages would “largely undermine the purposes served by an immunity”
BaselineA: Combination: Charter s. 24(1) as interpreted in common law (Vancouver (City) v. Ward, 2010 SCC 27). Statutory context: Energy Resources Conservation Act, R.S.A. 2000, c. E-10, s. 43 (immunity clause) informs the countervailing-factors analysis.
CaseB_TestB: Bird — Maybrun/Klippert framework for when an accused charged with breaching an administrative order may collaterally attack the order: determine legislative intent using five non-exhaustive factors (“important clues”): (1) wording of the enabling statute; (2) purpose of the legislation; (3) existence of a right of appeal/other effective review mechanisms; (4) nature of the attack in light of the expertise/raison d’être of the appeal tribunal or other forum; (5) penalty for non-compliance
BaselineB: Common law framework from R. v. Consolidated Maybrun Mines Ltd., [1998] 1 S.C.R. 706 and R. v. Al Klippert Ltd., [1998] 1 S.C.R. 737, applied in statutory context (Corrections and Conditional Release Act, S.C. 1992, c. 20, including s. 134.1(2); Criminal Code, s. 753.3(1)).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Art. 2930 C.C.Q. applies (3-year prescription) where the action is for “the direct and immediate consequences of interference with a person’s physical integrity”: the court must “characterize the basis for the action”, and “it is the nature of the initial interference rather than the head of damages being claimed” that makes it an action “based on the obligation to make reparation for bodily injury caused to another” (paras. 26, 55).
BaselineA: Statute: Civil Code of Québec, arts. 2925 and 2930 (in interaction with Cities and Towns Act, s. 586).
CaseB_TestB: Appellate non-intervention on trial judge’s factual findings/credibility: once the trial judge’s reasons are available, the Court of Appeal’s “substitution ... of its opinion for that of the trial judge is an unwarranted intrusion” into an area “exclusive to the trial judge” (citing Latour, Maze, Dorval, Métivier, etc.).
BaselineB: Common law / appellate practice doctrine from prior cases cited in the reasons (e.g., Latour v. Grenier; Maze v. Empson; Dorval v. Bouvier; Métivier v. Cadorette; Hood v. Hood).
