Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Schrenk ‘sufficient nexus with the employment context’ test for whether discrimination is ‘regarding employment’ under s. 13(1)(b): Tribunal conducts a contextual analysis considering all relevant circumstances; non-exhaustive factors include (1) whether the respondent was integral to the complainant’s workplace, (2) whether the impugned conduct occurred in the complainant’s workplace, and (3) whether the complainant’s work performance or work environment was negatively affected (paras. 67-68).
BaselineA: Statute: Human Rights Code, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 210, s. 13(1)(b) (and related definitions in s. 1).
CaseB_TestB: Groia in-court incivility/professional misconduct framework: a context-specific, multi-factor approach considering generally (i) what the lawyer said, including that integrity-impugning allegations cross the line unless made in good faith and with a reasonable basis, (ii) the manner and frequency of the conduct, and (iii) the presiding judge’s reaction and the lawyer’s response (paras. 59, 80-83, 98-110).
BaselineB: Statute/regulatory: Law Society Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. L.8 (discipline mandate) and Rules of Professional Conduct made under it (e.g., civility/competence rules referenced at paras. 47, 81, 114).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Ontario anti-SLAPP dismissal framework (CJA s. 137.1): (1) defendant shows proceeding arises from expression on a matter of public interest (s. 137.1(3)); then (2) plaintiff must show both (a) “grounds to believe” the proceeding has “substantial merit” and defendant has “no valid defence” (s. 137.1(4)(a)), and (b) harm is “sufficiently serious” that the public interest in allowing the proceeding to continue “outweighs” the public interest in protecting the expression (s. 137.1(4)(b)). Key SCC clarifications include: “grounds to believe” requires “a basis in the record and the law”; “substantial merit” means a “real prospect of success” supported by evidence “reasonably capable of belief”; and s. 137.1(4)(b) is an open-ended public-interest weighing where one interest must “outweigh” the other.
BaselineA: Statute: Courts of Justice Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.43, s. 137.1(3) and (4) (anti-SLAPP).
CaseB_TestB: Corporate attribution doctrine (including for one-person corporations) in the limitations/discoverability context: apply Aquino/Livent principles—attribution is purposive, contextual, and pragmatic; even if directing-mind conditions are met and fraud/no-benefit exceptions do not apply, courts have discretion to refuse attribution where it would not be “in the public interest”, i.e., would not “promote the purpose of the law under which attribution is sought” (here, Limitations Act discoverability and BIA purposes).
BaselineB: Common law corporate attribution doctrine from Canadian Dredge & Dock Co. v. The Queen; Deloitte & Touche v. Livent Inc. (Receiver of); Christine DeJong Medicine Professional Corp. v. DBDC Spadina Ltd.; as summarized in Aquino v. Bondfield Construction Co. (applied in the context of Limitations Act, 2002, ss. 4, 5, 12).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Duty to comment on Crown counsel’s prejudicial jury address: where remarks are “prejudicial to a degree sufficient to impose a legal duty on the trial judge to comment” to ensure the defence position is “fairly put to the jury”; failure is an error of law (and no curative proviso applied here).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, s. 686(1)(b)(iii) curative proviso) plus common-law principles governing fair jury trials and judicial duty to correct prejudicial advocacy (as adopted from Ayles J.A.’s dissent).
CaseB_TestB: “Identifiability” test for Federal Court in rem jurisdiction under s. 43(2): reject “physical nexus”; property is “subject of the action” if it is identifiable as the cargo designated in the contract of affreightment alleged to be breached.
BaselineB: Statute (Federal Courts Act, s. 43(2) — meaning of “ship, aircraft or other property that is the subject of the action”).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Threshold for summary dismissal of a criminal application: the underlying application may be summarily dismissed only if it is “manifestly frivolous”; on the motion the judge must assume alleged facts are true and take the applicant’s arguments “at their highest”, without weighing evidence or choosing among competing inferences (R. v. Haevischer, 2023 SCC 11, at paras. 3, 71, 82-85, 90).
BaselineA: Common law / judge-made criminal procedure (Vukelich-type screening power), with the Court selecting among competing common-law formulations (e.g., “no reasonable prospect of success”, “no reasonable likelihood of assistance”) and clarifying the governing threshold (paras. 63-80; considering R. v. Vukelich (1996) and related jurisprudence).
CaseB_TestB: Combined effect of Criminal Code s. 172.1(3) presumption and s. 172.1(4) “reasonable steps” requirement in child luring: where underage is represented, the accused is presumed to believe the interlocutor is underage; the presumption is rebutted only by “evidence to the contrary, which must include evidence that the accused took steps to ascertain the real age” and those steps must be “reasonable in the circumstances”; evidential burden on accused, persuasive burden on Crown (R. v. Levigne, 2010 SCC 25, at para. 32).
BaselineB: Statute — Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 172.1(3) and s. 172.1(4) (interpreted together and applied).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Two-step framework for whether legislation displaces the common law, applied to credit for pre-sentence driving prohibitions: (1) identify the applicable common law rule allowing credit; (2) specify the statute’s effect (expressly or by necessary implication). On the merits, s. 259(1)(a) imposes a minimum 'punishment' (global deprivation), not a minimum prospective 'sentence', so a judge must impose the one-year minimum but may then grant common law credit; credit is not 'backdating' and does not conflict with s. 719(1).
BaselineA: Combination of common law and statute: common law discretion to credit pre-sentence driving prohibitions (recognized in R. v. Lacasse, 2015 SCC 64, and analogized to pre-sentence custody credit discussed in R. v. Wust, 2000 SCC 18) + statutory provisions Criminal Code, ss. 259(1)(a) and 719(1) (and discussion of s. 719(3)).
CaseB_TestB: Mitigation in contract damages (including when specific performance is claimed): defendant must prove (i) plaintiff failed to take 'reasonable steps' and (ii) mitigation was possible; a plaintiff claiming specific performance may justify inaction only with a 'fair, real, and substantial justification' / 'substantial and legitimate interest' in specific performance—investment property generally requires showing land has 'peculiar and special value' such that damages are not a complete remedy.
BaselineB: Common law: mitigation principles from Asamera Oil Corp. v. Seal Oil & General Corp., [1979] 1 S.C.R. 633 (quoting British Westinghouse) and related SCC mitigation cases; specific performance context informed by Semelhago v. Paramadevan, [1996] 2 S.C.R. 415.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Hearsay admissibility under the principled approach (necessity + threshold reliability), which can override traditional hearsay exceptions (e.g., present intention) where the statement is made in “circumstances of suspicion” or is otherwise not sufficiently reliable/necessary
BaselineA: Common law (hearsay rule and exceptions; principled approach from R. v. Khan and R. v. Smith; present intentions exception discussed in R. v. Smith)
CaseB_TestB: Public interest standing (Downtown Eastside framework): court must cumulatively assess (i) serious justiciable issue, (ii) genuine interest, and (iii) reasonable and effective means; no single purpose/factor is determinative, and no directly affected co-plaintiff is required if a “sufficiently concrete and well-developed factual setting” will be forthcoming
BaselineB: Common law (public interest standing framework from Canada (Attorney General) v. Downtown Eastside Sex Workers United Against Violence Society, 2012 SCC 45)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Limited-liability/non-assessability constraint on corporate articles: a company cannot impose any pecuniary burden on holders of fully paid shares “in respect of those shares”; and a share transfer fee is valid only to the extent it reflects the “reasonable and proper cost of the transfer” (otherwise it is an “illegal levy”).
BaselineA: Statute + common law principle of limited liability (The Companies Act (Alberta), including s. 42(1) (alteration of articles), s. 61 (transferability per articles), s. 68(4) (shares without par value “fully paid and non-assessable”), and winding-up liability limit in s. 193(1)(d); plus authorities cited on non-assessability/limited liability such as Ooregum Gold Mining Co. v. Roper; Bisgood v. Henderson’s Transvaal Estates; Shalfoon v. Cheddar Valley Co-operative Dairy Co.).
JudgeA: Dickson J. (for Ritchie, Pigeon and Dickson JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Van der Peet aboriginal-rights identification test (as applied): to be an aboriginal right, the activity must be “an element of a practice, custom or tradition integral to the distinctive culture” of the group; the court must (1) “determine the precise nature of the claim” (considering the action, the impugned regulation, and the relied-on practice), and (2) ask whether, “prior to contact with Europeans,” the practice was a “central, significant or defining feature” of the society.
BaselineB: Constitution + common law/precedent: Constitution Act, 1982, s. 35(1) (aboriginal rights) applied through the framework articulated in R. v. Van der Peet (and referenced alongside Sparrow).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Reviewability of a consensual labour arbitrator’s award for error of law on the face: no “specific question of law” reference where the grievance arises in the ordinary course under a collective agreement that restricts the arbitrator from making any decision inconsistent with the agreement; therefore courts may review and quash for error of law on the face
BaselineA: Common law (judicial review of consensual arbitration awards; distinction between (i) specific question of law referred vs (ii) dispute where a question of law becomes material), as discussed via Government of Kelantan v. Duff Development Co. Ltd.; F.R. Absalom Ltd. v. Great Western (London) Garden Village Society Ltd.; Faubert and Watts v. Temagami Mining Co. Ltd.; Bell Canada v. Office and Professional Employees’ International Union, Local 131
CaseB_TestB: Morin framework for s. 11(b) “reasonable time” (length of delay minus waiver; then reasons for delay, prejudice, and s. 11(b) interests), including that “prejudice may be inferred from the length of the delay” and that scheduling does not require defence counsel to be in “a state of perpetual availability”
BaselineB: Statute/constitutional text (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 11(b)) as operationalized by common-law/precedential framework in R. v. Morin and R. v. Askov
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 3(4) test for establishing possession (including joint possession): for Code purposes, possession is personal possession or knowingly having it in another’s custody/possession or in any place for use/benefit; and where one of two or more persons, with the knowledge and consent of the rest, has it, it is deemed in the custody and possession of each and all
BaselineA: Statute — Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 3(4)(a)-(b) (interpreted as applying broadly “for the purposes of this Act” to all proceedings under the Code)
CaseB_TestB: Test for establishing adverse possession in British Columbia: possession must be “open and notorious, adverse, exclusive, peaceful (not by force), actual (generally), and continuous”; and the “inconsistent use” requirement is not part of BC law
BaselineB: Common law adverse possession elements as received/understood in BC, operating within BC limitations legislation (as discussed via the Real Property Limitation Act, 1833 (U.K.) and BC limitation statutes); SCC clarifies that “inconsistent use” is not required in BC
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Quantum meruit for services rendered without agreed remuneration: where a municipality continues to authorize and receive hospital services after termination of the prior agreement, the hospital has a quasi-contractual claim and the municipality "must pay reasonable rates" (subject only to valid statutory/regulatory bars).
BaselineA: Common law (quantum meruit / quasi-contract), applied with statutory interpretation of potential bars in Hospital Act s. 37(2) (as amended) and Residence and Responsibility Act s. 3 plus related Orders in Council (O.C. 3103, 4399, 4400); baseline case cited: King George Highway Hospital Ltd. v. District of Surrey, [1971] S.C.R. vi.
CaseB_TestB: Voluntariness/operating mind test for admissibility of inculpatory statements by an accused alleged to be insane: the "underlying and controlling question" is whether the statement was "freely and voluntarily made", including whether (even absent inducement) the accused’s mental condition meant the words were not "the utterances of an operating mind" / the accused was "so devoid of rationality and understanding, or so replete with psychotic delusions" that the words could not fairly be said to be his statement.
BaselineB: Common law confessions rule (voluntariness), drawing on Boudreau v. The King, [1949] S.C.R. 262 and Ward v. The Queen, [1979] 2 S.C.R. 30 (also discussing R. v. Santinon (BCCA)).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Effect of breach of a witness-exclusion order: witness not necessarily disqualified; admissibility discretionary; weight assessed by trier of fact (and no legal requirement that the judge expressly state a self-caution for each such witness)
BaselineA: Common law (practice/rule on exclusion of witnesses and consequences of breach, as reflected in cases cited such as Moore v. Lambeth County Court Registrar; Cook v. Nethercotte; Thomas v. David; Chandler v. Home; R. v. Carefoot)
CaseB_TestB: Crown immunity from discovery: immunity is overridden only by clear and unequivocal legislative language; CLPA s. 27 applies only where the Crown is a party, so discovery cannot be compelled when the Crown is not a party
BaselineB: Statute (Interpretation Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. I-21, s. 17; Crown Liability and Proceedings Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-50, s. 27) against the backdrop of common law Crown immunity
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Disqualification for bias in Law Society discipline: benchers who sat on the Discipline Committee are not disqualified from participating in Convocation’s consideration of the Committee report (a two-step process, not an appeal); express statutory disqualification in s. 39(4) applies only to s. 39 reprimand appeals (expressio unius).
BaselineA: Statute and regulation: The Law Society Act, 1970 (Ont.), ss. 33(12), 34, 37, 39 (esp. s. 39(4)); Reg. 556, s. 13(6)-(7); plus common-law natural justice/bias principles (nemo judex / reasonable apprehension of bias) discussed in dissent.
CaseB_TestB: Criminal Code s. 731(1)(b) probation eligibility: the “term not exceeding two years” refers to the imprisonment imposed by the sentencing court at that single sitting (not the aggregate of other sentences); but probation is unavailable if sentences imposed at the same session result in continuous custody over two years.
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 731(1)(b) (and related timing provisions in s. 732.2).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “operation of a mine” and when a separate “mine” exists for the 36‑month tax exemption: (1) “operation of a mine” refers only to extraction of ore (not processing); (2) there is “a mine” if there is “a body of ore together with the workings, equipment and machinery capable of producing it”; a separate ore body becomes a separate mine when it “commenced to be extracted by means of its separate and distinct extraction facilities” (shared milling does not matter).
BaselineA: Statute (Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1952, c. 148 as amended, s. 83(5) and s. 83(6)); interpreted in light of SCC authorities North Bay Mica Company Limited v. M.N.R., [1958] S.C.R. 597 and M.N.R. v. MacLean Mining Co., [1970] S.C.R. 877.
CaseB_TestB: Leave to sue a receiver/trustee under s. 215 BIA (Mancini test): leave should be refused only for “frivolous or vexatious” or “manifestly unmeritorious” claims; the evidence must “disclose a cause of action” and provide facts supporting it; the court “is not required to make a final assessment of the merits”; “If the evidence discloses a prima facie case, leave should be granted.”
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. B-3, s. 215 (leave requirement) as interpreted through the common-law/precedential Mancini (Bankrupt) v. Falconi (1993), 61 O.A.C. 332 (C.A.), adopted and applied by the SCC.
JudgeB: Abella J. (for McLachlin C.J. and Bastarache, Binnie, LeBel, Fish and Charron JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Education Act s. 373 roll-homologation duty: if municipal valuations are not uniform, school commissioners must amend the rolls to "re-establish on the basis of its real value the valuation of the taxable property of all the parts of the school municipality"—i.e., determine the real value of what is taxable in each municipality (no cross-municipal importation of another municipality’s decision to exempt machinery).
BaselineA: Statute (Education Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 235, s. 373; with context from Cities and Towns Act s. 488 (as amended) allowing a by-law excluding machinery from taxable immovables).
CaseB_TestB: Secret commissions offence (Criminal Code s. 426(1)(a)(ii))—actus reus elements for an agent/taker: (1) agency relationship; (2) acceptance of a benefit "as consideration" for acting/forbearing in relation to the principal’s affairs; (3) failure to make "adequate and timely disclosure"—"corruptly" in this context means "secretly or without the requisite disclosure" and no "corrupt bargain" with the giver is required.
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 426(1)(a), especially s. 426(1)(a)(ii)).
JudgeB: Cory J. (for L'Heureux-Dubé, Gonthier, Cory and Iacobucci JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Extradition-crime classification: “The test is what is the essence of the crime charged” (i.e., whether the offence is, in substance, a crime “against the laws for the suppression of the traffic in narcotics” under the extradition arrangement).
BaselineA: Statute + extradition arrangement: Extradition Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-21, s. 2 definition of “extradition crime”, as applied to the 1925 Supplementary Convention category “Crimes and offences against the laws for the suppression of the traffic in narcotics”.
CaseB_TestB: Section 13 Charter “incriminate” vs “impeach credibility” distinction: prior testimony may be used on cross-examination at a later proceeding if its purpose is only to impeach credibility, but not if used “to incriminate” (to establish guilt).
BaselineB: Constitution + statute: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 13 (interpreting “used to incriminate”); discussed alongside Canada Evidence Act, s. 5(2), and prior SCC cases R. v. Dubois and R. v. Mannion.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Negligence foreseeability/remoteness test for highway authority liability: “whether a reasonable person should have anticipated that what happened might be a natural result of that act or omission”; not necessary to foresee the “precise concatenation of events”, only “in a general way the class or character of injury”.
BaselineA: Common law foreseeability/remoteness in negligence (University Hospital Board v. Lépine; Wagon Mound No. 2 referenced/applied) alongside statutory highway-maintenance context (Highway Improvement Act, R.S.O. 1960, s. 33(1)).
CaseB_TestB: CEAA “tracking” rule: the environmental assessment track is determined by the “project as proposed” (not “project as scoped”); if the proposed project is listed in the Comprehensive Study List, s. 21 requirements are mandatory and the responsible authority cannot reduce the project below what is proposed.
BaselineB: Statutory interpretation/application of the Canadian Environmental Assessment Act, S.C. 1992, c. 37 (especially ss. 2 “project”, 15, 18, 21, 21.1, 58(1)(i)) and the Comprehensive Study List Regulations, SOR/94-638.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Using res ipsa loquitur to infer (gross) negligence: applies where (1) the thing causing damage was under defendant’s “sole management and control”; (2) the occurrence is such that it “would not have happened without negligence”; and (3) there is “no evidence as to why or how the occurrence took place” (or the defendant’s explanation is not a valid answer, leaving the presumption intact).
BaselineA: Common law rule of evidence (res ipsa loquitur), as accepted in Walker v. Coates et al., [1968] S.C.R. 599; applied in context of Ontario Highway Traffic Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 202, s. 132(3) (gross negligence requirement for gratuitous passengers).
CaseB_TestB: Criteria for recognizing a vested right (acquired right) and applying the presumption against legislative interference: a vested right exists where (1) the individual’s legal situation is “tangible and concrete rather than general and abstract”; and (2) it was “sufficiently constituted at the time of the new statute’s commencement”; absent “a clear indication in a statute to the contrary in light of the entire context”, legislation is presumed not to interfere with such vested rights.
BaselineB: Combination of statutory interpretation baseline (Interpretation Act, R.S.Q., c. I-16, s. 12) and common law presumption against interference with vested/accrued rights (e.g., Spooner Oils Ltd. v. Turner Valley Gas Conservation Board, [1933] S.C.R. 629; Gustavson Drilling (1964) Ltd. v. M.N.R., [1977] 1 S.C.R. 271).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Mechanics’ lien owner-liability/holdback test on contractor abandonment: s. 19(2) does not prevent the owner deducting completion costs from amounts otherwise payable to the contractor; owner liability remains limited by s. 6 to “the sum payable by the owner to the contractor” (so liens do not attach to a fund immune from completion-cost deductions beyond the statutory holdback). Key holding: “s. 19(2) ... does not bar the owner from deducting from the amounts payable upon the bankruptcy the cost of completion of the contract”.
BaselineA: Statute (Mechanics’ Lien Act, R.S.B.C. 1960, c. 238), especially ss. 6, 19(2), 21(1) and 21(6); interpreted in light of SCC approach in Canadian Comstock Co. Ltd. v. Toronto Transit Commission, [1970] S.C.R. 205 (following/approving Guttman/Freedman line).
CaseB_TestB: Choice-of-law rule for torts (interprovincial/international): apply the lex loci delicti as the general rule—“the law to be applied in torts is the law of the place where the activity occurred”; McLean v. Pettigrew overruled. Related characterization rule: foreign limitation periods are treated as substantive where they create “an accrued right in the defendant to plead a time bar”.
BaselineB: Common law conflict-of-laws (choice of law in tort), reformulating prior Canadian rule from McLean v. Pettigrew, [1945] S.C.R. 62 (overruled) and rejecting lex fori/double-actionability approaches; also applies/characterizes statutory limitation provisions (e.g., Vehicles Act, R.S.S. 1978, c. V-3, s. 180(1)).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Constitutional (territorial) validity test for provincial legislation: whether, in pith and substance, the law is directed at acts done outside the province / has impermissible extraterritorial operation (e.g., Manitoba cannot, via s. 4(2), nullify an out-of-province permission and thereby legislate in relation to conduct and rights outside Manitoba).
BaselineA: Statute + constitutional division of powers/territorial limits: The Fishermen’s Assistance and Polluters’ Liability Act, 1970 (Man.), especially s. 4(2) (and s. 4(1)); interpreted against B.N.A. Act, 1867 territorial limits on provincial heads of power (e.g., s. 92) and related constitutional principles.
JudgeA: Pigeon J. (for Martland, Pigeon and Beetz JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Privative-clause judicial review threshold: court may intervene only for jurisdictional error; an administrative decision loses protection only if it is "patently unreasonable" / an "unreasonable finding, whatever its origin, impairs the jurisdiction" (and, on Beetz J.'s approach, only an "abuse of authority amounting to fraud ... causing a flagrant injustice").
BaselineB: Statute + common-law administrative law: Act respecting labour standards, R.S.Q., c. N-1.1, ss. 124-129 (esp. s. 128, s. 129) and Labour Code, s. 139 (privative clause), plus the CUPE "patently unreasonable" line of cases cited in the reasons.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Collective agreement primacy in a statutory labour relations regime: common law repudiation/fundamental breach concepts are inapplicable to an unexpired collective agreement; an illegal strike does not per se terminate employment, and absent employer disciplinary action, plant closure triggers severance obligations under the agreement
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law labour jurisprudence: Mediation Services Act, 1968 (B.C.), ss. 6 (collective agreement binding) and 23(1) (prohibition on strike during term); SCC labour-law characterization of collective agreements (Syndicat catholique des employés de magasins de Québec Inc. v. Compagnie Paquet Ltée, [1959] S.C.R. 206; C.P.R. Co. v. Zambri, [1962] S.C.R. 609; with reference to Re Polymer Corp.)
CaseB_TestB: Limits on cross-examination using a complainant’s diary: Seaboyer/Osolin admissibility standard applies (not O’Connor production balancing); relevant defence evidence may be excluded only if its prejudicial effect “substantially outweighs” its probative value, and omissions are probative only if the defence establishes a “reasonable expectation” the event would have been recorded
BaselineB: Common law evidence principles governing cross-examination/admissibility (R. v. Seaboyer; R. v. Osolin) and clarification that O’Connor’s production test is not the admissibility test; Criminal Code ss. 278.1–278.9 held inapplicable to admissibility/use because they address production
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Admissibility of evidence that an accused refused to participate in a police line-up: admissible only where, in the circumstances, it is relevant (typically to explain the absence of a line-up) and not normally otherwise
BaselineA: Common law (evidence relevance/admissibility principles) informed by the common-law privilege against self-incrimination as limited to testimonial compulsion (citing Curr v. The Queen; A.-G. (Que.) v. Begin; and related authorities)
CaseB_TestB: Division of powers (pith and substance) limit on provincial commissions of inquiry: an inquiry is ultra vires if, in purpose/effect, it is a substitute police investigation/preliminary inquiry into specific Criminal Code offences by named individuals (circumventing federal criminal procedure)
BaselineB: Constitution Act, 1867, ss. 91(27) and 92 (division of powers) applied through the pith-and-substance doctrine; assessed against Ontario’s Public Inquiries Act order-in-council framework
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Punitive damages in tort: whether the circumstances justify an additional punitive award “in the interests of justice” (here, added $10,000) given the defendants’ tortious conduct and scheme to destroy the plaintiff’s business
BaselineA: common law (punitive/exemplary damages principles in tort; no specific baseline case articulated in the reasons)
CaseB_TestB: Anns/Cooper duty-of-care framework for pure economic loss in tendering: (1) does the claim fit a recognized category (incl. relational economic loss requiring third-party property damage); if not, (2) should a new duty be recognized under Anns (foreseeability + proximity, including party-specific policy at stage 1; residual policy like indeterminate liability at stage 2)
BaselineB: common law (Anns v. Merton; Kamloops v. Nielsen; Cooper v. Hobart; Childs v. Desormeaux; Norsk categories of pure economic loss)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory limits on Canadian Transport Commission power re freight-tariff effective dates: even if s. 275(2) allows extending the 30-day notice, any extension must be ordered before the tariff’s stated effective date; after that date, an ‘extension’ is an impermissible postponement (ultra vires).
BaselineA: Statute (Railway Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. R-2, ss. 275(2) and 275(4); also National Transportation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. N-17, s. 64(5))
CaseB_TestB: Palmer test for admitting fresh evidence on appeal: (1) due diligence (relaxed in criminal cases), (2) relevance to a decisive/potentially decisive issue, (3) credibility, and (4) whether, if believed, it could reasonably be expected to have affected the result (“interests of justice”).
BaselineB: Common law (Palmer v. The Queen, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 759) applied within Criminal Code appellate-evidence discretion (s. 683).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Effectiveness/finality of an order still within the appeal period: despite being appealable, it may be treated as fully effective (even against third parties) where there is only an “ephemeral prospect of an appeal”; assess “the purpose for which the finality or want of finality of an order is urged”, “who is affected”, and “in what context” finality is asserted before the appeal period expires.
BaselineA: Combination: statute (The Conveyancing and Law of Property Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 85, s. 62) plus general/common-law principles about the effect of appealable orders (as discussed via Re West and Leonard v. Wharton, distinguished).
CaseB_TestB: Preliminary inquiry committal test under Criminal Code s. 548(1) (Shephard): ask whether there is “any evidence upon which a reasonable jury properly instructed could return a verdict of guilty”; if Crown evidence is circumstantial, the judge must do a “limited weighing” of the whole evidence (including defence evidence) to see if, assuming Crown evidence is believed, it would be reasonable for a jury to infer guilt—without drawing inferences or assessing credibility.
BaselineB: Combination: statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 548(1)) and common law (United States of America v. Shephard; also Mezzo; Monteleone; Charemski).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Discretionary public-interest standing to challenge legislation: standing may be granted where (1) a “serious, a substantial constitutional issue” is raised; (2) the plaintiff has taken “all the steps that he could reasonably be required to take” to make standing “ripe for consideration”; (3) the plaintiff is arguably “directly affected” (here, as a member of the public affected by censorship); and (4) there is “no other way, practically speaking, to subject the challenged Act to judicial review”, making it appropriate to “exercise[] [the Court’s] discretion” to grant standing.
BaselineA: Common law (standing/locus standi doctrine), drawing on Smith v. Attorney General of Ontario, [1924] S.C.R. 331 and Thorson v. Attorney General of Canada, [1975] 1 S.C.R. 138.
CaseB_TestB: Interpretation of ASRA Program s. 88(3): the provision “does not specify how” government-assistance amounts are to be linked and, interpreted under C.C.Q. arts. 1425-1432 (especially arts. 1427 and 1426), it “does not require that amounts be linked individually” but instead “gives La Financière the discretion to decide what linkage method to employ”, subject to exercising that discretion in “good faith and contractual fairness” (C.C.Q. arts. 6, 7, 1375, 1434).
BaselineB: Regulation and civil law: Programme d’assurance stabilisation des revenus agricoles, s. 88(3), interpreted using Civil Code of Québec arts. 1425-1432 (interpretation) and arts. 6, 7, 1375, 1434 (good faith/contractual fairness).
JudgeB: Wagner and Gascon JJ. (for McLachlin C.J. and Abella, Cromwell and Karakatsanis JJ.)
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Rebuttable presumption of mens rea for drug trafficking once actus reus proved: when it is proved the accused trafficked in the restricted drug, “a rebuttable presumption arises” that the condition/act was voluntarily induced and the accused “must be convicted unless other evidence is adduced which raises a reasonable doubt” as to an honest belief negating mens rea (applied from R. v. King to trafficking facts).
BaselineA: Common law mens rea principles applied to statutory offence; Food and Drugs Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. F-27, ss. 40 (definitions) and 42 (trafficking in restricted drugs), with the rebuttable-presumption approach drawn from R. v. King, [1962] S.C.R. 746 and mens rea discussion in Beaver v. The Queen, [1957] S.C.R. 531.
CaseB_TestB: Limits on trial-judge intervention / appearance of impartiality: a judge may question and interrupt witnesses, but “must do so within certain limits and in such a way that justice is seen to be done”; alleged departures are assessed “with respect to [their] effect on the fairness of the trial”, and if the conduct raises “some doubt as to his impartiality”, a new trial is required.
BaselineB: Common law procedural fairness / judicial impartiality principle (justice must be seen to be done) from R. v. Sussex Justices; Ex parte McCarthy, [1924] 1 K.B. 256, and related common law guidance on judicial interventions (e.g., Torbiak; Darlyn; Yuill; Jones).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory-interpretation rule for “burglary” in Criminal Code constructive murder: despite later revisions, “burglary” in s. 213 retains the meaning of the offence “called burglary” in the 1892 Code (s. 410) (dwelling-house/night; with related definitions in s. 407), absent clear Parliamentary intent to change it
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 213; Interpretation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-23, s. 36(f); with recourse to prior Criminal Code enactments, especially Criminal Code, 1892, ss. 228, 407, 410)
CaseB_TestB: Damages for repudiation where contract has alternative modes of performance: assess damages on the basis of the mode “least profitable to the plaintiff, and the least burdensome to the defendant”; not on a factual inquiry into how the defendant would likely have performed but for repudiation
BaselineB: Common law (general principle traced to Cockburn v. Alexander (1848), and explained in Withers v. General Theatre Corp. (1933))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Lease interpretation test for shifting fire-loss risk to landlord where tenant covenants to pay “insurance rates”: applying “the ordinary test of reading it reasonably and in a business sense”, the tenant’s payment means “the risk of loss by fire passed to the landlord, at least upon the presentation by the landlord of the insurance bill”, so the landlord’s insurer has “no basis” for subrogation against the tenant for fire caused by the tenant’s negligence.
BaselineA: Common law contract/lease interpretation ("reading it reasonably and in a business sense") plus statutory insurance context (Ontario Insurance Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 224, s. 118 referenced as confirming usual coverage).
CaseB_TestB: Civil Code art. 1053 “fault–damage” basis for bank liability on unauthorized endorsements: a bank commits a compensable “fault” by accepting payment/crediting proceeds on an unauthorized endorsement “without examining it, and without verifying the sufficiency of the endorsement”; where this deprives the payee of money and the payee has no effective recourse against the drawer, damages are “equal to the amount of the cheques.”
BaselineB: Statute and civil law: Civil Code art. 1053 (fault causing damage) applied in the negotiable instruments context, with reference to Bills of Exchange Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. B-5, ss. 10 and 51, and Norwich Union Fire Insurance Society Ltd. v. La Banque Canadienne Nationale, [1934] S.C.R. 596.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 15(1) adverse-impact discrimination (prima facie breach): (1) law/policy has a disproportionate impact creating a distinction on an enumerated/analogous ground; and (2) it imposes burdens/denies a benefit in a way that reinforces, perpetuates, or exacerbates disadvantage (with flexible proof of disproportionate impact—statistics and/or group-context evidence; no intent or causation requirement beyond showing disproportionate impact).
BaselineA: Constitution (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 15(1); applied within the existing two-step s. 15 framework from cases such as Withler and Taypotat, as cited in the reasons).
JudgeA: Abella J. (for Wagner C.J. and Moldaver, Karakatsanis, Martin and Kasirer JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Division of powers “pith and substance” analysis: (1) determine the law’s essential character by purpose and legal effect; (2) classify that character under a head of power (here, whether s. 27 is in pith and substance related to federal fisheries power rather than provincial property and civil rights; efficacy generally irrelevant).
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine of pith and substance under the Constitution Act, 1867 (ss. 91(12), 91(27), 92(13)), as articulated in prior SCC cases cited (e.g., Reference re Firearms Act; Morgentaler).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Lease interpretation test for whether tenant’s covenant to pay “insurance rates” shifts the risk of fire loss (including tenant-negligence fire) to the landlord, barring insurer subrogation: apply “the ordinary test of reading [the lease] reasonably and in a business sense”; where tenant pays for fire insurance, it “is entitled to rest in respect of loss by fire on the discharge of its obligation to pay for fire insurance” (risk passes to landlord at least upon presentation of the insurance bill).
BaselineA: Common law contract/lease interpretation ("reading it reasonably and in a business sense"), in the landlord–tenant context; with statutory backdrop that fire insurance covers third-party negligence (The Insurance Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 224, s. 118).
CaseB_TestB: Warsaw Convention limitation entitlement based on ticket delivery/compliance: Art. 3(2) is applied literally—limitation is lost “only where no ticket is delivered” (ticket “absence, irregularity or loss” does not remove limitation if delivered); for baggage, Art. 4(4) sanction applies only if no luggage ticket delivered or it lacks required particulars, and compliance is satisfied where print is “legible by the ordinary person using ordinary diligence” and content is adequate.
BaselineB: Statute/treaty text: Carriage by Air Act, R.S.C. 1952, c. 45, Schedule I (Warsaw Convention), Arts. 3, 4, 22 (and interpretation of the sanction structure in Arts. 3(2) and 4(4)).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Negligent misrepresentation (opinion/estimate): plaintiff must prove more than that the estimate was wrong; must show the error resulted from a lack of "skill, competence or diligence" / "carelessness"—i.e., a failure to exercise "such care as the circumstances required" (Hedley Byrne).
BaselineA: Common law (negligent misrepresentation duty/standard of care), drawing on Hedley Byrne & Co. Ltd. v. Heller & Partners Ltd. and Mutual Life and Citizens’ Assurance Co. Ltd. v. Evatt as cited in the reasons.
CaseB_TestB: Extra-territoriality (s. 92): where a provincial law’s pith and substance is intangible, determine if it is "in the Province" by examining "the relationships among the enacting territory, the subject matter of the law, and the person[s] sought to be subjected to its regulation" to see if there is a "meaningful connection" and respect for other jurisdictions’ sovereignty.
BaselineB: Constitutional text and doctrine: Constitution Act, 1867, s. 92 (esp. s. 92(13) "Property and Civil Rights in the Province"), applying prior SCC approach to pith and substance and territoriality (e.g., Reference re Upper Churchill Water Rights Reversion Act; Unifund; Global Securities, as cited).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Habeas corpus review of parole detention confined to the face of the warrants (no certiorari into Parole Board’s administrative acts); parole revocation after sentence expiry permitted if inmate is in custody under s. 16
BaselineA: Statute (Parole Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. P-2; Federal Court Act, 1970-71-72 (Can.), c. 1) plus prior SCC case law on parole/administrative character and habeas corpus limits
JudgeA: Ritchie J. (for Judson, Ritchie, Pigeon and Beetz JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Approach to equitable compensation for Crown breach of fiduciary duty over reserve land: assess the beneficiary’s “lost opportunity” by first defining what the Crown “ought to have done” as fiduciary (not merely what it could have done legally), then valuing loss (with hindsight; no foreseeability/remoteness limit) including the land’s value to the hydroelectric project and presuming most favourable use
BaselineB: Common law equity/fiduciary remedies (Guerin; Canson; Blueberry River; Osoyoos; Wewaykum; Williams Lake) applied in the context of statutory/treaty framework (Indian Act, R.S.C. 1927, c. 98, ss. 48, 50, 51; Treaty No. 3; Royal Proclamation, 1763)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Sales tax exemption test for machinery/apparatus: whether the apparatus is used by a manufacturer/producer "directly in ... the manufacture or production of goods" (and not merely in distribution); gas pressure regulators are not "production" because they "merely cause the gas to pass ... from the higher pressure pipes to lower pressure pipes" and are "apparatus controlling the flow of gas in pipes" rather than producing something new.
BaselineA: Statute: Excise Tax Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-13, s. 29(1) and Schedule III, Part XIII, para. 1(a)(i) (exemption for machinery/apparatus used "directly in ... the manufacture or production of goods"); interpreted in light of Hydro-Québec v. Dep. Min. of Nat. Revenue for Customs and Excise, [1970] S.C.R. 30.
CaseB_TestB: Scope-of-retainer test (solicitor/counsel liability): whether, on the evidence, the adviser’s retainer included responsibility to advise on limitation periods (beyond assisting with proofs of loss); the scope of retainer is "purely a factual question" and appellate interference is limited to "error arising from misapprehension of the evidence".
BaselineB: Common law: characterization of the scope of a professional retainer as a factual issue, with appellate deference absent misapprehension of evidence (as stated in these reasons).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Patent Act s. 41(1) “chemical process” test: interpret “chemical process” in its “ordinary and popular sense” (not scientific) and decide, on an “informed layman” view of the whole process, whether chemical operations play a “significant” and “essential” part (not merely incidental) in producing the food substance
BaselineA: Statute (Patent Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. P-4, s. 41(1)) as interpreted through prior SCC cases (Continental Soya; Laboratoire Pentagone)
CaseB_TestB: Adequacy of indictment test (incl. multiple conspiracies context): an indictment is adequate if it gives the accused “reasonable information” to identify the transaction and prepare a defence; and a proven conspiracy lies within the indictment if it included some accused, occurred at some time within the alleged time span, and had as its object the type of crime alleged
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 510, 512, 516) plus common-law principles from SCC cases (e.g., Côté; Wis Development; Cotroni; B.(G.))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 1 Charter justification (Oakes proportionality) applied contextually: pressing and substantial objective + proportionality (rational connection, minimal impairment, overall proportionality), with emphasis that a total ban requires proof that only a full prohibition will achieve the objective and that justification must be “demonstrably” shown on a balance of probabilities
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 1; and the Oakes s. 1 framework from R. v. Oakes, [1986] 1 S.C.R. 103
CaseB_TestB: Duty to accommodate in the presence of a collectively bargained automatic-termination clause: the negotiated absence period is a relevant factor/evidence in assessing accommodation and undue hardship, but does not definitively determine entitlement; accommodation remains individualized and undue hardship is assessed globally from the start of the absence
BaselineB: Common law / jurisprudential framework: Meiorin (BCGSEU) test for justifying a discriminatory standard and the duty to accommodate/undue hardship analysis (with reference to Bergevin, O’Malley, Renaud); applied in the context of Quebec human rights legislation (Charter of human rights and freedoms, R.S.Q., c. C-12, ss. 10, 20) and a collective agreement clause (e.g., clause 12.11.5)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Indian Act s. 88 applicability/inconsistency analysis: provincial law of general application applies to Indians (via s. 88 reference) except to the extent it is "inconsistent with" the Indian Act or "make[s] provision for any matter for which provision is made by or under" the Indian Act; here, adoption does not remove the child’s entitlement to registration under Indian Act s. 11(1)(d) despite Adoption Act s. 10(2) severing parent-child ties "for all purposes".
BaselineA: Statute: Indian Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-6, s. 88 (and s. 11(1)(d) registrability definition of "Indian"), applied to provincial Adoption Act, R.S.B.C. 1960, c. 4, s. 10(2) ("for all purposes").
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 24(2) Collins framework (as organized in Greffe): whether admitting evidence would bring the administration of justice into disrepute by balancing three categories—(1) fairness of the trial, (2) seriousness of the Charter breach (including good/bad faith; here emphasizing need for proven "reasonable and probable grounds" and assessing informant tips), and (3) the effect of exclusion on the repute of the justice system (including long-term consequences).
BaselineB: Combination: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 24(2) ("shall be excluded if ... the admission of it ... would bring the administration of justice into disrepute"), structured by common-law framework from R. v. Collins (and related Charter evidence cases cited in the reasons).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Test for effective termination (“determination”) of a continuing guarantee by “notice in writing”: notice need not use set words, but must be explicit and unequivocal so the creditor is left in no doubt; an equivocal letter expressing only a “wish” or “preference” is insufficient.
BaselineA: Contract/common law interpretation of the guarantee’s clause (4) allowing termination “by notice in writing delivered to the Manager of the branch or agency of the Bank receiving this instrument”.
CaseB_TestB: Admissibility/handling of evidence of an accused’s post-caution silence: unless the Crown establishes “a real relevance and a proper basis” for admission, neither the incriminating questions nor “evidence as to the ensuing silence” should be admitted; if admitted, the jury must be instructed to ignore it (no adverse inference), and failure to do so may require a new trial.
BaselineB: Common law right to silence (as discussed via Rothman; Robertson; Symonds) and Charter s. 7 recognition of the right to silence; applied in the criminal trial context.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: S. 96 BNA Act validity of conferring remedial cease-and-desist power on an administrative labour board: assess the power in its statutory/institutional setting (not in isolation) and uphold where it is part of a specialized agency’s limited discretionary remedial authority supporting the legislative scheme (cease-and-desist differs from a court injunction).
BaselineA: Combination: Constitution (British North America Act, 1867, s. 96) as applied through prior s. 96 jurisprudence; and statute (Trade Union Act, 1972 (N.S.), ss. 48-49) defining the challenged power.
CaseB_TestB: YCJA youth sentencing: general deterrence is not a permissible sentencing principle because s. 50(1) excludes Criminal Code s. 718(b) and deterrence cannot be implied from YCJA ss. 3 and 38; additionally, s. 42(2)(o) does not require a fixed 2/3 custody and 1/3 supervision split (unlike s. 42(2)(n)).
BaselineB: Statute: Youth Criminal Justice Act, S.C. 2002, c. 1 (especially ss. 3, 38, 42(2)(n), 42(2)(o), 50(1)); with reference to Criminal Code sentencing provisions excluded by s. 50(1) (notably s. 718(b)).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Cities and Towns Act s. 622(4) excuse for failure to give municipal notice: if the victim proves they were prevented from giving notice within 15 days for a reason “deemed sufficient by the court or judge”, then the failure does not bar the action and (per SCC) the victim is permanently released from any obligation to give notice later
BaselineA: Statute: Cities and Towns Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 193, s. 622(1), (3), (4), (5) (especially s. 622(4) and its interaction with s. 622(5))
CaseB_TestB: Judicial review of a labour grievance arbitration award on collective agreement interpretation: courts must ask whether the arbitrator’s conclusion is a “patently unreasonable” interpretation / whether it is one the agreement would “reasonably bear” (and not re-decide correctness)
BaselineB: Common law standard of review for labour arbitration/collective agreement interpretation, relying on SCC authorities including Bell Canada v. Office and Professional Employees' Union, [1974] S.C.R. 335 and CUPE v. New Brunswick Liquor Corp., [1979] 2 S.C.R. 227 (as cited in the reasons)
JudgeB: Pigeon J. (reasons concurred in by Martland, Ritchie, Beetz and Pratte JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Admissibility of similar-fact evidence: other criminal acts are inadmissible to show propensity, but are admissible if relevant to an issue (e.g., whether the act was “designed or accidental” or “to rebut a defence which would otherwise be open”), and are admitted “not to prove commission of the crime… but to establish guilty intent” (Makin/Noor Mohamed/Wray line as applied).
BaselineA: Common law evidence rule on similar-fact evidence (general exclusionary rule and its exceptions) drawn from Makin v. A-G for New South Wales, Thompson v. The King, Noor Mohamed v. The King, and applied with reference to R. v. Wray.
CaseB_TestB: Municipal valuation where usual methods cannot be applied: “Where special circumstances make it impossible to fix the realizable value of property by the usual methods, whatever method is appropriate in the circumstances may be used to estimate the property at its actual value.”
BaselineB: Combination of statute and precedent: municipal valuation at “actual value” under the Charter of the City of Montreal (including appeal provisions ss. 873-874) as interpreted in Sun Life Assurance Co. of Canada v. City of Montreal and related valuation jurisprudence.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Admissibility of similar fact evidence: admissible only if relevant to an issue (e.g., designed vs accidental / to rebut a defence otherwise open), and not to show disposition; in criminal negligence, Crown may use similar conduct to prove mens rea (wanton or reckless disregard) beyond the act itself
BaselineA: Common law evidence rule on similar fact evidence (general exclusionary rule with Makin exception; discussed with Thompson, Noor Mohamed; and SCC’s approach in R. v. Wray)
CaseB_TestB: Issue estoppel on a subsequent perjury charge: Crown is estopped from re-litigating an issue decided in accused’s favour unless it tenders evidence that was not available by the exercise of reasonable diligence at the first trial
BaselineB: Common law res judicata/issue estoppel principles (as applied in criminal law; drawing on Gushue v. The Queen and DPP v. Humphrys)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory interpretation of “tetracycline and its derivatives”: apply the primary/common meaning in both official languages—“derivative” means a thing actually “obtained from” another (not merely in the same scientific ‘family’)
BaselineA: Regulation/statutory instrument and bilingual-interpretation statute: Order in Council SOR/69-8, s. 4 and Schedule A (tariff item 92944-1: “Tetracycline and its derivatives” / “dérivés”); Official Languages Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. O-2, s. 8(2)(b); plus common-law interpretive principle that statutes use common meaning even in technical contexts (citing Continental Soya; Laboratoire Pentagone; Burton Parsons).
CaseB_TestB: Inherent/implied jurisdiction limit re amici remuneration: absent statutory authority or a constitutional (Charter) basis, courts may appoint amici only exceptionally when “essential”, but do NOT have inherent/implied jurisdiction to fix amici’s rates and order the province to pay
BaselineB: Common law/constitutional doctrine of inherent and implied jurisdiction (as described in cases like MacMillan Bloedel; Caron; Cunningham) constrained by separation of powers and provincial responsibility for administration of justice (Constitution Act, 1867, ss. 92(14), 96).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Bankruptcy trustee’s duty to insure and keep insured all the bankrupt’s “insurable property” (including hypothecated property) and resulting personal liability for omission (including failure to notify secured creditor)
BaselineA: Statute (Bankruptcy Act, R.S.C. 1952, c. 14, ss. 9(1)-(2), 2(o) “property”, 2(r) “secured creditor”, and s. 171)
CaseB_TestB: Charitable status under the fourth Pemsel head for ITA registration: purposes must be of public benefit and “in a way the law regards as charitable”, assessed by analogy to prior cases (sport is charitable only if ancillary to a recognized charitable purpose, not “mere sport”)
BaselineB: Common law (Pemsel; Vancouver Society adopting D’Aguiar/Verge approach) applied within the statutory registration scheme (Income Tax Act, ss. 149.1(1), 248(1))
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Eligibility for Quebec seats on the SCC under Supreme Court Act s. 6: s. 6 narrows s. 5 and requires current membership in Quebec institutions (current Quebec CA/Superior Court judge or current Quebec bar member with 10 years standing). Key holding: “s. 6 narrows the pool from the four groups of people who are eligible under s. 5 to two groups who are eligible under s. 6” and “requires that, at the time of appointment, the appointee be a current member of the Quebec bar with at least 10 years standing” (paras. 17, 4).
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional text: Supreme Court Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. S-26, ss. 5 and 6 (interpreted together); Constitution Act, 1982, s. 41(d) (composition of the Supreme Court) for the entrenchment consequence.
JudgeA: The Chief Justice and LeBel, Abella, Cromwell, Karakatsanis and Wagner JJ.
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 15(1) equality test (as applied to Pay Equity Act s. 38 delay): two-step inquiry—(1) whether the law “on its face or in its impact, draw[s] a distinction based on an enumerated or analogous ground”; and (2) whether it “impose[s] burdens or den[ies] a benefit in a manner that has the effect of reinforcing, perpetuating or exacerbating … disadvantage” (para. 22, quoting Quebec v. A and Taypotat).
BaselineB: Constitutional text/common-law framework: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 15(1), applying the SCC’s established two-step s. 15(1) framework (cited in the reasons: Quebec (Attorney General) v. A; Kahkewistahaw First Nation v. Taypotat).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Highway Victims Indemnity Fund must satisfy a final judgment upon timely application: claimant must (i) be a creditor under a final judgment meeting s. 36 thresholds, (ii) apply within one year (s. 36), and (iii) file a sworn declaration under s. 37 establishing the judgment is unsatisfied and that “no insurer will benefit” (s. 37(b)), which is met because s. 39 transfers “all the creditor’s rights without restriction”; no need to exhaust remedies against the insurer; prescription is 30 years under art. 2265 C.C. because the action is “based on the judgments obtained, not on the liability”.
BaselineA: Statute and civil law: Highway Victims Indemnity Act (R.S.Q. 1964, c. 232, ss. 36-39) and Civil Code (arts. 2262, 2265).
CaseB_TestB: Fatal Accidents Act damages assessment framework: determine annual dependency (including deducting income tax from projected earnings), then award the present value of a lump sum that will replace that annual support over the relevant period, using a discount rate based on “present rates of return on long-term investments with an allowance for the effects of future inflation”, with “some reduction for contingencies”; appellate interference with quantum only for “error in principle” or if award is “so excessive that it could not be upheld”.
BaselineB: Statute plus common-law damages methodology: The Fatal Accidents Act (R.S.O. 1970, c. 164) (and related damages jurisprudence referenced, including Jennings and Gehrmann; and the contemporaneous trilogy Andrews/Thornton/Arnold for present-value methodology).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Equitable interest for improper withholding of a just debt: where payment of a just debt has been improperly withheld and it is fair and equitable to compensate, the court should award interest “for such time and at such rate as the Court may think right”; here, compensation set at the creditor’s bank borrowing rates (not the contract holdback rate).
BaselineA: Common law/equitable principle from Toronto Railway Co. v. City of Toronto, [1906] A.C. 117 (as followed in The Custodian v. Blucher, [1927] S.C.R. 420), applied alongside statutory context (Interest Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-18, ss. 3, 12, 13; Supreme Court Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. S-19, s. 52).
CaseB_TestB: Dixon two-step test for remedy (new trial) after Crown non-disclosure: (1) is there a reasonable possibility the undisclosed information, on its face, affects the reliability of the conviction? If yes, new trial. (2) if not, is there a reasonable possibility non-disclosure affected overall trial fairness (lost lines of inquiry/opportunities), considering defence due diligence and balancing materiality vs lost opportunities.
BaselineB: Common law/Charter disclosure framework from R. v. Stinchcombe, [1991] 3 S.C.R. 326 and related cases (Egger; Chaplin; Carosella), applying Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms ss. 7 and 24(1).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Doctrine/rule of recent possession (jury instruction): once Crown proves recent theft + accused’s possession, jury may infer guilt; if an explanation “may reasonably be true”, it must be considered and can raise a reasonable doubt; Crown need not adduce evidence of ‘no explanation’ and such an instruction is not a prohibited comment on silence
BaselineA: Common law rule of evidence (recent possession) as stated in R. v. Schama; R. v. Abramovitch and repeatedly approved; plus Canada Evidence Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-10, s. 4(5) (no comment on failure to testify)
CaseB_TestB: Imperial Tobacco extraterritoriality framework for provincial legislation: (1) identify pith and substance by purpose/effects; (2) for territorial limits, ask whether the law has a “meaningful connection” to the province and respects other governments’ sovereignty (applied to uphold ORA s. 11 as procedural under s. 92(14))
BaselineB: Common law constitutional division-of-powers framework from British Columbia v. Imperial Tobacco Canada Ltd., 2005 SCC 49 (applied to Constitution Act, 1867, s. 92 territorial limits; classification under s. 92(14) vs s. 92(13))
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Mulligan (majority): When psychiatric evidence of a dissociative state is directed to insanity (disease of the mind) and is not evidence of a pre-existing condition making the accused more likely to become incapable from alcohol, the trial judge need not relate that psychiatric evidence again when charging the jury on the separate defence of drunkenness; drunkenness is considered only if insanity is rejected.
BaselineA: Common law (drunkenness negating specific intent) as in Director of Public Prosecutions v. Beard; applied in context of Criminal Code s. 212(a) mens rea for murder
CaseB_TestB: Ibanescu: “Straddle evidence” is admissible and, per LeBel J. in Gibson, may rebut the Criminal Code s. 258(1)(d.1) presumption if, weighed with all the evidence, it is capable of raising a reasonable doubt that BAC exceeded 80 mg/100 mL at the time of driving.
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, s. 258(1)(d.1) presumption) as interpreted/applied through R. v. Gibson, 2008 SCC 16
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Drunkenness negating mens rea for murder: intoxication must render the accused “incapable of forming the specific intent” to kill (or to cause bodily harm known likely to cause death); psychiatric “dissociative reaction” evidence need not be re-put on drunkenness if it is directed to insanity and the jury is told to consider drunkenness only after rejecting insanity
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Criminal Code, s. 212 (murder intent) plus common law intoxication doctrine from Director of Public Prosecutions v. Beard, [1920] A.C. 479 (H.L.) (as adopted in the jury charge)
JudgeA: Martland J. (for Martland, Judson, Ritchie, Pigeon, Beetz and de Grandpré JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Section 23 “numbers warrant” sliding-scale placement: (1) determine long-term number who will eventually avail themselves of the service; (2) compare with majority-language schools to assess pedagogy/cost, with a rebuttable presumption from existence of comparably sized majority schools province-wide; (3) determine level of services (homogeneous school if comparable and presumption not rebutted; otherwise lower-scale services with deference to minority board)
BaselineB: Combination of constitutional text and common law: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 23 (and s. 1 context), building on Mahe v. Alberta, [1990] 1 S.C.R. 342 (sliding scale; pedagogy/cost factors)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Labour Code s. 108(1)(b) judicial review limit: court may intervene only for an "error of law affecting the jurisdiction" of a labour arbitrator; no such jurisdictional error where the arbitrator "applied himself to the problem at hand" and answered the question submitted (even if arguably right or wrong on the merits).
BaselineA: Statute: Labour Code of British Columbia Act, 1973, s. 108(1)(b) (limited appellate intervention only for "error of law affecting the jurisdiction of the arbitration board").
CaseB_TestB: Garofoli leave (threshold) test for cross-examining a wiretap affiant: defence must show a "reasonable likelihood" that cross-examination "will elicit testimony of probative value" on a material issue for the reviewing judge (relevance/materiality; focus on whether it may undermine the basis for authorization).
BaselineB: Common law: R. v. Garofoli, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 1421 (leave required; threshold showing before cross-examining affiant).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: ITA s. 83(3) “arrangement with the prospector” / “employer of the prospector” requirement for excluding consideration (mining property interest or shares) from income: whether the taxpayer advanced/paid prospecting expenses “either under an arrangement with the prospector made before the prospecting… work or as employer of the prospector” and received the consideration described in s. 83(3)(a)-(b) (unless rent/royalty).
BaselineA: Statute: Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1952, c. 148, s. 83(3) (as amended by 1965 (Can.), c. 18, s. 19) (and related definition in s. 83(1)(c) referenced in reasons).
JudgeA: de Grandpré J. (for Laskin C.J. and Judson, Beetz and de Grandpré JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: “Integral element” test for whether federal legislation affecting a s. 92(10) federal undertaking is within Parliament’s jurisdiction: Parliament may legislate only where the matter is an “integral part” of the federal core; here, a special limitation period for provincial personal-injury negligence actions is not “an integral part of federal jurisdiction” over railways, so Railway Act s. 342(1) is ultra vires to that extent (but can be read down to statutory causes of action under the Railway Act).
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine (division of powers) applying the “integral element” approach from Construction Montcalm Inc. v. Minimum Wage Commission and Northern Telecom Ltd. v. Communications Workers of Canada, in relation to Constitution Act, 1867, ss. 91(29) and 92(10); applied to Railway Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. R-2, s. 342(1).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Fire policy statutory condition 10(a): the insurer is not relieved of liability for property “owned by any other person than the assured” so long as the insured has an insurable interest; the insured need not state the nature of its interest in the policy unless required (i.e., “All that is necessary to satisfy statutory condition 10(a) of the policy is that the insured have an insurable interest.”).
BaselineA: Statute and civil law: Insurance Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 295, s. 240 (statutory conditions, including condition 10(a)); Civil Code art. 2571 (and related provisions discussed, incl. arts. 2480, 2572).
CaseB_TestB: Section 8 “piggybacking” principle for bodily samples: even if a coroner’s seizure is initially valid for non-criminal purposes, once the evidence (or information derived from it) is appropriated by the criminal law enforcement arm for use against the person, the seizure becomes unreasonable under s. 8; courts must “go beyond the initial non‑police seizure” to assess whether police conduct constitutes a seizure or makes the coroner’s seizure unreasonable.
BaselineB: Combination of constitutional and common law: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 8; prior SCC s. 8 framework from Hunter v. Southam Inc. (prior judicial authorization for criminal-law seizures) and R. v. Dyment (privacy in bodily samples/information).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Refusal of adjournment where counsel absent: discretion must be exercised judicially; adjournment needed to exercise right to counsel may be refused only for a reason based on established facts, and refusal is reviewable if based on reasons not well founded in law (especially where it deprives an accused of the right to make full defence by counsel).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 577(3) and 613) plus prior case law on adjournments/discretion (e.g., Spataro v. R.; Talbot v. R. (Que. C.A.) as applied).
JudgeA: Pigeon J. (for Laskin C.J. and Judson, Spence, Dickson and Beetz JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Equitable compensation for breach of fiduciary duty (non-disclosure by solicitor): losses are recoverable only if, on a 'common sense view of causation', they were caused by the breach; foreseeability is not required; losses from independent third-party wrongdoing are not recoverable absent a direct link permitted by the breach.
BaselineB: Common law/equity (fiduciary duty and equitable compensation), drawing on cases including Nocton v. Lord Ashburton and Guerin v. The Queen (as discussed), and related authorities on compensation/causation.
JudgeB: McLachlin J. (for Lamer C.J. and L'Heureux-Dubé J.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Quebec declinatory exception/jurisdiction based on defendant’s domicile or residence: filing a declinatory exception (even supported by an affidavit) does not automatically shift the burden to the plaintiff; court assesses the whole record to determine whether defendant resided in the district (art. 68 C.C.P.), with a statutory presumption from Canadian citizenship (Citizenship Act s. 10) supporting principal residence in Canada
BaselineA: Statute (Quebec Code of Civil Procedure, arts. 68 and 70; Canadian Citizenship Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-19, s. 10)
CaseB_TestB: When (and how) police/state misconduct can reduce a criminal sentence: sentencing judges may account for misconduct as a mitigating factor only where it relates to the circumstances of the offence or the offender; generally unnecessary to invoke Charter s. 24(1); sentence must remain within Criminal Code parameters (including mandatory minimums), with only a narrow possibility of exceptional s. 24(1) relief outside statutory limits for particularly egregious misconduct
BaselineB: Combination of statute and Constitution (Criminal Code ss. 718–718.2 and mandatory minimum scheme; Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms s. 24(1))
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Contractual interpretation of warranty: in para. 3(g) and the auditor’s letter, “depreciation” is an accounting concept (write-off over useful life) and cannot be construed as “full capital cost allowance” (a tax concept); the parenthetical “(using capital cost allowance rates)” refers to rates only, not adoption of the tax ‘system’, and the words “at least” reinforce that the warranty is not an identity-with-tax-returns promise.
BaselineA: Common law (contract interpretation of a share-sale warranty clause, read with incorporated letter terms).
CaseB_TestB: Youth court power under Young Offenders Act: despite s. 19(2) (“find ... guilty or not guilty or make an order dismissing the charge”), a youth court has no jurisdiction to dismiss a charge merely because it “ought never to have been laid”; absent clear statutory language, courts must respect prosecutorial discretion (subject only to exceptional remedies like abuse-of-process stays in the “clearest of cases”).
BaselineB: Statute (Young Offenders Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. Y-1, especially ss. 19(2) and 3(1), read with the background common-law principle of prosecutorial discretion).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Crown appeal from acquittal after legal error: Crown must satisfy the court that the verdict "would not necessarily have been the same" absent the misdirection (White v. R. test, applied in Vézeau); plus clarification that s. 4(5) Canada Evidence Act does not authorize telling the jury it cannot draw an inference from the accused’s failure to testify (especially on alibi).
BaselineA: Combination: statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 613(4) and s. 618(2); Canada Evidence Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-10, s. 4(5)) and common law (White v. R., [1947] S.C.R. 268; followed in R. v. Gauthier, [1977] 1 S.C.R. 441).
CaseB_TestB: Group defamation/personal injury in Quebec civil liability: plaintiff must prove that "an ordinary person would have believed that each of [the group members] personally sustained damage to his or her reputation"; to decide if personal injury is shown, the judge analyzes the impugned comments contextually using a non-exhaustive set of factors (e.g., group size, homogeneity/organization, identifiability/visibility, stigma, plaintiff’s relationship to group, precision of allegations, seriousness/extravagance, plausibility, and other extrinsic context).
BaselineB: Statute/civil code framework: Civil Code of Québec, art. 1457 (fault, injury, causal connection) and related CCQ provisions on compensable injury (arts. 1607, 1611), plus class action procedure does not alter substantive requirements (Code of Civil Procedure). Built on SCC defamation-injury objective standard from Prud’homme v. Prud’homme and Néron (as cited in the reasons).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Interpretation of standard auto policy exclusion: insured is excluded if, on the admitted facts, they are "entitled to receive the benefits of any workmen’s compensation law or plan"—entitlement does not depend on having applied for or obtained a compensation award
BaselineA: Statute (mandatory standard-form policy wording): Insurance Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 224, s. 232(1) and Schedule E, Exclusion 2(a)(ii), interpreted with reference to Workmen’s Compensation Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 505 (e.g., ss. 3, 4, 8)
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 8 reasonableness framework (mutatis mutandis) for cross-border disclosure under Criminal Code s. 193(2)(e): (1) disclosure authorized by law; (2) the law is reasonable; (3) disclosure carried out in a reasonable manner—authorization requires recipient be a foreign investigative/prosecutorial authority and disclosure be "intended to be in the interests of the administration of justice" (i.e., a legitimate law enforcement purpose)
BaselineB: Combination: Charter s. 8 reasonableness framework from R. v. Collins / R. v. Caslake applied to statutory disclosure under Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 193(2)(e)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Discretion to order service ex juris under Federal Court Rules, Rule 307 guided by forum conveniens: the “overriding consideration” is whether there exists “some other forum more convenient and appropriate for the pursuit of the action and for securing the ends of justice”; refusal is an error in principle if based solely on “no relation or connection with Canada”.
BaselineA: Statute and regulation: Federal Court Act, R.S.C. 1970 (2nd Supp.), c. 10, ss. 22(2)(a), 43(1), 44; Federal Court Rules, Rule 307 (service ex juris).
JudgeA: Ritchie J. (for Ritchie, Pigeon, Beetz and de Grandpré JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Quebec medical civil liability causation (rejecting “loss of chance” as a substitute for causation where death/sickness has occurred): causation “must be established on the balance of probabilities, taking into account all the evidence: factual, statistical and that which the judge is entitled to presume”; in some cases a court may presume causation where a fault creates “clear danger” and the danger materializes, “unless there is a demonstration or a strong indication to the contrary”; if not satisfied on the balance of probabilities that the fault caused “any real damage”, recovery is denied.
BaselineB: Civil law (Quebec delictual responsibility) with evidentiary presumptions under Civil Code of Lower Canada, art. 1205; SCC references to prior SCC causation approach including Snell v. Farrell, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 311.
JudgeB: Gonthier J. (for Lamer C.J. and L'Heureux-Dubé, Sopinka, Gonthier, Cory and McLachlin JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Breach of municipal development agreement sewer-servicing obligation: developer must prove a specific failure to provide sewers/enlargements “required to properly service” the project stage (i.e., evidence of existing or foreseeable inadequacy); a general sewer-upgrading report/charge is irrelevant absent evidence connecting it to serviceability
BaselineA: Common law (contract interpretation and breach) applied to s. 31(a)(iii) of the 1966 development agreement (covenant to construct/enlarge sewers “required to properly service” each stage)
CaseB_TestB: Presumption of advancement and rebuttal in husband-to-wife gratuitous transfer: presumption applies unless husband rebuts it; it is not rebutted by saying the transfer was only to defeat creditors, and surrounding conduct may confirm rather than rebut the presumption
BaselineB: Common law presumptions in property/trusts between spouses (presumption of advancement vs resulting trust), with statutory non-retroactivity principle applied to The Family Law Reform Act, 1975 (Ont.), s. 1(3)(d)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 613(1)(b)(iii) curative proviso: despite trial error(s), uphold conviction if the Crown satisfies the appellate court that the jury, properly charged, "could not, as reasonable men, have done otherwise than find the appellant guilty" (i.e., no "substantial wrong or miscarriage of justice")
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code s. 613(1)(b)(iii)) as applied through SCC precedent (Colpitts v. R. adopting Brooks v. The King formulation)
CaseB_TestB: Marshall treaty right framework: interpret Mi’kmaq Treaties of 1760-61 using extrinsic historical/cultural evidence (even absent facial ambiguity) to ascertain the parties’ common intention; recognize a treaty right to fish and trade for "necessaries" (modern "moderate livelihood"), subject to regulation and infringement/justification analysis under Sparrow/Badger
BaselineB: Common law/constitutional doctrine governing treaty interpretation and s. 35 treaty-rights infringement/justification (e.g., Sioui/Badger/Sparrow/Adams as cited in the reasons) applied to the Mi’kmaq Treaties of 1760-61
JudgeB: Binnie J. (for Lamer C.J. and L’Heureux-Dubé, Cory, Iacobucci and Binnie JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Hague Protocol ‘notice’ requirement as a precondition to invoking Art. 22 liability limits: the passenger ticket/baggage check must include a ‘notice’ in a form ‘calculated to attract attention’ (not merely readable fine print), otherwise the carrier cannot limit liability
BaselineA: Statute (Carriage by Air Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-14 incorporating the Hague Protocol/Warsaw Convention as amended): Hague Protocol Arts. 3(1)(c), 3(2), 4(1)(c), and 22 (contrasted with Warsaw Convention Arts. 3 and 4)
