CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 11(d) test for statutory presumptions in breathalyzer scheme and severance remedy: a presumption violates s. 11(d) if it can require conviction despite a reasonable doubt; under s. 258(1)(c) only the first rebuttal requirement (evidence raising doubt about malfunction/improper operation) is justified, while the 2nd and 3rd rebuttal requirements are unconstitutional and severed
BaselineB: Combination (statute + constitutional doctrine): Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, ss. 258(1)(c), (d.01), (d.1) interpreted under Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms ss. 11(d) and 1 (with the s. 11(d) presumption analysis drawn from cases such as Oakes/Whyte/Vaillancourt as discussed in the reasons)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Municipal notice-of-accident limitation period runs from the claimant’s date of discovery (when the relevant facts come to the claimant’s attention), not necessarily from the accident date, where starting from the accident date would make the right of action practically illusory
BaselineA: Statute: Charter of the City of Montreal, 1959-60 (Que.), c. 102, art. 1088 (15-day notice must be 'received'); interpreted in light of the notice regime and exceptions (including analogy to prescription principles and reference to City of Ile Perrot v. Goulet-Wiseman, [1977] 1 S.C.R. 175)
CaseB_TestB: Discretionary test for discharging a civil jury after a reference to insurance: discharge only if the reference likely caused real prejudice amounting to a 'substantial wrong or miscarriage of justice' and the prejudice cannot be cured (typically by instructions)
BaselineB: Common law (overruling prior SCC rule in Bowhey v. Theakston, [1951] S.C.R. 679, on automatic discharge); applied in the context of Supreme Court Rules, B.C. Reg. 310/76, Rule 41(6)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Admissibility of an accused’s prior in-court testimony (judicial statement under oath) at a later trial without a voir dire: such testimony is admissible as of right even if alleged to have been induced by unlawful threats/violence; voluntariness goes to weight for the jury, not admissibility, and the witness must claim statutory protection at the time of testifying (cannot do so after the event).
BaselineA: Common law (distinction between extra-judicial confessions to persons in authority requiring a voluntariness voir dire, and judicial statements under oath in prior proceedings). Key baseline authorities cited: R. v. Scott (1856) (compelled prior testimony admissible), and related line of cases following Scott; also references to Canada Evidence Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-10, s. 5(2) (protection against subsequent use if claimed at the time).
CaseB_TestB: Appellate intervention for trial judge’s failure to consider relevant evidence: an appellate court must review the record to ensure the trial court directed itself to all evidence bearing on the relevant issues; where the record discloses a lack of appreciation/complete disregard of relevant evidence, the reviewing court must intercede (new trial).
BaselineB: Common law principles on appellate review of reasons/evidence, relying on SCC authorities including MacDonald v. The Queen, [1977] 2 S.C.R. 665 and Ungaro v. R., [1950] S.C.R. 430 (manifest misdirection/self-misdirection; omission to deal with relevant issue/evidence can be reversible error).
JudgeB: Estey J. (for Martland, Dickson, Beetz, Estey, McIntyre and Lamer JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Admissibility of Crown rebuttal evidence against an alibi/credibility: Crown may contradict an alibi only by attacking its “material points”; and Crown cannot contradict a collateral fact elicited on cross-examination (no collateral-fact contradiction rule).
BaselineA: Common law evidence principles (rebuttal to alibi limited to material points; collateral fact rule against contradiction), with related Criminal Code appeal proviso context (s. 613(1)(b)(iii)).
CaseB_TestB: Drunkenness and rape (specific vs general intent): rape is an offence of general/basic intent, so self-induced intoxication is not a defence; only if an offence requires “specific intent” can intoxication be considered to negate that intent (per George/Beard/Majewski line).
BaselineB: Common law intoxication doctrine and the specific-intent/general-intent distinction (The Queen v. George; DPP v. Beard; DPP v. Majewski), with Criminal Code appeal proviso context (s. 613(1)(b)(iii)).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Applicability of mandatory supervision on release: if an inmate is released by remission with remission exceeding 60 days, s. 15(1) applies; where an inmate receives an additional term while confined, s. 14(1) deems all terms to be 'one sentence' for s. 15(1), and a post–Aug. 1, 1970 penitentiary sentence brings the inmate within the class to whom s. 15 applies (via s. 101(2) proclamation).
BaselineA: Statute (Parole Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. P-2, ss. 14(1), 15(1)-(2); Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1968-69 (Can.), c. 38, s. 101(2) and proclamation SOR/70-339; also references Criminal Code s. 659(2)).
CaseB_TestB: Succession duty inclusion for insurance proceeds: s. 26(1) applies to 'proceeds of insurance policies... due... by reason or on account of the death of the person on whose life the insurance was effected' and is not limited to life insurance; accidental death is still 'death' for the provision, so accident-policy proceeds payable on death are deemed property transmitted owing to death.
BaselineB: Statute (Succession Duties Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 70, s. 26(1); also discussed ss. 45(f), 46(1); interpretive support from Civil Code arts. 1902, 1903, 1905, 1906).
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Estate Tax Act “passing/competent to dispose” analysis for community of acquests with a full survivorship stipulation: if the survivor becomes owner of all community property “retroactively to the date of the marriage”, there is no “passing”; and the deceased is not “competent to dispose” of community assets in the sense of ss. 3(1)(a), 3(2)(a) and 58(1)(i) (even if he had administrative powers).
BaselineA: Statute (Estate Tax Act, 1958 (Can.), c. 29, especially ss. 3(1)(a), 3(2)(a), 3(2)(e), 58(1)(i); also the Act’s “passing” concept in ss. 2 and 3) as interpreted through SCC precedents Sura v. MNR, [1962] S.C.R. 65 and The Royal Trust Company et al. v. MNR, [1968] S.C.R. 505.
CaseB_TestB: Treaty 8/NRTA geographic-limit test for hunting on private land: the treaty/NRTA right of access to hunt for food is limited by “visible, incompatible land use”; if private land is “occupied, that is, put to visible use which is incompatible with hunting”, there is no right of access; if “unoccupied and not put to visible use”, there is a right of access (case-by-case).
BaselineB: Combination of constitutional instrument and treaty interpretation: para. 12 of the Natural Resources Transfer Agreement, 1930 (Constitution Act, 1930, Schedule 2) and Treaty No. 8 (1899), with interpretive principles and prior SCC cases (e.g., Horseman, Frank, Myran, Horse, Mousseau).
JudgeB: Cory J. (for La Forest, L'Heureux-Dubé, Gonthier, Cory and Iacobucci JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Contractual price-adjustment clause for tax/duty changes applies only where a “tax, duty, charge or fee” is imposed on the seller (Imperial) “in respect of bunker fuel oil” (the product) or its “production, manufacture, sale or delivery” by the seller; it does not cover upstream crude-oil cost increases from foreign taxes/royalties or affiliate supply arrangements.
BaselineA: Contract (interpretation of clause 9 of the parties’ supply agreement, governed by Nova Scotia law per clause 11).
CaseB_TestB: Van der Peet test (as applied to self-government/gambling claim under s. 35(1)): (1) characterize the claimed right by considering “the nature of the action”, “the nature of the governmental regulation… being impugned”, and “the practice, custom or tradition being relied upon”; (2) determine whether the activity is “an element of a practice, custom or tradition integral to the distinctive culture” and whether it was “a defining feature of the culture in question” prior to European contact.
BaselineB: Common law constitutional test under Constitution Act, 1982, s. 35(1), applying R. v. Van der Peet (and related s. 35 jurisprudence).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Foreseeability-based duty/causation limit for occupier/railway: no negligence liability unless the injury was a "reasonably foreseeable result" of the situation created by the defendant; here, "no reasonable occupier could have reasonably foreseen" a child leaving a place of safety to try to board a moving freight train
BaselineA: Common law negligence/occupier’s liability principles (foreseeability) with reference to prior SCC cases (e.g., Mitchell v. C.N.R.; Amos v. New Brunswick Electric Power Commission; Ouellet v. Cloutier; University Hospital Board v. Lepine) and a statutory fencing point under Railway Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. R-2, s. 214 (rejected as inapplicable on causation)
CaseB_TestB: Section 7 "fair hearing" requirements for IRPA security-certificate process: a fair judicial process must include (1) a hearing, (2) an independent and impartial magistrate, (3) a decision on the facts and the law, and (4) the right to know and answer the case; if full disclosure is impossible, "either the person must be given the necessary information, or a substantial substitute for that information must be found"
BaselineB: Constitutional (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7; also ss. 9 and 10(c) discussed) applied to the statutory IRPA security-certificate scheme (Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, S.C. 2001, c. 27, ss. 77-85, especially s. 78 (confidentiality/summary) and s. 80 (reasonableness determination))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Highway Victims Indemnity Fund liability for unknown-driver accidents: under Highway Victims Indemnity Act s. 43 the Fund must satisfy judgment only "to the same extent as if [judgment] had been rendered against the author of the accident", which imports the s. 14 cap ($35,000); prior payment by another liable party does not extinguish the Fund’s liability up to that cap (and s. 38 deduction does not apply where victim received nothing from the unknown driver).
BaselineA: Statute: Highway Victims Indemnity Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 232, especially ss. 43 (unknown driver), 14 (financial responsibility amount), 38 (deduction rule in Fund recourse), and 49 (Fund powers).
CaseB_TestB: Sentencing treatment of collateral immigration consequences and appellate intervention: a sentencing judge "may" consider collateral immigration consequences as part of individualization, but only if the sentence remains proportionate (Criminal Code s. 718.1); such consequences "must not be allowed to dominate" or be used to impose "inappropriate and artificial sentences"; an appellate court may vary sentence where the sentencing judge was unaware of the collateral immigration consequences or counsel failed to advise, and where not raised below and Crown does not consent, "some evidence should be adduced".
BaselineB: Statute-informed common law sentencing principles: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, ss. 718, 718.1, 718.2 (proportionality, parity, individualization) applied in context of IRPA, S.C. 2001, c. 27, s. 64 (immigration appeal bar at 2 years).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Whether the trial judge must give the accomplice-evidence caution (danger of convicting on uncorroborated testimony) when a key witness may be an accomplice and/or an accessory after the fact; and whether, on these facts, the jury could find the witness an accessory after the fact without also finding him an accomplice
BaselineA: Common law rule of practice/caution on accomplice testimony (corroboration warning), as discussed via Davies v. DPP and Horsburgh v. The Queen; plus Criminal Code s. 23 definition of accessory after the fact referenced in the jury instruction
CaseB_TestB: Interpretation/application of Criminal Code s. 212(c) murder: meaning of 'unlawful object' and how the objective 'knows or ought to know' standard must be applied (reasonable person standard applied using the accused’s actual knowledge of surrounding circumstances; intoxication relevant to that knowledge)
BaselineB: Statute—Criminal Code ss. 205(5)(a) and 212(c) (and related discussion of ss. 212(a)(i)-(ii)); interpreted in light of prior SCC cases including Graves v. The King and R. v. Hughes
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Construction of Manitoba auto insurance exclusion: s. 31(3)(h) (“death of an insured”) is applied by reference to the specific certificate/contract under which indemnity is claimed (owner’s vs driver’s), because the certificates evidence “separate contracts” with “distinct coverages”.
BaselineA: Regulation (Manitoba Automobile Insurance Regulation, Man. Reg. 333/74 under The Manitoba Public Insurance Corporation Act, C.S.M. c. A180), especially ss. 30, 31(1), 31(2), 31(3)(h).
CaseB_TestB: Treaty 8 / NRTA limit on protected hunting: para. 12 restricts Treaty 8 rights to hunting “for food” (i.e., “for sustenance for the individual Indian or the Indian’s family”); a “multi-stage process” involving sale of the product of the hunt is “an act of commerce” and not protected, so provincial Wildlife Act s. 42 applies via Indian Act s. 88.
BaselineB: Constitutional/treaty and statute: Treaty No. 8 (1899); Natural Resources Transfer Agreement, 1930 (Alberta), para. 12 (confirmed by Constitution Act, 1930); Indian Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-6, s. 88; Wildlife Act, R.S.A. 1980, c. W-9, ss. 1(s), 42.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 287 (as then worded): “telecommunication” requires transmission “by wire or cable” (not Hertzian waves/radio); no ‘partly by wire’ extension
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 287(1)(b) and definition in s. 287(2) (as at May 1972)
CaseB_TestB: Immigration Act s. 19(1)(a)(ii) “excessive demands” assessment: must be individualized and consider both medical and non-medical factors (including family ability/willingness to pay); threshold is “reasonable probability, not remote possibility”
BaselineB: Statute: Immigration Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. I-2, s. 19(1)(a)(ii) (and comparison to IRPA s. 38(1)(c))
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Limits on municipal council’s discretion to refuse a business licence under Municipal Act s. 455: discretion must be exercised “judicially”, not on “extraneous”/“irrelevant or alien” grounds, and refusal “in any particular case” must be peculiar to the applicant (not a blanket prohibition of a type of lawful business/land use)
BaselineA: Statute (Municipal Act, R.S.B.C. 1960, c. 255, s. 455) interpreted in light of common law limits on municipal licensing/prohibition powers (e.g., Municipal Corporation of the City of Toronto v. Virgo, [1896] A.C. 88; Sunshine Valley Co-operative Society v. City of Grand Forks, [1949] 1 W.W.R. 165)
CaseB_TestB: IRPA security-certificate disclosure/fairness standard under Charter s. 7: the named person must receive an “incompressible minimum” of disclosure—“reasonably informed” means enough disclosure to give “meaningful instructions” to public counsel and “meaningful guidance and information” to special advocates; if non-disclosure prevents this, the Minister must withdraw the information/evidence and the judge must quash the certificate
BaselineB: Combination of statute and constitutional common law: Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, ss. 77(2), 78, 83(1)(e), 83(1)(i) interpreted to comply with Charter s. 7 as explained in Charkaoui v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2007 SCC 9
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Appellate deference to trial findings of fact: an appellate court should not disturb a trial judge’s findings where there was “credible evidence before him on which he could reasonably base his conclusion”; it is “not the function of an appellate court to reconsider that evidence … and come to a different conclusion, unless it can be shown that the evidence reasonably could not result in justifying the conclusion of the trial judge.”
BaselineA: Common law (appellate review standard for findings of fact; referenced in the decision as a “well-known principle”).
CaseB_TestB: Bona fide occupational qualification (BFOQ) under Ontario Human Rights Code s. 4(6): (1) subjective good faith—must be imposed “honestly, in good faith, and in the sincerely held belief” it serves “adequate performance … with … dispatch, safety and economy” and not for “ulterior or extraneous reasons”; and (2) objective necessity—must be “objectively related” and “reasonably necessary to assure the efficient and economical performance of the job without endangering” the employee, co-workers, or the public; employer bears the burden on a balance of probabilities once prima facie discrimination is shown.
BaselineB: Statute: The Ontario Human Rights Code, R.S.O. 1970, c. 318, ss. 4(1) and 4(6) (and related procedure provisions including s. 14d).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal causation for unlawful act manslaughter: Crown must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the unlawful act was “at least a contributing cause of death, outside the de minimis range” (and the jury may consider all evidence, expert and lay, on factual causation).
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Criminal Code s. 205(1) (“A person commits homicide ... when directly or indirectly, by any means, he causes the death of a human being”) plus common-law causation principles (including thin-skull) as reflected in cases discussed (e.g., R. v. Larkin; R. v. Nicholson; R. v. Blaue).
CaseB_TestB: Anns two-stage duty-of-care framework for recognizing a novel duty for pure economic loss: (1) prima facie duty via foreseeability and “proximity”; (2) whether “policy considerations ... serve to negative or limit” the duty (applied to reject a duty of care in commercial negotiations and in drafting tender specifications).
BaselineB: Common law: Anns v. Merton London Borough Council two-stage duty-of-care analysis (as adopted in Canadian jurisprudence, e.g., Kamloops), applied to proposed new categories of pure economic loss.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Crown bound by legislation/regulations only if expressly mentioned or (at common law) by “necessary implication” (i.e., the statute’s purpose would be “wholly frustrated” unless the Crown were bound); SCC holds Interpretation Act s. 16 (“except only as therein mentioned or referred to”) excludes binding the Crown by necessary implication absent mention/reference
BaselineA: Statute (Interpretation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-23, s. 16; s. 28) plus common law rule from Bombay Province v. Bombay Municipal Corporation, [1947] A.C. 58 (necessary implication/wholly frustrated purpose)
CaseB_TestB: Breach of contract where a stipulated term (here, cargo weight) is “material if not a critical term”: delivering goods ~30% overweight contrary to the undertaking constitutes breach; not “mutual mistake”; remedy in damages under Civil Code art. 1065 (not nullity under art. 992)
BaselineB: Statute (Civil Code arts. 992 and 1065) applied to the contract’s stipulated terms (material term/breach analysis)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Scope of CTC’s exemption inquiry under Lord’s Day Act s. 11(x): determine only whether, “having regard to the object of this Act” (preventing Sunday gainful work) and “with the object of preventing undue delay”, the Commission “deems [the work] necessary to permit” in connection with freight traffic; evidence about local congestion/noise/safety is irrelevant.
BaselineA: Statute (Lord’s Day Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. L-13, ss. 4 and 11(x))
CaseB_TestB: Test for “bona fide pension plan” under Human Rights Code s. 3(6)(a) (Abella J., for the judgment): plan must be “subjectively and objectively bona fide”: “a legitimate plan, adopted in good faith and not for the purpose of defeating protected rights”; inquiry is into “the overall bona fides of the plan, not the actuarial details or mechanics”.
BaselineB: Statute (Human Rights Code, R.S.N.B. 1973, c. H-11, s. 3(6)(a))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Combines conspiracy “undueness” test: Crown must prove (1) intent to enter the agreement and (2) that, if carried into effect, it would “prevent or lessen competition unduly” — i.e., impose “improper, inordinate, excessive or oppressive restrictions” / make participants “virtually unaffected by the influence of competition”; reject any shortcut that “undueness” is established merely because a “meaningful segment” of the industry is involved.
BaselineA: Statute (Combines Investigation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-23, s. 32(1)(c)) as interpreted in prior SCC cases (Howard Smith Paper Mills; Weidman v. Shragge; Stinson-Reeb; Container Materials).
CaseB_TestB: Unreasonable verdict (Criminal Code s. 686(1)(a)(i)) test: appellate court asks whether the verdict is one a properly instructed jury or judge “could reasonably have rendered”; may find unreasonableness where an essential inference/finding is (1) “plainly contradicted” by the evidence relied on, or (2) “incompatible with evidence” not otherwise contradicted or rejected; credibility findings are not to be disturbed unless they “cannot be supported on any reasonable view of the evidence”.
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(a)(i)) as developed in SCC jurisprudence (Yebes; Biniaris; Sinclair; Beaudry; Burke).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Circumstantial-evidence instruction: Hodge’s Case formula applies to proving the act/identity, but not to proving intent; intent is assessed under the ordinary reasonable-doubt standard (and s. 110(1)(b) requires intent that the benefit be conferred “with respect to those dealings”).
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Criminal Code, s. 110(1)(b) (“with respect to those dealings”) plus the common-law circumstantial-evidence direction from Hodge’s Case as limited by R. v. Mitchell (SCC).
CaseB_TestB: Insurance contract interpretation where a clause is susceptible of two meanings: apply art. 1014 C.C. so the clause is understood “in that in which it may have some effect rather than in that in which it can produce none”; thus “See Garage Policy” in the fleet policy is construed as referring to limits/premium (not eliminating fleet third-party coverage), and the garage rider only excludes garage coverage for owned autos.
BaselineB: Statute/civil law: Quebec Civil Code arts. 1013 and 1014 (interpretation; give effect to clauses), applied to the insurance policies’ wording (with contextual reference to the garage-policy rider Q.E.F. 73).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Impossibility of performance as a defence in contractual mandate: plaintiff proves fault, damage, and causality; defendant who alleges impossibility to avoid the obligation bears the burden under art. 1203 C.C. to prove impossibility (not mere difficulty)
BaselineA: Statute (Civil Code of Quebec): arts. 1701 (mandate), 984 and 1062 (object must be possible), and 1203 (burden on party alleging facts in avoidance/extinction of obligation)
CaseB_TestB: Municipal disqualification for conflict of interest: under s. 6 Moncton Consolidation Act, a mayor/councillor is disqualified if he 'directly or indirectly ... have any interest in any contract' with the City (beyond mere shareholding); interpret 'interested in' broadly in 'common usage of men' so directors/officers are at least indirectly interested
BaselineB: Statute (Moncton Consolidation Act, 1946 (N.B.), c. 101, s. 6; interpretive aid: New Brunswick Interpretation Act, R.S.N.B. 1973, c. I-13, s. 17; supported by SCC approach in Angrignon (1935) on meaning of 'interested in')
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Interpretation of para. 12 Alberta Natural Resources Transfer Agreement: “Indians of the Province” (Alberta Indians) vs “Indians within the boundaries” (all Indians physically in Alberta, regardless of residence), so the proviso hunting-for-food right applies to any Indian within Alberta on “all unoccupied Crown lands” or other lands with a “right of access”.
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional instrument: Alberta Natural Resources Transfer Agreement, 1930, para. 12 (confirmed by British North America Act, 1930 (U.K.) c. 26), applied alongside Indian Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-6, s. 88 and Alberta Wildlife Act, R.S.A. 1970, c. 391, s. 16.
CaseB_TestB: Qualified privilege in libel: a communication is privileged where the maker has an “interest or a duty, legal, social or moral” to make it to a recipient with a corresponding interest/duty (Adam v. Ward); on such an occasion, liability requires malice, and the defendant is protected even if language is “violent or excessively strong” if, “having regard to all the circumstances”, he “might have honestly and on reasonable grounds believed” it was true/necessary.
BaselineB: Common law: qualified privilege and malice principles from Adam v. Ward (definition and scope of privilege) and Netupsky v. Craig (malice defeating privilege), as applied to a report to a government department.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory obscenity test and exclusivity: apply Criminal Code s. 159(8) (“any publication a dominant characteristic of which is the undue exploitation of sex… shall be deemed to be obscene”) as the exhaustive standard for sex-based obscenity across Code offences, displacing the common law Hicklin test
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, especially s. 159(8); also s. 159(1)(a), and interpretive context including s. 8). Prior SCC baseline discussion in Brodie v. The Queen on exclusivity for “publications”.
JudgeA: Laskin C.J. (for Laskin C.J. and Judson, Spence and Dickson JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Duty to accommodate in adverse-effect discrimination: employer (and, where it is a party to the discrimination, the union) must take “reasonable measures short of undue hardship”; undue hardship assessed contextually (e.g., cost, disruption of collective agreement, morale/rights of other employees), with union duty arising as co-discriminator or where it blocks reasonable accommodation
BaselineB: Combination: Statute (Human Rights Act, S.B.C. 1984, c. 22, ss. 8(1), 8(4), 9) as interpreted through common-law/precedential framework from O'Malley and Central Alberta Dairy Pool (duty to accommodate/undue hardship).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory obscenity definition is exclusive for Criminal Code sex-based obscenity: apply Criminal Code s. 159(8) (“any publication a dominant characteristic of which is the undue exploitation of sex ... shall be deemed to be obscene”) across Code provisions where the allegation “revolves around sex considerations”, displacing the common law Hicklin test; and do not revive Hicklin as a fallback when s. 159(8) is not met.
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, s. 159(8) definition of obscenity) plus prior common law obscenity test (R. v. Hicklin (1868)) and SCC discussion in Brodie v. The Queen, [1962] S.C.R. 681.
CaseB_TestB: Duty to accommodate in the presence of a collectively bargained time-limit/termination clause: the negotiated absence period (e.g., “after the thirty-sixth (36th) month of absence”) is a relevant factor/evidence in assessing accommodation and undue hardship, but is not determinative; accommodation must remain individualized, and undue hardship from absence is assessed globally from the beginning of the absence (Meiorin framework).
BaselineB: Common law / human rights jurisprudence (Meiorin test for BFOR and accommodation/undue hardship) applied in the labour-arbitration context; informed by Quebec Charter of human rights and freedoms (equality rights) and the collective agreement clause.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Federal jurisdiction over cable TV undertakings: a cable distribution system that receives extra-provincial/foreign signals and transmits them to subscribers is a single interprovincial/international “undertaking”, so federal power extends to both reception and subsequent transmission (and program-content regulation is “inseparable” from regulating the undertaking).
BaselineA: Constitution (B.N.A. Act), ss. 91 and 92(10)(a), as interpreted in the Radio Reference (In re Regulation and Control of Radio Communication in Canada, [1932] A.C. 304) and related “undertaking” jurisprudence (e.g., Winner).
CaseB_TestB: Proceeds of disposition and assumed obligations: include an assumed obligation in the vendor’s “proceeds of disposition” only if it is a distinct existing liability assumed as part of the sale price; exclude obligations that are “embedded” future costs tied to the property that merely depress its value (regardless of contingency or contractual valuation).
BaselineB: Statute: Income Tax Act, s. 13(21) (“proceeds of disposition” includes “the sale price of property that has been sold”), applied with the general principle that “the assumption of a vendor’s liability by a purchaser may constitute part of the sale price”.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Immovable by nature (Civil Code): a structure is immovable by nature where it “adheres to something that is immovable by nature, whether land or a building, and thereby acquires a fixed foundation”; for networks, “the vertical attachment of a network of wires to the ground is in itself enough to make these wires immovable”, and separation of ownership of poles/wires is “irrelevant to whether a thing is immovable by nature”.
BaselineA: Statute + civil law: Retail Sales Tax Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 71, ss. 2(3) (definition of “moveable property” by reference to what is not immovable “by the laws of this Province”) and 6 (tax on purchase of moveable property), interpreted by reference to Civil Code arts. 374 et seq. (esp. arts. 375-378/376 on immovables by nature). Key prior SCC authorities applied/clarified: Montreal Light, Heat and Power Consolidated v. Westmount, [1926] S.C.R. 515; Lower St. Lawrence Power Co. v. L’Immeuble Landry Ltée, [1926] S.C.R. 655; Bélair v. Ste-Rose (1922), 63 S.C.R. 526.
CaseB_TestB: Punitive damages for breach of contract (wrongful dismissal): punitive damages are available but “rare”; they require (i) an “actionable wrong” causing the injury complained of, and (ii) “extreme” conduct “deserving of punishment because of its harsh, vindictive, reprehensible and malicious nature” and “by any reasonable standard … deserving of full condemnation and punishment”; in contract, the plaintiff is entitled only to what the contract provides (e.g., notice/pay in lieu), making punitive awards exceptional.
BaselineB: Common law of damages for breach of contract/wrongful dismissal, drawing on Addis v. Gramophone Co. (H.L.) and SCC’s Peso Silver Mines Ltd. (N.P.L.) v. Cropper, [1966] S.C.R. 673, plus punitive-damages jurisprudence (e.g., Rookes v. Barnard; McElroy v. Cowper-Smith; H. L. Weiss Forwarding Ltd. v. Omnus).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Parent’s contributory negligence / duty of care assessed by the community standard of reasonable parenting: whether the parent departed from the “generally accepted standard of care by parents generally in the community” (i.e., the “standard to be expected from a reasonably prudent mother under the circumstances”).
BaselineA: Common law negligence (standard of care / contributory negligence), with the Court referencing Donoghue v. Stevenson for duty of care concepts and relying on prior negligence authorities (e.g., Ware’s Taxi Ltd. v. Gilliham) for using other parents’ conduct as a benchmark.
CaseB_TestB: Contractual election-after-damage clause and repudiation: under clause 5 the purchaser must elect either to “have the proceeds of the insurance and complete the purchase” or “cancel the Agreement”; attempting to impose additional conditions (e.g., restoration or sufficient insurance within a reasonable time) is not an election but “dictating different terms” and “constituted a repudiation” the vendor may accept.
BaselineB: Common law contract principles (repudiation/acceptance) applied through interpretation of the parties’ agreement of purchase and sale (standard form clause 5 and clause 9).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Matrimonial property beneficial interest via resulting trust from a joint account/common pool: where spouses intend a joint pool, “in the absence of agreement to the contrary, a one-half interest in any investment purchased by a husband from a common pool of funds … will be considered to be held by him for the benefit of his wife” (rebuttable only by evidence of contrary intention).
BaselineA: Common law (resulting trust/common intention presumptions in matrimonial property disputes; cases cited include Murdoch v. Murdoch, Pettitt v. Pettitt, Gissing v. Gissing; joint account authority Jones v. Maynard).
CaseB_TestB: Access to court exhibits test (post-trial): court must balance open court/access against privacy/protection of the innocent; “curtailment of public accessibility can only be justified where there is present the need to protect social values of superordinate importance … [including] the protection of the innocent” (MacIntyre), and the court may require the applicant to specify the proposed use and may regulate that use.
BaselineB: Common law (open courts/right of access framework from Attorney General of Nova Scotia v. MacIntyre; applied to exhibits; also considers Nova Scotia Civil Procedure Rule 30.11(6) on return of exhibits).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Limitation Act s. 6(4)(b) postponement test: time runs only when a properly advised reasonable person would conclude the plaintiff could, acting reasonably in light of their own circumstances and interests, bring an action; postponement only if those interests/circumstances are “serious, significant, and compelling” and not tactical
BaselineA: Statute (Limitation Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 266, s. 6(4)(b) (and the s. 6(4) framework))
CaseB_TestB: Arbitration Act s. 15 stay framework in receivership: (1) applicant shows an arguable case for four technical prerequisites; (2) stay is mandatory unless, on a balance of probabilities in a clear case, the arbitration agreement is “void, inoperative or incapable of being performed” — including where enforcing it would compromise the orderly and efficient resolution/integrity of a court-ordered receivership (non-exhaustive factors listed)
BaselineB: Statute (Arbitration Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 55, s. 15(1)-(2), interpreted alongside Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. B-3, ss. 183(1) and 243(1)(c))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: When extinctive prescription begins to run for engineers’ percentage-based fees: prescription runs only when the fee is due—either “(a) on completion of the work; or (b) at the time it was suspended, after a decision clearly communicated to [the engineers]” (i.e., when they learn their services are no longer required / contract terminated, making it possible to claim and calculate the fee).
BaselineA: Combination: Civil Code art. 2260(6) (five-year prescription) + general principles of bilateral contracts (payment not demandable until performance/delivery) + Tariff of fee for Professional Engineers of the Province of Quebec (O.C. 891, Sept. 4, 1957) adopted under s. 4(2) of the Professional Engineers’ Act (R.S.Q. 1941, c. 270).
CaseB_TestB: Discretionary test for enforcing foreign letters rogatory under Canada Evidence Act s. 43: even if statutory/regulatory bars are uncertain, a court “may, in its or his discretion” refuse enforcement where doing so would run counter to Canadian public policy/sovereignty; and “it is not for a Court…to take issue with the government’s determination of public policy or to measure its impact.”
BaselineB: Statute conferring discretion: Canada Evidence Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-10, s. 43 (court “may, in its or his discretion” order examination/production). The decision also considers the Uranium Information Security Regulations (C.R.C., c. 366) made under Atomic Energy Control Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. A-19, s. 9, but proceeds on the basis that even if invalid, discretion may still be exercised to refuse enforcement on public policy grounds.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “nude” in Criminal Code s. 170: complete nudity is captured without needing proof it offended public decency/order; s. 170(2) is a deeming (enlarging) provision for being “so clad as to offend against public decency or order”
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, s. 170(1)(a) and s. 170(2); interpreted as a deeming provision akin to former s. 205A)
CaseB_TestB: When Crown improperly “splits its case” by adducing reply evidence that raises new issues/attacks credibility, the curative proviso in Criminal Code s. 613(1)(b)(iii) cannot be applied because the appellate court cannot realistically assess the residual case after extracting the improper evidence
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, s. 613(1)(b)(iii) curative proviso; applied to trial error involving reply evidence/splitting the Crown’s case)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “nude” in Criminal Code s. 170: complete nudity is captured without needing proof it offended public decency/order; s. 170(2) is a deeming (enlarging) provision so that “a person is nude who is so clad as to offend against public decency or order” means “shall be deemed to be” nude when clothed offensively, while “nude” otherwise retains its ordinary meaning of “completely bare”.
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, s. 170(1)(a) and s. 170(2); interpreted as a deeming provision akin to former s. 205A).
CaseB_TestB: Availability of certiorari in criminal proceedings: for parties, certiorari lies only for a provincial court judge’s jurisdictional error (not mere legal error); jurisdictional errors occur where the court fails to observe a mandatory statutory provision or acts in breach of natural justice.
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law (Criminal Code, s. 674 general bar on interlocutory appeals; common-law limits on certiorari and definition of “jurisdictional error” drawn from cases such as Skogman, Patterson, Forsythe, Dubois, Deschamplain).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Workmen’s Compensation Act third-party recovery/subrogation where the worker was contributorily at fault: the dependant cannot claim an “additional sum” under s. 8 if the Commission’s compensation already equals/exceeds the dependant’s reduced civil claim (e.g., reduced to 50% under art. 1056 C.C.)
BaselineA: Statute + Civil Code (Workmen’s Compensation Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 159, ss. 7(3) (subrogation pleno jure) and 8 (additional sum); Civil Code arts. 1056 (wrongful death damages reduced for victim fault) and 1157 (partial payment/subrogation priority))
CaseB_TestB: Employee salary-guarantee/termination contract interpretation: employer’s obligation to pay depends on the employee being “available and willing to provide the services”; signing to play for another club is a breach that frees the employer from further payment
BaselineB: Common law contract principles applied to the parties’ written contract terms (including termination and “guaranteed” salary clauses)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Workmen’s compensation subrogation/“additional sum” test where victim partly at fault: the dependant can claim an “additional sum” under s. 8 only if the compensation received is less than the dependant’s reduced civil claim; if compensation meets/exceeds that reduced claim, the Commission is subrogated pleno jure to the full amount paid and the dependant gets nothing further.
BaselineA: Statute + Civil Code (Workmen’s Compensation Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 159, ss. 7(3), 8; Civil Code art. 1157; with the dependant’s underlying delict claim under Civil Code art. 1056 reduced for contributory fault per SCC jurisprudence).
CaseB_TestB: Institutional financial security trigger for judicial independence: any government measure affecting judges’ remuneration conditions (including benefits like supernumerary status) must be preceded by an “independent, effective and objective” commission process; if recommendations are ignored, the government must justify that decision on a “simple rationality test”.
BaselineB: Constitution + Charter doctrine (s. 11(d) Charter; Preamble to Constitution Act, 1867) as developed in Valente v. The Queen and the Provincial Court Judges Reference (Reference re Remuneration of Judges of the Provincial Court of Prince Edward Island).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Suspensive effect on an inferior criminal court’s power when served with a prohibition/quash application endorsed with a Rule 7 command to “return forthwith” (Ontario Criminal Rules 4-8): service (with the return command) suspends further steps until the superior court disposes of the application; non-return cannot improve the inferior court’s position
BaselineA: Statute and rules: Ontario Criminal Rules 4-8 (esp. Rules 6-8) and Criminal Code, s. 714; informed by common law certiorari suspension principle discussed in the reasons
CaseB_TestB: Section 15(1) equality analysis (La Forest J. majority): (1) distinction; (2) disadvantage (burden/withheld benefit); (3) whether the distinction is based on an enumerated/analogous ground and is an “irrelevant personal characteristic” assessed by “relevancy to the functional values underlying the law” in its larger context
BaselineB: Constitutional (Charter): Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 15(1) (and s. 1 in the background); framework drawn from Andrews v. Law Society of British Columbia and Miron v. Trudel as cited in the reasons
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Fair comment defence requires proof that the defamatory comment was the honest expression of the real opinion of the writer/publisher; absent evidence of honest belief, the defence should not go to the jury
BaselineA: Common law (defamation: fair comment defence)
CaseB_TestB: Section 2(a) infringement threshold for indirect burdens: state action that increases the cost of practising religion infringes only if the burden is non-trivial (not 'trivial or insubstantial'); then apply Oakes s. 1 proportionality (pressing and substantial objective; proportional means including minimal impairment)
BaselineB: Constitution/Charter (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms ss. 2(a) and 1; Oakes framework for s. 1)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Fair comment requires proof that the defamatory comment was an honest expression of the real opinion of the writer/publisher (each publisher stands in the writer’s shoes); absent evidence of the writers’ honest belief (and with the newspaper’s denial of belief), the defence is not left to the jury
BaselineA: Common law (defamation—fair comment), drawing on authorities including Turner v. Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer Pictures Ltd. and Silkin v. Beaverbrook Newspapers Ltd. (as discussed in the reasons)
JudgeA: Ritchie J. (with concurrence noted by Laskin C.J., Pigeon and Pratte JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Contempt of court: the alleging party must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the alleged contemnor had personal service or actual personal knowledge of the order; service on a solicitor does not, without supporting circumstances, establish actual knowledge for ministers, and vicarious liability does not apply
BaselineB: Common law contempt requirements (personal service/actual knowledge) plus interpretation of Federal Court Rules (C.R.C. 1978, c. 663, rr. 308, 311, 355) as not altering contempt’s knowledge element
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Fair comment in defamation requires proof that the impugned comment was an honest expression of the real opinion of the writer/publisher; absent evidence of the writers’ honest belief (and with the newspaper’s denial of belief), the defence cannot go to the jury
BaselineA: Common law defence of fair comment in defamation (as described via authorities cited in the reasons, including Turner v. Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer Pictures Ltd. and Jones v. Skelton; also discussed with reference to Gatley and Salmond)
CaseB_TestB: Garofoli review of wiretap authorizations: errors in the ITO are only factors and do not automatically vitiate; after excising tainted material, ask whether sufficient reliable, independently verifiable information remains on which an authorization could reasonably be based
BaselineB: Common law framework from R. v. Garofoli governing review/setting aside of wiretap authorizations (Criminal Code wiretap regime applied through Garofoli)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Intra vires test for CRTC regulations under Broadcasting Act s. 16: validity "must ... be tested by determining whether the regulation deals with a class of subject referred to in s. 3" (i.e., made "in furtherance of its objects" implementing the s. 3 broadcasting policy).
BaselineA: Statute (Broadcasting Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. B-11, ss. 3, 15, 16; applied to CRTC regulation: Radio (A.M.) Broadcasting Regulations, s. 5(1)(k)).
CaseB_TestB: Quasi-delict (art. 1053 C.C.) assessed by the "prudent and reasonable man" standard: whether conduct was that of "a reasonable person concerned about the interests of others and placed in the same external situation"; jury verdict stands unless "unreasonable" (C.C.P. art. 380).
BaselineB: Statute/civil law (Civil Code art. 1053; Code of Civil Procedure arts. 363, 380; with supporting jurisprudence including Metropolitan Railway Co. v. Jackson (1877) as cited).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Limits on a provincial commission of inquiry’s coercive powers vis-à-vis federal institutions/Crown: province may inquire into specific criminal acts by RCMP members as part of “administration of justice”, but cannot (directly or indirectly) inquire into RCMP administration/management; and a s. 41(2) Federal Court Act national-security certificate is binding on a commissioner (not a superior court) so production “shall be refused without any examination”.
BaselineA: Combination: Constitution (B.N.A. Act ss. 91, 92; esp. s. 92(14) “administration of justice” vs federal jurisdiction), statute (Federal Court Act, R.S.C. 1970 (2nd Supp.), c. 10, s. 41(1)-(2); Quebec Public Inquiry Commission Act, s. 7; C.C.P. arts. 846-850), and common law Crown prerogative/privilege (incl. Crown not compellable for discovery). Key prior SCC baselines cited: Di Iorio v. Warden of the Montreal Jail; Faber v. The Queen; Her Majesty in right of Alberta v. C.T.C.; Quebec North Shore Paper v. C.P. Ltd.
CaseB_TestB: Contested custody (natural parent vs prospective adoptive parents): under parens patriae/equity preserved by statute, the court “must consider the welfare of the child the predominant factor” and decide it on “all relevant factors” (including “psychological, spiritual and emotional welfare”); parental claims are considered but “must be set aside where the welfare of the child requires it”.
BaselineB: Combination: statute (Domestic Relations Ordinance, R.O.N.W.T. 1974, c. D-9, ss. 28(1), 35(2), 37, and especially s. 39 preserving equity) and equitable common law/parens patriae custody principles (discussing the “trilogy” Re Baby Duffell; Hepton v. Maat; Re Agar; and applying Re Moores and Feldstein; also relying on Beson and Racine).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Public Authorities Protection Act s. 11 applicability: whether the impugned act/omission falls within a "statutory or other public duty or authority" by classifying the statutory power/duty as having a "public aspect or connotation" versus being "private executive/administrative" or "subordinate or incidental" (operational/managerial) in nature
BaselineA: Statute: The Public Authorities Protection Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 374, s. 11 (as amended), interpreted in relation to The Housing Development Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 213, s. 6(2); with interpretive support from Bradford Corporation v. Myers and McGonegal v. Gray (as discussed in the reasons)
CaseB_TestB: Non-delegable statutory duty under the Indian Act: a non-delegable duty exists only if the statute’s language clearly imposes it; permissive "may" language and express power to contract with religious organizations indicate no mandatory non-delegable duty
BaselineB: Statute: Indian Act, S.C. 1951, c. 29, ss. 113-114 (and related context), applying the approach to non-delegable statutory duty referenced to E.D.G. v. Hammer and Lewis (Guardian ad litem of) v. British Columbia
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Exemption-from-seizure via insurance policy clause: only effective for a “true beneficiary” (a third party), not for a universal legatee/heir; therefore art. 553(3) C.C.P. cannot be invoked by the heir
BaselineA: Statute/civil code provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, art. 553(3) (exemption from seizure for property declared by donor/testator to be exempt); Civil Code (Quebec), arts. 597 (heir not a third party), 1028 (contract binds heirs/legal representatives), 735 (cannot bequeath property to protect from creditors). Also considers insurance-policy exemption clause and distinguishes stipulation for third party benefit.
CaseB_TestB: No-fault liability for neighbourhood disturbances under art. 976 C.C.Q.: liability turns on whether neighbours suffered “abnormal or excessive annoyances” beyond the “limit of tolerance” (result-focused, not conduct/fault-focused)
BaselineB: Statute: Civil Code of Québec, art. 976 ("Neighbours shall suffer the normal neighbourhood annoyances that are not beyond the limit of tolerance..."). The Court situates this alongside (but distinct from) fault-based liability under arts. 1457 and 7 C.C.Q.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Superior Court residual jurisdiction test in face of a specialized federal tribunal: a provincial superior court retains jurisdiction under art. 31 C.C.P. unless a “specific provision of law” assigns the matter “exclusively” elsewhere; the court may decide the meaning of Bell Act s. 5(4) when it arises in a properly brought tort/injunction action (no clear statutory indication of exclusive Commission jurisdiction).
BaselineA: Statute (Quebec Code of Civil Procedure art. 31; An Act respecting The Bell Telephone Company of Canada, s. 5(4)-(6) as substituted by 1967-68 (Can.), c. 48, s. 6; National Transportation Act, s. 45(1))
CaseB_TestB: Test governing whether the Crown may reopen its case: the “keystone principle” is whether the accused will be prejudiced in the defence; discretion narrows by trial stage—(1) before Crown closes: broad latitude; (2) after Crown closes but before defence elects: reopening to correct an “oversight or inadvertent omission” if “justice requires it” and “no prejudice”; (3) after defence has started to answer: discretion “very restricted” and reopening only in the “narrowest or most exceptional of circumstances” (e.g., defence contributed to omission or a matter of form).
BaselineB: Common law discretion on reopening (as discussed through cases including Robillard v. The Queen, Kishen Singh, etc.), informed by Charter self-incrimination principles (ss. 7, 11(c), 13)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Admissibility of cross-examining an accused on juvenile delinquencies as “convictions” under s. 12 Canada Evidence Act (and related proof by admission): “The word 'offence' as used in s. 12(1) ... includes a delinquency consisting in a violation of the Criminal Code ... and a finding of delinquency under this Act is equivalent to a conviction within the meaning of s. 12”; and an admitted conviction “does not need to be otherwise proven ... except possibly in exceptional circumstances showing clearly that the admission was made in error.”
BaselineA: Statute: Canada Evidence Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-10, s. 12(1)-(2); Juvenile Delinquents Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. J-3 (esp. ss. 2(1), 3, 20(1)); also discussed: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 593.
CaseB_TestB: Criminal Code indictment amendment for variance in a particular: under s. 529(4)-(5), the court’s key question is whether amendment would prejudice the accused—i.e., consider “whether the accused has been misled or prejudiced in his defence” and “whether ... the proposed amendment can be made without injustice”; if no prejudice, the indictment may be amended (including on appeal under s. 613(1)(b)(i) and (3)).
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 529(4)-(5), 613(1)(b)(i), 613(3); applied in context of Narcotic Control Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. N-1, ss. 2, 4 and Schedule item 3.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Coopers & Lybrand criteria for when an administrative decision/order is required by law to be made on a judicial or quasi-judicial basis (and thus reviewable under Federal Court Act s. 28): (1) whether the statutory language/context suggests a hearing; (2) whether the decision affects rights/obligations; (3) whether an adversary process is involved; (4) whether there is an obligation to apply substantive rules to many individual cases (vs broad policy). These are "factors to be weighed and evaluated, no one of which is necessarily determinative."
BaselineA: Statute (Federal Court Act, s. 28; definition in s. 2) interpreted using common-law/natural justice jurisprudence (e.g., Guay v. Lafleur; Russell v. Duke of Norfolk; Durayappah v. Fernando).
CaseB_TestB: Stillman s. 24(2) trial-fairness framework: classify Charter-breached evidence as "conscriptive" vs "non-conscriptive"; if conscriptive, ask whether Crown proves on a balance of probabilities it would have been discovered by alternative non-conscriptive means (independent source or inevitable discovery). If conscriptive and not discoverable, admission renders trial unfair and evidence is excluded "as a general rule" without weighing other Collins factors.
BaselineB: Statute (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 24(2)) building on prior SCC framework in R. v. Collins and related cases (e.g., Black, Colarusso, Burlingham).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory limits on interim rate-setting under s. 31 Gas Utilities Act: the Board cannot (absent s. 31) set rates to recover pre-application revenue shortfalls; the proper inquiry is whether interim rates will "produce an amount in excess of the estimated total revenue requirements" for the period because they include "revenue shortfalls which have occurred prior to the date of the application" (and s. 31 "losses" means "loss of revenue" from delay, not accounting net loss).
BaselineA: Statute (Alberta): The Gas Utilities Act, R.S.A. 1970, c. 158, ss. 27-28, 31; The Administrative Procedures Act, R.S.A. 1970, c. 2, s. 8; The Public Utilities Board Act, R.S.A. 1970, c. 302, ss. 52(2), 62.
CaseB_TestB: Cuerrier fraud-vitiated consent test (HIV non-disclosure): consent under Criminal Code s. 265(3)(c) is vitiated where (1) dishonesty (including non-disclosure) related to obtaining consent is proven (objective reasonable-person assessment), and (2) the dishonesty results in deprivation by exposing the complainant to a "significant risk of serious bodily harm"; plus the Crown must prove the complainant would have refused unprotected sex if informed of HIV-positive status.
BaselineB: Statute (federal): Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, ss. 265(1)(a), 265(3)(c) ("fraud"), 268(1). (Interprets "fraud" using criminal fraud jurisprudence: R. v. Olan; R. v. Théroux; R. v. Zlatic, as discussed in the reasons.)
JudgeB: Cory J. (for Cory, Major, Bastarache and Binnie JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory interpretation of Parole Act revocation provisions: after the 1977 amendments, “parole” (including day parole) may be revoked under s. 10(1)(e) and s. 20, triggering the s. 20(2) sentence-calculation consequences (subject to s. 20(3) recredit discretion), rather than being limited to termination under s. 10(2).
BaselineA: Statute: Parole Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. P-2 (as amended in 1977), especially ss. 2 (definition of “parole” includes day parole), 10(1)(e) (Board may revoke parole), 10(2) (Board may terminate day parole), and 20(1)-(3) (recommitment and sentence calculation on revocation).
CaseB_TestB: Palmer criteria (same on sentence appeals as verdict appeals) for admitting fresh evidence on appeal: (1) due diligence (generally not admitted if could have been adduced at trial); (2) relevance; (3) credibility; (4) if believed, could reasonably, with the trial record, be expected to have affected the result.
BaselineB: Common law: Palmer v. The Queen, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 759 (fresh-evidence test), applied in the statutory context of Criminal Code ss. 683 and 687 (interests of justice / evidence on sentence appeal).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: SCC discretion under Supreme Court Act s. 52 to vary interest on an SCC judgment: default interest runs as it would on the trial judgment unless the Court orders otherwise; here, discretion exercised to limit pre-SCC interest to the trial award amount ($250,000) due to appellant-caused delay, with interest on full SCC award only from SCC reasons date
BaselineA: Statute: Supreme Court Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. S-19, s. 52 (as amended 1976) and Interest Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-18, ss. 13-14
CaseB_TestB: Whether procedural fairness/natural justice applies to Governor in Council decisions under National Transportation Act s. 64(1): on proper construction, s. 64(1) confers complete discretion (subject only to jurisdictional boundaries/conditions precedent), so no implied duty to hold a hearing, disclose materials, or give reasons
BaselineB: Statute: National Transportation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. N-17, s. 64(1) (contrasted with s. 64(2)); interpreted in light of common-law fairness/natural justice jurisprudence (e.g., Nicholson v. Haldimand-Norfolk, Martineau v. Matsqui Institution (No. 2))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory-limit rule for groundwater pumping: s. 37 defines reasonableness—“any pumping above 10,000 gallons a day is unreasonable unless a permit has been granted”; “any pumping in violation of s. 37 is to be considered as a nuisance when causing damage to other properties” and no “right to pump” is a defence for pumping exceeding the authorized quantity.
BaselineA: Statute (Ontario Water Resources Commission Act / Ontario Water Resources Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 332, s. 37; also discussed: s. 47 and Expropriations Act definition of “injurious affection”) plus pre-existing common law “English Rule” on percolating water (e.g., Langbrook Properties; St. John Y.M.C.A. v. Hutchison).
CaseB_TestB: Criteria for assessing solatium doloris (moral prejudice from death of a loved one): courts should consider, “inter alia: the circumstances of the death, the ages of the deceased and the parent, the nature and quality of the relationship between the deceased and the parent, the parent’s personality and ability to manage the emotional consequences of the death, and the effect of the death on the parent’s life … (presence of other children or the possibility of having others)”.
BaselineB: Civil Code of Lower Canada (arts. 1053, 1056) recognizing compensable moral prejudice; SCC also situates the assessment within civil-law restitutio in integrum principles.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Highway Code s. 13(6) irrebuttable presumption: if the registered owner has not complied with s. 13(1)-(2) on transfer, they are "deemed to be the owner" for "responsibility" and for "insurance against the responsibility" from ownership/use; therefore, for liability coverage the transfer is treated as not having occurred and the buyer/driver with the deemed-owner’s consent is covered by the omnibus clause.
BaselineA: Statute (Highway Code, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 231, s. 13(6), with compliance duties in s. 13(1)-(2))
CaseB_TestB: Garofoli leave (threshold) test for cross-examining the wiretap affiant: defence must show a "reasonable likelihood" that cross-examination "will elicit testimony of probative value" on a material issue for the reviewing judge (i.e., tending to undermine a statutory precondition/basis for the authorization).
BaselineB: Common law (R. v. Garofoli, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 1421), applied in the context of Criminal Code wiretap authorizations (including s. 184.2) and Charter s. 8 review
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Direct action under Highway Victims Indemnity Act s. 6: insurer is directly liable to third parties only for damage that is actually "covered by liability insurance"; s. 6 removes only nullity/lapse defences and "does not extend the insurance contract to what it does not cover"—coverage turns on the policy’s definition of "automobile" (including when a trailer is included/excluded) and whether the damage was caused "first and foremost" by the trailer’s use rather than the insured automobile’s use.
BaselineA: Statute (Highway Victims Indemnity Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 232, s. 6) interpreted alongside the insurance contract’s defined terms; guided by General Security Insurance Company of Canada v. Bélanger, [1977] 1 S.C.R. 802 (scope of s. 6 exception).
CaseB_TestB: Lease fire-loss/subrogation: a landlord’s covenant to insure against fire presumptively enures to the tenant’s benefit (barring insurer subrogation against the tenant for negligently caused fire) unless there is "another explanation" in the lease (here, the option-to-purchase provisions) that is consistent with leaving the fire-risk on the tenant; i.e., the covenant runs to the tenant "unless the option to purchase provisions ... provide a sufficient explanation" to the contrary.
BaselineB: Common law of landlord-tenant/contract interpretation and subrogation; built from SCC precedents Agnew-Surpass Shoe Stores Ltd. v. Cummer-Yonge Investments Ltd., [1976] 2 S.C.R. 221 and Ross Southward Tire Ltd. v. Pyrotech Products Ltd., [1976] 2 S.C.R. 35 (and distinguishing United Motors Service Inc. v. Hutson, [1937] S.C.R. 294).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Qualified privilege in defamation defeated only by malice; privilege protects even excessive language if the defendant "might have honestly and on reasonable grounds believed" it was true (Adam v. Ward / Netupsky v. Craig)
BaselineA: Common law (qualified privilege and malice), drawing on Adam v. Ward, [1917] A.C. 309 and Netupsky v. Craig, [1973] S.C.R. 55
CaseB_TestB: Sufficiency of reasons (Sheppard/Braich): two-stage inquiry—(1) are the reasons inadequate; (2) if so, do they prevent appellate review (i.e., are they not "sufficiently amenable to appellate review")?
BaselineB: Common law appellate review doctrine on reasons (R. v. Sheppard; R. v. Braich) in the context of Criminal Code, s. 686 appeals
JudgeB: Bastarache and Abella JJ. (LeBel J. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Fault for unlawful arrest by police: (1) coroner’s s. 38 warrant is invalid if used to detain a suspect (abuse of power), and officers’ legal error is no excuse; and/or (2) warrantless arrest requires “reasonable and probable grounds” that must “take into account all the information available” (police may disregard only what they have good reason to believe is unreliable).
BaselineA: Combination of statute and civil law: Civil Code arts. 1053, 1054 (fault and employer liability); Coroners' Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 29, s. 38; Criminal Code 1953-54, c. 51, s. 435 (warrantless arrest on reasonable and probable grounds).
CaseB_TestB: Validity of dismissal of a probationary constable: dismissal is ineffective unless made by the Board (exclusive, non-delegable statutory/contractual authority); Board must actually exercise its function (cannot silently ‘confirm’ without informing the constable or considering the case with notice).
BaselineB: Statute/regulation and collective agreement: The Police Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 351, s. 29; Regulation 680, s. 27(b); plus s. 9 of the collective agreement (probationary dismissal clause).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Municipal office disqualification for having a direct or indirect “interest” in a municipal contract (broad, non-technical meaning of “interested in” applied to directors/officers)
BaselineA: Statute (Moncton Consolidation Act, 1946 (N.B.), c. 101, s. 6; interpreted using Angrignon v. Bonnier, [1935] S.C.R. 38 and the remedial-interpretation direction in Interpretation Act, R.S.N.B. 1973, c. I-13, s. 17)
CaseB_TestB: Statutory interpretation of whether a municipality is an “institution” bound by OLA s. 22 (and scope of “oral or written pleadings”/“process”)
BaselineB: Statute (Official Languages Act, S.N.B. 2002, c. O-0.5, ss. 1 “institution”, 22; applied with the modern principle of statutory interpretation and the Bell ExpressVu ‘Charter values only if genuine ambiguity’ constraint)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Qualified privilege—threshold for leaving express malice to the jury: malice must be supported by evidence that "raises a probability of its existence" (i.e., "more consistent with its existence than with its non-existence"; more than a "mere scintilla").
BaselineA: Common law (defamation/qualified privilege), drawing on Somerville v. Hawkins (1851) and applied in SCC in Sun Life Assurance Co. of Canada v. Dalrymple (1965), with references to Adam v. Ward and Turner v. M-G-M Pictures.
CaseB_TestB: Blood Tribe clear-intent requirement for statutory abrogation of solicitor-client privilege: only where "legislative language evinces a clear intent" to abrogate privilege may a court find the statute does so; here s. 232(1) ITA is "unequivocal" in excluding "an accounting record of a lawyer".
BaselineB: Statute (Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), ss. 231.2(1), 231.7(1), and definition in s. 232(1) "solicitor-client privilege"), interpreted using the Blood Tribe interpretive principle.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Priority of B.C. Payment of Wages Act s. 5A lien: lien arises "from the date wages were earned" and takes priority only over dispositions after it attaches; pre-existing mortgages are not affected, so the lien "will only attach to the employer’s equity" in the property
BaselineA: Statute — Payment of Wages Act, 1962 (B.C.), c. 45, ss. 5 and 5A (especially s. 5A(1)-(2))
CaseB_TestB: Forced dissolution of a Quebec legal person under the C.C.Q.: where no special statutory scheme applies, the C.C.Q. dissolution provisions apply suppletively to fill gaps (art. 334/300), and dissolution may be ordered if one of art. 355(2)’s grounds is met (e.g., "impossibility of accomplishing" the object or "some other legitimate cause")
BaselineB: Statute/Civil code — Civil Code of Québec, arts. 300, 334, 355 (and related arts. 355-364); considered alongside Companies Act (Quebec) and Code of Civil Procedure art. 829
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Residual discretion/inherent jurisdiction to remedy unfairness from Crown’s closing address: (1) usually by curative jury instruction; (2) in rare cases, grant a limited defence reply only in the clearest cases of unfairness (e.g., Crown dramatically changes/adds a substantive theory in closing or misleads defence), with reply confined to the improper issues
BaselineA: Combination: statute (Criminal Code, s. 651(3)-(4)) plus common law inherent jurisdiction to control process and ensure trial fairness
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 11(d) validity of a statutory presumption: a presumption is constitutional only if proof of the substituted fact leads “inexorably” (i.e., necessarily in all cases) to the essential element it replaces; otherwise it violates the presumption of innocence
BaselineB: Combination: statute (Criminal Code, s. 172.1(3)) interpreted under Charter s. 11(d), with the SCC’s prior presumption jurisprudence (Whyte; Downey; Audet) supplying the “inexorable connection” requirement
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Adjudicator’s remedial authority to substitute a lesser penalty for discharge where there is “just and sufficient cause” for some discipline but not for discharge (discipline as a continuum under PSLRA s. 92(1)(b))
BaselineA: Statute and collective agreement: Public Service Labour Relations Act, R.S.N.B. 1973, c. P-25, ss. 92(1)(b), 101; collective agreement art. V(d) (“Discipline, suspension, demotion or discharge ... shall be for just and sufficient cause”) and art. XVII(c). Prior SCC baseline discussed/distinguished: Port Arthur Shipbuilding Co. v. Arthurs, [1969] S.C.R. 85.
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 24(2) exclusion test (Collins guidelines): whether, “having regard to all the circumstances”, admission of evidence obtained via a Charter breach “would bring the administration of justice into disrepute”
BaselineB: Statute/constitutional text and common law framework: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 24(2) (and assumed s. 8 breach); applied framework from R. v. Collins, [1987] 1 S.C.R. 265.
JudgeB: Lamer J. (for Dickson C.J. and Lamer, Wilson, Le Dain and La Forest JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Will-construction test: give effect to the testator’s overriding intention on a fair reading of the clause, so that administrative/boilerplate provisions cannot defeat a clearly expressed intention (legacy payable on disposition of the business ‘however that disposition was made’).
BaselineA: Common law (will construction/ascertaining testator’s intention from the will read as a whole; no specific statutory provision identified in the reasons).
CaseB_TestB: Manslaughter legal causation with intervening acts: even where a novus actus is alleged, the test remains whether the accused’s dangerous and unlawful acts were a ‘significant contributing cause of death’; foreseeability and ‘independent act’ are non-determinative analytical aids.
BaselineB: Common law causation test from Smithers v. The Queen (contributing cause beyond de minimis) as confirmed/expressed in R. v. Nette (legal causation as moral/imputable responsibility), applied in the context of Criminal Code ss. 222, 224, 225.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Functional/operational test for whether labour relations fall under the federal exception: exclusive federal jurisdiction exists only where labour relations are an integral part of a federal undertaking; otherwise provincial jurisdiction is the rule (Indian ownership/location/funding do not change the operational nature of the business).
BaselineA: Common law constitutional division-of-powers doctrine for labour relations (functional test; “integral part” principle from the Stevedoring case and related jurisprudence).
CaseB_TestB: Section 15(1) Charter equality test (Withler/Kapp): (1) Does the law create a distinction based on an enumerated or analogous ground? (2) Does the distinction create a disadvantage by perpetuating prejudice or stereotyping? No need to identify a “mirror comparator group”.
BaselineB: Common law Charter s. 15(1) framework from Andrews, Law, and Kapp (two-step discrimination inquiry).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Bankruptcy Act s. 107(1)(j) override: Crown tax claims (not otherwise listed) rank pari passu in bankruptcy “notwithstanding any statutory preference to the contrary”, so a provincially created/registered tax “privilege” cannot elevate the Crown to secured-creditor priority to escape s. 107(1)(j).
BaselineA: Statute (Bankruptcy Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. B-3, ss. 2 and 107(1)(j), (3)) interpreting interaction with provincial tax “privilege” (Retail Sales Tax Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 71, s. 30; Civil Code art. 1989).
JudgeA: Pigeon J. (for Martland, Ritchie, Pigeon, Beetz, Pratte and McIntyre JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Public interest standing (purposive, flexible 3-factor approach): (1) serious justiciable issue; (2) plaintiff has a real stake/genuine interest/engagement; and (3) the proposed suit is, “in all of the circumstances”, a “reasonable and effective means” to bring the issue to court (not a strict ‘no other way’ requirement), assessed with discretionary considerations (judicial economy, adversarial suitability, legality, realistic alternatives, etc.).
BaselineB: Common law doctrine of public interest standing (as articulated in Borowski; Finlay; Canadian Council of Churches; Hy and Zel’s; Thorson; McNeil).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Crown prerogative priority applies only where Crown and subject claims are “of equal degree”; a prior registered second/collateral mortgage is of a higher degree than a later registered Crown judgment, so Registry Act registration-date priorities govern
BaselineA: Combination: common law Crown prerogative priority for debts “of equal degree” (The Queen v. Bank of Nova Scotia (1885), 11 S.C.R. 1) plus Nova Scotia Registry Act, R.S.N.S. 1967, c. 265, ss. 17-18 (and related civil procedure distribution rule 47.11)
CaseB_TestB: International jurisdiction by extension of domestic territorial jurisdiction: under art. 71 C.C.P., an incidental action in warranty “must be taken before the court in which the principal action is pending”, with no limitation, and this applies to a foreign (alien) defendant
BaselineB: Statute/civil law: Code of Civil Procedure (Quebec), art. 71 (and discussion of art. 75); Civil Code, art. 27; plus the private international law principle that international jurisdiction is determined by extending domestic territorial jurisdiction rules (as recognized in Alimport and Trower)
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “detained” under Canadian Bill of Rights s. 2(c): “detain”/“detention” “connote some form of compulsory restraint” and contemplate a person “detained by due process of law” (habeas corpus context); absent such custody/restraint, no Bill of Rights right-to-counsel trigger and thus no “reasonable excuse” to refuse a roadside breath demand
BaselineA: Statute: Canadian Bill of Rights, 1960 (Can.), c. 44, s. 2(c)(ii)-(iii), applied to Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 234.1(1)-(2) (roadside breath demand/refusal “without reasonable excuse”); informed by prior cases discussed in the reasons (e.g., Brownridge v. The Queen; Hogan v. The Queen)
CaseB_TestB: Two-branch test for the tort of civil conspiracy: liability exists (1) where “the predominant purpose of the defendants’ conduct is to cause injury to the plaintiff” (means lawful or unlawful); or (2) where “the conduct of the defendants is unlawful”, is “directed towards the plaintiff (alone or together with others)”, and defendants “should know in the circumstances that injury to the plaintiff is likely to and does result” (constructive intent), with actual damage required
BaselineB: Common law tort of conspiracy to injure, as discussed through authorities in the reasons (including Lonrho Ltd. v. Shell Petroleum Co. Ltd.; Crofter Hand Woven Harris Tweed Co. v. Veitch; Sorrell v. Smith; and SCC cases such as Gagnon v. Foundation Maritime Limited)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 492 re-election validity test: effective re-election occurs where the accused (1) gives notice to the sheriff of a desire to re-elect (s. 492(1)); (2) attends at the time/place fixed (s. 492(2)-(3)); and (3) after the charge is read, makes the re-election (which may be done through counsel in the accused’s presence). SCC also interprets s. 492(3) as requiring the accused to hear the actual charge faced at trial (the preferred indictment), and holds failure to prefer a new Form 4 indictment under s. 496 after re-election does not invalidate proceedings where the indictment is already in Form 4.
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, s. 492 (re-election procedure) and related s. 496 (Form 4 indictment after re-election).
CaseB_TestB: Injurious affection (no land taken) — Loiselle four conditions, with actionable-at-common-law requirement assessed via nuisance: claimant must satisfy (1) damage results from an act rendered lawful by statutory powers; (2) damage would have been actionable at common law but for statutory powers; (3) injury is to the land itself (not personal/business); and (4) damage is occasioned by construction, not use. For (2), nuisance turns on whether there is physical injury to land or a substantial interference with use/enjoyment that is unreasonable “in the light of all the surrounding circumstances” (reasonable user/balancing).
BaselineB: Statute plus common law: Expropriations Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 154, ss. 1(e)(ii), 21, incorporating the common-law actionability requirement; baseline four-part test from The Queen v. Loiselle, [1962] S.C.R. 624.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Scope of Ontario Municipal Board jurisdiction under s. 137(1): s. 14(11)(a),(b),(d) Municipal Act is incorporated only as those clauses (without the introductory limitation to annexation/amalgamation orders), so the Board may adjust assets/liabilities (as it considers equitable) “in relation to the dissolution of the County of Carleton”.
BaselineA: Statute: The Regional Municipality of Ottawa-Carleton Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 407, ss. 135-137, incorporating The Municipal Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 284, s. 14(11)(a),(b),(d) (notably: Board may “make all such adjustments of assets and liabilities... as the Board may consider equitable”).
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 7/11(d) minimum mens rea for murder: “a conviction for murder cannot rest on anything less than proof beyond a reasonable doubt of subjective foresight of death”; therefore s. 213(a) (constructive murder) is unconstitutional because it removes the Crown’s burden to prove subjective foresight of death.
