BaselineB: Combination: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 7 and 11(d), applied to Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 213(a); built on SCC precedent R. v. Vaillancourt, [1987] 2 S.C.R. 636 (objective foreseeability as constitutional minimum, with Martineau adopting subjective foresight as required).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Validity of consent to intercept a private communication under Criminal Code s. 178.11(2)(a): consent must be "voluntary (i.e. free from coercion)" and "made knowingly, with an awareness of the significance of the consent"; promises/expected leniency do not by themselves amount to coercion, and consent is valid if it is the "conscious act" of the consenter and "not under external coercion".
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, Part IV.1 as enacted by the Protection of Privacy Act): ss. 178.1 (definition of private communication), 178.11(2)(a) (consent interception), 178.16(1)(a) (admissibility if interception "lawfully made").
JudgeA: McIntyre J. (for Martland, Ritchie, Pigeon, Dickson, Beetz, Estey, Pratte and McIntyre JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Proof that hate speech targeted the identifiable group particularized in the information (s. 319(2)): the trial judge must consider the "totality of the evidence" to decide whether the statements "as a matter of fact, promoted hatred" of the particularized group; it is "not necessary" to prove strict "interchangeability" between the hateful term used (e.g., "gypsies") and the group name ("Roma").
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code): s. 319(2) (wilful promotion of hatred) and s. 318(4) (definition of identifiable group), with interpretive context from Keegstra on the offence’s elements.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Audi alteram partem / no ex parte evidence rule for appellate tribunals: unless expressly or by necessary implication empowered to act ex parte, a tribunal must not hear evidence or receive representations from one side “behind the back of the other”; the affected party must know the case and have a fair opportunity to correct or contradict, and the court need not find actual prejudice—“it is sufficient if it might have done so”.
BaselineA: Common law (procedural fairness / natural justice), applied in a statutory university appeal context (Universities Act, 1974 (B.C.), ss. 58(1)-(3), 61) but not displaced by it.
CaseB_TestB: Workers’ compensation occupational-disease causation under s. 250(4): (i) apply the “evenly weighted” evidence rule—if evidence on causation is evenly weighted, resolve “in a manner that favours the worker”; and (ii) causation may be inferred from other (including circumstantial) evidence—“even in the face of inconclusive or contrary expert evidence”—and is not determined by the mere presence/absence of expert opinion evidence.
BaselineB: Statute and policy: Workers Compensation Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 492, ss. 6 and 250(4) (and s. 250(2) requiring application of Board policy), plus RSCM II policy defining “causative significance” and explaining s. 250(4).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Appellate intervention in damages: an appellate court may not substitute its own figure unless a wrong principle of law was applied or the overall award is a wholly erroneous estimate of damages (Andrews v. Grand & Toy).
BaselineA: Common law (as stated in Andrews et al. v. Grand & Toy Alberta Ltd. et al., [1978] 2 S.C.R. 229, at p. 235).
JudgeA: Martland J. (for the Court, oral reasons)
CaseB_TestB: Videotape-only identification: once it is established the videotape has not been altered/changed and depicts the crime, it is admissible; identity may be proven on the videotape alone if the trier of fact, considering clarity/quality (and to a lesser extent time depicted), is satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt it identifies the accused (no corroboration required).
BaselineB: Common law evidence principles (building on R. v. Leaney, [1989] 2 S.C.R. 393, and general admissibility/authenticity concepts for real evidence).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Quebec Labour Code s. 16 rebuttal/jurisdiction test: employer rebuts the s. 16 presumption only by showing the “other” reason is “of a substantial nature and not a pretext” and is the “true reason” (causa causans) for dismissal; the commissioner/Labour Court cannot assess the proportionality or “severity of the penalty” once a real, serious reason is established
BaselineA: Statute (Quebec Labour Code, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 141 as am., ss. 13-16, especially s. 16 “another good and sufficient reason”; also discussed in relation to s. 14). The Court adopts the longstanding administrative/labour jurisprudence interpretation (e.g., Maresq et Brown Bovari; L’Industrielle v. Nadeau) that the inquiry is limited to sincerity/true reason, not penalty severity.
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 12 “gross disproportionality” test (and its application to mandatory minimums): assess whether punishment is “so excessive as to outrage standards of decency” / “grossly disproportionate”, considering “the gravity of the offence, the personal characteristics of the offender and the particular circumstances of the case”; plus a two-aspect approach—(1) as applied to the actual offender, and if no breach, (2) whether the law is unconstitutional in “reasonable hypothetical circumstances” (not “far-fetched or marginally imaginable”)
BaselineB: Combination: Constitutional text (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 12) applied to statute (Motor Vehicle Act, R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 288, s. 88(1)(c) in application to s. 88(1)(a) and s. 86(1)(a)(ii)). The governing s. 12 test is taken from SCC precedent R. v. Smith and reaffirmed in Lyons and Luxton.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Summary conviction appeal costs—courts’ discretion to order the Crown to pay costs under Criminal Code ss. 758 and 771(3) (binding on Her Majesty by contextual statutory interpretation)
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, Part XXIV; plus Interpretation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-23, s. 16)
CaseB_TestB: Mortgage prepayment under Interest Act s. 10(1) in renewal contexts—five-year prepayment right applies at end of each five-year period; renewal with a “deemed date” and term ≤ 5 years defers prepayment until end of renewal; no enforceable contracting-out of the statutory right
BaselineB: Statute (Interest Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-18, s. 10(1), (2); also Manitoba Mortgage Act s. 20(6), (7))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Wrongful dismissal damages: no deduction for (i) income tax not payable and (ii) unemployment insurance benefits arising from the employment contract (collateral benefits rule as applied to UI)
BaselineA: Common law contract damages for wrongful dismissal (mitigation/collateral benefits), with discussion of Income Tax Act (R.S.C. 1952, ss. 3, 5, 25) only to reject an income-tax deduction premise
CaseB_TestB: Identification of Criminals Act s. 2 applies to juveniles: a juvenile in lawful custody for a delinquency relating to a Criminal Code indictable offence is 'charged with'/'under conviction of' an indictable offence, so necessary reasonable force may be used to fingerprint
BaselineB: Statute: Identification of Criminals Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-1, s. 2(1)-(2), interpreted alongside the Juvenile Delinquents Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. J-3 (as informed by Morris v. The Queen, [1979] 1 S.C.R. 405)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: “Air of reality / sense of reality” threshold for whether a trial judge must leave a defence (here, mistake of fact as to consent) with the jury: there must be “in the record some evidence which would convey a sense of reality in the submission”; for mistake of fact as to consent, “there must be some evidence which, if believed, would support the existence of a mistaken but honest belief” in consent (and not merely counsel’s assertion).
BaselineA: Common law (jury-charge duty / leaving defences to the jury), drawing the “sense of reality” formulation from Kelsey v. The Queen and applied as in R. v. Workman and Huculak; applied in the context of rape under Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 143.
CaseB_TestB: Section 11(b) “reasonable time” analysis (Morin factors) and its application to appellate delay: the s. 11(b) principles are “(1) the length of the delay; (2) waiver, if any, of parts of the delay; (3) the reasons for the delay; and (4) prejudice to the subject of the criminal process.”
BaselineB: Constitutional (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 11(b); framework as articulated in R. v. Morin).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Presumption of reasonableness for an administrative decision-maker interpreting its home statute, rebutted only by Dunsmuir correctness categories (statutory appeal is not a new correctness category)
BaselineA: Common law (standard of review framework from Dunsmuir v. New Brunswick and subsequent SCC cases)
CaseB_TestB: Framework for Crown sui generis fiduciary duty: duty arises from Crown discretionary control over a specific/cognizable Aboriginal interest; breach assessed by whether Crown met fiduciary standard of conduct (loyalty/good faith/full disclosure/ordinary prudence), not by achieving a particular result
BaselineB: Common law fiduciary law (as applied in Wewaykum Indian Band v. Canada; Guerin v. The Queen; Haida Nation; Manitoba Metis Federation) plus statutory specific-claims context (Specific Claims Tribunal Act, s. 14(1)(b), (c))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Necessarily incidental doctrine for federalism: where legislation is prima facie provincial (property and civil rights), it is valid federally only if it is "necessarily incidental to effective legislation" on an enumerated federal head (here, s. 91(12) fisheries); s. 33(3) fails because it is a "blanket prohibition" with "no attempt to link the proscribed conduct to actual or potential harm to fisheries"
BaselineA: Common law constitutional doctrine (division of powers) grounded in B.N.A. Act, 1867 ss. 91(12) and 92(13), drawing on Lord Tomlin’s proposition (3) in Attorney-General for Canada v. Attorney-General for British Columbia, [1930] A.C. 111
CaseB_TestB: Colour of right in theft: the defence turns on whether the jury is satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused did NOT have, at the time of the taking/transfer, an "honest belief that he had the right to that money" (not on what the jury thinks the accused’s legal rights actually were)
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code theft definition/defence language: "fraudulently and without colour of right"), applied in the context of ss. 283 and 294 (as referenced in the reasons)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “unlawful purpose” in Criminal Code conspiracy (s. 423(2)(a)): the purpose must be “contrary to law”, i.e., prohibited by federal or provincial legislation (not merely conduct that interferes with a statutory right unless that interference is itself prohibited).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 423(2)(a); with interpretive context including s. 8 excluding common law offences, and discussion of related provisions such as s. 381).
CaseB_TestB: Quebec defamation fault under art. 1457 C.C.Q.: fault is determined contextually, with the “guiding principle” that there is no fault unless the journalist/media “has fallen below professional standards”; truth and public interest are relevant but not determinative.
BaselineB: Statute/civil code (Civil Code of Québec, art. 1457; applied through prior Quebec defamation jurisprudence cited in the reasons, especially Société Radio-Canada v. Radio Sept-Îles Inc. and Prud’homme v. Prud’homme).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Rabey (majority) automatism/insanity classification: the central question is whether the accused’s automatism was caused by a “disease of the mind”, generally distinguished as a malfunctioning “primarily internal to the accused” versus a “transient effect produced by some specific external factor”; “ordinary stresses and disappointments of life” are not an external cause taking it out of disease of the mind.
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 16 (insanity/disease of the mind) applied alongside common law automatism/insanity authorities (e.g., Bratty v. A.G. Northern Ireland, R. v. K.).
CaseB_TestB: Mortgage clause conflict/supremacy test: where the mortgage clause says its terms “shall supersede any policy provisions in conflict therewith BUT ONLY TO THE INTEREST OF THE MORTGAGEE”, Statutory Condition 4 cannot be used to void mortgagee coverage if it conflicts with the mortgage clause (including where SC4 would void coverage for an unnotified “change material to the risk” but the mortgage clause keeps coverage in force “notwithstanding” mortgagor acts, including “any vacancy or non-occupancy”).
BaselineB: Statute and contract interpretation: Insurance Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. I.8, Part IV (Statutory Condition 4) interpreted in light of the policy’s standard mortgage clause and prior SCC guidance (National Bank of Greece (Canada) v. Katsikonouris).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Single-cause vs multiple-causes characterization for prescription: if claimed damages "result from a single cause of action" (breach of a contractual obligation), they are contractual and prescribe in 30 years; if they "result from several separate and independent causes of action", each head is characterized as contractual or delictual and prescribes accordingly (e.g., separate torts like "bomb threats" are prescribed).
BaselineA: Statute/civil code (Civil Code arts. 2242, 2261(2), plus related provisions) as interpreted through the contractual nature of voluntary-association by-laws and natural justice obligations (e.g., art. 1024).
CaseB_TestB: Priority between mechanic’s lien and mortgage where s. 14(1) does not apply: an unregistered lien has no general priority; when priorities are not otherwise prescribed, resort is to registration—under s. 20 the lien claimant on registration is "deemed to be a purchaser pro tanto"—so (absent actual notice) priority follows "priority of registration" under Registry Act ss. 69(1) and 70.
BaselineB: Statute (The Mechanics’ Lien Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 267, ss. 14(1), 20, 16, 21, 22) and The Registry Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 409, ss. 69(1), 70.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Accrued-rights on statutory repeal/amendment (Interpretation Act, s. 35(c)): if, on the eve of repeal, the claimant was "enjoying a right or a privilege which had accrued under the repealed enactment", the repeal does not "affect" it; read the amending Act "in the light of s. 35(c)" so accrued benefits continue, but only to the point the pre‑repeal disqualification would have ended them (here, pension-payable date).
BaselineA: Statute (Interpretation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-23, s. 35(c), applied to the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, s. 31 as amended by S.C. 1974-75-76, c. 80, s. 10; also considering Unemployment Insurance Act, s. 38 and Unemployment Insurance Entitlements Adjustment Act, 1976-77, c. 11, s. 2).
CaseB_TestB: Compellability of superior court judges before a provincial inquiry under the Public Inquiries Act: read ss. 3 and 4 together so the Commission’s power to "summon" does not exceed a superior court’s power to "compel"; because of judicial independence, judges have immunity from being compelled to testify about (1) "how and why" they reached a decision (adjudicative process) and (2) "why a particular judge sat on a particular case" (assignment/composition as an institutional independence matter).
BaselineB: Combination of statute and constitutional/common law principles (Public Inquiries Act, R.S.N.S. 1967, c. 250, ss. 3-4, interpreted in light of judicial independence/judicial immunity as discussed with reference to Valente v. The Queen and Beauregard v. Canada).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Interpretation of Motor Vehicle Transport Act, s. 3(2): provincial board may license extra-provincial undertakings “into or through” a province as including operations “in, across, into and out of the province”, and provincial enforcement (including seizure) is not displaced by MVTA s. 6
BaselineA: Statute (Motor Vehicle Transport Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. M-14, ss. 2, 3, 5, 6; incorporating provincial licensing/enforcement via The Public Service Vehicles Act, R.S.A. 1970, c. 300, incl. s. 58)
CaseB_TestB: Charter standing/scope test for s. 12: a claimant (including a corporation) must show an interest within the scope and purpose of the guarantee; s. 12’s protection against “cruel and unusual treatment or punishment” is limited to human beings (corporations cannot claim s. 12)
BaselineB: Constitution (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 12) interpreted purposively (Big M Drug Mart framework; CIP Inc. scope/purpose requirement)
JudgeB: Brown and Rowe JJ. (Wagner C.J. and Moldaver and Côté JJ. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Fundamental breach and exclusionary clause: whether the exclusion/waiver clause remains applicable is determined by the “true construction of the contract” (not an automatic rule that fundamental breach nullifies the clause); here, the lien waiver ceased to bind once the subcontractor communicated its election to treat the contract as at an end.
BaselineA: Combination: common law contract doctrine on exclusionary clauses and fundamental breach (Suisse Atlantique; Photo Production) plus statutory lien context (The Mechanics’ Lien Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 267, s. 5(1)).
CaseB_TestB: Collateral attack on an administrative order in penal proceedings: whether a penal court may determine validity “depends on the statute” and is answered by focusing on “the legislature’s intention as to the appropriate forum,” assessed using non-exhaustive factors (statutory wording, legislative purpose, availability of appeal, nature of the collateral attack in light of the appeal tribunal’s expertise/raison d’être, and penalty).
BaselineB: Statutory interpretation of the Environmental Protection Act, R.S.O. 1980, c. 141 (notably ss. 17, 122-123, 146(1a)) informed by common law principles on collateral attack/exhaustion and rule of law concerns (e.g., Litchfield; Sarson).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Pettkus unjust enrichment test grounding constructive trust: (1) enrichment, (2) corresponding deprivation, and (3) absence of any juristic reason for the enrichment; plus inquiry whether retention is “unjust” (including reasonable expectation knowingly accepted) and a factual “causal connection” between contribution and asset; remedy proportionate to contribution
BaselineA: Common law (equity): constructive trust/unjust enrichment framework drawn from Rathwell v. Rathwell and related matrimonial property trust jurisprudence (also discussed: Murdoch v. Murdoch; English cases Pettitt v. Pettitt and Gissing v. Gissing)
CaseB_TestB: Descôteaux solicitor-client confidentiality/privilege framework for search warrants: confidentiality applies to communications made to obtain legal advice (even pre-retainer); exceptions for communications “criminal in themselves” or made to facilitate crime; justice has no jurisdiction to authorize seizure of privileged evidence; before searching a lawyer’s office for evidence, justice should refuse warrant unless “no reasonable alternative” and must impose execution terms to minimize intrusion
BaselineB: Combination: Criminal Code, s. 443(1)(b) (search warrant for things that “will afford evidence”) interpreted in light of common law solicitor-client privilege/confidentiality (including Solosky v. The Queen and common law privilege authorities)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Informed-consent causation in medical non-disclosure: whether “a reasonable person in the patient’s position” would have declined the treatment if “all material and special risks” of proceeding and foregoing had been disclosed (objective causation test).
BaselineA: Common law (medical negligence / duty to disclose and causation), drawing on Hopp v. Lepp, [1980] 2 S.C.R. 192 (duty to disclose “all material risks” and answer specific questions; scope depends on circumstances).
CaseB_TestB: Division-of-powers “integral element” test for federal jurisdiction over s. 92(10) undertakings: federal legislation displacing provincial law is valid only if it regulates a matter “integral” (i.e., “vital”, “essential”) to the “core” of the federal undertaking; otherwise provincial law of general application applies.
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine (division of powers) applying the “integral element” approach from Construction Montcalm Inc. v. Minimum Wage Commission, [1979] 1 S.C.R. 754 and Northern Telecom Ltd. v. Communications Workers of Canada, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 115, in the context of Railway Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. R-2, s. 342(1).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Natural Resources Agreement (para. 12) “right of access” test for treaty Indian hunting for food: a province may deny access for hunting to everyone, but “once any hunting is permitted, then Indians (and other members of the public) have a right of access for the purpose of hunting”; that “right of access” engages the proviso so Indians may hunt “for food at all seasons of the year” (not limited to the particular day’s open season).
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional instrument: para. 12 of the 1930 Natural Resources Agreement (confirmed by 1930 (Sask.), c. 87; 1930 (Can.), c. 41; British North America Act, 1930, 1930 (Imp.), c. 26), as interpreted in R. v. Sutherland, Wilson and Wilson, [1980] 2 S.C.R. 451 (and referenced R. v. Smith; R. v. Strongquill).
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 2(a) invalidity via “purpose-first” constitutionality test: “the legislation's purpose is the initial test of constitutional validity”; effects are considered only if the law “has passed the purpose test,” and “effects can never be relied on to save legislation with an invalid purpose.” A law with a “purely religious” purpose (here, “compulsion of religious observance”) infringes freedom of religion and is of no force or effect.
BaselineB: Constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 2(a) (and remedial supremacy via Constitution Act, 1982, s. 52(1)); the Court also situates the approach against prior Bill of Rights case law (Robertson and Rosetanni) and Charter interpretive method (Hunter v. Southam).
JudgeB: Dickson J. (for Dickson, Beetz, McIntyre, Chouinard and Lamer JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: No implied power for the Commission/officer/Review Panel to retroactively revoke an allowed premium reduction; an officer’s erroneous grant is not a “nullity” where the officer was properly seized and acted under prescribed regulatory standards (review is one-way at the employer’s instance only).
BaselineA: Statute and regulation: Unemployment Insurance Act, 1970-71-72 (Can.), c. 48 as amended, ss. 64(4), 64(6) (regulation-making re premium reductions) and Regulations s. 24 (decision and employer-initiated review/appeal); also considered but rejected as a basis: Act s. 70 (Minister’s assessment powers).
CaseB_TestB: Mens rea for Criminal Code s. 121(1)(a): Crown must prove intentional commission of the prohibited act plus knowledge of the circumstances; “corruption” is not an element. “Thus, to be guilty... the accused must know that he or she is an official; ... must intentionally demand or accept a loan, reward, advantage or benefit...; and ... must know that the reward is in consideration for cooperation, assistance or exercise of influence in connection with... business with or relating to the government.”
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 121(1)(a) (and s. 19 noted re ignorance of law); interpreted in light of SCC precedent including Martineau v. La Reine.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Ernst (Cromwell J.) categorical Ward s. 24(1) Charter-damages bar for this quasi-judicial regulator: even if Ward’s functional objectives are met, Charter damages are never an “appropriate and just” remedy against the Board because (collectively) (1) judicial review is an effective alternative remedy, (2) good-governance concerns (independence/impartiality, chilling effects, resource diversion, collateral attack) negate damages, and (3) case-by-case damages litigation would undermine the purpose of statutory immunity; therefore s. 43 cannot be unconstitutional for barring Charter damages.
BaselineA: Combination: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 24(1) ("appropriate and just" remedy) as structured by the common-law framework in Vancouver (City) v. Ward, 2010 SCC 27 (functional objectives + countervailing factors). Also engages Energy Resources Conservation Act, R.S.A. 2000, c. E-10, s. 43 (immunity clause) as the statutory context.
CaseB_TestB: Mikisew Cree (Karakatsanis J.) no-duty-to-consult-in-law-making rule: “no aspect of the law-making process — from the development of legislation to its enactment — triggers a duty to consult” because the duty to consult (from the honour of the Crown) has only applied to executive action or action taken on behalf of the executive, and extending it to legislation is barred/ill-suited given separation of powers, parliamentary sovereignty, and parliamentary privilege.
BaselineB: Common law / constitutional doctrine: duty to consult framework from Haida Nation v. British Columbia (Minister of Forests), 2004 SCC 73 (honour of the Crown; duty triggered by contemplated Crown conduct with potential adverse effects on s. 35 rights). Constitutional/statutory context includes Constitution Act, 1982, s. 35 and Federal Courts Act jurisdictional provisions, but the key test is the common-law duty-to-consult doctrine.
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Workers’ compensation statutory bar does not extend to a non-employer car owner deemed a driver’s ‘agent or servant’ under motor-vehicle vicarious-liability deeming provision: s. 10(1) WCA bars actions only against the worker’s employer/covered employers/workers; the owner remains suable in tort despite the driver’s compensation immunity (the tort ‘does not disappear’).
BaselineA: Statute (interaction of Workers’ Compensation Act, 1968 (B.C.), c. 59, s. 10(1) with Motor-vehicle Act, R.S.B.C. 1960, c. 253, s. 70(1))
CaseB_TestB: Operational-conflict framework for conflicting administrative tribunal decisions: an ‘operational conflict’ exists where ‘compliance with the decision of one tribunal necessitates violation of the other’; if both decisions would otherwise survive review, courts may intervene and, using a ‘pragmatic and functional’ approach, decide which decision the legislature intended to take precedence (considering factors like each tribunal’s legislative purpose, centrality of the decision to that purpose, and the policy-making/implementation role).
BaselineB: Common law administrative law (building on Domtar and the ‘pragmatic and functional’ approach from Bibeault) plus statutory context of the tribunals (e.g., Railway Act ss. 335, 340; NTPPA ss. 49, 50, 68(1); Canada Labour Code s. 58)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Priority between a mechanics’ lien and a subsequent collateral mortgage for past indebtedness: absent s. 14(1) application, an unregistered (or later-registered) lien has no priority; once the lien claimant registers and is deemed a “purchaser pro tanto” (Mechanics’ Lien Act, s. 20), priority is determined under the Registry Act by order of registration unless the prior registrant had actual notice (Registry Act, ss. 69(1), 70).
BaselineA: Statute (Ontario): Mechanics’ Lien Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 267, ss. 14(1), 16, 20, 21, 22 (and context ss. 7(3),(4)); Registry Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 409, ss. 69(1), 70.
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 1 proportionality (Oakes) as applied to PIPA’s restriction of union expression: even with a pressing and substantial objective and rational connection, the law fails because its limits on expression are “disproportionate” to the privacy benefits (no mechanism to balance expression with privacy; overbroad restrictions in the labour-picketing context).
BaselineB: Constitutional (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms): ss. 2(b) and 1, applied to the Personal Information Protection Act, S.A. 2003, c. P-6.5 (notably ss. 3, 4, 7 and exemptions) and regulation.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Quebec civil liability “choice” test: a plaintiff in contractual relations may sue in delict only if the contractual fault is independently a fault under art. 1053 C.C. (i.e., would exist even absent the contract)
BaselineA: Statute (Quebec Civil Code, art. 1053; and jurisdictional hook in Code of Civil Procedure, art. 68(2)) plus SCC jurisprudence recognizing possible delict alongside contract (Ross v. Dunstall; Ross v. Emery; Alliance Assurance Co. v. Dominion Electric Protection Co.)
CaseB_TestB: Reasonable apprehension of bias in a criminal trial: once demonstrated, the trial judge has no further jurisdiction and the only appropriate remedy is a new trial; orders made after the bias are retroactively void
BaselineB: Common law procedural fairness / impartial adjudicator doctrine, relying on Newfoundland Telephone Co. v. Newfoundland (Board of Commissioners of Public Utilities) for the effect of established apprehension of bias (voidness)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Bills of Exchange Act “sum certain”/negotiability requirement: a promissory note must be certain on its face as to principal and interest; interest must be ascertainable from materials contained in the instrument (not dependent on an uncertain “date of advance” requiring extrinsic evidence).
BaselineA: Statute (Bills of Exchange Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. B-5, ss. 28, 176(1), 186; plus s. 10 incorporating common law/law merchant where not inconsistent).
CaseB_TestB: Criminal Code s. 172(3) “disturbs” threshold: conduct is criminal only if it is “disorderly in itself or productive of disorder”; mere “annoyance, anxiety or emotional upset” from brief, passive, peaceful conduct voluntarily desisted from is insufficient.
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 172(3) (and context from ss. 169–175 heading “Disorderly Conduct”)).
JudgeB: Dickson J. (for Dickson, Beetz, McIntyre, Chouinard and Lamer JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Bills of Exchange Act “sum certain”/negotiability requirement: principal and interest must be ascertainable on the face of the instrument (no extrinsic evidence unless the Act necessarily implies it); uncertainty as to interest start date (e.g., “from the date of advance”) makes the instrument non-negotiable and not a promissory note
BaselineA: Statute: Bills of Exchange Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. B-5, ss. 28 (incl. s. 28(1)(a), 28(3)), 176(1), 186; plus s. 10 incorporating common law/law merchant
CaseB_TestB: Start of the Civil Code (C.C.L.C.) two-year suicide exclusion limit: determine the contract’s effective date under art. 2516 (three concurrent conditions) and allow retroactive effectiveness to a backdated policy date if favourable to the insured; the art. 2532 two-year period runs from that effective date and cannot run more than once within a single contract (policy changes vs new contract assessed case-by-case for continuity)
BaselineB: Statute (civil law): Civil Code of Lower Canada, arts. 2516, 2532 (and art. 2500(2) re non-derogation except if more favourable); interpretive support from prior SCC cases including General Trust of Canada v. Artisans Coopvie
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Declaratory judgment should not be used to decide matters the legislature has specifically assigned to another tribunal (and will be refused where it would be of little/no practical use)
BaselineA: Combination: statute (Code of Civil Procedure, art. 453) plus common-law/precedent discretion limiting declaratory relief where a statutory scheme assigns the issue to an inferior tribunal (e.g., Barraclough v. Brown; City of Lethbridge v. Canadian Western Natural Gas; Cassidy v. Stuart)
CaseB_TestB: Minister’s s. 7 Fisheries Act power to “authorize to be issued” licences is a continuing power, so the Minister may revoke an authorization any time before the licence is issued; discretion constrained only by natural justice (relevant considerations, no arbitrariness, good faith)
BaselineB: Statute: Fisheries Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. F-14, s. 7 (and contrast with s. 9); Interpretation Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. I-21, s. 31(3)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Excise Tax Act machinery exemption: claimant must be a “manufacturer or producer” and the machinery must be “used directly” in the manufacture/production of “goods”; “manufacture” not restrictively defined—operating generators to produce electricity qualifies as manufacturing
BaselineA: Statute: Excise Tax Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-13, ss. 27(1), 29(1), and Schedule III, Part XIII, s. 1(a) (machinery sold to/imported by manufacturers or producers for use directly in manufacture/production of goods); supported by SCC definitions in R. v. York Marble, Tile and Terrazzo Ltd., [1968] S.C.R. 140 and Bank of Nova Scotia v. The King, [1930] S.C.R. 174
CaseB_TestB: Vesting of appeal-as-of-right: a “right” is only “acquired, accrued or accruing” when all conditions precedent are fulfilled—here, only upon the court of appeal rendering judgment reversing the acquittal and ordering a new trial
BaselineB: Statute: Interpretation Act, R.S.C., 1985, c. I-21, ss. 43(c) and 44(c),(d), applied to amended Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 691(2)
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Implied civil cause of action / common law tort barred where a statute provides a comprehensive enforcement and remedial scheme (Ontario Human Rights Code forecloses civil action for discrimination)
BaselineA: Statute (Ontario Human Rights Code, R.S.O. 1970, c. 318) interacting with common law principles on when breach of statute supports civil liability
CaseB_TestB: ‘Undue obstacle’ / reasonable accommodation analysis under CTA s. 172: barrier must be removed unless carrier proves bona fide justification by showing accommodation would impose undue hardship (contextual factors like cost, economic viability, safety, quality of service)
BaselineB: Statute (Canada Transportation Act, S.C. 1996, c. 10, ss. 5, 170(1), 172) informed by human rights reasonable-accommodation jurisprudence (e.g., Meiorin/Grismer)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Bill of Rights limit on reverse onus: a reverse-onus provision (balance of probabilities) is compatible with s. 2(f) only if the fact the accused must prove/disprove is "rationally open" to them; if the accused "cannot reasonably be expected to prove" it (beyond their knowledge/means of knowledge), the burden is "impossible to meet" and becomes an (effectively) irrebuttable presumption of guilt. For Customs Act s. 248(1), Crown must first show, beyond mere possession + foreign origin, "some knowledge or means of knowledge of the circumstances of importation" on the accused’s part before the reverse onus can operate.
BaselineA: Statute (Customs Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-40, ss. 205(1),(3), 248(1)) as constrained by statute (Canadian Bill of Rights, R.S.C. 1970, App. III, s. 2(f)); relying on R. v. Appleby, [1972] S.C.R. 303 for the general reverse-onus compatibility principle.
CaseB_TestB: Interested-party status/right to be heard in bargaining-unit definition under Quebec Labour Code s. 32: employees included in the proposed unit are not "interested parties" for the bargaining-unit portion because s. 32 requires that investigation be held only "in the presence of every association concerned and the employer"; with a privative clause, judicial review by evocation is unavailable where the tribunal’s interpretation is "not patently unreasonable" (i.e., not "manifestly unreasonable").
BaselineB: Statute (Quebec Labour Code, especially s. 32; also ss. 28, 39, 129) and Code of Civil Procedure art. 846, applied through common-law/administrative-law principles of natural justice and privative-clause deference (CUPE v. New Brunswick Liquor Corp., [1979] 2 S.C.R. 227; Nipawin, [1975] 1 S.C.R. 382).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Intoxication (drunkenness) and mens rea for murder: intoxication is relevant only if it "rendered an accused incapable of forming the intent" to kill or to cause bodily harm known to be likely to cause death; "The accused’s capacity is a question of fact for you" and "The Crown is the one that must satisfy you that the accused had the capacity" (capacity test).
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Criminal Code, s. 212(a)(ii) (murder by intending bodily harm known likely to cause death and recklessness), plus the common-law intoxication 'capacity' approach from Director of Public Prosecutions v. Beard, as applied/clarified in MacAskill v. The King, Perrault v. The Queen, and Mulligan v. The Queen (all cited in the reasons).
CaseB_TestB: Interjurisdictional immunity (constitutional inapplicability) for provincial laws of general application: provincial law applies to federal works/undertakings/services unless it bears on what makes them "specifically of federal jurisdiction"; for a federal service, immunity applies if the provincial statute "touches on a vital or essential aspect of its establishment, management or operation".
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine (interjurisdictional immunity) as articulated in Construction Montcalm Inc. v. Minimum Wage Commission and Bell Canada v. Quebec (CSST) (both relied on), applied to the provincial Transport Act permit scheme (R.S.Q., c. T-12, including s. 36) and Bus Transport Regulation.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 116(1) availability test: a charge for disobeying a lawful court order lies unless statute law expressly provides a penalty/punishment/other mode of proceeding (common law contempt powers do not qualify as 'expressly provided by law')
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 116(1) (and interpretive context including s. 8; Manitoba Queen’s Bench Rules considered but found not to 'expressly provide')
CaseB_TestB: Public law promissory estoppel in penal/zoning enforcement: requires (1) a clear and unambiguous promise by a public authority intended to induce action, and (2) reliance/change of conduct, but estoppel cannot be invoked to prevent application of a clear legislative provision creating a strict-liability regulatory offence
BaselineB: Common law doctrine of public law promissory estoppel as described in Mount Sinai (quoting Maracle), plus statutory/by-law context: Cities and Towns Act, s. 576; zoning by-law VQZ-3 (arts. 40, 83, 359); Act respecting land use planning and development, s. 227
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Insurance policy interpretation to determine the policy’s “effective date” for time-limited clauses: construe the policy and application “in entirety” (not “mechanical[ly]” or “isolated[ly]”) and select the single effective date that governs “the purpose of calculating any of the time periods contemplated, including the application of the self-destruction clause”.
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law contract interpretation: Insurance Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 224, s. 148(2) (application + policy form the contract) and general contractual construction of the insurance contract as a whole.
CaseB_TestB: Access in conjunction with permanent guardianship: (1) court has jurisdiction to grant access when making a permanent guardianship order; (2) access is “the exception and not the rule” and is granted only if, after weighing the statutory “best interests of the child” factors, access is in the child’s best interests—particularly, it “should not be granted if its exercise would have negative effects on the physical or psychological health of the child” or would jeopardize an adoption that is in the child’s best interests.
BaselineB: Statute: Family Services Act, S.N.B. 1980, c. F-2.2, especially ss. 1 (definition of “best interests of the child”), 53(2) (best interests paramount), 56(1) (permanent guardianship), 60(2) and 60(6) (variation and court may make any appropriate order if in best interests), and 85(2) (court may preserve access after adoption).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 16(2) insanity: meaning of “incapable of appreciating the nature and quality of an act” — an accused appreciates if he “knows what he is doing” and “is aware of the physical consequences which will result from his acts” (i.e., can “estimate and ... understand the physical consequences” such as injury/death; emotional reactions/remorse are irrelevant).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 16(2)); interpreted consistently with SCC authorities including Cooper v. The Queen, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 1149 and R. v. Barnier, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 1124 (as discussed and applied in the reasons).
CaseB_TestB: Extradition Act committal/surrender framework: (1) Committal under s. 29(1)(a) is whether there is admissible evidence of conduct that “would justify committal for trial in Canada” (prima facie case; extradition judge generally does not consider defences; ROC is “presumptively reliable” and refusal for unreliability only if evidence is “so defective or appears so unreliable that it would be dangerous or unsafe to act on it”). (2) At surrender, a defence-gap claim triggers a 3-part threshold: person sought must show (1) a substantive defence difference (defence in Canada but no comparable defence abroad), (2) a “reasonable prospect of success” in Canada, and (3) “significantly greater jeopardy” abroad; if met, Minister then weighs this with all other circumstances under s. 44(1)(a).
BaselineB: Statute (Extradition Act, S.C. 1999, c. 18, ss. 29(1)(a), 32(1)(c), 44(1)(a)); built on prior SCC extradition jurisprudence including United States of America v. Ferras, 2006 SCC 33 and Lake v. Canada (Minister of Justice), 2008 SCC 23 (as discussed and applied).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: When (if ever) to exceed the $100,000 rough upper limit for non-pecuniary damages under the functional approach: exceed only rarely, and not merely because injuries seem worse than the trilogy; $100,000 may increase only on proof/agreement of inflation’s effect
BaselineA: Common law (damages for non-pecuniary loss) from the SCC “trilogy” and refinement in Lewis v. Todd: Andrews v. Grand & Toy Alberta Ltd.; Thornton v. Board of School Trustees; Arnold v. Teno; Lewis v. Todd
CaseB_TestB: OPCF 44R / Insurance Act s. 239(1)(a) ‘arising directly or indirectly from the use or operation of an automobile’ (indemnity context): coverage requires an unbroken chain of causation showing the tortfeasor was at fault as a motorist; an intervening, severable tort breaks the chain (not satisfied by mere ‘but for’ vehicle involvement)
BaselineB: Statutory/contractual interpretation: Insurance Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. I.8, s. 239(1)(a) (tracked by OPCF 44R wording) and prior SCC guidance in Amos v. ICBC (distinguished/limited to no-fault context)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Effect of workers’ compensation election/subrogation on who may sue and whether the Commission has an interest to intervene or benefit from interruption of prescription: once election for compensation is made, only the Commission may claim the compensated portion; the worker may claim only the s. 8 ‘additional sum’, and a worker’s overbroad claim does not create Commission interest or interrupt prescription for the Commission
BaselineA: Statute and civil law: Workmen’s Compensation Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 159, ss. 7(1)-(3) and 8 (plus s. 5 referenced); Civil Code art. 1056a; Code of Civil Procedure art. 208; (prescription context: Civil Code art. 2262(2))
CaseB_TestB: Collins/Jacoy s. 24(2) Charter exclusion framework: whether admission would bring the administration of justice into disrepute, organized into three categories—(1) fairness of the trial, (2) seriousness of the Charter breach, and (3) effect of exclusion on the repute of justice—applied with emphasis on seriousness and on whether the Crown proved reasonable and probable grounds
BaselineB: Constitution and common law framework under Charter s. 24(2), applying prior SCC cases (especially R. v. Collins; R. v. Jacoy; R. v. Simmons; R. v. Strachan) and related reasonable-grounds jurisprudence (Hunter v. Southam; Debot as discussed)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Public access to search-warrant materials: after execution and where items are brought before a justice, the public may inspect the warrant and supporting information, subject to overriding countervailing interests (notably protecting the innocent where nothing is found) and with issuance proceedings properly in camera
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law/open court principle: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 443 (issuance of warrant) and 446 (bringing seized objects before a justice), plus common law presumption of openness and court supervisory power over records
CaseB_TestB: Two-branch test for a bona fide occupational qualification/requirement (BFOQ): (1) subjective good-faith/improper-purpose inquiry; and (2) objective necessity inquiry—whether the requirement is reasonably necessary to accomplish the job’s (here, denominational school’s) objectives
BaselineB: Statute interpreted through prior SCC common-law-like framework: Human Rights Code, R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 186, s. 8 (esp. s. 8(1) and s. 8(2)(a)); test drawn from Ontario Human Rights Commission v. Etobicoke (Borough of), [1982] 1 S.C.R. 202
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Validity of a Quebec inter vivos trust for unborn (non-existent) beneficiaries: trustee acceptance suffices to perfect/irrevocably constitute the trust and the trustee is owner during the trust; therefore art. 981a’s reference to gift/legacy capacity is read subject to the trust’s special characteristics and does not bar unborn primary beneficiaries absent a public-order prohibition.
BaselineA: Statute (Civil Code of Quebec provisions on trusts and gifts): arts. 981a, 981b, 981l (trusts) read with arts. 754, 755, 758, 760, 782, 608, 771, 772, 929; plus prior SCC interpretation in Curran v. Davis, [1933] S.C.R. 283 (trust acceptance/irrevocability and nature of trustee’s rights).
CaseB_TestB: When an injunction in private litigation may effectively bind non-parties (enforceable by contempt): courts have jurisdiction to make such orders, but fairness requires that non-parties be apprised of the order and given an opportunity to comply, that it is desirable the order state the duty of non-parties to respect it, and that orders be carefully worded and constrained so they are fair and not unduly broad.
BaselineB: Common law/equitable jurisdiction and contempt principles (e.g., Seaward v. Paterson; Bartle & Gibson; International Longshoremen’s Association) supplemented by statute confirming injunction power and civil remedies: Law and Equity Act, R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 224, s. 36; Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 11.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory displacement of the Kienapple rule: s. 83 permits an additional conviction (and consecutive sentence) for using a firearm during an indictable offence, notwithstanding another conviction arising from the same event; and s. 21 party liability applies to s. 83. Key language: s. 83(2) contemplates the sentence for s. 83(1) “shall be served consecutively to any other punishment imposed on him for an offence arising out of the same event or series of events”; Dickson J.: “I do not know what clearer language could be used to negate the so-called Kienapple principle” and “Parliament has in the enactment of s. 83 departed from the fundamental common law principle ... elaborated in Kienapple.”
BaselineA: Combination of common law and statute: common law rule against multiple convictions for the same delict (Kienapple v. The Queen; also Cox and Paton v. The Queen; R. v. Quon) as the baseline principle, interpreted as displaced by Criminal Code ss. 83(1)-(2); plus application of Criminal Code s. 21 (parties) to s. 83.
CaseB_TestB: Pith and substance characterization (purpose + effects) for division of powers: “In analyzing the pith and substance ... a court must consider both its purpose and its effects” and effects include “both the legal ramifications ... and the practical consequences.” Applied to find the notice’s pith and substance was “the choice of the location of radiocommunication infrastructure” (ultra vires).
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine (division of powers) applying the pith and substance framework; articulated with reference to prior SCC cases (e.g., Goodwin; Marine Services; COPA; Lacombe; Morgentaler) and the Constitution Act, 1867 heads of power (ss. 91(29), 92(10)(a), 92(13), 92(16)).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Labour arbitration remedial authority under s. 25(3): where the collective agreement lacks a specific penalty for the infraction, an arbitration board that cannot sustain dismissal may substitute a lesser penalty (including reinstatement without back pay) that “seems just and reasonable in the circumstances”.
BaselineA: Statute — The Trade Union Act, R.S.S. 1978, c. T-17, s. 25(3) (interacting with the collective agreement’s dismissal/reinstatement provisions).
CaseB_TestB: Ezokola contribution-based complicity test (Refugee Convention art. 1F(a)/IRPA s. 98): exclusion requires “serious reasons for considering” the claimant “has voluntarily made a significant and knowing contribution to the organization’s crime or criminal purpose”, assessed contextually using non-exhaustive factors (size/nature of organization; relevant part; duties; rank; time in organization after knowledge; recruitment and opportunity to leave).
BaselineB: Statute/treaty — IRPA, S.C. 2001, c. 27, s. 98 incorporating Refugee Convention, art. 1F(a) (“serious reasons for considering”).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 43 Canada Evidence Act letters rogatory: s. 43 should be construed broadly in comity; it authorizes an order for production of documents alone (not only documents ancillary to viva voce testimony), subject to comity limits (e.g., trial-not-discovery; relevance; scope; adequate definition; and limits on use of illegally intercepted communications).
BaselineA: Statute: Canada Evidence Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-10, s. 43 (letters rogatory/judicial assistance), with related statutory constraints considered under Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 178.2 and 178.16 (intercepted private communications).
CaseB_TestB: Admissibility of defence-led unknown third party suspect evidence: admissible where (1) relevant to a fact in issue (logical relevance shown by a sufficient connection/similarity between the charged crime and another incident the accused could not have committed, giving the defence an air of reality), and (2) probative value is not substantially outweighed by prejudicial effects (Seaboyer balancing; no balance-of-probabilities proof of the other incident; no credibility weighing by the judge).
BaselineB: Common law evidence principles, especially R. v. Seaboyer (defence evidence excluded only if prejudice substantially outweighs value), plus related common law concepts of logical relevance (Corbett) and air of reality (Cinous), and sufficient connection for third-party suspect evidence (McMillan/Grandinetti).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Civil Code art. 1055 C.C. “purpose/intended use” limit on owner’s liability for ruin: “want of repairs must be looked at from the viewpoint of the purpose for which the building or part of building was intended”; if the victim uses the building/part “contrary to the purpose for which it was intended”, the owner is not liable under art. 1055.
BaselineA: Statute (Civil Code of Quebec (as then in force), art. 1055 C.C.), as interpreted in Leznek v. City of Verdun, [1940] S.C.R. 313 (and related Quebec authorities cited).
JudgeA: Beetz J. (for Beetz, Chouinard and Lamer JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: “Operating mind” / limited cognitive capacity standard for confessions, right to silence, and s. 10(b) waiver: accused must have “sufficient cognitive capacity to understand what he or she is saying and what is said”, including understanding a caution that it “can be used against” him; for counsel/waiver, accused must have the “limited cognitive capacity” for fitness—able to communicate with and instruct counsel, understand counsel’s function, and that he can dispense with counsel; no separate “awareness of consequences” test and no higher capacity required absent police conduct that “effectively and unfairly deprived” the suspect of choice.
BaselineB: Combination of common law confession rule/right to silence (Ward; Horvath; Nagotcha; Hebert) and constitutional/statutory sources: Charter ss. 7 and 10(b); Criminal Code s. 2 definition of “unfit to stand trial” used to set the competence threshold.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Judicial review of a labour board’s “home statute” interpretation under a privative clause: intervene only if the interpretation is “patently unreasonable” / “plainly unreasonable” (i.e., cannot be rationally supported by the legislation)
BaselineA: Combination: statute (The Public Service Employee Relations Act, 1977 (Alta.), ss. 9, 11, 89 (and s. 48)) plus common-law deference doctrine (CUPE v. New Brunswick Liquor Corp.; Volvo; Douglas Aircraft)
CaseB_TestB: Adverse-effect religious discrimination and duty to accommodate: once discrimination is shown, employer must take “reasonable steps to accommodate ... short of undue hardship” (no de minimis threshold); undue hardship assessed with non-exhaustive factors (e.g., financial cost, disruption of collective agreement, morale/impact on others, interchangeability, size, safety)
BaselineB: Combination: statute (Quebec Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms, ss. 10, 16; plus Labour Code privative clause for review) and common law human-rights framework (O'Malley; Central Alberta Dairy Pool; Renaud)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Similar fact evidence admissibility: requires an evidentiary link to the accused (and probative value must outweigh prejudice)
BaselineA: Common law (as stated in Makin v. The Attorney-General for New South Wales; supported by Boardman v. DPP; Harris v. DPP)
CaseB_TestB: Charter vagueness test: a law is unconstitutionally vague if it lacks precision so as not to give sufficient guidance for legal debate
BaselineB: Common law constitutional principle under Charter s. 7 (building on the Prostitution Reference and related SCC vagueness jurisprudence)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 16(2) insanity (first arm): “incapable of appreciating the nature and quality of an act” is limited to appreciating the physical character and physical consequences of the act (mens rea/actus reus consequences), not the penal consequences (punishment) to the accused
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 16(2)); interpreted in light of SCC cases including Cooper v. The Queen, R. v. Barnier, Kjeldsen v. The Queen, and Schwartz v. The Queen
CaseB_TestB: Administrative tribunal constitutional jurisdiction test: “the essential question is whether the empowering legislation implicitly or explicitly grants to the tribunal the jurisdiction to interpret or decide any question of law”; if yes, the tribunal is presumed to have jurisdiction to decide the issue “in light of s. 35 or any other relevant constitutional provision”, absent a “clear implication” rebutting that presumption
BaselineB: Common law / constitutional doctrine on tribunal jurisdiction to decide constitutional questions, applied through Nova Scotia (Workers’ Compensation Board) v. Martin; implemented by interpreting the Forest Practices Code of British Columbia Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 159 (notably s. 131(8))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Patentability of a new use for an old compound as a “new and useful art”: the “invention” is “the application of this new knowledge to effect a desired result which has an undisputed commercial value”, and the claim may be to compositions as the “practical embodiment of the new knowledge” even if mixing with inert carriers is not itself novel.
BaselineA: Statute (Patent Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. P-4), especially s. 2 (“invention” includes “any new and useful art”) and s. 36 (claiming requirement); interpreted against prior case law including Hickton’s Patent Syndicate v. Patents and Machine Improvements Co. (1909) and the Farbwerke Hoechst line.
CaseB_TestB: Party liability for drug trafficking by aiding/abetting: under Criminal Code s. 21(1), to “aid” is to “assist or help the actor” and to “abet” includes “encouraging, instigating, promoting or procuring”; for s. 21(1)(b) “purpose” means “intention” (not “desire”), i.e., Crown must prove the accused “intended the consequences that flowed from his or her aid”.
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, s. 21(1)(b),(c); Narcotic Control Act, ss. 2 “traffic”, 4(1)); with mens rea interpretation drawn from R. v. Hibbert and trafficking/purchaser context from Poitras.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory incompatibility/inconsistency test: whether a permissive municipal discretion (Police Act, s. 24(6)) excludes a collectively bargained/arbitrated clause authorized as a “working condition” under s. 29(2); held valid where there is “no incompatibility or inconsistency” and each provision has “its own area of operation”.
BaselineA: Statute (The Police Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 351, ss. 24(6) and 29(2))
CaseB_TestB: State Immunity Act exception analysis (s. 6(a) territorial tort/physical integrity limits): the “personal or bodily injury” exception applies only where “the tort causing the personal injury or death has occurred in Canada” and, for psychological harm, only where “mental distress and emotional upset were linked to a physical injury” such that “some form of a breach of physical integrity must be made out”.
BaselineB: Statute (State Immunity Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. S-18, ss. 3(1), 6(a))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory incompatibility/repugnancy test between Police Act s. 24(6) (permissive indemnification discretion) and s. 29(2) (collective bargaining over “working conditions”): s. 24(6) does not create exclusivity; if there is “no incompatibility or inconsistency” the collective agreement clause is valid and each provision has “its own area of operation”.
BaselineA: Statute: The Police Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 351, ss. 24(6) and 29(2) (interpreting whether s. 24(6) excludes bargaining under s. 29(2)).
CaseB_TestB: Corporate attribution test for BIA s. 96(1)(b)(ii)(B) (transfer at undervalue — intent to “defraud, defeat or delay”): for s. 96, the “fraud” and “no benefit” exceptions do not apply; “the test for corporate attribution under s. 96 is simply whether the person was the directing mind and whether their actions were performed within the sector of corporate responsibility assigned to them.”
BaselineB: Combination: Statute (Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act, s. 96(1)(b)(ii)(B), plus CCAA s. 36.1 incorporation) applied through the common law corporate attribution doctrine (Canadian Dredge; Livent; DeJong) as adapted for the s. 96 context.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Jennings test for establishing a constitutional convention: (1) what are the precedents; (2) did the actors in the precedents believe they were bound by a rule (recognition/acquiescence); and (3) is there a reason for the rule — with recognition by the actors treated as the “most important element”
BaselineA: Common law (constitutional conventions doctrine), adopting Sir W. Ivor Jennings’ three-question framework as approved in Re: Resolution to amend the Constitution, [1981] 1 S.C.R. 753 (First Reference) and the Manitoba Reference definition quoted there
CaseB_TestB: Reasonable suspicion standard for sniffer-dog searches under s. 8: police may deploy a drug detection dog without prior authorization where there is “reasonable suspicion based on objective, ascertainable facts” assessed on the “totality of the circumstances” (a sufficiently particularized “constellation of factors”), with exculpatory/neutral facts not disregarded but no duty to investigate to rule out innocent explanations
BaselineB: Common law Charter search framework (R. v. Collins) and prior sniffer-dog cases (R. v. Kang-Brown; R. v. A.M.) applying s. 8 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criteria for whether a labour arbitrator under the Canada Labour Code is a “statutory tribunal” subject to evocation/certiorari: not only whether “by statute the parties must resort to it”, but also whether the tribunal is “invested with wide powers by statute” (statutory duties/powers conferring binding authority).
BaselineA: Combination of common law and statute: prior certiorari/evocation jurisprudence (Howe Sound Co. v. International Union of Mine, Mill and Smelter Workers (Canada), Local 663; Port Arthur Shipbuilding Co. v. Arthurs; R. v. National Joint Council for the Craft of Dental Technicians) applied to Code of Civil Procedure, art. 846, in light of Canada Labour Code provisions (ss. 156(2), 157, 159, 160(5)).
CaseB_TestB: Test for whether an agreement creates a patent sublicence: whether the licensee granted the third party (expressly or impliedly) “the right to do something which [it] would otherwise be prohibited from doing, and which [the licensee] was permitted to do only by virtue of its [licence]”, either by express terms or by the agreement’s “actual legal effect”.
BaselineB: Common law (licence/sublicence and contract interpretation principles) applied in the statutory context of the Patent Act compulsory licensing regime and Patented Medicines (Notice of Compliance) Regulations (notably Patent Act ss. 39(4), 39.11, 39.14; PM(NOC) Regulations ss. 5-7).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Kienapple remedy modification: when Kienapple applies, enter a stay of proceedings rather than an acquittal
BaselineA: Common law (Kienapple v. The Queen, [1975] 1 S.C.R. 729)
CaseB_TestB: Criteria for appointing/removing a litigation guardian: best interests test informed by Szwydky criteria, including mandatory 'indifference' (no conflict) requirement
BaselineB: Combination of statute/rules and case law: Queen’s Bench Rules (Saskatchewan) r. 49(1) ('best interests'); Szwydky v. Magiera (1988) six criteria; Dependent Adults Act, S.S. 1989-90, c. D-25.1 (context for guardianship/conflict)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Contract interpretation of the 1905 power-supply agreement: the Town’s entitlement is limited to the expressly reserved 4,000 horsepower at the fixed ceiling price of $14 per horsepower per annum (and no broader ‘requirements’ entitlement). Key language: the Company must “retain and reserve for use on the Canadian side… Four Thousand Horse Power” and the Town’s price “shall not in any event exceed… Fourteen Dollars ($14.00)”; the Court declares the obligation is “to provide… to the extent of 4,000 horsepower per annum… at the contract price of $14 per horsepower per annum.”
BaselineA: Statute/contract instrument: interpretation and reconciliation of specific clauses of the January 9, 1905 agreement (esp. paras. 1, 5, 6, 8, 13) governing quantity and price of power; statutes discussed but held not determinative.
CaseB_TestB: General Motors indicia for validity under the general branch of the federal trade and commerce power (Constitution Act, 1867, s. 91(2)): ask (1) “part of a general regulatory scheme”; (2) “oversight of a regulatory agency”; (3) “concerned with trade as a whole rather than with a particular industry”; (4) provinces “constitutionally incapable of enacting it”; and (5) failure to include a province would “jeopardize its successful operation”. The indicia are “not exhaustive” and “not necessary that they be present in every case.”
BaselineB: Common law constitutional test: General Motors of Canada Ltd. v. City National Leasing, [1989] 1 S.C.R. 641 (applied) interpreting Constitution Act, 1867, s. 91(2) (general trade and commerce power).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Contract-interpretation rule for the Town’s entitlement: reconcile the general ‘to such an extent as the said Town… may require’ language with the specific reservation/distribution clauses, yielding a fixed entitlement of 4,000 horsepower per annum at $14 per horsepower per annum (and no broader right to all output). Key text: para. 1 ‘to such an extent as the said Town… may require’; para. 8 ‘retain and reserve… Four Thousand Horse Power… permanently available’; Court: ‘I cannot read the general provision in paragraph 1… as overriding the precise distribution arrangements made in paragraphs 6 and 8’ and declares the obligation ‘to the extent of 4,000 horsepower per annum… at… $14 per horsepower per annum.’
BaselineA: Common law (contract interpretation of the January 9, 1905 agreement; statutes found not to have direct bearing).
CaseB_TestB: Party liability for late-joining participants in a continuing kidnapping: (1) kidnapping under Criminal Code s. 279(1) is a continuing offence including ensuing unlawful confinement ‘[s]o long as the victim… remains unlawfully confined’; it ends when the victim is freed; and (2) s. 21(1) party liability applies where, ‘with knowledge of the principal’s intention to see a continuing offence through to its completion’, the accused does/omits something ‘with the intention of aiding or abetting the commission of the ongoing offence’ (including where the accused is wilfully blind).
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, ss. 279(1), 21(1)), interpreted in light of common law meaning of kidnapping and prior SCC party-liability principles (e.g., Briscoe).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Trigger for mandatory municipal acquisition under Planning Act s. 70(1): land must be “designated under a land use by-law” (not merely in statutory plans); statutory plans are policy/proposals and do not trigger the s. 70 duty to acquire within six months/within a reasonable time.
BaselineA: Statute: The Planning Act, 1977 (Alta.), s. 70(1) (and related scheme/definitions incl. s. 1(14) “land use by-law”; also discussed: ss. 61, 62(2), 65(d), 66-69, 83(3)).
CaseB_TestB: O’Connor framework for production of private third-party records in criminal cases: (1) accused must show records are “likely to be relevant” to an issue at trial or witness competence; (2) if so, court balances salutary vs deleterious effects (privacy/equality vs full answer and defence) to decide whether/what to produce (often via in camera review), with a multi-factor proportionality assessment.
BaselineB: Common law/constitutional baseline: Charter ss. 7 and 24(1) (and Charter values of privacy/equality), plus existing SCC abuse-of-process/stay jurisprudence (e.g., R. v. Jewitt) and disclosure jurisprudence (R. v. Stinchcombe) as context; procedural/statutory context includes Criminal Code subpoena provisions (e.g., ss. 698, 700).
JudgeB: L’Heureux-Dubé J. (reasons for La Forest, L’Heureux-Dubé and Gonthier JJ.; McLachlin J. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “has become regularly engaged in some other occupation” under Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, s. 44(1)(c): focuses on regularity of work schedule (a “fixed pattern”) rather than duration or intent to abandon former job; claimant must have worked and worked “regularly” (not merely be hired).
BaselineA: Statute: Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, s. 44(1)(c) (with contextual reference to Regulations s. 49 defining “bona fide employed” for s. 44(1)(b)).
CaseB_TestB: Whether an ISP is a “broadcasting undertaking” under the Broadcasting Act when providing Internet access: entities that “merely provide the mode of transmission” and take no part in “selection, origination, or packaging of content” (i.e., lack control over programming and do not contribute to s. 3(1) policy objectives) are not broadcasting undertakings.
BaselineB: Statute: Broadcasting Act, S.C. 1991, c. 11, ss. 2(1) (“broadcasting”), 2(3), 3(1) (interpreted contextually/purposively).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Cross-border fresh pursuit: an officer retains “peace officer” status for Criminal Code s. 25(4) if the pursuit began lawfully in the officer’s province and remains “fresh”; arrest authority depends on whether the suspect would appear to a reasonable person in the circumstances to be committing an offence (reasonable and probable grounds).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34), especially ss. 25(4), 450(1)(b), and related ss. 449(1)(b), 25(1), 25(3). The arrest standard is drawn from R. v. Biron, [1976] 2 S.C.R. 56 (and Pritchard as discussed in Biron).
CaseB_TestB: Arbitrator jurisdiction under Canada Labour Code s. 157(d): an arbitrator is deprived of substitution power only if the collective agreement contains a “specific penalty” for the particular infraction; a penalty is not “specific” if it is not in the collective agreement or if it can be chosen “indiscriminately” by the employer.
BaselineB: Statute (Canada Labour Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. L-1, s. 157(d)(i)-(ii)) interpreted alongside the collective agreement (Article XI(b)).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Availability and scope of the Crown’s per quod servitium amisit action for injuries to Canadian Forces members deemed “servants of the Crown”: master may recover “cost necessarily incurred” (including wages/allowances and medical/hospital expenses) for “loss of any services”, but the “master’s right of action ... is dependant on the servant in turn having a valid cause of action against the wrongdoer”; Armed Forces services are not excluded as non-menial/domestic.
BaselineA: Combination: statute deeming relationship (Federal Court Act, s. 37; historically Exchequer Court Act, s. 50) plus common law per quod servitium amisit as recognized in SCC precedents (The King v. Richardson; Attorney-General of Canada v. Jackson; Nykorak v. Attorney General of Canada; The Queen v. Murray).
JudgeA: Ritchie J. (for Ritchie, Estey, Lamer and Wilson JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Mens rea for Criminal Code s. 121(1)(a): no “corrupt” purpose required; guilt requires (1) accused knows he/she is an “official”; (2) intentionally demands/accepts (etc.) “a loan, reward, advantage or benefit of any kind” for self/another; and (3) knows the benefit is “as consideration for cooperation, assistance or exercise of influence” in connection with “the transaction of business with or relating to the government”.
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 121(1)(a) (interpreted in light of SCC authority including Martineau v. La Reine; and contrasted with Hinchey).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Timing/trigger for Attorney General stay under Criminal Code s. 508(1): stay power begins only once a summons or warrant has issued (i.e., after the justice has decided to issue process; laying an information is not “finding” it).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34 as amended), especially ss. 508(1), 455.3, plus definitional/context provisions ss. 2 and 503.
CaseB_TestB: Statutory eligibility for discharge under Criminal Code s. 662.1(1): discharge is unavailable if the offence is one “for which a minimum punishment is prescribed by law”; an offence with any prescribed minimum (e.g., s. 234(a) fine “not less than fifty dollars”) is excluded even if alternative penalties have no minimum.
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code), interpreting and applying ss. 662.1(1) and 234(a) (and considering s. 645).
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 508 stay power timing: Attorney General may direct a stay only "after a summons or warrant is issued"; an information is "found" only once the justice decides to issue process (not upon mere laying/receipt of the information).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34 as amended), interpreting ss. 2 ("indictment"), 503 ("finding an indictment"), 508 (stay of proceedings), in the context of ss. 455 and 455.3 (private informations/hearing and issuance of process).
CaseB_TestB: Procedural fairness (Baker factors) requiring reasons: when an administrative decision affects rights/interests, the duty of fairness varies with five factors—(1) nature of decision/process, (2) statutory scheme, (3) importance to affected person, (4) legitimate expectations, (5) deference—and here these factors required the municipality to "give reasons" for refusing the 2nd and 3rd rezoning applications.
BaselineB: Common law administrative law duty of procedural fairness, applying Baker v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), [1999] 2 S.C.R. 817 (five-factor framework), in the municipal rezoning context under the Act respecting land use planning and development, R.S.Q., c. A-19.1.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Jurisdictional rule against joint trial on separate informations/indictments: even with consent, a judge is "without jurisdiction to try together separate informations or indictments" (Crane applied), unless a statute "expressly provide[s] otherwise".
BaselineA: Common law rule from Crane v. Public Prosecutor, [1921] 2 A.C. 299 (as applied/confirmed by the SCC); applied across Criminal Code and provincial summary conviction procedure absent express statutory authorization.
CaseB_TestB: Credibility-assessment guidance on (i) absence of evidence of motive to lie and (ii) lack of embellishment: motive-to-lie absence may be relevant but judges must avoid (1) treating "no evidence either way" as proof disproving a motive and (2) reversing the burden; lack of embellishment "cannot be used to bolster" credibility and "simply does not weigh against it" (may relate to motive-to-lie assessment).
BaselineB: Common law credibility/reasoning principles in criminal trials, drawing on R. v. W.(D.), R. v. Stirling, and related appellate guidance (as cited in the reasons).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Marine insurance “perils of the seas” causation test for negligent acts: a loss is by perils of the seas where the proximate cause is a “fortuitous accident or casualty of the seas”; specifically, “An act is not negligent in itself but only in relation to a foreseeable risk of harm. If that foreseeable risk of harm is a peculiarly marine risk, then the act, coupled with its foreseeable consequence, is a fortuitous accident of the seas and a peril of the seas and the proximate cause of the loss.”
BaselineA: Statute (Insurance (Marine) Act, R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 203, Schedule “Rules for Construction of Policy” defining perils of the seas as “fortuitous accidents or casualties of the seas”; and Marine Insurance Act, R.S.B.C. 1960, c. 231, s. 57(2)(a) (now s. 56(2)(a)) on insurer liability despite crew negligence) plus common-law/authorities (Canada Rice Mills, Ld. v. Union Marine & General Insurance Co., [1941] A.C. 55; Cohen, Sons & Co. v. National Benefit Assurance Co. (1924), 18 Ll. L. Rep. 199).
CaseB_TestB: Section 35(1) threshold test for who qualifies as an “aboriginal peopl[e] of Canada”: “the Aboriginal peoples of Canada under s. 35(1) are the modern successors of those Aboriginal societies that occupied Canadian territory at the time of European contact. This may include Aboriginal groups that are now outside Canada.” (If threshold met, proceed to Van der Peet.)
BaselineB: Constitutional text (Constitution Act, 1982, s. 35(1): “The existing aboriginal and treaty rights of the aboriginal peoples of Canada are hereby recognized and affirmed.”) interpreted purposively in light of prior SCC s. 35 jurisprudence (e.g., Sparrow; Van der Peet; Mitchell) as discussed in the reasons.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory “bridging” test for post-expiry interest arbitration: s. 70(1) preserves the right to invoke interest arbitration after a collective agreement expires if (i) notice to bargain has been given and no collective agreement is in operation, and (ii) the notice to arbitrate is served within the s. 70(1)(a) status-quo period; the right “need exist only at the time of the notice to arbitrate and not at the time the award is handed down.”
BaselineA: Statute: The Labour Relations Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 232, s. 70(1) (now R.S.O. 1980, c. 228, s. 79), applied to preserve contractual rights (interest arbitration clauses) beyond expiry; also considered s. 34c.
CaseB_TestB: Directed verdict / non-suit test: whether there is “any admissible evidence, whether direct or circumstantial, which, if believed by a properly charged jury acting reasonably, would justify a conviction” (from Monteleone/Shephard).
BaselineB: Common law test as stated in R. v. Monteleone (deriving from United States of America v. Shephard), applied in the criminal procedure context.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: McKibbon conditions for when an Attorney General’s agent (or other s. 507(2) actor) may prefer an indictment adding counts after a preliminary inquiry (Criminal Code, s. 507(2)-(3))
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 507(1)-(3); interpreted in light of related provisions ss. 504-505 and prior SCC discussion in R. v. Chabot, [1980] 2 S.C.R. 985; Re Criminal Code (1910), 43 S.C.R. 434)
JudgeA: Lamer J. (for Ritchie, Estey and Lamer JJ.)
