CaseB_TestB: Van der Peet test (as applied/clarified in Mitchell) for establishing an Aboriginal right under s. 35(1): (1) ancestral practice/custom/tradition; (2) integral to distinctive culture; (3) reasonable continuity; plus evidentiary approach to oral history (useful and reasonably reliable; due weight but proof on balance of probabilities)
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine under Constitution Act, 1982, s. 35(1), applying/clarifying R. v. Van der Peet, [1996] 2 S.C.R. 507 and Delgamuukw v. British Columbia, [1997] 3 S.C.R. 1010 (and related s. 35 jurisprudence)
JudgeB: McLachlin C.J. (for McLachlin C.J. and Gonthier, Iacobucci, Arbour and LeBel JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: First degree murder classification under Criminal Code ss. 212(b) + 214(2): if the murder (including a s. 212(b) “accident or mistake” killing of B) was “planned and deliberate” in relation to the s. 212(b) mens rea (intent to kill A), it is first degree; the victim’s identity is irrelevant.
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 212(b) and 214(2), within the homicide scheme including s. 205; classification approach confirmed in R. v. Farrant).
CaseB_TestB: Interpretation/application of Alberta Limitations Act s. 12 in conflicts cases: s. 12 applies Alberta limitation law to bar a claim only if a live cause of action exists under the applicable foreign substantive law; s. 12 does not revive an action already time-barred by the foreign limitation period (per Tolofson lex loci delicti).
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: Limitations Act, R.S.A. 2000, c. L-12, s. 12, interpreted against the Tolofson v. Jensen common-law conflicts rule (lex loci delicti includes foreign limitation as substantive).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Mens rea for attempted murder: Crown must prove a specific intent to kill (no lesser/constructive murder intent suffices)
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code) interpreted against prior SCC precedent (Lajoie v. The Queen, [1974] S.C.R. 399)
CaseB_TestB: “Same establishment” under CHRA s. 11 / Guidelines s. 10: whether employees are subject to a “common personnel and wage policy” (a factual inquiry into common employer policies/objectives, not a term-by-term collective agreement comparison)
BaselineB: Statute and regulation (Canadian Human Rights Act, s. 11, read with Equal Wages Guidelines, 1986, SOR/86-1082, s. 10)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Matrimonial property distribution under Saskatchewan’s Matrimonial Property Act: equal distribution presumption, with pre-marital property exempt only to its fair market value at marriage under s. 23; courts cannot use “Capital Base Theory” or s. 21(2)(q) to exempt more than that value (s. 23(4)-(5) discretion only to reduce/deny the exemption if it would be “unfair and inequitable” to exempt).
BaselineA: Statute: The Matrimonial Property Act, 1979 (Sask.), c. M-6.1, especially ss. 20, 21, 23 (and interaction with s. 21(2)(q)).
CaseB_TestB: Aggravated assault (Criminal Code, s. 268(1)) in HIV non-disclosure cases: because aggravated assault is consequence-based, the Crown must prove the aggravating consequence (“endangers the life”) beyond a reasonable doubt; if there is a reasonable doubt the complainant’s life was capable of being endangered (e.g., complainant may already have been HIV-positive), there is no aggravated assault (though attempt may be made out).
BaselineB: Statute interpreted/applied: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 268(1) (with related provisions on assault/consent and attempt: ss. 265(1)(a), 265(3)(c), 24(1), 660; and prior SCC guidance in R. v. Cuerrier and others).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Mechanics’ lien “owner” test under s. 1(1)(d): a person is an owner if they (a) have “any estate or interest in the land”, (b) the work is done “at whose request”, and (c) the work is done “upon whose credit, or … on whose behalf, or … with whose privity or consent, or … for whose direct benefit” (with the Court stressing an “overall view” of complex development arrangements to determine “request”/credit/benefit).
BaselineA: Statute: The Mechanics’ Lien Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 267, s. 1(1)(d) (and applied with s. 5(1) lien entitlement limits: “sum justly due” and “sum justly owing”).
CaseB_TestB: Challenge for cause (juror partiality) test under s. 638(1)(b): to show a “realistic potential for juror partiality” generally requires (1) “that a widespread bias exists in the community” and (2) “that some jurors may be incapable of setting aside this bias, despite trial safeguards, to render an impartial decision” (overarching question: “whether there exists a realistic potential for partial juror behaviour”).
BaselineB: Statute interpreted through prior SCC/common law: Criminal Code, s. 638(1)(b), applying/clarifying Sherratt and Williams (and related jurisprudence) on “realistic potential” and the two-part attitudinal/behavioural inquiry.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Anns-based duty of care for public authorities: (1) proximity/foreseeability — “is there a sufficiently close relationship… so that… carelessness… might cause damage”; and (2) residual policy considerations — “are there any considerations which ought to negative or limit (a) the scope of the duty (b) the class of persons… (c) the damages…”. Applied through the policy/operational distinction: “the more ‘operational’ a power or duty may be, the easier it is to superimpose upon it a common law duty of care.”
BaselineA: Common law (adopting/applying Anns v. Merton London Borough Council, [1978] A.C. 728; also drawing on Donoghue v. Stevenson; Hedley Byrne; Dorset Yacht) alongside statutory context (Municipal Act, R.S.B.C. 1960, c. 255, s. 714 and the City’s building by-law imposing an enforcement duty).
CaseB_TestB: Implied-limit framework for roadside sobriety screening under Charter s. 10(b): a limit is “prescribed by law” if it “results by necessary implication… from [a statute’s] operating requirements”; police sobriety-screening measures (asking about drinking; requesting roadside sobriety tests) are lawful if “reasonable and necessary” to fulfill the duty to check sobriety and are “incompatible with the exercise of the right to counsel”; then the implied limit is justified under s. 1 using Oakes proportionality (pressing objective, rational connection, minimal impairment, overall proportionality).
BaselineB: Statute + constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms ss. 10(b) and 1; Manitoba Highway Traffic Act, s. 76.1(1); Criminal Code, ss. 253 and 254; plus prior SCC interpretation of “prescribed by law”/operating requirements (Therens; Thomsen).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Perka necessity defence (excuse): moral/normative involuntariness requiring (i) “urgent situation of clear and imminent peril”, (ii) “no reasonable legal alternative”/“compliance with the law is demonstrably impossible”, and (iii) proportionality (“harm inflicted must be less than the harm sought to be avoided”), with Crown bearing burden once air of reality raised
BaselineA: Common law necessity preserved via Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 7(3); baseline formulation drawn from Morgentaler v. The Queen, [1976] 1 S.C.R. 616 (“urgent situations of clear and imminent peril when compliance with the law is demonstrably impossible”)
CaseB_TestB: Section 8 reasonable expectation of privacy (REP) test (totality of circumstances): four inquiries—(1) subject matter, (2) direct interest, (3) subjective expectation, (4) objective reasonableness (normative) — applied to determine whether police sting screenshotting engages s. 8
BaselineB: Constitutional (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 8) REP framework from prior SCC cases (e.g., Edwards/Spencer/Cole/Marakah) plus interaction with Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, Part VI (ss. 183, 184.2) via the concept of “private communication” depending on REP
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 613(1)(b)(iii) proviso: Crown must satisfy appellate court the verdict “would necessarily have been the same” absent the legal error; where the error is exclusion of exculpatory evidence, assess the whole record including the reasonable possible effect of the excluded evidence, with any reasonable effect enuring to the accused
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 613(1)(b)(iii)), as interpreted in Colpitts v. The Queen, [1965] S.C.R. 739
CaseB_TestB: Appellate court raising a new issue: may do so only rarely where failing to do so would risk an injustice (i.e., good reason to believe the result would realistically have differed absent the potential error), and only if the court has jurisdiction, the record is sufficient, and no procedural prejudice results; plus notice and opportunity to respond
BaselineB: Common law (appellate process/adversarial system principles drawing on cases such as R. v. W. (G.) and Quan v. Cusson) and statutory limits on Crown appeals (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, ss. 676(1)(a), 686(4))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Threshold s. 96 characterization: a power is not “judicial” (and thus does not trigger the s. 96 analysis) where there is “no real lis between the parties” and the decision is based “not on considerations of legality but on considerations of expediency” (administrative vs judicial power).
BaselineA: Common law / constitutional jurisprudence under Constitution Act, 1867, s. 96 (drawing on Re Residential Tenancies Act, 1979; Massey-Ferguson; Grondin; and the John East Iron Works two-fold approach to identifying 'judicial power').
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 12 mandatory-minimum framework (as applied to robbery MMPs): two-stage inquiry—(1) determine a “fit and proportionate sentence”; (2) ask whether the mandatory minimum “requires” a sentence that is “grossly disproportionate”, assessed via “scope and reach of the offence”, “effects of the penalty on the offender”, and “the penalty and its objectives”; may be assessed on the actual offender or a “reasonably foreseeable case”.
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 12; Criminal Code sentencing provisions (including s. 718.2(e)); and prior SCC s. 12 mandatory-minimum jurisprudence (especially R. v. Hills, 2023 SCC 2; R. v. Nur; R. v. Lloyd; R. v. Smith).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 93(1) denominational schools infringement test: a provincial education law is invalid if it "prejudicially affect[s] any Right or Privilege with respect to Denominational Schools which any Class of Persons have by Law in the Province at the Union"; applied via the agreed conditions: (a) a right/privilege affecting a denominational school; (b) enjoyed by a class of persons; (c) by law; (d) in effect at Union; and (e) prejudicially affected.
BaselineA: Constitution Act, 1867, s. 93(1) (and s. 93(2)); baseline content of protected rights identified by reference to law in force at Confederation (e.g., C.S.L.C. 1861, c. 15) and Privy Council jurisprudence cited in the reasons.
CaseB_TestB: Young Offenders Act non-disclosure test (records/reports): the "nub" is whether the information/disclosure "links the identity of the young person with a charge, proceeding or disposition"; if the prohibited link is made, disclosure/publication is barred unless it fits a specific statutory exception (e.g., s. 44.1(1)(k) requires judicial authorization and disclosure only to the extent directed; s. 38(1.13) requires disclosure be "necessary" for compliance/safety and limited to the relevant school board).
BaselineB: Statute: Young Offenders Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. Y-1, especially ss. 38(1), 38(1.1), 38(1.13)-(1.15), 40, 44.1, and 46.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 93(1) denominational schools guarantee: a provincial education law is unconstitutional if it "prejudicially affect[s]" a protected denominational-school "Right or Privilege" that a "Class of Persons" had "by Law" "at the time of the Union" (conditions: (a) right/privilege affecting a denominational school; (b) enjoyed by a particular class of persons; (c) by law; (d) in effect at the time of the Union; (e) prejudicially affected).
BaselineA: Constitution Act, 1867, s. 93(1) (and s. 93(2)); applied through Privy Council/SCC jurisprudence cited in the reasons (e.g., City of Winnipeg v. Barrett; Brophy; Ottawa Separate Schools Trustees v. Ottawa Corporation; Hirsch; Tiny).
CaseB_TestB: Ambit of federal maritime law (navigation and shipping): "the mere involvement of a pleasure craft in an incident is not sufficient"; courts must examine the "factual context" and ask whether the allegedly negligent act is "so integrally connected" to navigation/shipping (i.e., "integrally connected with the act of navigating the pleasure craft on Canadian waterways") that it is a "practical necessity" for Parliament to have jurisdiction.
BaselineB: Common law constitutional characterization of Canadian maritime law’s scope under Constitution Act, 1867, ss. 91(10) and 92(13), drawing on ITO — International Terminal Operators Ltd. v. Miida Electronics Inc.; Whitbread v. Walley; Ordon Estate v. Grail (as cited in the reasons).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Certiorari review of a preliminary inquiry committal: a committal is a jurisdictional error reviewable on certiorari where there is “no evidence” on an essential element (since “no evidence” can never be “sufficient evidence” under s. 475); reviewing court must independently assess whether there was “any evidence” on each essential element
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 475) as interpreted through prior SCC/PC certiorari jurisprudence (Patterson v. The Queen; Martin v. The Queen; Forsythe v. The Queen; Nat Bell Liquors)
JudgeA: Estey J. (for Dickson, Estey, Lamer and Wilson JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Criteria for a compensatory allowance under art. 559 C.C.Q.: claimant must establish (1) contribution, (2) enrichment of spouse’s patrimony, (3) causal link, and (4) proportion; elements “must be evaluated with great flexibility”; enrichment must “subsist” and is evaluated “at the time of the divorce”
BaselineB: Statute (Civil Code of Quebec, art. 559) informed by unjust enrichment principles (e.g., Cie Immobilière Viger Ltée v. Lauréat Giguère Inc.) and interaction with Bankruptcy Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. B-3, ss. 2 and 148
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Estoppel by representation (including by silence): requires a representation (words/conduct, or silence only where there is a legal duty to speak) that induces detrimental reliance; absent these conditions, estoppel cannot preclude denial of contractual liability
BaselineA: Common law (estoppel by representation; as summarized from Spencer Bower & Turner and cases such as Greenwood v. Martins Bank, Ltd.)
CaseB_TestB: Rebutting the Criminal Code s. 212(3) presumption: jury considers all the evidence about cohabitation and financial arrangements; trial judge need not identify a single “particular and severable” item as “evidence to the contrary”
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 212(3))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Municipal tax ultra vires where council sets a tax rate by resolution when enabling legislation requires the rate be imposed by by-law (self-redelegation/acting by wrong instrument)
BaselineA: Statute (Cities and Towns Act, R.S.Q. 1941, c. 233, s. 526 as amended for Dorval; plus procedural requirements in Cities and Towns Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 193 (e.g., ss. 385, 395))
CaseB_TestB: Causation in negligent blood-donor screening: whether the defendant’s negligence “materially contributed” to the occurrence of the injury (not a rebuttable presumption; not strict but-for)
BaselineB: Common law causation in negligence (but-for as general test; material contribution concept referenced via Snell v. Farrell and Athey v. Leonati; Hollis distinguished)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 13 bar on using an accused’s prior testimony to incriminate them in a retrial: s. 13 applies at the moment of attempted use; “incriminating” is assessed in the second proceeding; and a retrial is “any other proceedings”.
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 13 (interpreted purposively in light of ss. 11(c) and 11(d)).
CaseB_TestB: Reformed rule for substantive admissibility of a non-accused witness’s prior inconsistent statement: admissible for truth if (threshold) it would be admissible as the witness’s sole testimony, and (principled hearsay) necessity + reliability shown—typically via (1) oath/affirmation/solemn declaration plus explicit warning, (2) videotaped in entirety, and (3) full opportunity to cross-examine at trial; with a voir dire assessing indicia and voluntariness/administration-of-justice concerns.
BaselineB: Combination: Canada Evidence Act, s. 9 (procedure for cross-examining own witness) plus common law “orthodox rule” from Deacon v. The King (prior inconsistent statements only for credibility), modified using the principled hearsay approach from R. v. Khan and R. v. Smith.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: When a trial judge’s acquittal can be appealed by the Crown as an “error of law alone”: a “total absence of evidence” is an error of law only where the law shifts the burden of proof to the accused on the fact in issue; otherwise (given the presumption of innocence) “it can sometimes be said as a matter of law that there is no evidence on which the Court can convict but never that there is no evidence on which it can acquit”.
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 605(1)(a) (Crown appeal on a question of law alone)) as interpreted through SCC precedent (Sunbeam Corporation (Canada) Ltd. v. The Queen; Lampard v. The Queen; discussion of Wild v. The Queen).
CaseB_TestB: Test for interim relief (stay/interim release) under Supreme Court Act s. 65.1: the RJR—MacDonald criteria—(1) “a serious question” to be tried, (2) “irreparable harm”, and (3) “balance of convenience”.
BaselineB: Statute (Supreme Court Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. S-26, s. 65.1) applying the common-law/interlocutory injunction framework reaffirmed in RJR—MacDonald Inc. v. Canada (Attorney General).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: When a trial judge’s finding supporting an acquittal can be treated as an error of law ("no evidence"/"total absence of a foundation") for Crown appeal jurisdiction: intention is fact; "total absence of a foundation for a finding of fact" is an error of law, but for acquittals this "may only occur if there has been a transfer to the accused by the law of the burden of proof of a given fact"; otherwise "there is always some evidence" because of the presumption of innocence.
BaselineA: Combination: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 605(1)(a) (Crown appeal on "a question of law alone") plus SCC common-law appellate-jurisdiction principles from Sunbeam Corporation (Canada) Ltd. v. The Queen, [1969] S.C.R. 221 and Lampard v. The Queen, [1969] S.C.R. 373 (also discussing Wild v. The Queen, [1971] S.C.R. 101).
CaseB_TestB: Ontario anti-SLAPP dismissal framework under Courts of Justice Act s. 137.1: (1) moving party must "satisf[y]" the judge (balance of probabilities) that the proceeding "arises from" an "expression" that "relates to a matter of public interest" (broad, non-qualitative); if met, (2) responding party must show under s. 137.1(4)(a) "grounds to believe" the proceeding has "substantial merit" (legally tenable + evidence reasonably capable of belief; "real prospect of success") and the moving party has "no valid defence"; and (3) under s. 137.1(4)(b) the harm and public interest in allowing the proceeding to continue must "outweigh" the public interest in protecting the expression (a public-interest weighing exercise).
BaselineB: Statute: Courts of Justice Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.43, s. 137.1(3) and (4) (and related ss. 137.1(2), 137.2).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Lawfulness of warrantless arrest on private premises (forcible entry) under s. 450(1)(a): arrest is lawful if all four questions are answered “yes” (indictable offence; reasonable and probable grounds suspect committed/was about to commit; reasonable and probable grounds suspect is within premises; proper announcement before entry).
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 450(1)(a) (arrest without warrant) plus common law entry limits from Eccles v. Bourque, [1975] 2 S.C.R. 739 (itself grounded in Semayne’s Case (1604)).
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 15 discrimination analysis (as applied here): after showing a denial of an equality right (equality before the law), claimant must also show the distinction is “discriminatory” by being based on personal characteristics (enumerated or analogous grounds) in its social/political/legal context; geographic distinction for murder-mode-of-trial did not meet this discrimination requirement.
BaselineB: Constitutional/common law framework: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 15(1), as interpreted in Andrews v. Law Society of British Columbia, [1989] 1 S.C.R. 143 (definition of discrimination; enumerated/analogous grounds approach).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code indictment amendment for variance: court should amend a particular (e.g., drug specified) to conform to the evidence if it does not mislead or prejudice the accused (s. 529(4)-(5)); SCC may amend on appeal (s. 613(1)(b)(i), (3))
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 529(4)-(5) (amendment considering prejudice/misleading and injustice; possible adjournment to cure), and appellate power ss. 613(1)(b)(i), 613(3); applied in context of Narcotic Control Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. N-1, ss. 2, 4 and Schedule item 3 (what counts as a 'narcotic')
CaseB_TestB: Ineffective assistance of counsel test (G.D.B.): appellant must show (1) counsel’s acts or omissions constituted incompetence, and (2) a miscarriage of justice resulted
BaselineB: Common law: R. v. G.D.B., 2000 SCC 22, [2000] 1 S.C.R. 520 at para. 26 (two-part test for ineffective assistance of counsel)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Concurrent liability of a solicitor in tort and contract: a common law duty of care may arise from a contractual retainer where there is sufficient proximity, but tort cannot be used to circumvent contractual limits/exclusions
BaselineA: Common law (duty of care/proximity and negligent misstatement principles from Donoghue v. Stevenson; Hedley Byrne; Anns v. Merton; plus SCC treatment in Nunes Diamonds and Smith v. McInnis)
CaseB_TestB: Enforcement of exclusive choice-of-forum clause in an action in warranty: art. 3148(2) C.C.Q. prevails over art. 3139 C.C.Q. where the clause clearly ousts Quebec jurisdiction; forum non conveniens (art. 3135) applies only if Quebec jurisdiction is first established
BaselineB: Statute (Civil Code of Québec, arts. 3148 para. 2, 3139, and 3135)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Scope of Quebec Construction Industry Labour Relations Act/Decree: coverage turns on the “nature of the work done” (whether it is statutory “construction”), not the parties’ status; and Decree minimums are mandatory with no “total wage” set-off
BaselineA: Statute and regulation/decree: Construction Industry Labour Relations Act, S.Q. 1968, c. 45 (esp. ss. 1(e), 1(i), 1(j), 1(r), 2(2), 20; also s. 1(p) definition of “wage”) and Decree respecting the construction industry (ss. 3.01, 3.02, 18.06, 32.03)
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 12 mandatory-minimum analysis and remedy: punishment violates s. 12 only if “grossly disproportionate”; if a mandatory minimum is unconstitutional, the remedy is s. 52(1) invalidity (no stand-alone constitutional exemption under Charter s. 24(1))
BaselineB: Combination of constitutional text and common law: Charter ss. 12 and 24(1) and Constitution Act, 1982, s. 52(1); gross disproportionality test from R. v. Smith and related s. 12 jurisprudence cited in the reasons
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Parens patriae limit: a court should never authorize non-therapeutic sterilization of a mentally incompetent person (because it can never safely be determined to be for the person’s benefit)
BaselineA: Common law (parens patriae jurisdiction of superior courts, derived from the Crown/Chancery tradition; exercised on necessity for the protected person’s benefit)
CaseB_TestB: Residual management rights—“balancing of interests” assessment: arbitrator considers all surrounding circumstances and whether the employer policy strikes a reasonable balance between management and employees’ interests
BaselineB: Common law labour-arbitration framework (KVP; endorsed in Irving) applied to a collective agreement management-rights clause requiring the employer to act “reasonably, fairly and in good faith”
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Kienapple (rule against multiple convictions) applicability test: requires (1) sufficient factual nexus (usually: “Does the same act of the accused ground each of the charges?”) and (2) sufficient legal nexus such that “there is no additional and distinguishing element that goes to guilt” in the offence sought to be barred; with guidance that an element is not “distinct or additional” where (1) it is a “particularization” of another element, (2) there are multiple statutory methods to prove a single delict, or (3) Parliament deems an element satisfied by proxy proof; plus the overarching inquiry whether the same “cause, matter or delict” underlies both charges.
BaselineA: Common law (Kienapple v. The Queen) rule against multiple convictions, developed in SCC jurisprudence (including Côté v. The Queen; Krug v. The Queen).
CaseB_TestB: “Services … to the public” under Yukon Human Rights Act s. 8(a): two-part analysis—(1) determine what constitutes the “service” on the facts; (2) determine whether the service creates a “public relationship” between provider and user (with “public” defined relationally), assessed contextually using non-determinative criteria including “selectivity”, “diversity”, “involvement of non-members”, “commercial nature”, “intimate nature”, and “purpose” of offering the service.
BaselineB: Statute: Yukon Human Rights Act, R.S.Y. 1986 (Supp.), c. 11, ss. 8(a) (and related context ss. 6, 11; discussed alongside analogous human rights provisions and Berg).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Ensite test for whether property is “used or held ... in the course of carrying on a business” (ITA s. 129(4)): property must be “truly employed and risked” in the business; the test asks whether the property was “used to fulfil a requirement which had to be met in order to do business” (not whether the taxpayer was forced to use that property), with the threshold met when withdrawal would “have a decidedly destabilizing effect on the corporate operations themselves”.
BaselineA: Statute — Income Tax Act, s. 129(4) (especially the parenthetical exclusion in s. 129(4)(a)(ii): “other than a property used or held by the corporation in the year in the course of carrying on a business”).
CaseB_TestB: Crown appeal/new trial test under Criminal Code s. 686(4): to obtain a new trial after an acquittal, “it was the duty of the Crown ... to satisfy the Court that the verdict would not necessarily have been the same if the trial judge had properly directed the jury” (a “very heavy onus”, requiring “a reasonable degree of certainty”).
BaselineB: Statute — Criminal Code, s. 686(4), as interpreted through SCC precedent (Vézeau v. The Queen; R. v. Morin).
JudgeB: Cory J. (for Sopinka, Cory, Iacobucci and Major JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Public interest immunity for Cabinet documents: court must (i) conduct a preliminary judicial inspection and then (ii) balance the public interest in confidentiality against the public interest in the administration of justice, considering variables like the level of decision-making, nature of the policy, timing/recency, and importance/need for the documents in the litigation
BaselineA: Common law (public interest immunity/Crown privilege jurisprudence, especially Smallwood v. Sparling, [1982] 2 S.C.R. 686; also discussed: R. v. Snider, Gagnon v. Commission des valeurs mobilières du Québec; and comparative authorities such as Conway v. Rimmer and Burmah Oil)
CaseB_TestB: Review of jury charge (pre-Lifchus/W.(D.)): whether the charge, read as a whole, creates a 'reasonable likelihood that the jury misapprehended' (i) the standard of proof beyond a reasonable doubt and (ii) how to deal with conflicting versions of events (including the W.(D.) 'third alternative')
BaselineB: Common law (jury-instruction standards from R. v. Lifchus, [1997] 3 S.C.R. 320; R. v. W. (D.), [1991] 1 S.C.R. 742; and the 'substantial compliance' approach referenced via R. v. Starr and R. v. Russell)
JudgeB: Major J. (for Major, Binnie, Arbour and LeBel JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 7 limit on extradition/surrender: courts may intervene only where surrender would, in the particular circumstances, violate the principles of fundamental justice (judicial intervention limited to 'cases of real substance')
BaselineA: Statute/treaty framework for extradition (Extradition Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-21, ss. 13, 18; Extradition Treaty Between Canada and the United States of America, art. 4(1)(i)) plus Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7
CaseB_TestB: Crown appeal jurisdiction test: a Court of Appeal may interfere with an acquittal only if the trial court erred 'on a question of law alone' (Criminal Code s. 605(1)(a), applying Schuldt)
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 605(1)(a)) as interpreted in Schuldt v. The Queen, [1985] 2 S.C.R. 592
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 7 limit on extradition: courts may intervene only where surrender would, in the particular circumstances, violate the principles of fundamental justice (intervention limited to 'cases of real substance')
BaselineA: Statute/treaty plus Constitution: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7 (and context of Extradition Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-21 and Canada–U.S. Extradition Treaty)
CaseB_TestB: ITA s. 20(1)(c)(i) interest deductibility (purpose element): whether, considering all the circumstances, the taxpayer had a reasonable expectation of income at the time the investment was made (income = taxable income, not net income; ancillary income-earning purpose suffices absent sham/window dressing)
BaselineB: Statute: Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), s. 20(1)(c)(i) (interpreting 'purpose' and 'income')
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Injurious affection (no land taken): claimant must show the construction-caused loss would have been actionable at common law (nuisance), i.e., an “unreasonable” “substantial[] interfer[ence] with the use or enjoyment of land” (loss of view/prospect not actionable; balance of reasonable user/public utility).
BaselineA: Statute (Expropriations Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 154, ss. 1(e)(ii), 21) incorporating common-law nuisance actionability requirement; four conditions from The Queen v. Loiselle, [1962] S.C.R. 624 at 627.
CaseB_TestB: Adequacy of jury instructions on alternative routes to murder liability: charge is sufficient if, read as a whole and in context, it required proof beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused “actively participated”/“acted in concert with others” in the killing; trial judge may correct an erroneous “actual shooter” direction by adding “or was otherwise an active participant in her killing”.
BaselineB: Common law on appellate review of jury charges/fair trial (miscarriage of justice) applied in context of Criminal Code party liability (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, ss. 21, 229, 686(1)(b)(iii)); key prior SCC authority discussed: R. v. Thatcher, [1987] 1 S.C.R. 652.
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 10(b) right-to-counsel: absent circumstances showing non-understanding, accused must prove he asked for counsel and was denied (or denied any opportunity to ask); otherwise, once police promptly advise of the right, no further correlative duties arise until the accused indicates a desire to exercise it
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 10(b) (and remedy context s. 24(2)); applied approach from R. v. Anderson (Ont. C.A.)
CaseB_TestB: Employee/representative disgorgement for secret profits: where an employee acting in a representative capacity (or using employer funds/credit without authority) profits through bad faith/abuse of position, the employee must account for and turn over the profits to the employer (via C.C.L.C. arts. 411 and/or 1713 principles)
BaselineB: Statute/civil code: Civil Code of Lower Canada, arts. 411 (possessor in bad faith) and 1713 (mandatary must render account and deliver/pay over all received under authority of mandate)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Wigglesworth s. 11 Charter applicability test: a matter falls within s. 11 either (1) "because by its very nature it is a criminal proceeding" (public, criminal/quasi-criminal/regulatory) or (2) because conviction may lead to a "true penal consequence"; and "in cases where the two tests conflict the 'by nature' test must give way to the 'true penal consequence' test". "True penal consequence" includes "imprisonment or a fine which by its magnitude would appear to be imposed for the purpose of redressing the wrong done to society at large".
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 11 (opening words "Any person charged with an offence"); applied in context of s. 11(h).
CaseB_TestB: Functional approach to reviewing jury charges: "As long as an appellate court, when looking at a trial judge’s charge to the jury as a whole, concludes that the jury was left with a sufficient understanding of the facts as they relate to the relevant issues, the charge is proper" (juries must be "properly -- not perfectly -- instructed").
BaselineB: Common law appellate review standard for jury charges (as stated through prior SCC authorities cited in the reasons, including Azoulay v. The Queen; Cluett v. The Queen; John v. The Queen).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: s. 577(1) Criminal Code “whole of the trial” includes jury selection; accused must be able to hear/participate in any juror examination for partiality after plea, and breach is fundamental (not curable by proviso)
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 577(1), with related jury-selection provisions incl. ss. 569(2), 598-600, 613(1)(b)(iii)) interpreted in light of prior SCC guidance (Basarabas and Spek v. The Queen; Vézina and Côté v. The Queen) and appellate authority (Hertrich; Meunier)
CaseB_TestB: Common-law test for when an appellate court may set aside an acquittal and enter a conviction (instead of ordering a new trial): Crown must show verdict would not have been the same but for error of law, accused should have been found guilty but for that error, and all necessary findings of fact were made (explicitly/implicitly) or are not in issue
BaselineB: Common law (as stated in Vézeau v. The Queen; Courville v. The Queen) applied alongside Criminal Code s. 613(4)(b)(ii)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: When a trial judge quashes a voidable charge under Criminal Code s. 529, the quashing is tantamount to an acquittal (triggering autrefois acquit) if, as a matter of law, the required amendment cannot be made without injustice/irreparable prejudice; otherwise the judge should amend and not quash. Key formulation: the judge may quash only if the amendment "cannot be made without injustice being done"; and "if having determined, as a matter of law, that an amendment cannot be made without causing irreparable prejudice, his quashing of the charge at the trial is then ... tantamount to an acquittal" (Lamer J.).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34), especially ss. 529(3)-(6) (amendment/quash powers) and the special-plea provisions ss. 535 and 537; interpreted against prior SCC cases including Petersen v. The Queen and Doyle v. The Queen.
CaseB_TestB: Framework to define the scope of an acquired right (legal non-conforming use) and decide whether a changed use remains protected: (1) characterize the purpose of the pre-existing use actually carried on; (2) mere intensification is usually protected unless it becomes a different use; (3) added activities beyond prior ones may be too remote (no need to assess neighbourhood effects); (4) if added/altered within original purpose, balance landowner vs community considering nature of pre-existing use, remoteness, and new/aggravated neighbourhood effects; (5) neighbourhood effects should be proven by evidence unless obvious; (6) definition not too broad or too narrow; (7) criteria aim to ground the decision in objective facts and avoid personal value judgments (Binnie J.).
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law principles: Act Respecting Land Use Planning and Development, R.S.Q., c. A-19.1, s. 113(18) (acquired rights/non-conforming uses) and related municipal by-law context; informed by prior SCC/common law non-conforming use jurisprudence including Central Jewish Institute v. City of Toronto.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Workmen’s privilege against an owner’s immovable where work is ordered by a lessee: the lessee is only a “builder/contractor” for arts. 2013e/2013f C.C.L.C. if there is a construction contract including an owner-to-builder claim/undertaking to pay a construction contract price (a price fund from which the owner can retain to satisfy privileges); absent such a claim/price, no privilege lies against the owner’s immovable.
BaselineA: Statute (Civil Code of Lower Canada, arts. 2013e and 2013f (and related contract provisions arts. 984 et seq., 1060))
CaseB_TestB: Mental distress damages for breach of contract: recoverable where (1) “an object of the contract was to secure a psychological benefit that brings mental distress upon breach within the reasonable contemplation of the parties” and (2) “the degree of mental suffering caused by the breach was of a degree sufficient to warrant compensation”; no independent actionable wrong is required (Hadley v. Baxendale remoteness/foreseeability governs).
BaselineB: Common law (contract damages/remoteness under Hadley v. Baxendale; discussed with reference to Vorvis v. I.C.B.C.)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Unequal division of marital property under NB Marital Property Act s. 7(f): despite the equal-division principle, a court may depart where it is of the opinion equal division would be inequitable; specifically, "where the property has been acquired exclusively or almost wholly through the efforts of one spouse and there has been no, or a negligible contribution to child care, household management or financial provision by the other" (circumstances relating to acquisition/maintenance/improvement) the court may exercise discretion under s. 7(f).
BaselineA: Statute: Marital Property Act, S.N.B. 1980, c. M-1.1, ss. 2, 3, 7 (especially s. 7(f) and the equal-division principle in s. 2 as implemented by s. 3).
CaseB_TestB: Interjurisdictional immunity (constitutional inapplicability) for federal services: provincial laws of general application apply unless they "bear upon those subjects in what makes them specifically of federal jurisdiction"; for a federal service, its specific nature is affected if the provincial statute touches a "vital or essential aspect of its establishment, management or operation"—here, the provincial transport permit system is constitutionally inapplicable to the federal sightseeing service because of its "massive and intrusive impact" on those vital/essential aspects.
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine (interjurisdictional immunity) as articulated in prior SCC cases cited in the reasons, especially Bell Canada v. Quebec (CSST), Construction Montcalm Inc. v. Minimum Wage Commission, and Clark v. Canadian National Railway Co.; applied to the Quebec Transport Act permit scheme (R.S.Q., c. T-12, s. 36 etc.) and Bus Transport Regulation.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “financing” in Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971 s. 44(2)(a): claimant “finances” a labour dispute only where there is “active and voluntary involvement” and a “meaningful connection between the payment and the dispute” (mandatory union dues alone are insufficient).
BaselineA: Statute — Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, S.C. 1970-71-72, c. 48, s. 44(2)(a) (exception to disentitlement where claimant proves he is not “participating in or financing or directly interested in” the labour dispute).
CaseB_TestB: Enforceability/scope of waiver (exclusion) clause for negligence in a sporting event: in the “context in which it was signed”, determine whether the clause (though framed as indemnity) was intended as a release and whether the accident/negligence was within what the parties reasonably contemplated; clause upheld where it is not “unfair” or “unreasonable” in the circumstances.
BaselineB: Common law — contractual interpretation/enforcement of exclusion/waiver clauses (including arguments framed as fundamental breach, unconscionability, and public policy) as applied to the signed entry-form waiver.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “financing” in Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971 s. 44(2)(a): claimant is “financing” a labour dispute only where the payment reflects “active and voluntary involvement” and a “meaningful connection between the payment and the dispute” (mere mandatory union dues diverted to an international strike fund are insufficient).
BaselineA: Statute: Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, S.C. 1970-71-72, c. 48, s. 44(2)(a) (exception to disentitlement where claimant proves he is not “participating in or financing or directly interested in” the labour dispute).
CaseB_TestB: Extradition surrender review: whether surrender would be contrary to s. 7 fundamental justice so as to “shock the conscience” or be “unjust or oppressive” under Extradition Act s. 44(1); this requires the Minister to conduct a “balancing exercise”, with refusal only where the requesting state’s “particular treatment” sufficiently violates fundamental justice to tilt the balance against extradition.
BaselineB: Statute + Charter: Extradition Act, S.C. 1999, c. 18, s. 44(1) (“unjust or oppressive”) interpreted in light of Charter s. 7 (“shock the conscience”) and prior SCC guidance (e.g., Burns; Lake).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 10 “detention” test (Therens restatement): detention exists where (1) s. 10 targets a “restraint of liberty other than arrest” where one may reasonably need counsel; (2) beyond physical constraint, detention occurs when the state “assumes control over the movement of a person by a demand or direction which may have significant legal consequence and which prevents or impedes access to counsel”; and (3) the needed “compulsion or coercion” may arise from “criminal liability for refusal” or a “reasonable belief” there is no choice (applied to a s. 234.1(1) roadside breath demand).
BaselineA: Common law/Charter interpretation drawing from R. v. Therens, [1985] 1 S.C.R. 613 (interpreting Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 10(b) “detention”), applied in the statutory context of former Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 234.1(1)-(2).
CaseB_TestB: Criminal Code s. 150.1(4) “all reasonable steps” (mistake of age) framework: once the defence has an “air of reality”, the Crown must prove beyond a reasonable doubt either (1) the accused “did not honestly believe the complainant was at least 16” or (2) the accused “did not take ‘all reasonable steps’ to ascertain the complainant’s age”; the reasonable-steps inquiry is “highly contextual, fact-specific”, and “the more reasonable an accused’s perception of the complainant’s age, the fewer steps reasonably required of them.”
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 150.1(4) (and related scheme including ss. 150.1(1), 150.1(2.1)); SCC clarifies how the statutory “all reasonable steps” requirement operates and what evidence may be considered.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Extradition specialty/immunity duration: an undertaking not to prosecute for pre-surrender offences lasts only until the extraditee has been “restored or has had an opportunity of returning” (i.e., a reasonable opportunity to return); it does not confer perpetual immunity once the person remains/returns to Canada by choice
BaselineA: Statute (Extradition Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-21, s. 33) interpreted in light of the extradition arrangement/undertaking and international law interpretive principles (Vienna Convention, art. 31, cited)
CaseB_TestB: Intertwining principle for criminal appeals: where an appeal is properly before the SCC on an alleged error of law, the Court may also address whether the error is saved by the curative proviso; “the provisions for taking account of the severity of errors (s. 686(1)(b)(iii) ...) will always be intertwined with any error of law considered by this Court”
BaselineB: Common law clarification from R. v. Keegstra, [1995] 2 S.C.R. 381, applied alongside Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(b)(iii)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “anything” in Criminal Code theft (s. 283(1)): to be the object of theft, the thing must (1) be property capable of a proprietary right and (2) be capable of being taken/converted so as to cause deprivation; confidential information per se fails (and thus cannot be stolen).
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 283(1) (theft definition) (with related discussion of s. 338(1) fraud, but the key test is for theft).
CaseB_TestB: Interpretation of “assets” in MVHC rent-assistance application: “assets” means property/interests that can actually be used to discharge debts (including rent); a Henson trust interest (a “mere hope” with no enforceable right) is not an “asset” for eligibility/disclosure.
BaselineB: Common law (contractual interpretation principles, incl. Sattva) applied to the Assistance Application/Tenancy Agreement; plus trust-law characterization of Henson trusts (applied from Ontario (Director) v. Henson).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 7 analysis for compelled fingerprinting after charge: even if liberty is deprived, the deprivation accords with fundamental justice where the fingerprinting process does not "unduly invade the rights of the accused" and is not arbitrary (discretion to fingerprint is permissible within the criminal justice system).
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7; Identification of Criminals Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-1, s. 2; Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 453.3(3) and 455.5(5). The Court also draws on common-law/Charter baselines for "principles of fundamental justice" (e.g., Re B.C. Motor Vehicle Act; R. v. Lyons; Hunter v. Southam).
CaseB_TestB: Sheppard/Braich test for appellate intervention based on insufficient reasons: (1) are the reasons inadequate; and (2) if so, do they prevent appellate review (i.e., are they "inscrutable" / do they create an "impediment to appellate review")?
BaselineB: Common law: R. v. Sheppard, 2002 SCC 26 and R. v. Braich, 2002 SCC 27 (also applied alongside deference principles from cases like Burke/Housen/H.L.).
JudgeB: Bastarache and Abella JJ. (LeBel J. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Detention at the border for s. 10(b): a traveller is “detained” when customs “assumes control over the movement of a person by a demand or direction which may have significant legal consequence” (Therens), i.e., when “taken out of the normal course and forced to submit to a strip search” and cannot refuse/leave (Customs Act s. 203 offence to resist).
BaselineA: Common law / constitutional interpretation of Charter s. 10(b) “detention”, based on R. v. Therens, [1985] 1 S.C.R. 613 (definition of detention later affirmed in Hufsky and Thomsen).
CaseB_TestB: s. 11(b) unreasonable delay framework (Morin factors + institutional-delay guideline): determine unreasonableness by a “judicial determination balancing” the s. 11(b) interests using (1) length of delay; (2) waiver; (3) reasons for delay (inherent time requirements; actions of accused; actions of Crown; limits on institutional resources; other reasons); and (4) prejudice; with an administrative guideline of “between 8 and 10 months for institutional delay in Provincial Courts” (not a fixed ceiling and not to be applied mechanically).
BaselineB: Common law / constitutional interpretation of Charter s. 11(b), distilled from Mills, Rahey, Conway, Smith, and Askov (including Askov’s institutional-delay guideline concept).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Leary intoxication rule for general-intent offences (and the limited ‘extreme intoxication’ gateway): voluntary intoxication is not a defence to general-intent crimes; mens rea is inferred from the actus reus, and only in rare cases of extreme intoxication akin to insanity/automatism can intoxication evidence go to the trier of fact on minimal intent
BaselineA: Common law (Leary v. The Queen, [1978] 1 S.C.R. 29; also relying on R. v. George, [1960] S.C.R. 871; Swietlinski v. The Queen, [1980] 2 S.C.R. 956; and Majewski (H.L.)) applied in the context of Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 246.2(c)
CaseB_TestB: Appellate ‘error of law’ threshold for setting aside an acquittal where the trial judge failed to address a necessary issue: an appellate court may overturn where the trial judge “has not directed his mind to an issue or issues that require determination in order to reach the verdict” (as applied to the ‘global count’ proceeds charge)
BaselineB: Common law appellate review principles (including Schuldt v. The Queen, [1985] 2 S.C.R. 592) applied within the statutory criminal appeal framework (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 675 (and appeal context discussed under s. 676)) and the elements of proceeds offences under the Narcotic Control Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. N-1, ss. 11.1, 11.2
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Appellate intervention in a trial judge’s discretionary reapportionment of matrimonial property: intervene only if the judge “misdirects himself” or the decision is “so clearly wrong as to amount to an injustice” (and s. 51 does not require asset-by-asset contribution comparisons or separate ‘business’/‘domestic’ pools).
BaselineA: Combination: statute (Family Relations Act, R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 121, ss. 43 and 51) plus common-law appellate deference standard (as applied in Harper v. Harper, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 2; also citing Re Hull Estate).
CaseB_TestB: Duty to correct prejudicial Crown jury address: where Crown remarks are “prejudicial to a degree sufficient to impose a legal duty on the trial judge to comment” to ensure the defence is “fairly put to the jury”; failure is an error of law and (here) not cured by the s. 686(1)(b)(iii) proviso.
BaselineB: Combination: statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(b)(iii)) plus common-law fairness control of jury addresses/charge (articulated via adoption of Ayles J.A.’s formulation).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Wigmore/Slavutych four-part test for recognizing a (qualified) common law privilege against compelled disclosure of communications (including claimed journalist-source privilege): (1) communication originates in confidence; (2) confidentiality essential to the relationship; (3) relationship ought to be sedulously fostered; (4) injury from disclosure greater than benefit to correct disposal of litigation
BaselineA: Common law (Wigmore criteria as discussed/approved in Slavutych v. Baker, [1976] 1 S.C.R. 254)
CaseB_TestB: Reasonableness review of Crown corporations’ discretionary PILT calculations: discretion exists but must be exercised within the statutory/regulatory framework—effective rate must be based on the municipality’s actual existing tax system (as if the property were taxable private property), not a 'fictitious tax system'; reintroducing an abolished occupancy tax in the calculation is unreasonable
BaselineB: Statute and regulation (Payments in Lieu of Taxes Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. M-13, esp. ss. 2 (definitions incl. 'effective rate'), 2.1, 4(1), sch. II item 10; and Crown Corporation Payments Regulations, SOR/81-1030, esp. s. 2 (definitions), s. 7(1))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Patent Act s. 36(1) disclosure/sufficiency test: applicant must disclose “everything that is essential for the invention to function properly”; completeness requires two conditions — (1) “describe the invention and define the way it is produced or built” (ambiguity if not) and (2) “define the nature of the invention and describe how it is put into operation” (insufficiency if not); disclosure must enable a skilled person “to produce it using only the instructions contained in the disclosure” and, after expiry, “to use the invention as successfully as the inventor could at the time of his application”; deposit of seed “by itself does not comply” with s. 36(1).
BaselineA: Statute: Patent Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. P-4, s. 36(1) (as interpreted with reference to Consolboard; Minerals Separation; Burton Parsons; Monsanto).
CaseB_TestB: Standard of review for labour arbitral awards applying common law/equitable doctrines: apply Dunsmuir categories/context; arbitral use of estoppel is not automatically correctness—correctness only for Dunsmuir correctness categories (e.g., constitutional, central importance/outside expertise, true jurisdiction, competing tribunals); otherwise reasonableness applies, confirmed by contextual factors (privative clause, tribunal purpose, nature of question, expertise).
BaselineB: Common law administrative law framework from Dunsmuir v. New Brunswick and Smith v. Alliance Pipeline Ltd., applied in labour arbitration context; supported by statute context (Labour Relations Act, R.S.M. 1987, c. L10, ss. 121, 128(2)).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 96 / Residential Tenancies three-stage test as refined: (1) historical inquiry with narrow characterization and an exclusivity/concurrency gloss (shared jurisdiction valid only if inferior-court involvement was “broadly co-extensive”); (2) whether the tribunal function is judicial; (3) whether, in institutional context, the judicial power is “necessarily incidental”/ancillary to a broader policy scheme
BaselineA: Constitution Act, 1867, s. 96; common-law constitutional framework from Re Residential Tenancies Act, 1979, [1981] 1 S.C.R. 714
CaseB_TestB: Downtown Eastside public interest standing framework (discretionary, cumulative weighing of three factors): (i) serious justiciable issue; (ii) genuine interest; (iii) reasonable and effective means — with clarifications that legality/access to justice get no “particular weight”, no individual co-plaintiff is required if a “sufficiently concrete and well-developed factual setting” will be forthcoming, and standing may be revisited only after a “material change” raising serious doubt about that factual setting
BaselineB: Common law test from Canada (Attorney General) v. Downtown Eastside Sex Workers United Against Violence Society, 2012 SCC 45
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Bankruptcy priority for provincial “deemed trusts”: s. 47(a) applies only if the tax money is identifiable/traceable trust property under general trust law; otherwise the province has only a Crown claim under s. 107(1)(j). As McLachlin J. puts it: if the money is “identifiable or traceable” it is “exempt from distribution to creditors by reason of s. 47(a)”; if it “cannot be traced, there is no ‘property held . . . in trust’ under s. 47(a)” and “s. 107(1)(j) applies.”
BaselineA: Statute (Bankruptcy Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. B-3, ss. 47(a) and 107(1)(j)) interpreted alongside provincial Social Service Tax Act, R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 388, s. 18; informed by general principles of trust law and SCC cases Deputy Minister of Revenue v. Rainville and Deloitte Haskins and Sells Ltd. v. Workers' Compensation Board.
CaseB_TestB: Section 23 “numbers warrant” / facilities-location analysis (sliding scale): relevant numbers are “somewhere between the known demand and the total number of persons who could potentially take advantage of the service”; determining what numbers warrant requires (from Mahe) “a determination of the appropriate services, in pedagogical terms, for the number of students involved” and “an examination of the costs of the contemplated service”; and where a minority-language board exists, defining the relevant area and choosing the location of classes/facilities falls within the minority’s “exclusive powers of management and control”, with the Minister’s role limited to verifying compliance with “objective provincial norms and guidelines consistent with s. 23” (he has “no power to substitute his own criteria or decision”).
BaselineB: Constitution (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 23) as interpreted through the Mahe v. Alberta “sliding scale” framework; applied in the statutory/regulatory context of P.E.I.’s School Act and School Act Regulations (e.g., Reg. s. 6.01(f) threshold; ss. 6.07, 6.08, 6.11; School Act s. 128(2)).
JudgeB: Major and Bastarache JJ. (for the Court)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Young Offenders Act s. 16 transfer to ordinary court: whether the judge is satisfied, after "weighing and balancing all the relevant considerations" in s. 16(2), that transfer is appropriate (onus on applicant, but "not ... a heavy one")
BaselineA: Statute: Young Offenders Act, S.C. 1980-81-82-83, c. 110, s. 16(1) and s. 16(2) (factors), with the SCC applying/confirming its companion decision R. v. M. (S.H.), [1989] 2 S.C.R. 000
CaseB_TestB: Damages for repudiation where contract has alternative modes of performance: adopt the mode "least profitable to the plaintiff, and the least burdensome to the defendant"; not a factual inquiry into how defendant would likely have performed but for repudiation
BaselineB: Common law rule on damages for contracts with alternative performances, traced to Cockburn v. Alexander (1848) and explained in Withers v. General Theatre Corp. (1933) (as adopted/confirmed in Canadian appellate authority cited in the reasons)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Canadian maritime law test for agent liability on a contract with an unnamed/partially disclosed principal: personal liability turns on the parties’ intention as shown by the contract’s terms and surrounding circumstances (no prescribed formality of naming the principal; contract construction). Key formulations: whether the agent contracted personally or 'solely in the capacity of agent ... is a matter of construction of a particular contract' (La Forest J.); and 'there is no prescribed formality for disclosure and ... responsibility ... depends on the will of the contracting parties' (L'Heureux-Dubé J.).
BaselineA: Common law (contract/agency) as part of Canadian maritime law under Federal Court Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. F-7, ss. 2 and 22(2)(m), with the Court relying on ITO—International Terminal Operators Ltd. v. Miida Electronics Inc., [1986] 1 S.C.R. 752 as the key maritime-law baseline and drawing on common-law agency authorities (e.g., Universal Steam Navigation; The 'Swan'; The 'Santa Carina').
CaseB_TestB: Statutory 'reasonable cause' threshold for immunity from suit for reporting suspected child abuse under Child Welfare Act, s. 38: s. 38(6) immunity applies unless the report is made 'maliciously or without reasonable cause'; 'reasonable cause' is an objective threshold meaning the informant must have 'reasonable cause to ask CPS to consider looking into the matter' (not reasonable grounds to believe abuse occurred).
BaselineB: Statute: Child Welfare Act, R.S.N. 1990, c. C-12, ss. 38(1) and 38(6) (interpreting the scope of the reporting duty and the immunity/exception).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Common-law limits on a warrantless frisk search incident to a lawful arrest: (1) discretionary (no duty to search); (2) must be for a valid criminal-justice objective (safety/escape/evidence) and not an improper purpose; (3) must not be abusive—force/constraint must be proportionate to objectives and circumstances
BaselineA: Common law (search incident to arrest), as discussed through cases including R. v. Brezack (Ont. C.A.), R. v. Morrison (Ont. C.A.), and R. v. Miller (Ont. C.A.)
CaseB_TestB: Section 7 minimum procedural requirements for warrantless child apprehension in non-emergency situations: balance (1) seriousness of interests; (2) difficulty distinguishing emergency/non-emergency; (3) risks to children of an emergency-only threshold vs benefits of prior authorization; constitutional minimum is apprehension without prior authorization permitted where there is serious harm or risk of serious harm, plus a fair and prompt post-apprehension hearing
BaselineB: Statute and Charter: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7; Child and Family Services Act (Manitoba), S.M. 1985-86, c. 8, ss. 21(1), 17, 27(1), 29(1)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal negligence: whether the accused’s conduct is a “marked departure from the norm” such that “wanton or reckless disregard” can be inferred; consequences (death) generally add nothing unless “so interwoven” with the conduct as to help characterize it
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 202(1)-(2), 203 (now ss. 219-220)) as interpreted in R. v. Tutton, [1989] 1 S.C.R. 1392 (marked departure central under both objective and subjective approaches)
CaseB_TestB: Standing/jurisdiction before the CITT under the AIT: a procurement complaint under AIT is only available where the supplier is a “Canadian supplier” (has a “place of business in Canada”), because only then is the procurement “within Canada” under AIT Article 502
BaselineB: Statute and regulation incorporating a trade agreement: Canadian International Trade Tribunal Act, ss. 30.1, 30.11(1) and Canadian International Trade Tribunal Procurement Inquiry Regulations, s. 3(1), interpreted by reference to the Agreement on Internal Trade, arts. 501, 502, 518
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 8 reasonableness of compelled document production in a regulatory tax audit: s. 231(3) demand is a “seizure” but is reasonable given the regulatory scheme, low privacy expectation, and need for random monitoring; Hunter criteria are ill-suited outside criminal/quasi-criminal context
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law/constitutional doctrine: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 8 applied to Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1952, c. 148, ss. 231(3), 238(2) (and privacy protection context in s. 241); baseline s. 8 framework from Hunter v. Southam Inc. (criteria for reasonableness) and related s. 8 cases (e.g., Simmons)
CaseB_TestB: Public interest standing test (purposive, flexible weighing): (1) serious justiciable issue; (2) real stake/genuine interest/engagement; (3) whether the proposed suit is, “in all of the circumstances”, a “reasonable and effective means” to bring the issue to court (not a strict ‘no other way’ requirement), assessed with discretionary considerations (judicial economy, adversarial suitability, legality principle, realistic alternatives)
BaselineB: Common law doctrine of standing from SCC precedents (notably Borowski; Finlay; Canadian Council of Churches; Hy and Zel’s; Thorson; McNeil)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Duty to defend is determined by the pleadings: the insurer must defend only where the pleadings allege claims seeking damages that "are or may be payable under" the policy (i.e., potentially within coverage); no duty where allegations are clearly outside coverage (e.g., only fraud alleged and fraud is excluded).
BaselineA: Contract (insurance policy interpretation) informed by common-law insurance principles (e.g., "[t]he pleadings govern the duty to defend"; duty triggered by the "mere possibility" a covered claim may succeed).
CaseB_TestB: Air of reality threshold for honest but mistaken belief in consent under Criminal Code s. 265(4): the defence goes to the jury only if there is "sufficient evidence" such that a "reasonable jury properly instructed" could acquit; requires evidence beyond a "mere assertion" of belief (no need for evidence independent of the accused).
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 265(4)) codifying/reflecting common-law "air of reality" threshold for defences (citing Pappajohn, Bulmer, Robertson, etc.).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Collateral wage benefits and loss of earnings in tort: as a general rule, wage benefits paid while plaintiff is unable to work must be deducted from lost-earnings damages, subject to limited subrogation/trust exceptions
BaselineA: Common law (tort damages / collateral benefits doctrine), drawing on SCC personal injury damages principles in Andrews v. Grand & Toy Alberta Ltd.; Thornton v. Prince George School Board; Arnold v. Teno, and collateral benefits authorities including Parry v. Cleaver and Bradburn v. Great Western Rail. Co.
CaseB_TestB: Constitutional 'necessarily incidental' (integration) test for federal provisions intruding on provincial jurisdiction: impugned provisions must be sufficiently integrated with a valid federal scheme to be upheld
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine (division of powers / ancillary powers), as articulated in General Motors of Canada Ltd. v. City National Leasing and Reference re Exported Natural Gas Tax, applied in relation to Constitution Act, 1867 ss. 91(3) and 92(13)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Test for entitlement to a compensatory allowance under art. 559 C.C.Q.: claimant must prove (1) contribution, (2) enrichment of spouse’s patrimony, (3) causal link/correlation, and (4) proportion; enrichment must “subsist” and is evaluated “at the time of the divorce”, with “great flexibility” in evaluating the elements (bankruptcy is not irrefutable proof of no subsisting enrichment).
BaselineA: Statute (Civil Code of Quebec, art. 559) informed by civil-law unjust enrichment principles (e.g., Cie Immobilière Viger Ltée v. Lauréat Giguère Inc.).
CaseB_TestB: Test to set aside a conviction for misapprehension of evidence: misapprehension must go to “the substance” not “detail”, be “material” not “peripheral”, and the errors must play an “essential part” in the reasoning process leading to conviction (a “stringent” conjunctive standard).
BaselineB: Common law appellate standard adopted from R. v. Morrissey (Ont. C.A.) and endorsed with reference to R. v. C. (R.); applied within Criminal Code, s. 686(1)(a)(iii).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Copyright protection for computer programs embodied in silicon chips: whether the chip-embedded program is a “reproduction” of the copyrightable program in a “material form” under s. 3(1) (viewing the chip as a static object encoded with written instructions, not a dynamic sequence of electrical impulses).
BaselineA: Statute (Copyright Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-30, s. 3(1))
CaseB_TestB: Common law de facto taking (constructive expropriation) requiring compensation: two requirements—“(1) an acquisition of a beneficial interest in the property or flowing from it, and (2) removal of all reasonable uses of the property”.
BaselineB: Common law (as stated with reference to Mariner Real Estate; Manitoba Fisheries; Tener) and statutory overlay (Vancouver Charter, s. 569 deeming no “taking”/no compensation)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Novation (mortgage/assumption context): three-part test—(1) new debtor assumes complete liability; (2) creditor accepts new debtor as principal debtor (not agent/guarantor); (3) creditor accepts new contract “in full satisfaction and substitution for the old contract” (novation not found absent “really compelling” circumstances showing creditor assent).
BaselineA: Common law (novation doctrine), as stated in Polson v. Wulffsohn (1890) and applied/clarified in this decision; discussed alongside statutory context (The Limitation of Civil Rights Act, R.S.S. 1978, c. L-16, ss. 2, 40).
CaseB_TestB: De facto taking (constructive expropriation) at common law: two requirements—(1) “an acquisition of a beneficial interest in the property or flowing from it”; and (2) “removal of all reasonable uses of the property”.
BaselineB: Common law (de facto taking), drawn from Mariner Real Estate Ltd. v. Nova Scotia (Attorney General), Manitoba Fisheries Ltd. v. The Queen, and The Queen in Right of British Columbia v. Tener; applied in light of Vancouver Charter, S.B.C. 1953, c. 55, s. 569 (deeming no taking/compensation).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Applicability of Criminal Code s. 443 (now s. 487) search warrant power to offences under "any other Act of Parliament" even where that other Act (e.g., Bankruptcy Act s. 6) also contains search-and-seizure provisions: on a plain reading, s. 443(1)(a)-(b) applies to proceedings under any federal statute; only express limiting language (e.g., s. 443(1)(e) "subject to any other Act of Parliament") restricts it.
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 443(1)(a)-(b) as amended in 1985 to add "or any other Act of Parliament"; considered alongside Bankruptcy Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. B-3, s. 6 and Interpretation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-23, s. 27(2).
CaseB_TestB: Meaning of "risks willingly assumed" in Occupiers' Liability Act s. 4(1): s. 4(1) embodies the volenti doctrine, so more than mere knowledge/appreciation of risk is required; the plaintiff must have accepted the legal risk/waived recourse (i.e., assumed "the entire risk of injury ... without recourse to any contribution or liability" from the occupier).
BaselineB: Statute interpreted in light of common law: Occupiers' Liability Act, R.S.O. 1980, c. 322, ss. 2-4 (especially s. 4(1) "risks willingly assumed"); common law volenti as described in SCC cases Dube v. Labar and Crocker v. Sundance Northwest Resorts Ltd.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 32 applicability to an entity: whether the entity is part of “government” (La Forest J.: focus on whether government controls the entity’s core functions; distinction between “ultimate or extraordinary control” and “routine or regular control”).
BaselineA: Common law / constitutional interpretation of Charter s. 32(1), applying McKinney v. University of Guelph and referencing RWDSU v. Dolphin Delivery Ltd.
CaseB_TestB: Arbitration Act s. 31(2)(a) leave-to-appeal test: leave only on a “question of law”; plus (i) importance to the parties and (ii) determination “may prevent a miscarriage of justice” (requires a material legal error with “arguable merit”); with residual discretion factors (conduct, alternative remedies, undue delay, urgent need for final answer).
BaselineB: Statute: Arbitration Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 55, s. 31(2)(a) (formerly Commercial Arbitration Act), as interpreted with reference to BCIT and related cases.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Limits on applying the Paré “single transaction” analysis: it applies only to murder classification under Criminal Code s. 214(5) and requires first proving the accused committed (or was a party to) both the underlying offence and the murder, before asking whether they were “sufficiently closely connected in time” to classify the murder as first degree
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 214(5) (now s. 231(5))) as interpreted in R. v. Paré, [1987] 2 S.C.R. 618 ("single transaction" meaning of “while committing”); also engages party-liability concepts under Criminal Code s. 21
CaseB_TestB: Forum non conveniens test (post-Van Breda): once jurisdiction is properly assumed, the moving party must show the alternative forum is “clearly more appropriate”; the court considers multiple contextual factors (e.g., CJPTA s. 11(2) list) and one forum must “ultimately emerge as clearly more appropriate”
BaselineB: Common law (Club Resorts Ltd. v. Van Breda, 2012 SCC 17) forum non conveniens framework; supported by statutory codifications used as reference points (e.g., Court Jurisdiction and Proceedings Transfer Act, S.B.C. 2003, c. 28, s. 11(2); Civil Code of Québec, art. 3135)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Abuse of process stay test (Keyowski/Jewitt/Young): a stay is granted only in the “clearest of cases” where compelling the accused to stand trial would violate fundamental principles of justice/fair play and decency, or where proceedings are “oppressive or vexatious” (and, per Conway, where the “affront to fair play and decency is disproportionate to the societal interest” in prosecution).
BaselineA: Common law (as summarized from R. v. Keyowski adopting R. v. Jewitt, which adopted R. v. Young; also framed with R. v. Conway).
CaseB_TestB: When the curative proviso applies (Criminal Code, s. 686(1)(b)(iii)): an appellate court asks whether there is “any reasonable possibility that the verdict would have been different had the error at issue not been made” (i.e., whether the verdict would “necessarily have been the same” absent the error).
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(b)(iii)), interpreted through prior SCC cases (Colpitts; Wildman; R. v. S. (P.L.); Broyles; R. v. B. (F.F.)).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Lippé institutional impartiality test for part-time judges’ outside occupations: (1) whether a fully informed person would have a reasonable apprehension of bias in a substantial number of cases; if yes, the occupation is per se incompatible unless (2) safeguards sufficiently minimize the risk so that a fully informed person would not have that apprehension in a substantial number of cases
BaselineA: Common law test for reasonable apprehension of bias (Committee for Justice and Liberty v. National Energy Board) as adopted in Valente v. The Queen for independence/impartiality; applied within Charter s. 11(d) and Quebec Charter s. 23 context
CaseB_TestB: Zundel s. 1 objective-identification constraint (“no shifting purpose”): for s. 1, the Court must look to Parliament’s intention when the provision was enacted/amended and “cannot assign objectives, nor invent new ones according to the perceived current utility of the impugned provision”
BaselineB: Common law/constitutional doctrine under Charter s. 1 (Oakes framework) and prior SCC authority rejecting shifting purposes (R. v. Big M Drug Mart Ltd.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 96 ‘core jurisdiction’ / Residential Tenancies historical inquiry: characterize the impugned jurisdiction and ask whether it was exercised exclusively by s. 96 superior courts at Confederation (if not, the grant to an inferior court is valid)
BaselineA: Common law constitutional test applying Constitution Act, 1867, s. 96 (as developed in Re Residential Tenancies Act, 1979 and Sobeys Stores Ltd. v. Yeomans)
CaseB_TestB: Interpretation of “sold in any market in Canada” (Patent Act ss. 80(1)(b), 83(1), 85): includes sales regulated by Canadian public law, delivered/dispensed in Canada, and whose cost is borne by Canadians
BaselineB: Statutory interpretation of Patent Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. P-4, ss. 80(1)(b), 83(1), 85 (using the Canada Trustco textual-contextual-purposive approach)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Adequacy/sufficiency of an indictment (including when proof shows multiple conspiracies): indictment is adequate if it gives the accused reasonable notice and identifies the transaction; and a proven conspiracy falls within the indictment if it included some accused, occurred sometime within the alleged time span, and had as its object the type of crime alleged
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 510, 512, 516) as interpreted through SCC/common-law principles (cited: R. v. Côté; R. v. Wis Development Corp.; R. v. B. (G.); R. v. Cotroni)
CaseB_TestB: Constitutional validity of the Canada Evidence Act s. 38 national security disclosure scheme: (i) s. 96 analysis under Re Residential Tenancies Act, 1979 (historical conformity inquiry; if no conformity, inquiry ends) and (ii) fair-trial safeguard via s. 38.14—trial judge may order any remedy necessary to protect trial fairness, and the s. 38.14 stay is not constrained by the Charter/common-law 'clearest of cases' stay test
BaselineB: Statute (Canada Evidence Act, ss. 38 to 38.16, especially ss. 38.04, 38.06, 38.14) plus constitutional/common-law baselines for review (Constitution Act, 1867, s. 96; Charter, s. 7; Re Residential Tenancies Act, 1979; MacMillan Bloedel; Babcock)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Entrapment (random virtue-testing) under Mack: entrapment where police provide an opportunity without (a) reasonable suspicion the person is already engaged in the crime, or (b) acting pursuant to a bona fide inquiry into a sufficiently precise location reasonably suspected of the crime; Barnes clarifies that mere presence in the defined area is enough to be 'associated' with it, and that 'randomness' is permissible within a bona fide inquiry.
