"Random virtue-testing... only arises when... without a reasonable suspicion that: (a) the person is already engaged... or (b) the physical location... is a place where the particular criminal activity is likely occurring."
BaselineA: Common law (entrapment doctrine) from R. v. Mack, [1988] 2 S.C.R. 903
CaseB_TestB: Appellate intervention with trial judge’s voluntariness ruling: a court of appeal may not reweigh the voir dire evidence on whether a statement was "free and voluntary" absent a "serious, specific and determining error"; otherwise it "reassessed the weighing of the evidence as a whole" impermissibly.
BaselineB: Common law (confession voluntariness and appellate review principles; specific baseline cases not cited in the reasons provided)
JudgeB: LeBel J. (for the Court, oral reasons)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: When prejudicial Crown jury-address remarks create a legal duty on the trial judge to comment (and whether failure is an error of law not curable by the s. 686(1)(b)(iii) proviso)
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, s. 686(1)(b)(iii)) plus common-law fairness duty in jury trials (as reflected in the Court adopting Ayles J.A.’s formulation)
CaseB_TestB: Broker commission triggers under a Quebec brokerage contract: (1) no “agreement to sell” unless the accepted promise to purchase is unconditional and specific performance (transfer of title) is available; and (2) “voluntarily prevents free performance” requires seller fault (mirroring art. 1503 C.C.Q.)
BaselineB: Statute and contract interpretation (Civil Code of Québec, arts. 1396 and 1503; interpreted through the brokerage contract clauses 6.1(3o) and 6.1(4o))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 16(2) insanity test — clarify that the first branch (“incapable of appreciating the nature and quality”) is limited to incapacity to appreciate the physical character/consequences of the act; moral wrongfulness belongs (post-Chaulk) under the second branch (“incapable ... of knowing ... is wrong”). Key quotes: first branch “only protects an accused who, because of a disease of the mind, was incapable of appreciating the physical consequences of his act”; second branch (via Chaulk) “redefined the word ‘wrong’ in s. 16(2) to mean ‘morally wrong’ rather than ‘legally wrong’.
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 16(2)); interpreted in light of SCC precedents cited in the reasons (Cooper v. The Queen; Kjeldsen v. The Queen; R. v. Abbey; and the contemporaneous interpretive change in R. v. Chaulk).
CaseB_TestB: Reasonable suspicion standard for sniffer-dog search (and linked investigative detention) — must be more than a hunch: “reasonable suspicion must be grounded in objectively discernible facts”; assessed on “the totality of the circumstances”; “We are looking here at possibilities, not probabilities. Are the facts objectively indicative of the possibility of criminal behaviour... ? If so... met. If not, the inquiry is at an end.” Objective assessment is “through the lens of a reasonable person standing in the shoes of the police officer” (training/experience relevant but not accepted uncritically).
BaselineB: Common law Charter s. 8 / s. 9 framework for sniffer-dog searches and investigative detention, building on SCC precedents cited in the reasons (R. v. Kang-Brown; R. v. A.M.; R. v. Mann; and companion clarification in R. v. Chehil).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Legitimate expectations cannot constrain the legislative process: the doctrine is procedural only (consultation/representations), creates no substantive rights (no consent/veto), and does not apply to introducing legislation (especially money bills)
BaselineA: Common law administrative-law doctrine of legitimate expectations as an aspect of procedural fairness (natural justice), as described in Old St. Boniface Residents Assn. Inc. v. Winnipeg (City) and related cases (also relying on the principle that procedural fairness does not apply to purely legislative functions: Bates v. Lord Hailsham; Inuit Tapirisat; Martineau; Penikett)
CaseB_TestB: Divorce Act s. 17 variation framework: court must be satisfied of a post-order 'change in the condition, means, needs or other circumstances' (s. 17(4)) and then vary in light of that change considering the s. 17(7) objectives; pension income may be treated as 'means' and 'double dipping' depends on whether the pension was truly valued/divided as future property
BaselineB: Statute (Divorce Act, 1985), especially s. 17(4) (threshold change in circumstances) and s. 17(7) (objectives for varying spousal support)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Extradition under s. 7: surrender is unconstitutional only if it places the fugitive in a situation that “sufficiently shocks” the Canadian conscience / is “simply unacceptable”, assessed contextually (offence/penalty, foreign justice system safeguards, comity and security) with “due latitude” to the Minister’s balancing discretion.
BaselineA: Combination: statute (Extradition Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. E-23, s. 25) + Charter (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7) + common law/precedent (Canada v. Schmidt; United States v. Allard; Argentina v. Mellino).
CaseB_TestB: Search warrants for media premises: after meeting Criminal Code s. 487(1)(b), the justice must assess overall “reasonableness” under s. 8 in light of s. 2(b), considering a non-exhaustive list of factors (including impact on news-gathering, alternative sources ordinarily disclosed, possible conditions), with the “essential question” being whether “taking into account all the circumstances… the search was reasonable.”
BaselineB: Combination: statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 487(1)(b), (d), (e)) + Charter (ss. 2(b), 8) + prior case law (Re Pacific Press; Descôteaux v. Mierzwinski).
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Reasonable apprehension of bias (pecuniary interest) test for tribunal impartiality: “Would a reasonably well-informed person consider that the interest might have an influence on the exercise of the official’s public duty?” (Old St. Boniface formulation applied to Law Society costs provision).
BaselineA: Common law (administrative law / natural justice), applied as a principle of fundamental justice under Charter s. 7; test taken from Old St. Boniface Residents Assn. Inc. v. Winnipeg (City), [1990] 3 S.C.R. 1170.
CaseB_TestB: Nelles malicious prosecution / lifting prosecutorial immunity test (4 elements): (1) prosecution initiated by defendant; (2) terminated in plaintiff’s favour; (3) absence of reasonable and probable cause (subjective + objective); (4) malice / improper purpose (“deliberate and improper use of the office … inconsistent with the status of ‘minister of justice’”).
BaselineB: Common law tort framework from Nelles v. Ontario, [1989] 2 S.C.R. 170 (applied to Crown/prosecutors; balance of probabilities).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Colour of right / mistake of law bar: colour of right is unavailable unless the offence definition embraces it; and in any event a mistaken belief that the Criminal Code is inoperative on a reserve is a mistake of law, and "[s]ection 19 of the Code expresses the long recognized principle that a mistake about the law is no defence".
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, ss. 19 and 206(1)(d); plus the common-law principle codified by s. 19 that ignorance/mistake of law is no excuse).
CaseB_TestB: Modified Taylor definition/test for "hatred" under s. 14(1)(b): apply objectively whether "a reasonable person, aware of the context and circumstances" would view the expression as likely to expose a person/group to the extreme "detestation" and "vilification" (focus on likely effects; intent irrelevant), with the statutory words "ridicules, belittles or otherwise affronts the dignity of" struck as unconstitutional.
BaselineB: Statute as interpreted (Saskatchewan Human Rights Code, S.S. 1979, c. S-24.1, s. 14(1)(b)); built on prior SCC interpretation in Canada (Human Rights Commission) v. Taylor, [1990] 3 S.C.R. 892 (definition of hatred) as modified in this case.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Test for granting intervener status and managing prejudice from a new Charter argument/fresh evidence: intervener must have a sufficient interest and bring a special perspective; Court considers whether raising a new Charter issue would prejudice the respondent (e.g., if it would have been affected by additional trial evidence); proposed materials should be filed only on consent or, if objected to as fresh evidence, only with leave at the hearing.
BaselineA: Common law / SCC practice on intervention and fresh evidence (no specific statutory provision identified in the reasons).
CaseB_TestB: Interpretation of Criminal Code s. 182(b) (offering indignities to human remains): (1) physical interference/contact is sufficient but not necessary; (2) the offence targets indignities offered to a dead body/human remains, not monuments per se; (3) where a monument marks the presence/final resting place of human remains, offering indignities to the monument constitutes offering indignities to the human remains.
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 182(b) (with related appellate powers in ss. 683(1)(g) and 695(1) discussed).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: When the federal Environmental Assessment and Review Process Guidelines Order applies: there must be a “proposal” (an “initiative, undertaking or activity for which the Government of Canada has a decision making responsibility”), meaning an affirmative federal “legal duty or obligation” under an Act of Parliament; once that duty exists, the responsible “initiating department” must apply the Guidelines Order
BaselineA: Regulation and statute: Environmental Assessment and Review Process Guidelines Order, SOR/84-467 (ss. 2 “proposal”, “initiating department”; s. 6; also s. 3) made under Department of the Environment Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. E-10, s. 6; applied in context of Navigable Waters Protection Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. N-22, s. 5
CaseB_TestB: Curative proviso (harmless error) test under Criminal Code s. 686(1)(b)(iii): uphold conviction despite an error of law if the Crown shows either (1) the error was “so harmless, and so insignificant, that it could not have affected the verdict”; or (2) despite the serious error, the case was “so overwhelming that a conviction would have been inevitable even if the error had not been made”
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(b)(iii), as interpreted through SCC precedent cited in the reasons (notably R. v. Khan, 2001 SCC 86; R. v. Trochym, 2007 SCC 6)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 133 “legislative nature” test (including anti-circumvention principle): an instrument is legislative if (1) it embodies a rule of conduct, (2) has the force of law, and (3) applies to an undetermined number of persons; and if “the net effect of a series of discrete acts has a legislative character, then each of these component acts will also be imbued with this same character” and must comply with s. 133 bilingual enactment/publication requirements.
BaselineA: Constitution Act, 1867, s. 133, as interpreted in Reference re Manitoba Language Rights, [1992] 1 S.C.R. 000 and Reference re Manitoba Language Rights, [1985] 1 S.C.R. 721; also applied by analogy to Quebec (Attorney General) v. Brunet, [1990] 1 S.C.R. 260.
CaseB_TestB: Responsive-answer requirement on a jury question about reasonable doubt: even where the main charge follows Lifchus and is “unassailable”, if the jury asks about the standard of proof, “the trial judge must attempt to answer the jury’s question”; repeating the charge may suffice in some cases, but the judge must not discourage further questions and must provide meaningful assistance responsive to the confusion revealed by the question.
BaselineB: Common law governing jury instructions on reasonable doubt and recharges, principally R. v. Lifchus, [1997] 3 S.C.R. 320 and R. v. S. (W.D.), [1994] 3 S.C.R. 521 (with reference to R. v. Starr, 2000 SCC 40).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Mistaken transfer + recipient knowledge + transferor right of recovery ⇒ property does not pass for criminal theft; subsequent fraudulent conversion with intent to deprive constitutes theft (Criminal Code s. 322(1))
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 322(1)) interpreted in light of property-law principles about mistaken transfers and rights of recovery; prior cases discussed include R. v. Stewart, Brochu v. The King, R. v. Johnson; R. v. Dawood overruled
CaseB_TestB: Khosa/Dunsmuir approach to standard of review under Federal Courts Act s. 18.1: apply correctness vs reasonableness (two standards), with reasonableness requiring deference and asking whether the outcome falls within a 'range of possible, acceptable outcomes'
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: Federal Courts Act, R.S.C., 1985, c. F-7, ss. 18.1(3)-(4) (judicial review grounds) plus common-law standard-of-review framework from Dunsmuir v. New Brunswick (2008 SCC 9); applied in context of IRPA s. 67(1)(c)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 11(b) unreasonable delay analysis: a non-mathematical "balancing" of (1) length of delay; (2) waiver; (3) reasons for delay (incl. inherent requirements, accused/Crown actions, institutional limits, other); and (4) prejudice, with an institutional-delay guideline of 8–10 months in Provincial Court that is not a fixed ceiling and must yield to other factors
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional text (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 11(b), with remedy application under s. 24(1)) plus prior SCC s. 11(b) framework (Mills v. The Queen; R. v. Rahey; R. v. Conway; R. v. Smith; R. v. Askov)
CaseB_TestB: Contractor/subcontractor liability for collapse under Quebec Civil Code: even if supports yielded first, the subcontractor is not liable where the general contractor’s own fault imposed an unforeseeable overload; the subcontractor may rely on the contractor’s fault as a defence (by analogy to the builder’s defences in Hill, Clarke-Francis), and the contractor is liable under the contract’s overloading clause
BaselineB: Civil law/statute (Civil Code arts. 1684, 1688, 1065) and SCC articulation in Hill, Clarke-Francis Ltd. v. Northland Groceries (Quebec) Ltd. that a builder can avoid responsibility by proving force majeure/Act of God/owner’s fault/third party act
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Secret commissions offence (Criminal Code s. 426(1)(a)(ii)): actus reus requires (1) agency relationship; (2) agent accepts a benefit as consideration for an act/forbearance in relation to the principal’s affairs; and (3) failure to make “adequate and timely disclosure of the source, amount and nature of the benefit”; mens rea requires awareness of each element, and “corruptly” means “secretly or without the requisite disclosure” (no “corrupt bargain” requirement).
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 426(1)(a) (as applied to s. 426(1)(a)(ii)); interpreted/following R. v. Kelly, [1992] 2 S.C.R. 000.
CaseB_TestB: Criminal Code s. 686(1)(b)(iii) curative proviso: ask “whether a jury properly instructed could, acting reasonably, have come to a different conclusion absent the error”; jury findings may inform the hypothetical reasonable jury if “not tainted by the error.”
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(b)(iii).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: State Immunity Act s. 5 “commercial activity” exception (La Forest J.): two-step, contextual inquiry—(1) determine the “nature” of the foreign state activity (with purpose relevant as part of context), and (2) assess whether the Canadian proceedings “relate” to the commercial aspect by a sufficient “nexus” (more than merely “touch on” or “incidentally affect”); in multifaceted activity, identify the facets relevant to the proceedings and assess the proceedings’ impact on those facets as a whole.
BaselineA: Statute: State Immunity Act, S.C. 1980-81-82-83, c. 95, ss. 2 (definition of “commercial activity”), 3(1), 5; interpreted as codifying the common law restrictive immunity approach (acts jure imperii vs jure gestionis) and applied through a contextual approach (citing I Congreso del Partido).
CaseB_TestB: Compatibility test for provincial “pay/reimburse/retain” mechanisms with the BIA distribution scheme (Deschamps J.): characterize the provincial mechanism (subrogation/compensation/solidarity) and determine whether it “subvert[s] the scheme of distribution” under the BIA; specifically, compensation/retention is permitted only within BIA s. 97(3) set-off and Quebec civil law limits—pre-bankruptcy payment may allow legal compensation if mutual debts are “certain, liquid and exigible” (C.C.Q. arts. 1672-1673), but post-bankruptcy subrogatory payment cannot create compensation (mutual debts must exist before bankruptcy), leaving only a proof of claim (BIA s. 121).
BaselineB: Statutes/civil law: Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. B-3, ss. 97(3), 121, 136–147 (scheme of distribution); Quebec provisions s. 316 AIAOD and s. 54 ALRCI; Civil Code of Québec arts. 1651, 1656(3), 1672-1673, 1681; applied in light of Husky Oil Operations Ltd. v. M.N.R.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Quebec civil law “obligation to inform” (duty of disclosure) in contracts: main elements are (1) debtor’s knowledge (actual or presumed), (2) information of “decisive importance”, and (3) creditor’s inability to inform itself or legitimate reliance on the debtor; in large construction projects the content varies with allocation of risk, relative expertise, and the contract’s “continuing formation”.
BaselineA: Civil Code of Lower Canada (arts. 1024 good faith; 1053 delictual fault) and existing Quebec civil law jurisprudence on the obligation to inform (e.g., Ross v. Dunstall; Air Canada v. McDonnell Douglas; National Bank of Canada v. Soucisse; Houle v. Canadian National Bank).
CaseB_TestB: Test for judicial reform of the common law (maritime context) to abolish the contributory-negligence bar: courts may make incremental change where (1) change is necessary to keep the common law in step with the “dynamic and evolving fabric of our society”, and (2) the change will not have “unforeseeable or complex ramifications beyond the cognizance of the judiciary” (Watkins; Salituro).
BaselineB: Common law (Canadian maritime law) contributory negligence bar, with the SCC’s common-law reform framework from Watkins v. Olafson and R. v. Salituro.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Duty to accommodate (employer/union/complainant) in adverse-effect discrimination: take "reasonable measures short of undue hardship"; union liable if it (1) "cause[s] or contribute[s]" to the discriminatory rule (e.g., collective agreement term) or (2) "impedes the reasonable efforts of an employer to accommodate"; undue hardship assessed contextually (e.g., "financial cost, disruption of a collective agreement, problems of morale of other employees"), with "more than minor inconvenience" required to defeat accommodation.
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Human Rights Act, S.B.C. 1984, c. 22, ss. 8(1)(a),(b),(4) and 9(a)-(c), as interpreted through prior SCC duty-to-accommodate jurisprudence (Ontario Human Rights Commission and O'Malley v. Simpsons-Sears Ltd.; Central Alberta Dairy Pool v. Alberta (Human Rights Commission)).
CaseB_TestB: Exclusive arbitral jurisdiction under s. 45(1) OLRA: adopt the "exclusive jurisdiction model"—courts are ousted where the dispute, in its "essential character", "arises from the interpretation, application, administration or violation of the collective agreement"; analysis looks to "the facts surrounding the dispute" rather than legal labels; extends to Charter remedies if the arbitrator has jurisdiction over parties/subject matter and is empowered to grant the remedy.
BaselineB: Statutory interpretation of Ontario Labour Relations Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. L.2, s. 45(1), informed by prior SCC labour-arbitration exclusivity jurisprudence (notably St. Anne Nackawic Pulp & Paper Co. v. Canadian Paper Workers Union, Local 219) and Mills v. The Queen for 'court of competent jurisdiction' analysis on Charter remedies.
JudgeB: McLachlin J. (for L'Heureux-Dubé, Gonthier, McLachlin and Major JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Trial judge’s discretion to exclude cross-examination on a collateral credibility matter where its relevance does not outweigh its prejudicial effect (relevance vs. prejudice balancing).
BaselineA: Common law (discretionary admissibility control over cross-examination on collateral matters), applied via R. v. Meddoui, [1991] 3 S.C.R. 320.
JudgeA: McLachlin J. (for the Court, oral reasons)
CaseB_TestB: Interest deductibility under Income Tax Act s. 20(1)(c)(i): for the “purpose” element, the test is whether, considering all the circumstances, the taxpayer had a reasonable expectation of income at the time the investment was made (income = taxable income, not net income; ancillary income-earning purpose suffices absent sham/window dressing).
BaselineB: Statute (Income Tax Act, s. 20(1)(c)(i)), interpreted in light of prior SCC cases including Shell Canada Ltd. v. Canada and Bronfman Trust v. The Queen.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 10(b) “detention” at a port of entry: routine secondary immigration examination is not detention unless state action goes beyond what is required for processing entry and becomes a restraint of liberty (Therens/Simmons applied; factors include routine screening purpose and absence of stigma)
BaselineA: Combination: constitutional text (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 10(b)) interpreted through common-law/Charter jurisprudence on “detention” (R. v. Therens; R. v. Simmons; also discussed: R. v. Jacoy; R. v. Kwok)
CaseB_TestB: Elements of civil contempt: proof beyond a reasonable doubt of (1) a clear and unequivocal order, (2) actual knowledge of the order, and (3) an intentional act/omission that breaches the order; no “contumacious intent” required (goes to penalty, not liability)
BaselineB: Common law (civil contempt doctrine) as synthesized from prior authorities cited in the reasons (e.g., Bhatnager v. Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration); Pro Swing Inc. v. Elta Golf Inc.; United Nurses of Alberta v. Alberta (Attorney General); and appellate authorities such as Prescott-Russell and Sheppard)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Admissibility of bad-character/disposition evidence: admissible only if (1) relevant to an issue other than disposition/character and (2) its probative value outweighs its prejudicial effect (with heightened scrutiny for “morally repugnant” acts).
BaselineA: Common law (as stated in Morris v. The Queen; also applied with the probative/prejudicial balancing approach referenced in R. v. B. (C.R.) and the jury-instruction requirement in R. v. D. (L.E.)).
CaseB_TestB: Recent fabrication exception for prior consistent statements: where cross-examination amounts to an allegation of recent fabrication, prior complaint evidence is admissible to rebut it, but only to prove the fact the complaint was made (not the truth of its contents).
BaselineB: Common law (prior consistent statements generally inadmissible; admissible to rebut an allegation of recent fabrication).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Substantive admissibility of a non-accused witness’s prior inconsistent statement (B.(K.G.) reformed rule): prior statement admissible for its truth on a principled hearsay basis (reliability + necessity), with a threshold that it would have been admissible as the witness’s sole testimony; reliability is met where there are sufficient circumstantial guarantees (typically: (1) statement made under oath/affirmation/solemn declaration after an explicit warning about criminal sanctions for falsehood, (2) statement videotaped in its entirety, and (3) full opportunity to cross-examine the witness at trial), or equivalent substitutes; plus a voir dire where the judge must be satisfied the indicia are genuine and then examine voluntariness (if to a person in authority) and whether admission would bring the administration of justice into disrepute.
BaselineA: Common law hearsay/prior inconsistent statement doctrine (orthodox rule from Deacon v. The King) as modified by the principled hearsay approach in R. v. Khan and R. v. Smith; applied procedurally through Canada Evidence Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-5, s. 9 (voir dire/cross-exam of own witness).
CaseB_TestB: Interpretation of “interest” in a motor vehicle liability policy: insurer’s promise to pay “interest accrued on the amount of its guarantee from the date when the action was instituted” includes the art. 1056c C.C. additional indemnity because both the first-paragraph “interest” and second-paragraph “indemnity” are “damages due to delay” computed as a percentage of the capital sum; therefore the additional indemnity is included in the policy’s “interest” obligation (up to the policy limit).
BaselineB: Statutory civil law damages provision (Civil Code art. 1056c) applied through interpretation of the insurance contract’s “interest” clause; supported by characterization analysis in R. v. Nord-Deutsche Versicherungs-Gesellschaft and discussion of Highway Victims Indemnity Fund v. Martineau.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal fraud (Criminal Code s. 380(1)) — “other fraudulent means”: actus reus is conduct that a reasonable person would “properly ... stigmatize as dishonest”, i.e., the “wrongful use of something in which another person has an interest” that extinguishes or puts that interest at risk; mens rea requires subjective knowledge of the act and subjective knowledge that it could cause deprivation (including risk).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 380(1)) as interpreted through SCC/common-law fraud jurisprudence (notably R. v. Théroux and R. v. Olan).
CaseB_TestB: Union duty of representation in collective bargaining (Labour Code s. 47.2): union must not act “in bad faith or in an arbitrary or discriminatory manner or show serious negligence”; duty is generally an “obligation of means” and, in bargaining, union may have to consider former employees’ interests but they have no acquired right to retroactivity and the union has no “obligation of result” to obtain it.
BaselineB: Statute (Quebec Labour Code, R.S.Q., c. C-27, s. 47.2; also discussed alongside ss. 67, 53, 59, 62) with supporting SCC labour-law jurisprudence on the duty of representation.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Crown appeal from acquittal/new trial test under Criminal Code s. 686(4): Crown must show the verdict “would not necessarily have been the same” but for the legal error (a “very heavy onus”, requiring “a reasonable degree of certainty”).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(4)) as interpreted in prior SCC cases (Vézeau v. The Queen; R. v. Morin).
JudgeA: Cory J. (for Sopinka, Cory, Iacobucci and Major JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Implied contractual duty of reasonable notice before enforcing security/appointing a receiver: creditor must give “reasonable notice of its intention to enforce the security” and “reasonable time to pay”; reasonableness assessed using the Mister Broadloom criteria (loan amount, risk, relationship length, debtor reputation, ability to raise funds quickly, surrounding circumstances, and other relevant factors).
BaselineB: Common law (Lister (R.E.) Ltd. v. Dunlop Canada Ltd.; Mister Broadloom criteria adopted/used; also Massey v. Sladen quoted).
JudgeB: McLachlin and Bastarache JJ. (for the Court)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Engineer/design professional preparing tender documents owes no duty to advise/warn bidders about permits or difficulties tied to the contractor’s chosen method of performing the work, absent specific arrangements to the contrary (method is contractor’s responsibility).
BaselineA: Common law (construction/tendering negligence duty/standard of care allocating responsibility for means and methods to the contractor), relying on R. v. Paradis and Farley Inc., [1942] S.C.R. 10; Vermont Construction Inc. v. Beatson, [1977] 1 S.C.R. 758; and Temar Construction Ltd. v. West Hill Redevelopment Co. (1986), 21 C.L.R. 156 (Ont. H.C.).
CaseB_TestB: Framework for reviewing Crown decisions: (1) classify the decision as prosecutorial discretion (decisions about the “nature and extent of the prosecution”) vs tactics/conduct before the court; (2) if prosecutorial discretion, it is reviewable only for abuse of process (egregious conduct seriously compromising trial fairness or integrity), and the accused must first establish a proper evidentiary foundation (balance of probabilities) before the Crown may be required to justify its decision.
BaselineB: Common law/constitutional doctrine on prosecutorial discretion and abuse of process, clarifying Krieger v. Law Society of Alberta, 2002 SCC 65, and applying abuse-of-process review (also referencing Nixon, Power, Beare).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Constitutional limits on warrantless searches under s. 10 NCA: warrantless search is authorized only where “exigent circumstances render it impracticable to obtain prior judicial authorization” (otherwise not “authorized by law” and violates Charter s. 8).
BaselineA: Combination: Charter s. 8 reasonableness framework from R. v. Collins, [1987] 1 S.C.R. 265 (“A search will be reasonable if it is authorized by law, if the law itself is reasonable and if the manner in which the search was carried out is reasonable.”) plus statutory search power in Narcotic Control Act, R.S.C., 1985, c. N-1, s. 10 (as interpreted through R. v. Grant, [1993] 3 S.C.R. 000).
CaseB_TestB: ITA s. 241(3) disclosure exception: whether the confidentiality bar “do[es] not apply in respect of proceedings relating to the administration or enforcement of” the Income Tax Act—interpreted broadly using the “widest possible scope” of “in respect of”/“relating to” to include trustee-initiated bankruptcy proceedings connected to tax collection/enforcement.
BaselineB: Statute: Income Tax Act, S.C. 1970-71-72, c. 63, s. 241(1)-(4), especially s. 241(3) (“do not apply in respect of … proceedings relating to the administration or enforcement of this Act …”).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 486(2.1) screen order: judge may order a child complainant (under 18) testify behind a screen if the judge is of the opinion the exclusion is "necessary to obtain a full and candid account of the acts complained of"; this does not, in itself, breach Charter ss. 7 or 11(d) because confrontation is not absolute and remains in a limited form (accused can still see the witness) and cross-examination remains intact.
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 486(2.1)) applied/assessed under Charter ss. 7 and 11(d).
CaseB_TestB: Similar fact (identity) admissibility—use of prior conviction: where the accused puts identity for the prior act in issue, the Crown may tender the prior conviction as "some evidence" linking the accused to the similar act (Arp second test); verdicts are "presumptively reliable" and treated as such on identity unless overturned or later shown wrong; challenge to conviction on voir dire is rare and may be refused where there is "no reasonable likelihood" it will affect admissibility.
BaselineB: Common law similar fact framework from R. v. Arp and R. v. Handy (with SCC clarification of how prior convictions fit the Arp "some evidence" link requirement).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Party liability for manslaughter (where principal is guilty of murder): under s. 21(1) aiding/abetting or s. 21(2) common purpose, manslaughter mens rea is objective—i.e., a reasonable person in all the circumstances would have foreseen at least non-trivial bodily harm (not death).
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, ss. 21(1)(b),(c) and 21(2), as informed by SCC unlawful-act manslaughter jurisprudence (R. v. Creighton; R. v. DeSousa) and party-liability cases (R. v. Kirkness; R. v. Trinneer).
CaseB_TestB: Entitlement to GST rebate for overpayment under Excise Tax Act: if a person "has paid an amount" as or on account of tax "in circumstances where the amount was not payable", the Minister "shall" pay a rebate (s. 261(1)), and in assessment the Minister must apply an "allowable rebate" even if not claimed in time (s. 296(2.1)).
BaselineB: Statute: Excise Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. E-15, ss. 261(1)-(3) and 296(2.1) (with interaction discussed with ss. 215.1, 216(6), and definition of "net tax" in s. 225(1)).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Government tort liability: classify the impugned conduct as a non-justiciable “true policy decision” (immune) versus “operational implementation” (subject to negligence). Cory J.: policy decisions are those “which involve or are dictated by financial, economic, social or political factors or constraints” (Just, quoted), and “decisions concerning budgetary allotments… will be classified as policy decisions”; operational matters are those where courts apply negligence standards to action/inaction that is “merely the product of administrative direction, expert or professional opinion, technical standards or general standards of reasonableness.” Policy decisions remain reviewable only if not made in the “bona fide exercise of discretion” or are “so irrational as to constitute an improper exercise of governmental discretion.”
BaselineA: Common law (Anns v. Merton; Kamloops v. Nielsen; Just v. British Columbia) applied in the context of highway maintenance; with statutory context from Public Highways Act, R.S.N.S. 1989, c. 371, ss. 4-5 and Proceedings against the Crown Act, R.S.N.S. 1989, c. 360, s. 5(1)(a).
CaseB_TestB: Damages in lieu of specific performance: where the plaintiff maintains a claim for specific performance until trial and then elects damages, it is permissible to assess damages as of the date of trial/judgment (not necessarily the date of breach) so the award is a “true substitute for specific performance.” Sopinka J.: “it is not inconsistent with the rules of the common law to assess damages as of the date of trial” in such circumstances; and “Specific performance should… not be granted as a matter of course absent evidence that the property is unique to the extent that its substitute would not be readily available.”
BaselineB: Combination: statute conferring jurisdiction to award damages in substitution (Courts of Justice Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.43, s. 99; rooted in Lord Cairns’ Act) plus common law damages principles (Johnson v. Agnew; Wroth v. Tyler) and equitable specific performance doctrine (uniqueness/adequacy of damages).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Abuse of process threshold in criminal proceedings: stay/remedy only in the “clearest of cases” (conduct that “shocks the conscience of the community” with “overwhelming evidence” of unfairness) and no residual appellate discretion under Criminal Code s. 686(4) beyond abuse of process
BaselineA: Combination: statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(4)) plus common law abuse of process doctrine (as affirmed in R. v. Jewitt; reiterated in R. v. Keyowski; discussed with R. v. Conway, R. v. Mack, R. v. Scott, R. v. Potvin)
CaseB_TestB: Mr. Big confessions admissibility rule: presumptively inadmissible unless Crown proves (balance of probabilities) probative value (reliability) outweighs prejudicial effect; reliability assessed via operation circumstances and confession “markers of reliability”; plus separate abuse-of-process backstop for coercive/abusive operations
BaselineB: Common law evidence: party admissions exception to hearsay (R. v. Evans) and existing exclusion discretion (probative vs prejudicial; bad character principles in R. v. Handy), with abuse of process doctrine (R. v. Mack; R. v. Babos) as a separate control
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 16(1) “knowing it was wrong” (NCRMD) requires not just abstract knowledge of right/wrong, but capacity to rationally apply that knowledge to the particular act at the time — i.e., whether mental disorder deprived the accused of “capacity for rational perception and hence rational choice about the rightness or wrongness of the act”.
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 16(1)) interpreted in light of prior insanity jurisprudence (notably R. v. Chaulk) and the M'Naghten Rules.
CaseB_TestB: Palmer criteria (applied to sentence appeals): fresh evidence on appeal is admitted only if (1) generally not available with due diligence (flexible factor in criminal cases), (2) relevant, (3) credible, and (4) if believed, could reasonably, with the trial record, be expected to have affected the result.
BaselineB: Common law test from Palmer v. The Queen, applied under Criminal Code appellate evidence powers (especially ss. 683 and 687) and framed by the “interests of justice”.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Mohan test for admissibility of expert evidence (relevance; necessity; no other exclusionary rule; properly qualified expert), with added threshold for expert disposition/profile evidence requiring “distinctive behavioural characteristics” and a “standard profile” accepted as reliable
BaselineA: Common law (expert evidence admissibility and character/disposition evidence), drawing on R. v. Abbey (necessity/helpfulness), Kelliher (Village of) v. Smith (subject-matter outside ordinary experience), and the “abnormal group”/distinctiveness line from R. v. Lupien and R. v. Morin
CaseB_TestB: Section 745 Criminal Code parole ineligibility reduction decision: jury must consider statutory factors (character; conduct in custody; nature of offence; and “such other matters as the judge deems relevant”) and “weigh[] as a whole” in a discretionary determination whether ineligibility “ought to be reduced”
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 745(1)-(4), especially s. 745(2) (listed factors and two‑thirds jury requirement)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: s. 10(b) informational/implementational duties: no duty-counsel advice required where no duty counsel exists; further police duties are triggered only if detainee asserts desire to speak to a lawyer (a clear “No” triggers no further obligations)
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 10(b) (right to counsel) (with reference to prior SCC articulation in R. v. Brydges and R. v. Bartle; applied alongside the concurrent decision in R. v. Prosper)
CaseB_TestB: Criminal Code s. 347 framework for late payment penalties: (1) is the charge “interest” (i.e., a charge/expense “paid or payable for the advancing of credit under an agreement or arrangement”, with “credit advanced” including deferral of payment for goods/services/benefits); and (2) if so, does it offend s. 347(1)(a) or (b), including the Nelson ‘voluntary act of the debtor’ limitation for s. 347(1)(b)
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 347(1)-(2) (interpreting defined terms “interest”, “credit advanced”, “criminal rate” and applying Nelson v. C.T.C. Mortgage Corp.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 7 overbreadth (principles of fundamental justice): a law that deprives life/liberty/security violates s. 7 if it is "unnecessarily broad, going beyond what is needed to accomplish the governmental objective"; courts ask whether the means are "reasonably tailored" and "necessary to achieve the State objective" (Heywood).
BaselineA: Combination: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7 (principles of fundamental justice) applied to Criminal Code, s. 179(1)(b); baseline jurisprudence referenced includes Re B.C. Motor Vehicle Act and R. v. Nova Scotia Pharmaceutical Society (overbreadth/vagueness discussion).
CaseB_TestB: Income Tax Act s. 69(2) transfer-pricing reasonableness: determine whether the non-arm’s-length price exceeds the "reasonable amount" that "would have been reasonable in the circumstances" at arm’s length; "economically relevant characteristics" must be "sufficiently comparable" and, where linked, "transactions other than the purchasing transaction" (e.g., a Licence Agreement conferring rights/benefits) "must not be ignored" (GlaxoSmithKline).
BaselineB: Statute: Income Tax Act, s. 69(2) (now s. 247(2)).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Inference of possession from fingerprint evidence: whether an accused’s fingerprint on an article supports an inference of possession is “not subject to a hard and fast rule” but “a question of fact which depends on all of the circumstances of the case and all of the evidence adduced”; once the Crown proves a prima facie case, the absence of an accused’s explanation “merely failed to provide any basis to conclude otherwise”.
BaselineA: Common law (circumstantial evidence/inference of possession from fingerprints; adverse inference principles), with statutory context for “possession” (Criminal Code, s. 4(3) incorporated via Food and Drugs Act, s. 46). Key cases discussed: R. v. O'Keefe (Ont. C.A.); approved/referred to R. v. Mehrabnia; R. v. Johnson (Ont. C.A.) (cited with approval in R. v. François).
CaseB_TestB: Scope of Review Board power under Criminal Code s. 672.54: Boards may make conditions binding on hospital authorities and may impose conditions “regarding”/supervising treatment (including ordering re-evaluations and exploration of alternatives) but have “no power to ‘prescribe’ treatment”; s. 672.55(1) is not a true exception but an example of supervisory power.
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, Part XX.1), primarily ss. 672.54 and 672.55(1) (with related appeal/enforcement provisions such as s. 672.78).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 7 compellability / exemption from compulsion test: whether the "predominant purpose" of compelling the witness is to obtain incriminating evidence against them rather than to further a legitimate public purpose (with burden on the witness; possible justification by the party seeking compulsion; and consideration of other significant prejudice beyond derivative use).
BaselineA: Common law / Charter-based doctrine from R. v. S. (R.J.) interpreting and applying Charter ss. 7 and 13 in the context of compelled testimony (and related use/derivative-use immunity concepts).
CaseB_TestB: Timing rule for Corbett applications: the defence should bring, and the trial judge should decide, a Corbett application "immediately after the close of the Crown’s case"; if needed, a pre-defence-case voir dire may be held to inform the ruling, with possible later modification if defence evidence departs significantly from what was disclosed.
BaselineB: Statute plus common law: Canada Evidence Act, s. 12 (as interpreted in R. v. Corbett) conferring discretion to exclude prior convictions where probative value is outweighed by prejudicial effect; plus common-law/Charter-informed "case-to-meet" principle (Charter s. 7).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 7 compellability / self-incrimination framework for compelled testimony (and related derivative-use immunity): the “crucial question is whether the predominant purpose for seeking the evidence is to obtain incriminating evidence against the person compelled to testify or rather some legitimate public purpose”; if predominant purpose is incrimination, compulsion must be justified and the witness is not compellable if there is “any other significant prejudice ... such that his right to a fair trial will be jeopardized” (with derivative-use immunity triggered on a “plausible connection” showing, then Crown must prove on a balance of probabilities it “would have discovered” the evidence absent the compelled testimony).
BaselineA: Combination: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms (ss. 7 and 13) plus common-law/Charter doctrine as developed in R. v. S. (R.J.), [1995] 1 S.C.R. 451; applied in the statutory context of Securities Act, S.B.C. 1985, c. 83, s. 128(1) (testimonial/documentary compulsion).
CaseB_TestB: Section 15(1) Charter equality (prima facie discrimination) test from Quebec v. A: (1) whether the law “creates a distinction on the basis of an enumerated or analogous ground”; and (2) whether it imposes “arbitrary — or discriminatory — disadvantage”, i.e., fails to respond to actual capacities/needs and “reinforc[es], perpetuat[es] or exacerbat[es]” disadvantage; claimant must show the law has a “disproportionate effect ... based on ... membership in an enumerated or analogous group”.
BaselineB: Combination: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 15(1), as interpreted in Quebec (Attorney General) v. A, 2013 SCC 5 (and related s. 15 jurisprudence).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Tax-treaty residency under Canada–U.S. Convention (Art. IV(1)): entity is a “resident of a Contracting State” only if it is “liable to tax therein by reason of … domicile, residence, place of management, place of incorporation or any other criterion of a similar nature”, where “any other criterion of a similar nature” is limited to grounds for “full tax liability on world-wide income” (not mere source taxation); and a factor that merely informs domestic tax liability (e.g., place of management as a factor in ‘engaged in trade or business’) cannot be treated as the ‘by reason of’ basis for liability.
BaselineA: Statute (treaty incorporated into Canadian law): Canada-United States Tax Convention Act, 1984, S.C. 1984, c. 20, Schedule I (Canada–U.S. Income Tax Convention (1980)), Article IV(1) (definition of “resident of a Contracting State”), applied in context of Article XII; also interacts with Income Tax Act, s. 212(1)(d) withholding tax.
CaseB_TestB: Trigger for Ontario auto-insurance limitation period: the two-year period in Insurance Act, s. 281(5) “only begins to run upon the issuance by the insurer of a valid refusal”; “No such refusal is given if there has not been adequate compliance with s. 71” of the SABS, which requires notice of the dispute-resolution process in “straightforward and clear language, directed towards an unsophisticated person” and, “At a minimum”, including key steps (mediation; arbitration/litigation if mediation fails; mediation prerequisite; and “relevant time limits”).
BaselineB: Statute and regulation: Insurance Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. I.8, s. 281(5) (two-year limit from “insurer’s refusal”); Statutory Accident Benefits Schedule, O. Reg. 776/93, s. 71 (duty to inform of dispute-resolution procedure under ss. 279–283 of the Act).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Weber exclusive-arbitration jurisdiction test: courts are ousted if the dispute’s “essential character” arises from the “interpretation, application, administration or alleged violation” of the collective agreement (s. 45(1)); focus on facts, not legal labels
BaselineA: Statute: Ontario Labour Relations Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. L.2, s. 45(1) (mandatory “final and binding” arbitration of “all differences” arising from the collective agreement), informed by SCC approach in St. Anne Nackawic Pulp & Paper Co. v. Canadian Paper Workers Union, Local 219
CaseB_TestB: Criminal Code s. 744 parole-ineligibility extension framework: as a general rule 10 years, but may be “ousted” if, having regard to (1) character of offender, (2) nature of offence, and (3) circumstances surrounding its commission, the judge deems a longer period fit; appellate intervention only if sentence is “clearly unreasonable”
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 744 (and related sentencing appeal provision s. 687(1))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “loss of employment” for a retiring allowance: an employee is only “in the service” of the employer once under an obligation to provide services; therefore “loss of employment” cannot occur before that moment (no prospective/intended employment)
BaselineA: Statute (Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1952, c. 148 (now R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.)), ss. 56(1)(a)(ii) and 248(1) definitions of “employment” and “retiring allowance”)
CaseB_TestB: Trial fairness/miscarriage of justice assessment for improper Crown closing submissions (personal anecdote): apply contextual “relevant factors” (from R. v. Stephan) to decide whether the error rendered the trial unfair
BaselineB: Common law (improper jury address/trial fairness principles; factors referenced from R. v. Stephan and related cases such as Pisani and Boucher)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Pragmatic and functional approach to whether a labour board has jurisdiction (and resulting deference): reviewing courts consider (a) wording of the enactment conferring jurisdiction; (b) purpose of the statute; (c) reason for the tribunal’s existence; (d) tribunal members’ expertise; and (e) nature of the problem (Bibeault factors). If within jurisdiction, decision upheld unless “patently unreasonable” (i.e., “clearly irrational”).
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Canada Labour Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. L-2 (esp. ss. 22, 24, 27, 28, 33) plus the common-law/jurisprudential standard-of-review framework from U.E.S., Local 298 v. Bibeault, [1988] 2 S.C.R. 1048 and CUPE, [1979] 2 S.C.R. 227.
CaseB_TestB: Section 8 reasonableness of retrospective DNA data bank orders under Criminal Code s. 487.055: apply the Collins/Stillman framework—(a) authorized by law; (b) law itself reasonable; (c) manner reasonable—focusing on (b) and assessing “reasonableness” contextually by balancing the state interest in identification against the individual’s privacy interests (Hunter v. Southam balancing). Court holds Hunter ‘reasonable and probable grounds’ paradigm inapplicable; DNA data bank use is analogous to fingerprinting; no requirement to link offender to a particular investigation; ex parte procedure assessed under contextual procedural fairness.
BaselineB: Combination of statute and constitutional/common law: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 487.055 (and related ss. 487.06(2), 487.07, 487.057(1), 487.04) and DNA Identification Act, S.C. 1998, c. 37, ss. 3-4, interpreted through Charter s. 8 jurisprudence (Hunter v. Southam; R. v. Collins; R. v. Stillman; R. v. McKinlay Transport; R. v. Beare).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Gladstone refinement of Sparrow s.35 justification/priority for commercial Aboriginal rights: government must show (1) valid legislative objective and (2) consistency with fiduciary duty; where the Aboriginal right has no internal limit, “priority” is not exclusivity but requires the Crown to show both the allocation process and the resulting allocation “reflect the prior interest of aboriginal rights holders” (content of priority “must remain somewhat vague” and assessed case-by-case).
BaselineA: Common law constitutional framework under Constitution Act, 1982, s. 35(1) as set out in R. v. Sparrow (two-part justification test and priority concept), elaborated with reference to R. v. Van der Peet and Jack v. The Queen.
CaseB_TestB: Admissibility of Crown rebuttal evidence: rebuttal may be admitted where it is “clearly relevant to an issue raised in the defence” (here, going to “the context and the essential fabric of the alibi defence”) and the Crown “could not have known in advance” the defence evidence; admission is within the trial judge’s discretion.
BaselineB: Common law discretion governing admissibility of rebuttal evidence (as applied/endorsed from the Alberta Court of Appeal majority; no specific SCC precedent named in the reasons).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Implied waiver of Charter s. 11(d) rights by inaction in a no-imprisonment regulatory ticket scheme: waiver may be inferred from failure to pay and failure to appear only if the accused is fully aware of the consequences and the scheme has sufficient safeguards to ensure the omission was not due to events beyond the accused’s control
BaselineA: Combination of constitutional text (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 11(d)) and common law/Charter waiver principles as discussed in prior SCC cases (especially R. v. Lee) applied to a statutory ticketing scheme (Provincial Offences Procedure Act, S.N.B. 1987, c. P-22.1, s. 16 and related safeguards such as ss. 10(1)(h), 11(1), 117)
CaseB_TestB: Procedural fairness for Canadian Human Rights Commission dismissal of a complaint as unsubstantiated: before deciding, the Commission must give parties an opportunity to make submissions (at least in writing; a hearing not necessarily required) and must disclose the substance of its case so submissions are informed
BaselineB: Combination of statute (Canadian Human Rights Act, ss. 35 and 36(3)(b)) and common law natural justice/procedural fairness principles (as accepted and applied by the Court in this context)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Patently unreasonable standard on judicial review of labour arbitration: intervention only where the tribunal’s inference/finding is supported by “no evidence” or the evidence is “incapable of supporting” it (applied to the arbitrators’ inference that misconduct was temporary, justifying reinstatement).
BaselineA: Common law administrative law / labour arbitration judicial review standards (esp. CUPE v. New Brunswick Liquor; PSAC No. 2; Lester; Douglas Aircraft; Bradco).
CaseB_TestB: Statutory “equivalent in value” test under Reorg. Act s. 15(2)(a): equivalency requires comparing both (1) benefits paid and (2) the funding mechanism/contributions as of the implementation date; if employee contributions exceed employer’s (e.g., unmatched Initial Surplus), the plan complies only if the surplus is reserved exclusively for members or members receive compensatory benefits of equivalent value.
BaselineB: Statute: Manitoba Telephone System Reorganization and Consequential Amendments Act, S.M. 1996, c. 79, s. 15(2)(a) (interpreting “equivalent in value”); related context includes s. 15(3)-(4), (11) and CSSA definitions.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Doctrine of part performance overriding a statutory writing requirement (Statute of Frauds analogue): where an oral agreement for an interest in land has been carried out/partly performed, equity will enforce it and prevent the Crown from relying on the absence of writing (“equity recognizes as done that which ought to have been done”; writing requirement cannot be used as an “engine of fraud”).
BaselineA: Combination of statute and equitable common law: Public Highways Act, R.S.N.S. 1954, c. 235, s. 21(1)(a) (written permit requirement) interpreted as reflecting the Statute of Frauds; equitable doctrine of part performance as described via Steadman v. Steadman and related authorities.
CaseB_TestB: Quebec arbitration/public order validity-review framework: (1) arbitrator’s mandate is interpreted liberally to include matters “closely connected” to the arbitration agreement; (2) s. 37 Copyright Act does not bar arbitration; (3) on homologation/annulment for public order under art. 946.5 C.C.P., the court examines the award “as a whole” and will not annul for mere legal error unless the outcome conflicts with “fundamental principles of public order”.
BaselineB: Statutory: Civil Code of Québec art. 2639; Code of Civil Procedure (Québec) arts. 946.2, 946.4, 946.5, 947.2; Copyright Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-42, s. 37; Act respecting the professional status of artists, R.S.Q., c. S-32.01, s. 37.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Reasonableness simpliciter standard of review for statutory appeals from expert tribunals: reviewing court asks whether the tribunal decision was "unreasonable" — i.e., "in the main, ... not supported by any reasons that can stand up to a somewhat probing examination"; contrasted with patent unreasonableness where the defect is "apparent on the face" of the reasons.
BaselineA: Common law (standard of review doctrine) applied in the context of a statutory right of appeal under the Competition Tribunal Act, especially ss. 12-13; key prior SCC baseline case cited: Pezim v. British Columbia (Superintendent of Brokers).
CaseB_TestB: Temporal-effect test for suspended s. 52(1) declarations: declarations are presumptively retroactive, but the presumption is rebutted "explicitly or by necessary implication"; where "retroactivity would undermine" the purpose/compelling public interest that justified the suspension, "the declaration must apply purely prospectively".
BaselineB: Constitutional text and remedial doctrine: Constitution Act, 1982, s. 52(1) and Charter, s. 24(1), building on prior SCC remedial jurisprudence including Ontario (Attorney General) v. G and Canada (Attorney General) v. Hislop (and applied to Bedford).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Hickman Motors “purpose of producing income” test for CCA eligibility: (1) “Does the property produce income? In the affirmative, the deduction is allowable.” (2) If not, “was it acquired for the purpose of producing income?”, determined by “an objective evaluation of the specific facts and circumstances ... having regard to whether the taxpayer acted in accordance with reasonably acceptable principles of commerce and business practices.”
BaselineA: Statute and regulation: Income Tax Act, s. 20(1)(a) (deductions “allowed by regulation” and “applicable to that source”); Income Tax Regulations, s. 1102(1)(c) (property excluded if “not acquired ... for the purpose of gaining or producing income”).
CaseB_TestB: Hall test for denying bail to “maintain confidence in the administration of justice”: after severing the open-ended words, detention may be ordered “where the detention is necessary in order to maintain confidence in the administration of justice, having regard to all the circumstances, including” (i) “the apparent strength of the prosecution’s case”, (ii) “the gravity of the nature of the offence”, (iii) “the circumstances surrounding its commission”, and (iv) “the potential for a lengthy term of imprisonment”; the judge may deny bail only if “a reasonable member of the community would be satisfied that denial of bail is necessary”.
BaselineB: Statute (as constitutionally constrained): Criminal Code, s. 515(10)(c), interpreted under Charter, s. 11(e) (“not to be denied reasonable bail without just cause”) and s. 1; remedy via Constitution Act, 1982, s. 52 (severance).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Vesting/accrual of an appeal-as-of-right: a right is only “acquired”, “accrued” or “accruing” once all conditions precedent to exercising it are fulfilled (here, only when the court of appeal reverses the acquittal and orders a new trial)
BaselineA: Statute (Interpretation Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. I-21, ss. 43(c) and 44(c),(d), applied to Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 691(2) as amended)
CaseB_TestB: Sherman Estate test for discretionary limits on the open court principle (publication bans): (1) serious risk to an important public interest; (2) necessity because reasonable alternatives won’t prevent the risk; (3) proportionality—benefits outweigh negative effects
BaselineB: Common law (Sherman Estate v. Donovan, 2021 SCC 25, para. 38)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Income-tax profit computation framework under ITA s. 9(1): taxpayer may use any method consistent with the Act, case law, and well-accepted business principles that yields an “accurate picture” of profit; on reassessment the onus shifts to the Minister to show inaccuracy or a more accurate alternative method
BaselineA: Statute (Income Tax Act, s. 9(1) profit concept; limiting provisions incl. s. 18(1)(a) and s. 18(9)) plus prior case law on profit computation (e.g., M.N.R. v. Irwin; Associated Investors; Symes; Friesen)
CaseB_TestB: Interpretation/application of Partnership Act s. 55(b): without unanimous limited-partner consent, a general partner lacks authority to “do any act which makes it impossible to carry on the ordinary business” of the limited partnership; “impossible” means not possible and does not require all facets—only a substantial portion—of the ordinary business to be rendered impossible
BaselineB: Statute (Partnership Act, R.S.A. 1980, c. P-2, s. 55(b)) interpreted in light of the partnership’s constitutive documents defining its “ordinary business”
JudgeB: Estey J. (for Beetz, Estey, McIntyre and Lamer JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Dixon two-step test for post-conviction remedy for Crown non-disclosure: (1) reasonable possibility undisclosed info affects reliability of conviction; if not, (2) reasonable possibility non-disclosure affected overall fairness via lost lines of inquiry/opportunities, with defence due diligence weighed
BaselineA: Combination of common law Charter disclosure jurisprudence (R. v. Stinchcombe; R. v. Egger; R. v. C. (M.H.); R. v. Carosella) and Charter provisions (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 7 and 24(1))
CaseB_TestB: Standard-form insurance interpretation (Ledcor framework) applied to SEF 44 cl. 4(b)(vii): if language is unambiguous, give effect to its ordinary meaning as understood by the average insured; here “policy of insurance” means a private insurance contract and does not include CPP
BaselineB: Common law principles of standard-form insurance contract interpretation (Ledcor; Progressive Homes; Scalera; Gibbens) applied to the SEF 44 Endorsement, specifically cl. 4(b)(vii) (and related cl. 4(a), 4(b))
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Search incident to arrest must be “truly incidental”: police must have a purpose related to the arrest (within Cloutier purposes or other valid purpose) and it must be objectively reasonable; delay/distance may support a negative inference rebuttable by explanation
BaselineA: Common law (search incident to arrest doctrine from Cloutier v. Langlois; also framed within Charter s. 8 reasonableness via Hunter v. Southam and Collins)
CaseB_TestB: Admissibility of defence-led unknown third party suspect evidence: (1) relevance to a fact in issue/available defence (air of reality supported by a “sufficient connection”/similarity between crimes plus evidence accused could not have committed the other offence), and (2) admit unless prejudicial effects substantially outweigh probative value (Seaboyer balancing); no balance-of-probabilities proof of the other incident
BaselineB: Common law evidence principles (Seaboyer relevance + probative/prejudicial balancing; Cinous air of reality; Grandinetti/McMillan sufficient connection concept adapted to unknown suspect context)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 8 engagement for foreign evidence-gathering: a Canadian “letter of request” to foreign authorities, by itself, does not constitute a search or seizure and therefore does not engage s. 8; the compelled search/seizure abroad by foreign officials is not subject to Charter scrutiny
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional text (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 8 and 32(1)) informed by prior SCC s. 8 jurisprudence (e.g., Hunter v. Southam) and foreign-investigation cases (e.g., R. v. Terry)
CaseB_TestB: Anns/Cooper duty of care framework (foreseeability + proximity, then residual policy) for negligence claims alleging failure to prevent harm caused by a third party’s intentional wrongdoing
BaselineB: Common law (Cooper v. Hobart / Anns framework as developed in Cooper, Edwards, Odhavji, Childs, Hill)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Pushpanathan Art. 1F(c) exclusion test: Art. 1F(c) applies where there is (1) an explicit international-law designation (treaty/UN resolution) that the act is contrary to UN purposes and principles, or (2) the court can itself characterize the act as a “serious, sustained and systemic” violation of fundamental human rights “constituting persecution” (with universal-jurisdiction status as a compelling indicator); otherwise no exclusion.
BaselineA: Statute/treaty incorporated into statute: Immigration Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. I-2, s. 2(1) (definition of “Convention refugee” incorporating Refugee Convention exclusions) and Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees, Art. 1F(c) (“acts contrary to the purposes and principles of the United Nations”).
CaseB_TestB: Hadley v. Baxendale remoteness test for contract damages (as applied to employment implied duties): damages are those that arise “either naturally” or that “may reasonably be supposed to have been in the contemplation of both parties, at the time they made the contract, as the probable result of a breach”.
BaselineB: Common law: Hadley v. Baxendale (1854) remoteness/foreseeability rule for contract damages.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Hodgson framework for (1) who is a “person in authority” and (2) when a trial judge must hold a voir dire on voluntariness/person-in-authority absent a defence request (the “close connection/spectrum” trigger)
BaselineA: Common law confessions rule (voluntariness requirement for statements to a person in authority), drawing on prior SCC authority including Erven v. The Queen, [1979] 1 S.C.R. 926 and Rothman v. The Queen, [1981] 1 S.C.R. 640; voluntariness definition from Ibrahim v. The King, [1914] A.C. 599 (P.C.) adopted in Prosko v. The King (1922), 63 S.C.R. 226
CaseB_TestB: McClurg approach to Income Tax Act s. 56(2): dividends (including those allocated under a discretionary dividend clause) are generally outside s. 56(2) because they are not “diverted” amounts the taxpayer would otherwise have received
BaselineB: Statute—Income Tax Act, S.C. 1970-71-72, c. 63, s. 56(2) (attribution rule for a “payment or transfer of property” made “pursuant to the direction of, or with the concurrence of, a taxpayer” to another person “for the benefit of the taxpayer”); interpreted in light of prior case law including Miller v. M.N.R., 62 D.T.C. 1139 (Ex. Ct.) and Perrault v. The Queen, [1979] 1 F.C. 155 (C.A.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Depletion allowance profit computation under Reg. 1201(2): determine profits “reasonably attributable” to production by “ascertaining the difference between the receipts reasonably attributable to the production ... and the expenses of earning those receipts”, and deduct only the items enumerated in Reg. 1201(4) (no implied deduction for long-term research expenses).
BaselineA: Regulation (Income Tax Regulations (Can.), Reg. 1201(2) and 1201(4)) interpreting interaction with Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1952, c. 148, ss. 11(1)(j) and 72; approach referenced from Minister of National Revenue v. Imperial Oil Ltd., [1960] S.C.R. 735.
CaseB_TestB: Sherman Estate test for discretionary limits on the open court principle (publication bans): applicant must establish (1) openness poses a “serious risk to an important public interest”; (2) the order is “necessary” because “reasonably alternative measures will not prevent this risk”; and (3) proportionality: benefits outweigh negative effects.
BaselineB: Common law discretionary framework from Sherman Estate v. Donovan, 2021 SCC 25 (applied).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Kienapple/res judicata in multi-count prosecutions with different gravity: if same delict underlies both counts, convict on the more serious and acquit/hold in abeyance the less serious (cannot use a guilty plea to the lesser to bar trial/conviction on the greater).
BaselineA: Common law (Kienapple v. The Queen, [1975] 1 S.C.R. 729 rule against multiple convictions for the same delict/res judicata), applied in the context of Criminal Code charges (ss. 83, 302(d), 421(a)).
CaseB_TestB: Availability of habeas corpus to challenge continued detention in parole context: continuation is challengeable only if it becomes unlawful, which occurs only once the inmate has acquired parolee status (i.e., when the parole decision takes effect; if conditional, only when the condition is fulfilled).
BaselineB: Common law habeas corpus principles as expanded in R. v. Miller, [1985] 2 S.C.R. 613 (and related cases), applied in the statutory parole context (Parole Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. P-2 as amended).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: NCR disposition under Criminal Code s. 672.54: absolute discharge is mandatory unless the court/Review Board makes a positive finding on the evidence that the NCR accused poses a “significant threat to the safety of the public”; if a significant threat is found, impose the “least onerous and least restrictive” conditional discharge or detention (with “significant threat” defined as a real risk of serious physical/psychological harm, beyond “merely trivial or annoying”, from criminal conduct).
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, Part XX.1, especially s. 672.54 (and related provisions governing NCR dispositions).
CaseB_TestB: Westbank test for characterizing a levy under Constitution Act, 1867 s. 125: ask whether the charge is “(1) compulsory and enforceable by law; (2) imposed under the authority of the legislature; (3) levied by a public body; (4) intended for a public purpose; and (5) unconnected to any form of a regulatory scheme”; if all are yes, it will “generally be described as a tax” (and thus inapplicable to the other level of government under s. 125).
BaselineB: Constitutional text and doctrine: Constitution Act, 1867, s. 125 (and related taxation heads of power), building on prior SCC tax/fee indicia (e.g., Lawson; Re Exported Natural Gas Tax; Eurig Estate).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 2(d) freedom of association (labour context): s. 2(d) protects only (1) the freedom to establish/belong to/maintain an association and (2) the exercise in association of members’ lawful rights; it does not include a right to inclusion in a particular statutory labour-relations regime (no general positive obligation). Key quoted formulation: “first, that s. 2(d) protects the freedom to establish, belong to and maintain an association; second, that s. 2(d) does not protect an activity solely on the ground that the activity is a foundational or essential purpose of an association; third, that s. 2(d) protects the exercise in association of the constitutional rights and freedoms of individuals; and fourth, that s. 2(d) protects the exercise in association of the lawful rights of individuals.”
BaselineA: Combination: constitutional text (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 2(d), with s. 32(1) context) plus SCC common-law/constitutional jurisprudence (1987 labour trilogy; Professional Institute of the Public Service of Canada v. Northwest Territories (Commissioner); Canadian Egg Marketing Agency v. Richardson quoting Sopinka J.). Also applied to statutory exclusion in Public Service Staff Relations Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. P-35, s. 2 “employee” (e) (and discussed alongside Canada Labour Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. L-2, s. 6).
CaseB_TestB: Joint/co-principal liability in group assaults (Criminal Code s. 21(1)(a)): co-principal liability “flows whenever two or more individuals come together with an intention to commit an offence, are present during the commission of the offence, and contribute to its commission”; for manslaughter, focus is whether the accused’s actions were “a significant contributing cause of death” (and in group assaults, “absent a discrete or intervening event, the actions of all assailants can constitute a significant contributing cause to all injuries sustained”).
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 21(1)(a) (joint/co-principal liability) (context also mentions s. 21(1)(c) abetting). The SCC also situates the clarification as consistent with R. v. Pickton, 2010 SCC 32, and correcting an implication from R. v. Cabrera (ABCA) as affirmed in R. v. Shlah.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Federal Child Support Guidelines s. 4 ‘inappropriate’ analysis for incomes over $150,000: Table amount presumptively applies; deviation (up or down) only if rebutted by evidence showing the Table amount is ‘unsuitable’, assessed on all circumstances including s. 4(b)(ii) factors (condition, means, needs and other circumstances of the children; spouses’ financial ability).
BaselineA: Regulation (Federal Child Support Guidelines, SOR/97-175, ss. 3 and 4; especially s. 4(b) and s. 4(b)(ii)), under the Divorce Act framework (Divorce Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 3 (2nd Supp.), s. 26.1(2)).
CaseB_TestB: Categorization test for whether an all-risks/multi-peril policy falls under B.C. Insurance Act Part 5 (Fire Insurance) via s. 119: if the policy cannot coherently fit within Part 5’s category-based scheme, it is governed by Part 2 (general provisions), so the Part 2 limitation period applies; contractual shorter limitation cannot undercut Part 2 due to s. 3(a).
BaselineB: Statute (Insurance Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 226, ss. 119 and 3(a); interaction with Part 2 vs Part 5 and statutory condition 14).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meiorin unified BFOR test (3-step): employer must prove (1) standard adopted for a purpose “rationally connected to the performance of the job”; (2) adopted “in an honest and good faith belief” it was necessary; and (3) standard is “reasonably necessary” — i.e., “impossible to accommodate individual employees sharing the characteristics of the claimant without imposing undue hardship upon the employer”.
BaselineA: Statute (British Columbia Human Rights Code, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 210, s. 13(1)(a), (b), (4)) interpreted in light of prior SCC human-rights/BFOR and accommodation cases (e.g., O’Malley; Etobicoke; Central Alberta Dairy Pool; Renaud).
CaseB_TestB: Stewart source-of-income test (2-stage) replacing REOP as a stand-alone test: (i) “Is the activity ... undertaken in pursuit of profit, or is it a personal endeavour?” (only relevant where there is a personal/hobby element); (ii) if not personal, “is the source of the income a business or property?”; commerciality requires “subjective intention to profit” plus “evidence of businesslike behaviour” supporting that intention (REOP is only “a single factor, among others”).
BaselineB: Statute (Income Tax Act, especially ss. 3(a) and 9(1)-(2); also discussed: ss. 18(1)(a), (h), 20(1)(c)(i), 67, 248(1)) and prior SCC/common-law usage of REOP from Moldowan v. The Queen.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Staged analysis for whether a conditional sentence is available/appropriate under Criminal Code s. 742.1, including when and how s. 718.2(e) (Gladue factors) must be considered for Aboriginal offenders
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, ss. 742.1 and 718-718.2, especially s. 718.2(e)), as interpreted in R. v. Proulx and R. v. Gladue
CaseB_TestB: Quebec Charter s. 9.1 balancing of a freedom of religion claim (s. 3) against countervailing rights/values/harm to determine whether a party is immune from civil liability for breach of a contract with religious aspects
BaselineB: Statute (Charter of human rights and freedoms, R.S.Q., c. C-12, ss. 3 and 9.1; informed by SCC freedom of religion jurisprudence such as Syndicat Northcrest v. Amselem)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Unreasonable verdict review under Criminal Code s. 686(1)(a)(i): whether the verdict is one that a properly instructed jury (or trial judge) acting judicially could reasonably have rendered; appellate court must thoroughly re-examine the evidence and cannot intervene based only on a vague “lurking doubt” without articulating why the verdict is inconsistent with a judicial appreciation of the evidence
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, s. 686(1)(a)(i)) as interpreted in common law jurisprudence (R. v. Yebes; reaffirmed/clarified in R. v. Biniaris)
CaseB_TestB: Institutional consultation / natural justice framework: full-board consultation is permissible only if (1) it is not imposed by a superior authority, (2) it is limited to questions of policy and law (not re-assessment of evidence), and (3) decision-makers remain free to decide; for audi alteram partem on judicial review, an applicant must show an actual breach (not merely an apprehended breach), and a presumption of regularity applies absent further evidence
BaselineB: Common law procedural fairness/natural justice framework from IWA v. Consolidated-Bathurst Packaging Ltd. and Tremblay v. Quebec (Commission des affaires sociales), applied in the context of the Labour Relations Act, 1995 (notably ss. 114(1), 117)
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Functional and structural approach to whether a statutory court/tribunal has “power to grant the remedy sought” (and thus is a “court of competent jurisdiction”) under Charter s. 24(1) — focusing on the tribunal’s function and structure to infer implied remedial jurisdiction (here, costs against the Crown). Key formulation: “the paramount question remains whether the court or tribunal, by virtue of its function and structure, is an appropriate forum for ordering the Charter remedy in issue” (para. 35); the inquiry is “contextual” and considers (function) “what is the court or tribunal’s function within the legislative scheme?” and (structure) “the compatibility of the institution and its processes with the remedy sought” (paras. 43-45).
BaselineA: Combination: Charter s. 24(1) (“court of competent jurisdiction”) plus common-law/constitutional baseline from Mills v. The Queen (three-part test: jurisdiction over person, subject matter, and remedy) as affirmed in Weber and Mooring; applied to a statutory tribunal under the Provincial Offences Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. P.33.
