CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 11(d) test for validity of a statutory presumption: a presumption is constitutional “solely if proof of the substituted fact leads ‘inexorably’ to the existence of the essential element that it replaces” (para. 52); the “nexus requirement … is strict … nothing less than ‘inexorable’” (para. 53). Applied to Criminal Code s. 172.1(3) (presumption of belief from representation of age) and held unconstitutional because representation online does not “lead inexorably” to belief (paras. 55-62).
BaselineB: Combination: statute and Charter. Statutory presumption in Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 172.1(3), assessed under Charter s. 11(d) (and s. 1). Baseline SCC jurisprudence on presumptions: Whyte, Downey, Audet (inexorable-connection requirement).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Existence of a valid partnership for income tax purposes: at formation, evidence must show alleged partners were “(1) carrying on a business, (2) in common, (3) with a view to profit”; tax motivation does not negate partnership if these essentials are present, and “view to profit” is not a strictly quantitative net-gain inquiry (ancillary profit intention can suffice).
BaselineA: Combination: Income Tax Act, s. 96 (deduction of partnership losses) applied through common-law partnership test from Continental Bank Leasing Corp. v. Canada (1998 SCC) (as reiterated with Backman v. Canada (2001 SCC)).
CaseB_TestB: Adequacy of jury instructions on credibility and reasonable doubt (W.(D.) context): where credibility is central, the judge must explain the relationship between credibility assessment and the Crown’s burden; the charge is sufficient if, read as a whole, it is “crystal clear” the burden never shifts and the jury is not left with a “credibility contest” choice; no “magic incantation” is required.
BaselineB: Combination: common-law jury-charge framework from R. v. W.(D.) (1991 SCC) and related cases, applied in a Criminal Code prosecution (s. 271(1)(a) sets the offence but the test concerns common-law instruction requirements).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Customs Act s. 48(5)(a)(iv) “condition of sale” test for dutiable royalties/licence fees: royalties are dutiable only if the vendor could refuse to sell or repudiate the sale contract upon non-payment (i.e., payment is a true contractual condition of the sale for export)
BaselineA: Statute (Customs Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (2nd Supp.), s. 48(5)(a)(iv), interpreted using common law/sale of goods concepts of “condition of sale”)
CaseB_TestB: ITA s. 224(1) “requirement to pay” trigger in cheque-deposit context: a bank is “liable to make a payment” to the tax debtor only if, under BEA presentment/holder rules and the deposit instructions, the bank owes money to the tax debtor personally (not merely to joint account holders); payee status alone is insufficient
BaselineB: Statute (Income Tax Act, s. 224(1)) interpreted through Bills of Exchange Act rules (e.g., ss. 84(1), 84(3), 86(1), 126, 138(2), 165(3)) and banking common law principles
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Quebec Labour Code s. 45 successorship via subcontracting: s. 45 may apply where the transferee (1) performs functions similar to those performed by the transferor to which the certification applied and (2) receives a 'right to operate part of the transferor’s undertaking'; autonomy assessed contextually (no 'total control' requirement), including by the 'criterion of the subordination of the employees to the contractors' to determine whether the transferee has 'sufficient authority' to be the new employer operating that part of the undertaking.
BaselineA: Statute (Labour Code, R.S.Q., c. C-27, ss. 45-46) as interpreted in SCC jurisprudence (U.E.S., Local 298 v. Bibeault; Lester (W.W.) (1978) Ltd.)
CaseB_TestB: Jarvis 'predominant purpose' test for when a tax audit becomes a penal investigation: the adversarial relationship is engaged where the 'predominant purpose of an inquiry is the determination of a taxpayer’s penal liability' under s. 239; 'no one factor is determinative' and the judge must assess the 'totality of the circumstances' (with Jarvis factors applied) to decide when requirement powers (ss. 231.1/231.2) can no longer be used.
BaselineB: Common law Charter framework from R. v. Jarvis (applied to statutory audit powers in Income Tax Act, ss. 231.1(1), 231.2(1), and penal liability under s. 239; Charter ss. 7, 8, 24(2))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Anns/Cooper duty of care test for statutory regulators: (1) prima facie duty—foreseeability + proximity (starting with analogous categories; if none, whether a new duty should be recognized, with proximity grounded in the statute); (2) residual policy considerations may negate the duty
BaselineA: Common law (Anns v. Merton London Borough Council; Kamloops (City of) v. Nielsen), as clarified/applied in Cooper v. Hobart
JudgeA: The Chief Justice and Major J.
CaseB_TestB: Section 1 (Oakes) justification analysis, emphasizing that budgetary constraints can justify limits only in exceptional fiscal crises and rejecting an added 'separation of powers' step; applied through the proportionality sequence (pressing/substantial objective; rational connection; minimal impairment; overall proportionality including salutary vs deleterious effects)
BaselineB: Constitution (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 1) and common law framework from R. v. Oakes
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Pragmatic and functional approach to standard of review (correctness here): four factors—(1) privative clause/statutory appeal, (2) relative expertise, (3) purpose of the Act/provision, (4) nature of the problem
BaselineA: Common law (Pushpanathan v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration); Dr. Q v. College of Physicians and Surgeons of British Columbia) applied in light of Telecommunications Act, s. 64(1) (statutory right of appeal)
CaseB_TestB: When collateral consequences/mistake of law/non-impairment may mitigate sentence for refusal causing death: (i) collateral consequences must relate to the offence/offender and cannot make sentence disproportionate; (ii) mistake of law requires an honest but mistaken belief in legality (mere confusion/uncertainty insufficient); (iii) non-impairment is mitigating but its effect must be limited and offender bears onus on balance of probabilities
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, ss. 255(3.2), 718-718.2, 718.1; plus s. 19 for mistake of law not being a defence) with common-law sentencing principles (e.g., Lacasse; Pham) applied
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 2(b) infringement and s. 1 justification for a sign by-law restricting “counter-advertising” (Oakes proportionality: pressing objective; rational connection; minimal impairment; overall proportionality)
BaselineA: Combination: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms ss. 2(b), 1; and the s. 1 framework from R. v. Oakes (as refined in Dagenais and Thomson Newspapers, per Sharpe).
CaseB_TestB: Canadian Bill of Rights property “due process” analysis: (1) no right to notice/hearing before Parliament enacts expropriative legislation; (2) procedural protections only in individualized adjudication; (3) no substantive protection against clear, unambiguous legislative expropriation; plus s. 2(e) fair-hearing applies only to tribunals, not Parliament
BaselineB: Statute: Canadian Bill of Rights ss. 1(a) (enjoyment of property; not deprived except by due process of law) and 2(e) (fair hearing for determination of rights/obligations), applied to Department of Veterans Affairs Act s. 5.1(4).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Copyright Act s. 3(1) “reproduction” requires copying (typically the making of an additional/new copy); a mere physical transfer of the same ink layer to a new substrate, with no multiplication, is not “production (or reproduction) ... in any material form” and thus is not an infringing copy for s. 38(1) seizure
BaselineA: Statute (Copyright Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-42, ss. 3(1), 38(1); definition of “infringing” in s. 2; also interacts with Code of Civil Procedure, R.S.Q., c. C-25, art. 734 for seizure before judgment)
CaseB_TestB: Reasonableness simpliciter on judicial review: a decision is unreasonable only if “there is no line of analysis within the given reasons that could reasonably lead the tribunal from the evidence before it to the conclusion at which it arrived”; if any sufficient reasons are “tenable” on a “somewhat probing examination”, the court must not interfere
BaselineB: Common law (standards of review framework from SCC cases including Pushpanathan v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) and Canada (Director of Investigation and Research) v. Southam Inc.; applied in context of statutory appeal under Law Society Act, 1996, S.N.B. 1996, c. 89, ss. 66(1), 68)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Privacy Act s. 22(1)(b) exemption: government may refuse access only if disclosure “could reasonably be expected to be injurious” to the conduct of lawful investigations; requires a “clear and direct connection” between disclosure of the specific information and the alleged injury, based on “real grounds” tied to the case (not general assertions or mere lack of consent), and applies even after an investigation has concluded
BaselineA: Statute (Privacy Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. P-21, ss. 12(1), 22(1)(b), 22(3), 47, 49; reconciled with Official Languages Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 31 (4th Supp.), ss. 60(1), 72-74)
CaseB_TestB: Adverse inference / presumption of fact in medical causation: no rule requires the trier of fact to draw an adverse inference of causation where defendant negligence undermines proof and plaintiff adduces “some” evidence; the inference is discretionary as a presumption of fact under CCQ art. 2849 and must be assessed on all the evidence, within the “serious, precise and concordant” criteria, without altering the burden of proof
BaselineB: Statute/civil code (Civil Code of Québec, art. 2849 (and arts. 2846-2849 generally) governing presumptions of fact), informed by SCC causation jurisprudence (Snell v. Farrell; St-Jean v. Mercier)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Validity/effect of a zoning “holding regulation”: despite inelegant drafting, give effect to the substance of a clear municipal “freeze” policy where the by-law says “Notwithstanding any other provisions... no building... may be... erected to contain three or more dwelling units until this by-law has been amended...”
BaselineA: Statute + municipal by-law: The Planning Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 349, s. 35(1) (zoning power) and s. 35(22) (appeal to Municipal Board), applied to City of London zoning by-law 306-480 as amended by by-law 306(bc)-504, s. 4 (new s. 11 “Holding Regulation”). Prior SCC authority distinguished: Verdun v. Sun Oil Co. Ltd., [1952] 1 S.C.R. 222.
CaseB_TestB: Custody decision-making: under s. 1(1) of The Infants Act the judge must consider parental conduct only as one factor bearing on relative fitness; “the paramount consideration... [is] the welfare of the children”, and “each particular case must be judged on its own circumstances.”
BaselineB: Statute + common law: The Infants Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 222, s. 1(1) (welfare/fitness direction), informed by custody jurisprudence referenced in reasons (e.g., McKee v. McKee; Bickley v. Bickley; Retzer v. Retzer; and discussion in contemporaneous Talsky v. Talsky).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: OSC disclosure of compelled investigation material under Securities Act s. 17(1): apply Stinchcombe-style relevance (“reasonable possibility of being relevant” to full answer and defence) and order disclosure only if, balancing confidentiality/privacy against fairness, disclosure is “in the public interest” and “necessary to carry out [the OSC’s] mandate” (global disclosure permissible unless no reasonable possibility a particular item is relevant).
BaselineA: Statute (Ontario Securities Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. S.5, ss. 16-17; OSC Rules of Practice r. 3.3(2)) interpreted with reference to common-law disclosure relevance from R. v. Stinchcombe.
CaseB_TestB: Framework to classify requested state-held records as first-party (Stinchcombe) or third-party (O’Connor): consider (1) whether the information is in the possession/control of the prosecuting Crown; and (2) if not, whether police/another Crown entity ought to have supplied it because it is part of the “fruits of the investigation” or “obviously relevant”; if neither, O’Connor applies and the accused must show the record is “likely relevant” (“reasonable possibility” it is logically probative to an issue at trial or witness competence).
BaselineB: Common law (Stinchcombe; O’Connor; McNeil) applied in the context of Criminal Code s. 258(1)(c).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Misfeasance in public office: plaintiff must prove (1) “deliberate and unlawful conduct in [the defendant’s] capacity as a public officer” and (2) the officer was “aware both that his or her conduct was unlawful and that it was likely to harm the plaintiff” (plus causation and compensable loss).
BaselineA: Common law tort (misfeasance in public office), drawing on prior authorities including Roncarelli v. Duplessis and Three Rivers District Council v. Bank of England (No. 3); applied in context of statutory duties under Ontario Police Services Act, ss. 113(9) and 41(1)(b).
CaseB_TestB: Eligibility for Quebec seats under Supreme Court Act, s. 6: appointee must be a current member “from among” the Quebec institutions (Quebec CA/Superior Court or Barreau du Québec) and meet the 10-year standing requirement; former advocates are excluded.
BaselineB: Statutory interpretation of Supreme Court Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. S-26, ss. 5 and 6 (and constitutional constraints under Constitution Act, 1982, s. 41(d) for amendments to Court composition).
JudgeB: The Chief Justice and LeBel, Abella, Cromwell, Karakatsanis and Wagner JJ.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Reasonableness review of a securities commission’s s. 162 administrative-penalty order: ask whether there is a “rational basis” for the order “in light of the statutory framework and the circumstances”, reviewing the order “globally” and allowing consideration of “general deterrence” (a relevant but non-dispositive factor) in the “public interest” analysis.
BaselineA: Statute (Securities Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 418, s. 162; plus administrative-law standard-of-review framework from prior SCC cases such as Dr. Q and Pezim as cited in the reasons).
CaseB_TestB: Adequacy of jury instructions on alternative routes to murder liability where others may have participated: the charge is sufficient if, read as a whole and in context, it adequately conveys that it is not necessary the accused acted alone and that guilt may follow if he “acted in concert with others” and “actively participated in the killing”; correcting an erroneous “actual shooter” direction to include “or was otherwise an active participant in her killing” does not necessarily cause a miscarriage of justice.
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: Criminal Code party-liability provisions (notably s. 21; also ss. 229, 231(5), 686(1)(b)(iii)) applied through the common-law framework for assessing jury-charge adequacy/miscarriage of justice (as discussed with reference to cases such as Thatcher and Rose).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Cross-examination on unproven facts requires only a “good faith basis” (no evidentiary foundation required); judge may inquire only where the factual predicate is “manifestly tenuous or suspect”
BaselineA: Common law (scope/limits of cross-examination; clarified against misreadings of R. v. Howard and consistent with the good-faith approach reflected in R. v. Bencardino and related authorities)
CaseB_TestB: Federal paramountcy test: provincial law is inoperative only if (1) operational conflict (impossible dual compliance) or (2) frustration of federal purpose (clear proof of federal purpose + incompatibility)
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine of federal paramountcy (applied to Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act, s. 243 and Saskatchewan Farm Security Act, ss. 9-22)
JudgeB: Abella and Gascon JJ. (Cromwell, Moldaver, Karakatsanis and Wagner JJ. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Vaid framework for determining existence/scope of parliamentary privilege: (1) ask whether the claimed category/scope of privilege has been “authoritatively established” for Canada or Westminster; if not, (2) apply the necessity doctrine—privilege exists only if the activity is “so closely and directly connected” to legislative/deliberative functions (including holding government to account) that outside interference would undermine required autonomy; once established, courts do not review the merits of its exercise in a particular case.
BaselineA: Combination: constitutional text and inherited common law of parliamentary privilege (Constitution Act, 1867, s. 18; Parliament of Canada Act, s. 4; prior SCC privilege cases such as New Brunswick Broadcasting and Harvey).
CaseB_TestB: Oakes proportionality (s. 1) justification analysis for limits on expression: pressing and substantial objective; proportional means via (i) rational connection, (ii) minimal impairment, and (iii) proportionality of effects (balancing salutary vs deleterious effects).
BaselineB: Common law/constitutional doctrine under the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 1, applying the Oakes test (R. v. Oakes) and related Charter jurisprudence (e.g., RJR-MacDonald).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: GAAR “abusive tax avoidance” (s. 245(4)) via unified textual, contextual and purposive interpretation: GAAR applies where “it cannot be reasonably concluded that a tax benefit would be consistent with the object, spirit or purpose of the provisions relied upon by the taxpayer” and abuse may be found where transactions “lack a proper basis relative to the object, spirit or purpose” or are “wholly dissimilar” to what the provisions contemplate (applied to deny arm’s-length purchase of losses preserved under s. 18(13) through partnership rules).
BaselineA: Statute: Income Tax Act, ss. 245(1)-(4) (GAAR, especially s. 245(4) misuse/abuse), applied with ss. 18(13) and 96(1); interpretive approach and GAAR framework followed from Canada Trustco Mortgage Co. v. Canada, 2005 SCC 54 (as summarized and applied at paras. 31-32, 57-58).
CaseB_TestB: Vancouver Sun informer-privilege procedure and “single guiding rule”: (1) court verifies existence of informer privilege (in camera/ex parte if needed; “evidence that a person is a police informer automatically engages the privilege”); (2) once established, court must conduct proceedings “without violating the privilege while at the same time accommodating, to the greatest extent possible, the open court principle” — including, in informer-on-trial cases, generally proceeding totally in camera but (per SCC clarification) ensuring at least the existence of the in camera hearing and any decision is public, typically by creating a separate “parallel proceeding” with its own record number and a redacted public judgment where feasible.
BaselineB: Common law: Named Person v. Vancouver Sun, 2007 SCC 43 (informer privilege and the Vancouver Sun two-stage procedure/guiding rule), as applied and clarified; also grounded in the common-law open court principle jurisprudence (e.g., Sherman Estate v. Donovan, CBC v. Manitoba) as context for minimizing impairment.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “lawful authority” for whistleblower protection under s. 74(1)(a): includes not only police/public officials but also internal persons who “exercise lawful authority over the employee(s) complained about, or over the activity that is or is likely to result in the offence” (i.e., an “up the ladder” internal reporting route can qualify).
BaselineA: Statute: The Labour Standards Act, R.S.S. 1978, c. L-1, s. 74(1)(a) (and s. 74(2) vexatious exception), interpreted using the modern principle of statutory interpretation (Driedger/Rizzo/Bell ExpressVu).
CaseB_TestB: Waiver of insurer’s right to rely on dishonoured-cheque non-payment rule: despite demand for replacement cheque, “before waiver can be found there must be express and unequivocal language or conduct”; s. 238(1) deems the premium “not to have been made” if the cheque is dishonoured.
BaselineB: Combination: Statute (The Alberta Insurance Act, R.S.A. 1970, c. 187, s. 238(1)) plus common-law waiver requirement as applied/followed from McGeachie v. North American Life Insurance Company (1893), 23 S.C.R. 148.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “lawful authority” for whistleblower protection under s. 74(1)(a): includes not only police/state agents but also internal persons who exercise lawful authority over the employee(s) or over the activity likely to result in an offence (the “up the ladder” approach). Key holding: “the expression ‘lawful authority’ in s. 74 includes not only the police or other agents of the state ... but also individuals within the employer organization who exercise lawful authority over the employee(s) complained about, or over the activity that is or is likely to result in the offence” (para. 38).
BaselineA: Statute: The Labour Standards Act, R.S.S. 1978, c. L-1, s. 74(1)(a) (and s. 74(2) vexatious exception), interpreted using the modern principle of statutory interpretation (Rizzo; Bell ExpressVu).
CaseB_TestB: Common law joinder test (Clunas) applied to joint trials of provincial offences and summary conviction Criminal Code offences: (1) offences “could initially have been jointly charged” understood functionally as requiring a “sufficient factual nexus” (paras. 39-40); and (2) joinder must be “in the interests of justice” (para. 41), involving “a weighing of the costs and benefits of a joint trial” (para. 42) with consent relevant but not determinative (para. 43).
BaselineB: Common law: R. v. Clunas, [1992] 1 S.C.R. 595 (two-part joinder test), reaffirmed in R. v. S.J.L., 2009 SCC 14; applied in the statutory context of the Criminal Code and Ontario’s Provincial Offences Act (no express prohibition).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Two-step harm-based test for criminal indecency (Labaye/Butler framework): Crown must prove beyond a reasonable doubt (1) conduct “causes harm or presents a significant risk of harm” to individuals or society (e.g., “significantly interferes with [public] autonomy and liberty”, “predisposing others to anti-social behaviour”, or “physically or psychologically harming” participants) and (2) the harm/risk is “of a degree that is incompatible with the proper functioning of society” (Kouri, para. 10).
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 210(1) (keeping a common bawdy-house for “acts of indecency”), with the indecency analysis structured “based on the guidelines emerging from R. v. Butler, [1992] 1 S.C.R. 452” and developed in the companion case R. v. Labaye, 2005 SCC 80 (Kouri, paras. 1, 9-10).
CaseB_TestB: Pointe Gourde / s. 27(1)(a) “scheme to be ignored” test: for whether a land-use enactment’s value effects are ignored in expropriation compensation, “the key question is whether the enactment was made with a view to the expropriation or, conversely, was an independent enactment” (Lynch, para. 46); the inquiry “involves examining the purposes and effects of the enactment” (para. 48) and “causation does not drive the inquiry” (paras. 50-54).
BaselineB: Statute informed by common law: Expropriation Act, R.S.N.L. 1990, c. E-19, s. 27(1)(a) (“no account shall be taken of the compulsory acquisition of the land”), incorporating the common law “Pointe Gourde principle” from Pointe Gourde Quarrying and Transport Co. v. Sub-Intendent of Crown Lands, [1947] A.C. 565 (Lynch, paras. 2, 34-38).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Interpretation of Alberta Limitations Act, s. 12: it applies Alberta’s limitation law only to "live" foreign causes of action and does not revive claims already time-barred under the applicable foreign substantive law (lex loci delicti, including its limitation period)
BaselineA: Combination: statute (Limitations Act, R.S.A. 2000, c. L-12, s. 12) interpreted against common-law conflicts rule from Tolofson v. Jensen (lex loci delicti includes the foreign limitation period as substantive)
CaseB_TestB: Ancillary powers doctrine (Waterfield/Dedman framework) for common-law police powers: define the asserted power and liberty interest; then (1) does the conduct fall within the general scope of a police duty; (2) is it a justifiable exercise—i.e., "reasonably necessary"—weighing (a) importance of the duty, (b) necessity of the liberty interference, and (c) extent of the interference; onus on the state; applied to reject any common-law power to arrest a lawful actor to prevent an apprehended breach of the peace by others
BaselineB: Common law: Waterfield as adopted/used in Dedman v. The Queen and subsequent SCC cases (e.g., R. v. MacDonald); applied to a proposed arrest power
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Palmer/Lévesque test for admitting fresh evidence on a sentence appeal (interests of justice): (1) due diligence; (2) relevance to a decisive/potentially decisive sentencing issue; (3) credibility; (4) could reasonably be expected to have affected the result
BaselineA: Common law (Palmer v. The Queen; adapted to sentence appeals in R. v. Lévesque) applied under Criminal Code, s. 687(1) (appellate court may 'require or receive additional evidence')
CaseB_TestB: Section 8 reasonable expectation of privacy (REP) framework: REP assessed on the 'totality of the circumstances' via four inquiries—(1) subject matter; (2) direct interest; (3) subjective expectation; (4) objective reasonableness (normative) — with Brown J. holding no objectively reasonable REP in an adult–unknown-child sting
BaselineB: Common law Charter s. 8 jurisprudence (e.g., Edwards; Tessling; Spencer; Cole; Marakah) plus statutory interpretation link to Criminal Code, ss. 183 ('private communication') and 184.2
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Secondary infringement by importation under Copyright Act s. 27(2)(e) requires “hypothetical infringement”; no liability where the foreign maker would not infringe if it made the copy in Canada because it is the Canadian copyright owner (and an exclusive licensee cannot sue the owner-licensor for infringement).
CaseB_TestB: Section 11(h) “punished . . . again” test for retrospective parole changes: the “dominant consideration” is the extent to which an offender’s “settled expectation of liberty has been thwarted”; automatic lengthening of incarceration is a “clearest of cases” of double punishment; otherwise ask whether the change “substantially increase[s] the risk of additional incarceration” (with indicators including continued individualized decision-making and procedural safeguards).
BaselineB: Constitution (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 11(h); applied to Abolition of Early Parole Act, S.C. 2011, c. 11, s. 10(1))
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Sentencing/appellate intervention for hybrid offences prosecuted summarily: sentencing court bound by Crown election and appellate court intervenes only for error of principle (etc.) or demonstrably unfit sentence (including maximum)
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code sentencing provisions and summary conviction maximums) plus SCC sentencing jurisprudence on appellate intervention
CaseB_TestB: Mr. Big confessions admissibility rule: presumptive inadmissibility rebutted only if Crown proves (balance of probabilities) probative value (reliability) outweighs prejudicial effect; plus separate abuse-of-process scrutiny for coercive/abusive operations
BaselineB: Common law evidence (party admissions/hearsay; probative value vs prejudicial effect; abuse of process) with SCC precedents including Evans, Handy, Mohan, Mack, Babos, Oickle, Khelawon
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Adequacy of jury charge on evidence: trial judge must (except in rare needless cases) review the substantial parts of the evidence and present the defence theory so jurors understand the value/effect of the evidence and how law applies; judge has “considerable latitude” as to how much evidence to review, so long as jurors get an “adequate understanding” of the relationship between essential evidence and issues.
BaselineA: Common law (jury-charge adequacy principles from Azoulay v. The Queen and R. v. Jacquard).
CaseB_TestB: Trade-marks Act confusion test (s. 6): confusion exists if, considering “all the surrounding circumstances” (including s. 6(5) factors), it is likely the “casual consumer somewhat in a hurry” will draw the mistaken inference that the wares/services come from the same source; no requirement of “resemblance or linkage” between wares/services, and neither fame nor product-line difference “trumps” the totality-of-circumstances analysis.
BaselineB: Statute (Trade-marks Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. T-13, ss. 6(2) and 6(5)).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Elements of the Criminal Code child-luring offence (s. 172.1(1)(c)): Crown must prove (1) an intentional communication by computer; (2) with a person the accused knows or believes is under 14; (3) "for the specific purpose of facilitating" a listed secondary offence with respect to that person; "facilitating" includes "helping to bring about and making easier or more probable" and the inquiry is subjective intent assessed on the evidence as a whole (content not necessarily determinative; no need to intend to meet).
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 172.1(1)(c) (as it read at the time), with listed secondary offences including ss. 151 and 152.
CaseB_TestB: Enforcement of a forum selection clause: per Pompey, absent specific legislation, the court should hold parties to their bargain unless there is "strong cause" to displace the chosen forum; the test is "discretionary in nature" (and a Rule 21.01(3)(a) motion may be brought after delivering a statement of defence if brought promptly).
BaselineB: Common law: Z.I. Pompey Industrie v. ECU-Line N.V., 2003 SCC 27 ("strong cause" test), applied within the procedural framework of Ontario Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 21.01(3)(a).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Leave to appeal under Supreme Court Act s. 40(1): SCC may grant leave only if it is of the opinion the question is “by reason of its public importance or the importance of any issue of law or any issue of mixed law and fact… one that ought to be decided by the Supreme Court or is, for any other reason, of such a nature or significance as to warrant decision by it” (s. 40(1)); Cromwell J. adds that “only in very rare circumstances would a proposed appeal from an order granting an extension of time for appealing meet this test” (para. 12).
BaselineA: Statute: Supreme Court Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. S-26, s. 40(1) (and jurisdictional context in ss. 2, 40(3), with Criminal Code ss. 691-693).
CaseB_TestB: Access to Information Act s. 27(1) third-party notice threshold (Cromwell J.): disclosure without notice only in “clear cases” where the head “concludes that there is no reason to believe that the record might contain” s. 20(1) material (para. 72); refusal without notice where “there is no reason to believe that the information is subject to disclosure” (para. 72); otherwise notice is required, summarized as: the head “must give notice if he or she (i) is in doubt about whether the information is exempt…; (ii) intends to disclose exempted material… pursuant to s. 20(6); or (iii) intends to disclose severed material pursuant to s. 25” (para. 84).
BaselineB: Statute: Access to Information Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. A-1, especially ss. 20(1), 25, 27(1), 28, 44.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Reasonableness of unannounced/forced entry (departure from “knock and announce”): police must ordinarily give (i) notice of presence, (ii) notice of authority, and (iii) notice of purpose; if they depart, “there is an onus on them to explain why” and the Crown must show “reasonable grounds to be concerned about the possibility of harm ... or about the destruction of evidence” (Cornell, paras. 18-20).
BaselineA: Common law “knock and announce” rule (Eccles v. Bourque) applied within Charter s. 8 reasonableness framework (R. v. Collins).
CaseB_TestB: Implied assertions are hearsay when tendered for their truth; admissible only if within a traditional exception or, under the principled approach, if “sufficient indicia of reliability and necessity are established on a voir dire” (Baldree, paras. 34, 48).
BaselineB: Common law hearsay rule and the SCC’s “principled approach” (Khan; Mapara; Khelawon) defining hearsay by purpose (truth of contents) and requiring necessity and reliability.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: State Immunity Act “commercial activity” exception (s. 5): determine whether the proceeding “relate[s] to any commercial activity of the foreign state” by examining the “nature of the acts ... in their full context, which includes the purpose of the acts” (not merely whether the acts were state-authorized or pursued public interests).
BaselineA: Statute: State Immunity Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. S-18, ss. 2 (“commercial activity”), 3 (general immunity), 5 (commercial activity exception); applied through C.C.Q. art. 3076 (and recognition context under arts. 3155, 3158 C.C.Q.).
CaseB_TestB: Whether a procedural irregularity (jury exposure to inadmissible/tainted material) requires a mistrial / amounts to a miscarriage of justice: assess if the irregularity was “severe enough to render the trial unfair or create the appearance of unfairness”, using non-exhaustive “reference points” (centrality to the case, gravity/likely influence, jury vs judge-alone, whether remedied, effect on fairness/appearance, and defence counsel’s response).
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1) (especially s. 686(1)(a)(iii) “miscarriage of justice” and related curative proviso structure).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Journalist-source privilege in civil proceedings (Quebec): threshold relevance + four Wigmore factors, with context-specific balancing at factor 4
BaselineA: Common law (Wigmore case-by-case privilege framework as applied to journalist-source privilege in R. v. National Post, 2010 SCC 16) plus Quebec civil evidence/procedure context (C.C.Q. art. 2857 relevance; C.C.P. art. 46 general powers)
CaseB_TestB: Court jurisdiction to review decisions of voluntary associations: requires an underlying legal right; contract exists only if general contract formation (especially objective intention to create legal relations) is shown
BaselineB: Common law (Highwood Congregation of Jehovah’s Witnesses (Judicial Committee) v. Wall, 2018 SCC 26; general contract formation principles including objective intention to create legal relations)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Quebec Charter s. 49(2) exemplary (punitive) damages: (1) “unlawful” interference with a Charter right + (2) “intentional” interference; plus SCC clarification that punitive damages are autonomous (not barred by absence of compensatory damages) and may be awarded against a deceased wrongdoer’s succession for denunciation
BaselineA: Statute (Quebec Charter, s. 49(2), read with C.C.Q. art. 1621; and prior SCC interpretation in St-Ferdinand and Béliveau St-Jacques)
CaseB_TestB: YCJA jurisdiction for youth judicial interim release on s. 469 charges after election: interpret “the proceeding” in YCJA ss. 13(2)-(3) to include all steps after election (including pre-trial bail), and hold jurisdiction under YCJA s. 33(8) is concurrent between superior court judges deemed youth justice court judges and provincially designated youth justice court judges
BaselineB: Statute (Youth Criminal Justice Act ss. 13(1)-(3), 28, 33(8), 67; Criminal Code ss. 469, 522; Interpretation Act s. 33(2))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Miscarriage of justice on appeal: whether trial shortcomings "affected the trial judge’s appreciation of the evidence or rendered the proceedings unfair, so as to give rise to a miscarriage of justice" (including that leading questions are those that "suggest an answer or assume a state of facts that is in dispute")
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code appeal power) plus common-law/Charter-informed appellate concept of "miscarriage of justice"
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 13 engagement turns on whether prior compelled testimony is "incriminating evidence": evidence that the Crown could use at the later proceeding, if permitted, "to prove guilt, i.e., to prove or assist in proving one or more of the essential elements of the offence"; if not, s. 13 is not engaged and the evidence may be used for impeachment
BaselineB: Statute/constitutional text (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 13) interpreted in light of prior SCC cases (notably R. v. Henry; also Kuldip, Noël, Dubois)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 467.12 “in association with” a criminal organization: requires (1) a nexus between the predicate offence and the organization (not merely between the accused and the organization) and (2) subjective mens rea that the accused knowingly dealt with a criminal organization; “in association with” captures offences that “advance, at least to some degree, the interests of a criminal organization” (Venneri, paras. 54-58).
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 467.12(1) (interpreting the phrase “in association with” within “for the benefit of, at the direction of, or in association with, a criminal organization”).
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 7 use-immunity for compelled accident reports: a statement is “compelled” under Motor Vehicle Act s. 61(1) if, “at the time that the accident was reported by the driver, the driver gave the report on the basis of an honest and reasonably held belief that he or she was required by law to report the accident to the person to whom the report was given” (White, para. 75); accused bears the onus on a balance of probabilities to show compulsion (para. 81).
BaselineB: Combination: Statute (Motor Vehicle Act, R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 288, s. 61(1)) plus constitutional law (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7) establishing use immunity where the statement is compelled.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 8 sniffer-dog search: “reasonable suspicion” requires (1) a subjective belief and (2) objective grounds—“objectively discernible facts”—assessed on the “totality of the circumstances” through the lens of a reasonable officer; the question is whether facts indicate the “possibility of criminal behaviour” (not probability).
BaselineA: Common law Charter s. 8 framework for sniffer-dog searches from R. v. Kang-Brown and R. v. A.M., as clarified in companion R. v. Chehil (reasonable suspicion standard).
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 11(i) “punishment” test (reformulated): a measure is punishment if (1) it is a consequence of conviction forming part of the “arsenal of sanctions”, and either (2) it is imposed in furtherance of sentencing purposes/principles, or (3) it has a “significant impact” on liberty/security (significantly constrains lawful conduct or imposes significant burdens).
BaselineB: Combination of common law Charter interpretation and statutory context: builds on R. v. Rodgers (two-part punishment test) while applied to Criminal Code s. 161(1)(c), (d) (as amended by Safe Streets and Communities Act, 2012, c. 1, s. 16(1)).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: CCQ art. 1425 contract-interpretation/rectification approach: where evidence proves a discrepancy between the parties’ proven “common intention” and their “declared will” in the writings, the court may intervene to recognize the parties’ consensual amendments and ensure the error is remedied, subject to third-party rights (e.g., “the determination of the common intention… represents a true exercise of interpretation” and if a private writing contains an error “the court must… note the error and ensure that it is remedied”; “tax authorities do not have an acquired right to benefit from an error… after the parties have corrected the error by mutual consent”).
BaselineA: Statute (Civil Code of Québec, art. 1425; also relies on CCQ consensualism/contract principles and evidentiary rules referenced at arts. 2818, 2829, and modification at art. 1439).
CaseB_TestB: Bank ‘put upon inquiry’ constructive-trust test: “A banker may be a constructive trustee of money in his customer’s account and in breach of that trust if he pays the money away… in circumstances which put him upon inquiry”; once the bank has “sufficient notice… to put the Bank on its inquiry”, it must take steps “to ascertain the character of the funds” before dealing with them.
BaselineB: Common law (constructive trustee/bank on inquiry doctrine; SCC cites Halsbury’s Laws of England and discusses prior cases such as White v. Dominion Bank and Cartwright v. Lyster & Bank of Nova Scotia).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Whether a post–Court of Appeal Quebec statute (1974, c. 80, s. 5) applies so as to render C.C. art. 2262(2) (one-year prescription) inapplicable to a suit that was “pending before a court on 1 January 1975”, even though the case was then pending in the Supreme Court of Canada (and thus the appeal must be dismissed).
BaselineA: Statute: Supreme Court Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. S-19, s. 47 (power to dismiss appeal / give judgment the court below should have given), with discussion of ss. 50 and 67; plus Quebec Act to amend certain prescriptions, 1974 (Que.), c. 80, ss. 1, 3, 5 and Civil Code arts. 2261(2), 2262(2).
CaseB_TestB: Extradition refusal threshold: the person must show surrender would “shock the conscience” (s. 7 Charter) or be “unjust or oppressive” (Extradition Act, s. 44(1)); the Minister’s core inquiry is whether surrender to the “particular treatment” awaiting the person would be contrary to Canadian principles of fundamental justice.
BaselineB: Statute/constitutional: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7; Extradition Act, S.C. 1999, c. 18, s. 44(1), applying prior SCC guidance (United States v. Burns; Argentina v. Mellino).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: R. v. Hart (Moldaver J.) — New common law admissibility rule for “Mr. Big” confessions: presumptive inadmissibility rebutted only if Crown shows (balance of probabilities) probative value (as a function of reliability) outweighs prejudicial effect; reliability assessed via (i) circumstances of the operation and (ii) markers of reliability in the confession itself; plus separate abuse-of-process backstop for coercive/abusive operations
BaselineA: Common law evidence (party admissions exception to hearsay) and trial judge discretion to exclude prejudicial evidence; SCC notes Mr. Big confessions were routinely admitted as party admissions (citing R. v. Evans; R. v. Osmar) and that existing protections (right to silence; confessions rule) were inoperative (citing R. v. McIntyre; R. v. Hebert; R. v. Grandinetti)
CaseB_TestB: R. v. Borowiec (Cromwell J.) — Statutory interpretation of Criminal Code s. 233 “her mind is then disturbed”: apply “disturbed” in its ordinary sense (not a medical/legal term of art), meaning e.g. “mentally agitated/unstable/mental discomposure”; no need for a defined mental illness or s. 16 mental disorder; disturbance must exist at the time of the act/omission and be “by reason of” childbirth effects or lactation; no causal link required between disturbance and the killing (disturbance is actus reus, not mens rea)
BaselineB: Statute — Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 233 (infanticide), interpreted using the modern approach to statutory interpretation
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Penile swab incident to arrest is Charter-compliant only if (1) police have independent “reasonable grounds to believe that a penile swab will afford evidence of the offence for which the accused was arrested” and (2) the swab is conducted “in a reasonable manner” guided by 10 enumerated factors (e.g., station-house as general rule, supervisory authorization, same-gender officers, privacy, minimal force, record-keeping).
BaselineA: Common law (search incident to arrest framework from R. v. Fearon; reasonableness requirements from R. v. Caslake; strip-search modifications/guidelines from R. v. Golden; distinguished from R. v. Stillman).
CaseB_TestB: Co-principal (joint) liability in group assaults: “Joint/co‑principal liability flows whenever two or more individuals come together with an intention to commit an offence, are present during the commission of the offence, and contribute to its commission”; for manslaughter, focus is whether the accused’s actions were “a significant contributing cause of death”, not “which perpetrator inflicted which wound”.
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, s. 21(1)(a) (parties—common intention/co-principal liability); applied/clarified with reference to R. v. Pickton).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Whether a damages claim for breach/violation of a collective agreement is a “grievance” (i.e., a “disagreement respecting the interpretation or application of a collective agreement”) and therefore within mandatory grievance arbitration jurisdiction; no distinction between “application/interpretation” and “violation” (they are “two ways of looking at the same problem”).
BaselineA: Statute (Quebec Labour Code, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 141, ss. 1(g) definition of “grievance” and s. 88 mandatory arbitration), as interpreted in SCC precedent (General Motors of Canada Ltd. v. Brunet, [1977] 2 S.C.R. 537; also Imbleau et al. v. Laskin et al., [1962] S.C.R. 338).
CaseB_TestB: Enforceability/scope of a waiver (exclusion) clause for negligence: construed in its context to determine whether it exonerates the defendant(s), and whether the negligence was within the clause’s contemplation; attempts to avoid the clause via “unfair, unreasonable and inapplicable” arguments (including fundamental breach/unconscionability/public policy) fail where the clause is “reasonable in the circumstances” and the risk was known/voluntarily assumed.
BaselineB: Common law (contractual interpretation and enforceability of exclusion/waiver clauses; doctrines discussed include fundamental breach, unconscionability, and public policy—no specific statutory baseline identified in the reasons).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: When a CLRB s. 119 review of a certification order must be treated like a new certification: only if the review would “enlarge or otherwise alter” the unit so the revised order is “substantially different”; mere “clerical or technical changes”/“clarification” that do not “substantially affect[] the nature or effect” of the original order only require the Board be “satisfied that these changes are in order”
BaselineA: Statute (Canada Labour Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. L-1, s. 119) as interpreted through CLRB jurisprudence quoted and applied by the SCC (The Employees of the Regional Comptroller (1975), 9 D.I. 20; also referenced: Canadian Overseas Telecommunications Union (1979), 32 D.I. 270)
CaseB_TestB: Appellate intervention with trial findings: it is wrong to set aside a trial judgment absent “palpable and overriding error” where the only issue is “the interpretation of the evidence as a whole” (i.e., unless the trial judge was “plainly wrong” on the facts)
BaselineB: Common law (SCC appellate review standard drawn from Schreiber Brothers Ltd. v. Currie Products Ltd. and Gulf Oil Canada Ltd., [1980] 2 S.C.R. 78; Stein v. "Kathy K.", [1976] 2 S.C.R. 802; Lewis v. Todd, [1980] 2 S.C.R. 694)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Ernst (Cromwell J.) categorical Ward-based bar: Charter damages are never an “appropriate and just” remedy (Charter, s. 24(1)) against this quasi-judicial regulator, because Ward countervailing factors (effective alternative remedy + good governance + immunity’s purpose) collectively negate damages in every case
BaselineA: Common law (Charter remedial framework) applying Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 24(1), as interpreted in Vancouver (City) v. Ward, 2010 SCC 27
CaseB_TestB: Maybrun framework (as applied in Bird) for whether an accused charged with breaching an administrative order may collaterally attack the order: determine legislative intent using five non-exhaustive factors (wording; purpose; appeal/other review mechanisms; expertise/raison d’être; penalty), with an effective-remedy requirement in Charter contexts
BaselineB: Common law framework from R. v. Consolidated Maybrun Mines Ltd., [1998] 1 S.C.R. 706 and R. v. Al Klippert Ltd., [1998] 1 S.C.R. 737 (applied in context of CCRA s. 134.1(2) and Criminal Code s. 753.3(1))
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Art. 2930 C.C.Q. applies (three-year prescription) where the action is based on the wrongful act that caused interference with another’s physical integrity, and the plaintiff claims reparation for the direct and immediate consequences of that interference ("the nature of the initial interference rather than the head of damages being claimed"; "direct and immediate consequences").
BaselineA: Statute: Civil Code of Québec, arts. 2925 and 2930 (in interaction with Cities and Towns Act, s. 586).
CaseB_TestB: Appellate non-intervention on trial judge’s assessment of evidence/credibility: once the trial judge’s reasons are available, the Court of Appeal should not substitute its view of the evidence; doing so is an "unwarranted intrusion" into an area "exclusive to the trial judge" (especially given the trial judge’s advantage of seeing/hearing witnesses).
BaselineB: Common law principle of appellate deference/non-intervention on findings of fact and credibility (as reflected in cases cited: Latour v. Grenier; Maze v. Empson; Dorval v. Bouvier; Métivier v. Cadorette; Hood v. Hood).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Schrenk “sufficient nexus with the employment context” test for whether discrimination is “regarding employment” under s. 13(1)(b): Tribunal must conduct a “contextual analysis” considering all relevant circumstances; non-exhaustive factors include “(1) whether the respondent was integral to the complainant’s workplace; (2) whether the impugned conduct occurred in the complainant’s workplace; and (3) whether the complainant’s work performance or work environment was negatively affected” (para. 67).
BaselineA: Statute: Human Rights Code, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 210, s. 13(1)(b) (“discriminate against a person regarding employment”), with interpretive baseline from human rights/statutory interpretation principles (e.g., Rizzo; Berg) and workplace-discrimination jurisprudence (e.g., Robichaud; Janzen).
CaseB_TestB: Groia in-court incivility/professional misconduct framework: a “context-specific” approach considering “what the lawyer said, the manner and frequency in which it was said, and the presiding judge’s reaction” (paras. 59, 80). For integrity-impugning allegations, they “cross the line into professional misconduct unless they are made in good faith and have a reasonable basis” (para. 81), where “reasonable basis” is not met by “speculative or entirely lacking a factual foundation” and is not defeated merely by “legal error” if there is “a sufficient factual foundation” (paras. 88-89).
BaselineB: Statute/regulatory: Law Society Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. L.8 (home statute) and Law Society Rules of Professional Conduct/Professional Conduct Handbook (e.g., duties of civility/courtesy and professional conduct), applied through administrative-law reasonableness review (Ryan; Doré).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Ontario anti-SLAPP dismissal framework under CJA s. 137.1: (1) moving party must show on a balance of probabilities the proceeding “arises from an expression” that “relates to a matter of public interest” (s. 137.1(3)); then (2) responding party must show both (a) “grounds to believe” the proceeding has “substantial merit” and the moving party has “no valid defence” (s. 137.1(4)(a)), and (b) the harm is “sufficiently serious that the public interest in permitting the proceeding to continue outweighs the public interest in protecting that expression” (s. 137.1(4)(b)). Key SCC gloss: “grounds to believe” requires “a basis in the record and the law”; “substantial merit” means “a real prospect of success” supported by evidence “reasonably capable of belief”; and s. 137.1(4)(b) is a public-interest weighing where one interest must “outweigh” the other (paras. 39, 49, 61-67).
BaselineA: Statute: Courts of Justice Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.43, s. 137.1(3)-(4) (anti-SLAPP).
CaseB_TestB: Corporate attribution doctrine (including for one-person corporations) and the discretionary “public interest/purpose of the law” limit: attribution generally applies if (1) the wrongdoer was the corporation’s directing mind and (2) acted within their sector of corporate responsibility; attribution is generally inappropriate under the “fraud” and “no benefit” exceptions; and, additionally, courts have discretion to refuse attribution where it would not be “in the public interest, in the sense that it would promote the purpose of the law under which attribution is sought” (paras. 62, 75). SCC holds the same purposive, contextual, pragmatic approach applies to one-person corporations and rejects an automatic attribution rule (paras. 64-71).
BaselineB: Common law corporate attribution doctrine from SCC cases cited in the decision: Canadian Dredge & Dock Co. v. The Queen; Deloitte & Touche v. Livent Inc. (Receiver of); Christine DeJong Medicine Professional Corp. v. DBDC Spadina Ltd.; and Aquino v. Bondfield Construction Co. (applied).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Duty of trial judge to comment on Crown counsel’s prejudicial jury address: where remarks are “prejudicial to a degree sufficient to impose a legal duty on the trial judge to comment” to ensure the defence position is “fairly put to the jury”; failure to do so is an error of law (with s. 686(1)(b)(iii) curative proviso not applicable on these facts).
BaselineA: Combination: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(b)(iii) (curative proviso) + common-law fairness requirements for jury addresses/charge (as reflected in the Court’s adoption of Ayles J.A.’s formulation).
CaseB_TestB: Federal Courts Act s. 43(2) in rem jurisdiction — “identifiability” test: reject “physical nexus”; property is “subject of the action” if it is identifiable as the cargo designated in the contract of affreightment alleged to be breached.
BaselineB: Statute: Federal Courts Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. F-7, s. 43(2) (“against the ship, aircraft or other property that is the subject of the action”).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Threshold for summary dismissal of a criminal application: the underlying application may be summarily dismissed only if it is “manifestly frivolous” (judge must assume alleged facts are true and take the applicant’s arguments “at their highest”; no weighing of evidence; moving party bears burden).
BaselineA: Common law (criminal procedure/case management power to screen applications, developed in cases such as R. v. Vukelich (1996 BCCA) and R. v. Kutynec (1992 ONCA), with SCC context references to Jordan/Cody).
CaseB_TestB: Combined effect of Criminal Code s. 172.1(3) presumption and s. 172.1(4) “reasonable steps” requirement in child luring: if underage is represented, accused is presumed to believe underage; presumption rebutted only by “evidence to the contrary” that includes objectively reasonable steps to ascertain age; evidential burden on accused, persuasive burden on Crown.
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 172.1(3) and s. 172.1(4), read with s. 172.1(1)(a) and (c)).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Two-step framework for whether legislation displaces the common law (and, on the merits, whether a sentencing judge may grant credit for a pre-sentence driving prohibition despite a mandatory minimum): (1) identify the applicable common law rule; (2) specify the statute’s effect on that rule, including whether it displaces it expressly or by necessary implication. Applied to s. 259(1)(a) and s. 719(1) Cr. C., the Court holds the judge must impose the one-year minimum but may then grant credit because s. 259(1)(a) sets a minimum 'punishment' not a minimum 'sentence' (so no conflict with s. 719(1)). Key quotes: 'The two-step framework ... is well settled. The first step is “analysing, identifying and setting out the applicable common law”; and then, at the second step, “the statute law’s effect on the common law must be specified”' (para. 45). 'At the time of sentencing, the court is required to impose the one-year mandatory minimum punishment, but there is nothing in the statute that prevents it from then granting credit' (para. 10). 's. 259(1)(a) can be read in only one way: it provides for the imposition of a mandatory minimum punishment' (para. 74).
BaselineA: Combination of common law and statute: common law discretion to credit pre-sentence driving prohibitions recognized in R. v. Lacasse, 2015 SCC 64 (and analogy to credit for pre-sentence custody in R. v. Wust, 2000 SCC 18), interpreted alongside Criminal Code ss. 259(1)(a) and 719(1) (and considering s. 719(3)).
CaseB_TestB: Mitigation in contract where plaintiff claims specific performance: defendant must prove (i) plaintiff failed to take reasonable steps to mitigate and (ii) mitigation was possible; but a plaintiff seeking specific performance may justify inaction only if it had 'some fair, real, and substantial justification' / 'a substantial and legitimate interest' in specific performance. For investment land, that requires showing damages are inadequate because the land has 'a peculiar and special value'. Key quotes: 'As a general rule, a plaintiff will not be able to recover for those losses which he could have avoided by taking reasonable steps' (para. 24). 'Where it is alleged that the plaintiff has failed to mitigate, the burden of proof is on the defendant, who needs to prove both that the plaintiff has failed to make reasonable efforts to mitigate and that mitigation was possible' (para. 24). 'Before a plaintiff can rely on a claim to specific performance ... some fair, real, and substantial justification ... must be found' (para. 35, quoting Asamera). 'A plaintiff deprived of an investment property does not have a “fair, real, and substantial justification” ... unless he can show that money is not a complete remedy because the land has “a peculiar and special value” to him' (para. 41).
BaselineB: Common law mitigation doctrine and the Asamera Oil Corp. v. Seal Oil & General Corp. framework for when a specific-performance claim can justify mitigatory inaction; read with Semelhago v. Paramadevan on when land is sufficiently 'unique' / of 'peculiar and special value' such that damages are inadequate.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Hearsay admissibility under the “principled approach”: hearsay (including hearsay said to fit a traditional exception) is admissible only if it meets the twin requirements of “reliability and necessity”; traditional exceptions “must therefore yield to comply with the principled approach” where they conflict (e.g., statements of present intention inadmissible if made in “circumstances of suspicion”; statements of intention cannot be used to prove a third party’s intentions absent an exception for each hearsay level).
BaselineA: Common law (hearsay rule and exceptions; principled approach from R. v. Khan and R. v. Smith; present intentions exception discussed in R. v. Smith).
CaseB_TestB: Public interest standing (Downtown Eastside framework): a court must “assess and weigh three factors” cumulatively—(i) “serious justiciable issue”; (ii) “genuine interest”; and (iii) “reasonable and effective means” of bringing the case—applied “flexibly and purposively”; no one purpose (including legality/access to justice) has “particular weight”, and no directly affected co-plaintiff is required if a “sufficiently concrete and well-developed factual setting” will be forthcoming.
BaselineB: Common law (test from Canada (Attorney General) v. Downtown Eastside Sex Workers United Against Violence Society, 2012 SCC 45).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Limited-liability/non-assessability constraint on corporate article amendments: a company cannot impose any pecuniary obligation on holders of fully paid shares; and any transfer fee is unlawful to the extent it exceeds the reasonable and proper cost of the transfer
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law principle of limited liability/non-assessability (Alberta Companies Act; plus company-law authorities cited in reasons)
CaseB_TestB: Van der Peet aboriginal-rights identification test (as applied): (1) characterize the precise claim; (2) ask whether the practice/custom/tradition was, prior to contact, integral (central, significant, defining) to the distinctive culture of the claimant group
BaselineB: Common law constitutional test from R. v. Van der Peet (applied under Constitution Act, 1982, s. 35(1))
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Reviewability of a consensual labour arbitrator’s award for error of law on the face: no “specific question of law” reference (binding/ouster) where the issue arises through the ordinary grievance process under a collective agreement that limits the arbitrator to decisions consistent with the agreement
BaselineA: Common law (scope of judicial review of consensual arbitration awards; distinction between specific question of law vs dispute where law becomes material), drawing on Government of Kelantan v. Duff Development, F.R. Absalom, Faubert and Watts v. Temagami Mining, and Bell Canada v. OPEIU (as cited in the reasons)
CaseB_TestB: Morin framework for s. 11(b) “unreasonable delay”: assess total delay minus defence waiver, then consider reasons for delay, prejudice (including inferred prejudice from length), and the interests protected by s. 11(b) in a contextual balancing (not a mathematical formula)
BaselineB: Statute/constitutional text plus common law framework: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 11(b), applied through R. v. Morin and R. v. Askov (as cited in the reasons)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 3(4) possession (including joint possession): for Code purposes, possession is established where a person has something in personal possession or knowingly has it in another’s custody or in any place for use/benefit (s. 3(4)(a)); and where one of two or more persons, with the knowledge and consent of the rest, has anything in custody/possession, it is deemed to be in the custody and possession of each and all (s. 3(4)(b)). SCC holds s. 3(4) applies in all proceedings under the Code, including where possession is used as a circumstantial evidentiary link.
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 3(4) (and its scope via the phrase “For the purposes of this Act”).
CaseB_TestB: Adverse possession in British Columbia: possession must be “open and notorious, adverse, exclusive, peaceful (not by force), actual (generally), and continuous”; and the SCC rejects any additional requirement that the possessor’s use be inconsistent with the true owner’s intended use (the “inconsistent use” doctrine forms no part of BC law).
BaselineB: Common law adverse possession test as received and applied through BC limitations legislation (received 1833 English codification via Law and Equity Act, s. 2; applied through BC limitation statutes).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Quantum meruit for services rendered without agreed remuneration: where a municipality continues to authorize and receive hospital services after termination of an agreement, the municipality “must pay reasonable rates” (and recovery is not barred unless a valid Order in Council/statutory authority clearly extinguishes the right).
BaselineA: Common law (quantum meruit/quasi-contract), as applied in King George Highway Hospital Ltd. v. District of Surrey, [1971] S.C.R. vi; plus statutory/regulatory interpretation of Hospital Act, R.S.B.C. 1960, c. 178, s. 37(2), Social Assistance Act, R.S.B.C. 1960, c. 360, and Residence and Responsibility Act, R.S.B.C. 1960, c. 340, s. 3 (and O.C. 3103, 4399, 4400).
CaseB_TestB: Voluntariness/admissibility of inculpatory statements by an accused alleged to be insane: the “underlying and controlling question” is whether the statement was “freely and voluntarily made”, including whether it was the product of an “operating mind” (not so irrational/delusional that the words cannot fairly be said to be the accused’s statement).
BaselineB: Common law confessions rule (voluntariness), drawing on Boudreau v. The King, [1949] S.C.R. 262 and Ward v. The Queen, [1979] 2 S.C.R. 30 (with discussion of R. v. Santinon (BCCA)).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Effect of breach of a witness-exclusion order: witness not necessarily disqualified; admissibility is discretionary; weight is for trier of fact
BaselineA: Common law (practice/rule on exclusion of witnesses, as reflected in cases cited such as Moore v. Lambeth County Court Registrar; Cook v. Nethercotte; Thomas v. David; Chandler v. Home; Black v. Besse; R. v. Carefoot)
CaseB_TestB: Crown immunity from discovery is lifted only by clear and unequivocal legislative language; CLPA s. 27 applies only when the Crown is a party
BaselineB: Statute + common law (Interpretation Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. I-21, s. 17; Crown Liability and Proceedings Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-50, s. 27; against the backdrop of common law Crown immunity from discovery)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Bencher disqualification/bias in Law Society discipline: whether members of the Discipline Committee may participate in Convocation when Convocation considers the Committee’s report (two-stage process vs appeal; expressio unius from s. 39(4))
BaselineA: Statute and regulation (The Law Society Act, 1970 (Ont.), ss. 33(12), 34, 37, 39; Reg. 556, s. 13(6)-(7)) plus common-law natural justice/bias principles (nemo judex / reasonable apprehension of bias)
CaseB_TestB: Criminal Code s. 731(1)(b) probation availability: “imprisonment for a term not exceeding two years” refers to the term imposed by the sentencing court at a single sitting (not aggregate across other occasions); but probation is barred if sentences imposed at the same session result in continuous custody over two years
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, ss. 731(1)(b) and 732.2 (coming into force of probation))
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “operation of a mine” and when a separate “mine” exists for the 36‑month exemption: (1) “operation of a mine” in s. 83(5) “refers only to the extraction of ore from an ore body and does not include the processing of the ore after it has been produced”; and (2) “there is ‘a mine’ within the meaning of s. 83(5) if there is a body of ore together with the workings, equipment and machinery capable of producing it” — a separate mine arises when a separate ore body “commenced to be extracted by means of its separate and distinct extraction facilities,” even if the same mill processes ore from both.
BaselineA: Statute (Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1952, c. 148 as amended, s. 83(5) and definition in s. 83(6)); interpreted in light of SCC authorities North Bay Mica Company Limited v. M.N.R., [1958] S.C.R. 597 and M.N.R. v. MacLean Mining Co., [1970] S.C.R. 877.
CaseB_TestB: Mancini test for leave under s. 215 BIA to sue a receiver/trustee: leave should be refused only for “frivolous or vexatious” or “manifestly unmeritorious” claims; the evidence (typically affidavit plus draft pleading) must disclose a cause of action and “supply facts to support the claim”; the court “is not required to make a final assessment of the merits”; “If the evidence discloses a prima facie case, leave should be granted.”
BaselineB: Statute (Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. B-3, s. 215) applying/endorsing the common-law/appellate framework from Mancini (Bankrupt) v. Falconi (1993), 61 O.A.C. 332.
JudgeB: Abella J. (McLachlin C.J. and Bastarache, Binnie, LeBel, Fish and Charron JJ. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Education Act s. 373 roll-homologation/adjustment test: if valuations across municipalities are not uniform, commissioners must amend the rolls “so as to re-establish on the basis of its real value the valuation of the taxable property of all the parts of the school municipality” (i.e., equalize by real value of what is taxable in each municipality, not by importing another municipality’s tax base such as machinery).
BaselineA: Statute (Education Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 235, s. 373; with context from Cities and Towns Act s. 488 re machinery exclusion).
CaseB_TestB: Secret commissions offence (Criminal Code s. 426(1)(a)(ii))—elements for convicting an agent/taker: (1) agency relationship; (2) agent accepts a benefit “as consideration” for acting/forbearing in relation to the principal’s affairs; (3) “corruptly” = failure to make “adequate and timely disclosure” of the benefit’s “source, amount and nature”; no requirement to prove a “corrupt bargain” with the giver.
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 426(1)(a), especially s. 426(1)(a)(ii)).
JudgeB: Cory J. (for L’Heureux-Dubé, Gonthier, Cory and Iacobucci JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Extradition-crime classification under the 1925 Supplementary Convention: “The test is what is the essence of the crime charged” (i.e., whether the charge is, in substance, a crime “against the laws for the suppression of the traffic in narcotics”).
BaselineA: Statute + extradition arrangement: Extradition Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-21, s. 2 (definition of “extradition crime”), and the 1925 Supplementary Convention category “Crimes and offences against the laws for the suppression of the traffic in narcotics” (added to the Act).
CaseB_TestB: Section 13 “incrimination” purpose test for use of prior testimony at a later proceeding: prior testimony may be used on cross-examination if its purpose is only to impeach credibility, but not if used “to incriminate” (i.e., to establish guilt).
BaselineB: Constitutional + statutory interpretation: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 13 (and discussion of Canada Evidence Act, s. 5(2)); building on SCC self-incrimination jurisprudence including R. v. Dubois and R. v. Mannion (as discussed in the reasons).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Foreseeability/remoteness test for highway authority negligence: liability turns on whether “a reasonable person should have anticipated that what happened might be a natural result of that act or omission”; it is enough to foresee “in a general way the class or character of injury” (not the “precise concatenation of events”).
BaselineA: Common law (negligence foreseeability/remoteness), applied in the highway-maintenance context alongside the Highway Improvement Act, R.S.O. 1960, s. 33(1). Baseline case cited: University Hospital Board v. Lépine, [1966] S.C.R. 561; also applied: Wagon Mound No. 2.
CaseB_TestB: CEAA “tracking” rule: the environmental assessment track is determined by the “project as proposed” (not “project as scoped”); if the proposed project is in the Comprehensive Study List, s. 21 requirements are mandatory and the responsible authority “cannot reduce the scope of the project to less than what is proposed by the proponent.”
BaselineB: Statute/regulation: Canadian Environmental Assessment Act, S.C. 1992, c. 37 (especially ss. 2 “project”, 15, 18, 21, 58(1)(i)) and Comprehensive Study List Regulations, SOR/94-638 (e.g., Sch., s. 16).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Using res ipsa loquitur to infer (and prove) gross negligence in a gratuitous-passenger motor vehicle claim: (1) defendant had sole management/control; (2) occurrence would not have happened without negligence; and (3) there is no evidence as to why/how it occurred — but if an explanation is given and is not a valid answer, the inference may still apply
BaselineA: Combination: statute (Highway Traffic Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 202, s. 132(3) requiring “gross negligence”) plus common law evidentiary rule (res ipsa loquitur as described via Clerk & Lindsell; applied in SCC in Walker v. Coates et al.)
CaseB_TestB: Test for recognizing a vested (acquired) right that triggers the presumption against legislative interference: (1) the individual’s legal situation is “tangible and concrete” (not general/abstract); and (2) it was “sufficiently constituted at the time of the new statute’s commencement”
BaselineB: Combination: statutory interpretation baseline (Interpretation Act, R.S.Q., c. I-16, s. 12; transitional provisions in the 1997/1998 amending Acts, especially s. 13 of S.Q. 1997, c. 90) plus common law presumption against interference with vested rights (e.g., Spooner Oils; Gustavson Drilling) as synthesized in the reasons
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Mechanics’ lien owner-liability/holdback interpretation: s. 19(2) does not prevent an owner from deducting completion costs from amounts otherwise payable to a bankrupt head contractor; s. 19(2) only bars deductions for extraneous set-off/counterclaims not arising under the contract (reconciling ss. 6, 19(2), 21). Key quotes: s. 6 limits liability to 'the sum payable by the owner to the contractor'; s. 19(2) says the contract price 'shall not be diminished by any prior or subsequent indebtedness, set-off, or counterclaim'; SCC holds this 'did not apply when the owner was obliged to furnish material and labour to complete a contract abandoned by the head contractor' and 'does not bar the owner from deducting ... the cost of completion of the contract'.
BaselineA: Statute: Mechanics’ Lien Act, R.S.B.C. 1960, c. 238, ss. 6, 19(2), 21(1), 21(6) (interpreted in light of Canadian Comstock Co. Ltd. v. Toronto Transit Commission, [1970] S.C.R. 205, and S.I. Guttman Ltd. v. Mokry).
CaseB_TestB: Choice of law in tort (general rule): apply lex loci delicti—'the law of the place where the activity occurred'—as the governing substantive law; McLean v. Pettigrew overruled. SCC also treats foreign limitation periods as substantive where they create an accrued right to plead a time bar. Key quotes: 'the law to be applied in torts is the law of the place where the activity occurred, i.e., the lex loci delicti'; and limitation period substantive because it 'created an accrued right in the defendant to plead a time bar'.
BaselineB: Common law (conflict of laws in tort), reformulating/overruling prior SCC approach in McLean v. Pettigrew, [1945] S.C.R. 62; applied alongside statutory provisions in issue (e.g., Vehicles Act, R.S.S. 1978, c. V-3, s. 180(1); Quebec Automobile Insurance Act, L.Q. 1977, c. 68, ss. 3-4).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Constitutional validity/inapplicability of provincial legislation with extraterritorial operation: Manitoba cannot, via s. 4(2) of The Fishermen’s Assistance and Polluters’ Liability Act, nullify permissions granted by another jurisdiction for out-of-province conduct; interprovincial river pollution is a matter of exclusive federal concern (pith and substance/territorial limits).
BaselineA: Statute + constitutional division of powers/territorial limits (B.N.A. Act, 1867; Manitoba’s The Fishermen’s Assistance and Polluters’ Liability Act, 1970 (Man.), especially s. 4(2); also relies on constitutional principles from cases such as Royal Bank of Canada v. The King and The King v. National Trust Co. as discussed in the reasons).
JudgeA: Pigeon J. (for Martland, Pigeon and Beetz JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Privative-clause judicial review of arbitral awards: court may intervene only for jurisdictional error; an award justifies intervention only if it is "patently unreasonable"/an "unreasonable finding" that impairs jurisdiction, and insufficiency of reasons is generally not jurisdictional where reasons remain intelligible (Act respecting labour standards ss. 128-129; Labour Code s. 139).
BaselineB: Statute + administrative law doctrine (Act respecting labour standards, R.S.Q., c. N-1.1, ss. 128-129; Labour Code, R.S.Q. 1977, c. C-27, s. 139 privative clause; C.U.P.E. patently unreasonable standard as applied/clarified).
JudgeB: Lamer J. (reasons for McIntyre and Lamer JJ.; adopted in substance by Beetz, Chouinard and Wilson JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Collective agreement governs; common-law repudiation/fundamental breach inapplicable during subsisting collective agreement; illegal strike does not itself terminate employment so employer remains bound by severance clause if it closes plant without disciplining/discharging strikers
BaselineA: Combination: labour relations statute + SCC labour-law common law on nature of collective agreements (esp. Paquet; also Zambri; Re Polymer referenced)
CaseB_TestB: Limits on cross-examination using complainant’s diary: relevant defence evidence may be excluded only if its prejudicial effect substantially outweighs its probative value; omission evidence is probative only if defence establishes a reasonable expectation the event would have been recorded; O’Connor production balancing is not the test for cross-examination
BaselineB: Common law (Seaboyer; Osolin) with statutory context rejected as inapplicable to admissibility/use (Criminal Code ss. 278.1-278.9 are production-only)
