Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Admissibility of evidence that an accused refused to participate in a police line-up: admissible where (given the circumstances at trial) the Crown must explain the absence of a line-up or risk an adverse inference; otherwise such refusal evidence should not normally be tendered due to prejudice to the presumption of innocence.
BaselineA: Common law evidence (relevance/admissibility) and common law privilege against self-incrimination (testimonial compulsion only), as discussed via Curr v. The Queen and Attorney-General of Quebec v. Begin; also informed by comparative authorities (e.g., Holt; Schmerber; Wade).
CaseB_TestB: Division of powers (pith and substance) limit on provincial commissions of inquiry: a provincial inquiry is ultra vires if, in purpose/effect, it is a coercive substitute police investigation/preliminary inquiry into specific Criminal Code offences by named private individuals (i.e., it circumvents federally prescribed criminal procedure).
BaselineB: Constitution Act, 1867 division of powers analysis (pith and substance) under ss. 91(27) and 92, applied to provincial inquiry power under Ontario’s Public Inquiries Act, R.S.O. 1980, c. 411 (especially s. 2), and developed through prior SCC inquiry jurisprudence (Faber; Di Iorio; Keable; O'Hara).
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Punitive damages appropriateness/quantum in tort: whether the circumstances justify an additional punitive award “in the interests of justice” (here, “a very proper case for punitive damages”) given the defendants’ tortious conduct and scheme to destroy the plaintiff’s business
BaselineA: Common law (punitive/exemplary damages in tort; no specific baseline case articulated in the reasons provided)
CaseB_TestB: Anns/Cooper duty-of-care framework for recognizing a new duty in negligence (pure economic loss): (1) foreseeability + proximity (including party-specific policy at stage 1) and (2) residual policy considerations; plus threshold requirement that claims fit within a recognized pure-economic-loss category (e.g., relational economic loss requires third-party property damage)
BaselineB: Common law (Anns v. Merton London Borough Council; Kamloops (City of) v. Nielsen; Cooper v. Hobart; Childs v. Desormeaux; Norsk categories for pure economic loss)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory limits on Canadian Transport Commission power under Railway Act s. 275: a duly filed/published freight tariff takes effect on its stated effective date under s. 275(4) unless disallowed; any Commission order extending the s. 275(2) notice period must be made before the tariff’s effective date (post-effective-date ‘extension’ is an impermissible postponement and ultra vires).
BaselineA: Statute (Railway Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. R-2, s. 275(2) and s. 275(4); also National Transportation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. N-17, s. 64(5))
CaseB_TestB: Palmer test for admitting fresh evidence on appeal: (1) due diligence (relaxed in criminal cases), (2) relevance to a decisive/potentially decisive issue, (3) credibility, and (4) whether, if believed, it could reasonably be expected to have affected the result (overriding consideration: ‘the interests of justice’).
BaselineB: Common law (Palmer v. The Queen, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 759; applied via Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 683)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Effectiveness/finality of an order still within the appeal period: despite being appealable, it may be treated as fully effective (even against third parties) where there is only an “ephemeral prospect of an appeal”; assess (1) the purpose for which finality is invoked, (2) who is affected, and (3) the context in which finality/lack of finality is asserted before the appeal period expires.
BaselineA: Statute (The Conveyancing and Law of Property Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 85, s. 62) plus general/common-law principles about the effect of appealable orders (with Re West (1928) and Leonard v. Wharton (1921) discussed/distinguished).
CaseB_TestB: Preliminary inquiry committal test under Criminal Code s. 548(1): ask whether there is “any evidence upon which a reasonable jury properly instructed could return a verdict of guilty”; if Crown evidence is circumstantial, the judge must do a “limited weighing” of the whole evidence (including defence evidence) to assess whether, if the Crown’s evidence is believed, it would be reasonable for a jury to infer guilt (without drawing inferences or assessing credibility).
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 548(1)) interpreted through common law directed-verdict/committal jurisprudence, especially United States of America v. Shephard, [1977] 2 S.C.R. 1067 (also Mezzo and Monteleone clarified).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Discretionary test for granting public-interest (taxpayer/citizen) standing to challenge legislation: standing may be granted where (1) a “serious, a substantial constitutional issue” is raised; (2) the plaintiff has taken “all the steps that he could reasonably be required to take” so the standing issue is “ripe”; and (3) there is “no other way, practically speaking, to subject the challenged Act to judicial review” (with an “arguable case” that the public is “directly affected”).
BaselineA: Common law (standing/locus standi doctrine), drawing on Smith v. Attorney General of Ontario, [1924] S.C.R. 331 and Thorson v. Attorney General of Canada, [1975] 1 S.C.R. 138.
CaseB_TestB: Interpretation of ASRA Program s. 88(3): applying C.C.Q. arts. 1425–1432 (esp. arts. 1427 and 1426), s. 88(3) “does not require that amounts be linked individually” and instead “gives La Financière the discretion to decide what linkage method to employ”, subject to exercising that discretion in “good faith and contractual fairness” (arts. 6, 7, 1375, 1434 C.C.Q.).
BaselineB: Statute/regulation and civil code interpretation: Programme d’assurance stabilisation des revenus agricoles, s. 88(3), interpreted through Civil Code of Québec arts. 1425–1432, plus good faith/fairness duties in arts. 6, 7, 1375, 1434.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Rebuttable presumption of mens rea for trafficking: once actus reus of trafficking in LSD is proved, a presumption arises that the condition/intent was voluntarily induced and the accused is guilty unless other evidence raises a reasonable doubt that he lacked an honest belief/ability to appreciate he was (or might become) trafficking in the prohibited drug
BaselineA: Common law mens rea principles applied to statutory offence; Food and Drugs Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. F-27, ss. 40 (definitions) and 42 (trafficking in restricted drugs); baseline presumption framework drawn from R. v. King, [1962] S.C.R. 746 and honest-belief mistake principle from Beaver v. The Queen, [1957] S.C.R. 531
CaseB_TestB: Limits on trial-judge intervention: a judge may question/interrupt to clarify and ensure justice, but must stay within limits and act so that justice is seen to be done; if the judge’s conduct creates “some doubt” as to impartiality (appearance of assisting the Crown), a new trial is required
BaselineB: Common law procedural fairness / judicial impartiality principle (appearance of justice): R. v. Sussex Justices; Ex parte McCarthy, [1924] 1 K.B. 256 (“justice should not only be done, but should manifestly and undoubtedly be seen to be done”), with further guidance from cases such as Jones v. National Coal Board and R. v. Darlyn
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “burglary” in Criminal Code constructive murder provision: despite later revisions, “burglary” in s. 213 retains the 1892 Code meaning—“the offence defined as such in s. 410 of the Criminal Code 1892, coupled with the definitions of ‘dwelling-house’ and ‘break’ in s. 407” (i.e., breaking and entering a dwelling-house by night, etc.).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 213; Interpretation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. 1-23, s. 36; interpreted by reference to Criminal Code, 1892, ss. 228, 410, 407 and successive revisions).
CaseB_TestB: Damages for repudiation where contract has alternative modes of performance: adopt the mode “least profitable to the plaintiff, and the least burdensome to the defendant”; “The test is not how the defendant would likely have performed ... but for ... repudiation”; plaintiff is restored to position “had the contract been performed” (minimum performance owed).
BaselineB: Common law (general principle from Cockburn v. Alexander (1848), as explained in Withers v. General Theatre Corp. (1933), and adopted in Canadian appellate jurisprudence).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Lease interpretation test for shifting fire-loss risk to landlord/insurer: applying “the ordinary test of reading [the lease] reasonably and in a business sense”, a tenant who covenants to “pay … insurance rates” is “entitled to rest in respect of loss by fire on the discharge of its obligation to pay for fire insurance”, so the landlord’s insurer has no subrogated claim against the tenant for fire loss (including tenant-negligence fire) once the insurance bill is presented/paid.
BaselineA: Common law contract/lease interpretation ("reading it reasonably and in a business sense") plus statutory context that standard fire coverage includes third-party negligence (Insurance Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 224, s. 118).
CaseB_TestB: Civil Code art. 1053 “fault” liability for bank paying on unauthorized endorsement: a bank commits a compensable “fault” where, by accepting cheques payable to a company for deposit to an individual’s personal benefit “without examining it, and without verifying the sufficiency of the endorsement”, it deprives the payee of its money; damages are the cheque amounts where the payee has no remaining recourse against the drawer.
BaselineB: Combination of statute and civil law: Bills of Exchange Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. B-5 (notably s. 51 on signature by procuration; also s. 10 noted) and Civil Code (Quebec) art. 1053, as developed in Norwich Union Fire Insurance Society Ltd. v. La Banque Canadienne Nationale, [1934] S.C.R. 596.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 15(1) adverse-impact discrimination (prima facie breach): (1) law creates a distinction on an enumerated/analogous ground, including by effects shown through “disproportionate impact”; and (2) the law “reinforc[es], perpetuat[es], or exacerbat[es] disadvantage” (with flexible proof of disproportionate impact—statistics and/or group-context evidence; no need to prove intent or that the protected characteristic ‘caused’ the disparity).
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional text + prior SCC framework: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 15(1) (and s. 1 for justification). Baseline two-step s. 15 test stated in Quebec (AG) v. Alliance, 2018 SCC 17 at para. 25 and Centrale des syndicats du Québec, 2018 SCC 18 at para. 22; also Withler v. Canada (AG), 2011 SCC 12 (two-stage approach; adverse effects at para. 64).
CaseB_TestB: Division of powers “pith and substance” analysis: (1) determine the law’s “essential character” by examining “purpose and the legal effect”; (2) classify whether that character relates to an enumerated head of power (here, fisheries under s. 91(12) or criminal law under s. 91(27)).
BaselineB: Constitution + prior SCC doctrine: Constitution Act, 1867, ss. 91(12), 91(27), 92(13). Baseline pith-and-substance test drawn from Reference re Firearms Act (Can.), 2000 SCC 31 and Global Securities Corp., 2000 SCC 21 (as cited at para. 16-18). Applied to Marine Mammal Regulations, SOR/93-56, s. 27 (made under Fisheries Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. F-14, s. 43).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Lease interpretation test for whether a tenant’s covenant to pay “insurance rates” shifts the risk of fire loss (including loss caused by the tenant’s negligence) to the landlord, thereby barring the landlord’s insurer’s subrogated claim: apply “the ordinary test of reading [the lease] reasonably and in a business sense”; here, “under the provision of the lease respecting payment of insurance rates by the tenant, the risk of loss by fire passed to the landlord, at least upon the presentation by the landlord of the insurance bill”.
BaselineA: Common law contract/lease interpretation ("reading it reasonably and in a business sense") applied to the lease covenant; statutory context noted (Ontario Insurance Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 224, s. 118, as confirming fire coverage for third-party negligence).
CaseB_TestB: Warsaw Convention limitation-of-liability entitlement turns on ticket delivery (Art. 3(2)) and, for baggage, on inclusion of specified particulars (Art. 4(4)): Art. 3(2) is categorical—“The benefit of the limitation will be lost only where no ticket is delivered”; Art. 4(4) imposes a sanction if luggage is accepted without a luggage ticket or if it lacks particulars “(d), (f) and (h)”.
BaselineB: Statute: Carriage by Air Act, R.S.C. 1952, c. 45, Schedule I (Warsaw Convention), especially Arts. 3, 4, 22 (and interpretation of those provisions).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Negligent misrepresentation re estimates: plaintiff must prove more than error—must show the estimate was wrong because of a lack of reasonable care (i.e., "lack of skill, competence or diligence" / failure to exercise "such care as the circumstances required").
BaselineA: Common law (negligent misrepresentation duty of care), relying on Hedley Byrne & Co. Ltd. v. Heller & Partners Ltd. (HL) and its "such care as the circumstances require" formulation; also referencing Mutual Life and Citizens’ Assurance Co. Ltd. v. Evatt (PC) on an "ascertainable standard of skill, competence and diligence".
CaseB_TestB: Extra-territoriality (s. 92) for intangible pith-and-substance: after identifying pith and substance and a provincial head of power, if the matter is intangible, locate it by examining "the relationships among the enacting territory, the subject matter of the legislation and the persons made subject to it" to see if the law has a "meaningful connection" to the province and respects other jurisdictions’ sovereignty.
BaselineB: Common law / constitutional doctrine interpreting Constitution Act, 1867, s. 92 (esp. s. 92(13) "Property and Civil Rights in the Province"), building from prior SCC cases including Reference re Upper Churchill Water Rights Reversion Act and Unifund Assurance Co. v. ICBC.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Scope of habeas corpus review of parole detention: on habeas corpus simpliciter the court is confined to the face of the warrants/committal and cannot go behind them with affidavit evidence; certiorari will not lie to review the Parole Board’s administrative acts
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Parole Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. P-2 (esp. ss. 10(1)(e), 16, 18, 20, 23) and Federal Court Act, 1970-71-72 (Can.), c. 1, s. 18; plus common-law limits on habeas corpus/certiorari (Re Shumiatcher; Security Export Co. v. Hetherington; Commonwealth of Puerto Rico v. Hernandez; Ex p. McCaud; Howarth)
JudgeA: Ritchie J. (for Judson, Ritchie, Pigeon and Beetz JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Equitable compensation for Crown breach of fiduciary duty over reserve land: assess the beneficiary’s ‘lost opportunity’ by first determining what the Crown ‘ought to have done as a fiduciary’ (not merely what it could have done legally), then valuing the lost opportunity (here, negotiation of a surrender) to reflect the land’s value to the hydroelectric project; factual causation required but not limited by foreseeability/remoteness; apply equitable presumptions (e.g., most favourable use)
BaselineB: Common law of Crown fiduciary duty and equitable compensation (Guerin; Canson; Osoyoos; Wewaykum; Blueberry River; Williams Lake; etc.), applied in the statutory/treaty context of Indian Act, R.S.C. 1927, c. 98, ss. 48, 50, 51 and Treaty No. 3 (1873)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Sales tax exemption test for machinery/apparatus: whether the apparatus is used by a manufacturer/producer "directly in ... the manufacture or production of goods" (and not merely in distribution); gas pressure regulators that "merely cause the gas to pass ... from the higher pressure pipes to lower pressure pipes" are not used in "production" within the usual meaning.
BaselineA: Statute: Excise Tax Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-13, s. 29(1) and Schedule III, Part XIII, para. 1(a)(i) (exemption for machinery/apparatus used directly in the manufacture or production of goods), interpreted in light of Hydro-Québec v. Dep. Min. of Nat. Revenue for Customs and Excise, [1970] S.C.R. 30.
CaseB_TestB: Appellate review test for scope of a solicitor’s retainer (and resulting duty): the "crucial question" is the "nature and scope" of the retainer, a "purely a factual question" whose findings "should not ordinarily be upset on appeal save for error arising from misapprehension of the evidence"; absent such error, no duty is imposed beyond the limited retainer found.
BaselineB: Common law appellate standard of review for factual findings (including inferences) and common law principles of solicitor-client retainer/duty; articulated as: findings on scope of retainer are factual and not to be disturbed absent misapprehension of evidence.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Whether an invention relates to a substance “prepared or produced by chemical processes” under Patent Act s. 41(1): apply the “popular” (ordinary) meaning to the process as a whole (informed layman), recognizing that (i) chemical reaction is neither necessary nor sufficient, and (ii) it is enough if chemical operations play a significant/essential part in producing the substance
BaselineA: Statute (Patent Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. P-4, s. 41(1)), as interpreted in Continental Soya Co. Ltd. v. J.R. Short Milling Co. (Canada) Ltd., [1942] S.C.R. 187 and Laboratoire Pentagone Ltée v. Parke, Davis & Co., [1968] S.C.R. 307
CaseB_TestB: Adequacy of an indictment (including in conspiracy/multiple-conspiracies situations): an indictment is adequate if it gives the accused “reasonable information” to identify the transaction and prepare a defence; and a specific conspiracy lies within the indictment if it included some accused, occurred at some time within the alleged time span, and had as its object the type of crime alleged
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 510, 512, 516) plus common-law guidance from SCC cases including R. v. Côté, [1978] 1 S.C.R. 8; R. v. Wis Development Corp., [1984] 1 S.C.R. 485; R. v. Cotroni, [1979] 2 S.C.R. 256; R. v. B. (G.), [1990] 2 S.C.R. 30
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 1 justification (Oakes proportionality) applied contextually: pressing and substantial objective + proportionality (rational connection, minimal impairment, overall proportionality), with emphasis that the state must show a total ban is necessary where it is a complete ban on expression
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 1 ("reasonable limits ... demonstrably justified") as interpreted through the Oakes framework (R. v. Oakes) and related SCC s. 1 jurisprudence
CaseB_TestB: Duty to accommodate/undue hardship in the presence of a collectively bargained automatic-termination clause: the negotiated period is a relevant factor but not determinative; accommodation remains individualized; undue hardship from absence assessed globally from the start of the absence
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: Quebec Charter of human rights and freedoms (ss. 10, 20) and the common-law/Charter human-rights duty-to-accommodate framework from Meiorin (BCGSEU) and related cases (e.g., Bergevin, Renaud, O'Malley)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Indian Act s. 88 provincial-law applicability/paramountcy inquiry: provincial law of general application applies to Indians (via s. 88) except where it is (i) inconsistent with the Indian Act (or instruments under it) or (ii) makes provision for a matter for which provision is made by or under the Indian Act; applied here by asking whether Adoption Act s. 10(2) (“for all purposes” severing natural-parent relationship) removes an adopted child’s entitlement to be registered under Indian Act s. 11(1)(d) (held: it does not, so no inconsistency on registrability).
BaselineA: Statute (Indian Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-6, s. 88 and s. 11; Adoption Act, R.S.B.C. 1960, c. 4, s. 10)
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 24(2) Collins framework (as organized in Greffe): whether admitting evidence “would bring the administration of justice into disrepute” assessed by balancing three categories—(1) fairness of the trial, (2) seriousness of the Charter breach (police conduct, incl. good/bad faith; here emphasizing need for proven “reasonable and probable grounds” and that a “mere conclusory statement” from an informer is insufficient), and (3) the effect of exclusion on the repute of justice (including long-term consequences).
BaselineB: Statute/constitutional text (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 24(2)) plus common-law/precedential framework from R. v. Collins (as applied/structured here)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Test for effective termination (“determination”) of a continuing guarantee by “notice in writing”: notice need not use set words, but must be explicit and unequivocal so the creditor is left in no doubt; an equivocal expression of “wish” or “preference” is insufficient.
BaselineA: Contract (guarantee instrument), clause (4): liability may be determined “by notice in writing delivered to the Manager of the branch or agency of the Bank receiving this instrument”.
CaseB_TestB: Admissibility/handling of evidence of an accused’s post-caution silence: unless the Crown establishes “a real relevance and a proper basis” for admission, questions about the accused’s silence and the ensuing silence should not be admitted; if such evidence is before the jury, the judge must instruct the jury to ignore it (no adverse inference), and failure to do so may require a new trial (curative proviso not available where Crown cannot show verdict necessarily same).
BaselineB: Common law right to silence (as discussed via Rothman; Symonds/Robertson) and Criminal Code curative proviso s. 613(1)(b)(iii) (now s. 686(1)(b)(iii)); Charter s. 7 recognized as protecting the right to silence.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Validity/regularity of an interim Labour Relations Board “cease and desist” order under Trade Union Act, s. 49(2): Board may issue ex parte interim order “notwithstanding any provision of this Act” if “satisfied after investigation” of complaint that s. 48 breached; investigation may be done through Board officers; interim order need not be limited to relief requested so long as related to the illegal work stoppage.
BaselineA: Statute (Trade Union Act, 1972 (N.S.), c. 19, ss. 48, 49(2), 15(9)-(10); plus constitutional constraint discussion under British North America Act, 1867, s. 96).
CaseB_TestB: YCJA youth-sentencing interpretation: (1) General (and specific) deterrence is not a sentencing principle under the YCJA because s. 50(1) excludes Criminal Code s. 718(b) and deterrence cannot be implied from YCJA ss. 3 and 38; (2) YCJA s. 42(2)(o) does not require a 2/3 custody and 1/3 supervision split—unlike s. 42(2)(n), s. 42(2)(o) imposes no fixed custody/supervision ratio.
BaselineB: Statute (Youth Criminal Justice Act, S.C. 2002, c. 1, ss. 3, 38, 42(2)(n), 42(2)(o), 50(1); contrasted with Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 718(b)).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Cities and Towns Act s. 622(4) excuse for failure to give municipal notice: if the victim proves they were prevented from giving notice within 15 days for a reason “deemed sufficient by the court or judge”, then the failure is excused and (once the 15 days have been exceeded) the victim is permanently released from any obligation to give notice and may sue without further notice.
BaselineA: Statute: Cities and Towns Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 193, s. 622(1), (3), (4), (5) (especially s. 622(4) and the prescription start-points in s. 622(5)).
CaseB_TestB: Judicial review standard for a consensual labour arbitrator’s construction of a collective agreement on a grievance: courts must ask whether the arbitrator’s conclusion is a “patently unreasonable” interpretation / whether it is one “which the agreement would reasonably bear”, rather than whether the court would interpret the agreement differently.
BaselineB: Common law (judicial review of consensual arbitration awards), drawing on SCC labour-arbitration review cases cited in the reasons (notably Bell Canada v. Office and Professional Employees' Union, [1974] S.C.R. 335; and CUPE v. New Brunswick Liquor Corp., [1979] 2 S.C.R. 227 for the “patently unreasonable” criterion).
JudgeB: Pigeon J. (reasons concurred in by Martland, Ritchie, Beetz and Pratte JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Admissibility of similar-fact evidence: other misconduct is inadmissible to show propensity, but is admissible if it is relevant to a live issue (e.g., whether the act was “designed or accidental” or “to rebut a defence which would otherwise be open”), and is admitted “not to prove commission of the crime mentioned in the indictment but to establish guilty intent”.
BaselineA: Common law evidence rule on similar-fact evidence (general exclusionary rule and its exception), as stated in Makin v. Attorney-General for New South Wales and discussed with Thompson v. The King, Noor Mohamed v. The King, and R. v. Wray.
CaseB_TestB: Municipal valuation where usual methods cannot be applied: “Where special circumstances make it impossible to fix the realizable value of property by the usual methods, whatever method is appropriate in the circumstances may be used to estimate the property at its actual value.”
BaselineB: Statutory municipal valuation requirement of “actual value” under the Charter of the City of Montreal (S.Q. 1959-60, c. 102), informed by prior SCC/PC valuation jurisprudence (e.g., Sun Life Assurance Co. of Canada v. City of Montreal).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Admissibility of similar fact evidence: other misconduct is inadmissible to show disposition, but admissible if relevant to an issue such as whether the act was “designed or accidental” or to rebut a defence; in criminal negligence, Crown may use similar “passes” to show mens rea (wanton or reckless disregard) where relevant
BaselineA: Common law evidence rule on similar fact evidence (general exclusionary rule and its exception), drawn from Makin v. Attorney General for New South Wales and refined through Thompson v. The King, Noor Mohamed v. The King, and SCC’s R. v. Wray
CaseB_TestB: Issue estoppel on a perjury prosecution after an acquittal: Crown is estopped from re-litigating an issue necessarily decided in the accused’s favour unless it tenders evidence that was not “available by the exercise of reasonable diligence” at the first trial
BaselineB: Common law doctrine of issue estoppel/res judicata and fraud exception (e.g., Duchess of Kingston’s Case; Gushue v. The Queen; DPP v. Humphrys) as applied in criminal proceedings
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory interpretation of technical terms: apply the common/primary meaning in both official languages; select the shared concept (here, “derivative” = a thing actually obtained from another)
BaselineA: Regulation/statutory interpretation: Order in Council SOR/69-8, Schedule A (tariff item 92944-1: “Tetracycline and its derivatives”); Official Languages Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. O-2, s. 8(2)(b). Interpreting approach supported by SCC cases cited: Continental Soya; Laboratoire Pentagone; Burton Parsons.
CaseB_TestB: Limits of inherent/implied jurisdiction re amici: courts may appoint amici only exceptionally when essential, but absent statutory/constitutional authority they cannot fix amici compensation rates or order payment at a particular rate
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine: inherent jurisdiction of superior courts and implied powers of statutory courts, constrained by separation of powers and provincial responsibility for administration of justice (Constitution Act, 1867, ss. 92(14), 96).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Bankruptcy trustee’s duty to insure (and notify secured creditor) under Bankruptcy Act s. 9; failure can ground personal liability and is not protected by s. 171 leave requirement for “action taken”
BaselineA: Statute: Bankruptcy Act, R.S.C. 1952, c. 14, ss. 9(1)-(2), 171; definitions in s. 2 (“property”, “secured creditor”)
CaseB_TestB: Charitable status under ITA via common law Pemsel/Vancouver Society (4th head): purposes must be (a) of public benefit and (b) beneficial “in a way the law regards as charitable”, assessed by analogy to prior cases; sport is charitable only if ancillary to a recognized charitable purpose
BaselineB: Combination: Statute (Income Tax Act, ss. 149.1(1), 248(1)) relying on common law charity definition (Pemsel; Vancouver Society; D’Aguiar framework for 4th head)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Eligibility for a Quebec seat under Supreme Court Act s. 6: appointee must be a current member of the Quebec bar or a current judge of the Quebec Court of Appeal/Superior Court (in addition to meeting s. 5’s 10-year requirement). The Court holds s. 6 requires current membership because three judges must be appointed “from among” those institutions, which “impliedly excludes former members of those institutions and imposes a requirement of current membership” (paras. 4, 42, 45, 70).
BaselineA: Statute (Supreme Court Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. S-26, ss. 5 and 6; also constitutional constraints discussed under Constitution Act, 1982, Part V, s. 41(d) re composition).
JudgeA: The Chief Justice and LeBel, Abella, Cromwell, Karakatsanis and Wagner JJ.
CaseB_TestB: Section 15(1) Charter equality test (as applied to Pay Equity Act s. 38): (1) does the law, on its face or in its impact, draw a distinction based on an enumerated/analogous ground; and (2) does it impose burdens/deny a benefit in a way that “reinforc[es], perpetuat[es] or exacerbat[es] . . . disadvantage” (Abella J., para. 22; see also Côté J., paras. 117, 134-135).
BaselineB: Common law / constitutional doctrine (Charter s. 15(1) framework from Quebec (Attorney General) v. A and Taypotat, as quoted at para. 22; applied to Pay Equity Act, CQLR, c. E-12.001, s. 38).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Highway Victims Indemnity Fund must satisfy a final judgment upon timely application: claimant must (1) be a creditor under a final judgment within s. 36, (2) apply within one year (s. 36), and (3) file a sworn declaration under s. 37 establishing the judgment is unsatisfied and that “no insurer will benefit” (s. 37(b)), which is met because s. 39 transfers “all the creditor’s rights without restriction”; the Fund then “has no choice” and “shall satisfy the judgment” within 7 days (s. 38) without requiring prior proceedings against the insurer.
BaselineA: Statute (Highway Victims Indemnity Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 232, ss. 36-39) plus Civil Code prescription provisions (arts. 2262, 2265) for limitation characterization
CaseB_TestB: Assessment of damages under The Fatal Accidents Act: determine the dependants’ annual “disposable income” (including deducting income tax), then calculate the present value of a lump sum that, if invested, would replace that annual support over the relevant period, using a discount rate based on “present rates of return on long-term investments with an allowance for the effects of future inflation,” and then make “some reduction for contingencies”; overall question is whether the final award is “fair and adequate.”
BaselineB: Statute (The Fatal Accidents Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 164) as interpreted through common-law damages methodology (present value/discounting/contingencies) discussed in the reasons
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Equitable interest for improper withholding of a just debt: where payment of a just debt has been improperly withheld and it is fair and equitable to compensate, the court should award interest for such time and at such rate as it thinks right (here: contractor’s bank borrowing rate).
BaselineA: Common law/equitable principle from Toronto Railway Co. v. City of Toronto, [1906] A.C. 117 (applied via The Queen’s Bench Act, R.S.S. 1965, c. 73, s. 46; and with discussion of Interest Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-18, ss. 3, 12, 13; plus authority to set interest in SCC judgment under Supreme Court Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. S-19, s. 52).
CaseB_TestB: Dixon two-step post-conviction non-disclosure test (s. 7 / s. 24(1)): (1) is there a reasonable possibility the undisclosed information affects the reliability of the conviction? If yes, new trial. (2) if not, is there a reasonable possibility non-disclosure affected overall trial fairness (lost lines of inquiry/opportunities)? Due diligence of defence counsel is a significant factor in stage (2).
BaselineB: Common law/Charter doctrine from R. v. Stinchcombe, [1991] 3 S.C.R. 326 (disclosure relevance threshold) and related SCC cases (Egger; Chaplin; Carosella), applying Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 7 and 24(1).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Doctrine/rule of recent possession: once the Crown proves (1) the goods were recently stolen and (2) the accused possessed them, the jury may (not must) infer guilt; if an explanation is given that "may reasonably be true", it must be considered and can raise a reasonable doubt; the Crown need not adduce evidence of absence of explanation
BaselineA: Common law rule of evidence (recent possession) as stated in R. v. Schama; R. v. Abramovitch (quoted/approved) and applied in SCC cases including R. v. Graham, [1974] S.C.R. 206
CaseB_TestB: Imperial Tobacco extraterritoriality framework (as applied to ORA s. 11): (1) identify pith and substance by purpose and effects; (2) assess territorial limits by asking whether the law has a "meaningful connection" to the province and respects other governments’ sovereignty
BaselineB: Common law constitutional framework from British Columbia v. Imperial Tobacco Canada Ltd., 2005 SCC 49 (applied to a statutory provision: Opioid Damages and Health Care Costs Recovery Act, S.B.C. 2018, c. 35, s. 11, in light of Constitution Act, 1867, s. 92(13), (14))
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Drunkenness and mens rea for murder: intoxication is relevant only if it renders the accused “incapable of forming the specific intent”; evidence “falling short of incapacity” (mere increased violence/impulsivity) is legally insufficient, and the jury considers drunkenness only after rejecting insanity on a balance of probabilities (as charged).
BaselineA: Combination: Criminal Code s. 212(a) (murder intent) plus common law intoxication principles as in Director of Public Prosecutions v. Beard (adopted in the charge).
CaseB_TestB: Rebutting the s. 258(1)(d.1) BAC presumption with “straddle evidence”: such evidence is admissible and, per Gibson (LeBel J.), “may be capable of raising a reasonable doubt” about whether BAC exceeded 80 mg at the time of driving, assessed in light of all the evidence.
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, s. 258(1)(d.1) (statutory presumption) as interpreted through R. v. Gibson, 2008 SCC 16.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Drunkenness negating mens rea for murder: whether intoxication rendered the accused incapable of forming the specific intent to kill (or to cause bodily harm known likely to cause death), and what evidence must be put to the jury on that issue
BaselineA: Combination: statute (Criminal Code, s. 212(a) (as referenced in the reasons)) plus common law intoxication doctrine (DPP v. Beard, [1920] A.C. 479 (H.L.), as adopted in the jury charge)
JudgeA: Martland J. (for Martland, Judson, Ritchie, Pigeon, Beetz and de Grandpré JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Section 23 “numbers warrant” sliding-scale placement: three-step approach (long-term numbers; comparative pedagogy/cost with rebuttable presumption; then determine level of services)
BaselineB: Combination: constitutional text (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 23) plus prior SCC framework (Mahe v. Alberta, [1990] 1 S.C.R. 342 (sliding scale; pedagogy and cost factors))
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Labour Code s. 108(1)(b) review: whether the arbitrator committed an "error of law affecting [his] jurisdiction" (i.e., failed to answer the question submitted by not addressing the real circumstances).
BaselineA: Statute: Labour Code of British Columbia Act, 1973 (B.C.) (2d Sess.), c. 122, s. 108(1)(b) (limited appellate intervention only for "an error of law affecting the jurisdiction of the arbitration board").
CaseB_TestB: Garofoli leave (threshold) test for cross-examining a wiretap affiant: defence must show a "reasonable likelihood" that cross-examination will elicit "testimony of probative value" on a material issue for the reviewing judge (relevance/materiality; likely to undermine a statutory precondition/basis for authorization).
BaselineB: Common law (Charter s. 8 admissibility review procedure) from R. v. Garofoli, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 1421; applied in the context of Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 184.2 (consent wiretap authorization).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Income Tax Act s. 83(3) “arrangement with the prospector” / “employer of the prospector” requirement for excluding consideration (mining property interest or shares) from income: whether the taxpayer advanced/paid prospecting expenses under a qualifying pre‑work arrangement with the prospector or as the prospector’s employer
BaselineA: Statute: Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1952, c. 148, s. 83(3) (as amended by 1965 (Can.), c. 18, s. 19); also engages s. 83(1)(c) definition of “prospector” as argued
JudgeA: de Grandpré J. (for Laskin C.J. and Judson, Beetz and de Grandpré JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: “Integral element” test for whether Parliament (under s. 92(10) railways) can constitutionally apply a federal provision to displace provincial law: federal jurisdiction over an ancillary matter exists only if it is an “integral part” of the core federal competence; otherwise provincial law of general application applies
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine (division of powers) applying the “integral element” approach from Construction Montcalm Inc. v. Minimum Wage Commission, [1979] 1 S.C.R. 754 (and affirmed in Northern Telecom Ltd. v. Communications Workers of Canada, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 115), in the context of Constitution Act, 1867 ss. 91(29) and 92(10); applied to Railway Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. R-2, s. 342(1)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory condition 10(a) / art. 2571 C.C. validity test for fire insurance where insured is not the civil-law owner: the policy is not invalid for failure to state the insured’s interest so long as the insured has an insurable interest (i.e., “All that is necessary to satisfy statutory condition 10(a) of the policy is that the insured have an insurable interest.”).
BaselineA: Statute and civil law: Insurance Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 295, s. 240 (statutory conditions, incl. 10(a)); Civil Code art. 2571 (and related arts. 2480, 2572). Also relies on prior SCC interpretation of analogous statutory condition (Wandlyn Motels v. Commerce General Insurance Company).
CaseB_TestB: Section 8 ‘piggyback’ rule for bodily samples seized by a coroner: when a bodily sample is seized by a non-police state actor but is ultimately used in a criminal prosecution, the court must assess whether police conduct constitutes an independent state seizure or renders the initial seizure unreasonable; once evidence is appropriated for criminal law enforcement, the seizure becomes unreasonable absent Hunter-style prior judicial authorization (i.e., police cannot “piggy back” the coroner’s investigation).
BaselineB: Common law Charter framework under s. 8 (Hunter v. Southam; R. v. Dyment) applied in the statutory context of Coroners Act, R.S.O. 1980, c. 93, s. 16(2), (5).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Judicial review of refusal of adjournment affecting right to counsel: an adjournment needed to exercise the s. 577(3) right may be refused only for a reason based on established facts; discretionary refusal is reviewable if based on reasons not well founded in law (especially where it deprives the accused of rights).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 577(3) (right to make full defence personally or by counsel) and appellate review context under s. 613), applied with reference to prior cases including Spataro v. Regina, [1974] S.C.R. 253 and Talbot v. Regina, [1965] Que. Q.B. 159.
JudgeA: Pigeon J. (for Laskin C.J. and Judson, Spence, Pigeon, Dickson and Beetz JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Equitable compensation for breach of fiduciary duty (non-trust): assess plaintiff’s actual loss with hindsight; foreseeability not required; but recovery limited to losses which, on a “common sense view of causation”, were caused by the breach (no recovery for unrelated third-party losses absent a direct link).
BaselineB: Common law/equity (fiduciary duty and equitable compensation), drawing on authorities including Nocton v. Lord Ashburton, [1914] A.C. 932 and Guerin v. The Queen, [1984] 2 S.C.R. 335.
JudgeB: McLachlin J. (for Lamer C.J. and L'Heureux-Dubé and McLachlin JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Quebec court jurisdiction in a personal action challenged by declinatory exception: jurisdiction lies in the court of the defendant’s domicile, or failing that, residence (art. 68 C.C.P.), assessed on the record as a whole; a bare affidavit denying Quebec residence is insufficient to negate jurisdiction
BaselineA: Statute (Quebec Code of Civil Procedure, art. 68; also discussed: art. 70; plus evidentiary presumption from Canadian Citizenship Act, s. 10)
CaseB_TestB: When (and how) state/police misconduct can reduce a criminal sentence: misconduct may be treated as a mitigating factor in the ordinary Criminal Code sentencing process if it relates to the circumstances of the offence or the offender; sentence must remain within statutory parameters (including mandatory minimums), with only a not-foreclosed possibility of exceptional s. 24(1) relief outside statutory limits for particularly egregious misconduct
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, ss. 718–718.2 and statutory minimums; Charter, s. 24(1) discussed as remedial backstop)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Contractual interpretation of warranty: construe “depreciation” in para. 3(g) and the auditor’s letter as an accounting concept (write-off over useful life), not “full capital cost allowance”; parenthetical “(using capital cost allowance rates)” refers to rates only, not the CCA system, and “at least” must be given effect
BaselineA: Common law (contract interpretation of a share sale agreement warranty clause, read with incorporated auditor’s letter)
CaseB_TestB: Youth court jurisdiction under Young Offenders Act: s. 19(2) does not authorize dismissing a charge merely because it “ought never to have been laid”; absent “irresistible clearness” from Parliament, courts must respect prosecutorial discretion (subject only to exceptional abuse-of-process stays in the “clearest of cases”)
BaselineB: Statute (Young Offenders Act, R.S.C., 1985, c. Y-1, ss. 3(1), 19(2) (and related ss. 19(1), 20(1)(a), 51)) plus common-law principles of prosecutorial discretion/abuse of process (e.g., Smythe; Jewitt; Keyowski; Conway, as cited)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Crown appeal from acquittal: after establishing an error of law, the Crown must satisfy the court that the verdict "would not necessarily have been the same if the trial judge had properly directed the jury" (White v. R. test as applied in Vézeau).
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 613(4) (appeal from acquittal) plus the common-law appellate test from White v. R., [1947] S.C.R. 268 (also applied in R. v. Gauthier, [1977] 1 S.C.R. 441).
CaseB_TestB: Group defamation in a class action (Quebec): plaintiff must prove personal injury to each member by showing that "an ordinary person would have believed that each of them personally sustained damage to his or her reputation"; assessed contextually using a non-exhaustive set of factors (size/nature of group, identifiability, precision of allegations, plausibility, etc.).
BaselineB: Statute/civil code framework: Civil Code of Québec, art. 1457 (fault, injury, causal connection) and the objective "ordinary person" injury standard from Prud’homme v. Prud’homme, 2002 SCC 85 and Néron, 2004 SCC 53; applied in the class action context with Code of Civil Procedure provisions (e.g., arts. 1002-1003, 1028, 1034, 1051).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of the standard auto policy exclusion for a person “who is entitled to receive the benefits of any workmen’s compensation law or plan”: entitlement exists on the admitted facts giving rise to workers’ compensation coverage and is “not dependent upon a formal application for workmen’s compensation having been made and approved”; therefore the exclusion applies even if no claim/award was sought.
BaselineA: Statute (mandatory standard-form auto policy exclusion): Insurance Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 224, s. 232(1) and Schedule E, Exclusion 2(a)(ii) (“who is entitled to receive the benefits of any workmen’s compensation law or plan”), interpreted in light of the Workmen’s Compensation Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 505 (notably ss. 3 and 8).
CaseB_TestB: Section 8 reasonableness framework (applied mutatis mutandis to cross-border wiretap disclosures under Criminal Code s. 193(2)(e)): (1) disclosure must be authorized by law (compliance with s. 193(2)(e)’s two requirements: recipient is a foreign investigative/prosecutorial authority and disclosure is “intended to be in the interests of the administration of justice in Canada or elsewhere”); (2) the authorizing law must be reasonable (not overbroad, not vague—“administration of justice” meaning a “legitimate law enforcement purpose”—and adequate accountability in the overall Part VI scheme); and (3) the disclosure must be carried out in a reasonable manner (including, in risky contexts, considering protocols/caveats; in extreme cases s. 8 may forbid disclosure).
BaselineB: Combination of common law Charter framework and statute: Charter s. 8 reasonableness test from R. v. Collins / R. v. Caslake applied to statutory disclosure under Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 193(2)(e).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Discretion to order service ex juris under Federal Court Rule 307 guided by forum conveniens: the “overriding consideration” is whether there exists “some other forum more convenient and appropriate for the pursuit of the action and for securing the ends of justice”; refusal is an error in principle if based solely on “no relation or connection with Canada” without assessing a more appropriate forum.
BaselineA: Statute and regulation: Federal Court Act, R.S.C. 1970 (2nd Supp.), c. 10, ss. 22(2)(a), 43(1), 44; Federal Court Rules, Rule 307 (service ex juris).
JudgeA: Ritchie J. (for Ritchie, Pigeon, Beetz and de Grandpré JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Quebec medical civil liability causation (rejecting “loss of chance” as a substitute for causation where death/sickness has occurred): causation “must be established on the balance of probabilities, taking into account all the evidence: factual, statistical and that which the judge is entitled to presume”; in some cases a judge may presume causation where a fault presents “clear danger” and the danger materializes, “unless there is a demonstration or a strong indication to the contrary”; if not satisfied the fault caused “any real damage”, recovery is denied.
BaselineB: Civil law (Civil Code of Lower Canada) principles of civil responsibility (fault, causation, damage), with reference to C.C.L.C., art. 1205 (presumptions).
JudgeB: Gonthier J. (for Lamer C.J. and L'Heureux-Dubé, Sopinka, Gonthier, Cory and McLachlin JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Breach of municipal development agreement sewer-servicing obligation: developer must prove a specific failure to provide sewers/enlargements “required to properly service” the redevelopment stage (i.e., evidence of existing or foreseeable inadequacy); a general city-wide sewer master plan/charge is not enough without evidence connecting it to serviceability of the project sewers
BaselineA: Common law (contract interpretation/application of the parties’ 1966 development agreement, especially s. 31(a)(iii))
CaseB_TestB: Presumption of advancement in husband-to-wife gratuitous transfer: presumption applies and is rebuttable, but is not rebutted merely by the husband asserting he transferred “only … to defeat his creditors”; also, statutory abolition of the presumption (Family Law Reform Act, 1975, s. 1(3)(d)) does not apply retrospectively absent express terms or necessary implication
BaselineB: Common law (presumption of advancement / resulting trust principles; SCC cites Goodfriend v. Goodfriend) plus statute (Family Law Reform Act, 1975 (Ont.), s. 1(3)(d) considered for temporal application)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 613(1)(b)(iii) curative proviso: uphold conviction despite trial error if the Crown satisfies the appellate court that a properly charged jury "could not, as reasonable men, have done otherwise than find the appellant guilty" (no "substantial wrong or miscarriage of justice")
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, s. 613(1)(b)(iii)) as applied through SCC precedent (Colpitts v. R. adopting Brooks v. The King formulation)
CaseB_TestB: Treaty right to fish and trade for "necessaries" ("moderate livelihood") under the Mi’kmaq Treaties of 1760-61, with regulatory limits only if justified under the Badger/Sparrow framework; treaty interpretation permits extrinsic evidence absent facial ambiguity
BaselineB: Constitutional/treaty framework (Mi’kmaq Treaties of 1760-61; Constitution Act, 1982 s. 35(1)) plus existing SCC doctrine on treaty interpretation and justification (e.g., Badger; Sparrow; Sioui; Sundown; Guerin; Adams)
JudgeB: Binnie J. (for Lamer C.J. and L’Heureux-Dubé, Cory, Iacobucci and Binnie JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Hague Protocol ‘notice’ requirement for carrier to invoke liability limitation: the passenger ticket/baggage check must include a ‘notice’ (not merely a ‘statement’) that is “in a form calculated to attract attention”; if the ticket “does not include the notice required” the carrier “shall not be entitled to avail himself of the provisions of Article 22” (liability limits). Four-and-a-half point type at the foot of the ticket, even if readable, is “not … noticeable” and therefore not a ‘notice’.
BaselineA: Statute (Carriage by Air Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-14 incorporating the Warsaw Convention as amended by the Hague Protocol): Hague Protocol Arts. 3(1)(c), 3(2), 4(1)(c), and Art. 22 (limitation of liability).
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 11(d) test for statutory presumptions in breathalyzer regime and the (post-severance) rebuttal requirement: a presumption violates s. 11(d) if it can lead to conviction “even though the trier of fact has a reasonable doubt”; under s. 258(1)(c) (after severance), the accused may rebut the presumptions of accuracy/identity only by raising a reasonable doubt that “the instrument was functioning and was operated properly” (i.e., evidence directed to malfunction/improper operation).
BaselineB: Combination of statute and constitutional doctrine: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, ss. 258(1)(c), (d.01), (d.1) (as interpreted and partially severed) assessed under Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 11(d) (and s. 1 justification framework).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Municipal notice-of-accident limitation period runs from discovery (not the accident date) where starting from the accident would make the right of action practically illusory
BaselineA: Statute (An Act to revise and consolidate the Charter of the City of Montreal, 1959-60 (Que.), c. 102, art. 1088; with interpretive context from the Interpretation Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 1, ss. 52 and 61)
CaseB_TestB: Discretionary test for discharging a civil jury after a reference to insurance: discharge only if the reference likely causes real prejudice (a substantial wrong/miscarriage of justice) that cannot be cured by instructions
BaselineB: Common law (overruling Bowhey v. Theakston, [1951] S.C.R. 679, which had required automatic discharge upon a reasonable inference of insurance)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Admissibility of an accused’s prior in-court testimony (judicial statement under oath) without a voir dire: such testimony is admissible as of right even if alleged to have been induced by unlawful compulsion; voluntariness goes to weight for the jury, not admissibility
BaselineA: Common law (distinction between extra-judicial confessions to persons in authority requiring a voluntariness voir dire, and prior judicial testimony under oath). Key baseline authorities cited: R. v. Scott (1856) (compelled prior testimony admissible), and the line of cases following it; also Canada Evidence Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-10, s. 5(2) (protection against subsequent use if claimed at the time).
CaseB_TestB: Appellate intervention for failure to consider relevant evidence: an appellate court must review the record to ensure the trial court directed itself to all evidence bearing on relevant issues; where reasons/record disclose a lack of appreciation or complete disregard of relevant evidence, the reviewing court must intercede (new trial)
BaselineB: Common law / appellate criminal procedure principles (as articulated in prior SCC cases). Key baseline authorities cited: MacDonald v. The Queen, [1977] 2 S.C.R. 665; Ungaro v. R., [1950] S.C.R. 430.
JudgeB: Estey J. (for Martland, Dickson, Beetz, Estey, McIntyre and Lamer JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Admissibility of Crown rebuttal evidence to an alibi/credibility: Crown may contradict an alibi only by attacking its “material points”; and the Crown cannot contradict a collateral fact elicited in cross-examination (no rebuttal on collateral matters).
BaselineA: Common law evidence principles (rebuttal to alibi; collateral fact rule; similar fact limits), with appeal-disposition context under Criminal Code s. 613(1)(b)(iii).
CaseB_TestB: Intoxication and rape via specific/general intent classification: rape is an offence of general (basic) intent, therefore self-induced intoxication is not a defence (subject to the narrow ‘incapable of forming specific intent’ doctrine for specific-intent crimes).
BaselineB: Common law intoxication doctrine and the specific/general intent distinction (R. v. George; DPP v. Beard; DPP v. Majewski), applied in the rape context; appeal context under Criminal Code s. 613(1)(b)(iii).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Applicability of mandatory supervision under Parole Act s. 15(1) to an inmate with a pre‑Aug. 1, 1970 sentence plus a later (post‑Aug. 1, 1970) penitentiary sentence: if s. 15(1) exists at release and no statutory bar applies, and the inmate falls within the proclamation class (sentenced after Aug. 1, 1970), then—because s. 14(1) deems multiple terms to be 'one sentence'—s. 15(1) applies to that single deemed sentence (including the earlier term).
BaselineA: Statute (Parole Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. P-2, ss. 14(1), 15(1)-(2); Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1968-69 (Can.), c. 38, s. 101(2) and proclamation SOR/70-339 bringing s. 11B/now s. 15 into force for persons sentenced on/after Aug. 1, 1970).
CaseB_TestB: Whether accident-insurance death proceeds are taxable as 'property' passing on death under Succession Duties Act s. 26(1): s. 26(1) applies to 'proceeds of insurance policies... due... by reason or on account of the death of the person on whose life the insurance was effected'—this includes accident insurance (the phrase 'sur la tête' / 'on whose life' is not limited to life insurance), and an accidental death is still a death 'by reason or on account of' which proceeds are due.
BaselineB: Statute (Succession Duties Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 70, s. 26(1); also discussed: ss. 45(f), 46(1); interpretive support from Civil Code arts. 1902, 1903, 1905, 1906).
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Estate Tax Act: no “passing” of community property to surviving spouse (and deceased not “competent to dispose”) where marriage contract gives survivor ownership retroactive to marriage
BaselineA: Statute (Estate Tax Act, 1958 (Can.), c. 29, especially ss. 3(1)(a), 3(2)(a), 3(2)(e) and 58(1)(i); applied with SCC precedents Sura v. MNR and Royal Trust v. MNR)
CaseB_TestB: Treaty/NRTA hunting right on private land: “visible, incompatible land use” determines whether land is “occupied”/“taken up” (case-by-case); if prima facie infringement, justify under Sparrow
BaselineB: Combination of constitutional/statutory instruments and common law: Treaty No. 8 and NRTA para. 12 (Constitution Act, 1930, Schedule 2), with justification framework from R. v. Sparrow
JudgeB: Cory J. (majority reasons on key test)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Contractual price-adjustment (tax-escalation) clause applies only where a “tax, duty, charge or fee” is imposed on the seller (Imperial) in respect of the contracted “product” (bunker fuel oil) or its “production, manufacture, sale or delivery” by the seller; it does not cover upstream cost increases (e.g., higher crude oil prices) from taxes borne by affiliates/suppliers
BaselineA: Common law (contract interpretation of the parties’ agreement, especially clause 9)
CaseB_TestB: Van der Peet test for an Aboriginal right under s. 35(1): (1) characterize the exact nature of the claimed activity; (2) determine whether the activity is “an element of a practice, custom or tradition integral to the distinctive culture” of the group—i.e., “a defining feature of the culture in question” prior to contact
BaselineB: Common law / constitutional doctrine applying Constitution Act, 1982, s. 35(1), using the test from R. v. Van der Peet
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Negligence duty/foreseeability limit for occupier/railway: liability only if the injury was a reasonably foreseeable result of the situation created by the defendant (no duty to guard against a child’s unforeseeable attempt to board a moving train from a place of safety)
BaselineA: Common law negligence/occupiers’ liability principles (foreseeability and duty of care), with a rejected/limited statutory fencing angle under Railway Act s. 214
CaseB_TestB: Section 7 fundamental justice (fair hearing) requirements for IRPA security-certificate reasonableness/detention review: a fair judicial process must include (in substance) a hearing, an independent and impartial decision-maker, a decision on facts and law, and the right to know and answer the case; if full disclosure is impossible, a substantial substitute is required
BaselineB: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7 (and related procedural fairness jurisprudence), applied to IRPA ss. 77-85 (esp. ss. 78-84)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory interpretation of Highway Victims Indemnity Act s. 43: Fund must satisfy judgment for unknown-driver accident only up to the s. 14 cap ($35,000) and that liability is not extinguished by payments from other liable parties (no s. 38 deduction where victim received nothing from unknown driver). Key language: Fund satisfies judgment 'to the same extent as if it had been rendered against the author of the accident' (s. 43), which 'inserts ... the idea of a limitation' and ties to s. 14's '$35,000' limit.
BaselineA: Statute: Highway Victims Indemnity Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 232, especially ss. 43 (unknown driver), 14 (financial responsibility cap), 38 (deduction rule in Division XII), and 49(b) ('to the extent prescribed').
CaseB_TestB: Sentencing discretion re collateral immigration consequences and appellate intervention: a judge 'may' consider collateral immigration consequences, but only if the sentence remains 'proportionate to the gravity of the offence and the degree of responsibility of the offender'; consequences are 'but one' factor and 'must not be allowed to ... skew the process'. Appellate court may intervene where sentencing judge was unaware of those consequences or counsel failed to advise (and evidence may be required if not raised below and Crown does not consent).
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: Criminal Code ss. 718, 718.1 (proportionality), 718.2 (parity/individualization) plus sentencing appellate review principles from R. v. M. (C.A.) and proportionality discussion in R. v. Ipeelee (as cited in the reasons).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Whether the trial judge must give the accomplice-evidence caution (danger of convicting on uncorroborated testimony) where a witness could be found to be an accomplice (and the related accomplice vs. accessory-after-the-fact corroboration/caution issue).
BaselineA: Common law (rule of practice on accomplice evidence/corroboration), as discussed via Horsburgh v. The Queen and Davies v. DPP; also engages Criminal Code s. 23 (accessory after the fact) in describing the category.
CaseB_TestB: Interpretation/application of Criminal Code s. 212(c) murder: meaning of 'unlawful object' and how the objective 'knows or ought to know' standard operates (including that the reasonable-person assessment uses the accused’s actual knowledge of surrounding circumstances; intoxication relevant to that knowledge).
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code ss. 205(5)(a) and 212(c), with related ss. 212(a)(i)-(ii)); interpreted in light of prior SCC cases including Graves v. The King and R. v. Hughes.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Construction of Manitoba auto insurance exclusion for death of “an insured”: interpret exclusion (Man. Reg. 333/74, s. 31(3)(h)) as contract-specific—i.e., “an insured” means an insured under the particular certificate/contract under which indemnity is claimed; owner’s and driver’s certificates are “separate contracts” providing “distinct coverages”.
BaselineA: Regulation/statutory scheme: The Manitoba Public Insurance Corporation Act, C.S.M. c. A180 and Manitoba Automobile Insurance Regulation (Man. Reg. 333/74), especially s. 30(a) (definition of “insured”), s. 31(1)-(3) including s. 31(3)(h).
CaseB_TestB: Treaty 8 / NRTA para. 12 “for food” limitation test: determine whether the impugned conduct falls within the protected right to hunt “for food” (i.e., “for sustenance for the individual Indian or the Indian’s family”) or instead is an “act of commerce” (e.g., sale as part of a “multi-stage process”); if it is commerce, provincial Wildlife Act s. 42 applies via Indian Act s. 88.
BaselineB: Constitutional/statutory interpretation: Treaty No. 8 (1899); Natural Resources Transfer Agreement, 1930 (Alberta), para. 12; Indian Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-6, s. 88; Wildlife Act, R.S.A. 1980, c. W-9, ss. 1(s), 42; plus prior SCC interpretations (Frank; Sutherland; Moosehunter).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 287 (pre-1975): “telecommunication”/“telecommunication service” requires transmission “by wire or cable” (not Hertzian waves/radio); no ‘partly wire’ vs ‘entirely wire’ distinction
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 287(1)(b) and definition in s. 287(2) (“telecommunication” means transmission “by wire or cable”)
CaseB_TestB: Immigration Act s. 19(1)(a)(ii) “excessive demands” assessment: must be individualized; assess likely (not merely eligible) demands on social services, considering both medical and non-medical factors including family ability/willingness to pay; threshold is “reasonable probability, not remote possibility” (“more likely than not” that contingencies will materialize)
BaselineB: Statute: Immigration Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. I-2, s. 19(1)(a)(ii) (and noted as substantially similar to IRPA s. 38(1)(c))
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Limits on municipal discretion to refuse a business licence under Municipal Act s. 455: discretion must be exercised “judicially”, not on “extraneous”/“irrelevant or alien” grounds; “in any particular case” means peculiar to the applicant (not a blanket prohibition of a business type), and refusal cannot be used to prohibit a lawful trade/land use absent express statutory power of prohibition.
BaselineA: Statute (Municipal Act, R.S.B.C. 1960, c. 255, s. 455) interpreted in light of municipal-law principles (including Municipal Corporation of the City of Toronto v. Virgo, [1896] A.C. 88, applied; and the principle that discretion must not rest on irrelevant/alien grounds, as reflected in Sunshine Valley Co-operative Society v. City of Grand Forks).
CaseB_TestB: IRPA security-certificate disclosure/fairness standard under Charter s. 7: a named person must receive an “incompressible minimum” of disclosure and is “reasonably informed” only if they have “sufficient disclosure to be able to give meaningful instructions” to public counsel and “meaningful guidance and information” to special advocates; only information that “would” (not merely “could”) be injurious may be withheld, and if non-disclosure prevents being reasonably informed the Minister must withdraw the information/evidence (potentially leading to quashing under IRPA s. 78).
BaselineB: Statute + Charter (Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, S.C. 2001, c. 27, ss. 77(2), 78, 83(1)(c),(d),(e),(i), 85.4(2); interpreted to comply with Charter s. 7 as explained in Charkaoui v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2007 SCC 9).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Appellate deference to trial findings of fact: an appellate court should not disturb a trial judge’s findings where there was “credible evidence before him on which he could reasonably base his conclusion”; it is not the appellate function to “reconsider that evidence … and come to a different conclusion, unless it can be shown that the evidence reasonably could not result in justifying the conclusion of the trial judge.”
BaselineA: Common law (appellate review standard for findings of fact; case cites include Cook v. Lewis, [1951] S.C.R. 830 (distinguished) and the general principle of non-interference with trial fact-finding as stated in the reasons).
CaseB_TestB: Bona fide occupational qualification (BFOQ) under Ontario Human Rights Code s. 4(6): (1) subjective good faith—limitation “must be imposed honestly, in good faith, and in the sincerely held belief” it serves “adequate performance … with … dispatch, safety and economy” and not for “ulterior or extraneous reasons”; and (2) objective necessity—must be “related in an objective sense” and “reasonably necessary to assure the efficient and economical performance of the job without endangering” the employee/others; employer bears burden on a balance of probabilities once prima facie discrimination is shown.
BaselineB: Statute (The Ontario Human Rights Code, R.S.O. 1970, c. 318, ss. 4(1) and 4(6), plus procedural provisions including s. 14d).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal causation for unlawful act manslaughter: Crown must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the unlawful act was “at least a contributing cause of death, outside the de minimis range” (not necessary to prove it was the sole cause; thin-skull applies; foreseeability not required).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code), especially s. 205(1) (“A person commits homicide ... when directly or indirectly, by any means, he causes the death of a human being”), with supporting common-law causation principles (incl. thin-skull) discussed via cases such as R. v. Larkin, R. v. Cato, R. v. Garforth, R. v. Blaue, R. v. Nicholson.
CaseB_TestB: Anns two-stage duty-of-care framework for recognizing a novel duty for pure economic loss (applied to reject a negligence duty in commercial negotiations and in drafting tender specifications): (1) prima facie duty via foreseeability + proximity; (2) residual policy considerations may “negative or limit” the duty.
BaselineB: Common law: Anns v. Merton London Borough Council (two-stage duty-of-care analysis), as adopted in Kamloops (City of) v. Nielsen and applied in later SCC cases (e.g., Hercules Managements; Winnipeg Condominium; Bow Valley).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Crown bound by legislation/regulations only if expressly mentioned or (at common law) by “necessary implication” (i.e., the statute’s purpose would be “wholly frustrated” unless the Crown were bound); SCC holds current Interpretation Act s. 16 requires the Crown be “mentioned or referred to,” excluding necessary implication
BaselineA: Statute (Interpretation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-23, s. 16; s. 28) plus common law doctrine from Bombay Province v. Bombay Municipal Corporation (necessary implication/wholly frustrated purpose)
CaseB_TestB: Breach of contract where a stipulated term (here, cargo weight) is “material if not a critical term”; excessive deviation from the stipulated weight constitutes breach, engaging Civil Code art. 1065 (damages for breach) rather than art. 992 (nullity for error)
BaselineB: Statute (Civil Code, arts. 992 and 1065) applied to contract of carriage
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Scope of CTC inquiry under Lord’s Day Act s. 11(x): Commission must decide only whether, “having regard to the object of this Act” (preventing Sunday gainful work) and “with the object of preventing undue delay”, the Sunday freight work is “necessary to permit”; evidence about local congestion/noise/pollution is irrelevant to that statutory issue.
BaselineA: Statute: Lord’s Day Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. L-13, ss. 4 and 11(x) (interpreting “object of this Act” and the Commission’s mandate under s. 11(x)).
CaseB_TestB: “Bona fide pension plan” under Human Rights Code s. 3(6)(a) (Abella J. for the majority): plan must be “subjectively and objectively bona fide”: “a legitimate plan, adopted in good faith and not for the purpose of defeating protected rights”; inquiry is into the plan’s overall bona fides (registration under pension legislation is a helpful indicator), not actuarial details or piecemeal scrutiny of particular terms.
BaselineB: Statute: New Brunswick Human Rights Code, R.S.N.B. 1973, c. H-11, s. 3(6)(a) (interpreting “bona fide retirement or pension plan”).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: “Undueness” in conspiracy to lessen competition under Combines Investigation Act s. 32(1)(c): Crown must prove (1) intent to enter the agreement and (2) that, if carried into effect, it would “prevent or lessen competition unduly”; “undueness” assessed by the agreement’s prospective effect on competition (not merely that a ‘meaningful segment’ agreed on prices).
BaselineA: Statute: Combines Investigation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-23, s. 32(1)(c), interpreted in light of SCC cases including Howard Smith Paper Mills v. The Queen, Weidman v. Shragge, Stinson-Reeb Builders Supply Co. v. The King, and Container Materials Ltd. v. The King.
JudgeA: Ritchie J. (for Martland, Ritchie, Pigeon, Dickson and Beetz JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Unreasonable verdict test on appeal (Criminal Code s. 686(1)(a)(i)): appellate court asks whether the verdict is one a “properly instructed jury or a judge could reasonably have rendered”; may also find unreasonableness where an essential inference/finding is (1) “plainly contradicted” by the evidence relied on, or (2) “incompatible” with uncontradicted/unrejected evidence; credibility findings are reviewable only if they “cannot be supported on any reasonable view of the evidence”.
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(a)(i), as applied/clarified through SCC precedent (Yebes; Biniaris; Sinclair; Beaudry; Burke).
JudgeB: Deschamps J. (Abella, Cromwell, Moldaver and Karakatsanis JJ. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Limitation of the Hodge’s Case circumstantial-evidence formula: it applies to proving the act/identity, not to proving intent; for intent the jury applies the ordinary reasonable-doubt standard (and, where applicable, it is enough that guilt is the only reasonable inference from proven facts).
BaselineA: Combination: Criminal Code, s. 110(1)(b) (offence element “with respect to those dealings”) plus common-law jury-charge doctrine on circumstantial evidence from R. v. Mitchell, [1964] S.C.R. 471 (and discussion of Hodge’s Case; reaffirmed in John, Bagshaw, Paul).
CaseB_TestB: Interpretation of linked insurance policies: where a fleet policy’s schedule says “See Garage Policy” under third-party liability, that reference should be construed as referring to the garage policy’s limits/premium (not importing its restrictive insuring agreement), so the fleet policy’s own third-party liability coverage (including omnibus clause) applies; interpret clauses to have effect (art. 1014 C.C.) and consider surrounding facts/intent (civil law approach).
BaselineB: Combination: Civil Code of Quebec (arts. 1013, 1014, 1234, 1705, 2480) and statutory context (Highway Victims Indemnity Act, ss. 10, 12; Insurance Act, s. 214) applied to construction of the insurance contracts/policies.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Contractual liability of mandatary/broker: plaintiff must prove fault, damage, and causality; if defendant alleges “impossibility of performance” to avoid the obligation, art. 1203 C.C. places the burden on the defendant to prove impossibility (not mere difficulty)
BaselineA: Statute (Civil Code of Québec): arts. 1701 (mandate), 984 and 1062 (object must be possible), and especially art. 1203 C.C. (“he who alleges facts in avoidance or extinction of the obligation must prove them”); applied within the general civil-liability triad of fault/damage/causality
CaseB_TestB: Municipal disqualification for conflict of interest: under Moncton Consolidation Act s. 6, a mayor/councillor is disqualified if he “directly or indirectly… have any interest in any contract” with the City (other than as a shareholder); “interested in” is given its ordinary meaning and includes a director/officer’s indirect interest in the company’s municipal contracts
BaselineB: Statute: Moncton Consolidation Act, 1946 (N.B.), c. 101, s. 6 (interpreted alongside Municipalities Act, R.S.N.B. 1973, c. M-22, ss. 71-72, and Interpretation Act, R.S.N.B. 1973, c. I-13, s. 17); interpretive guidance drawn from SCC precedent Angrignon (1935) (“interested in” has no technical signification; apply common usage)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Interpretation of para. 12 Alberta Natural Resources Transfer Agreement: “Indians of the Province” (Alberta Indians) vs “Indians within the boundaries” (all Indians physically in Alberta), so non-resident Indians are subject to provincial game laws but retain the proviso right to hunt “for food” on unoccupied Crown lands/lands of access
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional instrument and treaty: Indian Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-6, s. 88 (incorporating provincial laws of general application subject to treaties/other federal law) + Alberta Natural Resources Transfer Agreement, 1930, para. 12 (as confirmed by British North America Act, 1930) + Treaty No. 6
CaseB_TestB: Qualified privilege in libel: a communication is privileged where the maker has an “interest or a duty, legal, social or moral” to make it and the recipient has a corresponding interest/duty; on such an occasion the statement is actionable only on proof of malice, and privilege protects even “violent or excessively strong” language if the maker “might have honestly and on reasonable grounds believed” it true
BaselineB: Common law: definition of qualified privilege from Adam v. Ward, [1917] A.C. 309, and SCC discussion in Netupsky v. Craig, [1973] S.C.R. 55
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code obscenity test: s. 159(8) is the exclusive definition of obscenity for sex-based obscenity across the Code (Hicklin displaced); i.e., a work is obscene if it is a “publication a dominant characteristic of which is the undue exploitation of sex …” and this statutory test governs allied obscenity offences where “the allegation of obscenity revolves around sex considerations”.
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, s. 159(8), applied/interpreted alongside ss. 159(1), 163, 164; with the common law Hicklin test treated as displaced).
CaseB_TestB: Duty to accommodate (employer/union) in adverse-effect discrimination: the discriminator must take “reasonable measures short of undue hardship”; undue hardship assessed contextually (non-exhaustive factors like “financial cost, disruption of a collective agreement, problems of morale of other employees, interchangeability of work force and facilities… [and] safety”), with specific rules on when a union is a party to discrimination and when its duty to accommodate arises.
BaselineB: Statute (Human Rights Act, S.B.C. 1984, c. 22, ss. 8(1)(a),(b),(4) and 9(a)-(c)) as interpreted through SCC human-rights common law (O'Malley; Central Alberta Dairy Pool).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.
