CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code obscenity test: apply s. 159(8) “undue exploitation of sex” standard as the exhaustive definition of “obscene” for Criminal Code offences where the allegation “revolves around sex considerations” (displacing the common law Hicklin test); s. 159(8): “any publication a dominant characteristic of which is the undue exploitation of sex ... shall be deemed to be obscene.”
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, s. 159(8) (and its interaction with ss. 159(1), 163, 164) and the prior common law Hicklin test as discussed in Brodie v. The Queen and R. v. Hicklin).
CaseB_TestB: Duty to accommodate/undue hardship in the presence of a collectively bargained termination-after-absence clause: the negotiated period is “a factor to consider” but “does not definitively determine” accommodation; “each case must be evaluated on the basis of its particular circumstances”; undue hardship from absence must be assessed “globally starting from the beginning of the absence, not from the expiry” of the negotiated period (within the Meiorin framework).
BaselineB: Common law human-rights duty to accommodate/undue hardship under the Meiorin test (BCGSEU) as applied in the labour arbitration context, alongside the Quebec Charter of human rights and freedoms (ss. 10, 20) and the collective agreement clause.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Federal jurisdiction over cable distribution systems: cable TV is a single interprovincial/international “undertaking” so federal power extends beyond signal reception to transmission and program-content regulation (no demarcation at the antenna)
BaselineA: Constitution (B.N.A. Act), ss. 91 and 92(10)(a), interpreted through precedent (Radio Reference; Winner) and applied to the Broadcasting Act scheme
CaseB_TestB: Income tax proceeds of disposition: purchaser’s assumption of reforestation obligations is excluded from vendor’s “sale price” where the obligation is an embedded future cost of the tenure (not a distinct existing liability like a mortgage)
BaselineB: Statute: Income Tax Act, s. 13(21) (“proceeds of disposition” includes “the sale price of property that has been sold”), applied with the general principle that assumed liabilities can form part of sale price
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Civil Code test for whether a structure/network is an “immovable by nature”: a construction is immovable if it “adheres” to land (or to a building/structure that adheres to land) such that the attachment is “not purely transitory and accidental”; for networks, “the vertical attachment of a network of wires to the ground is in itself enough to make these wires immovable”, and separation of ownership of poles/land from wires is irrelevant.
BaselineA: Statute + civil law (Retail Sales Tax Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 71, ss. 2(3), 6, incorporating the Civil Code distinction between movable/immovable: arts. 374 et seq., incl. arts. 375-378/376 as discussed).
CaseB_TestB: Punitive damages in breach of contract (wrongful dismissal): punitive damages are available but “rare”; they require (i) an “actionable wrong” (typically the breach plus conduct that is also tortious) causing the injury, and (ii) “extreme” conduct “deserving of punishment” because of its “harsh, vindictive, reprehensible and malicious nature”; otherwise contract damages remain limited to notice/pay in lieu.
BaselineB: Common law (contract damages principles; authorities discussed include Addis v. Gramophone Co. and Peso Silver Mines Ltd. (N.P.L.) v. Cropper; punitive damages principles discussed with reference to Rookes v. Barnard and Canadian cases such as McElroy v. Cowper-Smith and Woodman and H. L. Weiss Forwarding Ltd. v. Omnus).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Negligence duty/standard of care for a business that attracts very young children into traffic danger: once the vendor/operator creates a relationship of proximity with child patrons, they "must take reasonable care to avoid acts or omissions which you can reasonably foresee would be likely to injure your neighbour" (Donoghue v. Stevenson), and failing to take obvious precautions (e.g., watching for traffic/warning children) is negligent.
BaselineA: Common law negligence duty of care/proximity and foreseeability (Donoghue v. Stevenson).
CaseB_TestB: Contract interpretation/repudiation in fire-damage clause: under clause 5 the purchaser must elect either to "have the proceeds of the insurance and complete the purchase" or "cancel the Agreement"; the clause gives time to assess and obtain insurance details but "does not accord [the purchaser] the right to wait and see if the insurer will pay"; insisting on different conditions is "dictating different terms" and "constituted a repudiation" the vendor may accept.
BaselineB: Common law contract principles of interpretation and repudiation applied to the parties’ agreement (standard-form clause 5 and time-is-of-the-essence clause 9).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Matrimonial property resulting trust from a joint account/common pool: where spouses intend a joint “common purse”, a spouse taking title to an investment bought from that pool holds the other spouse’s beneficial share (typically one-half absent contrary agreement); presumption rebuttable only by evidence of contrary intention
BaselineA: Common law (resulting trust/common intention in matrimonial property; joint account resulting trust principles)
CaseB_TestB: Common law access-to-exhibits balancing: court may curtail public access to filed exhibits where needed to protect superordinate values (especially protecting the “innocent”); court must inquire into proposed use and may regulate use; access may be denied where privacy/prejudice outweighs openness
BaselineB: Common law (open courts/access to judicial records; applied from Attorney General of Nova Scotia v. MacIntyre)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Limitation Act s. 6(4)(b) postponement test: time runs only when a properly advised reasonable person would conclude the plaintiff, in light of their own circumstances and interests, could reasonably bring an action; postponement requires interests/circumstances that are “serious, significant, and compelling” and excludes “purely tactical concerns” (Novak v. Bond, per McLachlin J., para. 39).
BaselineA: Statute (Limitation Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 266, s. 6(4)(b), within the s. 6(4) postponement scheme; also linked to s. 6(4)(a) and “appropriate advice” in s. 6(5)(a)).
CaseB_TestB: Two-part stay framework under Arbitration Act s. 15, with insolvency-based inoperability exception: (1) applicant shows an arguable case for four “technical prerequisites” to a mandatory stay; (2) resisting party proves on a balance of probabilities a s. 15(2) exception (e.g., arbitration agreement “void, inoperative or incapable of being performed”), including that an agreement may be “inoperative” in a receivership where enforcing arbitration would “compromise the orderly and efficient resolution of a receivership”; guided by non-exhaustive factors (effect on integrity of insolvency proceedings, relative prejudice, urgency, insolvency stay, other material factors) (Peace River Hydro Partners v. Petrowest, per Côté J., paras. 76-89, 155).
BaselineB: Statute (Arbitration Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 55, s. 15(1)-(2), interpreted alongside Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. B-3, ss. 183(1) and 243(1)(c)).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: When extinctive prescription begins to run for engineers’ fees under art. 2260(6) C.C.: prescription runs only when the fee is due—i.e., “on completion of the work” or, if suspended/terminated, “at the time it was suspended, after a decision clearly communicated” to the engineers (and, under the engineers’ tariff, generally not before the “call for tenders” stage or notice that there will be no tenders/contract termination).
BaselineA: Combination of statute/civil code and regulation: art. 2260(6) Civil Code (five-year prescription for certain claims) plus the Tariff of fee for Professional Engineers of the Province of Quebec (O.C. 891, Sept. 4, 1957) adopted under s. 4(2) of the Professional Engineers’ Act; also supported by general civil-law principles of bilateral contracts (payment not demandable before performance/delivery absent agreement).
CaseB_TestB: Discretionary test for enforcing foreign letters rogatory under s. 43 Canada Evidence Act: even if jurisdiction exists, the court “may, in its or his discretion” order examination/production, but should refuse enforcement where doing so would run counter to Canadian public policy/sovereignty (and the court should not “take issue with the government’s determination of public policy or to measure its impact”).
BaselineB: Statute plus common-law/comity discretion: Canada Evidence Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-10, s. 43 (discretion to order evidence for foreign proceedings), informed by comity principles and public policy limits (with discussion of related federal instruments like the Uranium Information Security Regulations and Atomic Energy Control Act, s. 9, but the dispositive framework is s. 43 discretion constrained by public policy).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “nude” in Criminal Code s. 170: complete nudity is captured without needing proof it offended public decency/order; s. 170(2) is a deeming (enlarging) provision for being ‘so clad as to offend against public decency or order’
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, s. 170(1)(a) and s. 170(2); interpreted as a deeming provision akin to former s. 205A)
CaseB_TestB: When the Crown improperly ‘splits its case’ by adducing reply evidence that raises new issues/attacks credibility and forces the accused to testify again, the curative proviso in Criminal Code s. 613(1)(b)(iii) (“no substantial wrong or miscarriage of justice”) cannot be applied because an appellate court cannot realistically assess the residual case after extracting the improper evidence
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, s. 613(1)(b)(iii) curative proviso) applied in light of common-law criminal trial fairness principles against splitting the Crown’s case
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 170 nudity offence: “nude” in s. 170(1)(a) means complete bareness; s. 170(2) is a deeming provision that extends nudity to being “so clad as to offend against public decency or order”, and the Crown need not prove offensiveness where there is total nudity
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, s. 170(1)(a) and s. 170(2); interpreted as a deeming provision akin to former s. 205A)
CaseB_TestB: Availability of certiorari in criminal proceedings: for parties, certiorari lies only for a provincial court judge’s “jurisdictional error” (i.e., failure to observe a mandatory statutory provision or breach of natural justice), not for mere errors of law (including disclosure/evidentiary rulings)
BaselineB: Combination (Criminal Code, s. 674 prohibition on interlocutory appeals + common law limits on certiorari/prerogative writs; definition of “jurisdictional error” drawn from SCC jurisprudence such as Skogman and natural justice cases)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Workmen’s Compensation Act s. 8 “additional sum” claim where Commission is subrogated: if the dependant’s civil claim against the third party (reduced for the victim’s contributory fault under Civil Code art. 1056) is fully met or exceeded by compensation, the dependant cannot claim any “additional sum”; the Commission has priority to recover up to what it paid (s. 7(3)).
BaselineA: Statute + Civil Code: Workmen’s Compensation Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 159, ss. 7(3) (subrogation pleno jure) and 8 (right to claim “any additional sum required”); Civil Code art. 1056 (wrongful death claim reduced by victim’s fault) and art. 1157 (partial payment rule for subrogation priority).
CaseB_TestB: Employer’s obligation to pay under a guaranteed-salary employment contract depends on the employee being “available and willing to provide the services”; entering a conflicting contract and playing for another team is a breach that frees the employer from further payment obligations.
BaselineB: Common law contract principles applied to an employment contract (repudiation/anticipatory breach and dependency of payment on readiness to perform), interpreted through the contract’s own terms (notably exclusivity/consent and termination/guarantee clauses).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Workmen’s Compensation Act s. 8 “additional sum” entitlement where Commission is subrogated: if the dependant’s civil claim (after reduction for the victim’s fault) is fully covered by compensation, there is no further “additional sum” claim against the third party; Commission has priority to recover up to the compensation paid (subrogation pleno jure).
BaselineA: Statute + Civil Code (Workmen’s Compensation Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 159, ss. 7(3) (subrogation pleno jure) and 8 (additional sum); Civil Code art. 1157 (partial payment/subrogation priority) and art. 1056 (wrongful death claim), applied with SCC authorities Rainville Automobile Ltd. v. Primiano; Hôpital Notre-Dame de l’Espérance and Théoret v. Laurent; Brink’s Express v. Plaisance distinguished.
CaseB_TestB: Institutional financial security requirement for judicial independence: any government measure affecting judges’ remuneration conditions (including elimination of an office conferring an economic benefit) must be preceded by an independent, effective and objective commission process; if recommendations are ignored, the decision must be justified on a “simple rationality test”.
BaselineB: Constitution + Charter/common law framework (Charter s. 11(d) and Constitution Act, 1867 Preamble; applying Valente v. The Queen and the Provincial Court Judges Reference (Reference re Remuneration of Judges of the Provincial Court of Prince Edward Island)).
JudgeB: Gonthier J. (for L’Heureux-Dubé, Gonthier, Iacobucci, Major and Arbour JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Suspensive effect of serving an originating notice for prohibition/quashing with a Rule 7 command to return the record “forthwith”: service triggers suspension of the inferior court’s power to proceed (and non-return cannot improve the inferior court’s position).
BaselineA: Regulation/rules + statute + common law (Ontario Criminal Rules 4-8; Criminal Code, s. 714; common law certiorari suspension on service)
CaseB_TestB: Section 15(1) equality analysis (La Forest J. majority): (1) distinction; (2) disadvantage; (3) whether the distinction rests on an enumerated/analogous ground and is an “irrelevant personal characteristic” assessed by “relevancy to the functional values underlying the law” in its larger context.
BaselineB: Constitution (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 15(1)) + common law equality jurisprudence (Andrews; Miron v. Trudel framework as adopted/applied)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Fair comment in defamation requires proof that the impugned comment was the honest expression of the real opinion of the writer/publisher; absent evidence of honest belief, the defence cannot go to the jury
BaselineA: Common law (defamation: defence of fair comment), drawing on authorities cited in the reasons including Turner v. Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer Pictures Ltd. and Slim v. Daily Telegraph Ltd.
CaseB_TestB: Section 2(a) infringement threshold for indirect burdens: state action that increases the cost of practising religion infringes only if the burden is not 'trivial or insubstantial' (and then proceeds to s. 1 justification)
BaselineB: Constitution (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 2(a) and s. 1), relying on R. v. Big M Drug Mart Ltd. and referencing R. v. Jones for the 'trivial or insubstantial' threshold
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Fair comment requires proof that the defamatory comment was an honest expression of the real opinion of the writer/publisher; absent evidence of the writers’ honest belief (and with the newspaper’s denial of belief), the defence is unavailable
BaselineA: Common law (defamation—fair comment defence), drawing on authorities including Turner v. Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer Pictures Ltd. and Slim v. Daily Telegraph Ltd. (as discussed in the reasons)
CaseB_TestB: Contempt of court: liability requires personal service or actual personal knowledge of the order (proved beyond a reasonable doubt); service on a solicitor does not, without more, fix ministers with knowledge, and vicarious liability does not apply
BaselineB: Common law contempt principles (knowledge/personal service requirement), with Federal Court Rules (Rules 308, 311, 355) held not to alter contempt’s elements absent explicit language
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Defence of fair comment requires proof that the defamatory comment was an honest expression of the real opinion of the writer/publisher; absent evidence of the writers’ honest belief (and with the newspaper’s denial of belief), the defence is unavailable
BaselineA: Common law (defamation/fair comment), drawing on authorities including Turner v. Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer Pictures Ltd. and Jones v. Skelton (as discussed in the reasons)
CaseB_TestB: Garofoli review of wiretap authorizations: errors in the information to the authorizing judge are factors only (not automatic vitiation); after excising tainted material, ask whether sufficient reliable, independently verifiable information remains to support an authorization
BaselineB: Common law framework from R. v. Garofoli (1990) governing challenges to wiretap authorizations
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Intra vires test for CRTC regulations under Broadcasting Act s. 16: validity is tested by whether the regulation, viewed objectively, is made 'in furtherance of [the Commission’s] objects'—i.e., whether it 'deals with a class of subject referred to in s. 3' (broadcasting policy).
BaselineA: Statute (Broadcasting Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. B-11, ss. 3, 15, 16(1) including 16(1)(b)(i) and 16(1)(b)(ix)) and the impugned subordinate legislation (Radio (A.M.) Broadcasting Regulations, s. 5(1)(k)).
CaseB_TestB: Appellate review of a civil jury verdict on quasi-delict/negligence: the verdict is binding 'unless it is unreasonable'; where fault is assessed by the 'prudent and reasonable man', the jury translates that standard to the case, but the court may set aside the verdict if it is 'unreasonable' (e.g., effectively creates fault/causation where none can exist in law).
BaselineB: Statute/civil law (Civil Code art. 1053; Code of Civil Procedure arts. 363, 380) plus common-law guidance on judge/jury roles and unreasonableness review (Metropolitan Railway Co. v. Jackson (1877), 3 A.C. 193, followed).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Limits on a provincial commission of inquiry’s coercive powers vis-à-vis federal institutions and the federal Crown: a province may inquire into specific criminal acts by RCMP members as part of “administration of justice”, but cannot (directly or indirectly) inquire into RCMP administration/management; and a minister’s s. 41(2) Federal Court Act national-security certificate is binding on a commissioner (not a superior court).
BaselineA: Combination: Constitution (B.N.A. Act, ss. 91/92, esp. s. 92(14) “Administration of Justice in the Province”); Quebec Public Inquiry Commission Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 11, s. 7; Federal Court Act, R.S.C. 1970 (2nd Supp.), c. 10, s. 41(1)-(2); common law Crown prerogative/immunity re compellability/discovery; prior SCC cases Di Iorio v. Warden of the Montreal Jail, [1978] 1 S.C.R. 152 and Faber v. The Queen, [1976] 2 S.C.R. 9.
CaseB_TestB: Contested custody (natural parent vs adoptive parents): under parens patriae/equity preserved by statute, the court must treat the child’s welfare as the “predominant”/“paramount” consideration, decided on “all relevant factors” (including psychological, spiritual and emotional welfare), with parental claims considered but set aside if welfare requires.
BaselineB: Statute plus equity/common law: Domestic Relations Ordinance, R.O.N.W.T. 1974, c. D-9, ss. 28(1), 35(2), 37, and especially s. 39 (equity rules prevail where not conflicting); equitable parens patriae jurisdiction; authorities discussed include Re Moores and Feldstein (1973), Beson v. Director of Child Welfare (Nfld.), [1982] 2 S.C.R. 716, and Racine v. Woods, [1983] 2 S.C.R. 173.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Public Authorities Protection Act s. 11 scope: whether the impugned act/omission is in the execution of a "statutory or other public duty or authority"—i.e., segregate statutory functions into (1) those with a "public aspect or connotation" vs (2) "private executive or private administrative"/"managerial, internal or operational" matters; only the former get s. 11’s six‑month limitation protection.
BaselineA: Statute: The Public Authorities Protection Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 374, s. 11, read with The Housing Development Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 213, s. 6(2) (and interpretive reliance on Bradford Corporation v. Myers; McGonegal v. Gray).
CaseB_TestB: Bazley vicarious liability "significant connection" test: vicarious liability where there is a significant connection between authorized enterprise conduct and the wrong, assessed via factors including (a) opportunity to abuse power; (b) furtherance of employer’s interests; (c) intimacy/conditions conducive to the wrong; (d) power conferred over the victim; (e) victim vulnerability.
BaselineB: Common law: Bazley v. Curry (and Jacobi v. Griffiths) vicarious liability framework (significant connection / enterprise risk factors).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Exemption-from-seizure for insurance proceeds: clause effective only for a “true beneficiary” (a third party), not for a universal legatee/heir; therefore art. 553(3) C.C.P. cannot be invoked
BaselineA: Statute/civil law codal provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, art. 553(3); Civil Code (Quebec), arts. 597, 735, 1028 (and related stipulation-for-third-party-benefit concept)
CaseB_TestB: Art. 976 C.C.Q. no-fault neighbourhood-disturbance liability: liability where neighbours suffer “abnormal or excessive annoyances” beyond the “limit of tolerance” (result-focused, not conduct/fault-focused)
BaselineB: Statute/civil code: Civil Code of Québec, art. 976 (with interaction discussed with arts. 7 and 1457 C.C.Q.)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Superior Court residual jurisdiction not ousted: a provincial superior court may decide a federal statutory issue (here, whether Bell has a legal obligation under s. 5(4) to prescribe “reasonable requirements”) when it arises incidentally in a properly constituted tort/injunction action, unless a “specific provision of law” assigns the matter exclusively elsewhere (art. 31 C.C.P.)
BaselineA: Statute (Quebec Code of Civil Procedure, art. 31; Bell Telephone Company of Canada Act, s. 5(4)-(6), as amended; National Transportation Act, s. 45(1))
CaseB_TestB: Reopening the Crown’s case: the “keystone principle” is prejudice to the accused; discretion narrows by trial stage—(1) before Crown closes: broad latitude; (2) after Crown closes but before defence elects: allowed to correct an “oversight or inadvertent omission” if “justice requires it” and “no prejudice”; (3) after defence has started to answer: reopening only in the “narrowest or most exceptional of circumstances” (e.g., defence contributed to omission or matter of form), because reopening then risks undermining the principle against self-incrimination
BaselineB: Common law discretion on reopening (considering Robillard v. The Queen; Kishen Singh; etc.), informed by Charter self-incrimination principles (ss. 7, 11(c), 13)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Admissibility of cross-examining an accused on juvenile delinquency findings as “convictions” under s. 12 Canada Evidence Act (and related proof by admission): “any offence” includes Criminal Code violations dealt with under the Juvenile Delinquents Act, and a juvenile “finding of delinquency” is “equivalent to a conviction” for s. 12 purposes; an admitted conviction need not be proved by the official record (absent exceptional circumstances showing the admission was made in error).
BaselineA: Statute: Canada Evidence Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-10, s. 12(1)-(2) (and interpretive interaction with Juvenile Delinquents Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. J-3, incl. ss. 2(1), 3, 20(1), 38; also discussed: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 593).
CaseB_TestB: When the Crown has particularized the narcotic in an indictment but the evidence proves a different scheduled form, the charge should be amended under Criminal Code s. 529 if the variance causes no prejudice: the court must consider s. 529(4) factors, especially whether the accused was “misled or prejudiced in his defence”; if no prejudice, amendment may be made (including by the SCC on appeal under s. 613(1)(b)(i) and (3)).
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 529(4)-(5), 613(1)(b)(i), 613(3); Narcotic Control Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. N-1, ss. 2 ("narcotic"), 4(2), schedule item 3.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Dickson J.’s four-factor test for whether an administrative decision/order is “required by law to be made on a judicial or quasi-judicial basis” for Federal Court Act s. 28 review (hearing contemplated; affects rights; adversary process; application of substantive rules to individual cases), with factors “to be weighed and evaluated, no one of which is necessarily determinative”.
BaselineA: Statute (Federal Court Act, s. 28; applied in context of Income Tax Act, s. 231(4)-(5))
CaseB_TestB: Stillman s. 24(2) “trial fairness” framework: classify Charter-breached evidence as non-conscriptive vs conscriptive; if conscriptive, Crown must prove on a balance of probabilities it was discoverable by an independent source or inevitable discovery—if not, evidence is excluded “as a general rule” without weighing other Collins factors.
BaselineB: Statute (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 24(2), building on Collins)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory limits on interim gas-utility rate orders under s. 31: “losses” means “lost revenue” after the rate application, and the key question is whether interim rates will “produce an amount in excess of the estimated total revenue requirements” by including pre-application revenue shortfalls (subject to s. 31’s limited power).
BaselineA: Statute (Alberta): The Gas Utilities Act, R.S.A. 1970, c. 158, ss. 27-28, 31, 35; plus The Administrative Procedures Act, R.S.A. 1970, c. 2, s. 8 (reasons requirement).
CaseB_TestB: Cuerrier fraud-vitiated consent test (s. 265(3)(c)): consent to sex is vitiated by fraud where (1) dishonesty (including non-disclosure) objectively exists and (2) it results in deprivation by exposing the complainant to a “significant risk of serious bodily harm”; Crown must also prove the complainant would have refused unprotected sex if informed of HIV status.
BaselineB: Statute (federal): Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, ss. 265(3)(c), 268; interpreted using criminal fraud principles (e.g., Olan; Théroux) as adapted to assault/consent.
JudgeB: Cory J. (for Cory, Major, Bastarache and Binnie JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory interpretation of Parole Act revocation provisions: after the 1977 amendments, “parole” (s. 2) “includes day parole”, so day parole may be ended either by revocation under s. 10(1)(e) triggering s. 20 consequences, or by termination under s. 10(2); “recommitment” wording in s. 20(1) does not create ambiguity preventing application of s. 20(2) to “any parole”.
BaselineA: Statute: Parole Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. P-2 (as amended effective Oct. 15, 1977), especially ss. 2 (definition of “parole”), 10(1)(e), 10(2), and 20(1)-(3).
CaseB_TestB: Palmer criteria (applied to sentence appeals) for admitting fresh evidence on appeal: (1) generally not admitted if, by due diligence, it could have been adduced at trial; (2) relevant to a decisive or potentially decisive issue; (3) credible; (4) if believed, could reasonably, taken with the other evidence, be expected to have affected the result.
BaselineB: Common law: Palmer v. The Queen, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 759 (fresh evidence test), applied in the statutory context of Criminal Code ss. 683 and 687.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Exercise of SCC discretion under Supreme Court Act s. 52 to vary interest on an SCC judgment (whether to limit interest that would otherwise run from the trial judgment date)
BaselineA: Statute (Supreme Court Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. S-19, s. 52 as amended; Interest Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-18, ss. 13-14; plus Supreme Court Rules, r. 61 procedure)
CaseB_TestB: Whether procedural fairness/natural justice applies to Governor in Council decisions under National Transportation Act s. 64(1): construe the statutory scheme; if s. 64(1) confers complete discretion (subject only to jurisdictional boundaries/conditions precedent), no implied duty of fairness/hearing/reasons
BaselineB: Statute (National Transportation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. N-17, s. 64(1)-(2), interpreted in light of common-law fairness/natural justice jurisprudence such as Nicholson v. Haldimand-Norfolk (cited))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory-limit rule for groundwater pumping: Ontario Water Resources Act s. 37 defines what is “reasonable”; pumping above 10,000 gallons/day without a permit is “unreasonable” and, if it causes damage, “is to be considered as a nuisance” and cannot be defended as an exercise of a right (also supports negligence).
BaselineA: Statute (Ontario Water Resources Commission Act / Ontario Water Resources Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 332, s. 37; also discussed: s. 47 and Expropriations Act definition of injurious affection).
CaseB_TestB: “Unlawful and intentional interference” for exemplary damages under Quebec Charter s. 49(2): intent exists where the actor “has a state of mind that implies a desire or intent to cause the consequences of his or her wrongful conduct, or ... acts with full knowledge of the immediate and natural or at least extremely probable consequences that his or her conduct will cause.”
BaselineB: Statute (Quebec Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms, s. 49(2), interpreted; test applied from Quebec (Public Curator) v. Syndicat national des employés de l’hôpital St-Ferdinand).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Effect of uncompleted vehicle-registration transfer: under Highway Code s. 13(6), the registered owner who has not complied with s. 13(1)-(2) "shall be deemed to be the owner" for liability responsibility and "for purposes of insurance against the responsibility resulting from the ownership or use"; therefore, for liability coverage the transfer is deemed not to have occurred and the buyer/driver with the deemed-owner’s consent is covered by the omnibus clause.
BaselineA: Statute (Highway Code, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 231, s. 13(6) (and compliance duties in s. 13(1)-(2)); applied to the civil-liability section/omnibus clause of the auto policy).
CaseB_TestB: Garofoli leave/threshold test for cross-examining a wiretap affiant: defence must show a "reasonable likelihood" that cross-examination "will elicit testimony of probative value" on the issue for the reviewing judge (i.e., tending to undermine a statutory precondition/basis for the authorization).
BaselineB: Common law (R. v. Garofoli, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 1421), applied in the context of Criminal Code wiretap authorizations (notably s. 184.2) and Charter s. 8 review.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Direct action under Highway Victims Indemnity Act s. 6: insurer is directly liable to third parties only for “damage covered by liability insurance”; s. 6 bars only nullity/lapse defences and “does not extend the insurance contract to what it does not cover” (coverage/excluded-risk analysis turns on the policy’s definition of “automobile” and whether the damage was caused “first and foremost” by use of an uninsured trailer).
BaselineA: Statute (Highway Victims Indemnity Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 232, s. 6) as interpreted in General Security Insurance Company of Canada v. Bélanger, [1977] 1 S.C.R. 802, applied through the insurance contract’s coverage definitions (policy definition of “automobile” for Section A “Civil Liability”).
CaseB_TestB: Landlord covenant-to-insure effect on subrogation against negligent tenant: tenant escapes liability for negligently caused fire only if the landlord’s covenant to insure “runs to the benefit of the tenant”; the covenant is treated as benefiting the tenant “unless the option to purchase provisions ... provide an explanation consistent with the risk of fires being on the tenant.”
BaselineB: Common law lease/insurance allocation principles from Ross Southward Tire Ltd. v. Pyrotech Products Ltd., [1976] 2 S.C.R. 35 and Agnew-Surpass Shoe Stores Ltd. v. Cummer-Yonge Investments Ltd., [1976] 2 S.C.R. 221 (and distinguishing United Motors Service Inc. v. Hutson, [1937] S.C.R. 294).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Qualified privilege in defamation defeated only by malice; privilege still protects even “violent or excessively strong” language if the defendant “might have honestly and on reasonable grounds believed that what he wrote or said was true” (Adam v. Ward as applied; Netupsky v. Craig).
BaselineA: Common law (qualified privilege and malice), drawing on Adam v. Ward and Netupsky v. Craig as cited in the reasons.
CaseB_TestB: Sheppard/Braich two-stage test for appellate intervention based on insufficient reasons: (1) “are the reasons inadequate”; (2) “if so, do they prevent appellate review” (i.e., are they “sufficiently amenable to appellate review”).
BaselineB: Common law (appellate review of sufficiency of reasons), based on R. v. Sheppard and R. v. Braich as applied in the reasons.
JudgeB: Bastarache and Abella JJ. (LeBel J. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Fault for unlawful arrest by police: (1) coroner’s s. 38 warrant is invalid if used to detain a suspect for interrogation (abuse of power), and officers’ legal error is no excuse; and (2) warrantless arrest power exists only where the officer has “reasonable and probable grounds” and that belief “must take into account all the information available to him” (may disregard only what he has good reason to believe unreliable).
BaselineA: Combination: Civil Code arts. 1053, 1054 (fault and vicarious liability) + Coroners' Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 29, s. 38 (detention of witnesses) + Criminal Code, 1953-54 (Can.), c. 51, s. 435 (warrantless arrest on reasonable and probable grounds).
CaseB_TestB: Validity of dismissal of a probationary constable: dismissal is ineffective unless made by the Board (exclusive, non-delegable statutory/contractual authority); a purported dismissal by the chief cannot stand, and the Board cannot validly ‘confirm’ it without itself acting as the decision-maker (including at least informing the constable that his case is being considered).
BaselineB: Statute/regulation: The Police Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 351, s. 29 and Regulation 680, s. 27(b) (authority of a board to dispense with services within 18 months), with reference to Nicholson v. Haldimand-Norfolk Regional Board of Commissioners of Police, [1979] 1 S.C.R. 311.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Municipal office disqualification for having a direct or indirect “interest in any contract” with the City (broad, ordinary-meaning approach to “interested in”)
BaselineA: Statute: Moncton Consolidation Act, 1946 (N.B.), c. 101, s. 6 (interpreted using the Angrignon principle that “interested in” has no technical meaning and is given its ordinary meaning); also considered Municipalities Act, R.S.N.B. 1973, c. M-22, ss. 71-72 (no displacement/conflict found). Key quoted baseline language: s. 6 disqualifies a person who “directly or indirectly otherwise than as a shareholder in an incorporated company, have any interest in any contract made with the City of Moncton”.
CaseB_TestB: Statutory interpretation of whether “institution” in OLA s. 22 includes municipalities (contextual/scheme-based coherence analysis; Charter values only if genuine ambiguity remains)
BaselineB: Statute: Official Languages Act, S.N.B. 2002, c. O-0.5, ss. 1 (“institution”), 22. Key quoted baseline language: s. 22: where “Her Majesty in right of the Province or an institution is a party to civil proceedings... [it] shall use... the official language chosen by the other party”; s. 1 defines “institution” by listing bodies and describing other bodies “established to perform a governmental function...”.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Qualified privilege in libel: malice goes to the jury only if the trial judge finds evidence raising a probability of express malice (more than a mere scintilla/possibility; more consistent with malice than non-malice).
BaselineA: Common law (defamation/qualified privilege and malice; drawing on authorities including Sun Life Assurance Co. of Canada v. Dalrymple and English cases such as Adam v. Ward and Somerville v. Hawkins).
CaseB_TestB: Blood Tribe clear-intent requirement for statutory abrogation of solicitor-client privilege: only clear, unequivocal legislative language can abrogate privilege; s. 232(1) ITA clearly excludes lawyers’ accounting records (though constitutionally invalid per Chambre des notaires).
BaselineB: Statute (Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), ss. 231.2(1), 231.7(1), and especially s. 232(1) definition of “solicitor-client privilege”), interpreted under the common-law/constitutional principle from Blood Tribe that privilege cannot be abrogated by inference.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Priority of B.C. Payment of Wages Act s. 5A lien: lien arises “from the date wages were earned”; it takes priority only over dispositions after it attaches, and “Where a mortgage has been made prior to the lien attaching, it is not affected. The lien will only attach to the employer’s equity in that property.”
BaselineA: Statute — Payment of Wages Act, 1962 (B.C.), c. 45, ss. 5 and 5A (especially s. 5A(1)-(2))
CaseB_TestB: Forced dissolution of a Quebec legal person under the C.C.Q.: where no special statutory scheme applies, the C.C.Q. suppletive scheme governs; dissolution may be ordered if the court confirms one of art. 355(2)’s grounds (fulfilled condition; object accomplished; impossibility of accomplishing object; or “some other legitimate cause”), including where the legal person is “incapable of accomplishing the objects for which it was constituted.”
BaselineB: Statute (civil code) — Civil Code of Québec, arts. 300, 334, 355 (and related arts. 355-364); interaction with Companies Act and Code of Civil Procedure art. 829
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Residual discretion/inherent jurisdiction to remedy unfairness from Crown’s closing address: (1) usually by curative jury instruction; (2) in rare ‘clearest cases of unfairness’, grant a limited defence reply confined to the improper issue(s)
BaselineA: Combination: statute (Criminal Code, s. 651(3)-(4)) plus common law inherent jurisdiction to control process and ensure trial fairness
JudgeA: Cory, Iacobucci and Bastarache JJ. (for Gonthier, Cory, Iacobucci and Bastarache JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Charter-validity test for a statutory presumption under s. 11(d): a presumption is constitutional only if proof of the substituted fact leads ‘inexorably’ (necessarily in all cases) to the essential element it replaces; otherwise it violates the presumption of innocence
BaselineB: Combination: statute (Criminal Code, s. 172.1(3)) interpreted under Charter s. 11(d), applying SCC presumption jurisprudence (e.g., Whyte; Downey; Audet)
JudgeB: Moldaver J. (Wagner C.J. and Gascon, Côté, Brown, Rowe and Martin JJ. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Adjudicator’s remedial power to substitute a lesser penalty for discharge where there is “just and sufficient cause for some disciplinary action, but not for discharge” (discipline as a continuum from financial penalty to suspension to discharge).
BaselineA: Statute + collective agreement: Public Service Labour Relations Act, R.S.N.B. 1973, c. P-25, s. 92(1)(b) (adjudication of “disciplinary action resulting in discharge, suspension or a financial penalty”) and the collective agreement’s “just and sufficient cause” clauses (Art. V(d), XVII(c)); distinguished from Port Arthur Shipbuilding Co. v. Arthurs, [1969] S.C.R. 85.
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 24(2) exclusion analysis (R. v. Collins guidelines): whether, “having regard to all the circumstances”, admission of evidence obtained in a Charter-breaching manner “would bring the administration of justice into disrepute”.
BaselineB: Statute/constitutional text + common law framework: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 24(2) (and ss. 7, 8 context) as applied through the SCC’s guidelines in R. v. Collins, [1987] 1 S.C.R. 265.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Will-construction test: give effect to the testator’s overriding intention on a fair reading of the will; administrative/boilerplate clauses should not defeat a clearly expressed intention (here, legacy payable on disposition of the business however effected, not only on a literal sale of shares).
BaselineA: Common law (will construction/ascertaining testator intention from the will read as a whole; no specific statutory provision identified in the reasons).
CaseB_TestB: Manslaughter legal causation with intervening acts: the Smithers/Nette test remains whether the accused’s dangerous unlawful acts were a “significant contributing cause of death” (i.e., “a contributing cause of death, outside the de minimis range”); foreseeability and ‘independent intentional act’ are non-determinative analytical aids.
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: Criminal Code ss. 222(1), 222(5)(a), 224, 225 (homicide/culpable homicide and non-breaking of causation in specified circumstances) plus common-law causation test from Smithers v. The Queen and R. v. Nette.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Functional (federal undertaking) test for labour-relations jurisdiction: provincial jurisdiction is the rule; federal jurisdiction is the exception for labour relations in undertakings/services/businesses that, having regard to the "functional test of the nature of their operations and their normal activities", can be characterized as federal; federal jurisdiction over labour relations arises only if it is "an integral part of primary federal jurisdiction over some other federal object" (Stevedoring case).
BaselineA: Common law constitutional division-of-powers doctrine for labour relations (functional/operational test; integral-to-federal-head principle), as stated with reference to Toronto Electric Commissioners v. Snider; the Stevedoring Reference; Bell Telephone; Letter Carriers; City of Yellowknife; Construction Montcalm.
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 15(1) two-part discrimination test (Withler/Kapp): (1) "Does the law create a distinction based on an enumerated or analogous ground?" and (2) "Does the distinction create a disadvantage by perpetuating prejudice or stereotyping?"; no need to identify a "mirror comparator group"; step two asks, "having regard to all relevant factors", whether the law perpetuates disadvantage/prejudice or stereotypes.
BaselineB: Common law/constitutional jurisprudence interpreting Charter s. 15(1), especially Andrews v. Law Society of British Columbia; Law v. Canada; R. v. Kapp (two-step formulation).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Bankruptcy Act s. 107(1)(j) overrides provincial Crown statutory preferences: provincial tax claims (not otherwise mentioned) rank pari passu notwithstanding any statutory preference, and cannot be elevated to 'secured creditor' status to escape s. 107(1)(j).
BaselineA: Statute (Bankruptcy Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. B-3, ss. 2 and 107(1)(j), (3))
JudgeA: Pigeon J. (for Martland, Ritchie, Pigeon, Beetz, Pratte and McIntyre JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Public interest standing test (purposive, flexible weighing): (1) serious justiciable issue; (2) plaintiff has a real stake or is engaged with the issues; (3) proposed suit is, in all the circumstances, a reasonable and effective means to bring the issue to court (not a strict 'no other way' requirement).
BaselineB: Common law (standing jurisprudence: Borowski; Finlay; Canadian Council of Churches; Hy and Zel’s; Thorson; McNeil)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Crown prerogative priority applies only where Crown and subject claims are “of equal degree”; a prior registered second/collateral mortgage is of a higher degree than a later-registered Crown judgment, so Registry Act registration-date priorities govern the surplus distribution
BaselineA: Combination of common law Crown prerogative priority for debts “of equal degree” (The Queen v. Bank of Nova Scotia (1885), 11 S.C.R. 1) and Nova Scotia statutory priorities under The Registry Act, R.S.N.S. 1967, c. 265, ss. 17-18 (plus Nova Scotia Civil Procedure Rule 47.11 on distributing surplus “according to their priorities”)
CaseB_TestB: International jurisdiction by extension of domestic territorial jurisdiction: under art. 71 C.C.P., an incidental action in warranty “must be taken before the court in which the principal action is pending”, and this rule applies to a foreign (alien) defendant without limitation
BaselineB: Statutory rule in Code of Civil Procedure, art. 71 (incidental warranty action must be brought where principal action is pending), interpreted in light of private international law principle that international jurisdiction is determined by extending domestic territorial jurisdiction rules (with support from Civil Code art. 27 and cases such as Alimport and Trower)
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “detained” under Canadian Bill of Rights s. 2(c): “detain”/“detention” “connote some form of compulsory restraint” (i.e., being “held in custody”/actual physical restraint), so a roadside stop/sobriety screening where the driver is then “allowed to go away” is not a detention and does not ground a “reasonable excuse” to refuse a breath demand
BaselineA: Statute (interpretation/application of Canadian Bill of Rights, 1960, s. 2(c)(ii)-(iii) in relation to Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 234.1(1)-(2) breath-demand/refusal scheme; with reference to prior SCC breath-demand cases including Brownridge v. The Queen and Hogan v. The Queen)
CaseB_TestB: Two-branch test for the tort of civil conspiracy: liability exists if (1) “whether the means used by the defendants are lawful or unlawful, the predominant purpose of the defendants’ conduct is to cause injury to the plaintiff”; or (2) “where the conduct of the defendants is unlawful, the conduct is directed towards the plaintiff (alone or together with others), and the defendants should know in the circumstances that injury to the plaintiff is likely to and does result” (constructive intent), with “actual damage” required in both situations
BaselineB: Common law (tort of conspiracy), drawing on authorities including Lonrho Ltd. v. Shell Petroleum Co. Ltd., Crofter Hand Woven Harris Tweed Co. v. Veitch, Sorrell v. Smith, and Canadian cases including Gagnon v. Foundation Maritime Limited
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 492 re-election validity test: effective re-election occurs where the accused (1) notifies the sheriff of the desire to re-elect (s. 492(1)); (2) attends at the time/place fixed (s. 492(2)-(3)); and (3) after the charge is read, makes the election (which may be through counsel in the accused’s presence). SCC also interprets s. 492(3) as requiring reading of the actual charge faced at trial (the preferred indictment), not the original information.
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, s. 492 (re-election procedure) and related s. 496 (post re-election indictment in Form 4).
CaseB_TestB: Injurious affection (no land taken) conditions + common-law actionability requirement: claimant must satisfy the four Loiselle conditions, including that the damage be such as would have been actionable at common law but for statutory authority, and (in this case) that turns on whether the construction constitutes an actionable private nuisance—i.e., an indirect interference that is a physical injury to land or a substantial interference with use/enjoyment which, “in the light of all the surrounding circumstances, ... is held to be unreasonable”.
BaselineB: Statute: Ontario Expropriations Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 154, ss. 1(e)(ii) and 21 (injurious affection where no land is acquired), incorporating common-law actionability; SCC relies on prior SCC articulation in The Queen v. Loiselle (1962) for the four conditions and applies common-law nuisance concepts.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Ontario Municipal Board jurisdiction to adjust assets/liabilities on dissolution: s. 137(1) incorporates only s. 14(11)(a),(b),(d) Municipal Act (without the prefatory limits), empowering the Board to make “adjustments of assets and liabilities…as the Board may consider equitable” in relation to the County’s dissolution
BaselineA: Statute: The Regional Municipality of Ottawa-Carleton Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 407, ss. 135-137, incorporating The Municipal Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 284, s. 14(11)(a),(b),(d)
CaseB_TestB: Charter fundamental justice mens rea for murder: “a conviction for murder cannot rest on anything less than proof beyond a reasonable doubt of subjective foresight of death” (therefore s. 213(a) is unconstitutional because it removes that requirement)
BaselineB: Constitution (Charter): Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 7 and 11(d), applied to Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 213(a) (constructive murder), building on R. v. Vaillancourt, [1987] 2 S.C.R. 636
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Validity of consent to intercept a private communication under Criminal Code s. 178.11(2)(a): consent must be “voluntary (i.e. free from coercion)” and “made knowingly, with an awareness of the significance of the consent”; and if there is valid consent, the interception is “lawfully made” for s. 178.16(1)(a) admissibility purposes.
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, Part IV.1 as enacted by the Protection of Privacy Act): ss. 178.1 (definition of “private communication”), 178.11(2)(a) (consent interception), 178.16(1)(a) (admissibility if interception “lawfully made”).
JudgeA: McIntyre J. (for Martland, Ritchie, Pigeon, Dickson, Beetz, Estey, Pratte and McIntyre JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Targeting an identifiable group under Criminal Code s. 319(2): the trial judge must assess “the totality of the evidence” to decide whether the accused’s statements, “as a matter of fact, promoted hatred” of the particularized group; it is not necessary to prove strict “interchangeability” between labels used (e.g., “gypsies”) and the group named in the information (“Roma”).
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code): s. 319(2) (wilful promotion of hatred), with “identifiable group” in s. 318(4).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Audi alteram partem / no ex parte evidence after the hearing: an appellate tribunal must not receive evidence or “necessary facts” in a party’s absence without disclosure and a real opportunity to respond; prejudice need only be possible
BaselineA: Common law (procedural fairness / natural justice), applied in a statutory university-appeal setting (Universities Act, 1974 (B.C.), ss. 58(1)-(3), 61)
CaseB_TestB: Workers’ compensation occupational-disease causation under s. 250(4): causation may be inferred from circumstantial evidence; expert opinion is not determinative; if evidence is “evenly weighted” the issue must be resolved in the worker’s favour
BaselineB: Statute and policy: Workers Compensation Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 492, ss. 6 and 250(4) (and s. 250(2) requiring application of Board policy on “causative significance”); plus common-law causation inference principles (Snell v. Farrell) as applied in this statutory context
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Appellate intervention in damages: an appellate court may not substitute its own figure unless a wrong principle of law was applied or the overall award is a wholly erroneous estimate of damages (Andrews v. Grand & Toy).
BaselineA: Common law (appellate review standard for damages) from Andrews et al. v. Grand & Toy Alberta Ltd. et al., [1978] 2 S.C.R. 229 at p. 235.
CaseB_TestB: Videotape-only identification: once it is established the videotape has not been altered and depicts the crime, it is admissible; the trier of fact may identify and convict on the videotape alone if satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt, assessing clarity/quality and (to a lesser extent) time of depiction, with appropriate cautions.
BaselineB: Common law evidence principles on admissibility/weight of recordings and videotape identification, drawing on R. v. Leaney, [1989] 2 S.C.R. 393 (and related authorities).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Quebec Labour Code s. 16 rebuttal/jurisdiction test: to rebut the presumption, the employer must satisfy the investigation commissioner that the employer’s “other” reason is “of a substantial nature and not a pretext” and is “the true reason for the dismissal”; the commissioner/Labour Court cannot assess the proportionality or “severity of the penalty” (cannot substitute their judgment for the employer’s once a real, non-pretext reason is shown).
BaselineA: Statute (Quebec Labour Code, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 141 as am., ss. 13-16, especially s. 16 “another good and sufficient reason”; also discussed alongside s. 14).
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 12 “gross disproportionality” test (and its two-aspect application): cruel and unusual punishment turns on whether the punishment is “so excessive as to outrage standards of decency” / “grossly disproportionate”, considering “the gravity of the offence, the personal characteristics of the offender and the particular circumstances of the case” (plus other non-decisive factors); if not grossly disproportionate on the actual facts, the court may assess validity on “reasonable hypothetical circumstances” (not “far-fetched”).
BaselineB: Combination: constitutional text (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 12) plus common-law/precedential framework from R. v. Smith (reaffirmed in Lyons and Luxton) applied to a statutory minimum sentence (Motor Vehicle Act, s. 88(1)(c) as applied with s. 88(1)(a) and s. 86(1)(a)(ii)).
JudgeB: Gonthier J. (for La Forest, L’Heureux-Dubé, Sopinka, Gonthier, Cory and Iacobucci JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Summary conviction appeal costs: under Criminal Code ss. 758 and 771(3), the appeal court "may make any order with respect to costs that it considers just and reasonable" / "proper" and these provisions implicitly bind Her Majesty when read in the context of Part XXIV (despite Interpretation Act s. 16).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 758 and 771(3), interpreted in the context of Part XXIV including ss. 720(1), 738(4), 748, 752.1, 755, 759; and Interpretation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-23, s. 16).
CaseB_TestB: Mortgage statutory prepayment timing under Interest Act s. 10(1): five-year prepayment right applies at the end of each five-year period; where a mortgagor enters a valid renewal that "deems" the mortgage date to the maturity of the existing loan and the renewal term does not exceed five years, the mortgagor cannot prepay until the end of that five-year renewal term; choosing to renew (with full knowledge) is not "waiver/contracting out".
BaselineB: Statute (Interest Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-18, s. 10(1) (and s. 10(2) exclusion); also considered alongside Manitoba Mortgage Act, s. 20(6) and Real Property Act, s. 103(1)(c)).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Wrongful dismissal damages: no deduction for (i) income tax not payable and (ii) unemployment insurance benefits that flow from the employment contract (collateral benefits rule as applied to UI)
BaselineA: Common law contract damages / collateral benefits principles (applied by analogy to contributory pension benefits in Guy v. Trizec Equities Ltd., and rejecting the Gourley income-tax deduction approach per R. v. Jennings)
CaseB_TestB: Identification of Criminals Act s. 2 applies to juveniles: a juvenile in lawful custody for a delinquency that relates to a Criminal Code indictable offence is a person 'charged with' (and may be 'under conviction of') an indictable offence, so reasonable force may be used to fingerprint
BaselineB: Statute—Identification of Criminals Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-1, s. 2(1)-(2), interpreted alongside the Juvenile Delinquents Act; relying on Morris v. The Queen for meaning of 'offence'/'conviction' in the juvenile context
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: “Air of reality / sense of reality” threshold for whether a trial judge must leave a defence (here, mistake of fact as to consent) with the jury: there must be “some evidence which would convey a sense of reality in the submission”; i.e., “some evidence which, if believed, would support the existence of a mistaken but honest belief” (and not “fantasy”).
BaselineA: Common law (jury-charge duty re defences), drawing the “sense of reality” formulation from Kelsey v. The Queen and applied in R. v. Workman and Huculak; also discussed alongside Wu v. The King.
CaseB_TestB: Section 11(b) “reasonable time” analysis (Morin factors): assess (1) “the length of the delay”; (2) “waiver, if any, of parts of the delay”; (3) “the reasons for the delay”; and (4) “prejudice to the subject of the criminal process” (and, in the majority’s holding, s. 11(b) does not apply to appellate delay).
BaselineB: Statute/constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 11(b) (and related discussion of ss. 7 and 24(1)); the four-factor framework is taken from R. v. Morin.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Standard of review framework: start with a presumption of reasonableness for a tribunal interpreting its home statute, rebutted only if the issue falls within a Dunsmuir correctness category; a statutory right of appeal is not a new correctness category
BaselineA: Common law (judicial review standard-of-review framework from Dunsmuir v. New Brunswick, plus subsequent SCC cases like Saguenay/McLean)
CaseB_TestB: Framework for Crown sui generis fiduciary duty (as applied in specific claims): (1) identify a specific/cognizable Aboriginal interest; (2) determine Crown discretionary control over that interest; (3) assess whether Crown met fiduciary standard of conduct (loyalty/good faith/full disclosure/ordinary prudence), recognizing competing interests do not absolve the duty
BaselineB: Common law fiduciary doctrine (especially Wewaykum Indian Band v. Canada; also Guerin, Haida Nation, Manitoba Metis Federation) applied within the Specific Claims Tribunal Act scheme
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Necessarily incidental doctrine for federal validity: where a law is prima facie provincial (property and civil rights), it is valid under s. 91(12) only if it is "necessarily incidental to effective" fisheries legislation and is sufficiently linked to actual or likely harm to fisheries (not a blanket prohibition).
BaselineA: Common law constitutional division-of-powers doctrine (Lord Tomlin’s proposition (3) in Attorney-General for Canada v. Attorney-General for British Columbia and others, [1930] A.C. 111) applied to s. 91(12) B.N.A. Act and s. 33(3) Fisheries Act.
CaseB_TestB: Colour of right in theft: the defence turns on whether the trier of fact is satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused did not have, at the time of the taking/transfer, an "honest belief" in a right to the property; it does not depend on what the accused’s rights actually were (e.g., when commissions were legally payable).
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code theft definition requiring taking "fraudulently and without colour of right" (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 283, 294).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “unlawful purpose” in Criminal Code s. 423(2)(a): it “means contrary to law, that is prohibited by federal or provincial legislation”; if the alleged purpose is not prohibited by legislation, the information does not disclose an offence under s. 423(2)(a).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 423(2)(a); also s. 8 excluding common law offences; discussed alongside Canada Labour Code, s. 110(1))
CaseB_TestB: Quebec defamation fault under art. 1457 C.C.Q.: fault is determined by a contextual analysis, where “the guiding principle of liability for defamation is that there will not be fault until it has been shown that the journalist or media outlet in question has fallen below professional standards”; “the conduct of the reasonable journalist becomes the all-important guidepost.”
BaselineB: Statute (Civil Code of Québec, art. 1457; applied with reference to prior Quebec jurisprudence including Société Radio-Canada v. Radio Sept-Îles and Prud’homme)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Automatism/insanity classification: whether the accused’s automatism is due to a “disease of the mind” (internal cause) versus a transient effect of a specific external factor; “ordinary stresses and disappointments of life” are not an external cause taking the condition out of disease of the mind
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 16) interpreted through common-law automatism/insanity jurisprudence (e.g., Bratty v. A.G. Northern Ireland, R. v. K.)
CaseB_TestB: Conflict/supersession analysis for mortgagee coverage: where the mortgage clause says it “shall supersede any policy provisions in conflict therewith”, Statutory Condition 4 cannot be used to void mortgagee coverage if it conflicts with the mortgage clause (including where the clause preserves coverage “notwithstanding ... any vacancy or non-occupancy”)
BaselineB: Statute and contract: Insurance Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. I.8, Part IV (Statutory Condition 4) and the policy’s standard mortgage clause, interpreted in light of National Bank of Greece (Canada) v. Katsikonouris
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Single-cause vs multiple-causes characterization for prescription: if claimed damages “result from a single cause of action, which is the breach of a contractual obligation”, they are contractual and prescribe in 30 years; if they “result from several separate and independent causes of action”, each is characterized as contractual or delictual and prescribes accordingly.
BaselineA: Civil Code (Quebec): arts. 2242 (30-year prescription residual), 2261(2) (2-year prescription for delict/quasi-delict), plus characterization of corporate by-laws/natural justice obligations as contractual (drawing on corporate-law concepts and cited jurisprudence such as Vancouver Real Estate Board v. Moscrop Realty Ltd.).
CaseB_TestB: Priority between mechanic’s lien and mortgage for past indebtedness: where s. 14(1) of The Mechanics’ Lien Act does not apply, “the present case must be decided on priority of registration” under The Registry Act (ss. 69(1), 70); an unregistered (or later-registered) lien has no general priority absent written notice/registration conditions in s. 14(1).
BaselineB: Statutory: The Mechanics’ Lien Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 267 (esp. ss. 14(1), 16, 20, 21, 22) and The Registry Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 409 (ss. 69(1), 70).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Accrued-rights/anti-retroactivity analysis on statutory repeal: apply Interpretation Act s. 35(c) so repeal does not “affect any right, privilege, obligation or liability acquired, accrued, accruing or incurred”; read the amending Unemployment Insurance Act s. 31 together with s. 35(c) to preserve only the pre-repeal accrued benefit (here, benefits through January 31, 1976) while keeping pre-repeal disqualifications (old s. 31(3)(b) pension-payable disentitlement).
BaselineA: Statute: Interpretation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-23, s. 35(c) (effect of repeal on accrued rights) applied to Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, S.C. 1970-71-72, c. 48, ss. 31, 38 as amended by S.C. 1974-75-76, c. 80, s. 10; also considers Unemployment Insurance Entitlements Adjustment Act, 1976-77, c. 11, s. 2.
CaseB_TestB: Judicial immunity/privilege against compelled testimony before a commission: under Public Inquiries Act ss. 3-4 (read together), a commission may “summon” persons (s. 3) but cannot “compel” judges to testify about (i) “how and why they arrived at their decisions” (adjudicative process) or (ii) “why a particular judge sat on a particular case” (assignment/composition), because vague general language is insufficient to override the fundamental principle of judicial independence and immunity.
BaselineB: Combination: Statute (Public Inquiries Act, R.S.N.S. 1967, c. 250, ss. 3-4) interpreted in light of constitutional/common-law principle of judicial independence and long-standing judicial immunity (supported by Valente v. The Queen; Beauregard v. Canada; Knowles' Trial and related authorities).
JudgeB: McLachlin J. (for L'Heureux-Dubé, Gonthier and McLachlin JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Interpretation of Motor Vehicle Transport Act, s. 3(2): provincial board may license an extra‑provincial undertaking “into or through” a province as encompassing operations “in, across, into and out of the province” (and provincial enforcement powers apply via “like terms and conditions”)
BaselineA: Statute: Motor Vehicle Transport Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. M-14, ss. 2 (definitions), 3(1)-(2), 5, 6; incorporating provincial scheme via The Public Service Vehicles Act, R.S.A. 1970, c. 300 (incl. s. 58 seizure power) through the “like terms and conditions and in the like manner” language in s. 3(2)
CaseB_TestB: Charter scope test for corporate claimants under s. 12: claimant must show an interest “falling within the scope of the guarantee, and one which accords with the purpose of that provision”; purposive interpretation begins with text, and “cruel and unusual” denotes protection “only human beings can enjoy” so corporations are outside s. 12’s protective scope
BaselineB: Constitutional text and purposive-interpretation framework: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 12; interpretive approach from R. v. Big M Drug Mart Ltd. (purposive interpretation) and CIP Inc. (scope/purpose requirement for claimants)
JudgeB: Brown and Rowe JJ. (Wagner C.J. and Moldaver and Côté JJ. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Fundamental breach and exclusionary clause: whether the exclusion/waiver clause remains applicable is determined by the “true construction of the contract” (not an automatic rule that fundamental breach nullifies the clause); here, the lien waiver ceased to bind once the subcontractor elected to treat the contract as at an end and communicated that election.
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Mechanics’ Lien Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 267, s. 5(1) (effect of signing an express agreement to the contrary) plus the common-law approach from Suisse Atlantique and Photo Production that applicability of an exclusion clause after fundamental breach is a matter of contractual construction.
CaseB_TestB: Collateral attack on an administrative order in penal proceedings: whether a penal court may determine validity “depends on the statute” and is answered by focusing on legislative intent as to the appropriate forum, using non-exhaustive factors (statutory wording, legislative purpose, availability of appeal, nature of the collateral attack in light of the appeal tribunal’s expertise/raison d’être, and penalty).
BaselineB: Statute-based: Environmental Protection Act, R.S.O. 1980, c. 141 (notably ss. 17, 122-123, 146(1a)) interpreted to determine the proper forum and whether collateral attack is permitted.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Constructive trust based on unjust enrichment in a spousal/common-law relationship: claimant must show (1) an enrichment, (2) a corresponding deprivation, and (3) absence of any juristic reason; and it is unjust where one party prejudices herself in a reasonable expectation of an interest and the other knowingly accepts the benefit (plus a factual ‘causal connection’ between contribution and asset; remedy proportionate to contribution).
BaselineA: Common law (equitable constructive trust/unjust enrichment), drawing on Rathwell v. Rathwell and Murdoch v. Murdoch (and discussion of Pettitt v. Pettitt; Gissing v. Gissing).
CaseB_TestB: Solicitor-client confidentiality/privilege and search warrants: (i) confidentiality may be raised whenever disclosure is likely without consent; (ii) conflicts are resolved in favour of confidentiality unless law provides otherwise; (iii) exercises of statutory authority must impair confidentiality only to the extent ‘absolutely necessary’; (iv) enabling statutes derogating from confidentiality are interpreted restrictively; plus (a) a justice has no jurisdiction to authorize seizure of privileged (inadmissible) evidence, and (b) before searching a lawyer’s office for evidence under Criminal Code s. 443(1)(b), the justice should refuse the warrant unless there is ‘no reasonable alternative’ and must impose protective execution terms.
BaselineB: Combination: statute (Criminal Code, s. 443(1)(b)) interpreted in light of common law solicitor-client privilege/confidentiality (including Solosky v. The Queen and common law crime/fraud exception).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Reibl v. Hughes informed-consent negligence causation test: whether “a reasonable person in the patient’s position would have done if there had been proper disclosure of attendant risks” (objective test, accounting for the patient’s particular position but “objectively assessed in terms of reasonableness”).
BaselineA: Common law (medical negligence duty of disclosure and causation in non-disclosure cases), drawing on Hopp v. Lepp (duty to disclose “all material risks” and answer specific questions) and developing the causation approach for non-disclosure.
CaseB_TestB: Clark v. CNR division-of-powers “integral element” test: federal legislation affecting a s. 92(10) undertaking is valid/applicable only if it regulates an “integral” (i.e., “vital”, “essential” or “integral”) aspect of the core federal undertaking; otherwise provincial laws of general application apply.
BaselineB: Combination of constitutional text and doctrine: Constitution Act, 1867 ss. 91(29), 92(10), 92(13), 92(14), applying the “integral element” approach from Construction Montcalm Inc. v. Minimum Wage Commission and Northern Telecom Ltd. v. Communications Workers of Canada.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: “Right of access” under para. 12 of the Saskatchewan Natural Resources Agreement: the Province may deny access for hunting to everyone, but “once any hunting is permitted, then Indians (and other members of the public) have a right of access for the purpose of hunting”, which engages the proviso and guarantees hunting “for food at all seasons of the year” (i.e., provincial season limits cannot apply once limited hunting is allowed).
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional instrument: para. 12 of the Natural Resources Agreement (confirmed by British North America Act, 1930) as applied/clarified in R. v. Sutherland, Wilson and Wilson, [1980] 2 S.C.R. 451 (and contrasted with R. v. Smith).
CaseB_TestB: Charter “purpose-first” constitutionality test (s. 2(a)): “The legislation's purpose is the initial test of constitutional validity”; effects are considered only if the law “has passed the purpose test”; and “effects can never be relied on to save legislation with an invalid purpose.”
BaselineB: Constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 2(a) (and remedial/supremacy context in Constitution Act, 1982, s. 52(1)); building on purposive Charter interpretation (Hunter v. Southam Inc., [1984] 2 S.C.R. 145) and distinguishing Robertson and Rosetanni v. The Queen, [1963] S.C.R. 651.
JudgeB: Dickson J. (for Dickson, Beetz, McIntyre, Chouinard and Lamer JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: No implied power for the Commission/officer/Review Panel to retroactively revoke an allowed premium reduction; an officer’s erroneous grant is not a “nullity” where the officer was properly seized and acted under prescribed regulatory standards (review is one-way at the employer’s instance only).
BaselineA: Statute and regulation: Unemployment Insurance Act, 1970-71-72 (Can.), c. 48 as amended, ss. 64(4), 64(6) (regulation-making and prescribed standards/appeals) and related scheme; Regulations s. 24 (decision and employer-initiated review/appeal).
CaseB_TestB: Mens rea for Criminal Code s. 121(1)(a): no “corrupt” purpose required; guilt requires intentional commission of the prohibited act plus knowledge of the circumstances—(1) know one is an official, (2) intentionally demand/accept a loan/reward/advantage/benefit, and (3) know it is “in consideration for” cooperation/assistance/exercise of influence in connection with government business.
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 121(1)(a) (and s. 19 noted re ignorance of law).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Ernst (Cromwell J.) categorical Ward-based rule: Charter damages are never an “appropriate and just” remedy (Charter, s. 24(1)) for Charter breaches by this quasi-judicial regulator, because countervailing factors (alternative remedy of judicial review + good governance/immunity rationales + case-by-case inquiry undermining immunity) collectively negate damages
BaselineA: Combination: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 24(1) (remedial discretion) + common law Charter damages framework from Vancouver (City) v. Ward, 2010 SCC 27 (functional purposes and countervailing factors) + statutory immunity clause Energy Resources Conservation Act, R.S.A. 2000, c. E-10, s. 43
CaseB_TestB: Mikisew Cree (Karakatsanis J.) rule: the duty to consult does not apply to the law-making process—“no aspect of the law-making process — from the development of legislation to its enactment — triggers a duty to consult”
BaselineB: Combination: common law duty-to-consult doctrine from Haida Nation v. British Columbia (Minister of Forests), 2004 SCC 73 (duty triggered by contemplated Crown conduct with potential adverse effects) + constitutional principles (separation of powers, parliamentary sovereignty/privilege) + Constitution Act, 1867, Part IV (legislative power) + Constitution Act, 1982, s. 35
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory interaction test: whether Workers’ Compensation Act s. 10(1) bars a tort action against a vehicle owner who is only a deemed employer/servant-master under Motor-vehicle Act s. 70(1) (answer: no, because the owner is not an “employer” within s. 10(1))
BaselineA: Statute (Workers’ Compensation Act, 1968 (B.C.), c. 59, s. 10(1) and Motor-vehicle Act, R.S.B.C. 1960, c. 253, s. 70(1); with discussion of Co-Operators Insurance Association v. Kearney, [1965] S.C.R. 106 and Harrison v. Toronto Motor Car Limited and Krug, [1945] O.R. 1)
CaseB_TestB: Operational conflict / precedence framework for conflicting administrative decisions: (1) determine if there is “operational conflict” (i.e., “compliance with the decision of one tribunal necessitates violation of the other”); (2) if so, first ask whether either decision could be overturned under its normal standard of review; (3) if both would stand, courts may declare one decision inoperative to the extent of conflict and decide precedence using a “pragmatic and functional” approach considering factors like legislative purpose, centrality to tribunal purpose, and policy-making/implementation role
BaselineB: Common law administrative law (building from Domtar Inc. v. Quebec (Commission d'appel en matière de lésions professionnelles), [1993] 2 S.C.R. 756 and the “pragmatic and functional” approach from U.E.S., Local 298 v. Bibeault, [1988] 2 S.C.R. 1048; applied in the context of statutory schemes including Railway Act, R.S.C., 1985, c. R-3, ss. 335, 340 and NTPPA, ss. 49-50)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Priority between a mechanics’ lien and a subsequent collateral mortgage for past indebtedness: where the Mechanics’ Lien Act does not prescribe priority (s. 14(1) inapplicable), an unregistered lien has no general priority and the contest is resolved by registration priority under the Registry Act once the lien is registered and deemed a purchaser (s. 20).
BaselineA: Statute (Ontario): Mechanics’ Lien Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 267, ss. 14(1) and 20 (and related registration provisions ss. 16, 21, 22), interacting with the Registry Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 409, ss. 69(1) and 70.
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 1 justification (Oakes proportionality) applied to PIPA’s restriction on union expression: even with a pressing and substantial objective and rational connection, the law fails because its limits on expression are disproportionate (no mechanism to balance union expression in labour disputes with privacy interests).
BaselineB: Constitution (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms): ss. 2(b) and 1 (Oakes proportionality framework), applied to the Personal Information Protection Act, S.A. 2003, c. P-6.5.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Quebec “choice” between contractual and delictual liability: a plaintiff may sue in delict despite a contract if the alleged contractual fault is independently a delictual fault under art. 1053 C.C. (i.e., it would be a fault “even in the absence of a contract”)
