BaselineA: Statute (Quebec Civil Code, art. 1053; Code of Civil Procedure, art. 68) as interpreted through SCC/civil-law authorities (e.g., Ross v. Dunstall; Alliance Assurance)
CaseB_TestB: Reasonable apprehension of bias in a criminal trial: where it is demonstrated, the trial judge has “no further jurisdiction” and “the only appropriate remedy is a new trial”; appellate finding of apprehension of bias retroactively renders trial orders “void and without effect”
BaselineB: Common law procedural fairness / bias doctrine, relying on Newfoundland Telephone Co. v. Newfoundland (Board of Commissioners of Public Utilities), [1992] 1 S.C.R. 623
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Bills of Exchange Act “sum certain”/negotiability requirement: a promissory note must be certain on its face as to principal and interest; interest must be “ascertained in gross on the face of the document, or ... capable of being ascertained by numerical calculation from materials contained in the document”, and (generally) certainty must appear on the face of the instrument (no extrinsic evidence unless necessary to implement a specific Act provision).
BaselineA: Statute (Bills of Exchange Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. B-5, ss. 28, 176(1), 186; plus s. 10 incorporating common law/law merchant where not inconsistent).
CaseB_TestB: Criminal Code s. 172(3) “disturbs” threshold: to convict, the accused’s wilful act must be “disorderly in itself or productive of disorder”; mere “annoyance, anxiety or emotional upset” is insufficient, and where acts are “brief, essentially passive and peaceful ... and ... voluntarily desisted from, upon request ... then there is no crime”; “some activity in the nature of a disorder must occur”.
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 172(3) (and context ss. 169-175 heading “Disorderly Conduct”)).
JudgeB: Dickson J. (for Dickson, Beetz, McIntyre, Chouinard and Lamer JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Bills of Exchange Act “sum certain”/negotiability requirement: principal and interest must be ascertainable on the face of the instrument (or by numerical calculation from materials in it); recourse to extrinsic evidence is generally not permitted unless necessary to implement a specific Act provision
BaselineA: Statute (Bills of Exchange Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. B-5, ss. 28, 176(1), 186; plus s. 10 incorporating common law/law merchant where not inconsistent)
CaseB_TestB: Start of life-insurance suicide exclusion period (arts. 2516 & 2532 C.C.L.C.): determine the contract’s effective date (including permissible retroactive effect from a backdated policy date if favourable and if art. 2516 conditions are later met with no change in insurability); exclusion period cannot run more than once within a single contract and increases in coverage may be mere variations depending on continuity factors
BaselineB: Statute (Civil Code of Lower Canada, arts. 2500, 2516, 2532; interpretive rule art. 1018; related discussion of art. 2524)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: When a statute creates a special tribunal/procedure to decide an issue, the Superior Court should not intervene by declaratory judgment to decide that very issue (and may also refuse declarations that would be of little or no practical use).
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Code of Civil Procedure, art. 453 (declaratory judgment) applied alongside the principle from Barraclough v. Brown and City of Lethbridge that courts should not bypass a legislatively-prescribed specialized forum/procedure.
CaseB_TestB: Minister’s s. 7 Fisheries Act power to 'authorize to be issued' licences is a continuing power; therefore the Minister may revoke an authorization any time before the licence is actually issued, subject only to natural justice (relevant considerations, non-arbitrariness, good faith).
BaselineB: Statute: Fisheries Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. F-14, s. 7 (and contrast with s. 9 for issued licences), plus Interpretation Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. I-21, s. 31(3) ('from time to time as occasion requires').
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Excise Tax Act machinery exemption: taxpayer must be a “manufacturer or producer of goods” and the machinery must be “purchased and used directly in the manufacture of goods”; “manufacture” not restrictively defined—operating generators to produce electricity is manufacturing
BaselineA: Statute: Excise Tax Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-13, ss. 27(1), 29(1), and Schedule III, Part XIII, s. 1(a) (machinery sold to/imported by manufacturers or producers for use directly in manufacture/production of goods); interpretive support from R. v. York Marble, Tile and Terrazzo Ltd., [1968] S.C.R. 140 and Bank of Nova Scotia v. The King, [1930] S.C.R. 174
CaseB_TestB: When an appeal-as-of-right is “acquired/accrued/accruing” under a repealed enactment: the right arises only when all conditions precedent are fulfilled—here, only upon the court of appeal’s judgment reversing the acquittal and ordering a new trial
BaselineB: Statute: Interpretation Act, R.S.C., 1985, c. I-21, ss. 43(c) and 44(c),(d), applied to Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 691(2) (as amended effective May 14, 1997)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: No common law tort/civil action for discrimination where a comprehensive human rights code provides the enforcement and remedial scheme (the Code “foreclose[s] any civil action based directly upon a breach thereof” and “also excludes any common law action based on an invocation of the public policy expressed in the Code”).
BaselineA: Statute — The Ontario Human Rights Code, R.S.O. 1970, c. 318 (especially the employment non-discrimination provisions in s. 4(1)(a)-(b) and the Code’s administrative/board-of-inquiry and appeal scheme, including s. 14b(6), s. 14c, s. 14d(4)).
CaseB_TestB: Undue obstacle/undue hardship (reasonable accommodation) analysis under CTA s. 172: discriminatory barriers must be removed unless the carrier proves “undue hardship”/a “bona fide justification”; “What constitutes undue hardship depends on factors relevant to the circumstances and legislation governing each case” (including CTA s. 5 factors like cost, economic viability, safety, and quality of service).
BaselineB: Statute interpreted in light of human rights principles — Canada Transportation Act, S.C. 1996, c. 10, ss. 5, 170(1), 171, 172 (and the Court’s human-rights accommodation jurisprudence, e.g., Meiorin/Grismer, as incorporated into the CTA ‘undue obstacle’ inquiry).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Bill of Rights limit on reverse onus: a reverse onus (balance of probabilities) is compatible with s. 2(f) only if the fact the accused must prove/disprove is "rationally open" to them; if the Crown’s proved facts have "no rational or necessary connection" to the presumed conclusion and the accused cannot "reasonably be expected to prove" lawful importation, the reverse onus is inoperative unless the Crown also shows the accused had "some knowledge or means of knowledge" of the importation circumstances
BaselineA: Statute (Customs Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-40, ss. 205(1),(3), 248(1)) as construed/applied under the Canadian Bill of Rights, R.S.C. 1970, App. III, s. 2(f), with reference to R. v. Appleby, [1972] S.C.R. 303
CaseB_TestB: Privative-clause judicial review threshold: on an evocation/judicial review, the labour commissioner/Labour Court’s interpretation of s. 32 Labour Code (who is an "interested party" and who may be present/heard) is immune unless it is "patently unreasonable"/"manifestly unreasonable"; here, employees are not interested parties for bargaining-unit definition because s. 32 exhaustively specifies presence of "associations concerned" and "the employer"
BaselineB: Statute (Quebec Labour Code, especially s. 32; also arts. 846 C.C.P. and related Labour Code provisions) plus common-law administrative law deference under a privative clause (CUPE v. N.B. Liquor Corp.; Nipawin)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Intoxication (“capacity”) test for mens rea of murder: intoxication is relevant only if it rendered the accused “incapable of forming the intent to kill or to cause bodily harm that he knew was likely to cause death”; Crown must satisfy jury beyond a reasonable doubt that accused had that capacity
BaselineA: Common law (as adopted/clarified in prior cases) applied to Criminal Code murder mens rea (R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 212(a)(ii))
CaseB_TestB: Interjurisdictional immunity (constitutional inapplicability) for provincial laws affecting federal services: a provincial law of general application is inapplicable if it “touches on a vital or essential aspect of [the federal service’s] establishment, management or operation” (i.e., bears on what makes it “specifically of federal jurisdiction”)
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine of interjurisdictional immunity (as stated in Bell Canada v. Quebec (CSST), Construction Montcalm, Clark, Dick, etc.)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 116(1) availability test: a charge for disobeying a lawful court order lies unless statute law (not common law/inherent contempt power) "expressly" provides a penalty/punishment or other mode of proceeding; "by law" means "by statute law"
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 116(1) (and related discussion of s. 8; Manitoba Queen’s Bench Rules 483, 485, 492 considered but found not to qualify)
CaseB_TestB: Public law promissory estoppel in penal/zoning context: requires (1) a clear and unambiguous promise by a public authority intended to induce action, plus (2) reliance and change of conduct, but estoppel cannot be invoked to prevent application of a clear express legislative provision (e.g., strict-liability zoning offence)
BaselineB: Common law doctrine of promissory estoppel as applied in public law (Mount Sinai; Maracle), constrained by the principle that estoppel cannot override express legislation; applied alongside municipal zoning by-law offence provisions (By-law VQZ-3, art. 359; Cities and Towns Act, s. 576)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Insurance policy interpretation to determine the policy’s single “effective date” for time-limited clauses: construe the policy and application “in entirety” and identify the date the policy is “entirely structured around” for “calculating any of the time periods contemplated” (including the suicide clause).
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law contract interpretation: Insurance Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 224, s. 148(2) (application + policy form the contract) (with background reference to s. 154 on when a contract takes effect), plus general contractual interpretation principles applied to the insurance contract.
CaseB_TestB: Access in conjunction with permanent guardianship: (1) court has jurisdiction under the Family Services Act to grant/deny access when making or varying a permanent guardianship order; (2) access is decided by a best-interests analysis where “access is the exception and not the rule” and “should not be granted if its exercise would have negative effects on the physical or psychological health of the child” or would jeopardize adoption.
BaselineB: Statute: Family Services Act, S.N.B. 1980, c. F-2.2, especially s. 1 (“best interests of the child” factors), s. 53(2) (best interests paramount), ss. 56, 60(2), 60(6), 61(1), and s. 85(2) (post-adoption access preservation).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 16(2) insanity: meaning of being “incapable of appreciating the nature and quality of an act” — the accused appreciates if he “knows what he is doing” and “is aware of the physical consequences which will result from his acts” (i.e., can “estimate and understand the physical consequences”); emotional indifference/remorselessness is irrelevant.
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 16(2)); interpreted consistently with SCC authorities including Cooper v. The Queen, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 1149 and R. v. Barnier, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 1124 (and discussion of Schwartz v. The Queen, [1977] 1 S.C.R. 673).
CaseB_TestB: Extradition Act committal/surrender frameworks: (1) Committal under s. 29(1)(a) — extradition judge applies the preliminary-inquiry committal test and must take a “restrained view” of reliability: the requesting state’s certified ROC evidence is “presumptively reliable” and committal may be refused for unreliability only where evidence is “so defective or appears so unreliable that it would be dangerous or unsafe to act on it”; defences/exculpatory evidence generally not considered. (2) Surrender under s. 44(1)(a) — unavailability of a Canadian defence in the requesting state triggers a 3-part threshold: (1) a substantive difference (defence available in Canada but no comparable defence abroad); (2) a reasonable prospect of success in Canada; and (3) significantly greater jeopardy abroad; if met, the Minister must weigh this with all circumstances.
BaselineB: Statute (Extradition Act, S.C. 1999, c. 18, ss. 29(1)(a), 32(1)(c), 44(1)(a)); built on prior SCC extradition jurisprudence including United States of America v. Ferras, 2006 SCC 33 and Lake v. Canada (Minister of Justice), 2008 SCC 23.
JudgeB: Cromwell J. (McLachlin C.J. and Moldaver and Wagner JJ. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: When (if ever) to exceed the $100,000 rough upper limit for non-pecuniary damages under the functional approach: exceed only rarely, and not merely because injuries seem worse than the trilogy; $100,000 may increase only on proof/agreement of inflation’s effect
BaselineA: Common law (damages for non-pecuniary loss) as set out in the “trilogy” and refined in Lewis v. Todd: Andrews v. Grand & Toy Alberta Ltd.; Arnold v. Teno; Thornton v. Board of School Trustees; Lewis v. Todd
CaseB_TestB: OPCF 44R / Insurance Act s. 239(1)(a) ‘arising directly or indirectly from the use or operation of an automobile’ (indemnity context): require an unbroken chain of causation showing the tortfeasor is liable ‘as a motorist’; coverage denied where the tort is an intervening, severable act (not mere ‘but for’ vehicle involvement)
BaselineB: Statute/contract interpretation: Insurance Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. I.8, s. 239(1)(a) (and tracking language in OPCF 44R s. 3); distinguished from the no-fault ‘relaxed causation’ approach in Amos v. ICBC
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Effect of workers’ compensation election/subrogation on (i) who may sue the tortfeasor and for what, and (ii) whether the Commission has “interest” to intervene / can benefit from interruption of prescription: once election for compensation is made, only the Commission may claim amounts it paid/will pay; the worker may claim only the s. 8 “additional sum”; a worker’s overbroad action does not create Commission interest or interrupt prescription for the Commission
BaselineA: Statute and civil law: Workmen’s Compensation Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 159, ss. 7(1)-(3) (subrogation “by the mere making of the election”), 8 (worker’s residual claim for “additional sum”); Civil Code art. 1056a (recourse only to extent permitted by the Act); Code of Civil Procedure art. 208 (intervention by “any person interested”); (prescription context: Civil Code art. 2262(2))
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 24(2) exclusion (Collins framework) with emphasis on assessing “seriousness of the Charter violations”: balance three categories—(1) fairness of trial, (2) seriousness of the Charter breach (incl. good/bad faith, reasonable and probable grounds, intrusiveness), and (3) effect of exclusion/admission on repute of justice—asking whether “having regard to all the circumstances, the admission ... would bring the administration of justice into disrepute”
BaselineB: Combination of constitutional text and common law framework: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 24(2) (and related ss. 8, 10); common-law/precedential framework from R. v. Collins (as organized in Simmons/Jacoy)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Public access to executed search warrants/informations: general rule of access after execution (and items brought before a justice), subject to denial only where needed to protect 'social values of superordinate importance'—notably 'protection of the innocent' where 'nothing is found'; issuance proceedings may be in camera to protect the administration of justice
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law/open court principle: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 443 and 446, plus common law policy of openness in judicial acts (e.g., Scott v. Scott; McPherson v. McPherson; Gazette Printing Co. v. Shallow, as discussed in the reasons)
CaseB_TestB: Two-branch test for a bona fide occupational qualification/requirement (BFOQ): (1) subjective—imposed 'honestly, in good faith, and in the sincerely held belief' it is for adequate performance and 'not for ulterior or extraneous reasons'; and (2) objective—'reasonably necessary' to assure performance (here reframed as necessity to accomplish the Church’s objectives in operating a Catholic school)
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law test: Human Rights Code, R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 186, s. 8 (and related s. 22 context), applying the common-law/precedential BFOQ framework from Ontario Human Rights Commission v. Etobicoke (Borough of), [1982] 1 S.C.R. 202
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Validity of a Quebec deed of donation and trust benefiting unborn (non-existent) primary beneficiaries: interpret Civil Code art. 981a “subject to the special characteristics of the trust” so that (i) trustee acceptance suffices to make the trust irrevocable and (ii) trustee holds ownership during the trust, meaning it is “not necessary that there be beneficiaries in whom ownership of the property conveyed is vested”; arts. 981a et seq. must be given a “wide and liberal interpretation” to permit benefits for non-existent persons unless barred by public order.
BaselineA: Statute (Civil Code of Quebec provisions on trusts and gifts): arts. 981a, 981b, 981l (trusts) read with arts. 754, 755, 765, 771, 772, 929 (gifts/substitutions/capacity). Key prior SCC baseline cases discussed: Curran v. Davis (trustee acceptance suffices; nature of trust gift) and related jurisprudence on trust property/beneficiaries.
CaseB_TestB: When an injunction in private civil litigation may effectively bind non-parties (enforceable by contempt): courts have jurisdiction to make orders binding on non-parties; because non-parties may be held in contempt, they must (i) be “apprised of the existence and terms of the order” and (ii) be “given an opportunity to comply”; it is “desirable” that the order speak of non-parties’ duty to respect it; and it is “necessary” that orders be “carefully worded and constrained” so they are “fair and not unduly broad.”
BaselineB: Combination of common law equitable/inherent jurisdiction principles (injunctions and contempt) and statute: Law and Equity Act, R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 224, s. 36 (“just or convenient” interlocutory injunctions) and Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 11 (civil remedies not suspended by criminality). Key prior SCC baseline case cited on practice: International Longshoremen's Association, Local 273 v. Maritime Employers' Association.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: When Parliament has given a “clear indication” of intent to permit multiple convictions/punishments for the same delict, the Kienapple bar does not apply (applied to Criminal Code s. 83(2) consecutive-sentence scheme for using a firearm while committing/attempting an indictable offence).
BaselineA: Combination of common law and statute: common law rule against multiple convictions from Kienapple v. The Queen (and Cox and Paton v. The Queen), applied/limited by interpretation of Criminal Code ss. 83(1)-(2) (use of a firearm; consecutive sentence) and s. 21 (parties).
CaseB_TestB: Interjurisdictional immunity two-step test: (1) does the provincial/municipal measure trench on the “core” of a federal power; and (2) is the effect sufficiently serious to “impair” (not merely “affect”) that core (here, siting of radiocommunication infrastructure; “seriously and significantly impaired”).
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine (interjurisdictional immunity) as articulated in Canadian Western Bank and COPA, applied with reference to precedent (Toronto Corporation v. Bell Telephone) and to the federal radiocommunication power (Constitution Act, 1867 ss. 91(29), 92(10)(a)).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: When s. 25(3) of Saskatchewan’s Trade Union Act permits an arbitrator to substitute a lesser penalty in a discharge grievance (cause/penalty interrelated; applies unless the infraction carries a specified penalty of discharge)
BaselineA: Statute: The Trade Union Act, R.S.S. 1978, c. T-17, s. 25(3), applied alongside the collective agreement’s dismissal/reinstatement provisions (arts. 6(4) and 12(12)(a))
CaseB_TestB: Article 1F(a) complicity (refugee exclusion) contribution-based test: exclusion only if there are serious reasons for considering the claimant voluntarily made a knowing and significant contribution to the group’s crime or criminal purpose (guided by non-exhaustive contextual factors)
BaselineB: Statute + treaty: Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, s. 98 incorporating Refugee Convention, art. 1F(a) (with interpretation informed by international criminal law sources such as the Rome Statute)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 43 Canada Evidence Act letters rogatory: (i) s. 43 permits an order for production of documents alone (not only documents ancillary to viva voce testimony) and (ii) comity-based guidelines for granting judicial assistance (trial not discovery; relevancy for commissioner/foreign court; scope permitted domestically; documents adequately defined).
BaselineA: Statute (Canada Evidence Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-10, s. 43) interpreted in light of comity and prior guidance (including Zingre v. The Queen, [1981] 2 S.C.R. 392).
CaseB_TestB: Admissibility of defence-led unknown third party suspect evidence: (1) evidence must be relevant to a fact in issue (logical relevance shown by a sufficient connection/similarity between the charged crime and another incident plus evidence the accused could not have committed the other offence); and (2) evidence is admissible unless its prejudicial effects substantially outweigh its probative value (Seaboyer balancing), without the judge weighing credibility or requiring proof on a balance of probabilities.
BaselineB: Common law evidence principles, especially R. v. Seaboyer, [1991] 2 S.C.R. 577 (defence evidence excluded only if prejudice substantially outweighs value), plus logical relevance (Corbett) and air of reality (Cinous) as supporting concepts.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Civil Code art. 1055 “ruin of a building” liability limited by intended purpose: owner not liable where the victim used the building/part for a purpose contrary to that for which it was intended (and, separately, a “trap” under art. 1053 requires a hidden, non-apparent danger)
BaselineA: Statute (Quebec Civil Code, arts. 1053, 1054, 1055), as interpreted in prior SCC authority including Leznek v. City of Verdun, [1940] S.C.R. 313 and Curley v. Latreille (1920), 60 S.C.R. 131
JudgeA: Beetz J. (for Beetz, Chouinard and Lamer JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Mental capacity standard for confessions/right to silence/s.10(b) waiver: the accused must have an “operating mind” (limited cognitive capacity) — understand what is being said and that it can be used against him; no separate “awareness of consequences” test; inner compulsion alone doesn’t negate voluntariness absent police conduct
BaselineB: Combination of common law confession/voluntariness doctrine and Charter standards (ss. 7, 10(b)), building on SCC cases including Ward, Horvath, Nagotcha, Clarkson, and Hebert
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Judicial review of a labour board’s “home statute” interpretation under a privative clause: intervene only if the interpretation is “patently unreasonable” / “plainly unreasonable” (i.e., cannot be rationally supported by the legislation)
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law (administrative law deference under privative clauses). Statutory baseline: The Public Service Employee Relations Act, 1977 (Alta.), c. 40, ss. 9, 11, 89 (review by certiorari/mandamus) and s. 48 (non-arbitral items). Common-law baseline as cited: Canadian Union of Public Employees Local 963 v. New Brunswick Liquor Corporation, [1979] 2 S.C.R. 227; Volvo Canada Ltd. v. U.A.W., Local 720, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 178; Douglas Aircraft Co. of Canada v. McConnell, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 245.
CaseB_TestB: Duty to accommodate adverse-effect religious discrimination: once adverse-effect discrimination is shown, the employer must take “reasonable steps to accommodate … short of undue hardship” (no de minimis threshold); undue hardship assessed with non-exhaustive factors (e.g., financial cost, disruption of collective agreement, morale/impact on others, interchangeability, size, safety)
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law. Statutory baseline: Quebec Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms, R.S.Q., c. C-12, ss. 3, 10, 16 (and related provisions); also Labour Code, R.S.Q., c. C-27, ss. 139, 139.1 (privative clause context). Common-law baseline as cited: Ontario Human Rights Commission and O'Malley v. Simpsons-Sears Ltd., [1985] 2 S.C.R. 536 (adverse-effect discrimination and accommodation); Central Okanagan School District No. 23 v. Renaud, [1992] 2 S.C.R. 970; Central Alberta Dairy Pool v. Alberta (Human Rights Commission), [1990] 2 S.C.R. 489.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Similar fact evidence admissibility: (1) apply the Makin/Boardman principle that admissibility depends on probative value balanced against prejudice; and (2) as a threshold, "Before evidence may be admitted as evidence of similar facts, there must be a link between the allegedly similar facts and the accused"—i.e., "some evidentiary link, direct or circumstantial, with the accused" (similarity alone is insufficient).
BaselineA: Common law (Makin v. A-G for New South Wales; Boardman v. DPP; Harris v. DPP; Thompson v. The King)
CaseB_TestB: Charter vagueness test (s. 7 / s. 1 in limine): "a law will be found unconstitutionally vague if it so lacks in precision as not to give sufficient guidance for legal debate" (fair notice + limiting enforcement discretion).
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine under the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7 (building on the Prostitution Reference and related SCC vagueness jurisprudence)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 16(2) insanity (first arm): “incapable of appreciating the nature and quality of an act” is limited to appreciating the physical character and physical consequences of the act (mens rea/actus reus consequences), and does NOT include failure to appreciate “penal sanctions” or “consequence of punishment”.
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 16(2)), interpreted in light of SCC cases including Cooper v. The Queen, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 1149; R. v. Barnier, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 1124; Kjeldsen v. The Queen, [1981] 2 S.C.R. 617; Schwartz v. The Queen, [1977] 1 S.C.R. 673.
CaseB_TestB: Administrative tribunal jurisdiction to apply the Constitution (including s. 35): “the essential question is whether the empowering legislation implicitly or explicitly grants to the tribunal the jurisdiction to interpret or decide any question of law”; if yes, the tribunal is presumed to have “concomitant jurisdiction” to decide the issue in light of s. 35 (or other constitutional provisions) unless a “clear implication” rebuts it.
BaselineB: Common law presumption about tribunal constitutional jurisdiction as articulated with reference to Nova Scotia (Workers’ Compensation Board) v. Martin, 2003 SCC 54, and related tribunal-jurisdiction jurisprudence, applied to the Forest Practices Code of British Columbia Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 159 (notably s. 131(8) allowing submissions as to “facts, law and jurisdiction”).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Patentable “invention” as a “new and useful art”: discovery of a new use for an old compound is patentable where it is an “application of this new knowledge to effect a desired result which has an undisputed commercial value”, and the claimed compositions are the “practical embodiment of the new knowledge” (no separate inventive ingenuity required in mixing with conventional adjuvants if mixing is necessary to give practical effect to the new use).
BaselineA: Statute (Patent Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. P-4), especially s. 2 definition of “invention” and s. 36 claiming/specification requirements; interpreted against prior case law including Farbwerke Hoechst, Ciba, and Hickton’s Patent Syndicate.
CaseB_TestB: Party liability for drug trafficking by aiding/abetting: under Criminal Code s. 21(1), to aid is “to assist or help the actor” and to abet includes “encouraging, instigating, promoting or procuring”; an agent/assistant of a purchaser can be guilty as a party to trafficking if they in fact assist/encourage the sale, and for s. 21(1)(b) the Crown need prove only that the accused intended the consequences of their aid (“purpose” = “intention”, not “desire”).
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, s. 21(1)(b),(c); Narcotic Control Act, ss. 2 “traffic”, 3(1), 4(1),(2)), as interpreted with prior SCC authority (notably Hibbert on “purpose” and Poitras on purchaser not trafficking by purchase alone).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory incompatibility/repugnancy test for whether a permissive municipal discretion (Police Act, s. 24(6)) excludes a collectively-bargained/arbitrated working-condition clause authorized by s. 29(2): ask whether the provisions are “incompatible or inconsistent”; if not, “each has its own area of operation” and the clause is valid.
BaselineA: Statute (The Police Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 351, ss. 24(6) and 29(2))
CaseB_TestB: State Immunity Act interpretation test for the s. 6(a) “death or personal or bodily injury … that occurs in Canada” exception: (1) the exception applies only where “the tort causing the personal injury or death” occurred in Canada; and (2) “some form of a breach of physical integrity must be made out” (psychological distress qualifies only if linked to physical injury).
BaselineB: Statute (State Immunity Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. S-18, ss. 3(1), 6(a); relying on Schreiber v. Canada (Attorney General), 2002 SCC 62 for the physical-integrity requirement)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory incompatibility/repugnancy test for whether a permissive municipal discretion (Police Act, s. 24(6)) excludes a collectively bargained/arbitrated clause under s. 29(2): s. 24(6) is an 'empowering provision only' and does not preclude bargaining unless the provisions are 'incompatible or inconsistent'; if not, 'each has its own area of operation'.
BaselineA: Statute (The Police Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 351, ss. 24(6) and 29(2))
CaseB_TestB: Corporate attribution under BIA s. 96(1)(b)(ii)(B) (transfer at undervalue): for this statutory context, the 'fraud' and 'no benefit' exceptions do not apply; 'the test for corporate attribution under s. 96 is simply whether the person was the directing mind and whether their actions were performed within the sector of corporate responsibility assigned to them'.
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act, s. 96(1)(b)(ii)(B) (and CCAA, s. 36.1) applied with the common law corporate attribution doctrine from Canadian Dredge & Dock Co. v. The Queen; Deloitte & Touche v. Livent; DeJong
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Jennings test for establishing a constitutional convention: (1) what are the precedents; (2) did the actors in the precedents believe they were bound by a rule (recognition/acceptance); and (3) is there a reason for the rule — with recognition by the actors emphasized as the “most important element”
BaselineA: Common law (constitutional conventions doctrine), adopting Sir W. Ivor Jennings’ three-question test as approved in Re: Resolution to amend the Constitution, [1981] 1 S.C.R. 753 (and the Manitoba Reference definition quoted there)
CaseB_TestB: Reasonable suspicion standard authorizing sniffer-dog searches: police may deploy a drug detection dog without prior authorization where there is “reasonable suspicion based on objective, ascertainable facts” assessed on the “totality of the circumstances” (a sufficiently particularized ‘constellation of factors’), with reliability of the dog relevant to reasonableness
BaselineB: Common law Charter s. 8 framework for warrantless searches (R. v. Collins) as applied to sniffer dogs in R. v. Kang-Brown and R. v. A.M.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory tribunal (art. 846 C.C.P.) test for labour arbitrators: even if parties were not compelled to arbitrate, an arbitrator is a “statutory tribunal” where, once arbitration is chosen, the arbitrator is “invested with wide duties and powers by statute” (e.g., Canada Labour Code s. 157) and thus subject to evocation; refusal to hear “admissible and relevant evidence” is “so clear a case of excess or refusal to exercise jurisdiction” that it justifies evocation.
BaselineA: Combination of common law criteria for certiorari/evocation against arbitrators (Howe Sound Co. v. International Union of Mine, Mill and Smelter Workers; Port Arthur Shipbuilding Co. v. Arthurs; R. v. National Joint Council for the Craft of Dental Technicians) and statutory provisions: Code of Civil Procedure (Quebec) art. 846 (and art. 33 discussed) plus Canada Labour Code ss. 156(2), 157, 159, 160(5).
CaseB_TestB: Sublicence characterization test in patent licensing: a sublicence exists only if the licensee “grant[ed], either expressly or impliedly, the right to do something which [the third party] would otherwise be prohibited from doing, and which [the licensee] was permitted to do only by virtue of its compulsory licence”; assess from the contract’s text (subjective intention inadmissible if unambiguous) and its “actual legal effect”.
BaselineB: Common law principles of patent licensing and contractual interpretation (e.g., Consolidated-Bathurst Export Ltd. v. Mutual Boiler; Lampson v. City of Quebec; Indian Molybdenum Ltd. v. The King) applied in the statutory context of the Patent Act compulsory licensing regime (notably s. 39(4), and timing limits in ss. 39.11 and 39.14) and related NOC Regulations context.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Kienapple remedy direction: where Kienapple applies, enter a stay of proceedings rather than an acquittal
BaselineA: Common law (Kienapple v. The Queen, [1975] 1 S.C.R. 729 double-conviction principle)
CaseB_TestB: Removing/replacing a litigation guardian: the Rule 49(1) test turns on the dependent adult’s “best interests”, guided by the Szwydky criteria (including required “indifference”/no conflict)
BaselineB: Combination of regulation/rules and common law: Queen’s Bench Rules (Saskatchewan) r. 49(1) (“best interests”) as informed by Szwydky v. Magiera (1988) (six criteria, including “indifferent as to the outcome”)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Contract-interpretation test for the extent of the Company’s supply obligation: reconcile the general words in para. 1 (“to such an extent as the said Town… may require”) with the specific allocation provisions in paras. 6 and 8, holding the Town’s entitlement is capped at the para. 8 reserve (“retain and reserve… Four Thousand Horse Power… permanently available”) at the para. 5 ceiling price (“shall not in any event exceed… Fourteen Dollars ($14.00) per Horse Power per annum”).
BaselineA: Statute/contract instrument: the January 9, 1905 agreement (especially paras. 1, 5, 6, 8, 13). The Court held the federal/provincial statutes had no direct bearing on the dispositive issue.
CaseB_TestB: General Motors indicia for validity under the general branch of the federal trade and commerce power (Constitution Act, 1867, s. 91(2)): ask (1) part of a general regulatory scheme; (2) oversight of a regulatory agency; (3) concerned with trade as a whole rather than a particular industry; (4) provinces acting alone or together would be constitutionally incapable of enacting it; (5) failure to include one or more provinces would jeopardize successful operation elsewhere (indicia “not exhaustive” and “not necessary that they be present in every case”).
BaselineB: Common law constitutional test from General Motors of Canada Ltd. v. City National Leasing, [1989] 1 S.C.R. 641, applying Constitution Act, 1867, s. 91(2) (general trade and commerce power).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Contract-interpretation test for the extent of the Company’s obligation to supply Fort Frances power at the contract rate: reconcile the general ‘to such an extent as the said Town… may require’ language with the specific reservation/distribution clauses, yielding a fixed entitlement of 4,000 horsepower per annum at $14 per horsepower per annum (and no more at that rate). Key provisions: para. 1 (‘to such an extent as the said Town… may require’), para. 5 (price ‘shall not in any event exceed… Fourteen Dollars ($14.00) per Horse Power per annum’), and para. 8 (‘retain and reserve… Four Thousand Horse Power… permanently available’).
BaselineA: Common law (contract interpretation) applied to the January 9, 1905 agreement (especially paras. 1, 5, 6, 8, 13).
CaseB_TestB: Continuing-offence/party-liability test for kidnapping: (1) Kidnapping under Criminal Code s. 279(1) is a continuing offence that includes ensuing unlawful confinement—‘So long as the victim of the kidnapping remains unlawfully confined, the crime of kidnapping continues’ and ‘continues until the victim is freed’; and (2) latecomer party liability under s. 21(1) is established where, ‘with knowledge of the principal’s intention to see a continuing offence through to its completion’, the accused does (or omits) something ‘with the intention of aiding or abetting the commission of the ongoing offence’.
BaselineB: Statute interpreted in light of common law: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, ss. 279(1), 279(2), 21(1), informed by the common law understanding of kidnapping as an aggravated form of false imprisonment/unlawful confinement.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Trigger for mandatory municipal acquisition under Planning Act s. 70(1): land must be “designated under a land use by-law” (not merely in statutory plans) for park/public use, which then triggers the council’s duty to acquire within six months or amend the by-law
BaselineA: Statute: The Planning Act, 1977 (Alta.), s. 70(1) (and definition of “land use by-law” in s. 1(14))
CaseB_TestB: O’Connor stay-for-non-disclosure framework: s. 7 breach requires proof (balance of probabilities) that non-disclosure prejudiced/adversely affected full answer and defence; remedy is disclosure/adjournment unless prejudice is irremediable—only in the “clearest of cases” is a stay appropriate
BaselineB: Combination: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms ss. 7 and 24(1), building on common law abuse-of-process jurisprudence (e.g., R. v. Jewitt) and disclosure doctrine (R. v. Stinchcombe)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “has become regularly engaged in some other occupation” under Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, s. 44(1)(c): claimant must have worked in the new occupation on a regular (fixed-pattern) schedule; “regularly” concerns regularity/continuity of the work schedule (contrasted with “casual”/“intermittent”), not long-term duration or an intention to abandon the prior job/strike (employment may be only for the strike so long as it is regular during that period).
BaselineA: Statute: Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, s. 44(1)(c) (and interpretive context including s. 44(1)(b) and Regulations s. 49 defining “bona fide employed” as “not less than two weeks duration”).
CaseB_TestB: Whether an ISP “carr[ies] on ... ‘broadcasting undertakings’” under the Broadcasting Act when providing Internet access: interpret “broadcasting”/“broadcasting undertaking” in statutory context and purpose; entities that “merely provide the mode of transmission” and “take no part in the selection, origination, or packaging of content” (i.e., have no measure of control over programming and no role in advancing s. 3(1) content-focused policy objectives) are not “broadcasting undertakings”.
BaselineB: Statute: Broadcasting Act, S.C. 1991, c. 11, ss. 2(1) (“broadcasting”), 2(3), 3(1) (purposive/contextual interpretation of defined terms).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 450(1)(b) arrest-without-warrant test (and related s. 25(4) protection): validity turns on whether, on the circumstances apparent at the time, the suspect would have appeared to a reasonable person in the officer’s position to be committing an offence; plus cross-border fresh pursuit rule that the officer retains s. 25(4) ‘peace officer’ status if the pursuit commenced lawfully in-province and remains ‘fresh’ (until local authorities take over).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 450(1)(b) and 25(4); also ss. 449(1)(b), 25(1),(3)) as interpreted in R. v. Biron, [1976] 2 S.C.R. 56 (and discussion of Pritchard).
CaseB_TestB: Canada Labour Code s. 157(d)(ii) ‘specific penalty’ jurisdiction test: an arbitrator is deprived of substitution power only if “a specific penalty must be assigned to the particular infraction in the collective agreement”; a penalty is not ‘specific’ if it “can be chosen indiscriminately by the employer” or is only in an employer rule book rather than the collective agreement.
BaselineB: Statute (Canada Labour Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. L-1, s. 157(d), especially s. 157(d)(ii)) applied to the collective agreement terms.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Availability and scope of the Crown’s per quod servitium amisit action for injuries to Canadian Forces members deemed “servants of the Crown” (master may recover necessary expenses for loss of services, dependent on servant’s valid cause of action)
BaselineA: Combination: statute (Federal Court Act, R.S.C. 1970 (2nd Supp.), c. 10, s. 37 deeming Forces members servants of the Crown) plus common law per quod servitium amisit as recognized in SCC cases (The King v. Richardson; Nykorak v. Attorney General of Canada; Attorney-General of Canada v. Jackson; The Queen v. Murray)
CaseB_TestB: Mens rea for Criminal Code s. 121(1)(a): no “corrupt” purpose required; guilt requires intentional acceptance/demand of a benefit with knowledge of the circumstances (official status and quid pro quo for cooperation/assistance/influence re government business)
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 121(1)(a) (interpreted in light of Martineau v. La Reine and distinguished from Hinchey)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Timing rule for Attorney General stay under Criminal Code s. 508(1): the stay power begins only once a summons or warrant has issued (i.e., after the justice has decided to issue process; laying/receiving an information is not “finding” it).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 2, 455, 455.3, 503, 508)
CaseB_TestB: Statutory eligibility rule for discharge under Criminal Code s. 662.1(1): a discharge is unavailable if the offence is one “for which a minimum punishment is prescribed by law”; an offence has a minimum punishment if any minimum penalty is prescribed (e.g., s. 234(a) minimum $50 fine), even if an alternative punishment has no minimum.
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, ss. 234, 662.1(1) (and discussed: s. 645(2), s. 592))
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Timing/trigger for Attorney General’s Criminal Code s. 508 stay power: an information is “found” (and stay power begins) only after the justice decides to issue process (summons or warrant), not upon mere laying/receipt of the information
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34 as amended), especially ss. 455, 455.3, 503, 508
CaseB_TestB: Baker procedural fairness framework applied to municipal rezoning refusals: content of duty of fairness varies with five factors and, on these facts, required careful evaluation and reasons for refusing the 2nd and 3rd rezoning applications
BaselineB: Common law administrative law duty of procedural fairness (Baker v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration))
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Jurisdictional rule against joint trial on separate informations/indictments: even with consent, a judge is "without jurisdiction to try together separate informations or indictments" (Crane applied), unless a statute "expressly provide[s] otherwise".
BaselineA: Common law rule from Crane v. Public Prosecutor, [1921] 2 A.C. 299 (as applied/confirmed by the SCC); applied across Criminal Code and provincial summary conviction procedure absent express statutory authorization.
CaseB_TestB: Credibility-assessment guidance on (i) absence of evidence of motive to lie and (ii) lack of embellishment: motive-to-lie evidence may be considered but judges must avoid (1) treating "no evidence either way" as proof disproving a motive, and (2) reversing the burden by requiring the accused to show a motive; lack of embellishment "cannot be used to bolster" credibility and "simply does not weigh against it" (may relate to motive-to-lie assessment).
BaselineB: Common law credibility/W.(D.) framework from R. v. W.(D.) and related SCC authority (including Stirling; Vuradin; G.F.).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Marine insurance “perils of the seas” causation test for negligent acts: a loss is by perils of the seas where the proximate cause is a “fortuitous accident or casualty of the seas”; negligence does not bar recovery if the negligent act is tied to a foreseeable, peculiarly marine risk (“An act is not negligent in itself but only in relation to a foreseeable risk of harm. If that foreseeable risk of harm is a peculiarly marine risk, then the act, coupled with its foreseeable consequence, is a fortuitous accident of the seas and a peril of the seas and the proximate cause of the loss.”).
BaselineA: Statute (Insurance (Marine) Act, R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 203, Schedule “Rules for Construction of Policy” defining perils of the seas as “fortuitous accidents or casualties of the seas”; and Marine Insurance Act, R.S.B.C. 1960, c. 231, s. 57(2)(a) (now s. 56(2)(a)) on insurer liability despite crew negligence) plus common-law/authorities applied (Canada Rice Mills, Ld. v. Union Marine & General Insurance Co., [1941] A.C. 55; Cohen, Sons & Co. v. National Benefit Assurance Co. (1924), 18 Ll. L. Rep. 199).
CaseB_TestB: Section 35(1) threshold for who can claim Aboriginal rights: to be an “aboriginal peopl[e] of Canada”, a group must be “the modern-day successors of Aboriginal societies that occupied Canadian territory at the time of European contact” (which “may include Aboriginal groups that are now outside Canada”); if the threshold is met, apply the Van der Peet test (characterize right; prove integral pre-contact practice; prove modern right is “demonstrably connected to, and reasonably regarded as a continuation of,” the pre-contact practice).
BaselineB: Constitution (Constitution Act, 1982, s. 35(1)) and existing Aboriginal-rights common-law framework (R. v. Van der Peet, [1996] 2 S.C.R. 507, as restated in Lax Kw’alaams Indian Band v. Canada (Attorney General), 2011 SCC 56 at para. 46).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory “bridging” of an expired collective agreement: s. 70(1) preserves the parties’ right to invoke interest arbitration (and the right need exist only when notice to arbitrate is served, not when the award issues).
BaselineA: Statute (Ontario Labour Relations Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 232, s. 70(1) (now R.S.O. 1980, c. 228, s. 79)), applied alongside the collective agreement’s interest-arbitration provisions; supported by Bradburn v. Wentworth Arms Hotel Limited, [1979] 1 S.C.R. 846.
CaseB_TestB: Directed verdict / non-suit test: whether there is “any admissible evidence, whether direct or circumstantial, which, if believed by a properly charged jury acting reasonably, would justify a conviction”.
BaselineB: Common law test from United States of America v. Shephard, [1977] 2 S.C.R. 1067, as applied/confirmed in R. v. Monteleone, [1987] 2 S.C.R. 154.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: McKibbon conditions for when a non-AG (an AG’s agent) may prefer an indictment in a non-grand-jury province under Criminal Code s. 507(2)-(3), including additional counts disclosed by preliminary inquiry evidence
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 507(1)-(3))
CaseB_TestB: Van der Peet / Mitchell test for establishing an Aboriginal right under Constitution Act, 1982, s. 35(1): (1) ancestral practice/custom/tradition; (2) integral to distinctive culture; (3) reasonable continuity; plus 3-factor characterization of the claimed right
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine under s. 35(1), applying R. v. Van der Peet and Delgamuukw (and related s. 35 jurisprudence)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: First degree murder under Criminal Code ss. 212(b) + 214(2): planning and deliberation attaches to the intended killing (mens rea) and can classify as first degree even if an unintended victim is killed by accident or mistake; victim identity is irrelevant
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 212(b) and 214(2), within the homicide scheme including s. 205; classification principle from R. v. Farrant applied)
CaseB_TestB: Interpretation of Alberta Limitations Act s. 12 in conflicts cases: it applies Alberta limitation law only to "live" causes of action and does not revive an action already time-barred by the applicable foreign substantive law (lex loci delicti, including its limitation period)
BaselineB: Statute (Limitations Act, R.S.A. 2000, c. L-12, s. 12) interpreted against the common-law conflicts rule from Tolofson v. Jensen that lex loci delicti governs, including the foreign limitation period as substantive
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Mens rea for attempted murder: the Crown must prove a specific intent to kill; constructive/lesser murder intents (including s. 212(a)(ii) or s. 213 constructive murder) cannot ground an attempt
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code) interpreted in light of prior SCC authority
CaseB_TestB: “Establishment” under CHRA s. 11 / Guidelines s. 10: employees are in the same establishment if they are subject to a “common personnel and wage policy”; this is a factual inquiry into the employer’s common principles/approach (not a term-by-term comparison of collective agreements)
BaselineB: Statute plus regulation/guidelines (Canadian Human Rights Act, s. 11; Equal Wages Guidelines, 1986, s. 10)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Matrimonial property distribution under Saskatchewan’s Matrimonial Property Act: equal distribution presumption, with pre-marital property exempt only to its fair market value at marriage (s. 23), and no additional exemption via “capital base theory” or s. 21(2)(q); s. 23(4)-(5) discretion only to reduce (not increase) the exemption if it would be “unfair and inequitable” to exempt.
BaselineA: Statute: The Matrimonial Property Act, 1979 (Sask.), c. M-6.1, ss. 20, 21, 23 (and related distribution scheme).
CaseB_TestB: Aggravated assault (Criminal Code, s. 268(1)) in HIV non-disclosure cases: because s. 268(1) is consequence-based, the Crown must prove the aggravating consequence (“endangers the life”) beyond a reasonable doubt; if there is a reasonable doubt the complainant was capable of being endangered (e.g., could already have been HIV-positive), no aggravated assault, though attempted aggravated assault may be made out if intent and more-than-preparatory acts are proven.
BaselineB: Statute (as interpreted through prior SCC authority): Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, ss. 268(1), 24(1), 265(1)(a), 265(3)(c), 660; applying/clarifying Cuerrier and related mens rea/actus reus principles.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Mechanics’ lien “owner” test under s. 1(1)(d): a person is an owner if they (a) have an estate or interest in the land, (b) requested the work, and (c) the work was done “upon whose credit, or … on whose behalf, or … with whose privity or consent, or … for whose direct benefit” (with “request” assessed by taking an “overall view” of complex development arrangements, including agency).
BaselineA: Statute: The Mechanics’ Lien Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 267, s. 1(1)(d) (and applied with s. 5(1) lien entitlement/limits).
CaseB_TestB: Challenge for cause (Criminal Code s. 638(1)(b)) “realistic potential for juror partiality” test: generally requires (1) “that a widespread bias exists in the community”; and (2) “that some jurors may be incapable of setting aside this bias, despite trial safeguards, to render an impartial decision” (with the “overarching consideration… whether there exists a realistic potential for partial juror behaviour”).
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 638(1)(b) (as interpreted through prior SCC cases including R. v. Sherratt and R. v. Williams).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Anns-based duty of care for public authorities: (1) proximity/foreseeability between public authority and plaintiff; (2) whether considerations should “negative or limit” the duty (scope/class/damages), with a key limit that bona fide “policy” decisions are immune but “operational” implementation attracts a duty of reasonable care; nonfeasance/misfeasance is irrelevant where there is a duty to act (or at least to make a bona fide policy decision not to act).
BaselineA: Common law (Anns v. Merton London Borough Council, [1978] A.C. 728) applied alongside the Municipal Act, R.S.B.C. 1960, c. 255, s. 714 and the City’s building by-law imposing an enforcement duty on the building inspector.
CaseB_TestB: Implied s. 1 “prescribed by law” limit on Charter s. 10(b) at roadside sobriety screening: a limit may arise “by necessary implication” from a statute’s “operating requirements”; police sobriety-check measures are authorized if “reasonable and necessary” to fulfill the duty and are “incompatible with the exercise of the right to counsel,” and the resulting limit is then assessed under Oakes proportionality.
BaselineB: Constitutional + statutory interpretation: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms ss. 1 and 10(b), applying the “prescribed by law” concept from R. v. Therens and the implied-limit approach from R. v. Thomsen, in the context of Highway Traffic Act (Man.), s. 76.1(1) and Criminal Code ss. 253-254.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal defence of necessity (as an excuse): requires moral/normative involuntariness shown by (i) “urgent situation of clear and imminent peril”, (ii) “compliance with the law [is] demonstrably impossible” including “no reasonable legal alternative”, and (iii) proportionality (“harm inflicted must be less than the harm sought to be avoided”); Crown must disprove voluntariness beyond a reasonable doubt once properly raised.
BaselineA: Common law defence preserved by Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 7(3), drawing on Morgentaler v. The Queen, [1976] 1 S.C.R. 616 (necessity limited to “urgent situations of clear and imminent peril when compliance with the law is demonstrably impossible”).
CaseB_TestB: Section 8 Charter “reasonable expectation of privacy” (objective reasonableness) in undercover online sting: assessed on the “totality of the circumstances” via four inquiries (subject matter; direct interest; subjective expectation; and whether that expectation is objectively reasonable), with the majority holding that in these circumstances “adults cannot reasonably expect privacy online with children they do not know”, so s. 8 is not engaged and Criminal Code s. 184.2 is inapplicable absent a “private communication”.
BaselineB: Constitutional/common law Charter framework for s. 8 reasonable expectation of privacy (e.g., Edwards; Tessling; Spencer; Cole; Marakah) and statutory definitions in Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, Part VI, ss. 183 (“private communication”, “intercept”) and 184.2.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 613(1)(b)(iii) proviso: Crown must satisfy appellate court the verdict “would necessarily have been the same” absent the legal error; where the error is exclusion of exculpatory evidence, assess the whole record including the reasonable possible effect of the excluded evidence, with any reasonable effect enuring to the accused
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 613(1)(b)(iii)) as interpreted in Colpitts v. The Queen, [1965] S.C.R. 739 (Cartwright J. at p. 744: Crown must show verdict “would necessarily have been the same if such error had not occurred”)
CaseB_TestB: When an appellate court may raise a new issue: only in rare circumstances—only when failing to do so would risk an injustice (i.e., there is “good reason to believe” the result would realistically have differed absent the potential error), and the court should also consider jurisdiction, sufficiency of the record, and procedural prejudice; if raised, there must be notice and opportunity to respond
BaselineB: Common law appellate procedure principles (party presentation/adversarial system; prior SCC guidance including R. v. W. (G.) and Quan v. Cusson) refined into an articulated threshold and considerations
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Two-criteria test for whether a provincial decision-maker is exercising a “judicial power” for s. 96 purposes: (1) whether there is a real “lis between the parties”; and (2) whether the decision is based on “considerations of legality” or instead on “considerations of expediency” (if not judicial, s. 96 is not infringed).
BaselineA: Common law / constitutional jurisprudence under Constitution Act, 1867, s. 96 (drawing on Re Residential Tenancies Act, 1979; Grondin; Coopers and Lybrand; and the John East Iron Works two-fold approach).
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 12 mandatory-minimum framework (as applied to robbery MMPs): two-stage inquiry—(1) determine a “fit and proportionate sentence”; (2) ask whether the law requires a sentence that is “grossly disproportionate” compared to that fit sentence, assessed via (i) “scope and reach of the offence”, (ii) “effects of the penalty on the offender”, and (iii) “the penalty and its objectives”; analysis may be based on the actual offender or a “reasonably foreseeable case”.
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 12; Criminal Code sentencing provisions (including ss. 718.1 and 718.2(e)); and SCC s. 12 jurisprudence (especially Hills, Smith, Nur, Lloyd, Bissonnette, Boudreault).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 93(1) denominational schools protection: a provincial education law is invalid if it "prejudicially affect[s]" a denominational-school "Right or Privilege" that a "Class of Persons" had "by Law" "at the time of the Union" (conditions: (a) right/privilege affecting a denominational school; (b) enjoyed by a class of persons; (c) by law; (d) in effect at Union; (e) prejudicially affected).
BaselineA: Constitution Act, 1867, s. 93(1) (and s. 93(2)); applied against Quebec's Act respecting municipal taxation and providing amendments to certain legislation, 1979 (Que.), c. 72 (school financing amendments to the Education Act).
CaseB_TestB: Young Offenders Act non-disclosure analysis: focus on whether the communication "create[s] a link between the identity of a young person and an (alleged) offence or hearing"; if the prohibited link is made, disclosure/publication is barred unless a specific statutory exception applies (e.g., s. 44.1(1)(k) requires judicial authorization and disclosure only to the extent directed; s. 38(1.13) requires disclosure be "necessary" for compliance or safety and directed to the responsible school board).
BaselineB: Statute: Young Offenders Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. Y-1, especially ss. 38(1), 38(1.1), 38(1.13) and ss. 40-46 (including s. 44.1 and s. 46).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 93(1) denominational schools guarantee: a provincial education law is invalid if it "prejudicially affect[s]" a protected denominational-school "Right or Privilege" that a "Class of Persons" had "by Law" "at the Union" (conditions: (a) right/privilege affecting denominational school; (b) class of persons; (c) by law; (d) in effect at Union; (e) prejudicially affected).
BaselineA: Constitution Act, 1867, s. 93(1) (and s. 93(2)); applied through Privy Council/SCC s. 93 jurisprudence (e.g., Barrett; Brophy; Hirsch; Tiny; Ottawa Separate Schools Trustees).
CaseB_TestB: Canadian maritime law scope (navigation and shipping): "the mere involvement of a pleasure craft in an incident is not sufficient"; court must examine the "factual context" and ask whether the allegedly negligent act is "integrally connected" to navigating the pleasure craft on Canadian waterways such that it is a "practical necessity" for Parliament to have jurisdiction (otherwise provincial property and civil rights applies).
BaselineB: Common law constitutional/maritime-law framework from ITO — International Terminal Operators Ltd. v. Miida Electronics Inc.; Whitbread v. Walley; Ordon Estate v. Grail (applied to ss. 91(10) and 92(13) of the Constitution Act, 1867).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Certiorari review of a preliminary inquiry committal: a committal is a reviewable jurisdictional error where there is "no evidence" on an essential element (" 'No evidence' on an essential element of the charge can never amount to 'sufficient evidence' under s. 475"; reviewing court must determine whether there was "any evidence at all" on each essential element).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, s. 475) as interpreted through SCC/PC certiorari jurisprudence (Patterson v. The Queen; Martin v. The Queen; Forsythe v. The Queen; Nat Bell Liquors).
CaseB_TestB: Criteria for compensatory allowance under art. 559 C.C.Q.: claimant must establish (1) contribution; (2) enrichment of spouse's patrimony; (3) causal link; and (4) proportion; "Each of these elements must be evaluated with great flexibility"; enrichment must "subsist" and be evaluated "at the time of the divorce".
BaselineB: Statute (Civil Code of Quebec, art. 559) informed by unjust enrichment principles (e.g., Cie Immobilière Viger Ltée v. Lauréat Giguère Inc.) and interaction with Bankruptcy Act, ss. 2 and 148.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Estoppel by representation (including by silence): requires a representation (words/conduct, or silence only where there is a legal duty to speak) that induces detrimental reliance; absent these conditions, estoppel does not preclude denial of contractual liability
BaselineA: Common law (estoppel by representation; contract inferred from conduct)
CaseB_TestB: Rebutting the s. 212(3) Criminal Code presumption: jury considers all the evidence about cohabitation and financial arrangements to decide whether there is 'evidence to the contrary'; no need to identify a single 'particular and severable' item
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 212(3))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Ultra vires municipal taxation where enabling statute requires a by-law: council cannot set a tax rate by resolution (self-redelegation) when the Legislature required exercise of the taxing power by by-law; resulting by-law/resolutions are void and excess of jurisdiction supports art. 33 C.C.P. nullity action
BaselineA: Statute (Cities and Towns Act, R.S.Q. 1941, c. 233, art. 526 as amended for Dorval; plus procedural requirements in Cities and Towns Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 193, including s. 395; and Code of Civil Procedure, art. 33 (formerly art. 50))
CaseB_TestB: Causation in negligent blood donor screening: apply the 'material contribution' test (not a rebuttable presumption and not strict 'but-for')—ask whether the defendant’s negligence 'materially contributed' to the injury; 'A contributing factor is material if it falls outside the de minimis range'
BaselineB: Common law (causation in negligence; but-for test and material-contribution line of cases, including Snell v. Farrell and Athey v. Leonati, as cited in the reasons)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 13 bar on using an accused’s prior testimony at a retrial: s. 13 applies at the moment the Crown attempts to use prior testimony; “any evidence the Crown tenders as part of its case against an accused is, for the purpose of s. 13, incriminating evidence”; and a retrial is “any other proceedings” (so the prior testimony is inadmissible except for perjury/contradictory evidence).
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 13 (interpreted in light of ss. 11(c) and 11(d)).
CaseB_TestB: Reformed rule for substantive admissibility of a non-accused witness’s prior inconsistent statement: admissible for truth if (threshold) it “would have been admissible as the witness’s sole testimony”; and on a s. 9 Canada Evidence Act voir dire the judge finds sufficient “circumstantial guarantees of reliability” (typically: (1) oath/affirmation/solemn declaration plus explicit warning of criminal sanctions, (2) videotaped in entirety, (3) full opportunity to cross-examine at trial), plus necessity (flexibly defined), and no voluntariness/administration-of-justice concerns.
BaselineB: Combination: statutory procedure (Canada Evidence Act, s. 9) plus common law hearsay/prior-inconsistent-statement doctrine (the “orthodox rule” from Deacon v. The King) reformed using the principled hearsay approach (Khan; Smith).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: When a trial judge’s acquittal can be appealed by the Crown as an “error of law alone”: a “total absence of evidence/foundation” is an error of law only where the law shifts the burden of proof to the accused on the fact in issue; otherwise (given the presumption of innocence) there is always some evidence on which to acquit and any mistake is an error of fact
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 605(1)(a) (Crown appeal on a question of law alone)) interpreted through SCC precedent (Sunbeam Corporation (Canada) Ltd. v. The Queen; Lampard v. The Queen; discussion of Wild v. The Queen and rejection of Lemire’s broader approach)
CaseB_TestB: Test for interim relief/stay (interim release) under Supreme Court Act s. 65.1: the RJR—MacDonald criteria—(1) serious question, (2) irreparable harm, (3) balance of convenience
BaselineB: Statute (Supreme Court Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. S-26, s. 65.1) applying the common-law/interlocutory-relief framework reaffirmed in RJR—MacDonald Inc. v. Canada (Attorney General)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: When a trial judge’s factual finding (supporting an acquittal) can be treated as an error of law for Crown appeal: only where there is a “total absence of a foundation” and, for acquittals, this occurs only if the law shifts the burden of proof to the accused on that fact
BaselineA: Combination: statute (Criminal Code appeal-from-acquittal jurisdiction) plus SCC common law on fact/law distinction and “no evidence” errors
CaseB_TestB: Ontario anti-SLAPP dismissal framework under Courts of Justice Act s. 137.1: (1) defendant shows on balance of probabilities the proceeding “arises from” its “expression” that “relates to a matter of public interest”; then (2) plaintiff must show “grounds to believe” the claim has “substantial merit” and defendant has “no valid defence”, and (3) the harm/public-interest in continuing the proceeding “outweighs” the public interest in protecting the expression
BaselineB: Statute: Courts of Justice Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.43, s. 137.1(3) and s. 137.1(4)(a)-(b) (and related ss. 137.1(2), 137.2)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Lawfulness of warrantless arrest on private premises (forcible entry) under s. 450(1)(a): arrest is lawful only if all four questions are answered “yes” (indictable offence; reasonable and probable grounds re offence; reasonable and probable grounds suspect is within; proper announcement before entry).
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 450(1)(a) (arrest without warrant for indictable offence) plus common law entry limits from Eccles v. Bourque, [1975] 2 S.C.R. 739 (itself drawing on Semayne’s Case).
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 15 discrimination analysis (as applied here): even if a law denies “equality before the law”, it violates s. 15 only if the distinction is discriminatory—i.e., a distinction “based on grounds relating to personal characteristics” that imposes burdens/withholds benefits; requires examining the “larger social, political and legal context” and typically a showing of pre-existing disadvantage.
BaselineB: Constitutional baseline: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 15(1), interpreted through Andrews v. Law Society of British Columbia, [1989] 1 S.C.R. 143 (definition/approach to discrimination).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 529 amendment test for variance between indictment particulars and proof: court should amend unless the accused was “misled or prejudiced in his defence” and the amendment cannot be made “without injustice being done” (with possible adjournment to cure prejudice).
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 529(4)-(5) (amendment considering (a)-(e), including prejudice/misleading and injustice; adjournment to cure prejudice) and appellate amendment power under ss. 613(1)(b)(i), 613(3); applied alongside the Narcotic Control Act definition of “narcotic” (ss. 2, 4, schedule item 3).
CaseB_TestB: Ineffective assistance of counsel (G.D.B.) test: appellant must show (1) counsel’s acts/omissions constituted “incompetence” and (2) “a miscarriage of justice resulted”.
BaselineB: Common law: R. v. G.D.B., 2000 SCC 22, [2000] 1 S.C.R. 520 at para. 26 (two-part incompetence + miscarriage of justice test).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Concurrent liability in tort and contract for professional negligence: a common law duty of care may arise from a contractual relationship of sufficient proximity, but tort cannot be used to circumvent contractual limits. Key limits include: the tort duty must not depend on express contractual specifications (“between what is to be done and how it is to be done”); and “A concurrent or alternative liability in tort will not be admitted if its effect would be to permit the plaintiff to circumvent or escape a contractual exclusion or limitation of liability”.
BaselineA: Common law (duty of care/proximity and negligent misrepresentation principles from Donoghue v. Stevenson; Hedley Byrne; Anns v. Merton London Borough Council; and SCC discussion of Nunes Diamonds).
CaseB_TestB: Jurisdiction in an action in warranty where there is an exclusive choice-of-forum clause: art. 3148 para. 2 C.C.Q. prevails over art. 3139 C.C.Q. if the clause shows a “clear intention to oust the jurisdiction of the Quebec authority”; then “the Quebec authority must decline jurisdiction”. Forum non conveniens (art. 3135) is “applicable only where the jurisdiction of the Quebec court has first been established”.
BaselineB: Statute (Civil Code of Québec, especially arts. 3148 para. 2, 3139, and 3135).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Scope of Quebec Construction Industry Labour Relations Act/Decree turns on the nature of the work ("look at the nature of the work done and not simply at the status of the parties"); if work is "construction" and no s. 2 exception applies, the Decree’s specific minimum conditions must be paid and no "total wage" set-off/equivalency is permitted
BaselineA: Statute and regulation: Construction Industry Labour Relations Act, S.Q. 1968, c. 45 (ss. 1(e),(i),(j),(p),(r), 2(2)) and Decree respecting the construction industry (ss. 3.01, 3.02; plus public-order clauses such as Act s. 20 and Decree ss. 18.06, 32.03)
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 12 mandatory-minimum analysis and remedy: a sentence violates s. 12 only if "grossly disproportionate" ("so excessive as to outrage standards of decency" / "abhorrent or intolerable"); if a mandatory minimum is unconstitutional in a particular case, the proper remedy is s. 52 invalidity (no stand-alone constitutional exemption under Charter s. 24(1))
BaselineB: Combination of constitutional text and common-law Charter doctrine: Charter ss. 12 and 24(1) and Constitution Act, 1982 s. 52(1); gross disproportionality test from R. v. Smith and related cases; remedial framework from Schachter/Seaboyer/Osborne/Corbiere (as discussed in the reasons)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Parens patriae limit: a court may not authorize non-therapeutic sterilization of a mentally incompetent person; parens patriae discretion must be exercised only for the protected person’s benefit and with great caution
BaselineA: Common law (parens patriae jurisdiction as inherited from the English Court of Chancery/Lord Chancellor; referenced through historical Chancery/parens patriae authorities such as Wellesley v. Duke of Beaufort and Re X (a minor))
CaseB_TestB: Residual management rights ‘balancing of interests’ test: whether a unilaterally imposed workplace policy is a reasonable (and here, also fair) exercise of management rights, assessed by considering all surrounding circumstances and whether the policy strikes a reasonable balance between employer and employee interests
BaselineB: Common law / labour arbitration doctrine (KVP test; endorsed in Irving Pulp & Paper and applied to interpret collective agreement clause requiring employer to act “reasonably, fairly and in good faith”)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Kienapple (rule against multiple convictions) applicability: requires (1) sufficient factual nexus (usually: “Does the same act of the accused ground each of the charges?”) and (2) sufficient legal nexus—“only be satisfied if there is no additional and distinguishing element that goes to guilt” in the second offence; plus guidance on when elements are not “distinct or additional” (particularization; alternative methods to prove a single delict; evidentiary proxy/deeming).
BaselineA: Common law (Kienapple v. The Queen) as refined through SCC cases (e.g., Côté; Krug) and framed against Criminal Code overlap concepts (e.g., s. 11; included offence under s. 589).
JudgeA: The Chief Justice (Dickson C.J., for the Court)
CaseB_TestB: Meaning of “services … to the public” under Yukon Human Rights Act s. 8(a): two-part analysis—(1) identify the “service” on the facts; (2) determine whether it creates a “public relationship” between provider and user, assessed contextually using non-determinative criteria (e.g., “selectivity… diversity… involvement of non-members… commercial nature… intimate nature… purpose”).
BaselineB: Statutory interpretation of Yukon Human Rights Act, R.S.Y. 1986 (Supp.), c. 11, s. 8(a) (and context including ss. 1–6, 10), guided by analogous Canadian human rights provisions and Berg.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Ensite test for whether property is “used or held ... in the course of carrying on a business” (ITA s. 129(4)(a)(ii)): property must be “truly employed and risked in the business”; the inquiry is “whether the property was used to fulfil a requirement which had to be met in order to do business” and the “threshold ... is met when the withdrawal of the property would ‘have a decidedly destabilizing effect on the corporate operations themselves’.”
BaselineA: Statute (Income Tax Act, s. 129(4)(a)(ii) exclusion for “a property used or held ... in the course of carrying on a business”; interpreted with reference to Marsh & McLennan and March Shipping)
CaseB_TestB: Crown appeal from acquittal/new trial test under Criminal Code s. 686(4): the Crown must satisfy the court that “the verdict would not necessarily have been the same if the trial judge had properly directed the jury” (Vézeau; reaffirmed in Morin).
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, s. 686(4), applying the Vézeau v. The Queen / R. v. Morin formulation)
JudgeB: Cory J. (for Sopinka, Cory, Iacobucci and Major JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Public interest immunity for Cabinet documents: court must (i) conduct a preliminary judicial inspection and then (ii) balance the public interest in confidentiality against the public interest in the administration of justice, considering variables like the level/nature of policy, timing (contemporary vs stale), and importance/needs of the litigation
BaselineA: Common law (public interest immunity/Crown privilege doctrine), drawing particularly on Smallwood v. Sparling, [1982] 2 S.C.R. 686; also discussed: R. v. Snider, [1954] S.C.R. 479; Gagnon v. Commission des valeurs mobilières du Québec, [1965] S.C.R. 73; and Commonwealth authorities (e.g., Conway v. Rimmer; Burmah Oil; Sankey v. Whitlam)
CaseB_TestB: Adequacy review of a (pre-Lifchus) jury charge: whether the charge, read as a whole, shows “substantial compliance” with Lifchus/W.(D.) and whether there is a “reasonable likelihood that the jury misapprehended” the reasonable-doubt standard or the approach to conflicting evidence
