BaselineB: Common law (jury-instruction requirements) from R. v. Lifchus, [1997] 3 S.C.R. 320; R. v. W. (D.), [1991] 1 S.C.R. 742; and the appellate review framing in R. v. Starr, 2000 SCC 40
JudgeB: Major J. (for Major, Binnie, Arbour and LeBel JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 7 Charter limit on extradition: courts may intervene in surrender only where, in the particular circumstances, surrender would violate the principles of fundamental justice; intervention must be exercised with caution and limited to cases of “real substance” (generally after the executive surrender decision).
BaselineA: Constitution (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7) applied in the extradition context (with reference to the executive’s surrender discretion under the Extradition Act and treaty framework).
CaseB_TestB: Crown appeal jurisdiction test: a Court of Appeal may interfere with an acquittal on a Crown appeal only if the trial court erred “on a question of law alone” (Criminal Code, s. 605(1)(a); applying Schuldt).
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 605(1)(a)) as interpreted/applied in Schuldt v. The Queen, [1985] 2 S.C.R. 592.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 7 limit on extradition: courts may intervene only where surrender would, in the particular circumstances, violate the principles of fundamental justice (intervention limited to 'cases of real substance')
BaselineA: Constitution (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7) applied to extradition/surrender decisions; extradition framework under Extradition Act and treaty context
CaseB_TestB: Income Tax Act s. 20(1)(c)(i) purpose test for interest deductibility: whether, considering all the circumstances, the taxpayer had a reasonable expectation of income at the time the investment was made (income = taxable income, not net income)
BaselineB: Statute (Income Tax Act, s. 20(1)(c)(i)) interpreted in light of prior SCC interest-deductibility jurisprudence (e.g., Bronfman Trust; Shell Canada) and statutory interpretation principles
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Injurious affection where no land is taken: claimant must show the construction-caused damage would have been actionable at common law (nuisance), i.e., an indirect physical injury to land or a substantial interference with use/enjoyment that is unreasonable in all the circumstances; no recovery for mere loss of prospect/amenities from highway construction
BaselineA: Statute (Ontario Expropriations Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 154, ss. 1(e)(ii), 21) incorporating a common-law actionability requirement; the four conditions for injurious affection when no land is taken are taken from The Queen v. Loiselle, [1962] S.C.R. 624 at p. 627, including that the damage must be actionable at common law but for statutory authority, and must be from construction not use
CaseB_TestB: Adequacy of jury instructions on identity/party liability in murder: trial judge must instruct on all routes to liability arising on the evidence; it is sufficient if the charge, read as a whole, required the Crown to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused "actively participated" (had a physical role) in the killings, whether acting alone or "in concert with others"; correcting an erroneous "actual shooter" instruction to include "or was otherwise an active participant" does not necessarily cause a miscarriage of justice
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, especially s. 21 (parties), and appellate miscarriage-of-justice/curative proviso framework in s. 686(1)(b)(iii)); applied through common-law principles on jury-charge adequacy and routes to liability (e.g., R. v. Thatcher, [1987] 1 S.C.R. 652)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: s. 10(b) right-to-counsel compliance: absent proof the detainee did not understand the right, the detainee must show they asked for counsel and were denied (or denied any opportunity to ask); otherwise, once police promptly advise of the right, no further correlative duties arise until the detainee indicates a desire to exercise it
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 10(b) (with remedy context in s. 24(2)); applied approach drawn from R. v. Anderson (Ont. C.A.) as adopted by the SCC
CaseB_TestB: Disgorgement/accounting for employee’s secret profits: where an employee acting in a representative capacity (and/or without authority using employer funds) profits through bad faith/abuse of position, the employee must account for and remit the profits to the employer (via C.C.L.C. arts. 411 and 1713 principles and the broader good-faith/loyalty obligation)
BaselineB: Statute/civil code: Civil Code of Lower Canada, arts. 411 (possessor in bad faith) and 1713 (mandatary must render account and deliver/pay over all received under authority of mandate), extended by the Court to the employment/representative-capacity context
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Wigglesworth s. 11 Charter applicability test: a matter falls within s. 11 either (1) because "by its very nature it is a criminal proceeding" (public nature/public order and welfare) or (2) because conviction may lead to a "true penal consequence" (imprisonment or a fine of such magnitude as to redress a wrong to society at large); where the two conflict, the "by nature" test "must give way" to the "true penal consequence" test.
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 11 (opening words "Any person charged with an offence"); interpretive context includes the marginal note "Proceedings in criminal and penal matters".
CaseB_TestB: Functional approach to appellate review of jury charges: a charge is proper "[a]s long as" read "as a whole" it leaves the jury with a "sufficient understanding of the facts as they relate to the relevant issues"; juries must be "properly -- not perfectly -- instructed" (including relating crucial defence evidence to live issues, without unnecessary repetition).
BaselineB: Common law (jury-charge review principles) drawing on prior SCC authorities cited (e.g., Azoulay v. The Queen; Cluett v. The Queen; John v. The Queen).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: s. 577(1) Criminal Code “whole of the trial” / right to be present test: s. 577 is “triggered whenever the ‘vital interests’ of the accused are at stake” and includes jury selection; accused must be able to hear; breach is fundamental and not cured by s. 613(1)(b)(iii)
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 577(1); also discussed: ss. 569(2), 598, 599, 600, 613(1)(b)(iii)) plus prior SCC/CA interpretations (Basarabas and Spek v. The Queen; Vézina and Côté v. The Queen; Hertrich; Meunier v. The Queen)
CaseB_TestB: Common-law test for when an appellate court may set aside an acquittal and enter a conviction (instead of ordering a new trial): Crown must show (1) “had there been a proper application of the law, the verdict would not have been the same”, (2) the accused “should have been found guilty but for the error of law”, and (3) “all the findings necessary to support a verdict of guilty must have been made, either explicitly or implicitly, or not be in issue”
BaselineB: Common law (as stated in Vézeau v. The Queen; R. v. Courville/Courville v. The Queen) applied alongside Criminal Code, s. 613(4)(b)(ii)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: When a trial judge quashes a voidable charge under Criminal Code s. 529, the quashing is tantamount to an acquittal (triggering autrefois acquit) unless the charge was an absolute nullity/lack of jurisdiction; quashing is only permitted where the required amendment cannot be made without injustice/irreparable prejudice
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 529, 535, 537) informed by common law autrefois acquit principles and SCC cases (e.g., Riddle; Petersen; Doyle; Jewitt)
CaseB_TestB: Scope of acquired rights / legal non-conforming use: characterize the pre-existing use and assess whether changes are protected by considering intensification (difference in kind), remoteness of added/modified activities, and (where within original purpose) balancing remoteness with neighbourhood effects (7-step framework)
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: Act Respecting Land Use Planning and Development, R.S.Q., c. A-19.1, s. 113(18) (and s. 227) plus common law/non-conforming use jurisprudence (e.g., Central Jewish Institute v. City of Toronto)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Workmen’s privilege against an owner’s immovable where work is contracted through a lessee: a lessee is not a “builder/contractor” for arts. 2013e/2013f unless the owner–lessee agreement is a true construction contract that includes an owner-to-builder claim/undertaking to pay a construction contract price (a price fund from which the owner can retain to satisfy privileges).
BaselineA: Statute (Civil Code of Lower Canada), especially arts. 2013e and 2013f (and the construction-contract concept in art. 1060).
CaseB_TestB: Mental distress damages for breach of contract (Hadley v. Baxendale application): plaintiff must show (1) an object of the contract was to secure a psychological benefit bringing mental distress on breach within the parties’ reasonable contemplation at contract formation, and (2) the mental suffering was of a degree sufficient to warrant compensation (no independent actionable wrong required).
BaselineB: Common law (Hadley v. Baxendale remoteness/foreseeability; discussed through Vorvis and related authorities).
JudgeB: McLachlin C.J. and Abella J. (for the Court)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Unequal division of marital property under Marital Property Act s. 7(f): despite the equal-division principle in s. 2, a court may depart where it is of the opinion equal division would be inequitable; specifically, "where the property has been acquired exclusively or almost wholly through the efforts of one spouse and there has been no, or a negligible contribution to child care, household management or financial provision by the other" (circumstances relating to acquisition/maintenance/improvement) the court may exercise discretion under s. 7(f).
BaselineA: Statute: Marital Property Act, S.N.B. 1980, c. M-1.1, ss. 2, 3, 7 (especially s. 7(f) residual factor permitting unequal division where equal division would be "inequitable").
CaseB_TestB: Interjurisdictional immunity (constitutional inapplicability) for federal services: provincial laws of general application apply unless they "bear upon those subjects in what makes them specifically of federal jurisdiction"; for a federal service, its specific nature is affected if the provincial statute touches a "vital or essential aspect of its establishment, management or operation"—if so, the provincial scheme (here, the permit system) is constitutionally inapplicable to the federal service.
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine (interjurisdictional immunity) as articulated in prior SCC cases cited, especially Bell Canada v. Quebec (CSST), [1988] 1 S.C.R. 749 and Construction Montcalm Inc. v. Minimum Wage Commission, [1979] 1 S.C.R. 754; applied to provincial Transport Act/Bus Transport Regulation permit scheme.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “financing” in Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971 s. 44(2)(a): claimant is “financing” only where there is “active and voluntary involvement” and a “meaningful connection between the payment and the dispute” (mere mandatory union dues diverted to a strike fund are insufficient).
BaselineA: Statute: Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, S.C. 1970-71-72, c. 48, s. 44(2)(a) (exception to disentitlement where claimant proves he is not “participating in or financing or directly interested in” the labour dispute).
CaseB_TestB: Enforceability/scope of waiver (exclusion) clause for negligence in a race entry form: construed in its context to determine whether it releases the defendant(s) for the type of negligence that occurred; clause upheld where the negligence falls within what was contemplated and the clause is not shown to be “unfair” or “unreasonable” in the circumstances.
BaselineB: Common law contract interpretation/enforcement of exclusion/waiver clauses (including arguments framed as fundamental breach/unconscionability/public policy, treated as unnecessary on these facts).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “financing” in Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971 s. 44(2)(a): claimant is “financing” a labour dispute only where there is an active and voluntary contribution with a “meaningful connection” between the payment and the dispute (mandatory union dues alone are insufficient).
BaselineA: Statute: Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, S.C. 1970-71-72, c. 48, s. 44(2)(a) (exception where claimant proves he is not “participating in or financing or directly interested in” the labour dispute).
CaseB_TestB: Extradition surrender review: whether extradition would be contrary to s. 7 fundamental justice so as to “shock the conscience” or otherwise be “unjust or oppressive” under Extradition Act s. 44(1), assessed through a Ministerial balancing exercise (with deference/comity; intervention only in exceptional cases).
BaselineB: Statute (informed by Charter values): Extradition Act, S.C. 1999, c. 18, s. 44(1) (“unjust or oppressive”); Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7 (“principles of fundamental justice”), as applied in Burns and Lake.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 10 “detention” test (Therens criteria): detention occurs when the state assumes control over a person’s movement by a demand/direction with significant legal consequence, with compulsion/coercion (incl. criminal liability for refusal or reasonable belief of no choice), in a situation where counsel may reasonably be required and access to counsel is impeded
BaselineA: Common law/Charter jurisprudence interpreting Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 10 (b), principally R. v. Therens, [1985] 1 S.C.R. 613 (as restated and applied); applied to Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 234.1(1) demand context
CaseB_TestB: Mistake-of-age “all reasonable steps” framework under Criminal Code s. 150.1(4): once an air of reality exists, Crown must prove beyond a reasonable doubt either no honest belief complainant was at least 16 or failure to take “all reasonable steps”; what steps are required is contextual—“the more reasonable an accused’s perception of the complainant’s age, the fewer steps reasonably required of them”
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 150.1(4) (and related scheme); SCC clarifies application and evidentiary relevance within the statutory “all reasonable steps” requirement
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Extradition specialty/immunity duration: an undertaking not to prosecute for pre-surrender offences does not confer perpetual immunity; it ends once the extraditee has been "restored or has had an opportunity of returning" (i.e., a reasonable opportunity to return) and remains in Canada by choice rather than by reason of the surrender
BaselineA: Statute (Extradition Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-21, s. 33) interpreted in light of the extradition arrangement/undertaking and international law interpretive principles (Vienna Convention, art. 31)
CaseB_TestB: Criminal appeal scope/leave: where an appeal as of right is founded on a dissent on a question of law, the appellant may address all aspects of that question; the curative proviso in Criminal Code s. 686(1)(b)(iii) is "always intertwined" with the alleged error of law, so the Crown need not seek separate leave to appeal the refusal to apply the proviso
BaselineB: Common law principle from R. v. Keegstra, [1995] 2 S.C.R. 381, applied alongside Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(b)(iii)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code theft: whether an item falls within “anything” in s. 283(1) — it must (1) be “property of some sort” and (2) be “capable of being taken or converted in a manner that results in the deprivation of the victim”; confidential information per se fails (not property for policy reasons and, in any event, not capable of taking/conversion with deprivation).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 283(1)); interpretive backdrop includes R. v. Scallen (property requirement for “anything”) and the Code’s actus reus of “takes” or “converts” plus intent in s. 283(1)(a)-(d).
CaseB_TestB: Contractual interpretation of “assets” in MVHC’s Assistance Application: give the word its “ordinary and grammatical meaning” in context; a reasonable person would understand “assets” to mean “property or interest(s) in property that can actually be used to discharge ... debts and liabilities, including ... monthly rent”; a Henson trust interest (a “mere hope”) is not an asset because the beneficiary has “no enforceable right” and cannot use it to pay rent unless distributions are made.
BaselineB: Common law contractual interpretation (Sattva Capital Corp. v. Creston Moly Corp.; Ledcor Construction Ltd. v. Northbridge Indemnity Insurance Co.) applied to the tenancy agreement/assistance application documents (private contract instruments).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 7 two-step analysis applied to compelled fingerprinting: (1) deprivation of “life, liberty and security of the person”; (2) whether the deprivation is “contrary to the principles of fundamental justice” (including whether fingerprinting “unduly invades the rights of the accused” and whether the scheme is arbitrary).
BaselineA: Statute + constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7; Identification of Criminals Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-1, s. 2; Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 453.3(3) and 455.5(5). The Court frames the s. 7 method as: “The analysis of s. 7 of the Charter involves two steps” (para. 28).
CaseB_TestB: Sheppard/Braich test for appellate intervention based on insufficient reasons: two stages—“(1) are the reasons inadequate; (2) if so, do they prevent appellate review?”; the functional question is whether the reasons are “sufficiently amenable to appellate review” / whether there is “an impediment to appellate review”.
BaselineB: Common law framework from SCC precedents on sufficiency of reasons, especially R. v. Sheppard, 2002 SCC 26 and R. v. Braich, 2002 SCC 27 (as summarized at para. 13). (Criminal Code, s. 686 provides the appellate powers context but the operative “sufficiency of reasons” test is articulated through the case law.)
JudgeB: Bastarache and Abella JJ. (LeBel J. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Detention at the border (s. 10(b) Charter): a traveller is “detained” when a state agent “assumes control over the movement of a person by a demand or direction which may have significant legal consequence” (Therens) — applied here to a compelled customs strip search where the person “could not have refused and continued on her way” and was “subject to external restraint”.
BaselineA: Common law/constitutional interpretation of Charter s. 10(b) “detention”, based on R. v. Therens, [1985] 1 S.C.R. 613 (definition of detention) and applied in the customs-search context alongside Customs Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-40, ss. 143, 144, 203.
CaseB_TestB: Section 11(b) “reasonable time” analysis (Morin factors + institutional-delay guideline): determine unreasonableness by a non-formulaic balancing of (1) length of delay; (2) waiver; (3) reasons for delay (inherent requirements, actions of accused, actions of Crown, limits on institutional resources, other reasons); and (4) prejudice — with an administrative guideline of “between 8 and 10 months for institutional delay in Provincial Courts” (and 6–8 months post-committal).
BaselineB: Constitutional/common law framework interpreting Charter s. 11(b), drawing on prior SCC cases including R. v. Smith, [1989] 2 S.C.R. 1120 and R. v. Askov, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 1199 (and earlier Mills/Rahey/Conway), and applying Charter ss. 11(b) and 24(1).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Leary intoxication rule for general-intent offences (as applied to sexual assault causing bodily harm): intoxication generally irrelevant to mens rea except possibly where it raises doubt about voluntariness/automatism; Crown may prove mens rea by inference from actus reus or, in extreme cases, by proving voluntary self-induced intoxication
BaselineA: Common law (Leary v. The Queen; also relying on R. v. George and DPP v. Majewski) applied alongside Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 246.2(c) (offence definition)
CaseB_TestB: Appellate review of acquittal: (1) appellate court cannot overturn a trial judge’s inferences of fact on a Crown appeal merely because it would draw different inferences (Schuldt); but (2) it may intervene for an error of law where the trial judge failed to direct his or her mind to an issue requiring determination to reach the verdict
BaselineB: Common law (Schuldt v. The Queen; also referencing R. v. Morin and R. v. C.(R.))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Appellate intervention in a trial judge’s discretionary reapportionment of matrimonial property under s. 51: intervene only if the trial judge “misdirects himself” or the decision is “so clearly wrong as to amount to an injustice”
BaselineA: Combination: statute (Family Relations Act, R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 121, ss. 43 and 51) plus common-law appellate deference principles (applied from Harper v. Harper, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 2; also citing Re Hull Estate (Ont. C.A.))
CaseB_TestB: Duty to comment on prejudicial Crown jury-address remarks: where remarks are “prejudicial to a degree sufficient to impose a legal duty on the trial judge to comment” to ensure the defence is “fairly put to the jury”; failure is an error of law, and the curative proviso (s. 686(1)(b)(iii)) applies only if no substantial wrong/miscarriage of justice
BaselineB: Combination: statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(b)(iii)) plus common-law fairness control of jury addresses/charge (as adopted via the dissenting reasons of Ayles J.A. quoted and applied by the SCC)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Wigmore/Slavutych four-part test for recognizing a (qualified) common law privilege against compelled disclosure of communications: (1) communication originates in confidence; (2) confidentiality is essential to the relationship; (3) relationship is one the community ought to foster; (4) injury from disclosure outweighs benefit for correct disposal of litigation
BaselineA: Common law (Wigmore criteria as discussed/approved in Slavutych v. Baker, [1976] 1 S.C.R. 254)
CaseB_TestB: Reasonableness review of Crown corporations’ discretionary PILT calculations: discretion exists to choose the “effective rate”, but calculations must be based on the municipality’s actual existing tax system (as if the federal property were taxable private property) and cannot be based on a “fictitious tax system” (e.g., reintroducing an abolished occupancy tax)
BaselineB: Statute and regulation (Payments in Lieu of Taxes Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. M-13, ss. 2 (definitions incl. “effective rate”), 2.1, 4(1), sch. II item 10; Crown Corporation Payments Regulations, SOR/81-1030, ss. 2, 7(1))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Patent disclosure/sufficiency under Patent Act s. 36(1): applicant must disclose everything essential so a person skilled in the art can make/produce and use the invention; completeness requires two conditions—(1) describe the invention and define how it is produced or built; and (2) define the nature of the invention and describe how it is put into operation; mere deposit of a sample (here, seeds) is not, by itself, sufficient disclosure.
BaselineA: Statute (Patent Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. P-4, s. 36(1)), as interpreted through prior patent-law disclosure cases cited (e.g., Minerals Separation; Burton Parsons; Monsanto; Consolboard).
CaseB_TestB: Standard of review for labour-arbitration awards applying common law/equitable remedies: reasonableness remains the presumptive standard; correctness applies only to established Dunsmuir categories (constitutional questions, questions of general law of central importance outside expertise, true jurisdiction/vires, or competing-tribunal jurisdictional lines). Arbitrators may adapt doctrines like estoppel within a bounded ‘sphere of arbitral creativity’, subject to reasonableness review.
BaselineB: Common law administrative-law standard of review framework (Dunsmuir; Smith) applied in the labour arbitration context, alongside the statutory scheme (Labour Relations Act, R.S.M. 1987, c. L10, ss. 121, 128(2)).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 96 ‘Residential Tenancies’ three-stage test, clarified: (1) historical inquiry with narrow characterization and a ‘shared jurisdiction’ gloss requiring inferior-court involvement to be ‘broadly co-extensive’; (2) whether tribunal function is judicial; (3) whether, in institutional context, the judicial power is merely ancillary/necessarily incidental to a broader policy goal
BaselineA: Constitution Act, 1867, s. 96; common-law/constitutional doctrine from Re Residential Tenancies Act, 1979, [1981] 1 S.C.R. 714 (three-step framework), with related s. 96 jurisprudence (e.g., Grondin, Farrah, Tomko) as discussed in the reasons
CaseB_TestB: Public interest standing (Downtown Eastside) framework applied/clarified: court ‘must assess and weigh three factors’—(i) serious justiciable issue, (ii) genuine interest, (iii) reasonable and effective means—‘cumulatively, flexibly and purposively’; no ‘particular weight’ to legality/access to justice; no requirement of a directly affected co-plaintiff if a ‘sufficiently concrete and well-developed factual setting’ will be forthcoming; standing may be revisited only on a ‘material change’ raising serious doubt and where other litigation tools are inadequate
BaselineB: Common law doctrine of public interest standing from Canada (Attorney General) v. Downtown Eastside Sex Workers United Against Violence Society, 2012 SCC 45 (three-factor discretionary framework), as interpreted and applied in this decision
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Bankruptcy priority for provincial “statutory trust” tax funds: s. 47(a) applies only if the tax money is identifiable/traceable as trust property under general trust law; otherwise the province has only a Crown claim under s. 107(1)(j)
BaselineA: Statute (Bankruptcy Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. B-3, ss. 47(a) and 107(1)(j)) interpreted alongside provincial statute (Social Service Tax Act, R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 388, s. 18); SCC trust-law baseline referenced via Deputy Minister of Revenue v. Rainville and Deloitte Haskins and Sells Ltd. v. Workers' Compensation Board
CaseB_TestB: Section 23 “numbers warrant” / local facilities and management-control analysis: relevant numbers are between known demand and potential demand; defining the service area is case-by-case within minority management and control (subject to objective provincial norms consistent with s. 23), and the Minister’s approval role is limited to verifying compliance (no substitution of his own criteria)
BaselineB: Constitution (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 23) plus statutory/regulatory scheme (P.E.I. School Act and School Act Regulations) interpreted through Mahe v. Alberta (sliding scale; numbers warrant; management and control)
JudgeB: Major and Bastarache JJ. (for the Court)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Young Offenders Act s. 16 transfer to ordinary court: transfer is ordered if, after considering the s. 16(2) factors, the judge is satisfied (on a not-“heavy” onus) that transfer is appropriate, i.e., “after weighing and balancing all the relevant considerations”
BaselineA: Statute: Young Offenders Act, S.C. 1980-81-82-83, c. 110, s. 16 (especially ss. 16(1), 16(2), 16(9)-(10)); applied/clarified via R. v. M. (S.H.), [1989] 2 S.C.R. 000
CaseB_TestB: Contract damages where defendant had alternative modes of performance: assess damages on the basis of the mode “least profitable to the plaintiff, and the least burdensome to the defendant”; “The test is not how the defendant would likely have performed ... but for ... repudiation”
BaselineB: Common law principle from Cockburn v. Alexander (1848) and related authorities (e.g., Withers v. General Theatre Corp.) as adopted/confirmed in Canadian law
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Canadian maritime law test for an agent’s personal liability when principal is unnamed/partially disclosed: liability turns on the parties’ intention as shown by the contract—“the issue whether an agent contracted personally, or solely in the capacity of agent ... is a matter of construction of a particular contract”; “there is no prescribed formality for disclosure ... [it] depends on the will of the contracting parties.”
BaselineA: Common law (contract/agency) as part of Canadian maritime law under Federal Court Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. F-7, ss. 2 and 22(2)(m), building on ITO—International Terminal Operators Ltd. v. Miida Electronics Inc., [1986] 1 S.C.R. 752; also informed comparatively by C.C.L.C. arts. 1715-1716 (per L’Heureux-Dubé J.)
CaseB_TestB: Statutory “reasonable cause” threshold for immunity/duty-to-report child abuse: s. 38(6) protects an informant only if the report is not made “maliciously or without reasonable cause”; “Reasonable cause” is an objective threshold meaning the informant must have “reasonable cause to ask CPS to consider looking into the matter” (not reasonable grounds to believe abuse occurred).
BaselineB: Statute: Child Welfare Act, R.S.N. 1990, c. C-12, ss. 38(1) and 38(6) (interpreting the scope of the statutory duty to report and the immunity bar)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Common-law limits on a warrantless “frisk” search incident to a lawful arrest: no reasonable/probable grounds prerequisite, but search must (1) be discretionary and assessed case-by-case, (2) pursue a valid criminal-justice objective (safety/escape/evidence) and not an improper purpose, and (3) be conducted non-abusively with force/constraint proportionate to the objectives and circumstances
BaselineA: Common law (search incident to arrest), drawing on authorities discussed in the reasons including Leigh v. Cole (1853) and Canadian cases such as R. v. Brezack (1949) and R. v. Morrison (1987)
CaseB_TestB: Section 7 minimum procedural standard for warrantless child apprehension: the principles of fundamental justice do not require prior judicial authorization if the statutory scheme permits apprehension without prior authorization only where there is “serious harm or risk of serious harm” to the child, and it must be followed by a “fair and prompt post-apprehension hearing”
BaselineB: Statute interpreted/assessed under Charter s. 7: Child and Family Services Act, S.M. 1985-86, c. 8, s. 21(1) (with related context in ss. 17, 27(1), 29(1))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal negligence (s. 219): whether the accused’s conduct is a “marked departure from the norm” such that “the conclusion that there is a wanton or reckless disregard is to be drawn from the conduct which falls below the standard”; consequences generally add nothing unless “so interwoven” with the conduct as to help characterize it
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 202(1)-(2), 203 (now Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, ss. 219, 220); interpreted in light of R. v. Tutton, [1989] 1 S.C.R. 1392 (marked departure central under both objective and subjective approaches)
CaseB_TestB: Standing/jurisdiction before the CITT under the AIT: a complainant must be a “potential supplier” on a “designated contract”, and for AIT coverage the procurement must be “within Canada”, which requires the supplier to be a “Canadian supplier” (AIT art. 518: supplier with “a place of business in Canada”); non-Canadian suppliers therefore lack standing
BaselineB: Combination of statute/regulation and incorporated trade agreement: Canadian International Trade Tribunal Act, ss. 30.1 (definitions), 30.11(1); Canadian International Trade Tribunal Procurement Inquiry Regulations, ss. 3(1), 7(1), 11; interpreted with Agreement on Internal Trade, arts. 501, 502, 518
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 8 reasonableness of compelled document production in a regulatory/tax audit context: Hunter criteria are not "hard and fast"; reasonableness turns on a flexible, context-specific assessment (regulatory vs criminal), including the taxpayer’s relatively low expectation of privacy and the scheme’s need for random monitoring (s. 231(3) is the "least intrusive means").
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law/constitutional doctrine: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 8 applied to Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1952, c. 148, ss. 231(3), 238(2) (and privacy safeguard in s. 241), with baseline s. 8 reasonableness framework from Hunter v. Southam Inc. and related cases (e.g., R. v. Simmons).
CaseB_TestB: Public interest standing test (purposive, flexible, discretionary): courts weigh three interrelated factors—(1) serious justiciable issue; (2) plaintiff has a real stake/genuine interest; and (3) whether the proposed suit is, "in all of the circumstances", a "reasonable and effective means" to bring the case—rejecting a rigid requirement to show "no other" reasonable and effective means.
BaselineB: Common law doctrine of public interest standing from Borowski / Finlay / Canadian Council of Churches (reformulated/clarified here as a discretionary weighing of factors rather than a strict checklist).
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Duty to defend is determined by the pleadings: insurer must defend only claims that, on the pleadings, seek damages that "are or may be payable" under the policy (i.e., potentially within coverage); no duty where allegations are clearly outside coverage (e.g., only fraud alleged and fraud excluded).
BaselineA: Contract (insurance policy) interpreted using common-law insurance contract construction principles; key policy language: insurer must "[d]efend any suit... seeking damages which are or may be payable under the terms of this Policy"; exclusion for "dishonest, fraudulent, criminal or malicious act or omission". Supporting common-law principle cited: "[t]he pleadings govern the duty to defend" (Bacon v. McBride) and no duty where pleadings clearly fall within an exclusion (Opron Maritimes).
CaseB_TestB: Criminal Code s. 265(4) “air of reality” threshold for honest but mistaken belief in consent: defence goes to jury only if there is "sufficient evidence" such that "if believed" a reasonable jury properly instructed could acquit; requires evidence beyond a bare assertion of belief (though it need not be independent of the accused).
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 265(4)) interpreted in light of common-law “air of reality” jurisprudence on when defences are left to the jury (e.g., Pappajohn; Bulmer; Robertson; Brisson).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Collateral wage benefits and tort damages for lost earnings: “As a general rule, wage benefits paid while a plaintiff is unable to work must be brought into account and deducted from the claim for lost earnings”, with a limited exception where the payor has a subrogation/reimbursement entitlement (statute, valid third-party claim; rarely a trust where “necessary and appropriate in the interests of justice”).
BaselineA: Common law damages principles (compensation for “actual loss” and no double recovery) as articulated in Andrews v. Grand & Toy Alberta Ltd.; Thornton v. Prince George School Board; Arnold v. Teno, and collateral-benefit authorities including Parry v. Cleaver and Bradburn v. Great Western Rail. Co.
CaseB_TestB: Constitutional validity of GST collection scheme under the “necessarily incidental”/integration analysis: where a valid federal objective exists, impugned provisions affecting provincial jurisdiction are upheld if “sufficiently integrated with the scheme that [they] can be upheld by virtue of that relationship.”
BaselineB: Constitution Act, 1867 (especially ss. 91(3) and 92(13)) plus the SCC’s “necessarily incidental” doctrine as framed in General Motors of Canada Ltd. v. City National Leasing and Reference re Exported Natural Gas Tax.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Test for entitlement to a compensatory allowance under art. 559 C.C.Q.: claimant must establish (1) contribution, (2) enrichment of the other spouse’s patrimony, (3) causal link/correlation between the two, and (4) the proportion in which the contribution made possible the enrichment; the enrichment must subsist and is evaluated at the time of the divorce, with the elements assessed “with great flexibility”.
BaselineA: Statute (Civil Code of Quebec, art. 559), informed by unjust enrichment principles (e.g., “correlation” from Cie Immobilière Viger Ltée v. Lauréat Giguère Inc.).
CaseB_TestB: Morrissey test for setting aside a conviction for misapprehension of evidence: the misapprehension must go to “the substance” not “detail”, be “material” not “peripheral”, and the errors must play an “essential part” in the reasoning process resulting in conviction (a “stringent” conjunctive standard).
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: Criminal Code, s. 686(1)(a)(iii) (miscarriage of justice) (and interaction with s. 686(1)(a)(i)), applying/endorsing R. v. Morrissey and R. v. C. (R.).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Copyright infringement for software embedded in a silicon chip: a program in chip form is protected if it is a “reproduction” of the copyrightable program in written/assembly form (i.e., the chip is a “static object encoded with written instructions”, not merely a “dynamic interchange of electrical impulses”).
BaselineA: Statute — Copyright Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-30, s. 3(1) (including s. 3(1)(a) and (d) discussed but not decided).
CaseB_TestB: Common law de facto taking (constructive expropriation) requiring compensation: two requirements must be met — “(1) an acquisition of a beneficial interest in the property or flowing from it, and (2) removal of all reasonable uses of the property”.
BaselineB: Common law — test drawn from Mariner Real Estate Ltd. v. Nova Scotia (Attorney General) (N.S.C.A.), Manitoba Fisheries Ltd. v. The Queen, and The Queen in Right of British Columbia v. Tener; applied alongside statute (Vancouver Charter, s. 569) which deems no taking/compensation.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Novation (substitution of debtors) test: (1) new debtor assumes complete liability; (2) creditor accepts new debtor as principal debtor (not agent/guarantor); (3) creditor accepts new contract in full satisfaction and substitution for the old; and, absent express agreement, courts should be "loath to find novation unless the circumstances are really compelling"
BaselineA: Common law (novation doctrine), with the three-part test stated as being "set out in Polson v. Wulffsohn (1890)"; applied in mortgage context alongside statutory background
CaseB_TestB: De facto taking (constructive expropriation) test: compensation at common law requires (1) "an acquisition of a beneficial interest in the property or flowing from it" and (2) "removal of all reasonable uses of the property"
BaselineB: Common law (de facto taking) as articulated via Mariner Real Estate (N.S.C.A.) and SCC authorities Manitoba Fisheries and Tener; applied alongside statute (Vancouver Charter, especially s. 569 deeming no taking)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Applicability of Criminal Code s. 443 (now s. 487) search warrant power to offences under any federal statute: on a plain reading, after the 1985 amendment adding "or any other Act of Parliament" to s. 443(1)(a)-(b), a justice may issue a warrant where there are "reasonable ground[s] to believe" items are connected to or will afford evidence of an offence under "this Act or any other Act of Parliament", regardless of whether the other statute (e.g., Bankruptcy Act s. 6) also contains search-and-seizure provisions; only express statutory limits (e.g., s. 443(1)(e) "subject to any other Act of Parliament") restrict s. 443.
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 443(1)(a)-(b) as amended in 1985 (adding "or any other Act of Parliament"), and s. 443(1)(e) ("subject to any other Act of Parliament"); considered alongside Bankruptcy Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. B-3, s. 6.
CaseB_TestB: Meaning of "risks willingly assumed" in Occupiers' Liability Act s. 4(1): s. 4(1) embodies the volenti doctrine, so more than mere knowledge/appreciation of danger is required; the plaintiff must have knowledge of the risk and, from conduct/circumstances, have assumed it "in the sense of being prepared to accept the entire risk of injury ... without recourse"—i.e., consent to the legal risk/waiver of legal rights—making s. 4(1) a "very narrow exception" to the s. 3(1) duty of reasonable care.
BaselineB: Statute interpreted in light of common law: Occupiers' Liability Act, R.S.O. 1980, c. 322, ss. 3(1) and 4(1), with the common law volenti doctrine as articulated in SCC cases (Dube v. Labar; Crocker v. Sundance Northwest Resorts Ltd.).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 32 applicability to a university: distinction between “ultimate or extraordinary control” and “routine or regular control” over the entity’s “core functions” (government control/connection test from McKinney/Stoffman applied to UBC)
BaselineA: Common law / constitutional doctrine interpreting Charter s. 32(1), applied from McKinney v. University of Guelph and Stoffman v. Vancouver General Hospital (also referencing RWDSU v. Dolphin Delivery’s government-action connection concept)
JudgeA: La Forest J. (for Dickson C.J. and La Forest and Gonthier JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Leave to appeal a commercial arbitral award under Arbitration Act s. 31(2)(a): must raise a question of law; “may prevent a miscarriage of justice” requires a material legal issue with “arguable merit” (and residual discretion factors may still justify denying leave)
BaselineB: Statute: Arbitration Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 55, s. 31(2)(a) (interpreted and operationalized by the SCC, drawing on BCIT and related cases)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Limits on applying the Paré “single transaction” analysis: it applies only to murder classification under Criminal Code s. 214(5) (now s. 231(5)), not to manslaughter; to use it the Crown must first prove the accused committed (or was a party to) both the underlying offence and the murder, and only then ask whether the offences were “sufficiently closely connected in time” to classify the murder as first degree
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 214(5) (now s. 231(5))) as interpreted in R. v. Paré, [1987] 2 S.C.R. 618 (single transaction meaning of “while committing”); applied alongside party-liability provisions in Criminal Code s. 21
CaseB_TestB: Assumption of jurisdiction and forum non conveniens in multistate defamation: jurisdiction is established via a presumptive connecting factor (tort committed in Ontario through publication/republication), rebuttable by the defendant; even if jurisdiction exists, a stay requires the defendant to show another forum is “clearly more appropriate” based on a variable, non-exhaustive set of factors assessed globally
BaselineB: Common law framework from Club Resorts Ltd. v. Van Breda, 2012 SCC 17 (presumptive connecting factors; forum non conveniens with “clearly more appropriate forum” and discretionary stay), applied to defamation publication/republication principles; referenced statutory analogues include CJPTA s. 11 and Civil Code of Québec art. 3135 (as comparative guides)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Abuse of process stay test: a stay should be granted only in the “clearest of cases” where compelling the accused to stand trial would violate “fundamental principles of justice”/community “sense of fair play and decency”, or where proceedings are “oppressive or vexatious” (Jewitt/Young as affirmed in Keyowski; Conway proportionality language).
BaselineA: Common law (abuse of process stay doctrine from R. v. Jewitt adopting R. v. Young; applied/confirmed in R. v. Keyowski and R. v. Conway) alongside the statutory stay/recommencement power in Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 508 (now s. 579).
CaseB_TestB: When a Vetrovec “clear and sharp warning” is required: trial judge has discretion to warn where a witness is “for some reason untrustworthy to such an extent that a warning to the jury is necessary”, but in some cases the circumstances are such that a Vetrovec caution “must be given”; warning need not always detail corroborative evidence.
BaselineB: Common law (Vetrovec v. The Queen; refined with R. v. Babinski; related accomplice/accessory caution context in Sellars v. The Queen).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Two-step test for institutional impartiality (institutional reasonable apprehension of bias): (1) whether the judge’s outside occupation creates a reasonable apprehension of bias in a substantial number of cases; (2) if yes (occupation per se incompatible), whether safeguards sufficiently minimize the risk so that a fully informed person would not still apprehend bias in a substantial number of cases
BaselineA: Common law/Charter jurisprudence: reasonable apprehension of bias test from Committee for Justice and Liberty v. National Energy Board, adopted in Valente v. The Queen for s. 11(d) independence/impartiality
CaseB_TestB: Irwin Toy s. 2(b) infringement inquiry applied to Criminal Code s. 181: (1) does the activity convey/attempt to convey meaning (content irrelevant unless violent form); (2) does the law’s purpose or effect restrict that expression
BaselineB: Common law/Charter jurisprudence: Irwin Toy Ltd. v. Quebec (Attorney General) framework for s. 2(b) (and related s. 2(b) cases like Keegstra/Butler as cited)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 96 ‘core jurisdiction’ / Residential Tenancies historical inquiry: characterize the impugned jurisdiction and ask whether it was exercised exclusively by superior courts at Confederation (if not, s. 96 not infringed)
BaselineA: Common law constitutional test from Re Residential Tenancies Act, 1979, [1981] 1 S.C.R. 714 (as refined in Sobeys Stores Ltd. v. Yeomans, [1989] 1 S.C.R. 238) applying s. 96 of the Constitution Act, 1867
CaseB_TestB: Interpretation of “sold in any market in Canada” (Patent Act ss. 80(1)(b), 83(1), 85): includes sales regulated by Canadian public law, delivered/dispensed in Canada, and whose cost is borne by Canadians
BaselineB: Statutory interpretation of Patent Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. P-4, ss. 80(1)(b), 83(1), 85 (using the Canada Trustco textual-contextual-purposive approach)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Adequacy of an indictment (including where evidence shows multiple conspiracies): indictment is adequate if it gives the accused reasonable information and identifies the transaction; and a proven conspiracy falls within the indictment if it included some accused, occurred sometime within the alleged time span, and had as its object the type of crime alleged
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code indictment provisions) interpreted and applied with supporting SCC/common-law principles
CaseB_TestB: Constitutional validity of the Canada Evidence Act s. 38 national security disclosure scheme: (i) s. 96 analysis under Re Residential Tenancies Act, 1979 begins with whether the power broadly conforms to a superior court power at Confederation (if not, inquiry ends); and (ii) trial judges must retain adequate means (via s. 38.14/Charter remedies) to prevent an unfair trial
BaselineB: Combination of statute and constitutional/common-law tests (CEA ss. 38-38.16; Constitution Act, 1867 s. 96; Charter s. 7; Re Residential Tenancies Act, 1979 framework)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Entrapment (random virtue-testing) — first branch of Mack: police may offer an opportunity only with (a) reasonable suspicion the person is already engaged in the particular criminal activity, OR (b) pursuant to a bona fide inquiry into a sufficiently precise area reasonably suspected of that activity; “random virtue-testing” arises only if neither (a) nor (b) is present, and “associated” with the area requires no more than presence
BaselineA: Common law (R. v. Mack, [1988] 2 S.C.R. 903)
CaseB_TestB: Appellate review of trial judge’s voluntariness ruling on a voir dire — a court of appeal should not reweigh the evidence absent a “serious, specific and determining error”
BaselineB: Common law (standard of appellate intervention on evidentiary/voir dire findings; no specific prior case cited in the reasons provided)
JudgeB: LeBel J. (for the Court, oral reasons)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Duty of trial judge to comment on Crown counsel’s prejudicial jury address: where remarks are “prejudicial to a degree sufficient to impose a legal duty on the trial judge to comment” so the defence position is “fairly put to the jury”; failure is an error of law (then consider whether s. 686(1)(b)(iii) ‘no substantial wrong or miscarriage of justice’ applies).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, s. 686(1)(b)(iii)) plus common-law fairness principles governing jury charges and improper jury addresses (as reflected through adoption of Ayles J.A.’s formulation).
CaseB_TestB: Broker’s commission under clause 6.1(4o)/art. 1503 C.C.Q. (“seller voluntarily prevents free performance”): broker must prove a valid brokerage contract, performance of broker’s obligations, and that fulfilment of the preconditions to compensation “was prevented through the fault of the seller”; fault may be failing to do what the seller was obliged to do or doing what it was obliged not to do.
BaselineB: Statute (Civil Code of Québec, art. 1503; also art. 1396) and contractual clauses 6.1(3o) and 6.1(4o) of the brokerage contract (interpreted as mirroring art. 1503).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 16(2) insanity test — (1) incapacity to appreciate the nature and quality (limited to physical character/consequences) OR (2) incapacity to know the act is “wrong” (per Chaulk: morally wrong)
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 16(2)); interpreted in light of SCC precedents Cooper v. The Queen, Kjeldsen v. The Queen, R. v. Abbey (first branch) and R. v. Chaulk (meaning of “wrong” in second branch)
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 8 sniffer-dog search: “reasonable suspicion” requires a subjective belief grounded in “objectively discernible facts” assessed on the “totality of the circumstances” (possibilities, not probabilities), through the lens of a reasonable officer’s training/experience
BaselineB: Common law Charter s. 8 search-and-seizure doctrine on sniffer dogs and reasonable suspicion (R. v. Kang-Brown; R. v. A.M.; clarified with R. v. Chehil) applying Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 8 (and relatedly s. 9)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Limits of the doctrine of legitimate expectations: it is procedural only (consultation/representations), creates no substantive rights (no consent/veto), and does not apply to the legislative process (including introducing a money bill)
BaselineA: Common law administrative law doctrine of legitimate expectations as an aspect of procedural fairness/natural justice (as summarized in Old St. Boniface Residents Assn. Inc. v. Winnipeg (City))
CaseB_TestB: Divorce Act s. 17 variation framework: court must be satisfied of a post-order change in the parties’ condition/means/needs/other circumstances (s. 17(4)) and then exercise discretion considering the s. 17(7) objectives; pension income may be treated as “means” and “double dipping” is not engaged where the pension was not truly valued/divided as future property
BaselineB: Statute (Divorce Act, 1985, s. 17(4) and s. 17(7))
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Extradition under s. 7: surrender is unconstitutional only if the foreign penalty/circumstances “sufficiently shocks” the Canadian conscience / is “simply unacceptable” (contextual balancing with deference to Minister)
BaselineA: Combination: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7 applied to extradition under Extradition Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. E-23, s. 25; common-law/Charter baseline from Canada v. Schmidt ("shock the conscience") and United States v. Allard ("simply unacceptable")
CaseB_TestB: Search warrants for media premises: after meeting Criminal Code s. 487(1)(b), the justice must assess overall reasonableness by balancing all circumstances (press interests as backdrop); alternative sources are not mandatory prerequisites
BaselineB: Combination: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 487(1)(b), (d), (e) plus Charter backdrop (ss. 2(b), 8); informed by Re Pacific Press Ltd. and Descôteaux v. Mierzwinski
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Reasonable apprehension of bias (pecuniary interest) test: “Would a reasonably well-informed person consider that the interest might have an influence on the exercise of the official’s public duty?” (Old St. Boniface), applied to whether s. 52(4) costs power creates an apprehension of bias
BaselineA: Common law (administrative law/natural justice) test adopted from Old St. Boniface Residents Assn. Inc. v. Winnipeg (City), [1990] 3 S.C.R. 1170, applied as a principle of fundamental justice under Charter s. 7
CaseB_TestB: Nelles malicious prosecution test (lifting Crown’s relative immunity): plaintiff must prove (1) prosecution initiated by defendant; (2) terminated in plaintiff’s favour; (3) absence of reasonable and probable cause (subjective + objective); and (4) malice/improper purpose
BaselineB: Common law test from Nelles v. Ontario, [1989] 2 S.C.R. 170 (four-part malicious prosecution framework, including definition of reasonable and probable cause and malice/improper purpose)
JudgeB: Iacobucci and Binnie JJ. (for McLachlin C.J. and Iacobucci, Major and Binnie JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Colour of right / mistake of law bar: colour of right is unavailable unless the offence definition embraces it; and a belief that the Criminal Code is inoperative on a reserve is a mistake of law, which is no defence (Criminal Code, s. 19).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, ss. 19 and 206(1)(d)); plus common-law understanding that colour of right is offence-specific (e.g., theft-type offences) as reflected in cited cases.
CaseB_TestB: Modified Taylor ‘hatred’ test under Saskatchewan Human Rights Code s. 14(1)(b): apply objectively whether “a reasonable person, aware of the context and circumstances” would view the expression as “likely to expose” a protected group to “detestation and vilification”; focus on effects, not intent; and strike “ridicules, belittles or otherwise affronts the dignity of”.
BaselineB: Statute (Saskatchewan Human Rights Code, S.S. 1979, c. S-24.1, s. 14(1)(b)) interpreted through prior SCC common-law/constitutional framework in Canada (Human Rights Commission) v. Taylor (definition of hatred) and Charter analysis context.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Test for granting leave to intervene (sufficient interest + special perspective; manage prejudice from new issues/evidence by deferring to appeal panel and requiring consent/leave for proposed materials)
BaselineA: Common law (SCC practice on intervention and prejudice from new issues/fresh evidence) applied in an application to intervene; no specific statutory provision articulated as the governing test
CaseB_TestB: Interpretation of Criminal Code s. 182(b): (1) physical contact not required; (2) indignities must be to human remains, not monuments per se; (3) but indignities to monuments marking human remains count as indignities to the remains
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 182(b); also ss. 683(1)(g) and 695(1) re amending indictments)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: When the federal Environmental Assessment and Review Process Guidelines Order applies: there must be a “proposal” (an “initiative, undertaking or activity for which the Government of Canada has a decision making responsibility”), meaning an affirmative federal “legal duty or obligation” under an Act of Parliament; then the responsible “initiating department” must run the assessment process
BaselineA: Regulation + statute: Environmental Assessment and Review Process Guidelines Order, SOR/84-467 (esp. ss. 2 “proposal”/“initiating department”, 3, 6) made under Department of the Environment Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. E-10, s. 6; applied alongside Navigable Waters Protection Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. N-22, s. 5
CaseB_TestB: Curative proviso (Criminal Code, s. 686(1)(b)(iii)) test: despite an error of law, uphold conviction if Crown shows either (1) the error was “so harmless, and so insignificant, that it could not have affected the verdict”; or (2) the case was “so overwhelming that a conviction would have been inevitable even if the error had not been made”
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(b)(iii) (as explained by SCC precedent cited in the reasons, including R. v. Khan and R. v. Trochym)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 133 “legislative nature” test + anti-circumvention principle: an instrument is legislative if (1) it “embodies a rule of conduct”, (2) “has the force of law”, and (3) “applies to an undetermined number of persons”; and “if the net effect of a series of discrete acts has a legislative character, then each of these component acts will also be imbued with this same character” (so each must comply with s. 133 bilingualism).
BaselineA: Constitution Act, 1867, s. 133, as interpreted in Reference re Manitoba Language Rights (1985; 1992) and applied with analogy to Quebec (Attorney General) v. Brunet.
CaseB_TestB: Responsive-answer requirement to jury questions on reasonable doubt: even with an “unassailable” Lifchus/model charge, if the jury asks about the standard of proof the trial judge “must attempt to answer the jury’s question”; repeating the charge may suffice in some cases, but the judge must not discourage further questions and must provide meaningful assistance responsive to the confusion.
BaselineB: Common law on jury instructions and recharges, especially R. v. Lifchus and R. v. S. (W.D.) (with reference to Starr and related jury-charge jurisprudence).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Theft by conversion of mistakenly transferred property: where a transferor mistakenly transfers property and the recipient knows of the mistake, property does not pass for criminal-law purposes if the law of property gives the transferor a right of recovery (void/voidable distinction irrelevant); if the recipient then converts it "fraudulently and without colour of right" with intent to deprive, theft is made out.
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 322(1)) interpreted with reference to property-law principles about mistake and rights of recovery; prior SCC context noted (R. v. Stewart, [1988] 1 S.C.R. 963).
CaseB_TestB: Judicial review standard for IAD humanitarian-and-compassionate relief decisions: apply Dunsmuir’s two standards and select "reasonableness" for IRPA s. 67(1)(c) decisions; on reasonableness, courts ask whether the outcome falls within "a range of possible, acceptable outcomes" and must not reweigh evidence.
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: Federal Courts Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. F-7, s. 18.1 (esp. s. 18.1(4)) and Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, S.C. 2001, c. 27, s. 67(1)(c), applied through the common-law standard-of-review framework in Dunsmuir v. New Brunswick, 2008 SCC 9.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 11(b) unreasonable delay analysis (Morin factors + institutional-delay guideline): a "judicial determination balancing" the s. 11(b) interests against four factors—(1) length of delay; (2) waiver; (3) reasons for delay (including inherent time requirements, actions of accused, actions of Crown, limits on institutional resources, other reasons); and (4) prejudice—plus a non-binding administrative guideline of 8–10 months for institutional delay in Provincial Court (6–8 months post-committal).
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional text (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 11(b) and remedial trigger via s. 24(1)) as developed in SCC jurisprudence (Mills v. The Queen; R. v. Rahey; R. v. Conway; R. v. Smith; R. v. Askov).
CaseB_TestB: Contractor/subcontractor liability where loss is caused by overloading: even if the subcontractor’s supports "yielded first", the subcontractor is not liable if the "true cause" was the general contractor’s fault in overloading contrary to contract/specifications; the subcontractor "was under no obligation to furnish supports capable of withstanding this overload" where it was not forewarned and not obliged to foresee it (fault of the contractor as a defence).
BaselineB: Civil Code (Quebec) provisions governing contractor liability and contractual damages (arts. 1684, 1688, 1065 C.C.), informed by SCC statement in Hill, Clarke-Francis Ltd. v. Northland Groceries (Quebec) Ltd. (builder can avoid responsibility by proving damage due to force majeure/Act of God/fault of owner/act of third party).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Secret commissions offence (Criminal Code s. 426(1)(a)(ii)): actus reus requires (1) agency relationship; (2) agent accepts a benefit as consideration for an act/forbearance in relation to principal’s affairs; and (3) failure to make “adequate and timely disclosure of the source, amount and nature of the benefit”; mens rea requires awareness of each element, and if some disclosure was made “it will be for the court to determine whether, in all the circumstances of the particular case, it was in fact adequate and timely”; “corruptly” means “secretly or without the requisite disclosure” and there is no “corrupt bargain” requirement.
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 426(1)(a) (as applied to s. 426(1)(a)(ii)); framework followed from R. v. Kelly (released concurrently).
CaseB_TestB: Criminal Code s. 686(1)(b)(iii) curative proviso: ask “whether a jury properly instructed could, acting reasonably, have come to a different conclusion absent the error”; jury findings may be considered if “not tainted by the error”.
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(b)(iii).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: State Immunity Act s. 5 “commercial activity” exception (La Forest J.): two-step, contextual inquiry—(1) determine the “nature” of the foreign state activity (with purpose relevant as part of context), and (2) assess whether the Canadian proceedings “relate” to the commercial aspect by a sufficient “nexus” (more than merely “touch on” or “incidentally affect”); in multifaceted activities, identify the facets relevant to the proceedings and assess the proceedings’ impact on those facets as a whole.
BaselineA: Statute: State Immunity Act, S.C. 1980-81-82-83, c. 95, ss. 2 (definition of “commercial activity”) and 5 (“proceedings that relate to any commercial activity”); interpreted as codifying the common law restrictive immunity approach (acts jure imperii vs jure gestionis) and applied contextually (citing I Congreso del Partido).
CaseB_TestB: Compatibility test for provincial “pay-and-retain/compensation” mechanisms with the BIA distribution scheme (Deschamps J.): characterize the provincial mechanism (subrogation/compensation/solidarity) and determine whether it “subvert[s] the scheme of distribution” under the BIA; for s. 316 AIAOD, apply a structured timing-based set-off analysis—(1) if employer pays before bankruptcy and mutual debts are “certain, liquid and exigible”, legal compensation operates (C.C.Q. arts. 1672-1673) and the trustee has no claim; (2) if payment is before bankruptcy but the contractor’s claim is not liquid, compensation may be set up via BIA s. 97(3); (3) if payment is after bankruptcy, subrogatory payment cannot give rise to compensation (s. 97(3) read narrowly with ss. 121, 136(3), 141), though employer may file a proof of claim (s. 121). Equitable set-off is inapplicable in Quebec bankruptcy.
BaselineB: Statutes and civil law: Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. B-3, ss. 97(3), 121, 136–147 (scheme of distribution) and related provisions; provincial statutes s. 316 AIAOD and s. 54 ALRCI; suppletive Quebec civil law rules on subrogation/compensation (C.C.Q. arts. 1651, 1656(3), 1672-1673, 1681) as applicable in Quebec bankruptcy.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Quebec civil law “obligation to inform” (duty of disclosure) in contracts of enterprise: (1) debtor’s knowledge (actual or presumed) of the information; (2) information is of “decisive importance”; and (3) creditor cannot inform itself or is legitimately relying on the debtor; with the obligation’s content in large projects varying with (a) allocation of risk, (b) relative expertise, and (c) the contract’s “continuing formation” via change orders.
BaselineA: Civil Code of Lower Canada (arts. 1024 good faith; 1053 delictual fault) and existing Quebec jurisprudence recognizing a contractual duty to inform; SCC also draws on Houle v. Canadian National Bank and other cases to situate delictual liability to third parties.
CaseB_TestB: Judicial-reform test for changing Canadian maritime common law (to remove the contributory-negligence bar): courts may make incremental common-law change where it is “clearly necessary to keep the law in step with the ‘dynamic and evolving fabric of our society’” and where the change’s ramifications are not “unforeseeable or complex” (i.e., are assessable within judicial competence).
BaselineB: Common law (Canadian maritime law incorporating common-law tort principles) and prior SCC guidance on judicial law reform: Watkins v. Olafson and R. v. Salituro (as cited in the reasons).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Duty to accommodate (employer/union/complainant) in adverse-effect discrimination: take "reasonable measures short of undue hardship"; union duty arises as co-discriminator or where it impedes accommodation; complainant must facilitate/accept reasonable accommodation
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: British Columbia Human Rights Act, S.B.C. 1984, c. 22, ss. 8(1)(a),(b),(4) and 9(a)-(c), as interpreted through SCC duty-to-accommodate jurisprudence (Ontario Human Rights Commission and O'Malley v. Simpsons-Sears Ltd.; Central Alberta Dairy Pool v. Alberta (Human Rights Commission))
CaseB_TestB: Exclusive arbitral jurisdiction under s. 45(1) OLRA: courts are ousted if the dispute, in its "essential character", arises from the "interpretation, application, administration or alleged violation" of the collective agreement
BaselineB: Statute interpreted in light of SCC labour-arbitration exclusivity jurisprudence: Ontario Labour Relations Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. L.2, s. 45(1), building on St. Anne Nackawic Pulp & Paper Co. v. Canadian Paper Workers Union, Local 219
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Trial judge’s discretion to exclude cross-examination on a collateral credibility matter where its (tenuous) relevance does not outweigh its prejudicial effect/misleading potential
BaselineA: Common law (trial management/evidence discretion; applied from R. v. Meddoui, [1991] 3 S.C.R. 320)
CaseB_TestB: Income Tax Act s. 20(1)(c)(i) interest deductibility: whether, considering all the circumstances, the taxpayer had a reasonable expectation of income at the time the investment was made (and “income” means income subject to tax, not net income)
BaselineB: Statute (Income Tax Act, s. 20(1)(c)(i); interpreted with reference to Bronfman Trust v. The Queen and related SCC tax jurisprudence)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 10(b) “detention” at a port of entry: routine secondary immigration examination is not detention unless state action goes beyond what is required for processing entry and becomes a restraint of liberty (Therens/Simmons applied; factors include routine screening purpose and absence of stigma). Key quotes: detention requires state agent assuming control by a demand/direction with significant legal consequence and compulsion; but at the border, “routine questioning... do[es] not constitute detention” and there must be “some action... to indicate that the restriction... has gone beyond that required for the processing of his application for entry and has become a restraint of liberty”.
BaselineA: Combination: constitutional text (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 10(b)) interpreted through common-law/precedential definition of “detention” from R. v. Therens and border-screening framework from R. v. Simmons (also discussed: R. v. Jacoy; R. v. Kwok).
CaseB_TestB: Elements of civil contempt (common law): three elements proved beyond a reasonable doubt — (1) the order “must state clearly and unequivocally what should and should not be done”; (2) the alleged contemnor must have actual knowledge of the order; (3) the alleged contemnor must have intentionally done the prohibited act or intentionally failed to do the compelled act. Key quote: “all that is required to establish civil contempt is proof beyond a reasonable doubt of an intentional act or omission that is in breach of a clear order of which the alleged contemnor has notice”; contumacious intent is not required for liability.
BaselineB: Common law (civil contempt doctrine), drawing on prior authorities cited in the reasons (e.g., Bhatnager v. Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration); Prescott-Russell; Sheppard). Procedural context referenced: Rules of Civil Procedure, R.R.O. 1990, Reg. 194, r. 60.11 (but the liability test is articulated as common law).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Admissibility of bad-character/disposition evidence: admissible only if (1) relevant to an issue other than disposition/character, and (2) its probative value outweighs its prejudicial effect (with especially high probative value required for “morally repugnant” acts).
BaselineA: Common law (as stated in Morris v. The Queen; also applied with the probative/prejudicial balancing approach referenced in R. v. B. (C.R.) and the jury-instruction requirement in R. v. D. (L.E.)).
CaseB_TestB: Recent-fabrication exception for prior consistent statements: where cross-examination amounts to an allegation of recent fabrication, prior consistent statements are admissible to rebut it, but only to prove the fact the complaint was made, not the truth of its contents.
BaselineB: Common law (prior consistent statements generally inadmissible, with an exception to rebut an allegation of recent fabrication).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Substantive admissibility of a non-accused witness’s prior inconsistent statement on a principled hearsay basis (reliability + necessity), with a threshold requirement that the statement would have been admissible as the witness’s in-court testimony, and a voir dire screening for reliability indicia (oath/solemn affirmation/solemn declaration + explicit warning; videotaped in entirety; full opportunity to cross-examine at trial) or adequate substitutes, plus voluntariness/administration-of-justice safeguards
BaselineA: Common law hearsay/orthodox rule limiting prior inconsistent statements to credibility only (e.g., Deacon v. The King), modified through the principled hearsay approach in R. v. Khan and R. v. Smith; applied in the context of Canada Evidence Act, s. 9 voir dire procedure
CaseB_TestB: Characterization/coverage test: whether the art. 1056c C.C. second-paragraph “additional indemnity” is of the same nature as the first-paragraph “interest” (both being “damages due to delay”) such that an insurance promise to pay “interest accrued on the amount of its guarantee from the date when the action was instituted” includes the additional indemnity
BaselineB: Statutory baseline: Civil Code art. 1056c (interest from institution of action; plus optional additional indemnity computed as a percentage equal to the excess of a specified rate over legal interest). Interpreted in light of prior SCC discussion of art. 1056c’s first paragraph in R. v. Nord-Deutsche Versicherungs-Gesellschaft
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal fraud by “other fraudulent means” (Criminal Code, s. 380(1)): actus reus requires conduct that a reasonable person would “properly ... stigmatize as dishonest” (objective dishonesty), i.e., “the wrongful use of something in which another person has an interest ... extinguished or put at risk”; mens rea requires subjective knowledge of the prohibited act and subjective knowledge that it “could have as a consequence” deprivation (including risk to pecuniary interests), without needing subjective appreciation of dishonesty.
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 380(1)), as interpreted through SCC precedent (R. v. Théroux; R. v. Olan).
CaseB_TestB: Union duty of representation in collective bargaining (Labour Code, s. 47.2): the duty is generally an “obligation of means”; the union must not act “in bad faith or in an arbitrary or discriminatory manner or show serious negligence”, and while it may have to consider interests of employees who left the unit, their prior work “would not ... create rights ... that would take precedence” and does not impose an “obligation of result” to obtain retroactivity for them.
BaselineB: Statute (Quebec Labour Code, R.S.Q., c. C-27, s. 47.2; also discussed alongside ss. 67, 59 and Charter ss. 10, 19, 46).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Crown appeal from acquittal/new trial test under Criminal Code s. 686(4): Crown must show the verdict “would not necessarily have been the same” but for the legal error (a “very heavy onus”, requiring “a reasonable degree of certainty”).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(4)) as interpreted in SCC precedent (Vézeau v. The Queen; reaffirmed in R. v. Morin).
JudgeA: Cory J. (for Sopinka, Cory, Iacobucci and Major JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Reasonable notice before enforcing security/calling a demand loan and seeking a receiver: creditor must give “reasonable notice of its intention to enforce the security” and “reasonable time to pay”; reasonableness assessed using the Mister Broadloom criteria (7 factors).
BaselineB: Common law (Lister (R.E.) Ltd. v. Dunlop Canada Ltd.; Mister Broadloom criteria; Massey v. Sladen quoted for “some notice on which he might reasonably expect to be able to act”).
JudgeB: McLachlin and Bastarache JJ. (for the Court)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Engineer/design professional preparing tender documents owes no duty to advise/warn bidders about permits or difficulties tied to the contractor’s chosen method of performing the work, absent specific arrangements to the contrary (method is contractor’s responsibility).
BaselineA: Common law (construction/tendering duty of care allocation): R. v. Paradis and Farley Inc., [1942] S.C.R. 10; Vermont Construction Inc. v. Beatson, [1977] 1 S.C.R. 758; and related authorities cited.
CaseB_TestB: Framework for reviewing Crown decisions: (1) classify the decision as prosecutorial discretion vs. tactics/conduct before the court; (2) if prosecutorial discretion, it is reviewable only for abuse of process—i.e., conduct that is “egregious and seriously compromises trial fairness and/or the integrity of the justice system”—and the accused must first establish a “proper evidentiary foundation” before the Crown may be required to justify its decision.
BaselineB: Combination of common law constitutional doctrine and Charter/statutory context: Krieger v. Law Society of Alberta, 2002 SCC 65; R. v. Nixon, 2011 SCC 34; abuse of process jurisprudence; applied in the context of Criminal Code ss. 255 and 727(1) and Charter s. 7.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Constitutional applicability of NCA s. 10 to warrantless searches: s. 10 can justify a warrantless search only where “exigent circumstances render it impracticable to obtain prior judicial authorization”; otherwise the search is not “authorized by law” and is unreasonable under s. 8 (Collins framework).
BaselineA: Combination of common law Charter s. 8 reasonableness framework from R. v. Collins, [1987] 1 S.C.R. 265 (“A search will be reasonable if it is authorized by law, if the law itself is reasonable and if the manner in which the search was carried out is reasonable.”) and statutory search power in Narcotic Control Act, R.S.C., 1985, c. N-1, s. 10 (as limited by the Charter).
CaseB_TestB: ITA s. 241(3) disclosure exception: whether the confidentiality bar in ss. 241(1)-(2) is lifted because the evidence is sought “in respect of proceedings relating to the administration or enforcement of” the Income Tax Act—interpreted broadly to include bankruptcy-related proceedings aimed at tax collection.
BaselineB: Statutory interpretation of Income Tax Act, S.C. 1970-71-72, c. 63, s. 241(1)-(4), especially s. 241(3) (“in respect of proceedings relating to the administration or enforcement of this Act”).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.
