CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 486(2.1) screen order: judge may order complainant under 18 (for enumerated offences) to testify behind a screen/device if the judge is of the opinion the exclusion is "necessary to obtain a full and candid account of the acts complained of"; constitutionally valid because it preserves core confrontation/cross-examination and does not make the trial unfair
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 486(2.1)) applied/assessed under Charter ss. 7 and 11(d)
CaseB_TestB: Similar fact (identity) admissibility — use of prior conviction to satisfy Arp's "some evidence" link: if the accused puts identity for the prior act in issue, the Crown may tender the prior conviction as "some evidence" linking the accused to the similar act; verdicts are "presumptively reliable" on identity unless overturned or later shown wrong; challenge to conviction on voir dire only in rare cases where it could reasonably affect admissibility
BaselineB: Common law (similar fact evidence framework from R. v. Arp and R. v. Handy; plus Mahalingan on ability to challenge prior convictions) with reference to Criminal Code s. 696.3(3)(a) as an example of setting aside a conviction
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Party liability for manslaughter (even if principal is guilty of murder): under Criminal Code s. 21(1) aiding/abetting and s. 21(2) common unlawful purpose, mens rea is objective—manslaughter where a reasonable person in all the circumstances would foresee non-trivial bodily harm from the dangerous act/common purpose (no foreseeability of death required). Key formulations: unlawful act manslaughter is objective; "Nor is it necessary that the risk of death be foreseeable"; "As long as the unlawful act is inherently dangerous and harm to another which is neither trivial nor transitory is its foreseeable consequence"; and under s. 21(2) manslaughter where the accused "did not foresee the probability of murder but a reasonable person in all the circumstances would have foreseen at least a risk of harm".
BaselineA: Combination of statute and SCC common-law mens rea for unlawful act manslaughter: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, ss. 21(1)(b),(c) and 21(2); baseline SCC authorities applied/clarified include R. v. Kirkness, [1990] 3 S.C.R. 74; R. v. Creighton, [1993] 3 S.C.R. 3; R. v. Trinneer, [1970] S.C.R. 638; R. v. DeSousa, [1992] 2 S.C.R. 944.
CaseB_TestB: Entitlement to GST rebate for overpayment under Excise Tax Act: s. 261(1) applies based on actual payment (not legal liability) where a person "has paid an amount" as/on account of tax "in circumstances where the amount was not payable or remittable"; s. 261(2)(c) only bars double recovery where a rebate "is payable" under ss. 215.1 or 216(6), not merely available; and s. 296(2.1) requires the Minister on assessment to apply an "allowable rebate" even if not claimed within s. 261(3)'s two-year limit (relief via s. 296(2.1)(c)).
BaselineB: Statute: Excise Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. E-15, ss. 261(1)-(3), 296(2.1), 215.1(1),(2), 216(6), 225(1) (and related Customs Act procedures referenced).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Policy vs. operational decision framework for governmental tort liability in highway maintenance (policy decisions immune; operational implementation subject to negligence standard). Key guidance: a public authority is under no duty of care for decisions “which involve or are dictated by financial, economic, social or political factors or constraints” (policy), but may be liable where courts apply a negligence standard to “administrative direction, expert or professional opinion, technical standards or general standards of reasonableness” (operational).
BaselineA: Common law (Just v. British Columbia, [1989] 2 S.C.R. 1228; also discussed via Anns v. Merton; Kamloops v. Nielsen) applied in the context of highway maintenance; with statutory context considered (Public Highways Act, ss. 4-5; Proceedings against the Crown Act, s. 5(1)(a); Expropriation Act, ss. 70(f), 71).
CaseB_TestB: Damages in lieu of specific performance—date of assessment and uniqueness. Where a purchaser has a legitimate claim to specific performance and elects damages instead, it may be appropriate to assess damages “as of the date of trial” (technically judgment) rather than breach; and “specific performance should ... not be granted as a matter of course absent evidence that the property is unique to the extent that its substitute would not be readily available.”
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law/equity: Courts of Justice Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.43, s. 99 (damages in substitution for specific performance) applied alongside common law flexibility on assessment date (Johnson v. Agnew; Wroth v. Tyler) and the compensatory principle.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Abuse of process threshold in criminal proceedings: stay/remedy only in the “clearest of cases” (conduct that “shocks the conscience of the community” and is “so detrimental to the proper administration of justice” that intervention is warranted; requires “overwhelming evidence” the proceedings are unfair “to the point that they are contrary to the interest of justice”).
BaselineA: Common law (abuse of process doctrine as recognized in SCC cases such as R. v. Jewitt and R. v. Keyowski, as discussed in the reasons).
CaseB_TestB: Mr. Big confessions admissibility rule: confessions to the state during a Mr. Big operation are “presumptively inadmissible”; Crown must show (on a balance of probabilities) that “the probative value of the confession outweighs its prejudicial effect”, with probative value assessed via reliability (circumstances of the operation + markers of reliability in the confession).
BaselineB: Common law (new evidentiary rule qualifying the party admissions exception to hearsay; draws on common law probative value vs prejudicial effect balancing and related evidence doctrines).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 16(1) “knowing that it was wrong”: incapacity includes inability to rationally apply right/wrong to the particular act (capacity for rational perception and rational choice about wrongness at the time)
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 16(1)) interpreted in light of M'Naghten's Case and SCC authority (R. v. Chaulk)
CaseB_TestB: Palmer criteria for admitting fresh evidence on appeal (applies equally to sentence appeals): (1) due diligence (flexible factor), (2) relevance, (3) credibility, (4) could reasonably be expected to have affected the result
BaselineB: Common law test from Palmer v. The Queen, applied/confirmed under Criminal Code ss. 683 and 687 (“interests of justice” discretion)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Mohan test for admissibility of expert evidence (relevance; necessity; no other exclusionary rule; properly qualified expert), with added threshold for expert disposition/profile evidence requiring “distinctive behavioural characteristics” and a “standard profile” accepted as reliable
BaselineA: Common law (law of evidence): expert opinion admissibility and character/disposition evidence rules, drawing on cases including R. v. Abbey, R. v. Morin, and the “abnormal group” line from R. v. Lupien / R. v. McMillan / R. v. Robertson
CaseB_TestB: Section 745 Criminal Code parole ineligibility review framework: jury must decide whether ineligibility “ought to be reduced” by weighing listed factors (character, conduct in custody, nature of offence, and “such other matters as the judge deems relevant”) as a whole; burden-of-proof concepts are of “very limited value” in this discretionary decision
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 745(1)-(4) (especially s. 745(2))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 10(b) informational/implementational duties: no duty-counsel advice required where no duty counsel exists; further police duties are only triggered if detainee asserts a desire to speak to counsel (a clear 'No' does not trigger).
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 10(b) (and related jurisprudence on informational/implementational components: R. v. Brydges; confirmed in R. v. Bartle; addressed alongside R. v. Prosper).
CaseB_TestB: Criminal Code s. 347 framework for late payment penalties: (1) determine if charge is 'interest'—i.e., a charge/expense (including a 'penalty') 'paid or payable for the advancing of credit under an agreement or arrangement' (with 'credit advanced' including deferral of payment for goods/services/benefits); (2) apply s. 347(1)(a) ex ante (requires criminal-rate interest on face of agreement) vs s. 347(1)(b) ex post (payment received; calculate effective annual rate over period credit actually outstanding); (3) Nelson 'voluntary act of debtor' exception to s. 347(1)(b).
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 347(1)-(2) (interpreting defined terms 'interest', 'credit advanced', 'criminal rate'); incorporating Nelson v. C.T.C. Mortgage Corp. and Degelder Construction Co. v. Dancorp Developments Ltd. principles on s. 347(1)(a)/(b) and voluntariness.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 7 overbreadth (PFJ) test: a law violates s. 7 if it deprives life/liberty/security in a manner that is "unnecessarily broad, going beyond what is needed to accomplish the governmental objective"; courts ask whether the means are "necessary" and "reasonably tailored" to the objective (overbreadth = means "broader than is necessary").
BaselineA: Constitution (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7) applied to Criminal Code s. 179(1)(b); overbreadth/vagueness discussion drawing on R. v. Nova Scotia Pharmaceutical Society and Re B.C. Motor Vehicle Act (as cited in the reasons).
CaseB_TestB: Transfer pricing “reasonable amount in the circumstances” under ITA s. 69(2): determine whether the non-arm’s length price exceeds what would be "reasonable in the circumstances" at arm’s length; consider "all the circumstances" relevant to price, including linked agreements conferring rights/benefits, and ensure comparators are "sufficiently comparable" having regard to "economically relevant characteristics"; if needed, consider transactions other than the purchasing transaction.
BaselineB: Statute: Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), s. 69(2) (transfer pricing).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Inference of possession from fingerprint evidence: whether an accused’s fingerprint on an article supports an inference of possession is “not subject to a hard and fast rule” but “depends on all of the circumstances of the case and all of the evidence adduced” (a totality-of-the-evidence assessment); once the Crown proves a prima facie case, the accused’s silence may simply “fail[] to provide any basis to conclude otherwise”.
BaselineA: Common law evidentiary principles on circumstantial proof of possession and adverse inference from silence, drawing on R. v. O'Keefe (1958) (Ont. C.A.) and approving the contextual approach in R. v. Mehrabnia (1993) (Ont. Prov. Div.); also relies on the prima facie-case/absence-of-defence-evidence approach from R. v. Johnson (1993) (Ont. C.A.), cited with approval in R. v. François, [1994] 2 S.C.R. 827.
CaseB_TestB: Scope of Review Board power under Criminal Code s. 672.54: Boards may impose binding conditions on hospital authorities and may make conditions “regarding”/supervising treatment (including ordering re-evaluations and exploration of alternatives), but have no power to “prescribe”/impose treatment; s. 672.55(1) is interpreted narrowly as not creating a true exception to the no-prescription rule.
BaselineB: Statutory interpretation of Criminal Code Part XX.1, especially ss. 672.54 and 672.55(1) (with related context from ss. 672.1, 672.38-672.42, 672.72-672.78, 672.58-672.62).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 7 compellability / exemption from compulsion test: whether the "predominant purpose" of compelling the witness is to obtain incriminating evidence against them rather than to further a legitimate public purpose (with justification and prejudice analysis if predominant purpose is incrimination).
BaselineA: Common law / Charter-based doctrine from R. v. S. (R.J.), [1995] 1 S.C.R. 451 (principle against self-incrimination under Charter s. 7; derivative use immunity; exemptions from compulsion).
CaseB_TestB: Timing rule for Corbett applications: the defence should bring, and the trial judge should decide, a Corbett application "immediately after the close of the Crown’s case" (with a possible pre-defence-case voir dire to inform the ruling, and possible later modification if defence evidence departs significantly).
BaselineB: Statute interpreted through common law discretion: Canada Evidence Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-5, s. 12 as construed in R. v. Corbett, [1988] 1 S.C.R. 670 (discretion to exclude prior convictions where probative value is outweighed by prejudicial effect).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 7 compellability / exemption from compulsion test: whether the "predominant purpose" of compelling the witness is to obtain incriminating evidence against them rather than to further a legitimate public purpose; if predominant purpose is incrimination, compulsion must be justified and the witness is not compellable if there is other significant prejudice to fair trial beyond derivative use (with derivative-use immunity governed by a "plausible connection" trigger and Crown "would have discovered" burden).
BaselineA: Combination of Charter and common law: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms ss. 7 and 13, applied and refined from R. v. S. (R.J.), [1995] 1 S.C.R. 451 (derivative use immunity and exemptions from compulsion).
CaseB_TestB: Section 15(1) prima facie discrimination test (Quebec v. A framework): (1) does the law create a distinction on an enumerated or analogous ground (on its face or in impact); and (2) does it impose "arbitrary — or discriminatory — disadvantage" by failing to respond to actual capacities/needs and instead "reinforcing, perpetuating or exacerbating" disadvantage; claimant must show a "disproportionate effect" based on group membership.
BaselineB: Combination of Charter and common law: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms s. 15(1), applying the SCC’s existing s. 15 framework as set out in Quebec (Attorney General) v. A, 2013 SCC 5 (and related s. 15 jurisprudence).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Tax-treaty residency under Article IV: a person is a “resident of a Contracting State” only if “liable to tax therein by reason of ... domicile, residence, place of management, place of incorporation or any other criterion of a similar nature”; “any other criterion of a similar nature” is limited to criteria grounding comprehensive (world-wide) tax liability, not mere source taxation (e.g., being “engaged in a trade or business” effectively connected to the U.S.).
BaselineA: Statute/treaty: Canada-United States Tax Convention Act, 1984, Schedule I (Canada-United States Income Tax Convention (1980)), Article IV(1) (definition of “resident of a Contracting State”), applied in the context of Article XII (withholding rate).
CaseB_TestB: Valid-refusal trigger for limitation period: the two-year limitation in Insurance Act, s. 281(5) “only begins to run upon the issuance by the insurer of a valid refusal”; “No such refusal is given if there has not been adequate compliance with s. 71” of the SABS, which requires notice of the dispute-resolution process “in straightforward and clear language, directed towards an unsophisticated person” and, “At a minimum”, including key steps (mediation; arbitration/litigation if mediation fails; mediation prerequisite; and “relevant time limits”).
BaselineB: Statute/regulation: Insurance Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. I.8, s. 281(5) (two-year limit runs from “insurer’s refusal”); Statutory Accident Benefits Schedule, O. Reg. 776/93, s. 71 (duty to inform of dispute-resolution procedure under ss. 279-283 of the Insurance Act).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Weber exclusive-arbitration jurisdiction test: courts are ousted if the dispute’s “essential character” arises from the “interpretation, application, administration or alleged violation” of the collective agreement (s. 45(1)); focus on facts, not legal labels
BaselineA: Statute: Ontario Labour Relations Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. L.2, s. 45(1) (mandatory “final and binding” arbitration of “all differences” arising from the collective agreement), informed by SCC approach in St. Anne Nackawic Pulp & Paper Co. v. Canadian Paper Workers Union, Local 219
CaseB_TestB: Criminal Code s. 744 parole-ineligibility extension framework: trial judge may extend beyond 10 years by considering (1) character of the offender, (2) nature of the offence, and (3) circumstances surrounding its commission; “general rule” 10 years, ousted if judge determines longer is fit under s. 744 criteria
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 744 (and related sentencing provisions including s. 742(b))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “loss of employment” for a retiring allowance: an employee is only “in the service” of the employer once under an obligation to provide services; therefore “loss of employment” cannot occur before that moment (no retiring allowance for loss of intended/prospective employment)
BaselineA: Statute (Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1952, c. 148 (now R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.)), ss. 56(1)(a)(ii) and 248(1) definitions of “retiring allowance”, “employment”, “employee”)
CaseB_TestB: Trial fairness/miscarriage of justice assessment for improper Crown closing submissions: apply the contextual “relevant factors” (from R. v. Stephan) to decide whether the improper comment rendered the trial unfair
BaselineB: Common law (contextual factors approach referenced from R. v. Stephan; also guided by Pisani and Boucher on improper submissions)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Pragmatic and functional approach to whether a labour board has jurisdiction (and, if within jurisdiction, review only for patent unreasonableness/clear irrationality)
BaselineA: Combination of common law administrative-law standards of review (pragmatic and functional approach; patent unreasonableness) and statute (Canada Labour Code privative clause and certification provisions)
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 8 reasonableness of DNA data bank sampling under Criminal Code s. 487.055: contextual balancing of state interest in identification vs privacy/physical integrity, with statutory safeguards limiting use to identification
BaselineB: Combination of statute (Criminal Code, s. 487.055; DNA Identification Act, ss. 3-4) and common law/constitutional doctrine (Charter s. 8 reasonableness framework from Hunter v. Southam; Collins/Stillman reasonableness requirements; Beare fingerprinting analogy)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Gladstone refinement of Sparrow s.35 justification: two-part justification plus modified “priority” where the Aboriginal right has no internal limit (priority is “something less than exclusivity” assessed case-by-case)
BaselineA: Common law / constitutional doctrine applying Constitution Act, 1982, s. 35(1) (Sparrow framework) and refining Sparrow’s justification/priority analysis
CaseB_TestB: Admissibility of Crown rebuttal evidence: rebuttal may be admitted where it is relevant to an issue raised by the defence and the Crown could not have known in advance the defence evidence; admission is within the trial judge’s discretion
BaselineB: Common law (trial judge’s discretion over rebuttal evidence) plus Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(b)(iii) (curative proviso on appeal)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Implied waiver of Charter s. 11(d) in ticketed regulatory offences: legislature may infer waiver from failure to pay and failure to appear only if the accused is "fully aware of the consequences" and the scheme has "sufficient safeguards" to ensure the omission was not due to events beyond the accused’s control
BaselineA: Combination: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 11(d) (and contextual s. 7 liberty analysis) plus common-law/Charter waiver principles as applied in R. v. Lee (SCC) and general waiver doctrine (voluntary + full knowledge)
CaseB_TestB: Procedural fairness for CHRC dismissal of a complaint as unsubstantiated (CHRA s. 36(3)(b)): before deciding, the Commission must give an opportunity to make submissions ("at least in writing") and must disclose "the substance of the case" so submissions are informed
BaselineB: Combination: Canadian Human Rights Act, ss. 35 and 36(3)(b) (Commission investigation/dismissal power) interpreted through common-law natural justice/procedural fairness requirements for quasi-judicial decisions
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Patently unreasonable standard on judicial review of labour arbitration (including the “no evidence” basis for finding patent unreasonableness)
BaselineA: Common law (administrative law / labour arbitration judicial review standards), applied in light of a strong privative clause in School Boards and Teachers Collective Negotiations Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. S.2, s. 72
CaseB_TestB: Statutory test for whether successor pension plan benefits are “equivalent in value” on the implementation date (requires comparing both benefits and their funding; prima facie breach if employee contribution not matched unless offset by exclusive/compensatory benefits)
BaselineB: Statute: Manitoba Telephone System Reorganization and Consequential Amendments Act, S.M. 1996, c. 79, s. 15(2)(a) (“equivalent in value”); interpreted with statutory context including s. 15(3), and related pension-plan statutory background (CSSA definition provisions referenced)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Doctrine of part performance prevents the Crown from relying on a statutory writing requirement (s. 21(1)(a) Public Highways Act) to deny an equitable permission/right of way created and carried out in fact
BaselineA: Combination: statute (Public Highways Act, R.S.N.S. 1954, c. 235, s. 21(1)(a) writing/permit requirement; Expropriation Act, R.S.N.S. 1954, c. 91, s. 1(c) definition of “land”) and equitable common law doctrine (part performance as an exception to Statute of Frauds-type writing requirements, discussed via Steadman v. Steadman (H.L.))
CaseB_TestB: Arbitrability / annulment-public-order framework: (1) interpret arbitrator’s mandate liberally to include matters “closely connected” to the arbitration agreement; (2) s. 37 Copyright Act does not exclude arbitration; (3) under art. 946.5 C.C.P., an award is annulled for public order only if the outcome (disposition) conflicts with fundamental public order, not merely because of an error of law
BaselineB: Statutory/civil code framework: Civil Code of Québec arts. 2639-2643; Code of Civil Procedure arts. 946.2, 946.4, 946.5, 947.2; Copyright Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-42, s. 37; Act respecting the professional status of artists, R.S.Q., c. S-32.01, s. 37
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Reasonableness simpliciter standard of review for statutory appeals from expert tribunals: reviewing court asks whether the tribunal decision was "unreasonable" — i.e., "in the main, ... not supported by any reasons that can stand up to a somewhat probing examination"; contrasted with patent unreasonableness where the defect is "apparent on the face" of the reasons.
BaselineA: Common law (standard of review doctrine) applied in the context of a statutory right of appeal under the Competition Tribunal Act, especially ss. 12-13; key prior SCC baseline case cited: Pezim v. British Columbia (Superintendent of Brokers).
CaseB_TestB: Temporal-effect test for suspended s. 52(1) declarations: declarations are presumptively retroactive, but the presumption is rebutted "explicitly or by necessary implication"; where "retroactivity would undermine" the purpose/compelling public interest justifying the suspension, "the declaration must apply purely prospectively".
BaselineB: Constitutional text and remedial doctrine: Constitution Act, 1982, s. 52(1) and Charter, s. 24(1), building on prior SCC remedial jurisprudence including Canada (Attorney General) v. Hislop and Ontario (Attorney General) v. G.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: CCA “purpose of producing income” test under Reg. 1102(1)(c): (1) “Does the property produce income? In the affirmative, the deduction is allowable.” (2) If not, “was it acquired for the purpose of producing income?”, determined by “an objective evaluation of the specific facts and circumstances ... having regard to whether the taxpayer acted in accordance with reasonably acceptable principles of commerce and business practices.” (L’Heureux‑Dubé J.)
BaselineA: Statute and regulation: Income Tax Act, s. 20(1)(a) (deductions “as is allowed by regulation”) and Income Tax Regulations, s. 1102(1)(c) (property excluded if “not acquired ... for the purpose of gaining or producing income”).
CaseB_TestB: Bail denial under Criminal Code s. 515(10)(c) (post-severance): detention may be ordered “where the detention is necessary in order to maintain confidence in the administration of justice”, assessed objectively “having regard to all the circumstances, including” four listed factors (strength of Crown’s case, gravity of offence, circumstances of commission, potential for lengthy imprisonment), and only if “a reasonable member of the community would be satisfied that denial of bail is necessary” (McLachlin C.J.).
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, s. 515(10)(c), interpreted/limited to comply with Charter s. 11(e) (“not to be denied reasonable bail without just cause”) by severing “on any other just cause being shown, and without limiting the generality of the foregoing”.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Vesting/accrual of an appeal-as-of-right: a right is only “acquired”, “accrued” or “accruing” once all conditions precedent are fulfilled (here, upon the court of appeal’s judgment reversing the acquittal and ordering a new trial)
BaselineA: Statute (Interpretation Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. I-21, ss. 43(c) and 44(c),(d), applied to Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 691(2) (as amended))
CaseB_TestB: Sherman Estate v. Donovan test for discretionary limits on the open court principle (publication bans): (1) serious risk to an important public interest; (2) necessity because reasonable alternatives won’t prevent the risk; (3) proportionality—benefits outweigh negative effects
BaselineB: Common law (Sherman Estate v. Donovan, 2021 SCC 25, para. 38)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Income-tax profit computation framework under ITA s. 9(1): taxpayer may use any method consistent with the Act, case law, and well-accepted business principles that yields an “accurate picture” of profit; on reassessment the onus shifts to the Minister to show inaccuracy or a more accurate alternative method
BaselineA: Statute (Income Tax Act, s. 9(1) profit concept; limiting provisions incl. s. 18(1)(a) and s. 18(9)) plus prior case law on profit computation (e.g., Symes v. Canada; M.N.R. v. Irwin; Associated Investors)
CaseB_TestB: Interpretation/application of Partnership Act s. 55(b): without unanimous written consent/ratification, a general partner has no authority to “do any act which makes it impossible to carry on the ordinary business” of the limited partnership; “impossible” means not possible and refers to a substantial portion (not every facet) of the ordinary business
BaselineB: Statute (Partnership Act, R.S.A. 1980, c. P-2, s. 55(b)) interpreted in light of the partnership’s constitutive documents defining its “ordinary business”
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Post-conviction Crown non-disclosure: two-step “reasonable possibility” test for impairment of full answer and defence/new trial (reliability of verdict, then overall trial fairness, with defence due diligence as a significant factor)
BaselineA: Combination: Charter ss. 7 and 24(1) plus SCC common law disclosure jurisprudence (R. v. Stinchcombe; R. v. Egger; R. v. C. (M.H.); R. v. Carosella). Key formulation: impairment shown where there is a “reasonable possibility the non-disclosure affected the outcome at trial or the overall fairness of the trial process” and the Court mandates a “two-step analysis” (first reliability; second fairness, including lost investigative opportunities) with defence counsel due diligence considered.
CaseB_TestB: Standard-form insurance interpretation of SEF 44 cl. 4(b)(vii): “policy of insurance” has its ordinary meaning (private insurance contract) and does not include CPP; apply clear language if unambiguous
BaselineB: Common law contract/insurance interpretation principles for standard form policies (Ledcor; Progressive Homes; Scalera; Gibbens) applied to SEF 44 Endorsement cl. 4(b)(vii) (“any policy of insurance providing disability benefits...”). SCC contribution: fixes the ordinary-meaning rule for this clause—“policy of insurance” refers to a private policy and “does not include the CPP regime”.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Search incident to arrest must be “truly incidental”: police must have a purpose related to the arrest (within Cloutier purposes or other valid purpose) and it must be objectively reasonable; delay/distance may support a negative inference rebuttable by explanation
BaselineA: Common law (search incident to arrest doctrine from Cloutier v. Langlois; also framed within Charter s. 8 reasonableness via Hunter v. Southam and Collins)
CaseB_TestB: Admissibility of defence-led unknown third party suspect evidence: (1) relevance to a fact in issue/available defence shown by a “sufficient connection” (similarity) between the charged crime and another incident plus evidence the accused could not have committed the other offence; and (2) admit unless prejudicial effects “substantially outweigh” probative value (Seaboyer balancing), without credibility findings or balance-of-probabilities proof of the other incident
BaselineB: Common law evidence principles (Seaboyer probative vs prejudicial balancing; Corbett relevance; Cinous air of reality; Grandinetti sufficient connection for known third party suspects)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Schreiber (Lamer C.J.) — s. 8 Charter is only triggered if claimant shows a reasonable expectation of privacy; in foreign-search context, expectation generally corresponds to protection provided by foreign law (Plant contextual factors; replace “seriousness of crime” with “activity bringing individual into contact with the state”).
BaselineA: Combination: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 8 (and s. 32(1) on application) + common-law/constitutional jurisprudence on reasonable expectation of privacy (Hunter v. Southam; R. v. Plant; Terry; Harrer).
CaseB_TestB: Fullowka (Cromwell J.) — Anns/Cooper duty-of-care framework for negligence (foreseeability + proximity → prima facie duty; then residual policy may negate/limit), applied to omissions to prevent third-party intentional harm (with proximity informed by Childs factors such as control, autonomy, reliance).
BaselineB: Common law: Anns/Cooper duty-of-care framework (Cooper v. Hobart; Edwards; Odhavji; Childs; Hill) as applied to negligence/duty to prevent third-party harm.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Pushpanathan Art. 1F(c) exclusion test: Art. 1F(c) applies where there is (1) an international-law consensus that the acts are “sufficiently serious and sustained violations of fundamental human rights as to amount to persecution”, or (2) an explicit international designation that the acts are “contrary to the purposes and principles of the United Nations”; includes (i) explicit UN/international declarations (determinative if reflecting “reasonable consensus”), and (ii) acts a court can itself characterize as “serious, sustained and systemic violations of fundamental human rights constituting persecution” (even an isolated violation if near the core of human rights and subject to international condemnation/punishment, e.g., universal jurisdiction offences).
BaselineA: Statute + incorporated treaty: Immigration Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. I-2, s. 2(1) (definition of “Convention refugee” incorporating Refugee Convention Art. 1F(c)); interpreted using Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, Arts. 31-32 (as applied in Ward/Thomson).
CaseB_TestB: Hadley v. Baxendale remoteness/proximity test for contract damages: damages are those that “arise either naturally” or that “may reasonably be supposed to have been in the contemplation of both parties, at the time they made the contract, as the probable result of a breach”; applied to assess damages for breach of an implied contractual duty of good faith by a branch manager who orchestrated a mass exit.
BaselineB: Common law: Hadley v. Baxendale (1854) remoteness rule for contract damages (as adopted/applied in Canadian contract law).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Hodgson framework for (1) who is a “person in authority” and (2) when a trial judge must hold a confession voir dire on their own motion: person in authority includes those the accused reasonably believes can influence/control proceedings; defence must raise the issue, but in “extremely rare cases” the judge must order a voir dire if the record objectively shows a clear, close connection to authorities along a spectrum from “conventional” authority figures.
BaselineA: Common law confessions rule (voluntariness requirement for statements to a person in authority), drawing on cases including Erven v. The Queen, [1979] 1 S.C.R. 926; Rothman v. The Queen, [1981] 1 S.C.R. 640; Ibrahim v. The King, [1914] A.C. 599; Prosko v. The King (1922), 63 S.C.R. 226; Boudreau v. The King, [1949] S.C.R. 262.
CaseB_TestB: McClurg interpretation of Income Tax Act s. 56(2) (diversion/attribution): s. 56(2) targets diversion of amounts the taxpayer “otherwise would have obtained”; as a general rule dividends (including allocations under a discretionary dividend clause) are outside s. 56(2) because, absent declaration/allocation, profits remain corporate retained earnings and are not amounts the taxpayer would otherwise receive.
BaselineB: Statutory interpretation of Income Tax Act, S.C. 1970-71-72, c. 63, s. 56(2) (with corporate-law context from Saskatchewan Business Corporations Act, R.S.S. 1978, c. B-10, including ss. 24(4), 40, 97, 234). Prior interpretive guidance cited includes Miller v. M.N.R., 62 D.T.C. 1139; Stubart Investments Ltd. v. The Queen, [1984] 1 S.C.R. 536; The Queen v. Golden, [1986] 1 S.C.R. 209; Bronfman Trust v. The Queen, [1987] 1 S.C.R. 32.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Depletion allowance profit computation under Income Tax Regulations, reg. 1201: determine profits “reasonably attributable” to production and deduct only the amounts enumerated in reg. 1201(4) (courts cannot read in additional deductions such as long-term scientific research expenses)
BaselineA: Regulation/statute: Income Tax Regulations (Can.), reg. 1201(2) and 1201(4), in relation to Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1952, c. 148, ss. 11(1)(j) and 72; interpretive approach referenced from Minister of National Revenue v. Imperial Oil Ltd., [1960] S.C.R. 735
CaseB_TestB: Sherman Estate v. Donovan test for discretionary limits on the open court principle (publication bans): applicant must establish (1) serious risk to an important public interest; (2) necessity because reasonable alternatives will not prevent the risk; and (3) proportionality—benefits outweigh negative effects
BaselineB: Common law: Sherman Estate v. Donovan, 2021 SCC 25 (para. 38) governing discretionary orders limiting court openness
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Kienapple (res judicata) in unequal-gravity offences: if same delict underlies two counts of different gravity, convict on the more serious and acquit/hold in abeyance the less serious (a guilty plea to the less serious cannot bar trial/conviction on the more serious).
BaselineA: Common law (Kienapple v. The Queen, [1975] 1 S.C.R. 729) applied in the context of Criminal Code charges (ss. 83, 302(d), 421(a)).
CaseB_TestB: Habeas corpus for continued detention in parole context: continuation of valid detention is challengeable only if it becomes unlawful; in parole, unlawfulness arises only once inmate has acquired parolee status (when parole takes effect, including fulfillment of any condition).
BaselineB: Common law habeas corpus doctrine as developed in R. v. Miller, [1985] 2 S.C.R. 613; applied alongside the Parole Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. P-2 (as amended).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: NCR disposition under Criminal Code s. 672.54: absolute discharge is mandatory unless the court/Review Board makes a positive finding that the NCR accused poses a “significant threat to the safety of the public”; if significant threat is found, impose the “least onerous and least restrictive” conditional discharge or detention after considering the four statutory factors (public protection, mental condition, reintegration, other needs). Key definition: “significant threat” = “a real risk of physical or psychological harm ... that is serious ... beyond the merely trivial or annoying” and “conduct ... must be criminal in nature”.
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, Part XX.1, especially s. 672.54 (and related NCR regime provisions).
CaseB_TestB: Westbank levy characterization for Constitution Act, 1867 s. 125: determine whether a levy is, in pith and substance, (1) a tax, (2) a regulatory charge (financing/constituting or ancillary to a regulatory scheme), or (3) a user fee. For “tax” vs “regulatory charge”, ask: is the charge “(1) compulsory and enforceable by law; (2) imposed under the authority of the legislature; (3) levied by a public body; (4) intended for a public purpose; and (5) unconnected to any form of a regulatory scheme?” If all yes, it “will generally be described as a tax.”
BaselineB: Constitution (Constitution Act, 1867, s. 125; also s. 91(3)) and statute (Indian Act, s. 83(1)(a)); building on prior SCC tax/charge jurisprudence (e.g., Lawson; Re Exported Natural Gas Tax; Eurig Estate).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 2(d) freedom of association (labour context): s. 2(d) protects only (1) the freedom to establish/belong to/maintain an association and (2) the exercise in association of members’ lawful rights; it does not include a right to a particular statutory labour-relations regime or official recognition (no general positive obligation of inclusion).
BaselineA: Combination: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 2(d) (and s. 32(1) re government actors) as interpreted in prior SCC cases cited in the reasons, especially the 1987 labour trilogy (Reference re Public Service Employee Relations Act (Alta.); PSAC v. Canada; RWDSU v. Saskatchewan) and Professional Institute of the Public Service of Canada v. Northwest Territories (Commissioner), confirmed in Canadian Egg Marketing Agency v. Richardson.
CaseB_TestB: Joint/co-principal liability in group assaults (Criminal Code, s. 21(1)(a)): co-principal liability applies where “two or more individuals come together with an intention to commit an offence, are present during the commission of the offence, and contribute to its commission”; for manslaughter, focus on whether the accused’s acts were a “significant contributing cause of death” (not on who inflicted which wound), and in group assaults “absent a discrete or intervening event” all assailants’ actions can be such a cause.
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 21(1)(a)) as informed by SCC party-liability jurisprudence referenced in the reasons (notably R. v. Pickton).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Federal Child Support Guidelines s. 4 ‘inappropriateness’ framework for incomes over $150,000: Table amount presumptively applies; deviation only if rebutted by evidence showing the Table amount is ‘inappropriate’ meaning ‘unsuitable’, assessed after examining all circumstances including s. 4(b)(ii) factors
BaselineA: Regulation/statute: Federal Child Support Guidelines, SOR/97-175, s. 4 (esp. s. 4(b)(i)-(ii)) under the Divorce Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 3 (2nd Supp.), s. 26.1(2)
CaseB_TestB: Classification rule for all-risks/multi-peril policies under the B.C. Insurance Act: if the policy does not fit coherently within Part 5 (fire insurance) via s. 119, it is governed by Part 2 (general provisions), so the Part 2 limitation period applies; contractual shorter limitation cannot undercut Part 2 due to s. 3(a)
BaselineB: Statute/regulation: Insurance Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 226, ss. 119 and 3(a) (and Part 2 vs Part 5 scheme; statutory condition 14 in Part 5)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meiorin unified BFOR test (3-step): employer must prove (1) standard adopted for a purpose “rationally connected to the performance of the job”; (2) adopted “in an honest and good faith belief” it was necessary; and (3) standard is “reasonably necessary” — i.e., “impossible to accommodate individual employees sharing the characteristics of the claimant without imposing undue hardship upon the employer”.
BaselineA: Statute (Human Rights Code, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 210, ss. 13(1)(a), (b), (4)) plus prior SCC human-rights BFOR/accommodation jurisprudence (e.g., O’Malley; Etobicoke; Central Alberta Dairy Pool; Renaud).
CaseB_TestB: Stewart source-of-income test (2-stage): (i) “Is the taxpayer’s activity undertaken in pursuit of profit, or is it a personal endeavour?”; (ii) if not personal, “is the source of the income a business or property?”; with stage (i) only engaged where there is a personal/hobby element, requiring “subjective intention to profit” supported by “evidence of businesslike behaviour”.
BaselineB: Statute (Income Tax Act, especially ss. 3(a), 9(1)-(2); also discussed: ss. 18(1)(a), (h), 20(1)(c)(i), 67, 248(1)) and prior SCC case law on “reasonable expectation of profit” (Moldowan v. The Queen).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Staged analysis for whether a conditional sentence is appropriate for an Aboriginal offender (s. 742.1 + mandatory consideration of s. 718.2(e)/Gladue factors once incarceration is in play)
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, ss. 742.1 and 718-718.2(e)) as interpreted in R. v. Proulx and R. v. Gladue
CaseB_TestB: Balancing under Quebec Charter s. 9.1 to determine whether a freedom of religion claim (s. 3) immunizes a party from civil liability for breaching a valid contract with religious aspects
BaselineB: Statute (Quebec Charter of human rights and freedoms, ss. 3 and 9.1) informed by SCC freedom of religion jurisprudence (e.g., Syndicat Northcrest v. Amselem) and Quebec civil law contract validity rules (C.C.Q., arts. 1378, 1385, 1412-1413)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Unreasonable verdict review under Criminal Code s. 686(1)(a)(i): whether the verdict is one that a properly instructed jury (or trial judge) acting judicially could reasonably have rendered; appellate court must thoroughly re-examine the evidence and cannot overturn based only on a vague “lurking doubt” without articulating why the verdict is inconsistent with a judicial appreciation of the evidence.
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(a)(i)) as interpreted in common law jurisprudence (R. v. Yebes; reaffirmed/clarified in R. v. Biniaris).
CaseB_TestB: Institutional consultation / natural justice test: full-board consultation is permissible only if (1) it is not imposed by a superior authority, (2) it is limited to questions of policy and law, and (3) decision-makers remain free to decide; for audi alteram partem, an applicant must show an actual breach (not merely an apprehended breach), and a presumption of regularity applies such that a change from draft to final reasons alone does not imply impropriety.
BaselineB: Common law procedural fairness/natural justice doctrine, especially IWA v. Consolidated-Bathurst Packaging Ltd. and Tremblay v. Quebec (Commission des affaires sociales), applied in the context of the Labour Relations Act, 1995 (notably ss. 114(1), 117).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: “Functional and structural” approach to the third branch of the Mills ‘court of competent jurisdiction’ test (power to grant the Charter remedy sought under s. 24(1))
BaselineA: Combination: Charter s. 24(1) plus common-law/constitutional jurisprudence defining “court of competent jurisdiction” (Mills v. The Queen three-part test; affirmed in Weber and Mooring) applied to a statutory court (Provincial Offences Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. P.33).
JudgeA: The Chief Justice (McLachlin C.J., for the Court)
CaseB_TestB: Section 11(d) ‘inexorable connection’ test for statutory presumptions (and resulting invalidity of Criminal Code s. 172.1(3) in sting operations)
BaselineB: Combination: statute and Charter. Statutory presumption in Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 172.1(3) assessed under Charter s. 11(d) (with s. 1 analysis). The governing presumption-validity rule comes from SCC cases cited in the reasons (Whyte; Downey; Audet; St-Onge Lamoureux; Vaillancourt).
JudgeB: Moldaver J. (Wagner C.J. and Gascon, Côté, Brown, Rowe and Martin JJ. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Existence of a valid partnership for income tax loss deduction: at formation, evidence must show (1) “carrying on a business”, (2) “in common”, (3) “with a view to profit”; tax motivation does not negate partnership if these essentials are present (ancillary profit intention can suffice).
BaselineA: Common law partnership test (Continental Bank Leasing Corp. v. Canada, [1998] 2 S.C.R. 298; applied via Backman v. Canada, 2001 SCC 10) applied in the context of Income Tax Act, s. 96 loss deductions.
CaseB_TestB: Adequacy of jury instructions on credibility and reasonable doubt (W.(D.) context): where credibility is central, the judge must explain the relationship between credibility assessment and the Crown’s burden; the charge is sufficient if, read as a whole, it is “crystal clear” the burden never shifts and the jury is not left with a “credibility contest” choice between versions.
BaselineB: Common law jury-charge framework from R. v. W. (D.), [1991] 1 S.C.R. 742 (and subsequent SCC applications such as S. (W.D.) and Avetysan).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Customs Act s. 48(5)(a)(iv) “condition of sale” test for dutiable royalties/licence fees: royalties/licence fees are added to value for duty only if the purchaser “must pay, directly or indirectly, as a condition of the sale of the goods for export to Canada”; “Unless a vendor is entitled to refuse to sell licensed goods to the purchaser or repudiate the contract of sale where the purchaser fails to pay royalties or licence fees, s. 48(5)(a)(iv) is inapplicable.”
BaselineA: Statute (Customs Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (2nd Supp.), s. 48(5)(a)(iv), with interpretive reliance on common law/sale of goods concepts of “condition of sale”).
CaseB_TestB: ITA s. 224 “requirement to pay” trigger (bank liability to tax debtor): s. 224(1) applies only where the person served is “liable to make a payment” to the tax debtor; for cheques deposited to a joint account, “the fact that a person is designated as payee on the face of a cheque does not on its own mean that the bank is liable to make a payment to the person”; liability turns on cheque mechanics (e.g., presentment/holder status and deposit instructions).
BaselineB: Statute (Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), s. 224(1)) interpreted in light of Bills of Exchange Act provisions governing cheques/presentment/holder status (e.g., BEA ss. 2, 20(3), 84(1),(3), 86(1), 126, 138(2), 165(3)).
JudgeB: Deschamps J. (Binnie, Rothstein and Cromwell JJ. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Quebec Labour Code s. 45 “transfer of the operation of part of an undertaking” in subcontracting: s. 45 may apply where the transferee (1) performs similar functions and (2) “receives a right to operate part of the transferor’s undertaking”, with “sufficient degree of autonomy” assessed contextually (including the “criterion of the subordination of the employees to the contractors”).
BaselineA: Statute — Labour Code, R.S.Q., c. C-27, ss. 45-46, as interpreted in SCC jurisprudence (notably U.E.S., Local 298 v. Bibeault and Lester (W.W.) (1978) Ltd.).
CaseB_TestB: Jarvis “predominant purpose” test for when a CCRA audit becomes a penal investigation: the adversarial relationship is engaged where “the predominant purpose of an inquiry is the determination of a taxpayer’s penal liability”, assessed on the “totality of the circumstances” (no single factor determinative).
BaselineB: Common law/constitutional doctrine applying Charter ss. 7 and 8 to Income Tax Act audit powers, following R. v. Jarvis; applied in the context of Income Tax Act, ss. 231.1(1) and 231.2(1) (requirement powers) and s. 239 (tax offences).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Anns/Cooper duty of care test for statutory regulators: (1) prima facie duty based on foreseeability + proximity (including whether the case fits/analogizes to an existing category; if not, whether a new duty should be recognized, with proximity grounded in the statute); (2) if prima facie duty, whether residual policy considerations negate the duty
BaselineA: Common law (Anns v. Merton London Borough Council; Kamloops (City of) v. Nielsen), as clarified in Cooper v. Hobart (2001 SCC 79); applied in light of the governing statute (Law Society Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. L.8, esp. ss. 9, 33, 51, 61)
JudgeA: The Chief Justice and Major J.
CaseB_TestB: Section 1 (Oakes) justification analysis, including the Court’s articulation of five related questions: (1) pressing and substantial objective; (2) rational connection; (3) minimal impairment (as little as reasonably necessary); (4) proportionality between effects and objective; (5) whether deleterious effects outweigh salutary effects; and rejection of adding a separate “separation of powers” step
BaselineB: Constitutional (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 1) and common law framework from R. v. Oakes; applied to Public Sector Restraint Act, S.N. 1991, c. 3, s. 9
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Pragmatic and functional approach to select the standard of review (correctness here): assess (1) privative clause/statutory appeal, (2) relative expertise, (3) purpose of the Act/provision, (4) nature of the problem
BaselineA: Common law (standard of review framework from Pushpanathan v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), [1998] 1 S.C.R. 982; also referenced: Dr. Q v. College of Physicians and Surgeons of British Columbia, 2003 SCC 19)
CaseB_TestB: When collateral consequences/mistake of law/non-impairment may mitigate sentence for refusal causing death: (i) collateral consequences include consequences from commission/conviction/sentence that impact offender; must relate to offence/offender; no rigid formula; cannot make sentence disproportionate; vigilante violence considered only to a limited extent; (ii) mistake of law mitigates only if 'honest but mistaken belief in the legality'—'confusion or uncertainty' is not enough; (iii) non-impairment can mitigate but 'must be limited' and offender bears onus on balance of probabilities
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46: ss. 255(3.2), 718 to 718.2, 718.1; plus s. 19 re mistake of law not a defence) with common-law sentencing principles/cases (e.g., Lacasse, Pham, Ipeelee)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 2(b) infringement for sign restrictions: a by-law that restricts the use of an “optimum means of expression” (posting signs) to designated places “directly infringes freedom of expression” (para. 26), especially where its practical effect is to make it “impossible for any individual to post signs criticising” a business (para. 27).
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 2(b) (freedom of expression), applied to municipal by-law definitions and prohibition (Règlement d’urbanisme no 1200, ss. 2.2.4, 14.1.5(p)); SCC baseline approach to s. 2(b) includes Irwin Toy and related expression jurisprudence cited in the reasons.
CaseB_TestB: Canadian Bill of Rights due process/property analysis: s. 1(a) and s. 2(e) do not require (i) notice/hearing before Parliament enacts expropriative legislation; (ii) an adjudicative hearing where a law applies non-discretionarily to “incontestable facts”; and (iii) do not protect against expropriation by “clear and unambiguous” legislation—Parliament may expropriate property (even without compensation) if its intent is “clear and unambiguous” (paras. 37, 45, 51-57).
BaselineB: Statute: Canadian Bill of Rights, ss. 1(a) and 2(e), and the interpretive/paramountcy rule in s. 2 (unless expressly declared to operate notwithstanding). Applied to Department of Veterans Affairs Act, s. 5.1(4).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Copyright Act s. 3(1) “reproduction” requires copying (typically multiplication/new copies); mere physical transfer of the same ink layer to a new substrate is not “production (or reproduction) ... in any material form” and thus not an infringing copy for s. 38(1) seizure
BaselineA: Statute (Copyright Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-42, ss. 3(1), 38(1); definition of “infringing” in s. 2; moral rights context in s. 28.2; Quebec C.C.P. art. 734 for seizure before judgment)
CaseB_TestB: Reasonableness simpliciter on judicial review: a decision is unreasonable only if “there is no line of analysis within the given reasons that could reasonably lead the tribunal from the evidence ... to the conclusion”; if any sufficient reasons are “tenable” on a “somewhat probing examination”, the court must not interfere
BaselineB: Common law (standards of review framework from SCC cases, especially Canada (Director of Investigation and Research) v. Southam Inc. and Pushpanathan v. Canada; applied within statutory appeal under Law Society Act, 1996 (N.B.), ss. 66(1), 68)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Privacy Act s. 22(1)(b) exemption: government institution may refuse access only if disclosure “could reasonably be expected to be injurious” to the conduct of lawful investigations; requires a “clear and direct connection” between disclosure of the specific information and the alleged injury, supported by “concrete reasons” tied to the case (not mere general assertions or lack of consent).
BaselineA: Statute (Privacy Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. P-21, ss. 12(1), 22(1)(b), 22(3), 47, 49; reconciled with Official Languages Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 31 (4th Supp.), ss. 60(1), 72-74).
CaseB_TestB: Adverse inference / presumption of fact in medical causation: where defendant’s negligence undermines proof of causation and plaintiff adduces some evidence, the trier of fact is not required to draw an adverse inference; it is a discretionary presumption of fact under CCQ art. 2849, available only if “serious, precise and concordant”, assessed legally (not scientifically) and weighed with all the evidence.
BaselineB: Statute and jurisprudence: Civil Code of Québec, art. 2849 (presumptions of fact) as informed by SCC causation/inference cases Snell v. Farrell and St-Jean v. Mercier.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Validity/interpretation of a zoning “holding regulation”: a by-law clause stating “Notwithstanding any other provisions... no building... may be... erected to contain three or more dwelling units” operates as a lawful freeze on apartment development; added language about future amendment/schedules is treated as “superfluous words” that do not invalidate the effective prohibitory words (i.e., read the provision as a prohibition rather than an ad hoc discretionary licensing scheme).
BaselineA: Statute + municipal by-law: The Planning Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 349, s. 35(1) (zoning power) and s. 35(22) (appeal to Municipal Board), applied to City of London zoning by-law 306-480 as amended by by-law 306(bc)-504, s. 4 (new s. 11 “Holding Regulation”).
CaseB_TestB: Custody assessment under the Infants Act: the court “must consider the conduct of the parties” as it bears on “relative fitness” to have custody, but conduct/fault is “only one factor” and “each particular case must be judged on its own circumstances” with “the paramount consideration... the welfare of the children.”
BaselineB: Statute + prior custody jurisprudence: The Infants Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 222, s. 1(1) (welfare paramount; direction to consider conduct), informed by cases cited in the reasons (e.g., McKee v. McKee; Bickley v. Bickley; Retzer v. Retzer; Re L.; and Spence J.’s contemporaneous discussion in Talsky v. Talsky).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: OSC disclosure of compelled investigation material under Securities Act s. 17(1): apply Stinchcombe-style relevance (“reasonable possibility of being relevant to full answer and defence”) and then decide if disclosure is “in the public interest” by balancing confidentiality/privacy against fairness/full answer and defence; disclosure should be limited to what is necessary to carry out the OSC’s mandate
BaselineA: Statute (Ontario Securities Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. S.5, ss. 16-17) plus common-law relevance standard from R. v. Stinchcombe
CaseB_TestB: Framework to classify requested state-held records as first-party (Stinchcombe/McNeil) or third-party (O’Connor) disclosure: consider (1) whether the information is in the possession/control of the prosecuting Crown; and (2) if not, whether the police/other Crown entity ought to have supplied it because it is part of the “fruits of the investigation” or “obviously relevant”; if neither, O’Connor applies and the accused must show the record is “likely relevant” (“reasonable possibility” it is logically probative)
BaselineB: Common law (Stinchcombe; McNeil; O’Connor) applied in the context of Criminal Code s. 258(1)(c)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Misfeasance in public office (Iacobucci J.): plaintiff must prove (1) “deliberate unlawful conduct in the exercise of public functions”; and (2) “awareness that the conduct is unlawful and likely to injure the plaintiff” (plus causation and compensable loss).
BaselineA: Common law tort (as discussed through cases such as Roncarelli v. Duplessis; Three Rivers District Council v. Bank of England (No. 3); and others cited in the reasons).
CaseB_TestB: Eligibility for Quebec seats under Supreme Court Act s. 6: appointee must be a current member “from among” the Quebec Court of Appeal/Superior Court or “from among the advocates of [Quebec]” (i.e., current membership; former advocates excluded).
BaselineB: Statute/constitutional text: Supreme Court Act, ss. 5 and 6 (interpreted in light of Constitution Act, 1982, Part V, including s. 41(d)).
JudgeB: The Chief Justice and LeBel, Abella, Cromwell, Karakatsanis and Wagner JJ.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Securities Act s. 162 administrative penalty: after a contravention, the Commission may impose up to $100,000 if it "considers it to be in the public interest"; in assessing public interest it may consider the full context, including general deterrence (a permissible factor) and settlements (relevant but not binding), and courts review the order "globally" for reasonableness (rational basis in light of statutory framework and circumstances).
BaselineA: Statute (Securities Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 418, s. 162; also s. 167(3) on appeal powers).
CaseB_TestB: Adequacy of jury instructions on alternative routes to murder liability where others may have participated: the charge must adequately convey that it is not necessary the accused acted alone; the jury may convict if satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt the accused "acted in concert with other persons" and "actively participated in the killing"; the trial judge may correct an erroneous "actual shooter" instruction by adding "or was otherwise an active participant" so the instructions are consistent and responsive to the evidence.
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, including ss. 21 and 229; appeal/miscarriage framework in s. 686(1)(b)(iii)).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Good-faith basis requirement for cross-examination on unproven facts (no evidentiary foundation required unless predicate is manifestly tenuous/suspect)
BaselineA: Common law (cross-examination ethics/limits), as reflected in R. v. Bencardino (Ont. C.A.) and discussed alongside R. v. Howard and Browne v. Dunn
CaseB_TestB: Federal paramountcy test (operational conflict vs. frustration of federal purpose; clear proof of federal purpose; restrained/cooperative-federalism approach)
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine of federal paramountcy (as summarized from SCC precedents such as Canadian Western Bank, COPA, Rothmans, and Ryan Estate)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Parliamentary privilege existence/scope test (authoritative precedent first; otherwise necessity): if not authoritatively established for Canada/Westminster, the claimant must show the activity is "so closely and directly connected" to legislative/deliberative functions (including holding government to account) that outside interference would undermine the autonomy needed for Parliament to do its work "with dignity and efficiency" (Vaid, paras. 39-40, 46).
BaselineA: Combination of constitutional text and common law: Constitution Act, 1867, s. 18; Parliament of Canada Act, s. 4; and prior SCC privilege jurisprudence (notably New Brunswick Broadcasting Co. v. Nova Scotia (Speaker of the House of Assembly) and Harvey v. New Brunswick (Attorney General)).
CaseB_TestB: Interpretive test for Tobacco Act s. 22(3) (ads appealing to young persons): s. 22(3) "requires the prosecution in a given case to prove that there are reasonable grounds to believe that the advertisement ... could be appealing to young persons", meaning "particularly attractive and of interest to young persons, as distinguished from the general population" (JTI-Macdonald, para. 89).
BaselineB: Statute (Tobacco Act, S.C. 1997, c. 13, s. 22(3)) interpreted in light of Charter s. 1/2(b) proportionality framework (Oakes) and bilingual statutory interpretation principles.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: GAAR “abusive tax avoidance” (s. 245(4)) test: after tax benefit and avoidance transaction are established, ask whether it “cannot be reasonably concluded that a tax benefit would be consistent with the object, spirit or purpose of the provisions relied upon by the taxpayer” (para. 31(1)(3)); apply a “unified textual, contextual and purposive analysis” of the provisions conferring the benefit (para. 31(4)) and deny the benefit where the transactions “frustrate or defeat the object, spirit or purpose” of those provisions (paras. 2, 35, 58).
BaselineA: Statute — Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), especially ss. 245(1)-(4) (GAAR) applied to benefits claimed under ss. 18(13) and 96(1); interpretive approach and GAAR framework followed from Canada Trustco Mortgage Co. v. Canada, 2005 SCC 54 (paras. 1-2, 31).
CaseB_TestB: Vancouver Sun informer-privilege procedure / guiding rule for in camera proceedings: a two-stage approach—(1) verify privilege; “evidence that a person is a police informer automatically engages the privilege” (para. 48) and “even the claim of informer privilege must not be disclosed” (para. 48); (2) once privilege exists, conduct proceedings giving “full effect” to the “complete and total bar” on disclosure while “limiting, as much as possible, any impairment of the open court principle” (paras. 47, 49, 72-73), generally ensuring at least public notice of the existence of the in camera hearing/decision and, where needed, creating a sealed “parallel proceeding” with a record number and a redacted public judgment (paras. 73-75, 82).
BaselineB: Common law — informer privilege and the procedural framework from Named Person v. Vancouver Sun, 2007 SCC 43 (paras. 5-6, 47-51).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “lawful authority” for whistleblower protection under s. 74(1)(a): includes not only police/agents of the state but also “individuals within the employer organization who exercise lawful authority over the employee(s) complained about, or over the activity that is or is likely to result in the offence” (para. 38).
BaselineA: Statute: The Labour Standards Act, R.S.S. 1978, c. L-1, s. 74(1)(a) (and interpretive direction/context including The Interpretation Act, 1995, S.S. 1995, c. I-11.2, s. 10; applied using the Driedger/Rizzo/Bell ExpressVu modern principle).
CaseB_TestB: Waiver of insurer’s right to rely on dishonoured-cheque non-payment rule: “Before one can find waiver there must be express and unequivocal language or conduct” (Dickson J.), in the context of s. 238(1) deeming a dishonoured premium cheque “not to have been made”.
BaselineB: Combination: Statute and common law. Statute: The Alberta Insurance Act, R.S.A. 1970, c. 187, s. 238(1) (dishonoured cheque deemed not payment). Common law: waiver principle as applied/followed from McGeachie v. North American Life Insurance Company (1893), 23 S.C.R. 148.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Whistleblower protection under Labour Standards Act s. 74(1)(a): whether the employee “has reported ... to a lawful authority” an activity “that is or is likely to result in an offence”; “lawful authority” includes internal workplace authorities who can lawfully address the wrongdoing (the “up the ladder” approach). Key holding: “the expression ‘lawful authority’ in s. 74 includes not only the police or other agents of the state ... but also individuals within the employer organization who exercise lawful authority over the employee(s) complained about, or over the activity that is or is likely to result in the offence” (para. 38).
BaselineA: Statute: The Labour Standards Act, R.S.S. 1978, c. L-1, s. 74(1)(a) (and s. 74(2) vexatious exception).
CaseB_TestB: Common-law joinder test (Clunas) for trying provincial charges with summary conviction criminal charges: two-part test requiring (1) the offences “could initially have been jointly charged” (interpreted functionally as requiring a “sufficient factual nexus” rather than the same physical charging document) and (2) a joint trial is “in the interests of justice” (a weighing of costs and benefits; consent relevant but not determinative). Key passages: Clunas test at para. 35; “functional approach ... asks ... whether there is a sufficient factual nexus” (paras. 39-40); and “The second element requires that a joint trial be in the interests of justice ... weighing of the costs and benefits” (para. 41-43).
BaselineB: Common law: R. v. Clunas, [1992] 1 S.C.R. 595 (two-part joinder test), as reaffirmed in R. v. S.J.L., 2009 SCC 14. Applied in the statutory context of the Provincial Offences Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. P.33 (notably ss. 2(1), 23, 47(1)) and the Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46 (notably ss. 591(3), 788(1)).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Two-step harm-based test for criminal indecency under s. 210(1): Crown must prove beyond a reasonable doubt (1) conduct "causes harm or presents a significant risk of harm" (e.g., to public autonomy/liberty, by predisposing anti-social behaviour, or by physical/psychological harm) and (2) the harm/risk is "of a degree that is incompatible with the proper functioning of society" (R. v. Kouri, paras. 9-10).
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 210(1) (and related definition in s. 197(1) "public place"), interpreted through the indecency jurisprudence; the Court states the structure is "[b]ased on the guidelines emerging from R. v. Butler" and elaborated in the companion case R. v. Labaye (paras. 1, 9-10).
CaseB_TestB: Pointe Gourde / s. 27(1)(a) compensation inquiry: when deciding whether a land-use enactment’s effect on value must be ignored, "the key question is whether the enactment was made with a view to the expropriation or, conversely, was an independent enactment"; the inquiry examines "the purposes and effects of the enactment" and "causation does not drive the inquiry" (St. John’s (City) v. Lynch, paras. 46, 48, 50-54).
BaselineB: Statute informed by common law: Expropriation Act, R.S.N.L. 1990, c. E-19, s. 27(1)(a) ("no account shall be taken of the compulsory acquisition of the land"), incorporating the common law Pointe Gourde principle (Pointe Gourde Quarrying and Transport Co. v. Sub-Intendent of Crown Lands) and related jurisprudence (paras. 2, 34-38, 46).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Interpretation of Limitations Act, s. 12: forum limitation law applies only to "live" foreign causes of action; s. 12 does not revive a claim already time-barred under the applicable foreign substantive law (including its limitation period under lex loci delicti). Key holding: "Section 12 does not purport to revive an action time-barred by the substantive law of the place where the accident occurred" and where the foreign limitation has expired "there was no right of action".
BaselineA: Combination: statute (Limitations Act, R.S.A. 2000, c. L-12, s. 12) interpreted against common law conflict-of-laws baseline from Tolofson v. Jensen (lex loci delicti includes foreign limitation period as substantive).
CaseB_TestB: Ancillary powers doctrine (Waterfield/Dedman framework) for common law police powers interfering with liberty: preliminary definition of asserted power and liberty interests; then (1) whether conduct falls within scope of a police duty; (2) whether conduct is a justifiable exercise of powers—i.e., "reasonably necessary"—weighing three factors: "(1) the importance of the performance of the duty to the public good, (2) the necessity of the interference with individual liberty for the performance of the duty, and (3) the extent of the interference with individual liberty"; onus on the state throughout. Applied to reject a purported power to arrest a lawful actor to prevent others’ breach of the peace.
BaselineB: Common law: ancillary powers doctrine from R. v. Waterfield as adopted/applied in SCC jurisprudence including Dedman v. The Queen and R. v. MacDonald (three-factor reasonable necessity analysis).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Palmer/Lévesque test for admitting fresh evidence on a sentence appeal (interests of justice): (1) due diligence; (2) relevance to a decisive/potentially decisive sentencing issue; (3) credibility; (4) could reasonably be expected to have affected the result
BaselineA: Common law (Palmer v. The Queen; adapted to sentence appeals in R. v. Lévesque) applied under Criminal Code, s. 687(1) (power to receive additional evidence)
CaseB_TestB: Section 8 reasonable expectation of privacy (REP) test: REP assessed on the 'totality of the circumstances' via four inquiries—(1) subject matter of the alleged search; (2) claimant’s direct interest; (3) subjective expectation of privacy; (4) whether that expectation is objectively reasonable
BaselineB: Common law Charter s. 8 framework (as reiterated in Marakah/Cole/Spencer/Tessling/Edwards) applied to Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 8 (and consequentially Criminal Code, ss. 183, 184.2)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Copyright Act s. 27(2)(e) secondary infringement requires “hypothetical infringement”: the importer must have imported a copy that “would infringe copyright if it had been made in Canada by the person who made it”; no liability where the hypothetical maker would be the Canadian copyright owner (owner cannot infringe its own copyright, and an exclusive licensee cannot sue the owner-licensor for infringement).
BaselineA: Statute (Copyright Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-42), especially ss. 27(2)(e), 27(1), 2.7, 13(5), 13(7), 36(1)-(2). Also relies on CCH’s three elements of secondary infringement, with s. 27(2)(e) as the “hypothetical” variant.
CaseB_TestB: Section 11(h) “punished … again” test for retrospective parole changes: the “dominant consideration” is “the extent to which an offender’s settled expectation of liberty has been thwarted by retrospective legislative action”; a retrospective change is not punitive if it “does not substantially increase the risk of additional incarceration”, but a change that “automatically lengthen[s] the offender’s period of incarceration” is a “clearest of cases” of double punishment.
BaselineB: Constitution (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 11(h), with s. 1 justification). Built from prior SCC punishment/double jeopardy jurisprudence (e.g., Wigglesworth, Shubley, Rodgers) but reformulated for retrospective parole-eligibility changes.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Sentencing of hybrid offences prosecuted summarily; appellate intervention standard: sentencing court must sentence within summary-conviction limits and, absent "an error of principle, failure to consider a relevant factor, or overemphasis of the appropriate factors", a sentence within range ("including the maximum") is varied only if "demonstrably inadequate or excessive"; "worst offender, worst offence" no longer constrains maximum sentences
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, Part XXIII) plus SCC sentencing jurisprudence rejecting the "worst offender, worst offence" constraint
CaseB_TestB: Mr. Big confession admissibility (new common law evidentiary rule): confessions to the state during a Mr. Big operation are "presumptively inadmissible" unless Crown proves (balance of probabilities) "the probative value of the confession outweighs its prejudicial effect"; probative value turns on reliability assessed via non-exhaustive circumstances and "markers of reliability"; separate abuse-of-process backstop for coercive/abusive operations
BaselineB: Common law evidence (party admissions exception to hearsay) and existing exclusionary doctrines (probative vs prejudicial discretion; abuse of process), with the SCC creating a new qualification for Mr. Big confessions
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Adequacy of jury charge (Azoulay/Jacquard): trial judge must (except rare needless cases) review the substantial parts of the evidence and give the jury the theory of the defence so they can appreciate the evidence and apply the law; the judge should “decant and simplify”, with latitude as to how much evidence to review so long as jurors get an “adequate understanding” of the relationship between essential evidence and the issues they must decide.
BaselineA: Common law (Azoulay v. The Queen; R. v. Jacquard)
CaseB_TestB: Trade-marks Act confusion test (s. 6): confusion exists if, considering “all the surrounding circumstances” (including the s. 6(5) factors), it is likely the “casual consumer somewhat in a hurry” will be led to the mistaken inference that the wares/services come from the same source; no requirement of “resemblance or linkage” between wares/services, and neither fame nor product-line difference “trumps” the totality-of-circumstances assessment.
BaselineB: Statute (Trade-marks Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. T-13, ss. 6(2) and 6(5))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Elements of the Criminal Code child-luring offence (s. 172.1(1)(c)): Crown must prove (1) intentional computer communication; (2) with a person the accused knows or believes is under 14; (3) for the specific purpose of facilitating a listed secondary offence; “facilitating” means “helping to bring about and making easier or more probable”, and the key question is whether “the evidence as a whole establishes beyond a reasonable doubt” the accused’s subjective purpose.
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 172.1(1)(c) (as then numbered); related secondary offences include ss. 151 and 152).
CaseB_TestB: Enforcement of a forum selection clause: absent legislation, the court should enforce the clause unless there is “strong cause” to displace the chosen forum; delivery of a statement of defence does not, by itself, bar a prompt Rule 21.01(3)(a) motion relying on the clause.
BaselineB: Common law (Z.I. Pompey Industrie v. ECU-Line N.V., 2003 SCC 27 “strong cause” test) applied within a procedural framework under Ontario Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 21.01(3)(a).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: SCC leave-to-appeal test under Supreme Court Act s. 40(1): leave only if the Court is of the opinion the question is of sufficient importance (public importance/importance of an issue of law or mixed fact and law, or otherwise warrants decision), and jurisdiction exists for “any final or other judgment” not excluded by s. 40(3).
BaselineA: Statute (Supreme Court Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. S-26, ss. 2, 40(1), 40(3); with interaction of Criminal Code ss. 691-693 for exclusions).
CaseB_TestB: Access to Information Act s. 27(1) third-party notice threshold: disclose without notice only in “clear cases” where there is “no reason to believe” the record might contain s. 20(1) material; refuse without notice where there is “no reason to believe” it is subject to disclosure; otherwise notice is required (including where the head is “in doubt” or intends severance under s. 25).
BaselineB: Statute (Access to Information Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. A-1, especially ss. 20(1), 25, 27(1), 28, 44).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.
