CaseA_TestA: Reasonableness of an unannounced forced entry (departure from “knock and announce”): police must ordinarily give (i) notice of presence, (ii) notice of authority, and (iii) notice of purpose; if they depart, the Crown must show an evidentiary basis that police had “reasonable grounds to be concerned” about harm or destruction of evidence, assessed on what was (or should reasonably have been) known at the time
BaselineA: Common law + constitutional (Charter s. 8) + statute. Baseline includes: (a) Charter s. 8 reasonableness framework from R. v. Collins (search must be authorized by law; law reasonable; search conducted reasonably); (b) common law “knock and announce” rule from Eccles v. Bourque; (c) justification/onus language from R. v. Genest and R. v. Gimson; and (d) Criminal Code, s. 29(1) (warrant must be had/produced where feasible) as interpreted in multi-officer execution.
CaseB_TestB: Implied assertions are hearsay when tendered for the truth of their contents; admissible only if within a traditional exception or, failing that, if the principled approach is satisfied on a voir dire by showing “sufficient indicia of reliability and necessity”
BaselineB: Common law. Baseline includes: (a) definition/features of hearsay from R. v. Khelawon (statement tendered for truth + no contemporaneous cross-examination); and (b) the principled hearsay framework summarized in R. v. Mapara (traditional exceptions remain; otherwise admissible only if necessity and reliability established).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: State Immunity Act commercial activity exception (s. 5): determine whether proceedings “relate to any commercial activity” by examining the “nature of the acts ... in their full context, which includes the purpose of the acts”; not enough that acts were “authorized or desired” by the state or done to preserve “public interests” (contextual nature/purpose characterization; accept foreign court’s findings of fact on recognition).
BaselineA: Statute — State Immunity Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. S-18, ss. 2 (“commercial activity”), 3 (general immunity), 5 (commercial activity exception); applied with reference to Re Canada Labour Code, [1992] 2 S.C.R. 50 (contextual nature/purpose approach).
CaseB_TestB: Miscarriage of justice / mistrial from procedural irregularity (tainted material to jury): assess whether the irregularity was “severe enough to render the trial unfair or create the appearance of unfairness”, using non-exhaustive reference points (centrality to case, gravity/likely influence, jury vs judge-alone, whether remedied, appearance of fairness, counsel’s response).
BaselineB: Statute — Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(a)(iii) (miscarriage of justice) and related curative provisions; framework articulated in these reasons (with supporting case law cited in the decision).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Journalist-source privilege (Quebec civil litigation): threshold relevance + Wigmore 4-factor test with context-specific balancing at factor 4
BaselineA: Common law (Wigmore privilege framework as applied to journalist-source privilege in R. v. National Post, 2010 SCC 16) applied within Quebec’s civil evidence/procedure context (notably C.C.Q., art. 2857 on relevance/admissibility; C.C.P., art. 46 general powers)
CaseB_TestB: Court jurisdiction to review voluntary association decisions: requires an underlying legal right; contract exists only if general contract formation (especially objective intention to create legal relations) is shown
BaselineB: Common law (voluntary associations justiciability/jurisdiction from Highwood Congregation of Jehovah’s Witnesses (Judicial Committee) v. Wall, 2018 SCC 26; contract formation principles including objective intention to create legal relations)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Quebec Charter s. 49(2) punitive (exemplary) damages: admissible autonomously (not dependent on compensatory damages) where there is (1) “unlawful interference” with a Charter right and (2) “intentional” interference; punitive damages may serve denunciation even if the wrongdoer is deceased
BaselineA: Statute (Quebec Charter, s. 49(2)) interpreted alongside Civil Code of Québec, art. 1621; prior SCC Charter-damages jurisprudence (Béliveau St-Jacques; St-Ferdinand; Augustus) on the relationship between compensatory and exemplary damages and the meaning of “unlawful and intentional interference”
CaseB_TestB: YCJA jurisdiction for youth judicial interim release on s. 469 charges after election: (1) “the proceeding” in YCJA ss. 13(2)-(3) includes all steps after election (including pre-trial bail) until trial; (2) YCJA s. 33(8) gives release power to “a youth justice court judge” (including both s. 13(1) designated youth court judges and ss. 13(2)-(3) deemed superior court judges), so jurisdiction is concurrent
BaselineB: Statute (Youth Criminal Justice Act, ss. 13(1)-(3), 28, 33(8), 67; Criminal Code, ss. 469, 522; Interpretation Act, s. 33(2)) interpreted using modern statutory interpretation principles
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Miscarriage of justice on appeal: whether trial shortcomings "affected the trial judge’s appreciation of the evidence or rendered the proceedings unfair, so as to give rise to a miscarriage of justice" (including that leading questions are those that "suggest an answer or assume a state of facts that is in dispute").
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code appeal jurisdiction) plus common-law/Charter-informed appellate concept of "miscarriage of justice"
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 13 engagement turns on whether the prior compelled testimony is "incriminating evidence": evidence from the prior proceeding that the Crown could use at the later proceeding, if permitted, "to prove or assist in proving one or more of the essential elements of the offence"; if not, s. 13 is not engaged and the evidence may be used for impeachment.
BaselineB: Statute/constitutional text (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 13) as interpreted in prior SCC cases (notably R. v. Henry; also Kuldip, Noël, Dubois)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 467.12 “in association with” test: the phrase captures predicate offences that “advance, at least to some degree, the interests of a criminal organization”; it “requires a connection between the predicate offence and the organization, as opposed to simply an association between the accused and the organization”; and the Crown “must also demonstrate that an accused knowingly dealt with a criminal organization” (including wilful blindness).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 467.12(1) phrase “for the benefit of, at the direction of, or in association with, a criminal organization”; related definition in s. 467.1).
CaseB_TestB: Compulsion test for Motor Vehicle Act accident reports (Charter s. 7 use-immunity context): “whether, at the time that the accident was reported by the driver, the driver gave the report on the basis of an honest and reasonably held belief that he or she was required by law to report the accident to the person to whom the report was given” (and the accused bears the onus on a balance of probabilities to show compulsion).
BaselineB: Combination: Statute (Motor Vehicle Act, R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 288, s. 61(1)) interpreted through Charter baseline (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7 principle against self-incrimination; remedy discussion under s. 24(1)).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Reasonable suspicion standard for sniffer-dog search (and related investigative detention): requires a subjective suspicion grounded in “objectively discernible facts” assessed on the “totality of the circumstances” (a “constellation of factors”), through the lens of a reasonable officer; asks whether facts indicate the “possibility of criminal behaviour” (not probability) and must be more than a “hunch” (R. v. MacKenzie, 2013 SCC 50, paras. 41, 63, 71-73).
BaselineA: Common law Charter s. 8 sniffer-dog jurisprudence: R. v. Kang-Brown, 2008 SCC 18; R. v. A.M., 2008 SCC 19; companion clarification in R. v. Chehil, 2013 SCC 49 (as relied on in MacKenzie).
CaseB_TestB: Section 11(i) “punishment” test (reformulated): a measure is punishment if (1) it is a consequence of conviction forming part of the “arsenal of sanctions” and either (2) it is imposed in furtherance of sentencing purposes/principles, or (3) it has a “significant impact on an offender’s liberty or security interests” by significantly constraining lawful conduct or imposing significant burdens (R. v. K.R.J., 2016 SCC 31, paras. 28, 41-42).
BaselineB: Common law Charter s. 11(i) punishment framework from R. v. Rodgers, 2006 SCC 15 (two-part test at para. 63), as modified in K.R.J.; applied in relation to Criminal Code, s. 161(1)(c), (d).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: CCQ art. 1425 contract-interpretation/rectification: where evidence shows a discrepancy between the parties’ proven “common intention” and the “declared will” in the written instruments, the court may recognize and give effect to amendments correcting the writings once the error is proved and third-party rights are not affected (i.e., the court must “note the error and ensure that it is remedied”).
BaselineA: Statute (Civil Code of Québec, art. 1425; also relies on CCQ evidence provisions arts. 2818, 2829 and contract principles such as art. 1439).
CaseB_TestB: Bank ‘put upon inquiry’ constructive trust test: “A banker may be a constructive trustee of money in his customer’s account and in breach of that trust if he pays the money away, even on the customer’s mandate, in circumstances which put him upon inquiry.”
BaselineB: Common law (as summarized from Halsbury’s Laws of England and illustrated by cases cited in the reasons, including White v. Dominion Bank and Cartwright v. Lyster & Bank of Nova Scotia).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Whether a retrospective Quebec prescription amendment (1974, c. 80, s. 5) applies to a case pending in the Supreme Court of Canada so as to render Civil Code art. 2262(2) inapplicable and defeat a prescription defence (i.e., SCC may dismiss an appeal on the basis of a post-CA provincial statute).
BaselineA: Statute (Supreme Court Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. S-19, s. 47; plus Quebec Act to amend certain prescriptions, 1974 (Que.), c. 80, ss. 1, 3, 5; and Civil Code arts. 2261(2), 2262(2))
CaseB_TestB: Extradition refusal threshold on ministerial surrender: the person must show surrender would “shock the conscience” (s. 7 Charter) or be “unjust or oppressive” (Extradition Act, s. 44(1)); otherwise the Minister’s surrender decision is upheld if reasonable, with due process concerns generally left to the foreign court.
BaselineB: Statute and Constitution (Extradition Act, S.C. 1999, c. 18, s. 44(1); Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7; as applied through SCC precedents including United States v. Burns and Argentina v. Mellino)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Hart framework for admissibility of “Mr. Big” confessions: presumptive inadmissibility rebutted only if Crown shows (on balance) probative value (reliability) outweighs prejudicial effect; plus separate abuse-of-process backstop for coercive/abusive operations
BaselineA: Common law (party admissions exception to hearsay; trial judge discretion to exclude evidence more prejudicial than probative; abuse of process doctrine)
CaseB_TestB: Meaning of “her mind is then disturbed” in Criminal Code s. 233 (infanticide): apply “disturbed” in its ordinary sense with listed interpretive points (no need for mental disorder; must be present at time; must be “by reason of” childbirth/lactation; no causation requirement between disturbance and act)
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 233)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Penile swab as a search incident to arrest is Charter-compliant only if police (1) have reasonable grounds to believe the swab will reveal and preserve evidence of the offence of arrest, and (2) conduct the swab in a reasonable manner guided by specified safeguards (e.g., station-house, supervisory authorization, privacy, same-gender officers, minimal force, record-keeping).
BaselineA: Common law (search incident to arrest framework from R. v. Fearon; reasonableness requirements and strip-search tailoring from R. v. Golden; s. 8 reasonableness structure from R. v. Caslake; Stillman distinguished).
CaseB_TestB: Joint/co-principal liability in group assaults: liability “flows whenever two or more individuals come together with an intention to commit an offence, are present during the commission of the offence, and contribute to its commission”; for manslaughter, focus is whether the accused’s actions were “a significant contributing cause of death” (not who inflicted which wound), absent a discrete/intervening event.
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: Criminal Code, s. 21(1)(a) (co-principal) and related party-liability jurisprudence (Pickton; clarification of Cabrera/Shlah implication).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Whether a damages claim for breach/violation of a collective agreement clause (e.g., no-strike clause) is a statutory “grievance” that must go to arbitration: no distinction between “interpretation/application” and “violation” (they are “two ways of looking at the same problem”), and no distinction between employer and employee monetary claims.
BaselineA: Statute (Quebec Labour Code, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 141, ss. 1(g) definition of “grievance” as a “disagreement respecting the interpretation or application of a collective agreement”, and s. 88 mandatory arbitration of “Every grievance”), as interpreted in SCC precedents General Motors of Canada Ltd. v. Brunet, [1977] 2 S.C.R. 537 and Imbleau et al. v. Laskin et al., [1962] S.C.R. 338.
CaseB_TestB: Enforceability/scope of a waiver (exclusion) clause for negligence in a race entry form: construed in its context as a release; the clause applies unless the alleged negligence is outside what reasonable parties would have contemplated, and it will not be set aside as “unfair” or “unreasonable” absent factors like pressure/unconscionability/public policy concerns.
BaselineB: Common law (contractual interpretation/enforcement of exclusion/waiver clauses; doctrines argued included fundamental breach, unconscionability, and public policy—treated as common-law constraints).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: When a CLRB s. 119 ‘review’ application must be treated like a new certification: only if the Board’s review order would “enlarge or otherwise alter” the bargaining unit so that the “revised order will be substantially different”; otherwise it is merely an update/clarification and “the Board must simply be satisfied that these changes are in order.”
BaselineA: Statute — Canada Labour Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. L-1, s. 119 (Board may “review, rescind, amend, alter or vary any order or decision made by it”), as applied through the Board’s own s. 119 framework quoted from The Employees of the Regional Comptroller (1975), 9 D.I. 20; with judicial review route under Federal Court Act, s. 28(1)(a)-(c).
CaseB_TestB: Appellate intervention standard on factual findings: it is wrong for an appellate court to set aside a trial judgment where there is not “palpable and overriding error” and “the only point at issue is the interpretation of the evidence as a whole”; the appellate court must be able to say the trial judge was “plainly wrong.”
BaselineB: Common law — appellate review standard drawn from Schreiber Brothers Ltd. v. Currie Products Ltd. and Gulf Oil Canada Ltd., [1980] 2 S.C.R. 78; Stein v. "Kathy K.", [1976] 2 S.C.R. 802; and Lewis v. Todd, [1980] 2 S.C.R. 694.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Ernst (Cromwell J.) categorical Ward-based bar: Charter damages can never be an “appropriate and just” remedy (Charter, s. 24(1)) against this quasi-judicial regulator because countervailing factors (effective alternative remedy + good governance + immunity’s purpose) collectively negate damages
BaselineA: Common law / constitutional remedial framework under Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 24(1), as set out in Vancouver (City) v. Ward, 2010 SCC 27 (plus statutory context: Energy Resources Conservation Act, s. 43 immunity clause)
CaseB_TestB: Maybrun framework (as applied in Bird) for whether an accused charged with breaching an administrative order may collaterally attack the order: determine legislative intent using five non-exhaustive factors
BaselineB: Common law test from R. v. Consolidated Maybrun Mines Ltd., [1998] 1 S.C.R. 706 and R. v. Al Klippert Ltd., [1998] 1 S.C.R. 737 (applied in statutory context of Corrections and Conditional Release Act, s. 134.1(2), and Criminal Code, s. 753.3)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Art. 2930 C.C.Q. applies (3-year prescription) where the action is based on the obligation to make reparation for the direct and immediate consequences of interference with a person’s physical integrity; the court must characterize the action’s basis by the nature of the initial interference (bodily injury), not by the heads of damages claimed (paras. 26, 55).
BaselineA: Statute: Civil Code of Québec, arts. 2925 and 2930 (in interaction with Cities and Towns Act, s. 586).
CaseB_TestB: Appellate non-intervention in trial fact-finding/credibility: once the trial judge’s oral reasons are in the record, the Court of Appeal’s substitution of its view of the evidence for the trial judge’s is an “unwarranted intrusion” into the trial judge’s exclusive domain (citing Latour v. Grenier; Maze v. Empson; Dorval v. Bouvier; Métivier v. Cadorette; Hood v. Hood).
BaselineB: Common law principle of appellate deference to trial judges on assessment of evidence/credibility, as reflected in SCC precedents cited in the reasons (Latour; Maze; Dorval; Métivier; Hood).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Schrenk “sufficient nexus” test for discrimination “regarding employment”: Tribunal must conduct a contextual analysis to decide whether the discriminatory conduct has a “sufficient nexus with the employment context”, with non-exhaustive factors including “(1) whether the respondent was integral to the complainant’s workplace; (2) whether the impugned conduct occurred in the complainant’s workplace; and (3) whether the complainant’s work performance or work environment was negatively affected” (para. 67).
BaselineA: Statute: Human Rights Code, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 210, s. 13(1)(b) (“discriminate against a person regarding employment”), interpreted using modern statutory interpretation and human-rights interpretive principles.
CaseB_TestB: Groia in-court incivility/professional misconduct framework: a “context-specific” inquiry considering (generally) “what the lawyer said, the manner and frequency in which it was said, and the presiding judge’s reaction” (para. 80). For integrity-impugning allegations, they “cross the line into professional misconduct unless they are made in good faith and have a reasonable basis” (para. 81), with “reasonable basis” meaning not speculative and having “a sufficient factual foundation” even if based on a sincerely held but mistaken legal belief (paras. 88-89).
BaselineB: Regulatory/statutory: Law Society Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. L.8 (home statute) and Law Society Rules of Professional Conduct (incl. civility obligations), as applied through administrative-law reasonableness review.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Ontario anti-SLAPP dismissal framework under CJA s. 137.1: (1) defendant must show on a balance of probabilities the proceeding “arises from” an “expression” that “relates to a matter of public interest” (s. 137.1(3)); then (2) plaintiff must show “grounds to believe” the claim has “substantial merit” and defendant has “no valid defence” (s. 137.1(4)(a)), and (3) that the harm is “sufficiently serious” that the public interest in allowing the proceeding to continue “outweighs” the public interest in protecting the expression (s. 137.1(4)(b)) — the “fundamental crux of the analysis”. Key clarifications include: “grounds to believe” requires “a basis in the record and the law”; “substantial merit” means a “real prospect of success”; and s. 137.1(4)(b) is an open-ended public-interest weighing exercise.
BaselineA: Statute: Courts of Justice Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.43, s. 137.1(3) and (4) (anti-SLAPP).
CaseB_TestB: Corporate attribution doctrine (applied to one-person corporations) for limitation/discoverability purposes: corporate attribution provides “guiding principles” and must be applied “purposively, contextually, and pragmatically” to the purpose of the law under which attribution is sought; even where the directing mind test is met, courts have discretion to refuse attribution when it would not be “in the public interest” (i.e., would not promote the purpose of the relevant law). The SCC holds the same principles apply to one-person corporations and rejects any automatic attribution rule.
BaselineB: Common law: corporate attribution doctrine from Canadian Dredge & Dock Co. v. The Queen; Deloitte & Touche v. Livent Inc. (Receiver of); Christine DeJong Medicine Professional Corp. v. DBDC Spadina Ltd.; summarized in Aquino v. Bondfield Construction Co. Statutory context: Limitations Act, 2002, ss. 4, 5, 12; Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act, ss. 71, 97(3).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Duty-to-comment test for improper Crown jury address: whether Crown counsel’s remarks were “prejudicial to a degree sufficient to impose a legal duty on the trial judge to comment” to ensure the defence position was “fairly put to the jury” (failure to do so is an error of law).
BaselineA: Common law (trial fairness / jury charge principles) applied through Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(b)(iii) (curative proviso).
CaseB_TestB: “Identifiability” test for Federal Court in rem jurisdiction under s. 43(2): reject “physical nexus”; cargo is “subject of the action” if it is “the cargo designated in the contract of affreightment alleged to be breached”.
BaselineB: Statute: Federal Courts Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. F-7, s. 43(2) (“against the ship, aircraft or other property that is the subject of the action”).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Threshold for summary dismissal of criminal applications: an application may be summarily dismissed only if it is “manifestly frivolous”; on the motion the judge must “assume the facts alleged by the applicant to be true” and “take the applicant’s arguments at their highest”, without weighing evidence or choosing among competing inferences (R. v. Haevischer, 2023 SCC 11 at paras. 3, 66, 71, 82-85, 90).
BaselineA: Common law criminal procedure (case-management/summary dismissal power discussed through Vukelich/Kutynec line; SCC clarifies national threshold).
CaseB_TestB: Combined effect of Criminal Code s. 172.1(3) presumption and s. 172.1(4) “reasonable steps” requirement: if the interlocutor is represented as underage, the accused is presumed to believe they are underage; the presumption is rebutted only by “evidence to the contrary, which must include evidence that the accused took steps to ascertain the real age” and those steps must be “reasonable in the circumstances”; evidential burden on accused, persuasive burden on Crown (R. v. Levigne, 2010 SCC 25 at para. 32).
BaselineB: Statute — Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 172.1(3) and s. 172.1(4) (interpreted together).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Two-step framework for whether legislation displaces a common law sentencing rule (and its application to credit for pre-sentence driving prohibitions despite a mandatory minimum): (1) identify the applicable common law; (2) specify the statute’s effect (expressly or by necessary implication). Applied to hold that s. 259(1)(a) sets a minimum 'punishment' (not a minimum 'sentence'), so a judge must impose the one-year minimum but may then grant credit for pre-sentence prohibition time.
BaselineA: Combination of common law and statute: common law discretion to credit pre-sentence driving prohibitions (R. v. Lacasse, 2015 SCC 64) plus the settled two-step common law/statute interaction framework (2747-3174 Québec Inc. v. Quebec (Régie des permis d’alcool), [1996] 3 S.C.R. 919, para. 97), interpreted alongside Criminal Code provisions (notably ss. 259(1)(a) and 719(1)).
CaseB_TestB: Mitigation in contract where plaintiff claims specific performance: defendant must prove plaintiff failed to take 'reasonable steps' and that mitigation was possible; plaintiff’s refusal to mitigate may be reasonable only if it had a 'fair, real, and substantial justification' / 'substantial and legitimate interest' in specific performance—i.e., for investment land, only if damages are inadequate because the land has 'a peculiar and special value' to the plaintiff.
BaselineB: Common law mitigation doctrine and the specific-performance/mitigation qualification from Asamera Oil Corp. v. Seal Oil & General Corp., [1979] 1 S.C.R. 633 (pp. 668-69), read with Semelhago v. Paramadevan, [1996] 2 S.C.R. 415 (paras. 20-21) on when land is sufficiently unique that damages are inadequate.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Principled hearsay admissibility (and conformity of traditional exceptions): hearsay is admissible only if it meets the twin criteria of necessity and threshold reliability; even evidence within a traditional exception may be excluded if it fails necessity/reliability (e.g., statements of present intention inadmissible if made under “circumstances of suspicion”; statements cannot be used to prove a third party’s intentions absent an exception for each hearsay level). Key quotes: “Hearsay evidence may only be admitted if it is necessary and reliable” and “in the event of a conflict between the two, it is the principled approach that must prevail”; “the statement was made under ‘circumstances of suspicion’, and therefore does not fall within the present intentions exception.”
BaselineA: Common law (hearsay rule and traditional exceptions; principled approach from R. v. Khan and R. v. Smith; also references to R. v. B. (K.G.), R. v. Hawkins).
CaseB_TestB: Downtown Eastside public interest standing framework: discretionary, cumulative weighing of three factors — “(i) whether the case raises a serious justiciable issue; (ii) whether the party bringing the action has a genuine interest in the matter; and (iii) whether the proposed suit is a reasonable and effective means of bringing the case to court” — applied “flexibly and purposively”; legality/access to justice are relevant but do not get “particular weight”; no requirement of an individual co-plaintiff if a “sufficiently concrete and well-developed factual setting” will be forthcoming.
BaselineB: Common law (public interest standing doctrine; test from Canada (Attorney General) v. Downtown Eastside Sex Workers United Against Violence Society, 2012 SCC 45).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Limited-liability / non-assessability constraint on corporate articles: a company cannot, by amending articles or resolution, impose any pecuniary burden on holders of fully paid shares “in respect of those shares”; and a share transfer fee is valid only to the extent it reflects the “reasonable and proper cost of the transfer” (any excess is an illegal levy).
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law principle: The Companies Act (Alberta) (notably s. 42(1) alteration power “subject to the provisions of this Act and to the conditions contained in its memorandum”; plus limited-liability/non-assessability provisions including s. 68(4) deeming no-par shares “fully paid and non-assessable” and defining member liability as limited to unpaid amounts) together with the common-law ‘basic jural principle’ of limited liability (citing Ooregum Gold Mining Co. of India v. Roper; Bisgood v. Henderson’s Transvaal Estates; Shalfoon v. Cheddar Valley Co-operative Dairy Co.).
JudgeA: Dickson J. (for Ritchie, Pigeon and Dickson JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Van der Peet aboriginal-rights identification test (as applied): to be an aboriginal right, the activity must be “an element of a practice, custom or tradition integral to the distinctive culture of the aboriginal group”; the court (1) determines the “precise nature of the claim” (considering the action, the impugned regulation, and the relied-on practice), then (2) asks whether, “prior to contact with Europeans,” the practice was a “central, significant or defining feature” of the group’s distinctive culture.
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine under Constitution Act, 1982, s. 35(1), applying the SCC’s contemporaneous framework from R. v. Van der Peet (and situated within Sparrow’s s. 35 structure, though this case is resolved at the rights-identification stage).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Reviewability of a consensual labour arbitrator’s award for error of law on the face: no “specific question of law” reference where the issue arises in the ordinary grievance process under a collective agreement that limits the arbitrator to decisions consistent with the agreement
BaselineA: Common law (judicial review of consensual arbitration awards; distinction between a specific question of law referred vs. a general dispute where law arises incidentally), applied in the labour-arbitration/collective agreement context
CaseB_TestB: Morin framework for s. 11(b) “reasonable time” (length of delay minus defence waiver; then reasons for delay, prejudice, and s. 11(b) interests; prejudice may be inferred from length of delay)
BaselineB: Statute/constitutional text (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 11(b)) as operationalized by SCC common-law framework in R. v. Morin and R. v. Askov
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 3(4) “possession” framework (including joint possession): for Code purposes, possession is personal possession or knowingly having an item in another’s custody or in any place for use/benefit; and where one of two or more persons, with the knowledge and consent of the rest, has anything in custody/possession, it is deemed in the custody and possession of each and all
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 3(4)(a)-(b))
CaseB_TestB: Test for establishing adverse possession in British Columbia: possession must be “open and notorious, adverse, exclusive, peaceful (not by force), actual (generally), and continuous”; SCC also holds the “inconsistent use” requirement is not part of BC law
BaselineB: Common law adverse possession test as received/embedded through BC limitations legislation (received 1833 English codification; applied under BC limitation statutes such as Statute of Limitations (1924), ss. 16-17)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Quantum meruit for services accepted without agreed remuneration: where a party continues to request/authorize and accept services with no agreement on price, it is obligated to pay a reasonable rate (and statutory/regulatory instruments only bar recovery if they validly and clearly fix/limit the rate).
BaselineA: Common law (quasi-contract/quantum meruit), with statutory/regulatory interpretation of Hospital Act s. 37(2) and Orders in Council 3103, 4399, 4400 (and related Social Assistance Act and Residence and Responsibility Act provisions) to assess any bar/limit on recovery; King George Highway Hospital Ltd. v. District of Surrey, [1971] S.C.R. vi applied.
CaseB_TestB: Voluntariness/operating mind test for admissibility of inculpatory statements by an allegedly insane accused: the controlling question is whether the statement was "freely and voluntarily made", including whether it represents the utterances of an "operating mind" (not so devoid of rationality/understanding or so replete with psychotic delusions that it cannot fairly be said to be the accused’s statement).
BaselineB: Common law confessions rule (voluntariness) as articulated in Boudreau v. The King, [1949] S.C.R. 262 and Ward v. The Queen, [1979] 2 S.C.R. 30 (with discussion of R. v. Santinon (BCCA) and other authorities).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Effect of breach of a witness-exclusion order: witness not necessarily disqualified; admissibility is discretionary; weight is for trier of fact
BaselineA: Common law (practice/rule on exclusion of witnesses, as reflected in cases cited in the reasons: Moore v. Lambeth County Court Registrar; Cook v. Nethercotte; Thomas v. David; Chandler v. Home; R. v. Briggs; R. v. Thompson; Black v. Besse; R. v. Carefoot)
CaseB_TestB: Clear-and-unequivocal-language requirement to lift Crown immunity from discovery; CLPA s. 27 applies only when the Crown is a party
BaselineB: Combination of common law Crown immunity from discovery plus statute (Interpretation Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. I-21, s. 17; Crown Liability and Proceedings Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-50, s. 27 (and related context in Part II))
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory disqualification/bias rule for Law Society discipline: benchers who sat on the Discipline Committee are not barred from participating in Convocation’s consideration of the Committee’s report (a two-step process, not an appeal), and s. 39(4)’s express disqualification applies only to the specific s. 39 reprimand appeal (expressio unius est exclusio alterius).
BaselineA: Statute/regulation: The Law Society Act, 1970 (Ont.), c. 19, ss. 33(12), 34, 37, 39 (especially s. 39(4) disqualification on appeal from reprimand) and Reg. 556, s. 13(6)-(7) (report to Convocation).
CaseB_TestB: Criminal Code s. 731(1)(b) probation availability rule: “imprisonment for a term not exceeding two years” refers to the term imposed by the sentencing court at a single sitting; it does not include other outstanding or later sentences, but probation is unavailable if sentences imposed at the same session result in continuous custody exceeding two years.
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 731(1)(b) (with related context in s. 732.2 on when probation comes into force).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “operation of a mine” and when a separate “mine” exists for the 36‑month tax exemption: “operation of a mine” refers only to extraction of ore (not processing), and there is “a mine” if there is “a body of ore together with the workings, equipment and machinery capable of producing it”; a separate mine arises when a separate ore body “commenced to be extracted by means of its separate and distinct extraction facilities” (shared mill does not matter).
BaselineA: Statute: Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1952, c. 148 as amended, s. 83(5) (exemption for income “derived from the operation of a mine” for 36 months after it “came into production”) and s. 83(6) (definitions of “mine” and “production”); interpreted in light of SCC authorities North Bay Mica Co. Ltd. v. M.N.R., [1958] S.C.R. 597 and M.N.R. v. Maclean Mining Co., [1970] S.C.R. 877.
CaseB_TestB: Mancini test for leave under s. 215 BIA to sue a receiver/trustee: leave should be refused only for “frivolous or vexatious” or “manifestly unmeritorious” claims; leave should be denied if the supporting evidence (including draft pleading) “does not disclose a cause of action”; the court “is not required to make a final assessment of the merits”; if the evidence discloses a “prima facie case”, leave should be granted.
BaselineB: Statute: Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. B-3, s. 215 (leave required before an action lies against an interim receiver/trustee for actions taken under the Act), with the governing leave framework taken from Mancini (Bankrupt) v. Falconi (1993), 61 O.A.C. 332 (C.A.) as adopted/applied by the SCC.
JudgeB: Abella J. (McLachlin C.J. and Bastarache, Binnie, LeBel, Fish and Charron JJ. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Education Act s. 373 school-tax roll equalization: if municipal valuations are not uniform, commissioners must amend the rolls "so as to re-establish on the basis of its real value the valuation of the taxable property of all the parts of the school municipality"—i.e., equalize by valuing only what is taxable in each municipality (no importing another municipality’s choice to exempt machinery).
BaselineA: Statute (Education Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 235, s. 373; with municipal taxability of machinery governed by Cities and Towns Act, s. 488 (as amended 1959, now R.S.Q. c. 193)).
CaseB_TestB: Criminal Code s. 426(1)(a)(ii) secret commission offence (agent/taker): actus reus requires (1) agency relationship; (2) agent accepts a benefit "as consideration" for acting in relation to the principal’s affairs; and (3) "failure ... to make adequate and timely disclosure"—with "corruptly" meaning "secretly or without the requisite disclosure" and no requirement to prove a "corrupt bargain" with the giver.
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 426(1)(a), especially s. 426(1)(a)(ii)).
JudgeB: Cory J. (for L'Heureux-Dubé, Gonthier, Cory and Iacobucci JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Extradition-crime classification under an extradition arrangement: “The test is what is the essence of the crime charged” (i.e., whether the charged offence is, in substance, a crime “against the laws for the suppression of the traffic in narcotics”).
BaselineA: Statute + treaty/arrangement incorporated into statute: Extradition Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-21, s. 2 (definition of “extradition crime”), and the 1925 Supplementary Convention category “Crimes and offences against the laws for the suppression of the traffic in narcotics” (added to the Act).
CaseB_TestB: Section 13 Charter / s. 5(2) Canada Evidence Act distinction: prior testimony may be used on retrial in cross-examination if its purpose is to impeach credibility, but not if it is used “to incriminate” (to establish guilt).
BaselineB: Constitution + statute: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 13; Canada Evidence Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-10, s. 5(2) (as interpreted alongside prior SCC cases including R. v. Dubois and R. v. Mannion).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Negligence/causation foreseeability test for highway authority liability: “whether a reasonable person should have anticipated that what happened might be a natural result of that act or omission”; not necessary to foresee the “precise concatenation of events”, only “in a general way the class or character of injury which occurred”.
BaselineA: Common law foreseeability/remoteness in negligence (University Hospital Board v. Lépine; Wagon Mound No. 2; Hoffer). Also applied in the context of the Highway Improvement Act, R.S.O. 1960, s. 33(1) (duty to maintain).
CaseB_TestB: CEAA “tracking” rule: the environmental assessment track is determined by the “project as proposed” (not “project as scoped”); if the proposed project is in the Comprehensive Study List, s. 21 requirements are mandatory and the responsible authority “cannot reduce the scope of the project to less than what is proposed by the proponent” (though it may enlarge scope under s. 15(2)-(3)).
BaselineB: Statutory interpretation/application of the Canadian Environmental Assessment Act, S.C. 1992, c. 37, especially ss. 2 (“project”), 15, 18, 21, 21.1, 58(1)(i), and the Comprehensive Study List Regulations, SOR/94-638 (Sch., s. 16).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Using res ipsa loquitur to infer (and support a finding of) gross negligence for a gratuitous passenger claim: applies where (1) the thing causing damage was under defendant’s “sole management and control”; (2) the occurrence is such that it “would not have happened without negligence”; and (3) there is “no evidence as to why or how the occurrence took place” — but if an explanation is given and is “no answer, even if believed in full”, the maxim may still apply.
BaselineA: Combination: statute (Highway Traffic Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 202, s. 132(3) gross negligence requirement for gratuitous passengers) + common law evidentiary rule (res ipsa loquitur as described via Clerk & Lindsell; SCC recognition in Walker v. Coates).
CaseB_TestB: Vested-rights (acquired-rights) test for whether new legislation can affect an existing legal position: a vested right exists where (1) the individual’s legal situation is “tangible and concrete rather than general and abstract”; and (2) the situation was “sufficiently constituted at the time of the new statute’s commencement”. Absent clear legislative intent, legislation is presumed not to interfere with such vested rights.
BaselineB: Combination: statutory interpretation baseline (Interpretation Act, R.S.Q., c. I-16, s. 12; transitional provision in Amending Act, 1998, s. 13 re “juridical situations in progress”) + common law/civil-law interpretive presumption against interference with vested/acquired rights (e.g., Spooner Oils; Gustavson Drilling).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Mechanics’ lien owner-liability/holdback test on contractor abandonment: s. 19(2) does not prevent the owner deducting completion costs from amounts otherwise payable to the head contractor; owner liability remains limited by s. 6 to “the sum payable by the owner to the contractor” (so liens do not attach to a broader ‘fund’ immune from completion-cost deductions).
BaselineA: Statute (Mechanics’ Lien Act, R.S.B.C. 1960, c. 238, especially ss. 6, 19(2), 21(1), 21(6); interpreted in light of Comstock following Guttman/Freedman).
CaseB_TestB: Choice-of-law rule for torts: “as a general rule, the law to be applied in torts is the law of the place where the activity occurred, i.e., the lex loci delicti”; with only a narrowly confined possibility of rare exceptions (and foreign limitation periods treated as substantive where they create an accrued right to plead a time bar).
BaselineB: Common law (conflict of laws in tort: Phillips v. Eyre; McLean v. Pettigrew (overruled); related double-actionability jurisprudence) plus characterization principles applied to limitation statutes.
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Constitutional (territorial) validity test for provincial legislation with extraterritorial operation: a province cannot legislate in relation to conduct/rights outside its territory; Manitoba’s s. 4(2) was ultra vires because it purported to nullify an out-of-province permission/licence. Key formulation: s. 4(2) 'purported to nullify the effect of permission duly granted by the regulatory authority of another jurisdiction' and thus 'purported to legislate with respect to conduct and rights of the [defendants] outside the territorial limits of the Province of Manitoba' (Ritchie J.).
BaselineA: Statute (The Fishermen’s Assistance and Polluters’ Liability Act, 1970 (Man.), especially s. 4(2)) plus constitutional limits under the B.N.A. Act, 1867 (territorial limits on s. 92 powers; discussion also engages s. 91(12) and POGG).
JudgeA: Pigeon J. (for Martland, Pigeon and Beetz JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Privative-clause judicial review threshold: court may intervene only if the tribunal’s decision is 'patently unreasonable' / an 'unreasonable finding' that 'impairs the jurisdiction of the tribunal'. Key quote: 'was the Board's interpretation so patently unreasonable that its construction cannot be rationally supported by the relevant legislation and demands intervention by the court upon review?' (adopting CUPE).
BaselineB: Common law administrative law doctrine on privative clauses and jurisdictional review (CUPE and related SCC jurisprudence) applied in the statutory setting of Act respecting labour standards, R.S.Q., c. N-1.1, ss. 124-129 (esp. s. 128) and Labour Code s. 139 (privative clause).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Collective agreement not terminable by common-law repudiation/fundamental breach during its term; an illegal strike does not per se terminate employment, and absent employer disciplinary discharge the employer remains bound by collective-agreement severance obligations upon plant closure
BaselineA: Combination: statute (Mediation Services Act, 1968 (B.C.), ss. 6, 8, 23) plus SCC/common-law labour jurisprudence rejecting individual-contract framing (Syndicat catholique des employés de magasins de Québec Inc. v. Compagnie Paquet Ltée; C.P.R. Co. v. Zambri) and related authority (Re Polymer)
JudgeA: Laskin C.J. (for Laskin C.J. and Martland, Judson, Dickson and Beetz JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Limits on cross-examination using a complainant’s diary: relevant defence evidence may be excluded only if its prejudicial effect substantially outweighs probative value; omission evidence is probative only if the defence establishes a reasonable expectation the event would have been recorded; O’Connor production balancing is not the admissibility/cross-examination test
BaselineB: Common law (Seaboyer; Osolin; O’Connor distinguished) with statutory context rejected as inapplicable to admissibility (Criminal Code, ss. 278.1–278.9)
JudgeB: Binnie J. (for McLachlin C.J. and Iacobucci, Major, Bastarache, Binnie, Arbour and LeBel JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Admissibility of evidence that an accused refused to participate in a police line-up: admissible only where, in the circumstances, it is relevant (typically to explain the absence of a line-up) and not merely to suggest guilt
BaselineA: Common law (evidence relevance/admissibility principles; privilege against self-incrimination limited to testimonial compulsion as discussed via Curr v. The Queen and Attorney-General of Quebec v. Begin)
CaseB_TestB: Division of powers (pith and substance) limit on provincial commissions of inquiry: an inquiry is ultra vires if, in purpose/effect, it is a substitute police investigation/preliminary inquiry into specific Criminal Code offences by named private individuals (i.e., circumvents federal criminal procedure)
BaselineB: Constitution Act, 1867 (ss. 91(27), 92) and the pith-and-substance doctrine; applied to a provincial Order in Council under the Public Inquiries Act, R.S.O. 1980, c. 411, s. 2
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Punitive damages in tort: whether the circumstances justify an additional punitive award (here, where tortious conduct was coupled with a scheme to take over and end the plaintiff as a going concern), assessed as required by the 'interests of justice'/'substantial justice' in the circumstances
BaselineA: common law (punitive/exemplary damages principles in tort; no specific baseline case articulated in the reasons provided)
CaseB_TestB: Anns/Cooper duty-of-care framework for recognizing a new duty of care in negligence (pure economic loss): Stage 1—(1) reasonable foreseeability and (2) proximity including party-specific policy reasons; Stage 2—residual policy considerations (e.g., indeterminate liability) that may negate the duty
BaselineB: common law (Anns v. Merton London Borough Council; adopted in Kamloops (City of) v. Nielsen; refined in Cooper v. Hobart and Childs v. Desormeaux)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory limits on Canadian Transport Commission power re freight-tariff notice/effective date: even assuming s. 275(2) allows extending the 30-day notice, any extension must be ordered before the tariff’s stated effective date; a post-effective-date ‘extension’ is an impermissible indirect postponement and is ultra vires (tariff takes effect on stated date under s. 275(4)).
BaselineA: Statute: Railway Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. R-2, s. 275(2) and s. 275(4) (with context from National Transportation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. N-17, s. 3(a) and s. 64(5)). Key statutory language: s. 275(2) requires filing/publishing an advancing tariff 'at least thirty days before its effective date' 'Unless otherwise ordered by the Commission'; s. 275(4) provides tolls 'shall take effect on the date stated in the tariff' and are 'conclusively deemed to be the lawful tolls' unless disallowed.
CaseB_TestB: Palmer test for admitting fresh evidence on appeal (criminal): overriding consideration is 'in the interests of justice' and requires (1) due diligence (relaxed in criminal cases), (2) relevance to a decisive/potentially decisive issue, (3) credibility, and (4) whether, if believed, it 'could reasonably ... be expected to have affected the result'.
BaselineB: Common law: Palmer v. The Queen, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 759 (fresh-evidence criteria), applied under Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 683 (appellate power to admit fresh evidence). Quoted formulation: 'The overriding consideration ... is “the interests of justice” ... (1) ... due diligence ... (2) ... relevant ... (3) ... credible ... (4) ... could reasonably ... be expected to have affected the result.'
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Contextual approach to whether an order discharging a restriction is sufficiently “final” (despite an unexpired appeal period) to answer a purchaser’s title requisition: consider “the purpose for which the finality or want of finality of an order is urged”, “who is affected”, and “in what context” it is asserted; the order may be fully effective if there is only an “ephemeral prospect of an appeal”.
BaselineA: Statute (The Conveyancing and Law of Property Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 85, s. 62) plus general/common-law principles about the effect of appealable orders (with Ontario authorities Re West (1928) and Leonard v. Wharton (1921) discussed/distinguished).
CaseB_TestB: Sufficiency of evidence for committal at a preliminary inquiry (s. 548(1) Criminal Code): ask “whether or not there is any evidence upon which a reasonable jury properly instructed could return a verdict of guilty”; if Crown evidence is circumstantial, the judge must do a “limited weighing” of the whole record (including defence evidence) to assess whether the evidence, if believed, could reasonably support the inference of guilt, without drawing inferences or assessing credibility.
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 548(1) (and Part XVIII generally), interpreted through the common law rule from United States of America v. Shephard, [1977] 2 S.C.R. 1067 (also relying on Mezzo v. The Queen and R. v. Monteleone).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Discretionary test for granting public-interest/taxpayer standing to challenge legislation (McNeil/Thorson): serious constitutional issue + plaintiff has taken reasonable steps and is arguably directly affected + no other practical way to bring the issue before the courts
BaselineA: Common law (standing/locus standi doctrine), drawing on Smith v. Attorney General of Ontario, [1924] S.C.R. 331 and Thorson v. Attorney General of Canada, [1975] 1 S.C.R. 138
CaseB_TestB: Interpretation of ASRA Program s. 88(3): applying C.C.Q. arts. 1425-1432 (esp. 1426, 1427), s. 88(3) gives La Financière discretion to choose collective or individual linkage, constrained by good faith and contractual fairness (C.C.Q. arts. 6, 7, 1375, 1434)
BaselineB: Statute/regulation and civil-law codal interpretation: Programme d’assurance stabilisation des revenus agricoles, s. 88(3) (and related structure), interpreted through Civil Code of Québec arts. 1425-1432; discretion constrained by C.C.Q. arts. 6, 7, 1375, 1434
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Rebuttable presumption of mens rea for trafficking in LSD once actus reus proved: when it is proved the accused trafficked in LSD, a rebuttable presumption arises that the condition was voluntarily induced/that he intended to traffic in LSD and he "must be convicted unless other evidence is adduced which raises a reasonable doubt" that he lacked mens rea (e.g., an honest belief amounting to non-existence of mens rea).
BaselineA: Common law (mens rea/mistake of fact principles) applied to statutory offence under Food and Drugs Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. F-27, ss. 40, 42 (restricted drugs/trafficking); baseline authorities include Beaver v. The Queen and R. v. King (rebuttable presumption approach).
CaseB_TestB: Limits on trial judge intervention—new trial where conduct creates doubt about impartiality: although a judge may question/interrupt witnesses "within certain limits", the interventions must be such that "justice is seen to be done"; if the judge's conduct gives the impression of assisting the prosecution and "raised some doubt as to his impartiality", a new trial is required.
BaselineB: Common law procedural fairness/natural justice (appearance of justice and judicial impartiality), drawing on R. v. Sussex Justices; Ex parte McCarthy and related authorities on permissible judicial intervention.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory-interpretation rule for s. 213 constructive murder: “burglary” retains its 1892 Criminal Code meaning (burglary = breaking and entering a dwelling-house by night, etc.), despite later revision ambiguities; therefore “burglary” in s. 213 “still means the offence defined as such in s. 410 of the Criminal Code 1892, coupled with the definitions of ‘dwelling-house’ and ‘break’ in s. 407.”
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 213; Interpretation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-23, s. 36(f) (repeal-and-substitution/consolidation principle), plus historical Criminal Code provisions (1892 Code ss. 228, 410, 407) used to resolve ambiguity).
CaseB_TestB: Damages for breach where contract has alternative modes of performance: adopt the mode “least profitable to the plaintiff, and the least burdensome to the defendant”; “The test is not how the defendant would likely have performed ... but for ... repudiation”; plaintiff is restored to the position it “would have been in had the contract been performed.”
BaselineB: Common law (general principle traced to Cockburn v. Alexander (1848) and explained in Withers v. General Theatre Corp. (1933), adopted in Canadian appellate jurisprudence).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Lease interpretation test for shifting fire-loss risk to landlord: applying “the ordinary test of reading [the lease] reasonably and in a business sense”, a tenant covenant to “pay… insurance rates” means the fire-loss risk (including tenant-negligence fire) passes to the landlord (at least once the landlord presents the insurance bill), barring the landlord’s insurer’s subrogated claim.
BaselineA: Common law contract/lease interpretation ("reading it reasonably and in a business sense"), applied in the landlord-tenant/insurance context; with reference to Ontario Insurance Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 224, s. 118 (fire coverage includes third-party negligence).
CaseB_TestB: Civil Code art. 1053 “fault-damage” basis for bank liability on unauthorized endorsements: a bank commits a compensable “fault” by accepting/processing cheques payable to a company for deposit to an individual’s personal benefit “without examining it, and without verifying the sufficiency of the endorsement”; if this deprives the payee of its money and it has no remaining recourse against the drawer, damages equal the cheque amounts.
BaselineB: Statute and civil law: Civil Code art. 1053 (fault causing damage) applied alongside Bills of Exchange Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. B-5, ss. 10 and 51 (including s. 51 on signatures by procuration as notice of limited authority), building on Norwich Union Fire Insurance Society Ltd. v. La Banque Canadienne Nationale, [1934] S.C.R. 596.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 15(1) adverse-impact discrimination (prima facie breach): (1) law creates a distinction on an enumerated/analogous ground through its effects by having a “disproportionate impact” on a protected group; and (2) it “imposes burdens or denies a benefit” in a way that “reinforc[es], perpetuat[es], or exacerbat[es] disadvantage” (with flexible proof of disproportionate impact—statistics and/or group-context evidence; no intent; no need to prove the protected characteristic ‘caused’ the disparity).
BaselineA: Combination: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 15(1) (and s. 1 for justification) as interpreted in prior SCC cases (e.g., Withler; Taypotat; Alliance; Centrale).
CaseB_TestB: Division of powers “pith and substance” analysis for validity of legislation: (1) determine the law’s “essential character” by examining “purpose and the legal effect”; then (2) ask whether that character relates to an enumerated head of power (here, whether s. 27 is in pith and substance fisheries under s. 91(12) rather than property and civil rights under s. 92(13), and not criminal law under s. 91(27)).
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine of pith and substance under the Constitution Act, 1867 (ss. 91(12), 91(27), 92(13)), applied to Marine Mammal Regulations, s. 27 (made under Fisheries Act, s. 43).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Lease interpretation test for whether tenant’s covenant to pay “insurance rates” shifts the fire-loss risk (including tenant-negligence fire) to the landlord, barring the landlord/insurer’s subrogated claim: apply “the ordinary test of reading [the lease] reasonably and in a business sense”; here, “under the provision of the lease respecting payment of insurance rates by the tenant, the risk of loss by fire passed to the landlord, at least upon the presentation by the landlord of the insurance bill”.
BaselineA: Common law contract/lease interpretation ("reading it reasonably and in a business sense"), applied in the landlord-tenant/insurance context; with statutory backdrop noted (Ontario Insurance Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 224, s. 118, on standard fire coverage) and prior SCC authority discussed (United Motors Service, Inc. v. Hutson).
CaseB_TestB: Warsaw Convention limitation entitlement based on ticket delivery/content: for passenger death claims under Art. 3(2), limitation is lost “only where no ticket is delivered” (irregularity/illegibility does not equal non-delivery); for baggage claims under Art. 4(4), limitation is lost if luggage accepted without a luggage ticket or if the ticket lacks particulars (d), (f), (h), and compliance turns on whether the print is “legible by the ordinary person using ordinary diligence” and content is adequate.
BaselineB: Statute: Carriage by Air Act, R.S.C. 1952, c. 45, Schedule I (Warsaw Convention), especially Arts. 3(1)-(2), 4(1)-(4), and 22 (limitations).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Negligent misrepresentation (heating-cost estimate): plaintiff must prove more than a wrong estimate—must show the error resulted from a lack of "skill, competence or diligence" / failure to exercise "such care as the circumstances required"; care level depends on what advice was sought and what the defendant represented it could give.
BaselineA: Common law (negligent misrepresentation / duty of care for advice), drawing on Hedley Byrne & Co. Ltd. v. Heller & Partners Ltd. and Mutual Life and Citizens’ Assurance Co. Ltd. v. Evatt (as cited in the reasons).
CaseB_TestB: Extra-territoriality (s. 92 limits) for provincial laws with an intangible pith and substance: (1) identify pith and substance and a provincial head of power; (2) if intangible, determine whether it is "in the Province" by examining "the relationships among the enacting territory, the subject matter of the legislation and the persons made subject to it" to ensure a "meaningful connection" and respect for other jurisdictions’ sovereignty.
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine interpreting Constitution Act, 1867, s. 92 territorial limits (including s. 92(13)), relying on prior SCC cases cited (e.g., Churchill Falls; Unifund; Global Securities).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Parole suspension power under Parole Act s. 16(1): a designated person may suspend parole and authorize apprehension only "by a warrant in writing signed by him" and only when "he is satisfied that the arrest of the inmate is necessary or desirable" for specified purposes (prevent breach of conditions, rehabilitation, or protection of society).
BaselineA: Statute (Parole Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. P-2, ss. 16(1)-(2); also referenced: s. 10(1)(e), s. 20(1))
CaseB_TestB: Equitable compensation for Crown breach of fiduciary duty over reserve land: (1) identify fiduciary obligations; (2) identify the beneficiary’s "lost opportunity" caused in fact by the breach; (3) assess (not precisely calculate) loss with "benefit of hindsight" and without common-law remoteness/foreseeability limits; (4) apply equitable presumptions (e.g., "most favourable use"); and (5) value the lost opportunity consistently with what the Crown "ought to have done" as fiduciary (here, negotiate compensation reflecting the land’s value to hydroelectric generation).
BaselineB: Common law (equitable compensation for breach of fiduciary duty: Guerin v. The Queen; Canson Enterprises Ltd. v. Boughton & Co.; Blueberry River; Osoyoos; etc.) plus statutory/treaty context informing obligations (Indian Act, R.S.C. 1927, c. 98, ss. 48, 50, 51; Treaty No. 3 (1873))
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Sales tax exemption test for whether machinery/apparatus is used “directly in … the manufacture or production of goods” (Excise Tax Act, Sch. III, Part XIII, para. 1(a)(i)): regulators not exempt because they are “apparatus controlling the flow of gas in pipes” and “cannot be considered as used in the ‘production of gas’ within the usual meaning of those words”; Hydro-Québec distinguished because transformers were exempt where their operation was “no mere transmission” and was seen as “producing a new current at a different voltage”.
BaselineA: Statute: Excise Tax Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-13, s. 29(1) and Schedule III, Part XIII, para. 1(a)(i) (exemption for machinery/apparatus used directly in the manufacture or production of goods), interpreted in light of Hydro-Québec v. Dep. Min. of Nat. Revenue for Customs and Excise, [1970] S.C.R. 30.
JudgeA: Pigeon J. (for Martland, Judson, Pigeon, Dickson and Beetz JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Scope-of-retainer test for allocating responsibility between solicitors: the “crucial question” is “the nature and scope of [counsel’s] retainer”, treated as “purely a factual question” and not to be disturbed on appeal absent “error arising from misapprehension of the evidence”; on the facts, Matthews’ retainer was limited to assisting with proofs of loss and did not include responsibility to alert Meehan to limitation periods that were “obvious”.
BaselineB: Common law (solicitor/counsel professional responsibility framed through the contractual retainer and appellate deference to trial findings of fact: findings on scope of retainer not to be upset absent misapprehension of evidence).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Whether an invention relates to a food substance “prepared or produced by chemical processes” under Patent Act s. 41(1): apply the term in its “ordinary and popular sense” (as an informed layman), looking at the process “as a whole”; chemical reactions are neither necessary nor sufficient, but it is enough if chemical operations play a “significant part” in producing the substance
BaselineA: Statute: Patent Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. P-4, s. 41(1), as interpreted in Continental Soya Co. Ltd. v. J.R. Short Milling Co. (Canada) Ltd., [1942] S.C.R. 187 and Laboratoire Pentagone Ltée v. Parke, Davis & Co., [1968] S.C.R. 307
CaseB_TestB: Adequacy of an indictment (including in conspiracy cases): an indictment is adequate if it gives the accused “reasonable information” to identify the transaction and prepare a defence; exact time need not be precise unless essential and no prejudice results; where multiple conspiracies are proven, a conspiracy lies within the indictment if it included some accused, occurred within the time frame alleged, and had as its object the type of crime alleged
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 510, 512, 516; plus SCC/common-law guidance including R. v. Côté, [1978] 1 S.C.R. 8; R. v. Wis Development Corp., [1984] 1 S.C.R. 485; R. v. Cotroni, [1979] 2 S.C.R. 256
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 1 justification (Oakes proportionality) applied contextually: pressing and substantial objective; proportionality via (1) rational connection, (2) minimal impairment, (3) proportionality of effects; with emphasis that a total ban requires proof that only a full prohibition will achieve the objective and that justification must be “demonstrably” shown on a balance of probabilities
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 1 ("reasonable limits ... demonstrably justified") interpreted through the Oakes framework (R. v. Oakes, [1986] 1 S.C.R. 103) and related s. 2(b)/s. 1 jurisprudence
CaseB_TestB: Meiorin duty-to-accommodate/justification framework applied to an absence-termination clause: employer must justify the standard by showing (1) rational connection to job performance, (2) adopted in good faith, and (3) reasonably necessary—i.e., “impossible to accommodate ... without imposing undue hardship”; a collectively bargained maximum-absence period is a relevant factor but not determinative; undue hardship assessed globally from the start of the absence
BaselineB: Common law / Charter human rights jurisprudence: Meiorin (BCGSEU) test for justifying a discriminatory standard and duty to accommodate; also informed by Quebec Charter of human rights and freedoms (R.S.Q., c. C-12) equality principles and collective agreement provisions (e.g., clause 12.11.5)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Indian Act s. 88 “inconsistency” analysis for applying provincial laws of general application to Indians: provincial law applies (via s. 88 incorporation) except to the extent it is “inconsistent with” the Indian Act; here, Adoption Act s. 10(2) (“for all purposes” severing natural-parent relationship) does not remove an adopted child’s entitlement to be registered under Indian Act s. 11(1)(d).
BaselineA: Statute: Indian Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-6, s. 88 (and s. 11(1)(d) registrability definition of “Indian”); interacting with Adoption Act, R.S.B.C. 1960, c. 4, s. 10(2) (“for all purposes”).
CaseB_TestB: Collins s. 24(2) exclusion framework (as organized in Greffe): balance three categories—(1) fairness of the trial, (2) seriousness of the Charter breach (including whether police had “reasonable and probable grounds” and indicia of informant reliability), and (3) effect of exclusion/admission on the repute of the administration of justice—applied to decide whether admitting the evidence would “bring the administration of justice into disrepute”.
BaselineB: Statute/constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 24(2), applying the common-law/Charter framework from R. v. Collins, [1987] 1 S.C.R. 265.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Termination (“determination”) of a continuing guarantee by “notice in writing”: notice need not use set words but must be explicit and unequivocal (a mere expression of “wish” or “preference” is insufficient; creditor must not be left in doubt).
BaselineA: Contract/common law interpretation of the guarantee instrument (clause (4) allowing determination “by notice in writing delivered to the Manager of the branch or agency of the Bank receiving this instrument”).
CaseB_TestB: Admissibility/use of an accused’s post-caution silence: unless the Crown establishes “a real relevance and a proper basis”, questions about silence and evidence of ensuing silence should not be admitted; if admitted, the jury must be instructed to ignore it (no adverse inference).
BaselineB: Common law right to silence (as discussed via Rothman; Robertson; Symonds) and Charter s. 7 protection of the right to silence; applied in the context of Criminal Code s. 613(1)(b)(iii) (curative proviso).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: s. 96 BNA Act validity test (institutional setting approach): whether conferring s. 49 ‘cease and desist’/mandatory remedial power on a labour board is permissible because the power must be assessed in its ‘setting in the institutional arrangements’ and as part of a specialized administrative scheme, not by ‘detached jurisdiction or power alone’
BaselineA: Combination: Constitution (British North America Act, 1867, s. 96) + prior jurisprudence on s. 96 limits (Labour Relations Board of Saskatchewan v. John East Iron Works; Tremblay v. Commission des Relations de Travail du Québec; also Dupont v. Inglis; Display Services; Brooks v. Pavlick)
CaseB_TestB: YCJA youth-sentencing principle: general (and specific) deterrence is not a permissible sentencing principle under the YCJA because s. 50(1) excludes Criminal Code s. 718(b) and deterrence cannot be found or implied from YCJA ss. 3 and 38; additionally, s. 42(2)(o) does not require a 2/3 custody and 1/3 supervision split
BaselineB: Statute: Youth Criminal Justice Act, S.C. 2002, c. 1 (especially ss. 3, 38, 42(2)(o), 50(1)); interpretive contrast with Criminal Code s. 718(b) (excluded by s. 50(1))
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Relief from municipal notice requirement: failure to give notice under Cities and Towns Act s. 622(1) does not bar the action if the plaintiff proves they were prevented from giving notice for a reason “deemed sufficient by the court or judge” (s. 622(4)); if so, the plaintiff is “permanently released from the obligation to give notice” and may sue without later giving notice.
BaselineA: Statute: Cities and Towns Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 193, s. 622(1), (3), (4), (5) (especially s. 622(4) “any reason deemed sufficient by the court or judge” and s. 622(5) prescription starting points).
CaseB_TestB: Judicial review of a labour grievance arbitration award on collective agreement interpretation: courts should ask whether the arbitrator’s interpretation is “patently unreasonable” / “one which the agreement would reasonably bear,” rather than whether it is correct.
BaselineB: Common law (judicial review of arbitration awards) as applied in labour arbitration; key SCC baseline cases cited include Bell Canada v. Office and Professional Employees' Union, [1974] S.C.R. 335 and CUPE v. New Brunswick Liquor Corp., [1979] 2 S.C.R. 227 (patently unreasonable standard).
JudgeB: Pigeon J. (reasons concurred in by Martland, Ritchie, Beetz and Pratte JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Admissibility of similar-fact evidence: other criminal acts are inadmissible to show propensity, but are admissible if relevant to an issue (e.g., whether the act was “designed or accidental” or “to rebut a defence which would otherwise be open”), and (per Noor Mohamed/Wray as adopted) should not be excluded merely because prejudicial if relevant and of probative value (only a very limited exclusionary discretion).
BaselineA: Common law evidence rule on similar-fact evidence (Makin v. A-G for New South Wales; Thompson v. The King; Noor Mohamed v. The King) as received in Canada; plus SCC approach to exclusion of admissible evidence in R. v. Wray.
CaseB_TestB: Municipal valuation in exceptional cases: where “special circumstances make it impossible to fix the realizable value of property by the usual methods”, “whatever method is appropriate in the circumstances may be used” to estimate “actual value” (including the ‘developer’s approach’).
BaselineB: Statutory requirement to value property at “actual value” under the Charter of the City of Montreal (including appeal provisions ss. 873-874), interpreted through prior valuation jurisprudence (e.g., Sun Life Assurance Co. of Canada v. City of Montreal).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Admissibility of similar fact evidence to prove mens rea in criminal negligence: similar acts admissible if relevant to an issue (e.g., designed vs accidental / to rebut a defence otherwise open), not to show disposition
BaselineA: Common law evidentiary rule on similar fact evidence (general exclusionary rule and its exception), as stated in Makin v. Attorney General for New South Wales and discussed with Thompson v. The King, Noor Mohamed v. The King, and R. v. Wray
CaseB_TestB: Issue estoppel on a perjury charge after an acquittal: Crown estopped from re-litigating an issue decided in accused’s favour unless it tenders evidence not available by reasonable diligence at the first trial
BaselineB: Common law doctrine of issue estoppel / res judicata in criminal proceedings (building on Gushue v. The Queen and DPP v. Humphrys, and related authorities)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory interpretation of technical terms: apply the primary/common-language meaning (in both official languages) — here, “derivative/dérivé” means a thing actually “obtained from” another, not merely in the same scientific ‘family’
BaselineA: Combination: (1) statutory/regulatory text (Customs Tariff Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-41, s. 12, Schedule A, tariff item 92944-1 as amended by Order in Council SOR/69-8, Schedule A: “Tetracycline and its derivatives”); and (2) statutory bilingual-interpretation rule (Official Languages Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. O-2, s. 8(2)(b)); plus common-law interpretive principle that statutes use common-language meaning (cited: Continental Soya; Laboratoire Pentagone; Burton Parsons)
CaseB_TestB: Scope of inherent/implied jurisdiction re amici: courts may appoint amici only exceptionally where “essential” to just adjudication, but (absent statutory authority or a constitutional/Charter basis) inherent/implied jurisdiction does not extend to fixing amici’s rates of compensation and ordering the province to pay
BaselineB: Common law / constitutional doctrine: inherent jurisdiction of superior courts and implied powers of statutory courts, constrained by separation of powers and provincial responsibility for administration of justice (Constitution Act, 1867, ss. 92(14), 96, etc., discussed as constitutional framework rather than a direct statutory test). Key baseline authorities discussed include MacMillan Bloedel and R. v. Caron (inherent jurisdiction), and separation-of-powers jurisprudence (e.g., New Brunswick Broadcasting)
JudgeB: Karakatsanis J. (McLachlin C.J. and Rothstein, Moldaver and Wagner JJ. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Bankruptcy trustee’s statutory duty to insure: under Bankruptcy Act s. 9(1)-(2), trustee must keep existing insurance in force and insure all “insurable property of the bankrupt” (including hypothec-encumbered property), and if insurance is cancelled must replace it or at least notify the secured (hypothecary) creditor; failure can ground personal liability (and s. 171 leave requirement does not apply to omissions).
BaselineA: Statute: Bankruptcy Act, R.S.C. 1952, c. 14, ss. 9(1)-(2), 2(o) (“property”), 2(r) (“secured creditor”), and s. 171.
CaseB_TestB: Charitable status under ITA via common law Pemsel (4th head): organization must show its purposes are (a) for “public benefit/beneficial to the community” and (b) “in a way the law regards as charitable”; under Vancouver Society/D’Aguiar, assess (1) trend of prior cases and reasonable extension/analogy, (2) accepted anomalies, and (3) cross-check whether purposes allow non-charitable application—sport is charitable only if ancillary to another recognized charitable purpose, not “mere sport”.
BaselineB: Combination: Statute (Income Tax Act, ss. 149.1(1), 248(1) and related provisions) relying on common law definition of charity (Pemsel; Vancouver Society adopting D’Aguiar framework).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Eligibility for a Quebec seat on the SCC under Supreme Court Act s. 6: appointee must be a current member of the Quebec Court of Appeal/Superior Court or a current Quebec advocate (with 10 years standing via s. 5); former Quebec advocates (including Federal Court judges who were formerly Quebec advocates) are ineligible
BaselineA: Statute (Supreme Court Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. S-26, ss. 5 and 6; plus constitutional constraint in Constitution Act, 1982, s. 41(d) re amendments to Court composition)
JudgeA: McLachlin C.J. and LeBel, Abella, Cromwell, Karakatsanis and Wagner JJ. (Joint Reasons)
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 15(1) equality test (as applied to Pay Equity Act s. 38 delay): (1) does the law create a distinction on an enumerated/analogous ground (on its face or in impact)? (2) does it impose a discriminatory disadvantage by ‘reinforcing, perpetuating or exacerbating’ disadvantage?
BaselineB: Common law / constitutional doctrine (Charter s. 15(1) framework from Quebec (AG) v. A and Taypotat, applied to Pay Equity Act, CQLR c. E-12.001, s. 38)
JudgeB: Côté J. (Wagner, Brown and Rowe JJ. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Entitlement to payment from the Highway Victims Indemnity Fund and applicable prescription: claimant must hold a final judgment meeting s. 36 thresholds, apply within 1 year, file the s. 37 sworn declaration (incl. judgment unsatisfied and “no insurer will benefit”), and the Fund must pay within 7 days under s. 38; any action on the Fund’s obligation is prescribed by 30 years (art. 2265 C.C.), not bodily-injury prescription (art. 2262(2) C.C.), and the remedy is not conditional on exhausting remedies against the insurer
BaselineA: Statute (Highway Victims Indemnity Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 232, ss. 36-40) plus Civil Code prescription provisions (arts. 2262(2), 2265 C.C.)
CaseB_TestB: Method for assessing Fatal Accidents Act damages (dependency) including income tax: determine annual dependency (net of income tax and personal expenditures), then calculate the present value of a lump sum that will replace that stream over the relevant period using a discount rate based on long-term investment returns adjusted for inflation, with a reduction for contingencies (overall award must be “fair and adequate”)
