BaselineB: Statute (The Fatal Accidents Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 164) as interpreted through SCC damages jurisprudence (including reconsideration of Gehrmann v. Lavoie and reference to Andrews/Thornton/Arnold methodology)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Equitable interest for improper withholding of a just debt: where payment of a just debt has been improperly withheld and it is fair and equitable to compensate, the court should award interest for such time and at such rate as it thinks right (here, contractor’s bank borrowing rate).
BaselineA: Common law/equitable principle (Toronto Railway Co. v. City of Toronto, [1906] A.C. 117; followed in The Custodian v. Blucher, [1927] S.C.R. 420) applied alongside statutory context (Interest Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-18, ss. 3, 12, 13; Supreme Court Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. S-19, s. 52).
CaseB_TestB: Two-step post-conviction non-disclosure/new trial test: (1) reasonable possibility undisclosed info affects reliability of conviction → new trial; (2) if not, assess reasonable possibility non-disclosure affected overall fairness via lost lines of inquiry/opportunities, weighing defence due diligence.
BaselineB: Common law/Charter disclosure jurisprudence under Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms ss. 7 and 24(1), building on R. v. Stinchcombe and related cases (Egger, Chaplin, Carosella).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Doctrine/rule of recent possession: once Crown proves (1) goods were recently stolen and (2) accused possessed them, jury may infer guilt; if an explanation is given that “may reasonably be true”, it must be considered and acquittal follows if it raises a reasonable doubt; Crown need not adduce evidence of absence of explanation and the instruction is not barred by Canada Evidence Act s. 4(5).
BaselineA: Common law rule of evidence (recent possession) as stated in R. v. Schama; R. v. Abramovitch (quoted/approved) and applied/confirmed in SCC cases including R. v. Graham, [1974] S.C.R. 206 (also Richler v. The King; Ungaro v. The King; Graham v. The Queen; Tremblay v. The Queen). Statutory issue addressed: Canada Evidence Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-10, s. 4(5) (no comment on failure to testify).
CaseB_TestB: Imperial Tobacco extraterritoriality framework (as applied to ORA s. 11): (1) identify pith and substance by purpose and effects; (2) assess territorial limits by asking whether the law has a “meaningful connection” to the province and “respects the legislative sovereignty” of other provinces.
BaselineB: Common law constitutional division-of-powers framework from British Columbia v. Imperial Tobacco Canada Ltd., 2005 SCC 49 (two-stage pith-and-substance/territoriality analysis), applied to Constitution Act, 1867, s. 92(13) and s. 92(14) and to Opioid Damages and Health Care Costs Recovery Act, S.B.C. 2018, c. 35, s. 11 (with CPA, s. 16 referenced).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Mulligan (majority): psychiatric “dissociative reaction” evidence need not be specifically re-put on the drunkenness issue where it is directed to insanity and the jury is told to consider drunkenness only if insanity is not made out (i.e., if the dissociative-reaction thesis is rejected)
BaselineA: Common law (drunkenness and specific intent as in DPP v. Beard) plus Criminal Code s. 212(a) mens rea for murder; applied through jury-instruction/charge adequacy principles
CaseB_TestB: Ibanescu: “straddle evidence” is admissible to rebut the Criminal Code s. 258(1)(d.1) presumption, and its probative value is assessed by whether it “may be capable of raising a reasonable doubt” when weighed with all the evidence (per LeBel J. in Gibson)
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, s. 258(1)(d.1) presumption re BAC at time of driving) as interpreted in R. v. Gibson, 2008 SCC 16
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Drunkenness negating mens rea for murder: whether intoxication rendered the accused incapable of forming the specific intent to kill (or to cause bodily harm known likely to cause death) — and whether psychiatric “dissociative reaction” evidence must be related to that issue in the jury charge
BaselineA: Combination: statute (Criminal Code, s. 212(a) (as referenced: “means to cause his death”)) plus common law intoxication doctrine (DPP v. Beard, [1920] A.C. 479 (H.L.), adopted in the charge)
JudgeA: Martland J. (for Martland, Judson, Ritchie, Pigeon, Beetz and de Grandpré JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Section 23 “numbers warrant” sliding-scale placement framework (three-step approach with a rebuttable presumption from province-wide comparator schools) to determine entitlement to minority-language educational facilities/services
BaselineB: Combination: constitutional text (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 23(3)(a) and s. 23(3)(b)) plus prior SCC framework (Mahe v. Alberta, [1990] 1 S.C.R. 342)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Labour Code s. 108(1)(b) judicial review threshold: court may intervene only for an "error of law affecting the jurisdiction" of a labour arbitrator; no such jurisdictional error where the arbitrator "applied himself to the problem at hand" and answered the question submitted on the whole award read fairly
BaselineA: Statute: Labour Code of British Columbia Act, 1973, s. 108(1)(b) (limited Court of Appeal review to "error of law affecting the jurisdiction of the arbitration board")
CaseB_TestB: Garofoli leave/threshold test for cross-examining a wiretap affiant: defence must show a "reasonable likelihood" that cross-examination "will elicit testimony of probative value" on a material issue for the reviewing judge (relevance/materiality), i.e., likely to undermine a statutory precondition/basis for the authorization
BaselineB: Common law: R. v. Garofoli, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 1421 (threshold/leave requirement for cross-examining affiant on a wiretap review); applied in the context of Criminal Code, s. 184.2 and Charter s. 8
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Income Tax Act s. 83(3) “arrangement with the prospector” / “employer of the prospector” requirement for excluding consideration (mining property interest or shares) from income: whether the prospector was acting “on behalf of himself” or was the taxpayer’s employee/employer under an arrangement made before the work
BaselineA: Statute: Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1952, c. 148, s. 83(3) (as amended by 1965 (Can.), c. 18, s. 19); also s. 83(1)(c) referenced for “prospector”
JudgeA: de Grandpré J. (for Laskin C.J. and Judson, Beetz and de Grandpré JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: “Integral element” test for whether Parliament (under s. 92(10) railways) can validly legislate in an area otherwise provincial: federal jurisdiction displaces provincial law only where the matter is an “integral part” of the core federal undertaking; applied to hold Railway Act s. 342(1) ultra vires as applied to provincial personal-injury negligence actions
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine (division of powers) applying the “integral element” approach from Construction Montcalm Inc. v. Minimum Wage Commission and Northern Telecom Ltd. v. Communications Workers of Canada; applied to Railway Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. R-2, s. 342(1) and Constitution Act, 1867, ss. 91(29), 92(10), 92(13), 92(14)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory condition 10(a) (fire policy): the insurer is only exempt for loss of property “owned by any other person than the assured” if the insured lacks an insurable interest; “all that is necessary to satisfy statutory condition 10(a) ... is that the insured have an insurable interest” (so the insured need not state the nature of its interest when not required).
BaselineA: Statute (Quebec Insurance Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 295, s. 240; statutory condition 10(a) in the fire policy) and Civil Code art. 2571 C.C. (requirement that the nature of the interest be specified).
CaseB_TestB: Non-police seizure later used in criminal prosecution: courts must “go beyond the initial non‑police seizure” and decide whether police conduct (i) constitutes an independent state seizure or (ii) makes the initial seizure unreasonable; if evidence is “appropriated by the state's criminal law enforcement arm” for use against the person, the seizure becomes unreasonable under s. 8 (no “piggy back” on the coroner to avoid Hunter prior-authorization).
BaselineB: Common law/constitutional doctrine under Charter s. 8 (Hunter v. Southam; R. v. Dyment) applied in the statutory context of the Coroners Act, R.S.O. 1980, c. 93, s. 16(2) and related provisions.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Refusing an adjournment that is necessary to exercise the accused’s right to counsel: the refusal must rest on established facts and be a judicial discretion reviewable for legally unfounded reasons (with prejudice/fair-trial implications)
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 577(3) and 613) applied through appellate review principles; with supporting case law including Spataro v. Regina, [1974] S.C.R. 253 and Talbot v. Regina, [1965] Que. Q.B. 159
JudgeA: Pigeon J. (for Laskin C.J. and Judson, Spence, Pigeon, Dickson and Beetz JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Equitable compensation for breach of fiduciary duty (non-disclosure by solicitor): recover losses caused by the breach on a common-sense view of causation (not foreseeability), with limits for third-party losses lacking a causal link and for losses attributable to the plaintiff’s clearly unreasonable conduct
BaselineB: Common law / equity (fiduciary duty and equitable compensation), drawing on authorities including Nocton v. Lord Ashburton, [1914] A.C. 932 and Guerin v. The Queen, [1984] 2 S.C.R. 335
JudgeB: McLachlin J. (for Lamer C.J. and L'Heureux-Dubé and McLachlin JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Declinatory exception to territorial jurisdiction: filing an exception (even supported by an affidavit) does not automatically shift the burden to the plaintiff; jurisdiction is assessed on the whole record, and a bare affidavit asserting foreign domicile/residence carries little weight against contrary indicia (including a statutory presumption from Canadian citizenship).
BaselineA: Statute (Quebec Code of Civil Procedure, arts. 68 and 70; plus Canadian Citizenship Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-19, s. 10 presumption)
CaseB_TestB: When (and how) police/state misconduct can reduce sentence: if the misconduct (even if a Charter breach) relates to the circumstances of the offence or the offender, it may be treated as a mitigating factor within the Criminal Code sentencing regime; generally unnecessary to invoke Charter s. 24(1), and sentence must still respect statutory minimums (save possibly exceptional egregious cases).
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, ss. 718–718.2 and statutory minimums; Charter, s. 24(1) as remedial backdrop)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Contractual interpretation of warranty: construe “depreciation” in para. 3(g) and the auditor’s letter as an accounting concept (write-off over useful life), not “full capital cost allowance”; the parenthetical “(using capital cost allowance rates)” refers to rates only, not the tax ‘system’, and “at least” must be given effect—so no breach if the books show full depreciation for the period assets were in service at those rates.
BaselineA: Common law (contract interpretation of a share sale agreement warranty clause, read with the incorporated auditor’s letter).
CaseB_TestB: Youth court power under Young Offenders Act: s. 19(2) does not authorize dismissing a charge merely because the judge thinks it “ought never to have been laid”; absent clear statutory language, courts must respect prosecutorial discretion (subject only to exceptional remedies like a stay for abuse of process in the “clearest of cases”).
BaselineB: Statute (Young Offenders Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. Y-1, especially ss. 19(2) and 3(1); interpreted against the background common-law principle of prosecutorial discretion and the stay-for-abuse-of-process jurisprudence).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Crown appeal from acquittal: after establishing an error of law, the Crown must satisfy the court that “the verdict would not necessarily have been the same if the trial judge had properly directed the jury” (White v. R. test as applied in Vézeau).
BaselineA: Common law test from White v. R., [1947] S.C.R. 268, applied in the context of Criminal Code appeal powers (s. 613(4)).
CaseB_TestB: Group defamation/personal injury in Quebec civil liability: plaintiff must prove that “an ordinary person would have believed that each of them personally sustained damage to his or her reputation”; court assesses this contextually using a “non-exhaustive” set of factors (size/nature of group, identifiability, precision of allegations, plausibility, etc.).
BaselineB: Statutory civil liability under Civil Code of Québec, art. 1457 (fault, injury, causal connection), building on SCC defamation cases (Prud’homme; Néron) for the “ordinary person” injury standard.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Interpretation of the standard auto policy exclusion for a person “who is entitled to receive the benefits of any workmen’s compensation law or plan”: entitlement does not depend on making a claim/obtaining an award; if admitted facts establish statutory entitlement, the exclusion applies
BaselineA: Statute (Ontario): Insurance Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 224, s. 232(1) and Schedule E, Exclusion 2(a)(ii) (mandatory standard policy wording), interpreted with reference to Workmen’s Compensation Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 505 (esp. ss. 3 and 8)
CaseB_TestB: Section 8 (Charter) framework applied mutatis mutandis to cross-border disclosure under Criminal Code s. 193(2)(e): (1) disclosure authorized by law (recipient is proper foreign authority + disclosure intended to be in the interests of the administration of justice), (2) the law is reasonable (not overbroad/vague; accountability within Part VI), and (3) disclosure carried out in a reasonable manner (including case-specific safeguards where serious risks are known/foreseeable)
BaselineB: Combination: Charter s. 8 reasonableness framework from R. v. Collins / R. v. Caslake, applied to statutory disclosure power in Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 193(2)(e)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Discretion to order service ex juris under Federal Court Rules, Rule 307 guided by forum conveniens: the “overriding consideration” is whether there exists “some other forum more convenient and appropriate for the pursuit of the action and for securing the ends of justice” (with factors like participation/attornment and enforceability of judgment/security).
BaselineA: Statute and regulation: Federal Court Act, R.S.C. 1970 (2nd Supp.), c. 10, ss. 22(2)(a), 43(1), 44; Federal Court Rules, Rule 307 (service ex juris).
JudgeA: Ritchie J. (for Ritchie, Pigeon, Beetz and de Grandpré JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Medical-malpractice causation in Quebec civil responsibility (rejecting loss of chance as a substitute for causation where death/sickness has occurred): plaintiff must prove fault, damage, and causation “on the balance of probabilities, taking into account all the evidence: factual, statistical and that which the judge is entitled to presume”; in some cases a court may presume causation where a fault creates “clear danger” and the danger materializes, unless there is a “strong indication to the contrary”; if not satisfied causation of “any real damage” is shown, recovery is denied.
BaselineB: Civil law (Quebec delictual liability) principles of fault–damage–causation; evidentiary presumptions under Civil Code of Lower Canada, art. 1205; SCC causation approach referenced in Snell v. Farrell, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 311.
JudgeB: Gonthier J. (for Lamer C.J. and L'Heureux-Dubé, Sopinka, Gonthier, Cory and McLachlin JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Breach of municipal development agreement sewer-servicing obligation: developer must prove a specific failure to provide sewers/enlargements “required to properly service” the redevelopment stage (i.e., evidence of existing or foreseeable inadequacy); a general city-wide long-term sewer master plan/charge is not enough
BaselineA: Common law (contract interpretation/application of s. 31(a)(iii) of the 1966 development agreement)
CaseB_TestB: Presumption of advancement and rebuttal in husband-to-wife gratuitous transfer: presumption applies unless husband rebuts it; he does not rebut it by saying he transferred “only ... to defeat his creditors” (and post-trial statutory abolition of the presumption is ignored absent express/necessary retrospective application)
BaselineB: Common law (presumption of advancement / resulting trust principles; discussed with reference to Goodfriend v. Goodfriend and Tinker v. Tinker) plus statutory interpretation of The Family Law Reform Act, 1975 (Ont.), c. 41, s. 1(3)(d) on non-retrospectivity
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 613(1)(b)(iii) curative proviso: despite trial error(s), uphold conviction if the Crown satisfies the court that “the jury, charged as it should have been, could not, as reasonable men, have done otherwise than find the appellant guilty” (Brooks v. The King, quoted via Colpitts v. R.)—i.e., no “substantial wrong or miscarriage of justice”.
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code s. 613(1)(b)(iii)) as applied through SCC precedent (Colpitts v. R., adopting Brooks v. The King formulation).
CaseB_TestB: Marshall treaty right and infringement analysis: (1) interpret the 1760-61 Mi’kmaq treaties (including extrinsic evidence) to recognize a treaty right to obtain “necessaries” (modern “moderate livelihood”) through hunting/fishing and trading; (2) assess prima facie infringement under Sparrow (“is the limitation unreasonable?”, “does the regulation impose undue hardship?”, “does the regulation deny… their preferred means”); (3) if infringed, Crown must justify under the Badger/Sparrow justificatory standard.
BaselineB: Combination: constitutional and common law (Constitution Act, 1982 s. 35(1); Sparrow infringement test; Badger justification framework) applied to the Mi’kmaq Treaties of 1760-61 and to fisheries legislation/regulations (Fisheries Act s. 7(1); Maritime Provinces Fishery Regulations ss. 4(1)(a), 20; Fishery (General) Regulations s. 35(2)).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Carrier can invoke Hague Protocol liability limits only if the passenger ticket/baggage check includes the required Art. 3(1)(c)/4(1)(c) “notice” — i.e., something “in a form calculated to attract attention”; a 4.5-point, inconspicuous printing is “not a ‘notice’ within the meaning of the Article”
BaselineA: Statute (Carriage by Air Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-14, incorporating the Warsaw Convention as amended by the Hague Protocol): Hague Protocol Arts. 3(1)(c), 3(2), 4(1)(c) and the limitation in Art. 22
CaseB_TestB: Rebutting Criminal Code breathalyzer presumptions after St‑Onge Lamoureux: for s. 258(1)(c) (after severance), accused must raise a reasonable doubt that “the approved instrument was malfunctioning or was operated improperly” (with s. 258(1)(d.01) excluding Carter consumption evidence for that purpose); for s. 258(1)(d.1), accused must adduce evidence tending to show consumption consistent with both (i) BAC not exceeding .08 at time of offence and (ii) the test results
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, ss. 258(1)(c), 258(1)(d.01), 258(1)(d.1)) as assessed under Charter s. 11(d) and remedied by severance under Charter s. 1
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Municipal notice-of-accident limitation period runs from discovery (not the accident date) where starting from the accident date would make the right of action practically illusory; thus the 15-day period in Charter art. 1088 did not start until the claimant learned the true cause of death ("the period did not start to run until February 5").
BaselineA: Statute: An Act to revise and consolidate the Charter of the City of Montreal, 1959-60 (Que.), c. 102, art. 1088 (15-day notice must be "received"), with related interpretive context from the Interpretation Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 1, ss. 52 and 61; and the Charter’s exception clause (valid reason/irresistible force) in art. 1088.
CaseB_TestB: Discretionary test for discharging a civil jury after a reference to insurance: no automatic discharge; trial judge assesses whether the reference likely caused "a substantial wrong or miscarriage of justice" making it unfair to continue, considers whether insurance is "well known", and discharges only if prejudice "cannot be cured" (usually by instructions).
BaselineB: Common law baseline from Bowhey v. Theakston, [1951] S.C.R. 679 (automatic discharge rule), which the SCC overrules in favour of a discretionary prejudice/miscarriage-of-justice approach; applied in the context of Supreme Court Rules, B.C. Reg. 310/76, Rule 41(6).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Admissibility of an accused’s prior in-court testimony (judicial statement under oath) without a voir dire: such testimony is admissible as of right even if alleged to have been induced by unlawful threats/violence; voluntariness goes to weight, not admissibility, and the witness must claim statutory protection at the time of testifying (cannot do so after the fact). Key statements: “Scott laid down the principle that a statement made under oath by the accused during an earlier judicial proceeding is admissible in evidence against him although it was obtained under compulsion of the law and by authority of the court”; “it is never necessary to hold a voir dire with respect to the voluntariness of a previous statement of the accused given in court”; “the witness may request the protection of the law at the time of his testimony, but he may not do so after the event”.
BaselineA: Common law rule on admissibility of prior judicial testimony (distinguished from extra-judicial confessions requiring a voir dire), relying especially on R. v. Scott (1856) and the line of cases following it; interacts with Canada Evidence Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-10, s. 5(2) (protection against subsequent use if claimed).
CaseB_TestB: Appellate intervention for trial judge’s failure to consider relevant evidence: an appellate court does not reassess guilt, but must review whether the trial court directed itself to all evidence on relevant issues; if the record shows “a lack of appreciation of relevant evidence” or “complete disregard of such evidence”, the reviewing court “must intercede” and order a new trial. Key statements: “An appellate tribunal has neither the duty nor the right to reassess evidence… Its duty… includes a review of the record… to determine whether the trial court has properly directed itself to all the evidence bearing on the relevant issues”; “Where the record… discloses a lack of appreciation of relevant evidence… the reviewing tribunal [must] intercede.”
BaselineB: Common law appellate review principles as articulated in prior SCC cases, especially MacDonald v. The Queen, [1977] 2 S.C.R. 665 and Ungaro v. R., [1950] S.C.R. 430 (misdirection/overlooking relevant issues/evidence).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Admissibility of Crown rebuttal evidence to an alibi/credibility: Crown may contradict an alibi only by attacking its “material points”; and the Crown may not contradict a “collateral fact” elicited on cross-examination (so rebuttal evidence on a collateral point is inadmissible).
BaselineA: Common law evidence rules (rebuttal to alibi; collateral-fact rule), with related statutory context for harmless error under Criminal Code s. 613(1)(b)(iii). Cases cited: R. v. Cargill; R. v. Hrechuk; R. v. Rafael; R. v. Rosik; The Queen v. Vézeau.
CaseB_TestB: Drunkenness and rape via the specific-intent/general-intent distinction: rape is an offence of “general or basic intent”, therefore “the defence of drunkenness can have no application” (subject to the general rule that extreme intoxication may matter only where a specific intent is required).
BaselineB: Common law intoxication doctrine and the specific-intent/general-intent framework as stated in The Queen v. George and DPP v. Beard, and affirmed in DPP v. Majewski; applied in the appeal context with Criminal Code s. 613(1)(b)(iii).
JudgeB: Pigeon J. (for Martland, Judson, Ritchie, Pigeon, Beetz and de Grandpré JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Applicability of Parole Act mandatory supervision: an inmate is subject to mandatory supervision under Parole Act s. 15(1) if (i) s. 15(1) is in force at release, (ii) the inmate falls within the proclamation class under Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1968-69, c. 38, s. 101(2) (here, "persons who are sentenced to imprisonment in ... any class of penitentiary on and after the first day of August, 1970"), and (iii) by Parole Act s. 14(1) multiple terms are "deemed to constitute one sentence" so that s. 15(1) applies to the single deemed sentence at release.
BaselineA: Statute (Parole Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. P-2, ss. 14(1), 15(1)-(2); Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1968-69 (Can.), c. 38, s. 101(2) and proclamation SOR/70-339; also referenced: Criminal Code s. 659(2))
CaseB_TestB: Succession Duties Act s. 26(1) inclusion rule: "the proceeds of insurance policies ... due by an insurer by reason or on account of the death of the person on whose life the insurance was effected" are deemed property transmitted on death and taxable; this applies to accident insurance as well as life insurance, because nothing in s. 26(1) limits it to life insurance and "a death does not cease to be a death because it is accidental".
BaselineB: Statute (Succession Duties Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 70, s. 26(1); also discussed: ss. 45(f), 46(1); interpretive support from Civil Code arts. 1902, 1903, 1905, 1906)
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Estate Tax Act: whether community property with a survivorship stipulation is “property passing on death” / “property of which the deceased was ... competent to dispose” (no passing; not competent to dispose in the Act’s sense)
BaselineA: Statute (Estate Tax Act, 1958 (Can.), c. 29, ss. 3(1)(a), 3(2)(a), 3(2)(e), 58(1)(i); applied with SCC precedents Sura v. MNR, [1962] S.C.R. 65 and Royal Trust Co. v. MNR, [1968] S.C.R. 505)
CaseB_TestB: Treaty/NRTA hunting on private land: geographic limit based on “visible, incompatible land use” (case-by-case) to determine whether land is “taken up/occupied” so as to defeat a treaty/NRTA right of access to hunt for food
BaselineB: Constitutional/statutory instruments (Treaty No. 8; Natural Resources Transfer Agreement, 1930, para. 12; applied alongside prior SCC cases including R. v. Horseman, [1990] 1 S.C.R. 901; R. v. Horse, [1988] 1 S.C.R. 187; Myran v. The Queen, [1976] 2 S.C.R. 137; R. v. Mousseau, [1980] 2 S.C.R. 89)
JudgeB: Cory J. (for La Forest, L'Heureux-Dubé, Gonthier, Cory and Iacobucci JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Interpretation of contractual tax-adjustment clause: Clause 9 applies only to a “tax, duty, charge or fee imposed upon [the Seller] in respect of bunker fuel oil, or the production, manufacture, sale or delivery by [the Seller] of bunker fuel oil”, and “does not apply to increases in the cost price of crude oil purchased” under affiliate supply contracts; crude-oil imports are not deliveries of “the product”.
BaselineA: Contract (common law contractual interpretation applied to the parties’ agreement, especially clause 9; also interacts with the Canada Shipping Act levy only as a factual trigger for whether clause 9 is engaged).
CaseB_TestB: Van der Peet test for an Aboriginal right under s. 35(1): “in order to be an aboriginal right an activity must be an element of a practice, custom or tradition integral to the distinctive culture of the aboriginal group claiming the right”; court must (1) “identify the exact nature of the activity claimed” and (2) determine whether it was “a defining feature of the culture in question” prior to European contact (applied to claimed right to participate in and regulate gambling).
BaselineB: Common law constitutional test from R. v. Van der Peet (applied to s. 35(1) of the Constitution Act, 1982).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Foreseeability-based duty/causation limit for occupier/railway: liability only if the injury was a “reasonably foreseeable result” of the situation created by the defendant; no duty where “no reasonable occupier could have reasonably foreseen” a child leaving a place of safety to attempt to board a moving train
BaselineA: Common law negligence/occupier’s liability principles (foreseeability of risk) with reference to prior SCC cases on foreseeability (e.g., Ouellet v. Cloutier; University Hospital Board v. Lepine) and railway-duty context (e.g., Paskivski; Mitchell); statutory context noted but not determinative (Railway Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. R-2, s. 214 fencing duty)
CaseB_TestB: Section 7 “fair hearing” requirements for IRPA security-certificate process: a fair judicial process must include “the right to a hearing”, “an independent and impartial magistrate”, a decision “on the facts and the law”, and “the right to know the case put against one, and the right to answer that case”; if full disclosure is impossible, “either the person must be given the necessary information, or a substantial substitute for that information must be found”
BaselineB: Constitutional (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7) applied to the statutory IRPA security-certificate scheme (Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, S.C. 2001, c. 27, ss. 77-85, especially s. 78 secrecy provisions and s. 80 reasonableness determination)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Highway Victims Indemnity Fund liability for unknown-driver accidents: under Highway Victims Indemnity Act s. 43 the Fund must satisfy judgment only "to the same extent as if [judgment] had been rendered against the author of the accident", which imports the s. 14 cap ($35,000); prior payment by another liable party does not extinguish the Fund’s liability up to that cap (and s. 38 deduction does not apply where victim received nothing from the unknown driver).
BaselineA: Statute (Highway Victims Indemnity Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 232, especially ss. 43, 14, 38, 49; also read with ss. 36-42 and 40).
CaseB_TestB: Sentencing—collateral immigration consequences: a judge "may" consider collateral immigration consequences as part of individualization/parity, but only if the sentence remains proportionate (Criminal Code s. 718.1); consequences "must not be allowed to dominate" or "skew" sentencing; appellate intervention is available where the sentencing judge was unaware of those consequences or counsel failed to advise, and (absent Crown consent) evidence should be adduced on appeal.
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law principles: Criminal Code ss. 718, 718.1, 718.2 (proportionality/parity/individualization) applied in light of prior SCC sentencing jurisprudence (e.g., Ipeelee; M. (C.A.)); immigration consequence arises under IRPA s. 64.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Whether the accomplice corroboration 'rule of caution' applies to an accessory after the fact (and related direction to the jury on accomplice/accessory status)
BaselineA: Common law (rule of practice/caution on uncorroborated accomplice evidence; accomplice definition from Davies v. DPP as accepted in Horsburgh v. The Queen; debate reflected in R. v. Gratton and R. v. Riezebos)
JudgeA: Pigeon J. (reasons for Spence, Pigeon and de Grandpré JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Interpretation/application of Criminal Code s. 212(c) murder: meaning of 'unlawful object' and how 'knows or ought to know' is applied (objective reasonable-person foresight based on the accused’s actual knowledge; intoxication relevant to that knowledge)
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, ss. 205(5)(a) and 212(c), with related context from s. 212(a)(i)-(ii)); interpreted in light of prior SCC cases including Graves v. The King and R. v. Hughes
JudgeB: Lamer J. (for Martland, Dickson, Estey, McIntyre, Chouinard and Lamer JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Construction of Manitoba auto insurance exclusion: in s. 31(3)(h) (“death of an insured”), “an insured” is read as referring to an insured under the particular certificate/contract under which indemnity is claimed (owner’s vs driver’s), because the owner’s and driver’s certificates evidence separate contracts with distinct coverages.
BaselineA: Regulation/Statute: The Manitoba Public Insurance Corporation Act, C.S.M. c. A180 and Manitoba Automobile Insurance Regulation (Man. Reg. 333/74), especially ss. 30 (definition of “insured”), 31(1), 31(2), and 31(3)(h).
CaseB_TestB: Treaty 8 / NRTA para. 12 limitation test: determine whether the impugned conduct is hunting “for food” (i.e., “for sustenance for the individual Indian or the Indian’s family”) or instead an “act of commerce”; if it is commerce, it is not protected by Treaty No. 8 as limited by the 1930 Natural Resources Transfer Agreement and provincial Wildlife Act s. 42 applies via Indian Act s. 88.
BaselineB: Combination of constitutional/statutory instruments: Treaty No. 8 (1899); Natural Resources Transfer Agreement, 1930, para. 12 (confirmed by Constitution Act, 1930); Indian Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-6, s. 88; Wildlife Act, R.S.A. 1980, c. W-9, ss. 42 and 1(s) (“traffic”).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 287 (pre-1975): “telecommunication” requires transmission “by wire or cable” (not Hertzian waves/radio); no ‘partly wire’ vs ‘entirely wire’ distinction
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 287(1)(b) and definition in s. 287(2) (“telecommunication” means transmission “by wire or cable”)
CaseB_TestB: Immigration Act s. 19(1)(a)(ii) “excessive demands” assessment: must be individualized; consider both medical and non-medical factors (including family ability/willingness to pay) and apply a “reasonable probability” (more-likely-than-not) threshold, not remote possibility
BaselineB: Statute: Immigration Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. I-2, s. 19(1)(a)(ii) (and interpretive link to similar IRPA s. 38(1)(c))
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Limits on municipal discretion to refuse a business licence under Municipal Act s. 455: discretion must be exercised “judicially”, not on “extraneous”/“irrelevant or alien” grounds; “in any particular case” means peculiar to the applicant (not a blanket prohibition of a business type), and refusal cannot be used to prohibit a lawful trade/land use absent express statutory power of prohibition.
BaselineA: Statute (Municipal Act, R.S.B.C. 1960, c. 255, s. 455) interpreted in light of the Act’s overall scheme; supported by common law/authority that licensing/regulation does not imply prohibition absent express power (Municipal Corporation of the City of Toronto v. Virgo, [1896] A.C. 88; and the “irrelevant or alien grounds” constraint noted in Sunshine Valley Co-operative Society v. City of Grand Forks).
CaseB_TestB: IRPA security-certificate disclosure/fairness standard under Charter s. 7: the named person must receive an “incompressible minimum” of disclosure—i.e., is “reasonably informed” only if they have “sufficient disclosure to be able to give meaningful instructions” to public counsel and “meaningful guidance and information” to special advocates; if non-disclosure prevents this, the Minister must withdraw the essential information/evidence and the judge must quash the certificate.
BaselineB: Combination of statute and constitutional common law: Immigration and Refugee Protection Act provisions on summaries and closed evidence (notably ss. 77(2), 78, 83(1)(e), 83(1)(i)) interpreted to comply with Charter s. 7 principles of fundamental justice as articulated in Charkaoui v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2007 SCC 9 (Charkaoui I).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Appellate deference to trial findings of fact: an appellate court should not disturb a trial judge’s findings where there was “credible evidence before him on which he could reasonably base his conclusion”; it is “not the function of an appellate court to reconsider that evidence … and come to a different conclusion, unless it can be shown that the evidence reasonably could not result in justifying the conclusion of the trial judge.”
BaselineA: Common law (appellate review standard for findings of fact; articulated as a “well-known principle” rather than tied to a statute).
CaseB_TestB: Bona fide occupational qualification (BFOQ) under Ontario Human Rights Code s. 4(6): a mandatory retirement limit must be imposed “honestly, in good faith, and in the sincerely held belief” it serves “adequate performance … with all reasonable dispatch, safety and economy” and “not for ulterior or extraneous reasons”; and it must be objectively related to the job—“reasonably necessary to assure the efficient and economical performance of the job without endangering the employee, his fellow employees and the general public.”
BaselineB: Statute (The Ontario Human Rights Code, R.S.O. 1970, c. 318, ss. 4(1) and 4(6); also discusses burden after prima facie discrimination and standard of proof on balance of probabilities).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Unlawful-act manslaughter causation: Crown must prove the unlawful act was “at least a contributing cause of death, outside the de minimis range” (and causation is for the jury on all the evidence, not experts alone).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code) plus common-law causation principles (incl. thin skull). Criminal Code s. 205(1): homicide where one “directly or indirectly, by any means, ... causes the death of a human being”; applied with prior case law cited in the reasons (e.g., R. v. Larkin; R. v. Cato; R. v. Nicholson; R. v. Blaue).
CaseB_TestB: Anns two-stage duty-of-care framework for recognizing a novel duty for pure economic loss (prima facie duty via proximity/foreseeability, then residual policy considerations may negate/limit it).
BaselineB: Common law: Anns v. Merton London Borough Council (two-stage duty of care), as adopted in Kamloops (City of) v. Nielsen and applied in later SCC negligence/economic loss cases (e.g., Hercules; Winnipeg Condominium; Bow Valley).
JudgeB: Iacobucci and Major JJ. (for the Court)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Crown bound by legislation/regulations only if expressly mentioned or (at common law) by “necessary implication” (i.e., the statute’s purpose would be “wholly frustrated” unless the Crown were bound); s. 16 Interpretation Act requires the Crown be “mentioned or referred to”
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Interpretation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-23, s. 16 (and s. 28 definition of “Her Majesty”); common law “necessary implication” rule from Bombay Province v. Bombay Municipal Corporation, [1947] A.C. 58
CaseB_TestB: Breach of contract where a stipulated term (here, cargo weight) is “a material if not a critical term” and is excessively departed from; not “mutual mistake” where the promisor was in a position to know the true facts; damages under Civil Code art. 1065 for breach (not nullity under art. 992)
BaselineB: Statute (Civil Code of Quebec): art. 1065 (damages for breach) contrasted with art. 992 (error as cause of nullity)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Lord’s Day Act s. 11(x) exemption: CTC’s inquiry is limited to whether (having regard to the Act’s object of preventing Sunday gainful work) an exemption is needed “with the object of preventing undue delay” in freight traffic; evidence about local congestion/noise/safety is irrelevant to that mandate
BaselineA: Statute: Lord’s Day Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. L-13, ss. 4 and 11(x) (plus relevance of evidence tied to the statutory mandate)
CaseB_TestB: Meaning of “bona fide pension plan” under Human Rights Code s. 3(6)(a): plan must be “subjectively and objectively bona fide” — “a legitimate plan, adopted in good faith and not for the purpose of defeating protected rights” (overall plan bona fides, not actuarial details)
BaselineB: Statute: Human Rights Code, R.S.N.B. 1973, c. H-11, s. 3(6)(a) (interpreting “bona fide” in the pension-plan exemption)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Combines conspiracy: Crown must prove (1) intent to enter an agreement and (2) that, if carried into effect, the agreement would "prevent or lessen competition unduly"; "undueness" is assessed by the agreement’s prospective effect on competition (not merely that a "meaningful segment" agreed on prices).
BaselineA: Statute — Combines Investigation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-23, s. 32(1)(c) ("Every one who conspires... (c) to prevent, or lessen, unduly, competition... or in the price of insurance...") as construed in prior SCC cases (notably Howard Smith Paper Mills; Weidman v. Shragge; Stinson-Reeb; Container Materials).
CaseB_TestB: Unreasonable verdict (Criminal Code s. 686(1)(a)(i)): appellate court asks whether the verdict is one a properly instructed jury or judge "could reasonably have rendered"; may find unreasonableness where an essential inference/finding is (1) "plainly contradicted" by the evidence relied on, or (2) "incompatible" with uncontradicted/unrejected evidence; credibility findings are not disturbed unless they "cannot be supported on any reasonable view of the evidence".
BaselineB: Statute — Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(a)(i), as interpreted in SCC jurisprudence (Yebes; Biniaris; Sinclair; Beaudry; Burke).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Circumstantial-evidence instruction: Hodge’s Case formula does not apply to proving mens rea/intent; for intent the jury applies the ordinary reasonable-doubt standard (Hodge’s applies, if at all, to proof of the act/identity where guilt must be the only reasonable inference).
BaselineA: Common law (jury-charge rule on circumstantial evidence from Hodge’s Case, as interpreted in R. v. Mitchell and reaffirmed in R. v. John/Bagshaw/Paul) plus statutory offence element of “with respect to those dealings” in Criminal Code s. 110(1)(b).
CaseB_TestB: Insurance contract interpretation/coverage where policies cross-reference: apply Civil Code art. 1014 so a clause is construed to have effect; thus “See Garage Policy” in the fleet policy is read as referring to limits/premium (not importing the garage policy’s restrictive coverage), and the garage rider excluding owned autos does not negate fleet third-party liability coverage.
BaselineB: Civil law/statutory interpretation of contract terms under Civil Code arts. 1013 and 1014 (and related insurance context), applied to the garage and fleet policies’ wording and cross-references.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Civil liability of mandatary/broker: plaintiff must prove fault, damage, and causality; if defendant alleges “impossibility of performance” to avoid the obligation, defendant bears the burden under art. 1203 C.C. to prove impossibility (difficulty is insufficient)
BaselineA: Statute (Civil Code of Quebec): arts. 1701 (mandate), 984 and 1062 (object must be possible), and 1203 (“he who alleges facts in avoidance or extinction of the obligation must prove them”); applied within the general fault-damage-causality framework
CaseB_TestB: Municipal disqualification for conflict: under Moncton Consolidation Act s. 6, an elected official is disqualified if he “directly or indirectly… have any interest in any contract” with the City (beyond mere shareholding); “interested in” is given its ordinary meaning and includes a director/officer’s indirect interest in the company’s municipal contracts
BaselineB: Statute: Moncton Consolidation Act, 1946 (N.B.), c. 101, s. 6 (interpreted with reference to Interpretation Act, R.S.N.B. 1973, c. I-13, s. 17; and considered alongside Municipalities Act, R.S.N.B. 1973, c. M-22, ss. 71-72)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Interpretation of para. 12 of the Alberta Natural Resources Transfer Agreement: “Indians of the Province” (Alberta Indians) vs “Indians within the boundaries” (all Indians physically in Alberta, irrespective of residence), so the para. 12 hunting-for-food proviso applies to the latter group
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional instrument and treaty: Indian Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-6, s. 88; Alberta Natural Resources Transfer Agreement, 1930, para. 12 (confirmed by British North America Act, 1930 (U.K.)); Treaty No. 6 hunting clause
CaseB_TestB: Qualified privilege in libel: a communication is privileged where the maker has an “interest or a duty, legal, social or moral, to make it” and the recipient has a corresponding interest/duty; if privileged, liability requires malice, and the publisher is protected even if language is “violent or excessively strong” if he “might have honestly and on reasonable grounds believed that what he wrote or said was true”
BaselineB: Common law: definition of qualified privilege from Adam v. Ward, [1917] A.C. 309; malice/privilege analysis as discussed in Netupsky v. Craig, [1973] S.C.R. 55 (as quoted/applied)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory obscenity test in Criminal Code s. 159(8) as the exclusive standard for sex-based obscenity across the Code: a work is obscene if it is a “publication a dominant characteristic of which is the undue exploitation of sex, or of sex and … crime, horror, cruelty and violence” and the Hicklin common-law test is displaced/should not be used as a fallback.
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, s. 159(8) definition of obscenity; interpreted in light of Criminal Code s. 8 and prior SCC treatment in Brodie v. The Queen, [1962] S.C.R. 681, and the common-law Hicklin test from R. v. Hicklin (1868)).
CaseB_TestB: Duty to accommodate (employer and union) in adverse-effect discrimination: the discriminator must take “reasonable measures short of undue hardship”; “undue” means more than de minimis, and undue hardship is assessed contextually (e.g., cost, disruption of collective agreement, morale/rights of other employees, interchangeability, size, safety). Union liability arises if it (1) helped create the discriminatory rule (e.g., in the collective agreement) or (2) blocks a reasonable accommodation; complainant must facilitate and accept reasonable accommodation.
BaselineB: Statute interpreted through common-law human rights jurisprudence (Human Rights Act, S.B.C. 1984, c. 22, ss. 8(1)(a),(b),(4) and 9(a)-(c), building on O'Malley v. Simpsons-Sears and Central Alberta Dairy Pool).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory obscenity definition is exclusive for all Criminal Code sexual-obscenity offences: apply Criminal Code s. 159(8) (“any publication a dominant characteristic of which is the undue exploitation of sex ... shall be deemed to be obscene”) across the Code and do not apply the common law Hicklin test as a fallback
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, especially ss. 159(1)(a) and 159(8); interpretive reliance on s. 8) plus prior SCC treatment in Brodie v. The Queen; common law Hicklin test discussed as displaced
CaseB_TestB: Duty to accommodate where a collective agreement has an automatic termination clause: the negotiated absence period is a relevant factor but not determinative; accommodation must remain individualized and undue hardship must be assessed globally from the start of the absence (not only after the clause’s expiry)
BaselineB: Common law / human rights framework (Meiorin duty-to-accommodate/undue hardship test) applied in the collective bargaining context; informed by Quebec Charter of human rights and freedoms (ss. 10, 20) and collective agreement clause 12.11.5
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Federal jurisdiction over cable TV as a single interprovincial/international “undertaking” (no constitutional demarcation at the antenna/technology change)
BaselineA: Constitution (B.N.A. Act/Constitution Act, 1867 ss. 91 and 92(10)(a)) interpreted through precedent (especially the Privy Council’s Radio Reference, [1932] A.C. 304, and Winner, [1954] A.C. 541)
CaseB_TestB: Proceeds of disposition: purchaser’s assumption of an obligation is included only if it is a distinct existing liability; embedded future costs (like reforestation obligations running with a tenure) are excluded
BaselineB: Statute (Income Tax Act, s. 13(21) definition of “proceeds of disposition” as including “the sale price of property that has been sold”) plus general tax principle that assumed liabilities can be part of sale price
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Immovable by nature (Civil Code): a structure is immovable where it adheres (directly or indirectly) to land or a building so as to acquire a fixed foundation; vertical attachment of a wire network to the ground is sufficient, and separation of ownership of poles/land is irrelevant
BaselineA: Statute + civil law: Retail Sales Tax Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 71, ss. 2(3) ("moveable property" = all property not considered immoveable by the laws of Quebec) and 6 (tax on purchase of moveable property), interpreted by reference to Civil Code arts. 374 et seq. (immovables), and SCC precedents on networks as immovables by nature (Montreal Light, Heat and Power Consolidated v. Westmount; Lower St. Lawrence Power Co. v. L’Immeuble Landry Ltée; Bélair v. Ste-Rose)
CaseB_TestB: Punitive damages for breach of contract/wrongful dismissal: available but rare; require an actionable wrong (typically a tort) and conduct that is "extreme" and "deserving of punishment" ("harsh, vindictive, reprehensible and malicious"), not merely offensive pre-dismissal conduct
BaselineB: Common law of contract damages (wrongful dismissal) drawing on Addis v. Gramophone Co. and Peso Silver Mines Ltd. (N.P.L.) v. Cropper; punitive damages principles discussed with reference to Rookes v. Barnard and Restatement (Second) of Contracts s. 355 (punitive damages not recoverable for breach of contract unless the conduct is also a tort)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Parent’s contributory negligence / contribution: whether the parent departed from the “generally accepted standard of care” (i.e., the standard of a “reasonably prudent” parent in the community) in supervising the child
BaselineA: Common law negligence (standard of care / contributory negligence), with the Court expressly grounding duty/standard analysis in Donoghue v. Stevenson and treating parental contribution as turning on the community-accepted standard of parental care (also referencing Ware’s Taxi Ltd. v. Gilliham on using other parents’ conduct as a benchmark).
CaseB_TestB: Clause-5 election/repudiation framework in a real estate sale after fire: purchaser must elect either (i) complete and take insurance proceeds or (ii) cancel; attempting to impose additional conditions is a repudiation the vendor may accept
BaselineB: Common law contract/real property principles (including repudiation) as modified by the parties’ contract (standard-form agreement clause 5 and clause 9). The Court contrasts the clause-5 regime with the harsher common law position absent such a clause.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Matrimonial property beneficial interest via resulting trust from contribution to purchase price/common pool: if a spouse contributes (directly or indirectly) in “money or money’s worth” to acquisition/improvement, a resulting trust is presumed; in a joint “common purse” account, “in the absence of agreement to the contrary, a one-half interest in any investment purchased by a husband from a common pool of funds… will be considered to be held by him for the benefit of his wife” (rebuttable by proof of contrary intention).
BaselineA: Common law (resulting trust/common intention presumptions in matrimonial property disputes), drawing on Murdoch v. Murdoch, Pettitt v. Pettitt, Gissing v. Gissing, Thompson v. Thompson; joint account trust reasoning from Jones v. Maynard and Re Daly; Daly v. Brown.
CaseB_TestB: Access to court exhibits (post-trial) balancing test: court has supervisory power over its records and may curtail access where needed to protect superordinate values (especially “the protection of the innocent”); for exhibits, the court “is bound to inquire into the use to be made of them” and may regulate use; here, an acquitted person’s privacy interests outweigh public access to exhibits judicially determined inadmissible.
BaselineB: Common law open court/access doctrine from Attorney General of Nova Scotia v. MacIntyre (supervisory power; curtailment only to protect superordinate values like protection of the innocent), applied in the context of exhibits; procedural context includes Nova Scotia Civil Procedure Rule 30.11(6) (return of exhibits).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Limitation Act s. 6(4)(b) postponement test: when a properly advised reasonable person would conclude the plaintiff could reasonably bring an action, given the plaintiff’s serious, significant, and compelling interests/circumstances (no tactical delay)
BaselineA: Statute (Limitation Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 266, s. 6(4)(b) (and the s. 6(4) framework including s. 6(4)(a) and s. 6(5) definitions))
CaseB_TestB: Arbitration Act s. 15 stay framework in receivership: (1) technical prerequisites (arguable case) then (2) exceptions—stay refused only in a clear case where the arbitration agreement is “void, inoperative or incapable of being performed”; in receivership, “inoperative” if enforcing arbitration would compromise the orderly and efficient resolution/integrity of the receivership (non-exhaustive factors)
BaselineB: Statute (Arbitration Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 55, s. 15(1)-(2), interpreted alongside Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. B-3, ss. 183(1) and 243(1)(c))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: When does extinctive prescription begin to run for engineers’ fees on a percentage basis? Prescription runs only when the fee is "due": either (a) "on completion of the work" or (b) "at the time it was suspended, after a decision clearly communicated" to the engineers; until then (e.g., before tenders/termination is known), the engineer cannot require payment.
BaselineA: Combination of statute/regulation and civil law principles: Civil Code art. 2260(6) (five-year prescription) plus the Tariff of fee for Professional Engineers of the Province of Quebec (O.C. 891, Sept. 4, 1957, adopted under s. 4(2) of the Professional Engineers’ Act), applied through general principles of bilateral contracts (payment not demandable until the work owed is delivered/contract terminated).
CaseB_TestB: Discretionary test for enforcing foreign letters rogatory under Canada Evidence Act s. 43: even if jurisdiction exists, the court "may, in its or his discretion" order evidence; enforcement should be refused where it would run counter to Canadian public policy/sovereignty, and the court should not "take issue with the government’s determination of public policy or to measure its impact" when deciding whether to enforce.
BaselineB: Statute-based discretion under Canada Evidence Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-10, s. 43 (court/judge "may, in its or his discretion" order examination/production), informed by comity principles and public policy limits discussed in prior authorities (e.g., Re Westinghouse; Rio Tinto Zinc v. Westinghouse).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “nude” in Criminal Code s. 170: s. 170(2) is a deeming (enlarging) provision; for complete nudity under s. 170(1)(a) the Crown need not prove the nudity “offend[ed] against public decency or order” (that phrase only deems certain clothing to be nudity).
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, s. 170(1)(a) and s. 170(2) (interpreting “a person is nude who is so clad as to offend against public decency or order” as “shall be deemed to be”); historical predecessor s. 205A.
CaseB_TestB: When Crown improperly “splits its case” by adducing reply evidence that raises a new issue/forces the accused back into the witness box, the s. 613(1)(b)(iii) proviso (“no substantial wrong or miscarriage of justice”) cannot be applied because the appellate court cannot realistically assess the verdict after extracting the improper evidence.
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 613(1)(b)(iii) (curative proviso) applied to trial error involving reply evidence/splitting the Crown’s case.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “nude” in Criminal Code s. 170: complete nudity is captured without needing proof it offended public decency/order; s. 170(2) is a deeming (enlarging) provision for being “so clad as to offend against public decency or order”
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, s. 170(1)(a) and s. 170(2); interpreted as a deeming provision akin to predecessor s. 205A)
CaseB_TestB: Availability of certiorari in criminal proceedings: for parties, certiorari lies only for a provincial court judge’s jurisdictional error (not mere error of law on the face of the record); jurisdictional error is failure to observe a mandatory statutory provision or breach of natural justice
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law (Criminal Code, s. 674 prohibition on interlocutory appeals; common-law extraordinary remedy of certiorari as constrained by SCC jurisprudence such as Cohen/Skogman/Dagenais)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Workmen’s Compensation Act s. 8 “additional sum” claim where Commission is subrogated: if the dependant’s civil claim (reduced for the victim’s contributory fault) is fully met or exceeded by compensation, there is no entitlement to any “additional sum”; Commission has priority to recover up to what it paid (s. 7(3) subrogation pleno jure).
BaselineA: Statute + Civil Code: Workmen’s Compensation Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 159, ss. 7(3) (subrogation pleno jure) and 8 (right to claim “any additional sum required”); Civil Code art. 1157 (partial payment and creditor priority) and art. 1056 (wrongful death claim reduced by victim fault).
CaseB_TestB: Contract salary-guarantee enforceability depends on employee’s continued availability/willingness to perform: employer’s obligation to pay “depended upon the plaintiff’s being available and willing to provide the services”; signing/playing for another club without consent is a breach that “freed the respondent of any further obligation to pay salary under the contract.”
BaselineB: Common law contract principles applied to the parties’ written contract terms (especially exclusivity/consent and termination/guarantee clauses).
JudgeB: McIntyre J. (for Dickson, Beetz and McIntyre JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Workmen’s Compensation Act s. 8 “additional sum” entitlement where the Commission is subrogated: if the dependant’s civil claim (after reduction for the victim’s fault) is fully covered by compensation, there is no “additional sum” recoverable from the third party
BaselineA: Statute + Civil Code: Workmen’s Compensation Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 159, ss. 7(3) (subrogation “pleno jure”) and 8 (“additional sum required ... an indemnification proportionate to the loss actually sustained”); Civil Code art. 1157 (partial payment rule) and art. 1056 (wrongful death claim).
CaseB_TestB: Institutional financial security requirement for judicial independence: any government measure affecting judges’ remuneration conditions must be preceded by an “independent, effective and objective” commission process; if recommendations are ignored, the government must justify that decision on a “simple rationality test”
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine under Charter s. 11(d) and the Constitution Act, 1867 Preamble, as articulated in Valente v. The Queen and the Provincial Court Judges Reference (Reference re Remuneration of Judges of the Provincial Court of Prince Edward Island).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Suspensive effect of serving an originating notice for prohibition and/or to quash with a Rule 7 command to “return forthwith”: the inferior criminal court’s jurisdiction is suspended (and it cannot proceed) pending disposition; non-compliance with the return obligation cannot improve the inferior court’s position
BaselineA: Combination of procedural rules and statute: Ontario Criminal Rules 4-8 (esp. Rules 6-8 requiring a “return forthwith” and equating the return to a certiorari return) plus Criminal Code, s. 714; informed by common law certiorari suspension principles discussed in the reasons
CaseB_TestB: Section 15(1) Charter equality analysis (La Forest J. majority): three-step test—(1) distinction, (2) disadvantage, (3) whether distinction is based on an enumerated/analogous ground and is an “irrelevant personal characteristic” assessed by “relevancy to the functional values underlying the law” in its larger context
BaselineB: Common law/constitutional jurisprudence interpreting Charter s. 15(1), especially Andrews v. Law Society of British Columbia and Miron v. Trudel (as applied to Charter s. 15(1))
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Fair comment in defamation requires proof that the defamatory comment was the honest expression of the publisher/writer’s real opinion; absent evidence of the writers’ honest belief (and with the newspaper’s denial of belief), the defence cannot go to the jury.
BaselineA: Common law (defamation—defence of fair comment), drawing on authorities cited in the reasons (e.g., Turner v. Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer Pictures Ltd.; Jones v. Skelton; Slim v. Daily Telegraph; Globe and Mail Ltd. v. Boland; and Silkin v. Beaverbrook Newspapers Ltd.).
CaseB_TestB: Section 2(a) freedom of religion: indirect state-imposed burdens are covered if non-trivial; a burden is not prohibited if “trivial or insubstantial”; if infringed, the limit is assessed under s. 1 using the Oakes proportionality framework (pressing and substantial objective; rational connection; minimal impairment; proportionality of effects).
BaselineB: Statute/constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms ss. 2(a) and 1 (with the s. 1 framework from R. v. Oakes), applied to the Retail Business Holidays Act, R.S.O. 1980, c. 453 (notably ss. 2(1) and 3(4)).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Fair comment requires proof that the defamatory comment was an honest expression of the real opinion of the writer/publisher; absent evidence of the writers’ honest belief (and where the newspaper disavows belief), the defence is not left to the jury
BaselineA: Common law (defamation—fair comment), drawing on authorities cited in the reasons including Turner v. Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer Pictures Ltd. and Slim v. Daily Telegraph Ltd.
CaseB_TestB: Contempt of court (knowledge element): the party alleging contempt must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the alleged contemnor had personal service or actual personal knowledge of the order; service on a solicitor does not, without supporting circumstances, fix ministers with knowledge; no vicarious liability for contempt
BaselineB: Common law contempt (knowledge requirement) plus interpretation of Federal Court Rules (C.R.C. 1978, c. 663, rr. 308, 311, 355) as not altering contempt elements
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Defence of fair comment requires proof that the defamatory comment was an honest expression of the real opinion of the person (including each publisher) relying on the defence; absent evidence of the writers’ honest belief (and where publisher/editor deny belief), the defence is unavailable
BaselineA: Common law defamation (fair comment) as described in authorities cited in the reasons, including Silkin v. Beaverbrook Newspapers Ltd.; Turner v. Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer Pictures Ltd.; Jones v. Skelton; Slim v. Daily Telegraph Ltd.
CaseB_TestB: Garofoli review of wiretap authorizations: errors (even fraudulent) in the ITO are only factors and do not automatically vitiate; court must excise tainted material and ask whether remaining independent information provides sufficient reliable grounds on which an authorization could reasonably be based
BaselineB: Common law/Charter criminal procedure framework for reviewing wiretap authorizations from R. v. Garofoli, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 1421 (applied to Criminal Code wiretap authorizations)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Intra vires test for CRTC regulations under Broadcasting Act s. 16: validity "must be tested by determining whether the regulation deals with a class of subject referred to in s. 3" (applied objectively, in furtherance of the Commission’s objects/policy in s. 3).
BaselineA: Statute (Broadcasting Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. B-11, ss. 3, 15, 16; applied to Radio (A.M.) Broadcasting Regulations, s. 5(1)(k))
CaseB_TestB: Appellate review of jury verdict on quasi-delict/negligence: verdict is binding "unless it is unreasonable"; judge states the legal criterion (prudent and reasonable person) and jury applies it, but verdict set aside if it is "unreasonable" (e.g., effectively creates fault/causation where none can exist in law).
BaselineB: Statute/civil law (Civil Code art. 1053; Code of Civil Procedure arts. 363, 380) with supporting jurisprudence (e.g., Metropolitan Railway Co. v. Jackson (1877))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Constitutional limits on a provincial commission of inquiry vis-à-vis federal institutions and Crown privilege: a province may inquire into specific criminal acts by RCMP members as part of provincial 'administration of justice', but cannot (directly or by colourability) inquire into RCMP administration/management (e.g., 'frequency of their use' of methods) or make recommendations affecting RCMP practices; and a minister’s s. 41(2) Federal Court Act national-security certificate binds the commissioner (not a superior court) so production 'shall be refused without any examination'.
BaselineA: Combination of constitutional division of powers (B.N.A. Act ss. 91, 92) and statute (Federal Court Act, R.S.C. 1970 (2nd Supp.), c. 10, s. 41(2)), with supporting common-law Crown/prerogative principles (as discussed in the reasons, including that commissions have no inherent power to compel discovery against the Crown).
CaseB_TestB: Custody contest (natural parent vs adoptive parents): under s. 39 equity/parens patriae, the court must treat the child’s welfare as the 'predominant factor'—decided on 'all relevant factors' (including 'psychological, spiritual and emotional welfare')—and parental claims 'must be set aside where the welfare of the child requires it'.
BaselineB: Statute (Domestic Relations Ordinance, R.O.N.W.T. 1974, c. D-9, ss. 28(1), 35(2), 37, 39) incorporating equitable parens patriae principles; supported by prior custody jurisprudence cited (e.g., Racine v. Woods; Beson; Re Moores and Feldstein; and the SCC 'trilogy' cases).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Public Authorities Protection Act s. 11 scope: whether the impugned act/omission is in the execution of a "statutory or other public duty or authority"—i.e., segregate statutory functions into (1) those with a "public aspect or connotation" vs (2) "private executive or private administrative"/"managerial, internal or operational" matters; only the former get s. 11’s six-month bar
BaselineA: Statute (Ontario): The Public Authorities Protection Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 374, s. 11, interpreted in relation to The Housing Development Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 213, s. 6(2) (and informed by prior case law including McGonegal et al. v. Gray et al., [1952] 2 S.C.R. 274 and Bradford Corporation v. Myers, [1916] 1 A.C. 242)
CaseB_TestB: Non-delegable statutory duty inquiry: whether the statute’s language "clearly places" the defendant under a non-delegable duty—starting with the words of the statute; permissive "may" and express power to contract out indicate no mandatory non-delegable duty (Indian Act ss. 113-114)
BaselineB: Statute (federal): Indian Act, S.C. 1951, c. 29, ss. 113-114 (interpreted using the approach in E.D.G. v. Hammer, 2003 SCC 52, and contrasted with Lewis (Guardian ad litem of) v. British Columbia, [1997] 3 S.C.R. 1145)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Exemption-from-seizure for insurance proceeds claimed by a universal legatee: the policy’s exemption clause can operate only in favour of a “true beneficiary” (a third party); a universal legatee/heir is not a third party and therefore cannot invoke the exemption (including under art. 553(3) C.C.P.)
BaselineA: Statute/civil law codal provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, art. 553(3) (exemption from seizure for property declared exempt by donor/testator); Civil Code (C.C.) arts. 597 (heir not a third party), 1028 (contract binds heirs/legal representatives), 735 (limits on bequeathing property to defeat creditors). Also discussed: Husbands and Parents Life Insurance Act, s. 30; Supplemental Pension Plans Act, s. 31 (as contrast).
CaseB_TestB: No-fault liability for neighbourhood disturbances under art. 976 C.C.Q.: liability turns on whether neighbours suffered “abnormal or excessive annoyances” beyond the “limit of tolerance” owed “according to the nature or location of their land or local custom,” not on proof of fault
BaselineB: Statute/civil code: Civil Code of Québec, art. 976 (neighbourhood annoyances). Contextual interaction with arts. 1457 (fault-based liability) and 7 (abuse of rights), but the no-fault regime is grounded in art. 976 itself as interpreted.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Superior Court residual jurisdiction not ousted absent clear exclusive assignment: Superior Court may decide the meaning/obligation under Bell Act s. 5(4) when the issue arises in properly brought tort/injunction proceedings (art. 31 C.C.P.), despite CTC’s regulatory role
BaselineA: Statute (Quebec Code of Civil Procedure, art. 31; An Act respecting The Bell Telephone Company of Canada, s. 5(4)-(6) as substituted by 1967-68, c. 48, s. 6; National Transportation Act, s. 45(1))
CaseB_TestB: Reopening Crown’s case: “keystone principle” is prejudice to the defence; discretion narrows by trial stage—after Crown closes and defence has started to answer, reopening permitted only in the “narrowest or most exceptional of circumstances” (e.g., defence contributed to omission or matter of form)
BaselineB: Common law discretion on reopening (considering Robillard v. The Queen; R. v. Kishen Singh; related reopening jurisprudence) informed by Charter self-incrimination principles (ss. 7, 11(c), 13)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Admissibility of cross-examining an accused on juvenile delinquency record as “convictions” under s. 12 Canada Evidence Act (and character-in-issue under s. 593 Cr.C.): “any offence” includes Criminal Code delinquencies enforceable under the Juvenile Delinquents Act, and a finding of delinquency is “equivalent to a conviction” for s. 12 purposes; admissions on cross-examination can prove the convictions unless exceptional circumstances show error.
BaselineA: Statute: Canada Evidence Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-10, s. 12(1)-(2) ("A witness may be questioned as to whether he has been convicted of any offence..."); plus Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 593 (Crown may adduce prior convictions where accused adduces evidence of good character); interpreted alongside Juvenile Delinquents Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. J-3 (esp. ss. 3, 20(1), 38).
CaseB_TestB: Criminal Code indictment amendment for variance in a particular (drug specified) where no prejudice: under s. 529(4)-(5) the court must consider listed factors including whether the accused was “misled or prejudiced” and whether amendment can be made “without injustice”; if no (irreparable) prejudice, the indictment should be amended, and SCC may amend on appeal under s. 613(1)(b)(i) and (3).
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 529(4)-(5) (mandatory considerations for amendment; adjournment to cure prejudice) and ss. 613(1)(b)(i), 613(3) (SCC appellate powers to amend/substitute); applied in context of Narcotic Control Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. N-1, ss. 2, 4 and Schedule item 3.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Coopers & Lybrand criteria for when an administrative decision/order is required by law to be made on a judicial or quasi-judicial basis (and thus reviewable): (1) whether the statutory language/context suggests a hearing; (2) whether the decision affects rights/obligations; (3) whether an adversary process is involved; (4) whether there is an obligation to apply substantive rules to many individual cases (vs broad policy implementation) — “These are all factors to be weighed and evaluated, no one of which is necessarily determinative.”
BaselineA: Common law (duty to act judicially / natural justice; judicial vs administrative classification) as discussed through prior cases cited in the reasons (e.g., Guay v. Lafleur; Randolph; Howarth; Martineau; Durayappah; Ridge v. Baldwin; Wiseman; Pearlberg; Russell v. Duke of Norfolk).
CaseB_TestB: Stillman s. 24(2) trial-fairness framework for Charter-breached evidence: (1) classify evidence as “conscriptive” vs “non-conscriptive” based on how obtained; (2) if conscriptive, Crown must prove on a balance of probabilities the evidence was “discoverable” by alternative non-conscriptive means (independent source or inevitable discovery); if not discoverable, “the court, as a general rule, will exclude the evidence without considering” other Collins factors.
BaselineB: Statute/constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 24(2), building on the Collins s. 24(2) framework (as cited and elaborated in the reasons).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory-limit test for whether interim rates unlawfully recover pre-application “losses” under Gas Utilities Act s. 31: the question is whether “the interim rates prospectively applied will produce an amount in excess of the estimated total revenue requirements for the same period ... by reason of the inclusion ... of revenue shortfalls which have occurred prior to the date of the application” (not whether the “rate base includes” such losses).
BaselineA: Statute (Alberta): The Gas Utilities Act, R.S.A. 1970, c. 158, ss. 28, 31; plus The Public Utilities Board Act, R.S.A. 1970, c. 302, s. 62; and The Administrative Procedures Act, R.S.A. 1970, c. 2, s. 8.
CaseB_TestB: Cuerrier fraud-vitiated-consent test under Criminal Code s. 265(3)(c): fraud requires (1) dishonesty (including non-disclosure) assessed objectively (“whether a reasonable person would find [the accused’s actions] to be dishonest”) and (2) deprivation/risk—Crown must prove the dishonesty exposed the complainant to a “significant risk of serious bodily harm”; plus proof the complainant would have refused unprotected sex if informed of HIV-positive status.
BaselineB: Statute (federal): Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, ss. 265(3)(c), 268, informed by criminal fraud jurisprudence (e.g., R. v. Olan; R. v. Théroux; R. v. Zlatic) as adopted/modified in the reasons.
JudgeB: Cory J. (for Cory, Major, Bastarache and Binnie JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory interpretation of Parole Act revocation provisions: after the 1977 amendments, day parole may be ended either by (i) revocation under s. 10(1)(e) triggering s. 20 consequences, or (ii) termination under s. 10(2); and s. 20 applies to “any parole” (including day parole) despite “recommitment” wording (no sufficient ambiguity). Key language: “parole… includes day parole”; “when any parole is revoked”; and no “real ambiguities… or doubts of substance” (Marcotte).
BaselineA: Statute: Parole Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. P-2 (as amended effective Oct. 15, 1977), especially ss. 2 (definition of parole), 10(1)(e), 10(2), 20(1)-(3) (revocation/recommitment and remission credits).
CaseB_TestB: Palmer criteria (same on sentence appeals) for admitting fresh evidence on appeal: (1) due diligence (generally not admitted if could have been adduced at trial, applied flexibly in criminal cases); (2) relevance to a decisive/potentially decisive issue; (3) credibility (reasonably capable of belief); (4) if believed, could reasonably, with the trial record, be expected to have affected the result. Key quote (Palmer): “(1)… due diligence… (2) …relevant… (3) …credible… (4) …could reasonably… be expected to have affected the result.”
BaselineB: Common law test from Palmer v. The Queen, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 759, applied in the statutory context of Criminal Code ss. 683 and 687 (fresh evidence powers on appeal).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Exercise of SCC discretion under Supreme Court Act s. 52 to vary interest on an SCC judgment: default interest runs as it would on the trial judgment unless the Court orders otherwise; here, limit pre-SCC interest to the trial award amount due to litigation delay attributable to the successful appellant
BaselineA: Statute (Supreme Court Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. S-19, s. 52 as amended by 1974-75-76, c. 18, s. 7; Interest Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-18, ss. 13-14)
CaseB_TestB: Whether procedural fairness/natural justice applies to Governor in Council review under National Transportation Act s. 64(1): construe the statutory scheme; where s. 64(1) grants complete discretion with no procedural standards, courts confine review to jurisdictional boundaries/conditions precedent and do not imply a fairness hearing duty
BaselineB: Statute (National Transportation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. N-17, s. 64(1); with context from Railway Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. R-2, ss. 320-321(1))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.
