CaseA_TestA: Statutory-limit rule for groundwater pumping: under Ontario Water Resources Commission Act s. 37, pumping above 10,000 gallons/day (absent a permit) is per se “unreasonable” and thus can ground nuisance/negligence; no pumping right is a defence for excess pumping (“The statute has defined what is reasonable… any pumping above 10,000 gallons a day is unreasonable unless a permit has been granted… any pumping in violation of s. 37 is to be considered as a nuisance when causing damage”).
BaselineA: Statute (Ontario Water Resources Commission Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 332, s. 37 (and discussion of s. 47); interacting with common-law nuisance/negligence and the prior “English Rule” on percolating water).
CaseB_TestB: Criteria-based assessment of solatium doloris (moral prejudice from death of a loved one): in assessing the moral prejudice, courts should consider factors “inter alia: the circumstances of the death, the ages of the deceased and the parent, the nature and quality of the relationship… the parent’s personality and ability to manage… and the effect of the death on the parent’s life…”.
BaselineB: Civil law/statute (Civil Code of Lower Canada, arts. 1053, 1056) as interpreted by the SCC; the SCC articulates assessment criteria for quantum.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Highway Code s. 13(6) irrebuttable presumption: if the registered owner has not complied with s. 13(1)-(2) on transfer, they are “deemed to be the owner” for liability responsibility and liability insurance purposes; therefore, for civil-liability coverage the transfer is treated as not having occurred and the buyer/driver with the deemed owner’s consent is covered under the omnibus clause.
BaselineA: Statute (Highway Code, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 231, s. 13(6) (and related compliance duties in s. 13(1)-(2)); applied in the context of the policy’s civil liability/omnibus clause).
CaseB_TestB: Garofoli leave threshold for cross-examining a wiretap affiant: the defence must show a “reasonable likelihood” that cross-examination “will elicit testimony of probative value to the issue for consideration by the reviewing judge” (i.e., tending to discredit a statutory precondition for the authorization).
BaselineB: Common law (R. v. Garofoli, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 1421), applied in the statutory/Charter context of wiretap authorizations (Criminal Code, s. 184.2; Charter, s. 8).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: s. 6 Highway Victims Indemnity Act direct action: insurer directly liable to third party only for “damage covered by liability insurance”; s. 6 does not extend coverage to an excluded/non-insured risk, so court must interpret policy’s defined “automobile” and ask whether the loss was caused “first and foremost” by use of an uninsured trailer rather than the insured automobile
BaselineA: Statute (Highway Victims Indemnity Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 232, s. 6) as interpreted in General Security Insurance Company of Canada v. Bélanger, [1977] 1 S.C.R. 802, together with the insurance contract’s definition of “automobile” governing the scope of liability coverage
CaseB_TestB: Lease/insurance subrogation: tenant escapes liability for negligently caused fire only if the landlord’s covenant to insure “runs to the benefit of the tenant”; this is presumed where landlord covenants with tenant to insure against fire unless there is “another explanation” (e.g., option-to-purchase provisions) consistent with leaving the risk on the tenant
BaselineB: Common law of landlord-tenant/fire loss and subrogation, applying and distinguishing Agnew-Surpass Shoe Stores Ltd. v. Cummer-Yonge Investments Ltd., [1976] 2 S.C.R. 221; Ross Southward Tire Ltd. v. Pyrotech Products Ltd., [1976] 2 S.C.R. 35; and distinguishing United Motors Service Inc. v. Hutson, [1937] S.C.R. 294
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Qualified privilege in defamation defeated only by malice; privilege protects even “violent or excessively strong” language if the defendant “might have honestly and on reasonable grounds believed that what he wrote or said was true” (Adam v. Ward, applied via Netupsky v. Craig).
BaselineA: Common law (qualified privilege and malice), drawing on Adam v. Ward [1917] A.C. 309 and Netupsky v. Craig [1973] S.C.R. 55.
CaseB_TestB: Sheppard/Braich test for insufficient reasons: two stages—(1) are the reasons inadequate; (2) if so, do they prevent appellate review (i.e., are they not “sufficiently amenable to appellate review” / do they create an “impediment to appellate review”).
BaselineB: Common law (appellate review of sufficiency of reasons), from R. v. Sheppard, 2002 SCC 26 and R. v. Braich, 2002 SCC 27 (also situated within Criminal Code s. 686 appeal powers).
JudgeB: Bastarache and Abella JJ. (LeBel J. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Fault for unlawful arrest by police: (1) coroner’s s. 38 warrant is invalid if used to detain a suspect for interrogation rather than to secure attendance as a witness; and (2) warrantless arrest power requires “reasonable and probable grounds” that must “take into account all the information available” (police may disregard only what they have good reason to believe is unreliable).
BaselineA: Combination: Civil Code arts. 1053, 1054 (fault and employer liability) + Coroners' Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 29, s. 38 (detention of witnesses) + Criminal Code 1953-54, c. 51, s. 435 (warrantless arrest on reasonable and probable grounds).
CaseB_TestB: Validity of dismissal of a probationary constable: dismissal is ineffective unless made by the Board (the power to dismiss is exclusively vested in the Board and cannot be delegated to the chief), and the Board must actually exercise that function (it cannot validly ‘confirm’ a chief’s dismissal without engaging the constable—here, not even informing him his case would be considered).
BaselineB: Statute/regulation: The Police Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 351, s. 29 + Regulation 680, s. 27(b) (authority of a board to dispense with services within 18 months).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Disqualification for municipal office under s. 6 Moncton Consolidation Act: whether an office-holder has a direct or indirect “interest in any contract” with the City (beyond mere shareholding), interpreted broadly by “common usage of men”
BaselineA: Statute (Moncton Consolidation Act, 1946 (N.B.), c. 101, s. 6), interpreted using the SCC’s approach in Angrignon (1935) (“interested in” has no technical signification; apply common usage) and the remedial construction direction in Interpretation Act, R.S.N.B. 1973, c. I-13, s. 17
CaseB_TestB: Statutory interpretation of OLA s. 22: whether a municipality is an “institution” (OLA s. 1) obliged to use the other party’s chosen official language in “oral or written pleadings” and “process” in civil proceedings; and scope excludes evidence and case-law translations
BaselineB: Statute (Official Languages Act, S.N.B. 2002, c. O-0.5, ss. 1 “institution”, 22) interpreted under the modern principle (Driedger) and Bell ExpressVu (Charter values only if genuine ambiguity)
JudgeB: Charron J. (McLachlin C.J. and Major, Fish and Abella JJ. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Qualified privilege in libel: malice goes to the jury only if the evidence “raises a probability” of express malice (more than a “mere scintilla” and “more consistent with [malice’s] existence than with its non-existence”)
BaselineA: Common law (defamation/qualified privilege). Authorities cited include Somerville v. Hawkins (1851) (probability standard), Spill v. Maule (1869), Adam v. Ward (1917), and SCC adoption in Sun Life Assurance Co. of Canada v. Dalrymple (1965).
CaseB_TestB: Blood Tribe clear-intent requirement for statutory abrogation of solicitor-client privilege: only “where legislative language evinces a clear intent” may privilege be abrogated; s. 232(1) ITA is “unequivocal” in excluding “an accounting record of a lawyer”
BaselineB: Statute (Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), ss. 231.2(1), 231.7(1), and especially s. 232(1) definition of “solicitor-client privilege”), interpreted through the common-law/constitutional interpretive principle from Canada (Privacy Commissioner) v. Blood Tribe Department of Health, 2008 SCC 44.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Priority of B.C. Payment of Wages Act s. 5A wage lien: lien arises "from the date wages were earned" and takes priority only over dispositions after attachment; pre-existing mortgages are not affected, so the lien "will only attach to the employer’s equity" in the property
BaselineA: Statute — Payment of Wages Act, 1962 (B.C.), c. 45, ss. 5 and 5A(1)-(2) (as amended/re-enacted)
CaseB_TestB: Suppletive dissolution framework for Quebec legal persons: apply C.C.Q. arts. 355-364 to "fill the gaps" of special statutes (art. 334), and order dissolution under art. 355(2) where the corporation is "incapable of accomplishing the objects for which it was constituted" (impossibility of accomplishing object/other legitimate cause)
BaselineB: Statute (Civil Code of Québec) — C.C.Q. arts. 300, 334, 355 (and related arts. 355-364); interaction with Companies Act and C.C.P. art. 829 addressed
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Residual discretion/inherent jurisdiction to remedy unfairness from Crown’s closing address: (1) usually by curative jury instruction; (2) in rare cases, a limited defence reply only in the clearest cases of unfairness (e.g., Crown dramatically changes/adds legal theory or misleads defence), confined to the improper issues
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 651(3)-(4) (order of addresses) plus common-law inherent jurisdiction to control process and ensure trial fairness (e.g., cited: R. v. Osborn; Amato v. The Queen; Selvey v. DPP)
JudgeA: Cory, Iacobucci and Bastarache JJ. (for Gonthier, Cory, Iacobucci and Bastarache JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Charter-validity test for a statutory presumption under s. 11(d): a presumption is constitutional only if proof of the substituted/basic fact leads 'inexorably' to the essential element it replaces (an 'inexorable' link 'necessarily holds true in all cases'); applied to strike down Criminal Code s. 172.1(3)
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law/constitutional doctrine: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 172.1(3) (presumption re age) assessed under Charter s. 11(d) using prior SCC presumption jurisprudence (cited: Whyte; Downey; Audet; St-Onge Lamoureux; Vaillancourt)
JudgeB: Moldaver J. (Wagner C.J. and Gascon, Côté, Brown, Rowe and Martin JJ. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Adjudicator’s remedial authority to substitute a lesser penalty for discharge where there is “just and sufficient cause” for some discipline but not for discharge (discipline as a continuum).
BaselineA: Statute and collective agreement: Public Service Labour Relations Act, R.S.N.B. 1973, c. P-25, s. 92(1)(b) (adjudication of “disciplinary action resulting in discharge, suspension or a financial penalty”) plus collective agreement art. V(d) (“Discipline, suspension, demotion or discharge ... shall be for just and sufficient cause”). Prior SCC baseline discussed/distinguished: Port Arthur Shipbuilding Co. v. Arthurs, [1969] S.C.R. 85.
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 24(2) exclusion analysis (Collins guidelines): whether, “having regard to all the circumstances”, admission of evidence obtained in a Charter-infringing manner would “bring the administration of justice into disrepute”.
BaselineB: Statute/constitutional text plus common law framework: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 24(2) (and assumed s. 8 breach), applied through the common-law/Charter framework in R. v. Collins, [1987] 1 S.C.R. 265.
JudgeB: Lamer J. (for Dickson C.J. and Lamer, Wilson, Le Dain and La Forest JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Will-construction test: give effect to the testator’s overriding intention on a fair reading of the clause, and do not let administrative/boilerplate provisions defeat a clearly expressed intention (legacy payable on disposition of the business, however effected).
BaselineA: Common law (will construction/ascertaining testator’s intention from the will read as a whole; no specific statutory provision identified in the reasons).
CaseB_TestB: Manslaughter legal causation with intervening acts: the Smithers/Nette test remains whether the accused’s dangerous unlawful acts were a “significant contributing cause of death”; foreseeability and “independent act” are non-determinative analytical aids.
BaselineB: Common law causation test from Smithers v. The Queen and R. v. Nette, applied in the context of Criminal Code ss. 222, 224, 225 (and discussion of s. 21).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Functional (and traditional) test for whether labour relations fall under the federal exception: exclusive federal jurisdiction only where the undertaking can be characterized as a federal undertaking/service/business; otherwise provincial jurisdiction applies
BaselineA: Common law constitutional division-of-powers doctrine for labour relations (functional characterization of the undertaking), as reflected in cases cited including Toronto Electric Commissioners v. Snider and the Stevedoring Reference
CaseB_TestB: Two-part s. 15(1) Charter equality test: (1) distinction based on an enumerated/analogous ground; (2) disadvantage by perpetuating prejudice or stereotyping (no need for a mirror comparator group)
BaselineB: Common law Charter jurisprudence interpreting s. 15(1), especially Andrews v. Law Society of British Columbia and R. v. Kapp (two-step discrimination framework)
JudgeB: McLachlin C.J. and Abella J. (for the Court)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Bankruptcy Act s. 107(1)(j) overrides provincial Crown statutory preferences: provincial tax claims (not otherwise mentioned) rank pari passu notwithstanding any statutory preference, even if a provincial ‘privilege’ was registered; the opening ‘Subject to the rights of secured creditors’ yields where the ‘notwithstanding’ clause applies.
BaselineA: Statute (Bankruptcy Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. B-3, ss. 2 and 107(1)(j), (3); interacting with Quebec Retail Sales Tax Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 71, s. 30 and Civil Code art. 1989)
JudgeA: Pigeon J. (for Martland, Ritchie, Pigeon, Beetz, Pratte and McIntyre JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Public interest standing (purposive, flexible): court weighs (1) serious justiciable issue; (2) plaintiff has a real stake or is engaged; and (3) proposed suit is, ‘in all of the circumstances’, a ‘reasonable and effective means’ to bring the issue to court (not a strict “no other way” requirement), assessed with considerations like judicial economy, adversarial suitability, and legality.
BaselineB: Common law (standing framework from Borowski; Finlay; Canadian Council of Churches; Hy and Zel’s; Thorson; McNeil)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Crown prerogative priority applies only where Crown and subject claims are “of equal degree”; foreclosure surplus is distributed by Registry Act priorities so a prior registered second/collateral mortgage is of a higher degree than a later registered Crown judgment
BaselineA: Combination: common law Crown prerogative priority for debts/claims “of equal degree” (The Queen v. Bank of Nova Scotia (1885), 11 S.C.R. 1) plus Nova Scotia Registry Act, R.S.N.S. 1967, c. 265, ss. 17-18 (and related civil procedure distribution rule 47.11)
CaseB_TestB: International jurisdiction for an incidental action in warranty is determined by extending domestic territorial jurisdiction rules: art. 71 C.C.P. applies to a foreign defendant, so the warranty action “must be taken before the court in which the principal action is pending” and is “not subject to any limitation”
BaselineB: Statute/codified procedure: Code of Civil Procedure (Quebec), art. 71 (incidental action in warranty must be brought where principal action pending), supported by Civil Code art. 27 and the private international law principle that international jurisdiction is defined by extension of domestic territorial jurisdiction rules (as recognized in Alimport, [1977] 2 S.C.R. 858; Trower and Sons, Ld. v. Ripstein, [1944] A.C. 254)
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “detained” under Canadian Bill of Rights s. 2(c): “detain”/“detention” “connote some form of compulsory restraint” (i.e., being “held in custody”/actual physical restraint), so a roadside stop/sobriety screening where the driver is then “allowed to go away” is not detention and does not trigger the right to counsel as a “reasonable excuse” for refusing a breath demand
BaselineA: Statute: Canadian Bill of Rights, 1960 (Can.), c. 44, s. 2(c)(ii)-(iii), applied in the context of Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 234.1(1)-(2) (roadside breath demand and offence of refusal “without reasonable excuse”); prior SCC context discussed: Brownridge v. The Queen, [1972] S.C.R. 926; Hogan v. The Queen, [1975] 2 S.C.R. 574
CaseB_TestB: Two-branch test for the tort of civil conspiracy: (1) liability where “the predominant purpose of the defendants’ conduct is to cause injury to the plaintiff” (means lawful or unlawful); or (2) where “the conduct of the defendants is unlawful”, is “directed towards the plaintiff (alone or together with others)”, and defendants “should know in the circumstances that injury to the plaintiff is likely to and does result” (constructive intent), with “actual damage” required in both
BaselineB: Common law tort of conspiracy, drawing on and synthesizing prior authorities discussed in the reasons (including Lonrho Ltd. v. Shell Petroleum Co. Ltd., Crofter Hand Woven Harris Tweed Co. v. Veitch, Sorrell v. Smith, and Canadian cases such as Gagnon v. Foundation Maritime Limited and International Brotherhood of Teamsters v. Therien); statutory illegality context considered: Combines Investigation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-23, s. 32
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 492 re-election validity test: effective re-election occurs where the accused (1) gives notice to the sheriff of a desire to re-elect (s. 492(1)); (2) attends at the time/place fixed (s. 492(2)-(3)); and (3) after the charge is read, communicates the re-election (which may be done through counsel in the accused’s presence). SCC also interprets s. 492(3) as requiring the reading of the actual charge the accused faces (the preferred indictment), and holds failure to prefer a new Form 4 indictment under s. 496 after re-election does not invalidate proceedings where the indictment is already in Form 4.
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, s. 492 (re-election procedure) and related s. 496 (indictment after re-election).
CaseB_TestB: Injurious affection (no land taken) actionable-at-common-law requirement: to obtain compensation under Expropriations Act s. 1(e)(ii) and s. 21, the claimant must show the construction-caused damage “would have been actionable at common law”; here, the only possible cause is private nuisance, assessed by whether there is “physical injury to land or substantially interfering with the use or enjoyment of land ... where, in the light of all the surrounding circumstances, this injury or interference is held to be unreasonable” (Street), i.e., a reasonable-user/balancing inquiry; loss of prospect/view is not actionable and highway construction is not an unreasonable use in this context.
BaselineB: Combination: Statute (Expropriations Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 154, ss. 1(e)(ii), 21) incorporating common law (private nuisance) as the actionable-wrong requirement; injurious affection conditions referenced from The Queen v. Loiselle, [1962] S.C.R. 624.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Ontario Municipal Board jurisdiction to adjust assets/liabilities on dissolution: s. 137(1) incorporates only s. 14(11)(a),(b),(d) of The Municipal Act (without the prefatory limits tied to annexation/amalgamation), empowering the Board to make “adjustments of assets and liabilities…as the Board may consider equitable” in relation to the County’s dissolution
BaselineA: Statute: The Regional Municipality of Ottawa-Carleton Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 407, ss. 135-137, incorporating The Municipal Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 284, s. 14(11)(a),(b),(d) (especially s. 14(11)(a): Board may “make all such adjustments of assets and liabilities…as the Board may consider equitable”)
JudgeA: Estey J. (for Dickson, Estey and McIntyre JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Charter fundamental justice mens rea requirement for murder: “a conviction for murder cannot rest on anything less than proof beyond a reasonable doubt of subjective foresight of death” (therefore s. 213(a) constructive murder is unconstitutional)
BaselineB: Constitution + statute: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 7 and 11(d), applied to Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 213(a) (with Vaillancourt as the immediate doctrinal baseline discussed in the reasons)
JudgeB: Lamer C.J. (for Dickson C.J. and Lamer C.J. and Wilson, Gonthier and Cory JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Validity of consent to intercept a private communication under Criminal Code s. 178.11(2)(a): consent must be "voluntary (i.e. free from coercion)" and "made knowingly, with an awareness of the significance of the consent"; promises/expected leniency do not by themselves amount to coercion, and consent may be express or implied.
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code (as amended by the Protection of Privacy Act), especially ss. 178.1 ("private communication"), 178.11(2)(a) (consent interception), and 178.16(1)(a) (admissibility if interception "lawfully made").
CaseB_TestB: Proof that hate speech targeted the identifiable group particularized in the information (s. 319(2)): the trier must assess the "totality of the evidence" to decide whether the statements "as a matter of fact, promoted hatred" of the group; it is not necessary to prove strict "interchangeability" of labels (e.g., "gypsies" and "Roma").
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, s. 319(2) (wilful promotion of hatred) and s. 318(4) ("identifiable group"); plus evidentiary doctrine of judicial notice as summarized from R. v. Find (facts "so notorious" or "capable of immediate and accurate demonstration").
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Audi alteram partem / no ex parte evidence rule for appellate tribunals: unless expressly or by necessary implication empowered to act ex parte, an appellate authority must not hear evidence or receive representations from one side in the absence of the other; the affected party must know the case and have a fair opportunity to correct or contradict; prejudice need not be shown—enough that the evidence 'might' have prejudiced
BaselineA: Common law (procedural fairness / natural justice), applied in a statutory appeal setting under the Universities Act, 1974 (B.C.), c. 100 (notably ss. 58(1)-(3) and s. 61) but not abrogated absent 'express language or necessary implication'
CaseB_TestB: Workers’ compensation occupational-disease causation under s. 250(4): causation may be inferred from other (including circumstantial) evidence and is not determined by the presence/absence of expert opinion; where evidence on causation is 'evenly weighted', the issue must be resolved in the worker’s favour
BaselineB: Statute (Workers Compensation Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 492, ss. 6 and 250(4)) plus mandatory policy incorporated by statute (s. 250(2) requiring application of RSCM II 'causative significance' policy)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Appellate intervention in a trial damages award: an appellate court may not substitute its own figure unless a wrong principle of law was applied or the overall award is a wholly erroneous estimate of damages (Andrews v. Grand & Toy).
BaselineA: Common law (as stated in Andrews et al. v. Grand & Toy Alberta Ltd. et al., [1978] 2 S.C.R. 229, at p. 235).
JudgeA: Martland J. (for the Court, oral reasons)
CaseB_TestB: Videotape-only identification: once it is established the videotape has not been altered and depicts the crime, it is admissible; a trier of fact may identify and convict on the videotape alone if satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt, assessing weight mainly by the tape’s clarity/quality and (to a lesser extent) time of depiction, with cautions to exercise care.
BaselineB: Common law evidence principles (admissibility/relevance of real evidence; reliance on R. v. Leaney, [1989] 2 S.C.R. 393) plus the criminal standard of proof (beyond a reasonable doubt).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Quebec Labour Code s. 16 rebuttal/jurisdiction test: employer rebuts the presumption only by showing the alleged “other good and sufficient reason” is (1) substantial, (2) not a pretext, and (3) the true/real determining reason (causa causans) for dismissal; the commissioner/Labour Court cannot assess the proportionality or “severity of the penalty” once a real, serious reason is established
BaselineA: Statute (Quebec Labour Code, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 141 as am., ss. 13-16, especially s. 16; also s. 14 remedial scheme)
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 12 “gross disproportionality” test (with two-aspect analysis): cruel and unusual punishment is established only where the punishment is “so excessive as to outrage standards of decency”/“grossly disproportionate”, assessed by considering “the gravity of the offence, the personal characteristics of the offender and the particular circumstances of the case” (plus other non-decisive factors), and if not grossly disproportionate on the actual facts, the challenger must show gross disproportionality in a “reasonable hypothetical” (not far-fetched) scenario
BaselineB: Combination: constitutional text (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 12) plus common law/precedent (R. v. Smith; reaffirmed in Lyons and Luxton) applied to a statutory minimum sentence (Motor Vehicle Act, s. 88(1)(c) as applied with s. 86(1)(a)(ii))
JudgeB: Gonthier J. (for La Forest, L'Heureux-Dubé, Sopinka, Gonthier, Cory and Iacobucci JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Summary conviction appeal costs: under Criminal Code ss. 758 and 771(3), the appeal court "may make any order with respect to costs that it considers just and reasonable" / "proper" and these provisions are interpreted as implicitly binding the Crown (Her Majesty) in Part XXIV context
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, Part XXIV), interpreted alongside Interpretation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-23, s. 16
CaseB_TestB: Mortgage statutory prepayment right (Interest Act s. 10(1)) in renewals: mortgagor may prepay at end of each five-year period; if renewal "deems" a new mortgage date and renewal term ≤ 5 years, mortgagor cannot prepay until end of that renewal; contracting out of the statutory right is unenforceable, but a fully informed choice not to exercise the right is not a waiver
BaselineB: Statute (Interest Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-18, s. 10(1), (2); also considered: Manitoba Mortgage Act s. 20(6), (7))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Wrongful dismissal damages: collateral benefits (income tax and unemployment insurance) are not deducted—no deduction for income tax not payable; unemployment insurance benefits are a consequence of the employment contract and therefore not deductible
BaselineA: Common law contract damages principles for wrongful dismissal (including the compensatory principle from Livesley v. Horst) and the SCC’s collateral benefits approach in Guy v. Trizec Equities Ltd.
CaseB_TestB: Statutory authorization to fingerprint juveniles: under Identification of Criminals Act s. 2(1)-(2), a juvenile in lawful custody for a delinquency relating to a Criminal Code indictable offence is treated as 'charged with'/'under conviction of' an indictable offence, so necessary force may be used to take fingerprints
BaselineB: Statute—Identification of Criminals Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-1, s. 2(1)-(2), interpreted in light of the Juvenile Delinquents Act and applied using Morris v. The Queen
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: “Air of reality / sense of reality” threshold for whether a trial judge must leave a defence (here, mistake of fact as to consent) with the jury: there must be “in the record some evidence which would convey a sense of reality in the submission”; for mistake-of-fact-as-to-consent, “there must be some evidence which, if believed, would support the existence of a mistaken but honest belief” in consent, and (on these facts) the Court adds that to require the alternative defence, the evidence must be “from or be supported by sources other than the appellant” to give it “any air of reality.”
BaselineA: Common law (jury-charge duty / defences left to jury) drawing the “sense of reality” formulation from Kelsey v. The Queen, [1953] 1 S.C.R. 220, and applied in R. v. Workman and Huculak, [1963] S.C.R. 266 (in the context of a rape charge under Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 143).
CaseB_TestB: Morin s. 11(b) “reasonable time” framework (as adopted/used in Potvin): assess reasonableness of delay by considering “(1) the length of the delay; (2) waiver, if any, of parts of the delay; (3) the reasons for the delay; and (4) prejudice to the subject of the criminal process.”
BaselineB: Constitutional text (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 11(b)) as structured by R. v. Morin, [1992] 1 S.C.R. 771 (and related s. 11 interpretation cases such as R. v. Kalanj, [1989] 1 S.C.R. 1594).
JudgeB: McLachlin J. (for Lamer C.J. and McLachlin and Major JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Standard of review framework: start with a presumption of reasonableness for a tribunal interpreting its home statute; rebut only if a Dunsmuir correctness category applies (and a statutory right of appeal is not a new correctness category)
BaselineA: Common law (judicial review standard-of-review framework from Dunsmuir v. New Brunswick, plus subsequent SCC cases such as Saguenay/McLean)
CaseB_TestB: Sui generis Crown fiduciary duty framework: fiduciary duty arises from Crown discretionary control over a specific/cognizable Aboriginal interest; breach assessed by whether Crown met fiduciary standard of conduct (loyalty/good faith/full disclosure/ordinary prudence), not by achieving a particular result
BaselineB: Common law (Crown–Indigenous fiduciary duty jurisprudence, especially Wewaykum; applied within the statutory specific-claims scheme)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Necessarily-incidental (ancillary) powers test for validity of federal legislation that prima facie intrudes on provincial jurisdiction: where a provision is not directly about a s. 91 head of power, it is valid only if it is "necessarily incidental to effective legislation" on that federal subject; here, s. 33(3) failed because it was a "blanket prohibition" that "makes no attempt to link the proscribed conduct to actual or potential harm to fisheries" and was therefore not "necessarily incidental" to s. 91(12) fisheries power.
BaselineA: Common law constitutional doctrine (ancillary/necessarily-incidental doctrine) drawn from Attorney-General for Canada v. Attorney-General for British Columbia and others, [1930] A.C. 111 (Lord Tomlin’s proposition (3)), applied to Parliament’s s. 91(12) fisheries power under the British North America Act, 1867.
CaseB_TestB: Colour of right in theft: "colour of right" means a "bona fide"/"honest belief"; the defence turns on whether the jury is satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused did NOT have, "at the time of the transfers, an honest belief that he had the right to that money" (not on what the jury thinks the accused’s legal rights actually were).
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code theft provisions using the phrase "without colour of right"), specifically ss. 283 and 294 (as referenced in the reasons).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “unlawful purpose” in Criminal Code conspiracy (s. 423(2)(a)): the purpose must be “contrary to law”, i.e., prohibited by federal or provincial legislation (not merely conduct that interferes with a statutory right unless that interference is itself prohibited).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 423(2)(a); also considers s. 8 excluding common law offences; and contrasts with s. 423(2)(b) and s. 381).
CaseB_TestB: Quebec defamation fault under art. 1457 C.C.Q.: a contextual analysis where “there will not be fault until it has been shown that the journalist or media outlet in question has fallen below professional standards”; the “conduct of the reasonable journalist” is the “all-important guidepost”.
BaselineB: Statute (Civil Code of Québec, art. 1457; with guidance drawn from Quebec jurisprudence including Société Radio-Canada v. Radio Sept-Îles and Prud’homme).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Automatism/insanity classification: whether the accused’s automatism is due to a “disease of the mind” (internal cause) versus a transient effect of a specific external factor; “ordinary stresses and disappointments of life” are not an external cause taking it out of disease-of-the-mind
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 16) interpreted through common-law automatism/insanity jurisprudence (e.g., Bratty v. A.G. Northern Ireland, R. v. K.)
CaseB_TestB: Conflict/supersession analysis in fire insurance: where a standard mortgage clause says it “shall supersede any policy provisions in conflict therewith”, Statutory Condition 4 cannot be used to void mortgagee coverage if it conflicts with the mortgage clause (including where the alleged material change is vacancy/non-occupancy covered by the clause)
BaselineB: Statute and contract: Insurance Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. I.8, Part IV (Statutory Condition 4) plus the policy’s standard mortgage clause; interpreted with reference to National Bank of Greece (Canada) v. Katsikonouris
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Single-cause vs multiple-causes characterization for prescription: if claimed damages “result from a single cause of action, which is the breach of a contractual obligation”, they are contractual and prescribe in 30 years; if they “result from several separate and independent causes of action”, each is characterized as contractual or delictual and prescribes accordingly
BaselineA: Statute/civil code (Civil Code of Quebec provisions on prescription: arts. 2242 (30 years), 2261(2) (2 years for delict/quasi-delict), with characterization of obligations informed by corporate/by-law context and art. 1024 (contract consequences))
CaseB_TestB: Priority between mechanic’s lien and mortgage where s. 14(1) does not apply: an unregistered lien has no general priority; when priorities are not otherwise prescribed, resort is to registration—upon registration the lien claimant is “deemed to be a purchaser pro tanto” (s. 20), and under Registry Act ss. 69(1) and 70 “priority [is] according to priority of registration” (absent actual notice)
BaselineB: Statute (The Mechanics’ Lien Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 267, ss. 14(1), 20 (and related registration/expiry provisions ss. 16, 21, 22) interpreted alongside The Registry Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 409, ss. 69(1), 70)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Accrued-rights on statutory repeal/amendment (Interpretation Act, s. 35(c)): if, on the eve of repeal, the claimant was "enjoying a right or a privilege which had accrued under the repealed enactment", the repeal does not "affect" it; read the amending Act "in the light of s. 35(c)" so accrued benefits continue, but only to the extent of the pre-repeal entitlement (here, benefits continued for January 1976 but remained subject to the old disqualification when a pension "becomes payable").
BaselineA: Statute (Interpretation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-23, s. 35(c)) applied to the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, S.C. 1970-71-72, c. 48, s. 31 (as amended by S.C. 1974-75-76, c. 80, s. 10) and s. 38; also considers Unemployment Insurance Entitlements Adjustment Act, 1976-77, c. 11, s. 2.
CaseB_TestB: Compellability of superior court judges before a provincial inquiry under the Public Inquiries Act: read ss. 3 and 4 together so the Commission’s power to compel is no greater than a superior court judge in a civil case; because of judicial independence/immunity, judges cannot be compelled to testify "as to how and why" they reached a decision or "as to why a particular judge sat on a particular case" (general statutory language is "not specific enough" to override this immunity).
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law/constitutional principle: Public Inquiries Act, R.S.N.S. 1967, c. 250, ss. 3-4, interpreted in light of the constitutional principle of judicial independence (as summarized in Valente v. The Queen and Beauregard v. Canada) and the common law immunity tradition (e.g., Knowles' Trial).
JudgeB: McLachlin J. (for L'Heureux-Dubé, Gonthier and McLachlin JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Interpretation of Motor Vehicle Transport Act, s. 3(2): provincial board may license extra-provincial undertakings “into or through” a province as including operations “in, across, into and out of the province”, and provincial enforcement (including seizure) is not displaced by MVTA s. 6
BaselineA: Statute (Motor Vehicle Transport Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. M-14, ss. 2, 3, 5, 6; incorporating provincial licensing/enforcement via The Public Service Vehicles Act, R.S.A. 1970, c. 300, incl. s. 58)
CaseB_TestB: Charter standing/scope test for s. 12: claimant must show an interest within the guarantee’s scope and purpose; s. 12’s “cruel and unusual” is limited to human beings (corporations cannot claim s. 12 protection)
BaselineB: Constitution (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 12) interpreted purposively (Big M Drug Mart framework; CIP standing principle)
JudgeB: Brown and Rowe JJ. (Wagner C.J. and Moldaver and Côté JJ. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Fundamental breach and exclusionary clause: whether the exclusion/waiver clause remains applicable is determined by the “true construction of the contract” (not an automatic rule that fundamental breach nullifies the clause); here, the lien waiver ceased to bind once the subcontractor communicated its election to treat the contract as at an end.
BaselineA: Combination: common law (Suisse Atlantique; Photo Production) plus statute interpreted in context (The Mechanics’ Lien Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 267, s. 5(1)).
CaseB_TestB: Collateral attack on administrative order in penal proceedings: whether a penal court may determine an order’s validity “depends on the statute” and is answered by focusing on “the legislature’s intention as to the appropriate forum”, assessed using non-exhaustive factors (statutory wording, legislative purpose, availability of appeal, nature of the collateral attack in light of the appeal tribunal’s expertise/raison d’être, and penalty).
BaselineB: Statute-focused framework under the Environmental Protection Act, R.S.O. 1980, c. 141 (notably ss. 17, 122-123, 146(1a)), informed by prior collateral-attack jurisprudence (e.g., Wilson; Litchfield; Sarson) and comparative authorities.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Pettkus unjust enrichment test for constructive trust: (1) enrichment, (2) corresponding deprivation, and (3) absence of any juristic reason; plus the Court’s articulation that it is unjust where a spouse-like partner prejudices herself in a reasonable expectation of an interest and the other knowingly (or ought to have known) accepts the benefit
BaselineA: Common law (equitable constructive trust/unjust enrichment), drawing from Rathwell v. Rathwell and Murdoch v. Murdoch (and related trust jurisprudence discussed in the reasons)
CaseB_TestB: Descôteaux framework for solicitor-client confidentiality/privilege in search warrants: confidentiality applies to communications made to obtain legal advice (even pre-retainer) unless crime/fraud exception; and for Criminal Code s. 443(1)(b) a justice lacks jurisdiction to authorize seizure of privileged material and should refuse a warrant to search a lawyer’s office unless there is no reasonable alternative, with protective execution terms
BaselineB: Combination: statute (Criminal Code, s. 443(1)(b)) interpreted in light of common law solicitor-client privilege/confidentiality (including Solosky v. The Queen and other privilege authorities cited)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Informed-consent causation test in medical non-disclosure: whether “a reasonable person in the patient’s position would have done if there had been proper disclosure of attendant risks” (objective test, with the patient’s particular circumstances considered objectively and reasonably).
BaselineA: Common law (medical negligence duty of disclosure and causation), drawing on Hopp v. Lepp (duty to disclose “all material risks” and answer specific questions) and developing the causation approach for non-disclosure.
CaseB_TestB: “Integral element” test for federal legislative competence over s. 92(10) undertakings: Parliament may displace provincial law only where the matter is an “integral part” of the core federal undertaking; otherwise provincial laws of general application apply (here, a federal railway limitation period is ultra vires as applied to provincial personal-injury negligence actions).
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine (division of powers) applying the “integral element” approach from Construction Montcalm Inc. v. Minimum Wage Commission and Northern Telecom Ltd. v. Communications Workers of Canada, in the context of Railway Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. R-2, s. 342(1).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Natural Resources Agreement (para. 12) “right of access” test for treaty Indian hunting for food: if provincial law contemplates any (even limited) hunting on the land, that constitutes a “right of access” and the para. 12 proviso is engaged, so Indians may hunt for food “at all seasons of the year” (province may totally deny hunting to all, but if any hunting is permitted, the proviso applies).
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional instrument: Natural Resources Agreement, 1930 (Canada–Saskatchewan), para. 12 (confirmed by British North America Act, 1930). Interpreted and applied in light of R. v. Sutherland, Wilson and Wilson, [1980] 2 S.C.R. 451 (definition of “right of access”).
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 2(a) invalid-purpose framework: “The legislation's purpose is the initial test of constitutional validity”; if the law’s purpose is invalid (e.g., “compulsion of religious observance”), it violates s. 2(a) and “effects can never be relied on to save legislation with an invalid purpose.”
BaselineB: Constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 2(a) (and related remedial/supremacy provisions, especially Constitution Act, 1982, s. 52(1)). The Court articulates a general purpose/effects approach to Charter validity (not the Oakes s. 1 test).
JudgeB: Dickson J. (for Dickson, Beetz, McIntyre, Chouinard and Lamer JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: No implied retroactive revocation power: where the Act/Regulations provide only employer-initiated review, the Commission/officer/review panel cannot “undo retroactively and suo motu” previously granted premium reductions; an erroneous grant is not a “nullity” absent jurisdictional defect or express authority
BaselineA: Statute and regulation: Unemployment Insurance Act, 1970-71-72 (Can.), c. 48 as amended, ss. 64(4), 64(6) (regulation-making and prescribed standards/appeals) and related scheme; Unemployment Insurance Regulations, s. 24(2)-(4) (officer decides; employer may seek review/appeal). Also considered but rejected as a basis: Act, s. 70 (Minister of National Revenue assessment powers).
CaseB_TestB: Mens rea for Criminal Code s. 121(1)(a): Crown must prove the accused (1) knew he/she was an official, (2) intentionally demanded/accepted a loan, reward, advantage or benefit, and (3) knew it was “in consideration for cooperation, assistance or exercise of influence” in connection with “the transaction of business with or relating to the government”; no additional “corrupt” purpose required
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 121(1)(a) (and s. 19 noted re ignorance of law). Interpreted in light of SCC precedent (Martineau v. La Reine) and distinguished from Hinchey.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Ernst (Cromwell J.) categorical Ward-based rule: Charter damages are never an “appropriate and just” remedy against this quasi-judicial regulator because countervailing factors (alternative remedy of judicial review + good governance/immunity rationales + futility of case-by-case inquiry) collectively negate damages
BaselineA: Common law Charter remedial framework under Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 24(1), as set out in Vancouver (City) v. Ward, 2010 SCC 27 (plus statutory context: Energy Resources Conservation Act, s. 43 immunity clause)
CaseB_TestB: Mikisew Cree (Karakatsanis J.) rule on scope of duty to consult: “no aspect of the law-making process — from the development of legislation to its enactment — triggers a duty to consult”; duty to consult applies only to executive action or action taken on behalf of the executive
BaselineB: Common law duty to consult doctrine from Haida Nation v. British Columbia (Minister of Forests), 2004 SCC 73, grounded in the honour of the Crown and s. 35 of the Constitution Act, 1982; applied alongside statutory jurisdiction limits in the Federal Courts Act (ss. 2(1), 2(2), 17, 18, 18.1)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory interaction test: whether Workers’ Compensation Act s. 10(1) bars a tort action against a vehicle owner who is only a deemed employer/servant-master under Motor-vehicle Act s. 70(1) (answer: no, because the owner is not an “employer” within s. 10(1))
BaselineA: Statute (Workers’ Compensation Act, 1968 (B.C.), c. 59, s. 10(1) and Motor-vehicle Act, R.S.B.C. 1960, c. 253, s. 70(1); with discussion of Co-Operators Insurance Association v. Kearney, [1965] S.C.R. 106)
CaseB_TestB: Operational conflict framework for conflicting administrative decisions: (1) is there an “operational conflict” (i.e., “compliance with one necessitates violation of the other” / inability to fulfil both legal obligations)? (2) if so, can either decision be overturned on its ordinary standard of review? (3) if both are otherwise valid, courts may declare one inoperative to the extent of conflict, choosing precedence via a “pragmatic and functional” analysis of legislative intent (purpose, centrality, policy-making role, etc.)
BaselineB: Common law administrative law (building on pragmatic and functional approach in U.E.S., Local 298 v. Bibeault, [1988] 2 S.C.R. 1048; and conflict discussion in Domtar Inc. v. Quebec (Commission d'appel en matière de lésions professionnelles), [1993] 2 S.C.R. 756)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Priority between a mechanics’ lien and a subsequent collateral mortgage for past indebtedness: where the Mechanics’ Lien Act does not prescribe priority (s. 14(1) inapplicable), the lien claimant must register and priority is determined by Registry Act registration priority (absent actual notice).
BaselineA: Statute (Ontario): Mechanics’ Lien Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 267, ss. 14(1), 16, 20, 21, 22; and Registry Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 409, ss. 69(1), 70.
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 1 proportionality (Oakes) as applied to PIPA’s restriction on union expression: whether the statute achieves a “constitutionally acceptable balance” between privacy control and freedom of expression; here, the infringement is “disproportionate” and not justified.
BaselineB: Constitution (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms): ss. 2(b) and 1 (Oakes/Charter justification framework) applied to Personal Information Protection Act, S.A. 2003, c. P-6.5.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Quebec civil liability “choice” test: a plaintiff in contractual relations may sue in delict only if the alleged contractual fault is independently a fault under art. 1053 C.C. (i.e., it would be actionable “even in the absence of a contract”)
BaselineA: Statute (Civil Code art. 1053; Code of Civil Procedure art. 68(2) on “place where the whole cause of action has arisen”), as interpreted in SCC cases including Ross v. Dunstall; Ross v. Emery and Alliance Assurance v. Dominion Electric
CaseB_TestB: Reasonable apprehension of bias rule in criminal trials: once a reasonable apprehension of bias is demonstrated, the trial judge has “no further jurisdiction” and “the only appropriate remedy is a new trial”; appellate finding of bias retroactively renders trial orders “void and without effect”
BaselineB: Common law procedural fairness / bias doctrine (as applied via Newfoundland Telephone Co. v. Newfoundland (Board of Commissioners of Public Utilities))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Bills of Exchange Act “sum certain”/negotiability requirement: a promissory note must be certain on its face as to principal and interest; interest must be ascertainable from the instrument (no extrinsic evidence for an inherently uncertain interest start date like “from the date of advance”).
BaselineA: Statute: Bills of Exchange Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. B-5, ss. 28, 176(1), 186 (and s. 10 incorporating common law/law merchant).
CaseB_TestB: Criminal Code s. 172(3) “disturbs” threshold: to convict, the accused’s wilful act must be disorderly in itself or productive of disorder; mere annoyance/anxiety/emotional upset from brief, passive, peaceful conduct voluntarily desisted from is insufficient.
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 172(3) (interpreted in context, including the “Disorderly Conduct” heading).
JudgeB: Dickson J. (for Dickson, Beetz, McIntyre, Chouinard and Lamer JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: “Sum certain”/negotiability test for promissory notes: principal and interest must be ascertainable on the face of the instrument (or by numerical calculation from materials in it); recourse to extrinsic evidence to fix an uncertain interest-accrual date (e.g., “from the date of advance”) defeats negotiability
BaselineA: Statute (Bills of Exchange Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. B-5, ss. 28, 176(1), 186; plus s. 10 incorporating common law/law merchant)
CaseB_TestB: Start of the art. 2532 C.C.L.C. two-year suicide exclusion: determine the contract’s effective date (including permissible retroactivity from backdating) and whether later changes are a mere variation or a new contract; the exclusion period cannot run more than once within a single insurance contract
BaselineB: Statute (Civil Code of Lower Canada, arts. 2516, 2532; also art. 2500(2) and interpretive art. 1018 referenced)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Declaratory judgment should not be used to decide issues the legislature has specifically confided to another tribunal (here, the Olympic Village arbitration committee), especially where the declaration would be of limited usefulness
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law principles: Code of Civil Procedure, art. 453 (declaratory judgment) applied alongside the principle from Barraclough v. Brown that where a statute creates a specific tribunal/procedure, parties should not seek to have the superior court determine the very matter assigned to that tribunal
CaseB_TestB: Minister’s s. 7 Fisheries Act power to “authorize to be issued” licences is a continuing power, so the Minister may revoke an authorization any time before the licence is actually issued; discretion is constrained only by natural justice (relevant considerations, no arbitrariness, good faith)
BaselineB: Statutory interpretation of Fisheries Act, R.S.C., 1985, c. F-14, s. 7 (and interaction with s. 9) plus Interpretation Act, R.S.C., 1985, c. I-21, s. 31(3) (“from time to time as occasion requires”)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Excise Tax Act machinery exemption: claimant must be a “manufacturer or producer” of “goods” and the machinery must be used “directly” in that manufacture; “manufacturing” cannot be restrictively defined where the Act does not do so (operating generators manufactures electricity).
BaselineA: Statute: Excise Tax Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-13, ss. 27(1), 29(1), and Schedule III, Part XIII, s. 1(a) (plus acceptance that electricity is “goods” under Schedule III).
CaseB_TestB: Vesting/accrual of appeal-as-of-right: a right is “acquired, accrued or accruing” only when all conditions precedent are fulfilled; for former Criminal Code s. 691(2), the right to appeal as of right arises only when the court of appeal reverses the acquittal and orders a new trial.
BaselineB: Statute: Interpretation Act, R.S.C., 1985, c. I-21, ss. 43(c) and 44(c),(d), applied to Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 691(2) (as amended effective May 14, 1997).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: No common-law tort or direct civil action for discrimination where a comprehensive human rights code provides the enforcement/remedial scheme (the Code 'foreclose[s] any civil action based directly upon a breach thereof' and 'also excludes any common law action based on an invocation of the public policy expressed in the Code').
BaselineA: Statute (Ontario Human Rights Code, R.S.O. 1970, c. 318, especially s. 4(1)(a)-(b) and the Code’s board-of-inquiry/appeal/remedy scheme (e.g., ss. 14b(6), 14c, 14d(4))).
CaseB_TestB: Undue-obstacle/undue-hardship (reasonable accommodation) analysis under CTA s. 172: remove the barrier unless the carrier proves a bona fide justification by establishing accommodation would impose 'undue hardship' (factors include cost, economic viability, safety, quality of service), with the onus on the carrier to show the obstacle is not 'undue'.
BaselineB: Statute (Canada Transportation Act, S.C. 1996, c. 10, ss. 5, 170(1), 171, 172(1), 172(3)), interpreted consistently with human rights reasonable-accommodation principles (e.g., Meiorin/Grismer line).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Bill of Rights s. 2(f) limit on reverse onus: a reverse onus (balance of probabilities) is compatible only if the fact is "rationally open" to the accused to prove/disprove; if the accused "cannot reasonably be expected to prove" it (beyond his knowledge/means of knowledge), the onus is "impossible to meet" and becomes an "irrebuttable presumption of guilt". For Customs Act s. 248(1), the Crown must first prove foreign origin + possession and also "show some knowledge or means of knowledge of the circumstances of importation on the part of the accused" before the reverse onus applies; otherwise the Crown must prove unlawful importation beyond a reasonable doubt.
BaselineA: Statute: Customs Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-40, ss. 205(1),(3), 248(1) interpreted/limited by Canadian Bill of Rights, R.S.C. 1970, App. III, s. 2(f); prior SCC guidance referenced: R. v. Appleby, [1972] S.C.R. 303.
CaseB_TestB: Privative-clause judicial review / natural justice claim: where employees allege denial of audi alteram partem based on being "interested parties" under Labour Code s. 32, the commissioners/Labour Court’s interpretation is immune from review unless it is "patently unreasonable" ("not manifestly unreasonable"). On the merits of s. 32, employees are not "interested part[ies]" for bargaining-unit definition because s. 32 specifies the investigation is held in the presence of "every association concerned and the employer", indicating legislative intent to exclude employees from that status.
BaselineB: Statute: Quebec Labour Code, R.S.Q. 1977, c. C-27, s. 32 (and related provisions) plus Code of Civil Procedure, art. 846; common-law/admin-law baseline for deference under privative clause drawn from CUPE v. New Brunswick Liquor Corp., [1979] 2 S.C.R. 227 and related cases cited.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Intoxication (drunkenness) and mens rea for murder: intoxication is relevant only if it raises a reasonable doubt that alcohol "destroyed [the accused’s] capacity" to form the specific intent to kill or to cause bodily harm "that he knew was likely to cause death" (capacity test).
BaselineA: Common law (as adopted/clarified in prior cases) applied to the Criminal Code murder mens rea provision (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 212(a)(ii)). Key authorities cited: Director of Public Prosecutions v. Beard; MacAskill v. The King; Perrault v. The Queen; Mulligan v. The Queen.
CaseB_TestB: Interjurisdictional immunity (constitutional inapplicability) for federal services: a provincial law of general application applies unless it bears on what makes the federal subject specifically federal; for a federal service, inapplicability arises if the provincial law "touches on a vital or essential aspect of its establishment, management or operation".
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine (interjurisdictional immunity) as articulated in cases cited in the reasons, especially Construction Montcalm Inc. v. Minimum Wage Commission; Bell Canada v. Quebec (CSST); Clark v. Canadian National Railway Co.; Dick v. The Queen.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Availability of Criminal Code s. 116(1) charge for disobeying a court order: s. 116(1) applies unless statute law (not common law/inherent contempt power) "expressly" provides a "penalty or punishment or other mode of proceeding"; "by law" in the exception means "by statute law"
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 116(1); also considers s. 8 and Manitoba Queen’s Bench Rules 483, 485, 492)
CaseB_TestB: Public law promissory estoppel in penal enforcement of zoning by-laws: requires (1) a "clear and unambiguous promise" by a public authority intended to induce action, and (2) reliance/change of conduct; but estoppel "must yield" to overriding public interest and cannot prevent application of a "clear"/"express legislative provision" (so it is unavailable to defeat a strict-liability zoning offence)
BaselineB: Common law doctrine of promissory estoppel as applied in public law (Mount Sinai; Maracle), constrained by the principle that estoppel cannot override express legislation; applied in context of municipal by-law enforcement (Cities and Towns Act, s. 576; zoning by-law penal provisions; Act respecting land use planning and development, s. 227)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Insurance policy interpretation to determine the policy’s “effective date”: read the policy and application “in entirety” and, on the “true construction of the entire contract”, select the single effective date that governs “the purpose of calculating any of the time periods contemplated, including the application of the self-destruction clause”.
BaselineA: Statute + contract terms: Insurance Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 224, s. 148(2) (application and policy form the contract) (with interpretive backdrop including s. 154 discussed) and the policy/application wording (“effective date”, Declaration).
CaseB_TestB: Access in conjunction with permanent guardianship: access is discretionary and “the exception and not the rule”; it may be granted only if, after weighing the statutory “best interests of the child” factors, access is in the child’s best interests and should be refused where it would harm the child’s physical/psychological health or jeopardize adoption.
BaselineB: Statute: Family Services Act, S.N.B. 1980, c. F-2.2, especially s. 1 (“best interests of the child” factors (a)-(g)), s. 53(2) (best interests paramount), s. 60(6) (court may make any appropriate order if satisfied it is in best interests), and s. 85(2) (court may preserve access after adoption).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 16(2) insanity: meaning of being “incapable of appreciating the nature and quality of an act” — the accused appreciates if he “knows what he is doing” and is “aware of the physical consequences which will result from his acts” (excluding mere emotional/moral indifference).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 16(2)); interpreted consistently with Cooper v. The Queen, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 1149 and R. v. Barnier, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 1124 (also Schwartz v. The Queen, [1977] 1 S.C.R. 673).
CaseB_TestB: Extradition Act committal/surrender framework: (1) Committal—under s. 29(1)(a), the extradition judge applies the preliminary-inquiry committal test and starts from a presumption that the requesting state’s certified ROC evidence is reliable; refusal for unreliability only if evidence is “so defective or appears so unreliable that it would be dangerous or unsafe to act on it”. (2) Surrender—where a Canadian defence is allegedly unavailable abroad, the person sought must show three threshold elements: (1) a substantive difference (defence available in Canada but no comparable defence abroad), (2) a reasonable prospect of success in Canada, and (3) significantly greater jeopardy abroad; if met, the Minister must then weigh this with all other circumstances under s. 44(1)(a).
BaselineB: Statute (Extradition Act, S.C. 1999, c. 18, ss. 29(1)(a), 32(1)(c), 44(1)(a)); building on United States of America v. Ferras, 2006 SCC 33 and related committal/preliminary inquiry jurisprudence (e.g., Arcuri).
JudgeB: Cromwell J. (McLachlin C.J. and Moldaver and Wagner JJ. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: When (if ever) to exceed the $100,000 rough upper limit for non-pecuniary damages under the functional approach: exceed only rarely, and not merely because injuries seem worse than the trilogy; $100,000 may increase only on proof/agreement of inflation’s effect
BaselineA: Common law (damages for personal injury; non-pecuniary loss) as set out in the “trilogy” and refined in Lewis v. Todd: Andrews v. Grand & Toy Alberta Ltd.; Arnold v. Teno; Thornton v. Board of School Trustees; Lewis v. Todd
CaseB_TestB: OPCF 44R / Insurance Act s. 239(1)(a) ‘arising directly or indirectly from the use or operation of an automobile’ test for indemnity coverage: (1) vehicle used as a vehicle (ordinary use), and (2) an unbroken chain of causation showing the tortfeasor is liable ‘as a motorist’; coverage fails if the tort is an intervening, severable act (not mere ‘but for’ connection)
BaselineB: Statutory/contractual interpretation of Ontario Insurance Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. I.8, s. 239(1)(a) (and parallel OPCF 44R wording), with Amos v. ICBC distinguished as a no-fault benefits context
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Effect of workers’ compensation election/subrogation on who may sue and whether the Commission has an 'interest' to intervene or benefit from interruption of prescription: once election for compensation is made, 'only the Commission can claim the amounts which it has paid or will have to pay' and the victim may claim only the s. 8 'additional sum'; a victim’s full-damages action 'does not have the effect of validly introducing' the Commission’s claim so as to create intervention interest or interrupt prescription for the Commission.
BaselineA: Statute and civil law: Workmen’s Compensation Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 159, ss. 7(1)-(3) and 8 (subrogation 'by the mere making of the election'); Civil Code art. 1056a (recourse only to extent permitted by the Act); Code of Civil Procedure art. 208 (intervention by 'Any person interested in an action').
CaseB_TestB: Collins s. 24(2) framework for excluding evidence: whether admission would bring the administration of justice into disrepute, organized into three categories—(1) fairness of the trial, (2) seriousness of the Charter violation, and (3) effect of exclusion on the repute of the justice system—applied 'having regard to all the circumstances'.
BaselineB: Statute/constitutional text and common law framework: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 24(2) ('shall be excluded if it is established that, having regard to all the circumstances, the admission of it ... would bring the administration of justice into disrepute'), as structured by R. v. Collins, [1987] 1 S.C.R. 265 (and related cases such as Simmons).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Public access to search-warrant materials: after execution and where items are brought before a justice, the public may inspect the warrant and supporting information, subject to overriding countervailing interests (notably protection of the innocent where nothing is found) and with issuance proceedings properly in camera
BaselineA: Combination of statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 443, 446) and common law/open court principle (public access to judicial records subject to court’s supervisory power)
CaseB_TestB: Bona fide occupational qualification (BFOQ) test (Etobicoke) as applied to denominational-school teachers: (1) subjective good-faith/improper-purpose branch; and (2) objective branch requiring the requirement be reasonably necessary to accomplish the employer’s legitimate objectives (here, religious conformity to provide Catholic education)
BaselineB: Statute (Human Rights Code, R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 186, s. 8) interpreted through the common-law/precedential BFOQ framework from Ontario Human Rights Commission v. Etobicoke (Borough of), [1982] 1 S.C.R. 202
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Validity of a Quebec deed of donation and trust benefiting unborn (non-existent) primary beneficiaries: trustee acceptance suffices to perfect/irrevocabilize the trust; trustee is owner during the trust; and art. 981a’s reference to gift/legacy rules is read subject to the trust’s special characteristics (liberal interpretation), so non-existence of beneficiaries at creation is not an impediment absent a public-order prohibition.
BaselineA: Statute (Civil Code of Quebec provisions on trusts and gifts): arts. 981a, 981b, 981l (trusts) read alongside arts. 754, 755, 758, 760, 782, 608, 771, 772, 929. Key common-law/civil-law baseline cases discussed: Curran v. Davis, [1933] S.C.R. 283 (trustee acceptance; nature of trust gift) and related jurisprudence on trustee ownership/seizin (e.g., Greenshields; Reford).
CaseB_TestB: When an injunction in private litigation may effectively bind non-parties (enforceable by contempt): courts have jurisdiction to make such orders; but fairness requires (i) non-parties must be apprised of the order’s existence and terms and given an opportunity to comply, (ii) it is desirable the order’s terms speak to non-parties’ duty to respect it, and (iii) the order must be carefully worded and constrained so it is fair and not unduly broad.
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: Law and Equity Act, R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 224, s. 36 (interlocutory injunctions “just or convenient” on terms the court thinks just) and Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 11 (civil remedies not suspended by criminality), plus contempt/injunction jurisprudence cited (e.g., International Longshoremen’s Association, [1979] 1 S.C.R. 120; Bartle & Gibson; English authorities on contempt).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory displacement of the Kienapple rule against multiple convictions: whether Parliament has given a “clear indication that multiple prosecutions and, indeed, multiple convictions are envisaged” such that a s. 83 firearm-use conviction may stand in addition to the underlying offence (and s. 21 party liability applies unless expressly/necessarily excluded).
BaselineA: Combination: common law principle from Kienapple v. The Queen (rule against multiple convictions for the same delict) plus statutory interpretation/application of Criminal Code ss. 83 and 21 (and comparison to former s. 122 and Quon).
JudgeA: Dickson J. (for Martland, Dickson, Estey, McIntyre and Chouinard JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Pith and substance analysis of an impugned municipal measure: characterize the measure by considering both “its purpose and its effects” (including “legal ramifications” and “practical consequences”) to determine whether it is ultra vires as trenching on exclusive federal jurisdiction (here, radiocommunication siting).
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine (division of powers) applying the pith and substance framework; informed by precedent (e.g., COPA, Lacombe) and applied in the context of federal radiocommunication jurisdiction under the Constitution Act, 1867.
JudgeB: Wagner and Côté JJ. (for McLachlin C.J. and Abella, Cromwell, Moldaver, Karakatsanis and Brown JJ. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: When s. 25(3) of Saskatchewan’s Trade Union Act applies to discharge grievances: if the collective agreement lacks a specific penalty for the infraction, the arbitrator may substitute a lesser penalty (including reinstatement without back pay) when dismissal is not sustainable; if the cause is not established, reinstatement with full compensation; if the cause is established under a clause specifying dismissal-for-cause, dismissal must be sustained.
BaselineA: Statute: The Trade Union Act, R.S.S. 1978, c. T-17, s. 25(3) (interacting with the collective agreement’s dismissal/remedy provisions, including art. 6(4) and art. 12(12)(a)).
CaseB_TestB: Contribution-based test for complicity under Refugee Convention art. 1F(a)/IRPA s. 98: exclusion requires “serious reasons for considering” the claimant “has voluntarily made a significant and knowing contribution to the organization’s crime or criminal purpose”; contextual factors may guide the assessment (size/nature of organization; part involved; duties; rank; time in organization after knowledge; recruitment and opportunity to leave).
BaselineB: Statute/treaty: Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, S.C. 2001, c. 27, s. 98 incorporating Refugee Convention, art. 1F(a) (interpreted in light of international criminal law sources).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 43 Canada Evidence Act letters rogatory: (i) s. 43 is broad enough to order production of documents alone (not only documents ancillary to viva voce testimony) and (ii) comity-based discretionary guidelines for granting judicial assistance (trial not discovery; relevance; scope permitted domestically; adequate precision of request).
BaselineA: Statute — Canada Evidence Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-10, s. 43 (letters rogatory/judicial assistance), with related consideration of Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 178.2 and 178.16 (intercepted private communications).
CaseB_TestB: Admissibility of defence-led unknown third party suspect evidence: admissible where (1) relevant to a fact in issue (logical relevance shown by a sufficient connection/similarity between the charged crime and another incident plus evidence the accused could not have committed the other offence), and (2) probative value is not substantially outweighed by prejudicial effects (Seaboyer balancing); no balance-of-probabilities proof of the other incident and no credibility weighing by the trial judge.
BaselineB: Common law — general admissibility principles and balancing from R. v. Seaboyer, [1991] 2 S.C.R. 577 (and logical relevance from Corbett), with the SCC adapting the 'sufficient connection' idea from known third-party suspect cases (McMillan; Grandinetti) to the unknown-suspect context.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Civil Code art. 1055 “ruin of a building” liability applies only where the defect/want of repairs is assessed in light of the building’s intended purpose; if the victim used the building/part for a purpose contrary to that for which it was intended, the owner is not liable under art. 1055. Related: art. 1054 presumption applies only where damage is caused by the “positive and independent action” of the thing (not the user’s action).
BaselineA: Statute (Quebec Civil Code, arts. 1054 and 1055; also art. 1053). Baseline authorities cited for the purpose-limitation under art. 1055 include Leznek v. City of Verdun, [1940] S.C.R. 313 and Bourassa v. Grégoire (1926), 42 Que. K.B. 154; for art. 1054 “independent action of the thing” include Curley v. Latreille (1920), 60 S.C.R. 131.
CaseB_TestB: Mental-capacity standard for confessions/right to silence/s.10(b) waiver: the accused must have an “operating mind” (limited cognitive capacity) — i.e., sufficient capacity to understand what is being said and said to him, including understanding a caution that the statement can be used against him; no separate “awareness of consequences” test and no higher capacity than fitness-to-stand-trial is required for s.10(b) waiver.
BaselineB: Combination of common law and constitutional/statutory sources: common law confession voluntariness/“operating mind” line (Ward v. The Queen; Horvath v. The Queen; Nagotcha v. The Queen; Hebert) and Charter ss. 7 and 10(b); fitness-to-stand-trial definition in Criminal Code s. 2 (“unfit to stand trial”).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Judicial review of labour board decisions under a privative clause: intervene only if the board’s interpretation is “plainly unreasonable” / “patently unreasonable” (certiorari is “a long way from an appeal”)
BaselineA: Combination: statute (The Public Service Employee Relations Act, 1977 (Alta.), c. 40, ss. 9, 11, 48, 89) + common-law/precedent on deference (CUPE v. New Brunswick Liquor Corp. adopting “patently unreasonable” review; also Volvo; Douglas Aircraft; Bradley)
CaseB_TestB: Adverse-effect religious discrimination and duty to accommodate: discrimination established by the 3-part Quebec Charter s. 10 test; once adverse-effect discrimination is shown, employer must take “reasonable steps to accommodate … short of undue hardship” (no de minimis threshold)
BaselineB: Combination: statute (Quebec Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms, ss. 10, 16; plus Labour Code privative clause context) + common law (O’Malley; Central Alberta Dairy Pool; Renaud on accommodation/undue hardship factors)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Similar fact evidence admissibility: (1) apply the Makin/Boardman principle that admissibility depends on probative value balanced against prejudice; and (2) as a threshold, "Before evidence may be admitted as evidence of similar facts, there must be a link between the allegedly similar facts and the accused"—i.e., "some evidentiary link, direct or circumstantial, with the accused" (similarity alone is insufficient).
BaselineA: Common law (Makin v. A-G for New South Wales; Boardman v. DPP; Harris v. DPP; Thompson v. The King)
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 7 vagueness test: "a law will be found unconstitutionally vague if it so lacks in precision as not to give sufficient guidance for legal debate" (i.e., meaning cannot be reached by reasoned legal analysis applying legal criteria).
BaselineB: Common law / constitutional doctrine under Charter s. 7 (building on the Prostitution Reference and related SCC vagueness jurisprudence)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 16(2) insanity (first arm): “incapable of appreciating the nature and quality of an act” is limited to appreciating the physical character and physical consequences of the act (mens rea/actus reus consequences), and does NOT include failure to appreciate “the penal sanctions” or “consequence of punishment”.
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 16(2)); interpreted in light of SCC cases including Cooper v. The Queen, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 1149; Schwartz v. The Queen, [1977] 1 S.C.R. 673; R. v. Barnier, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 1124; Kjeldsen v. The Queen, [1981] 2 S.C.R. 617.
CaseB_TestB: Administrative tribunal constitutional jurisdiction (Martin/Paul test): the “essential question is whether the empowering legislation implicitly or explicitly grants to the tribunal the jurisdiction to interpret or decide any question of law”; if yes, the tribunal is presumed to have “concomitant jurisdiction” to decide the issue in light of s. 35 (and other constitutional provisions) unless there is a “clear implication” in the statutory scheme excluding it.
BaselineB: Common law / constitutional supremacy framework as articulated in Nova Scotia (Workers’ Compensation Board) v. Martin, 2003 SCC 54, applied to s. 35; applied to Forest Practices Code of British Columbia Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 159, especially s. 131(8) (submissions as to “facts, law and jurisdiction”).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Patentability of a new use for an old compound as a “new and useful art” (and permissibility of claiming compositions as the practical embodiment): the invention is “the application of this new knowledge to effect a desired result which has an undisputed commercial value” and falls within “any new and useful art”; once the new use is discovered, mixing with appropriate carriers to realize that use need not itself be novel, and s. 36 does not bar composition claims that embody the invention.
BaselineA: Statute (Patent Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. P-4), especially s. 2 (“invention” includes “any new and useful art...”) and s. 36 (specification/claiming requirements), with prior case context including Commissioner of Patents v. Farbwerke Hoechst, [1964] S.C.R. 49 and related composition-claim cases; Hickton’s Patent Syndicate v. Patents and Machine Improvements Co. (1909) applied by analogy.
CaseB_TestB: Party liability for drug trafficking by aiding/abetting: under Criminal Code s. 21(1), to aid is to “assist or help the actor” and requires doing something “for the purpose of aiding” (purpose = intention, not desire); to abet includes “encouraging, instigating, promoting or procuring” and requires intention to encourage. Applied to drug trafficking (Narcotic Control Act), a purchaser cannot be guilty of aiding/abetting trafficking “on the basis of the purchase alone,” but an agent/assistant to the purchaser can be a party where their acts assist/encourage the sale and they intend the consequences of that assistance.
