BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 21(1)(b),(c); Narcotic Control Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. N-1, ss. 2 “traffic”, 3(1), 4(1)), with mens rea clarification drawn from R. v. Hibbert, [1995] 2 S.C.R. 973 and purchaser exception context from Poitras v. The Queen, [1974] S.C.R. 649.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory incompatibility/repugnancy test for whether a permissive municipal discretion (Police Act, s. 24(6)) excludes a collectively-bargained/arbitrated working-condition clause under s. 29(2): s. 24(6) is an 'empowering provision only' and does not preclude bargaining unless the provisions are 'incompatible or inconsistent'; here 'there is no incompatibility or inconsistency ...; each has its own area of operation.'
BaselineA: Statute (The Police Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 351, ss. 24(6) and 29(2))
CaseB_TestB: State Immunity Act interpretation test for the s. 6(a) 'death or personal or bodily injury ... that occurs in Canada' exception: (1) the exception applies only where 'the tort causing the personal injury or death' occurred in Canada; and (2) 'personal or bodily injury' requires a 'physical breach of personal integrity'—'only when psychological distress manifests itself after a physical injury will the exception ... be triggered' (Schreiber).
BaselineB: Statute (State Immunity Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. S-18, ss. 3(1), 6(a); with reliance on SCC precedent Schreiber v. Canada (Attorney General), 2002 SCC 62 for the physical-injury requirement)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory incompatibility/repugnancy test between Police Act s. 24(6) (permissive indemnification discretion) and s. 29(2) (collective bargaining over “working conditions”): s. 24(6) does not exclude a bargained/arbitrated clause unless the provisions are “incompatible or inconsistent”; s. 24(6) is “an empowering provision only” and “does not prescribe exclusivity”.
BaselineA: Statute: The Police Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 351, ss. 24(6) and 29(2) (interpreting whether s. 24(6) precludes bargaining/arbitration under s. 29(2)).
CaseB_TestB: Corporate attribution test for BIA s. 96(1)(b)(ii)(B) (transfer at undervalue): for attributing a directing mind’s intent to “defraud, defeat or delay a creditor” to the corporate debtor, “the test for corporate attribution under s. 96 is simply whether the person was the directing mind and whether their actions were performed within the sector of corporate responsibility assigned to them”, with the “fraud” and “no benefit” exceptions inapplicable in this context.
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act, s. 96(1)(b)(ii)(B) (and related s. 2 definition; CCAA s. 36.1 incorporation) plus common-law corporate attribution doctrine from Canadian Dredge & Dock Co. v. The Queen, Deloitte & Touche v. Livent Inc. (Receiver of), and Christine DeJong Medicine Professional Corp. v. DBDC Spadina Ltd., as adapted for the s. 96 context.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Jennings test for establishing a constitutional convention: (1) what are the precedents; (2) did the actors in the precedents believe they were bound by a rule (recognition/acceptance); and (3) is there a reason for the rule — with recognition by the actors treated as the “most important element”
BaselineA: Common law (constitutional conventions doctrine) as adopted in Re: Resolution to amend the Constitution, [1981] 1 S.C.R. 753, approving Jennings’ three questions and the Manitoba Reference definition (via Freedman C.J.M./Hogg).
CaseB_TestB: Reasonable suspicion standard for sniffer-dog (sniff) searches under s. 8: police may deploy a drug detection dog without prior authorization where there is “reasonable suspicion based on objective, ascertainable facts” assessed on the “totality of the circumstances” (a ‘constellation’), with exculpatory/neutral facts not disregarded but no duty to investigate to rule out innocent explanations
BaselineB: Common law Charter search framework (R. v. Collins) and prior sniffer-dog cases (R. v. Kang-Brown; R. v. A.M.) applying s. 8 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criteria for when a labour arbitrator is a “statutory tribunal” subject to evocation/certiorari: not only whether “by statute the parties are bound to resort to it”, but also whether the arbitrator is “invested with wide powers by statute” (i.e., has “duties and powers conferred by statute” such that, once arbitration is chosen under the Canada Labour Code, the arbitrator is statutory).
BaselineA: Common law test for statutory tribunals in certiorari/evocation (R. v. National Joint Council for the Craft of Dental Technicians; Howe Sound; Port Arthur Shipbuilding; Rivando) applied within Quebec Code of Civil Procedure art. 846, with statutory context from Canada Labour Code ss. 156(2), 157, 159, 160(5).
CaseB_TestB: Test for whether an agreement creates a patent sublicence: a sublicence exists only if the licensee “granted, either expressly or impliedly, the right to do something which [the third party] would otherwise be prohibited from doing, and which [the licensee] was permitted to do only by virtue of its [licence]”; assessed from the contract’s text (no subjective intention evidence if unambiguous) and its “actual legal effect”.
BaselineB: Common law principles of patent licensing/sublicensing and contractual interpretation (including Consolidated-Bathurst; Lampson; Joy Oil; Indian Molybdenum) applied in the statutory setting of the Patent Act compulsory-licence regime and NOC proceedings.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Kienapple remedy modification: when Kienapple applies, enter a stay of proceedings rather than an acquittal
BaselineA: Common law (Kienapple v. The Queen, [1975] 1 S.C.R. 729)
CaseB_TestB: Removing/replacing a litigation guardian: the Rule 49(1) 'best interests' test, guided by the Szwydky criteria (including the 'indifference' / no-conflict requirement)
BaselineB: Combination of statute/rules and prior case law: Queen’s Bench Rules (Saskatchewan) r. 49(1) ('best interests'); Szwydky v. Magiera (1988) criteria as guiding framework; also Dependent Adults Act, S.S. 1989-90, c. D-25.1 (context for guardianship)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Contract interpretation of the 1905 power-supply agreement: the Town’s entitlement is limited to the expressly reserved 4,000 horsepower at the fixed $14/hp/year rate (general words in para. 1 do not override the specific allocation in paras. 6 and 8). Key language: para. 8 requires the Company to “retain and reserve for use on the Canadian side ... Four Thousand Horse Power” and para. 5 sets a ceiling price that “shall not in any event exceed ... Fourteen Dollars ($14.00) per Horse Power per annum”; the Court declares the Company’s commitment “is to provide ... to the extent of 4,000 horsepower per annum ... at the contract price of $14 per horsepower per annum.”
BaselineA: Common law (contract interpretation) applied to the January 9, 1905 agreement (especially paras. 1, 5, 6, 8, 13).
CaseB_TestB: General Motors indicia for validity under the general branch of the federal trade and commerce power (Constitution Act, 1867, s. 91(2)): ask (1) “part of a general regulatory scheme”; (2) “oversight of a regulatory agency”; (3) “concerned with trade as a whole rather than with a particular industry”; (4) provinces “constitutionally incapable of enacting it”; and (5) failure to include a province would “jeopardize its successful operation” (indicia “not exhaustive” and “not necessary that they be present in every case”).
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine interpreting Constitution Act, 1867, s. 91(2) (general trade and commerce power), applying General Motors of Canada Ltd. v. City National Leasing, [1989] 1 S.C.R. 641.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Contract-interpretation rule for extent/price of power supply obligation under the 1905 agreement: reconcile general 'to such an extent as the said Town… may require' with specific reserve/availability clauses; obligation fixed at 4,000 horsepower/year at $14 per horsepower/year
BaselineA: Common law (contract interpretation) applied to the January 9, 1905 agreement (esp. paras. 1, 5, 6, 8, 13); statutes held not to govern the issue
CaseB_TestB: Continuing-offence/party-liability framework for kidnapping: (1) kidnapping under s. 279(1) is a continuing offence including ensuing confinement 'until the victim is freed'; (2) latecomer party liability under s. 21(1) where, with knowledge of the ongoing offence, the accused acts (or omits) with intent to aid/abet its completion
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, ss. 279(1), 279(2), 21(1)) interpreted in light of common law meaning of kidnapping/false imprisonment and prior SCC party-liability principles (notably Briscoe)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Trigger for municipality’s mandatory acquisition duty under Planning Act s. 70(1): land must be “designated under a land use by-law” (not merely in statutory plans); statutory plans are policy proposals and do not trigger s. 70
BaselineA: Statute: The Planning Act, 1977 (Alta.), s. 70(1) (and definition of “land use by-law” in s. 1(14))
CaseB_TestB: O’Connor framework for production of private third-party records: (1) accused must show records are “likely to be relevant”; (2) if so, judge balances salutary vs deleterious effects (privacy/equality vs full answer and defence) and, after in camera review, orders only what has significant probative value not substantially outweighed by prejudice/harm
BaselineB: Combination: Charter (ss. 7, 24(1)) and common law/precedent (notably R. v. Stinchcombe; also Jewitt/Keyowski abuse-of-process line) plus Criminal Code subpoena provisions (e.g., ss. 698, 700) as procedural context
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “has become regularly engaged in some other occupation” under Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, s. 44(1)(c): focuses on regularity of work schedule (a “fixed pattern”) rather than duration or intent to abandon former job; claimant must have worked and worked “regularly” (not merely be hired).
BaselineA: Statute: Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, s. 44(1)(c) (with contextual reference to s. 44(1)(b) and Regulations s. 49 defining “bona fide employed” as “not less than two weeks duration”).
CaseB_TestB: Whether an ISP “carr[ies] on … ‘broadcasting undertakings’” under the Broadcasting Act when providing Internet access: entities that “merely provide the mode of transmission” and take no part in “selection, origination, or packaging of content” (i.e., lack “some measure of control over programming”) are not broadcasting undertakings.
BaselineB: Statute: Broadcasting Act, S.C. 1991, c. 11, ss. 2(1) (“broadcasting”), 2(3), 3(1) (interpreted in light of statutory purposes).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Cross-border fresh pursuit: an officer retains “peace officer” status for Criminal Code s. 25(4) if the pursuit began lawfully in the officer’s province and remains “fresh”; arrest authority depends on whether the suspect would appear to a reasonable person in the circumstances to be committing an offence (reasonable and probable grounds).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34), especially ss. 25(4), 450(1)(b), and related ss. 449, 25(1), 25(3). The arrest standard is drawn from R. v. Biron, [1976] 2 S.C.R. 56 (and Pritchard as discussed in Biron).
CaseB_TestB: Arbitrator jurisdiction under Canada Labour Code s. 157(d): a collective agreement contains a “specific penalty” (thus barring substitution) only if a penalty is assigned to the particular infraction in the collective agreement; a penalty is not “specific” if it can be chosen indiscriminately by the employer or is only in an employer rule book.
BaselineB: Statute (Canada Labour Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. L-1, s. 157(d)(i)-(ii)) interpreted alongside the collective agreement (Article XI(b)).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Availability and scope of the Crown’s per quod servitium amisit action for injuries to Canadian Forces members deemed “servants of the Crown”: master may recover “cost necessarily incurred” (including wages/allowances and medical/hospital expenses) for “loss of any services”, but the “master’s right of action… is dependant on the servant in turn having a valid cause of action against the wrongdoer”; Armed Forces services are not excluded as non-menial/domestic.
BaselineA: Combination: statute deeming relationship (Federal Court Act, R.S.C. 1970 (2nd Supp.), c. 10, s. 37; with reference to Exchequer Court Act, R.S.C. 1952, c. 98, s. 50) plus common law per quod servitium amisit as recognized in SCC cases (The King v. Richardson; Attorney-General of Canada v. Jackson; Nykorak v. Attorney General of Canada; The Queen v. Murray).
CaseB_TestB: Mens rea for Criminal Code s. 121(1)(a): no “corrupt” purpose required; guilt requires (1) accused knows he/she is an official, (2) intentionally demands/accepts a “loan, reward, advantage or benefit of any kind”, and (3) knows the benefit is “in consideration for cooperation, assistance or exercise of influence in connection with the transaction of business with or relating to the government”; intention + knowledge of relevant circumstances is sufficient.
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 121(1)(a) (and s. 19 noted re ignorance of law), interpreted in light of SCC authority (Martineau v. La Reine; distinguished R. v. Hinchey).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Timing rule for Attorney General stay under Criminal Code s. 508: stay power arises only after process issues (summons or warrant); laying/receiving an information is not the “finding” of an information
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34 as amended), especially ss. 455, 455.3, 508 (and related definitions in ss. 2, 503)
CaseB_TestB: Statutory eligibility rule for discharge under Criminal Code s. 662.1(1): discharge unavailable if the offence is one “for which a minimum punishment is prescribed by law”; s. 234(a) prescribes a minimum ($50 fine) so no discharge
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code), ss. 234 and 662.1(1) (with discussion of s. 645 and related sentencing provisions)
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 508 stay power timing: the Attorney General may direct a stay only "after a summons or warrant is issued"; an information is "found" only once the justice decides to issue process (not upon mere laying/receiving of the information).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34 as amended): ss. 455, 455.3, 503, 508 (interpreting when an "indictment has been found" includes an information).
CaseB_TestB: Procedural fairness (Baker) content test: whether reasons are required is assessed by the five Baker factors—(1) nature of decision/process, (2) statutory scheme, (3) importance to affected person, (4) legitimate expectations, (5) deference—leading here to a duty to give reasons for refusing rezoning.
BaselineB: Common law administrative law duty of fairness framework from Baker v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), [1999] 2 S.C.R. 817 (five-factor test), applied to municipal rezoning decisions.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Jurisdictional rule against joint trial of separate informations/indictments: even with consent, a judge is "without jurisdiction to try together separate informations or indictments" (a joint trial on more than one information/indictment is a nullity), unless a provincial statute "expressly provide[s] otherwise".
BaselineA: Common law rule from Crane v. Public Prosecutor, [1921] 2 A.C. 299 (applied/confirmed as Canadian law; also treated as incorporated by implication into Criminal Code procedure).
CaseB_TestB: Credibility-assessment directions re (i) absence of evidence of motive to lie and (ii) lack of embellishment: motive-to-lie evidence may be relevant but judges must avoid (1) treating "absence of evidence" as "evidence disproving" a motive, and (2) reversing the burden by requiring the accused to show a motive; "lack of embellishment cannot be used to bolster" credibility (it "simply does not weigh against it"), though it may be considered on the motive-to-lie question.
BaselineB: Common law (credibility assessment principles; W.(D.) framework and related appellate guidance as discussed through R. v. Stirling and other cases).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Marine insurance “perils of the seas” causation test for negligent acts: an act is negligent only relative to a foreseeable risk of harm; if that foreseeable risk is a “peculiarly marine risk”, then the act plus its foreseeable consequence is a “fortuitous accident of the seas” and thus a “peril of the seas” and the proximate cause of the loss (i.e., “If that foreseeable risk of harm is a peculiarly marine risk, then the act, coupled with its foreseeable consequence, is a fortuitous accident of the seas and a peril of the seas and the proximate cause of the loss.”).
BaselineA: Statute (Insurance (Marine) Act, R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 203, Schedule “Rules for Construction of Policy” defining perils of the seas as “fortuitous accidents or casualties of the seas”; and Marine Insurance Act, R.S.B.C. 1960, c. 231, s. 57(2)(a) (now s. 56(2)(a)) on liability despite crew negligence) plus common-law/UK authority (Canada Rice Mills; Cohen).
CaseB_TestB: Section 35(1) threshold test for who qualifies as an “aboriginal peopl[e] of Canada”: on a purposive interpretation, “aboriginal peoples of Canada” “must mean the modern-day successors of Aboriginal societies that occupied Canadian territory at the time of European contact” (and if the threshold is met, proceed to the Van der Peet Aboriginal-rights test).
BaselineB: Constitution (Constitution Act, 1982, s. 35(1)) interpreted purposively in light of existing s. 35 jurisprudence (e.g., Sparrow; Van der Peet; Mitchell) and the doctrinal structure of Aboriginal rights.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory “bridging” of an expired collective agreement: s. 70(1) preserves the parties’ right to invoke interest arbitration if (i) notice to bargain has been given and no collective agreement is in operation, and (ii) the notice to arbitrate is served within the s. 70(1)(a) status-quo period; the right “need exist only at the time of the notice to arbitrate and not at the time the award is handed down.”
BaselineA: Statute: The Labour Relations Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 232, s. 70(1) (now R.S.O. 1980, c. 228, s. 79), applied to preserve contractual interest-arbitration rights post-expiry; also considered s. 34c.
CaseB_TestB: Directed verdict / non-suit test: whether there is “any admissible evidence, whether direct or circumstantial, which, if believed by a properly charged jury acting reasonably, would justify a conviction” (from Monteleone/Shephard).
BaselineB: Common law test as stated in R. v. Monteleone (deriving from United States of America v. Shephard).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: McKibbon conditions for when a non-AG (including an AG’s agent) may prefer an indictment with additional counts in a non-grand-jury jury trial under Criminal Code s. 507(2): (1) a preliminary inquiry has been held; (2) the accused has been committed for trial on at least one charge inquired into; and (3) each count must be either (a) an offence for which the accused was committed, or (b) an offence disclosed by the evidence at the preliminary inquiry and not an offence for which the accused was discharged.
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 507(1)-(3), with comparison to ss. 496, 504, 505).
JudgeA: Lamer J. (for Ritchie, Estey and Lamer JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Van der Peet / Delgamuukw test (as applied/clarified in Mitchell) to establish an Aboriginal right under Constitution Act, 1982, s. 35(1): claimant must prove (1) an ancestral practice/custom/tradition; (2) that it was “integral to the distinctive culture” (a “defining feature” such that the culture would be “fundamentally altered” without it); and (3) “reasonable continuity” between the pre-contact practice and the modern claim; plus the initial characterization step using Van der Peet factors: (1) nature of the action claimed; (2) nature of the impugned governmental action/legislation; (3) ancestral practices relied on.
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine under s. 35(1), primarily from R. v. Van der Peet and Delgamuukw v. British Columbia (applied to Constitution Act, 1982, s. 35(1)).
JudgeB: McLachlin C.J. (for McLachlin C.J. and Gonthier, Iacobucci, Arbour and LeBel JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: First-degree murder classification under Criminal Code ss. 212(b) and 214(2): where murder is made out by intending to kill A but by accident/mistake killing B, the s. 214(2) “planned and deliberate” element attaches to the s. 212(b) mens rea (intent to kill A), so victim identity is irrelevant and the murder is first degree if the intent to kill was planned and deliberate.
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 205, 212(b), 214(2); with s. 214 treated as a sentencing-classification provision per R. v. Farrant, [1983] 1 S.C.R. 24).
CaseB_TestB: Interpretation of Alberta Limitations Act s. 12 in conflicts cases: s. 12 applies Alberta’s limitation law only to “live” causes of action; it “does not purport to revive an action time-barred by the substantive law of the place where the accident occurred”, so if the lex loci delicti limitation has expired, “no right of action existed” and the claim is barred.
BaselineB: Statute (Limitations Act, R.S.A. 2000, c. L-12, s. 12) interpreted against the common-law conflicts rule from Tolofson v. Jensen, [1994] 3 S.C.R. 1022 (lex loci delicti includes the foreign limitation period as substantive).
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Mens rea for attempted murder: the Crown must prove a specific intent to kill; lesser mental states (including constructive murder intents under ss. 212/213) cannot ground an attempt
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code) interpreted against prior SCC precedent (Lajoie v. The Queen, [1974] S.C.R. 399)
CaseB_TestB: “Same establishment” under CHRA s. 11 / Guidelines s. 10: determine whether employees are subject to a “common personnel and wage policy” (a factual inquiry into the employer’s common principles/approach, not a term-by-term comparison of collective agreements); if established, a notional establishment exists for comparator selection
BaselineB: Statute plus regulation/guidelines (Canadian Human Rights Act, s. 11, read with Equal Wages Guidelines, 1986, s. 10)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory matrimonial property distribution: equal division presumption with limited pre-marital exemption—s. 23 exemption capped at fair market value at marriage; s. 21(2)(q) cannot be used to expand the exemption (rejecting the “Capital Base Theory”).
BaselineA: Statute: The Matrimonial Property Act, 1979 (Sask.), c. M-6.1, especially ss. 20, 21(1)-(2), 23(1)-(6).
CaseB_TestB: Aggravated assault (s. 268(1)) in HIV non-disclosure: Crown must prove the aggravating consequence (“endangers the life”) beyond a reasonable doubt; no conviction where there is a reasonable doubt the complainant was already HIV-positive at the relevant time (but attempt may be made out).
BaselineB: Statute (with common-law interpretation): Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, ss. 268(1) (aggravated assault), 265(1)(a) and 265(3)(c) (assault/consent vitiated by fraud), plus attempt provisions ss. 24(1) and 660; interpreted with reference to Cuerrier, Godin, DeSousa, Cooper, Ewanchuk, Ancio, Dynar (as cited in the reasons).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Mechanics’ lien “owner” test under s. 1(1)(d): a party is an owner if it (a) has an estate or interest in the land, (b) requested the work, and (c) the work was done “upon whose credit, or on whose behalf, or with whose privity or consent, or for whose direct benefit” (with “request” assessed by taking an “overall view” of the arrangements, not “dissected into [their] minute parts”).
BaselineA: Statute: The Mechanics’ Lien Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 267, s. 1(1)(d) (and applied with s. 5(1) lien entitlement limits: “sum justly due” and “sum justly owing”).
CaseB_TestB: Challenge for cause (juror partiality) test under Criminal Code s. 638(1)(b): to show a “realistic potential for juror partiality” generally requires (1) “that a widespread bias exists in the community” and (2) “that some jurors may be incapable of setting aside this bias, despite trial safeguards, to render an impartial decision”, with the “overarching consideration” being “whether there exists a realistic potential for partial juror behaviour”.
BaselineB: Statute plus prior SCC framework: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 638(1)(b), applying/clarifying the “realistic potential” approach from R. v. Sherratt and R. v. Williams (as cited in the reasons).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Anns-based duty of care for public authorities: (1) proximity/foreseeability — “is there a sufficiently close relationship… so that… carelessness… might cause damage”; and (2) residual policy considerations — “are there any considerations which ought to negative or limit (a) the scope of the duty (b) the class of persons… (c) the damages…”. Applied through the policy/operational distinction: “the more ‘operational’… the easier it is to superimpose… a common law duty of care”; and where there is a duty to act, “the non-feasance/misfeasance dichotomy becomes irrelevant.”
BaselineA: Common law (adopting/applying Anns v. Merton London Borough Council; also drawing on Donoghue v. Stevenson / Hedley Byrne / Dorset Yacht) alongside interpretation of municipal enabling legislation and by-law (Municipal Act, R.S.B.C. 1960, c. 255, s. 714; and Kamloops building by-law imposing enforcement duty).
CaseB_TestB: Implied-limit framework for s. 10(b) at roadside sobriety screening: a s. 10(b) limit is “prescribed by law” if it “results by necessary implication… from [a statute’s] operating requirements”; police sobriety-screening measures (asking about drinking; requesting roadside sobriety tests) are lawful if “reasonable and necessary” to fulfill the duty to check sobriety and are “incompatible with the exercise of the right to counsel”; then the implied limit is justified under s. 1 using the Oakes proportionality criteria (objective, rational connection, minimal impairment, proportionality).
BaselineB: Statutory/constitutional interpretation: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms ss. 10(b) and 1; Manitoba Highway Traffic Act s. 76.1(1) (general stop power) read with Criminal Code s. 254 (breath demands), applying the Therens/Thomsen ‘operating requirements’ doctrine.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal defence of necessity (as an excuse): requires “urgent situation of clear and imminent peril when compliance with the law is demonstrably impossible”, i.e., moral/normative involuntariness shown by (i) imminent risk/direct and immediate peril, (ii) no reasonable legal alternative (“no legal way out”), and (iii) proportionality (harm inflicted less than harm avoided); plus limits re foreseeability/contributory fault and Crown must disprove beyond a reasonable doubt once air of reality raised
BaselineA: Common law defence preserved by Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 7(3), drawing on Morgentaler v. The Queen, [1976] 1 S.C.R. 616 (necessity limited to “urgent situations of clear and imminent peril when compliance with the law is demonstrably impossible”)
CaseB_TestB: Section 8 reasonable expectation of privacy (REP) “totality of the circumstances” framework: four inquiries—(1) subject matter of alleged search, (2) claimant’s direct interest, (3) subjective expectation of privacy, and (4) whether that expectation is objectively reasonable (a normative assessment of when Canadians “ought” to expect privacy); in this sting context, no objectively reasonable REP where an adult communicates online with a child stranger and police know this from the outset
BaselineB: Common law/Charter framework for s. 8 REP analysis (e.g., Hunter v. Southam; Edwards; Tessling; Spencer; Cole; Marakah), applied to Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 8; with related statutory context in Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, Part VI (ss. 183, 184.2) for “private communication”
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 613(1)(b)(iii) proviso (harmless error): Crown must satisfy the court the verdict “would necessarily have been the same if such error had not occurred”; where the error is exclusion of exculpatory evidence, assess the entirety of the evidence including the reasonable possible effect of the excluded evidence, with any reasonable effect enuring to the accused
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 613(1)(b)(iii)) as interpreted in Colpitts v. The Queen, [1965] S.C.R. 739 (test: Crown must show verdict would necessarily have been the same absent the error)
CaseB_TestB: Appellate court raising a new issue on appeal: an issue is “new” if it provides a new basis to find error beyond the parties’ grounds; discretion to raise it should be exercised only rarely—only when failing to do so would risk an injustice (i.e., “good reason to believe” the result would realistically have differed), and only if the court has jurisdiction, the record is sufficient, and procedural prejudice can be avoided with notice and opportunity to respond
BaselineB: Common law / appellate practice principles (drawing on prior SCC guidance such as R. v. W. (G.) and Quan v. Cusson) governing appellate courts’ role in an adversarial system; applied in the context of Criminal Code appeal jurisdiction (ss. 676(1)(a), 686(4))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Threshold s. 96 characterization: a power is administrative (not judicial) where there is no real "lis between the parties" and the decision is based on "considerations of expediency" rather than "considerations of legality"; if not judicial, s. 96 is not infringed
BaselineA: Common law / constitutional jurisprudence under Constitution Act, 1867, s. 96 (drawing on Re Residential Tenancies Act, 1979; Massey-Ferguson; Grondin; and the John East Iron Works two-fold approach to 'judicial power')
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 12 mandatory-minimum framework (as applied to robbery MMPs): two-stage inquiry—(1) determine a "fit and proportionate sentence" under Criminal Code sentencing principles; (2) ask whether the mandatory minimum requires a sentence that is "grossly disproportionate" compared to the fit sentence, assessed via "scope and reach of the offence", "effects of the penalty on the offender", and "the penalty and its objectives"; may be assessed on the actual offender or a "reasonably foreseeable" case
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 12; Criminal Code sentencing provisions (including ss. 718.1 and 718.2(e)); and prior SCC s. 12 mandatory-minimum jurisprudence (especially R. v. Hills, 2023 SCC 2; also Smith, Nur, Lloyd, Bissonnette, Boudreault)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 93(1) denominational schools infringement test: s. 93 protection applies where (a) there is a right/privilege affecting a denominational school, (b) enjoyed by a particular class of persons, (c) by law, (d) in effect at the time of the Union, and (e) which is “prejudicially affected” (and, on the merits here, rights included proportionate grants and taxation within the board’s own district).
BaselineA: Constitution Act, 1867, s. 93(1) (and s. 93(2)); applied using Privy Council/SCC s. 93 jurisprudence cited in the reasons (e.g., Barrett; Hirsch; Tiny; Ottawa Separate Schools Trustees).
CaseB_TestB: Young Offenders Act non-disclosure ‘link’ test: the “nub” is whether the disclosure “links the identity of the young person with a charge, proceeding or disposition under the Act”; if the prohibited link is made, disclosure/publication is barred unless a specific statutory exception is satisfied (e.g., s. 44.1(1)(k) requires judge authorization; s. 38(1.13) requires necessity for compliance/safety and disclosure to the responsible school board).
BaselineB: Statute: Young Offenders Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. Y-1, especially ss. 38(1), 38(1.1), 38(1.13) and ss. 40-46 (including s. 44.1 and s. 46).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 93(1) denominational schools protection test: s. 93 applies where (a) there is a "right or privilege affecting a denominational school" (b) "enjoyed by a particular class of persons" (c) "by law" (d) "in effect at the time of the Union" and (e) "which is prejudicially affected" (trial judge’s formulation adopted as undisputed at para. 16).
BaselineA: Constitution Act, 1867, s. 93(1) (and s. 93(2)); baseline articulation of the conditions for s. 93 protection drawn from Privy Council jurisprudence cited in the reasons (e.g., Barrett; Brophy; Hirsch; Tiny).
CaseB_TestB: Canadian maritime law / navigation and shipping scope test: "the mere involvement of a pleasure craft in an incident is not sufficient"; courts must examine the "factual context" and ask whether the allegedly negligent act is "so integrally connected" to navigation/shipping "such that it is a practical necessity for Parliament to have jurisdiction" (paras. 20-25).
BaselineB: Common law constitutional/maritime-law framework from SCC cases cited and applied: ITO — International Terminal Operators Ltd. v. Miida Electronics Inc. ("so integrally connected"), Whitbread v. Walley (practical necessity for uniform law re pleasure craft navigation), and Ordon Estate v. Grail (examine factual context).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Certiorari review of a preliminary inquiry committal: a committal is a reviewable jurisdictional error where there is "no evidence" on an essential element ("'No evidence' on an essential element of the charge against the accused cannot amount to 'sufficient evidence' under s. 475").
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 475) interpreted through prior SCC/PC certiorari jurisprudence (Patterson v. The Queen; Martin v. The Queen; Forsythe v. The Queen; Nat Bell Liquors).
CaseB_TestB: Criteria for compensatory allowance under art. 559 C.C.Q.: claimant must establish (1) contribution, (2) enrichment of spouse’s patrimony, (3) causal link, and (4) proportion; "[e]ach of these elements must be evaluated with great flexibility" and enrichment must "subsist" and be evaluated "at the time of the divorce".
BaselineB: Statute (Civil Code of Quebec, art. 559) informed by unjust enrichment principles (e.g., Cie Immobilière Viger Ltée v. Lauréat Giguère Inc.) and interaction with Bankruptcy Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. B-3, ss. 2 and 148.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Estoppel by representation (including by silence): requires a representation (words/conduct, or silence only where there is a duty to speak) that induces detrimental reliance; silence/inaction is a representation only if the representor owes a legal duty to disclose
BaselineA: Common law (estoppel by representation; definition drawn from Spencer Bower & Turner and cases such as Greenwood v. Martins Bank, Ltd.)
CaseB_TestB: Rebutting the Criminal Code s. 212(3) presumption: jury may consider all the evidence about cohabitation and financial arrangements; trial judge need not identify a single 'particular and severable' item as 'evidence to the contrary'
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 212(3))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Municipal taxing power must be exercised in the form required by the enabling legislation (where the statute requires a by-law, the municipality cannot set the tax rate by resolution; doing so is an ultra vires self-redelegation/excess of jurisdiction, remediable by art. 33 C.C.P.)
BaselineA: Statute (Cities and Towns Act, R.S.Q. 1941, c. 233, art. 526 as amended for Dorval; plus procedural provisions in Cities and Towns Act and Code of Civil Procedure, art. 33)
CaseB_TestB: Causation in negligent blood-donor screening: apply the 'materially contributed' test (not a rebuttable presumption and not strict 'but-for') — i.e., whether the defendant’s negligence 'materially contributed' to the injury, where 'A contributing factor is material if it falls outside the de minimis range'
BaselineB: Common law causation in negligence (but-for as general rule; material contribution as exception/alternative), drawing on Snell v. Farrell and Athey v. Leonati; Hollis distinguished
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 13 bar on using an accused’s prior testimony to incriminate them in a retrial: s. 13 applies at the moment of attempted use; “incriminating” is assessed in the second proceeding; and a retrial is “any other proceedings”.
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 13 (interpreted purposively in light of ss. 11(c) and 11(d)).
CaseB_TestB: Reformed rule for substantive admissibility of a non-accused witness’s prior inconsistent statement: admissible for truth if (threshold) it would be admissible as the witness’s sole testimony and (reliability) sufficient guarantees exist—typically (1) oath/affirmation/solemn declaration plus explicit warning, (2) videotaped in entirety, and (3) full opportunity to cross-examine at trial—plus (necessity) flexible necessity satisfied by recantation; with a voir dire assessing indicia and voluntariness/justice-disrepute factors.
BaselineB: Combination: statutory procedure (Canada Evidence Act, s. 9) plus common law hearsay/prior-inconsistent-statement doctrine (the “orthodox rule” from Deacon v. The King) reformed via the principled hearsay approach (R. v. Khan; R. v. Smith).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: When a trial judge’s acquittal can be appealed by the Crown as an “error of law alone”: a “total absence of evidence/foundation” for a finding of fact is an error of law only where the law has shifted the burden of proof to the accused; otherwise (given the presumption of innocence) “it can sometimes be said as a matter of law that there is no evidence on which the Court can convict but never that there is no evidence on which it can acquit”.
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 605(1)(a) (Crown appeal on a question of law alone)) plus common-law/jurisprudential principles from Lampard v. The Queen, Sunbeam Corporation (Canada) Ltd. v. The Queen, and discussion of Wild v. The Queen and Lemire.
CaseB_TestB: Test for interim relief/stay under Supreme Court Act s. 65.1 (as reaffirmed in RJR—MacDonald): (1) serious question, (2) irreparable harm, and (3) balance of convenience.
BaselineB: Common law (RJR—MacDonald Inc. v. Canada (Attorney General)) applied in the statutory context of Supreme Court Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. S-26, s. 65.1.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: When a trial judge’s finding supporting an acquittal can be treated as an error of law ("no evidence"/"total absence of a foundation") for Crown appeal jurisdiction: intention is fact; "total absence of a foundation for a finding of fact" is an error of law, but for an acquittal this "may only occur if there has been a transfer to the accused by the law of the burden of proof of a given fact"; otherwise "there is always some evidence" because of the presumption of innocence.
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 605(1)(a) (Crown appeal on "a question of law alone")) interpreted in light of SCC precedent (Lampard v. The Queen; Sunbeam Corporation (Canada) Ltd. v. The Queen; discussion of Wild v. The Queen and rejection of Lemire to the extent inconsistent).
CaseB_TestB: Ontario anti-SLAPP dismissal framework under Courts of Justice Act s. 137.1: (1) moving party must show on balance of probabilities the proceeding "arises from" its "expression" that "relates to a matter of public interest" (s. 137.1(3)); if met, (2) responding party must satisfy the judge that (a) there are "grounds to believe" the proceeding has "substantial merit" and the moving party has "no valid defence" (s. 137.1(4)(a)), and (b) the harm likely suffered "is sufficiently serious that" the public interest in permitting the proceeding to continue "outweighs" the public interest in protecting the expression (s. 137.1(4)(b)), described as an open-ended "public interest weighing exercise" and the "crux" of the analysis.
BaselineB: Statute (Courts of Justice Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.43, s. 137.1(3)-(4) (and related ss. 137.1-137.5)) interpreted and operationalized by the SCC.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Lawfulness of warrantless arrest on private premises (forcible entry) under s. 450(1)(a): arrest is lawful only if all four questions are answered “yes” (indictable offence; reasonable and probable grounds re commission; reasonable and probable grounds suspect is within; proper announcement before entry).
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 450(1)(a) (arrest without warrant for indictable offence) plus common law “standards enunciated in Eccles v. Bourque” governing entry onto private premises (including Semayne’s Case as historical source discussed).
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 15 discrimination analysis (as applied here): even if a law denies an equality right (equality before the law), it violates s. 15 only if the distinction is “discriminatory” in purpose or effect—i.e., a distinction “based on grounds relating to personal characteristics” that imposes burdens/withholds benefits; requires examining the “larger social, political and legal context” and typically a showing of pre-existing disadvantage.
BaselineB: Constitutional baseline: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 15(1) (and related discussion of s. 11(f) and s. 24(1) in the case). The Court applies and builds on Andrews v. Law Society of British Columbia (definition/approach to discrimination).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code indictment amendment for variance: court should amend a particular (e.g., specified narcotic) to conform to the evidence unless the accused was misled or prejudiced (and if prejudice exists, consider whether it can be cured, e.g., by adjournment) (Criminal Code, s. 529(4)-(5))
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 529(4)-(5); also applied via appellate powers in s. 613(1)(b)(i) and s. 613(3))
CaseB_TestB: Ineffective assistance of counsel (G.D.B.) test: appellant must show (1) counsel’s acts or omissions constituted incompetence and (2) a miscarriage of justice resulted
BaselineB: Common law (R. v. G.D.B., 2000 SCC 22, at para. 26)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Concurrent liability in tort and contract for professional negligence: a common law duty of care may arise from a contractual relationship if proximity exists, but tort cannot be used to circumvent contractual limits; plaintiff may elect tort/contract where concurrent liability exists
BaselineA: Common law (duty of care/proximity from Donoghue v. Stevenson; Hedley Byrne & Co. v. Heller & Partners Ltd.; Anns v. Merton London Borough Council; plus contractual-limitation principle from Elder, Dempster & Co. v. Paterson, Zochonis & Co.)
CaseB_TestB: Enforcement of exclusive choice-of-forum clauses in Quebec private international law: art. 3148(2) C.C.Q. prevails over art. 3139 C.C.Q. for warranty/incidental actions where the clause clearly ousts Quebec jurisdiction; forum non conveniens (art. 3135) applies only after Quebec jurisdiction is first established
BaselineB: Statute (Civil Code of Québec, arts. 3148 para. 2, 3139, 3135)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Scope of Quebec Construction Industry Labour Relations Act/Decree: coverage turns on the “nature of the work done” (activities within statutory definition of “construction”), not the status of the employer/employee; and Decree conditions are mandatory (no “total wage” set-off). Key holding: “in order to determine whether a particular employer or employees are covered, one must look at the nature of the work done and not simply at the status of the parties” and “The question is not one of the total wage but of the specific conditions determined by the decree.”
BaselineA: Statute and regulation/decree: Construction Industry Labour Relations Act, S.Q. 1968, c. 45 (esp. ss. 1(e),(i),(j),(p),(r), 2(2), 20) and Decree respecting the construction industry (1973) 105 O.G. II 5837 (esp. ss. 3.01, 3.02, 18.06, 32.03).
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 12 mandatory-minimum analysis and remedy: (1) s. 12 test is “grossly disproportionate” (“so excessive as to outrage standards of decency” / “abhorrent or intolerable”); (2) if a mandatory minimum is unconstitutional in a particular case, the proper remedy is s. 52(1) invalidity, not a s. 24(1) constitutional exemption (“If a mandatory minimum sentence would create an unconstitutional result in a particular case, the minimum sentence must be struck down.”).
BaselineB: Combination of constitutional text and common-law Charter doctrine: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms ss. 12, 24(1) and Constitution Act, 1982 s. 52(1), applying/confirming prior SCC tests (R. v. Smith for gross disproportionality; Goltz/Morrisey for mandatory minimum review).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Parens patriae limit: a court may not authorize non-therapeutic sterilization of a mentally incompetent person; parens patriae discretion must be exercised only for the protected person’s benefit and with great caution, and here “should never be authorized for non-therapeutic purposes” because it “can never safely be determined that such a procedure is for the benefit of that person”.
BaselineA: Common law (parens patriae/Chancery jurisdiction as received in provincial superior courts; discussed via English Chancery/wardship authorities such as Wellesley v. Duke of Beaufort and Re X (a minor))
CaseB_TestB: Residual management rights “balancing of interests” assessment: to decide if a unilateral workplace policy is a reasonable exercise of management rights, arbitrators must “consider all of the surrounding circumstances” and determine whether the policy “strikes a reasonable balance between management and employees’ interests”.
BaselineB: Common law / labour-arbitration doctrine (KVP test; endorsed in Irving Pulp & Paper) applied to interpretation of collective agreement clause requiring employer to act “reasonably, fairly and in good faith”
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: R. v. Prince refinement of the Kienapple rule against multiple convictions: Kienapple applies only where there is (1) a sufficient factual nexus (usually “Does the same act of the accused ground each of the charges?”) and (2) a sufficient legal nexus such that “there is no additional and distinguishing element that goes to guilt” in the offence sought to be barred; plus guidance on when elements are not “distinct or additional” (particularization; multiple methods to prove a single delict; evidentiary proxy).
BaselineA: Common law (Kienapple v. The Queen, [1975] 1 S.C.R. 729; also discussed through Côté v. The Queen, [1975] 1 S.C.R. 303 and Krug v. The Queen, [1985] 2 S.C.R. 255).
JudgeA: The Chief Justice (Dickson C.J., for the Court)
CaseB_TestB: Gould v. Yukon Order of Pioneers test for whether a “service … to the public” under Yukon Human Rights Act s. 8(a) exists: a two-part analysis—(1) determine what constitutes the “service” on the facts; (2) determine whether the service creates a “public relationship” between provider and user, with “public” defined relationally; relevant (non-determinative) criteria include “selectivity”, “diversity”, “involvement of non-members”, “commercial nature”, “intimate nature”, and “purpose” of offering the service, assessed contextually.
BaselineB: Statute (Yukon Human Rights Act, R.S.Y. 1986 (Supp.), c. 11, s. 8(a); interpreted in light of analogous human rights provisions and UBC v. Berg, [1993] 2 S.C.R. 353).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Ensite test for whether property is “used or held ... in the course of carrying on a business” (ITA s. 129(4)): property must be “truly employed and risked” in the business; “risk” is more than a remote risk or mere business purpose; threshold met when withdrawal would “have a decidedly destabilizing effect on the corporate operations themselves”; focus is whether property was used to fulfil a requirement that had to be met to do business (not whether taxpayer was forced to use that particular property).
BaselineA: Statute: Income Tax Act, s. 129(4)(a)(ii) (as amended) exclusion for “a property used or held ... in the course of carrying on a business” (in defining investment income/foreign investment income).
CaseB_TestB: Crown appeal from acquittal/new trial test under Criminal Code s. 686(4): Crown must satisfy the court that “the verdict would not necessarily have been the same if the trial judge had properly directed the jury” (a “very heavy onus” requiring “a reasonable degree of certainty”).
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, s. 686(4), as interpreted in prior SCC cases (Vézeau v. The Queen; R. v. Morin).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Public interest immunity for Cabinet documents: court (not Crown) decides by balancing the public interest in confidentiality against the public interest in the administration of justice, ordinarily after judicial inspection of the documents
BaselineA: Common law (public interest immunity/Crown privilege doctrine), drawing on SCC authority that courts decide the claim (e.g., Smallwood v. Sparling; also referencing R. v. Snider; Gagnon v. Commission des valeurs mobilières du Québec) and Commonwealth developments (e.g., Conway v. Rimmer; Burmah Oil; Sankey v. Whitlam)
CaseB_TestB: Appellate review of a (pre-Lifchus) jury charge: whether the charge, read as a whole, shows 'substantial compliance' with Lifchus/W.(D.) and whether there is a 'reasonable likelihood that the jury misapprehended' the correct standard of proof/approach to conflicting evidence
BaselineB: Common law (jury-instruction standards from R. v. Lifchus; R. v. Starr; and the W.(D.) framework for conflicting evidence/credibility)
JudgeB: Major J. (for Major, Binnie, Arbour and LeBel JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 7 extradition intervention test: courts may intervene against surrender only in compelling cases where surrender would, in the particular circumstances, violate the principles of fundamental justice (judicial intervention limited to cases of “real substance”).
BaselineA: Combination: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7 (and s. 32 scope), applied in the extradition context under the Extradition Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-21 and the Canada–U.S. Extradition Treaty; informed by Operation Dismantle Inc. v. The Queen, [1985] 1 S.C.R. 441 (Charter binds executive).
CaseB_TestB: Crown appeal jurisdiction test: a Court of Appeal may interfere with an acquittal on a Crown appeal only where the trial court erred “on a question of law alone” (Criminal Code, s. 605(1)(a); applied via Schuldt v. The Queen).
BaselineB: Statute/common law application: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 605(1)(a), as interpreted/applied in Schuldt v. The Queen, [1985] 2 S.C.R. 592.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 7 limit on extradition: courts may intervene only where surrender would, in the particular circumstances, violate the principles of fundamental justice (judicial intervention limited to 'cases of real substance')
BaselineA: Statute/Constitution (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7; applied in extradition context alongside Extradition Act and treaty framework)
CaseB_TestB: Income Tax Act s. 20(1)(c)(i) interest deductibility (purpose element): whether, considering all the circumstances, the taxpayer had a reasonable expectation of income at the time the investment was made (ancillary income-earning purpose suffices absent sham/window dressing)
BaselineB: Statute (Income Tax Act, s. 20(1)(c)(i); interpreted with reference to prior SCC tax cases including Bronfman Trust and Shell Canada)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Injurious affection where no land is taken: claimant must show the construction-caused loss would be actionable at common law (nuisance), applying the Loiselle four conditions and excluding non-compensable heads like loss of prospect; nuisance turns on “substantially interfering with the use or enjoyment of land ... [and] ... unreasonable” in all the circumstances.
BaselineA: Statute (Ontario Expropriations Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 154, ss. 1(e)(ii), 21) incorporating common-law nuisance/actionability requirement; SCC baseline test referenced from The Queen v. Loiselle, [1962] S.C.R. 624 (four conditions for injurious affection when no land is taken).
CaseB_TestB: Adequacy of jury instructions on identity/party participation in murder: it is not necessary the accused acted alone; jury may convict if satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt he “actively participated in the killing” (not merely present/minor role), and the trial judge may correct an erroneous “actual shooter” direction by adding “shot ... or was otherwise an active participant in her killing”.
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, especially s. 21 party liability; appeal/miscarriage framework under s. 686(1)(b)(iii) discussed but not the core test applied by the majority).
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 10(b) right-to-counsel: absent circumstances showing non-understanding, accused must prove he asked for counsel and was denied (or denied any opportunity to ask); otherwise, once police promptly advise of the right, no further correlative duties arise until the accused indicates a desire to exercise it
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 10(b) (with remedy context under s. 24(2)); applied approach from R. v. Anderson (Ont. C.A.) as adopted by the SCC
CaseB_TestB: Employee/representative secret-profit disgorgement: where an employee acts in a representative capacity (or without authority using employer funds) and receives profits/secret commissions through abuse of position or bad faith, the employee must account for and remit those profits to the employer (via C.C.L.C. arts. 411 and 1713 principles)
BaselineB: Statute (civil law codal): Civil Code of Lower Canada, arts. 411 (possessor in bad faith) and 1713 (mandatary must render account and deliver/pay over all received under authority of mandate), extended by the Court to analogous employment/representative relationships grounded in good faith/loyalty
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Wigglesworth s. 11 Charter applicability test: a matter falls within s. 11 either (1) because "by its very nature it is a criminal proceeding" (the "by nature" test) or (2) because conviction may lead to a "true penal consequence"; where they conflict, the "by nature" test "must give way" to the "true penal consequence" test. A "true penal consequence" includes "imprisonment" or a fine whose magnitude appears aimed at "redressing the wrong done to society at large" rather than internal discipline.
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 11 (opening words "Any person charged with an offence").
CaseB_TestB: Jacquard functional approach to reviewing jury charges: "As long as an appellate court, when looking at a trial judge’s charge to the jury as a whole, concludes that the jury was left with a sufficient understanding of the facts as they relate to the relevant issues, the charge is proper" (juries must be "properly -- not perfectly -- instructed").
BaselineB: Common law (jury-charge review doctrine), relying on prior SCC authorities cited in the reasons (e.g., Azoulay v. The Queen; Cluett v. The Queen; John v. The Queen).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: s. 577(1) Criminal Code “whole of the trial” includes jury selection; accused must be able to hear/participate in any juror examination on partiality after plea, and breach is fundamental (not curable)
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 577(1), with related provisions ss. 569(2), 598, 599, 600, 613(1)(b)(iii)); interpreted in light of SCC/CA jurisprudence cited (Basarabas and Spek v. The Queen; Vézina and Côté v. The Queen; Meunier v. The Queen; Hertrich (Ont. C.A.))
CaseB_TestB: Common-law test for when an appellate court may set aside an acquittal and enter a conviction (instead of ordering a new trial): Crown must show verdict would not have been the same but for error of law, and all findings necessary for guilt were made (explicitly/implicitly) or are not in issue
BaselineB: Common law (as stated in Vézeau v. The Queen; R. v. Courville/Courville v. The Queen), applied alongside Criminal Code, s. 613(4)(b)(ii)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: When a trial judge quashes a voidable charge under Criminal Code s. 529, the quashing is tantamount to an acquittal (triggering autrefois acquit) unless the charge was an absolute nullity/lack of jurisdiction; quashing is only permitted where the required amendment cannot be made without injustice/irreparable prejudice
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 529 and 535–537) informed by common law autrefois acquit principles and SCC cases (e.g., Petersen v. The Queen; Doyle v. The Queen)
CaseB_TestB: Scope of acquired rights / legal non-conforming use: characterize the pre-existing use and assess whether changes are protected by considering intensification, remoteness, and neighbourhood effects in a structured multi-step approach
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: Act Respecting Land Use Planning and Development, R.S.Q., c. A-19.1, s. 113(18) (and related municipal by-law powers) plus common law non-conforming use doctrine (e.g., Central Jewish Institute v. City of Toronto)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Workmen’s privilege against an owner’s immovable where work is ordered by a lessee: the lessee is only a “builder/contractor” for arts. 2013e/2013f C.C.L.C. if there is a construction contract including an owner-to-builder claim/undertaking to pay a construction contract price (a price fund from which the owner can retain to satisfy privileges); absent such a claim/price, no privilege lies against the owner’s immovable.
BaselineA: Statute (Civil Code of Lower Canada, arts. 2013e and 2013f (and related contract provisions arts. 984 et seq., 1060))
CaseB_TestB: Mental distress damages for breach of contract (Hadley v. Baxendale application): recoverable where (1) an object of the contract was to secure a psychological benefit so that mental distress on breach was within the reasonable contemplation of the parties at contract formation, and (2) the plaintiff proves mental suffering of a degree sufficient to warrant compensation; no independent actionable wrong required.
BaselineB: Common law (Hadley v. Baxendale foreseeability/remoteness principle; discussed with reference to Vorvis v. I.C.B.C.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Unequal division of marital property under NB Marital Property Act s. 7(f): court may depart from equal division where it is of the opinion equal division would be inequitable; in particular, where property was acquired "exclusively or almost wholly" through one spouse’s efforts and the other made "no, or a negligible" contribution to child care/household management/financial provision, there are "circumstances relating to the acquisition, maintenance and improvement" justifying discretion to depart.
BaselineA: Statute (Marital Property Act, S.N.B. 1980, c. M-1.1, especially ss. 2, 3, 7 and residual factor s. 7(f))
CaseB_TestB: Interjurisdictional immunity (constitutional inapplicability) for federal services: provincial laws of general application apply unless they bear on what makes the matter specifically federal; for a federal service, provincial law is inapplicable if it touches a "vital or essential aspect" of the service’s "establishment, management or operation" (here, the provincial transport permit system is inapplicable to the federal sightseeing service).
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine (interjurisdictional immunity) as articulated in prior SCC cases (e.g., Bell Canada v. Quebec (CSST); Construction Montcalm; Clark v. CNR; Dick v. The Queen) and applied to provincial Transport Act/Regulation permit scheme
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “financing” in Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971 s. 44(2)(a): claimant is “financing” only where there is “active and voluntary involvement” and a “meaningful connection between the payment and the dispute”; mandatory union dues diverted to a strike fund are not enough
BaselineA: Statute: Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, S.C. 1970-71-72, c. 48, s. 44(2)(a) (exception to disentitlement where claimant proves he is not “participating in or financing or directly interested in” the labour dispute)
CaseB_TestB: Enforceability/scope of a waiver (exclusion) clause for negligence in a race entry form: construed in its context to determine whether it covers the accident and is not avoided as “unfair, unreasonable and inapplicable” (including whether the negligence was within the parties’ contemplation; and whether unconscionability/public policy concerns apply)
BaselineB: Common law: contractual interpretation and enforceability of exclusion/waiver clauses (including arguments framed in terms of fundamental breach, unconscionability, and public policy) as applied to the entry-form waiver
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “financing” in Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971 s. 44(2)(a): claimant “finances” a labour dispute only with an “active and voluntary involvement” and a “meaningful connection between the payment and the dispute” (i.e., not mere mandatory union dues indirectly used for strike pay).
BaselineA: Statute: Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, S.C. 1970-71-72, c. 48, s. 44(2)(a) (exception to disentitlement where claimant proves he is not “participating in or financing or directly interested in” the labour dispute).
CaseB_TestB: Extradition surrender review: Minister must balance comity/international cooperation against s. 7 fundamental justice; surrender should be refused only where the “particular treatment” in the requesting state would “shock the conscience” or be “unjust or oppressive” under Extradition Act s. 44(1).
BaselineB: Statute + Charter: Extradition Act, S.C. 1999, c. 18, s. 44(1) (“unjust or oppressive”); Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7; as framed by United States v. Burns and Lake v. Canada (Minister of Justice).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 10 “detention” test (Therens criteria): detention exists where the state assumes control over a person’s movement by a demand/direction with significant legal consequence, with compulsion/coercion (e.g., criminal liability for refusal or reasonable belief of no choice), in a situation where the person may reasonably require counsel and access to counsel is prevented/impeded
BaselineA: Common law/Charter interpretation based on R. v. Therens, [1985] 1 S.C.R. 613 (applied to Criminal Code s. 234.1(1) roadside breath demand and Charter s. 10(b))
CaseB_TestB: Mistake-of-age “all reasonable steps” framework under Criminal Code s. 150.1(4): once an air of reality exists, Crown must prove beyond a reasonable doubt either no honest belief complainant was at least 16 or failure to take “all reasonable steps”; the inquiry is “highly contextual, fact-specific”, with the general rule that “the more reasonable an accused’s perception of the complainant’s age, the fewer steps reasonably required”
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 150.1(4) (and related burden articulation once an air of reality exists)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Extradition specialty/undertaking immunity ends once the extradited person has been “restored or has had an opportunity of returning” to the surrendering state; an unqualified specialty undertaking is construed (in context, object/purpose, and international-law principles) as not conferring perpetual immunity where the person remains in Canada by choice
BaselineA: Statute + international agreement interpretation: Extradition Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-21, s. 33 (and related interpretive context including s. 3 and the Canada–Brazil extradition arrangement/undertaking; interpreted in light of Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, Art. 31, and general principles of international law)
CaseB_TestB: Intertwining principle for criminal appeals: where an appeal is properly before the SCC on an alleged error of law, the Court may also determine (if the Crown invoked it) whether the error is curable under Criminal Code s. 686(1)(b)(iii); the Crown need not seek separate leave to appeal the refusal to apply the proviso
BaselineB: Statute as interpreted through precedent: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(b)(iii), applying R. v. Keegstra, [1995] 2 S.C.R. 381 (paras. 30-31)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “anything” in Criminal Code s. 283(1) (theft): to be the object of theft, the thing must (1) be “property of some sort” and (2) be “capable of being taken or converted in a manner that results in the deprivation of the victim”; confidential information per se fails (not property for policy reasons and, in any event, not capable of taking/conversion with deprivation).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 283(1)); with reference to prior interpretation that “anything” includes some intangibles (R. v. Scallen; followed in R. v. Hardy).
CaseB_TestB: Interpretation of “assets” in MVHC rent-subsidy Assistance Application: objectively, “assets” means an applicant’s “property or interest(s) in property that can actually be used to discharge his or her debts and liabilities, including the monthly rent”; a Henson trust interest is a “mere hope” and therefore not an “asset” for eligibility-to-be-considered.
BaselineB: Common law (contractual interpretation: ordinary and grammatical meaning read in context and surrounding circumstances, per Sattva; plus trust-law characterization of Henson trusts).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 7 analysis for compelled fingerprinting: (1) deprivation of life/liberty/security; (2) whether deprivation accords with the principles of fundamental justice — here, fingerprinting of a person charged on reasonable and probable grounds does not violate fundamental justice because it does not “unduly invade the rights of the accused” and the scheme is not arbitrary despite police discretion
BaselineA: Combination: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7 (two-step framework) plus statutory fingerprinting scheme (Identification of Criminals Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-1, s. 2; Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 453.3(3), 455.5(5))
CaseB_TestB: Sufficiency of reasons (Sheppard/Braich): two-stage inquiry — “(1) are the reasons inadequate; (2) if so, do they prevent appellate review?”; even if “objectively inadequate”, review may proceed if the basis for the verdict is “obvious on the face of the record”, but if reasons are “both inadequate and inscrutable, a new trial is required”
BaselineB: Common law (as summarized from R. v. Sheppard, 2002 SCC 26 and R. v. Braich, 2002 SCC 27; also tied to appellate review under Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686)
JudgeB: Bastarache and Abella JJ. (LeBel J. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 10(b) “detention” test applied to customs strip searches: detention exists where a state agent “assumes control over the movement of a person by a demand or direction which may have significant legal consequence” (Therens), and Simmons holds that when a traveller is “taken out of the normal course and forced to submit to a strip search that person is detained” and must be informed of the right to counsel “at that time”.
BaselineA: Common law/constitutional interpretation of Charter s. 10(b) based on R. v. Therens, [1985] 1 S.C.R. 613 (definition of detention).
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 11(b) unreasonable delay framework (Morin): “not by the application of a mathematical or administrative formula but rather by a judicial determination balancing” the relevant factors: (1) length of delay; (2) waiver; (3) reasons for delay (inherent requirements, actions of accused, actions of Crown, limits on institutional resources, other reasons); and (4) prejudice; with a non-binding institutional-delay guideline of “between 8 and 10 months for institutional delay in Provincial Courts”.
BaselineB: Combination of Charter s. 11(b) and common-law/constitutional framework developed in prior SCC cases (notably R. v. Smith, [1989] 2 S.C.R. 1120 and R. v. Askov, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 1199).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Voluntary intoxication and mens rea for general-intent offences (Leary rule preserved): intoxication evidence is excluded unless it is so extreme as to negate the minimal intent/voluntariness; Crown may prove mens rea by inference from actus reus or, in extreme cases raising doubt about voluntariness, by proving voluntary self-induced intoxication as the blameworthy mental state. Key formulations: (1) general vs specific intent: a general intent offence involves intent only as to doing the act, with no ulterior purpose; (2) for general intent, mens rea can be proved because "in most cases can be inferred from the actus reus itself" ("a person is presumed to have intended the natural and probable consequences of his actions"); and (3) only where intoxication is "so intoxicated as to raise doubt as to the voluntary nature of his conduct" may the Crown establish the blameworthy mental state by proving "voluntary self-induced intoxication"; Wilson J. adds intoxication should go to the trier of fact only if it is "evidence of extreme intoxication involving an absence of awareness akin to a state of insanity or automatism".
BaselineA: Common law (intoxication defence / general vs specific intent) as set out in Leary v. The Queen, [1978] 1 S.C.R. 29 (and discussed with Majewski; also relying on R. v. George, [1960] S.C.R. 871; Swietlinski v. The Queen, [1980] 2 S.C.R. 956). Applied in context of Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 246.2(c) (sexual assault causing bodily harm).
CaseB_TestB: Appellate intervention on Crown appeal from acquittal: (i) an appellate court cannot interfere with a trial judge’s inferences of fact "simply because the appellate court would draw different inferences" (Schuldt); but (ii) it may overturn where the trial judge "has not directed his mind to an issue or issues that require determination in order to reach the verdict"—here, the judge had to consider whether, even if reasonable doubt existed on particularized proceeds counts, the Crown proved the broader "global count" beyond a reasonable doubt (it was "open" to convict on the global count if at least one transaction involved proceeds).
BaselineB: Common law appellate review limits on Crown appeals from acquittal, relying on Schuldt v. The Queen, [1985] 2 S.C.R. 592; applied within the statutory appeal framework (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 675) and in relation to proceeds offences under the Narcotic Control Act, ss. 11.1 and 11.2 (now ss. 19.1 and 19.2).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Appellate intervention in a trial judge’s discretionary reapportionment of matrimonial property: intervene only if the trial judge “misdirects himself” or the decision is “so clearly wrong as to amount to an injustice” (in applying Family Relations Act, s. 51 unfairness-based reapportionment).
BaselineA: Common law standard of appellate deference to discretionary decisions (as applied in Harper v. Harper, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 2; also citing Re Hull Estate (Ont. C.A.)) in the statutory context of the Family Relations Act, R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 121, ss. 43 and 51.
CaseB_TestB: Duty to correct prejudicial Crown jury address and curative proviso: where Crown remarks are “prejudicial to a degree sufficient to impose a legal duty on the trial judge to comment” to ensure the defence is “fairly put to the jury”, failure is an error of law; then consider whether s. 686(1)(b)(iii) (no substantial wrong/miscarriage of justice) applies.
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(b)(iii) (curative proviso) applied to trial error; common law principles of fair trial/jury instruction as reflected in the Court’s adoption of Ayles J.A.’s formulation.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Wigmore/Slavutych four-part test for recognizing a (qualified) common law privilege against compelled disclosure of communications (including claimed journalist-source privilege): (1) communication originates in confidence; (2) confidentiality essential to the relationship; (3) relationship one the community ought to foster; (4) injury from disclosure greater than benefit for correct disposal of litigation
BaselineA: Common law (Wigmore criteria as discussed/approved in Slavutych v. Baker, [1976] 1 S.C.R. 254)
CaseB_TestB: Reasonableness review of Crown corporations’ discretionary decisions setting PILT “effective rate”: discretion exists but must be exercised within the statutory/regulatory framework—rate must be calculated “as if the federal property were taxable property belonging to a private owner” and cannot be based on a “fictitious tax system” (must use the tax system that actually exists in the municipality)
BaselineB: Statute and regulation (Payments in Lieu of Taxes Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. M-13, esp. ss. 2 (definitions incl. “effective rate”), 2.1, 4(1), sch. II; and Crown Corporation Payments Regulations, SOR/81-1030, esp. s. 2 (definitions incl. “corporation effective rate”), s. 7(1))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Patent disclosure/sufficiency under Patent Act s. 36(1): applicant must disclose everything essential for the invention to function; completeness requires two conditions — (1) “describe the invention and define the way it is produced or built” and (2) “define the nature of the invention and describe how it is put into operation”; disclosure must enable a person skilled in the art “to produce it using only the instructions contained in the disclosure”; mere deposit of a sample “by itself, does not comply” with s. 36(1).
BaselineA: Statute (Patent Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. P-4, s. 36(1)), as interpreted through prior patent-law disclosure cases cited (e.g., Minerals Separation; Burton Parsons; Monsanto; Consolboard).
CaseB_TestB: Standard of review for labour arbitral awards applying common law/equitable doctrines: correctness applies only to Dunsmuir correctness categories (constitutional questions; general law of central importance outside expertise; true jurisdiction/vires; competing tribunal jurisdiction lines); otherwise reasonableness applies, including where an arbitrator imposes an “estoppel” as a labour-relations remedy, assessed contextually and for whether it “reasonably respond[s] to the distinctive nature of labour relations”.
BaselineB: Common law administrative-law standard of review framework (Dunsmuir; Smith) applied in the labour arbitration context, alongside the statutory scheme (Labour Relations Act, R.S.M. 1987, c. L10, ss. 121, 128(2)).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Residential Tenancies s. 96 test as refined in Sobeys: (1) historical inquiry with narrow characterization of the jurisdiction and an exclusivity/concurrency gloss (shared jurisdiction validates only if inferior-court involvement was “broadly co-extensive”); (2) whether the tribunal is exercising a “judicial function”; (3) whether, in institutional context, the judicial power is “necessarily incidental to the achievement of a broader policy goal” (or merely ancillary) rather than the tribunal’s “sole or central function”. Key quotes: stage 1 asks whether the challenged power “broadly conform[s]” to s. 96 courts at Confederation; if shared, only sufficient where inferior-court work was “broadly co-extensive”; stage 2: “The primary issue is the nature of the question which the tribunal is called upon to decide”; stage 3: “What must be considered is the ‘context’ in which this power is exercised” and the scheme is invalid only when adjudication is a “sole or central function”.
BaselineA: Common law constitutional doctrine applying Constitution Act, 1867, s. 96; baseline framework from Re Residential Tenancies Act, 1979, [1981] 1 S.C.R. 714 (three-stage test).
CaseB_TestB: Downtown Eastside public interest standing test as clarified: courts “must assess and weigh three factors” — (i) “serious justiciable issue”; (ii) “genuine interest”; (iii) “reasonable and effective means” — and must weigh them “cumulatively, flexibly and purposively”; legality/access to justice get no “particular weight” and are not “hard and fast requirements” or “freestanding, independently operating tests”. The Court also clarifies the ‘sufficient factual setting’ aspect of factor (iii): an “individual co-plaintiff [is] not required” if a “sufficiently concrete and well-developed factual setting” will be forthcoming, and sets a rule for revisiting standing: a defendant may seek to revisit only if a “material change has occurred” raising “a serious doubt” about the forthcoming factual setting and other case-management tools are inadequate.
