BaselineB: Common law doctrine of public interest standing; baseline test from Canada (Attorney General) v. Downtown Eastside Sex Workers United Against Violence Society, 2012 SCC 45 (three-factor discretionary framework).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Bankruptcy Act s. 47(a) vs s. 107(1)(j) characterization: a provincial “deemed trust” only removes assets from the bankrupt’s estate under s. 47(a) if the tax money is “identifiable or traceable”; if it “cannot be traced”, there is no “property held ... in trust” and the province is left with a Crown claim governed by s. 107(1)(j).
BaselineA: Statute (Bankruptcy Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. B-3, ss. 47(a), 107(1)(j)) interpreted alongside provincial statute (Social Service Tax Act, R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 388, s. 18) and “general principles of trust law” (identifiability/traceability).
CaseB_TestB: Section 23 “numbers warrant” / local facilities & management-and-control approach: the relevant number is “somewhere between the known demand and the total number of persons who could potentially take advantage of the service”; defining the relevant “area” is case-by-case and within the minority’s management and control (subject to objective provincial norms consistent with s. 23), and the Minister’s approval role is limited to verifying provincial requirements (no substitution of his own criteria).
BaselineB: Constitution (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 23) as developed through Mahe v. Alberta’s “sliding scale” and applied alongside provincial statute/regulations (P.E.I. School Act and School Act Regulations).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Young Offenders Act s. 16 transfer to ordinary court: whether the judge is satisfied, after "weighing and balancing all the relevant considerations" in s. 16(2), that transfer is appropriate (onus on applicant, but "not ... a heavy one")
BaselineA: Statute: Young Offenders Act, S.C. 1980-81-82-83, c. 110, s. 16 (especially s. 16(1) and the s. 16(2) factors; review provisions in s. 16(9)-(10) discussed but the key test is the transfer decision under s. 16)
CaseB_TestB: Damages for repudiation where contract has alternative modes of performance: adopt the mode "least profitable to the plaintiff, and the least burdensome to the defendant"; not a factual inquiry into how defendant would likely have performed but for repudiation
BaselineB: Common law principle on damages for breach with alternative performances, traced to Cockburn v. Alexander (1848) and explained in Withers v. General Theatre Corp. (1933) (as adopted/recognized in Canadian appellate authority cited)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Canadian maritime law (agency/mandate): whether an agent of an unnamed/partially disclosed principal is personally liable turns on the parties’ intention as shown by the contract—“a matter of construction of a particular contract”; “there is no prescribed formality for disclosure” and liability “depends on the will of the contracting parties” (e.g., “as agent only” indicates no personal liability).
BaselineA: Combination: Federal Court Act, R.S.C., 1985, c. F-7, ss. 2 (definition of “Canadian maritime law”) and 22(2)(m) (stevedoring within maritime law) + common law of contract/agency (as incorporated into Canadian maritime law; discussed with reference to ITO—International Terminal Operators Ltd. v. Miida Electronics Inc.).
CaseB_TestB: Child Welfare Act reporting immunity threshold: s. 38(6) protects an informant unless the report is made “maliciously or without reasonable cause”; “reasonable cause” is an objective threshold meaning “reasonable cause to ask CPS to consider looking into the matter” (not reasonable grounds to believe abuse occurred).
BaselineB: Statute: Child Welfare Act, R.S.N. 1990, c. C-12, ss. 38(1) (duty to report) and 38(6) (immunity unless “maliciously or without reasonable cause”).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Common-law limits on a warrantless frisk search incident to a lawful arrest: no reasonable/probable grounds prerequisite, but (1) discretionary (not a duty), (2) must be for a valid criminal-justice objective (safety/escape/evidence) and not an improper purpose, and (3) must be conducted non-abusively with proportionate physical/psychological constraint
BaselineA: Common law (search incident to arrest), as discussed through authorities including R. v. Brezack (Ont. C.A.), R. v. Morrison (Ont. C.A.), and R. v. Miller (Ont. C.A.)
CaseB_TestB: Section 7 minimum procedural requirements for warrantless child apprehension: no prior judicial authorization required where apprehension is in situations of “serious harm or risk of serious harm” to the child, but a “fair and prompt post-apprehension hearing” is constitutionally required
BaselineB: Statute + Charter: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7 applied to Child and Family Services Act, S.M. 1985-86, c. 8, ss. 17 and 21(1) (and post-apprehension process ss. 27(1), 29(1))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal negligence (s. 219): whether the accused’s conduct is a “marked departure from the norm” such that “wanton or reckless disregard” can be inferred; consequences (death) generally add nothing unless “so interwoven” with the conduct as to help characterize it
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 202(1)-(2), 203 (now ss. 219-220)), as interpreted in R. v. Tutton, [1989] 1 S.C.R. 1392 (marked departure central under both objective and subjective approaches)
CaseB_TestB: CITT standing/jurisdiction under AIT procurement regime: a non-Canadian supplier has no standing; for AIT to apply the procurement must be “within Canada”, which requires the supplier to be a “Canadian supplier” (AIT art. 518: “a place of business in Canada”)
BaselineB: Statute and regulation incorporating a trade agreement: Canadian International Trade Tribunal Act, ss. 30.1, 30.11(1) and Canadian International Trade Tribunal Procurement Inquiry Regulations, s. 3(1), interpreted in light of the Agreement on Internal Trade, especially arts. 501, 502 and 518
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 8 reasonableness of compelled document production in a regulatory/tax audit: s. 231(3) demand is a “seizure” but is reasonable under a flexible, context-specific standard (Hunter criteria not mechanically required in regulatory schemes).
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law/constitutional doctrine: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 8 applied to Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1952, c. 148, ss. 231(3) (demand for information/documents), 238(2) (offence for non-compliance), and privacy protection in s. 241; baseline s. 8 framework from Hunter v. Southam Inc. and related s. 8 cases (e.g., Simmons, Hufsky) as discussed in the reasons.
CaseB_TestB: Public interest standing test (purposive, flexible weighing): (1) serious justiciable issue; (2) plaintiff has a real stake/genuine interest; (3) proposed suit is, “in all of the circumstances”, a “reasonable and effective means” to bring the issue to court (not a strict ‘no other way’ requirement).
BaselineB: Common law doctrine of standing from SCC precedents, especially Minister of Justice of Canada v. Borowski and Canadian Council of Churches v. Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration) (three-factor standing framework), as refined/clarified in this decision.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Duty to defend is determined by the pleadings: the insurer must defend only where the suit seeks “damages which are or may be payable under the terms of this Policy”; “the pleadings govern the duty to defend”, and the duty does not arise for allegations “clearly beyond the scope of the policy”.
BaselineA: Common law principles of insurance contract interpretation applied to the policy’s defence clause and exclusions (including the pleaded-claims approach: “the pleadings govern the duty to defend”).
CaseB_TestB: Criminal Code s. 265(4) “air of reality” threshold for honest but mistaken belief in consent: a defence is left to the jury only if there is “sufficient evidence” such that “a reasonable jury properly instructed could acquit”; requires evidence “beyond the mere assertion” of belief (no need for evidence independent of the accused).
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 265(4)) interpreted as codifying the common-law ‘air of reality’ requirement for defences (citing Pappajohn, Bulmer, Robertson, etc.).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Deductibility of wage-continuation benefits from tort damages for lost earnings (collateral benefits rule for wages): “As a general rule, wage benefits paid while a plaintiff is unable to work must be brought into account and deducted from the claim for lost earnings”, with a limited subrogation/trust exception where the payer is entitled to reimbursement.
BaselineA: Common law damages principles (compensation for “actual loss” and no double recovery), drawing on the SCC personal injury damages trilogy (Andrews v. Grand & Toy Alberta Ltd.; Thornton v. Prince George School Board; Arnold v. Teno) and collateral benefits authorities (e.g., Parry v. Cleaver; Bradburn v. Great Western Rail. Co.).
CaseB_TestB: Restitution/unjust enrichment preconditions (used to reject suppliers’ claim for GST collection costs): restitution requires “(1) an enrichment, (2) a corresponding deprivation, and (3) a lack of any juridical reason for the enrichment” (Pettkus v. Becker), and a valid statute supplies the “juridical reason”.
BaselineB: Common law restitution/unjust enrichment test from Pettkus v. Becker (three-part test: enrichment, corresponding deprivation, absence of juristic/juridical reason).
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Test for entitlement to a compensatory allowance under art. 559 C.C.Q.: claimant must prove (1) contribution, (2) enrichment of spouse’s patrimony, (3) causal link/correlation, and (4) proportion; enrichment must “subsist” and is evaluated “at the time of the divorce”, with “great flexibility” in evaluating the elements (bankruptcy is not irrefutable proof of no subsisting enrichment).
BaselineA: Statute (Civil Code of Quebec, art. 559) informed by civil-law unjust enrichment principles (e.g., Cie Immobilière Viger Ltée v. Lauréat Giguère Inc.).
CaseB_TestB: Misapprehension-of-evidence test for setting aside a conviction: misapprehension must go to “the substance” not “detail”, be “material” not “peripheral”, and (conjunctively) the errors must play an “essential part” in the reasoning process resulting in conviction (miscarriage of justice under Criminal Code s. 686(1)(a)(iii)).
BaselineB: Common law test adopted from R. v. Morrissey (Ont. C.A.) and endorsed with reference to R. v. C. (R.), applied within the statutory appeal grounds in Criminal Code, s. 686(1)(a)(iii) (and interaction with s. 686(1)(a)(i)).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Copyright infringement for software embedded in ROM: a computer program originating in copyrightable written form remains protected when replicated in a silicon chip if the chip embodies a reproduction of the program in a material form (a “static object encoded with written instructions”, not merely a “dynamic interchange of electrical impulses”).
BaselineA: Statute (Copyright Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-30, s. 3(1), especially the right to “produce or reproduce the work ... in any material form whatever”).
CaseB_TestB: Common law de facto taking (constructive expropriation) test: compensation is owed only if (1) there is “an acquisition of a beneficial interest in the property or flowing from it”, and (2) there is “removal of all reasonable uses of the property”.
BaselineB: Common law (as stated in the decision, drawing on Manitoba Fisheries Ltd. v. The Queen; The Queen in Right of British Columbia v. Tener; and Mariner Real Estate Ltd. v. Nova Scotia (Attorney General)).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Novation (mortgage/assumption context): three-part test—(1) new debtor assumes complete liability; (2) creditor accepts new debtor as principal debtor (not agent/guarantor); (3) creditor accepts new contract “in full satisfaction and substitution for the old contract” (novation not found absent “really compelling” circumstances showing creditor assent).
BaselineA: Common law (novation doctrine), as stated in Polson v. Wulffsohn (1890) and applied/clarified in this decision; discussed alongside statutory context (The Limitation of Civil Rights Act, R.S.S. 1978, c. L-16, ss. 2, 40).
CaseB_TestB: De facto taking (constructive expropriation) test: compensation at common law requires (1) “an acquisition of a beneficial interest in the property or flowing from it”, and (2) “removal of all reasonable uses of the property”.
BaselineB: Common law (de facto taking), drawn from Mariner Real Estate Ltd. v. Nova Scotia (A.G.), Manitoba Fisheries Ltd. v. The Queen, and The Queen in Right of British Columbia v. Tener; applied in statutory setting (Vancouver Charter, especially s. 569).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Applicability of Criminal Code s. 443 (now s. 487) search-warrant power to offences under “any other Act of Parliament” even where that other Act (e.g., Bankruptcy Act) has its own search provisions: on a plain reading, s. 443(1)(a)-(b) applies to proceedings under any federal statute; only para. (e) is expressly “subject to any other Act of Parliament”.
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 443(1)(a)-(b) as amended in 1985 to add “or any other Act of Parliament” (and relatedly s. 443(1)(e) “subject to any other Act of Parliament”); considered alongside Bankruptcy Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. B-3, s. 6.
CaseB_TestB: Meaning of “risks willingly assumed” in Occupiers’ Liability Act s. 4(1): s. 4(1) embodies the volenti doctrine, requiring more than mere knowledge—i.e., knowledge plus consent/waiver of legal rights (“the plaintiff has assumed both the physical and the legal risk”); the exception is “very narrow”.
BaselineB: Statute interpreted in light of common law: Occupiers’ Liability Act, R.S.O. 1980, c. 322, ss. 2, 3(1), 4(1); common-law volenti as articulated in SCC cases cited in the reasons (Dube v. Labar; Crocker v. Sundance Northwest Resorts Ltd.).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 32 applicability to non-core government entities (universities): focus on whether government control is merely “ultimate or extraordinary” versus “routine or regular” over the entity’s “core functions” (and thus whether the impugned policy is government action)
BaselineA: Common law constitutional doctrine interpreting Charter s. 32(1), applied from McKinney v. University of Guelph (1990) and referencing RWDSU v. Dolphin Delivery Ltd. (1986) (government action / sufficient connection analysis)
CaseB_TestB: Leave to appeal a commercial arbitral award under Arbitration Act s. 31(2)(a): threshold question of law; “may prevent a miscarriage of justice” requires a material legal error with “arguable merit” (some possibility of success), plus residual discretion factors
BaselineB: Statute (Arbitration Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 55, s. 31(2)(a)); with common-law framing of what counts as a “question of law” in contractual interpretation (abandoning the historical rule; relying on Housen and Southam) and BCIT for leave considerations
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Limit on using the Paré “single transaction” analysis: it applies only to murder classification under Criminal Code s. 214(5) (now s. 231(5)), and only after the Crown first proves the accused committed (or was a party to) both the underlying offence and the murder; only then may the court ask whether the offences were “sufficiently closely connected in time” to classify the murder as first degree.
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 214(5) (now R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 231(5))) as interpreted in R. v. Paré, [1987] 2 S.C.R. 618 (single transaction / meaning of “while committing”).
CaseB_TestB: Forum non conveniens test: once jurisdiction is properly assumed, the party seeking a stay must show another forum is “clearly a more appropriate forum”; the court considers multiple, context-specific factors and asks whether “one forum ultimately emerge[s] as clearly more appropriate,” with the stay decision being discretionary and owed deference absent legal error or serious factual error.
BaselineB: Common law (Club Resorts Ltd. v. Van Breda, 2012 SCC 17) governing forum non conveniens; with reference to codified factor-lists (e.g., CJPTA s. 11; C.C.Q. art. 3135) as persuasive guides rather than the direct legal source in Ontario.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Abuse of process stay test (Keyowski/Jewitt/Young): a stay is granted only in the “clearest of cases” where compelling the accused to stand trial would violate fundamental principles of justice/fair play and decency, or where proceedings are “oppressive or vexatious” (and, per Conway, where the “affront to fair play and decency is disproportionate to the societal interest” in prosecution).
BaselineA: Common law (as summarized from R. v. Jewitt adopting R. v. Young; reaffirmed in R. v. Keyowski; explained in R. v. Conway).
CaseB_TestB: When the curative proviso applies (Criminal Code, s. 686(1)(b)(iii)): an appellate court asks whether there is “any reasonable possibility that the verdict would have been different had the error at issue not been made” (i.e., whether the verdict would “necessarily have been the same” absent the error).
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(b)(iii)), interpreted through prior SCC cases (e.g., Colpitts; Wildman; S.(P.L.); Broyles; B.(F.F.)).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Two-step test for institutional impartiality (structural bias) of part-time judges’ outside occupation: (1) would a fully informed person have a reasonable apprehension of bias in a substantial number of cases? (2) if yes (occupation per se incompatible), do safeguards sufficiently minimize the risk so that a fully informed person would not have that apprehension in a substantial number of cases?
BaselineA: Common law / Charter jurisprudence: reasonable apprehension of bias test from Committee for Justice and Liberty v. National Energy Board, adopted in Valente v. The Queen for s. 11(d) independence/impartiality; applied to Charter s. 11(d) and Quebec Charter s. 23.
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 2(b) infringement and s. 1 justification analysis for Criminal Code s. 181 (false news): determine if expression is protected under Irwin Toy (all meaning-conveying expression unless violent form), then whether s. 181’s purpose/effect restricts it; if so, assess s. 1 (including identifying a pressing and substantial objective tied to Parliament’s original purpose and proportionality/minimal impairment).
BaselineB: Common law / constitutional doctrine: Irwin Toy Ltd. v. Quebec (Attorney General) framework for s. 2(b) infringement; R. v. Oakes framework for s. 1 justification; applied to Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 181 and Charter ss. 2(b) and 1.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 96 “core jurisdiction” / Residential Tenancies step-one historical inquiry (as applied to youth courts): properly characterize the impugned jurisdiction, then ask whether it was exercised exclusively by s. 96 courts at Confederation; if the jurisdiction is novel (did not exist in 1867), it is not within the s. 96 core and may be conferred on an inferior court
BaselineA: Common law constitutional test from Re Residential Tenancies Act, 1979, [1981] 1 SCR 714 (three-step s. 96 analysis), as refined in Sobeys Stores Ltd. v. Yeomans, [1989] 1 SCR 238; applied to s. 96 of the Constitution Act, 1867
CaseB_TestB: Interpretation of “sold in any market in Canada” (Patent Act ss. 80(1)(b), 83(1), 85): for PMPRB jurisdiction, “sold in any market in Canada” includes sales of medicines “regulated by the public laws of Canada”, “delivered in Canada”, “dispensed in Canada”, and where “the cost of the medicine will be borne by Canadians”
BaselineB: Statutory interpretation of Patent Act, RSC 1985, c P-4, ss. 80(1)(b), 81(1)(a), 83(1), 85, applying the modern principle of interpretation (Canada Trustco Mortgage Co. v. Canada, 2005 SCC 54)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Adequacy of an indictment / whether a proven conspiracy falls within the scope of the conspiracy charged: indictment is adequate if it gives the accused “reasonable information” to identify the transaction and prepare a defence; and, for multiple-conspiracy proof, “it is sufficient if the evidence adduced demonstrates that the conspiracy proven included some of the accused, establishes that it occurred at some time within the time frame alleged in the indictment, and had as its object the type of crime alleged.”
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 510, 512, 516(1)(g)) as interpreted through SCC/common-law principles (notably R. v. Côté; R. v. Wis Development Corp.; R. v. B.(G.); and conspiracy-indictment construction principles from R. v. Cotroni).
CaseB_TestB: Section 96 (Residential Tenancies) analysis for conferral of jurisdiction + core jurisdiction characterization: apply Re Residential Tenancies Act, 1979—first ask whether the power “broadly conforms to a power or jurisdiction exercised by a superior, district or county court at the time of Confederation”; if not, “the inquiry ends”; and even if it passes, assess whether the legislation removes a matter within the superior courts’ protected “core” (requiring a narrow characterization of the subject matter).
BaselineB: Common law constitutional test (Re Residential Tenancies Act, 1979; MacMillan Bloedel; Reference re Amendments to the Residential Tenancies Act (N.S.)) applied to a statutory scheme (Canada Evidence Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-5, ss. 38 to 38.16) and constitutional text (Constitution Act, 1867, s. 96).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Entrapment (random virtue-testing) under Mack: police may offer an opportunity only with (i) reasonable suspicion about the person, OR (ii) a bona fide inquiry into a sufficiently precise area where the offence is likely occurring; random virtue-testing exists only if neither (i) nor (ii) is present
BaselineA: Common law (R. v. Mack, [1988] 2 S.C.R. 903)
CaseB_TestB: Appellate review of trial judge’s voluntariness ruling on a statement: a court of appeal should not reweigh the evidence from the voir dire absent a “serious, specific and determining error”
BaselineB: Common law (admissibility of statements/voluntariness; specific baseline cases not identified in the reasons provided)
JudgeB: LeBel J. (for the Court, oral reasons)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Duty of trial judge to comment on Crown counsel’s improper jury address: where Crown remarks are “prejudicial to a degree sufficient to impose a legal duty on the trial judge to comment” to ensure the defence position is “fairly put to the jury”; failure to do so is an error of law (with no curative proviso applied here under s. 686(1)(b)(iii)).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, s. 686(1)(b)(iii)) plus common-law principles on fair trial/jury instructions (as reflected through adoption of Ayles J.A.’s formulation).
CaseB_TestB: Broker commission triggers under brokerage contract: (1) no “agreement to sell” unless the accepted promise to purchase is “unconditional” — i.e., “so long as a promise to purchase is not unconditionally binding ... and it is not yet possible ... to bring an action to compel transfer of title, there is no ‘agreement to sell’”; and (2) “voluntarily prevents the free performance” requires proof that fulfilment was prevented “through the fault of the seller” (mirroring art. 1503 C.C.Q.).
BaselineB: Statute and contract interpretation (Civil Code of Québec, arts. 1396 and 1503; interpreted alongside standard-form brokerage contract clauses 6.1(3o) and 6.1(4o)).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 16(2) insanity test — meaning of the two branches: (1) incapacity to appreciate the “nature and quality” of the act (physical character/consequences only) vs. (2) incapacity to know the act is “wrong” (as redefined in Chaulk to mean morally wrong). Key clarifications: first branch is limited to “incapable of appreciating the physical consequences of his act”; second branch turns on incapacity to know the act was “morally wrong”.
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 16(2)); prior SCC interpretations in Cooper v. The Queen, Kjeldsen v. The Queen, R. v. Abbey (first branch) and R. v. Chaulk (meaning of “wrong” in second branch).
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 8 sniffer-dog search authorization — “reasonable suspicion” standard: must be more than a hunch; must be grounded in “objectively discernible facts” assessed on the “totality of the circumstances”, through the lens of a reasonable officer with training/experience; asks whether facts indicate the “possibility” (not probability) of criminal behaviour (“We are looking here at possibilities, not probabilities. Are the facts objectively indicative of the possibility of criminal behaviour... If so... met. If not, the inquiry is at an end.”).
BaselineB: Common law Charter s. 8 framework for sniffer-dog searches from R. v. Kang-Brown and R. v. A.M., clarified with R. v. Chehil; applied under Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 8 (and related discussion of s. 9 detention).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Legitimate expectations doctrine limits: it is procedural only (consultation/representations), creates no substantive rights (no consent/veto), and does not apply to the legislative process (so cannot bar introducing a money bill). Key quotes: legitimate expectations is "simply an extension of the rules of natural justice and procedural fairness" and "can only create a right to make representations or to be consulted"; "There is no support... that the doctrine of legitimate expectations can create substantive rights"; and "the doctrine does not apply to the legislative process" (including bill formulation/introduction).
BaselineA: Common law administrative law doctrine of legitimate expectations as procedural fairness (as summarized from Old St. Boniface Residents Assn. Inc. v. Winnipeg (City) and related cases such as Inuit Tapirisat; also tied to constitutional principles of parliamentary sovereignty/lex parliamenti).
CaseB_TestB: Divorce Act s. 17 variation framework for spousal support: before varying, court "shall satisfy itself" there has been a "change in the condition, means, needs or other circumstances" since the order (s. 17(4)) and, in making the variation, "shall take into consideration that change"; variation order "should" pursue objectives in s. 17(7) (recognize economic advantages/disadvantages, apportion child-care financial consequences, relieve economic hardship, and promote self-sufficiency "in so far as practicable").
BaselineB: Statute (Divorce Act, 1985, s. 17(4) and s. 17(7)).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Extradition under s. 7: surrender is unconstitutional only if it places the fugitive in a situation that “sufficiently shocks” the Canadian conscience / is “simply unacceptable”, assessed contextually (offence/penalty, foreign justice system safeguards, comity and security) with “due latitude” to the Minister’s balancing discretion.
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law/Charter: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7; Extradition Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. E-23, s. 25; and the s. 7 extradition standard from Canada v. Schmidt ("shock the conscience") and United States v. Allard ("simply unacceptable").
CaseB_TestB: Search warrants for media premises: after meeting Criminal Code s. 487(1)(b), the justice must assess the “overall reasonableness” of the search under s. 8 in light of s. 2(b), considering all circumstances and striking a “delicate balance”; alternative sources are ordinarily disclosed but are not a mandatory prerequisite.
BaselineB: Statute plus Charter overlay: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 487(1)(b), (d), (e) (warrant preconditions and discretion), interpreted in light of Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 2(b) and 8; drawing on Re Pacific Press Ltd. and The Queen and Descôteaux v. Mierzwinski for the discretionary balancing approach.
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Reasonable apprehension of bias (pecuniary interest) test: “Would a reasonably well-informed person consider that the interest might have an influence on the exercise of the official’s public duty?” (applied to whether Law Society costs power creates institutional bias)
BaselineA: Common law (administrative law/natural justice), applying Old St. Boniface Residents Assn. Inc. v. Winnipeg (City), [1990] 3 S.C.R. 1170 (and the broader reasonable apprehension of bias jurisprudence)
CaseB_TestB: Nelles malicious prosecution test (lifting prosecutorial immunity): plaintiff must prove (1) prosecution initiated by defendant; (2) terminated in plaintiff’s favour; (3) absence of reasonable and probable cause (subjective + objective); and (4) malice/improper purpose (“deliberate and improper use of the office… inconsistent with the status of ‘minister of justice’”)
BaselineB: Common law, following Nelles v. Ontario, [1989] 2 S.C.R. 170
JudgeB: Iacobucci and Binnie JJ. (for McLachlin C.J. and Iacobucci, Major and Binnie JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Colour of right / mistake of law bar: colour of right is unavailable unless the offence definition embraces it; and a mistaken belief that the law is inoperative is a mistake of law and no defence (Criminal Code, s. 19).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, ss. 19 and 206(1)(d)) plus common-law principle that mistake of law is no defence (as expressed in s. 19).
CaseB_TestB: Modified Taylor ‘hatred’ test under Saskatchewan Human Rights Code s. 14(1)(b): apply objectively whether a reasonable person, aware of context, would view the expression as likely to expose a protected group to ‘detestation’ and ‘vilification’ (effects-focused; intent irrelevant), and strike ‘ridicules, belittles or otherwise affronts the dignity of’.
BaselineB: Statute (Saskatchewan Human Rights Code, s. 14(1)(b)) interpreted through prior SCC common-law/constitutional framework in Canada (Human Rights Commission) v. Taylor (definition of hatred) and Charter analysis context.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Test for granting leave to intervene: applicant must have a “sufficient interest” and “bring a special perspective”; intervention may be limited/conditioned where a new Charter issue or new evidentiary material could prejudice a party (e.g., if the Charter argument “would have been affected by additional evidence at trial”; proposed material not filed if it is “fresh evidence” absent consent/leave).
BaselineA: Common law / SCC practice on intervention and prejudice from raising new issues; applied in the context of a proposed Charter interpretive argument and proposed extra-record materials.
CaseB_TestB: Interpretation of Criminal Code s. 182(b) (“offers any indignity”): (1) physical interference/contact is sufficient but not necessary; (2) the indignity must be offered to “a dead human body or human remains” (not “monuments per se”); (3) where monuments mark the presence/final resting place of human remains, indignities to those monuments constitute indignities to the human remains.
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 182(b); also ss. 683(1)(g) and 695(1) re amendment power, though the key test is s. 182(b) scope).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: When the federal Environmental Assessment and Review Process Guidelines Order applies: there must be a “proposal” (an “initiative, undertaking or activity for which the Government of Canada has a decision making responsibility”), meaning an affirmative federal “regulatory duty” (a “legal duty or obligation”) under an Act of Parliament; the department with that duty is the “initiating department” and must run the self-assessment process (screening and, if significant, panel review).
BaselineA: Regulation and statute: Environmental Assessment and Review Process Guidelines Order, SOR/84-467 (ss. 2 “proposal”/“initiating department”, 3, 6) made under Department of the Environment Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. E-10, s. 6; applied alongside Navigable Waters Protection Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. N-22, s. 5.
CaseB_TestB: Appellate review of alleged jury-charge error re post-offence conduct and intent: determine whether the impugned instruction is an error justifying intervention under Criminal Code s. 686(1)(a) (unreasonable verdict / error of law / miscarriage of justice), reading the charge “as a whole” and “in its entire context”; if error, apply the curative proviso in s. 686(1)(b)(iii) (harmless error or overwhelming evidence).
BaselineB: Statute and common law: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, ss. 686(1)(a) and 686(1)(b)(iii); post-offence conduct limits from R. v. Arcangioli, [1994] 1 S.C.R. 129 and R. v. White, [1998] 2 S.C.R. 72; curative proviso framework from R. v. Khan, 2001 SCC 86.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 133 applies to all instruments of a legislative nature; courts look to substance over form: if the net effect of a series of discrete acts is legislative, then each component act is also legislative and must be printed/published in both languages (badges: rule of conduct, force of law, applies to an undetermined number of persons).
BaselineA: Constitution Act, 1867, s. 133, as interpreted in Reference re Manitoba Language Rights (1985; 1992) (legislative nature inquiry: connection to legislature; badges: (1) embodies a rule of conduct, (2) has force of law, (3) applies to an undetermined number of persons).
CaseB_TestB: Responsive-answer requirement on jury questions about reasonable doubt: even with an unassailable Lifchus charge, when the jury asks about the standard of proof the trial judge must attempt to answer and must not discourage further questions; repeating the charge may suffice in some cases but not where it is non-responsive and closes the door to follow-up.
BaselineB: Common law on jury instructions/recharge, especially R. v. Lifchus (1997) (model reasonable doubt charge) and R. v. S. (W.D.) (1994) (jury questions must be answered “in a complete and careful manner”; recharge must be “correct and comprehensive”).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Mistaken transfer + recipient knowledge + transferor right of recovery ⇒ property does not pass for criminal-law theft; subsequent fraudulent conversion with intent to deprive constitutes theft
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 322(1)) interpreted with reference to property-law concepts of mistake and recovery rights
CaseB_TestB: Dunsmuir standard-of-review selection and application: only correctness or reasonableness; for IAD s. 67(1)(c) H&C decisions, apply reasonableness and ask whether outcome falls within a range of acceptable outcomes (no reweighing of evidence)
BaselineB: Combination of common law (Dunsmuir v. New Brunswick) and statute (Federal Courts Act, R.S.C., 1985, c. F-7, s. 18.1; IRPA, S.C. 2001, c. 27, s. 67(1)(c))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 11(b) unreasonable delay analysis (Morin factors + institutional-delay guideline): a "judicial determination balancing" the s. 11(b) interests against four factors—(1) length of delay; (2) waiver; (3) reasons for delay (incl. inherent requirements, actions of accused/Crown, institutional limits, other); and (4) prejudice—plus a non-mechanical administrative guideline of "between 8 and 10 months" for institutional delay in Provincial Courts (influenced by prejudice).
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional text (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 11(b) and remedial trigger via s. 24(1)) as developed in prior SCC jurisprudence (Mills v. The Queen; R. v. Rahey; R. v. Conway; R. v. Smith; R. v. Askov).
CaseB_TestB: Contractor/subcontractor liability where loss caused by overloading: even if supports yielded first, the subcontractor is not liable where the "true cause" is the general contractor’s fault in overloading contrary to contract/specs; the subcontractor "must at least be entitled" to defend by showing the damage was due to "the fault of the [general] contractor himself" and had "no obligation to furnish supports capable of withstanding this overload" that it was not forewarned of and not obliged to foresee.
BaselineB: Civil Code (Quebec) arts. 1684, 1688, 1065, and the SCC-stated principle in Hill, Clarke-Francis Ltd. v. Northland Groceries (Quebec) Ltd. that a builder can avoid liability by proving the damage is due to force majeure/Act of God/"fault of the owner"/act of a third party; applied by analogy to contractor–subcontractor relations.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Secret commissions offence (Criminal Code s. 426(1)(a)(ii)): actus reus requires (1) agency relationship; (2) agent accepts a benefit as consideration for an act/forbearance in relation to the principal’s affairs; and (3) failure to make “adequate and timely disclosure of the source, amount and nature of the benefit”; mens rea requires awareness of each element; “corruptly” means “secretly or without the requisite disclosure” and there is no “corrupt bargain” requirement.
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 426(1)(a) (as applied to s. 426(1)(a)(ii) secret commissions); as interpreted in R. v. Kelly (released concurrently and followed).
CaseB_TestB: Criminal Code s. 686(1)(b)(iii) curative proviso: ask “whether a jury properly instructed could, acting reasonably, have come to a different conclusion absent the error”; jury findings may be considered if not tainted by the error.
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(b)(iii).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: State Immunity Act s. 5 “commercial activity” exception: two-step, contextual inquiry—(1) determine the nature of the foreign state’s activity (considering its context, including purpose where helpful), and (2) assess whether the Canadian proceedings “relate” to the commercial aspect by a sufficient “nexus” (more than merely ‘touch on’ or ‘incidentally affect’), considering competing nexus to sovereign aspects and the practical consequences of the proceedings
BaselineA: Statute (State Immunity Act, S.C. 1980-81-82-83, c. 95, ss. 2 and 5) codifying the common law restrictive immunity approach (acts jure imperii vs. jure gestionis; contextual approach discussed via I Congreso del Partido)
CaseB_TestB: Compatibility of provincial “pay-and-retain/compensation” mechanisms with the BIA scheme of distribution: determine whether the provincial mechanism goes beyond BIA s. 97(3) set-off; apply a timing-based framework—(i) if payment and mutual debts are certain, liquid, and exigible pre-bankruptcy, legal compensation operates and the trustee takes no claim; (ii) if payment is pre-bankruptcy but the contractor’s claim is not liquid, compensation may be set up via BIA s. 97(3); (iii) if payment is post-bankruptcy, subrogatory payment cannot give rise to compensation (mutual debts must exist pre-bankruptcy), though the payer may prove a claim under BIA s. 121; equitable set-off is inapplicable in Quebec bankruptcy
BaselineB: Statutes and civil law rules: Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. B-3 (esp. ss. 97(3), 121, 136-147) interacting with Quebec provisions (AIAOD s. 316; ALRCI s. 54) and Civil Code of Québec rules on subrogation/compensation (arts. 1651, 1656(3), 1672-1673, 1681)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Quebec civil law “obligation to inform” (duty of disclosure) in contracts of enterprise: (1) debtor’s knowledge (actual or presumed) of the information; (2) information is of “decisive importance”; and (3) creditor cannot inform itself or is “legitimately relying” on the debtor; with the obligation’s content in large projects varying with (a) allocation of risk, (b) relative expertise, and (c) the contract’s “continuing formation” via change orders.
BaselineA: Civil Code of Lower Canada arts. 1024 (good faith), 1053 (delictual fault) (and related Quebec jurisprudence on the obligation to inform; SCC examples discussed include Ross v. Dunstall (1921), Air Canada v. McDonnell Douglas Corp., National Bank of Canada v. Soucisse, Houle v. Canadian National Bank).
CaseB_TestB: Judicial reform test for changing Canadian maritime common law (to remove the contributory-negligence bar): courts may make incremental change where (1) it is “clearly necessary to keep the law in step with the ‘dynamic and evolving fabric of our society’” and (2) the change’s ramifications are not “unforeseeable or complex”/“beyond the cognizance of the judiciary” (Watkins v. Olafson; R. v. Salituro).
BaselineB: Common law (Canadian maritime law/common law of tort), with the reform framework drawn from Watkins v. Olafson and R. v. Salituro; applied to the maritime contributory-negligence bar.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Duty to accommodate (employer/union/complainant) in adverse-effect discrimination: take "reasonable measures short of undue hardship"; union liable if it (1) "cause[s] or contribute[s]" to the discriminatory rule or (2) "impedes" reasonable accommodation; complainant must "facilitate" and accept reasonable accommodation
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Human Rights Act, S.B.C. 1984, c. 22, ss. 8(1)(a),(b),(4) and 9(a)-(c), as interpreted through SCC duty-to-accommodate jurisprudence (Ontario Human Rights Commission and O'Malley v. Simpsons-Sears Ltd.; Central Alberta Dairy Pool v. Alberta (Human Rights Commission))
CaseB_TestB: Exclusive arbitral jurisdiction under s. 45(1) OLRA: courts are ousted if the dispute, in its "essential character", arises from the "interpretation, application, administration or alleged violation" of the collective agreement
BaselineB: Statute interpreted in light of SCC labour-arbitration exclusivity jurisprudence: Ontario Labour Relations Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. L.2, s. 45(1), building on St. Anne Nackawic Pulp & Paper Co. v. Canadian Paper Workers Union, Local 219
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Trial judge’s discretion to exclude cross-examination on a collateral credibility matter where its (tenuous) relevance does not outweigh its prejudicial effect/misleading potential
BaselineA: Common law (trial management/evidence discretion; applied R. v. Meddoui, [1991] 3 S.C.R. 320)
CaseB_TestB: Interest deductibility under ITA s. 20(1)(c)(i): whether, considering all the circumstances, the taxpayer had a reasonable expectation of income at the time the investment was made (and “income” means income subject to tax, not net income)
BaselineB: Statute (Income Tax Act, s. 20(1)(c)(i); interpreted with reference to Bronfman Trust v. The Queen and Shell Canada Ltd. v. Canada)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 10(b) “detention” at a port of entry: routine secondary immigration questioning is not “detention” unless the restriction goes beyond what is required for processing entry and becomes a restraint of liberty (Therens/Simmons applied; factors include routine screening purpose and absence of stigma). Key quotes: detention requires an agent of the state assuming control over movement by a demand/direction with significant legal consequence; but at the border, “routine questioning ... do[es] not constitute detention” and there must be “some action ... to indicate that the restriction ... has gone beyond that required for the processing ... and has become a restraint of liberty”.
BaselineA: Common law constitutional interpretation of Charter s. 10(b) “detention”, baseline from R. v. Therens and R. v. Simmons (also discussed: R. v. Jacoy; R. v. Kwok (Ont. C.A.)).
CaseB_TestB: Elements of civil contempt (common law): three elements proved beyond a reasonable doubt — (1) the order “must state clearly and unequivocally what should and should not be done”; (2) the alleged contemnor had actual knowledge of the order; and (3) the alleged contemnor “intentionally” did the prohibited act or failed to do the compelled act. SCC clarifies no “contumacious intent”/intent to interfere with administration of justice is required: “All that is required ... is proof beyond a reasonable doubt of an intentional act or omission that is in breach of a clear order of which the alleged contemnor has notice.”
BaselineB: Common law of civil contempt (elements drawn from cases cited in reasons, including Bhatnager v. Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration) and other appellate authorities; applied alongside Ontario Rules of Civil Procedure r. 60.11 governing procedure).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Admissibility of bad-character/disposition evidence: admissible if (1) relevant to an issue other than disposition/character and (2) its probative value outweighs its prejudicial effect (with heightened concern where the act is “morally repugnant”); plus the requirement for a limiting jury instruction against propensity reasoning
BaselineA: Common law (bad character/disposition exclusion and probative value vs prejudicial effect balancing), as stated in Morris v. The Queen and applied with guidance from R. v. B. (C.R.) and R. v. D. (L.E.)
CaseB_TestB: Recent fabrication exception for prior consistent statements: where cross-examination amounts to an allegation of recent fabrication, prior complaint evidence is admissible only to rebut it, and only to prove the fact the complaint was made (not the truth of its contents)
BaselineB: Common law (rule against prior consistent statements and the recent-fabrication exception)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: R. v. B. (K.G.) reformed rule for substantive admissibility of a non-accused witness’s prior inconsistent statement (principled hearsay: necessity + threshold reliability with specified safeguards, plus voir dire screening)
BaselineA: Common law hearsay/orthodox prior-inconsistent-statement rule (Deacon v. The King) as applied through Canada Evidence Act, s. 9 procedure; principled hearsay approach from R. v. Khan and R. v. Smith
CaseB_TestB: Interpretive test for whether the art. 1056c C.C. second-paragraph “additional indemnity” is included within an insurer’s contractual obligation to pay “interest” (i.e., characterize both as delay damages and treat indemnity as part of interest payable under the policy)
BaselineB: Statute and contract interpretation: Civil Code art. 1056c (both paragraphs) applied to an insurance policy clause promising to pay “interest accrued on the amount of its guarantee from the date when the action was instituted”
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal fraud (Criminal Code, s. 380(1)) — “other fraudulent means”: actus reus requires conduct that a reasonable person would “properly ... stigmatize as dishonest” (objective dishonesty), and deprivation by actual loss or “placing of the victim’s pecuniary interests at risk”; mens rea requires subjective knowledge of the prohibited act and subjective knowledge that it could cause deprivation (including risk).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 380(1)), as interpreted through SCC/common law definitions in R. v. Théroux (1993) and R. v. Olan (1978) ("other fraudulent means" = means "properly ... stigmatized as dishonest").
CaseB_TestB: Union duty of representation in collective bargaining (Labour Code, s. 47.2): union must not act “in bad faith or in an arbitrary or discriminatory manner or show serious negligence”; duty is generally an “obligation of means” and, in bargaining, may require considering former employees’ interests but creates no “obligation of result” to secure retroactivity for them.
BaselineB: Statute (Labour Code, R.S.Q., c. C-27, s. 47.2; also discussed alongside ss. 67, 53, 59, 62) with supporting SCC jurisprudence on the duty of representation (Noël v. Société d’énergie de la Baie James; Centre hospitalier Régina Ltée).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Crown appeal from acquittal/new trial test under Criminal Code s. 686(4): Crown must show the verdict "would not necessarily have been the same" but for the legal error
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(4)) as interpreted in SCC precedent (Vézeau v. The Queen; reaffirmed in R. v. Morin)
JudgeA: Cory J. (for Sopinka, Cory, Iacobucci and Major JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Implied contractual notice requirement before enforcing security/appointing receiver: debtor must receive "reasonable notice" of intention to enforce security and "reasonable time to pay"; reasonableness assessed by multi-factor criteria (Mister Broadloom factors)
BaselineB: Common law (Lister (R.E.) Ltd. v. Dunlop Canada Ltd.; reasonableness criteria from Mister Broadloom; also citing Massey v. Sladen)
JudgeB: McLachlin and Bastarache JJ. (for the Court)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Engineer/design professional preparing tender documents owes no duty to advise/warn bidders about permits or difficulties tied to the contractor’s chosen method of performing the work, absent specific arrangements to the contrary (method is contractor’s responsibility).
BaselineA: Common law (construction/tendering negligence duty/standard of care allocating responsibility for means and methods to the contractor), relying on R. v. Paradis and Farley Inc., [1942] S.C.R. 10; Vermont Construction Inc. v. Beatson, [1977] 1 S.C.R. 758 (also citing Temar Construction Ltd. v. West Hill Redevelopment Co. (Ont. H.C.)).
CaseB_TestB: Framework for reviewing Crown decisions: (1) classify the decision as prosecutorial discretion (decisions about the “nature and extent of the prosecution”) vs tactics/conduct before the court; (2) if prosecutorial discretion, it is reviewable only for abuse of process (egregious conduct seriously compromising trial fairness or integrity of the justice system), with a threshold requirement that the accused first establish a proper evidentiary foundation before the Crown must justify its decision.
BaselineB: Common law/constitutional doctrine on prosecutorial discretion and judicial review, clarifying Krieger v. Law Society of Alberta, 2002 SCC 65, and applying the abuse of process standard (with threshold evidentiary foundation) from cases including R. v. Nixon, 2011 SCC 34; also in statutory context of Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 727(1) (Notice) and s. 255 (mandatory minimums).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Constitutional limits on warrantless searches under s. 10 NCA: warrantless search is authorized only where “exigent circumstances render it impracticable to obtain prior judicial authorization” (otherwise not “authorized by law” and violates Charter s. 8).
BaselineA: Combination: Charter s. 8 reasonableness framework from R. v. Collins, [1987] 1 S.C.R. 265 (search reasonable if “authorized by law”, law reasonable, manner reasonable) + statutory search power in Narcotic Control Act s. 10 (as constrained by R. v. Grant, [1993] 3 S.C.R. 000).
CaseB_TestB: ITA s. 241(3) disclosure exception: whether disclosure is permitted “in respect of proceedings relating to the administration or enforcement of” the Income Tax Act—interpreted broadly via the “widest possible scope” of “in respect of”/“relating to”, capturing bankruptcy-related proceedings connected to tax enforcement.
BaselineB: Statute: Income Tax Act, S.C. 1970-71-72, c. 63, s. 241(1)-(4) (especially s. 241(3)); interpreted in light of s. 222 (tax debts recoverable in court) and prior case law (e.g., Glover; Nowegijick).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Screen order for child complainant under Criminal Code s. 486(2.1): judge may order testimony behind a screen if (1) accused is charged with an enumerated offence, (2) complainant is under 18, and (3) the judge is of the opinion the exclusion is “necessary to obtain a full and candid account of the acts complained of from the complainant”; this discretion is constitutionally valid under Charter ss. 7 and 11(d).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 486(2.1)) applied/assessed against Charter ss. 7 and 11(d).
CaseB_TestB: Use of a prior conviction on a similar fact (identity) voir dire: where the accused puts identity for the prior act in issue, the Crown may tender the prior conviction as “some evidence” linking the accused to the similar act; challenging the conviction on the voir dire is not automatically barred but will be rare and may be refused where there is “no reasonable likelihood” the challenge will affect admissibility; overall, similar fact evidence remains presumptively inadmissible and is admitted only if probative value exceeds prejudicial effect.
BaselineB: Common law similar fact framework (R. v. Arp; R. v. Handy; and related admissibility principles) with limited statutory reference (Criminal Code s. 696.3(3)(a) as an example of a basis to show a conviction set aside).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Party liability for manslaughter (even if principal is guilty of murder): under s. 21(1) aiding/abetting or s. 21(2) common purpose, manslaughter mens rea is objective foreseeability of non-trivial harm (not death) from an inherently dangerous unlawful act; i.e., "the test is objective" and "[a]s long as the unlawful act is inherently dangerous and harm to another which is neither trivial nor transitory is its foreseeable consequence, the resultant death amounts to manslaughter"; under s. 21(2) a party is guilty of manslaughter if he did not foresee murder but "a reasonable person in all the circumstances would have foreseen at least a risk of harm".
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, ss. 21(1)(b),(c) and 21(2)) as interpreted through SCC unlawful-act manslaughter jurisprudence (R. v. Creighton; R. v. DeSousa; R. v. Kirkness; R. v. Trinneer).
CaseB_TestB: Entitlement to GST rebate for overpayment under Excise Tax Act: s. 261(1) turns on actual payment (not legal liability) of an amount "as or on account of" GST "in circumstances where the amount was not payable"; s. 261(2)(c) only bars a s. 261 rebate where a rebate "is payable" under ss. 215.1/216(6) (not merely available); and s. 296(2.1) requires the Minister on assessment to apply an "allowable rebate" even if not claimed within s. 261(3)'s two-year limit (since s. 296(2.1)(c) relieves against that limitation).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Policy vs. operational decision framework for Crown negligence in highway maintenance: a public authority owes a duty of care unless excluded by (i) an explicit statutory exemption or (ii) the impugned conduct being a “pure policy decision”; “budgetary allocations and the constraints which they entail in terms of allocation of resources cannot be made the subject of a duty of care”, while operational implementation may attract liability if negligent (Just v. British Columbia applied).
BaselineA: Common law (governmental liability in negligence) from Just v. British Columbia, [1989] 2 S.C.R. 1228 (also drawing on Anns v. Merton and Kamloops v. Nielsen); applied alongside interpretation of Public Highways Act, R.S.N.S. 1989, c. 371, ss. 4-5 and Proceedings against the Crown Act, R.S.N.S. 1989, c. 360, s. 5(1)(a).
CaseB_TestB: Damages in lieu of specific performance—assessment date and uniqueness: where a purchaser has a legitimate claim to specific performance and elects damages, it may be appropriate to assess damages at the date of trial/judgment (not necessarily breach) so damages are a “true substitute for specific performance”; additionally, “specific performance should ... not be granted as a matter of course absent evidence that the property is unique to the extent that its substitute would not be readily available.”
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: Courts of Justice Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.43, s. 99 (damages in substitution for specific performance) applied with common-law damages principles (Johnson v. Agnew; Wroth v. Tyler; and SCC guidance in Asamera Oil Corp. v. Seal Oil & General Corp.).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Abuse of process threshold in criminal proceedings: stay/remedy only in the “clearest of cases” (conduct that “shocks the conscience of the community”, with “overwhelming evidence” of unfairness; courts intervene only with “conspicuous evidence of improper motives or of bad faith” or an act “so wrong that it violates the conscience of the community”)
BaselineA: Common law doctrine of abuse of process (as affirmed in R. v. Jewitt; reiterated in R. v. Keyowski; discussed with R. v. Conway, R. v. Mack, R. v. Scott)
CaseB_TestB: Mr. Big confessions admissibility rule: presumptively inadmissible; Crown must show on a balance of probabilities that probative value (reliability) outweighs prejudicial effect, assessed via listed reliability circumstances and “markers of reliability” plus prejudice (moral/reasoning) considerations
BaselineB: Common law evidence (party admissions exception to hearsay) and existing exclusionary discretion; SCC creates a new common law rule specific to Mr. Big confessions
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 16(1) “knowing that it was wrong”: incapacity includes inability to rationally apply right/wrong to the particular act (capacity for rational perception and rational choice)
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 16(1)), interpreted in light of M'Naghten's Case and R. v. Chaulk
CaseB_TestB: Palmer criteria for admitting fresh evidence on appeal (including sentence appeals): (1) due diligence (flexible factor), (2) relevance, (3) credibility, (4) could reasonably be expected to have affected the result
BaselineB: Common law test from Palmer v. The Queen, applied within Criminal Code appellate-evidence discretion (ss. 683 and 687) under the overriding “interests of justice”
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Mohan test for admissibility of expert opinion evidence (relevance; necessity; no exclusionary rule; properly qualified expert), with added threshold scrutiny for novel science and for “expert disposition/profile” evidence requiring distinctive behavioural characteristics and a standardized, reliable profile
BaselineA: Common law (expert opinion and character evidence rules; prior SCC and other appellate authorities cited in the reasons, including R. v. Abbey, R. v. Béland, R. v. Morin, and R. v. Lupien)
CaseB_TestB: Section 745 Criminal Code parole-ineligibility review: jury must decide whether ineligibility “ought to be reduced” by weighing listed factors (character, conduct in custody, nature of offence, and other relevant matters) as a whole in a discretionary decision; fairness requires Crown not to undermine the statutory process with improper/inflammatory submissions
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 745(1)-(4), especially s. 745(2) listing factors and conferring discretion)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: s. 10(b) informational/implementational duties: no duty-counsel advice required where no duty counsel exists; further police duties are only triggered if detainee asserts desire to speak to a lawyer (a clear 'No' triggers no further obligations)
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 10(b) (as interpreted in R. v. Brydges and confirmed in R. v. Bartle; applied alongside the concurrent holding in R. v. Prosper that s. 10(b) imposes no positive obligation to provide duty counsel)
CaseB_TestB: Criminal Code s. 347 framework for late-payment penalties: (1) is the charge 'interest'—i.e., a charge (including a 'penalty') 'paid or payable for the advancing of credit under an agreement or arrangement' (with 'credit advanced' including deferral of payment for goods/services/benefits); and (2) s. 347(1)(b) liability assessed at time of payment using effective annual rate over period credit actually outstanding, except where criminal-rate payment arises from a 'voluntary act of the debtor' (Nelson) as defined
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 347(1)-(2) (interpreting 'interest', 'credit advanced', 'agreement or arrangement', and applying Nelson v. C.T.C. Mortgage Corp. as refined via Degelder Construction Co. v. Dancorp Developments Ltd.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 7 overbreadth (principles of fundamental justice) test: a law that deprives life/liberty/security violates s. 7 if it is "unnecessarily broad, going beyond what is needed to accomplish the governmental objective"; courts ask whether the means are "necessary" and "reasonably tailored" to the objective (overbreadth).
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7 (principles of fundamental justice) applied to Criminal Code, s. 179(1)(b). Key baseline articulation drawn from Re B.C. Motor Vehicle Act (s. 7 scope) and R. v. Nova Scotia Pharmaceutical Society (overbreadth/vagueness discussion) as cited in the reasons.
CaseB_TestB: Transfer pricing “reasonable amount in the circumstances” test under s. 69(2): determine whether the non-arm’s-length price exceeds what "would have been reasonable in the circumstances" at arm’s length; consider all relevant circumstances, including "agreements that may confer rights and benefits in addition to the purchase of property where those agreements are linked to the purchasing agreement"; ensure comparators are "sufficiently comparable" having regard to "economically relevant characteristics".
BaselineB: Statute: Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), s. 69(2) (now replaced by s. 247(2)).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Inference of possession from fingerprint evidence: whether an accused’s fingerprint on an article supports an inference of possession is “not subject to a hard and fast rule” but “a question of fact which depends on all of the circumstances of the case and all of the evidence adduced”; adverse inference from silence only once Crown proves a prima facie case supporting guilt beyond a reasonable doubt
BaselineA: Common law (circumstantial evidence/inference of possession from fingerprints; adverse inference from failure to testify once Crown case is strong). Key authorities discussed: R. v. O'Keefe (Ont. C.A.); R. v. Mehrabnia (Ont. Prov. Div.); R. v. Johnson (Ont. C.A., cited with approval in R. v. François, SCC).
CaseB_TestB: Review Board jurisdiction under Criminal Code Part XX.1: Boards may impose binding conditions on hospital authorities and may make conditions “regarding”/supervising treatment (including ordering re-evaluations and exploration of alternatives) but have no power to “prescribe”/“impose” treatment; s. 672.55(1) is not a true exception but an example of supervisory power
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, Part XX.1), especially ss. 672.54 and 672.55(1) (also discussed: ss. 672.1, 672.38-672.42, 672.58-672.62, 672.72-672.78).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 7 compellability / exemption from compulsion test: whether the “predominant purpose” of compelling the witness is to obtain incriminating evidence against them or to further a legitimate public purpose (with justification and prejudice analysis if predominant purpose is incrimination)
BaselineA: Combination: Charter (ss. 7 and 13) plus common-law/Charter self-incrimination jurisprudence, chiefly R. v. S. (R.J.), [1995] 1 S.C.R. 451 (as applied/clarified in the regulatory inquiry context under Securities Act, S.B.C. 1985, c. 83, s. 128(1))
CaseB_TestB: Timing rule for Corbett applications: the defence’s application to exclude prior convictions must be decided “immediately after the close of the Crown’s case,” with an optional pre-defence-case voir dire to inform the ruling (and possible later modification if defence evidence departs significantly)
BaselineB: Combination: statute (Canada Evidence Act, s. 12 discretion as interpreted in R. v. Corbett, [1988] 1 S.C.R. 670) plus common-law/Charter “case-to-meet” fairness principle under Charter s. 7
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 7 compellability / exemption from compulsion test: whether the “predominant purpose” of compelling the witness is to obtain incriminating evidence against them or “some legitimate public purpose”; if predominant purpose is to incriminate, compulsion must be justified and the witness may be non-compellable if there is “any other significant prejudice” beyond derivative use (Sopinka & Iacobucci JJ., relying on R. v. S. (R.J.))
BaselineA: Combination: Charter (s. 7, with s. 13 in the background) + common law/Charter doctrine from R. v. S. (R.J.), [1995] 1 S.C.R. 451; applied in the statutory regulatory setting of Securities Act, S.B.C. 1985, c. 83, s. 128(1)
CaseB_TestB: Section 15(1) prima facie discrimination test (Quebec v. A framework): (1) does the law create a distinction on an enumerated or analogous ground (on its face or in impact)? (2) does it impose “arbitrary — or discriminatory — disadvantage” by reinforcing/perpetuating/exacerbating disadvantage; claimant must show “disproportionate effect” linked to group membership
BaselineB: Common law/constitutional doctrine interpreting Charter s. 15(1), as set out in Quebec (Attorney General) v. A, 2013 SCC 5 (and related s. 15 cases such as Withler, Kapp, Andrews)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Tax-treaty residency under Canada–U.S. Income Tax Convention (1980) Art. IV(1): entity must be “liable to tax” in the contracting state “by reason of” an enumerated residence-type criterion (or one “of a similar nature”), which the Court interprets as requiring full (worldwide) tax liability rather than mere source-based liability
BaselineA: Statute/treaty: Canada-United States Tax Convention Act, 1984, Schedule I (Canada–U.S. Income Tax Convention (1980)), Art. IV(1) (“liable to tax therein by reason of ... domicile, residence, place of management, place of incorporation or any other criterion of a similar nature”) and Art. XII; applied against Income Tax Act, s. 212(1)(d)
CaseB_TestB: Trigger for Ontario Insurance Act limitation period: the two-year period in Insurance Act s. 281(5) runs only after a “valid refusal”; no valid refusal exists without adequate compliance with SABS s. 71, requiring notice of the dispute-resolution process “in straightforward and clear language, directed towards an unsophisticated person” and, “at a minimum”, including key steps and time limits
BaselineB: Statute/regulation: Insurance Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. I.8, s. 281(5) (two years after “insurer’s refusal”); Statutory Accident Benefits Schedule, O. Reg. 776/93, s. 71 (duty to inform of dispute-resolution procedure under Insurance Act ss. 279–283) (also discussed: SABS ss. 62(8), 72, 94)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Weber exclusive arbitral jurisdiction test: courts are ousted where the dispute’s “essential character” arises from the “interpretation, application, administration or alleged violation” of the collective agreement (s. 45(1)); focus on facts of the dispute, not legal labels (tort/Charter).
BaselineA: Statute (Ontario Labour Relations Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. L.2, s. 45(1)) interpreted in light of SCC labour-arbitration exclusivity jurisprudence (notably St. Anne Nackawic Pulp & Paper Co. v. Canadian Paper Workers Union, Local 219).
CaseB_TestB: Criminal Code s. 744 parole-ineligibility extension framework: judge may extend beyond 10 years “having regard to (1) the character of the offender, (2) the nature of the offence, and (3) the circumstances surrounding its commission”; 10 years is the general rule but can be “ousted” if those criteria justify longer; no “unusual circumstances” requirement.
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 744 (and related sentencing appeal provision s. 687(1))).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “loss of employment” for a retiring allowance: an employee is only “in the service” of the employer once under an obligation to provide services; therefore “loss of employment” cannot occur before that moment (no retiring allowance for loss of intended/prospective employment)
BaselineA: Statute (Income Tax Act): s. 56(1)(a)(ii) and s. 248(1) definitions of “retiring allowance”, “employment”, and “employee”
CaseB_TestB: Whether improper Crown closing submissions (personal anecdote not in evidence) caused an unfair trial/miscarriage of justice, assessed contextually using the “relevant factors” (from R. v. Stephan) including seriousness, prominence, objections, and adequacy of the jury charge
BaselineB: Common law (improper jury address/trial fairness): Pisani v. The Queen; Boucher v. The Queen; contextual-factor approach referenced from R. v. Stephan and R. v. Manasseri
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Pragmatic and functional approach to whether a labour board has jurisdiction (and resulting deference): reviewing courts consider (a) wording of the enactment conferring jurisdiction; (b) purpose of the statute; (c) reason for the tribunal’s existence; (d) tribunal expertise; and (e) nature of the problem (Bibeault factors). If within jurisdiction, decision stands unless “patently unreasonable” (i.e., “clearly irrational”).
BaselineA: Combination: statute (Canada Labour Code, especially ss. 24, 27, 28, 22, 33) plus common-law/admin-law standard of review framework from U.E.S., Local 298 v. Bibeault (pragmatic and functional approach) and CUPE (patently unreasonable deference).
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 8 reasonableness of DNA data bank sampling under Criminal Code s. 487.055: a seizure is reasonable where, in context, the law strikes an “appropriate balance” between the state’s identification interest and the individual’s privacy/physical integrity; Hunter v. Southam’s investigative ‘reasonable and probable grounds’ paradigm is “not applicable” because data bank sampling is for identification (analogous to fingerprinting), and offenders have a reduced/no reasonable expectation of privacy in identifying information.
BaselineB: Combination: statute (Criminal Code s. 487.055 and related DNA provisions; DNA Identification Act ss. 3-4) plus Charter s. 8 reasonableness framework from Hunter v. Southam and related s. 8 jurisprudence (e.g., Collins/Stillman).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Gladstone refinement of Sparrow justification for infringements of Aboriginal rights lacking internal limits: government must show (1) a valid legislative objective and (2) consistency with fiduciary duty, including a non-exclusive but priority-respecting allocation process and outcome
BaselineA: Common law / constitutional framework: Sparrow justification test under s. 35(1) Constitution Act, 1982 (two-part test: valid legislative objective + fiduciary duty/priority); also draws on Jack v. The Queen on priority
CaseB_TestB: Admissibility of Crown rebuttal evidence: rebuttal may be admitted where it is relevant to an issue raised by the defence and the Crown could not have known in advance the defence evidence; admission is within the trial judge’s discretion
BaselineB: Common law discretion over rebuttal evidence (as applied by the Court; no specific prior SCC case named in the reasons)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Implied waiver of Charter s. 11(d) rights by inaction in a no-imprisonment regulatory ticket scheme: waiver may be inferred from failure to pay and failure to appear only if the accused is fully aware of the consequences and the scheme has sufficient safeguards to ensure the inaction was not due to events beyond the accused’s control
BaselineA: Combination: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 11(d) (and contextual link to s. 7 liberty), plus common-law/Charter waiver principles as discussed through SCC cases (notably R. v. Lee) applied to the statutory ticketing scheme in the Provincial Offences Procedure Act (NB), especially ss. 10(1)(h), 11(1)-(2), 16, 48(1), 117
CaseB_TestB: Procedural fairness requirements for CHRC rejection of a complaint as unsubstantiated: before deciding, the Commission must give parties an opportunity to make submissions (at least in writing; a hearing not necessarily required) and must disclose the substance of the case against the party so submissions are informed
BaselineB: Combination: Canadian Human Rights Act, 1976-77 (Can.), c. 33, ss. 35 and 36(3)(b), interpreted through common-law natural justice/procedural fairness principles (quasi-judicial decision-making)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Patently unreasonable standard on judicial review of labour arbitration (including the “no evidence” basis for finding patent unreasonableness)
BaselineA: Common law (administrative law standard of review) applied in the labour-arbitration/privative-clause context; key sources cited include CUPE v. New Brunswick Liquor Corp. (patently unreasonable interpretation), PSAC No. 2 (meaning of patently unreasonable), and Lester (findings of fact/inferences: evidence incapable of supporting finding)
CaseB_TestB: Statutory “equivalent in value” test under Reorg. Act s. 15(2)(a): equivalence requires comparing both benefits and the funding mechanism as of the implementation date
BaselineB: Statute: The Manitoba Telephone System Reorganization and Consequential Amendments Act, S.M. 1996, c. 79, s. 15(2)(a) (and related context in s. 15(3), (4), (11)); interpreted alongside the Civil Service Superannuation Act definition of “pension benefit” (s. 1(1)) but with the key interpretive focus on “equivalent in value”
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Doctrine of part performance overriding a statutory writing requirement (Statute of Frauds analogue): where an oral agreement for an interest in land has been carried out/partly performed, equity will enforce it and prevent the Crown from relying on the absence of writing (“equity recognizes as done that which ought to have been done”; writing requirement cannot be used as an “engine of fraud”).
BaselineA: Combination of statute and equitable common law: Public Highways Act, R.S.N.S. 1954, c. 235, s. 21(1)(a) (written permit requirement) interpreted as reflecting the Statute of Frauds; equitable doctrine of part performance as described via Steadman v. Steadman and related authorities.
CaseB_TestB: Quebec arbitration/public order validity-review framework: (1) arbitrator’s mandate is interpreted liberally to include matters “closely connected” to the arbitration agreement; (2) s. 37 Copyright Act does not bar arbitration; (3) on homologation/annulment for public order under art. 946.5 C.C.P., the court examines the award “as a whole” and will not annul for mere legal error unless the outcome conflicts with “fundamental principles of public order” (no merits review per art. 946.2 C.C.P.).
BaselineB: Statutory: Civil Code of Québec art. 2639; Code of Civil Procedure (Québec) arts. 946.2, 946.4, 946.5, 947.2; Copyright Act, s. 37; Act respecting the professional status of artists, s. 37.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Reasonableness simpliciter standard of appellate review for expert tribunal decisions on questions of mixed law and fact: uphold unless the decision is “unreasonable” (i.e., “in the main, is not supported by any reasons that can stand up to a somewhat probing examination”); contrasted with “patently unreasonable” where the defect is “apparent on the face of the tribunal’s reasons”.
BaselineA: Combination: statute (Competition Tribunal Act, ss. 12-13; Competition Act purpose in s. 1.1) plus common-law standard-of-review jurisprudence (Pezim; CUPE; Bell Canada; Bradco).
CaseB_TestB: Temporal-effect test for suspended s. 52(1) declarations: declarations are presumptively retroactive, but the presumption is rebutted “explicitly or by necessary implication”; where “retroactivity would undermine [the] purpose” of the suspension (protecting a compelling public interest), “the declaration must apply purely prospectively”.
BaselineB: Combination: Constitution Act, 1982, s. 52(1) and Charter, s. 24(1), interpreted through prior SCC remedial jurisprudence (Ontario (AG) v. G; Hislop; Manitoba Language Reference; Big M Drug Mart; Ferguson; Bedford).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: CCA “purpose of producing income” test under Reg. 1102(1)(c): (1) “Does the property produce income? In the affirmative, the deduction is allowable.” (2) If not, “was it acquired for the purpose of producing income?”, determined by “an objective evaluation of the specific facts and circumstances ... having regard to whether the taxpayer acted in accordance with reasonably acceptable principles of commerce and business practices.” (L’Heureux-Dubé J.)
BaselineA: Statute and regulation: Income Tax Act, s. 20(1)(a) (deductions “as is allowed by regulation”) and Income Tax Regulations, s. 1102(1)(c) (“property ... not acquired ... for the purpose of gaining or producing income”).
CaseB_TestB: Bail denial under Criminal Code s. 515(10)(c) (post-severance): detention may be ordered “where the detention is necessary in order to maintain confidence in the administration of justice”, assessed objectively “having regard to all the circumstances, including” four listed factors (strength of Crown’s case, gravity of offence, circumstances of commission, potential for lengthy imprisonment), and only if “a reasonable member of the community would be satisfied that denial of bail is necessary” (McLachlin C.J.).
