BaselineB: Statute and constitutional constraint: Criminal Code, s. 515(10)(c) interpreted in light of Charter s. 11(e) (“not to be denied reasonable bail without just cause”) and prior SCC bail jurisprudence (Pearson; Morales).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Vesting/accrual of an appeal-as-of-right: a right is only “acquired”, “accrued” or “accruing” once all conditions precedent to exercising it are fulfilled (here, only when the court of appeal renders judgment reversing an acquittal and ordering a new trial)
BaselineA: Statute (Interpretation Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. I-21, ss. 43(c) and 44(c),(d), applied to Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, former/amended s. 691(2))
CaseB_TestB: Sherman Estate test for discretionary limits on the open court principle (publication bans): applicant must show (1) serious risk to an important public interest; (2) necessity because reasonable alternatives won’t prevent the risk; and (3) proportionality—benefits outweigh negative effects
BaselineB: Common law (Sherman Estate v. Donovan, 2021 SCC 25, para. 38)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Canderel profit-computation framework under ITA s. 9(1): taxpayer may use any method consistent with the Act, case law, and well-accepted business principles that yields an “accurate picture” of profit; on reassessment, once taxpayer shows an accurate picture, the onus shifts to the Minister to show it is not accurate or that another method is more accurate
BaselineA: Statute (Income Tax Act, S.C. 1970-71-72, c. 63, ss. 9(1), 18(1)(a), 18(9)) plus prior SCC/common-law principles on profit computation (cited in the decision: Symes v. Canada; Friesen v. Canada; M.N.R. v. Irwin; Johnston v. M.N.R.)
CaseB_TestB: Interpretation/application of Partnership Act s. 55(b): a general partner breaches the statute only if it does an act that “makes it impossible to carry on the ordinary business of the limited partnership”, meaning impossibility as to a “substantial portion” of the partnership’s ordinary business (not every facet)
BaselineB: Statute (Partnership Act, R.S.A. 1980, c. P-2, s. 55(b)) interpreted in light of the partnership’s constitutive documents defining its “ordinary business”
JudgeB: Estey J. (for Beetz, Estey, McIntyre and Lamer JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Two-step test (post-conviction) for whether Crown non-disclosure impaired full answer and defence and warrants a new trial: (1) reasonable possibility undisclosed info affects reliability of conviction; if not, (2) reasonable possibility non-disclosure affected overall fairness via lost lines of inquiry/opportunities, with defence due diligence weighed
BaselineA: Combination of Charter and common law: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms ss. 7 and 24(1), building on disclosure jurisprudence in R. v. Stinchcombe, R. v. Egger, R. v. C. (M.H.), and R. v. Carosella
CaseB_TestB: Standard-form insurance interpretation applied to SEF 44 cl. 4(b)(vii): give effect to clear, unambiguous language as understood by the average insured; “policy of insurance” means a private insurance contract and does not include CPP disability benefits
BaselineB: Common law contract/insurance interpretation principles (Ledcor; Progressive Homes; Scalera; Gibbens) applied to the SEF 44 Endorsement, specifically cl. 4(b)(vii) (“any policy of insurance providing disability benefits...”)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Caslake ‘truly incidental to arrest’ limit on the common-law search-incident-to-arrest power: police must have a purpose connected to the arrest (e.g., “protecting the police, protecting the evidence, discovering evidence”) and “must have had some reason related to the arrest ... and that reason must be objectively reasonable”; delay/distance may support a negative inference rebuttable by explanation.
BaselineA: Common law (search incident to arrest doctrine from Cloutier v. Langlois; also framed within Charter s. 8 reasonableness via Hunter v. Southam and R. v. Collins).
CaseB_TestB: Grant (2015) framework for admissibility of defence-led unknown third party suspect evidence: admissible where (1) relevant to a fact in issue and (2) “probative value ... is not substantially outweighed by its prejudicial effects”; relevance/air-of-reality foundation shown by “a sufficient connection ... between the [charged] crime and the allegedly similar incident(s) ... coupled with evidence that the accused could not have committed the other offence”; no balance-of-probabilities proof of the other incident and no credibility weighing by the judge.
BaselineB: Common law evidence principles (R. v. Seaboyer probative-prejudice balancing; R. v. Corbett relevance; R. v. Cinous air of reality; draws on Grandinetti’s “sufficient connection” concept but adapts it for unknown suspects).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 8 engagement for foreign evidence via letter of request: the sending of a letter of request, by itself, does not constitute a Canadian 'search or seizure' and therefore does not engage s. 8; Charter scrutiny stops at the request and does not extend to foreign officials’ compelled acts abroad
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional text (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 8 and 32(1)) informed by prior SCC s. 8 jurisprudence (notably Hunter v. Southam Inc.; also Terry/Harrer on non-application to foreign officials)
CaseB_TestB: Anns/Cooper duty of care framework (foreseeability + proximity, then residual policy) for negligence claims alleging failure to prevent third-party intentional harm
BaselineB: Common law (Cooper v. Hobart / Anns-style duty of care analysis as applied and developed in Cooper, Edwards, Odhavji Estate, Childs, Hill)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Pushpanathan Art. 1F(c) exclusion test: Art. 1F(c) applies where there is (1) an international-law consensus that the acts are “sufficiently serious and sustained violations of fundamental human rights as to amount to persecution”, or (2) the acts are “explicitly recognized as contrary to the purposes and principles of the United Nations”; with two main categories: (i) a widely accepted international agreement/UN resolution explicitly so declaring (a “reasonable consensus” designation is “determinative”), or (ii) acts a court can itself characterize as “serious, sustained and systemic violations of fundamental human rights constituting persecution” (even an isolated violation may suffice if the violated rule is near the core of human rights and e.g. a universal-jurisdiction offence).
BaselineA: Statute incorporating treaty: Immigration Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. I-2, s. 2(1) (definition of “Convention refugee” incorporating Refugee Convention Art. 1F(c)); interpreted using Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, Arts. 31-32.
CaseB_TestB: Hadley v. Baxendale remoteness/proximity test for contract damages: damages are those that “arise either naturally” or “may reasonably be supposed to have been in the contemplation of both parties, at the time they made the contract, as the probable result of a breach”; applied to uphold loss-of-profits damages for breach of an implied duty of good faith by a branch manager who orchestrated a mass exit.
BaselineB: Common law contract damages (Hadley v. Baxendale (1854), as cited and applied).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Hodgson framework for (1) who is a “person in authority” and (2) when a trial judge must hold a confession voir dire on their own motion: person in authority includes those the accused reasonably believes can influence/control proceedings; defence must raise the issue, but in “extremely rare cases” the judge must order a voir dire if the record objectively shows a clear, close connection to authorities along a spectrum from “conventional” authority figures.
BaselineA: Common law confessions rule (voluntariness requirement for statements to a person in authority), drawing on prior SCC authority including Erven v. The Queen, [1979] 1 S.C.R. 926 and Rothman v. The Queen, [1981] 1 S.C.R. 640; classic voluntariness formulation from Ibrahim v. The King, [1914] A.C. 599 (P.C.) adopted in Canada in Prosko v. The King (1922), 63 S.C.R. 226.
CaseB_TestB: McClurg approach to Income Tax Act s. 56(2) in the corporate-dividend context: as a general rule, a dividend (including one allocated under a valid discretionary dividend clause) is not a “payment or transfer” diverted from the taxpayer because, until declaration, profits belong to the corporation; s. 56(2) targets diversion of amounts the taxpayer “otherwise would have obtained.”
BaselineB: Statute—Income Tax Act, S.C. 1970-71-72, c. 63, s. 56(2) (attribution rule for payments/transfers made “pursuant to the direction of, or with the concurrence of, a taxpayer”); interpreted in light of prior case law on s. 56(2)’s purpose including Miller v. M.N.R., 62 D.T.C. 1139 (Ex. Ct.) and Perrault v. The Queen, [1979] 1 F.C. 155 (C.A.).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Depletion allowance profit computation under Reg. 1201(2): determine profits “reasonably attributable” to production by “ascertaining the difference between the receipts reasonably attributable to the production ... and the expenses of earning those receipts”, and deduct only the items enumerated in Reg. 1201(4) (no implied deduction for long-term research expenses deductible for income under ITA ss. 11(1)(j) and 72).
BaselineA: Regulation (Income Tax Regulations (Can.), Reg. 1201(2) and 1201(4)) interpreting interaction with Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1952, c. 148, ss. 11(1)(j) and 72; approach referenced from Minister of National Revenue v. Imperial Oil Ltd., [1960] S.C.R. 735.
CaseB_TestB: Sherman Estate test for discretionary limits on the open court principle (publication bans): applicant must establish (1) openness poses a “serious risk to an important public interest”; (2) the order is “necessary” because “reasonably alternative measures will not prevent this risk”; and (3) proportionality: “the benefits of the order outweigh its negative effects”.
BaselineB: Common law discretionary framework from Sherman Estate v. Donovan, 2021 SCC 25 (applied).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Kienapple/res judicata in multi-count prosecutions with different gravity: if same delict underlies both counts, convict on the more serious and acquit/hold in abeyance the less serious (cannot use a guilty plea to the lesser to bar trial/conviction on the greater)
BaselineA: Common law (Kienapple v. The Queen, [1975] 1 S.C.R. 729 rule against multiple convictions for the same delict/matter; applied in context of Criminal Code charges)
CaseB_TestB: Availability of habeas corpus to challenge continued detention in parole context: continuation is challengeable only if it becomes unlawful, which occurs only once the inmate has acquired parolee status (i.e., when the parole decision takes effect; if conditional, only when the condition is fulfilled)
BaselineB: Combination of common law habeas corpus principles as expanded in R. v. Miller, [1985] 2 S.C.R. 613 (and Cardinal; Morin) and statutory parole framework (Parole Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. P-2 as amended)
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: NCR disposition under Criminal Code s. 672.54: absolute discharge is mandatory unless the court/Review Board makes a positive finding that the NCR accused poses a “significant threat to the safety of the public”; if significant threat is found, impose the “least onerous and least restrictive” conditional discharge or detention after considering the four statutory factors (public protection, mental condition, reintegration, other needs). Key definition: “significant threat” = “a real risk of physical or psychological harm ... that is serious ... beyond the merely trivial or annoying” and the conduct “must be criminal in nature”.
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, Part XX.1, especially s. 672.54; interpreted against Charter s. 7 principles and Swain).
CaseB_TestB: Westbank test for characterizing a levy as a “tax” (vs regulatory charge/user fee) for Constitution Act, 1867 s. 125: ask whether the charge is “(1) compulsory and enforceable by law; (2) imposed under the authority of the legislature; (3) levied by a public body; (4) intended for a public purpose; and (5) unconnected to any form of a regulatory scheme”; if all are yes, “the levy in question will generally be described as a tax.”
BaselineB: Constitution Act, 1867, s. 125 (and related heads of power), plus statutory authority under Indian Act, s. 83(1)(a); builds on prior SCC tax/fee jurisprudence (e.g., Lawson; Eurig Estate; Re Exported Natural Gas Tax).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 2(d) scope/violation test for exclusion from a statutory labour-relations regime: s. 2(d) protects only (1) “the freedom to establish, belong to and maintain an association” and (2) “the exercise in association of the lawful rights of individuals”; it “does not include the right to establish a particular type of association defined in a particular statute”, and (absent exceptional circumstances) imposes no positive obligation on government to provide a legislative framework; thus exclusion from the PSSRA does not itself infringe s. 2(d).
BaselineA: Combination: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 2(d) (and s. 32(1) re government action), interpreted through prior SCC jurisprudence (notably the 1987 labour trilogy and Professional Institute of the Public Service of Canada v. Northwest Territories (Commissioner), as reaffirmed in Canadian Egg Marketing Agency v. Richardson).
CaseB_TestB: Co-principal (joint) liability in group assaults: “Joint/co‑principal liability flows whenever two or more individuals come together with an intention to commit an offence, are present during the commission of the offence, and contribute to its commission.” For manslaughter, focus on whether the accused’s actions were “a significant contributing cause of death” (and in group assaults, absent a “discrete or intervening event”, all assailants’ actions can be such a cause).
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, s. 21(1)(a) (and related party provision s. 21(1)(c)); clarified in light of prior case law including R. v. Pickton and correcting an implication from R. v. Cabrera.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Federal Child Support Guidelines s. 4 ‘inappropriateness’ framework for incomes over $150,000: Table amount presumptively applies; deviation only if Table amount shown ‘inappropriate’ (= ‘unsuitable’), assessed on all circumstances including s. 4(b)(ii) factors
BaselineA: Regulation/statute: Federal Child Support Guidelines, SOR/97-175, s. 4 (and related ss. 1, 3, 7, 21) under the Divorce Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 3 (2nd Supp.), s. 26.1(2)
CaseB_TestB: Categorization test for whether an all-risks/multi-peril policy falls under B.C. Insurance Act Part 5 (fire) or Part 2 (general): if the policy does not fit a specific Part 5 category under s. 119, it is governed by Part 2 (including Part 2 limitation period); contractual shorter limitation cannot undercut Part 2 due to s. 3(a)
BaselineB: Statute/regulation: Insurance Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 226, ss. 119 and 3(a) (and statutory condition 14; Insurance Classes Regulation, B.C. Reg. 337/90, s. 2)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meiorin unified BFOR test (3-step justification of a prima facie discriminatory employment standard): employer must prove (1) purpose “rationally connected to the performance of the job”; (2) standard adopted “in an honest and good faith belief” it was necessary; and (3) standard “reasonably necessary” — i.e., “impossible to accommodate” affected employees “without imposing undue hardship upon the employer”.
BaselineA: Statute (Human Rights Code, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 210, s. 13(1)(a), (b), (4)) plus prior SCC human-rights BFOR/accommodation jurisprudence (e.g., O’Malley; Etobicoke; Central Alberta Dairy Pool; Renaud).
CaseB_TestB: Stewart source-of-income test under the Income Tax Act (2-stage): (i) “Is the activity ... undertaken in pursuit of profit, or is it a personal endeavour?”; (ii) if not personal, “is the source of the income a business or property?”; where personal/hobby is in issue, ask: “Does the taxpayer intend to carry on an activity for profit and is there evidence to support that intention?” (REOP only a factor).
BaselineB: Statute (Income Tax Act, especially ss. 3(a), 9(1)-(2), 18(1)(a), (h), 20(1)(c)(i), 248(1) “personal or living expenses”) and prior SCC case law on “reasonable expectation of profit” (Moldowan v. The Queen).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Staged analysis for whether a conditional sentence is available/appropriate for an Aboriginal offender (s. 742.1 with mandatory consideration of s. 718.2(e) once the choice narrows to incarceration): (1) preliminarily exclude probation/suspended sentence and a penitentiary term; (2) confirm s. 742.1 prerequisites (no minimum; <2 years; community safety—risk of reoffending and gravity of harm); (3) then determine whether a conditional sentence is consistent with ss. 718–718.2, and at that stage the judge is 'required to consider s. 718.2(e)' including 'the unique systemic or background circumstances' and 'the types of practicable procedures and sanctions' (Gladue).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, ss. 742.1 and 718–718.2, especially s. 718.2(e)), as interpreted in R. v. Proulx and R. v. Gladue
CaseB_TestB: Quebec Charter s. 9.1 balancing of a freedom of religion claim against countervailing rights/values in enforcing a civil obligation: the religious-freedom claim 'must be balanced and reconciled with countervailing rights, values, and harm' and deciding when it yields is a 'complex, nuanced, fact-specific exercise'; (in addition, the contract is valid under C.C.Q. arts. 1378, 1385, 1412–1413 unless its object is prohibited by law or contrary to public order).
BaselineB: Statute (Quebec Charter of human rights and freedoms, ss. 3 and 9.1; applied with the Amselem freedom-of-religion framework) and Civil Code of Québec contract-formation provisions (arts. 1378, 1385, 1412–1413)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Unreasonable verdict review under Criminal Code s. 686(1)(a)(i): whether the verdict is one that a properly instructed jury (or trial judge) acting judicially could reasonably have rendered; appellate court must thoroughly re-examine the evidence and cannot intervene based only on a vague “lurking doubt” without articulating why the verdict is inconsistent with a judicial appreciation of the evidence.
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(a)(i)) as interpreted in common law authorities including R. v. Yebes and reaffirmed/applied via R. v. Biniaris.
CaseB_TestB: Institutional consultation / natural justice limits (Consolidated-Bathurst rules) and judicial review threshold: full-board consultation is permissible only if (1) not imposed by superiors, (2) limited to questions of policy and law (not re-assessing evidence), and (3) decision-makers remain free to decide; for audi alteram partem, applicant must show an actual breach (not merely an apprehended breach), and a change from draft to final reasons alone does not rebut the presumption of regularity.
BaselineB: Common law procedural fairness/natural justice framework from IWA v. Consolidated-Bathurst Packaging Ltd. and Tremblay v. Quebec (Commission des affaires sociales), applied in the context of judicial review (with statutory backdrop including Labour Relations Act, 1995, ss. 114(1), 117).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: “Functional and structural” approach to whether a statutory court/tribunal has the s. 24(1) Charter “power to grant the remedy sought” (and thus is a “court of competent jurisdiction” under the Mills three-part test)
BaselineA: Combination: Charter s. 24(1) plus common-law/constitutional jurisprudence defining “court of competent jurisdiction” (Mills v. The Queen) and related SCC cases (Weber; Mooring). Also considers the tribunal’s enabling statute (Provincial Offences Act) for implied remedial power.
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 11(d) validity test for statutory presumptions: a presumption is constitutional “solely if proof of the substituted fact leads inexorably to the existence of the essential element it replaces” (the “inexorable connection” requirement)
BaselineB: Combination: Criminal Code, s. 172.1(3) (statutory presumption) interpreted under Charter s. 11(d), applying prior SCC presumption cases (Whyte; Downey; Audet) and related s. 11(d) principles (Vaillancourt; St-Onge Lamoureux).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Existence of a valid partnership for Income Tax Act s. 96 loss deductions: at formation, evidence must show (1) “carrying on a business”, (2) “in common”, (3) “with a view to profit” (Continental Bank, para. 22; applied). Tax motivation does not negate partnership if these ingredients are present; “view to profit” is not a strictly quantitative net-gain test and may be supported by ancillary profit intention assessed pragmatically on the whole facts.
BaselineA: Combination: Income Tax Act, s. 96 (loss deduction through partnership) + common law partnership test from Continental Bank Leasing Corp. v. Canada, [1998] 2 S.C.R. 298 (three essential ingredients) as reiterated in Backman v. Canada, 2001 SCC 10.
CaseB_TestB: Adequacy of jury instructions on credibility and reasonable doubt (W.(D.) context): where credibility is central, the judge must explain the relationship between credibility assessment and the Crown’s burden; the charge must make it “crystal clear” the burden never shifts and avoid the “credibility contest” (not a required “magic incantation” of W.(D.)). The ultimate test is whether, read as a whole, “the jury could not have been under any misapprehension as to the correct burden and standard of proof to apply”.
BaselineB: Common law: R. v. W. (D.), [1991] 1 S.C.R. 742 (and subsequent SCC applications such as S. (W.D.) and Avetysan) governing credibility/reasonable doubt jury instructions; applied in the context of a Criminal Code s. 271(1)(a) prosecution.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Customs Act s. 48(5)(a)(iv) “condition of sale” test for dutiable royalties/licence fees: royalties/licence fees are added to value for duty only if they are paid “as a condition of the sale of the goods for export to Canada”; i.e., “Unless a vendor is entitled to refuse to sell licensed goods to the purchaser or repudiate the contract of sale where the purchaser fails to pay royalties or licence fees, s. 48(5)(a)(iv) is inapplicable” (para. 68).
BaselineA: Statute — Customs Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (2nd Supp.), s. 48(5)(a)(iv) (and related valuation provisions in ss. 45(1), 48(4)-(5)).
CaseB_TestB: ITA s. 224 “requirement to pay” trigger (bank liability) in cheque-deposit context: a bank is subject to a requirement to pay only if it is “liable to make a payment” to the tax debtor; “the mere fact that cheques payable to [the tax debtor] were delivered to the Bank for deposit did not make the latter liable to make a payment to the former within the meaning of s. 224(1) of the ITA” (para. 46).
BaselineB: Statute — Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), s. 224, interpreted alongside Bills of Exchange Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. B-4 (notably ss. 84(1), 84(3), 86(1), 126, 138(2), 165(3)).
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Quebec Labour Code s. 45 successorship via subcontracting: s. 45 may apply where the transferee, beyond performing similar functions, receives a "right to operate part of the transferor’s undertaking" and has a "sufficient degree of autonomy" assessed contextually (here using the "criterion of the subordination of the employees" to the contractor) to show the contractor can be the effective employer controlling working conditions.
BaselineA: Statute (Labour Code, R.S.Q., c. C-27, ss. 45-46) as interpreted in U.E.S., Local 298 v. Bibeault and Lester (W.W.) (1978) Ltd.
CaseB_TestB: Jarvis/Ling audit-to-investigation line: an inquiry becomes a criminal investigation when the "predominant purpose" is determining penal liability under Income Tax Act s. 239; "no one factor is determinative" and the judge assesses the "totality of the circumstances" (Jarvis factors) to decide when the adversarial relationship crystallized, after which use of ss. 231.1/231.2 requirement powers violates Charter ss. 7 and 8.
BaselineB: Common law/Charter framework following R. v. Jarvis, applying Charter ss. 7, 8, 24(2) to the statutory audit powers in Income Tax Act, ss. 231.1(1), 231.2(1), and offences in s. 239(1).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Anns/Cooper duty of care test (stage 1: foreseeability + proximity, including statutory proximity; stage 2: residual policy considerations negating duty)
BaselineA: Common law (Anns v. Merton London Borough Council; Kamloops (City of) v. Nielsen), as clarified in Cooper v. Hobart; applied with close attention to the governing statute (Law Society Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. L.8, esp. s. 9)
JudgeA: The Chief Justice and Major J.
CaseB_TestB: Section 1 Charter justification (Oakes) analysis for whether a fiscal crisis can justify limiting Charter rights; rejection of adding a separate 'separation of powers' step
BaselineB: Constitution (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 1) and common law framework from R. v. Oakes (and subsequent s. 1 jurisprudence)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Pragmatic and functional approach to select the standard of review (privative clause/appeal; relative expertise; purpose of the Act/provision; nature of the problem), applied to hold correctness for the CRTC’s interpretation of s. 43(5)
BaselineA: Common law (standard of review doctrine) applied to a statutory appeal under the Telecommunications Act
CaseB_TestB: Sentencing treatment of collateral consequences and related mitigating considerations: collateral consequences may be considered if they relate to the offence/offender, but proportionality prevails; plus mistake-of-law mitigation requires an 'honest but mistaken belief' and non-impairment mitigation must be limited (onus on offender on balance of probabilities)
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code sentencing provisions) interpreted and applied: ss. 718 to 718.2 (including s. 718.1 proportionality) and refusal offence s. 255(3.2)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 2(b) infringement for sign restrictions: a by-law that restricts an “optimum means of expression” (posting signs) to certain places, and in effect makes it “impossible for any individual to post signs criticising” a business, directly infringes freedom of expression; the government then bears the s. 1 burden (Oakes/Dagenais/Thomson proportionality) to justify the limit.
BaselineA: Combination: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms ss. 2(b) and 1 (with s. 1 justification under R. v. Oakes as refined in Dagenais and Thomson Newspapers); applied to a municipal zoning by-law (Règlement d’urbanisme no 1200, ss. 2.2.4 and 14.1.5(p)).
CaseB_TestB: Canadian Bill of Rights “due process” limits on property expropriation: s. 1(a) does not require notice/hearing before Parliament enacts expropriative legislation; procedural due process applies only in an individualized adjudicative setting, and “no adjudicative procedure is necessary for the non-discretionary application of a law to incontestable facts”; substantively, the Bill of Rights “does not protect against the expropriation of property by the passage of unambiguous legislation” where Parliament’s intent is “clear and unambiguous”.
BaselineB: Statute: Canadian Bill of Rights ss. 1(a) and 2(e), applied to Department of Veterans Affairs Act s. 5.1(4) (and the Bill of Rights’ inoperability mechanism in s. 2).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Copyright infringement by “reproduction” under Copyright Act s. 3(1): “Reproduction” generally requires “producing additional or new copies”; a mere physical transfer of the same ink layer to a new substrate, with “no multiplication”, is not a “production (or reproduction) of a new artistic work ‘in any material form’” (so s. 38(1) seizure remedy unavailable absent “infringing copies”).
BaselineA: Statute (Copyright Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-42, especially ss. 3(1), 2 “infringing”, 27(1), 38(1); with related moral-rights provisions ss. 14.1, 28.2 discussed to maintain separation of economic vs moral rights).
CaseB_TestB: Reasonableness simpliciter on judicial review: the standard is constant (does not “float”); a decision is unreasonable “only if there is no line of analysis within the given reasons that could reasonably lead the tribunal from the evidence before it to the conclusion at which it arrived”; if any sufficient reasons are “tenable” on a “somewhat probing examination”, the court must not interfere.
BaselineB: Common law (standards of review framework from SCC cases including Pushpanathan v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) and Canada (Director of Investigation and Research) v. Southam Inc.; applied in context of statutory appeal under Law Society Act, 1996, S.N.B. 1996, c. 89).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Privacy Act s. 22(1)(b) exemption: refusal to disclose personal information only if disclosure “could reasonably be expected” to be injurious to the conduct of lawful investigations, requiring a “clear and direct connection” between the specific disclosure and the alleged injury, on “real grounds” tied to the specific case
BaselineA: Statute (Privacy Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. P-21, ss. 12(1), 22(1)(b), 22(3), 47, 49; reconciled with Official Languages Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 31 (4th Supp.), ss. 60, 72-74)
CaseB_TestB: Adverse inference / presumption of fact in medical causation: no rule requires drawing an adverse inference of causation; under C.C.Q. art. 2849, a presumption of fact is discretionary and may be drawn only if “serious, precise and concordant”, assessed on a legal (not scientific) standard and weighed with all the evidence
BaselineB: Statute and common law (Civil Code of Québec, art. 2849; interpreted in light of SCC causation/inference jurisprudence including Snell v. Farrell and St-Jean v. Mercier)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Validity/effect of a zoning “holding regulation”: interpret the by-law so that, despite superfluous drafting about future amendment, the operative words impose a general freeze (i.e., “Notwithstanding any other provisions… no building… may be… erected to contain three or more dwelling units”) and therefore do not create an invalid discretionary/spot-zoning regime
BaselineA: Statute + municipal by-law: The Planning Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 349, s. 35(1) (zoning power) and the City of London zoning by-law 306-480 as amended by by-law 306(bc)-504, s. 4 (new s. 11 “Holding Regulation”); contrasted with common-law limits on discretionary licensing/regulation in Toronto v. Mandelbaum and Verdun v. Sun Oil Co. Ltd.
CaseB_TestB: Custody decision-making under s. 1(1) of The Infants Act: the trial judge “must consider the conduct of the parties” as it bears on “relative fitness” (including conduct making two-parent family life impossible), but it is “only one factor” and “each particular case must be judged on its own circumstances” with “the paramount consideration… the welfare of the children”
BaselineB: Statute + best-interests common law: The Infants Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 222, s. 1(1) (direction to consider conduct) applied within the overarching common-law ‘welfare/best interests of the child’ approach (with references to McKee v. McKee, Bickley v. Bickley, Retzer v. Retzer, and Re L.)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: OSC s. 17(1) disclosure of compelled investigation material: apply Stinchcombe relevance (“reasonable possibility of being relevant” to full answer and defence) within the statutory “public interest” discretion; disclosure improper if “no reasonable possibility” a particular item is relevant
BaselineA: Statute (Ontario Securities Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. S.5, ss. 16-17) plus common-law relevance standard from R. v. Stinchcombe
CaseB_TestB: Framework to classify requested state-held records as first-party (Stinchcombe/McNeil) vs third-party (O’Connor): ask (1) is the information in the possession/control of the prosecuting Crown?; and (2) if not, ought police/another Crown entity to have supplied it because it is part of the “fruits of the investigation” or “obviously relevant”? If neither, O’Connor applies and accused must show “likely relevance” (“reasonable possibility” of logical probativeness)
BaselineB: Common law (Stinchcombe; O’Connor; McNeil) applied in context of Criminal Code, s. 258(1)(c)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Misfeasance in public office (defining elements): (1) “deliberate and unlawful conduct in the exercise of public functions”; and (2) “awareness that the conduct is unlawful and likely to injure the plaintiff” (plus causation and compensable loss).
BaselineA: Common law tort (misfeasance in public office), with unlawfulness often supplied by statutory duties (here Police Services Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. P.15, ss. 41(1)(b), 113(9)); key cases discussed include Roncarelli v. Duplessis and Three Rivers District Council v. Bank of England (No. 3).
CaseB_TestB: Eligibility for Quebec seats under Supreme Court Act, s. 6: s. 6 “narrows the pool” and requires “current membership” — appointees must be current members of the Barreau du Québec or current judges of the Quebec Court of Appeal/Superior Court (and meet s. 5’s 10-year standing requirement).
BaselineB: Statutory interpretation of Supreme Court Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. S-26, ss. 5 and 6 (and constitutional constraint analysis under Constitution Act, 1982, s. 41(d) re “composition” of the Court).
JudgeB: McLachlin C.J. and LeBel, Abella, Cromwell, Karakatsanis and Wagner JJ.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Securities Act s. 162 administrative-penalty ‘public interest’ analysis: once a contravention is found, the Commission may impose up to $100,000 if it ‘considers it to be in the public interest’, and may consider general deterrence (as a preventative factor) and the full context; reviewing courts assess whether there is a ‘rational basis’ and review the order ‘globally’ without isolating any one factor.
BaselineA: Statute (Securities Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 418, s. 162 (and related public-interest context under ss. 161-162))
CaseB_TestB: Adequacy of jury instructions on routes to criminal liability where other participants may be involved: the trial judge must instruct on all routes to liability arising on the evidence; it is not necessary to find the accused acted alone—jury may convict if satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt the accused ‘actively participated in the killing’/‘acted in concert with others’ (and the ‘actual shooter’ instruction was legally erroneous and properly corrected).
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, especially s. 21 party liability; also appellate miscarriage-of-justice framework including s. 686(1)(b)(iii))
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Good-faith basis standard for putting unproven factual suggestions in cross-examination (no evidentiary foundation required; judge may require assurance only if predicate is manifestly tenuous or suspect)
BaselineA: Common law (cross-examination ethics/limits), as reflected in R. v. Bencardino and clarified against misreadings of R. v. Howard; also linked to Charter-protected full answer and defence (ss. 7, 11(d))
CaseB_TestB: Federal paramountcy test: provincial law is inoperative only if (1) operational conflict (impossible dual compliance) or (2) frustration of federal purpose (clear proof of purpose and incompatibility)
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine of federal paramountcy (as articulated in cases such as Rothmans, Canadian Western Bank, COPA, Ryan Estate) applied to BIA ss. 243-244 and provincial SFSA Part II
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Vaid parliamentary privilege existence/scope test (authoritative precedent first; otherwise necessity): court asks if the claimed privilege’s “existence and scope ... have been authoritatively established” for Canada/Westminster; if not, the claimant must show the activity is “so closely and directly connected” to legislative/deliberative functions (including holding government to account) that outside interference would undermine the autonomy needed for Parliament to work “with dignity and efficiency” (paras. 39-40, 46).
BaselineA: Combination: constitutional/statutory privilege framework (Constitution Act, 1867, s. 18; Parliament of Canada Act, s. 4) plus common-law doctrine of necessity as the “foundation of all parliamentary privilege” (paras. 33-40).
CaseB_TestB: Interpretive test for Tobacco Act s. 22(3) (“appealing to young persons”): s. 22(3) “requires the prosecution ... to prove that there are reasonable grounds to believe that the advertisement ... could be appealing to young persons, in the sense that it could be particularly attractive and of interest to young persons, as distinguished from the general population” (para. 89).
BaselineB: Statute: Tobacco Act, S.C. 1997, c. 13, s. 22(3) (interpreted bilingually/purposively to fix meaning and application).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: GAAR “abusive tax avoidance” (s. 245(4)) — deny a tax benefit where it “cannot be reasonably concluded that a tax benefit would be consistent with the object, spirit or purpose of the provisions relied upon by the taxpayer” (three-part GAAR framework from Canada Trustco, applied in Mathew)
BaselineA: Statute: Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), especially ss. 245(1)-(4) (GAAR), 18(13) (superficial loss rule for money-lending business), and 96(1) (partnership loss flow-through). The GAAR framework is taken from the companion SCC decision Canada Trustco Mortgage Co. v. Canada, 2005 SCC 54 (summarized and applied at paras. 31-32).
CaseB_TestB: Vancouver Sun informer-privilege procedure and “single guiding rule”: (1) verify existence of informer privilege (in camera/ex parte if needed; evidence of informer status “automatically engages the privilege”); (2) once established, conduct proceedings giving “full effect” to the “complete and total bar” on disclosure of identity while “limiting, as much as possible, any impairment of the open court principle” (including, generally, using a parallel sealed proceeding with a public docket entry and a redacted public judgment)
BaselineB: Common law: Named Person v. Vancouver Sun, 2007 SCC 43 (procedure for informer privilege claims; reiterated and applied). The decision also relies on the common-law rule that informer privilege is non-discretionary/near-absolute once status is established.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “lawful authority” for whistleblower protection under s. 74(1)(a): includes internal authorities who can address the wrongdoing (“up the ladder” reporting). The Court held that “the expression ‘lawful authority’ in s. 74 includes not only the police or other agents of the state… but also individuals within the employer organization who exercise lawful authority over the employee(s) complained about, or over the activity that is or is likely to result in the offence” (para. 38).
BaselineA: Statute: The Labour Standards Act, R.S.S. 1978, c. L-1, s. 74(1)(a) (as am. 1994, c. 39, s. 41) (interpreting “lawful authority”).
CaseB_TestB: Waiver of insurer’s right to rely on statutory non-payment rule for dishonoured premium cheque: “Before one can find waiver there must be express and unequivocal language or conduct” (Dickson J.). Applied alongside s. 238(1) deeming a dishonoured cheque not to be payment.
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: The Alberta Insurance Act, R.S.A. 1970, c. 187, s. 238(1) (dishonoured cheque deemed not to be payment) plus common-law waiver principle as applied/followed from McGeachie v. North American Life Insurance Company (1893), 23 S.C.R. 148.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “lawful authority” for whistleblower protection under s. 74(1)(a): includes internal authorities who can address the wrongdoing (“up the ladder” reporting)
BaselineA: Statute: The Labour Standards Act, R.S.S. 1978, c. L-1, s. 74(1)(a) (and s. 74(2))
CaseB_TestB: Common law joinder (Clunas) applied to provincial + summary conviction criminal charges: (1) sufficient factual nexus (functional approach to “could initially have been jointly charged”); and (2) joint trial is in the interests of justice (weighing costs/benefits)
BaselineB: Common law: R. v. Clunas, [1992] 1 S.C.R. 595 (two-part joinder test), applied alongside statutory context (POA s. 2(1), s. 47(1); Criminal Code summary conviction procedure)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Two-step harm-based test for criminal indecency (Labaye/Butler framework): Crown must prove beyond a reasonable doubt (1) conduct "causes harm or presents a significant risk of harm" to individuals/society undermining a constitutionally-endorsed value (e.g., (a) unwanted public exposure interfering with autonomy/liberty; (b) predisposing to anti-social behaviour; (c) physical/psychological harm), and (2) the harm/risk is "of a degree that is incompatible with the proper functioning of society" (Kouri, para. 10).
BaselineA: Combination: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 210(1) (keeping a common bawdy-house for acts of indecency) interpreted through common-law indecency jurisprudence; Court states the two-step structure is "[b]ased on the guidelines emerging from R. v. Butler" and elaborated in the companion case R. v. Labaye (Kouri, paras. 1, 9-10).
CaseB_TestB: Pointe Gourde / s. 27(1)(a) compensation inquiry: when deciding whether a land-use enactment’s effect on value must be ignored, "the key question is whether the enactment was made with a view to the expropriation or, conversely, was an independent enactment"; the inquiry examines the enactment’s "purposes and effects" and "causation does not drive the inquiry" (Lynch, paras. 46, 48, 50-54).
BaselineB: Statute interpreted in light of common law: Expropriation Act, R.S.N.L. 1990, c. E-19, s. 27(1)(a) ("no account shall be taken of the compulsory acquisition of the land") incorporating the common-law Pointe Gourde principle (Pointe Gourde Quarrying and Transport Co. v. Sub-Intendent of Crown Lands) (Lynch, paras. 2, 34-38).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Interpretation of Limitations Act, s. 12: forum limitation law applies only to "live" foreign causes of action; s. 12 does not revive claims already time-barred under the applicable foreign substantive law (lex loci delicti, including its limitation period)
BaselineA: Combination: statute (Limitations Act, R.S.A. 2000, c. L-12, s. 12) interpreted against common law conflicts rule from Tolofson v. Jensen (lex loci delicti includes the foreign limitation period as substantive)
CaseB_TestB: Ancillary powers doctrine (Waterfield/Dedman framework) for common law police powers: define the asserted power and liberty interest; then (1) within scope of police duty; (2) "reasonably necessary" assessed by weighing (i) importance of duty, (ii) necessity of liberty interference, (iii) extent of interference; onus on the state
BaselineB: Common law: ancillary powers doctrine from R. v. Waterfield as adopted/applied in Dedman v. The Queen and refined in R. v. MacDonald (three-factor weighing at stage two)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Palmer/Lévesque test for admitting fresh evidence on a sentence appeal (interests of justice): (1) due diligence; (2) relevance; (3) credibility; (4) could reasonably be expected to have affected the result
BaselineA: Common law test from Palmer v. The Queen, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 759, as adapted to sentence appeals in R. v. Lévesque, 2000 SCC 47 (applied under Criminal Code, s. 687(1))
CaseB_TestB: Section 8 reasonable expectation of privacy (REP) test: totality of circumstances assessed along four lines of inquiry—(1) subject matter; (2) direct interest; (3) subjective expectation; (4) objective reasonableness
BaselineB: Common law/Charter framework for s. 8 REP (as reiterated in Marakah, Cole, Spencer, Tessling, Edwards, etc.)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Copyright Act s. 27(2)(e) “hypothetical infringement” requirement: secondary infringement by importation requires that the foreign maker “would have infringed copyright if [the copy] had been made in Canada by the person who made it”; a copyright owner cannot be the hypothetical infringer vis-à-vis its exclusive licensee, so the licensee cannot establish hypothetical infringement where the maker is the owner-licensor.
CaseB_TestB: Section 11(h) Charter test for when retrospective parole changes amount to being “punished ... again”: the “dominant consideration” is “the extent to which an offender’s settled expectation of liberty has been thwarted”; automatic lengthening of incarceration is a “clearest of cases”, while other changes depend on whether they “substantially increase the risk of additional incarceration” (with indicators including individualized decision-making and procedural safeguards).
BaselineB: Constitution (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 11(h); applied to Abolition of Early Parole Act, S.C. 2011, c. 11, s. 10(1))
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Sentencing of hybrid offences prosecuted summarily: treat as summary conviction for sentencing; maximum may be imposed without “worst offender/worst offence”; appellate intervention only for error in principle/relevant factor/overemphasis or if sentence is demonstrably unfit
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, Part XXIII sentencing principles and summary conviction limit) plus SCC sentencing appellate review framework
CaseB_TestB: Mr. Big confessions admissibility rule: presumptive inadmissibility rebutted only if Crown proves (balance of probabilities) probative value (reliability) outweighs prejudicial effect; plus separate abuse-of-process backstop for coercive/abusive operations
BaselineB: Common law evidence (party admissions/hearsay exception; probative value vs prejudicial effect discretion) and abuse of process doctrine
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Adequacy of jury charge (Azoulay/Jacquard): trial judge must (except rare needless cases) review the substantial parts of the evidence and give the jury the theory of the defence so they can appreciate the evidence and apply the law; judge has 'considerable latitude' in how much evidence to review, provided jurors get an 'adequate understanding' of the relationship between essential evidence and the issues they must decide.
BaselineA: Common law (Azoulay v. The Queen; R. v. Jacquard)
CaseB_TestB: Trade-marks Act confusion test (s. 6): confusion exists if, considering 'all the surrounding circumstances' (including s. 6(5) factors), it is likely the 'casual consumer somewhat in a hurry' will be led to the mistaken inference that the wares/services come from the same source; no requirement of 'resemblance or linkage' between wares/services, and neither fame nor difference in wares/services 'trumps' the totality-of-circumstances analysis.
BaselineB: Statute (Trade-marks Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. T-13, ss. 6(2) and 6(5))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Elements of the Criminal Code child-luring offence (s. 172.1(1)(c)): Crown must prove (1) intentional communication by computer; (2) with a person the accused knows or believes is under 14; (3) "for the specific purpose of facilitating" a listed secondary offence; "facilitating" includes "helping to bring about and making easier or more probable" and the accused’s purpose is assessed subjectively on the evidence as a whole.
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 172.1(1)(c) (and related secondary offences ss. 151, 152, etc.).
CaseB_TestB: Enforcement of a forum selection clause: absent "strong cause" to displace the chosen forum, courts should hold parties to their bargain; the "strong cause" test is discretionary (Pompey) and a Rule 21.01(3)(a) motion may be brought after delivery of a statement of defence if brought promptly.
BaselineB: Common law: Z.I. Pompey Industrie v. ECU-Line N.V., 2003 SCC 27 ("strong cause" test), applied within the procedural framework of Ontario Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 21.01(3)(a).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: SCC leave-to-appeal test under Supreme Court Act s. 40(1): leave only if the Court is of the opinion the question is of sufficient importance (public importance/important issue of law or mixed fact and law, or otherwise warrants decision), and jurisdiction exists for “any final or other judgment” not excluded by s. 40(3)
BaselineA: Statute (Supreme Court Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. S-26, ss. 40(1), 40(3); definition of “judgment” in s. 2; interaction with Criminal Code ss. 691-693)
CaseB_TestB: Access to Information Act third-party notice threshold under s. 27(1): disclose without notice only in clear cases; refuse without notice only if clearly exempt; otherwise give notice (including where severance under s. 25 is intended), with a serious record-by-record review by the institutional head
BaselineB: Statute (Access to Information Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. A-1, ss. 20(1), 25, 27(1), 28, 44)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Reasonableness of unannounced forced entry (departure from “knock and announce”): police must ordinarily give “(i) notice of presence… (ii) notice of authority… (iii) notice of purpose” (Eccles), but if they depart, “the Crown must lay an evidentiary framework” showing “reasonable grounds to be concerned about… harm… or… destruction of evidence”; decision judged by what was “known… at the time” (no ex post facto justifications).
BaselineA: Common law + constitutional baseline (Charter s. 8 reasonableness) with related statutory context. Baseline sources cited: R. v. Collins (s. 8 requires search be authorized by law, law reasonable, and search conducted reasonably); Eccles v. Bourque (knock-and-announce content); R. v. Genest / R. v. Gimson (onus/evidentiary framework; no ex post facto justifications).
CaseB_TestB: Implied assertions are hearsay when tendered for truth; admissible only if within a traditional exception or, failing that, under the principled approach requiring “indicia of reliability and necessity” on a voir dire (Mapara). Court holds “no principled… distinction between express and implied assertions” when offered for truth.
BaselineB: Common law hearsay rule and the SCC’s principled hearsay framework. Baseline cases cited: R. v. Khelawon (defining features/dangers of hearsay); R. v. Mapara (principled approach structure); R. v. Khan / R. v. Starr (development of principled approach).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: State Immunity Act commercial activity exception (s. 5): determine whether proceedings “relate to any commercial activity” by examining the “nature of the acts ... in their full context, which includes the purpose of the acts”; not enough that acts were “authorized or desired” by the state or done to preserve “public interests” (contextual nature/purpose characterization; accept foreign court’s findings of fact on recognition).
BaselineA: Statute — State Immunity Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. S-18, ss. 2 (“commercial activity”), 3 (general immunity), 5 (commercial activity exception); applied with reference to Re Canada Labour Code, [1992] 2 S.C.R. 50 (contextual nature/purpose approach).
CaseB_TestB: Miscarriage of justice / mistrial from procedural irregularity (tainted material to jury): assess whether the irregularity was “severe enough to render the trial unfair or create the appearance of unfairness”, using non-exhaustive reference points (centrality to case, gravity/likely influence, jury vs judge-alone, whether remedied, appearance of fairness, counsel’s response).
BaselineB: Statute — Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(a)(iii) (miscarriage of justice) and related curative provisions; framework articulated in these reasons (with supporting case law cited in the decision).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Journalist-source privilege in civil proceedings (Quebec): threshold relevance + Wigmore factors with context-specific balancing at factor 4. As summarized by the Court: to compel answers that may disclose a confidential source, the requesting party must first show the questions are relevant; if relevant, the court applies Wigmore: (1) relationship originates in confidence; (2) anonymity essential; (3) relationship should be sedulously fostered in the public interest; (4) public interest in protecting identity outweighs public interest in getting at the truth; at factor 4 the court must balance “the importance of disclosure to the administration of justice” against “the public interest in maintaining journalist-source confidentiality”, considering context (e.g., stage of proceedings, centrality, whether journalist is party, alternative sources, public importance, publication).
BaselineA: Common law (Wigmore case-by-case privilege framework as applied to journalist-source privilege in R. v. National Post, 2010 SCC 16, adopting the four Wigmore factors; also incorporates a threshold relevance gatekeeping requirement consistent with civil evidence principles (e.g., C.C.Q. art. 2857 on relevance/admissibility).
CaseB_TestB: Court jurisdiction to review decisions of voluntary associations: jurisdiction exists only if a legal right is at stake; where contract is alleged, contract formation requires objective intention to create legal relations. The Court states: “Jurisdiction to intervene in the affairs of a voluntary association depends on the existence of a legal right”; and for intention to create legal relations, “the test ... is whether parties have indicated to the outside world, in the form of the objective reasonable bystander, their intention to contract and the terms of such contract.”
BaselineB: Common law (justiciability/jurisdiction over voluntary associations from Highwood Congregation of Jehovah’s Witnesses (Judicial Committee) v. Wall, 2018 SCC 26; and general contract formation principles including objective intention to create legal relations, drawing on Scotsburn Co-operative Services Ltd. v. W. T. Goodwin Ltd., 1985 and Owners, Strata Plan LMS 3905 v. Crystal Square Parking Corp., 2020).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Quebec Charter s. 49(2) punitive (exemplary) damages: admissible autonomously (no compensatory damages required) and available against a deceased wrongdoer’s succession; award requires (1) unlawful interference with a Charter right and (2) intentional interference (intent to cause the result), with denunciation recognized as a valid objective
BaselineA: Statute (Quebec Charter, s. 49(2), interpreted alongside Civil Code of Québec art. 1621; informed by SCC precedents Augustus, St-Ferdinand, Béliveau St-Jacques)
CaseB_TestB: YCJA jurisdiction for youth judicial interim release on s. 469 charges after election: “the proceeding” in YCJA ss. 13(2)-(3) includes pre-trial steps (including bail), and YCJA s. 33(8) gives release power to any “youth justice court judge” (including both s. 13(1) designated youth court judges and s. 13(2)-(3) deemed superior court judges), creating concurrent jurisdiction
BaselineB: Statute (Youth Criminal Justice Act ss. 13(1)-(3), 28, 33(8), 67; Criminal Code ss. 469, 522; Interpretation Act s. 33(2))
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Miscarriage of justice from trial conduct: whether trial shortcomings “affected the trial judge’s appreciation of the evidence or rendered the proceedings unfair, so as to give rise to a miscarriage of justice” (para. 8); leading questions are impermissible only if they “suggest an answer or assume a state of facts that is in dispute” (para. 9).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 693(1)(a)) plus common-law appellate standard for “miscarriage of justice”/trial fairness (not specifically sourced to a named SCC precedent in these reasons).
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 13 “incriminating evidence” threshold: s. 13 is engaged only if the prior compelled testimony is “incriminating evidence”, meaning evidence from the prior proceeding that the Crown could use at the later proceeding “to prove or assist in proving one or more of the essential elements of the offence” (paras. 8-10); using non-incriminating discovery evidence “for impeachment purposes, and nothing else,” does not trigger s. 13 (paras. 22, 25).
BaselineB: Statute/constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 13 (interpreting “incriminating evidence” and “used to incriminate”); prior SCC jurisprudence discussed as baseline context includes R. v. Henry, 2005 SCC 76; R. v. Kuldip, [1990] 3 S.C.R. 618; R. v. Noël, 2002 SCC 67; Dubois v. The Queen, [1985] 2 S.C.R. 350.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 467.12 “in association with” a criminal organization: requires (1) a nexus between the predicate offence and the organization (not merely between the accused and the organization) and (2) subjective mens rea that the accused knowingly dealt with a criminal organization; “in association with” captures offences that “advance, at least to some degree, the interests of a criminal organization” (Venneri, paras. 54-57).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 467.12(1) (and related definition in s. 467.1))
CaseB_TestB: Test for compulsion under Motor Vehicle Act s. 61(1) (for Charter s. 7 use-immunity): whether, at the time of reporting, the driver gave the report on the basis of “an honest and reasonably held belief that he or she was required by law to report the accident to the person to whom the report was given” (White, para. 75); accused bears the onus on a balance of probabilities to show compulsion (para. 81).
BaselineB: Combination of statute and constitutional law (Motor Vehicle Act, R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 288, s. 61(1) and Charter s. 7 principle against self-incrimination as applied to compelled statements)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Reasonable suspicion standard for sniffer-dog searches: suspicion must be grounded in “objectively discernible facts” assessed on the “totality of the circumstances” (a “constellation of factors”), through the lens of a reasonable officer; the question is whether facts are “objectively indicative of the possibility of criminal behaviour” (not probability).
BaselineA: Common law Charter s. 8 sniffer-dog search framework from R. v. Kang-Brown and R. v. A.M., clarified with R. v. Chehil; investigative detention authority from R. v. Mann (reasonable suspicion).
CaseB_TestB: Reformulated s. 11(i) “punishment” test: a measure is punishment if (1) it is a consequence of conviction forming part of the “arsenal of sanctions”, and either (2) it is imposed in furtherance of sentencing purposes/principles, or (3) it has a “significant impact” on liberty/security (significantly constrains otherwise lawful conduct or imposes significant burdens not imposed on the public).
BaselineB: Common law Charter s. 11(i) punishment test from R. v. Rodgers (two-part test), applied to Criminal Code s. 161(1)(c),(d) (as amended by Safe Streets and Communities Act, 2012).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: CCQ art. 1425 “common intention” interpretation/rectification: where writings misstate the parties’ proven common intention due to error, the court may recognize the parties’ corrective amendments (including retroactive dating) as “legitimate and necessary”, subject to third-party rights; “If a private writing contains an error, the court must, once the error is proved ... note the error and ensure that it is remedied.”
BaselineA: Statute (Civil Code of Québec, art. 1425; also relies on CCQ contract-law principles such as consensualism and the negotium/instrumentum distinction)
CaseB_TestB: Bank “put upon inquiry” constructive trust test: “A banker may be a constructive trustee of money in his customer’s account and in breach of that trust if he pays the money away, even on the customer’s mandate, in circumstances which put him upon inquiry.”
BaselineB: Common law (constructive trustee/bank on inquiry doctrine; as summarized from Halsbury’s Laws of England and illustrated by cases such as White v. Dominion Bank and Cartwright v. Lyster & Bank of Nova Scotia, as cited in the reasons)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Applicability of Quebec’s 1974 retrospective prescription amendments to a case pending in the Supreme Court of Canada: s. 5 makes art. 2262(2) C.C. inapplicable to a “suit pending before a court on 1 January 1975”, so the SCC may dismiss the appeal on that basis (SCC Act s. 47 does not bar dismissal on new law).
BaselineA: Statute (Supreme Court Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. S-19, s. 47; plus Quebec Act to amend certain prescriptions, 1974 (Que.), c. 80, ss. 1, 3, 5; Civil Code arts. 2261(2), 2262(2))
CaseB_TestB: Ministerial refusal-of-surrender threshold in extradition: extradition should be refused only if surrender would “shock the conscience” (s. 7 Charter) or be “unjust or oppressive” (Extradition Act, s. 44(1)); otherwise it is reasonable to leave due process concerns (including delay) to the foreign court.
BaselineB: Combination (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7; Extradition Act, S.C. 1999, c. 18, s. 44(1); common law/precedent including United States v. Burns and Argentina v. Mellino)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Hart ‘Mr. Big’ confessions admissibility framework: presumptive inadmissibility rebutted only if Crown shows (on balance) probative value (reliability) outweighs prejudicial effect; plus separate abuse-of-process backstop for coercive/abusive operations
BaselineA: Common law (law of evidence): party admissions exception to hearsay (R. v. Evans; R. v. Osmar) and the trial judge’s residual discretion to exclude evidence where prejudicial effect exceeds probative value (e.g., R. v. Mohan; R. v. Handy); abuse of process doctrine (e.g., R. v. Babos; R. v. Mack)
CaseB_TestB: Borowiec interpretation of Criminal Code s. 233 ‘her mind is then disturbed’: apply ‘disturbed’ in its ordinary sense (low threshold), with six clarifications (no need for mental disorder; must exist at time; must be ‘by reason of’ birth/lactation; no causation requirement between disturbance and act)
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 233 (infanticide) (with contextual comparison to ss. 2, 16, 663(b), 672.11(c))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Penile swab as a search incident to arrest is Charter-compliant only if (1) police have independent “reasonable grounds to believe that a penile swab will afford evidence of the offence for which the accused was arrested” and (2) the swab is “conducted in a reasonable manner” guided by enumerated factors (e.g., station-house, supervisory authorization, privacy, same gender, minimal officers, record-keeping).
BaselineA: Common law (search incident to arrest under s. 8 Charter reasonableness). Baseline framework: R. v. Fearon, 2014 SCC 77 (general search-incident-to-arrest framework) and R. v. Golden, 2001 SCC 83 (strip-search modifications: reasonable grounds + manner guidelines); also distinguishes R. v. Stillman, [1997] 1 S.C.R. 607.
CaseB_TestB: Joint/co-principal liability in group assaults: it “flows whenever two or more individuals come together with an intention to commit an offence, are present during the commission of the offence, and contribute to its commission”; for manslaughter, focus is whether the accused’s actions were “a significant contributing cause of death” (not which perpetrator inflicted which wound), and “absent a discrete or intervening event, the actions of all assailants can constitute a significant contributing cause to all injuries sustained.”
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, s. 21(1)(a) (co-principal) and s. 21(1)(c) (abetting) as the party-liability baseline) as interpreted through common law; relies on/clarifies against R. v. Pickton, 2010 SCC 32 and corrects an implication from R. v. Cabrera (ABCA), aff’d R. v. Shlah, 2019 SCC 56.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Whether a damages claim for breach/violation of a collective agreement clause (e.g., no-strike clause) is a statutory “grievance” that must go to arbitration: no distinction between (i) employer vs employee monetary claims and (ii) “interpretation/application” vs “violation” of the agreement (they are “two ways of looking at the same problem”).
BaselineA: Statute (Quebec Labour Code, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 141, ss. 1(g) definition of “grievance” as a “disagreement respecting the interpretation or application of a collective agreement”, and s. 88 mandatory arbitration of “Every grievance”), as interpreted in SCC precedent General Motors of Canada Ltd. v. Brunet, [1977] 2 S.C.R. 537 (and supported by Imbleau et al. v. Laskin et al., [1962] S.C.R. 338).
CaseB_TestB: Enforceability/scope of a waiver (exclusion) clause for negligence in a race entry form: construed in its context as a release; the clause applies unless the alleged negligence is outside what reasonable parties would have contemplated, and it will not be avoided as “unfair” or “unreasonable” on these facts (no need to decide fundamental breach; no unconscionability/public policy bar here).
BaselineB: Common law (contractual interpretation/enforcement of exclusion/waiver clauses; doctrines argued included fundamental breach, unconscionability, and public policy—no specific statutory basis identified in the reasons).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: When a CLRB s. 119 application is merely an updating/clarification versus a de facto new certification: if the Board’s changes “do not alter the nature and scope of the certificate of certification and of the bargaining unit”, it is a review/clarification (not a new certification requiring full ss. 124+ representativeness/appropriateness inquiries).
BaselineA: Statute (Canada Labour Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. L-1, s. 119 (Board may “review, rescind, amend, alter or vary any order or decision made by it”); contrasted with certification requirements under ss. 124 et seq. as argued).
CaseB_TestB: Appellate intervention standard on factual findings: it is wrong to set aside a trial judgment absent “palpable and overriding error” where the only issue is “the interpretation of the evidence as a whole”; the appellate court must be able to say the trial judge was “plainly wrong”.
BaselineB: Common law (as stated to follow prior SCC authority: Schreiber Brothers Limited v. Currie Products Limited and Gulf Oil Canada Limited; Stein v. "Kathy K."; Lewis v. Todd).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Ernst (Cromwell J.) categorical Ward-based rule: Charter damages can never be an “appropriate and just” remedy (s. 24(1)) for Charter breaches by this quasi-judicial regulator, given countervailing factors (alternative remedy + good governance + immunity purpose)
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 24(1) (“appropriate and just” remedy) as interpreted in Vancouver (City) v. Ward, 2010 SCC 27 (framework for Charter damages); applied in context of Energy Resources Conservation Act, s. 43 (immunity clause).
CaseB_TestB: Maybrun framework (as applied in Bird) for when an accused charged with breaching an administrative order may collaterally attack the order: infer legislative intent using five non-exhaustive factors
BaselineB: Common law framework from R. v. Consolidated Maybrun Mines Ltd., [1998] 1 S.C.R. 706 and R. v. Al Klippert Ltd., [1998] 1 S.C.R. 737, applied in the statutory context of Corrections and Conditional Release Act, s. 134.1(2) (LTSO conditions) and Criminal Code, s. 753.3(1) (offence for breach).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Art. 2930 C.C.Q. applies (3-year prescription) where the action is based on the obligation to make reparation for the direct and immediate consequences of interference with a person’s physical integrity: the court must “characterize the basis for the action” by looking to “the nature of the initial interference rather than the head of damages being claimed” (paras. 26-27, 55).
BaselineA: Statute: Civil Code of Québec, arts. 2925 and 2930 (in interaction with Cities and Towns Act, s. 586).
CaseB_TestB: Appellate non-intervention on trial judge’s factual findings/credibility: once the trial judge’s oral reasons are in the record, the Court of Appeal’s substitution of its view of the evidence is an “unwarranted intrusion” into an area “exclusive to the trial judge”.
BaselineB: Common law principle of appellate deference/non-intervention on findings of fact and credibility (as reflected in Latour v. Grenier; Maze v. Empson; Dorval v. Bouvier; Métivier v. Cadorette; Hood v. Hood, cited in the reasons).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Schrenk “sufficient nexus” test for discrimination “regarding employment”: Tribunal must conduct a contextual analysis of whether the discrimination has a “sufficient nexus with the employment context”, with non-exhaustive factors including (1) whether the respondent was “integral to the complainant’s workplace”; (2) whether the conduct occurred “in the complainant’s workplace”; and (3) whether the complainant’s “work performance or work environment was negatively affected” (paras. 67-68).
BaselineA: Statute: Human Rights Code, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 210, s. 13(1)(b) (“discriminate against a person regarding employment or any term or condition of employment”), with interpretive context from ss. 1 (“person”, “employment”) and 3 (purposes).
CaseB_TestB: Groia in-court incivility/professional misconduct framework: a context-specific inquiry considering “what the lawyer said, the manner and frequency in which it was said, and the presiding judge’s reaction” (para. 80). Within this, allegations impugning opposing counsel’s integrity “cross the line into professional misconduct unless they are made in good faith and have a reasonable basis” (para. 81), where “reasonable basis” focuses on whether allegations are “speculative or entirely lacking a factual foundation” and not merely based on legal error (paras. 88-91).
BaselineB: Statute/regulatory: Law Society Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. L.8 (discipline mandate) and Law Society Rules of Professional Conduct (made under the Act) governing civility/professional conduct.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Ontario anti-SLAPP dismissal framework under CJA s. 137.1: (1) defendant must show on a balance of probabilities the proceeding “arises from an expression” that “relates to a matter of public interest” (s. 137.1(3)); if met, (2) plaintiff must satisfy the judge that (a) there are “grounds to believe” the proceeding has “substantial merit” and the defendant has “no valid defence” (s. 137.1(4)(a)), and (b) the harm from the expression is “sufficiently serious” that the public interest in permitting the proceeding to continue “outweighs” the public interest in protecting the expression (s. 137.1(4)(b)). Key SCC clarifications include: “grounds to believe” requires “a basis in the record and the law”; “substantial merit” means a “real prospect of success” (legally tenable + evidence “reasonably capable of belief”); and s. 137.1(4)(b) is an open-ended public-interest weighing where one side must “outweigh” the other.
BaselineA: Statute: Courts of Justice Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.43, s. 137.1(3) and (4) (and related ss. 137.1(2), 137.2).
CaseB_TestB: Corporate attribution doctrine (including one-person corporations): whether a directing mind’s knowledge/acts are attributed to the corporation depends on purposive, contextual application of Aquino principles, including a discretionary “public interest” refusal. SCC summary: (a) attribution generally if (1) wrongdoer was directing mind and (2) acted within assigned corporate responsibility; (b) generally inappropriate if “totally in fraud of the corporation” or “not by design or result partly for the benefit of the corporation”; (c) courts also have discretion to refrain where attribution would not be “in the public interest, in the sense that it would promote the purpose of the law under which attribution is sought”; (d) always apply purposively/contextually/pragmatically. Applied to Limitations Act discoverability: court may decline attribution where it would undermine the purposes of the Limitations Act discoverability rules and the BIA.
BaselineB: Common law: corporate attribution doctrine from Canadian Dredge & Dock Co. v. The Queen; Deloitte & Touche v. Livent Inc. (Receiver of); Christine DeJong Medicine Professional Corp. v. DBDC Spadina Ltd.; summarized in Aquino v. Bondfield Construction Co. (applied in this case).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Duty of trial judge to comment on Crown counsel’s improper jury address: where remarks are “prejudicial to a degree sufficient to impose a legal duty on the trial judge to comment” to ensure the defence position is “fairly put to the jury”; failure to do so is an error of law (then consider whether s. 686(1)(b)(iii) ‘no substantial wrong or miscarriage of justice’ applies).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(b)(iii)) plus common-law fairness requirements for jury charges/addresses (as reflected in the Court’s adoption of Ayles J.A.’s formulation).
CaseB_TestB: “Identifiability” test for Federal Court in rem jurisdiction under s. 43(2): reject a narrow “physical nexus” approach; property is “subject of the action” if it is identifiable as the cargo designated in the contract of affreightment alleged to be breached.
BaselineB: Statute (Federal Courts Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. F-7, s. 43(2) — meaning of “ship, aircraft or other property that is the subject of the action”).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Threshold for summary dismissal of criminal applications: an application may be summarily dismissed only if it is “manifestly frivolous”; on the motion the judge must “assume the facts alleged ... to be true” and “take the applicant’s arguments at their highest”, without weighing evidence, and the moving party bears the burden (R. v. Haevischer, 2023 SCC 11 at paras. 3, 66, 71, 82-85, 90).
BaselineA: Common law / judge-made criminal procedure (Vukelich-type summary dismissal power; prior varied formulations in cases such as Vukelich, Kutynec, Cody, Jordan, Pires).
CaseB_TestB: Combined effect of Criminal Code s. 172.1(3) presumption and s. 172.1(4) “reasonable steps” requirement: if underage is represented, accused is presumed to believe underage; presumption is rebutted only by “evidence to the contrary, which must include evidence that the accused took steps to ascertain the real age ... [that] must be reasonable in the circumstances”; evidential burden on accused, persuasive burden on Crown (R. v. Levigne, 2010 SCC 25 at para. 32).
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 172.1(3) and s. 172.1(4) (interpreted harmoniously with s. 172.1’s purpose).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Two-step framework for whether legislation displaces a common law sentencing rule (and its application to credit for pre-sentence driving prohibitions despite a mandatory minimum): (1) identify the applicable common law rule; (2) specify the statute’s effect on that rule (expressly or by necessary implication).
BaselineA: Combination of common law and statute: common law discretion to credit pre-sentence driving prohibitions (R. v. Lacasse, 2015 SCC 64; analogy to pre-sentence custody credit discussed in R. v. Wust, 2000 SCC 18) plus interpretation of Criminal Code ss. 259(1)(a) and 719(1) (and discussion of s. 719(3)).
CaseB_TestB: Mitigation in breach of contract where plaintiff sought specific performance: defendant must prove (i) plaintiff failed to take reasonable steps to mitigate and (ii) mitigation was possible; plaintiff’s inaction may be reasonable only if it had a “fair, real, and substantial justification” / “substantial and legitimate interest” in specific performance (typically requiring land’s “peculiar and special value” such that damages are inadequate).
BaselineB: Common law mitigation doctrine and specific-performance-related mitigation exception from Asamera Oil Corp. v. Seal Oil & General Corp., [1979] 1 S.C.R. 633, read with Semelhago v. Paramadevan, [1996] 2 S.C.R. 415 (uniqueness/“peculiar and special value” for specific performance).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Hearsay admissibility under the principled approach (necessity and threshold reliability) applies even to traditional exceptions; statements of present intention are inadmissible if made in “circumstances of suspicion” and cannot be used to prove a third party’s intentions absent an exception for each hearsay level
BaselineA: Common law (hearsay rule and exceptions; principled approach from R. v. Khan and R. v. Smith; present intentions exception discussed in Smith)
CaseB_TestB: Public interest standing (Downtown Eastside) — discretionary, cumulative weighing of three factors: (i) serious justiciable issue; (ii) genuine interest; (iii) reasonable and effective means (including whether a sufficiently concrete and well-developed factual setting will be forthcoming, without requiring an individual co-plaintiff)
BaselineB: Common law (public interest standing framework from Canada (Attorney General) v. Downtown Eastside Sex Workers United Against Violence Society, 2012 SCC 45)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.
