CaseA_TestA: Limited-liability / non-assessability constraint: a company cannot, by altering articles or passing resolutions, impose any pecuniary burden on holders of fully paid shares (and a transfer fee is invalid to the extent it exceeds the reasonable and proper cost of the transfer).
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common-law company-law principle: The Companies Act (Alberta) (notably ss. 42(1), 68(4), 193(1)(d) and related limited-liability definitions) plus the fundamental principle that “there can be no pecuniary assessment in respect of fully paid shares”.
JudgeA: Dickson J. (for Ritchie, Pigeon and Dickson JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Van der Peet aboriginal-rights test (as applied): an activity is an aboriginal right only if it is “an element of a practice, custom or tradition integral to the distinctive culture” of the group; court must (1) characterize the precise claim, then (2) ask whether, prior to contact, the practice was a “central, significant or defining feature” of the society.
BaselineB: Common law / constitutional interpretation baseline from R. v. Van der Peet (1996) interpreting Constitution Act, 1982, s. 35(1) (applied to charges under Fisheries Act s. 61(1) and BC Fishery (General) Regulations ss. 4(5), 27(5)).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Reviewability of a consensual labour arbitrator’s award for error of law on the face of the award: no “specific question of law” reference (binding/ouster) where the issue arises in the ordinary grievance process under a collective agreement that limits the arbitrator to decisions consistent with the agreement
BaselineA: Common law (scope of court review of consensual arbitration awards), drawing on Government of Kelantan v. Duff Development Co. Ltd. and the SCC’s approach in Faubert and Watts v. Temagami Mining Co. Ltd. and Bell Canada v. Office and Professional Employees’ International Union, Local 131
CaseB_TestB: Morin framework for s. 11(b) “reasonable time” (as applied/clarified): assess total delay minus defence waiver, then consider reasons for delay, prejudice (including inferred prejudice from length), and s. 11(b) interests; defence scheduling does not require “perpetual availability”
BaselineB: Statute/constitutional text (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 11(b)) as operationalized by common-law framework in R. v. Morin (and R. v. Askov)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 3(4) test for establishing (joint) possession: possession exists where a person has something in personal possession or knowingly has it in another’s custody/possession or in any place for use/benefit (s. 3(4)(a)); and where one of two or more persons, with the knowledge and consent of the rest, has anything in custody/possession, it is deemed to be in the custody and possession of each and all of them (s. 3(4)(b)). SCC holds this applies 'for the purposes of this Act' to all proceedings under the Code, including when possession is used as a circumstantial evidentiary link.
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 3(4) (now s. 4(3) in later consolidations).
CaseB_TestB: Test for establishing adverse possession in British Columbia: possession must be 'open and notorious, adverse, exclusive, peaceful (not by force), actual (generally), and continuous'; and the 'inconsistent use' requirement (use inconsistent with the true owner’s intended present/future enjoyment) is not part of BC law.
BaselineB: Combination: common law adverse possession elements as received/understood in BC, and BC limitations legislation reproducing the 1833 English codification (e.g., Statute of Limitations (1924) ss. 16-17; Law and Equity Act s. 2 receiving Real Property Limitation Act, 1833).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Quantum meruit for services rendered without agreed remuneration: where a municipality continues to authorize and accept services after termination of an agreement, it is obligated to pay “reasonable rates” (and recovery is not barred unless a valid Order in Council/statutory authority clearly extinguishes the right).
BaselineA: Common law (quantum meruit / quasi-contract), with statutory interpretation of delegated regulation powers under the Hospital Act s. 37(2) (as amended), the Social Assistance Act, and the Residence and Responsibility Act s. 3 to assess whether Orders in Council could bar recovery.
CaseB_TestB: Admissibility/voluntariness of inculpatory statements by an allegedly insane accused: the “underlying and controlling question” is whether the statement was “freely and voluntarily made”, including whether it reflects an “operating mind” (not a fixed formula; trial judge must address the proper considerations).
BaselineB: Common law confessions rule on voluntariness (Boudreau v. The King; Ward v. The Queen; with guidance from R. v. Santinon).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Effect of breach of a witness-exclusion order: witness not necessarily disqualified; admissibility discretionary; weight assessed by trier of fact (and no legal requirement that the judge expressly state a self-caution for each such witness)
BaselineA: Common law (practice/rule on exclusion of witnesses and consequences of breach, as reflected in cases cited such as Moore v. Lambeth County Court Registrar; Cook v. Nethercotte; Thomas v. David; Chandler v. Home; Black v. Besse; R. v. Carefoot)
CaseB_TestB: Clear-and-unequivocal-language requirement to lift Crown immunity from discovery: s. 27 CLPA applies only where the Crown is a party; otherwise common law immunity from discovery remains
BaselineB: Statute interpreted against common law backdrop (Interpretation Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. I-21, s. 17; Crown Liability and Proceedings Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-50, s. 27 (and related structure/ss. 23-27, 34))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Whether members of the Law Society Discipline Committee are disqualified (for bias/natural justice) from participating in Convocation when Convocation considers the Committee’s report and recommendation (two-stage process vs appeal; expressio unius from s. 39(4))
BaselineA: Statute and regulation (The Law Society Act, 1970 (Ont.), ss. 33(12), 34, 37, 39; Reg. 556, s. 13(6)-(7)) plus common-law natural justice/bias principles (nemo judex / reasonable apprehension of bias)
CaseB_TestB: Criminal Code s. 731(1)(b) probation eligibility: “imprisonment for a term not exceeding two years” refers to the term imposed by the sentencing court at a single sitting (not the aggregate of other sentences), with the caveat that probation cannot attach where sentences imposed at the same session result in continuous custody over two years
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 731(1)(b), with related context in ss. 732.2 and 743.1)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “operation of a mine” and when a separate “mine” exists for the 36‑month exemption: (1) “operation of a mine” in s. 83(5) “refers only to the extraction of ore from an ore body and does not include the processing of the ore after it has been produced”; and (2) “there is ‘a mine’ within the meaning of s. 83(5) if there is a body of ore together with the workings, equipment and machinery capable of producing it” — a separate mine arises when a separate ore body “commenced to be extracted by means of its separate and distinct extraction facilities” (shared milling does not matter).
BaselineA: Statute: Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1952, c. 148 as amended, s. 83(5) and s. 83(6) (definitions of “mine” and “production”); interpreted in light of SCC authorities North Bay Mica Company Limited v. M.N.R., [1958] S.C.R. 597 and M.N.R. v. MacLean Mining Co., [1970] S.C.R. 877.
CaseB_TestB: Leave to sue a receiver/trustee under s. 215 BIA (Mancini test): leave should be refused only for frivolous/vexatious or manifestly unmeritorious claims; the evidence must provide the required support and disclose a cause of action; the court “is not required to make a final assessment of the merits” — “If the evidence discloses a prima facie case, leave should be granted.”
BaselineB: Statute: Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. B-3, s. 215 (leave requirement), applied through the common-law/precedential framework from Mancini (Bankrupt) v. Falconi (1993), 61 O.A.C. 332 (C.A.) as adopted/endorsed by the SCC in this case.
JudgeB: Abella J. (McLachlin C.J. and Bastarache, Binnie, LeBel, Fish and Charron JJ. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Education Act s. 373 school-tax roll equalization: commissioners must amend non-uniform municipal rolls only to "re-establish on the basis of its real value the valuation of the taxable property" in each part of the school municipality (i.e., value what is taxable in each municipality; no priority to another municipality’s choice to exempt machinery).
BaselineA: Statute: Education Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 235, s. 373 (with context from Cities and Towns Act s. 488 re municipal option to exclude machinery; and prior SCC treatment in Protestant School Board of Greater Montreal v. Jenkins Bros. Ltd., [1967] S.C.R. 739 distinguished).
CaseB_TestB: Criminal Code s. 426(1)(a)(ii) “secret commission” offence (agent/taker): actus reus requires (1) agency relationship; (2) agent accepts a benefit "as consideration" for acting/forbearing in relation to the principal’s affairs; and (3) "failure ... to make adequate and timely disclosure"—because "corruptly" in this context means "secretly or without the requisite disclosure"; no corrupt bargain required.
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 426(1)(a) (formerly s. 383(1)(a)); interpreting "corruptly" and elements of the offence.
JudgeB: Cory J. (for L’Heureux-Dubé, Gonthier, Cory and Iacobucci JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Extradition-crime characterization: “The test is what is the essence of the crime charged” (i.e., whether the charged conduct falls within the extradition arrangement category, here “against the laws for the suppression of the traffic in narcotics”).
BaselineA: Statute + extradition arrangement: Extradition Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-21, s. 2 (definition of “extradition crime”), including crimes “described in such arrangement”; Supplementary Convention (1925) category added to the Act: “Crimes and offences against the laws for the suppression of the traffic in narcotics”.
CaseB_TestB: Section 13 “incriminate” vs credibility-use distinction: prior testimony may be used on cross-examination at a later proceeding if used only to impeach credibility, but not if used “to incriminate” (establish guilt).
BaselineB: Constitution + statute: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 13 (and its interpretation in Dubois and Mannion as discussed in the reasons); Canada Evidence Act, s. 5(2) (as interpreted alongside s. 13).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Negligence foreseeability/remoteness test for highway authority liability: whether a reasonable person should have anticipated the harm as a natural (probable) result of the act/omission; need not foresee the “precise concatenation of events”, only the general “class or character of injury”.
BaselineA: Common law foreseeability/remoteness in negligence (University Hospital Board v. Lépine; Wagon Mound No. 2). Also applied in the context of the Highway Improvement Act, R.S.O. 1960, s. 33(1) (failure to maintain highway at a dangerous point).
CaseB_TestB: CEAA “tracking” rule: the environmental assessment track is determined by the “project as proposed” (not “project as scoped”); if the proposed project is listed in the Comprehensive Study List, s. 21 requirements are mandatory and the responsible authority cannot reduce the project below what is proposed.
BaselineB: Statutory interpretation/application of the Canadian Environmental Assessment Act, S.C. 1992, c. 37 (especially ss. 2 “project”, 15, 18, 21, 58(1)(i)) and the Comprehensive Study List Regulations, SOR/94-638.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Res ipsa loquitur as a rule of evidence to infer (and support a finding of) gross negligence in a gratuitous-passenger motor vehicle claim: applies where (1) the thing causing damage was under the defendant’s “sole management and control”; (2) the occurrence is such that it “would not have happened without negligence”; and (3) there is “no evidence as to why or how the occurrence took place” (but if an explanation is given and is not a “valid explanation”, the maxim may still apply).
BaselineA: Common law (res ipsa loquitur), applied in the statutory context of Ontario Highway Traffic Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 202, s. 132(3) (gratuitous passenger requires proof that loss was “caused or contributed to by the gross negligence of the driver”).
CaseB_TestB: Two-part criteria for recognizing a vested (acquired) right, triggering the presumption against legislative interference: a vested right exists where (1) the individual’s legal situation is “tangible and concrete rather than general and abstract”; and (2) the situation was “sufficiently constituted at the time of the new statute’s commencement”.
BaselineB: Statutory interpretation/common law presumption against interference with vested rights, codified in Interpretation Act, R.S.Q., c. I-16, s. 12; applied to amendments to the Act respecting financial assistance for students (including s. 13 “juridical situations in progress”).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Mechanics’ lien owner-liability/holdback test on contractor abandonment: s. 19(2) does not prevent the owner deducting completion costs from amounts otherwise payable to the head contractor; s. 19(2) only bars deductions for “prior or subsequent indebtedness, set-off, or counterclaim” extraneous to the contract (so owner liability remains limited by s. 6 to “the sum payable by the owner to the contractor”).
BaselineA: Statute (Mechanics’ Lien Act, R.S.B.C. 1960, c. 238, ss. 6, 19(2), 21(1), 21(6))
CaseB_TestB: Choice-of-law rule for torts: “as a general rule, the law to be applied in torts is the law of the place where the activity occurred, i.e., the lex loci delicti” (overruling McLean v. Pettigrew); and, for conflicts purposes, the foreign limitation period is treated as substantive where it “created an accrued right in the defendant to plead a time bar.”
BaselineB: Common law (conflict of laws in tort; overruling McLean v. Pettigrew and rejecting lex fori/double-actionability approaches)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Constitutional (territorial) validity test for provincial legislation with extra-provincial effects: a province cannot legislate in relation to conduct/rights outside its territory (e.g., cannot nullify another jurisdiction’s permission/licence); interprovincial pollution is a matter of federal concern
BaselineA: Combination: statute (B.N.A. Act, 1867 ss. 91–92; Manitoba’s The Fishermen’s Assistance and Polluters’ Liability Act, 1970, especially s. 4(2)) plus common-law/conflict-of-laws principles and prior cases cited (e.g., Royal Bank of Canada v. The King; Phillips v. Eyre; The King v. National Trust Co.)
JudgeA: Pigeon J. (for Martland, Pigeon and Beetz JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Judicial review under a privative clause: court may intervene only for jurisdictional error; an administrative decision warrants intervention only if it is “patently unreasonable”/an “unreasonable finding” (and, in Beetz J.’s framing, only if it amounts to an abuse of authority causing “flagrant injustice”)
BaselineB: Combination: statute (Act respecting labour standards, R.S.Q., c. N-1.1, ss. 124–129, especially s. 128; Labour Code, s. 139 privative clause; Code of Civil Procedure, art. 846) plus SCC administrative-law jurisprudence (e.g., CUPE v. NB Liquor)
JudgeB: Lamer J. (reasons; with Beetz J. concurring in result and adding observations)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Collective agreement primacy: common law repudiation/fundamental breach concepts are inapplicable to an unexpired collective agreement; an illegal strike does not, by itself, terminate the employment relationship or severance-pay obligations absent employer disciplinary termination
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law labour jurisprudence: Mediation Services Act, 1968 (B.C.), ss. 6 (collective agreement binding) and 23 (prohibition on strike during term), plus SCC labour-law characterization of collective agreements (Syndicat catholique des employés de magasins de Québec Inc. v. Compagnie Paquet Ltée; C.P.R. Co. v. Zambri) and related authority (Re Polymer Corp.)
CaseB_TestB: Limits on cross-examination using a complainant’s diary: relevant defence cross-examination should be allowed unless its prejudicial effect substantially outweighs its probative value; omission evidence is probative only if the defence establishes a reasonable expectation the event would have been recorded
BaselineB: Common law evidence principles governing defence evidence/cross-examination limits: R. v. Seaboyer and R. v. Osolin ("prejudice must substantially outweigh" probative value); clarification that R. v. O’Connor (production balancing) is not the admissibility/cross-examination test
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Admissibility of evidence that an accused refused to participate in a police line-up: admissible only where, in the circumstances, it is relevant (typically to explain the absence of a line-up) and not merely to suggest guilt
BaselineA: Common law evidence (relevance/admissibility) informed by the common law privilege against self-incrimination (testimonial compulsion) and related jurisprudence (e.g., Curr v. The Queen; A.-G. (Que.) v. Begin; U.S. cases on testimonial vs physical evidence)
CaseB_TestB: Division of powers (pith and substance) limit on provincial commissions of inquiry: an inquiry is ultra vires if, in purpose/effect, it is a substitute police investigation/preliminary inquiry into specific alleged Criminal Code offences by named private individuals (i.e., circumvents federal criminal procedure)
BaselineB: Constitution Act, 1867 (ss. 91(27), 92) division-of-powers pith-and-substance analysis, applied to a provincial Order in Council under the Public Inquiries Act, R.S.O. 1980, c. 411, and assessed against Criminal Code context (notably s. 121 and preliminary inquiry provisions such as ss. 535, 548)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Punitive damages in tort: whether the circumstances justify an additional punitive award “in the interests of justice” (here, tortious inducement/conspiracy aimed at taking over and ending the plaintiff’s business), and if so, the quantum
BaselineA: Common law (punitive/exemplary damages principles; no specific baseline case articulated in the reasons provided)
CaseB_TestB: Duty of care for pure economic loss: (1) does the claim fit within a recognized duty category (including relational economic loss requiring third-party property damage), and if not (2) should a new duty be recognized under the two-stage Anns/Cooper test (foreseeability + proximity, then residual policy such as indeterminate liability)
BaselineB: Common law (Anns v. Merton; Kamloops v. Nielsen; Cooper v. Hobart; Childs v. Desormeaux; Norsk categories of pure economic loss)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory limits on Canadian Transport Commission power under Railway Act s. 275: a tariff filed/published in compliance takes effect on its stated effective date; any Commission order extending the s. 275(2) notice period must be made before that effective date (post‑effective-date “extension” is an impermissible postponement and ultra vires).
BaselineA: Statute (Railway Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. R-2, s. 275(2) and s. 275(4); also National Transportation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. N-17, s. 64(5) considered re effect of invalid orders).
CaseB_TestB: Palmer test for admitting fresh evidence on appeal (“interests of justice”): (1) due diligence (less strict in criminal cases), (2) relevance to a decisive/potentially decisive issue, (3) credibility, and (4) could reasonably be expected to have affected the result if believed.
BaselineB: Common law (Palmer v. The Queen, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 759, at p. 775) applied within the statutory discretion to admit fresh evidence (Criminal Code, s. 683; predecessor s. 610).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Effectiveness/finality of an order still within the appeal period: even though an order subject to appeal is not effective for all purposes before the appeal time runs, lack of finality will not invariably prevent full effectiveness (even against third parties) where there is only an “ephemeral prospect of an appeal”; the court must consider “the purpose for which the finality or want of finality of an order is urged”, “who is affected”, and “in what context” finality is asserted before the appeal period expires.
BaselineA: Statute (The Conveyancing and Law of Property Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 85, s. 62) applied in the vendor–purchaser context; with the Court distinguishing Re West (1928) and Leonard v. Wharton (1921) on the effect of non-final orders.
CaseB_TestB: Preliminary inquiry committal/sufficiency test with defence evidence: under Criminal Code s. 548(1), ask whether there is “any evidence upon which a reasonable jury properly instructed could return a verdict of guilty” (Shephard). If Crown evidence is direct on all elements, committal follows regardless of defence evidence; if Crown evidence is (in whole or part) circumstantial, the judge must do a “limited weighing” of the whole evidence to decide whether, if the Crown’s evidence is believed, it would be reasonable for a properly instructed jury to infer guilt (without drawing inferences or assessing credibility).
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 548(1) (and related preliminary inquiry provisions) interpreted through the common law sufficiency rule from United States of America v. Shephard, [1977] 2 S.C.R. 1067 (also discussed with Mezzo and Monteleone).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Discretionary public-interest standing (taxpayer/citizen) to challenge legislation: standing may be granted where (1) a “serious, a substantial constitutional issue” is raised; (2) the plaintiff has taken “all the steps that he could reasonably be required to take” so the issue is “ripe”; (3) the plaintiff is arguably “directly affected” (here, as a member of the public affected by censorship); and (4) “there appears to be no other way, practically speaking, to subject the challenged Act to judicial review”, making it appropriate to “exercise[] its discretion” to grant standing.
BaselineA: Common law (standing/locus standi doctrine), drawing on Smith v. Attorney General of Ontario, [1924] S.C.R. 331 and Thorson v. Attorney General of Canada, [1975] 1 S.C.R. 138
CaseB_TestB: Interpretation of ASRA Program s. 88(3) and linkage discretion: applying C.C.Q. arts. 1425-1432 (esp. art. 1427 ‘contract as a whole’ and art. 1426 ‘past practice/usage’), s. 88(3) (“[a]ny amounts to which a participant is entitled”) “does not require that amounts be linked individually but, on the contrary, gives La Financière the discretion to decide what linkage method to employ”; that discretion must be exercised “in accordance with the requirements of good faith and contractual fairness” (arts. 6, 7, 1375, 1434 C.C.Q.).
BaselineB: Statute/regulation and civil code interpretation: Programme d’assurance stabilisation des revenus agricoles, s. 88(3) (and related structure), interpreted under Civil Code of Québec arts. 1425-1432; discretion constrained by arts. 6, 7, 1375, 1434 C.C.Q.
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Rebuttable presumption of mens rea for drug trafficking once actus reus proved: when trafficking in LSD is proved, a presumption arises that the condition/intent was voluntarily induced and the accused "must be convicted unless other evidence is adduced which raises a reasonable doubt"; here, with no defence evidence, "it is not possible to find that he had an honest belief amounting to a non-existence of mens rea" (applying R. v. King).
BaselineA: Common law mens rea principles applied to statutory drug-trafficking offence; Food and Drugs Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. F-27, ss. 40 (definitions) and 42 (trafficking in restricted drugs), with mens rea framework drawn from Beaver v. The Queen and the rebuttable-presumption approach from R. v. King.
CaseB_TestB: Limits on trial-judge intervention / appearance of impartiality: although a judge may and sometimes must question and interrupt witnesses, he must do so "within certain limits and in such a way that justice is seen to be done"; if the judge's conduct "raised some doubt as to his impartiality", a new trial is required.
BaselineB: Common law procedural fairness / judicial impartiality principle ("justice should not only be done, but should manifestly and undoubtedly be seen to be done" from R. v. Sussex Justices; Ex parte McCarthy), with guidance from cases like Jones v. National Coal Board, Yuill v. Yuill, and R. v. Darlyn.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “burglary” in the constructive murder provision (Criminal Code s. 213): despite later revisions, “burglary” retains the 1892 Code meaning—i.e., “the offence defined as such in s. 410 of the Criminal Code 1892, coupled with the definitions of ‘dwelling-house’ and ‘break’ in s. 407” (so limited to breaking/entering a dwelling-house by night, etc.).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 213; Interpretation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. 1-23, s. 36; with historical reference to Criminal Code, 1892, ss. 228, 407, 410).
CaseB_TestB: Damages for repudiation where contract has alternative modes of performance: adopt the mode “least profitable to the plaintiff, and the least burdensome to the defendant”; “The test is not how the defendant would likely have performed ... but for ... repudiation” and the plaintiff is restored to the position “had the contract been performed” (minimum performance).
BaselineB: Common law (general principle traced to Cockburn v. Alexander (1848) and explained in Withers v. General Theatre Corp. (1933), as adopted/confirmed in Canadian appellate jurisprudence cited).
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Lease interpretation test for shifting fire-loss risk to landlord: applying “the ordinary test of reading [the lease] reasonably and in a business sense”, a tenant’s covenant to “pay … insurance rates” means the fire-loss risk (including tenant-negligence fire) passes to the landlord “at least upon the presentation by the landlord of the insurance bill”, barring the landlord’s insurer’s subrogated claim.
BaselineA: Common law contract/lease interpretation ("reading it reasonably and in a business sense"), applied to the lease covenant; with statutory context that standard fire coverage includes third-party negligence (Insurance Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 224, s. 118).
CaseB_TestB: Civil Code art. 1053 “fault causing damage” basis for bank liability on unauthorized endorsements: a bank that accepts company cheques for deposit to an officer’s personal benefit “without examining it, and without verifying the sufficiency of the endorsement” commits a “fault” under art. 1053; where this deprives the payee company of its money and it has no remaining recourse against the drawer, damages are “equal to the amount of the cheques”.
BaselineB: Statute and civil law: Civil Code art. 1053 (fault/damage/causation) applied in the negotiable instruments context, with reference to Bills of Exchange Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. B-5, ss. 10 and 51, and Norwich Union Fire Insurance Society Ltd. v. La Banque Canadienne Nationale, [1934] S.C.R. 596.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 15(1) adverse-impact discrimination (prima facie breach): (1) law creates a distinction on an enumerated/analogous ground through its effects by showing a “disproportionate impact” on a protected group; (2) the law imposes a burden/denies a benefit in a way that “reinforc[es], perpetuat[es], or exacerbat[es] disadvantage” (with flexible proof of disproportionate impact: group-situation evidence and/or outcome/statistical evidence; no intent requirement; no need to prove the protected characteristic ‘caused’ the disparity).
BaselineA: Combination: constitutional text (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 15(1)) plus SCC common-law/constitutional jurisprudence (two-step s. 15 framework from cases cited in the reasons, including Quebec (AG) v. Alliance du personnel professionnel et technique de la santé et des services sociaux, 2018 SCC 17; Centrale des syndicats du Québec v. Quebec (AG), 2018 SCC 18; Withler v. Canada (AG), 2011 SCC 12; Kahkewistahaw First Nation v. Taypotat, 2015 SCC 30).
CaseB_TestB: Division of powers “pith and substance” analysis: (1) determine the law’s “essential character” by examining its “purpose and the legal effect”; (2) determine whether that character “relate[s] to an enumerated head of power” (here, whether s. 27 of the Marine Mammal Regulations is in pith and substance connected to the federal fisheries power rather than provincial property and civil rights).
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine (pith and substance test) applied to a regulation: Marine Mammal Regulations, SOR/93-56, s. 27, made under Fisheries Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. F-14, s. 43; heads of power in Constitution Act, 1867, ss. 91(12), 91(27), 92(13).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Lease interpretation test for whether tenant’s covenant to pay “insurance rates” shifts the fire-loss risk (including tenant-negligence fires) to the landlord, barring the landlord/insurer’s subrogated claim: apply “the ordinary test of reading [the lease] reasonably and in a business sense”; where the tenant pays for fire insurance, it “is entitled to rest in respect of loss by fire on the discharge of its obligation to pay for fire insurance” (risk passes to landlord at least once the insurance bill is presented/paid).
BaselineA: Common law contract/lease interpretation (reasonably and in a business sense) applied to lease covenants allocating fire-loss risk; background landlord-tenant liability principles referenced (e.g., United Motors Service Ltd. v. Hutson; Canada Steamship Lines Ltd. v. The King) and statutory context noted (Ontario Insurance Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 224, s. 118, as to standard fire coverage).
CaseB_TestB: Warsaw Convention Art. 3(2) limitation entitlement rule: “The benefit of the limitation will be lost only where no ticket is delivered”; “The absence, irregularity or loss of the passenger ticket does not affect the existence or the validity of the contract of carriage” and does not remove limitation if a ticket was delivered. (For baggage, Art. 4 sanction applies only if luggage ticket not delivered or missing required particulars; compliance assessed by whether print/content is legible/adequate to an ordinary person using ordinary diligence.)
BaselineB: Statute/treaty text: Carriage by Air Act, R.S.C. 1952, c. 45, Schedule I (Warsaw Convention), especially Arts. 3, 4, and 22 (limitations of liability).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Negligent misrepresentation (opinion/estimate): plaintiff must prove more than that the estimate was wrong; must show the error resulted from a lack of "skill, competence or diligence" / "carelessness or a failure to exercise such care as the circumstances required" (failure to qualify is not itself a separate head of negligence, but affects responsibility).
BaselineA: Common law (negligent misrepresentation duty of care), drawing on Hedley Byrne & Co. Ltd. v. Heller & Partners Ltd. and Mutual Life and Citizens’ Assurance Co. Ltd. v. Evatt as discussed in the reasons.
CaseB_TestB: Extra-territoriality / s. 92 territorial limits for intangible pith-and-substance: after identifying pith and substance and a provincial head of power, if the matter is intangible the court "must look to the relationships among the enacting territory, the subject matter of the legislation and the persons made subject to it" to decide whether there is a "meaningful connection" and respect for other jurisdictions’ sovereignty (if so, the matter is "in the Province").
BaselineB: Common law / constitutional doctrine interpreting Constitution Act, 1867, s. 92 (including s. 92(13)) and prior SCC cases (e.g., Churchill Falls; Unifund) on territorial limits and pith and substance.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Parole suspension/revocation under the Parole Act: suspension requires a written warrant and may be issued when the decision-maker is "satisfied" arrest is "necessary or desirable" for specified purposes; revocation may occur ("in its discretion") even after sentence expiry if the inmate is in custody under s. 16
BaselineA: Statute (Parole Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. P-2, ss. 10(1)(e), 16(1)-(5); also discussed: Canadian Bill of Rights, s. 2(c)(i), s. 2(e)) plus prior SCC authority (Ex p. McCaud; Howarth v. National Parole Board)
JudgeA: Ritchie J. (for Judson, Ritchie, Pigeon and Beetz JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Equitable compensation for Crown breach of fiduciary duty over reserve land: assess the beneficiary’s "lost opportunity" by first determining what the Crown "ought to have done as a fiduciary"; loss must be caused in fact (not limited by foreseeability/remoteness), assessed with hindsight, applying equitable presumptions (e.g., most favourable use), and here requires valuing the land based on its use/value to the hydroelectric project and the lost opportunity to negotiate a surrender at the best price
BaselineB: Common law (fiduciary duty and equitable compensation principles from Guerin; Canson; Osoyoos; Blueberry River; etc.) applied in the statutory/treaty context (Indian Act, R.S.C. 1927, c. 98, ss. 48, 50, 51; Treaty No. 3)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Sales tax exemption test for whether machinery/apparatus is used “directly in the manufacture or production of goods” (gas pressure regulators held not to qualify because they are mere transmission/flow control, not “production”)
BaselineA: Statute: Excise Tax Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-13, s. 29(1) and Schedule III, Part XIII, para. 1(a)(i) (exemption for machinery/apparatus used directly in “the manufacture or production of goods”); interpreted in light of Hydro-Québec v. Dep. Min. of Nat. Revenue for Customs and Excise, [1970] S.C.R. 30
JudgeA: Pigeon J. (for Martland, Judson, Pigeon, Dickson and Beetz JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Appellate review test for interfering with a trial judge’s finding on the scope of a solicitor’s retainer: it is “purely a factual question” and “should not ordinarily be upset on appeal save for error arising from misapprehension of the evidence”
BaselineB: Common law appellate standard of review for findings of fact (as stated in the reasons: deference to trial judge; interference only for error such as misapprehension of evidence)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Whether an invention relates to a food substance “prepared or produced by chemical processes” under Patent Act s. 41(1): apply the term “chemical process” in its ordinary/popular sense (as understood by an informed layman) by assessing the character of the entire process; chemical reactions are neither necessary nor sufficient, but it is enough if chemical operations play a significant/essential part in producing the substance.
BaselineA: Statute (Patent Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. P-4, s. 41(1)) as interpreted through prior SCC cases (Continental Soya Co. Ltd. v. J.R. Short Milling Co. (Canada) Ltd., [1942] S.C.R. 187; Laboratoire Pentagone Ltée v. Parke, Davis & Co., [1968] S.C.R. 307).
JudgeA: Dickson J. (for Laskin C.J. and Martland, Judson, Spence and Dickson JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Adequacy of an indictment (including in multiple-conspiracy situations): an indictment is adequate if it contains sufficient detail to give the accused “reasonable information” about the charge and to “identify the transaction” to permit preparation of the defence; sufficiency depends on the offence and facts, time need not be exact unless essential/no prejudice, and a conspiracy proven falls within the indictment if it included some accused, occurred sometime within the alleged time span, and had as its object the type of crime alleged (with the Crown’s opening address relevant to construing the charge).
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 510, 512, 516(1)(g)) informed by prior SCC guidance (e.g., R. v. Cotroni, [1979] 2 S.C.R. 256; R. v. Côté, [1978] 1 S.C.R. 8; R. v. Wis Development Corp., [1984] 1 S.C.R. 485; R. v. B. (G.), [1990] 2 S.C.R. 30).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 1 Charter justification (Oakes proportionality) applied contextually: pressing and substantial objective + proportionality (rational connection, minimal impairment, overall proportionality), with emphasis that the state must show a total ban is necessary and that justification must be “reasonable” and “demonstrably justified”.
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional text (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 1) as structured by common-law Oakes framework (R. v. Oakes). Key language: s. 1 requires limits “prescribed by law as can be demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society”; Oakes requires objective of sufficient importance and proportionality (rational connection, minimal impairment, proportionality of effects).
CaseB_TestB: Meiorin duty-to-accommodate / BFOR justification test applied to termination-after-absence clauses: employer must show (1) purpose rationally connected to job performance; (2) adopted in honest and good faith belief it was necessary; (3) reasonably necessary—i.e., “impossible to accommodate ... without imposing undue hardship”; collective-agreement absence period is a relevant factor but not determinative; undue hardship assessed globally from start of absence.
BaselineB: Common law (Meiorin/BCGSEU test for BFOR justification and duty to accommodate; also O’Malley and Renaud on accommodation/undue hardship) applied in the labour-arbitration context; informed by Quebec Charter of human rights and freedoms (equality/discrimination) but the operative test is the Meiorin common-law framework.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Indian Act s. 88 provincial-law applicability / inconsistency analysis: provincial law applies to Indians (via s. 88) except to the extent it is "inconsistent with" the Indian Act or "make[s] provision for any matter for which provision is made by or under" the Indian Act; applied by asking whether Adoption Act s. 10(2) ("for all purposes" severing natural-parent relationship) removes an adopted child’s entitlement to be registered under Indian Act s. 11(1)(d) (held: it does not, so no inconsistency on registrability).
BaselineA: Statute (Indian Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-6, s. 88 and s. 11; Adoption Act, R.S.B.C. 1960, c. 4, s. 10)
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 24(2) Collins framework (as organized in Greffe): exclude evidence if, "having regard to all the circumstances", its admission would bring the administration of justice into disrepute; factors organized into three categories—(1) fairness of the trial, (2) seriousness of the Charter violation (including whether police had "reasonable and probable grounds"; and informant-tip sufficiency: not a "mere conclusory statement"; consider detail, source/means of knowledge, and indicia of reliability), and (3) effect of exclusion on the repute of justice.
BaselineB: Statute/constitutional text (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 24(2)) plus common-law/precedential framework (R. v. Collins, as applied/organized)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Termination of a continuing guarantee by “notice in writing”: notice need not use set words but must be explicit and unequivocal (a mere “wish” or “preference” in equivocal terms is insufficient and the creditor must not be left in doubt).
BaselineA: Contract (guarantee instrument), cl. (4): guarantor may “by notice in writing delivered to the Manager ... determine ... liability ... in respect of liabilities thereafter incurred or arising”.
CaseB_TestB: Admissibility/use of an accused’s post-caution silence: unless the Crown establishes “real relevance and a proper basis”, questions about silence and evidence of ensuing silence should not be admitted; if admitted, the jury must be instructed to ignore it (no adverse inference).
BaselineB: Common law right to silence as recognized in prior cases (e.g., Rothman; Symonds/Robertson line) and its Charter protection under s. 7; applied in the context of Criminal Code s. 613(1)(b)(iii) (now s. 686(1)(b)(iii)).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Validity/regularity of an interim cease-and-desist order under Trade Union Act, s. 49(2): Board may issue ex parte interim order if "satisfied after investigation" of complaint that s. 48 breached; investigation may be done through Board officers; interim order need not be limited to relief requested so long as related to the illegal work stoppage
BaselineA: Statute (Trade Union Act, 1972 (N.S.), c. 19, ss. 48, 49(2), 15(9)-(10))
CaseB_TestB: YCJA youth-sentencing interpretation: general (and specific) deterrence is not a sentencing principle under the YCJA; and s. 42(2)(o) does not require a 2/3 custody and 1/3 supervision split (unlike s. 42(2)(n))
BaselineB: Statute (Youth Criminal Justice Act, S.C. 2002, c. 1, ss. 3, 38, 42(2)(n), 42(2)(o), 50(1); Criminal Code, s. 718(b) excluded by YCJA s. 50(1))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Relief from municipal notice requirement: failure to give notice under Cities and Towns Act s. 622(1) does not bar the action if the plaintiff proves they were prevented from giving notice for a reason 'deemed sufficient' by the court; once so justified, the plaintiff is permanently released from any obligation to give notice and may sue without further condition.
BaselineA: Statute (Cities and Towns Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 193, s. 622(1), (3), (4), (5))
CaseB_TestB: Judicial review standard for labour grievance arbitration award: court asks whether the arbitrator’s interpretation is 'patently unreasonable' / whether it is an interpretation the collective agreement 'would reasonably bear' (and not whether the court would decide differently).
BaselineB: Common law (judicial review of arbitration awards), drawing on SCC labour-arbitration review jurisprudence including Bell Canada v. Office and Professional Employees' Union, [1974] S.C.R. 335 and CUPE v. New Brunswick Liquor Corp., [1979] 2 S.C.R. 227
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Admissibility of similar fact evidence: other acts evidence is inadmissible to show propensity, but is admissible if it is relevant to an issue (e.g., whether the act was “designed or accidental” or “to rebut a defence which would otherwise be open”), and is admitted “not to prove commission of the crime… but to establish guilty intent” (Makin/Noor Mohamed/Wray line as applied).
BaselineA: Common law evidence rule on similar fact evidence (general exclusionary rule and its exception), as stated in Makin v. Attorney-General for New South Wales and discussed with Thompson v. The King, Noor Mohamed v. The King, and R. v. Wray.
CaseB_TestB: Municipal valuation—special circumstances: where “special circumstances make it impossible to fix the realizable value of property by the usual methods… whatever method is appropriate in the circumstances may be used to estimate the property at its actual value.”
BaselineB: Statutory municipal valuation requirement of “actual value” under the Charter of the City of Montreal, S.Q. 1959-60, c. 102 (appeal structure noted via ss. 873-874), as interpreted through prior valuation jurisprudence (notably Sun Life Assurance Co. of Canada v. City of Montreal).
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Admissibility of similar-fact evidence: admissible only if relevant to an issue (e.g., designed vs accidental / to rebut a defence otherwise open), and not to show disposition; in criminal negligence, Crown may use similar conduct to show mens rea (wanton or reckless disregard) beyond the act itself
BaselineA: Common law evidence rule and exception from Makin v. Attorney-General for New South Wales (1894) (as developed in Thompson v. The King; Noor Mohamed v. The King) and SCC approach in R. v. Wray
CaseB_TestB: Issue estoppel on a perjury charge: Crown is estopped from re-litigating an issue decided in accused’s favour unless it tenders evidence that was not available by the exercise of reasonable diligence at the first trial
BaselineB: Common law res judicata/issue estoppel and fraud principles (e.g., Duchess of Kingston’s Case; Gushue v. The Queen; DPP v. Humphrys)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory interpretation of technical terms: construe words in their primary/common meaning (in both official languages); “derivative/dérivé” means a thing actually obtained from another (not merely in the same scientific ‘family’).
BaselineA: Combination: (1) statutory/regulatory text creating the tariff exception for “tetracycline and its derivatives” (Customs Tariff Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-41, s. 12, Schedule A, item 92944-1, as implemented by Order in Council SOR/69-8, Schedule A; and Tariff Board Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. T-1, s. 5(9)); plus (2) bilingual interpretation rule in Official Languages Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. O-2, s. 8(2)(b); plus (3) common-law interpretive principle that statutes are construed according to common language meaning (citing Continental Soya; Laboratoire Pentagone; Burton Parsons).
CaseB_TestB: Limits of inherent/implied jurisdiction re amici remuneration: courts may appoint amici only exceptionally where “essential” to just adjudication, but (absent statutory authority or a constitutional/Charter basis) inherent/implied jurisdiction does not extend to fixing rates of compensation and ordering the Attorney General to pay a particular rate; if impasse, judge may stay until an amicus can be found.
BaselineB: Common law / constitutional principles governing inherent jurisdiction and separation of powers (as described through prior SCC jurisprudence, e.g., MacMillan Bloedel; Provincial Judges Reference; Caron; Cunningham) rather than a specific statutory test; the majority frames the limit as applying “absent authority flowing from a constitutional challenge or a statutory provision”.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Bankruptcy trustee’s duty to insure (and notify) secured creditors: under Bankruptcy Act s. 9(1)-(2), trustee must keep existing insurance in force and, if cancelled/insufficient, insure all the bankrupt’s insurable property (including hypothec-encumbered property) and notify the hypothecary creditor if insurance cannot be obtained; failure can ground personal liability (and s. 171 leave requirement does not apply to omissions).
BaselineA: Statute — Bankruptcy Act, R.S.C. 1952, c. 14, ss. 9(1)-(2) (duty to insure; insurance payable to trustee), s. 171 (leave to sue trustee), and s. 2 definitions of “property” and “secured creditor”.
CaseB_TestB: Charitable status under ITA via common-law Pemsel (4th head) as applied to sports: to be charitable, an organization’s purposes must be (a) of “public benefit” and (b) “in a way the law regards as charitable”; under the 4th head this requires analogy to prior recognized charitable purposes (Vancouver Society/D’Aguiar approach), and “public benefit alone does not equal charity” — sport is charitable only if ancillary to another recognized charitable purpose, not “sport in itself”.
BaselineB: Combination — Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), ss. 149.1(1) (charitable organization) and 248(1) (RCAAA/registered charity), relying on common law charity definition (Pemsel; Vancouver Society; D’Aguiar test quoted in Vancouver Society).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Eligibility for a Quebec seat on the SCC under Supreme Court Act s. 6 requires current membership in a listed Quebec institution (Quebec CA/Superior Court or Barreau du Québec) plus the s. 5 10-year standing requirement; former Quebec advocates are excluded
BaselineA: Statute (Supreme Court Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. S-26, ss. 5 and 6; constitutional constraint discussed under Constitution Act, 1982, s. 41(d))
JudgeA: The Chief Justice and LeBel, Abella, Cromwell, Karakatsanis and Wagner JJ.
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 15(1) two-step equality test applied to Pay Equity Act s. 38: (1) distinction on an enumerated/analogous ground (on its face or in impact); (2) discriminatory disadvantage by reinforcing/perpetuating/exacerbating disadvantage
BaselineB: Constitution (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 15(1); framework drawn from Quebec (AG) v. A and Kahkewistahaw First Nation v. Taypotat as cited in the reasons)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Entitlement to payment from the Highway Victims Indemnity Fund and applicable prescription: claimant must (i) be a creditor under a final judgment within s. 36, (ii) apply within one year (s. 36) by sworn declaration meeting s. 37 (unsatisfied judgment; “no insurer will benefit”; other claims), after which the Fund “shall satisfy the judgment” within seven days (s. 38); the action against the Fund is prescribed by 30 years under art. 2265 C.C. (not art. 2262(2) C.C.), and the claimant need not first exhaust remedies against the insurer.
BaselineA: Statute (Highway Victims Indemnity Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 232, ss. 36-39) plus Civil Code prescription provisions (arts. 2262(2), 2265).
CaseB_TestB: Method for assessing Fatal Accidents Act damages (dependency) including tax and discounting: determine annual “disposable income for dependants” (including deducting income tax), then award the present value of a lump sum that will replace that annual amount over the relevant period, using a discount rate based on “present rates of return on long-term investments with an allowance for the effects of future inflation,” with “some reduction for contingencies.”
BaselineB: Statute (The Fatal Accidents Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 164) as interpreted through common-law damages principles (including discussion of Gehrmann v. Lavoie and Jennings).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Discretionary award of pre-judgment interest as compensation where payment of a just debt has been improperly withheld: if (in the court’s opinion) a just debt was improperly withheld and it is fair and equitable to compensate, the court should allow interest “for such time and at such rate as the Court may think right”; here, proper rate = creditor’s bank borrowing rate
BaselineA: Common law/equitable principle (Toronto Railway Co. v. City of Toronto, [1906] A.C. 117; followed in The Custodian v. Blucher, [1927] S.C.R. 420) applied alongside statutory context (Interest Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-18, ss. 3, 12, 13; Supreme Court Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. S-19, s. 52)
CaseB_TestB: Dixon two-step test for remedy (new trial) after Crown non-disclosure: (1) examine undisclosed info to see if there is a reasonable possibility it affects reliability of conviction; if yes, order new trial; (2) if not, assess reasonable possibility non-disclosure affected overall fairness via lost lines of inquiry/opportunities, weighing defence due diligence
BaselineB: Common law/Charter jurisprudence on disclosure and full answer and defence (R. v. Stinchcombe; R. v. Egger; R. v. Chaplin; R. v. Carosella) applying Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 7 and 24(1)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Doctrine/rule of recent possession: once Crown proves (1) goods were recently stolen and (2) accused possessed them, jury may infer guilt; if no explanation advanced, possession alone raises a prima facie case; Crown need not prove absence of explanation and jury instruction is not barred by Canada Evidence Act s. 4(5).
BaselineA: Common law rule of evidence (doctrine of recent possession) as stated in R. v. Schama; R. v. Abramovitch and repeatedly approved (e.g., Richler v. The King; Ungaro v. The King; Graham v. The Queen; Tremblay v. The Queen; R. v. Graham). Also considered alongside Canada Evidence Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-10, s. 4(5) (no comment on failure to testify).
CaseB_TestB: Imperial Tobacco extraterritoriality framework for provincial legislation: (1) identify pith and substance by purpose and effects; (2) ensure territorial limits respected by asking whether the law has a “meaningful connection” to the province and “respects the sovereignty of other provinces”.
BaselineB: Common law constitutional framework from British Columbia v. Imperial Tobacco Canada Ltd., 2005 SCC 49, applied to Constitution Act, 1867, s. 92 (esp. s. 92(14) and territorial limits “in the Province”) and to the impugned statute Opioid Damages and Health Care Costs Recovery Act, S.B.C. 2018, c. 35, s. 11.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Mulligan (majority) approach to when psychiatric “dissociative reaction” evidence must be put to the jury on the defence of drunkenness: if the medical evidence is directed to insanity (disease of the mind arising at the time of the offence) and would, if accepted, establish insanity, the trial judge need not re-instruct the jury to consider it again under drunkenness; it would matter for drunkenness only where a pre-existing condition makes the accused more likely to become incapable from alcohol.
BaselineA: Combination: Criminal Code s. 212(a) (mens rea for murder) and common law intoxication doctrine as in Director of Public Prosecutions v. Beard (1920) (as adopted in the jury charge).
JudgeA: Martland J. (for Martland, Judson, Ritchie, Pigeon, Beetz and de Grandpré JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Test for probative value of “straddle evidence” to rebut the Criminal Code s. 258(1)(d.1) presumption: straddle evidence is admissible and, when weighed “in the light of all of the evidence at trial”, it “may be capable of raising a reasonable doubt” that BAC exceeded 80 mg/100 mL at the time of driving.
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, s. 258(1)(d.1) (statutory presumption from breathalyzer readings), as interpreted through R. v. Gibson, 2008 SCC 16.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Drunkenness negating mens rea for murder: intoxication must render the accused incapable of forming the specific intent to kill (or to cause bodily harm known likely to cause death); mere impairment/greater propensity to violence is insufficient
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, s. 212(a) (as referenced)) applied through common law intoxication doctrine (DPP v. Beard)
JudgeA: Martland J. (for Martland, Judson, Ritchie, Pigeon, Beetz and de Grandpré JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Section 23 “numbers warrant” sliding-scale placement: (1) determine long-term number of students who will eventually avail themselves; (2) compare to majority-language schools (local first, otherwise province-wide) with a rebuttable presumption from comparable majority schools; (3) determine level of services (homogeneous school if comparable and presumption not rebutted; otherwise lower-level services with deference to minority board)
BaselineB: Constitution (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 23) as interpreted in Mahe v. Alberta (sliding scale; pedagogy and cost factors)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Labour Code s. 108(1)(b) review: whether the arbitrator committed an "error of law affecting the jurisdiction" (i.e., failed to answer the question submitted/failed to consider the real circumstances), as opposed to merely being right or wrong on the merits
BaselineA: Statute: Labour Code of British Columbia Act, 1973, s. 108(1)(b) (court may intervene only for "an error of law affecting the jurisdiction of the arbitration board")
CaseB_TestB: Garofoli leave threshold to cross-examine wiretap affiant: defence must show a "reasonable likelihood" that cross-examination will elicit testimony of "probative value" on a material issue for the reviewing judge (relevance/materiality; whether it may undermine a statutory precondition for authorization)
BaselineB: Common law: R. v. Garofoli, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 1421 (leave required; threshold showing before cross-examining affiant on a wiretap authorization review)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: ITA s. 83(3) mining-share exclusion: whether the taxpayer advanced/paid prospecting expenses "either under an arrangement with the prospector made before the prospecting... work or as employer of the prospector" (incl. whether the prospector was the syndicate’s employee/employer relationship existed)
BaselineA: Statute: Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1952, c. 148, s. 83(3) (as amended by 1965 (Can.), c. 18, s. 19); also engages s. 83(1)(c) definition of prospector
JudgeA: de Grandpré J. (for Laskin C.J. and Judson, Beetz and de Grandpré JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Division of powers “integral element” test: Parliament may legislate for s. 92(10) undertakings only where the matter is an "integral part" of the core federal competence; otherwise provincial laws of general application apply (used to hold Railway Act s. 342(1) ultra vires as applied to provincial personal-injury negligence actions)
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine (division of powers) applying the "integral element" approach from Construction Montcalm Inc. v. Minimum Wage Commission and Northern Telecom Ltd. v. Communications Workers of Canada; applied to Railway Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. R-2, s. 342(1) and Constitution Act, 1867, ss. 91(29), 92(10), 92(13), 92(14)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory condition 10(a) (fire insurance): the policy is not void for failure to state the insured’s interest so long as the insured has an insurable interest (i.e., “All that is necessary to satisfy statutory condition 10(a) of the policy is that the insured have an insurable interest.”).
BaselineA: Statute + civil law: Insurance Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 295, s. 240 (statutory conditions) including statutory condition 10(a) (“For the loss of property owned by any other person than the assured, unless the interest of the assured is stated in or upon the policy”); Civil Code art. 2571 (interest must be specified). Also relies on SCC/common-law interpretation of similar statutory condition (Wandlyn Motels v. Commerce General Insurance Company, [1970] S.C.R. 992).
CaseB_TestB: Section 8 ‘coroner-to-police bodily sample’ framework: where a bodily sample is seized by a non-police actor but used in a criminal prosecution, the court must assess whether police conduct constitutes an independent state seizure or renders the initial seizure unreasonable (“go beyond the initial non‑police seizure and determine whether the actions of the police constitute a seizure by the state or make the initially valid seizure by the coroner unreasonable”).
BaselineB: Common law + constitutional text: Charter s. 8 (unreasonable search or seizure) as interpreted in Hunter v. Southam Inc. (prior judicial authorization for criminal-law seizures) and R. v. Dyment (privacy in bodily samples). Applied in context of Coroners Act, R.S.O. 1980, c. 93, s. 16(2) and related provisions.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Refusal of adjournment that forces an accused to proceed without counsel: discretion must be exercised judicially; an adjournment needed to exercise the s. 577(3) right may be refused only for a reason based on established facts, and appellate review is available where reasons are not well founded in law (with particular concern where the refusal deprives the accused of the right to counsel/full defence).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 577(3) right to make full defence personally or by counsel; appellate review context under s. 613) plus common-law principles on judicial discretion/review (as discussed through cases like Spataro v. R.).
JudgeA: Pigeon J. (for Laskin C.J. and Judson, Spence, Pigeon, Dickson and Beetz JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Equitable compensation for breach of fiduciary duty (solicitor non-disclosure): assess the plaintiff’s actual loss with hindsight; foreseeability is not required, but recovery is limited to losses which, on a common-sense view of causation, were caused by the breach (no recovery for independent third-party losses absent a direct link).
BaselineB: Common law/equity (fiduciary duty and equitable compensation), drawing on authorities including Nocton v. Lord Ashburton and Guerin v. The Queen (as discussed in the reasons).
JudgeB: McLachlin J. (for Lamer C.J. and L'Heureux-Dubé and McLachlin JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Quebec court jurisdiction on a declinatory exception in a personal action: jurisdiction lies in the court of the defendant’s domicile, or failing that, residence (art. 68 C.C.P.); filing a declinatory exception does not automatically shift the burden to the plaintiff, and the court assesses the evidence as a whole to determine the defendant’s (principal) residence
BaselineA: Statute (Quebec Code of Civil Procedure, arts. 68 and 70; plus a statutory presumption in Canadian Citizenship Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-19, s. 10)
CaseB_TestB: When (and how) state/police misconduct can reduce a criminal sentence: if the misconduct relates to the circumstances of the offence or the offender, it may be treated as a mitigating factor within the Criminal Code sentencing regime; generally unnecessary to invoke Charter s. 24(1), and sentence reductions must stay within statutory limits (no going below mandatory minimums absent a constitutional challenge), save possibly in exceptional egregious cases
BaselineB: Combination (statute and constitutional text): Criminal Code sentencing provisions (ss. 718 to 718.2 and related limits, including mandatory minimums) and Charter s. 24(1) (with discussion of Charter s. 7 context)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Contractual warranty interpretation: construe “depreciation” in the warranty/letter as an accounting concept (write-off over useful life) and not “full capital cost allowance”; the parenthetical “(using capital cost allowance rates)” refers to rates only, not the tax ‘system’, and “at least” means the tax returns may claim more than book depreciation—so no breach if books show full depreciation over time-in-service at those rates.
BaselineA: Common law (contract interpretation of a share-sale warranty clause, read with the incorporated auditor’s letter).
CaseB_TestB: Youth court power under Young Offenders Act: s. 19(2) does not authorize dismissing a charge merely because the judge thinks it “ought never to have been laid”; absent “manifest”/“irresistible clearness” from Parliament, courts must respect prosecutorial discretion (subject only to exceptional remedies like abuse of process/stay in the “clearest of cases”).
BaselineB: Statute (Young Offenders Act, R.S.C., 1985, c. Y-1, especially ss. 19(2) and 3(1), read against the common-law/constitutional principle of prosecutorial discretion and limited judicial control via abuse of process/stay: Smythe; Jewitt; Keyowski; Conway).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Crown appeal from acquittal after legal error: Crown must satisfy the court that the verdict "would not necessarily have been the same if the trial judge had properly directed the jury" (White v. R. test, applied in Vézeau); plus clarification that s. 4(5) Canada Evidence Act does not authorize telling the jury it "may not draw" an unfavourable inference from the accused’s failure to testify (jury may draw a "logical conclusion", especially re alibi).
BaselineA: Combination: statute (Canada Evidence Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-10, s. 4(5); Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 613(4), 618(2)) plus common law appellate test from White v. R., [1947] S.C.R. 268 (also followed in R. v. Gauthier, [1977] 1 S.C.R. 441).
CaseB_TestB: Group defamation/personal injury in Quebec civil liability: plaintiff must prove that "an ordinary person would have believed that each of them personally sustained damage to his or her reputation"; determination is contextual using a non-exhaustive set of factors (e.g., group size, homogeneity/organization, identifiability/visibility, historical stigma, plaintiff’s relationship to group, precision of allegations, seriousness/extravagance, plausibility, and other extrinsic context).
BaselineB: Statute/civil code framework: Civil Code of Québec, art. 1457 (fault, injury, causal connection) and related CCQ damages provisions (arts. 1607, 1611) plus procedural context under Code of Civil Procedure class action provisions; built on SCC defamation-injury objective standard from Prud’homme v. Prud’homme, 2002 SCC 85 and Néron, 2004 SCC 53.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Interpretation of standard auto policy exclusion for a person “who is entitled to receive the benefits of any workmen’s compensation law or plan”: entitlement does not depend on making a claim/obtaining an award; if the admitted facts establish statutory entitlement, the exclusion applies (and contra proferentem does not apply where the wording is statutorily mandated).
BaselineA: Statute (Ontario): Insurance Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 224, s. 232(1) and Schedule E, Exclusion 2(a)(ii) (mandated wording), interpreted in light of the Workmen’s Compensation Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 505 (e.g., ss. 3, 8).
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 8 reasonableness framework applied (mutatis mutandis) to cross-border disclosure under Criminal Code s. 193(2)(e): (1) disclosure must be authorized by law (recipient is a foreign investigative/prosecutorial authority and disclosure is “intended to be in the interests of the administration of justice”); (2) the authorizing law must be reasonable (not overbroad/vague; adequate safeguards/accountability in context); and (3) the disclosure must be carried out in a reasonable manner (in serious risk cases, s. 8 may forbid disclosure; otherwise protocols/caveats may mitigate).
BaselineB: Combination: Statute and constitutional doctrine. Statutory baseline is Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 193(2)(e). Constitutional baseline is the established s. 8 framework from R. v. Collins and R. v. Caslake (“authorized by law / law reasonable / manner reasonable”), applied to disclosures.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Discretion to order service ex juris under Federal Court Rules, Rule 307 guided by forum conveniens: the "overriding consideration" is whether there exists "some other forum more convenient and appropriate for the pursuit of the action and for securing the ends of justice"; refusal is an error in principle if based solely on "no relation or connection with Canada".
BaselineA: Statute and regulation: Federal Court Act, R.S.C. 1970 (2nd Supp.), c. 10, ss. 22(2)(a), 43(1), 44; Federal Court Rules, Rule 307 (service ex juris).
JudgeA: Ritchie J. (for Ritchie, Pigeon, Beetz and de Grandpré JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Medical civil liability causation (rejecting loss of chance as a substitute for causation where death/sickness has occurred): plaintiff must prove fault, damage, and causation "on the balance of probabilities" using "all the evidence: factual, statistical and that which the judge is entitled to presume"; in some cases a court may presume causation where a fault creates a "clear danger" that materializes, unless there is a "strong indication to the contrary"; if not satisfied causation of "any real damage" is shown, recovery is denied.
BaselineB: Civil law (Quebec delictual liability) principles of fault-causation-damage; evidentiary presumptions under Civil Code of Lower Canada, art. 1205; SCC causation approach referenced in Snell v. Farrell and other SCC cases cited in the reasons.
JudgeB: Gonthier J. (for Lamer C.J. and L'Heureux-Dubé, Sopinka, Gonthier, Cory and McLachlin JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Breach of municipal development-agreement sewer obligation: developer must prove an actual (or foreseeable) inadequacy in sewer service showing the City failed to provide sewers/enlargements “required to properly service” the redevelopment stage; a general long-term sewer master plan/charge is irrelevant absent evidence connecting it to serviceability of the project sewers
BaselineA: Common law (contract interpretation/application of the parties’ 1966 development agreement, especially s. 31(a)(iii))
CaseB_TestB: Presumption of advancement and rebuttal on gratuitous husband-to-wife transfer: presumption of intent to advance applies unless rebutted; it is not rebutted by the husband asserting he transferred “only ... to defeat his creditors” (and the court assesses surrounding conduct/intent). Also, statutory abolition of the presumption is not applied retrospectively absent express terms or necessary implication
BaselineB: Common law (presumption of advancement/resulting trust principles; referenced SCC authority includes Goodfriend v. Goodfriend) plus statutory interpretation of The Family Law Reform Act, 1975 (Ont.), s. 1(3)(d) on temporal application
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 613(1)(b)(iii) curative proviso: uphold conviction despite trial error only if the Crown satisfies the appellate court that a properly charged jury "could not, as reasonable men, have done otherwise than find the appellant guilty" (i.e., no substantial wrong or miscarriage of justice).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, s. 613(1)(b)(iii)) as applied through SCC precedent (Colpitts v. R., quoting Brooks v. The King).
CaseB_TestB: Treaty right to fish and trade for "necessaries" (modern "moderate livelihood") and resulting s. 35 infringement analysis: discretionary licensing/close season/sales bans prima facie infringe where they interfere with the treaty right, applying Sparrow’s infringement questions (unreasonable limitation/undue hardship/denial of preferred means) and requiring justification under the Badger test.
BaselineB: Combination: constitutional and common law framework for s. 35 (Sparrow infringement test; Badger justification test) applied to the Mi’kmaq Treaties of 1760-61; plus relevant fisheries legislation/regulations (Fisheries Act s. 7(1); Maritime Provinces Fishery Regulations ss. 4(1)(a), 20; Fishery (General) Regulations s. 35(2)).
JudgeB: Binnie J. (for Lamer C.J. and L’Heureux-Dubé, Cory, Iacobucci and Binnie JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Hague Protocol notice requirement for carrier to invoke liability limitation: the passenger ticket/baggage check must include a “notice” (not merely a “statement”) that is “in a form calculated to attract attention”; if the ticket “does not include the notice required” by Art. 3(1)(c) (and similarly Art. 4(1)(c)), the carrier “shall not be entitled to avail himself of the provisions of Article 22” limiting liability.
BaselineA: Statute (Carriage by Air Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-14, incorporating the Hague Protocol amending the Warsaw Convention): Hague Protocol Arts. 3(1)(c), 3(2), 4(1)(c), and 22 (and comparison to Warsaw Convention Arts. 3 and 4).
CaseB_TestB: Rebutting Criminal Code breathalyzer presumptions (post-severance upheld under Charter s. 1): to rebut the s. 258(1)(c) presumption of accuracy/identity, the accused must raise a reasonable doubt that “the instrument was functioning and was operated properly” (i.e., evidence directed to deficiencies in maintenance/operation); and to rebut the s. 258(1)(d.1) presumption of identity, the accused’s evidence must tend to show (1) consumption consistent with BAC not exceeding .08 at the time of the offence and (2) consumption consistent with the test results.
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, ss. 258(1)(c), 258(1)(d.01), 258(1)(d.1)) as assessed under Charter ss. 11(d) and 1 (Oakes framework referenced but not treated as the key test).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Municipal notice-of-accident limitation period runs from the claimant’s discovery of the accident’s causal significance (not necessarily the accident date) where starting from the accident date would make the right of action practically illusory
BaselineA: Statute: Charter of the City of Montreal, 1959-60 (Que.), c. 102, art. 1088 (15-day notice must be 'received'); interpreted in light of the heavy-burden/anti-aleatory approach and analogy to prescription suspension; also references to Interpretation Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 1, ss. 52, 61 and Code of Civil Procedure art. 165(4) (pleaded facts assumed true on motion to dismiss)
CaseB_TestB: Discretionary test for discharging a civil jury after a reference to insurance: discharge only if the reference likely caused real prejudice (a 'substantial wrong or miscarriage of justice') and the prejudice cannot be cured by instructions
BaselineB: Common law (overruling prior SCC rule in Bowhey v. Theakston on automatic discharge); applied within the trial judge’s discretion in jury management (with reference to B.C. Supreme Court Rules, Rule 41(6), but the discharge test itself is common-law/discretionary)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Admissibility of an accused’s prior in-court testimony (judicial statement under oath) without a voir dire: such testimony is admissible as of right even if alleged to have been induced by unlawful threats/violence; voluntariness goes to weight for the jury, not admissibility
BaselineA: Common law (distinction between extra-judicial confessions requiring a voluntariness voir dire vs. statements made in a judicial proceeding). Key baseline authorities cited: R. v. Scott (1856) (compelled prior testimony admissible), and related line including Tass v. The King, [1947] S.C.R. 103; also Canada Evidence Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-10, s. 5(2) (witness protection against subsequent use if claimed at the time).
CaseB_TestB: Appellate intervention for trial judge’s failure to consider relevant evidence: appellate courts do not reassess guilt, but must review whether the trial court directed itself to all evidence bearing on relevant issues; where reasons/record disclose a 'lack of appreciation' or 'complete disregard' of relevant evidence, the reviewing court must intercede (new trial)
BaselineB: Common law principles on appellate review of reasons/evidence, as articulated in MacDonald v. The Queen, [1977] 2 S.C.R. 665 and Ungaro v. R., [1950] S.C.R. 430 (misdirection/overlooking relevant issues/evidence can vitiate conviction).
JudgeB: Estey J. (for Martland, Dickson, Beetz, Estey, McIntyre and Lamer JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Admissibility of Crown rebuttal evidence to an alibi/credibility: Crown may contradict an alibi only by attacking its “material points”; and the Crown may not contradict a “collateral fact” elicited on cross-examination (so rebuttal evidence on a collateral fact is inadmissible).
BaselineA: Common law evidence principles (rebuttal to alibi; collateral-fact rule), with appellate-harmless-error overlay under Criminal Code s. 613(1)(b)(iii). Cases cited: R. v. Cargill; R. v. Hrechuk; R. v. Rafael; R. v. Rosik; The Queen v. Vézeau.
CaseB_TestB: Drunkenness and rape (specific vs general intent): rape is an offence of “general intent” so “the defence of drunkenness can have no application” (subject to the general rule that intoxication is relevant only where a specific intent is required).
BaselineB: Common law intoxication doctrine and the specific-intent/general-intent distinction (DPP v. Beard; adopted/clarified in R. v. George; reinforced by DPP v. Majewski). Also considers Criminal Code s. 613(1)(b)(iii) on miscarriage of justice.
JudgeB: Pigeon J. (for Martland, Judson, Ritchie, Pigeon, Beetz and de Grandpré JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Applicability of Parole Act mandatory supervision: an inmate is subject to mandatory supervision under s. 15(1) if (i) s. 15(1) is in force at release, (ii) the inmate falls within the proclamation class under Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1968-69, c. 38, s. 101(2) (i.e., “sentenced to imprisonment in a penitentiary on and after the first day of August, 1970”), and (iii) by s. 14(1) the multiple terms are “deemed to constitute one sentence” to which s. 15(1) applies at release (release “as a result of remission… and the term of such remission exceeds sixty days”).
BaselineA: Statute (Parole Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. P-2, ss. 14(1), 15(1)-(2); Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1968-69 (Can.), c. 38, s. 101(2) and proclamation SOR/70-339 bringing s. 11B/15 into force for persons sentenced on/after Aug. 1, 1970).
CaseB_TestB: Succession Duties Act s. 26(1) inclusion rule: “the proceeds of insurance policies… due by an insurer by reason or on account of the death of the person on whose life the insurance was effected” are deemed property transmitted on death and taxable; this applies to accident insurance as well as life insurance, because nothing in s. 26(1) limits “insurance policies” to life insurance and “a death does not cease to be a death because it is accidental.”
BaselineB: Statute (Succession Duties Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 70, s. 26(1) (and related discussion of ss. 45(f), 46(1)); interpretive use of Civil Code arts. 1902, 1903, 1905, 1906 for bilingual/terminological context).
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Estate Tax Act: no taxable “passing” (and no inclusion under s. 3(1)(a)) where a marriage contract gives the survivor ownership of all community property retroactive to marriage; deceased not “competent to dispose” of community assets in the statutory sense
BaselineA: Statute (Estate Tax Act, 1958 (Can.), c. 29, ss. 2, 3(1)(a), 3(2)(a), 3(2)(e), 58(1)(i)) as applied through SCC precedents Sura v. MNR, [1962] S.C.R. 65 and The Royal Trust Company v. MNR, [1968] S.C.R. 505
CaseB_TestB: Treaty 8/NRTA geographic limit: “right of access” to hunt for food on private land turns on “visible, incompatible land use” assessed case-by-case (occupied if put to visible use incompatible with hunting; unoccupied if not)
