BaselineB: Constitutional/treaty text (NRTA, 1930, para. 12; Treaty No. 8) interpreted using treaty-interpretation principles and prior cases (e.g., Frank v. The Queen; Horseman; Horse; Myran; Mousseau; Sparrow (by analogy for justification))
JudgeB: Cory J. (for La Forest, L'Heureux-Dubé, Gonthier, Cory and Iacobucci JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Contract interpretation of a tax-escalation/price-adjustment clause: clause 9 applies only to a “tax, duty, charge or fee imposed upon [the Seller] in respect of bunker fuel oil, or the production, manufacture, sale or delivery by [the Seller] of bunker fuel oil”, and “does not apply to increases in the cost price of crude oil purchased by [the Seller] under supply contracts” (including from affiliates).
BaselineA: Common law (contract interpretation) applied to the parties’ agreement, specifically clause 9 (price adjustment for taxes/duties/charges/fees) and the contract definition of “the product” (bunker fuel oil).
CaseB_TestB: Van der Peet test (as applied to asserted self-government/gambling): “in order to be an aboriginal right an activity must be an element of a practice, custom or tradition integral to the distinctive culture of the aboriginal group claiming the right”; the Court must (1) “identify the exact nature of the activity claimed to be a right” and then (2) determine whether it was “a defining feature of the culture in question” prior to contact with Europeans.
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine under Constitution Act, 1982, s. 35(1), applying the test from R. v. Van der Peet, [1996] 2 S.C.R. 507 (including its claim-characterization guidance).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Foreseeability-based duty/breach limit for occupier/railway: liability only if the injury was a reasonably foreseeable result of the situation created by the defendant (no duty to guard against a child’s unforeseeable attempt to board a moving train between crossings).
BaselineA: Common law negligence/occupier’s liability principles (foreseeability of risk; reasonable person standard), with a rejected/limited statutory angle re Railway Act s. 214 fencing duty.
CaseB_TestB: Section 7 ‘fair hearing’ requirements in security-certificate proceedings: a fair judicial process must include (in substance) a hearing, an independent and impartial judge, a decision on facts and law, and the right to know and answer the case; if full disclosure is impossible, a ‘substantial substitute’ must be provided.
BaselineB: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7 (principles of fundamental justice) applied to IRPA certificate/detention scheme (IRPA ss. 77-85, especially s. 78).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Highway Victims Indemnity Fund liability for unknown-driver accidents: under Highway Victims Indemnity Act s. 43 the Fund must satisfy judgment only "to the same extent as if [judgment] had been rendered against the author of the accident", meaning (i) liability is capped at the s. 14 amount ($35,000) and (ii) the Fund’s liability is not extinguished by payments from other liable parties; s. 38 deduction applies only to amounts received from the same (unknown) driver/author
BaselineA: Statute: Highway Victims Indemnity Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 232, especially ss. 43 (unknown driver), 14 (financial responsibility cap), 38 (deduction rule in Fund recourse), and 49 (Fund powers/"extent prescribed")
CaseB_TestB: Sentencing and immigration collateral consequences: a judge may consider collateral immigration consequences as part of individualized sentencing, but only if the final sentence remains proportionate (Criminal Code s. 718.1); immigration consequences are "but one" factor and must not "skew" sentencing; appellate intervention is permitted where the sentencing judge was unaware of those consequences or counsel failed to advise, and (absent Crown consent) evidence should be adduced on appeal
BaselineB: Statute-informed common law sentencing framework: Criminal Code, ss. 718, 718.1, 718.2 (proportionality, parity, individualization) applied alongside IRPA, s. 64 (loss of immigration appeal right at 2 years or more)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Whether the accomplice corroboration 'rule of caution' applies to an accessory after the fact (and related direction that the jury decides accomplice status on the explained legal factors)
BaselineA: Common law (rule of practice/caution on uncorroborated accomplice evidence; definition of 'accomplice' from Davies v. DPP as accepted in Horsburgh v. The Queen; debate in lower courts including R. v. Gratton and R. v. Riezebos)
JudgeA: Pigeon J. (reasons for Spence, Pigeon and de Grandpré JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Interpretation/application of Criminal Code s. 212(c) murder: meaning of 'unlawful object' and how the objective 'ought to know' standard interacts with the accused’s actual knowledge (including relevance of drunkenness to that knowledge)
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, ss. 205(5)(a) and 212(c), with related ss. 212(a)(i)-(ii)); interpreted in light of prior SCC cases including Graves v. The King and R. v. Hughes
JudgeB: Lamer J. (for Martland, Dickson, Estey, McIntyre, Chouinard and Lamer JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Construction of Manitoba auto insurance exclusion: in s. 31(3)(h) (“death of, an insured”), “an insured” is read as referring to an insured under the particular certificate/contract under which indemnity is claimed (owner’s and driver’s certificates are separate contracts with distinct coverages).
BaselineA: Regulation/statutory scheme: The Manitoba Public Insurance Corporation Act, C.S.M. c. A180, and Man. Reg. 333/74 (Manitoba Automobile Insurance Regulation), especially ss. 30 (definition of “insured”), 31(1), 31(2) (“DRIVER’S POLICY”), and 31(3)(h) (exclusion).
CaseB_TestB: Treaty 8/NRTA limitation test for provincial game-law applicability: Treaty 8 hunting rights are limited by NRTA 1930, para. 12 to hunting “for food” (i.e., “for sustenance for the individual Indian or the Indian’s family”); if the activity is part of a “multi-stage process” involving sale/trafficking, it is an “act of commerce” and not protected, so provincial Wildlife Act s. 42 applies via Indian Act s. 88.
BaselineB: Constitutional/statutory instruments: Treaty No. 8 (1899); Natural Resources Transfer Agreement, 1930 (Alberta), para. 12; Indian Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-6, s. 88; Wildlife Act, R.S.A. 1980, c. W-9, ss. 42 and 1(s) (“traffic”).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 287(2) definition of “telecommunication”: whether the transmission/emission/reception is “by wire or cable” (excludes Hertzian-wave radio transmission; no ‘partly by wire’ distinction).
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 287(1)(b) and definition in s. 287(2) (“telecommunication” means transmission etc. “by wire or cable”).
CaseB_TestB: Immigration Act s. 19(1)(a)(ii) “excessive demands” assessment: determine whether admission “would cause or might reasonably be expected to cause excessive demands” on social services, requiring an individualized assessment of likely demands (not mere eligibility) and considering both medical and non-medical factors (including family ability/willingness to pay); threshold is “reasonable probability, not remote possibility” (more likely than not).
BaselineB: Statute: Immigration Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. I-2, s. 19(1)(a)(ii) (and noted parallel in IRPA s. 38(1)(c)).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Limits on municipal council’s discretion to refuse a business licence under Municipal Act s. 455: discretion must be exercised “judicially”, not on “extraneous”/“irrelevant or alien” grounds; “in any particular case” means peculiar to the applicant (not a blanket prohibition of a business type), and refusal cannot be used to prohibit a lawful trade absent express statutory power of prohibition.
BaselineA: Statute (Municipal Act, R.S.B.C. 1960, c. 255, s. 455) interpreted in light of municipal-law principles and authorities (including Municipal Corporation of the City of Toronto v. Virgo, [1896] A.C. 88; Sunshine Valley Co-operative Society v. City of Grand Forks; Wilcox v. Township of Pickering).
CaseB_TestB: IRPA security-certificate disclosure/fairness standard under Charter s. 7: the named person must receive an “incompressible minimum” of disclosure—i.e., be “reasonably informed” by receiving “sufficient disclosure to be able to give meaningful instructions” to public counsel and “meaningful guidance and information” to special advocates; if non-disclosure prevents this, the Minister must withdraw the information/evidence (and the judge must quash the certificate).
BaselineB: Statute + constitutional overlay: Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, ss. 77(2), 78, 83(1)(e), 83(1)(i) interpreted to comply with Charter s. 7 as explained in Charkaoui v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2007 SCC 9.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Appellate deference to trial findings of fact: an appellate court should not disturb a trial judge’s findings where there was “credible evidence before him on which he could reasonably base his conclusion”; it is “not the function of an appellate court to reconsider that evidence… and come to a different conclusion, unless it can be shown that the evidence reasonably could not result in justifying the conclusion of the trial judge.”
BaselineA: Common law (appellate review standard for findings of fact; referenced generally as a “well-known principle” and discussed alongside Cook v. Lewis, [1951] S.C.R. 830, though Cook held inapplicable on these facts).
CaseB_TestB: Bona fide occupational qualification (BFOQ) under Ontario Human Rights Code s. 4(6): (1) subjective good faith—limitation “must be imposed honestly, in good faith, and in the sincerely held belief” it serves “adequate performance… with all reasonable dispatch, safety and economy” and not for “ulterior or extraneous reasons”; and (2) objective necessity—must be “related in an objective sense” and “reasonably necessary to assure the efficient and economical performance of the job without endangering” the employee, co-workers, or the public; employer bears the burden on a balance of probabilities once prima facie discrimination is shown.
BaselineB: Statute: The Ontario Human Rights Code, R.S.O. 1970, c. 318, ss. 4(1) and 4(6) (and procedural context under ss. 14a, 14d).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal causation for unlawful act manslaughter: Crown must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the unlawful act was “at least a contributing cause of death, outside the de minimis range” (not necessary to prove it caused each intermediate mechanism like vomiting/aspiration).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code) interpreted through common-law causation principles; especially s. 205(1) (“A person commits homicide ... when directly or indirectly, by any means, he causes the death of a human being”).
CaseB_TestB: Anns/Kamloops two-stage duty-of-care framework for novel pure economic loss claims (applied to proposed negligence duty in commercial negotiations): (1) proximity/foreseeability prima facie duty; (2) residual policy considerations may negate/limit the duty.
BaselineB: Common law (Anns v. Merton London Borough Council; adopted in Kamloops (City of) v. Nielsen) duty-of-care analysis for negligence, applied in the pure economic loss context.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Crown bound by legislation/regulations only if expressly mentioned or (at common law) by “necessary implication” (i.e., the statute’s purpose would be “wholly frustrated” unless the Crown were bound); SCC holds Interpretation Act s. 16 excludes binding the Crown by mere necessary implication unless the Crown is “mentioned or referred to”.
BaselineA: Combination of common law (Bombay Province v. Bombay Municipal Corporation: Crown bound only by express words or “necessary implication” where purpose would be “wholly frustrated”) and statute (Interpretation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-23, s. 16; applied in context of Aeronautics Act and Air Carrier Regulations).
CaseB_TestB: Breach of contract where a stipulated term (here, cargo weight) is “material if not a critical term”; excessive deviation from the stipulated weight constitutes breach, engaging Civil Code art. 1065 (damages for breach) rather than nullity for error under art. 992.
BaselineB: Statute (Civil Code, arts. 992 and 1065) applied to a contract of carriage by sea; contractual term interpretation (weight as a material term).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Scope of CTC inquiry under Lord’s Day Act s. 11(x): Commission must identify the Act’s object (preventing gainful Sunday work) and then decide whether to exempt “any work” it “deems necessary to permit” to prevent “undue delay” in freight traffic; evidence about general Sunday impacts on the city is irrelevant to that mandate.
BaselineA: Statute: Lord’s Day Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. L-13, ss. 4 and 11(x) (interpreting “having regard to the object of this Act” and the Commission’s limited mandate).
CaseB_TestB: Meaning of “bona fide pension plan” in NB Human Rights Code s. 3(6)(a): plan must be “subjectively and objectively bona fide” — “a legitimate plan, adopted in good faith and not for the purpose of defeating protected rights”; inquiry is into the plan’s overall bona fides, not actuarial details; registration is a helpful indicator.
BaselineB: Statute: Human Rights Code, R.S.N.B. 1973, c. H-11, s. 3(6)(a) (interpreting “bona fide retirement or pension plan”).
JudgeB: Abella J. (Binnie, LeBel and Rothstein JJ. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: “Undueness” in conspiracy to lessen competition under Combines Investigation Act s. 32(1)(c): Crown must prove (1) an agreement/conspiracy and (2) that, if carried into effect, it would “prevent or lessen competition unduly” — i.e., impose “improper, inordinate, excessive or oppressive restrictions” / “virtually reliev[e] the conspirators from the influence of free competition”; not established merely because a “meaningful segment” is involved.
BaselineA: Statute (Combines Investigation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-23, s. 32(1)(c)) interpreted through prior SCC cases (Howard Smith Paper Mills; Weidman v. Shragge; Stinson-Reeb; Container Materials).
CaseB_TestB: Unreasonable verdict review (Criminal Code s. 686(1)(a)(i)): appellate court asks whether the verdict is one “that a properly instructed jury or a judge could reasonably have rendered”; may find unreasonableness if an essential inference/finding is (1) “plainly contradicted” by the evidence relied on, or (2) “incompatible with evidence that has not otherwise been contradicted or rejected”; credibility findings are not disturbed unless they “cannot be supported on any reasonable view of the evidence”.
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(a)(i)) as developed in SCC jurisprudence (Yebes; Biniaris; Sinclair; Beaudry; Burke).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Hodge’s Case circumstantial-evidence formula does not apply to proving mens rea/intent; intent must be proved beyond a reasonable doubt without requiring that the circumstances be “inconsistent with any other rational conclusion”
BaselineA: Common law (jury-charge approach to circumstantial evidence) as clarified in R. v. Mitchell, [1964] S.C.R. 471, and applied to the statutory offence in Criminal Code s. 110(1)(b)
CaseB_TestB: Interpretation of linked insurance policies: where a clause is susceptible of two meanings, prefer the meaning that gives it effect (art. 1014 C.C.), so “See Garage Policy” in the fleet policy is construed as referring to limits/premium (not importing the garage policy’s restrictive coverage), leaving fleet third-party liability coverage intact
BaselineB: Statute/civil law—Civil Code of Quebec art. 1014 (and related contract-interpretation provisions) applied to the insurance contracts/policies
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Contractual liability of mandatary/broker: plaintiff must prove fault, damage, and causality; if defendant alleges impossibility of performance (object of obligation impossible), defendant bears the burden under art. 1203 C.C. to prove impossibility (difficulty is insufficient)
BaselineA: Statute (Civil Code of Quebec): arts. 1701 (mandate), 984 and 1062 (object must be possible), and 1203 (burden: 'he who alleges facts in avoidance or extinction of the obligation must prove them')
CaseB_TestB: Municipal disqualification for conflict of interest: under s. 6 Moncton Consolidation Act, an elected official is disqualified if he 'directly or indirectly... have any interest in any contract' with the City (other than as a shareholder); 'interested in' is given its ordinary meaning and includes a director/officer’s indirect interest in the company’s municipal contracts
BaselineB: Statute (Moncton Consolidation Act, 1946 (N.B.), c. 101, s. 6), interpreted using the Angrignon principle that 'interested in' has no technical signification and must be given effect 'according to the common usage of men'
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Interpretation of para. 12 of the Alberta Natural Resources Transfer Agreement: “Indians within the boundaries” includes all Indians physically in Alberta (not only Alberta residents), so they are subject to provincial game laws but retain the proviso right to hunt “for food” on “unoccupied Crown lands” and other lands of access
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional instrument: Indian Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-6, s. 88 (provincial laws of general application apply to Indians “subject to the terms of any treaty”); Alberta Natural Resources Transfer Agreement, 1930, para. 12 (as confirmed by the British North America Act, 1930 (U.K.) c. 26); Treaty No. 6 (1876) hunting clause
CaseB_TestB: Qualified privilege in libel: a communication is privileged where the maker has an “interest or a duty, legal, social or moral” to make it and the recipient has a corresponding interest/duty; if privileged, the statement is actionable only on proof of malice, and the publisher is protected even if language is “violent or excessively strong” if, “having regard to all the circumstances”, he “might have honestly and on reasonable grounds believed” it true
BaselineB: Common law: definition of qualified privilege from Adam v. Ward, [1917] A.C. 309; SCC discussion applied via Netupsky v. Craig, [1973] S.C.R. 55
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory obscenity test in Criminal Code s. 159(8) is exhaustive for sex-based obscenity across the Code (displacing Hicklin): a work is obscene if it is a “publication a dominant characteristic of which is the undue exploitation of sex, or of sex and … crime, horror, cruelty and violence” and it “shall be deemed to be obscene”; Hicklin should not be used as a back-up where s. 159(8) is not met.
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, s. 159(8) (and its interaction with ss. 159(1), 163, 164) against the background of the common law Hicklin test (R. v. Hicklin) and Brodie v. The Queen.
CaseB_TestB: Duty to accommodate in employment discrimination: employer (and, in defined circumstances, union) must take “reasonable measures short of undue hardship”; “undue” means more than de minimis, and undue hardship is assessed contextually (e.g., financial cost, disruption of collective agreement, morale/rights of other employees, interchangeability, size, safety). Union is a party to discrimination (and must accommodate) if it (1) helped create the discriminatory rule (e.g., in the collective agreement) or (2) blocks the employer’s reasonable accommodation where union cooperation is required; complainant must facilitate and accept reasonable accommodation.
BaselineB: Statute interpreted/applied: British Columbia Human Rights Act, S.B.C. 1984, c. 22, ss. 8(1), 8(4), 9; building on SCC common law/precedent on accommodation and undue hardship (O’Malley; Central Alberta Dairy Pool).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 159(8) statutory obscenity test is exclusive for sex-based obscenity across the Code: a thing is obscene if it is a “publication” whose “dominant characteristic” is the “undue exploitation of sex” (alone or with “crime, horror, cruelty and violence”); the common law Hicklin test is displaced and should not be used as a fallback where s. 159(8) is not met.
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, s. 159(8) (and its interaction with ss. 159(1), 163, 164); contrasted with common law Hicklin test as discussed in Brodie v. The Queen and R. v. Hicklin).
CaseB_TestB: Role of a collectively-negotiated time-limit termination clause in the duty to accommodate: the negotiated period is a relevant factor/evidence in assessing reasonable accommodation and undue hardship, but is not determinative; accommodation must remain individualized and undue hardship is assessed globally from the start of the absence, not from expiry of the negotiated period.
BaselineB: Common law / human rights jurisprudence (Meiorin duty-to-accommodate/undue hardship framework) applied in the labour arbitration context; informed by Quebec Charter equality principles.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Federal jurisdiction over cable TV as a single interprovincial/international “undertaking” (no constitutional demarcation at the antenna/technology change point)
BaselineA: Constitution (B.N.A. Act ss. 91 and 92(10)(a)) interpreted through precedent, especially the Radio Reference (In re Regulation and Control of Radio Communication in Canada, [1932] A.C. 304) and Winner ([1954] A.C. 541)
CaseB_TestB: Income Tax Act s. 13(21) “proceeds of disposition”: purchaser’s assumed obligation is included only if it is a distinct existing vendor liability; embedded future costs that depress value are excluded
BaselineB: Statute (Income Tax Act, s. 13(21) definition of “proceeds of disposition” including “the sale price of property that has been sold”), applied with the general principle that assumed liabilities can be part of sale price (e.g., mortgage analogy discussed via Telus, Loyens, Lord Elgin Hotel)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Immovable by nature (Civil Code) for utility-style networks: a structure is immovable by nature where it is a 'construction attached to the ground'—it is enough that the attachment is 'not purely transitory and accidental'; the 'criterion for being immovable by nature is met when a structure that may be described as a building adheres to something that is immovable by nature, whether land or a building', and separation of ownership of the supporting immovable is irrelevant.
BaselineA: Statute + civil law: Retail Sales Tax Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 71, ss. 2(3) ("moveable property" = not immoveable by the laws of the Province) and 6 (tax on purchase of moveable property), interpreted by reference to Civil Code arts. 374 et seq. (incl. arts. 375-378/376 on immovables by nature). Key baseline cases applied: Montreal Light, Heat and Power Consolidated v. City of Westmount, [1926] S.C.R. 515; Lower St. Lawrence Power Co. v. L’Immeuble Landry Ltée, [1926] S.C.R. 655; Bélair v. City of Ste-Rose (1922), 63 S.C.R. 526.
CaseB_TestB: Punitive damages in breach of contract (wrongful dismissal): punitive damages may be awarded for breach of contract but 'will be rare'; they require (1) an 'actionable wrong' causing the injury complained of, and (2) 'extreme' misconduct 'deserving of punishment because of its harsh, vindictive, reprehensible and malicious nature'—conduct must be 'sufficiently offensive, standing alone, to constitute actionable wrong' to justify punitive damages.
BaselineB: Common law of contract damages and wrongful dismissal, relying on Addis v. Gramophone Co. (H.L.) and SCC authority Peso Silver Mines Ltd. (N.P.L.) v. Cropper, [1966] S.C.R. 673; also draws on punitive damages jurisprudence (e.g., Rookes v. Barnard; McElroy v. Cowper-Smith and Woodman; H. L. Weiss Forwarding Ltd. v. Omnus) and Restatement (Second) of Contracts s. 355 (as persuasive).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Parent’s contributory negligence / contribution: whether the parent departed from the “generally accepted standard of care” of parents in the community (i.e., the conduct expected of a “reasonably prudent” parent in the circumstances)
BaselineA: Common law negligence (standard of care) as framed in the decision by reference to community parental practice; discussed alongside cases including Ware’s Taxi Ltd. v. Gilliham (SCC) and other negligence authorities cited in the reasons
CaseB_TestB: Clause-5 election/repudiation framework in a real estate APS after fire: purchaser must elect either (i) take insurance proceeds and complete, or (ii) cancel; attempting to impose different conditions is a refusal to perform as written and constitutes repudiation that the vendor may accept
BaselineB: Common law contract (repudiation) plus interpretation/application of the parties’ Agreement of Purchase and Sale (standard form), especially clause 5 (risk/insurance/election) and clause 9 (time of the essence)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Matrimonial property beneficial interest via resulting trust from contribution to purchase price/common pool: if a spouse contributes (directly or indirectly) in “money or money’s worth” to acquisition/improvement, a resulting trust is presumed (rebuttable by proof of contrary intention); in a joint “common purse” account, “in the absence of agreement to the contrary, a one-half interest in any investment purchased by a husband from a common pool of funds … will be considered to be held by him for the benefit of his wife.”
BaselineA: Common law (resulting trust/common intention presumptions in matrimonial property disputes), drawing on Murdoch v. Murdoch, Pettitt v. Pettitt, Gissing v. Gissing, and joint-account resulting trust reasoning (e.g., Jones v. Maynard as discussed).
CaseB_TestB: Discretionary access-to-exhibits balancing test: court (as custodian) must balance the strong presumption of openness against countervailing interests (especially protecting the “innocent”/privacy), may inquire into and regulate the proposed use; “curtailment of public accessibility can only be justified where there is present the need to protect social values of superordinate importance … [including] the protection of the innocent.”
BaselineB: Common law open court/access doctrine from Attorney General of Nova Scotia v. MacIntyre (applied), with reference to Nova Scotia Civil Procedure Rule 30.11(6) on return of exhibits (context for custody/ownership, not the core test).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Limitation Act s. 6(4)(b) postponement test: time runs only when a properly advised reasonable person would conclude the plaintiff could, acting reasonably in light of their own circumstances and interests, bring an action; postponement beyond accrual requires interests/circumstances that are “serious, significant, and compelling” and excludes “purely tactical concerns” (Novak v. Bond, per McLachlin J., para. 39).
BaselineA: Statute (Limitation Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 266, s. 6(4)(b) (and the s. 6(4) structure including s. 6(4)(a) and “appropriate advice” in s. 6(5)(a))).
CaseB_TestB: Arbitration Act s. 15 stay framework in receivership: (1) applicant shows an arguable case for four “technical prerequisites” (arbitration agreement; court proceeding by a party; matter within scope; stay sought before any “step”); (2) resisting party must prove a s. 15(2) exception—“void, inoperative or incapable of being performed”—and in receivership an agreement may be “inoperative” where enforcing it would “compromise the orderly and efficient resolution of a receivership”, assessed via a non-exhaustive factor list (effect on integrity of insolvency proceedings; relative prejudice; urgency; effect of insolvency stay; other material factors) (Peace River, per Côté J., paras. 76-89, 155).
BaselineB: Statute (Arbitration Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 55, s. 15(1)-(2), interpreted alongside Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. B-3, ss. 183(1) and 243(1)(c)).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: When 5-year extinctive prescription begins for engineers’ percentage-based fees: prescription runs only when the fee is due—either “on completion of the work” or, if suspended/terminated, “at the time it was suspended, after a decision clearly communicated” to the engineers (and, under the tariff, generally not before the call for tenders or notice that there will be no tenders/termination).
BaselineA: Combination of statute/regulation and civil-law principles: Civil Code art. 2260(6) (5-year prescription) plus the Tariff of fee for Professional Engineers of the Province of Quebec (O.C. 891, Sept. 4, 1957, esp. “General Conditions of Agreement”, s. 3 “Payment of Engineers’ Fee”), interpreted alongside general principles of bilateral contracts (as discussed with reference to Mignault and Lalonde v. La Ville de Mont-St-Hilaire).
CaseB_TestB: Discretionary test for enforcing foreign letters rogatory under Canada Evidence Act s. 43: even if statutory/regulatory bars are uncertain, a court “may, in its or his discretion” refuse enforcement where doing so would run counter to Canadian public policy/sovereignty; it is “not for a Court…to take issue with the government’s determination of public policy or to measure its impact.”
BaselineB: Statute-based discretion: Canada Evidence Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-10, s. 43 (court “may, in its or his discretion” order examination/production). Considered alongside the Uranium Information Security Regulations (C.R.C., c. 366) made under Atomic Energy Control Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. A-19, s. 9, and comity/public policy principles (including Rio Tinto Zinc v. Westinghouse and Re Westinghouse).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “nude” in Criminal Code s. 170: complete nudity is captured without needing proof it “offend[s] against public decency or order”; s. 170(2) is a deeming extension for being “so clad as to offend against public decency or order” (i.e., “is” = “shall be deemed to be”).
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, s. 170(1)(a) and s. 170(2) (with historical comparison to former s. 205A deeming language).
CaseB_TestB: When the Crown improperly “split[s] its case” by adducing reply evidence that raises new issues/attacks credibility and forces the accused to testify again, the curative proviso in Criminal Code s. 613(1)(b)(iii) (“no substantial wrong or miscarriage of justice”) cannot be applied because the appellate court cannot realistically assess the verdict after extracting the improper evidence.
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, s. 613(1)(b)(iii) (application of the curative proviso on appeal) in the context of the common-law rule against splitting the Crown’s case.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “nude” in Criminal Code s. 170: s. 170(2) is a deeming provision (“is” = “shall be deemed to be”) that extends nudity to being “so clad as to offend against public decency or order”; for complete nudity under s. 170(1)(a), the Crown need not prove offence to public decency/order (and the accused cannot defend by proving compatibility with decency/order absent a separate “lawful excuse”).
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, s. 170(1)(a) and s. 170(2) (interpreting s. 170(2) as a deeming/fiction provision; contrasted with predecessor s. 205A).
CaseB_TestB: Availability of certiorari in criminal proceedings: for parties, certiorari lies only for a provincial court judge’s jurisdictional error (not for mere errors of law on the face of the record); “jurisdictional errors occur where the court fails to observe a mandatory provision of a statute or where a court acts in breach of the principles of natural justice”.
BaselineB: Combination: Criminal Code s. 674 (no interlocutory appeals) plus common law limits on extraordinary remedies/certiorari in criminal proceedings (as synthesized from prior SCC jurisprudence).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Workmen’s Compensation Act s. 8 “additional sum” claim where Commission is subrogated: if, due to the victim’s contributory fault, the dependant’s civil claim against the third party is reduced (e.g., to 50%), and the compensation paid is equal to or exceeds that reduced civil claim, the dependant cannot claim any “additional sum” because they have not received only “part payment” (and the Commission’s s. 7(3) subrogation takes priority).
BaselineA: Statute + Civil Code: Workmen’s Compensation Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 159, ss. 7(3) (subrogation pleno jure) and 8 (right to claim “any additional sum required...”), and Civil Code art. 1157 (partial payment rule) and art. 1056 (wrongful death claim reduced by victim fault).
CaseB_TestB: Employee’s right to guaranteed salary after being “cut”: the club’s obligation to pay “depended upon the plaintiff’s being available and willing to provide the services mentioned in the contract”; by signing/playing for another team without consent, the player “effectively breached the contractual arrangement... and freed the respondent of any further obligation to pay salary under the contract.”
BaselineB: Common law contract principles applied to the parties’ written employment contract (interpretation/enforcement of contractual terms; breach/repudiation concepts as discussed in the reasons).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Workmen’s Compensation Act “additional sum”/subrogation priority where victim contributorily at fault: claimant cannot recover any additional amount under s. 8 if compensation received is not merely “part payment” of the reduced civil claim (i.e., where victim’s fault reduces the art. 1056 claim and the Commission’s payment meets/exceeds that reduced amount, the Commission is subrogated pleno jure and has priority to recover from the third party).
BaselineA: Statute + Civil Code (Workmen’s Compensation Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 159, ss. 7(3), 8; Civil Code arts. 1056, 1157) as applied with SCC authorities on contributory fault and quantum (Rainville Automobile Ltd. v. Primiano; Hôpital Notre-Dame de l’Espérance and Théoret v. Laurent; Brink’s Express v. Plaisance distinguished).
CaseB_TestB: Institutional financial security requirement for judicial independence: any government measure affecting judges’ remuneration conditions (including elimination of an office conferring a clear economic benefit) must be preceded by an “independent, effective and objective” commission process; if recommendations are ignored, the decision must be justified on a “simple rationality test”.
BaselineB: Constitution + Charter doctrine (Charter s. 11(d) and Constitution Act, 1867 Preamble) building on Valente v. The Queen and the Provincial Court Judges Reference (Reference re Remuneration of Judges of the Provincial Court of Prince Edward Island).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Suspensive effect of serving a prohibition/quash notice endorsed with a Rule 7 command to make a return “forthwith”: the inferior court’s jurisdiction is suspended (and non-compliance cannot improve its position).
BaselineA: Statute + court rules + common law (Ontario Criminal Rules 4-8; Criminal Code, s. 714; common law certiorari suspension principle discussed via cases like R. v. Foster and R. v. Titchmarsh).
CaseB_TestB: Section 15(1) equality analysis (La Forest J.): (1) distinction; (2) disadvantage; (3) whether distinction is based on an enumerated/analogous ground and is an “irrelevant personal characteristic” assessed for relevance to the law’s “functional values” in its larger context.
BaselineB: Common law Charter doctrine (Andrews v. Law Society of British Columbia; Miron v. Trudel; related s. 15 jurisprudence) applied to the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 15(1).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Defence of fair comment requires proof that the defamatory comment is the honest expression of the real opinion of the writer/publisher; absent evidence of the writers’ honest belief (and where the newspaper disavows the opinion), the defence is not available and need not be left to the jury.
BaselineA: Common law (defamation: fair comment defence). Key authorities relied on include Turner v. Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer Pictures Ltd. and Slim v. Daily Telegraph Ltd. (as cited in the reasons).
CaseB_TestB: Section 2(a) infringement threshold for indirect burdens: state action that increases the cost of practising/manifesting religious belief infringes freedom of religion only if the burden is non-trivial (i.e., not “trivial or insubstantial”); all coercive burdens (direct/indirect, intentional/unintentional) are potentially within s. 2(a).
BaselineB: Statute/constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 2(a) (interpreted in light of s. 27). Built from prior SCC interpretation in R. v. Big M Drug Mart Ltd. (as cited).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Fair comment defence requires proof that the defamatory comment was an honest expression of the real opinion of the writer/publisher (each publisher in same position as original writer); absent evidence of the writers’ honest belief (and with publisher/editor denying honest belief), the defence is unavailable
BaselineA: Common law (defamation—fair comment defence), drawing on authorities including Silkin v. Beaverbrook Newspapers Ltd.; Turner v. Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer Pictures Ltd.; Jones v. Skelton; Slim v. Daily Telegraph Ltd.; Lyon & Lyon v. Daily Telegraph Ltd.
CaseB_TestB: Contempt of court: the party alleging contempt must prove beyond a reasonable doubt the constituent elements, including personal service or actual personal knowledge of the order; service on a solicitor does not, without supporting circumstances, fix ministers with knowledge, and vicarious liability does not apply
BaselineB: Common law contempt principles (knowledge/personal service requirement) plus interpretation of Federal Court Rules (C.R.C. 1978, c. 663, Rules 308, 311, 355) as not altering contempt elements
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Fair comment in defamation requires proof that the impugned comment was an honest expression of the real view of the person making/publishing the comment; absent evidence of the writers' honest belief (and with the newspaper/editor denying such belief), the defence cannot go to the jury
BaselineA: Common law (defamation—defence of fair comment), drawing on authorities cited in the reasons including Turner v. Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer Pictures Ltd. and Slim v. Daily Telegraph Ltd.
CaseB_TestB: Garofoli review of wiretap authorizations: errors or even fraud in the ITO are not automatically fatal; the court must excise the tainted material and ask whether the remaining, independent information provides sufficient reliable grounds on which an authorization could reasonably be based
BaselineB: Common law framework from R. v. Garofoli (review of wiretap authorizations under the Criminal Code interception regime)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Intra vires test for CRTC regulations under Broadcasting Act s. 16: validity “must be tested by determining whether the regulation deals with a class of subject referred to in s. 3” (i.e., made “in furtherance of its objects” implementing the s. 3 broadcasting policy).
BaselineA: Statute (Broadcasting Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. B-11, ss. 3, 15, 16(1) incl. 16(1)(b)(i) and 16(1)(b)(ix)) and the impugned regulation (Radio (A.M.) Broadcasting Regulations, s. 5(1)(k)).
CaseB_TestB: Quasi-delict (art. 1053 C.C.) assessed by the “prudent and reasonable man” standard, with appellate review of a jury verdict limited to whether the verdict is “unreasonable” (jury translates the reasonable-person criterion into the concrete standard for the case).
BaselineB: Statute/civil law (Civil Code art. 1053; Code of Civil Procedure arts. 363, 380) plus prior authority on jury/court roles (e.g., Metropolitan Railway Co. v. Jackson (1877), 3 A.C. 193; Gagné v. Côté, [1970] S.C.R. 25; C.N.R. v. Lancia, [1949] S.C.R. 177).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Constitutional limits on a provincial commission of inquiry: it may investigate specific criminal acts within provincial 'administration of justice' but cannot, under the guise of that inquiry, intrude into the administration/management of a federal institution (RCMP); relatedly, a minister’s s. 41(2) Federal Court Act national-security certificate is binding on a commissioner
BaselineA: Combination: Constitution (B.N.A. Act ss. 91, 92) + statute (Federal Court Act, s. 41(2)) + common law Crown immunity/privilege principles; applied with reference to Di Iorio v. Warden of the Montreal Jail and Faber v. The Queen
CaseB_TestB: Contested custody between natural parent and adoptive parents: exercising parens patriae (via s. 39), the court must treat the child’s welfare as the predominant/paramount consideration, decided on 'all relevant factors' (including psychological, spiritual and emotional welfare), with parental claims subordinate where welfare requires
BaselineB: Statute (Domestic Relations Ordinance, R.O.N.W.T. 1974, c. D-9, ss. 28(1), 35(2), 37, 39) informed by equitable parens patriae principles and prior custody jurisprudence (incl. Re Moores and Feldstein; Racine v. Woods; Beson v. Director of Child Welfare)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Public Authorities Protection Act s. 11 applicability: segregate statutory functions into (1) those with a “public aspect or connotation” vs (2) “private executive or private administrative”/“managerial, internal or operational” matters; only the former are protected by the six-month limitation
BaselineA: Statute: The Public Authorities Protection Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 374, s. 11, interpreted in relation to The Housing Development Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 213, s. 6(2) (and informed by cases like Bradford Corporation v. Myers and McGonegal v. Gray discussed in the reasons)
CaseB_TestB: Bazley v. Curry vicarious liability “significant connection” framework (with enumerated factors): vicarious liability may be imposed where there is a “significant connection” between the enterprise/employment and the wrong; factors include (a) opportunity to abuse power, (b) furtherance of employer’s interests, (c) intimacy/conditions conducive to the wrong, (d) power conferred, (e) vulnerability of victims
BaselineB: Common law: vicarious liability framework from Bazley v. Curry (and Jacobi v. Griffiths) as applied/affirmed; the decision also rejects a proposed common-law “charitable immunity” exemption
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Exemption-from-seizure via insurance clause requires a true third-party beneficiary; a universal legatee/heir is not a beneficiary and cannot invoke art. 553(3) C.C.P. or the policy’s exemption clause
BaselineA: Statute/civil code provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, art. 553(3) (property declared by donor/testator to be exempt from seizure); Civil Code (Quebec), arts. 597 (heir not a third party), 1028 (contract binds heirs/legal representatives), 735 (cannot bequeath property to shield from creditors)
CaseB_TestB: No-fault liability for neighbourhood disturbances under art. 976 C.C.Q.: liability turns on whether neighbours suffered 'abnormal or excessive annoyances' beyond the 'limit of tolerance' (result-focused, not conduct/fault)
BaselineB: Statute: Civil Code of Québec, art. 976 (duty to tolerate normal neighbourhood annoyances not beyond the limit of tolerance, considering nature/location of land or local custom)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Superior Court residual jurisdiction not ousted: a provincial superior court may decide a federal statutory issue (here, whether Bell has a legal obligation under s. 5(4) to prescribe “reasonable requirements”) when it arises incidentally in a properly constituted tort/injunction action, absent a “specific provision of law” assigning the matter exclusively to another tribunal
BaselineA: Statute (Quebec Code of Civil Procedure, art. 31; An Act respecting The Bell Telephone Company of Canada, s. 5(4)-(6) as amended; National Transportation Act, s. 45(1))
CaseB_TestB: Test for permitting the Crown to reopen its case: the “keystone principle” is prejudice to the accused; discretion narrows by trial stage—(1) before Crown closes: broad latitude; (2) after Crown closes but before defence elects: allowed to correct an “oversight or inadvertent omission” if “justice requires it” and “no prejudice”; (3) after defence has started to answer: reopening only in the “narrowest or most exceptional of circumstances” (e.g., defence contributed to omission, or correction of a matter of form)
BaselineB: Common law discretion on reopening (as discussed through cases including Robillard v. The Queen; plus Charter-informed rationale re self-incrimination)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Admissibility of cross-examining an accused on juvenile delinquencies as “convictions” under s. 12 Canada Evidence Act (and related character rebuttal under s. 593 Cr.C.): (1) “any offence” in s. 12(1) includes a Juvenile Delinquents Act delinquency that is a Criminal Code violation; (2) “a finding of delinquency under this Act is equivalent to a conviction within the meaning of s. 12”; (3) an admitted juvenile record is sufficient proof (“a conviction does not need to be proven by the production of the official record; it is just as validly proven by the admission of the convicted party”), absent “exceptional circumstances showing clearly that the admission was made in error”; and (4) the accused “put his character in issue when he stated that he had never been convicted nor arrested,” permitting contradiction by proof of prior convictions under s. 593.
BaselineA: Statute: Canada Evidence Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-10, s. 12(1)-(2); Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 593; interpreted in light of Juvenile Delinquents Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. J-3 (e.g., ss. 2(1), 3, 20(1), 38).
CaseB_TestB: When the Crown particularizes a narcotic in an indictment but proves a different scheduled form, the charge should be amended under Criminal Code s. 529 if it can be done without prejudice: the “gravamen of the offence is the possession of a narcotic for the purpose of trafficking”; the court “shall… consider” s. 529(4) factors including “whether the accused has been misled or prejudiced in his defence” and “whether… the proposed amendment can be made without injustice”; if prejudice exists but is curable, s. 529(5) permits adjournment; if “irreparable prejudice” exists, “there can be no amendment… and an acquittal must be entered.” Where no prejudice is apparent, an appellate court (including SCC) may amend and dismiss the appeal under ss. 613(1)(b)(i) and 613(3).
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 529(4)-(5), 613(1)(b)(i), 613(3); Narcotic Control Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. N-1, ss. 2 ("narcotic"), 4(2), schedule item 3.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Coopers & Lybrand criteria for when an administrative decision/order is required by law to be made on a judicial or quasi-judicial basis (for Federal Court Act s. 28 review): (1) whether the statutory language/context suggests a hearing; (2) whether the decision affects rights/obligations; (3) whether an adversary process is involved; (4) whether there is an obligation to apply substantive rules to individual cases rather than implement broad policy — “These are all factors to be weighed and evaluated, no one of which is necessarily determinative.”
BaselineA: Common law (duty to act judicially / natural justice) as discussed through prior cases cited in the reasons (e.g., Guay v. Lafleur; Randolph; Wiseman v. Borneman; Pearlberg v. Varty; Cooper v. Wandsworth; Russell v. Duke of Norfolk; Durayappah v. Fernando; Ridge v. Baldwin) applied within the statutory framework of Federal Court Act s. 28 and Income Tax Act s. 231(4)-(5).
CaseB_TestB: Stillman s. 24(2) “trial fairness” framework: classify evidence as non-conscriptive vs conscriptive; if conscriptive, Crown must prove on a balance of probabilities it would have been discovered by alternative non-conscriptive means (independent source or inevitable discovery) — otherwise admission renders trial unfair and evidence is excluded “as a general rule” without weighing other Collins factors.
BaselineB: Statute/constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 24(2), building on the Collins s. 24(2) framework (R. v. Collins) and related SCC jurisprudence (e.g., Black, Colarusso, Burlingham).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory limit on interim rate-setting: s. 31 “losses” means “lost revenue” after the rate application, and the legality question is whether interim rates will prospectively produce revenue in excess of estimated revenue requirements by including pre-application shortfalls (beyond s. 31’s limited reach).
BaselineA: Statute (Alberta): The Gas Utilities Act, R.S.A. 1970, c. 158, ss. 27-28, 31; plus The Administrative Procedures Act, R.S.A. 1970, c. 2, s. 8 (reasons requirement).
CaseB_TestB: Cuerrier fraud-vitiated consent test (s. 265(3)(c)): consent to sexual intercourse is vitiated by fraud where (1) dishonesty (including non-disclosure) relates to obtaining consent, assessed objectively, and (2) the dishonesty results in deprivation by exposing the complainant to a “significant risk of serious bodily harm”; Crown must also prove the complainant would have refused unprotected sex if informed of HIV-positive status.
BaselineB: Statute (federal): Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, ss. 265(3)(c), 268; informed by criminal fraud jurisprudence (e.g., R. v. Olan; R. v. Théroux; R. v. Zlatic) as adapted to s. 265.
JudgeB: Cory J. (for Cory, Major, Bastarache and Binnie JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory interpretation of Parole Act ss. 10 and 20 (as amended in 1977): day parole may be ended either by termination under s. 10(2) (then s. 20 consequences do not apply) or by revocation under s. 10(1)(e), in which case s. 20 applies to “any parole” (including day parole) and the inmate’s post-revocation custody/remission is calculated under s. 20(2) subject to the Board’s recredit discretion in s. 20(3). Key language: “ ‘parole’ means ... and includes day parole”; “when any parole is revoked”; and “the Board may recredit the whole or any part of the statutory and earned remission ...”.
BaselineA: Statute: Parole Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. P-2, ss. 10(1)(e), 10(2), 20(1)-(3) (as amended effective Oct. 15, 1977, by Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1977).
CaseB_TestB: Palmer criteria (applied to sentence appeals) for admitting fresh evidence on appeal: (1) generally not admitted if, by due diligence, it could have been adduced at trial (flexibly applied in criminal cases); (2) relevant to a decisive or potentially decisive issue; (3) credible (reasonably capable of belief); (4) if believed, could reasonably, taken with the other trial evidence, be expected to have affected the result. Overriding consideration: “the interests of justice”.
BaselineB: Common law: Palmer v. The Queen, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 759 (criteria for fresh evidence), applied within the statutory appellate-evidence framework of Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, ss. 683 and 687.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Exercise of SCC discretion under Supreme Court Act s. 52 to vary interest: default interest runs from the trial judgment date unless the Court orders otherwise; here, limit pre-SCC-judgment interest to the trial award amount due to litigation delay attributable to the successful appellant
BaselineA: Statute: Supreme Court Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. S-19, s. 52 (as amended by 1974-75-76, c. 18, s. 7) and Interest Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-18, ss. 13-14
CaseB_TestB: Whether procedural fairness/natural justice applies to Governor in Council review under National Transportation Act s. 64(1): construe the statutory scheme; because s. 64(1) confers complete discretionary, quasi-legislative power with no procedural standards, courts review only for jurisdictional boundaries/conditions precedent, not for fairness-based hearing requirements
BaselineB: Statute: National Transportation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. N-17, s. 64(1) (contrasted with s. 64(2)); plus general common-law fairness/natural justice jurisprudence (e.g., Nicholson v. Haldimand-Norfolk; Martineau v. Matsqui Institution (No. 2)) used to interpret whether any duty is implied
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory-limit rule for groundwater pumping: pumping above 10,000 gallons/day (unless permitted) is per se “unreasonable” and thus can ground nuisance/negligence; no pumping right is a defence for excess pumping
BaselineA: Combination of common law (private nuisance/negligence; the “English Rule” on percolating water) and statute (Ontario Water Resources Commission Act, s. 37; also discussed: s. 47 and Expropriations Act definition of “injurious affection”)
CaseB_TestB: Criteria-based assessment of solatium doloris (moral prejudice from death of a loved one): consider factors including “the circumstances of the death”, “the ages of the deceased and the parent”, “the nature and quality of the relationship”, “the parent’s personality and ability to manage the emotional consequences”, and “the effect of the death on the parent’s life”
BaselineB: Civil law/statutory baseline under Civil Code of Lower Canada, arts. 1053 and 1056 (recognizing compensable moral prejudice), with SCC overruling prior SCC authority denying solatium doloris (Canadian Pacific Railway Co. v. Robinson (1887))
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Effect of uncompleted vehicle-registration transfer on liability insurance: under Highway Code s. 13(6), if the registered owner has not complied with s. 13(1)-(2), he "shall be deemed to be the owner for purposes of responsibility and for purposes of insurance"; for liability coverage the transfer is treated as not having occurred, so the buyer/driver with the deemed owner’s consent is covered by the omnibus clause.
BaselineA: Statute (Highway Code, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 231, s. 13(6) (and non-compliance with s. 13(1)-(2)); applied to the civil-liability section/omnibus clause of the auto policy).
CaseB_TestB: Garofoli leave (threshold) test for cross-examining a wiretap affiant: the defence must show a "reasonable likelihood" that cross-examination "will elicit testimony of probative value to the issue for consideration by the reviewing judge" (i.e., likely to undermine a statutory precondition/basis for the authorization).
BaselineB: Common law (R. v. Garofoli, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 1421), applied in the context of Criminal Code wiretap authorizations (including s. 184.2) and Charter s. 8 review hearings.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Direct action under Highway Victims Indemnity Act s. 6: insurer is directly liable to third parties only for “damage covered by liability insurance”; s. 6 bars nullity/lapse defences but “does not extend the insurance contract to what it does not cover” (coverage determined by the policy’s definition of “automobile” and whether the damage was caused “first and foremost” by an excluded trailer risk).
BaselineA: Statute (Highway Victims Indemnity Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 232, s. 6) interpreted alongside the insurance contract’s coverage/definition clauses; guided by General Security Insurance Company of Canada v. Bélanger, [1977] 1 S.C.R. 802.
CaseB_TestB: Lease interpretation re fire-loss subrogation: a landlord’s covenant “with the Lessee” to keep premises “insured against loss by fire” runs to the tenant’s benefit (precluding insurer subrogation for tenant-negligence fire) unless there is “another explanation” in the lease (e.g., option-to-purchase provisions) sufficient to show the risk of negligently caused fire remains on the tenant.
BaselineB: Common law of landlord-tenant/insurance subrogation and lease interpretation, applying Agnew-Surpass Shoe Stores Ltd. v. Cummer-Yonge Investments Ltd., [1976] 2 S.C.R. 221 and Ross Southward Tire Ltd. v. Pyrotech Products Ltd., [1976] 2 S.C.R. 35 (and distinguishing United Motors Service Inc. v. Hutson, [1937] S.C.R. 294).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Qualified privilege in defamation defeated only by malice; privilege protects even excessive language if the defendant "might have honestly and on reasonable grounds believed" it was true (Adam v. Ward / Netupsky v. Craig)
BaselineA: Common law (qualified privilege and malice), drawing on Adam v. Ward, [1917] A.C. 309 and Netupsky v. Craig, [1973] S.C.R. 55
CaseB_TestB: Sufficiency of reasons (Sheppard/Braich): two-stage inquiry—(1) are the reasons inadequate; (2) if so, do they prevent appellate review (i.e., are they "sufficiently amenable to appellate review")
BaselineB: Common law (appellate review of reasons), relying on R. v. Sheppard, 2002 SCC 26 and R. v. Braich, 2002 SCC 27
JudgeB: Bastarache and Abella JJ. (LeBel J. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Reasonable and probable grounds for warrantless arrest must consider all information available (police cannot ignore exculpatory information); coroner’s s. 38 warrant cannot be used to detain a suspect for interrogation (abuse of power/invalid warrant)
BaselineA: Combination: statute (Criminal Code 1953-54, c. 51, s. 435; Coroners' Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 29, s. 38) plus civil liability under Civil Code arts. 1053-1054
CaseB_TestB: Validity of dismissal of a probationary constable: dismissal must be effected by the Board (non-delegable) and the Board must actually exercise its function by considering the case with notice to the constable; otherwise there is no effective discharge
BaselineB: Statute/regulation: The Police Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 351, s. 29; Regulation 680, s. 27(b) (and related collective agreement term, s. 9, made under s. 29)
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Municipal office disqualification for having a direct or indirect “interest in any contract” with the city (broad, ordinary-meaning approach): applying Angrignon, “interested in” has “no technical signification” and must be given effect “according to the common usage of men”; thus a municipal officer who is a director/officer of a contracting company is “most certainly ‘interested’ in his company entering into profitable contracts” and therefore has an (at least) indirect interest.
BaselineA: Statute (Moncton Consolidation Act, 1946 (N.B.), c. 101, s. 6), interpreted using the Angrignon approach to “interested in” (J.B. Arthur Angrignon v. Bonnier, [1935] S.C.R. 38) and supported by the remedial-interpretation direction in the New Brunswick Interpretation Act, R.S.N.B. 1973, c. I-13, s. 17.
CaseB_TestB: Statutory interpretation of whether a municipality is an “institution” for s. 22 OLA language-of-pleadings duty: read “institution” in its entire context and harmoniously with the scheme of the Act; because including municipalities would create “incoherent and illogical consequences”, “institution” in s. 22 (as defined in s. 1) does not include municipalities; Charter values apply only in cases of “genuine ambiguity”.
BaselineB: Statute (Official Languages Act, S.N.B. 2002, c. O-0.5, ss. 1 “institution” and 22), applying the modern principle of statutory interpretation (Driedger) and the Bell ExpressVu limit on Charter-values interpretation to genuine ambiguity.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Qualified privilege—threshold for leaving express malice to the jury: malice must be supported by evidence that “raises a probability of its existence” (more than a “mere scintilla” or “mere possibility”; evidence must be “more consistent with [malice’s] existence than with its non-existence”).
BaselineA: Common law (defamation/libel: qualified privilege and malice), drawing on Adam v. Ward and applied/confirmed in Sun Life Assurance Co. of Canada v. Dalrymple; also relying on Somerville v. Hawkins and related authorities.
CaseB_TestB: Blood Tribe clarity requirement for statutory abrogation of solicitor-client privilege: only where “legislative language evinces a clear intent to abrogate solicitor-client privilege” may a court find the statute does so; applied to s. 232(1) ITA’s express exclusion of “an accounting record of a lawyer”.
BaselineB: Statute (Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), ss. 231.2(1), 231.7(1), and especially s. 232(1) definition of “solicitor-client privilege”), interpreted through the common-law/constitutional interpretive principle from Blood Tribe.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Priority of B.C. Payment of Wages Act s. 5A lien: lien arises "from the date wages were earned" and takes priority only over dispositions after attachment; if a mortgage predates attachment, it is "not affected" and the lien "will only attach to the employer’s equity" in the property.
BaselineA: Statute — Payment of Wages Act, 1962 (B.C.), c. 45, ss. 5 and 5A (especially s. 5A(1)-(2)).
CaseB_TestB: Forced dissolution of a Quebec legal person under C.C.Q.: where no special statutory scheme applies, the C.C.Q. dissolution provisions apply suppletively to fill gaps (art. 334/300), and dissolution may be ordered under art. 355(2) if (i) condition fulfilled, (ii) object accomplished, (iii) impossibility of accomplishing the object, or (iv) "some other legitimate cause".
BaselineB: Statute/codified law — Civil Code of Québec, arts. 300, 334, 355 (and related arts. 355-364); considered alongside Quebec Companies Act and Code of Civil Procedure art. 829.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Residual discretion/inherent jurisdiction to grant a limited right of reply (or curative instruction) where Crown’s closing address causes prejudice: (1) usually cure by specific correcting reference in the jury charge; (2) if curative instructions will not suffice, in “relatively rare situations” grant a limited reply, only in the “clearest cases of unfairness”, confined to the improper issues and not to restate the defence or raise new theories.
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Criminal Code, s. 651(3)-(4) (order of addresses) plus common law inherent jurisdiction of superior courts to ensure trial fairness (citing, e.g., R. v. Osborn; Selvey v. DPP; Amato v. The Queen).
CaseB_TestB: Charter-validity test for a statutory presumption under s. 11(d): a presumption is constitutional “solely if proof of the substituted fact leads inexorably to the existence of the essential element it replaces”; the nexus must be “nothing less than inexorable” (i.e., necessarily true in all cases).
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law/Charter doctrine: Criminal Code, s. 172.1(3) (presumption re age) assessed under Charter, s. 11(d), applying SCC precedents on presumptions (Whyte; Downey; Audet; St-Onge Lamoureux; Vaillancourt).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Adjudicator’s remedial authority to substitute a lesser penalty for discharge: where the adjudicator finds “just and sufficient cause for some disciplinary action, but not for discharge”, the adjudicator may “substitute some lesser penalty for discharge”.
BaselineA: Statute + collective agreement: Public Service Labour Relations Act, R.S.N.B. 1973, c. P-25, s. 92(1)(b) (adjudication of “disciplinary action resulting in discharge, suspension or a financial penalty”) and s. 101 (privative clause), plus collective agreement art. V(d) (“Discipline, suspension, demotion or discharge ... shall be for just and sufficient cause”) and art. XVII(c) (management rights “for just and sufficient cause”). Prior SCC baseline discussed/distinguished: Port Arthur Shipbuilding Co. v. Arthurs, [1969] S.C.R. 85.
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 24(2) exclusion test (Collins guidelines): exclude evidence obtained in a Charter breach only if, “having regard to all the circumstances”, its admission “would bring the administration of justice into disrepute” (applied via Collins factors such as trial fairness and seriousness of the violation).
BaselineB: Statute/constitutional text + common law framework: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 24(2) (“shall be excluded if ... admission ... would bring the administration of justice into disrepute”), as structured by the SCC’s common-law guidelines in R. v. Collins, [1987] 1 S.C.R. 265 (applied).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Will-construction test: give effect to the testator’s overriding intention on a fair reading of the clause, so administrative/boilerplate provisions cannot defeat a clearly expressed intention (legacy payable on disposition of the business, however effected)
BaselineA: Common law (principles of will construction/ascertaining testator’s intention from the will read as a whole; no specific statutory provision identified in the reasons)
CaseB_TestB: Manslaughter legal causation with intervening acts: the Smithers/Nette test remains whether the accused’s dangerous unlawful acts were a “significant contributing cause of death”; foreseeability and “independent act” are non-determinative analytical aids
BaselineB: Combination: Criminal Code ss. 222, 224, 225 (homicide/causation context) plus common law causation test from Smithers v. The Queen and R. v. Nette
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Functional/operational test for whether labour relations fall under exclusive federal jurisdiction (exception) or provincial jurisdiction (rule): labour relations are provincially regulated unless the undertaking’s “nature of [its] operations and [its] normal activities” can be characterized as a federal undertaking/service/business; Indian ownership, reserve location, and federal funding do not change the undertaking’s operational nature.
BaselineA: Common law constitutional division-of-powers doctrine for labour relations (functional/operational characterization), as stated through cases like Toronto Electric Commissioners v. Snider and the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act Reference (Stevedoring).
CaseB_TestB: Section 15(1) Charter equality test (post-Kapp/Withler): (1) Does the law create a distinction based on an enumerated or analogous ground? (2) Does the distinction create a disadvantage by perpetuating prejudice or stereotyping, assessed contextually without requiring a “mirror comparator group”.
BaselineB: Common law/constitutional doctrine interpreting Charter s. 15(1), drawing on Andrews v. Law Society of British Columbia, Law v. Canada, and R. v. Kapp.
JudgeB: McLachlin C.J. and Abella J. (for the Court)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Interpretation of Bankruptcy Act s. 107(1)(j): Crown tax claims rank pari passu notwithstanding provincial statutory preferences; provincial registered tax “privilege” cannot elevate the Crown to “secured creditor” status to escape s. 107(1)(j)
BaselineA: Statute (Bankruptcy Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. B-3, ss. 2 and 107(1)(j), (3); interacting with Quebec Retail Sales Tax Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 71, s. 30 and Civil Code art. 1989)
JudgeA: Pigeon J. (for Martland, Ritchie, Pigeon, Beetz, Pratte and McIntyre JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Public interest standing test (purposive, flexible): (1) serious justiciable issue; (2) plaintiff has a real stake/genuine interest; (3) proposed suit is, in all the circumstances, a reasonable and effective means to bring the issue to court (not a strict ‘no other way’ requirement)
BaselineB: Common law (standing jurisprudence: Borowski; Finlay; Canadian Council of Churches; Thorson; McNeil; Hy and Zel’s; etc.)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Crown prerogative priority applies only where Crown and subject claims are “of equal degree”; a prior registered second/collateral mortgage is of a higher degree than a later-registered Crown judgment, so Registry Act registration-date priorities govern the surplus distribution
BaselineA: Combination: common law Crown prerogative priority for debts “of equal degree” (The Queen v. Bank of Nova Scotia (1885), 11 S.C.R. 1) plus Nova Scotia Registry Act, R.S.N.S. 1967, c. 265, ss. 17-18 (and related civil procedure distribution rule 47.11)
CaseB_TestB: International jurisdiction by extension of domestic territorial jurisdiction: art. 71 C.C.P. applies to foreign defendants, so an incidental action in warranty “must be taken before the court in which the principal action is pending” and is “not subject to any limitation”
BaselineB: Statute/civil code: Code of Civil Procedure (Quebec), art. 71 (and discussion of arts. 68-75, incl. art. 75) and Civil Code, art. 27; applied through the private international law principle that international jurisdiction is defined by extension of domestic territorial jurisdiction (citing Alimport; Trower and Sons)
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “detained” under Canadian Bill of Rights s. 2(c): detention requires “some form of compulsory restraint”/being “held in custody” (not mere compliance with police directions), so roadside breath-demand context here was not detention and thus no counsel-based “reasonable excuse” for refusal
BaselineA: Statute (Canadian Bill of Rights, 1960, s. 2(c)(ii)-(iii), applied to Criminal Code breath-demand/refusal scheme in s. 234.1(1)-(2))
CaseB_TestB: Tort of civil conspiracy (Estey J.): liability exists (1) where “the predominant purpose of the defendants’ conduct is to cause injury to the plaintiff” (means lawful or unlawful), or (2) where defendants’ conduct is unlawful, “directed towards the plaintiff (alone or together with others)”, and defendants “should know” injury to plaintiff is likely to and does result (constructive intent), with actual damage required
BaselineB: Common law (conspiracy tort jurisprudence, including Crofter Hand Woven Harris Tweed Co. v. Veitch and related authorities discussed in the reasons; comparative reliance on Lonrho)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 492 re-election validity test: effective re-election occurs where the accused (1) notifies the sheriff of the desire to re-elect (s. 492(1)); (2) attends at the time/place fixed (s. 492(2)-(3)); and (3) after the charge is read, makes the re-election (which may be communicated through counsel in the accused’s presence). The charge to be read is the actual charge faced at trial (the preferred indictment), and failure to prefer a new Form 4 indictment under s. 496 after re-election does not invalidate proceedings where the indictment is already in Form 4.
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, s. 492 (re-election procedure) and related s. 496 (Form 4 indictment after re-election).
CaseB_TestB: Injurious affection (no land taken) — actionable-at-common-law requirement: under Expropriations Act s. 1(e)(ii) and s. 21, compensation is available only if the construction-caused loss would have been actionable at common law; here, the only possible cause is private nuisance, requiring an unreasonable interference (a balancing of interests/‘reasonable user’), and loss of prospect/amenities from adjacent highway construction is not actionable.
BaselineB: Combination: Statute (Expropriations Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 154, ss. 1(e)(ii), 21) incorporating common law (private nuisance/actionable-at-common-law requirement; Loiselle conditions referenced).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Ontario Municipal Board jurisdiction to adjust assets/liabilities on dissolution under s. 137(1): s. 14(11)(a),(b),(d) is incorporated "entirely" without the qualifying words in the intro to s. 14(11), so the Board may "exercise" those powers "in relation to the dissolution of the County" and may make adjustments "as the Board may consider equitable"
BaselineA: Statute: The Regional Municipality of Ottawa-Carleton Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 407, ss. 135, 137 (incorporating The Municipal Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 284, s. 14(11)(a),(b),(d))
CaseB_TestB: Charter fundamental justice mens rea requirement for murder: "a conviction for murder cannot rest on anything less than proof beyond a reasonable doubt of subjective foresight of death"; s. 213(a) is unconstitutional because it removes the Crown’s burden to prove subjective foresight
BaselineB: Constitution + statute: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 7 and 11(d), applied to Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 213(a) (in light of R. v. Vaillancourt, [1987] 2 S.C.R. 636)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Valid consent to intercept a private communication under Criminal Code s. 178.11(2)(a): consent must be "voluntary (i.e. free from coercion)" and "made knowingly, with an awareness of the significance of the consent"; promised/expected leniency does not by itself amount to coercion, and consent may be express or implied.
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, Part IV.1 as enacted by the Protection of Privacy Act): ss. 178.1 ("private communication"), 178.11(2)(a) (consent interception), 178.16(1)(a) (admissibility if interception "lawfully made").
CaseB_TestB: Proving the target "identifiable group" under Criminal Code s. 319(2): the trial judge must consider the "totality of the evidence" to decide whether the statements, as a matter of fact, promoted hatred of the particularized group (here, Roma); it is not necessary to prove strict "interchangeability" of labels (e.g., "gypsies" and "Roma").
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code): s. 319(2) (wilful promotion of hatred) and s. 318(4) (definition of "identifiable group"), as interpreted in Keegstra.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Audi alteram partem in administrative appeals: an appellate authority must not receive evidence/representations ex parte after the hearing without disclosing it and giving the affected party a real opportunity to respond; prejudice need only be possible
BaselineA: Common law (procedural fairness / natural justice), applied in the statutory context of the Universities Act, 1974 (B.C.), c. 100 (ss. 58(1)-(3), 61) without express abrogation of natural justice
CaseB_TestB: Workers’ compensation occupational-disease causation under s. 250(4): causation may be inferred from circumstantial evidence even with inconclusive/contrary expert evidence; if evidence on causation is “evenly weighted”, the issue must be resolved in the worker’s favour
BaselineB: Statute (Workers Compensation Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 492, ss. 6 and 250(4)) plus mandatory policy baseline (RSCM II “causative significance” framework applied via s. 250(2))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Appellate intervention in damages: an appellate court may not substitute its own figure unless a wrong principle of law was applied or the overall award is a wholly erroneous estimate of damages
BaselineA: Common law (as stated in Andrews et al. v. Grand & Toy Alberta Ltd. et al., [1978] 2 S.C.R. 229, at p. 235)
JudgeA: Martland J. (for the Court, oral reasons)
CaseB_TestB: Videotape-only identification: once a videotape is shown not to be altered and to depict the crime, it is admissible; identity may be proven on the videotape alone if the trier of fact is satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt, considering the tape’s clarity/quality and (to a lesser extent) the time the perpetrator appears
BaselineB: Common law evidence principles (authentication/admissibility and proof beyond a reasonable doubt), drawing on R. v. Leaney, [1989] 2 S.C.R. 393 and related authorities; also discussed alongside Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(a)(i) (unreasonable verdict review)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Quebec Labour Code s. 16 rebuttal: employer must show the “other” reason is substantial, not a pretext, and the true (causa causans) reason for dismissal; commissioner/court cannot review the severity/appropriateness of the penalty once a real reason is established
BaselineA: Statute (Quebec Labour Code, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 141 as am., ss. 13-16, especially s. 16 “another good and sufficient reason” and the s. 16 presumption)
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 12 “gross disproportionality” analysis (as applied to a mandatory minimum): assess (1) gravity of the offence, (2) personal characteristics of the offender, (3) particular circumstances of the case, and (4) the effect of the sentence; if not grossly disproportionate on the facts, consider whether the law is grossly disproportionate in “reasonable hypothetical circumstances”
BaselineB: Combination (constitutional text + common law/precedent): Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 12; test drawn from and reaffirming R. v. Smith, [1987] 1 S.C.R. 1045 (also referencing Lyons and Luxton)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Summary conviction appeal costs: under Criminal Code ss. 758 and 771(3), the appeal court "may make any order with respect to costs that it considers just and reasonable" / "proper" and these provisions are interpreted as implicitly binding the Crown (Her Majesty) in Part XXIV context
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 758, 771(3), read in context of Part XXIV including s. 720(1) definitions; plus Interpretation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-23, s. 16)
CaseB_TestB: Mortgage prepayment under Interest Act s. 10(1): mortgagor may prepay at end of each five-year period; if mortgagor enters a valid renewal that "deems" the mortgage date to the existing loan’s maturity and the renewal term does not exceed five years, mortgagor cannot prepay until end of that five-year renewal; choosing not to exercise the right (with full knowledge) is not waiver/contracting out, but a clause purporting to relinquish the right at the end of any five-year period is unenforceable
BaselineB: Statute (Interest Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-18, s. 10(1) (and (2) exclusion); related provincial analogues discussed: Manitoba Mortgage Act s. 20(6) and Real Property Act s. 103(1)(c))
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.
