CaseA_TestA: Wrongful dismissal damages: no deduction for (i) income tax not payable and (ii) unemployment insurance benefits arising from the employment contract (collateral benefits rule as applied to UI contributions)
BaselineA: Common law contract damages for wrongful dismissal (mitigation/collateral benefits), applying Guy v. Trizec Equities Ltd. (contributory benefits not deductible) and rejecting a Gourley-style tax deduction approach (R. v. Jennings)
CaseB_TestB: Statutory authorization to fingerprint juveniles: under Identification of Criminals Act s. 2, a juvenile in lawful custody for a delinquency relating to a Criminal Code indictable offence is 'charged with'/'under conviction of' an indictable offence, so necessary reasonable force may be used
BaselineB: Statute—Identification of Criminals Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-1, s. 2(1)-(2), interpreted alongside the Juvenile Delinquents Act; relying on Morris v. The Queen for meaning of 'offence'/'conviction' in the juvenile context
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: “Air of reality / sense of reality” threshold for whether a trial judge must leave a defence (here, mistake of fact as to consent) with the jury: there must be “some evidence which would convey a sense of reality in the submission”; for mistake as to consent, “some evidence which, if believed, would support the existence of a mistaken but honest belief” in consent (and not merely counsel’s assertion).
BaselineA: Common law (jury-charge/defence-leaving threshold from Kelsey v. The Queen; also referenced in Wu v. The King and R. v. Workman and Huculak).
CaseB_TestB: Morin s. 11(b) “reasonable time” framework (as applied/assumed for trial delay): assess (1) length of delay, (2) waiver, (3) reasons for delay, and (4) prejudice; plus the holding (majority) that s. 11(b) does not apply to appellate delay (with any remedy for appellate delay proceeding, if at all, under s. 7 abuse of process).
BaselineB: Constitution (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 11(b) and s. 7) and prior SCC framework in R. v. Morin (for the four-factor s. 11(b) analysis).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Presumption of reasonableness standard of review for a tribunal interpreting its home statute, rebutted only by Dunsmuir correctness categories (statutory appeal is not a new correctness category)
BaselineA: Common law (judicial review standard of review framework from Dunsmuir v. New Brunswick, plus subsequent SCC cases on presumptive reasonableness for home-statute interpretation)
CaseB_TestB: Framework for Crown sui generis fiduciary duty: fiduciary duty arises from Crown discretionary control over a specific/cognizable Aboriginal interest; breach assessed by whether Crown acted with loyalty/good faith/full disclosure and 'ordinary prudence' toward beneficiary’s best interest (not guaranteeing a particular result)
BaselineB: Common law (fiduciary duty jurisprudence: Wewaykum; Guerin; Haida Nation; Manitoba Metis Federation; etc.) applied within a statutory specific-claims validity context (Specific Claims Tribunal Act, s. 14(1)(b), (c))
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Necessarily incidental (ancillary) doctrine for validating federal legislation that prima facie falls under provincial heads of power: to uphold such a provision, it "must be established that it provides for matters necessarily incidental to effective legislation" on an enumerated federal subject; here, s. 33(3) failed because it was a "blanket prohibition" that "makes no attempt to link the proscribed conduct to actual or potential harm to fisheries" and thus was not "necessarily incidental" to s. 91(12) fisheries power.
BaselineA: Common law constitutional division-of-powers doctrine (ancillary/incidental powers), articulated in A-G Canada v A-G British Columbia, [1930] A.C. 111 (Lord Tomlin proposition (3)), and applied to s. 91(12) fisheries power under the British North America Act, 1867.
CaseB_TestB: Colour of right in theft: the defence turns on whether the trier of fact is satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused did not have, at the time of the taking/transfer, "an honest belief that he had the right to that money"; it is not dependent on what the jury thinks the accused's legal rights actually were (e.g., when commissions were payable).
BaselineB: Statute — Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 283 (definition of theft including "fraudulently and without colour of right") and 294(a) (theft over $200).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “unlawful purpose” in Criminal Code s. 423(2)(a): it “means contrary to law, that is prohibited by federal or provincial legislation”; if the alleged purpose is not prohibited by legislation, the information does not disclose an offence under s. 423(2)(a).
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 423(2)(a) (conspiracy “to effect an unlawful purpose”); also considered in context with Criminal Code s. 8 (no common law offences) and Canada Labour Code s. 110(1). Prior SCC authority discussed: Wright, McDermott & Feeley v. The Queen, [1964] S.C.R. 192; Frey v. Fedoruk, [1950] S.C.R. 517.
CaseB_TestB: Quebec defamation fault under art. 1457 C.C.Q.: fault is determined by a “contextual analysis” and, for media defendants, “there will not be fault until it has been shown that the journalist or media outlet in question has fallen below professional standards”; “the conduct of the reasonable journalist becomes the all-important guidepost.”
BaselineB: Statute (civil law): Civil Code of Québec, art. 1457 (general extra-contractual liability), applied to defamation; jurisprudential baseline within the decision: Société Radio-Canada v. Radio Sept-Îles Inc., [1994] R.J.Q. 1811 (C.A.) and Prud’homme v. Prud’homme, 2002 SCC 85 (contextual defamation fault).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Rabey (majority) disease-of-the-mind classification for automatism: the key question is whether the accused’s automatism stems from a cause “primarily internal to the accused” (then a “disease of the mind”) versus a “transient effect produced by some specific external factor” (then not a disease of the mind); “ordinary stresses and disappointments of life” are not an external cause taking it out of disease of the mind.
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 16 (insanity/disease of the mind) applied alongside common-law automatism/insanity authorities (e.g., Bratty v. A.G. Northern Ireland).
CaseB_TestB: Mortgage clause conflict/supremacy test: where a standard mortgage clause says it “shall supersede any policy provisions in conflict therewith BUT ONLY TO THE INTEREST OF THE MORTGAGEE”, any conflicting policy term (including Statutory Condition 4) cannot be used to void the mortgagee’s coverage; in particular, SC4’s voiding for an unnotified “change material to the risk” conflicts with the clause’s “notwithstanding ... any vacancy or non-occupancy”.
BaselineB: Statute and contract: Insurance Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. I.8, Part IV (Statutory Condition 4) interpreted in light of the policy’s standard mortgage clause (and Katsikonouris).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Prescription characterization for damages: if damages flow from a single cause of action that is a breach of contractual obligation, they are contractual (30-year prescription); if they flow from several separate and independent causes, each head is characterized as contractual or delictual depending on its source and prescribed accordingly (e.g., separate ‘typical offences’ are delictual and prescribed in 2 years). Key formulation: “If the damages claimed result from a single cause of action, which is the breach of a contractual obligation, the damages will be characterized as contractual damages… If they result from several separate and independent causes of action… [they] must be regarded as contractual or delictual depending on whether they originate in the breach of a contract or in an offence or quasi-offence”.
BaselineA: Statute/civil code (Civil Code of Quebec provisions on prescription and obligations), especially arts. 2242 (30-year), 2261(2) (2-year for offences/quasi-offences), with characterization of corporate by-laws/natural justice as contractual in the voluntary-association context.
CaseB_TestB: Priority between mechanic’s lien and mortgage for past indebtedness: s. 14(1) gives lien priority only for “payments or advances made on account of any…mortgage” after written notice or after registration; otherwise it does not create general priority. Where the Act does not prescribe priorities, s. 20 deems a registered lien claimant a “purchaser pro tanto” so Registry Act ss. 69(1) and 70 apply and “priority [is] according to priority of registration” (absent actual notice).
BaselineB: Statute (The Mechanics’ Lien Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 267, ss. 14(1), 20 (and related registration/expiry provisions ss. 16, 21, 22)) interpreted together with The Registry Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 409, ss. 69(1), 70.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Accrued-rights/anti-retroactivity analysis on statutory repeal: apply Interpretation Act s. 35(c) so repeal does not “affect any right, privilege, obligation or liability acquired, accrued, accruing or incurred” under the repealed enactment; read the amending Unemployment Insurance Act s. 31 together with s. 35(c) to preserve only the pre‑repeal accrued entitlement (here, benefits through January 31, 1976) while leaving the claimant subject to the pre‑amendment disqualification (old s. 31(3)(b) pension-payable disentitlement).
BaselineA: Statute (Interpretation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-23, s. 35(c), applied to the repeal/substitution of Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, s. 31 by S.C. 1974-75-76, c. 80, s. 10; also considers Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, s. 38 and Unemployment Insurance Entitlements Adjustment Act, 1976-77, c. 11, s. 2).
CaseB_TestB: Judicial immunity/independence limit on compellability under a public inquiry statute: read Public Inquiries Act ss. 3-4 together so that, while the Commission may “summon” persons (s. 3), it cannot “compel” testimony beyond what a superior court judge could compel in a civil case (s. 4); because judicial independence requires that relations with other branches not impinge on the court’s “authority and function,” judges cannot be compelled to testify about (a) “how and why” they reached a decision (adjudicative process) or (b) “why a particular judge sat on a particular case” (assignment/composition of the panel).
BaselineB: Combination of statute and constitutional/common law principle (Public Inquiries Act, R.S.N.S. 1967, c. 250, ss. 3-4, interpreted in light of the constitutional principle of judicial independence and common law judicial immunity as discussed with reference to Valente v. The Queen and Beauregard v. Canada).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Interpretation of Motor Vehicle Transport Act, s. 3(2): provincial board may license an “extra‑provincial undertaking” “into or through the province” as including operations “in, across, into and out of the province”, and may apply provincial “terms and conditions” (including enforcement like seizure) “as if ... a local undertaking”
BaselineA: Statute: Motor Vehicle Transport Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. M-14, ss. 2 (definitions), 3(1)-(2), 5, 6; incorporating provincial scheme via The Public Service Vehicles Act, R.S.A. 1970, c. 300 (notably s. 58 seizure power) through the phrase “upon the like terms and conditions and in the like manner as if ... a local undertaking” in s. 3(2)
CaseB_TestB: Charter standing/scope test for corporate claim under s. 12: claimant must show an interest “falling within the scope of the guarantee, and one which accords with the purpose of that provision”; purposive interpretation begins with text, and “cruel and unusual” denotes protection only humans can enjoy, so corporations are outside s. 12’s protective scope
BaselineB: Constitutional text and purposive-interpretation framework: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 12; interpretive baseline from Big M Drug Mart (purposive interpretation) and CIP Inc. (must have an interest within scope/purpose), plus prior s. 12 jurisprudence on the “grossly disproportionate”/“outrage standards of decency” threshold (e.g., Smith (Edward Dewey); Boudreault) as context
JudgeB: Brown and Rowe JJ. (Wagner C.J. and Moldaver and Côté JJ. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Applicability of an exclusion/waiver clause after fundamental breach: whether the clause continues to bind is determined by the “true construction of the contract” (waiver clause’s fate tied to the contract’s fate; here it ceased to bind once the innocent party elected to treat the contract as at an end).
BaselineA: Combination: common law contract doctrine on exclusion clauses and fundamental breach (Suisse Atlantique; Photo Production) plus statutory lien context (The Mechanics’ Lien Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 267, s. 5(1) (“Unless he signs an express agreement to the contrary…”)).
CaseB_TestB: Collateral attack on an administrative order in penal proceedings: determine the legislature’s intended forum by considering (non-exhaustively) the statute’s wording, the legislation’s purpose, availability of appeal, the nature of the collateral attack in light of the appeal tribunal’s expertise/raison d’être, and the penal consequences; under the EPA, no collateral attack after failing to use the appeal mechanism.
BaselineB: Statutory/interpretive framework under the Environmental Protection Act, R.S.O. 1980, c. 141 (notably ss. 17, 122-123, 146(1a)), informed by prior SCC collateral-attack jurisprudence on court orders (Wilson; Litchfield; Sarson).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Constructive trust based on unjust enrichment: claimant must show (1) an enrichment, (2) a corresponding deprivation, and (3) absence of any juristic reason for the enrichment; and in spousal-like relationships it is unjust where one party prejudices herself in a reasonable expectation of an interest and the other freely accepts benefits knowing or ought to know of that expectation.
BaselineA: Common law (equitable constructive trust/unjust enrichment), drawing on Rathwell v. Rathwell and Murdoch v. Murdoch as discussed in the reasons.
CaseB_TestB: Solicitor-client confidentiality/privilege and search warrants: (i) confidentiality may be raised whenever communications are likely to be disclosed without consent; (ii) conflicts are resolved in favour of confidentiality unless law provides otherwise; (iii) exercises of legal authority must interfere with confidentiality only to the extent absolutely necessary; (iv) enabling legislation derogating from confidentiality is interpreted restrictively; plus for Criminal Code s. 443 searches of lawyers’ offices, the justice should refuse a warrant unless there is no reasonable alternative and must impose protective execution terms; crime/fraud communications are excepted.
BaselineB: Combination: statute (Criminal Code, s. 443) interpreted in light of common law solicitor-client privilege/confidentiality (including Solosky v. The Queen and common law crime/fraud exception).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Informed-consent negligence causation: whether “a reasonable person in the patient’s position would have done if there had been proper disclosure of attendant risks” (objective patient-position test, with the patient’s particular concerns considered only if “objectively assessed in terms of reasonableness”).
BaselineA: Common law (medical negligence / duty of disclosure and causation), drawing on Hopp v. Lepp, [1980] 2 S.C.R. 192 (duty to disclose “all material risks” and answer specific questions; scope depends on circumstances).
CaseB_TestB: Division-of-powers “integral element” test for federal jurisdiction over s. 92(10) undertakings: Parliament may displace provincial law only where the matter regulated is “an integral part” of the federal core (here, a special limitation period for personal-injury negligence claims is not “an integral part of federal jurisdiction”).
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine (division of powers) applying the “integral element” approach from Construction Montcalm Inc. v. Minimum Wage Commission, [1979] 1 S.C.R. 754 and Northern Telecom Ltd. v. Communications Workers of Canada, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 115, in the context of Railway Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. R-2, s. 342(1).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Natural Resources Agreement (para. 12) “right of access” test for treaty Indian hunting for food: a province may deny access for hunting to all, but “once any hunting is permitted, then Indians (and other members of the public) have a right of access for the purpose of hunting”; that right of access “engaged the proviso in paragraph 12” so Indians may hunt “for food at all seasons of the year” (not limited to the particular day’s open season).
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional instrument: para. 12 of the 1930 Natural Resources Agreement (confirmed by British North America Act, 1930) as applied/clarified in R. v. Sutherland, Wilson and Wilson, [1980] 2 S.C.R. 451 (and contrasted with R. v. Smith).
CaseB_TestB: Charter validity (s. 2(a)) purpose-first test: “the legislation's purpose is the initial test of constitutional validity”; effects are considered only if the law “has passed the purpose test”; and “effects can never be relied on to save legislation with an invalid purpose.”
BaselineB: Constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 2(a) (and s. 1 framework, excluding Oakes details), plus Constitution Act, 1982, s. 52(1) (supremacy/remedy).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: No implied power for the Commission/officer to retroactively revoke an employer’s previously granted premium reduction; errors in granting do not make the decision a “nullity” absent express statutory/regulatory authority (one-way employer-initiated review only).
BaselineA: Regulation/statute: Unemployment Insurance Act, 1970-71-72, ss. 64(4), 64(6) (regulation-making for premium reduction system) and Unemployment Insurance Regulations, s. 24 (decision and employer-only review/appeal).
CaseB_TestB: Mens rea for Criminal Code s. 121(1)(a): no “corrupt” purpose required; guilt requires (1) knowledge the accused is an official, (2) intentional demand/acceptance of a loan/reward/advantage/benefit, and (3) knowledge it is “in consideration for” cooperation/assistance/exercise of influence in connection with government business.
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 121(1)(a) (interpreting required mens rea; rejecting an added ‘corruption’ element).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Ernst (Cromwell J.) categorical Ward s. 24(1) Charter-damages analysis for quasi-judicial regulators: Charter damages are never an “appropriate and just” remedy against this Board because (collectively) (1) judicial review is an effective alternative remedy, (2) good-governance concerns (resource depletion, chilling effect, impartiality/collateral attack) negate damages, and (3) case-by-case damages litigation would undermine the purpose of statutory immunity
BaselineA: Combination: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 24(1) ("appropriate and just" remedy) + common-law Charter damages framework from Vancouver (City) v. Ward, 2010 SCC 27 (functional purposes of damages and countervailing factors) + statutory context of Energy Resources Conservation Act, R.S.A. 2000, c. E-10, s. 43 (immunity clause)
CaseB_TestB: Mikisew Cree (Karakatsanis J.) rule that the duty to consult does not apply to the law-making process: “no aspect of the law-making process — from the development of legislation to its enactment — triggers a duty to consult” because the duty to consult has only applied to executive action or action taken on behalf of the executive, and separation of powers/parliamentary sovereignty/privilege preclude applying it to legislative action
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine: duty to consult framework from Haida Nation v. British Columbia (Minister of Forests), 2004 SCC 73 (honour of the Crown; duty triggered by contemplated Crown conduct with potential adverse effects on s. 35 rights) + constitutional principles (separation of powers, parliamentary sovereignty/privilege) and constitutional text (Constitution Act, 1867, Part IV; Constitution Act, 1982, s. 35)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory interaction test for workers’ compensation bar vs. motor-vehicle owner’s vicarious liability: s. 10(1) WCA bars only actions against (i) the worker’s employer, (ii) any employer within the Act, or (iii) any worker; a vehicle owner deemed an employer/servant relationship under s. 70(1) MVA is still suable if the owner is not an employer within s. 10(1) (the tort ‘does not disappear’—remedy is compensation against the negligent worker, but court action against the non-covered owner).
BaselineA: Statute (Workers’ Compensation Act, 1968 (B.C.), c. 59, s. 10(1) and Motor-vehicle Act, R.S.B.C. 1960, c. 253, s. 70(1))
CaseB_TestB: Operational conflict / precedence framework for conflicting administrative decisions: (1) determine if there is a true ‘operational conflict’—i.e., ‘compliance with the decision of one tribunal necessitates violation of the other’; (2) if so, first ask whether either decision could be overturned under its ordinary standard of review; (3) if both would stand, courts may declare one decision inoperative to the extent of conflict and decide precedence using a ‘pragmatic and functional’ approach considering factors including ‘legislative purpose’ of each tribunal, how ‘central’ the decision is to each tribunal’s purpose, and the degree the decision reflects ‘policy-making or policy implementation’.
BaselineB: Combination of common law administrative law (pragmatic and functional approach; curial deference) and statute (Railway Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. R-3, ss. 335, 340; National Telecommunications Powers and Procedures Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. N-20, ss. 49, 50, 68(1))
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Priority between a mechanics’ lien and a subsequent collateral mortgage for past indebtedness: where the Mechanics’ Lien Act does not prescribe priority (s. 14(1) inapplicable), an unregistered lien has no priority and the contest is resolved by registration priority under the Registry Act (ss. 69(1), 70) once the lien is registered and deemed a purchaser pro tanto under s. 20.
BaselineA: Statute (Ontario): Mechanics’ Lien Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 267, ss. 14(1), 16, 20, 21, 22 (and s. 7(4) re when lien arises), plus Registry Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 409, ss. 69(1), 70.
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 1 proportionality (Oakes) as applied to PIPA’s restriction of union expression in a labour dispute: although PIPA has a pressing and substantial objective and is rationally connected, the infringement is not justified because the Act’s broad limits on expression are disproportionate (fails minimal impairment/proportionality of effects) given the lack of mechanisms to balance privacy with freedom of expression in lawful strikes.
BaselineB: Constitution (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 1 and 2(b)) applied to statute (Personal Information Protection Act, S.A. 2003, c. P-6.5, especially ss. 3, 4(1), 7(1) and exemptions; and Personal Information Protection Act Regulation, Alta. Reg. 366/2003, s. 7).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Election between contractual and delictual liability in Quebec: a plaintiff may sue in delict despite a contract if the alleged contractual fault is independently a delictual fault under art. 1053 C.C. (i.e., it would be a fault 'even in the absence of a contract')
BaselineA: Statute (Quebec Civil Code art. 1053; Quebec Code of Civil Procedure art. 68) as interpreted through SCC jurisprudence (Ross v. Dunstall; Alliance Assurance; etc.)
CaseB_TestB: Reasonable apprehension of bias in a criminal trial: where it is demonstrated, the trial judge has 'no further jurisdiction' and 'the only appropriate remedy is a new trial'; appellate finding of apprehension of bias retroactively renders trial orders 'void and without effect'
BaselineB: Common law procedural fairness / bias doctrine (as applied via Newfoundland Telephone Co. v. Newfoundland (Board of Commissioners of Public Utilities))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Bills of Exchange Act “sum certain” / negotiability requirement: a promissory note must be certain on its face as to principal and interest; interest must be ascertainable from the instrument without extrinsic evidence (except where the Act necessarily implies it).
BaselineA: Statute (Bills of Exchange Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. B-5, ss. 28, 176(1), 186; plus s. 10 incorporating common law/law merchant).
CaseB_TestB: Criminal Code s. 172(3) “disturbs” requirement: to convict, the conduct must be “disorderly in itself or productive of disorder”; mere “annoyance, anxiety or emotional upset” from brief, passive, peaceful conduct voluntarily desisted from is insufficient.
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 172(3) (and context of ss. 169–175 “Disorderly Conduct”)).
JudgeB: Dickson J. (for Dickson, Beetz, McIntyre, Chouinard and Lamer JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Bills of Exchange Act “sum certain”/negotiability requirement: principal and interest must be ascertainable on the face of the instrument (or by numerical calculation from materials in it); recourse to extrinsic evidence for an inherently uncertain interest-accrual date (e.g., “from the date of advance”) defeats promissory-note status
BaselineA: Statute: Bills of Exchange Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. B-5, ss. 28, 176(1), 186 (with s. 10 incorporating common law/law merchant where not inconsistent)
CaseB_TestB: Start of the Civil Code suicide-exclusion period (art. 2532 C.C.L.C.) in backdating/coverage-increase situations: determine the contract’s effective date under art. 2516 (concurrent conditions) while allowing retroactive effect to a policy date chosen by the parties if favourable and if no change in insurability; and decide whether later changes are a mere variation of the same contract or a new contract by assessing continuity in the particular circumstances
BaselineB: Statute (civil law): Civil Code of Lower Canada, arts. 2516, 2532 (and art. 2500(2) limiting derogations; interpretive support from art. 1018)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: When a statute creates a specific tribunal/procedure to decide an issue, the Superior Court should not intervene by declaratory judgment to decide that very issue (declaratory relief is discretionary and may be refused where another statutory mode of proceeding exists or the declaration would be of little use).
BaselineA: Combination: statute (Code of Civil Procedure, art. 453; Act respecting the Olympic Village, 1976 (Qué.), c. 43, esp. ss. 10, 27 and Division III arbitration scheme) plus common-law/discretionary principles on declaratory relief (e.g., Barraclough v. Brown; City of Lethbridge; Cassidy v. Stuart).
CaseB_TestB: Minister’s s. 7 Fisheries Act power to “authorize to be issued” licences is a continuing power: authorization may be revoked any time before the licence is actually issued, subject only to natural justice (relevant considerations, no arbitrariness, good faith).
BaselineB: Statute: Fisheries Act, R.S.C., 1985, c. F-14, s. 7 (and contrast with s. 9 for issued licences) interpreted with Interpretation Act, R.S.C., 1985, c. I-21, s. 31(3).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Excise Tax Act machinery exemption: taxpayer must be a “manufacturer or producer” and the machinery must be “used directly” in the manufacture/production of “goods”; “manufacture” not restrictively defined where the Act provides none (operating generators = manufacturing electricity).
BaselineA: Statute: Excise Tax Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-13, ss. 27(1), 29(1), and Schedule III, Part XIII, s. 1 (plus acceptance of prior case definition of “manufacture” from R. v. York Marble, Tile and Terrazzo Ltd.).
CaseB_TestB: Vesting of appeal-as-of-right: a right/privilege is only “acquired, accrued or accruing” when all conditions precedent are fulfilled; for former Criminal Code s. 691(2), the right arises only when the court of appeal reverses the acquittal and orders a new trial (so s. 44 Interpretation Act applies and the appeal is quashed).
BaselineB: Statute: Interpretation Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. I-21, ss. 43(c) and 44(c),(d), applied to Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 691(2) (as amended effective May 14, 1997).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Human rights code exclusivity / no parallel civil action: where a statute (Ontario Human Rights Code) provides a comprehensive administrative and adjudicative enforcement scheme, it forecloses (i) a civil action founded directly on breach of the statute and (ii) a common law tort action based on the statute’s public policy
BaselineA: Statute (The Ontario Human Rights Code, R.S.O. 1970, c. 318) plus common-law principles on when breach of statute can ground civil liability; SCC distinguishes statutory-duty tort cases (e.g., Halifax & South Western Railway v. Schwartz; Paskivski v. Canadian Pacific Ltd.) as inapplicable where there is “elaborate enforcement machinery”
CaseB_TestB: Undue obstacle / reasonable accommodation under CTA s. 172: the Agency must identify and remedy “undue obstacles” consistently with human rights reasonable-accommodation principles; the barrier must be removed unless the carrier proves accommodation would impose “undue hardship” (assessed contextually, including CTA s. 5 factors like cost, economic viability, safety, and quality of service)
BaselineB: Statute (Canada Transportation Act, S.C. 1996, c. 10, ss. 5, 172 (and Part V generally)) interpreted in light of human rights reasonable-accommodation jurisprudence (e.g., Meiorin/Grismer line) as incorporated into the CTA context
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Bill of Rights limit on reverse onus: a reverse-onus provision (balance of probabilities) is compatible with s. 2(f) only if the fact the accused must prove/disprove is "rationally open" to the accused; if the Crown’s proved facts lack a "rational or necessary connection" to the presumed conclusion, the Crown must first adduce at least some evidence of the accused’s "knowledge or means of knowledge" of the importation circumstances before the reverse onus can operate (otherwise it is an impossible burden/irrebuttable presumption).
BaselineA: Statute (Customs Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-40, ss. 205(1),(3), 248(1)) as constrained by statute (Canadian Bill of Rights, R.S.C. 1970, App. III, s. 2(f)); interpreted in light of R. v. Appleby, [1972] S.C.R. 303.
CaseB_TestB: Interested-party status/right to be heard in bargaining-unit definition: under Labour Code s. 32, employees are not "interested parties" for the bargaining-unit portion because the investigation is to be held only "in the presence of every association concerned and the employer"; on judicial review under a privative clause, the tribunal’s interpretation stands unless it is "patently unreasonable"/"manifestly unreasonable".
BaselineB: Statute (Quebec Labour Code, R.S.Q. 1977, c. C-27, s. 32 (and related scheme ss. 28, 39, 129)) plus common-law administrative law principles (audi alteram partem; privative-clause deference via CUPE v. N.B. Liquor, [1979] 2 S.C.R. 227).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Duty to leave defences to the jury: (1) ask whether a defence is revealed by the evidence or can reasonably be inferred; (2) if so, the trial judge must adequately put it to the jury (R. v. Squire).
BaselineA: Common law (as restated in R. v. Squire, citing Mancini v. DPP and other authorities)
CaseB_TestB: Interjurisdictional immunity (constitutional inapplicability): a valid provincial law of general application applies to federal works/undertakings/services unless it bears on what makes them specifically federal; for a federal service, inapplicability arises if the provincial law touches a 'vital or essential aspect' of its 'establishment, management or operation'.
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine (Construction Montcalm; Bell Canada v. Quebec (CSST); Clark v. CNR; Dick; Four B), applied to the provincial Transport Act permit scheme
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Availability of Criminal Code s. 116(1) charge for disobeying a court order: s. 116(1) applies unless statute law expressly provides a penalty/punishment or other mode of proceeding; inherent/common-law contempt powers are not an 'expressly provided' mode 'by law'.
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 116(1); also considers s. 8 and Manitoba Queen’s Bench Rules 483, 485, 492).
CaseB_TestB: Public law promissory estoppel in penal enforcement of zoning by-laws: requires a 'clear and unambiguous promise' intended to induce action plus reliance/change of conduct, but estoppel cannot be invoked to prevent application of a clear express legislative provision creating a strict-liability regulatory offence.
BaselineB: Common law (public law promissory estoppel as described in Mount Sinai, quoting Maracle) applied in light of express legislative/by-law provisions (Cities and Towns Act, s. 576; zoning by-law VQZ-3, art. 359; Act respecting land use planning and development, s. 227).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Insurance contract interpretation to fix a single “effective date”: read the policy and application “in entirety” (not “mechanical[ly]” or “isolated[ly]”) and, on the “true construction of the entire contract”, select the date the policy is “entirely structured around” for “calculating any of the time periods contemplated” (including the suicide clause).
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law contract interpretation: Insurance Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 224, s. 148(2) (application + policy form the contract) plus interpretation of the policy terms (including the self-destruction clause and the insured’s Declaration).
CaseB_TestB: Access alongside permanent guardianship: courts have jurisdiction to grant/deny access and the governing test is the child’s “best interests”; access is “the exception and not the rule” and “should not be granted if its exercise would have negative effects on the physical or psychological health of the child” or would jeopardize an adoption in the child’s best interests.
BaselineB: Statute: Family Services Act, S.N.B. 1980, c. F-2.2, especially s. 53(2) (court must “place above all other considerations the best interests of the child”), s. 1 (definition/factors for “best interests of the child”), and the variation/review/jurisdiction provisions (ss. 52(1), 59(4), 60(2), 60(6), 61(1), 85(2)).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 16(2) insanity: meaning of “incapable of appreciating the nature and quality of an act” — an accused “appreciates” if he “knows what he is doing” and “is aware of the physical consequences which will result from his acts” (not emotional/moral reactions).
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 16(2) (“incapable of appreciating the nature and quality of an act or omission”). Interpreted consistently with Cooper v. The Queen, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 1149 and R. v. Barnier, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 1124.
CaseB_TestB: Extradition Act committal/surrender framework: (1) Committal—under s. 29(1)(a), extradition judge applies preliminary-inquiry committal test and starts from a presumption that the certified ROC is reliable; refusal for unreliability only if evidence is “so defective or appears so unreliable that it would be dangerous or unsafe to act on it”. (2) Surrender—under s. 44(1)(a), unavailability of a Canadian defence in the requesting state triggers a 3-part threshold: (1) substantive difference (defence in Canada, no comparable defence abroad); (2) reasonable prospect of success in Canada; (3) significantly greater jeopardy abroad; if met, Minister must weigh this with all circumstances.
BaselineB: Statute: Extradition Act, S.C. 1999, c. 18, ss. 29(1)(a) (committal) and 44(1)(a) (surrender). Built on prior SCC guidance including United States of America v. Ferras, 2006 SCC 33 and Canada v. Schmidt, [1987] 1 S.C.R. 500.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Non-pecuniary damages in severe personal injury: apply the functional approach and a “rough upper limit” of $100,000, exceedable only rarely (e.g., on proof/agreement of inflation’s effect), not merely because injuries seem worse than the trilogy plaintiffs
BaselineA: Common law (damages assessment principles from the “trilogy”: Andrews v. Grand & Toy Alberta Ltd.; Arnold v. Teno; Thornton v. Board of School Trustees; and refined in Lewis v. Todd)
CaseB_TestB: OPCF 44R / Insurance Act s. 239(1)(a) “use or operation” for indemnity coverage: claimant must show an unbroken chain of causation linking the tortfeasor’s conduct as a motorist to the injury; coverage fails where the tort is an intervening, severable act (not satisfied by mere “but for” vehicle involvement)
BaselineB: Statute/contract interpretation: Insurance Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. I.8, s. 239(1)(a) (tracked by OPCF 44R s. 3); distinguished from Amos v. ICBC (no-fault “relaxed causation” test)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Effect of workers’ compensation election/subrogation on (i) who may sue the tortfeasor, and (ii) whether the Commission has an interest to intervene / can benefit from interruption of prescription: once the worker elects compensation, “only the Commission can claim the amounts which it has paid or will have to pay” and the worker “can claim ... only the additional sum provided for in s. 8”; a worker’s improper claim for the whole loss “does not have the effect of validly introducing ... the object of the Commission’s claim” for intervention or interruption purposes.
BaselineA: Statute and civil law: Workmen’s Compensation Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 159, ss. 7(1)-(3) (subrogation “by the mere making of the election”), 8 (worker may claim only the “additional sum”); Civil Code art. 1056a (recourse only to extent permitted by the Act); Code of Civil Procedure art. 208 (intervention by a person “interested in an action”).
CaseB_TestB: Collins s. 24(2) Charter exclusion framework (as applied/emphasized in Greffe): balance three categories—(1) fairness of the trial, (2) seriousness of the Charter violation, and (3) effect of exclusion on the repute of the justice system—asking whether, “having regard to all the circumstances, the admission ... would bring the administration of justice into disrepute.”
BaselineB: Constitution and common law framework: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 24(2) (exclusion if admission would bring administration of justice into disrepute), as structured by prior SCC jurisprudence (notably R. v. Collins; also discussed via Simmons/Jacoy).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Public access to executed search warrants/informations: presumption of openness after execution (and items brought before a justice), with curtailment only where needed to protect “social values of superordinate importance” (notably protecting the innocent where nothing is found); issuance may be in camera to protect the administration of justice
BaselineA: Combination: Criminal Code (R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 443, 446) plus common law/open court principle and courts’ supervisory power over records
CaseB_TestB: Bona fide occupational qualification (BFOQ) test (Etobicoke) as applied to denominational-school teachers: two branches—(1) subjective good faith (honestly imposed, not for ulterior/extraneous reasons) and (2) objective necessity (requirement “reasonably necessary” to accomplish the employer’s legitimate objectives)
BaselineB: Combination: statute (B.C. Human Rights Code, R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 186, s. 8) interpreted through SCC common-law/precedential BFOQ framework from Ontario Human Rights Commission v. Etobicoke (Borough of), [1982] 1 S.C.R. 202
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Validity of a Quebec deed of donation and trust benefiting unborn (non-existent) primary beneficiaries: interpret Civil Code art. 981a “subject to the special characteristics of the trust” and uphold validity where trustee acceptance makes the trust irrevocable and trustee ownership means beneficiaries need not exist at creation; plus related rule that a trust gift is not mortis causa unless the donor’s death is the essential condition (here the condition is absence of issue at trust termination). Key quotes: “acceptance by the trustee suffices to make the creation of the trust irrevocable”; “it is the trustee… who becomes owner of the property for the duration of the trust… it is not necessary that there be beneficiaries in whom ownership… is vested”; “arts. 981a et seq. must be given a wide and liberal interpretation… When article 981a refers to the provisions relating to gifts and legacies, it does so subject to the special characteristics of the trust”.
BaselineA: Statute (Civil Code of Quebec provisions on trusts and gifts): arts. 981a, 981b, 981l (trusts) and related gifts provisions including arts. 754, 755, 758, 760, 782, 608, 771, 772, 929; with prior SCC trust jurisprudence referenced (notably Curran v. Davis) as interpretive baseline.
CaseB_TestB: When a civil-court injunction in private litigation can effectively bind non-parties (members of the public) on pain of contempt: courts have jurisdiction to make such orders; enforceability rests on contempt for interfering with justice; fairness constraints require notice and opportunity to comply and careful, constrained wording. Key quotes: “Courts have jurisdiction to make orders binding on persons who are not parties to the action”; “enforceable on the long-standing principle that persons who are not parties… but who violate an order… may be found guilty of contempt”; “they must first be apprised of the existence and terms of the order and be given an opportunity to comply… [and] orders [must] be carefully worded and constrained to ensure that they are fair and not unduly broad.”
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law/equity: Law and Equity Act, R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 224, s. 36 (interlocutory injunctions) and Criminal Code, s. 11 (civil remedies not suspended by criminality), plus common law contempt/injunction principles (e.g., International Longshoremen’s Association; Bartle & Gibson; English contempt authorities).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory-displacement test for the Kienapple rule (multiple convictions): Kienapple applies unless Parliament gives a clear indication of intended multiple convictions; here, s. 83(2) is clear enough to permit a second conviction for using a firearm arising from the same event (and s. 21 party liability applies to s. 83 unless expressly/necessarily excluded). Key quotes: Kienapple principle applies 'unless there is a clear indication that multiple prosecutions and, indeed, multiple convictions are envisaged' (quoting Kienapple at p. 753); and s. 83(2) 'contemplates that the sentence imposed ... shall be served consecutively to any other punishment imposed on him for an offence arising out of the same event' such that 'I do not know what clearer language could be used to negate the so-called Kienapple principle.'
BaselineA: Combination of common law and statute: common law rule against multiple convictions from Kienapple v. The Queen (and Cox and Paton v. The Queen; R. v. Quon distinguished) plus Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 83(1)-(2) (use of a firearm; consecutive sentence) and s. 21 (parties).
JudgeA: Dickson J. (for Martland, Dickson, Estey, McIntyre and Chouinard JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Pith-and-substance characterization test (division of powers) for a municipal measure: determine the measure’s 'pith and substance' by considering both 'its purpose and its effects' (including 'legal ramifications' and 'practical consequences'); if its dominant purpose/effects fall within an exclusive federal head (here, siting radiocommunication infrastructure), it is ultra vires. Key quotes: 'In analyzing the pith and substance ... the Court must consider both its purpose and its effects' and effects include 'both the legal ramifications of the words used and the practical consequences of the application of the measure.'
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine (division of powers) applying the pith and substance framework from prior SCC cases cited in the reasons (e.g., Goodwin; Marine Services; COPA; Canadian Western Bank; Lacombe; Morgentaler) to a municipal notice issued under provincial statutes.
JudgeB: Wagner and Côté JJ. (joint reasons; McLachlin C.J. and Abella, Cromwell, Moldaver, Karakatsanis and Brown JJ. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: When s. 25(3) of Saskatchewan’s Trade Union Act applies in discharge grievances: if dismissal is not mandatory under a specified-penalty clause and the board cannot sustain dismissal, it may substitute a lesser penalty (including reinstatement without back pay) that “seems just and reasonable in the circumstances”.
BaselineA: Statute (The Trade Union Act, R.S.S. 1978, c. T-17, s. 25(3)) interpreted alongside the collective agreement’s dismissal/remedy clauses (arts. 6(4) and 12(12)(a)).
CaseB_TestB: Ezokola contribution-based complicity test under Refugee Convention art. 1F(a): exclusion requires “serious reasons for considering” the claimant “has voluntarily made a significant and knowing contribution to the organization’s crime or criminal purpose”, assessed contextually using non-exhaustive factors (size/nature of organization; part involved; duties; rank; time in organization after knowledge; recruitment/opportunity to leave).
BaselineB: Statute incorporating treaty (Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, s. 98 incorporating Refugee Convention art. 1F(a)); informed by international criminal law sources referenced in the reasons (e.g., Rome Statute arts. 25, 30, 31(1)(d)).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 43 Canada Evidence Act letters rogatory: (i) s. 43 permits an order for production of documents alone (not only documents ancillary to viva voce testimony) and (ii) comity-based guidelines for granting judicial assistance (trial not discovery; relevance for commissioner/foreign court; scope permitted domestically; documents adequately defined)
BaselineA: Statute — Canada Evidence Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-10, s. 43 (letters rogatory/judicial assistance), with related consideration of Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 178.2 and 178.16 (intercepted communications) and s. 446 (seized items)
JudgeA: The Chief Justice (Laskin C.J.), for the Court
CaseB_TestB: Admissibility of defence-led unknown third party suspect evidence: (1) relevance to a fact in issue/available defence, established by a “sufficient connection” (similarity) between the charged crime and another incident plus evidence the accused could not have committed the other offence; and (2) admissible unless prejudicial effects “substantially outweigh” probative value (Seaboyer balancing), without the judge weighing credibility or requiring proof on a balance of probabilities
BaselineB: Common law — general admissibility principles and Seaboyer balancing (R. v. Seaboyer) plus air of reality threshold (R. v. Cinous); discussion of (but rejection of importing) known third party suspect framework (R. v. Grandinetti) and Crown-led similar fact framework (R. v. Handy)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Civil Code art. 1055 C.C. “purpose of the building/part” limitation: owner liable for ruin from want of repairs/original defect only if the part was used for its intended purpose; if the victim uses it for a contrary purpose, art. 1055 does not apply
BaselineA: Statute (Civil Code of Quebec (as then in force), art. 1055 C.C.; interpreted through SCC precedent Leznek v. City of Verdun, [1940] S.C.R. 313)
CaseB_TestB: Mental capacity standard for confessions/right to silence/s. 10(b) waiver: the accused must have an “operating mind” (limited cognitive capacity) — understand what is said/said to him and that it can be used against him; no separate “awareness of consequences” test
BaselineB: Combination (common law confession voluntariness/“operating mind” line of cases: Ward, Horvath, Nagotcha, Hebert; plus statute/constitutional text: Charter ss. 7 and 10(b); Criminal Code s. 2 definition of “unfit to stand trial” used as benchmark for s. 10(b) capacity)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Judicial review of a labour board’s interpretation under a privative clause: intervene only if the interpretation is “patently unreasonable” (i.e., “so patently unreasonable that its construction cannot be rationally supported by the relevant legislation”).
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law (statutory privative/review provisions interpreted through the CUPE patently-unreasonable deference framework). Statute: The Public Service Employee Relations Act, 1977 (Alta.), c. 40, ss. 9, 11, 89 (reviewability) and s. 48 (arbitrable/non-arbitrable items). Common law baseline cited: Canadian Union of Public Employees Local 963 v. New Brunswick Liquor Corporation, [1979] 2 S.C.R. 227 (patently unreasonable standard), adopted in Volvo Canada Ltd. v. U.A.W., Local 720, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 178 and Douglas Aircraft Co. of Canada v. McConnell, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 245.
CaseB_TestB: Adverse-effect religious discrimination and duty to accommodate: discrimination is shown by the three s. 10 Quebec Charter elements (“distinction, exclusion or preference”; based on a listed ground; and having the effect of “nullifying or impairing” the right), triggering a duty to take “reasonable steps to accommodate … short of undue hardship”; no “de minimis” threshold applies.
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law. Statute: Quebec Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms, R.S.Q., c. C-12, ss. 10 and 16 (and related freedom provisions), plus Labour Code, R.S.Q., c. C-27, ss. 139 and 139.1 (privative clause) for the judicial review posture. Common law baseline cited: Ontario Human Rights Commission and O’Malley v. Simpsons-Sears Ltd., [1985] 2 S.C.R. 536 (adverse-effect discrimination and accommodation “short of undue hardship”); Central Okanagan School District No. 23 v. Renaud, [1992] 2 S.C.R. 970; Central Alberta Dairy Pool v. Alberta (Human Rights Commission), [1990] 2 S.C.R. 489 (undue hardship factors).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Similar fact evidence admissibility requires (1) relevance to an issue beyond propensity with probative value outweighing prejudice, and (2) a threshold evidentiary link connecting the alleged similar acts to the accused (not mere similarity).
BaselineA: Common law (similar fact evidence doctrine from Makin v. The Attorney-General for New South Wales; applied/endorsed with Boardman v. DPP and Harris v. DPP).
CaseB_TestB: Charter vagueness test: a law is unconstitutionally vague if it "so lacks in precision as not to give sufficient guidance for legal debate"; applied to uphold "unduly" in s. 32(1)(c) (with market-structure/behaviour inquiry) and to define mens rea as subjective entry/knowledge plus objective awareness/ought-to-have-known of undue lessening.
BaselineB: Statute + constitutional standard: Combines Investigation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-23, ss. 32(1)(c) and 32(1.1), interpreted under Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7 (vagueness and mens rea).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 16(2) insanity (first arm): “incapable of appreciating the nature and quality of an act” is limited to appreciating the physical character/consequences of the act (mens rea/actus reus consequences), not the accused’s appreciation of penal consequences (punishment).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 16(2)); interpreted in light of SCC cases including Cooper v. The Queen, Schwartz v. The Queen, R. v. Barnier, and Kjeldsen v. The Queen.
CaseB_TestB: Administrative tribunal constitutional jurisdiction test: the “essential question is whether the empowering legislation implicitly or explicitly grants to the tribunal the jurisdiction to interpret or decide any question of law”; if yes, the tribunal is presumed to have jurisdiction to decide the issue “in light of s. 35 or any other relevant constitutional provision”, unless a “clear implication” rebuts it.
BaselineB: Common law / constitutional doctrine on tribunal jurisdiction to decide constitutional questions, as reframed by Nova Scotia (Workers’ Compensation Board) v. Martin and discussed with Cooper v. Canada (Human Rights Commission); applied to Forest Practices Code of British Columbia Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 159, especially s. 131(8).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Patentability of a new use for an old compound as a “new and useful art”: the “invention” is “the application of this new knowledge to effect a desired result which has an undisputed commercial value” and the claimed compositions may be the “practical embodiment of the new knowledge” (Patent Act, s. 2; s. 36 not a bar where the combination is required to give effect to the new use).
BaselineA: Statute (Patent Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. P-4, ss. 2 and 36; with discussion of s. 41 and prior case law including Farbwerke Hoechst and Hickton’s Patent Syndicate).
CaseB_TestB: Party liability for trafficking by aiding/abetting: under Criminal Code s. 21(1)(b) “to aid ... means to assist or help the actor” and requires proof the accused acted “for the purpose of” aiding, i.e., “purpose” equated with “intention” (not “desire”); under s. 21(1)(c) abetting includes “encouraging, instigating, promoting or procuring” and requires intent to encourage; applied to determine when assisting a purchaser can amount to aiding/abetting trafficking.
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, s. 21(1)(b),(c); Narcotic Control Act, ss. 2 “traffic”, 3(1), 4(1),(2); interpretation informed by Hibbert and Poitras).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory-interpretation test for whether a permissive municipal discretion (Police Act, s. 24(6)) excludes/fetters a collectively bargained “working condition” under s. 29(2): ask whether the provisions are “incompatible or inconsistent”; if not, “each has its own area of operation” and the collective agreement clause stands.
BaselineA: Statute: The Police Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 351, ss. 24(6) and 29(2) (plus the arbitrated collective agreement clause).
CaseB_TestB: State Immunity Act framework (SIA) for barring civil claims: (1) s. 3(1) is exhaustive (“[e]xcept as provided by this Act”); (2) s. 6(a) territorial-tort/physical-integrity limits—exception applies only where the tort causing injury/death “occur[red] in Canada” and only where psychological harm is “linked to a physical injury” (“some form of a breach of physical integrity must be made out”); (3) “government” in s. 2 includes public officials acting in an official capacity, and torture can be an “official act”.
BaselineB: Statute: State Immunity Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. S-18, ss. 2, 3(1), 6(a) (interpreted with reference to Schreiber v. Canada (Attorney General), 2002 SCC 62, on s. 6(a)’s physical-injury requirement).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory incompatibility/inconsistency test for whether a permissive municipal discretion (Police Act, s. 24(6)) excludes a collectively bargained/arbitrated clause under s. 29(2): s. 24(6) is merely empowering and does not preclude bargaining unless the provisions are "incompatible or inconsistent"; here "there is no incompatibility or inconsistency" and "each has its own area of operation".
BaselineA: Statute: The Police Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 351, ss. 24(6) and 29(2) (plus the general statutory interpretation idea of repugnancy/inconsistency between provisions, discussed by analogy to IBEW v. Town of Summerside).
CaseB_TestB: Corporate attribution test under BIA s. 96 transfer-at-undervalue claims: for attribution of a directing mind’s intent to the corporate debtor, "the test for corporate attribution under s. 96 is simply whether the person was the directing mind and whether their actions were performed within the sector of corporate responsibility assigned to them"; the common-law "fraud" and "no benefit" exceptions "do not apply" in this context.
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act, s. 96(1)(b)(ii)(B) (and related s. 2 definition; CCAA s. 36.1 incorporation) plus the common law corporate attribution doctrine from Canadian Dredge & Dock Co. v. The Queen, Deloitte & Touche v. Livent, and DeJong (as discussed in the reasons).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Jennings test for establishing a constitutional convention (precedents; actors’ belief they were bound/recognition; reason for the rule), emphasizing recognition/acceptance as the key requirement
BaselineA: Common law (constitutional conventions doctrine) as articulated in Re: Resolution to amend the Constitution, [1981] 1 S.C.R. 753, adopting Sir W. Ivor Jennings’ three questions
CaseB_TestB: Reasonable suspicion standard authorizing sniffer-dog (sniff) searches: objective, ascertainable facts assessed on the totality of the circumstances (a sufficiently particularized ‘constellation’), plus dog reliability for reasonableness of the search
BaselineB: Common law Charter s. 8 search framework (R. v. Collins) and prior sniffer-dog cases (R. v. Kang-Brown; R. v. A.M.) defining reasonable suspicion for dog deployment
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criteria for when a labour arbitrator under the Canada Labour Code is a “statutory tribunal” subject to evocation/certiorari: not only whether “by statute the parties are bound to resort to it”, but also whether the tribunal is “invested with wide powers by statute” (i.e., has “duties and powers conferred by statute”).
BaselineA: Common law test for statutory tribunal (certiorari/evocation) from Howe Sound (adopting R. v. National Joint Council for the Craft of Dental Technicians) plus statutory context of Code of Civil Procedure, art. 846 and Canada Labour Code ss. 156(2), 157, 159, 160(5).
CaseB_TestB: Test for whether an agreement creates a patent sublicence: a sublicence exists only if the licensee “granted, either expressly or impliedly, the right to do something which [the third party] would otherwise be prohibited from doing, and which [the licensee] was permitted to do only by virtue of its [licence]”; interpret the contract from its text (no subjective-intent evidence if unambiguous) and ask whether licensed rights were actually transferred (as opposed to a purchase/sale supply arrangement).
BaselineB: Common law principles of patent licensing/sublicensing and contractual interpretation (including the parol evidence rule), as articulated in the reasons (e.g., Consolidated-Bathurst; Lampson; Indian Molybdenum; Joy Oil) and applied to the Patent Act compulsory-licence context.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Kienapple remedy modification: when Kienapple applies, enter a stay of proceedings rather than an acquittal
BaselineA: Common law (Kienapple v. The Queen, [1975] 1 S.C.R. 729)
CaseB_TestB: Criteria for appointing/removing a litigation guardian: best interests test informed by the Szwydky criteria, including the requirement that the guardian be 'indifferent' (no conflict of interest)
BaselineB: Combination of statute/rules and common law guidance: Queen’s Bench Rules (Saskatchewan) r. 49(1) ('best interests'); Szwydky v. Magiera (1988) (six criteria, including 'indifferent as to the outcome')
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Contract-interpretation test for the extent of a power-supply obligation: reconcile general language (“to such an extent as the said Town… may require”) with specific allocation clauses (paras. 6 and 8), yielding a fixed entitlement of 4,000 horsepower at $14 per horsepower per annum, with any further supply only if “unleased or not in permanent use”.
BaselineA: Contract (1905 agreement) — interpretation of key clauses, especially para. 1 (“to such an extent as the said Town… may require”), para. 5 (price ceiling “shall not in any event exceed… Fourteen Dollars ($14.00)”), para. 6 (“any power or energy reserved for use on the Canadian side… and not already in use”), and para. 8 (reserve of “Four Thousand Horse Power… permanently available…; PROVIDED FURTHER… any further power… which may be unleased or not in permanent use”).
CaseB_TestB: General Motors indicia for validity under the general trade and commerce power (Constitution Act, 1867, s. 91(2)): ask (1) general regulatory scheme; (2) oversight by regulatory agency; (3) trade as a whole vs particular industry; (4) provinces constitutionally incapable acting alone or in concert; (5) failure to include a province would jeopardize successful operation (not exhaustive; not all required).
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine applying Constitution Act, 1867, s. 91(2) (general trade and commerce power), using the test from General Motors of Canada Ltd. v. City National Leasing, [1989] 1 S.C.R. 641 (five indicia).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Contract-interpretation rule for the 1905 power agreement: reconcile general 'to such an extent as the said Town… may require' language with specific allocation clauses (paras. 6 & 8), yielding a fixed entitlement of 4,000 horsepower/year at $14 per horsepower/year (and no broader right to all output at that price)
BaselineA: Common law (contract interpretation principles) applied to the January 9, 1905 agreement (esp. paras. 1, 5, 6, 8, 13); related statutes found not to govern the issue
CaseB_TestB: Continuing-offence/party-liability framework for kidnapping: kidnapping under s. 279(1) continues while the victim remains unlawfully confined, and a latecomer is a party under s. 21(1) if, with knowledge (or wilful blindness) of the kidnapping and intent to assist its completion, they aid/abet the ongoing confinement
BaselineB: Statute interpreted in light of common law: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, ss. 279(1), 279(2), 21(1) (with common law understanding of kidnapping as aggravated false imprisonment)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Interpretation of Planning Act s. 70(1): land is “designated under a land use by-law” only when the designation is made in the land use by-law itself (not merely in statutory plans), triggering the mandatory acquire-or-amend duty within six months
BaselineA: Statute: The Planning Act, 1977 (Alta.), s. 70(1) (and definition of “land use by-law” in s. 1(14))
CaseB_TestB: O’Connor third-party records production framework: (1) accused must show records are “likely to be relevant” to an issue at trial or witness competence; (2) if so, judge balances salutary vs deleterious effects (privacy/equality vs full answer and defence) and, after in camera review, orders only what should be produced
BaselineB: Common law/Charter-based framework: Charter ss. 7 and 24(1) (and related abuse-of-process jurisprudence, e.g., R. v. Jewitt) plus the Court’s development of production procedure for third-party private records
JudgeB: L'Heureux-Dubé J. (reasons concurred in by La Forest and Gonthier JJ.; McLachlin J. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “has become regularly engaged in some other occupation” under Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, s. 44(1)(c): focuses on regularity of work schedule (a “fixed pattern”) rather than duration/permanence or intent to abandon former job
BaselineA: Statute (Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, s. 44(1)(c)) interpreted in light of related statutory context (including Regulations s. 49 defining “bona fide employed” for s. 44(1)(b))
CaseB_TestB: Whether an ISP “carr[ies] on ... ‘broadcasting undertakings’” under the Broadcasting Act when providing Internet access: entities that merely provide the mode of transmission (with no control over programming—no selection, origination, or packaging) are not “broadcasting undertakings”
BaselineB: Statute (Broadcasting Act, ss. 2(1) “broadcasting”, 2(3), 3(1)) interpreted purposively and contextually, with support from prior SCC interpretation of “transmit/communicate” (Electric Despatch; SOCAN v. CAIP)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Cross-border fresh pursuit: a peace officer who lawfully begins a warrantless-arrest pursuit in one province retains (for s. 25(4)) peace-officer status in another province so long as the pursuit is fresh; and the underlying arrest authority depends on whether, on the circumstances apparent at the time, the suspect would have appeared to a reasonable person in the officer’s position to be committing an offence (i.e., on 'reasonable and probable grounds').
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 25(4), 449(1)(b), 450(1)(b); with the 'reasonable and probable grounds/apparently committing' approach drawn from R. v. Biron, [1976] 2 S.C.R. 56 and Attorney General for Saskatchewan v. Pritchard (1961)).
CaseB_TestB: Arbitrator jurisdiction under Canada Labour Code s. 157(d)(ii): a 'specific penalty' that removes substitution power exists only if the collective agreement assigns a specific penalty to the particular infraction; a penalty is not 'specific' if it is discretionary/indiscriminately chosen by the employer or located only in an employer rule book rather than the collective agreement.
BaselineB: Statute (Canada Labour Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. L-1, s. 157(d)(i)-(ii)) interpreted alongside the collective agreement (Article XI(b)).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Availability of the Crown’s per quod servitium amisit action for injuries to Canadian Forces members deemed servants of the Crown: the action lies where (1) a master–servant relationship exists (here, by statute) and (2) the servant has a valid cause of action against the wrongdoer; damages are the master’s necessary costs from the loss of services (including wages/allowances and medical/hospital expenses).
BaselineA: Combination: statute (Federal Court Act, R.S.C. 1970 (2nd Supp.), c. 10, s. 37 deeming Forces/RCMP members servants of the Crown) plus common law per quod servitium amisit as recognized in SCC cases (The King v. Richardson; Nykorak v. Attorney General of Canada; Attorney-General of Canada v. Jackson; The Queen v. Murray).
JudgeA: Ritchie J. (for Ritchie, Estey, Lamer and Wilson JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: Mens rea for Criminal Code s. 121(1)(a): no “corrupt” purpose required; guilt requires (1) the accused knows he/she is an official, (2) intentionally demands/accepts a loan, reward, advantage or benefit, and (3) knows the benefit is “as consideration for cooperation, assistance or exercise of influence” in connection with “the transaction of business with or relating to the government”.
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 121(1)(a) (interpreted in light of SCC authority including Martineau v. La Reine; and distinguished from Hinchey).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Timing/trigger for Attorney General stay under Criminal Code s. 508(1): the stay power begins only once an information is "found"—i.e., after the justice has decided to issue process (summons or warrant), not merely when the information is laid/received.
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34 as amended), especially ss. 455, 455.3, 508 (and interpretive context from ss. 2 and 503).
CaseB_TestB: Statutory eligibility for absolute/conditional discharge under Criminal Code s. 662.1(1): discharge is unavailable if the offence is one "for which a minimum punishment is prescribed by law"; an offence has a minimum punishment if any minimum penalty is prescribed (e.g., s. 234(a) minimum $50 fine), even if an alternative punishment option has no minimum.
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code), primarily ss. 662.1(1) and 234(a) (with reference to s. 645 and s. 592 for context).
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Timing rule for Attorney General stay under Criminal Code s. 508(1): an information is “found” only after the justice decides to issue process; the stay power “starts as of the moment a summons or warrant is issued.”
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 2 (definition of “indictment”), 503 (“finding an indictment”), 508(1) (stay power), in relation to ss. 455 and 455.3 (private information and justice’s hearing/issuance of process)).
CaseB_TestB: Baker procedural fairness framework (five factors) applied to whether a municipality must give reasons: the duty’s content varies with (1) nature of decision/process, (2) statutory scheme, (3) importance to affected person, (4) legitimate expectations, and (5) deference; here these factors required reasons for refusing the 2nd and 3rd rezoning applications.
BaselineB: Common law administrative law duty of procedural fairness, structured by Baker v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), [1999] 2 S.C.R. 817 (five-factor framework), applied in the municipal rezoning context.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Jurisdictional rule against joint trials on separate informations/indictments: a trial judge is without jurisdiction to try together separate informations or indictments, even with consent, unless an applicable statute expressly provides otherwise
BaselineA: Common law (Crane v. Public Prosecutor, [1921] 2 A.C. 299; applied and confirmed as Canadian law; also treated as incorporated by implication into Criminal Code procedure)
CaseB_TestB: Credibility-assessment guidance on (i) absence of evidence of motive to lie and (ii) lack of embellishment: motive-to-lie absence may be considered but must not reverse burden; lack of embellishment cannot bolster credibility (only not weigh against it) though it may relate to motive-to-lie analysis
BaselineB: Common law (credibility/W.(D.) framework from R. v. W.(D.); appellate review/credibility principles from R. v. Vuradin and R. v. G.F.; motive-to-lie relevance from R. v. Stirling)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Marine insurance “perils of the seas” causation test for negligent acts: an act is negligent only relative to a foreseeable risk of harm; if that foreseeable risk is a “peculiarly marine risk”, then the act plus its foreseeable consequence is a “fortuitous accident of the seas” (a “peril of the seas”) and the proximate cause of the loss
BaselineA: Statute (Insurance (Marine) Act, R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 203, Schedule “Rules for Construction of Policy”: “The term ‘perils of the seas’ refers only to fortuitous accidents or casualties of the seas”; plus Marine Insurance Act, R.S.B.C. 1960, c. 231, s. 57(2)(a) (now s. 56(2)(a)): insurer liable for loss proximately caused by a peril insured against “even though the loss would not have happened but for the misconduct or negligence of the master or crew”); interpreted with common-law authorities Canada Rice Mills, Ld. v. Union Marine & General Insurance Co. and Cohen, Sons & Co. v. National Benefit Assurance Co.
CaseB_TestB: Section 35(1) threshold test for who qualifies as an “aboriginal peopl[e] of Canada”: “the modern-day successors of Aboriginal societies that occupied Canadian territory at the time of European contact” (which “may include Aboriginal groups that are now outside Canada”); if met, proceed to Van der Peet
BaselineB: Constitution Act, 1982, s. 35(1) (“The existing aboriginal and treaty rights of the aboriginal peoples of Canada are hereby recognized and affirmed.”) interpreted purposively; built on existing s. 35 jurisprudence (e.g., Sparrow; Van der Peet) but addressing a previously undecided threshold question
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory “bridging” of an expired collective agreement: s. 70(1) preserves the parties’ right to invoke interest arbitration if notice to arbitrate is given within the s. 70 status-quo period; the right need only exist at the time of the notice (not when the award issues).
BaselineA: Statute (Ontario Labour Relations Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 232, s. 70(1) (now R.S.O. 1980, c. 228, s. 79)) plus interpretation of the collective agreement’s interest-arbitration clauses (Haldimand art. 16; Perth art. 15).
CaseB_TestB: Criminal Code severance/division discretion: a court may divide or sever counts only where it is satisfied “that the ends of justice require it” (s. 590(3)) / “that the interests of justice so require” (s. 591(3)); appellate interference only if the judge acted unjudicially or the ruling resulted in an injustice.
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, ss. 590(3), 591(3)(a), 591(4)) with common-law appellate deference framing (unjudicial exercise / injustice).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: McKibbon (Lamer J.) conditions for when a non-AG actor (including an AG’s agent) may prefer an indictment with additional counts under Criminal Code s. 507(2) after the 1969 addition of s. 507(3): (1) a preliminary inquiry has been held; (2) the accused has been committed for trial on at least one charge inquired into; and (3) each count must be either (a) an offence for which the accused was committed, or (b) an offence disclosed by the evidence at the preliminary inquiry and not an offence for which the accused was discharged.
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 507(1)-(3); interpreted in light of related Code provisions ss. 504-505 and the Court’s approach in R. v. Chabot, [1980] 2 S.C.R. 985).
CaseB_TestB: Mitchell (McLachlin C.J.) Van der Peet test for establishing an Aboriginal right under Constitution Act, 1982, s. 35(1): claimant must prove (1) an ancestral practice/custom/tradition; (2) that it was “integral to the distinctive culture” (a “defining feature” such that the culture would be “fundamentally altered” without it); and (3) “reasonable continuity” between the pre-contact practice and the modern claim; plus the preliminary characterization step using three factors from Van der Peet (nature of the impugned action, nature of the alleged infringement, and ancestral practices relied on).
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine under s. 35(1) (test drawn from R. v. Van der Peet, [1996] 2 S.C.R. 507 and Delgamuukw v. British Columbia, [1997] 3 S.C.R. 1010; applied to Constitution Act, 1982, s. 35(1)).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: First degree murder classification under Criminal Code ss. 212(b) and 214(2): once murder is established under s. 212(b) (intent to kill A + by accident/mistake causes death of B), it is first degree under s. 214(2) if the planning and deliberation relates to the s. 212(b) mens rea (the intent to kill A); the identity of the actual victim is irrelevant.
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 212(b) and 214(2), within the homicide scheme including s. 205; applied with reference to R. v. Farrant).
CaseB_TestB: Interpretation/application of Alberta Limitations Act s. 12 in conflicts cases: s. 12 applies Alberta limitations law only to "live" causes of action; it "does not purport to revive an action time-barred by the substantive law of the place where the accident occurred" (so if the lex loci delicti limitation has expired, there is no right of action to pursue in Alberta).
BaselineB: Statute (Limitations Act, R.S.A. 2000, c. L-12, s. 12) interpreted against the conflicts baseline in Tolofson v. Jensen (lex loci delicti includes foreign limitation as substantive).
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Mens rea for attempted murder: the Crown must prove a specific intent to kill (no lesser/constructive murder intent suffices)
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code) interpreted against prior SCC authority (Lajoie v. The Queen, [1974] S.C.R. 399, overruled)
JudgeA: McIntyre J. (for Dickson, Beetz, Estey, McIntyre, Chouinard, Lamer and Wilson JJ.)
CaseB_TestB: “Establishment” for CHRA s. 11 pay equity: employees are in the same establishment if they are subject to a “common personnel and wage policy” (a factual inquiry into the employer’s common principles/approach, not a term-by-term collective agreement comparison)
BaselineB: Statute + regulation/guideline (Canadian Human Rights Act, s. 11 read with Equal Wages Guidelines, 1986, SOR/86-1082, s. 10)
JudgeB: LeBel and Abella JJ. (for the Court)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Saskatchewan Matrimonial Property Act pre-marital exemption: s. 23 limits exemption to the asset’s “fair market value ... at the time of the marriage”; s. 23(4)-(5) discretion only to decide whether it is “unfair and inequitable to exempt” (and thus reduce the exemption), and s. 21(2)(q) cannot be used to enlarge the exemption (rejecting the “Capital Base Theory”).
BaselineA: Statute — The Matrimonial Property Act, 1979 (Sask.), c. M-6.1, ss. 20-23 (especially s. 21(1)-(2) and s. 23(1), (4), (5)); interpretation rejecting use of s. 21(2)(q) to override s. 23.
CaseB_TestB: Aggravated assault (s. 268(1) “endangers the life”) in HIV non-disclosure: where the Crown alleges an offence “predicated on an aggravating consequence, it must prove the consequence beyond a reasonable doubt”; no aggravated assault if there is a reasonable doubt the complainant’s life was capable of being endangered (e.g., complainant could already have been HIV-positive), though attempt may be made out if intent plus more-than-preparatory steps are proven.
BaselineB: Statute — Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, ss. 268(1) (aggravated assault consequences), with related application of ss. 24(1) and 660 (attempt).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.
