CaseA_TestA: Mechanics’ lien Act “owner” test: a person is an “owner” if they (a) have an estate or interest in the land, (b) requested the work, and (c) the work was done “upon whose credit, or on whose behalf, or with whose privity or consent, or for whose direct benefit” (Mechanics’ Lien Act, s. 1(1)(d)); applied with an “overall view” of the transaction (not “dissected into [its] minute parts”).
BaselineA: Statute: The Mechanics’ Lien Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 267, s. 1(1)(d) (definition of “owner”) and s. 5(1) (lien attaches to the owner’s estate/interest, limited to sums “justly due” and “justly owing”).
CaseB_TestB: Challenge for cause (juror partiality) test under Criminal Code, s. 638(1)(b): to show a “realistic potential for juror partiality” generally requires (1) “that a widespread bias exists in the community”; and (2) “that some jurors may be incapable of setting aside this bias, despite trial safeguards, to render an impartial decision” (overarching question: “whether there exists a realistic potential for partial juror behaviour”).
BaselineB: Statute interpreted through common-law/Charter-informed jurisprudence: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 638(1)(b) (and related jury provisions), applying/clarifying R. v. Sherratt and R. v. Williams.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Anns-based duty of care for municipal building inspection/enforcement: (1) proximity — “a sufficiently close relationship between the parties ... so that, in the reasonable contemplation of the authority, carelessness on its part might cause damage”; and (2) residual policy considerations — “any considerations which ought to negative or limit (a) the scope of the duty (b) the class of persons ... (c) the damages”. Applied through the policy/operational distinction: “the more ‘operational’ a power or duty may be, the easier it is to superimpose upon it a common law duty of care”; no immunity for inaction where there is a duty to act or at least to make a bona fide policy decision not to act (“inaction for no reason or inaction for an improper reason cannot be a policy decision taken in the bona fide exercise of discretion”).
BaselineA: Common law (adopting/applying Anns v. Merton London Borough Council, [1978] A.C. 728, including proximity + residual policy stage and the policy/operational distinction), applied in light of Municipal Act, R.S.B.C. 1960, c. 255, s. 714 and the City’s building by-law imposing an enforcement duty on the building inspector.
CaseB_TestB: Implied s. 10(b) roadside-screening limit test: a limit is “prescribed by law” if it “results by necessary implication ... from [a statute’s] operating requirements”; police sobriety-screening measures are lawful if “reasonable and necessary” to fulfill the duty and fall within authorized police action, and the implied limit exists where the measures are “incompatible with the exercise of the right to counsel”. The limit is then justified under s. 1 using Oakes proportionality (pressing objective; rational connection; minimal impairment; proportionality of effects).
BaselineB: Statute/constitutional text and prior SCC Charter doctrine: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 1 and 10(b); Highway Traffic Act (Man.), s. 76.1(1); Criminal Code, ss. 254 (and related impaired-driving provisions). The “prescribed by law” operating-requirements approach is taken from R. v. Therens and the implied-limit reasoning from R. v. Thomsen.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal defence of necessity (as an excuse): requires “moral or normative involuntariness” shown by (i) “urgent situation of clear and imminent peril”/“direct and immediate peril”; (ii) “compliance with the law [is] demonstrably impossible” meaning “no reasonable legal alternative”; and (iii) proportionality (“harm inflicted must be less than the harm sought to be avoided”); plus limits re foreseeability and onus on Crown once air of reality raised
BaselineA: Common law defence preserved by Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 7(3), drawing on Morgentaler v. The Queen, [1976] 1 S.C.R. 616 (and discussion of Salvador etc.)
CaseB_TestB: Section 8 “reasonable expectation of privacy” (REP) inquiry for alleged search: objective reasonableness assessed on the “totality of the circumstances” via four lines of inquiry—(1) subject matter, (2) direct interest, (3) subjective expectation, and (4) whether that expectation is objectively reasonable (a “normative question about when Canadians ought to expect privacy”)—applied to undercover online communications
BaselineB: Common law Charter s. 8 framework for REP (as summarized in cases like Edwards/Spencer/Cole/Marakah, and applied to Charter, s. 8; with related statutory context in Criminal Code, ss. 183 and 184.2)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 613(1)(b)(iii) proviso (harmless error): Crown must satisfy the court the verdict “would necessarily have been the same if such error had not occurred”; where exculpatory evidence was excluded, assess the entirety of the evidence including the reasonable possible effect of the excluded evidence, with any reasonable effect enuring to the accused
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 613(1)(b)(iii)), as interpreted in Colpitts v. The Queen, [1965] S.C.R. 739
CaseB_TestB: Appellate court raising a new issue: may do so only in rare circumstances where failing to do so would risk an injustice (i.e., there is “good reason to believe” the result would realistically have differed absent the potential error), and only if the court has jurisdiction, the record is sufficient, and no procedural prejudice results; parties must receive notice and an opportunity to respond
BaselineB: Common law / appellate practice principles (drawing on cases such as R. v. W. (G.) and Quan v. Cusson) and constrained by statute on Crown appeals (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, ss. 676(1)(a), 686(4))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 96 ‘judicial power’ screening test: a power is administrative (not judicial) where there is no real lis between parties and the decision is based on expediency rather than legality
BaselineA: Common law constitutional doctrine under Constitution Act, 1867, s. 96 (drawing on Re Residential Tenancies Act, 1979; Massey-Ferguson; Grondin; and the ‘judicial power’ indicia from John East Iron Works and Coopers and Lybrand)
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 12 mandatory-minimum framework (as applied to robbery MMPs): (1) fix a fit and proportionate sentence; (2) ask whether the mandatory minimum is ‘grossly disproportionate’, assessed via (i) scope and reach of the offence, (ii) effects of the penalty on the offender, and (iii) the penalty and its objectives; analysis may be based on the actual offender or a reasonably foreseeable case
BaselineB: Combination of constitutional and statutory sources: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 12 (gross disproportionality jurisprudence, especially Smith, Nur, Lloyd, Bissonnette, Boudreault) and Criminal Code sentencing provisions (including ss. 718, 718.1, 718.2(e)) as integrated into the s. 12 analysis
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 93(1) denominational-schools protection: a provincial education law is invalid if it "prejudicially affect[s]" a protected denominational-school "Right or Privilege" that a "Class of Persons" had "by Law" "at the Union" (applied via the agreed five conditions: (a) right/privilege affecting a denominational school; (b) enjoyed by a class of persons; (c) by law; (d) in effect at the Union; (e) prejudicially affected).
BaselineA: Constitution Act, 1867, s. 93(1) (and s. 93(2)); baseline articulation of the conditions drawn from Privy Council jurisprudence (e.g., City of Winnipeg v. Barrett; Brophy; Ottawa Separate Schools Trustees v. Mackell/Ottawa Corporation; Hirsch; Tiny) and applied to rights shown in the 1861 Quebec education statute.
CaseB_TestB: Young Offenders Act non-disclosure analysis: the statutory ban turns on whether the communication "create[s] a link between the identity of a young person and an (alleged) offence or hearing"; if the link is made, disclosure is prohibited unless a specific statutory exception applies (e.g., s. 44.1(1)(k) requires judicial authorization and disclosure "desirable" for research/statistics or "proper administration of justice"; s. 38(1.13) requires disclosure be "necessary" for compliance or safety and be directed to the responsible school board).
BaselineB: Statute: Young Offenders Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. Y-1, especially ss. 38(1), 38(1.1), 38(1.13)-(1.15), 40-46 (including s. 44.1 and s. 46).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 93(1) denominational schools protection test: s. 93 applies only if (a) there is a right/privilege affecting a denominational school, (b) enjoyed by a particular class of persons, (c) by law, (d) in effect at the time of the Union, and (e) that is 'prejudicially affected' (trial judge’s conditions adopted at para. 16).
BaselineA: Constitution Act, 1867, s. 93(1) (and s. 93(2)); applied through Privy Council jurisprudence cited (e.g., City of Winnipeg v. Barrett; Brophy; Hirsch; Tiny; Ottawa Separate Schools Trustees cases).
CaseB_TestB: Canadian maritime law / navigation and shipping scope test: the 'mere involvement of a pleasure craft' is insufficient; courts must examine the 'factual context' and ask whether the allegedly negligent act is 'so integrally connected with the act of navigating the pleasure craft on Canadian waterways' that it is a 'practical necessity' for Parliament to have jurisdiction (paras. 21, 24).
BaselineB: Common law constitutional/maritime-law framework from ITO — International Terminal Operators Ltd. v. Miida Electronics Inc.; Whitbread v. Walley; Ordon Estate v. Grail, applied to ss. 91(10) and 92(13) of the Constitution Act, 1867.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Certiorari review of a preliminary inquiry committal: a committal is a reviewable jurisdictional error where there is “no evidence” on an essential element (since “no evidence” can never be “sufficient evidence” under s. 475); reviewing court must independently assess whether there was any evidence
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, s. 475) as interpreted through SCC/PC certiorari jurisprudence (Patterson v. The Queen; Martin v. The Queen; Forsythe v. The Queen; Nat Bell Liquors)
CaseB_TestB: Criteria for compensatory allowance under art. 559 C.C.Q.: claimant must establish (1) contribution, (2) enrichment of spouse’s patrimony, (3) causal link/correlation, and (4) proportion; elements assessed “with great flexibility”; enrichment must subsist and is evaluated at the time of divorce (bankruptcy not an irrefutable bar)
BaselineB: Statute (Civil Code of Quebec, art. 559) informed by unjust enrichment principles (e.g., Cie Immobilière Viger Ltée v. Lauréat Giguère Inc.) and Bankruptcy Act interpretation (ss. 2, 148)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Estoppel by representation (including by silence): requires a representation (words/conduct, or silence/inaction only where there is a legal duty to speak) that induces detrimental reliance; absent these conditions, estoppel cannot preclude denial of contractual liability
BaselineA: Common law (estoppel by representation; definition drawn from Spencer Bower & Turner and cases such as Greenwood v. Martins Bank, Ltd.)
CaseB_TestB: Rebutting the Criminal Code s. 212(3) presumption: jury considers all the evidence about cohabitation and financial arrangements; no need to identify a single “particular and severable” item as “evidence to the contrary”
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 212(3))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Municipal tax ultra vires where council sets a tax rate by resolution when enabling law requires the power be exercised by by-law (self-redelegation / wrong form of municipal act)
BaselineA: Statute (Cities and Towns Act, R.S.Q. 1941, c. 233, s. 526 as amended for Dorval; plus procedural requirements in Cities and Towns Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 193, including ss. 385 and 395; remedy under Code of Civil Procedure, art. 33)
CaseB_TestB: Causation in negligent blood-donor screening: whether the defendant’s negligence “materially contributed” to the occurrence of the injury (outside the de minimis range), rather than strict but-for causation
BaselineB: Common law (causation in negligence; but-for test and material contribution approach as discussed with reference to Snell v. Farrell and Athey v. Leonati; Hollis distinguished)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 13 bar on using an accused’s prior testimony at a retrial: s. 13 applies when the Crown attempts to use prior testimony to incriminate; incrimination assessed in the second proceeding; and a retrial is “any other proceedings”
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 13 (interpreted purposively in light of ss. 11(c) and 11(d))
CaseB_TestB: Reformed rule for substantive admissibility of a non-accused witness’s prior inconsistent statement: admissible for truth if (threshold) it would be admissible as the witness’s in-court testimony, and (principled hearsay) necessity + reliability shown—typically via (1) oath/affirmation/solemn declaration plus explicit warning, (2) videotaped in entirety, and (3) full opportunity to cross-examine at trial; with a voir dire assessing these indicia (or substitutes) and voluntariness/justice concerns
BaselineB: Combination: statute (Canada Evidence Act, s. 9) plus common law hearsay/prior-inconsistent-statement doctrine (the “orthodox rule” from Deacon v. The King) reformed using the principled hearsay approach (R. v. Khan; R. v. Smith)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: When a trial judge’s acquittal can be appealed by the Crown as a “question of law alone”: a “total absence of evidence” for a finding of fact is an error of law only where the law has shifted the burden of proof to the accused; otherwise “there is always some evidence upon which to make a finding of fact favourable to the accused” (presumption of innocence).
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 605(1)(a) (Crown appeal on “question of law alone”), plus SCC appellate-jurisdiction jurisprudence in Sunbeam Corporation (Canada) Ltd. v. The Queen, [1969] S.C.R. 221 and Lampard v. The Queen, [1969] S.C.R. 373 (and discussion of Wild v. The Queen, [1971] S.C.R. 101).
CaseB_TestB: Criteria for interim relief (stay/interim release) under Supreme Court Act s. 65.1 (RJR–MacDonald): (1) “a serious question” to be tried/raised; (2) “irreparable harm”; and (3) “balance of convenience”.
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: Supreme Court Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. S-26, s. 65.1, applying the common-law/interlocutory-relief framework reaffirmed in RJR–MacDonald Inc. v. Canada (Attorney General), [1994] 1 S.C.R. 311.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: When a trial judge’s factual finding (esp. reasonable doubt) can be treated as an error of law on a Crown appeal from acquittal: only where there is a ‘total absence of evidence’, which (for acquittals) occurs only if the law shifts the burden of proof to the accused on that fact
BaselineA: Combination: statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 605(1)(a) (Crown appeal on ‘question of law alone’)) plus common law on fact/law characterization and ‘no evidence’ error (Lampard v. The Queen; Sunbeam Corporation (Canada) Ltd. v. The Queen; discussion of Wild v. The Queen; Lemire not followed on this point)
CaseB_TestB: Ontario anti-SLAPP dismissal framework under CJA s. 137.1: (1) moving party shows on balance of probabilities the proceeding ‘arises from’ its ‘expression’ that ‘relates to a matter of public interest’ (s. 137.1(3)); then (2) responding party must show ‘grounds to believe’ the proceeding has ‘substantial merit’ and the moving party has ‘no valid defence’ (s. 137.1(4)(a)) and (3) the harm/public-interest weighing: harm causally linked to the expression is ‘sufficiently serious’ that the public interest in allowing the proceeding to continue ‘outweighs’ the public interest in protecting the expression (s. 137.1(4)(b))
BaselineB: Statute: Courts of Justice Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.43, s. 137.1(3) and (4) (and related ss. 137.1-137.5)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Lawfulness of warrantless arrest on private premises (forcible entry) under s. 450(1)(a): arrest is lawful if all four questions are answered “yes” (indictable offence; reasonable and probable grounds re offence; reasonable and probable grounds suspect is within; proper announcement before entry).
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 450(1)(a) (arrest without warrant) plus common law “standards enunciated in Eccles v. Bourque” (itself grounded in Semayne’s Case).
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 11(f) “benefit of trial by jury” and waiver: an accused may waive the s. 11(f) benefit, but “a constitutional right to waive is not a constitutional right to elect” and waiver does not create a right to judge-alone trial; s. 24(1) remedy requires an actual Charter infringement/denial.
BaselineB: Constitutional text and interpretation: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 11(f) and 24(1), interpreted in light of prior SCC waiver principles (Korponay v. Attorney General of Canada; Clarkson v. The Queen) and equality framework (Andrews v. Law Society of British Columbia).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 529 amendment test for variance between indictment particulars and proof: court must consider s. 529(4)(a)-(e) and, centrally, whether the accused was “misled or prejudiced in his defence” and whether the amendment can be made “without injustice”; if prejudice exists, consider whether it can be removed by adjournment under s. 529(5).
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 529(4)-(5) (amendment of indictment) and related appellate powers ss. 613(1)(b)(i), 613(3); applied in context of Narcotic Control Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. N-1, ss. 2, 4 and Schedule item 3.
CaseB_TestB: Ineffective assistance of counsel test (G.D.B.): to set aside a verdict, the appellant must show “first, that counsel’s acts or omissions constituted incompetence and second, that a miscarriage of justice resulted”.
BaselineB: Common law: R. v. G.D.B., 2000 SCC 22, [2000] 1 S.C.R. 520 at para. 26 (two-part test).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Concurrent liability in tort and contract for professional negligence: a common law duty of care may arise from a contractual relationship if the asserted tort duty does not depend on specific express contractual obligations; no tort claim to circumvent contractual limits; plaintiff may elect tort or contract
BaselineA: Common law (duty of care/proximity and negligent misrepresentation principles from Donoghue v. Stevenson; Hedley Byrne & Co. v. Heller; Anns v. Merton London Borough Council; plus SCC discussion of Nunes Diamonds and Smith v. McInnis)
CaseB_TestB: Enforcement of exclusive choice-of-forum clause in Quebec private international law: art. 3148(2) C.C.Q. prevails over art. 3139 C.C.Q. for warranty actions if the clause clearly ousts Quebec jurisdiction; forum non conveniens (art. 3135) applies only after Quebec jurisdiction is established
BaselineB: Statute (Civil Code of Québec, arts. 3148 para. 2, 3139, 3135; interpreted in light of Quebec’s international commitments re arbitration/choice clauses)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Scope of Quebec Construction Industry Labour Relations Act/Decree: coverage turns on the nature of the work ("construction" vs excluded "maintenance and repair"), not the status of the employer/employee; and no "total wage" set-off—Decree conditions must be paid as specified
BaselineA: Statute and regulation/decree: Construction Industry Labour Relations Act, S.Q. 1968, c. 45 (now R.S.Q., c. R-20), especially ss. 1(e) ("construction"), 1(i) ("employer"), 1(j) ("professional employer"), 1(r) ("permanent employee"), and s. 2(2) (exception for "maintenance and repair work" by permanent employees of non-professional employers); plus Decree respecting the construction industry (1973) 105 O.G. II 5837, including ss. 3.01-3.02 and public-order clauses (e.g., s. 18.06, s. 32.03)
CaseB_TestB: No stand-alone constitutional exemption for mandatory minimum sentences: if a mandatory minimum produces a s. 12 violation, the proper remedy is a s. 52(1) declaration that the law is of no force or effect (not a s. 24(1) exemption)
BaselineB: Constitutional text and Charter remedial structure: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms ss. 12 and 24(1), and Constitution Act, 1982 s. 52(1) (applied in context of Criminal Code s. 236(a) mandatory minimum)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Parens patriae limit: a court may not authorize non-therapeutic sterilization of a mentally incompetent person (parens patriae must be exercised only for the protected person’s benefit; here it can “never safely be determined” to be for that benefit, so it “should never be authorized”).
BaselineA: Common law (parens patriae jurisdiction) as received through provincial superior courts’ inherent/Chancery jurisdiction; discussed via English Chancery/wardship authorities (e.g., Wellesley v. Duke of Beaufort; Re X (a minor); Re D (a minor)).
CaseB_TestB: Residual management rights “balancing of interests” assessment: arbitrators must “consider all of the surrounding circumstances” and decide whether the employer policy “strikes a reasonable balance” between management and employees’ interests (including impact on employees and any less intrusive means).
BaselineB: Common law / labour-arbitration doctrine incorporated into collective agreement interpretation (KVP test; endorsed in Irving Pulp & Paper).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Kienapple (rule against multiple convictions) — applies only where there is (1) a sufficient factual nexus and (2) sufficient legal nexus (no additional and distinguishing element going to guilt); with guidance on when elements are not “distinct or additional”
BaselineA: Common law (Kienapple v. The Queen) as refined/clarified in SCC jurisprudence (e.g., Côté v. The Queen; Krug v. The Queen)
JudgeA: The Chief Justice (Dickson C.J., for the Court)
CaseB_TestB: “Services … to the public” under Yukon Human Rights Act s. 8(a): two-step analysis—(1) identify the “service”; (2) determine whether it creates a “public relationship” between provider and user, assessed contextually using non-determinative criteria (e.g., selectivity, diversity, non-member involvement, commercial nature, intimacy, purpose)
BaselineB: Statute (Yukon Human Rights Act, R.S.Y. 1986 (Supp.), c. 11, s. 8(a)) interpreted purposively in light of analogous human rights provisions and UBC v. Berg
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Ensite test for whether property is “used or held ... in the course of carrying on a business” (ITA s. 129(4)): property must be “truly employed and risked” in the business; “risk” is more than a remote risk or mere business purpose; threshold met when withdrawal would “have a decidedly destabilizing effect on the corporate operations themselves”; focus is whether property was used to fulfil a requirement that had to be met to do business (not whether taxpayer was forced to use that particular property).
BaselineA: Statute: Income Tax Act, s. 129(4)(a)(ii) (as incorporated into “foreign investment income” via s. 129(4)(b)); interpretive baseline informed by Marsh & McLennan (FCA) and March Shipping (TRB) as discussed in the reasons.
CaseB_TestB: Crown appeal/new trial test under Criminal Code s. 686(4): to obtain a new trial after an acquittal, the Crown must satisfy the court that “the verdict would not necessarily have been the same if the trial judge had properly directed the jury” (heavy onus; reaffirming Vézeau and Morin).
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, s. 686(4), applying the common-law articulation from Vézeau v. The Queen and reaffirmed in R. v. Morin.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Public interest immunity for Cabinet documents: court (not Crown) balances competing public interests; where Cabinet/high-level documents are sought, the court should first inspect them to decide whether disclosure is outweighed by the public interest in confidentiality (no need for requester to prove the documents will assist beyond relevance).
BaselineA: Common law public interest immunity ("Crown privilege"); baseline cases discussed/applied include Smallwood v. Sparling, [1982] 2 S.C.R. 686; R. v. Snider, [1954] S.C.R. 479; Gagnon v. Commission des valeurs mobilières du Québec, [1965] S.C.R. 73; and the modern balancing approach from Conway v. Rimmer, [1968] A.C. 910 (H.L.).
CaseB_TestB: Appellate review of (pre-Lifchus) jury instructions on reasonable doubt/competing evidence: the charge is adequate if, read as a whole, it shows "substantial compliance" with Lifchus/W.(D.) and does not create a "reasonable likelihood" the jury misapprehended the standard of proof (including the W.(D.) ‘third option’).
BaselineB: Common law jury-charge requirements from R. v. Lifchus, [1997] 3 S.C.R. 320 and R. v. W. (D.), [1991] 1 S.C.R. 742 (as applied through R. v. Starr, 2000 SCC 40).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 7 extradition intervention test: courts may intervene only where surrender, in the particular circumstances, would violate the principles of fundamental justice (a "compelling" case of "real substance"), and ordinarily only after the executive surrender decision
BaselineA: Constitution (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7; also s. 32 re Charter application to Canadian government action in extradition)
CaseB_TestB: Crown appeal jurisdiction limit: a Court of Appeal may interfere with an acquittal only if the trial court erred "on a question of law alone" (Criminal Code, s. 605(1)(a); applying Schuldt)
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 605(1)(a), as interpreted in Schuldt v. The Queen)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 7 limit on extradition: courts may intervene only where surrender would, in the particular circumstances, violate the principles of fundamental justice (intervention limited to 'cases of real substance')
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional text (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7; also extradition framework under Extradition Act and treaty context)
CaseB_TestB: Income Tax Act s. 20(1)(c)(i) purpose test: interest is deductible if, considering all the circumstances, the taxpayer had a reasonable expectation of income at the time the investment was made (income = taxable income, not net income; ancillary income-earning purpose suffices absent sham/window dressing)
BaselineB: Statute (Income Tax Act, s. 20(1)(c)(i))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Injurious affection (no land taken): claimant must satisfy the four Loiselle conditions, including that the damage would be actionable at common law (typically nuisance) but for statutory authority; nuisance requires an unreasonable substantial interference/physical injury, and loss of prospect/view is not compensable
BaselineA: Statute (Expropriations Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 154, ss. 1(e)(ii), 21) incorporating common-law actionability; four-condition test from The Queen v. Loiselle, [1962] S.C.R. 624 at p. 627; nuisance concepts discussed via Canadian Pacific Railway Co. v. Albin (1919) and general nuisance definitions
CaseB_TestB: Adequacy of jury instructions on identity/party liability in murder: it is not necessary to find the accused acted alone; jury may convict if satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused “actively participated”/“had a physical role” in the killing (including “acted in concert with others”), and the trial judge may correct an erroneous “actual shooter” instruction by adding “or was otherwise an active participant”
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, especially s. 21 (parties), with murder provisions ss. 229, 231(5); appellate miscarriage-of-justice context under s. 686(1)(b)(iii)); prior SCC guidance referenced including R. v. Thatcher, [1987] 1 S.C.R. 652 and R. v. Rose, [1998] 3 S.C.R. 262
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 10(b) right-to-counsel: once police promptly advise of the right, no further correlative duties arise unless the detainee indicates a desire to exercise it; absent circumstances showing non-understanding, the accused bears the onus to show he asked for counsel and was denied or denied any opportunity to ask
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 10(b) (and remedy context s. 24(2)); applied approach from R. v. Anderson (Ont. C.A.) as adopted by the SCC
CaseB_TestB: Disgorgement/accounting for employee’s secret profits: where an employee acts in a representative capacity and abuses position/bad faith (including using employer funds or taking secret commissions), the employee must account for and turn over profits to the employer under the principle in arts. 411 and 1713 C.C.L.C. (ill-gotten gains) tied to good faith/loyalty
BaselineB: Statute/civil code: Civil Code of Lower Canada, arts. 411 (possessor in bad faith) and 1713 (mandatary’s duty to render account and deliver what received under authority of mandate), extended by analogy to senior employees acting representatively
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Wigglesworth s. 11 Charter applicability test: a matter falls within s. 11 either (1) because "by its very nature it is a criminal proceeding" (a public proceeding "intended to promote public order and welfare") or (2) because conviction may lead to a "true penal consequence" ("imprisonment or a fine which by its magnitude would appear to be imposed for the purpose of redressing the wrong done to society at large"); where the two conflict, the "by nature" test "must give way" to the "true penal consequence" test.
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 11 (opening words "Any person charged with an offence").
CaseB_TestB: Jacquard functional approach to reviewing jury charges: "As long as an appellate court, when looking at a trial judge’s charge to the jury as a whole, concludes that the jury was left with a sufficient understanding of the facts as they relate to the relevant issues, the charge is proper" (juries must be "properly -- not perfectly -- instructed").
BaselineB: Common law (appellate review of jury instructions), drawing on prior SCC authorities cited in the reasons (e.g., Cluett v. The Queen; Azoulay v. The Queen).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Scope of s. 577(1) Criminal Code right to be present: “trial” includes jury selection and any judge examination of prospective jurors about impartiality after arraignment/plea; breach is fundamental and not cured by curative provisions
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 577(1) “present in court during the whole of his trial”), interpreted in light of prior SCC guidance that “trial” varies by provision (Basarabas and Spek v. The Queen, [1982] 2 S.C.R. 730) and SCC/CA jurisprudence on presence and juror impartiality (Vézina and Côté v. The Queen, [1986] 1 S.C.R. 2; Hertrich (Ont. C.A.))
CaseB_TestB: Common law test for when an appellate court may set aside an acquittal and enter a conviction (instead of ordering a new trial): Crown must show (1) with correct law the verdict would not have been the same, (2) accused should have been found guilty but for the error of law, and (3) all findings necessary for guilt were made explicitly/implicitly or are not in issue
BaselineB: Common law appellate remedial test, as stated with reference to Vézeau v. The Queen, [1977] 2 S.C.R. 277 and Courville v. The Queen, [1985] 1 S.C.R. 847 (via Ont. C.A. Courville), applied alongside Criminal Code, s. 613(4)(b)(ii)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: When a trial judge quashes a voidable charge under Criminal Code s. 529 after plea, the quashing is tantamount to an acquittal (supporting autrefois acquit) only where the required amendment cannot be made without injustice/irreparable prejudice; otherwise the judge must amend (and quashing is reversible error). Key formulation: the judge must not quash unless he concludes the amendment cannot "be made without injustice being done"; if amendment "cannot be made without causing irreparable prejudice", then quashing "is ... tantamount to an acquittal" (Lamer J.).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 529(3)-(6), 535, 537) interpreted against common law autrefois acquit principles (e.g., Riddle; Petersen; Doyle; Jewitt).
CaseB_TestB: Framework to define the scope of an acquired right/legal non-conforming use and decide whether a changed use remains protected: (1) characterize the purpose of the pre-existing use; (2) mere intensification is usually protected unless it becomes a different use; (3) added activities beyond prior ones may be too remote (no need to assess neighbourhood effects); (4) if added/altered within original purpose, balance landowner vs community considering remoteness and new/aggravated neighbourhood effects; (5) neighbourhood effects should be proven by evidence unless obvious; (6) definition not too broad or too narrow; (7) criteria aim to ground the inevitably subjective judgment in objective facts (Binnie J.).
BaselineB: Combination: Quebec statute (Act Respecting Land Use Planning and Development, R.S.Q., c. A-19.1, s. 113(18)) plus common law/non-Quebec jurisprudence on legal non-conforming uses (e.g., Central Jewish Institute v. City of Toronto) used to structure the acquired-rights analysis.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Workmen’s privilege against an owner’s immovable where work is done under a lease: a lessee is not a “builder/contractor” for arts. 2013e–2013f C.C.L.C. unless the owner–lessee agreement is a true construction contract that includes an owner’s undertaking to pay a construction-contract “price” (i.e., a claim by the builder against the owner). The Court held that factors like owner approval/knowledge, scale of work, retention of improvements, and notice are not conclusive; the “existence of a claim between the owner and the builder is of the very essence of the privilege mechanism”.
BaselineA: Statute: Civil Code of Lower Canada, arts. 2013e and 2013f (workmen/supplier/subcontractor privileges), with related contract provisions (arts. 984 et seq., 1060).
CaseB_TestB: Mental distress damages for breach of contract under Hadley v. Baxendale: recoverable where (1) “an object of the contract was to secure a psychological benefit that brings mental distress upon breach within the reasonable contemplation of the parties”; and (2) “the degree of mental suffering caused by the breach was of a degree sufficient to warrant compensation” (no independent actionable wrong required).
BaselineB: Common law: remoteness/foreseeability in contract damages from Hadley v. Baxendale, as developed in SCC jurisprudence including Vorvis v. I.C.B.C.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Unequal division of marital property under Marital Property Act s. 7(f): court may depart from equal division where it is of the opinion equal division would be inequitable, including where property was acquired 'exclusively or almost wholly through the efforts of one spouse' and the other made 'no, or a negligible contribution to child care, household management or financial provision'.
BaselineA: Statute (New Brunswick Marital Property Act, S.N.B. 1980, c. M-1.1, ss. 2, 3, 7; especially s. 7(f) 'any other circumstances ... rendering it inequitable for the division ... to be in equal shares').
CaseB_TestB: Interjurisdictional immunity (constitutional inapplicability) for a federal service: provincial law of general application applies unless it bears on what makes the matter specifically federal; for a federal service, inapplicability where the provincial statute 'touches on a vital or essential aspect of its establishment, management or operation'.
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine (interjurisdictional immunity) as articulated in prior SCC cases cited, especially Construction Montcalm and Bell Canada v. Quebec (CSST), plus application to provincial Transport Act permit scheme.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “financing” in Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971 s. 44(2)(a): claimant “finances” a labour dispute only where there is “active and voluntary involvement” and a “meaningful connection between the payment and the dispute”; mandatory union dues alone are not enough
BaselineA: Statute: Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, S.C. 1970-71-72, c. 48, s. 44(2)(a) (exception where claimant proves “he is not participating in or financing or directly interested in the labour dispute that caused the stoppage of work”)
CaseB_TestB: Enforceability/scope of a negligence waiver (exclusion) clause in a race entry form: construed in its context; effective where the parties intended a release and the accident falls within what was contemplated (not “radically different” from what reasonable persons could have contemplated); clause not avoided as “unfair” or “unreasonable” on these facts
BaselineB: Common law: contractual interpretation/enforcement of exclusion (waiver) clauses and related doctrines (fundamental breach/unconscionability/public policy) as applied to the entry-form waiver
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “financing” in Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971 s. 44(2)(a): claimant is “financing” only if there is a “meaningful connection” between the payment and the dispute and the claimant’s involvement is “active and voluntary” (mandatory union dues alone are not enough).
BaselineA: Statute: Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, S.C. 1970-71-72, c. 48, s. 44(2)(a) (disentitlement exception requiring claimant prove he is not “participating in or financing or directly interested in” the labour dispute).
CaseB_TestB: Extradition surrender review: whether extraditing the person sought would be contrary to s. 7 fundamental justice so as to “shock the conscience” or otherwise be “unjust or oppressive” under Extradition Act s. 44(1); requires a balancing exercise and refusal only where the “particular treatment” in the requesting state sufficiently violates fundamental justice.
BaselineB: Statute/constitutional: Extradition Act, S.C. 1999, c. 18, s. 44(1) (“unjust or oppressive”); Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7; as framed through Burns and Lake (balancing; refusal only where “particular treatment” sufficiently violates fundamental justice).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 10 “detention” test (Therens criteria): detention occurs when the state assumes control over a person’s movement by a demand/direction with significant legal consequence, with compulsion/coercion (e.g., criminal liability for refusal or reasonable belief of no choice), in a situation where the person may reasonably require counsel and access to counsel is impeded.
BaselineA: Common law/Charter jurisprudence interpreting Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 10 (b), especially R. v. Therens, [1985] 1 S.C.R. 613 (criteria restated and applied to Criminal Code s. 234.1(1) roadside demand).
CaseB_TestB: Mistake of age—Criminal Code s. 150.1(4) “all reasonable steps” framework: once the defence has an air of reality, the Crown must prove beyond a reasonable doubt either (1) no honest belief the complainant was at least 16, or (2) failure to take “all reasonable steps”; the inquiry is “highly contextual, fact-specific”, with the general rule that “the more reasonable an accused’s perception of the complainant’s age, the fewer steps reasonably required of them.”
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 150.1(4) (and related scheme), as interpreted/applied; SCC also clarifies evidentiary relevance in the reasonable-steps analysis (steps must precede sex, but evidence used to prove them need not).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Extradition specialty/immunity duration: an undertaking not to prosecute for pre-surrender offences does not confer perpetual immunity; it ends once the extraditee has been "restored or has had an opportunity of returning" (i.e., a reasonable opportunity to return) and is no longer in Canada "by reason of the surrender" but by choice
BaselineA: Statute (Extradition Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-21, s. 33) interpreted in light of the extradition arrangement/undertaking and international law interpretive principles (Vienna Convention, art. 31, cited)
CaseB_TestB: Criminal appeal scope/leave test: where an appeal lies as of right on a dissent on a question of law, the appellant may address all aspects of that question, and the s. 686(1)(b)(iii) curative proviso is "always intertwined" with the alleged error of law; therefore no separate leave is required to appeal the refusal to apply the proviso
BaselineB: Common law/doctrine from R. v. Keegstra, [1995] 2 S.C.R. 381, applied alongside Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(b)(iii)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “anything” in Criminal Code theft (s. 283(1)): to be stolen, the subject must (1) be property capable of a proprietary right and (2) be capable of being taken or converted so as to cause deprivation; confidential information per se fails (not property for theft and generally not capable of taking/conversion with deprivation).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 283(1) (theft); also discussed: s. 338(1) (fraud)).
CaseB_TestB: Interpretation of “assets” in MVHC rent-subsidy Assistance Application: “assets” means property/interests “that can actually be used to discharge ... debts and liabilities, including monthly rent”; a Henson trust interest is a “mere hope” and not an “asset” for eligibility to be considered for subsidy.
BaselineB: Common law contractual interpretation (ordinary and grammatical meaning in context/factual matrix) as per Sattva Capital Corp. v. Creston Moly Corp.; applied to the Tenancy Agreement/Assistance Application documents.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 7 analysis for compelled fingerprinting pre‑conviction: (1) deprivation of life/liberty/security; (2) whether deprivation accords with principles of fundamental justice — here, fingerprinting is constitutional if it does not "unduly invade the rights of the accused" and is not arbitrary, given "reasonable and probable grounds" for the charge and acceptance of police discretion
BaselineA: Combination: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7 (two-step framework) applied to statutory fingerprinting powers in Identification of Criminals Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-1, s. 2 and Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 453.3(3), 455.5(5); with interpretive guidance from Re B.C. Motor Vehicle Act and related s. 7 jurisprudence
CaseB_TestB: Sheppard/Braich test for appellate intervention based on insufficient reasons: two stages — "(1) are the reasons inadequate; (2) if so, do they prevent appellate review?"; if reasons are "both inadequate and inscrutable, a new trial is required"; overall question is whether reasons are "sufficiently amenable to appellate review" / whether there is "an impediment to appellate review"
BaselineB: Common law framework from R. v. Sheppard and R. v. Braich (as applied in this appeal), in the context of Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686 appellate review powers
JudgeB: Bastarache and Abella JJ. (LeBel J. concurring)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Detention at the border triggering s. 10(b): a traveller is “detained” when a state agent “assumes control over the movement of a person by a demand or direction which may have significant legal consequence” (Therens), applied here to a compelled customs strip search where the person “could not have refused and continued on her way” and was “subject to external restraint”.
BaselineA: Combination: Charter s. 10(b) (constitutional text) + common-law definition of “detention” from R. v. Therens, [1985] 1 S.C.R. 613 (affirmed in Hufsky and Thomsen).
CaseB_TestB: s. 11(b) unreasonable delay framework (Morin factors + institutional-delay guideline): determine unreasonableness by a “judicial determination balancing” four factors—(1) length of delay; (2) waiver; (3) reasons for delay (including inherent requirements, actions of accused, actions of Crown, institutional limits, other reasons); and (4) prejudice—plus a non-binding guideline of “between 8 and 10 months for institutional delay in Provincial Courts” (and 6–8 months post-committal), which “must not be applied in mechanical fashion but must yield to other factors”.
BaselineB: Combination: Charter s. 11(b) (constitutional text) + prior SCC s. 11(b) jurisprudence (Mills; Rahey; Conway; Smith; Askov) distilled into the multi-factor balancing approach and refined with institutional-delay guidelines.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Leary rule on self-induced intoxication and general-intent offences: intoxication is not a defence; mens rea is proved either (1) by inferring intent from the actus reus (“a person is presumed to have intended the natural and probable consequences of his actions”) or (2) in extreme cases raising doubt about voluntariness, by proving “voluntary self-induced intoxication” as the blameworthy mental state.
BaselineA: Common law (applied/affirmed from Leary v. The Queen, [1978] 1 S.C.R. 29; also discussed with R. v. George, [1960] S.C.R. 871; Swietlinski v. The Queen, [1980] 2 S.C.R. 956; and DPP v. Majewski, [1977] A.C. 443). Also applied in the context of Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 246.2(c) (sexual assault causing bodily harm).
CaseB_TestB: Appellate review of Crown appeal from acquittal / trial-judge error: an appellate court cannot overturn an acquittal merely because it would draw different inferences (“not open to an appellate court... to interfere with the inferences of fact... simply because the appellate court would draw different inferences”); but it may intervene where the trial judge “has not directed his mind to an issue... that require[s] determination” to reach the verdict (error of law).
BaselineB: Common law (limits on Crown appeals from acquittal and deference to trial inferences, relying on Schuldt v. The Queen, [1985] 2 S.C.R. 592; also referencing R. v. Morin, [1992] 3 S.C.R. 286 and R. v. C. (R.), [1993] 2 S.C.R. 226).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Appellate intervention in a trial judge’s discretionary reapportionment of family assets: intervene only if the judge “misdirects himself” or the decision is “so clearly wrong as to amount to an injustice” (and s. 51 does not require asset-by-asset contribution comparisons or separate ‘business’/‘domestic’ streams).
BaselineA: Combination: common law appellate deference to discretion (as applied in Harper v. Harper, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 2; Re Hull Estate (Ont. C.A.) quoted) + statute (Family Relations Act, R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 121, ss. 43 and 51).
CaseB_TestB: Duty to comment on Crown counsel’s improper jury-address remarks: where remarks are “prejudicial to a degree sufficient to impose a legal duty on the trial judge to comment” to ensure the defence is “fairly put to the jury”; failure is an error of law (with no s. 686(1)(b)(iii) cure on these facts).
BaselineB: Combination: common law fairness in jury trials/addresses to jury (as adopted via the dissenting reasons of Ayles J.A. and applied by the SCC) + statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(b)(iii)).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Wigmore/Slavutych four-part test for recognizing a (qualified) common law privilege against compelled disclosure of communications (including claimed journalist-source privilege): (1) communication originates in confidence; (2) confidentiality essential to the relationship; (3) relationship one the community ought to foster; (4) injury from disclosure greater than benefit for correct disposal of litigation.
BaselineA: Common law (Wigmore criteria as discussed/approved in Slavutych v. Baker, [1976] 1 S.C.R. 254).
CaseB_TestB: Reasonableness review of Crown corporations’ discretionary determination of the “effective rate” for PILTs: discretion exists, but calculations must be based on the municipality’s actual existing tax system and treat federal property “as if ... taxable property belonging to a private owner”; corporations cannot base calculations on a “fictitious tax system” (e.g., cannot reintroduce an abolished occupancy tax).
BaselineB: Statute and regulation: Payments in Lieu of Taxes Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. M-13 (esp. ss. 2 (definitions incl. “effective rate”), 2.1, 4(1), sch. II item 10) and Crown Corporation Payments Regulations, SOR/81-1030 (esp. ss. 2 ("corporation effective rate"), 7(1)).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Patent Act s. 36(1) disclosure/sufficiency test: applicant must disclose everything essential for the invention to function; disclosure is complete only if (1) it "describe[s] the invention and define[s] the way it is produced or built" and (2) "define[s] the nature of the invention and describe[s] how it is put into operation"; it must enable a skilled person "to produce it using only the instructions contained in the disclosure" (and seed deposit alone is not enough).
BaselineA: Statute (Patent Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. P-4, s. 36(1)), as interpreted through prior patent-law authorities cited in the reasons (e.g., Minerals Separation; Burton Parsons; Monsanto; Consolboard).
CaseB_TestB: Standard of review for labour-arbitration awards applying common law/equitable doctrines: reasonableness remains the presumptive standard; correctness applies only to Dunsmuir correctness categories (e.g., constitutional questions, questions of central importance to the legal system and outside expertise, true jurisdiction/vires, competing tribunals). An arbitrator may "adapt and apply" doctrines like estoppel within a "contained sphere of arbitral creativity", but must do so in a way that "reasonably respond[s] to the distinctive nature of labour relations".
BaselineB: Common law administrative-law standard of review framework (Dunsmuir; Smith) applied in the labour arbitration context, alongside the statutory scheme of The Labour Relations Act, R.S.M. 1987, c. L10 (notably ss. 121, 128(2)).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 96 ‘Residential Tenancies’ test (as glossed in Sobeys): (1) historical inquiry with narrow characterization and exclusivity/shared-jurisdiction analysis (shared only if inferior-court work was ‘broadly co-extensive’); (2) whether the tribunal function is judicial; (3) whether the power is exercised in a context where it is ‘necessarily incidental to the achievement of a broader policy goal’ (or merely ancillary) rather than the tribunal operating ‘like a s. 96 Court’.
BaselineA: Common law constitutional doctrine under Constitution Act, 1867, s. 96, applying the three-stage framework from Re Residential Tenancies Act, 1979, [1981] 1 S.C.R. 714.
CaseB_TestB: Public interest standing (Downtown Eastside framework, clarified): court ‘must assess and weigh three factors’—(i) serious justiciable issue; (ii) genuine interest; (iii) reasonable and effective means—‘cumulatively, flexibly and purposively’; legality/access to justice are not given ‘particular weight’; no directly affected co-plaintiff is required if a ‘sufficiently concrete and well-developed factual setting’ will be forthcoming, and standing may be revisited only on a ‘material change’ raising serious doubt about that setting.
BaselineB: Common law test for public interest standing from Canada (Attorney General) v. Downtown Eastside Sex Workers United Against Violence Society, 2012 SCC 45.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Bankruptcy priority for provincial “deemed trust” tax claims: s. 47(a) applies only if the tax money is identifiable/traceable as true trust property under general trust law; if not, the province has only a Crown claim under s. 107(1)(j)
BaselineA: Statute (Bankruptcy Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. B-3, ss. 47(a) and 107(1)(j)) interpreted alongside provincial statute (Social Service Tax Act, R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 388, s. 18)
CaseB_TestB: Section 23 “numbers warrant” / local facilities & management-control: relevant numbers are between known demand and potential demand; area is defined case-by-case by the minority board (subject to objective provincial norms consistent with s. 23); Minister’s approval power is limited to verifying compliance and cannot substitute his own criteria
BaselineB: Constitution (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 23) plus statutory/regulatory scheme (P.E.I. School Act and School Act Regulations) as informed by Mahe v. Alberta (sliding scale; numbers warrant; management and control)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Young Offenders Act s. 16 transfer to ordinary court: whether the judge is satisfied, after "weighing and balancing all the relevant considerations" (s. 16(2) factors), that transfer is appropriate; Crown bears a persuasive but "not ... heavy" onus
BaselineA: Statute: Young Offenders Act, S.C. 1980-81-82-83, c. 110, s. 16(1), (2) (transfer test and factors); applied/clarified in light of R. v. M. (S.H.), [1989] 2 S.C.R. 000
CaseB_TestB: Contract damages where defendant had alternative modes of performance: adopt the mode "least profitable to the plaintiff, and the least burdensome to the defendant"; not a factual inquiry into how defendant would likely have performed but for repudiation
BaselineB: Common law principle from Cockburn v. Alexander (1848) (as adopted/confirmed in Canadian and other authorities cited in the reasons)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Canadian maritime law (agency): whether an agent of an unnamed/partially disclosed principal is personally liable turns on the parties’ intention as shown by the contract—“a matter of construction of a particular contract”; “there is no prescribed formality for disclosure” and liability “depends on the will of the contracting parties” (e.g., “as agent only” indicates no personal liability).
BaselineA: Combination: statute + common law/civilian sources as comparative inputs. Statutory baseline is Federal Court Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. F-7, s. 2 (“Canadian maritime law”) and s. 22(2)(m) (stevedoring within maritime law). The agency/mandate baseline is drawn from common law agency/contract principles and (comparatively) C.C.L.C. arts. 1715-1716.
CaseB_TestB: Child Welfare Act reporting immunity threshold: s. 38(6) bars actions by informants unless the report is made “maliciously or without reasonable cause”; “reasonable cause” means having “reasonable cause to ask CPS to consider looking into the matter” (not reasonable grounds to believe abuse occurred).
BaselineB: Statute: Child Welfare Act, R.S.N. 1990, c. C-12, ss. 38(1) (duty to report) and 38(6) (immunity unless “maliciously or without reasonable cause”).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Common-law limits on a warrantless “frisk” search incident to a lawful arrest: no reasonable/probable grounds prerequisite, but (1) discretionary (not a duty), (2) must pursue a valid criminal-justice objective (safety/escape/evidence) and not an improper purpose, and (3) must be non-abusive with force/constraint proportionate to objectives and circumstances
BaselineA: Common law (search incident to arrest), drawing on Canadian and UK authorities; SCC relies in particular on Canadian appellate cases it applies: R. v. Brezack (Ont. C.A.), R. v. Morrison (Ont. C.A.), and R. v. Miller (Ont. C.A.)
CaseB_TestB: Section 7 minimum procedural standard for warrantless child apprehension in “non-emergency” situations: no prior judicial authorization required if apprehension is limited to “serious harm or risk of serious harm” to the child, but s. 7 requires a fair and prompt post-apprehension hearing as the minimum safeguard
BaselineB: Statute + Charter: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7 applied to Manitoba Child and Family Services Act, S.M. 1985-86, c. 8, ss. 17, 21(1), 27(1), 29(1)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal negligence: whether the accused’s conduct is a “marked departure from the norm” such that “wanton or reckless disregard” can be inferred; consequences (death) generally add nothing unless “so interwoven” with the conduct as to help characterize it
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 202(1) (now s. 219) and 203 (now s. 220)) as interpreted in R. v. Tutton, [1989] 1 S.C.R. 1392 (marked departure central under both objective and subjective approaches)
CaseB_TestB: Standing/jurisdiction before the CITT under the AIT: a procurement is covered by AIT Article 502 (“procurement within Canada”) only if the supplier is a “Canadian supplier” (AIT Art. 518: has a place of business in Canada); non-Canadian suppliers therefore lack standing
BaselineB: Statute and regulation incorporating a trade agreement: Canadian International Trade Tribunal Act, ss. 30.1 (definitions) and 30.11(1) (complaints by “potential supplier”), plus Canadian International Trade Tribunal Procurement Inquiry Regulations, s. 3(1) (designated contracts include those described in AIT Art. 502); interpreted through the Agreement on Internal Trade, especially Arts. 101(1), 501, 502 and 518
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 8 reasonableness of compelled document production in a regulatory scheme: Hunter criteria are not "hard and fast"; in the administrative/regulatory context a "lesser standard may apply" and reasonableness turns on balancing the state’s compliance-monitoring interest against the taxpayer’s (relatively low) privacy interest (e.g., random monitoring; least intrusive means; confidentiality safeguards).
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law/constitutional doctrine: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 8 applied to Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1952, c. 148, ss. 231(3), 238(2) (and privacy safeguard s. 241); baseline s. 8 framework from Hunter v. Southam Inc. (criteria for reasonableness) and related SCC cases noted (e.g., R. v. Simmons).
CaseB_TestB: Public interest standing (purposive, flexible, discretionary): courts weigh three interrelated factors—(1) serious justiciable issue; (2) plaintiff has a real stake/is engaged; and (3) the proposed suit is, "in all of the circumstances", a "reasonable and effective means" to bring the case—rejecting a rigid "no other" checklist and requiring a contextual assessment (economy of resources, adversarial suitability, legality principle, realistic alternatives).
BaselineB: Common law doctrine of standing from SCC jurisprudence (e.g., Borowski; Finlay; Canadian Council of Churches; Thorson; McNeil; Hy and Zel’s), refined/clarified in this decision.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Duty to defend is determined by the pleadings: insurer must defend only if the pleadings allege claims seeking damages that "are or may be payable under" the policy (i.e., potentially within coverage); no duty where allegations are clearly outside coverage (e.g., only fraud alleged and fraud excluded).
BaselineA: Contract (insurance policy) interpreted with insurance-contract principles; supported by common-law authorities cited in the reasons (e.g., "[t]he pleadings govern the duty to defend": Bacon v. McBride; and cases holding no duty where pleadings clearly fall outside coverage).
CaseB_TestB: Section 265(4) "air of reality" threshold for honest but mistaken belief in consent: a defence is left with the jury only if there is "sufficient evidence" such that a reasonable jury properly instructed could acquit; requires evidence beyond a bare assertion of belief (though it need not be independent of the accused).
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 265(4)) interpreted as codifying the common-law evidentiary threshold for leaving defences with the jury (cases discussed include Pappajohn, Bulmer, Robertson).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Deductibility of wage-continuation benefits from tort damages for lost earnings (collateral benefits rule): as a general rule, wage benefits paid while plaintiff is unable to work "must be brought into account and deducted"; exception where payer has a subrogation/reimbursement entitlement (and, rarely, a trust where "necessary and appropriate in the interests of justice").
BaselineA: Common law damages principles (compensation for "actual loss"; no double recovery) and prior collateral-benefits jurisprudence including Andrews v. Grand & Toy Alberta Ltd., Thornton v. Prince George School Board, Arnold v. Teno, and Parry v. Cleaver (as discussed in the reasons).
CaseB_TestB: No enforceable right of GST suppliers to reimbursement for collection/remittance costs: s. 103 is an appropriations provision and does not create a legally enforceable right; common law agency/restitution does not require remuneration absent contract, and statutory scheme (including limited transitional credit) displaces any broader common law claim.
BaselineB: Constitution Act, 1867, s. 103 (interpreted as an appropriations provision) and common law agency/restitution principles (e.g., remuneration requires express/implied contract; unjust enrichment framework from Pettkus v. Becker as applied).
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Test for entitlement to a compensatory allowance under art. 559 C.C.Q.: claimant must establish (1) contribution, (2) enrichment of spouse’s patrimony, (3) causal link/correlation, and (4) proportion; enrichment must “subsist” and be evaluated “at the time of the divorce”, with “great flexibility” in evaluating the elements (bankruptcy is not irrefutable proof of no subsisting enrichment).
BaselineA: Statute (Civil Code of Quebec, art. 559), informed by unjust enrichment principles (e.g., Cie Immobilière Viger Ltée v. Lauréat Giguère Inc. (SCC) on “correlation”).
CaseB_TestB: Morrissey test for setting aside a conviction for misapprehension of evidence: misapprehension must go to “the substance” not “detail”, be “material” not “peripheral”, and (conjunctively) the errors must play an “essential part” in the reasoning process resulting in conviction (miscarriage of justice under Criminal Code s. 686(1)(a)(iii)).
BaselineB: Common law appellate standard adopted from R. v. Morrissey (Ont. C.A.) and consistent with R. v. C. (R.) (SCC), applied within the statutory appeal grounds in Criminal Code, s. 686(1)(a)(iii) (and contrasted with s. 686(1)(a)(i)).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Copyright infringement for chip-embedded software: a computer program “replicated in the circuitry of a silicon chip” remains protected if the chip version is a “reproduction” of the copyrightable program in a “material form whatever” under Copyright Act, s. 3(1) (i.e., view the chip as a “static object encoded with written instructions”, not a “dynamic interchange of electrical impulses”).
BaselineA: Statute — Copyright Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-30, s. 3(1) (including the right to “produce or reproduce the work ... in any material form whatever”).
CaseB_TestB: Common law de facto taking (constructive expropriation) test for compensation: “two requirements must be met” — (1) “an acquisition of a beneficial interest in the property or flowing from it”, and (2) “removal of all reasonable uses of the property”.
BaselineB: Common law — de facto taking test drawn from Mariner Real Estate (N.S.C.A.) and SCC authorities Manitoba Fisheries and Tener; applied alongside statute (Vancouver Charter, s. 569) which deems affected property “not to have been taken”.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Interpretation of Limitation of Civil Rights Act waiver: a corporate mortgagor’s s. 40(2) waiver binds only corporate “successors”, and binds “assigns” only where the corporation unilaterally assigns to an individual without the mortgagee’s consent/assumption agreement; an individual who assumes by agreement with the mortgagee is protected by s. 2(2)(d) and is not bound by the waiver.
BaselineA: Statute (The Limitation of Civil Rights Act, R.S.S. 1978, c. L-16, ss. 2(2)(d), 40(1), 40(2))
CaseB_TestB: Common law de facto taking test (compensation): requires (1) “an acquisition of a beneficial interest in the property or flowing from it” and (2) “removal of all reasonable uses of the property”.
BaselineB: Common law (Manitoba Fisheries Ltd. v. The Queen; The Queen in Right of British Columbia v. Tener; applied via Mariner Real Estate Ltd. v. Nova Scotia (Attorney General))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Applicability of Criminal Code s. 443 (now s. 487) search-warrant power to offences under other federal statutes: on a plain reading, s. 443(1)(a)-(b) applies to proceedings under “any other Act of Parliament” even if that Act has its own search-and-seizure provisions; only express “subject to any other Act of Parliament” language (as in s. 443(1)(e)) restricts it.
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 443(1)(a)-(b),(e) (as amended 1985, c. 19, s. 69) (now s. 487); considered alongside Bankruptcy Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. B-3, s. 6 and Interpretation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-23, s. 27(2).
CaseB_TestB: Meaning of “risks willingly assumed” in Occupiers’ Liability Act s. 4(1): s. 4(1) embodies the volenti doctrine—more than mere knowledge/appreciation of danger is required; the plaintiff must accept the legal risk/waive legal rights (assume “the entire risk of injury ... without recourse” against the occupier).
BaselineB: Statute interpreted in light of common law: Occupiers’ Liability Act, R.S.O. 1980, c. 322, ss. 2, 3(1), 4(1); common-law volenti as clarified in SCC cases cited (Dube v. Labar; Crocker v. Sundance Northwest Resorts Ltd.).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 32 applicability to an entity: Wilson J.’s three-part ‘government’ criteria (general control; government function; statutory authority/public interest objective)
BaselineA: Constitution (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 32(1)) and SCC precedent (McKinney v. University of Guelph; RWDSU v. Dolphin Delivery Ltd.)
CaseB_TestB: Arbitration Act s. 31(2)(a) leave-to-appeal framework: threshold ‘question of law’ + ‘may prevent a miscarriage of justice’ (material issue + arguable merit) + residual discretion factors
BaselineB: Statute (Arbitration Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 55, s. 31(2)(a)) and B.C. appellate jurisprudence (BCIT) as interpreted/clarified by the SCC
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Limit on applying the Paré “single transaction” analysis: it applies only to murder classification under Criminal Code s. 214(5) (now s. 231(5)), and only after the Crown first proves the accused committed (or was a party to) both the underlying offence and the murder; only then may the court ask whether the offences were sufficiently closely connected in time to classify the murder as first degree.
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 214(5) (now s. 231(5))) as interpreted in R. v. Paré, [1987] 2 S.C.R. 618 ("single transaction" meaning of "while committing").
CaseB_TestB: Assumption of jurisdiction and forum non conveniens in multistate defamation: jurisdiction is established via a presumptive connecting factor (tort of defamation committed in Ontario upon publication there), and forum non conveniens requires the moving party to show another forum is "clearly more appropriate" by weighing multiple contextual factors; one forum must ultimately emerge as clearly more appropriate.
BaselineB: Common law framework from Club Resorts Ltd. v. Van Breda, 2012 SCC 17 (real and substantial connection; presumptive connecting factors; forum non conveniens with "clearly more appropriate" forum and multi-factor analysis).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Abuse of process stay of proceedings test: a stay is granted only in the “clearest of cases” where compelling the accused to stand trial would violate “fundamental principles of justice”/community “sense of fair play and decency”, or where proceedings are “oppressive or vexatious” (Jewitt/Young as affirmed in Keyowski; applied in Scott to Crown stay-and-recommence under Criminal Code s. 508).
BaselineA: Common law (abuse of process stay test from R. v. Jewitt adopting R. v. Young; reiterated in R. v. Keyowski and R. v. Conway) applied in the context of Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 508 (now s. 579).
CaseB_TestB: When a Vetrovec “clear and sharp warning” is required: trial judge has discretion to warn where a witness is “for some reason untrustworthy to such an extent that a warning to the jury is necessary”, but in some cases the circumstances are such that a Vetrovec caution “must be given”; warning need not always detail corroborative evidence, and whether/how to refer to supportive evidence is within trial judge discretion.
BaselineB: Common law (jury-warning framework from Vetrovec v. The Queen; refined with reference to R. v. Babinski and related cases).
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Test for institutional impartiality (institutional reasonable apprehension of bias): (1) ask whether, considering factors like the occupation and parties appearing, a fully informed person would have a reasonable apprehension of bias in a substantial number of cases; (2) if yes (occupation per se incompatible), assess whether safeguards sufficiently minimize the risk so that a fully informed person would not have such an apprehension in a substantial number of cases; otherwise challenges proceed case-by-case
BaselineA: Combination of common law and constitutional text: Committee for Justice and Liberty v. National Energy Board (reasonable apprehension of bias test) as adopted in Valente v. The Queen for s. 11(d); applied to Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 11(d) and Quebec Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms, s. 23; with statutory safeguards assessed under Cities and Towns Act, ss. 608 and 608.1 (plus related oath/ethics provisions)
CaseB_TestB: Section 1 justification analysis for Criminal Code s. 181 (false news): identify Parliament’s objective at enactment/amendment (no impermissible 'shifting purpose'); if no pressing and substantial objective, the limit fails; even if an objective is assumed, assess proportionality (including minimal impairment) given s. 181’s breadth (e.g., 'injury or mischief to a public interest')
BaselineB: Constitutional text and existing Charter framework: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 1 and 2(b), applying the Oakes s. 1 framework and Irwin Toy s. 2(b) approach; applied to Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 181
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 96 “core jurisdiction” / Residential Tenancies step-one historical inquiry (with required characterization): determine whether the impugned jurisdiction was exercised exclusively by superior courts at Confederation; if not, s. 96 is not infringed
BaselineA: Common law constitutional test from Re Residential Tenancies Act, 1979, [1981] 1 S.C.R. 714 (as refined in Sobeys Stores Ltd. v. Yeomans, [1989] 1 S.C.R. 238) applying Constitution Act, 1867, s. 96
CaseB_TestB: Interpretation of “sold in any market in Canada” (Patent Act ss. 80(1)(b), 83(1), 85): includes sales of medicines regulated by Canadian public law, delivered/dispensed in Canada, and whose cost is borne by Canadians
BaselineB: Statutory interpretation of Patent Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. P-4, ss. 80(1)(b), 83(1), 85 (textual/contextual/purposive approach per Canada Trustco)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Adequacy/sufficiency of an indictment (including where evidence shows multiple conspiracies): an indictment is adequate if it gives the accused “reasonable information” to identify the transaction and prepare a defence; and a proven conspiracy falls within the indictment if it “included some of the accused, occurred at some time within the span alleged in the indictment, and had as its object the type of crime alleged”.
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code indictment provisions) interpreted and applied, with common-law/jurisprudential gloss from SCC cases.
CaseB_TestB: Constitutional validity of the Canada Evidence Act s. 38 national security disclosure scheme: (i) apply the Re Residential Tenancies Act, 1979 s. 96 test (historical conformity inquiry first); and (ii) ensure criminal trial judges retain adequate remedial power (notably under CEA s. 38.14) to prevent an unfair trial, including staying proceedings where necessary.
BaselineB: Statute (Canada Evidence Act, ss. 38-38.16) assessed under constitutional doctrine (Constitution Act, 1867 s. 96; Charter s. 7) including the Re Residential Tenancies Act, 1979 framework.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Entrapment (random virtue-testing) — police may offer an opportunity only with (a) reasonable suspicion the person is already engaged in the particular criminal activity, OR (b) acting pursuant to a bona fide inquiry into a sufficiently precise location where the activity is likely occurring; mere presence in the area is enough to be 'associated' with it
BaselineA: Common law (entrapment test from R. v. Mack, [1988] 2 S.C.R. 903)
CaseB_TestB: Appellate review of trial judge’s voluntariness ruling on a statement — a court of appeal should not reweigh the voir dire evidence absent a 'serious, specific and determining error'
BaselineB: Common law (admissibility of statements/voluntariness; standard of appellate intervention framed in terms of requiring a serious, specific and determining error)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Duty of trial judge to comment on Crown counsel’s improper jury address: where remarks are “prejudicial to a degree sufficient to impose a legal duty on the trial judge to comment” to ensure the defence position is “fairly put to the jury”; failure to do so is an error of law (then consider whether s. 686(1)(b)(iii) ‘no substantial wrong or miscarriage of justice’ applies).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(b)(iii)) plus common-law fairness principles governing jury addresses/charge (as reflected in the Court’s adoption of Ayles J.A.’s formulation).
CaseB_TestB: Broker commission trigger under clause 6.1(3o) and 6.1(4o): (i) no “agreement to sell” unless the accepted promise to purchase is “unconditional” such that it is possible to compel transfer of title; and (ii) clause 6.1(4o)/art. 1503 C.C.Q. requires proof that fulfilment was prevented “through the fault of the seller” (i.e., breach of an obligation to do or not do something).
BaselineB: Statute and contract interpretation (Civil Code of Québec, arts. 1396 and 1503, applied to standard-form brokerage clauses 6.1(3o) and 6.1(4o)).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 16(2) insanity test — second branch: whether, due to “disease of the mind”, the accused was “incapable… of knowing that an act or omission is wrong”, with “wrong” (per Chaulk, applied here) meaning “morally wrong” (not merely “legally wrong”); first branch limited to inability to appreciate the “physical consequences” of the act
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 16(2)); interpreted in light of SCC precedents including R. v. Chaulk (redefining “wrong”), and Cooper/Kjeldsen/Abbey (limiting first branch to physical character/consequences)
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 8 sniffer-dog search threshold — “reasonable suspicion” requires a subjective suspicion plus “objectively discernible facts” assessed on the “totality of the circumstances” (a “constellation of factors”), asking whether facts are “objectively indicative of the possibility of criminal behaviour” (possibilities, not probabilities), viewed through the lens of a reasonable officer with relevant training/experience
BaselineB: Common law Charter s. 8 framework for sniffer-dog searches from R. v. Kang-Brown and R. v. A.M., clarified with R. v. Chehil; applied under Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 8 (and related detention analysis under s. 9/Mann)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Legitimate expectations doctrine limits: (1) creates no substantive rights (no consent/veto), only procedural rights (representations/consultation); and (2) does not apply to the legislative process (so cannot restrain government from introducing a bill, especially a money bill). Key quotes: doctrine is 'part of the rules of procedural fairness' and 'can only create a right to make representations or to be consulted' and 'does not create substantive rights'; further, 'the doctrine does not apply to the legislative process' and '[t]he formulation and introduction of a bill are part of the legislative process with which the courts will not meddle.'
BaselineA: Common law administrative law doctrine of legitimate expectations as an extension of procedural fairness/natural justice (citing Old St. Boniface Residents Assn. Inc. v. Winnipeg (City); also referencing Bates v. Lord Hailsham; Inuit Tapirisat; Martineau; Penikett).
CaseB_TestB: Divorce Act s. 17 variation framework for spousal support: court must be satisfied there has been 'a change in the condition, means, needs or other circumstances' since the order (s. 17(4)), then in making the variation considers the s. 17(7) objectives (recognize advantages/disadvantages, apportion child-related consequences, relieve hardship, and 'in so far as practicable, promote ... self-sufficiency').
