In this case, pension income could be treated as 'means' and no 'double dipping' injustice arose given the earlier rough contribution-based pension division.
BaselineB: Statute: Divorce Act, 1985, s. 17(4) and s. 17(7) (variation of support orders and objectives).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Extradition and s. 7: surrender is unconstitutional only if the foreign consequences are so unacceptable as to “shock the conscience” / be “simply unacceptable” (contextual balancing including comity and security, with deference to ministerial discretion)
BaselineA: Combination of Charter (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7) and common law extradition jurisprudence (Canada v. Schmidt; United States v. Allard; Argentina v. Mellino) applied to Extradition Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. E-23, s. 25 (and the discretionary assurance mechanism in Extradition Treaty Canada–U.S., Art. 6).
CaseB_TestB: Search warrants for media premises: overall “reasonableness” balancing under s. 8 (with s. 2(b) as backdrop), guided by a non-exhaustive list of factors; alternative sources are ordinarily disclosed but not a constitutional prerequisite
BaselineB: Statutory search-warrant standard in Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 487(1)(b), (d), (e), assessed through Charter reasonableness (ss. 8 and 2(b)) and prior cases (Re Pacific Press; Descôteaux v. Mierzwinski).
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Reasonable apprehension of bias (pecuniary interest) test for tribunal impartiality: “Would a reasonably well-informed person consider that the interest might have an influence on the exercise of the official’s public duty?” (Old St. Boniface formulation applied to Law Society costs provision).
BaselineA: Common law (administrative law/natural justice) as formulated in Old St. Boniface Residents Assn. Inc. v. Winnipeg (City), [1990] 3 S.C.R. 1170; applied within Charter s. 7 “principles of fundamental justice” analysis.
CaseB_TestB: Nelles malicious prosecution test (lifting Crown prosecutorial immunity): plaintiff must prove on a balance of probabilities (1) prosecution initiated by defendant; (2) terminated in plaintiff’s favour; (3) absence of reasonable and probable cause (subjective + objective); and (4) malice/improper purpose (“deliberate and improper use of the office ... inconsistent with the status of ‘minister of justice’”).
BaselineB: Common law (tort of malicious prosecution / prosecutorial immunity) from Nelles v. Ontario, [1989] 2 S.C.R. 170 (followed).
JudgeB: Iacobucci and Binnie JJ. (for McLachlin C.J. and Iacobucci, Major and Binnie JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Colour of right / mistake analysis for s. 206(1)(d) lottery offence: (1) colour of right is unavailable unless the offence definition “embrace[s] the concept”; and (2) a belief that the Criminal Code is inoperative is a mistake of law barred by s. 19 (“Ignorance of the law ... is not an excuse”).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, ss. 19 and 206(1)(d); plus common-law/precedential understanding that colour of right is only relevant where the offence definition includes it, as illustrated by theft cases cited).
CaseB_TestB: Modified Taylor hate-speech test under s. 14(1)(b): apply objectively whether “a reasonable person, aware of the context and circumstances” would view the expression as “likely to expose” a protected group to “detestation and vilification”; focus on likely effects, not intent; and strike “ridicules, belittles or otherwise affronts the dignity of” as unconstitutional.
BaselineB: Statute (Saskatchewan Human Rights Code, s. 14(1)(b)) interpreted through prior SCC precedent Canada (Human Rights Commission) v. Taylor, [1990] 3 S.C.R. 892.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Test for granting intervener status and managing prejudice from a new Charter argument/material: intervener must have “a sufficient interest” and “bring a special perspective”; Court considers whether raising the Charter “for the first time in this Court” would “occasion prejudice” (i.e., whether it “would have been affected by additional evidence at trial” / respondent “might have adduced other evidence”); proposed material should be filed only on respondent’s consent or, absent consent, “with leave of the Court” (especially if it is “fresh evidence”).
BaselineA: Common law / SCC practice on intervention and new issues/fresh evidence on appeal (as applied in an application to intervene, with reference to Charter use as an interpretive tool).
CaseB_TestB: Interpretation of Criminal Code s. 182(b) (“offering indignities”): (1) physical interference/contact is “sufficient but not a necessary element”; (2) s. 182(b) “does not apply to offering indignities to monuments per se”; but (3) it “does apply to offering indignities to monuments that mark human remains because to offer indignities to such monuments is to offer indignities to the remains themselves.”
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 182(b); also ss. 683(1)(g), 695(1) re amendment power).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: When the federal Environmental Assessment and Review Process Guidelines Order applies: there must be a “proposal” (an “initiative, undertaking or activity for which the Government of Canada has a decision making responsibility”), meaning an affirmative federal “legal duty or obligation” under an Act of Parliament; then the responsible “initiating department” must run the mandatory assessment process
BaselineA: Regulation and statute: Environmental Assessment and Review Process Guidelines Order, SOR/84-467 (esp. ss. 2 “proposal”/“initiating department”, 3, 6) made under Department of the Environment Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. E-10, s. 6; applied alongside Navigable Waters Protection Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. N-22, s. 5 and Fisheries Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. F-14, s. 37
CaseB_TestB: Appellate intervention/curative proviso framework for alleged jury-charge error: an error warrants intervention only if it fits Criminal Code s. 686(1)(a)(i)-(iii); even if there is an error of law, the conviction may be upheld under s. 686(1)(b)(iii) if (1) the error was harmless/insignificant and could not have affected the verdict, or (2) the case was so overwhelming that conviction was inevitable
BaselineB: Statute and prior SCC case law: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, ss. 686(1)(a) and 686(1)(b)(iii), as explained through R. v. Khan, 2001 SCC 86 and R. v. Trochym, 2007 SCC 6 (cited in the reasons)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 133 “legislative nature” / anti-circumvention test: if the net effect of a series of discrete acts is legislative, each component act is legislative and must be printed/published in both languages
BaselineA: Constitution Act, 1867, s. 133 as interpreted in Reference re Manitoba Language Rights (1985; 1992) (legislative instruments include statutes and other instruments of a legislative nature; badges include: (1) embodies a rule of conduct; (2) has the force of law; (3) applies to an undetermined number of persons; plus the “connection between the legislature and the instrument” indicates legislative nature)
CaseB_TestB: Responsive-answer requirement on jury question about reasonable doubt: after a proper Lifchus charge, if the jury asks about the standard of proof, the trial judge must attempt to answer and must not discourage further questions
BaselineB: Common law jury-instruction framework from R. v. Lifchus and the recharge duty in R. v. S. (W.D.) (a jury question indicates confusion and must be answered “in a complete and careful manner” and the recharge must be “correct and comprehensive” on the issue raised)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Mistaken transfer + recipient knowledge + transferor right of recovery ⇒ property does not pass (for criminal law); subsequent fraudulent conversion with intent to deprive ⇒ theft (Criminal Code s. 322(1))
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 322(1) (theft by fraudulent conversion without colour of right, with intent to deprive), applied with property-law concepts of mistake and right of recovery; SCC discusses R. v. Stewart, [1988] 1 S.C.R. 963 as context for property concepts in criminal law
CaseB_TestB: Dunsmuir standard-of-review framework applied under Federal Courts Act s. 18.1: determine correctness vs reasonableness; where reasonableness applies, court asks whether outcome falls within a “range of possible, acceptable outcomes” and must not reweigh evidence
BaselineB: Combination: common law (Dunsmuir v. New Brunswick, 2008 SCC 9) plus statute (Federal Courts Act, R.S.C., 1985, c. F-7, s. 18.1; and context of IRPA, S.C. 2001, c. 27, s. 67(1)(c))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 11(b) unreasonable delay analysis (Morin): a non-mathematical balancing of factors, with institutional-delay guidelines (8–10 months in Provincial Court; 6–8 months post-committal) that are not fixed ceilings and must yield to other factors like prejudice
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional text (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 11(b) and s. 24(1)) as developed in prior SCC cases (Mills; Rahey; Conway; Smith; Askov)
CaseB_TestB: Contractor/subcontractor liability for construction collapse: subcontractor can avoid liability where the loss was caused by the contractor’s own fault (e.g., overloading), i.e., builder can free itself by proving damage due to “force majeure… the fault of the owner or the act of a third party”, and at least these defences (including contractor’s own fault) are available against the contractor
BaselineB: Civil Code provisions and related contractual framework (C.C. arts. 1684, 1688, 1065; plus incorporated contract ‘General Conditions’ clause on overloading), with SCC authority in Hill, Clarke-Francis Ltd. v. Northland Groceries (Quebec) Ltd.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Secret commissions under Criminal Code s. 426(1)(a)(ii): actus reus requires (1) agency relationship; (2) agent accepts a benefit as consideration for an act/forbearance in relation to the principal’s affairs; and (3) failure to make “adequate and timely disclosure of the source, amount and nature of the benefit”; mens rea requires awareness of each element, including awareness of the extent of disclosure; “corruptly” means “secretly or without the requisite disclosure” and there is no “corrupt bargain” requirement.
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 426(1)(a) (as applied to s. 426(1)(a)(ii) secret commissions); framework followed from R. v. Kelly, [1992] 2 S.C.R. 000.
CaseB_TestB: Criminal Code s. 686(1)(b)(iii) curative proviso: ask “whether a jury properly instructed could, acting reasonably, have come to a different conclusion absent the error”; jury findings may be considered for the hypothetical reasonable jury if not tainted by the error.
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(b)(iii).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: State Immunity Act “commercial activity” exception (s. 5): two-step contextual inquiry—(1) determine the “nature” of the foreign state’s activity (with purpose/context relevant), then (2) assess whether the Canadian proceedings “relate to” that commercial activity by a sufficient “nexus” (more than merely “touch on” or “incidentally affect” it).
BaselineA: Statute (State Immunity Act, S.C. 1980-81-82-83, c. 95, ss. 2 and 5) codifying the common law restrictive immunity approach (acts jure imperii vs jure gestionis; contextual approach discussed via I Congreso del Partido).
CaseB_TestB: Whether Quebec “pay-and-retain/compensation” mechanisms (AIAOD s. 316; ALRCI s. 54) are inoperative in bankruptcy: analyze subrogation/compensation and apply a timing-based framework—pre-bankruptcy payment may permit compensation (if debts are “certain, liquid and exigible” or via BIA s. 97(3)); post-bankruptcy payment cannot create compensation and only supports a proof of claim (BIA s. 121).
BaselineB: Combination of statute and civil law: Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. B-3 (esp. ss. 97(3), 121, 136-147, 67, 71) plus Quebec statutes (AIAOD s. 316; ALRCI s. 54) and Civil Code of Québec rules on subrogation/compensation (arts. 1651, 1656(3), 1672-1673, 1681).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Quebec civil-law “obligation to inform” (duty of disclosure) in contracts of enterprise: duty arises where there is (1) “knowledge of the information, whether actual or presumed” by the debtor; (2) the information is “of decisive importance”; and (3) it is “impossible for the party to whom the duty to inform is owed to inform itself, or that the creditor is legitimately relying on the debtor of the obligation”; in large projects, the duty’s content varies with “allocation of risk”, “relative expertise”, and “continuing formation of the contract”.
BaselineA: Combination: Civil Code of Lower Canada arts. 1024 (good faith), 1053 (delictual fault) plus SCC/civil-law jurisprudence recognizing good faith and disclosure duties (cited in reasons: National Bank of Canada v. Soucisse; Bank of Montreal v. Kuet Leong Ng; Houle v. Canadian National Bank; also discussion of obligation to inform in Ross v. Dunstall; Air Canada v. McDonnell Douglas).
CaseB_TestB: Judicial-reform test for changing Canadian maritime common law (used to abolish the contributory-negligence bar): courts may make incremental common-law change where it is “clearly necessary to keep the law in step with the ‘dynamic and evolving fabric of our society’” and the change’s “ramifications ... are not incapable of assessment” (i.e., not “complex and far-reaching effects” beyond judicial cognizance).
BaselineB: Common law (Canadian maritime law/common law of tort), with the reform framework drawn from SCC precedents on judicial law reform: Watkins v. Olafson and R. v. Salituro (as cited).
JudgeB: McLachlin J. (reasons of La Forest and McLachlin JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Duty to accommodate in adverse-effect discrimination: employer/union must take "reasonable measures short of undue hardship"; union duty arises as co-discriminator or where it blocks reasonable accommodation; complainant must facilitate and accept reasonable accommodation
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Human Rights Act, S.B.C. 1984, c. 22, ss. 8(1)(a),(b),(4) (BFOR) and 9(a)-(c), interpreted through SCC duty-to-accommodate jurisprudence (Ontario Human Rights Commission and O'Malley v. Simpsons-Sears Ltd.; Central Alberta Dairy Pool v. Alberta (Human Rights Commission))
CaseB_TestB: Exclusive arbitral jurisdiction test under s. 45(1) OLRA: courts are ousted if the dispute, in its "essential character", arises from the "interpretation, application, administration or alleged violation" of the collective agreement
BaselineB: Statute interpreted in light of prior SCC labour-arbitration exclusivity jurisprudence: Ontario Labour Relations Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. L.2, s. 45(1), building on St. Anne Nackawic Pulp & Paper Co. v. Canadian Paper Workers Union, Local 219
JudgeB: McLachlin J. (for L'Heureux-Dubé, Gonthier, McLachlin and Major JJ.)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Trial judge’s discretion to exclude cross-examination on a collateral credibility matter where its (tenuous) relevance is outweighed by prejudicial effect/misleading the jury (relevance vs prejudicial value balancing).
BaselineA: Common law (evidentiary discretion re cross-examination on collateral matters), as applied in R. v. Meddoui, [1991] 3 S.C.R. 320.
CaseB_TestB: Income Tax Act s. 20(1)(c)(i) interest deductibility (purpose element): whether, considering all the circumstances, the taxpayer had a reasonable expectation of income at the time the investment was made; “income” means income subject to tax (not net income), and an ancillary income-earning purpose suffices absent sham/window dressing.
BaselineB: Statute: Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), s. 20(1)(c)(i) (with related interpretive context from Bronfman Trust v. The Queen, [1987] 1 S.C.R. 32; Shell Canada Ltd. v. Canada, [1999] 3 S.C.R. 622; Tennant v. M.N.R., [1996] 1 S.C.R. 305).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 10(b) “detention” at a port of entry: routine secondary immigration examination is not detention unless state action goes beyond what is required for processing entry and becomes a restraint of liberty (Therens/Simmons applied)
BaselineA: Combination: constitutional text (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 10(b)) interpreted through common law definition of “detention” from R. v. Therens and border-screening context from R. v. Simmons
CaseB_TestB: Elements of civil contempt: (1) clear and unequivocal order; (2) actual knowledge; (3) intentional act/omission that breaches the order — no requirement of contumacious intent; proof beyond a reasonable doubt
BaselineB: Common law (civil contempt doctrine) as summarized from cases including Bhatnager v. Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration) and other appellate authorities; applied alongside Ontario Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 60.11 (procedure/remedies, not elements)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 686(1)(b)(iii) curative proviso: Crown must satisfy the appellate court that the verdict "would necessarily have been the same" absent the legal error (i.e., that any other verdict would have been "unreasonable or not supported by the evidence" / no jury properly charged could reasonably acquit).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(b)(iii)), as interpreted in SCC cases including Colpitts v. The Queen; Wildman v. The Queen; Mahoney v. The Queen; R. v. Yebes; R. v. S. (P.L.); R. v. Broyles.
CaseB_TestB: Recent fabrication exception to the rule excluding prior consistent statements: where cross-examination amounts to an allegation of recent fabrication, prior consistent statements are admissible to rebut it, but only to prove the fact the complaint was made, not the truth of its contents.
BaselineB: Common law (rule on prior consistent statements and the recent-fabrication exception; no specific baseline case named in the reasons).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Substantive admissibility of a non-accused witness’s prior inconsistent statement (reformed rule): admissible for truth on a principled hearsay basis (reliability + necessity) with threshold safeguards and a voir dire. Threshold: statement admissible only if it "would have been admissible as the witness's sole testimony". Reliability satisfied where there are "sufficient circumstantial guarantees of reliability"—specifically: (1) statement made "under oath, solemn affirmation or solemn declaration" after an "explicit warning" about criminal sanctions for falsehood; (2) statement "videotaped in its entirety"; and (3) opposing party has "a full opportunity to cross-examine the witness at trial". Alternatively, "other circumstantial guarantees of reliability may suffice" if the judge is satisfied they provide "adequate assurances of reliability". Necessity is flexible: in recantation cases, evidence of the same value cannot be expected from the witness/other sources. Voir dire: judge must be satisfied indicia are "present and genuine" and then examine circumstances to ensure voluntariness (if to a person in authority) and no other factors tending to bring the administration of justice into disrepute; generally proved on a balance of probabilities.
BaselineA: Common law hearsay/prior inconsistent statement rule (the "orthodox rule" from Deacon v. The King) as applied through Canada Evidence Act, s. 9 procedure; principled hearsay approach from R. v. Khan and R. v. Smith (reliability and necessity).
CaseB_TestB: Interpretation of insurance policy obligation to pay "interest": where the policy covers "pecuniary consequences" of the insured’s civil liability and promises to pay "interest accrued on the amount of its guarantee from the date when the action was instituted", that interest is "necessarily the interest which the insured may be ordered to pay" under Civil Code art. 1056c; since art. 1056c ‘interest’ is "in reality damages due to delay", the second-paragraph "indemnity" (computed as a percentage of the capital sum, like the first-paragraph interest) is "of the same nature" and therefore "included in the interest" the insurer undertook to pay (up to the policy limit).
BaselineB: Statutory baseline: Civil Code of Québec (then C.C.), art. 1056c (interest and additional indemnity). Contractual baseline: insurance policy clause to pay "interest accrued on the amount of its guarantee from the date when the action was instituted".
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal fraud (Criminal Code, s. 380(1)) — “other fraudulent means”: actus reus is conduct that a reasonable person would “properly ... stigmatize as dishonest”, i.e., “the wrongful use of something in which another person has an interest ... extinguished or put at risk”; mens rea requires (1) “subjective knowledge of the prohibited act” and (2) “subjective knowledge that the prohibited act could have as a consequence the deprivation of another” (including risk to “pecuniary interests”), and “does not require that the accused subjectively appreciate the dishonesty of his or her acts”.
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 380(1)) as interpreted through SCC/common-law definitions in R. v. Théroux (released concurrently) and R. v. Olan (definition of “other fraudulent means” as conduct that can be “stigmatized as dishonest”).
CaseB_TestB: Union duty of representation (Labour Code, s. 47.2) in collective bargaining: the duty is “as a general rule ... an obligation of means”; breach requires proof the union acted “in bad faith or in an arbitrary or discriminatory manner or show[ed] serious negligence” toward employees in the bargaining unit (including, potentially, residual effects for employees who have left), but former employees have no “acquired rights in respect of retroactivity” and their presence “did not impose an obligation of result on the Union”.
BaselineB: Statute (Labour Code, R.S.Q., c. C-27, s. 47.2) and related labour-relations jurisprudence on the duty of representation (e.g., Noël; Centre hospitalier Régina) applied to collective bargaining context.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Crown appeal from acquittal/new trial test (Criminal Code s. 686(4)): Crown must show the verdict “would not necessarily have been the same” but for the legal error
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(4)) as interpreted in SCC precedent (Vézeau v. The Queen; reaffirmed in R. v. Morin)
CaseB_TestB: Reasonable notice before enforcing security/appointing receiver: debtor must receive “reasonable notice of intention to enforce the security” and “reasonable time to pay”; reasonableness assessed using the Mister Broadloom factors
BaselineB: Common law (Lister (R.E.) Ltd. v. Dunlop Canada Ltd.; reasonableness criteria from Mister Broadloom; also citing Massey v. Sladen)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Engineer/design professional preparing tender documents owes no duty to advise bidders about permits or execution methods chosen by the contractor, absent specific arrangements to the contrary (contractor bears responsibility for its chosen method).
BaselineA: Common law (construction/tendering negligence duty/standard of care), relying on the settled rule in R. v. Paradis and Farley Inc.; Vermont Construction Inc. v. Beatson; and Temar Construction Ltd. v. West Hill Redevelopment Co.
CaseB_TestB: Framework for reviewing Crown prosecutorial decisions: (1) identify whether the decision is prosecutorial discretion (decisions about the nature/extent of the prosecution) or tactics/conduct before the court; (2) if prosecutorial discretion, it is reviewable only for abuse of process (egregious conduct seriously compromising trial fairness or integrity of the justice system), with a threshold requirement that the accused first establish a proper evidentiary foundation before the Crown may be required to justify its decision.
BaselineB: Common law/constitutional doctrine on prosecutorial discretion and abuse of process, building on Krieger v. Law Society of Alberta and related SCC jurisprudence (e.g., Nixon; Power).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Constitutional limit on warrantless searches under s. 10 Narcotic Control Act: s. 10 is constitutionally applicable to warrantless searches only where “exigent circumstances render it impracticable to obtain prior judicial authorization”; absent such exigency, the search is not “authorized by law” and is unreasonable under s. 8 (Collins framework).
BaselineA: Combination of common law/Charter doctrine and statute: Charter s. 8 “reasonableness” test from R. v. Collins, [1987] 1 S.C.R. 265 (“A search will be reasonable if it is authorized by law, if the law itself is reasonable and if the manner in which the search was carried out is reasonable.”) applied to Narcotic Control Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. N-1, s. 10 (warrantless search power).
CaseB_TestB: Scope of Income Tax Act confidentiality exception: s. 241(1)-(2) non-disclosure “do not apply in respect of proceedings relating to the administration or enforcement” of the Act (s. 241(3)); “in respect of”/“relating to” are “of the widest possible scope”, so bankruptcy-related proceedings aimed at tax collection can qualify.
BaselineB: Statute: Income Tax Act, S.C. 1970-71-72, c. 63, s. 241(1)-(4), especially s. 241(3) (exception for “proceedings relating to the administration or enforcement” of the Act).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Screen order for child complainant under Criminal Code s. 486(2.1): judge may order testimony behind a screen if complainant is under 18, offence is enumerated, and judge is of the opinion the exclusion is "necessary to obtain a full and candid account of the acts complained of"; constitutionally valid because it does not make the trial "fundamentally unfair" and leaves cross-examination intact
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 486(2.1)) applied within Charter ss. 7 and 11(d) fair trial/fundamental justice analysis
CaseB_TestB: Use of a prior conviction on a similar fact voir dire to prove identity: where the accused puts identity for the prior act in issue, the Crown may tender the prior conviction as "some evidence" linking the accused to the similar act; verdicts are "presumptively reliable" and treated as such on identity unless overturned or later shown wrong; challenge to the conviction on the voir dire is allowed only rarely and may be refused where there is "no reasonable likelihood" it will affect admissibility
BaselineB: Common law similar fact admissibility framework (R. v. Arp; R. v. Handy) including the "some evidence" linkage requirement and probative value vs prejudicial effect balancing
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Party liability for manslaughter (where principal guilty of murder): under s. 21(1) aiding/abetting or s. 21(2) common purpose, manslaughter is available if the accused lacked murder mens rea but, objectively, a reasonable person would have foreseen non-trivial bodily harm from the dangerous act/common purpose (foreseeability of death not required).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, ss. 21(1)(b),(c) and 21(2)) as informed by SCC common-law mens rea for unlawful act manslaughter (R. v. Creighton; R. v. DeSousa) and party-liability cases (R. v. Kirkness; R. v. Trinneer).
CaseB_TestB: Entitlement to GST rebate for overpayment under Excise Tax Act: a person who actually paid an amount “as or on account of” GST that was “not payable” is entitled to a rebate under s. 261(1); s. 261(2)(c) only bars double payment where a rebate is actually payable under ss. 215.1/216(6); and s. 296(2.1) requires the Minister on assessment to apply an “allowable rebate” even if not claimed within s. 261(3)’s two-year limit.
BaselineB: Statute (Excise Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. E-15, ss. 261(1)-(3), 296(2.1), plus interaction with ss. 215.1, 216(6), and definition of “net tax” in s. 225(1)).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Government tort liability: classify the impugned conduct as a protected “policy decision” (immune) or an “operational” act (subject to negligence), per Just v. British Columbia; policy includes decisions “involv[ing] or [being] dictated by financial, economic, social or political factors or constraints” (e.g., “budgetary allocations”), while operational matters are those to which “the standard of negligence… can be applied”.
BaselineA: Common law (Just v. British Columbia, [1989] 2 S.C.R. 1228; also discussed via Anns v. Merton and Kamloops v. Nielsen) applied in the context of highway maintenance; with statutory context considered (Public Highways Act, R.S.N.S. 1989, c. 371, ss. 4-5; Proceedings against the Crown Act, R.S.N.S. 1989, c. 360, s. 5(1)(a); Expropriation Act, R.S.N.S. 1989, c. 156, ss. 70(f), 71).
CaseB_TestB: Damages in lieu of specific performance: where the plaintiff maintains a claim to specific performance and elects damages instead, damages may be assessed as of the date of trial/judgment so they are a “true substitute for specific performance”; “it is not inconsistent with the rules of the common law to assess damages as of the date of trial” in such circumstances, and specific performance “should not be granted as a matter of course absent evidence that the property is unique”.
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: Courts of Justice Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.43, s. 99 (damages “in substitution for… specific performance”), applied alongside common-law damages principles and authorities (Johnson v. Agnew; Wroth v. Tyler; and the traditional compensatory principle).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Abuse of process threshold in criminal proceedings: stay/remedy only in the “clearest of cases” (conduct that “shocks the conscience of the community” and is so unfair it is “contrary to the interest of justice”)
BaselineA: Common law (abuse of process doctrine as affirmed in R. v. Jewitt; reiterated in R. v. Keyowski, R. v. Conway, R. v. Scott, R. v. Potvin)
CaseB_TestB: Admissibility of “Mr. Big” confessions: presumptively inadmissible unless Crown proves (balance of probabilities) probative value (reliability) outweighs prejudicial effect; plus separate abuse-of-process backstop for coercive/abusive operations
BaselineB: Common law (new evidentiary rule as a qualification to the party admissions exception to hearsay; informed by existing common law evidence principles and abuse of process doctrine)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 16(1) “knowing that it was wrong”: an accused is not criminally responsible where, at the time of the act, mental disorder deprived them of the capacity for rational perception and thus rational choice about the act’s wrongness (not just abstract knowledge of right/wrong, but ability to apply it to the particular act).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 16(1)) interpreted in light of prior insanity jurisprudence (notably R. v. Chaulk) and the M’Naghten rules.
CaseB_TestB: Palmer criteria for admitting fresh evidence on appeal (including sentence appeals): (1) due diligence (flexible factor), (2) relevance, (3) credibility, and (4) could reasonably be expected to have affected the result when taken with the trial record.
BaselineB: Common law test from Palmer v. The Queen, applied/confirmed for sentence appeals under Criminal Code ss. 683 and 687 (interests of justice).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Mohan test for admissibility of expert evidence (relevance; necessity; no other exclusionary rule; properly qualified expert), with added gatekeeping for disposition/profile evidence requiring “distinctive behavioural characteristics” and a “standard profile” accepted as reliable
BaselineA: Common law (expert opinion and character evidence rules; prior SCC and other appellate authority including R. v. Abbey, R. v. Béland, R. v. Morin, and discussion of R. v. Lupien / McMillan / Robertson)
CaseB_TestB: Section 745(2) parole ineligibility reduction decision: jury must consider listed factors (character, conduct in custody, nature of offence, and other relevant matters) and “weigh[] as a whole” in a discretionary determination whether ineligibility “ought to be reduced”
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 745(2) (and related s. 745(1), (3), (4)))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 10(b) informational/trigger test in a no-duty-counsel jurisdiction: police satisfy the informational component by advising of the right to counsel and legal aid; if no 24-hour duty counsel exists, no duty to mention it; further implementational duties arise only if the detainee asserts the right to counsel (a clear 'No' does not trigger further duties).
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 10(b) (as interpreted in R. v. Brydges and confirmed in R. v. Bartle; applied alongside the concurrent holding in R. v. Prosper that s. 10(b) does not impose a positive obligation to provide duty counsel).
CaseB_TestB: Criminal Code s. 347 applicability to late payment penalties: a charge is 'interest' only if it is 'paid or payable for the advancing of credit under an agreement or arrangement'; 'credit advanced' includes deferral of payment for goods/services; s. 347(1)(a) assessed at time of contracting (narrow), s. 347(1)(b) assessed at time of payment (broad) with Nelson 'voluntary act of debtor' limitation.
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 347(1)-(2) (interpreting defined terms 'interest', 'credit advanced', and applying Nelson v. C.T.C. Mortgage Corp. as refined in the companion Degelder Construction Co. v. Dancorp Developments Ltd.).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 7 overbreadth (PFJ) test: a law violates s. 7 if it deprives life/liberty/security in a manner that is "unnecessarily broad, going beyond what is needed to accomplish the governmental objective"; courts ask whether the means are "necessary" and "reasonably tailored" to the objective (overbreadth).
BaselineA: Combination: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7 (principles of fundamental justice) + prior SCC s. 7 jurisprudence recognizing overbreadth/vagueness as PFJ tools (notably R. v. Nova Scotia Pharmaceutical Society; Re B.C. Motor Vehicle Act; also references to Lyons, Swain, Cunningham).
CaseB_TestB: Transfer pricing “reasonable amount in the circumstances” under s. 69(2): determine whether the non-arm’s length price exceeds what would be "reasonable in the circumstances" at arm’s length by considering all relevant circumstances, including linked agreements conferring rights/benefits; ensure arm’s length comparators are "sufficiently comparable" having regard to "economically relevant characteristics".
BaselineB: Statute: Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), s. 69(2) (now s. 247(2)); informed (not controlled) by OECD Transfer Pricing Guidelines (1979, 1995) on comparability and methods.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Inference of possession from fingerprint evidence: whether an accused’s fingerprint on an article supports an inference of possession is “not subject to a hard and fast rule” but “depends on all of the circumstances of the case and all of the evidence adduced” (including that once the Crown proves a prima facie case, the accused’s silence may simply “fail[] to provide any basis to conclude otherwise”).
BaselineA: Common law (circumstantial evidence/inference of possession from fingerprints; adverse inference principles), drawing on R. v. O'Keefe and approving the approach in R. v. Mehrabnia; also relies on R. v. Johnson (approved in R. v. François) for when silence may have adverse consequences.
CaseB_TestB: Scope of Review Board power under Criminal Code s. 672.54: Boards may make conditions binding on hospital authorities and may impose conditions “regarding”/supervising treatment, but have “no power to ‘prescribe’ treatment”; supervisory power includes ordering re-evaluations/exploration of alternatives “anything short of actually prescribing treatment”.
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, Part XX.1), primarily s. 672.54 and s. 672.55(1) (interpreted to distinguish prohibited directions that treatment “be carried out” from permissible conditions “regarding” treatment).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 7 compellability / exemption from compulsion test: whether the "predominant purpose" of compelling the witness is to obtain incriminating evidence against them rather than to further a legitimate public purpose; if predominant purpose is incrimination, compulsion must be justified and the witness is not compellable if there is other significant prejudice to fair trial (beyond derivative use, which is protected by derivative-use immunity).
BaselineA: Common law / Charter-based doctrine from R. v. S. (R.J.) (s. 7 self-incrimination; derivative use immunity and exemptions from compulsion), applied in the context of Securities Act, S.B.C. 1985, c. 83, s. 128(1).
CaseB_TestB: Timing rule for Corbett applications: a Corbett application to exclude an accused’s prior record (probative value vs prejudicial effect) "should be made after the close of the Crown’s case" and decided then; if necessary, hold a pre-defence voir dire where defence outlines intended evidence, with possible later modification if defence evidence departs significantly from what was disclosed.
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: Canada Evidence Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-5, s. 12 as interpreted in R. v. Corbett (trial-judge discretion to exclude where probative value is outweighed by prejudicial effect); procedural fairness grounded in common law and s. 7 Charter (case-to-meet principle).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 7 compellability / self-incrimination framework for compelled testimony (and related derivative-use immunity): the “crucial question is whether the predominant purpose for seeking the evidence is to obtain incriminating evidence against the person compelled to testify or rather some legitimate public purpose”; if predominant purpose is to incriminate, compulsion must be justified and the witness is not compellable if there is “any other significant prejudice ... such that his right to a fair trial will be jeopardized”.
BaselineA: Combination: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 7 and 13, applied through/with the common-law principle against self-incrimination as developed in R. v. S. (R.J.), [1995] 1 S.C.R. 451 (and related discussion of derivative use immunity and exemptions from compulsion).
CaseB_TestB: Section 15(1) prima facie discrimination test (Quebec v. A framework): (1) whether the law “creates a distinction on the basis of an enumerated or analogous ground”; and (2) whether it imposes “arbitrary — or discriminatory — disadvantage”, i.e., “fails to respond to the actual capacities and needs” and has the effect of “reinforcing, perpetuating or exacerbating” disadvantage; claimant must show “a disproportionate effect ... based on ... membership in an enumerated or analogous group”.
BaselineB: Combination: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 15(1), as interpreted in Quebec (Attorney General) v. A, 2013 SCC 5 (and related s. 15 jurisprudence cited, e.g., Withler, Kapp, Andrews).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Tax-treaty residency under Article IV: a person/entity is a “resident of a Contracting State” only if “liable to tax therein by reason of ... domicile, residence, place of management, place of incorporation or any other criterion of a similar nature”, where “criterion of a similar nature” means a basis for full (world-wide) tax liability, not mere source taxation; and a factor that merely informs domestic tax liability (e.g., place of management as a factor in ‘engaged in trade or business’) cannot be treated as the ‘by reason of’ basis for liability.
BaselineA: Statute/treaty: Canada-United States Tax Convention Act, 1984, Schedule I (Canada-United States Income Tax Convention (1980)), Article IV(1) (definition of “resident of a Contracting State”) and Article XII(2) (10% withholding cap for royalties paid to a resident).
CaseB_TestB: Trigger for Ontario Insurance Act limitation period: the two-year period in Insurance Act s. 281(5) “only begins to run upon the issuance by the insurer of a valid refusal”; “No such refusal is given if there has not been adequate compliance with s. 71” of the SABS, which requires notice of the dispute-resolution process in “straightforward and clear language, directed towards an unsophisticated person”; “At a minimum” it should include key steps (mediation; arbitration/litigation if mediation fails; mediation as prerequisite) and “the relevant time limits that govern the entire process.”
BaselineB: Statute/regulation: Insurance Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. I.8, s. 281(5) (two-year limit from “insurer’s refusal”); Statutory Accident Benefits Schedule, O. Reg. 776/93, s. 71 (duty to inform of dispute-resolution procedure under ss. 279-283 of the Act).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Exclusive arbitral jurisdiction under s. 45(1) OLRA: courts are ousted if the dispute’s “essential character” arises from the “interpretation, application, administration or alleged violation” of the collective agreement (focus on facts, not legal labels).
BaselineA: Statute (Ontario Labour Relations Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. L.2, s. 45(1)) interpreted in light of SCC labour-arbitration exclusivity jurisprudence (notably St. Anne Nackawic).
CaseB_TestB: s. 744 Criminal Code parole-ineligibility extension: as a general rule 10 years, but may be increased if, having regard to (1) character of the offender, (2) nature of the offence, and (3) circumstances surrounding its commission, the judge deems a longer period “fit in the circumstances” (no “unusual circumstances” requirement).
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 744 (and related sentencing scheme in ss. 742(b), 743)).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “loss of employment” for a retiring allowance: an employee is only “in the service” of the employer once obliged to provide services; therefore “loss of employment” cannot occur before that moment (no prospective/intended employment).
BaselineA: Statute (Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1952, c. 148 (now R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.)), ss. 56(1)(a)(ii) and 248(1) definitions of “retiring allowance”, “employment”, “employee”; interpretive context includes s. 80.4(1) “intended office or employment”).
CaseB_TestB: Trial fairness/miscarriage of justice assessment for improper Crown closing submissions (personal anecdote): apply the “relevant factors” (from R. v. Stephan) to decide whether the impropriety rendered the trial unfair.
BaselineB: Common law (improper jury addresses and trial fairness; factors referenced from R. v. Stephan; related guidance in Pisani v. The Queen, Boucher v. The Queen, and consideration of objection/curative instruction per Manasseri).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Pragmatic and functional approach to whether a labour board has jurisdiction (and, if within jurisdiction, review only for patent unreasonableness/clear irrationality)
BaselineA: Combination: common law administrative law standards of review + statute (Canada Labour Code privative clause and certification provisions). Key baseline cases cited: U.E.S., Local 298 v. Bibeault (pragmatic and functional approach); CUPE v. New Brunswick Liquor (deference/patently unreasonable). Statutory provisions applied: Canada Labour Code, ss. 22 (privative clause), 24, 27, 28 (certification/unit appropriateness), 33 (multi-employer units).
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 8 reasonableness test for DNA data bank orders under Criminal Code s. 487.055: balance state identification interest vs privacy; Hunter v. Southam criteria not required in this context; ex parte procedure assessed by contextual procedural fairness
BaselineB: Combination: constitutional common law under Charter s. 8 (reasonableness framework from Hunter v. Southam; Collins/Stillman three-part reasonableness requirements) + statute (Criminal Code s. 487.055 and related DNA provisions; DNA Identification Act purposes/safeguards). Key statutory provisions applied: Criminal Code, s. 487.055 (and s. 487.055(3.1) criteria), plus related ss. 487.06(2), 487.07, 487.057(1); DNA Identification Act, ss. 3-4.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Gladstone refinement of Sparrow justification/priority for infringements of Aboriginal commercial rights: government must show (1) valid legislative objective and (2) consistency with fiduciary duty, including a non-exclusive but priority-respecting allocation process and outcome where the right has no internal limit
BaselineA: Common law constitutional framework under Constitution Act, 1982 s. 35(1) (and s. 52), building on R. v. Sparrow (justification test and priority) and R. v. Van der Peet (definition of Aboriginal right)
CaseB_TestB: Admissibility of Crown rebuttal evidence: rebuttal may be admitted where it is clearly relevant to an issue raised by the defence (here, alibi) and the Crown could not have known in advance the accused would testify or what he would say; admission is within trial judge’s discretion
BaselineB: Common law trial-evidence principles on rebuttal evidence and trial judge discretion (as applied by the Court; no specific originating case named in the reasons)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Implied waiver of Charter s. 11(d) in regulatory (no-imprisonment) ticket schemes: legislature may infer waiver from failure to act only if (1) the accused is "fully aware of the consequences of failing to act" and (2) the scheme has "sufficient safeguards to ensure that the conduct of the accused was not due to events over which he or she had no control" (e.g., clear ticket warning, personal service, judicial checks for irregularities, and a set-aside mechanism where failure to appear was not the accused’s fault).
BaselineA: Combination: Charter s. 11(d) plus common-law/Charter waiver principles (as discussed via R. v. Lee and general waiver jurisprudence) applied to the statutory ticket-conviction procedure in Provincial Offences Procedure Act, S.N.B. 1987, c. P-22.1, s. 16 (and related safeguards such as ss. 10(1)(h), 11(1), 117).
CaseB_TestB: Procedural fairness for CHRC dismissal of a complaint as unsubstantiated (Canadian Human Rights Act, s. 36(3)(b)): the Commission must act "on a quasi-judicial basis" and fairness requires (1) an "opportunity to make submissions, at least in writing if not at a hearing, before any decision is made" and (2) prior disclosure of "the substance of its case" so submissions are informed.
BaselineB: Combination: statutory decision under Canadian Human Rights Act, 1976-77 (Can.), c. 33, ss. 35 and 36(3)(b), informed by common-law natural justice/procedural fairness requirements.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Patently unreasonable standard on judicial review of labour arbitration (including the 'no evidence' basis): decision must be 'not clearly irrational' / 'evidently not in accordance with reason'; a finding based on 'no evidence' is patently unreasonable
BaselineA: Common law (administrative law standard of review) applied in labour arbitration context; key baseline authorities cited include Canadian Union of Public Employees, Local 963 v. New Brunswick Liquor Corp. (CUPE) and PSAC No. 2; also Douglas Aircraft and Lester on 'no evidence'/incapable of supporting findings
CaseB_TestB: Statutory 'equivalent in value' test for successor pension plan under Reorg. Act s. 15(2)(a): equivalence requires comparing both benefits and the funding mechanism; prima facie breach if employee contributions exceed employer’s on implementation date unless surplus reserved exclusively for members or compensated by equivalent-value benefits
BaselineB: Statute: The Manitoba Telephone System Reorganization and Consequential Amendments Act, S.M. 1996, c. 79, s. 15(2)(a) ('benefits which on the implementation date are equivalent in value'); interpreted in statutory context including s. 15(3)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Doctrine of part performance defeats a statutory writing requirement (Statute of Frauds analogue): where an oral agreement for an interest in land has been carried out/partly performed so that insisting on writing would itself work a fraud, equity enforces the agreement and prevents the Crown from relying on the absence of writing (creating an 'equitable permission' to cross the highway).
BaselineA: Combination of statute and equitable/common law doctrine: Public Highways Act, R.S.N.S. 1954, c. 235, s. 21(1)(a) (written permit requirement) interpreted as reflecting the Statute of Frauds; equitable doctrine of part performance as described in Steadman v. Steadman, [1976] A.C. 536 (H.L.).
CaseB_TestB: Quebec arbitration/public order test for annulment or refusal of homologation: under art. 946.5 C.C.P., the court examines the award 'as a whole' and annuls/refuses only if the award’s disposition/outcome violates public order; mere legal error in applying a mandatory/public-order rule is insufficient unless the outcome conflicts with 'fundamental principles of public order'.
BaselineB: Statutory: Code of Civil Procedure, R.S.Q., c. C-25, arts. 946.2 and 946.5 (and related arts. 946.4, 947.2); Civil Code of Québec, art. 2639 (public order/arbitrability).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Standard of appellate review for Competition Tribunal decisions on questions of mixed law and fact: reasonableness simpliciter (a third standard between correctness and patent unreasonableness), i.e., whether the decision is "unreasonable"—"not supported by any reasons that can stand up to a somewhat probing examination"; patently unreasonable if the defect is "apparent on the face" of the reasons
BaselineA: Common law (standard-of-review jurisprudence) + statute (statutory right of appeal and tribunal structure under Competition Tribunal Act, ss. 12-13; context of Competition Act, s. 92(1))
CaseB_TestB: Temporal-effect test for suspended s. 52(1) declarations: declarations are presumptively retroactive, but the presumption is rebutted "explicitly or by necessary implication"; for suspended declarations, courts must look to the "purpose of the suspension"—if retroactivity would "defeat" the compelling public interests that justified the suspension, the declaration "must apply purely prospectively"
BaselineB: Constitution (Constitution Act, 1982, s. 52(1); Charter, s. 24(1)) + common law/precedent on constitutional remedies (e.g., Hislop; Ontario (AG) v. G; Manitoba Language Reference; Bedford)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: CCA “purpose of producing income” test under Reg. 1102(1)(c): (1) “Does the property produce income? In the affirmative, the deduction is allowable.” (2) If not, “was it acquired for the purpose of producing income?”, determined by “an objective evaluation of the specific facts and circumstances… having regard to whether the taxpayer acted in accordance with reasonably acceptable principles of commerce and business practices.” (L’Heureux‑Dubé J.)
BaselineA: Statute and regulation: Income Tax Act, s. 20(1)(a) (deduction “as is allowed by regulation”) and Income Tax Regulations, s. 1102(1)(c) (“property… not acquired… for the purpose of gaining or producing income”).
CaseB_TestB: Bail denial to “maintain confidence in the administration of justice” under Criminal Code s. 515(10)(c): detention only if “necessary… to maintain confidence in the administration of justice, having regard to all the circumstances, including” (i) “apparent strength of the prosecution’s case”, (ii) “gravity… of the offence”, (iii) “circumstances surrounding its commission”, and (iv) “potential for a lengthy term of imprisonment”; applied through whether “a reasonable member of the community would be satisfied that denial of bail is necessary” (McLachlin C.J.).
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, s. 515(10)(c), interpreted for Charter compliance with s. 11(e) (and s. 1) as per Pearson and Morales.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Vesting/accrual of an appeal-as-of-right: a right is only “acquired”, “accrued” or “accruing” once all conditions precedent to exercising it are fulfilled (here, upon the court of appeal’s judgment reversing the acquittal and ordering a new trial)
BaselineA: Statute (Interpretation Act, R.S.C., 1985, c. I-21, ss. 43(c) and 44(c),(d), applied to Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, former s. 691(2) as amended effective May 14, 1997)
CaseB_TestB: Sherman Estate test for discretionary limits on the open court principle (publication bans): (1) serious risk to an important public interest; (2) necessity because reasonable alternatives will not prevent the risk; (3) proportionality—benefits outweigh negative effects
BaselineB: Common law (Sherman Estate v. Donovan, 2021 SCC 25, para. 38)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Income Tax Act s. 9(1) profit computation framework: taxpayer may use any method consistent with the Act, case law, and well-accepted business principles that yields an “accurate picture” of profit; on reassessment, once taxpayer shows an accurate picture, onus shifts to Minister to show it is not accurate or another method is more accurate
BaselineA: Statute (Income Tax Act, S.C. 1970-71-72, c. 63, ss. 9(1), 18(1)(a), 18(9)) plus existing case law on profit computation (including Symes v. Canada; M.N.R. v. Irwin; Associated Investors of Canada Ltd. v. M.N.R.)
CaseB_TestB: Partnership Act s. 55(b) interpretation: breach occurs only if the general partner does an act that makes it impossible to carry on a “substantial portion” of the limited partnership’s ordinary business (not every facet); plus fiduciary self-dealing rule is voidable but subject to consent/exceptional-circumstances approval
BaselineB: Statute (Partnership Act, R.S.A. 1980, c. P-2, s. 55(b)) interpreted alongside common law/equity fiduciary principles (trustee self-dealing/voidable purchase: Ex p. James; Aberdeen Railway; Holder v. Holder; Regal (Hastings))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Dixon two-step test for post-conviction Crown non-disclosure: (1) reasonable possibility undisclosed info affects reliability of conviction; if not, (2) reasonable possibility non-disclosure affected overall fairness of trial process (including lost investigative opportunities), with defence due diligence as a significant factor
BaselineA: Combination of common law Charter disclosure jurisprudence (R. v. Stinchcombe; R. v. Egger; R. v. C. (M.H.); R. v. Carosella) and the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 7 and 24(1)
CaseB_TestB: Standard-form insurance contract interpretation (Ledcor framework) applied to SEF 44 cl. 4(b)(vii): if language is unambiguous reading the contract as a whole, give effect to its ordinary meaning as understood by the average insured; only if ambiguous use general rules, then contra proferentem—here, “policy of insurance” means private insurance contract and excludes CPP
BaselineB: Common law principles of standard-form insurance contract interpretation (Ledcor Construction Ltd. v. Northbridge Indemnity Insurance Co.; Progressive Homes; Scalera; Gibbens) applied to the SEF 44 Endorsement clause 4(b)(vii)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Search incident to arrest must be “truly incidental”: police must have a purpose connected to the arrest (e.g., “protecting the police, protecting the evidence, discovering evidence”) and “must have had some reason related to the arrest ... and that reason must be objectively reasonable”; delay/distance may support a negative inference rebuttable by explanation (Caslake, paras. 19-25).
BaselineA: Common law (search incident to arrest) as articulated in Cloutier v. Langlois, [1990] 1 S.C.R. 158 (and discussed with reference to R. v. Stillman, [1997] 1 S.C.R. 607).
CaseB_TestB: Admissibility of defence-led unknown third party suspect evidence: (1) evidence must be relevant to a fact in issue (logical relevance to an available defence), established by a “sufficient connection — or similarity — between the crime charged and another crime the accused could not possibly have committed”; and (2) admissible unless “its prejudicial effects substantially outweigh its probative value” (Seaboyer framework) (Grant 2015, paras. 7, 45, 54).
BaselineB: Common law evidence principles, especially R. v. Seaboyer, [1991] 2 S.C.R. 577 (probative value vs prejudicial effect for defence evidence), with related relevance/air-of-reality principles from R. v. Corbett, [1988] 1 S.C.R. 670 and R. v. Cinous, 2002 SCC 29.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Schreiber (L’Heureux‑Dubé J.) — s. 8 Charter is not engaged by merely sending a foreign “letter of request”; only the foreign authorities’ compelled search/seizure would engage s. 8 (but Charter does not apply extraterritorially)
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional text + prior SCC Charter jurisprudence: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms ss. 8 and 32(1), applying the s. 8 concept of “search or seizure” from Hunter v. Southam Inc. and the non-extraterritoriality principle from R. v. Terry / R. v. Harrer
CaseB_TestB: Fullowka — Anns/Cooper duty-of-care framework (foreseeability + proximity, then residual policy) for negligence claims alleging failure to prevent harm caused by a third party
BaselineB: Common law: Cooper v. Hobart / Edwards v. Law Society of Upper Canada / Odhavji Estate / Childs v. Desormeaux / Hill v. Hamilton‑Wentworth (Anns/Cooper duty framework)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Pushpanathan framework for applying Refugee Convention art. 1F(c): exclusion applies only where there is international-law consensus that the acts are "sufficiently serious and sustained violations of fundamental human rights as to amount to persecution", or where acts are "explicitly recognized as contrary to the purposes and principles of the United Nations" (two-category approach: explicit UN/international designation; or court characterization as serious/sustained/systemic human-rights violations amounting to persecution).
BaselineA: Statute incorporating treaty: Immigration Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. I-2, s. 2(1) (incorporating Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees, Art. 1F(c)); interpretive baseline includes Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, Arts. 31-32 (as applied in Ward and Thomson, cited in the reasons).
CaseB_TestB: Contract damages remoteness/proximity test (Hadley v. Baxendale) as applied to breach of implied employment duties: damages are those that "arise either naturally" or were "in the contemplation of both parties, at the time they made the contract, as the probable result of a breach"; applied to assess loss-of-profits damages for breach of an implied duty of good faith by a branch manager who orchestrated a mass exit.
BaselineB: Common law contract damages: Hadley v. Baxendale (1854) (expressly adopted and applied).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Hodgson framework for (i) who is a “person in authority” for the confessions rule and (ii) when a trial judge must hold a voir dire on their own motion: (a) “person in authority” includes those “formally engaged in the arrest, detention, examination or prosecution of the accused” and also those the accused “reasonably believes are acting on behalf of the police or prosecuting authorities and could therefore influence or control the proceedings”; (b) defence must raise the issue and meet an evidential burden; (c) only in “extremely rare cases” must the judge order a voir dire proprio motu where evidence “clearly demonstrates” the receiver was “closely connected to the authorities,” on a ‘spectrum’ from conventional authorities to less obvious cases.
BaselineA: Common law (confessions rule; voluntariness requirement; “person in authority” concept; voir dire practice)
CaseB_TestB: McClurg interpretation of Income Tax Act s. 56(2) (attribution for diverted payments) as generally inapplicable to ordinary corporate dividends: s. 56(2) targets situations where a taxpayer “seeks to avoid receipt of what in his hands would be income by arranging to have the amount received by some other person”; because “until a dividend is declared, the profits belong to a corporation as a juridical person,” “as a general rule, a dividend payment cannot reasonably be considered a benefit diverted from a taxpayer to a third party within the contemplation of s. 56(2).”
BaselineB: Statute (Income Tax Act, S.C. 1970-71-72, c. 63, s. 56(2); with corporate-law context from Saskatchewan Business Corporations Act, R.S.S. 1978, c. B-10, ss. 24(4), 40, 97, 234)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Reg. 1201 depletion-base profit computation: determine profits “reasonably attributable” to production by “ascertaining the difference between the receipts reasonably attributable to the production ... and the expenses of earning those receipts”, and deduct only the items enumerated in Reg. 1201(4) (no implied deduction for long-term research expenses deductible for income under ITA ss. 11(1)(j) and 72).
BaselineA: Regulation/statute: Income Tax Regulations, Reg. 1201(2) and 1201(4), interpreted alongside Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1952, c. 148, ss. 11(1)(j) and 72; with interpretive support from MNR v. Imperial Oil Ltd., [1960] S.C.R. 735.
CaseB_TestB: Sherman Estate test for discretionary limits on the open court principle (publication bans): applicant must establish (1) openness poses a “serious risk to an important public interest”; (2) the order is “necessary” because “reasonably alternative measures will not prevent this risk”; and (3) proportionality: “the benefits of the order outweigh its negative effects”.
BaselineB: Common law: Sherman Estate v. Donovan, 2021 SCC 25 (para. 38) governing discretionary publication bans/open court limits.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Guidelines for applying the Kienapple/res judicata rule against multiple convictions where counts differ in gravity (plea to lesser held in abeyance; convict on more serious and acquit/strike lesser if same delict underlies both)
BaselineA: Common law (Kienapple v. The Queen, [1975] 1 S.C.R. 729) applied in the context of Criminal Code charges (ss. 83, 302(d), 421(a))
CaseB_TestB: Habeas corpus availability to challenge continued detention in parole context: continuation is challengeable only if it becomes unlawful, which occurs only once the inmate has acquired parolee status (parole decision must have taken effect; conditions must be fulfilled)
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: Parole Act (R.S.C. 1970, c. P-2 as amended) plus habeas corpus principles as developed in R. v. Miller, [1985] 2 S.C.R. 613; Cardinal v. Director of Kent Institution, [1985] 2 S.C.R. 643; Morin v. National Special Handling Unit Review Committee, [1985] 2 S.C.R. 662
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: NCR disposition under Criminal Code s. 672.54: absolute discharge is mandatory unless the court/Review Board makes a positive finding that the NCR accused poses a “significant threat to the safety of the public”; if significant threat is found, impose the “least onerous and least restrictive” conditional discharge or detention (with “significant threat” defined as a real risk of serious physical/psychological harm, beyond “merely trivial or annoying”, from criminal conduct). Key quotes: “unless it makes a positive finding on the evidence that the NCR accused poses a significant threat to the safety of the public, the court or Review Board must order an absolute discharge”; “A ‘significant threat’ means a real risk of physical or psychological harm… serious… beyond the merely trivial or annoying… [and] criminal in nature.”
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, Part XX.1, especially s. 672.54 (and related disposition/review provisions).
CaseB_TestB: Westbank levy characterization for s. 125 immunity: determine whether a levy is, in pith and substance, (1) a tax, (2) a regulatory charge (financing/constituting or ancillary to a regulatory scheme), or (3) a user fee. For “tax” vs “regulatory charge” under s. 125, ask: is the charge “(1) compulsory and enforceable by law; (2) imposed under the authority of the legislature; (3) levied by a public body; (4) intended for a public purpose; and (5) unconnected to any form of a regulatory scheme? If the answers to all of these questions are affirmative, then the levy… will generally be described as a tax.” Regulatory-scheme indicia include: “(1) a complete, complex and detailed code of regulation; (2) a regulatory purpose which seeks to affect some behaviour; (3) … actual or properly estimated costs…; (4) a relationship between the person being regulated and the regulation…”.
BaselineB: Combination: Constitution Act, 1867, s. 125 (and related federalism/taxing-power provisions) plus common-law/precedent criteria for taxes vs regulatory charges (e.g., Lawson; Re Exported Natural Gas Tax; Eurig Estate) as synthesized in this decision.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 2(d) freedom of association (labour context): s. 2(d) protects only (1) the freedom to establish/belong to/maintain an association and (2) the exercise in association of members’ lawful rights; it does not include a right to be included in a particular statutory labour-relations regime (no general positive obligation). Key quoted formulation: “first, that s. 2(d) protects the freedom to establish, belong to and maintain an association; second, that s. 2(d) does not protect an activity solely on the ground that the activity is a foundational or essential purpose of an association; third, that s. 2(d) protects the exercise in association of the constitutional rights and freedoms of individuals; and fourth, that s. 2(d) protects the exercise in association of the lawful rights of individuals.”
BaselineA: Combination: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 2(d) (and s. 32(1) re government action), plus prior SCC common-law/constitutional jurisprudence (the 1987 labour trilogy; Professional Institute of the Public Service of Canada v. Northwest Territories (Commissioner); Canadian Egg Marketing Agency v. Richardson). Statutory context: Public Service Staff Relations Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. P-35, s. 2 “employee” (e) (exclusion of RCMP members).
CaseB_TestB: Joint/co-principal liability in group assaults (Criminal Code, s. 21(1)(a)): co-principal liability “flows whenever two or more individuals come together with an intention to commit an offence, are present during the commission of the offence, and contribute to its commission”; for manslaughter, focus is on whether the accused’s actions were “a significant contributing cause of death” (not on who inflicted the fatal wound), and in group assaults “absent a discrete or intervening event, the actions of all assailants can constitute a significant contributing cause to all injuries sustained.”
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 21(1)(a) (and related party provisions s. 21(1)(c) referenced). Common-law gloss from SCC jurisprudence referenced in the decision: R. v. Pickton.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Federal Child Support Guidelines s. 4 ‘inappropriate’ analysis for incomes over $150,000: (1) start from a presumption the Table amount is appropriate; (2) the party seeking deviation must rebut that presumption with evidence sufficient to raise a concern the Table amount is ‘inappropriate’ (i.e., ‘unsuitable’); (3) only after examining all the circumstances, including the s. 4(b)(ii) factors (‘condition, means, needs and other circumstances of the children’ and ‘financial ability of each spouse’), may the court find the Table amount inappropriate and set a more suitable amount (including possible downward variation).
BaselineA: Regulation (Federal Child Support Guidelines, SOR/97-175), interpreting and applying ss. 3 and 4 (especially s. 4(b)(ii)); also situated within the Divorce Act, s. 26.1(2).
CaseB_TestB: Classification rule for limitation periods under the B.C. Insurance Act for all-risks/multi-peril policies: determine whether the policy fits within Part 5 (Fire Insurance) via s. 119; if it does not ‘fit into a specific category’, it is governed by Part 2 (general provisions) and the Part 2 limitation period applies; additionally, even if Part 2 applies, s. 3(a) prevents contracting out to impose harsher terms than Part 2’s protections.
BaselineB: Statute (Insurance Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 226), interpreting ss. 119 and 3(a) (and the Part 2 vs Part 5 scheme, including statutory condition 14).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meiorin unified BFOR test (3 steps): employer must prove (1) standard adopted for a purpose “rationally connected to the performance of the job”; (2) adopted “in an honest and good faith belief” it was necessary; and (3) standard is “reasonably necessary” — i.e., “impossible to accommodate” affected employees “without imposing undue hardship upon the employer”.
BaselineA: Statute (British Columbia Human Rights Code, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 210, s. 13(1)(a), (b), (4)) plus prior SCC BFOR/accommodation jurisprudence (e.g., O’Malley; Etobicoke; Central Alberta Dairy Pool; Renaud).
CaseB_TestB: Stewart source-of-income test (2 stages): (i) “Is the activity ... undertaken in pursuit of profit, or is it a personal endeavour?” (only relevant where there is a personal/hobby element; requires “subjective intention to profit” plus “evidence of businesslike behaviour”); (ii) if not personal, is the source “a business or property?”. REOP is “no more than a single factor, among others”.
BaselineB: Statute (Income Tax Act, especially ss. 3(a), 9(1)-(2); also ss. 18(1)(a), (h), 20(1)(c)(i), 67, 248(1)) and prior SCC case law on “reasonable expectation of profit” (Moldowan).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Staged analysis for whether a conditional sentence is available/appropriate for an Aboriginal offender (s. 742.1 with mandatory consideration of s. 718.2(e)): (1) preliminarily exclude probation and a penitentiary term; (2) confirm s. 742.1 prerequisites; (3) determine under s. 742.1(b) whether a conditional sentence is consistent with ss. 718–718.2, including s. 718.2(e) Gladue factors when incarceration is in issue
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, ss. 742.1 and 718–718.2, especially s. 718.2(e)), as interpreted in R. v. Proulx and R. v. Gladue
CaseB_TestB: Quebec Charter s. 9.1 balancing for a freedom-of-religion claim raised to avoid civil liability: a religious-freedom claim must be "balanced and reconciled with countervailing rights, values, and harm" and may yield where outweighed by more pressing public interests/values (e.g., equality, autonomy, enforcement of contracts)
BaselineB: Statute (Charter of human rights and freedoms, R.S.Q., c. C-12, ss. 3 and 9.1), informed by SCC freedom-of-religion jurisprudence (e.g., Syndicat Northcrest v. Amselem; R. v. Big M Drug Mart)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Unreasonable verdict review under Criminal Code s. 686(1)(a)(i): whether the verdict is one that a properly instructed jury acting judicially could reasonably have rendered; appellate court must thoroughly re-examine the evidence and cannot overturn based on a mere “lurking doubt” without articulating why the verdict is inconsistent with a judicial appreciation of the evidence.
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(a)(i)) as interpreted in common law (R. v. Yebes; reaffirmed/applied via R. v. Biniaris).
CaseB_TestB: Institutional consultation / natural justice limits (Consolidated-Bathurst rules): consultation is permissible if (1) it is not imposed by a superior authority; (2) it is limited to questions of policy and law (no re-assessment of evidence); and (3) decision-makers remain free to decide; for audi alteram partem, an applicant must show an actual breach (not merely an apprehended breach), and a presumption of regularity applies absent further evidence.
BaselineB: Common law procedural fairness/natural justice framework from IWA v. Consolidated-Bathurst Packaging Ltd. and Tremblay v. Quebec (Commission des affaires sociales) (applied in context of judicial review; with statutory backdrop including Labour Relations Act, 1995, ss. 114(1), 117).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: “Functional and structural” approach to the third branch of the Mills test (whether a statutory court/tribunal has the “power to grant the remedy sought” under Charter s. 24(1) and is therefore a “court of competent jurisdiction”)
BaselineA: Combination: Charter s. 24(1) “court of competent jurisdiction” + common-law Mills framework. Baseline test: a “court of competent jurisdiction” possesses “(1) jurisdiction over the person; (2) jurisdiction over the subject matter; and (3) jurisdiction to grant the remedy” (Mills v. The Queen, [1986] 1 S.C.R. 863, as quoted/applied).
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 11(d) validity test for statutory presumptions: a presumption is constitutional “solely if proof of the substituted fact leads inexorably to the existence of the essential element it replaces” (the “inexorable connection”/strict nexus requirement)
BaselineB: Combination: Charter s. 11(d) + common-law/constitutional jurisprudence on presumptions. Baseline cases cited for the “inexorable” nexus requirement: R. v. Whyte, [1988] 2 S.C.R. 3; R. v. Downey, [1992] 2 S.C.R. 10; R. v. Audet, [1996] 2 S.C.R. 171. Statutory context: Criminal Code, s. 172.1(3).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Existence of a valid partnership for purposes of deducting losses under Income Tax Act s. 96: at formation, alleged partners must be (1) “carrying on a business”, (2) “in common”, (3) “with a view to profit” (Continental Bank, para. 22, as summarized at para. 15). SCC clarifies tax-motivation does not negate partnership if these ingredients are present (para. 17) and that “view to profit” is not a strictly quantitative net-gain inquiry; ancillary profit intention supported by objective evidence can suffice (paras. 26-27).
BaselineA: Combination: Income Tax Act, s. 96 (deduction of partnership losses) applied through common-law partnership test from Continental Bank Leasing Corp. v. Canada, [1998] 2 S.C.R. 298 (as reiterated with Backman v. Canada, 2001 SCC 10).
CaseB_TestB: Adequacy of jury instructions on credibility and reasonable doubt (W.(D.) context): where credibility is central, the judge must explain the relationship between credibility assessment and the Crown’s burden; instructions must make it “crystal clear” the burden never shifts and must avoid the “credibility contest” error (paras. 8-9, 13). Failure to use W.(D.)’s three-question formula is not fatal if, read as a whole, the charge makes clear “the jury could not have been under any misapprehension as to the correct burden and standard of proof to apply” (para. 9; applied at para. 14).
BaselineB: Common law: jury-charge framework from R. v. W. (D.), [1991] 1 S.C.R. 742 (and subsequent SCC applications such as Avetysan).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Customs Act s. 48(5)(a)(iv) “condition of sale” test for dutiable royalties/licence fees: royalties/licence fees are added to value for duty only if the purchaser “must pay, directly or indirectly, as a condition of the sale of the goods for export to Canada”; “Unless a vendor is entitled to refuse to sell licensed goods to the purchaser or repudiate the contract of sale where the purchaser fails to pay royalties or licence fees, s. 48(5)(a)(iv) is inapplicable.”
BaselineA: Statute (Customs Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (2nd Supp.), s. 48(5)(a)(iv) (and related definition in s. 45(1) “price paid or payable”)) plus incorporated common law/sale of goods concepts of “condition of sale”.
CaseB_TestB: ITA s. 224 “requirement to pay” trigger (bank liability) in cheque-deposit context: a bank is not “liable to make a payment” to a tax debtor merely because the debtor is named as payee; “The fact that a person is designated as payee on the face of a cheque does not on its own mean that the bank is liable to make a payment to the person”; liability turns on who is the holder entitled on presentment and on “What is on the back of the cheque — the instructions or the endorsement — [which] is crucial.”
BaselineB: Statute (Income Tax Act, s. 224(1)) interpreted through Bills of Exchange Act rules (notably ss. 84(1), 84(3), 86(1), 126, 138(2), 165(3)) and common law banking/bills principles (e.g., Foley v. Hill; Schroeder).
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Quebec Labour Code s. 45 successorship in subcontracting: s. 45 may apply where the transferee, beyond performing similar functions, receives a "right to operate part of the transferor’s undertaking" and has a "sufficient degree of autonomy" assessed contextually (including by the "criterion of the subordination of the employees" to the contractor).
BaselineA: Statute (Labour Code, R.S.Q., c. C-27, ss. 45-46) as interpreted in SCC jurisprudence (notably U.E.S., Local 298 v. Bibeault and Lester (W.W.) (1978) Ltd.).
CaseB_TestB: Jarvis/Ling audit vs. investigation test: an inquiry becomes a penal investigation when its "predominant purpose" is determining penal liability under ITA s. 239; "no one factor is determinative" and the judge assesses the "totality of the circumstances" (with non-exhaustive factors applied).
