BaselineB: Common law/Charter doctrine applying the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms (ss. 7, 8, 24(2)) to the statutory audit/requirement powers in the Income Tax Act (ss. 231.1(1), 231.2(1), 239), following R. v. Jarvis.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Anns/Cooper duty of care framework (stage 1 foreseeability + proximity grounded in statute; stage 2 residual policy considerations)
BaselineA: Common law (Anns v. Merton London Borough Council; Kamloops (City of) v. Nielsen), as clarified in Cooper v. Hobart; applied in statutory-regulator context with reference to the Law Society Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. L.8 (notably s. 9 immunity and the Act’s scheme).
JudgeA: The Chief Justice and Major J. (for the Court)
CaseB_TestB: Section 1 Charter justification (Oakes proportionality) applied to fiscal-crisis limits on s. 15(1) equality rights; rejection of adding a separate ‘separation of powers’ step
BaselineB: Constitution (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 1) and the Oakes test (R. v. Oakes).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory-interpretation test for whether CRTC has jurisdiction under Telecommunications Act s. 43(5): whether “the supporting structure of a transmission line” includes provincially regulated utilities’ power poles (read “in their entire context and in their grammatical and ordinary sense harmoniously with the scheme of the Act, the object of the Act, and the intention of Parliament”). Key constraints applied: (1) “constructed on a highway or other public place” qualifies “transmission line”; (2) “transmission line” is not “distribution line”; (3) “transmission” aligns with “transmission facility” (s. 2(1)) as transmission of “intelligence”, not electricity; therefore s. 43(5) “cannot bear the broad meaning given to it by the CRTC”.
BaselineA: Statute: Telecommunications Act, S.C. 1993, c. 38, especially s. 43(5) (and context in ss. 2(1) “transmission facility”, 43(1)-(4), 64(1)); modern statutory interpretation principle (Driedger) as applied in SCC jurisprudence.
CaseB_TestB: Sentencing framework for refusal causing death (Criminal Code s. 255(3.2))—how to treat (i) collateral consequences, (ii) mistake of law, and (iii) non-impairment as mitigating factors, subject to proportionality. Key formulations: collateral consequence “includes any consequence arising from the commission of an offence, the conviction for an offence, or the sentence imposed for an offence, that impacts the offender”; it “do[es] not need to be foreseeable” but “must relate to the offence and the circumstances of the offender”; and “proportionality must prevail” so they “cannot be used to reduce a sentence to a point where it becomes disproportionate”. Mistake of law “occurs only where a person has an honest but mistaken belief in the legality of his or her actions”; “confusion or uncertainty… does not… meet” mistake-of-law requirements (though may still mitigate). Non-impairment is relevant but its mitigating effect “must be limited”; and “the onus is on the offender to establish, on a balance of probability, that he or she was not impaired”.
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, ss. 255(3.2) and 718 to 718.2 (plus s. 19 re mistake of law not being a defence); SCC sentencing-appeal framework from R. v. Lacasse (demonstrably unfit / error in principle impacting sentence).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charter s. 2(b) infringement for sign restrictions: a by-law that restricts access to an “optimum means of communication” (posting signs) by confining it to designated places directly infringes freedom of expression, especially where its practical effect is to make it “impossible for any individual to post signs criticising the practices, products or services of a business” (paras. 26-27).
BaselineA: Statute/constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 2(b) (freedom of expression) (applied to a municipal zoning by-law).
CaseB_TestB: Canadian Bill of Rights “due process” limits on property deprivations: s. 1(a) and s. 2(e) do not require (i) notice/hearing before Parliament enacts expropriative legislation; (ii) an individual hearing where a law applies non-discretionarily to incontestable facts; and (iii) do not protect against expropriation by “clear and unambiguous” legislation (paras. 37, 45-46, 51-57, 59-61).
BaselineB: Statute: Canadian Bill of Rights, ss. 1(a) and 2(e), applied to Department of Veterans Affairs Act, s. 5.1(4).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Copyright infringement by “reproduction” under s. 3(1): “reproduction” generally means producing “additional or new copies” (i.e., multiplication); a literal physical transfer of the same ink layer to a new substrate, with “no new reproductions ... brought into existence”, is not a “production (or reproduction) ... in any material form” and therefore does not justify seizure under s. 38(1).
BaselineA: Statute: Copyright Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-42, ss. 3(1) (definition of copyright: “sole right to produce or reproduce ... in any material form whatever”), 27(1) (infringement), 38(1) (seizure of “infringing copies”); plus the statutory moral-rights scheme in ss. 14.1 and 28.2 used to maintain the economic/moral rights boundary.
CaseB_TestB: Reasonableness simpliciter on judicial review: the standard does not “float”; a decision is unreasonable “only if there is no line of analysis within the given reasons that could reasonably lead the tribunal from the evidence before it to the conclusion at which it arrived”; if any sufficient reasons are “tenable” and can “stand up to a somewhat probing examination”, the court must not interfere.
BaselineB: Common law: pragmatic and functional approach and the three standards of review framework (correctness, reasonableness simpliciter, patent unreasonableness) drawn from SCC jurisprudence including Pushpanathan v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) and Canada (Director of Investigation and Research) v. Southam Inc.; applied in the context of a statutory appeal under the Law Society Act, 1996, S.N.B. 1996, c. 89.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Privacy Act s. 22(1)(b) exemption: government institution may refuse access only if disclosure “could reasonably be expected to be injurious” to the conduct of lawful investigations; requires a “clear and direct connection” between disclosure of the specific information and the alleged injury, based on “real grounds” tied to the specific case (not general assertions or mere lack of consent).
BaselineA: Statute: Privacy Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. P-21, ss. 22(1)(b), 22(3), 47, 49 (read alongside Official Languages Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 31 (4th Supp.), ss. 60(1), 72-74).
CaseB_TestB: Adverse inference / presumption of fact on causation in medical liability: even where defendant’s negligence undermines proof and plaintiff adduces some evidence, the trier of fact is not required to draw an adverse inference; any presumption of fact under CCQ art. 2849 is discretionary and must be “serious, precise and concordant”.
BaselineB: Statute (civil law evidence): Civil Code of Québec, art. 2849 (presumptions of fact), informed by SCC causation/inference jurisprudence (Snell v. Farrell; St-Jean v. Mercier).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Validity/effect of a zoning “holding regulation”: a municipality may “freeze” development where the by-law provides that “no building or structure may be converted or erected to contain three or more dwelling units until this by-law has been amended…”, and superfluous wording about future amendment does not invalidate the operative prohibition if the City’s freeze policy is clear and within its powers.
BaselineA: Statute (The Planning Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 349, s. 35(1) and related appeal mechanism in s. 35(22)) applied through interpretation of the municipal zoning by-law (By-law 306-480 as amended by By-law 306(bc)-504, s. 4/para. 11 “Holding Regulation”).
CaseB_TestB: Custody assessment under the Infants Act: the trial judge “must consider the conduct of the parties” as part of assessing “relative fitness” for custody, but conduct/fault is “only one factor” and “each particular case must be judged on its own circumstances” with “the paramount consideration… the welfare of the children.”
BaselineB: Statute (The Infants Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 222, s. 1(1)) plus prior custody jurisprudence referenced (e.g., McKee v. McKee; Bickley v. Bickley; Retzer v. Retzer; and discussion alongside Talsky v. Talsky).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: OSC disclosure of compelled investigation material under Securities Act s. 17(1): apply Stinchcombe-style relevance (“reasonable possibility of being relevant” to full answer and defence) within an overall “public interest” balancing; disclosure improper if “no reasonable possibility” a particular item is relevant
BaselineA: Statute and regulation: Securities Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. S.5, ss. 16 (confidentiality) and 17(1) (OSC may order disclosure if “in the public interest”), plus OSC Rules of Practice r. 3.3(2) (staff must disclose all “relevant” material); SCC uses the Stinchcombe relevance standard (“reasonable possibility of being relevant”) as the meaning of “relevant” in this context
CaseB_TestB: Framework to classify requested state-held information as first-party (Stinchcombe) vs third-party (O’Connor) disclosure: ask (1) is it in prosecuting Crown’s possession/control? and (2) should police/another Crown entity have supplied it because it is “fruits of the investigation” or “obviously relevant”? If yes to either → first-party; otherwise → third-party and accused must show “likely relevance” (O’Connor: “reasonable possibility” the info is logically probative)
BaselineB: Common law disclosure regimes: R. v. Stinchcombe (first-party disclosure), R. v. O’Connor (third-party disclosure), and R. v. McNeil (duties re police-held material; “fruits of the investigation”/“obviously relevant”); applied in the context of Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 258(1)(c) (presumption of accuracy)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Misfeasance in public office (Iacobucci J.): plaintiff must prove (1) “deliberate, unlawful conduct in the exercise of public functions”; and (2) “awareness that the conduct is unlawful and likely to injure the plaintiff” (plus causation and compensable loss).
BaselineA: Common law tort (misfeasance in public office), developed through cases including Roncarelli v. Duplessis and discussed with reference to Three Rivers District Council v. Bank of England (No. 3).
CaseB_TestB: Eligibility for Quebec seats under Supreme Court Act, s. 6: s. 6 “impliedly excludes former members” and “imposes a requirement of current membership” in the Quebec bar or Quebec superior courts (reading ss. 5 and 6 together).
BaselineB: Statute/constitutional interpretation: Supreme Court Act, ss. 5 and 6 (and constitutional constraints under Constitution Act, 1982, Part V, especially s. 41(d)).
JudgeB: McLachlin C.J. and LeBel, Abella, Cromwell, Karakatsanis and Wagner JJ.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Securities Act s. 162 administrative penalty: after a contravention, Commission may impose up to $100,000 if it "considers it to be in the public interest"; in assessing public interest it may consider the full context, including general deterrence (a permissible factor) and settlements (relevant but not binding), and courts review the order "globally" for reasonableness
BaselineA: Statute (Securities Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 418, s. 162 (and related public-interest context in ss. 161-162))
CaseB_TestB: Adequacy of jury instructions on alternate routes to murder liability where others may have participated: jury may convict if satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt the accused "actively participated"/"acted in concert with" others in the killing; trial judge must correct an erroneous "actual shooter" instruction and ensure the charge as a whole conveys the essential elements needed to decide liability routes raised by the evidence
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, especially ss. 21 and 229) plus common-law principles on adequacy of jury charges (e.g., R. v. Thatcher, R. v. Rose, as cited)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Good-faith basis requirement for cross-examination on unproven facts (no evidentiary foundation required): counsel may ask an otherwise permissible question if they have a “good faith basis” for it; where the factual predicate is “manifestly tenuous or suspect”, the judge may seek assurance of good faith and, if satisfied, “counsel should be permitted to put the question” (paras. 47-48, 52, 66).
BaselineA: Common law (cross-examination practice/ethics), as reflected in authorities discussed in the reasons (e.g., R. v. Bencardino; R. v. Howard distinguished/limited; Browne v. Dunn held irrelevant to evidentiary-foundation requirement).
CaseB_TestB: Federal paramountcy (frustration of purpose) test with restrained approach: after confirming no operational conflict, the party invoking paramountcy must (1) establish the purpose of the federal law with “clear proof of purpose”, and (2) prove the provincial law is “incompatible with this purpose”; “provincial legislation restricting the scope of permissive federal legislation is insufficient on its own” (paras. 17, 26-27).
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine of federal paramountcy (as articulated in prior SCC cases cited, e.g., Rothmans; COPA; Canadian Western Bank; Ryan Estate).
JudgeB: Abella and Gascon JJ. (for the majority)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Vaid framework for existence/scope of parliamentary privilege: (1) ask whether the claimed category/scope of privilege has been “authoritatively established” for Canada or Westminster; if not, (2) apply the necessity doctrine—privilege exists only if the activity is “so closely and directly connected” to legislative/deliberative functions (including holding government to account) that outside interference would undermine required autonomy; once established, courts do not review the merits of its exercise
BaselineA: Combination: Constitution Act, 1867, s. 18 and Parliament of Canada Act, s. 4 (benchmarking Westminster privileges) plus common-law doctrine of necessity and prior SCC privilege cases (e.g., New Brunswick Broadcasting; Harvey)
CaseB_TestB: Oakes s. 1 proportionality analysis as applied to tobacco-expression limits: pressing and substantial objective; rational connection; minimal impairment (often satisfied if Parliament chose among “several reasonable alternatives” on complex social issues); proportionality of effects
BaselineB: Common law/constitutional doctrine under Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 1 (Oakes framework), applied to Tobacco Act, ss. 18-25 and Tobacco Products Information Regulations (e.g., interpreting “promotion” in s. 18 and “appealing to young persons” in s. 22(3))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: GAAR “abusive tax avoidance” (s. 245(4)) — three requirements, with abuse assessed by whether it “cannot be reasonably concluded that a tax benefit would be consistent with the object, spirit or purpose of the provisions relied upon by the taxpayer” (para. 31(1)(3)); determined through a “unified textual, contextual and purposive analysis” (para. 31(4)) and may be found where transactions “lack a proper basis relative to the object, spirit or purpose” or are “wholly dissimilar” to contemplated transactions (para. 31(6); para. 57).
BaselineA: Statute — Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), ss. 245(1)-(4) (GAAR), with interpretation of ss. 18(13) and 96(1) as the provisions generating the tax benefit; framework followed from Canada Trustco Mortgage Co. v. Canada, 2005 SCC 54 (paras. 31, 35, 57).
CaseB_TestB: Vancouver Sun informer-privilege procedure and “single guiding rule”: give “full effect” to informer privilege (a “complete and total bar on any disclosure of the informer’s identity”) while “limiting, as much as possible, any impairment of the open court principle” (para. 47). Two stages: (1) verify existence of privilege (in camera, possibly ex parte; “evidence that a person is a police informer automatically engages the privilege” (para. 48)); (2) once established, conduct proceedings and choose confidentiality measures to protect privilege while accommodating openness “to the greatest extent possible” (para. 49). In cases requiring total in camera, the Court adds that the guiding rule “will necessarily ensure that, at a minimum, the existence of the in camera hearing and of any decision rendered as a result will be made public” and endorses creating a “parallel proceeding” with its own record number and a redacted public judgment where feasible (paras. 73-75).
BaselineB: Common law — procedure from Named Person v. Vancouver Sun, 2007 SCC 43 (paras. 47-51), concerning informer privilege and court openness.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “reported ... to a lawful authority” under s. 74(1)(a): “lawful authority” includes not only police/agents of the state but also “individuals within the employer organization who exercise lawful authority over the employee(s) complained about, or over the activity that is or is likely to result in the offence” (para. 38).
BaselineA: Statute: The Labour Standards Act, R.S.S. 1978, c. L-1, s. 74(1)(a) (and s. 74(2)); interpreted using the modern principle of statutory interpretation (Driedger/Rizzo/Bell ExpressVu) as discussed in the reasons.
CaseB_TestB: Waiver of insurer’s right to rely on s. 238(1) (dishonoured premium cheque): “Before one can find waiver there must be express and unequivocal language or conduct”; a demand for a replacement cheque, without payment and acceptance in the insured’s lifetime, is not waiver (following McGeachie).
BaselineB: Combination: Statute (The Alberta Insurance Act, R.S.A. 1970, c. 187, s. 238(1) deeming dishonoured-cheque premium “not to have been made”) plus common-law waiver requirement as applied/confirmed with reference to McGeachie v. North American Life Insurance Company (1893), 23 S.C.R. 148.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “reported ... to a lawful authority” in Saskatchewan whistleblower protection: “lawful authority” includes not only state authorities but also “individuals within the employer organization who exercise lawful authority over the employee(s) complained about, or over the activity that is or is likely to result in the offence” (s. 74 LSA).
BaselineA: Statute — The Labour Standards Act, R.S.S. 1978, c. L-1, s. 74(1)(a) (as am. 1994, c. 39, s. 41) (interpreting “lawful authority”); interpretive direction also referenced from The Interpretation Act, 1995, S.S. 1995, c. I-11.2, s. 10.
CaseB_TestB: Common law joinder test (Clunas) as applied to joint trials of provincial offences and summary conviction Criminal Code charges: (1) offences “could initially have been jointly charged” understood functionally as requiring a “sufficient factual nexus”; and (2) joinder must be “in the interests of justice”, involving “a weighing of the costs and benefits of a joint trial” (with accused consent relevant but not determinative).
BaselineB: Common law (R. v. Clunas, [1992] 1 S.C.R. 595) applied alongside statutes conferring jurisdiction and not prohibiting joinder (Provincial Offences Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. P.33, including ss. 2(1), 23, 47(1); Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, including ss. 591(3), 788(1)).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Two-step harm-based test for criminal indecency (Labaye/Butler framework): Crown must prove beyond a reasonable doubt (1) conduct “causes harm or presents a significant risk of harm” in specified ways (autonomy/liberty; anti-social attitudes; physical/psychological harm) and (2) the harm/risk is “incompatible with the proper functioning of society” (R. v. Kouri, para. 10).
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 210(1) (keeping a common bawdy-house for “acts of indecency”), with the indecency analysis structured “based on the guidelines emerging from R. v. Butler, [1992] 1 S.C.R. 452” and as elaborated in the companion case R. v. Labaye, 2005 SCC 80 (Kouri, paras. 1, 9-10).
CaseB_TestB: Pointe Gourde / s. 27(1)(a) “scheme to be ignored” test: for whether a land-use enactment’s effect on value is ignored in compensation, “the key question is whether the enactment was made with a view to the expropriation or, conversely, was an independent enactment” (Lynch, para. 46), assessed by examining “the purposes and effects of the enactment” (para. 48); “causation does not drive the inquiry” (para. 50).
BaselineB: Statute incorporating common-law principle: Expropriation Act, R.S.N.L. 1990, c. E-19, s. 27(1)(a) (“no account shall be taken of the compulsory acquisition of the land”), reflecting the common-law “Pointe Gourde principle” (Pointe Gourde Quarrying and Transport Co. v. Sub-Intendent of Crown Lands, [1947] A.C. 565) (Lynch, paras. 2, 34-38).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Interpretation of Alberta Limitations Act, s. 12: it applies Alberta’s limitation law only to "live" foreign causes of action and does not revive an action already time-barred under the applicable foreign substantive law (lex loci delicti, including its limitation period)
BaselineA: Statute (Alberta Limitations Act, R.S.A. 2000, c. L-12, s. 12) interpreted against the common-law conflicts baseline from Tolofson v. Jensen (lex loci delicti includes the foreign limitation period as substantive)
CaseB_TestB: Ancillary powers doctrine (Waterfield/Dedman framework) for common-law police powers: define the asserted power and liberty interest; then (1) does the conduct fall within the scope of a police duty; (2) is it a justifiable exercise—i.e., "reasonably necessary"—weighing (i) importance of the duty, (ii) necessity of the interference, and (iii) extent of the interference; onus on the state
BaselineB: Common law (ancillary powers doctrine from Dedman v. The Queen / R. v. Waterfield, as applied and structured in later SCC cases such as R. v. MacDonald)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Palmer/Lévesque test for admitting fresh evidence on a sentence appeal (interests of justice): (1) due diligence; (2) relevance; (3) credibility; (4) could reasonably be expected to have affected the result
BaselineA: Common law (Palmer v. The Queen) as adapted for sentence appeals in R. v. Lévesque; applied under Criminal Code, s. 687(1) (court of appeal may 'require or receive additional evidence')
CaseB_TestB: Section 8 reasonable expectation of privacy test (totality of circumstances) with four lines of inquiry: (1) subject matter; (2) direct interest; (3) subjective expectation; (4) objective reasonableness
BaselineB: Common law/Charter jurisprudence under Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 8 (as synthesized from cases including Edwards, Tessling, Spencer, Cole, Patrick, Marakah)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Copyright Act s. 27(2)(e) “hypothetical infringement” requirement for secondary infringement by importation: the importer must have imported a copy that it knows “would infringe copyright if it had been made in Canada by the person who made it”; where the foreign maker is also the Canadian copyright owner, “a copyright owner cannot be liable to its exclusive licensee for infringement”, so hypothetical infringement is not established and s. 27(2)(e) is not violated.
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 11(h) “punished again” test for retrospective parole changes: “The dominant consideration ... will be the extent to which an offender’s settled expectation of liberty has been thwarted by retrospective legislative action”; “It is the retrospective frustration of an expectation of liberty that constitutes punishment.” Generally not punitive if it “does not substantially increase the risk of additional incarceration”; but a retrospective change that “automatically lengthen[s] the offender’s period of incarceration” is “one of the clearest of cases” of double punishment.
BaselineB: Constitution (Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 11(h); applied to Abolition of Early Parole Act, S.C. 2011, c. 11, s. 10(1))
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Sentencing of hybrid offences prosecuted summarily: treat as summary conviction for sentencing; appellate intervention only for error in principle/relevant factor/overemphasis or if sentence within range is demonstrably unfit; “worst offender, worst offence” no longer a constraint on imposing the maximum
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, Part XXIII sentencing principles and summary conviction maximums), with prior SCC clarification that “worst offender, worst offence” is not a constraint
CaseB_TestB: Admissibility of Mr. Big confessions (new common law rule): presumptively inadmissible unless Crown proves (balance of probabilities) probative value (reliability) outweighs prejudicial effect; plus separate abuse-of-process scrutiny for coercive/abusive operations
BaselineB: Common law evidence (party admissions exception to hearsay; trial judge discretion to exclude where prejudicial effect exceeds probative value; abuse of process doctrine)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Adequacy of jury charge (Azoulay principle): trial judge must (except rare needless cases) review the substantial parts of the evidence and present the defence theory so the jury can appreciate the evidence’s value/effect and how law applies; judge has “considerable latitude” on how much evidence to review, so long as jurors get an “adequate understanding” of the relationship between essential evidence and issues
BaselineA: Common law (Azoulay v. The Queen; R. v. Jacquard)
CaseB_TestB: Trade-marks Act s. 6 confusion test: whether, having regard to “all the surrounding circumstances” (including s. 6(5) factors), it is likely the “casual consumer somewhat in a hurry” would be led to the mistaken inference that the wares/services come from the same source; SCC rejects any added requirement of “resemblance or linkage” between wares/services and reaffirms a context-specific totality assessment where no factor (including fame or product difference) ‘trumps’
BaselineB: Statute (Trade-marks Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. T-13, ss. 6(2) and 6(5))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Elements of the Criminal Code child-luring offence (s. 172.1(1)(c)): Crown must prove beyond a reasonable doubt (1) an intentional computer communication; (2) with a person the accused knows or believes is under 14; (3) "for the specific purpose of facilitating" a listed secondary offence—where "facilitating" includes "helping to bring about and making easier or more probable" and the focus is the accused’s subjective intent at the time of the communication (content not necessarily determinative; no need to meet or intend to meet).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 172.1(1)(c) (as it read at trial), with listed secondary offences including ss. 151 and 152).
CaseB_TestB: Enforcement of a forum selection clause: absent legislation, a court should hold parties to their bargain unless there is "strong cause" to displace the chosen forum (a discretionary test), applied on a Rule 21.01(3)(a) motion even after delivery of a statement of defence if brought promptly.
BaselineB: Common law (forum selection clause enforcement under Z.I. Pompey Industrie v. ECU-Line N.V., 2003 SCC 27) applied within the procedural framework of Ontario Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 21.01(3)(a).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: SCC leave jurisdiction and leave-importance test under Supreme Court Act s. 40(1): (1) jurisdiction extends to “any final or other judgment” (incl. extension-of-time orders) unless excluded by s. 40(3); (2) leave only if the question is of “public importance” or otherwise “of such a nature or significance as to warrant decision”
BaselineA: Statute (Supreme Court Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. S-26, ss. 2, 40(1), 40(3); with Criminal Code, ss. 691-693, informing s. 40(3) exclusions)
CaseB_TestB: Access to Information Act third-party notice threshold under s. 27(1): disclose without notice only in “clear cases” where there is “no reason to believe” the record might contain s. 20(1) exempt material; refuse without notice where there is “no reason to believe” disclosure could be required; otherwise give notice (including whenever severance under s. 25 is intended, or where the head is “in doubt” about exemption)
BaselineB: Statute (Access to Information Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. A-1, ss. 20(1), 25, 27(1), 28, 44)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Reasonableness of an unannounced forced entry (departure from the common law “knock and announce” rule): police must ordinarily (i) give notice of presence, (ii) notice of authority, and (iii) notice of purpose; if they depart, the Crown must show police had “reasonable grounds to be concerned about the possibility of harm ... or about the destruction of evidence” based on what was (or should reasonably have been) known at the time
BaselineA: Common law + constitutional baseline (Charter s. 8 reasonableness) drawing on Eccles v. Bourque (knock-and-announce) and R. v. Collins (three-part s. 8 reasonableness framework); also interpreted alongside Criminal Code, s. 29(1) (warrant possession) in the execution context
CaseB_TestB: Implied assertions are hearsay when tendered for their truth; admissible only if within a traditional exception or, failing that, under the principled hearsay approach requiring “necessity and reliability” (Mapara framework) established on a voir dire
BaselineB: Common law hearsay rule and the SCC’s principled hearsay framework (Khan; Khelawon; Starr; Mapara) applied to implied assertions; no statutory baseline for the hearsay test itself
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: State Immunity Act commercial activity exception: determine whether proceedings “relate to any commercial activity” by examining the “nature of the acts ... in their full context, which includes the purpose of the acts” (not merely whether authorized by the state or pursuing public interests); apply s. 3 presumption of immunity with claimant bearing burden to show an exception.
BaselineA: Statute (State Immunity Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. S-18, ss. 2 “commercial activity”, 3, 5) as interpreted through SCC precedent (Re Canada Labour Code, [1992] 2 S.C.R. 50; Schreiber v. Canada (Attorney General), 2002 SCC 62).
CaseB_TestB: Criminal Code s. 686(1) curative proviso / miscarriage-of-justice framework: (i) miscarriage of justice if irregularity “severe enough to render the trial unfair or create the appearance of unfairness”; (ii) curative proviso applies only where conviction was “inevitable” / no “reasonable possibility that the verdict would have been different had the error ... not been made”.
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(a)(ii)-(iii), (b)(iii)-(iv)) building on SCC case law cited in the reasons (e.g., Bevan, [1993] 2 S.C.R. 599; S. (P.L.), [1991] 1 S.C.R. 909; Colpitts, [1965] S.C.R. 739; Wildman, [1984] 2 S.C.R. 311).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Journalist-source privilege (Quebec civil litigation): threshold relevance + Wigmore factors, with context-specific balancing at factor 4. To compel answers that may identify a confidential source, the requesting party must first show the questions are relevant; if relevant, the court applies Wigmore: (1) relationship originates in confidence; (2) anonymity essential; (3) relationship should be sedulously fostered in the public interest; (4) public interest in protecting identity outweighs public interest in getting at the truth. At factor 4, the court must balance “the importance of disclosure to the administration of justice” against “the public interest in maintaining journalist-source confidentiality”, considering context (e.g., stage of proceedings, centrality, whether journalist is party/witness, alternative sources, public importance, publication/public domain).
BaselineA: Common law (Wigmore case-by-case privilege framework as applied/confirmed in R. v. National Post, 2010 SCC 16) plus Quebec civil evidence/procedure context (Civil Code of Québec art. 2857 relevance/admissibility; Code of Civil Procedure art. 46 general powers).
CaseB_TestB: Court jurisdiction to review voluntary association decisions: jurisdiction exists only if a legal right is at stake; for contract, membership is contractual only if general contract formation is met, especially objective intention to create legal relations. “Jurisdiction to intervene ... depends on the existence of a legal right”; voluntary associations “may be constituted by contract ... [but] objective intention to enter into legal relations is required”; intention test: “whether parties have indicated to the outside world, in the form of the objective reasonable bystander, their intention to contract and the terms of such contract.”
BaselineB: Common law (justiciability/jurisdiction over voluntary associations from Highwood Congregation of Jehovah’s Witnesses (Judicial Committee) v. Wall, 2018 SCC 26; and general contract formation principles, including objective intention to create legal relations, drawn from Scotsburn Co-operative Services Ltd. v. W. T. Goodwin Ltd., and related authorities cited in the reasons).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Quebec Charter s. 49(2) punitive (exemplary) damages: admissible autonomously (not dependent on compensatory damages) where there is (1) “unlawful” and (2) “intentional” interference with a Charter right; punitive damages may serve denunciation even if the wrongdoer is deceased
BaselineA: Statute: Charter of human rights and freedoms, R.S.Q., c. C-12, s. 49(2) (exemplary damages for “unlawful and intentional interference”); Civil Code of Québec, art. 1621 (preventive purpose of punitive damages) and arts. 625, 1610 (transmission to heirs). Prior SCC guidance discussed: Béliveau St-Jacques (scope limited), St-Ferdinand (unlawful/intentional interference; intent standard), Augustus (context).
CaseB_TestB: YCJA jurisdiction for youth judicial interim release on s. 469 charges after election: a superior court judge deemed a “youth justice court judge” under s. 13(2)/(3) for “the proceeding” (meaning all steps after election up to trial, including bail), and jurisdiction to grant release under s. 33(8) is concurrent with provincially designated youth justice court judges under s. 13(1)
BaselineB: Statute: Youth Criminal Justice Act, S.C. 2002, c. 1, ss. 13(1)-(3), 28, 33(8), 67; Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, ss. 469, 522 (Part XVI); Interpretation Act, s. 33(2).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Miscarriage of justice from trial shortcomings: whether defects “affected the trial judge’s appreciation of the evidence or rendered the proceedings unfair, so as to give rise to a miscarriage of justice” (including the leading-question threshold: leading questions “suggest an answer or assume a state of facts that is in dispute”).
BaselineA: Combination: Criminal Code appeal power (s. 693(1)(a)) plus common-law appellate standard for identifying a “miscarriage of justice”/unfair trial; the decision applies these principles rather than creating a new multi-step test.
CaseB_TestB: Charter s. 13 engagement test (majority): s. 13 applies only if the prior compelled testimony is “incriminating evidence” — i.e., evidence the Crown could use at the later proceeding “to prove or assist in proving one or more of the essential elements of the offence”; using “non-incriminating” prior evidence “for impeachment purposes, and nothing else,” does not trigger s. 13.
BaselineB: Statute/constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 13 (interpreting “incriminating evidence” and when s. 13 is engaged), informed by prior SCC cases including R. v. Henry, R. v. Kuldip, R. v. Noël, and Dubois v. The Queen.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal Code s. 467.12 “in association with” test: the predicate offence must (1) have a nexus/connection to a criminal organization such that it “advance[s], at least to some degree, the interests of a criminal organization” (not merely an association between accused and group), and (2) the accused must have subjective knowledge (or wilful blindness) that they were dealing with a criminal organization
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 467.12(1) phrase “for the benefit of, at the direction of, or in association with, a criminal organization”; related definition in s. 467.1)
CaseB_TestB: Compulsion test for Motor Vehicle Act accident reports (s. 61) triggering Charter s. 7 use-immunity: “whether, at the time that the accident was reported by the driver, the driver gave the report on the basis of an honest and reasonably held belief that he or she was required by law to report the accident to the person to whom the report was given”
BaselineB: Combination (Charter s. 7 principle against self-incrimination applied to statutory reporting: Motor Vehicle Act, R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 288, s. 61(1); SCC contextual self-incrimination jurisprudence including R. v. Fitzpatrick (cited and distinguished))
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Reasonable suspicion standard for sniffer-dog searches: police must have a subjective suspicion grounded in “objectively discernible facts” assessed on the “totality of the circumstances” (a “constellation of factors”), asking whether facts are “objectively indicative of the possibility of criminal behaviour” (possibilities, not probabilities), viewed through the lens of a reasonable officer with relevant training/experience.
BaselineA: Common law Charter s. 8 sniffer-dog jurisprudence (R. v. Kang-Brown; R. v. A.M.; clarified alongside R. v. Chehil) and investigative detention authority in R. v. Mann (reasonable suspicion).
CaseB_TestB: Reformulated s. 11(i) “punishment” test: a measure is punishment if (1) it is a consequence of conviction forming part of the “arsenal of sanctions”, and either (2) it is imposed in furtherance of the purpose/principles of sentencing, or (3) it has a “significant impact” on liberty/security (i.e., “significantly constrain[s]” lawful conduct or imposes significant burdens not imposed on the public).
BaselineB: Combination of statute and Charter interpretation: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 11(i) (and s. 1) applied to Criminal Code, s. 161(1)(c), (d); built from the common-law s. 11(i) punishment test in R. v. Rodgers.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: CCQ art. 1425 “common intention” interpretation/rectification: where evidence shows a discrepancy between the parties’ proven common intention and the written instruments, and the parties mutually correct the error, courts may recognize the amendments as “legitimate and necessary” (subject to third-party rights) and ensure the error is remedied
BaselineA: Statute (Civil Code of Québec, art. 1425 (interpretation of contracts), with related CCQ provisions on contract formation/modification and civil evidence)
CaseB_TestB: Bank “put upon inquiry” constructive trust test: “A banker may be a constructive trustee of money in his customer’s account and in breach of that trust if he pays the money away, even on the customer’s mandate, in circumstances which put him upon inquiry” (i.e., sufficient notice requiring steps to ascertain the character of the funds)
BaselineB: Common law (constructive trust/bank on inquiry doctrine, as summarized from Halsbury’s and illustrated by cases such as White v. Dominion Bank and Cartwright v. Lyster & Bank of Nova Scotia, as cited in the reasons)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Whether a Quebec retrospective prescription amendment applies at the SCC stage: distinguish cases where the new law is invoked to obtain a different judgment from the court below (Veilleux/McKie) from cases where it is invoked simply to have the appeal dismissed; under s. 47 Supreme Court Act, there is no limit on the grounds to dismiss an appeal, so the Court may apply the new provincial Act to dismiss the appeal
BaselineA: Statute (Supreme Court Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. S-19, s. 47; also applied alongside Quebec prescription legislation: Act to amend certain prescriptions, 1974 (Que.), c. 80, ss. 1, 3, 5; Civil Code arts. 2261(2), 2262(2))
CaseB_TestB: Extradition refusal threshold on ministerial surrender: the person must show surrender would “shock the conscience” (s. 7 Charter) or be “unjust or oppressive” (Extradition Act, s. 44(1)); core inquiry is whether surrender to the “particular treatment” abroad would be contrary to Canadian principles of fundamental justice
BaselineB: Combination of statute and constitutional standard (Extradition Act, S.C. 1999, c. 18, s. 44(1); Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7; as framed through SCC precedents including United States v. Burns and Argentina v. Mellino)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: R. v. Hart “Mr. Big” confessions admissibility rule: confession is “presumptively inadmissible” unless Crown proves (on balance) “the probative value of the confession outweighs its prejudicial effect”, with probative value assessed via reliability (circumstances + markers) and prejudice assessed as moral/reasoning prejudice; plus separate abuse-of-process backstop for coercive/abusive operations
BaselineA: Common law evidence (party admissions exception to hearsay; discretionary exclusion where prejudicial > probative; abuse of process doctrine)
CaseB_TestB: R. v. Borowiec interpretation of Criminal Code s. 233 “her mind is then disturbed”: apply “disturbed” in its “grammatical and ordinary sense” (e.g., “mentally agitated”, “mentally unstable” or “mental discomposure”); no need for mental disorder or significant impairment; disturbance must exist at time of act/omission and be “by reason of” childbirth/lactation; no causation required between disturbance and act
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 233)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Penile swab as a search incident to arrest is Charter-compliant only if (1) police have "reasonable grounds to believe that a penile swab will afford evidence of the offence" (independent of arrest grounds) and (2) the swab is "conducted in a reasonable manner" guided by specified factors (e.g., station-house, supervisory authorization, privacy, same gender, minimal force, record-keeping).
BaselineA: Common law (search incident to arrest framework from R. v. Fearon; reasonableness requirements for s. 8 from R. v. Caslake; strip-search tailoring from R. v. Golden; distinguished limit in R. v. Stillman).
CaseB_TestB: Joint/co-principal liability in group assaults: liability "flows whenever two or more individuals come together with an intention to commit an offence, are present during the commission of the offence, and contribute to its commission"; for manslaughter, focus on whether the accused’s actions were a "significant contributing cause of death" (not on who inflicted which wound), and in group assaults "absent a discrete or intervening event" all assailants’ actions can be such a cause.
BaselineB: Statute (Criminal Code, s. 21(1)(a) and (c) party liability) as interpreted in SCC jurisprudence (notably R. v. Pickton, referenced as consistent).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Whether a damages claim for breach/violation of a collective agreement clause is a statutory “grievance” (i.e., a “disagreement respecting the interpretation or application of a collective agreement”) and therefore must go to arbitration; no distinction between “application/interpretation” and “violation” (they are “two ways of looking at the same problem”).
BaselineA: Statute (Quebec Labour Code, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 141, ss. 1(g) definition of “grievance” and s. 88 mandatory arbitration), as interpreted through SCC precedent (General Motors of Canada Ltd. v. Brunet, [1977] 2 S.C.R. 537; also Imbleau et al. v. Laskin et al., [1962] S.C.R. 338).
CaseB_TestB: Enforceability/scope of a waiver (exclusion) clause for negligence in a race entry form: construed in its context to determine whether it releases the defendant(s) from liability, and whether the negligence was within the clause’s contemplation; clause upheld where it is not “unfair” or “unreasonable” in the circumstances.
BaselineB: Common law (contractual interpretation/enforcement of exclusion/waiver clauses; discussion touches fundamental breach/unconscionability/public policy but treats them as unnecessary given the clause’s reasonableness).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: When a CLRB s. 119 application is merely an updating/clarification versus a de facto new certification: if the Board’s changes “do not alter the nature and scope of the certificate of certification and of the bargaining unit”, it remains an order of review (not a new certification requiring fresh representativeness/appropriateness determinations).
BaselineA: Statute — Canada Labour Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. L-1, s. 119 (Board may “review, rescind, amend, alter or vary any order or decision made by it”), applied against the Board’s own prior categorization of s. 119 review situations (The Employees of the Regional Comptroller and the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Brotherhood of Railway, Transport and General Workers (1975), 9 D.I. 20).
CaseB_TestB: Appellate intervention standard on factual findings: an appellate court should not set aside a trial judgment absent “palpable and overriding error” where the issue is only “the interpretation of the evidence as a whole” (i.e., unless the trial judge was “plainly wrong”).
BaselineB: Common law — prior SCC authorities cited for the standard of review: Schreiber Brothers Limited v. Currie Products Limited and Gulf Oil Canada Limited, [1980] 2 S.C.R. 78; Stein v. "Kathy K.", [1976] 2 S.C.R. 802; Lewis v. Todd, [1980] 2 S.C.R. 694.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Ernst (Cromwell J.) — Ward s. 24(1) Charter damages: even if damages are functionally justified, they are not “appropriate and just” where countervailing factors (effective alternative remedy + good governance + immunity’s purpose) collectively negate damages; for this Board, “Charter damages could never be an appropriate and just remedy” (paras. 26-31, 58).
BaselineA: Common law / constitutional remedial framework under Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 24(1), as set out in Vancouver (City) v. Ward, 2010 SCC 27 (esp. countervailing factors: alternative remedies; good governance). Also applied alongside statutory immunity clause: Energy Resources Conservation Act, R.S.A. 2000, c. E-10, s. 43.
CaseB_TestB: Bird — Maybrun framework for when an accused charged with breaching an administrative order may collaterally attack it: focus on legislative intent, assessed using five “non-exhaustive” factors (wording; purpose; appeal/other review mechanisms; expertise/raison d’être; penalty), which are “not independent and absolute criteria, but important clues” (paras. 25-32).
BaselineB: Common law framework from R. v. Consolidated Maybrun Mines Ltd., [1998] 1 SCR 706 and R. v. Al Klippert Ltd., [1998] 1 SCR 737, applied in the statutory context of Corrections and Conditional Release Act, S.C. 1992, c. 20, s. 134.1(2) (and related review mechanisms such as Federal Courts Act judicial review; habeas corpus).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Art. 2930 C.C.Q. applies (3-year prescription) where the action is based on the wrongful act that caused interference with a person’s physical integrity, and the plaintiff claims reparation for the “direct and immediate consequences” of that interference (even if the plaintiff’s own losses are moral/material): “any civil liability action instituted to claim reparation for the direct and immediate consequences of interference with a person’s physical integrity must be based on the obligation to make reparation for bodily injury caused to another” (para. 55); court must “characterize the basis for the action” and “it is the nature of the initial interference rather than the head of damages being claimed” (para. 26).
BaselineA: Statute: Civil Code of Québec, arts. 2925 and 2930 (in interaction with Cities and Towns Act, s. 586).
CaseB_TestB: Appellate non-intervention in trial judge’s assessment of evidence/credibility: once the trial judge’s reasons show a preference for one version based on having “the clear advantage of seeing and hearing the witnesses”, the Court of Appeal’s substitution of its view is “an unwarranted intrusion” into an area “exclusive to the trial judge”.
BaselineB: Common law/jurisprudential principle of appellate deference to trial findings of fact and credibility, as reflected in cited SCC authorities (e.g., Latour v. Grenier; Maze v. Empson; Dorval v. Bouvier; Métivier v. Cadorette; Hood v. Hood).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Schrenk “sufficient nexus” test for whether discrimination is “regarding employment” under s. 13(1)(b): Tribunal must conduct a contextual analysis of whether the discrimination has a “sufficient nexus with the employment context”, with non-exhaustive factors including “(1) whether the respondent was integral to the complainant’s workplace; (2) whether the impugned conduct occurred in the complainant’s workplace; and (3) whether the complainant’s work performance or work environment was negatively affected” (para. 67).
BaselineA: Statute: Human Rights Code, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 210, s. 13(1)(b) (“discriminate against a person regarding employment”), with related interpretive context from ss. 1 (“person”, “employment”) and 3 (purposes).
CaseB_TestB: Groia in-court incivility/professional misconduct framework: a “context-specific” approach considering “what the lawyer said, the manner and frequency in which it was said, and the presiding judge’s reaction” (paras. 59, 80). Integrity-impugning allegations “cross the line into professional misconduct unless they are made in good faith and have a reasonable basis” (para. 81), with “reasonable basis” meaning not an exacting standard and not defeated merely by a sincerely held legal error if there is “a sufficient factual foundation” (para. 88).
BaselineB: Statute/regulatory: Law Society Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. L.8 (discipline mandate) and Law Society Rules of Professional Conduct (ethical/civility obligations) as interpreted/applied by the SCC.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Ontario anti-SLAPP dismissal framework (CJA s. 137.1): (1) moving party must show on a balance of probabilities the proceeding “arises from an expression” that “relates to a matter of public interest” (s. 137.1(3)); then (2) responding party must satisfy the judge that (a) there are “grounds to believe” the proceeding has “substantial merit” and the moving party has “no valid defence” (s. 137.1(4)(a)), and (b) the harm from the expression is “sufficiently serious” that the public interest in permitting the proceeding to continue “outweighs” the public interest in protecting the expression (s. 137.1(4)(b)). Key SCC gloss includes: “grounds to believe” requires “a basis in the record and the law”; “substantial merit” means “a real prospect of success”; and s. 137.1(4)(b) is an open-ended “public interest weighing exercise” where one interest must “outweigh” the other.
BaselineA: Statute: Courts of Justice Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.43, s. 137.1(3) and (4) (anti-SLAPP).
CaseB_TestB: Corporate attribution doctrine (including for one-person corporations) for limitation/discoverability purposes: attribution may occur if (1) the wrongdoer was the corporation’s directing mind and (2) acted within their sector of corporate responsibility; attribution is generally inappropriate under the “fraud” or “no benefit” exceptions; and, additionally, courts have discretion to refuse attribution where it would not be “in the public interest”, i.e., would not “promote the purpose of the law under which attribution is sought” (applied to refuse attributing the sole directing mind’s knowledge so as not to undermine the Limitations Act discoverability purpose and BIA purposes).
BaselineB: Common law corporate attribution doctrine from SCC cases cited in the decision: Canadian Dredge & Dock Co. v. The Queen; Deloitte & Touche v. Livent Inc. (Receiver of); Christine DeJong Medicine Professional Corp. v. DBDC Spadina Ltd.; and the summary in Aquino v. Bondfield Construction Co. (applied in this case).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Duty to comment on Crown counsel’s prejudicial jury address: where remarks are “prejudicial to a degree sufficient to impose a legal duty on the trial judge to comment” to ensure the defence position is “fairly put to the jury”; failure to do so is an error of law (then consider whether s. 686(1)(b)(iii) cures it).
BaselineA: Statute (Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(b)(iii)) plus common-law fairness requirements for jury charges (as reflected in the Court adopting Ayles J.A.’s formulation).
CaseB_TestB: “Identifiability” test for Federal Court in rem jurisdiction under s. 43(2): reject “physical nexus”; cargo is “subject of the action” if it is “the cargo designated in the contract of affreightment alleged to be breached.”
BaselineB: Statute (Federal Courts Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. F-7, s. 43(2)) interpreted by the SCC (not following the FCA’s prior “physical nexus” approach).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Threshold for summary dismissal of a criminal application: the underlying application may be summarily dismissed only if it is “manifestly frivolous”, applied by assuming alleged facts and inferences are true and taking the applicant’s arguments “at their highest” (R. v. Haevischer, 2023 SCC 11, at paras. 3, 71, 83-85, 100-101).
BaselineA: Common law / judge-made criminal procedure (Vukelich-type summary dismissal power), with the underlying stay remedy governed by the common-law Babos test for abuse of process (R. v. Babos, 2014 SCC 16, at para. 32, as referenced at para. 16).

CaseA_TestA: Two-step framework for whether legislation displaces a common law sentencing discretion (and its application to credit for pre-sentence driving prohibitions despite a mandatory minimum): (1) identify the applicable common law; (2) specify the statute’s effect on it, including whether the statute provides a minimum 'punishment' (global) rather than a minimum 'sentence' (prospective), so that credit may still be granted. Key holdings include: the two-step framework is 'well settled' — first 'analysing, identifying and setting out the applicable common law' and second 'the statute law’s effect on the common law must be specified' (para. 45); and 's. 259(1)(a) can be read in only one way: it provides for the imposition of a mandatory minimum punishment' (para. 74), so the court must impose the one-year minimum but 'there is nothing in the statute that prevents it from then granting credit' (para. 10).
BaselineA: Combination of common law sentencing discretion to credit pre-sentence driving prohibitions (recognized in R. v. Lacasse, 2015 SCC 64) plus statutory provisions interpreted: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, ss. 259(1)(a) and 719(1) (and considered alongside s. 719(3)).
CaseB_TestB: Mitigation in contract where plaintiff claims specific performance: defendant must prove failure to mitigate and that mitigation was possible; but a plaintiff’s refusal to mitigate may be reasonable only if it had 'some fair, real, and substantial justification' or 'a substantial and legitimate interest' in specific performance (Asamera). The Court states: 'As a general rule, a plaintiff will not be able to recover for those losses which he could have avoided by taking reasonable steps' (para. 24); and 'If the plaintiff has a “substantial justification” or a “substantial and legitimate interest” in specific performance, its refusal to purchase other property may be reasonable, depending upon the circumstances of the case' (para. 37).
BaselineB: Common law mitigation doctrine and the specific-performance/mitigation interaction from Asamera Oil Corp. v. Seal Oil & General Corp., [1979] 1 S.C.R. 633 (plus related mitigation authorities cited in the reasons).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.
